pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Store separately verified anonymized outputs under data_extra/anonymized/pdf; preserve every original file.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: v1 claims demonstrated feasibility and leading performance on CARLA Town05 while leaving real-world effectiveness unexplored. v2 broadens its abstract, contributions and conclusion to multiple benchmarks, real-world applicability and claimed vehicle-deployment validation. It also omits v1's explicit claim to be the first work using probabilistic modeling for the continuous planning action space.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning multimodal candidate quality, traffic-density robustness, vocabulary coverage and transfer, and the distinction between similar open-loop accuracy and stronger closed-loop performance. The introduction replaces the richer-supervision rationale with simpler action ranking. The conclusion replaces the unexplored-real-world limitation with specific concerns about naive simulated agents and insufficient realism; Appendix A.3 discusses vocabulary-related latency.

D1.justification: v2 adds component-specific encoder details, vocabulary-sampling pseudocode and endpoint-distance selection, six-waypoint planning, feature dimension 256, 16 NVIDIA 4090 GPUs, and parameter/latency measurements. Appendix A supplies dataset composition and shared-backbone comparison details. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v1's Town05 route counts and lengths are omitted. The GitHub address is retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates CARLA Town05 Long and Short. v2 retains these and adds Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, NAVSIMv2 and a 3DGS benchmark involving 2000 hours of real-driving training data and 337 reconstructed evaluation scenarios. Appendix A.2 also uses nuScenes trajectories to construct a vocabulary evaluated on NAVSIM, substantially extending represented data and environments.

E2.justification: Town05 Long Table 1 removes CILRS and LBC and adds Rao et al. (2024), DriveCoT and LeapVAD. Town05 Short, moved to v2 Table 9, adds LeapVAD while retaining its previous comparators. New benchmark comparisons additionally include DiffusionDrive, PRIX, GenAD and ETA, among others, substantially expanding the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce NAVSIM navtest PDMS, NAVSIMv2 extended metrics, eight-second 3DGS scenarios with collision/deviation metrics, and controlled density, vocabulary-size and training-data experiments. The Town05 data description also changes from three million frames sampled at 2 Hz to three million clips containing 1.6-second histories at 10 Hz. This is a reported setting revision, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: The original component ablation and qualitative examples are retained. v2 adds top-five candidate evaluation, traffic-density robustness, vocabulary and training-data scaling, deterministic versus probabilistic comparisons in open and closed loop, and vocabulary sampling/transfer analyses (Tables 6, 8 and 10–13). Appendix A.3 also adds reconstruction-quality and computational-efficiency analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report performance point estimates without seed information, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. The expanded evaluations do not introduce uncertainty reporting for experimental performance.

E6.justification: The retained Town05 scores and component-ablation values are unchanged, including VADv2 driving scores of 85.1 on Long and 89.7 on Short. v2 adds substantial results, including NAVSIM PDMS 89.3, NAVSIMv2 EPDMS 85.8, Bench2Drive driving score 76.15 and 3DGS collision ratio 0.270 (Tables 2–5), plus new comparator, ablation and efficiency entries.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the stated training target: v1 inserts the ground-truth trajectory into the vocabulary and downweights nearby negatives; v2 labels the nearest existing vocabulary trajectory and estimates empirical action frequencies from these assignments. This is a localized supervision revision. The scene-token architecture, trajectory vocabulary, Transformer planner and PID inference remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related-work discussion undergo substantial rewriting. The scene encoder becomes a component-by-component explanation, terminology changes from environmental to scene tokens, and experimental discussion is reorganized across the main text and a new appendix. Author/header information also changes. The revision extends well beyond isolated wording edits.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format and substantially reorganizes its displays. Town05 Short moves to Appendix A, the original qualitative Figure 3 becomes a compact four-panel Figure 4, and Figure 1 is reduced beside text. Numerous benchmark and ablation tables, an algorithm box and a standalone vocabulary visualization are added.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially revised to discuss Trajeglish, MotionLM, Diffusion Planner, DiffusionDrive and GoalFlow, alongside newer driving benchmarks and methods. v2 explicitly positions complete-trajectory tokens against single-step tokenization and iterative rollout, while condensing the earlier LLM survey and removing the sweeping first-work claim.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 defines empirical action frequencies, derives the cross-entropy objective from KL divergence and supplies an explicit indicator-based conflict-loss equation. These are limited mathematical additions. The continuity assumption and probabilistic-field construction remain, and no theorem or proof-based guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through direct deterministic-planner controls, multimodal and vocabulary analyses, and evaluations beyond Town05 using NAVSIM and reconstructed real-driving environments. These additions test the central planning argument more directly and broaden its empirical support; implementation disclosures also improve reproducibility. Repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, and on-vehicle deployment outcomes are referenced rather than shown in the supplied PDF, limiting the strongest applicability claims. Nevertheless, the added controlled evidence constitutes a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VADv2 research, with clearly matchable methods and Town05 experiments. The supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v2 includes Appendix A; v1 contains no appendix. Referenced external demonstrations and supplementary deployment results are outside this comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original Town05 results and adds Bench2Drive, NAVSIM, NAVSIMv2 and 3DGS evaluations, together with original analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original CARLA Town05 Long/Short evaluations, component ablations and qualitative planning results in Tables 1–3 and Figure 3.

results.title: VADv2: End-to-End Vectorized Autonomous Driving via Probabilistic Planning

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes learning spectral algorithms for sparse-vector recovery. v2 reframes the empirical contribution around a general tensor-learning recipe demonstrated across materials science, path signatures, and sparse recovery, and explicitly claims novelty at this level of generality. The underlying characterization of orthogonal, Lorentz, and symplectic equivariance remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit discussion of practical output-order limits and memory costs relative to Clebsch–Gordan methods. It removes v1's discussion of joint permutation invariance and its graph-isomorphism difficulty, as well as the suggestion that learned sparse-vector algorithms could generate theoretical conjectures. The principal interpretation of the sparse-vector results remains.

D1.justification: New Appendices H–I document dataset access, path generation with Signax, normalization, augmentation, network sizes, optimizer schedules, hardware, and training time. Appendix J.4 additionally specifies covariance selection per experimental trial. The original repository link and most sparse-vector implementation details are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds Neo-Hookean stress-from-strain prediction and synthetic polynomial-path signature estimation, including three-dimensional orthogonal and four-dimensional Lorentz settings (Section 5; Appendices H–I). The four sparse-vector sampling families and three covariance settings remain.

E2.justification: New comparisons include TFENN using published scores, augmentation-trained MLPs, a discrete path-signature estimator, and MLPs matched by width or parameter count (v2 Tables 1–2). The sparse-vector comparators remain; combining their identical SoS test scores into one column does not remove a method.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce substantial protocols: stress–strain training at three dataset sizes with 4,000 validation/test samples and 1,500 epochs; path signatures with 1,024 trajectories per split, ten input points, signatures through order three, and 500 epochs. They introduce Frobenius-error metrics and augmentation controls. The reported sparse-vector training protocol is substantially retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a limited training-data-size sensitivity comparison for stress–strain prediction, evaluating 5,000, 20,000, and 40,000 samples (Table 1). The existing sparse-vector full-versus-diagonal comparison, covariance analyses, and training-versus-test evidence are retained.

E5.justification: Sparse-vector results retain five-trial means and standard deviations. The new path-signature comparison specifies three trials and reports standard deviations only when they reach 0.001 (Table 2), introducing a different reporting rule. Stress–strain results otherwise follow the existing five-trial reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for both new tasks: for example, stress–strain error of 4.057e-6 with 5,000 training samples, and path-signature errors of 0.002 and 0.005 for orthogonal and Lorentz settings (Tables 1–2). Sparse-vector numerical test and training results match v1 after accounting for renamed columns and merged identical SoS scores.

M1.justification: v2 adds a distinct symmetric-matrix architecture: decompose the input into eigenvalues and eigenvectors, process the eigenvalues with a permutation-equivariant network, and reconstruct the output matrix (Corollary 2; Appendix H.2). The existing sparse-vector models and spectral estimation procedure are retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Section 3 gains explanatory guidance and reordered exposition; the isotropic-tensor lemma moves to Appendix C. Much of the sparse-vector setup and model description moves into Appendix J, allowing the main experiments section to cover three applications.

P2.justification: v2 adopts conference typography, headers, and table styling; adds the explanatory architecture diagram in Figure 1 and four tables for new results and settings; and restructures retained tables. The sparse-vector test table merges identical SoS columns, and its parameter table changes orientation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against e3nn, escnn, Domina et al., and Pearce-Crump, explaining differences between invariant-theory and representation-theory constructions. It adds materials and path-signature literature while removing the earlier neural-algorithmic-reasoning framing and associated references. These changes exceed bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds the symmetric-matrix characterization in Corollary 2, with a simultaneous-diagonalization lemma and proof in Appendix F, plus an explicit computational-complexity bound in Section 3. It also corrects mathematical expressions, including the missing Kronecker delta in Example 1. The principal general tensor and other-group theorems are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between the general theory and practical tensor learning. The proved symmetric-matrix construction and new experiments demonstrate matrix inputs, higher-order outputs, and Lorentz equivariance beyond v1's sole sparse-vector application. Parameter-matched and augmentation comparisons strengthen the empirical evidence, while detailed appendices improve reproducibility. Some earlier limitations discussion is lost, and TFENN scores are imported rather than rerun, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same tensor-equivariance framework and sparse-vector application, despite the changed title and expanded scope. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices H–J report original stress–strain, path-signature, and retained sparse-vector experiments. The TFENN comparison scores are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix H report original sparse-vector-recovery experiments, including test and training results across sampling distributions and covariance settings.

results.title: Tensor learning with orthogonal, Lorentz, and symplectic symmetries

C1.justification: Both versions claim two Cholesky/SPD metric families with efficient, stable, closed-form operators. V2 extends the stated contributions to constructing residual blocks and elevates neural-network applications alongside the geometric contributions. The central metric-design and novelty claims remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 substantially extends v1's explanation that powers distort diagonal entries less than logarithms. It proposes dataset-specific explanations using diagonal imbalance, explains BWCM's greater tolerance of negative theta, interprets the limited benefit of learning M, and explicitly identifies instability near the logarithmic limit (Section 6.2 and Appendices E.3–E.6). These add mechanisms and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: V1 already specifies SPDNet widths, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and epochs. V2 adds detailed GyroSPD covariance construction, residual-network settings, FPHA processing, selected theta values, and the parameterization and initialization of learned M. Appendix E.7 newly discloses CPU, GPU, and memory information. Both versions advertise code, although v2 inconsistently also says release will follow acceptance.

E1.justification: Radar, HDM05, numerical-stability simulations, and tensor interpolation remain. V2 adds FPHA, extending action-recognition coverage to first-person hand actions: 1,175 sequences across 45 categories (Appendix E.1.2). Additional backbones primarily broaden evaluation within these retained classification tasks.

E2.justification: The SPDNet classifier comparison expands from vanilla SPDNet and LCM in v1 Table 6 to AIM, LEM, and LCM in v2 Table 2; the vanilla SPDNet result is removed. V2 also evaluates these competing geometries in GyroSPD and residual networks, and includes PEM and BWM in the new MLR runtime comparison (Table 13).

E3.justification: V2 replaces the sparse positive deformation choices with a sweep from -2 to 1.5 and different selected parameters. It adds one-block HDM05 evaluation, GyroSPD and residual-network protocols, and FPHA-specific preprocessing. Stability testing adds theta=0.15 and extends the smallest diagonal values from 1e-15 to 1e-30. Appendix E.5 introduces a 50-class, batch-30 forward/backward timing protocol over dimensions 32–512.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's stability, interpolation, and limited deformation comparisons, v2 adds systematic theta sweeps (Tables 9–10), fixed-versus-learned M ablations (Table 14), input/output diagonal-distribution analysis (Figure 3), and dimensional scalability tests (Table 13). Expanded stability tests investigate failure closer to the logarithmic-metric limit. The original interpolation analysis is retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Classifier summaries change from ten-fold averages in v1 to five-fold results in v2, retaining the plus/minus reporting format. V1's explicit randomized-initialization and split statement is no longer supplied. The new residual-network comparison reports the best of three trials without uncertainty intervals (v2 Table 4). These are reported aggregation changes, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive classifier, residual-network, sensitivity, scalability, and learned-M results. Its expanded stability table reports 100% failure for theta=0.15 DBWM at 1e-30, whereas v1 tested only theta=0.5 and 1.5 with zero failures. Retained stability entries also change, including the 256-dimensional CM/DLM result at 1e-1 from 14.05% to 14.29%. Classifier results use changed theta and repetition settings, preventing same-setting improvement claims. Interpolation determinants remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core metrics, deformations, operators, and MLR formulas are retained: CDEM and CDBWM become PCM and BWCM. The procedural extensions are residual blocks using the proposed exponential maps (Section 5, Eq. 16) and an evaluated variant learning diagonal M instead of fixing it to the identity (Appendix E.6).

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative. Main-text theory is condensed and reorganized, proofs move to Appendix F, the existing MLR theorem moves into Section 5, and interpolation moves into Appendix E.2. An appendix contents page and reproducibility, ethics, and language-model disclosures are added.

P2.justification: V2 adds a framework diagram and diagonal-distribution plots, restructures accuracy/timing tables, expands the stability grid, and introduces sensitivity and scalability tables. The original interpolation figure and determinant table are relocated rather than newly generated evidence. The conference layout replaces the manuscript format, but the new acronym-list page visibly contains a LaTeX glossary-generation error.

R1.justification: The introduction shifts from broad SPD-geometry applications toward metrics as building blocks for neural networks. It adds substantial positioning around residual networks, diffusion and flow models, and recent normalization and attention research, including Katsman et al. (2024), Li et al. (2024), and Chen and Lipman (2024). The foundational relationship to Lin's Cholesky geometry remains.

T1.justification: V2 adds an analytical comparison of matrix-function counts and per-sample computational costs for seven MLR geometries (Appendix E.5.1, Tables 11–12). Definition 3.1 explicitly formalizes weighted coordinate metrics. The principal metric, deformation, gyro-structure, and MLR results are retained, with their proofs largely relocated to Appendix F.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited learning validation through AIM/LEM comparisons, additional architectures and FPHA, and systematic deformation, learned-M, and scalability analyses. Identifying a stability failure boundary also makes the practical claims more informative. These gains outweigh fewer reported folds, best-of-three residual reporting, an overbroad GyroSPD superiority statement—BWCM trails LCM on Radar in Table 3—and the broken acronym list. The improvement comes principally from stronger validation and interpretation, while the core geometry remains stable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cholesky product-geometry framework, with identifiable corresponding metrics, theorems, experiments, and appendices. The scientific material supports reliable comparison. The failed acronym list in v2 is a presentation defect rather than an essential evidence gap.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix E report original classifier, residual-network, stability, interpolation, sensitivity, diagonal-distribution, and scalability results.

before.justification: Section 7 reports original numerical-stability simulations, tensor-interpolation results, and SPDNet accuracy and timing experiments on Radar and HDM05.

results.title: Fast and Stable Riemannian Metrics on SPD Manifolds via Cholesky Product Geometry

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: localized embeddings from a frozen backbone, efficient gradient decomposition, optional contextual regularization, and use across retrieval, captioning and generation. The added evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting convergence to semantic capture and later boundary refinement, alpha to the local/global tradeoff, and comparative scaling to better use of larger backbones. It also argues for overlapping-mask independence and multi-object relationship preservation. The original explainability-quality and small-object limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents explicit computational-graph detachment and configurations for the added runtime experiments. Conversely, it omits v1's project-page link and explicit LeGrad averaging/normalization description. Existing backbone weights, optimizer, default iteration count and positional-embedding interpolation details are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix G/Figure 8 adds qualitative generation cases using masks covering combinations of cartoon characters, extending the illustrated input scenarios. The seven quantitative benchmark datasets and established task families remain unchanged; medical and aerial imagery are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds evaluated comparisons with MaskCLIP, CLIPSurgery and SCLIP across seven retained benchmarks and three backbone sizes. These comparisons were absent from v1, substantially expanding the comparator coverage while retaining the earlier baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled protocols tracking PascalVOC loss and accuracy through 100 iterations, sweeping alpha from 0 to 20 on RefCOCO, and measuring runtime at resolutions from 224 to 768 pixels with 10 masks and 10 iterations. The original benchmark metrics, backbone configurations and default optimization settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices D-G examine convergence and the stopping budget, runtime versus resolution, regularization sensitivity, and multi-object representation. These substantially extend v1's analyses. The earlier optimization visualizations, mask-quality, explainability-method and gradient-decomposition ablations are retained under matched sections and figures.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. The added parameter sweeps and curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline scores, regularization sensitivities, convergence/runtime curves and multi-object outputs. Most original results remain unchanged, but Table 2 changes ViT-B/32 PascalVOC Acc@10 from 8.9 to 98.8. In the new Table 3, H/14 advantages over the best listed baseline, CLIPSurgery, are 25.5 points on VOC and 23.6 on COCO; the accompanying prose incorrectly states 31.7 and 32.8.

M1.justification: Both versions use a frozen backbone, a CLS-initialized token optimized against a query mask through explainability and Dice loss, optional cosine regularization, and gradient decomposition. The new explanations of overlapping masks and graph detachment do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 polishes wording, condenses the methodological background and conclusion, makes experimental setup a separate subsection, and moves ablations before captioning and diffusion. Gradient decomposition is incorporated into Section 3.2. These are limited editorial reorganizations within the retained overall narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3 and 7 and Figures 5-8, redraws Figure 2 as a horizontal workflow, moves Figure 1 into the introduction, and regroups the main comparison and ablation tables. Existing qualitative figures and analyses remain, often relocated and renumbered. The visual changes extend substantially beyond pagination.

R1.justification: v2 adds CLIPSurgery, SCLIP and GradCAM++ references and expands its positioning against training-free dense-token aggregation. It removes the Efficient Self-Ensemble citation. Updates to LeGrad, FGVP and lambda-ECLIPSE bibliographic information concern existing works; the central novelty positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix I.1 adds a focused product-rule derivation supporting gradient decomposition, formalizing stop-gradient initialization and the token's zero derivative with respect to backbone activations. v1 states the independence and decomposition without this proof. The new derivation explicitly omits cosine-normalization terms.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method: Table 3 supplies missing direct training-free comparisons, while Appendices D-F quantitatively support the iteration budget and regularization choice and examine resolution costs. These address important evidence gaps in v1. Overstated baseline margins and removal of the project link detract from the revision, and the added proof remains limited by omitted cosine normalization, but the comparative and design-choice evidence is substantially stronger.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MaskInversion. All 16 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including equations, tables, figures and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds training-free baseline comparisons, hyperparameter analyses, resolution-scaling measurements and multi-object examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval and captioning experiments, mask-quality and runtime ablations, and qualitative generation results.

results.title: MaskInversion: Localized Embeddings via Optimization of Explainability Maps

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from general-manifold federated averaging supporting multiple local updates to simultaneously handling heterogeneous data and unknown, unequal participation probabilities. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion claim convergence in this broader setting and superiority over existing Riemannian FL methods on its new benchmarks. v1's emphasis on theoretically choosing communication-saving local-update counts is reduced.

C2.justification: v2 explains how unweighted aggregation can target a different objective and interprets error terms arising from client drift, probability estimation, participation, and stochastic gradients. It adds explanations of straggler behavior and heterogeneity effects. The stated applicability boundary changes from v1's full-participation/IID restriction to time-invariant participation statistics and Assumption 3.8; time-varying participation becomes future work.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's Manopt and parameter descriptions, v2 documents hardware, Windows/MATLAB versions, timing conventions, new dataset preprocessing and partitions, and Cayley/projection implementations. Appendix C.2 specifies handling rounds without participating agents. However, v2 introduces a reproducibility ambiguity: Algorithm 1 includes the local step size inside the gradient stream, whereas Section 2 defines an unscaled stream and AGS-AP applies that step size again.

E1.justification: Principal-eigenvector and Frechet-mean tasks remain, but their synthetic datasets are replaced by MNIST and PATHMNIST. Stiefel experiments change from Brockett minimization to synthetic/CIFAR10 PCA. Synthetic/School multitask learning is removed, while WordNet hyperbolic prediction and synthetic/MovieLens matrix completion are added. Heterogeneous data, unequal participation, and stragglers introduce substantial new evaluation scenarios.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates RFedAvg and centralized RSD, RCG, and limited-memory BFGS. v2 adds actual comparisons against RFedSVRG on PCA, hyperbolic prediction, and Frechet means, and RFedProj on PCA. The centralized suite remains in the new matrix-completion comparison, without RFedAvg there. Appendix A.3 also documents retraction-based adaptations of RFedAvg/RFedSVRG for Stiefel experiments.

E3.justification: New protocols include participation schemes matched at expected rates 0.3/0.5/0.7, simulated tenfold straggler delays, and CPU-time measurements excluding communication. The retained sphere task changes from normalized retraction to exponential mapping. MovieLens introduces per-user 80/20 rating splits, RMSE, and different rank/local-update budgets; these are new evaluation settings rather than reruns of the School experiment.

E4.justification: v1 mainly examines local-update counts and fixed versus decaying step sizes. v2 Appendix A.1 adds comparisons of biased, true-probability, and estimated-probability aggregation; evaluates original and reweighted objectives; compares participation schemes with and without stragglers; and varies data heterogeneity. Local-update sensitivity is also revisited on MNIST and matrix completion.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's concentration bounds concern its participation-probability estimator and belong to the algorithmic theory, rather than uncertainty reporting for experimental outcomes.

E6.justification: v1 Table 2's School NMSE results, such as 0.470 for r=3 and K=10, are replaced by MovieLens RMSE results: v2 Table 2 reports 0.7948 for r=3 and K=16 versus 0.7925 for each centralized comparator. v2 also adds PCA/HSP/FMC comparisons and participation, bias, and heterogeneity findings. These concern different tasks and settings, so they do not establish a direct performance improvement over v1.

M1.justification: v1 uniformly averages gradient streams from all agents. v2 introduces inverse-participation-probability weighting through AGS-AP, frequency-based estimation of unknown participation probabilities, and a separate global step size. These substantially extend the aggregation procedure while retaining its gradient-stream foundation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Geometric preliminaries move to Appendix B, convergence proofs are consolidated in Appendix D, and most experimental settings and supplementary analyses move to Appendix A. References precede the appendices. The revision also contains inconsistent RFedPP naming in material otherwise identified as RFedAGS.

P2.justification: The original convergence and School displays are replaced by benchmark panels combining accuracy and CPU time, a hyperbolic embedding visualization, participation/heterogeneity plots, and dataset-distribution histograms. Tables change from an experimental parameter grid and School NMSE comparison to an algorithm-capability matrix and MovieLens RMSE comparison. This substantially revises the visual organization, beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially toward heterogeneous FL and arbitrary or unknown participation, including Wang and Ji's participation studies and newer Barzilai–Borwein Riemannian FL methods. The new Table 1 positions methods by participation, heterogeneity, manifold, and geometric-operator requirements. Appendix C additionally relates RFedAGS's Euclidean specialization to Wang and Ji's 2024 method, substantially revising the research positioning.

T1.justification: The analysis expands from full participation and IID data to heterogeneous objectives and Bernoulli participation under a probability-estimation accuracy assumption, while relaxing isometric transport to bounded transport. v2 adds aggregation-bias and probability-estimation theorems, explicit decaying-step convergence rates, and a strong-retraction-convexity-to-RPL proof. v1's optimal-K Theorems 4.6–4.7 are removed. Much basic geometric background is retained in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly leaves partial participation and non-IID data to future work. v2 substantially addresses that central applicability limitation through weighted aggregation, broader conditional convergence analysis, and targeted tests of bias, probability estimation, heterogeneity, and stragglers. These additions materially strengthen the connection between the method's intended use and its evidence. Removing the School study and optimal-K theorems reduces some coverage, and the new scaling/naming inconsistencies impair clarity, but the gains in applicability and validation outweigh these drawbacks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RFedAGS and retain its gradient-stream aggregation foundation. Their readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 Section 4 and Appendix A report original benchmark comparisons and experiments examining aggregation, participation, heterogeneity, stragglers, and local-update counts.

before.justification: v1 Section 5 reports original synthetic optimization experiments and School multitask-learning results, including convergence curves and numerical NMSE comparisons.

results.title: Riemannian Federated Learning via Averaging Gradient Streams

C1.justification: The contribution expands from a six-subject examination benchmark to multilingual, multi-source benchmarking and analysis of generalization across languages and evaluator families. v2 additionally emphasizes specialized evaluator training and test-time scaling, replacing v1's emphasis on limited prompting and agent benefits. The central claim that automatic evaluators fall short of humans remains.

C2.justification: The explanation based on missed key information is retained, but v2 adds interpretations involving tie aversion, temperature-sensitive reasoning models, reward-model generalization, and overconfident RL convergence. Recommendations shift from broadly seeking semantic-sensitive metrics and additional disciplines toward trained evaluators, hybrid workflows, and explicit cost–quality tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v2 supplies filtering/paraphrasing prompts, expanded annotation instructions and compensation details, language-specific preprocessing and BERTScore backbones, and TTRL hyperparameters such as batch size 8, 32 rollouts, and learning rate 5e-7. It adds inference-time and API-cost tables, while removing several detailed agent-specific implementation recipes. Both versions already advertise code and data access.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates English translations of Chinese examination material covering six subjects. v2 evaluates Chinese examination data and original English Reddit/ELI5 data across 15 topics, adding domains such as engineering, biology, physics, and mathematics. The human–human, human–model, and model–model comparison families remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen/Llama/DeepSeek judges, reasoning models, Skywork and RM-R1 reward models, Prometheus, FineSurE, and a separately measured human baseline. Several earlier comparators, including BLEU, BLEURT, CritiqueLLM, TIGERScore, and ReFeR, disappear. G-Eval and ChatEval remain in Appendix B.4, Table 13.

E3.justification: v2 adds macro-F1 alongside accuracy and changes scalar tie-rounding from two to three decimal places. The reported annotation pool increases from five to ten, fluency is explicitly excluded from judging, and three additional PhD annotators provide a human baseline. Temperature-zero controls and TTRL training/validation settings introduce further experimental protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds temperature sensitivity, contamination checks, efficiency comparisons, TTRL/clipping ablations, and quantified error categories with new case studies. Domain, response-origin, CoT, and tie-exclusion analyses are retained but revised. v1's five-vote consistency analysis and analyses conditioned on human annotator disagreement are removed.

E5.justification: Annotation reliability reporting changes from raw agreement rates by subject and comparison mode in v1 Table 2 to chance-corrected Cohen's kappa in v2: 0.78 for reference validation and approximately 0.65 for preference annotation. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based variability for evaluator performance.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. GPT-4o's average accuracy is 0.532 in v1 Table 3 versus 57.5% in v2 Table 2, but changed data and protocols prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. v2 adds bilingual F1 scores, human accuracy averaging 79.9%, and TTRL results, including 63.9 versus 66.5 with higher clipping for Qwen2.5-3B (Table 7).

M1.justification: The described construction pipeline adds question filtering and expert reference rejection, while text transformation shifts from expanding references to paraphrasing human responses. v2 also introduces evaluator adaptation using structured outputs, TTRL, and DAPO-style higher clipping (Section 5.7); v1 contains no corresponding evaluator-training procedure.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming, the abstract, introduction, methodology, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. A broad Analysis section replaces the dedicated agent section, Discussion moves to Appendix C, and the appendices are reorganized around additional results, discussion, cases, instructions, and annotation.

P2.justification: The overview figure is redesigned, the main results table changes from subject-level accuracy columns to bilingual accuracy/F1 columns, and agreement displays become paired kappa heatmaps. New analysis tables and an error-type chart appear; many earlier full-page diagrams are removed or replaced. The annotation screenshot is retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially extends positioning toward reasoning models, reward modeling, and reinforcement learning, adding work on Prometheus, Skywork, RM-R1, FActScore, contamination detection, TTRL, and DAPO. Section 5.6 explicitly positions LFQA-E against Expert, Feedback-Bench, RM-Bench, and Reward-Bench. Several earlier agent/planning references and discussions disappear.

T1.justification: Neither version develops substantive mathematical theory, formal assumptions, or proofs. v2's standard accuracy and macro-F1 formulas explain empirical scoring; they do not introduce new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: The broader language/domain coverage, separately measured human baseline, and focused sensitivity/error analyses substantially address v1's narrow coverage and limited support for human comparisons. These gains strengthen the paper's empirical foundation. Reporting weaknesses remain: the overview gives 1618 questions/7323 comparisons while the conclusion gives 1625/7649, and Appendix B.4's agent-leadership claim exceeds Table 13's average results. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial evidential improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same reference-based LFQA benchmarking work, renamed from CALF to LFQA-E and substantially expanded. Their text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original bilingual evaluator experiments, a human baseline, sensitivity analyses, contamination checks, and reinforcement-learning results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluator experiments, annotation agreement, agent comparisons, and supplementary analyses, including Tables 2–5 and 15–17.

results.title: LFQA-E: Carefully Benchmarking Long-form QA Evaluation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: joint forward and inverse modeling, disentanglement from neural-operator parameters, component-wise identifiability under sufficient variability, and utility across three supervision settings. Hypernetwork terminology and additional evidence do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendices B.4–B.5 explain probabilistic encoding, latent visualization, backbone dependence, scalability, and the accuracy–interpretability trade-off. They explicitly delimit applicability to parametric PDE families. The conclusion replaces the earlier limited-number-of-systems caveat with a boundary concerning untested high-dimensional PDEs. These substantially expand the paper's interpretations and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data repository link, extensive architecture and input specifications for the added baselines, fuller documentation of FNO inverse optimization, and per-epoch timings, including its forward/inverse timing breakdown. Appendix C.4 documents the synthetic generator and sampling procedure. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's shorter implementation appendix.

E1.justification: The HGO, Mechanical MNIST, and two heterogeneous-material scenarios are retained. Appendix C.4 adds a controlled synthetic mapping with known two-dimensional generative factors for identifiability evaluation, a limited extension beyond the existing physical datasets.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from five to fourteen baselines, adding UFNO, WNO, PIANO, CAMEL, SMDP, InVAErt, FUSE, FUSE-f, and convVAE. PIANO also joins the corresponding comparisons in Tables 2–3, and MetaUFNO appears in the new backbone comparison.

E3.justification: Appendices B.1–B.2 revise the reported first-experiment depth of DisentangO and MetaNO from 16 to 8 layers. The new synthetic protocol varies training tasks over 3, 5, 7, and 9, uses 100 validation and 500 test tasks, and evaluates MCC and R². Per-epoch timing comparisons are also added. These changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Existing latent-dimension, loss-weight, supervision, and traversal analyses remain. Table 4 newly tests dependence on the operator backbone. Appendix C.4, Table 5, and Figure 12 test how task variability affects recovery of known latent factors and the identifiability rank condition, substantially extending validation of central methodological claims.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The expanded discussion of Gaussian latent distributions concerns the model, rather than a new practice for reporting experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Original error entries are retained, but numerous results are added. Table 1 adds FUSE's 4.99% inverse error alongside DisentangO's retained 4.63%, reducing the reported nearest-comparator margin from 68.2% to 7.2%. PIANO adds 13.73% and 50.71% errors in Tables 2–3. Tables 4–5 add backbone results and synthetic recovery scores, including MCC increasing from 0.7836 to 0.9121 across 3 to 9 training tasks.

M1.justification: The core task-wise lifting adaptation, VAE, losses, and supervision procedures remain. Appendix B.2 adds DisentangO-UFNO, replacing the IFNO backbone with UFNO while retaining the surrounding framework. This is a limited architectural adaptation.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are extensively condensed and rewritten. Section 3.1 reorganizes the method around explicit notation, a data model, and the operator architecture before the learning objective; assumptions are consolidated and numbered. Supervision scenario numbering is reversed, and the appendices gain several structured explanatory subsections.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains clearer labels and a detailed caption. The earlier main-text Figures 2–5 are retained but moved after the references and renumbered. Tables are expanded and reformatted, replacing numeric model codes with names and adding a timing column to Table 1. Tables 4–5 and Figure 12 are new, alongside a document-wide conference-format layout change.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a substantive hypernetwork discussion, including Ha, Chauhan, Nguyen, Oh and Peng, and Lee, positioning DisentangO relative to weight-generating architectures. It also acknowledges additional physical disentanglement work by Fotiadis, Lingsch, and Tong and adds references supporting the expanded baseline comparisons.

T1.justification: The generative premise changes from the one-to-one relation b=m(z) in v1 Equation 3.5 to b sampled from a distribution and z sampled conditionally on b in v2 Equation 3.4. The observation model also explicitly incorporates discrete noisy measurements. New Appendix A.2 derives the linear-independence condition for conditional exponential-family distributions. The identifiability conclusions and proof arguments are retained, but their formal setup is substantially revised.

improvement.justification: The expanded comparisons address an important weakness in v1 by including much closer inverse competitors, making the performance evidence substantially more informative. The backbone experiment and controlled latent-recovery study test previously unsupported aspects of the method, while implementation details and access information improve reproducibility. Some inconsistencies remain, notably Section 4.3's retained 90.7% advantage despite the added PIANO result implying 89.6%. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DisentangO and retain matching methods, physical experiments, and theoretical results. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline evaluations, a UFNO backbone experiment, and synthetic latent-identifiability results in Tables 4–5.

before.justification: v1 reports original supervised HGO, semi-supervised Mechanical MNIST, and unsupervised heterogeneous-material experiments, including prediction errors, ablations, and latent visualizations.

results.title: Disentangled Representation Learning for Parametric Partial Differential Equations

C1.justification: The principal generation claim strengthens from O(L^(3/2) sqrt(log L)) to O(L log^2 L). Prompted generation improves from O(L log L + K^2) to O(L log L + K log^2 K). v3 also claims demonstrated efficiency in deep convolutional and hybrid models. Exactness, applicability to convolutional models and the O(K) prompt-cache claim are retained.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's hardware caveat, v3 discusses runtime–memory trade-offs, near-optimality up to logarithmic factors, unsupported quantization, and long-prompt GPU memory failures. Appendix A.1 explicitly qualifies that STU-T's approximation loses the original LDS learning guarantees. Section 5.2 adds explanations linking practical speedups to model scale and avoided prompt recomputation.

D1.justification: v1 discloses little beyond a single-layer CPU loop. v3 documents H100 and TPUv2 hardware, PyTorch and JAX implementations, precision choices, tokenizer, initialization, 48 filters, STU-T factorization, attention configuration, FFT padding and casting, and separate prefill timing. Appendices A.1 and B.1 also provide dependency source and licensing information, substantially improving reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: Coverage expands within autoregressive generation timing: v1 evaluates generation from scratch, while v3 also evaluates prompt-conditioned decoding, including prompts longer and shorter than the generated continuation (Section 5.2; Appendix A.3). Neither version reports a named language corpus or downstream accuracy benchmark. Larger and hybrid architectures primarily change model configurations.

E2.justification: Naive convolution remains the principal empirical baseline. v3 Appendix B and Figure 4 additionally evaluate a two-layer Transformer with a standard KV cache. Attention appears only in theoretical complexity comparisons in v1. Flash Inference and approximate inference methods are discussed in v3 but are not reported empirical comparators.

E3.justification: Beyond v1's single-layer CPU experiment, v3 introduces complete-forward-pass H100 timing protocols across model depths, widths and precisions, with prefill and decoding measured separately. Appendix B adds matched two-layer convolutional and Transformer configurations on TPUv2. The controlled timing plots also use a revised sequence-length sweep. These are new evaluation designs, not established reruns of v1 under identical conditions.

E4.justification: v1 mainly examines runtime scaling with sequence length. v3 Section 5.2 and Appendix A add systematic depth, width and prompt-length analyses, comparisons of fully convolutional and hybrid configurations, and a cache-length sweep testing the runtime trade-off at fixed generation length. Figure 2b and Table 15 directly examine the choice of epoch length K.

E5.justification: v1 provides no run counts or quantified timing uncertainty. v3 Section 5.2 and Appendix A.1 specify three timings per configuration, discard the first, and report the mean and sample standard deviation of the remaining two, omitting deviations below 0.01 seconds. This introduces systematic uncertainty reporting without establishing increased runs for the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds Continuous-FutureFill timings and extensive model, prompt and cache-sweep results. For the 670.75M STU-only model, Table 3 reports 1009.36 seconds versus 1731.67 for naive convolution at 126,976 tokens, but 17.07 versus 14.72 at 4096 tokens. These newly reported settings establish both gains and short-sequence slowdowns; they are not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The earlier periodic FFT-cache scheme becomes Epoched-FutureFill. v3 additionally introduces Continuous-FutureFill, which accumulates future contributions through power-of-two blocks. This new procedure is incorporated into prompted generation and offered as an online-convolution module for spectral filtering in Algorithms 3–4; it is more than a renaming or expanded explanation.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially reorganized around an explicit online-convolution problem and FutureFill primitive. Online algorithms now precede prompted generation; experiments become a standalone section; conclusions and limitations are added. Existing model background, related work and the spectral-filtering discussion move into appendices, alongside extensive rewriting of the introductory and technical narrative.

P2.justification: The complexity tables gain memory information and separate algorithm variants. Earlier timing plots are reworked into v3 Figure 1, while new model and cache plots, an architecture diagram and numerical tables expand the presentation. The earlier FutureFill schematic is redrawn and relocated, and Figure 7 adds a multiscale execution diagram. Typography and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v3 acknowledges independent Flash Inference work obtaining the same quasilinear bound and distinguishes FutureFill through its formulation, memory trade-offs and implementation (Section 1.1; Appendix C.1). It also positions exact inference against approximate cache compression and sparse attention, and adds FlashSTU and implementation-related references. Much of v1's related work is retained in Appendix C.

T1.justification: The periodic-cache runtime analysis is retained, but v3 adds the formal FutureFill decomposition in Proposition 1, the O(L log^2 L) runtime and O(L) additional-memory result in Theorem 3, and correctness arguments using binary decompositions in Appendix E. Prompt-generation and spectral-filtering corollaries are strengthened accordingly; the underlying spectral-filtering regret guarantee remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens both the theoretical contribution and its empirical support: it adds a quasilinear algorithm with correctness/runtime arguments and replaces v1's largely unsupported assertion of large-model benefits with accelerator measurements, ablations and uncertainty reporting for Epoched-FutureFill. Detailed implementation documentation further improves assessability. Reporting weaknesses remain, including conflicting baseline prefill times in Tables 2 and 6 (37.20 versus 32.70 seconds) and broad speedup wording despite short-sequence slowdowns. These defects qualify, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FutureFill and are fully readable, including equations, figures and tables. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes complete Appendices A–E. The substantial revision supports reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 Section 5 and Appendices A–B report original controlled timings, GPU model experiments, Transformer comparisons and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 Section 4.2 and Figures 3–4 report original CPU timing experiments comparing FutureFill with naive convolutional generation.

results.title: FutureFill: Fast Generation from Convolutional Sequence Models

C1.justification: The central claims of training-free visualization up to 100 frames, improved consistency, and better interactions remain. V2 explicitly elevates the curated long-story benchmark to a main contribution and removes v1's abstract-level characterization of the framework as computationally efficient, qualifying efficiency elsewhere.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands explanations involving embedding convergence, content-adaptive attention, and suppression of irrelevant references. It adds interpretations of editing-model failures and explicit diversity and runtime limitations. Appendix F changes v1's conclusion that ten iterations are optimal to suggesting fewer than ten suffice, and discusses adaptive stopping and weighting as future work.

D1.justification: V2 documents Grounding-DINO cropping and first-occurrence reference selection for the existing metrics, identifies NVIDIA RTX A6000 hardware, and specifies StoryDiffusion's four reference frames. It updates code-access instructions to a repository and supplementary material. Most original hyperparameters and the pseudocode are retained, with their relocation alone constituting no reproducibility addition.

E1.justification: StorySalon, the twenty GPT-4o-generated 50/100-frame stories, and the 2,000 subject-consistency prompts are retained. V2 adds pose-conditioned visualization examples in Figure 9 and additional comic, film, and monochrome style scenarios in Appendix H.3, modestly broadening evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds IP-Adapter and IP-AdapterXL to the regular-length comparison. Table 2 adds FLUX.1.Kontext, Nano Banana, DALL·E 3, SEED-LLaMA, ConsiStory, and 1prompt1story to the long-story comparison. The original subject-consistent generation comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds four-step LCM evaluation, pose-conditioned testing, embedding Jensen-Shannon divergence tracking, and full-story time/memory comparisons. The original model's 50-step sampling, guidance 7.5, and ten iterations remain unchanged. Appendix C also changes the reported human-evaluation rubric from five criteria to four by dropping image quality; this does not establish that the study was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds attention maps and embedding-convergence analysis, four additional linear-weight ranges in Table 5, and sliding-window, random-reference, and mean-pooled aggregation ablations in Table 7. It also adds editing-model failure cases and a third-iteration result. The original GRCA-versus-CSA analysis is retained and expanded in Appendix A.5, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 Section 4.1 newly states that experiments use a fixed random seed by default, while Appendix H.3 mentions examples spanning different seeds. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; the added disclosure does not demonstrate increased replication.

E6.justification: The proposed models' main benchmark scores are unchanged, but v2 adds extensive comparator, variant, efficiency, and ablation results. AR-LDM's StorySalon CLIP-T/aCCS/aFID changes from 0.237/0.683/40.25 to 0.239/0.684/42.55 in Table 1. Human image-quality scores are removed from v1 Table 5's counterpart, v2 Table 8, while the remaining ratings are retained.

M1.justification: The original initialization, GRCA, and linearly weighted external iteration remain substantively unchanged. However, v2 Section 4.4 adds an SDXL-LCM Fast variant using four diffusion steps and a ControlNet variant accepting pose maps. These introduce substantial extensions to inference and conditioning, beyond the method's renaming.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract and substantial introduction and method prose, consistently distinguishes external iterations from diffusion steps, and adds an explicit contribution list. Related work is reorganized, pseudocode and implementation details move to the appendix, and dedicated variants, reproducibility, limitations, and disclosure sections reshape the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds attention, convergence, pose-control, metric-extraction, and editing-failure displays, and replaces the main long-story comparison with a different illustrated comparison. The original combined ablation table is split and extended, while the human-evaluation table loses its image-quality column. Numerous retained figures and tables are also relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: The broad diffusion-model survey is replaced by substantially expanded story-visualization positioning, including DreamStory, StoryGPT-V, MovieDreamer, and interactive-generation literature. Appendix E expands subject-consistency coverage, while the introduction and Appendix D develop distinctions from IP-Adapter and reference-image editing models. These exceed citation or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 retain the same mathematical procedure. The explicit linear-weight formula restates the existing schedule, and Appendix B explains the previously used evaluation metrics. The new convergence discussion is empirical interpretation, without added formal assumptions, theorems, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for GRCA through controlled aggregation and weighting ablations and comparisons with relevant additional methods. Full-story timing and Fast-variant results expose the practical speed-quality tradeoff missing from v1's per-image efficiency analysis, while metric documentation improves transparency. These gains outweigh the removal of human image-quality ratings and unclear per-image versus per-story FLOP accounting in Table 6, although those issues limit the revision's quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same iterative story-visualization work, renamed from Story-Adapter to Story-Iter. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, variant evaluations, attention analyses, and further ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original story-visualization and subject-consistency experiments, component ablations, computational measurements, and human evaluations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Story-Iter: A Training-free Iterative Paradigm for Long Story Visualization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: explicit DiT scaling laws, compute-optimal model/data allocation, successful large-budget extrapolation, predictable generation quality and transfer, and inexpensive design assessment. The additional experiments principally support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4 corrects the cross-attention model-exponent interpretation from 'larger' to 'smaller,' matching Table 1's 0.54 versus 0.56. New Appendices I–J substantially expand applicability limits and explain why the simplified architecture comparison does not establish intrinsic conditioning-mechanism superiority. However, Appendix I's claim that all experiments are compute-limited conflicts with the new data-constrained ImageNet experiment in H.9.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents maintaining and saving model-EMA weights with coefficient 0.99 and supplies settings for added experiments. It drops v1's explicit identification of Euler as the image-generation sampler, although the 25-step, CFG-10 defaults remain in Appendix H.3. Most existing implementation details are retained.

E1.justification: Coverage expands beyond the original LAION-derived training data, COCO transfer evaluation, and JourneyDB ablations. v2 adds Flickr30k transfer, JourneyDB as an additional transfer target, data-constrained ImageNet experiments, and GenEval compositional-generation tasks (Appendices H.7, H.9, and H.10).

E2.justification: The in-context versus PixArt-style cross-attention comparison retains the same participants, as does the diffusion-formulation comparison in Table 5. Flux and SiT appear in separate scaling-law tests, rather than as added comparators in the retained comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces GenEval and HPSv2.1/ImageReward evaluation, 512-by-512 training, model-EMA evaluation, and guidance/sampling-step controls across compute budgets. It also replaces v1's stated 1B-model learning-rate schedule of 1e-4, 3.16e-5, then 1e-5 with a constant 1e-4 description. This establishes a reported protocol revision, without establishing that the original experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The original formulation, aspect-ratio, loss-smoothing, and sampling ablations remain. v2 substantially expands tests of scaling stability across guidance scales, sampling steps, model-weight averaging, architectures, resolution, and transfer domains. It also adds a sparse-versus-dense caption comparison and qualitative samples controlled by fixed prompts and seeds.

E5.justification: Appendix H.8 newly states that qualitative samples use fixed sampling seeds. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty across seeds; the addition is limited seed-control information.

E6.justification: The original fitted scaling equations and numerical entries in Tables 1 and 5 are retained. Figures 10–23 add extensive numerical and qualitative results, including additional architecture, transfer, ImageNet, GenEval, and preference-reward curves. The new caption experiment reports a FID scaling exponent of -0.216 for sparse captions versus -0.234 for the retained dense-caption setting.

M1.justification: The central rectified-flow velocity objective, transformer designs, isoFLOP optimization, and power-law fitting procedure are retained. Additional architecture and model-EMA experiments do not establish a redesign of the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. v2 creates dedicated scaling-metric subsections, moves diffusion-transformer background and limitations into appendices, clarifies 'vanilla in-context' terminology, and updates affiliations and publication information while adding acknowledgments and an LLM-use disclosure.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 10–23, including scaling comparisons, new evaluation curves, and a generated-image grid. Retained figures and tables receive panel labels, formatting changes, and relocation. The original guidance and sampling-step plots survive with their contents exchanged between Figures 8 and 9, leaving captions and textual references mismatched.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hu et al.'s statistical DiT theory, Fan et al.'s generative-model work, and references supporting the new datasets and evaluation metrics. Discussion of Flux and SD3/MMDiT expands architectural context, while the central novelty positioning and most related-work coverage remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The velocity objective, likelihood derivations, power-law formulation, and FLOP-counting mathematics are retained. v2 makes the loss's data expectation and minibatch indexing explicit and numbers more equations, without introducing a substantive new mathematical result or derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's existing claims. Appendix H.6 directly tests the data-quality application that v1 illustrated mainly through architecture comparisons; additional transfer, ImageNet, compositional-alignment, preference-reward, and robustness experiments address important gaps in generality and generation-quality validation. Appendix J also limits architectural overgeneralization. These gains outweigh the learning-rate reporting ambiguity, swapped figure captions, and contradictory finite-data limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same scaling-law study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds architecture, dataset-transfer, caption-quality, ImageNet, GenEval, and preference-reward evaluations in Appendix H.

before.justification: v1 reports original compute-budget training sweeps, approximately 1B-parameter extrapolation experiments, architecture comparisons, and diffusion-formulation and sampling ablations.

results.title: Scaling Laws for Diffusion Transformers

C1.justification: The central claims remain that SimpleToM tests explicit and applied ToM across diverse everyday scenarios and exposes a substantial capability gap. v2 foregrounds scenario diversity and generic-intervention failures, but retains the successful task-specific combined intervention in Appendix F. This changes emphasis rather than the underlying claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of human consistency, small-model judgment anomalies, and persona effects, plus a hypothesis involving backtracking or self-questioning for o1-preview (Appendices H, N, P). Appendices A–B also develop concrete deployment implications and explain the false-belief-only evaluation scope.

D1.justification: v1 already supplies dataset access, evaluation outputs, and detailed prompts. v2 additionally reports generation/inference code availability, documents added model identifiers and temperature requirements, and provides exact persona descriptions. Table 4 nevertheless lists the Qwen-2.5-14B full name as Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, leaving that identifier inconsistent.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 1,147 stories, ten information-asymmetry scenarios, and three question types, with identical dataset statistics. The human study samples existing stories, while persona prompts change model conditions rather than the represented story domains or tasks.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands from ten to 21 named LLMs, adding models including GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4.5-preview, o1, o3-mini, and smaller Llama, Qwen, and Ministral models. Appendix H adds a human comparator. The original intervention comparison sets remain in Appendix F.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a human evaluation using five stories per scenario, totaling 50 stories and 150 responses; five persona conditions for two LLMs; and an additional high-reasoning-effort o1 configuration. It also specifies temperature exceptions for added reasoning models. The original full-dataset accuracy evaluation is retained.

E4.justification: Appendix P adds a systematic persona sensitivity study, Table 2 adds an o1 reasoning-effort comparison, and Appendix N quantifies Llama-3.1-8B's inconsistent behavior-versus-judgment answers. These extend the original prompt-variation and scenario analyses, which remain available.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v2 adds 95% Wald intervals, paired task-gap bootstrap intervals and p-values using 10,000 resamples, and scenario-level intervals using 5,000 resamples (Appendix Q). These concern sampling uncertainty; they do not establish additional independent model runs.

E6.justification: Original Table 2 point estimates are retained, but substantial results are added for new models, personas, humans, and reasoning effort. Figure 10 reports human accuracies of 88%, 86%, and 70% on the sampled stories. A retained Llama-3.1-405B baseline entry changes from 58.3 to 58.2 in the reminder table (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 5).

M1.justification: v2 adds persona-conditioned inference by inserting role descriptions into system prompts (Appendix P). This is a limited prompting extension; benchmark construction, filtering, and the original mental-state reminder, system-prompt, chain-of-thought, and combined interventions remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, opening motivation, contribution list, intervention narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Detailed intervention discussion moves into Appendix F, while the appendices are reorganized and expanded with applications, psychological grounding, human evaluation, model interpretations, personas, and statistics.

P2.justification: v2 restructures Table 2 with uncertainty annotations and a reasoning-model block, creates a consolidated intervention Table 3, and relocates the original intervention tables. It adds human, persona, and statistical displays and scenario plots with error bars. Main-text Figure 5 excerpts an existing appendix example rather than introducing a new case.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands psychological grounding through Appendix D, connecting benchmark choices to work on explicit versus applied competence, perspective use, and conceptual versus procedural knowledge. It also adds research on social deployment failures and reasoning limitations. Publication updates to previously cited works are separate from these substantive additions.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal mathematical theory or proofs. The new psychological framework in Appendix D is conceptual, while Appendix Q adds statistical estimation rather than new theoretical results or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central capability gap through newer-model evaluations, a human reference, persona sensitivity tests, and paired confidence intervals, addressing v1's lack of human calibration and uncertainty analysis. Reported code availability also helps reproducibility. The human comparison uses only 50 stories versus full-dataset model scores, and Table 12's chance-comparison p-values conflict with the stated positive-gap testing direction. These limitations constrain parts of the added evidence but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SimpleToM and retain the same benchmark and experimental core. The main text, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds evaluations of further LLMs, a human baseline, persona interventions, and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of ten LLMs, including task accuracies, scenario analyses, and prompting interventions in Tables 2–5.

results.title: SimpleToM: Exposing the Gap between Explicit ToM Inference and Implicit ToM Application in LLMs

C1.justification: The central claims of last-iterate Nash convergence and compatibility with existing optimization methods remain. The abstract and introduction expand the empirical contribution from Qwen2-1.5B to larger models, explicitly claiming controlled win rates above 60.2% and 56.8% for Llama-3 and Qwen2.5, respectively.

C2.justification: New Appendix L explicitly acknowledges that nonconvex LLM optimization lacks guarantees of achieving the required prox solutions and discusses unresolved convergence-rate limitations. Section 5.2 adds interpretations of post-training instability, capability retention, and benchmark-objective mismatch, including COMAL's failure to outperform Iter-IPO on Arena-Hard. These materially qualify practical applicability.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds actionable solver pseudocode, while Sections 5.1 and J document the new oracle identities, training schedules, regularization settings, reference-update intervals, and compute requirements. Conversely, v2 omits v1's code-and-trained-model access footnote and detailed hyperparameter-search reporting; this establishes lost documentation, not that the resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 adds Tulu3 SFT training data and evaluation on GSM8K, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, and Arena-Hard, substantially extending coverage to mathematical reasoning, knowledge, coding, and additional alignment tasks. UltraFeedback, AlpacaEval, UltraChat, and the original synthetic game remain represented.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain the initial/SFT policy, DPO, IPO, iterative IPO, and INPO for LLMs, and MD, iterative DPO, iterative IPO, SPPO, and INPO for synthetic experiments. Iter-IPO-L is a regularization configuration; newly described GRPO, DRO, and REBEL integrations are not new empirical comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds 7B/8B experiments with 18 training iterations, a Skywork/ArmoRM mixture preference oracle, one-epoch cosine-schedule training, and reference updates every six iterations. It also introduces GPT-4 evaluations and best-versus-final checkpoint comparisons for the new experiments. The original 42-iteration Qwen2-1.5B protocol remains in Appendix K rather than being replaced.

E4.justification: v2 extends regularization-sensitivity testing to iterative IPO on Llama-3, comparing strengths 0.002 and 0.1 to examine training collapse and stability. The original synthetic and output-length analyses remain, but v1's detailed DPO/IPO hyperparameter sweep in Appendix G and Table 3 is omitted.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and training trajectories without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The additional results retain the same uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Tables 1–3 and Figure 2: COMAL beats Iter-IPO by win rates of 60.25% on Llama-3 and 56.89% on Qwen2.5, while standard-benchmark rankings are mixed. These are new experimental settings, not improvements to the original scores. v1 Tables 2 and 4 are numerically preserved as v2 Tables 5 and 6; the hyperparameter-sweep results are removed.

M1.justification: The COMAL outer loop and INPO solver remain unchanged. Appendix G.1 adds a GRPO-based instantiation using group-sampled win-rate rewards and relative advantages. The expanded SPPO/DRO/REBEL pseudocode largely documents integrations already described generically in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction and method motivation are substantially rewritten and expanded. Related work, Bradley-Terry background, prox details, detailed synthetic discussion, and the original small-model experiments move into reorganized appendices. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the addition of new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overview figure, larger-model training plots, and three main results tables; it redraws and relocates existing synthetic figures and moves the original LLM displays into Appendix K. The hyperparameter table disappears. The property comparison also loses its robust-alignment column and incorrectly merges DPO/IPO and SPPO/Nash-MD into shared rows.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against Magnetic Preference Optimization and concurrent or subsequent extragradient, Mirror-Prox, and optimistic alignment methods. It distinguishes its approximate-solver guarantee from exact-solver assumptions and connects COMAL to GRPO and clairvoyant prox methods. The INPO citation's change from 2024 to 2025b is a publication update to the same work.

T1.justification: The full-support assumption, Theorems 1–3, and exact- and approximate-solver convergence proofs are retained from v1. Section 3.2 newly states that choosing tau = O(epsilon) yields an epsilon-approximate equilibrium in O-tilde(1/epsilon squared) iterations. This is a limited additional rate statement, not a new approximate-solver convergence proof.

improvement.justification: v1's practical validation relied on one 1.5B model and its training oracle. v2 substantially strengthens validation through two larger models, capability-retention tests, and GPT-4 evaluations that reveal both transfer and limits to superiority. Appendix L also clarifies the theory-to-practice gap. These address important evidential and qualification gaps, outweighing the omitted access information and hyperparameter results and the misleading merged rows in Table 4.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COMAL research, with matching core algorithms, convergence proofs, and original experiments. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments in Appendices I and K and adds Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B experiments, including preference comparisons and standard-benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original three-action preference-game simulations and Qwen2-1.5B fine-tuning experiments, including training trajectories, pairwise comparisons, and hyperparameter-search results.

results.title: COMAL: A Convergent Meta-Algorithm for Aligning LLMs with General Preferences

C1.justification: The central efficiency and image/video protection claims remain, but v2 Section 5 broadens the claimed generalization to unseen editing-model versions and mismatched masks, and asserts a learnable structure of effective perturbations. v1 emphasized unseen-content generalization and separately trained editing tools. v2 still acknowledges model specificity while claiming substantially broader transfer capabilities.

C2.justification: v2 newly attributes robustness to spatially targeted, low-frequency perturbations and interprets generalization as evidence of learnable perturbation structure. It substantially expands the earlier per-tool limitation with concrete failures involving multiple small objects, extreme mask mismatch and perceptible noise, plus qualifications concerning architectural transfer and temporal modeling (Appendices A.4–A.9).

D1.justification: The principal training details, including UNet++, Adam, 350 epochs, batch size 5, A100 hardware and approximately 22 hours, were already supplied in v1. v2 adds mask-free loss handling, JPEG-strength disclosure, participant instructions and randomized presentation details. It also states that source code and reproduction guidelines are supplied in supplementary materials and adds a CCP dataset access reference.
