Human evaluation expands from 46 participants and 767 comparisons to 67 participants, 977 comparisons and 231 absolute judgments. The absolute study selects cases where the VLM triggered retrieval. Appendix E.5 introduces a controlled diagnostic protocol with 20 classes and 780 prompts.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled tests of VLM concept recognition, seed-based diversity comparisons, concrete retrieval/counting/text failure cases, and qualitative component-ablation examples. The original prompt-rephrasing, retrieval-caption, retriever-choice and retrieval-dataset-size ablations are retained, sometimes relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix E.6 newly reports generation with different seeds, showing five outputs per prompt in Figures 17–19. It does not provide seed identities or aggregate repeated-run uncertainty. Existing mean-plus-standard-error tables and comparative-study error bars remain; no new significance-testing procedure is specified.

E6.justification: Most retained OmniGen/SDXL scores and original ablation values are unchanged. v2 adds ImageRAG-F, GPTScore, additional-dataset, VLM-diagnostic and absolute-study results; the latter reports 92%, 90% and 84% concept presence for OmniGen, SDXL and FLUX on selected cases. FLUX baseline values also change, such as ImageNet CLIP from 0.262 to 0.271, but configuration equivalence is insufficiently documented to interpret this as a same-setting gain.

M1.justification: The core VLM diagnosis, caption generation, retrieval and reference-conditioning workflow remains unchanged, including the prompts and error fallback. v2 Section 3.2 adds optional similarity-threshold filtering and repeated generation until VLM-confirmed alignment. These are proposed procedural options; Appendix A explicitly states that experiments use no retrieval threshold.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method and experimental narrative are extensively revised. Method exposition is reorganized around guided chain-of-thought; implementation, error handling, personalization and proprietary-data experiments move into appendices. Related-work subsections are consolidated, and reproducibility and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensive figure and table restructuring. The teaser and qualitative comparison grids are revised, the user-study figure gains FLUX and absolute-evaluation panels, and new failure, ablation and diversity figures appear. Existing ablation and proprietary-result tables are split or regrouped, alongside new GPTScore and dataset tables.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates positioning against close alternatives: RealRAG's trained retrieval module and FineRAG's retrieval of all concepts with layout construction. These comparisons sharpen the distinction of training-free, gap-directed retrieval beyond v1's contrast with RAG-trained generators. It also adds relevant chain-of-thought, editing, conditioning and evaluation references; RealRAG and FineRAG are discussed rather than directly benchmarked.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theoretical proofs or formal guarantees. The prompt template is restated for the already-used one-image-per-concept setting. The added chain-of-thought and retrieval explanations introduce no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's similarity metrics and relative preferences: the absolute human study checks concept presence on retrieval-triggered cases, while the controlled VLM experiment tests a central diagnostic assumption. Additional backbone coverage and explicit failure and diversity analyses strengthen applicability assessment. Unexplained FLUX reporting inconsistencies—the LAION-F rows in Tables 6–7 repeat base-FLUX values rather than Table 2's ImageRAG-F values—and some omitted protocol details limit parts of the evidence, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ImageRAG by the same authors. Their text, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds FLUX-based results, additional datasets, VLM diagnostic tests and expanded human evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation benchmarks, ablations, proprietary-retrieval experiments and a user study with 46 participants and 767 comparisons.

results.title: ImageRAG: Dynamic Image Retrieval for Reference-Guided Image Generation

C1.justification: The central single-token representation, efficiency, perfect-arithmetic-accuracy and 64-fold data-efficiency claims remain. v2 explicitly scopes the introductory perfect-accuracy claim to Transformers trained from scratch and highlights the existing 38M-versus-fine-tuned-1B comparison in the abstract. The conclusion more cautiously frames broader downstream applications as future research.

C2.justification: v1 treats integration with pretrained LLMs as future work; v2 interprets its new MMLU and perplexity experiments as evidence that FoNE preserves or improves semantic abilities. It also adds substantive arguments about classification versus regression, alternative numerical embeddings, positional encodings, numeral-base alignment and NTL loss weighting. Some interpretations overstate the evidence: Appendix B describes period 8 as performing poorly on base-5 inputs, whereas Table 7 reports 99.97% accuracy.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies that digit limits are global hyperparameters, describes numeric-string parsing, distinguishes scratch training from the fine-tuned baseline, and adds training-time bounds and NTL implementation settings. Most original configuration details remain. However, v1's code-and-visualization access link is removed, as is its blanket A6000 hardware statement; A6000 details remain for the long-number and Abacus experiments.

E1.justification: v2 expands beyond the original predominantly synthetic evaluation to FineWeb language modeling and MegaMath-Web-Pro continual pretraining, with MMLU and zero-shot arithmetic evaluation. Appendix B adds modular addition and base-5 inputs; Appendix E.1 adds direct-prompting scenarios for production LLMs. The original binary-classification, 60-digit addition and Abacus tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Appendix K introduces substantial head-to-head comparisons against Number Token Loss with digit-wise and subword tokenization, each evaluated at three loss weights across two arithmetic tasks and multiple data sizes. Original comparators remain. The five production LLMs in Table 9 are evaluated separately, rather than in a matched comparison against FoNE.

E3.justification: New protocols include paired continual pretraining on 15B tokens and GPT-2–117M pretraining on 10B FineWeb tokens. Appendix K specifies an eight-layer, 512-dimensional model, 50 training epochs, varying training-set sizes and 1,000 held-out examples evaluated with accuracy, R2 and RMSE. Appendix E.1 adds two-shot, temperature-zero testing on 100 sampled problems per setting. The original arithmetic split and configuration tables are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix B extends the original period ablation with a base-7-to-13 sweep and tests matching FoNE periods to base-5 inputs. Appendix K analyzes sensitivity to NTL loss weights. Section 5 adds a targeted text-only perplexity analysis on sequences containing both text and numbers, examining possible interference with language modeling. Original ablations and generalization analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same three random-seed runs for the Abacus comparison. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting procedures for its new experiments. The 100-problem samples in Appendix E.1 describe evaluation sample sizes, not repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results, while v2 adds substantial new findings. Table 4 reports 59.00% versus 51.35% four-digit addition accuracy for simplified FoNE versus the regular model, with MMLU scores of 38.21% versus 38.10%. Table 5 reports text-only perplexity of 46.856 for FoNE versus 67.390 for BPE. Table 16 reports 89.3% multiplication accuracy for FoNE versus 16.3% for the best NTL variant at 75K samples. These are newly reported comparisons under added protocols.

M1.justification: The core Fourier encoder, digit-classification loss and decoder remain unchanged. Section 5 adds a simplified adaptation that computes FoNE for existing BPE numerical subwords and learns a projection into pretrained token-embedding space during continual pretraining. This changes the integration procedure without redesigning the core method.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: it rewrites the abstract and discussion, separates representational properties into Section 3.2, moves algorithms to Appendix A, and relocates the existing Abacus and long-number discussions into Section 4.4. It also replaces the appendix roadmap with a contents page and adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: v2 combines an encoder illustration with the original decimal-addition results in Figure 1, redraws main performance plots using logarithmic error axes, and adds a new integration diagram in Figure 2. The original pipeline becomes Figure 6, Figure 4's panels are reordered, and table layouts are reformatted. New language-modeling and NTL figures and multiple experimental tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The Fourier-based numeracy positioning remains, with targeted additions concerning NTL/regression losses, SALSA, sinusoidal positional encodings and newer numerical-representation and frequency-bias studies. The original Fourier-related-work discussion is moved to Appendix C and expanded. These changes refine the relationship to prior work without fundamentally redefining the contribution.

T1.justification: The mathematical encoding, loss and prediction definitions and the recovery and normalization proofs are substantively retained, with v1 Appendix C becoming v2 Appendix D. Former Lemma 3.5 appears as explanatory prose in Section 3.2 with the same reasoning. The added positional-encoding discussion introduces no new formal derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 largely supports its proposed usefulness for language models through synthetic tasks and leaves pretrained integration for future work. v2 substantially addresses this validation gap with actual continual-pretraining/MMLU experiments and 10B-token FineWeb training, including text-only perplexity evaluation. The NTL comparisons also strengthen assessment against an alternative numerical-learning approach. These gains outweigh the removed code-access pointer and new reporting inconsistencies, such as the conflict between Appendix B's period-8 description and Table 7, although uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FoNE research. All 28 pages of v1 and 32 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, support comparison. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds language-model pretraining, continual pretraining, modular arithmetic, base-sensitivity experiments and Number Token Loss comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original arithmetic experiments, efficiency measurements, ablations, binary classification, Fourier analyses, 60-digit addition and Abacus generalization results.

results.title: FoNE: Precise Single-Token Number Embeddings via Fourier Features

C1.justification: The main representation claim expands from approximate binary first-order smoothing to exact smoothing for arbitrary finite-state first-order processes. The introduction replaces the claim of introducing a novel Markov-ICL framework with applying an existing framework to Mamba, and emphasizes convolution together with selectivity and recurrence. The empirical higher-order learning claim remains.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies convolution's importance: additional layers can compensate for its removal, gating matters strongly in language modeling, and convolution's relative effect decreases in deeper models. It proposes that other layers approximate convolution, explains held-out behavior through asymptotic minimax optimality, and contrasts recurrent exponential memory requirements with transformer scaling. Learning dynamics are explicitly left outside scope.

D1.justification: Appendix F newly reports a single Nvidia A100 and 10-60 minutes per experiment. However, v1's explicit WikiText sequence length of 256, two-layer transformer with dimension 256, and four-layer Mamba configuration disappear; the replacement reference to Appendix F does not recover them. The code link and original Markov hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds PG-19 language modeling, first-order Markov evaluation with 4, 6, and 8 states, and fifth-order binary Markov evaluation. Appendix E.5 also tests generalization between disjoint transition-probability ranges. These substantially broaden the binary Markov, switching Markov, and WikiText-103 coverage in v1.

E2.justification: Figure 7 adds one- and two-layer linear-attention transformers to the Markov comparisons. Figure 11 adds a one-layer transformer with convolution on its query, key, and value representations, an important control for Mamba's apparent advantage. Convolution-augmented transformers already appeared in v1's WikiText experiment, but not its Markov comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include training on transition probabilities in [0, 0.5] and testing on [0.5, 1], depth comparisons through four layers, convolution-free widths of 10, 100, and 1000, and 12-layer language models with 110M or 200M parameters. Figure 8 also adds relative loss-gap evaluation. The original Markov hyperparameter grids remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds checks of learned count-selection inner products and smoothing constants, hidden-dimension scaling, depth and overparameterization, and held-out-distribution generalization. Appendix E.6 tests whether convolution or additional layers explain Markov performance; E.8 separately ablates convolution, gating, and nonlinearities in language models. These substantially extend v1's convolution-focused analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions already specify five repetitions and display error bars or shaded intervals. V2's Figure 1 caption newly identifies its intervals as standard deviations across five runs. This clarifies uncertainty reporting without establishing any increase in runs; the additional tables also report plus-minus values without consistently defining them.

E6.justification: Numerous results are added: convolution enables a one-layer transformer to solve the Markov task, and two-layer Mamba succeeds without convolution. Table 4 adds WikiText perplexities of 32.16 without gating and 28.98 without nonlinearities. Table 5 adds deeper-model and PG-19 results. Original Table 1 scores remain unchanged; the deeper-model scores are new settings, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed MambaZero retains the same selective recurrence, convolutions, residual embedding, linear output, and L1 normalization. The finite-state parameter construction extends the representation analysis without introducing a new learning or inference procedure. Additional architectural variants serve as experimental controls.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and theoretical narrative are substantially rewritten and condensed. V2 removes the contents page, moves detailed language-model equations into Appendix B, relocates the switching-process procedure and lower-bound intuition, and reorganizes the proofs around the general theorem and retained binary theorem. These are substantial structural changes beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts the ICLR layout, resizes and repositions existing displays, and adds Figures 5-12 and Tables 2-5. The switching result moves from main-text Figure 4 to appendix Figure 13, while the original transition-factor plot becomes Figure 4. Figure 1 receives a more informative caption, and existing hyperparameter tables are repacked.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly credits Edelman et al. for the Markov-ICL framework and positions its novelty as applying that framework to Mamba. Related work is substantively reframed around representation power rather than architectural superiority, adding work on ICL, transformer-recurrent separations, and SSM expressivity, including Park et al., Ekbote et al., and Wang and Xue.

T1.justification: V2 adds an exact finite-state representation theorem with N=S and d=2S and a new constructive argument in Appendix C.2. V1's binary approximation theorem survives as Theorem 4 with d=N=2. The explicit higher-order Conjecture 1 is removed, while the exponential-memory lower bound remains. The new construction contains inconsistent stated projection dimensions.

improvement.justification: The new controls substantially strengthen the central explanation: convolution-augmented transformers, deeper convolution-free Mamba, and language ablations establish clearer boundaries for v1's convolution-focused claims. Broader state-space and distribution-shift evidence, together with more careful research positioning, improve support and interpretation. Missing WikiText setup details and dimensional inconsistencies in the new proof are drawbacks, but the empirical and interpretive gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Mamba and Markov-chain study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, supplemented by experiments on larger state spaces, additional comparators, distribution shift, model capacity, and language-model ablations in Appendices C-E.

before.justification: Sections 3 and 5 report original training and evaluation results on random Markov chains, switching Markov sequences, and WikiText-103, including prediction plots, ablations, and perplexities.

results.title: From Markov to Laplace: How Mamba In-Context Learns Markov Chains

C1.justification: v1 principally contributes a particular recurrent Transformer derived from dual hyperspherical energies. v3's abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden this to a general MLE-grounded design principle supporting multiple attention/feedforward operators and depth-wise adaptation. Parameter efficiency and competitive performance remain central claims, but architectural generality becomes an explicit contribution.

C2.justification: v3 develops the mode-seeking/mass-covering interpretation and interprets the new shared-QKV controls as evidence about the architectural mechanism. Its new limitations discussion identifies potentially restrictive uniformity assumptions, heuristic subspace choices, modulation-network overhead, validation below 20 million parameters, and the absence of causal structure. These substantially extend v1's narrower scalability caveats.

D1.justification: v3 newly tabulates the adaptive-step network's matrix dimensions, separates CIFAR and ImageNet training/configuration recipes, and supplies ImageNet-specific hardware and sample counts. It documents learning-rate bounds and warmup, revises existing hyperparameters, and specifies adapter dimensions, Gaussian initialization with standard deviation 0.02, scaling factor 4, and joint training. These are substantial changes to the reproducibility information; the existing code/data links remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Sudoku with 17–34 given digits, CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-100 classification, and ImageNet-100 masked reconstruction at the same masking ratios. The new ablations and scaling studies use existing datasets. Moving the layer-iteration analysis from CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-100 does not expand the paper's overall coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Energy Transformer to the classification comparison and evaluates both Energy Transformer and CRATE on Sudoku, where v1 compared only against Transformer. Appendix F.3 also introduces shared-QKV Transformer controls with ordinary and reversed attention-update signs. These are reported comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: The classification protocol is substantially revised: CIFAR input/patch sizes change from 224/16 to 32/8, Adam betas from (0, 0.95) to (0.9, 0.999), learning rate from 1e-4 to a 1e-3 maximum, and weight decay from zero to 5e-5. v3's ImageNet table specifies batch size 256 versus v1's blanket 128. Sudoku and reconstruction recipes also change AdamW beta1 from 0 to 0.9; retained scores do not establish reruns. New rank and width sweeps extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's energy, rank, angle, masking-ratio, and layer-iteration analyses, v3 tests alternative attention/feedforward operators and learned versus fixed step sizes in Table 3. Appendix F.3 examines shared-QKV projections and attention-sign reversal. LoRA-rank and larger-width studies add scalability evidence, while the layer-iteration study is revised to CIFAR-100.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 4 adds error bars explicitly defined as standard deviations over five runs for the layer-iteration comparison; v1 Figure 6 provides neither these bars nor that specification. Five-run averaging for Sudoku was already reported in v1 and remains unchanged. An increase in runs for retained experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces classification scores under revised settings: scaled Hyper-SET's ImageNet-100 accuracy changes from 55.98 to 70.16, and Transformer's from 57.82 to 69.44. These are not same-setting gains. v3 adds baseline failures on Sudoku, operator/control results, and scaling results, including 72.20 accuracy with rank-32 LoRA versus 70.16 without adapters. The Sudoku extrapolation values and all masked-reconstruction table values are retained.

M1.justification: The original symmetric attention, ReLU feedforward, and adaptive-step updates remain. However, v3 Section 5.5 and Appendix G introduce sigmoid and linear attention variants, softmax and gated feedforward variants, and iteration-specific low-rank adapters trained jointly with shared parameters. These extend the actual procedures beyond v1's architecture.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and substantial method prose are rewritten around the new conceptual framework. Hopfield preliminaries move from Section 3 to Appendix B, metric definitions move to Appendix D.5, and previously distributed representation analyses become Section 5.4. The new limitations and discussion sections substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensively restyled and rearranged plots. Figure 1 gains an alignment sequence, Figure 3 gains Sudoku training curves, and new tables and shared-QKV plots present added studies. The original appendix reconstruction grid is retained as v3 Figure 8, while v1's separate main-text reconstruction panel is removed.

R1.justification: Energy Transformer changes from a briefly cited related method into a central comparison, with detailed distinctions in the introduction, related work, and Appendix H. v3 also positions its principle against contrastive alignment/uniformity and expands discussion of Hopfield memory capacity, shared projections, and recursive LoRA. Added references support these substantive positioning changes.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the MLE/KL objective in Section 3 and derives it in Appendix A using explicit independence, uniform-prior, and conditional-independence assumptions, followed by a von Mises–Fisher mixture interpretation. Appendix G adds generalized energy definitions and induced operators. The original Hopfield background, core gradient derivations, and rank/angle definitions are retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: The direct Energy Transformer comparisons, component ablations, and shared-QKV/sign controls address important gaps in v1's evidence for its design rationale. Explicit assumptions and concrete applicability limitations also make the claims substantially easier to assess. These gains are tempered by changed classification protocols and apparent negative-gradient sign and beta-scaling inconsistencies in the new Table 18 formulas. The revision nevertheless provides substantially stronger empirical scrutiny and clearer boundaries, without fully establishing its broader theoretical or large-scale claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hyper-SET research, retaining the core architecture and experiments despite the changed title and expanded scope. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional baseline comparisons, component ablations, shared-QKV analyses, and scaling experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Sudoku, image-classification, and masked-image reconstruction experiments, including numerical results and analyses of energy and token representations.

results.title: Hyper-SET: Designing Transformers via Hyperspherical Energy Minimization

C1.justification: The central claims of accurate, concise, diverse voxel captions remain. V2 additionally claims an interpretability advantage from decomposing captioning into interpretable stages in its first contribution, and its conclusion more explicitly states that the richer ROI representations challenge conventional assumptions about functional specialization.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning encoder-based noise suppression, the value of sentence context, robustness across model and prompt choices, and reproducibility of semantic organization across subjects and datasets. It attributes lower BOLD5000 accuracy to dataset quality rather than NSD overfitting. The existing limitations concerning local face features and multimodal applicability are retained in Appendix A.6.

D1.justification: V2 adds Composer scoring weights, feature normalization, expanded checkpoint information, encoder-training hyperparameters, and hardware, memory, and timing estimates, including approximately 83 hours for 20,000 voxels (A.2–A.3). It explicitly reports public source-code and script availability. These substantially improve documentation, although v1's specific TextGraphParser extraction settings are omitted.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates neural responses only on NSD. V2 adds BOLD5000 with four additional participants and different acquisition conditions and stimulus sets (Appendix A.5). This materially broadens empirical coverage, although BOLD5000 caption-prediction accuracy is evaluated only on held-out COCO-captioned stimuli.

E2.justification: V2 adds a one-keyword/no-Composer comparator to Table 1 and the top-N voxel comparisons; this differs from v1's one-keyword ablation retaining the Composer. It also adds a raw-beta/no-encoding baseline, alternative encoder comparisons, and evaluated SigLIP2, FG-CLIP, CLIP-Text, and BLIP configurations (Tables A3–A5). BrainSCUBA and Concat remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce matched training/validation allocations for encoder comparisons, alternative architectures and evaluation embeddings, training-sample and category-count sweeps, and noun clustering with k = 6. BOLD5000 adds its own preprocessing, 90/10 split, COCO-only test evaluation, and top-100/500/1000 voxel selections. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original NSD headline protocol remains.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's image-count, keyword-count, extractor, temperature, and ROI-shuffling analyses, v2 tests encoder necessity, encoder training and architecture, VLM/MLLM choices, prompting, Composer removal, and evaluator sensitivity. It also adds data-size sensitivity, cross-subject caption similarity, multi-concept cluster counts, and shared semantic-cluster analyses (Appendices A.3–A.5; Figures A11–A13; Table A12).

E5.justification: V1 constructs null correlations from independent Gaussian vectors. V2 instead specifies 1,000 activity-vector permutations per voxel, pooling null correlations across voxels, and explicitly names Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction (A.2.2). This refines the existing significance framework; SD/SE and paired-test reporting remain, without evidence of increased experimental repetitions.

E6.justification: Original headline NSD scores and matched diversity/shuffling tables are retained. V2 adds substantial results: for example, subj01 raw-beta versus full-pipeline accuracy is 0.201 versus 0.246 (Table A4), and BOLD5000 top-100 accuracies are 0.2655, 0.1927, 0.1525, and 0.2117 (Table A7). Additional ablation, sensitivity, and cross-subject findings expand the evidence rather than demonstrate version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed default pipeline retains ridge encoding, optimal-image selection, MiniCPM-V captioning, LLM keyword extraction and filtering, and MeaCap/CBART sentence composition. V2 provides more explicit specifications and evaluates alternative components and ablated variants, without establishing a revision to the default method.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the introduction, related work, and implementation explanation; reorganizes the prediction and ROI-analysis narratives; and restructures the appendix into more detailed subsections. Limitations and impact discussion move to the appendix, while ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figures 1 and 3 are revised, Table 1 is split into sentence/image panels with configuration columns, and Figure 5 replaces the OFA-only summary with four-ROI noun/verb displays. Numerous new tables, sensitivity plots, heatmaps, and cluster visualizations are added, while many original appendix figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds explicit positioning against brain decoding, including Tang et al. and Chen et al., and references supporting BOLD5000, additional backbones, prompting, and sentence embeddings. Several earlier citations are removed. The central relationship to BrainSCUBA and SASC and the full related-work appendix remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2.1 adds an explicit candidate-token scoring definition combining weighted log-likelihood, mean optimal-caption similarity, and voxel similarity (Equation A1), where v1 described the guidance verbally. This is a limited addition of mathematical specification, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited validation through component controls, robustness tests, BOLD5000 evaluation, and cross-subject semantic analyses. Together with expanded implementation, resource, and code-access documentation, these additions improve confidence in the method and its reproducibility without relying on higher original headline scores. The gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including COCO-only BOLD5000 evaluation and new reporting inconsistencies such as Table A2's learning-rate decay factor disagreeing with its formula.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LaVCa study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds BOLD5000 experiments, component controls, sensitivity tests, and cross-subject semantic analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original NSD analyses, including voxel-caption prediction, comparisons with BrainSCUBA, ablations, and lexical and semantic diversity results.

results.title: LaVCa: LLM-assisted Visual Cortex Captioning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains policy optimization using a pretrained, frozen GVM. v2 qualifies equivalence as reward pretraining plus value estimation versus direct value pretraining and adds policy-invariance motivation. Headline efficiency claims change from 40% memory and 35% time savings in v1's abstract to 30–40% and 30–45% in v2's introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of Chat versus Chat-Hard performance, critic generalization and distribution-shift robustness, and describes GVM as policy-agnostic despite retaining trajectory conditioning in Section 3.2. New limitations address dataset coverage, bounded approximation error, nonstationarity, unavailable adaptation to fresh feedback and preference-data biases, with periodic GVM refresh proposed as future work.

D1.justification: v2 discloses gamma=1, five GRPO responses per prompt, a scalar linear head and 10K RL prompts, and adds code-access statements and baseline-result provenance. It removes v1's LoRA rank/alpha/dropout specifications and explicit 30%/50% SFT/reward split proportions. These omissions do not establish actual changes to fine-tuning or splitting. Most existing hyperparameters and the judging prompt remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds RewardBench evaluation across Chat, Chat-Hard, Safety and Reasoning, plus HH-RLHF testing of value models trained on UltraFeedback under distribution shift (Section 6). UltraFeedback and the original MT-Bench, Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval policy evaluations remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds ReMax and GRPO to the Base comparison, PPO and GRPO to the Mistral Instruction comparison, and ReMax/GRPO to computational comparisons. It also directly compares GVM against ScalarRM and the converged PPO critic. The GPT-4 performance row in v1 Table 2 is removed; GPT-4-based judging remains.

E3.justification: v2 extends Instruction optimization to Llama3-8B-Instruct and GVM evaluation to a Llama2-13B configuration. New reward evaluations specify Bellman-style response-level aggregation and evaluation of the PPO critic at convergence. The reported KL coefficient changes from an initial 0.2 to a default 0.05, with a new three-value sweep. These descriptions do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds reward-source ablation comparing scalar rewards with binary preferences, KL sensitivity testing, HH-RLHF distribution-shift analysis, and model-size analysis of GVM accuracy (Section 6 and Appendices E, G and H). The original token-feedback example and GPT-4 judging case studies are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard errors or significance tests. GVM percentile tables summarize token-value aggregation choices, not uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Original Base scores and Mistral DVPO scores are retained, while numerous comparator, reward-evaluation and ablation results are added. Newly reported Llama3-8B-Instruct DVPO scores are 7.72/39.2/42.59 on MT-Bench/Arena-Hard/AlpacaEval2. The instruction baseline's AlpacaEval2 entry changes from 22.92 to 34.38, and reported 3B DVPO convergence changes from 450 to 350 steps. These are reported changes, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The TD-trained, trajectory-conditioned GVM and frozen-GVM PPO updates remain. v2 adds a tested preference-only training variant assigning +1/-1 returns to chosen/rejected responses (Appendix G). v1's explicit batch-normalization step disappears from the method description, although tilde-Q remains in the advantage equation; whether implementation also changed is unresolved.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and the experimental setup is reorganized. The proof moves into Appendix B, detailed computational analysis moves into Appendix F, and the conclusion becomes a Discussion section with limitations. New ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements further change the document structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Figure 1 is redrawn into a two-by-two arrangement, benchmark tables are reorganized by backbone, and six new analysis/ablation tables appear. The training plot changes from two dual-axis panels to four separate panels with revised DVPO step axes. The unchanged held-out win-rate chart moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to RewardBench, DAPO and VAPO, explicitly distinguishing DVPO from VAPO's continued actor–critic training. Several earlier background citations disappear, including IPO, SLiC-HF and reward-overoptimization work. The broader positioning against PPO, direct preference optimization and value-guided inference remains.

T1.justification: v1's equivalence theorem becomes Lemma 3.1 with revised assumptions explicitly bounding both reward-derived and pretrained value estimates. Appendix B expands the advantage-error argument. v2 also adds a convergence corollary asserting PPO-like monotonic improvement, a substantive new guarantee without a separate derivation. The original Bellman conversion argument is retained, not newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for replacing reward/critic training: Tables 1–5 and 9–10 add missing baselines, direct GVM comparisons, distribution-shift testing and controlled ablations. Explicit limitations also clarify applicability. These gains substantially strengthen the empirical case, although theoretical and documentation regressions temper the improvement: the new convergence guarantee lacks derivation, Appendix B's constant-gradient assertion conflicts with its policy-dependent equations, and normalization/LoRA details become less explicit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DVPO despite the changed title. All 16 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables and figures.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds reward-model comparisons, distribution-shift evaluation and ablations. Some baseline scores are explicitly attributed to external sources, but original results are clearly present.

before.justification: v1 reports original DVPO training experiments, benchmark scores, computational measurements, held-out comparisons and GVM analyses.

results.title: Pretrain Value, Not Reward: Decoupled Value Policy Optimization

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes computer-use agents matching or surpassing specialists without task-specific engineering and potentially superseding tool-based SWE. v2's abstract and conclusion instead emphasize poor visual-only performance, the importance of file/bash APIs, and benchmarking generalist agents against specialists. Rapid improvement across model releases becomes an additional central claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of API gains as bypassing visual-editing weaknesses and of interaction patterns as task-dependent tool selection. It qualifies the earlier broad error-recovery criticism with better Claude 4.0 behavior and discusses narrowing capability gaps. Appendix H adds substantive arguments about IDE versus bash interfaces and computational overhead.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly specifies exact model snapshots, temperature 0.3, Claude computer-use API flags, vLLM inference on eight L40 GPUs, and mini-sweagent's multimodal adaptation. Appendix B adds task counts and verification details for the custom tasks. These are substantial disclosures; relocated infrastructure descriptions and the existing release website are not new resources.

E1.justification: The evaluated SWE-Bench-Java task is replaced by SWE-Bench-Multilingual in Table 6. v2's Table 4 documents repository tasks covering C++, TypeScript, Rust, Go, C, Ruby, and PHP alongside Java and JavaScript, substantially broadening language coverage while retaining the 15-task organization.

E2.justification: The main evaluation expands from five model versions to nine, adding Claude Sonnet 3.7 and 4.0, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and GUI-Owl-32B. v2 also directly evaluates mini-sweagent with Claude Sonnet 4.0 across the benchmark, adding a specialized-agent comparator absent from v1's corresponding experiment.

E3.justification: The main 300-instance, 20-step evaluation is retained. v2 adds a 250-step protocol for three agent designs on SWE-Bench, SWE-Bench-Multimodal, and SWE-Bench-Multilingual, plus sampled trajectory audits and five suppressed-action scenarios. These add substantial experimental controls and testing procedures.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of visual versus file/bash interaction frequencies, progress across Claude releases, quantified visual-grounding errors, and sensitivity to a 250-step budget. It also extends the suppressed-action recovery probe to Claude 4.0. The earlier assisted-tool experiments and qualitative examples remain, often relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same Intercode McNemar test with p = 0.014. v2 introduces no new repeated-run reporting, seeds, confidence intervals, or uncertainty-estimation procedures; its new trajectory counts concern analysis sampling.

E6.justification: v2 adds Claude 4.0 scores of 22.9% for visual interaction and 50.7% with file/bash APIs, versus 48.8% for mini-sweagent, plus 250-step results. Existing entries also change: Claude 3.5's file/bash aggregate becomes 45.5% from 46.8%, and refactoring results become 25%/75% without/with guidance instead of 0%/50%. Changed coverage prevents interpreting aggregate differences as same-setting gains. The new grounding-error percentages conflict between Section 5.1 and Appendix F.

M1.justification: The VSCode environment, primitive keyboard/mouse interaction, SoM support, file/bash augmentation, and assisted IDE-tool construction are retained. New evaluated models and the mini-sweagent comparator do not establish a change to PwP's underlying method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, conclusion, and main related-work narrative are extensively rewritten. Agent descriptions and experiments are consolidated into Section 5, while detailed infrastructure, related work, and several analyses move to expanded appendices. This is substantial reorganization beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, Figure 1 is redrawn, and numerous figures and comparison tables move to appendices. v2 adds interaction-frequency and model-progress plots, task-count and long-horizon tables, and restructures the main results table. v1's assisted-results Table 4 is redisplayed with unchanged values as v2's Figure 8.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from challenging specialized tool-based SWE toward testing generalist CUAs against strong specialist baselines. v2 introduces substantive comparisons with Cradle and ScienceBoard and incorporates newer work including UI-TARS, AndroidWorld, mini-sweagent, TRAE, and METAL. Much of the earlier related work is retained in Appendix C.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation and initial/final task-state description are substantively unchanged. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 introduces no substantive mathematical development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central comparison by adding a directly evaluated mini-sweagent baseline and 250-step checks, addressing weaknesses in v1's reliance on differently configured published specialist scores. Clearer separation of visual-only and API-assisted performance, behavioral analyses, and reproducibility details better support the conclusions. Reporting defects remain, notably reversed grounding-error percentages between Section 5.1 and Appendix F and the stale Java label in Figure 10, but these do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PwP environment and PwP-Bench research. Their full text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material relocated between versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds model comparisons, a mini-sweagent baseline, interaction analyses, and 250-step experiments in Section 5 and Appendices E–F.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations on PwP-Bench-Lite, assisted-tool experiments, and qualitative and prompting analyses in Sections 6 and Appendices C–D.

results.title: Programming with Pixels: Can Computer-Use Agents do Software Engineering?

C1.justification: Both versions claim hierarchical whole-body control that balances task tracking and safety recovery across terrains, embodiments and deployment environments. v1's conclusion already claims applicability beyond locomotion; v3's expressive-motion experiments provide new support for that retained claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds explicit limitations concerning fixed low-level controllers and discrete switching, the deployed robot's 19 DoFs, and incomplete realism of simulated recovery disturbances. It also adds interpretations linking G1 performance to mass and joint flexibility, long observation histories to reduced adaptability, and motion-recovery behavior to sacrificing tracking for stability.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies VAE architecture and hyperparameters, PPO activation, recovery-policy velocity-error tolerances, RTX 4090 training hardware and per-policy training costs. It also documents JIT export and deployed model sizes, supplies additional robot specifications, and adds a project-page link. These are substantial disclosures; they do not establish corresponding changes to the original implementation.

E1.justification: v3 adds punching, dancing and expressive-walking tasks, outdoor locomotion including grassy surfaces, and outdoor disturbance scenarios. Simulated robustness coverage changes from maintaining a standing posture under directional impulses to locomotion under forces, CoM impulses and payloads. CMU locomotion data and the H1/G1 embodiments remain.

E2.justification: v3 Table 4 adds a domain-randomized Motion-tracking policy as the comparator for expressive-motion tasks. DreamWaQ, AHL, Goal-tracking Policy and HWC-Loco-l remain in corresponding locomotion comparisons. ExBody and ExBody2 supply methodological references, rather than separately evaluated baseline rows.

E3.justification: Section 5 changes the human-likeness metric from MSE to Wasserstein-1 distance. Robustness evaluation now uses commanded locomotion over uniformly mixed terrains, with specified force durations, CoM-velocity perturbation ranges and 0–5 or 0–10 kg payloads. Appendix A.8 adds evaluations at history lengths 1, 10, 20 and 40. The retained terrain benchmark still uses 1200-step evaluations.

E4.justification: v3 substantially broadens recovery stress testing from standing impulses to disturbances during locomotion, including persistent forces and payloads. It adds observation-history sensitivity analysis (Table 14), outdoor disturbance cases and a punching-recovery case study (Figure 14). Existing saliency and extreme-state distribution analyses are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report training with three random seeds and use ± values and graphical variability displays. v3 extends these practices to additional results without documenting increased replication, a new uncertainty estimator, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: For the matched high-speed stair setting, HWC-Loco success changes from 88.72 ± 0.42% to 84.34 ± 0.43%, while goal tracking changes from 0.99 ± 0.03 to 1.07 ± 0.03 (v1 Table 2; v3 Table 1). Separate flat/obstacle results disappear, standing-disturbance results are replaced, and new disturbance, motion-tracking and history-length results appear. Human-likeness values use different metrics and cannot be compared directly.

M1.justification: The goal-tracking and ZMP-based recovery policies, Double-DQN selector, Wasserstein imitation objective and VAE estimator are retained. Expressive-motion experiments explicitly reuse the training pipeline. Added VAE specifications and recovery-reward explanations disclose implementation details without establishing a changed control procedure.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is reorganized: policy sensitivity moves into Section 4.3, embodiment evaluation moves into the scalability section, and real-world terrain discussion joins effectiveness evaluation. Appendix methods are reordered and experiments divided into H1/G1 subsections. Several passages are tightened or rewritten; an explicit limitations section is added and the Impact Statement removed.

P2.justification: The two-column main text becomes predominantly single-column, with a redrawn framework overview and an opening recovery illustration. Tables are restructured, and VAE, history-length, motion-tracking and robot-configuration displays are added. New outdoor and motion-recovery figures accompany relocated existing demonstrations; the policy-sensitivity plot also changes its displayed iteration range.

R1.justification: v3 expands related work with simulated-avatar control and newer humanoid systems including ASAP, TWIST and AMO, and adds ExBody2 and disturbance-testing references. It removes the Tan et al. hierarchical-controller and Double-Q-learning references. The central positioning around recovery from safety-critical situations remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 corrects the discriminator's stated codomain from {0,1} to R, consistent with its Wasserstein-critic formulation. The POMDP definitions, robust optimization formulation, ZMP mathematics and duality discussion otherwise remain. Combining and renumbering equations does not introduce new theory.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central robustness claim by evaluating recovery during locomotion under persistent forces, impulses and payloads, beyond v1's quantified standing-disturbance test. Expressive-motion comparisons directly support the previously asserted extension beyond locomotion. The history ablation, implementation disclosures and explicit limitations further improve assessability. These gains outweigh losing separate flat/obstacle results, although the new motion-tracking protocol remains sparsely specified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same HWC-Loco research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and revised experiments.

after.justification: v3 reports original locomotion, disturbance and expressive-motion experiments in Tables 1–4, plus observation-history experiments and additional real-robot demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original terrain-navigation, embodiment and disturbance experiments in Tables 1–3, alongside policy-sensitivity analyses and real-robot demonstrations.

results.title: HWC-Loco: A Hierarchical Whole-Body Control Approach to Robust Humanoid Locomotion

C1.justification: v2 narrows v1's claim that automatic exposure-mapping learning had not been explicitly studied by acknowledging existing learners and emphasizing its specially designed expressive architecture. It also expands the claimed capabilities to node-attribute influence and higher-order motifs. The central peer-effect estimation objective remains, but novelty positioning and capability scope are substantively revised.

C2.justification: v1's brief conclusion becomes a substantial discussion of applicability and limitations. v2 addresses untestable unconfoundedness, possible exposure confounding even in experiments, continuous-exposure positivity, reliable-network requirements, computational costs, and multi-hop scalability. It also interprets component ablations, embedding-dimension tradeoffs, and the absence of monotonic degradation under edge noise.

D1.justification: v2 adds source-code access information and substantially expands implementation documentation: GNN depth, Adam optimization, weight decay, learning-rate decay, checkpointing, training duration, baseline implementation provenance, hardware, and execution times. These are largely newly disclosed details, not evidence that the corresponding settings changed. Some outcome-generation coefficient values explicitly stated in v1 are no longer specified in the PDF.

E1.justification: The three synthetic network families and BlogCatalog are retained. v2 adds attribute-similarity exposure mechanisms and evaluation with randomly added or removed edges, extending the influence mechanisms and input conditions tested. It also reports Flickr experiments in Section 4.2 and Appendix A.8, although Table 4's caption inconsistently identifies BlogCatalog.

E2.justification: AEMNet joins the synthetic comparisons, and AEMNet and CauGramer join the semi-synthetic comparisons. BlogCatalog also gains TNet and NetEst, which were absent from v1 Figure 5 despite appearing in its synthetic experiments. v2 Table 5 additionally evaluates modified INE-TARNet and motif baselines using EgoNetGNN's feature and outcome modules.

E3.justification: Appendix A.6 changes the stated INE-TARNet and motif-baseline tuning grids, including TARNet learning rate from 0.01 to 0.02, and replaces other baselines' learning-rate searches with defaults. New protocols include comparisons with shared feature/outcome modules and exposure evaluation using the highest absolute Pearson correlation among two embedding dimensions. PEHE, flipped-peer counterfactuals, and the 20% model-selection holdout are retained.

E4.justification: v1 provides benchmark comparisons but no comparable diagnostic suite. v2 adds mask and feature-encoder ablations (Table 2), correlations with true exposure (Table 3), shared-module controls (Table 5), loss-coefficient and embedding-dimension sensitivity studies (Tables 6–7), and robustness to 10% or 20% edge additions/removals (Table 8). These examine component contributions, representation quality, and robustness.

E5.justification: v1 already reports five seeds with means and standard-deviation error bars. v2 likewise reports five simulations with means and standard deviations; its reproducibility statement says at least five repetitions without establishing an increase. Additional result tables retain this reporting practice, with no newly documented confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 revises the benchmark plots and substantially expands numerical results through Tables 1–8. For example, the newly evaluated BlogCatalog attribute-similarity setting reports PEHE of 5.65±0.7 for EgoNetGNN-TARNet and 4.86±1.9 for EgoNetGNN-CFR in Table 1. The ablation, correlation, and robustness findings are also new. Changed architectures and evaluation settings prevent interpreting these as direct same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: v2 adds a feature-similarity encoder, masked weights, an expanded exposure encoder with logarithmic transformation, and entropy and sparsity losses. It also introduces a CFR outcome-model option with reconstruction and distribution-balancing losses. The original uniform-distribution balance loss is retained under the name coverage loss, rather than being a new component. These changes substantially extend v1's architecture and training objective.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, related work moves to the appendix, and identification material is reorganized between the main text and Appendix A.3. The method is restructured around architecture, training, and theory; experiments expand from two to four research questions. A discussion-and-limitations section and reproducibility statement replace the brief concluding structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column ACM layout to a single-column format. Figures 1 and 2 are substantially redrawn, including a revised exposure example and a detailed architecture/loss diagram. Benchmark plots are reorganized, the BlogCatalog bar chart becomes a numerical table, and motif illustrations plus multiple diagnostic tables are added. These are extensive display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Beyond relocating related work to Appendix A.2, v2 positions EgoNetGNN against automated exposure mapping by Mao et al., unknown-interference approaches by Wu et al. and Lin et al., and debates about misspecified exposure mappings and policymaking. The distinction shifts toward structural expressiveness relative to existing learning approaches. Publication updates to retained works, such as DWR, are not counted as new references.

T1.justification: v2 adds a pre-treatment-network assumption, revises unconfoundedness, and changes positivity from marginal probabilities to context-conditional densities. Appendix A.4 introduces a formal motif-expressiveness proposition and proofs, higher-order motif arguments, runtime analysis, and prediction-error decomposition/bound arguments absent from v1. The earlier identification derivation is revised in Appendix A.3, whose final equation incorrectly repeats the same exposure condition in both terms.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification for the exposure-learning module: v1 mainly supplied benchmark plots, whereas Tables 2 and 5 test component contributions and isolate exposure mappings using shared feature/outcome modules. Representation, sensitivity, and noisy-network analyses provide further diagnostic evidence, while Appendix A.6 greatly improves implementation documentation. These gains address important validation and reproducibility gaps. Changed baseline tuning limits performance comparisons, and Table 4's dataset-label conflict and Appendix A.3's equation error weaken reporting, but do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EgoNetGNN research, with matching authors, title, and heterogeneous peer-effect estimation problem. Their main text, equations, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments, plus component ablations, exposure-representation evaluations, sensitivity analyses, and noisy-network tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation results on three synthetic network families and semi-synthetic BlogCatalog data, including additional experimental plots in the appendix.

results.title: Learning Exposure Mapping Functions for Inferring Heterogeneous Peer Effects

C1.justification: The central shortest-path encoding and constrained acquisition-optimization contributions remain. v2 removes the explicit claim to be the first BO algorithm for general attributed graphs, states a focus on undirected graphs, and extends the abstract's empirical claim from molecular demonstrations to competitive synthetic and molecular optimization.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops applicability and limitations in Appendix B. Its time-budget analysis qualifies v1's expectation that longer computation could improve nonlinear-kernel BO: the tested budgets mostly improve optimality gaps rather than objective values. It also discusses alternative acquisitions, scalability strategies, kernel selection and the limited suitability of generic molecular baselines, explicitly disclaiming a state-of-the-art molecular-design claim.

D1.justification: v2 adds synthetic GNN architecture details, GraKel usage, an explicit molecular feature-vector example and a statement that implementations and models accompany the supplementary materials. However, the benchmark link remains a placeholder. v1's Gurobi v11.0.0 specification and detailed 20-molecule warm-start description disappear; this establishes a documentation loss, not removal of warm starts from the implementation.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates molecular prediction and design using QM7/QM9. v2 retains this coverage and adds optimization of randomly initialized GAT, GCN and GraphSAGE functions over general connected, undirected graphs with five node labels. These synthetic tasks extend evaluation beyond molecular feasibility constraints.

E2.justification: v2 adds RW, SM, WL and WLOA prediction comparators, including versions combined with the feature kernel. Existing molecular optimization comparisons gain RW-lime and WL-lime alongside Limeade and BoGrape. New synthetic comparisons evaluate Random, RW-rand, WL-rand and WL-evol; WL-evol was not an evaluated comparator in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces synthetic-oracle protocols and controlled experiments varying MIP limits across 60/600/1200 seconds, exploration coefficients, and baseline acquisition candidate counts from 20 to 100. It also specifies large sampling and mutation feasibility trials. The main molecular budget of 10 initial samples, 50 BO iterations and a 600-second MIP limit is retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's kernel and sampling comparisons, v2 tests the contribution of feature kernels, sensitivity to solver time and exploration settings, and whether larger candidate pools strengthen sampling baselines. Figures 5–7 and 9 examine these questions, while Appendix C.3 quantifies failures of random generation and mutation under molecular constraints.

E5.justification: The reported replication count for kernel-regression tables changes from 30 in v1 to 100 in v2. Figure 8 additionally displays distributions with medians and quartiles. BO curves retain means with 0.5 standard deviation over 10 replications; the PDFs do not establish that the original runs were simply supplemented with 70 additional runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds synthetic optimization results, additional comparator results, ablation outcomes and mutation feasibility rates, including 0.35% at N=10 and 3 successes in one million mutations at N=20. Regression values are also replaced: v1 Table 2 gives N=10 SSP RMSEs of 0.30 for QM7 and 1.20 for QM9, whereas v2 Table 3 gives one dataset-unlabeled value of 0.710. Changed replication counts and missing dataset grouping prevent interpreting this as a same-setting performance change.

M1.justification: The four kernels and GP–LCB–MIP procedure remain intact. The written binary-feature encoding changes the count-indicator domain and constraints from c in [M+1] to c in [n+1] (v1 Appendix A.4; v2 Appendix A.5), altering representable node counts. This is a local formulation revision; neighboring expressions retain inconsistent indices, and no broader implementation change is established.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and contribution presentation, consolidates the BO background and acquisition formulation, moves preliminary encoding constraints and detailed regression exposition into appendices, and gathers proofs into a dedicated subsection. It also condenses Algorithm 1 and reorganizes the experimental narrative, substantially changing how the argument is presented.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands from four prediction panels to twelve, molecular optimization plots gain comparator curves and shared legends, and v2 adds synthetic, ablation, optimality-gap and violin displays. Regression tables are substantially restructured into rotated kernel-by-size tables, losing the previous explicit QM7/QM9 grouping. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the comparison kernels, synthetic GNN architectures, GraKel and further MIP/GNN work. It explicitly positions the Ru et al. adaptation WL-evol as a strong graph-BO comparator and softens the priority claim, while retaining the underlying MIP-based positioning. Limeade's updated publication citation refers to the same work.

T1.justification: The positive-definiteness lemmas and graph-encoding bijection proofs are retained and reorganized. v2 corrects the missing-node condition from min{Au,u, Av,v}=1 in v1 Equation (7f) to zero in Equation (6f). Appendices B.3–B.4 add asymptotic analysis, including O(nL²) kernel evaluation after path-count preprocessing, without introducing a new central theorem.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation and reliance on a sampling baseline by adding general graph benchmarks, competing BO methods and targeted robustness tests. The computational and application limitations are also better qualified. Unclear dataset attribution in the revised regression tables and incomplete access information remain weaknesses, but the stronger comparative evidence and diagnostic analyses provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BoGrape and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The rotated tables in v2 are inspectable. Ambiguous dataset attribution in v2's regression tables limits direct numerical matching, but not the overall comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices B–C report original molecular and synthetic graph optimization experiments, kernel comparisons, ablations and feasibility measurements.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original GP prediction experiments, molecular optimization results and comparisons between Limeade and random sampling.

results.title: BoGrape: Bayesian optimization over graphs with shortest-path encoded

C1.justification: The three principal contributions and abstract/conclusion claims about interpretable, category-agnostic multilayer prompts remain. v2 additionally asserts in the introduction that cross-layer alignment emulates human visual reasoning. Renaming hierarchical concepts otherwise leaves the central contribution intact.

C2.justification: v2 retains the in-domain-prototype limitation but adds concrete explanations of background confusion, occlusion failures and degradation from prompting too many layers. It also develops interpretations concerning monosemanticity, human reasoning and transferable concepts, including domain-dependent concept priorities observed in separately fine-tuned VLCS models.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C add optimizer, learning rates, batch size, epochs, scheduling, initialization, trainable-parameter exceptions, hardware, timing and parameter accounting. Appendix B details the adopted loss implementation. The abstract also supplies a code-repository link absent from v1; these are substantial documentation additions, without independently establishing implementation changes.

E1.justification: v2 adds quantitative PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part evaluation, FGVC-Aircraft visualizations, broader CIFAR-100/ImageNet examples, VLCS domain studies and unseen-category CUB evaluation. It also introduces human concept-interpretation evaluation. CUB, Stanford Cars and Gleason-2019 coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains all twelve comparator rows. The added dataset comparisons reuse ProtoPool, Huang et al. and VPT-Deep, and the computational comparison uses existing VPT. Prompt-CAM receives related-work discussion but is not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include extracting representative part points for PartImageNet/PASCAL-Part, layer/prototype configuration sweeps, validation-set alignment IoU, and a 20-participant study using 100 regions and five-point ratings. Appendix A also reports unfrozen backbone tokens and position embeddings despite the frozen-backbone description retained from v1; this changes the reported setting without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: The existing component ablation gains a spatial-bias row. Appendices C–G add computational-cost analysis, layer/prototype sensitivity, cross-layer alignment measurements, domain and unseen-class analyses, concrete failure cases, grade-dependent pathology scores, and visual comparisons across prototype counts and backbones.

E5.justification: v1 supplies point estimates without uncertainty reporting. v2 Table 5 introduces ± values for alignment IoUs, including an overall 99.0% ± 0.6, but does not define the uncertainty measure or sampling unit. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds or significance tests.

E6.justification: All 195 Table 1 scores and the original component-ablation scores are unchanged. New results include IVPT consistency/stability/accuracy of 63.2/71.5/74.2% on PartImageNet and 72.6/77.4/86.4% on PASCAL-Part, 97.5% human annotation accuracy, alignment IoUs, overhead measurements and additional ablation and qualitative findings. These expand the evidence rather than demonstrate same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: CRD with spatial bias, region-based feature aggregation, Gumbel-Softmax grouping, KL alignment and prompt-score averaging are retained. The cross-layer terminology, explicit loss coefficients still set to one, and fuller descriptions of existing part-shaping losses do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and method explanations undergo substantial rewriting, with cross-layer terminology replacing hierarchical terminology throughout much of the paper. The VPT preliminary is condensed into prompt construction, qualitative discussions are reordered, the original region-map comparison moves to Appendix G.1, and the expanded material receives a new appendix structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. v1's introductory illustration is removed, the fusion diagram is redrawn, pathology and car displays are combined with aircraft examples, and the original qualitative comparison moves to v2 Figure 8. Additional tables and figures present alignment, sensitivity, generalization and failure analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds a direct discussion of Prompt-CAM and references for aircraft, VLCS and newer prompt-learning work, while removing LPT, PW-Net and S-Prompts references. Comparisons with prior approaches become more explicit, but the principal positioning around region grounding, shared concepts and multilayer interpretation is retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B supplies explicit mathematical definitions for the previously referenced part-shaping losses and radial background mask (Equations 11–17), expanding their formal specification. The core aggregation and fusion mathematics remains equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially reduces v1's reliance on one quantitative benchmark and sparse training documentation through additional benchmark comparisons, targeted ablations, human evaluation, explicit failure analysis and detailed implementation information. Human-study scoring and IoU uncertainty remain under-specified, and backbone-freezing descriptions conflict. Nevertheless, the broader testable evidence and improved reproducibility provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IVPT, with matching authors, core pipeline and retained experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–G, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds benchmark comparisons, human evaluation, alignment measurements, sensitivity experiments and additional qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original CUB-200-2011 comparisons, component ablations and qualitative experiments on birds, Stanford Cars and Gleason-2019.

results.title: Exploring Interpretability for Visual Prompt Tuning with Cross-layer Concepts

C1.justification: The central efficiency, effectiveness and description-noise robustness contributions remain. The abstract narrows the empirical claim from outperforming existing methods generally to outperforming methods using textual descriptions for item representation on real-world Amazon datasets.

C2.justification: v2 explains the Goodbooks disadvantage through weak visual information, qualifies robustness under poor image quality, and hypothesizes why longer user histories hurt performance. Section 5 develops the interpretation of modality overlap as an efficiency advantage, while Appendix G expands v1's brief acknowledgment of missing text-specific information into a substantive limitation and research direction.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the adaptor's 512-unit intermediate dimension, offline feature caching, 3.4 KB per-item cache size, video-feature construction, and scaling-related memory, storage, throughput and training costs. The original learning rate, training batch size, hardware and code URL are retained; caching disclosure does not establish a changed original procedure.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original four Amazon categories and COCO similarity analysis, while adding Amazon Automotive, Video and Clothing, H&M Fashion, MicroLens and Goodbooks. It also evaluates entirely unseen target items and low-resolution images, substantially extending domains and test conditions.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains its comparator set. Appendix D.3 newly evaluates LC-Rec and IDGenRec on Sport and Art, broadening comparison to competing semantic-ID and textual-identifier representations. IDGenRec was discussed but not experimentally compared in v1.

E3.justification: The original leave-one-out protocol, 100 sampled negatives and Hit/NDCG metrics remain unchanged. New protocols include full-catalog comparisons, unseen-item subsets containing 302 Sport and 29 Art users, user-history grouping, extraction-inclusive timing, and 5K–20K catalog simulations with top-100 reranking. These are additions rather than demonstrated revisions to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of entirely unseen items, cold/warm users, image-quality sensitivity, successful versus unsuccessful image cases, and expanding catalogs with model reuse. Existing module, LoRA, backbone and training-strategy ablations remain; the missing-image experiment moves from Section 4.5 to Appendix E.8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. The additional results continue the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: The retained tables preserve their numerical values, but v2 adds substantial new results. Examples include MicroLens Hit@5 of 0.4854 versus TALLRec's 0.4459 and Goodbooks Hit@5 of 0.4870 versus TRSR's 0.5100 (Tables 6–7). Full-catalog, robustness, timing and scaling outcomes are newly reported, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core adaptor, alignment and retrieval objectives, frozen LLM and score fusion remain unchanged; ILA and IRE become RISA and RERI. A limited input adaptation averages sampled-frame image features for MicroLens video recommendations (Appendix E.4).

P1.justification: v2 renames the paper and modules, edits the introduction, merges training and inference sections, and moves implementation details, baseline descriptions, missing-image analysis and sequential related work into appendices. The appendices are extensively regrouped, with a contents page and dedicated discussion and limitations sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column ACM formatting to single-column ICLR formatting, with extensively resized and repositioned displays. v1 Figures 1–2 merge into v2 Figure 1; several retained multipanel plots are rearranged. New benchmark and image-quality tables and user-group and image-case figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially through discussion of semantic IDs and textual identifiers, multimodal redundancy, and recent multimodal LLM recommenders such as MSRBench and MLLM-MSR (Section 5; Appendices D.3 and F). The earlier sequential-recommendation discussion is largely retained and relocated.

T1.justification: The original mathematical definitions, objectives and quadratic token-length complexity analysis remain equivalent. Appendix E.13 adds a limited complexity argument asserting O(1) visual-feature indexing and catalog-independent request cost under fixed top-100 reranking; no supporting proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1's recommendation evidence centered on four Amazon categories and left visual-extraction costs unspecified. v2 addresses important gaps through competing compact-representation baselines, extraction-inclusive timing, and tests that expose applicability limits, especially TRSR's advantage on Goodbooks and sensitivity to poor images. These additions substantially strengthen empirical support and qualification without changing the retained results. Ambiguous timing wording between Section 4.3 and Appendix E.5 remains, but does not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe I-LLMRec despite the changed title and module names. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds benchmark evaluations, comparator experiments, robustness analyses and catalog-scaling simulations.

before.justification: v1 reports original recommendation experiments, image-description similarity measurements, efficiency analyses and ablations, including appendix results.

results.title: Token-Efficient Item Representation via Images for LLM Recommender Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: SD2.1-VAE16, SR-specific CiD/CiDA, and a simplified one-step pipeline offering a favorable quality-efficiency tradeoff. Additional evidence and appendix extensions do not materially redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning unexplored larger latent spaces and CiDA's memory requirements restricting DiT extensions (Section 5). It qualifies SD2.1-VAE16's T2I performance and adds interpretations of semantic prompts, CFG's fidelity-quality tradeoff, and adversarial loss improving no-reference scores while worsening LPIPS (Appendix A.4). v1 provides substantially less qualification and component-level interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds training pseudocode and staged-training documentation, guidance and weighting parameters, the 19.2% data-selection retention rate, user-study sampling details, complete prompt alternatives, and TensorRT deployment information. These greatly expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that the original training procedure changed. However, v1's explicit LAION-5B/FLUX data-generation description and project-page pointer disappear.

E1.justification: The principal SR and text-to-image coverage is retained. v3 adds qualitative evaluation on KwaiSR user-generated content (Figure 17) and targeted tests with extremely degraded faces (Figure 10). These provide limited additional domain and degradation-scenario coverage.
