E2.justification: The main SR benchmark comparator set is unchanged. v3 adds HYPIR and SD3.5-large with ControlNeXt in Figure 15, and additional VAE comparators including SD3.5 and FLUX in Table 5. DALL-E is removed from the retained text-to-image comparison, matching v1 Table 1 to v3 Table 11.

E3.justification: The main SR protocol is retained, but v3 substantially extends evaluation settings. It adds DeQA scoring while retaining DepictQA in the appendix, and reports an expanded GenEval/FID comparison on 20k COCO prompts, whereas v1's T2I table specified 30k. New protocols include prompt and CFG sweeps, batch-size-8 training-cost measurements, multiple deployment precisions and resolutions, and the 10k-iteration SDXL extension.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's distillation, VAE-channel and prompt-extractor comparisons, v3 separately examines adversarial and representation-alignment losses (Table 8), positive/negative prompt combinations and CFG sensitivity (Tables 6-7), VAE reconstruction and latent distributions (Table 5; Figures 11-12), and difficult face-restoration cases. These substantially expand evidence about individual design choices.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and preference percentages without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3's disclosure of ten user-study images concerns sample selection, not repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Most headline SR scores and the 77 ms runtime remain unchanged. v3 adds DeQA results, including GenDR's 4.1289 on RealSet80, detailed GenEval scores, VAE/component/prompt/CFG results, computational measurements and SDXL-variant examples. Conversely, v1's RealLR200 benchmark table and VAE-specific 36.25%/63.75% human-preference results are removed. The DepictQA heatmap is retained unchanged in the appendix.

M1.justification: The original SD2.1-based GenDR and CiDA objectives remain essentially unchanged. However, Appendix A.5 introduces GenDR-1.3B: a pruned SDXL generator adapted to SD3.5's 16-channel VAE and flow-matching scheduler, with SD3.5 score networks and an adapted CiD objective. This is a substantive architecture and distillation extension.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and selected explanatory passages are revised. Preliminaries is integrated into Related Work, T2I and DepictQA material is reorganized, and limitations and appendices receive explicit sections. Most existing methodology and conclusion prose remains closely matched; the expansion is primarily additional scientific documentation.

P2.justification: v3 switches to a single-column ICLR layout, redesigns the opening comparison, expands the VAE/distillation visual comparison, and introduces algorithm boxes, diagnostic tables and extensive qualitative panels. The earlier T2I gallery/table and DepictQA heatmap are relocated and reformatted, while the RealLR200 comparison table is removed.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of Transfer VAE Training as a related fidelity solution with the same compression rate, plus references supporting HYPIR, ControlNeXt, KwaiSR and DeQA. Several earlier references, including DALL-E, LAION-5B and DepictQA, are removed. The broader positioning around GAN priors, diffusion restoration and score distillation remains stable.

T1.justification: v1 asserts the generated-to-ground-truth latent substitution underlying CiD without a formal proof. v3 Appendix A.1 adds Equations 12-15, characterizing an optimal MSE predictor through conditional expectation and deriving the corresponding expected-inner-product identity. This adds formal reasoning for a central step under an optimal-predictor assumption; the main equations remain essentially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves support for the central design choices through separate loss-component ablations, VAE/prompt/CFG analyses, an idealized CiD derivation, and measured training and deployment costs. Pseudocode and explicit limitations make the method more assessable. Removing the RealLR200 comparison and some data-provenance details weakens completeness, and the new warm-up prose specifies L1 while Algorithm 2 shows squared-L2 loss. These shortcomings temper but do not outweigh the substantial gains in diagnostic evidence and technical transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GenDR research, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends after its references; v3 includes Appendices A and B. Material relocated into those appendices can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and additionally reports component ablations, reconstruction tests, computational measurements and preliminary SDXL-based GenDR results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GenDR benchmark results, distillation ablations, human and MLLM preference evaluations, and SD2.1-VAE16 generation results.

results.title: GenDR: Lighten Generative Detail Restoration

C1.justification: The principal claims about robust inference-time alignment, convex weight optimization, analytic best responses and efficient blockwise decoding remain. v2 adds an abstract-level effectiveness claim for the distilled policy and extends its headline empirical claims to LLM-as-Judge evaluation, without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 argues that RMOD also works with positively correlated objectives, attributes high-K deterioration of some best-of-K baselines to reward overoptimization, and interprets distillation performance alongside policy divergence. Its qualitative explanations shift from conciseness to helpfulness and safety. It also removes v1's explicit concluding limitation about reward bias and value-function accuracy.

D1.justification: v2 documents distillation using 16000 HH prompts and three training epochs, the MAXMIN-GRPO implementation, approximate training/evaluation times, and additional hardware settings. Appendix C.5 supplies complete separate GPT-4o judging prompts and evaluation instructions. These materially expand reproducibility information; the repository URL itself is unchanged.

E1.justification: The same three datasets remain. Within UltraFeedback, v2 replaces the conciseness objective with safety and adds a four-objective scenario excluding safety to examine positively correlated objectives. Coverage changes are confined to task variants within an existing dataset.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 2 adds MAXMIN-GRPO, shown as the Maxmin GRPO bar, providing a robust fine-tuning comparator. UltraFeedback's CONCISENESS comparator is replaced by INSTRUCTION-FOLLOWING and SAFETY. Table 3 adds direct-reward best-of-K comparisons, including WORSTCASE selection. The CD- prefixes merely rename existing controlled-decoding baselines.

E3.justification: Reported UltraFeedback settings change from four to sixteen training responses per prompt and from 956 to 1000 test prompts; Figure 4 changes from worst-case win rate to reward improvement. v2 also introduces separate GPT-4o grading for helpfulness and harmlessness, KL estimation protocols, and length-normalized HH latency measurements on a 40GB A100. The original UltraFeedback latency protocol remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds the correlated-objective ablation, KL-divergence analysis, and direct-reward best-of-K sweeps examining reward overoptimization. It updates weight-trajectory examples and replaces the UltraFeedback conciseness case study with two HH cases. Existing block-size, lambda, ValuePrism reverse-order and UltraFeedback latency analyses are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions display error bars without explaining their construction and retain the same unelaborated latency-significance statement. v2's additional error bars accompany revised or new results; it does not document new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence-interval procedures or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 replaces UltraFeedback results under changed objectives and settings, so these do not establish a same-setting improvement over v1. It adds substantial results: Table 1 reports GPT-4o worst-case win rates of 59.1% for RMOD, 57.9% for DISTILL-RMOD and 57.6% for CD-UNIFORM. Tables 2-4 add latency, direct-reward best-of-K and KL results, alongside new ablation and qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The central maxmin decoding procedure remains, but v2 introduces DISTILL-RMOD, a policy trained by supervised fine-tuning on RMOD-generated responses. Appendix C.1 also changes UltraFeedback's value architecture from five separately trained models to one model with five outputs. These are substantive procedural and architectural changes.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around balancing critical objectives. Related Work becomes a separate section, the method exposition centers on one practical algorithm, blockwise decoding moves earlier, and the experimental appendix is extensively reorganized. Acknowledgement and reproducibility statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 changes document typography and page layout, condenses two algorithm displays into one, adds four tables, expands Figure 2 and redraws UltraFeedback plots with different axes and legends. v1's paired ValuePrism figure is split between the main text and appendix, and judging prompts and response examples receive boxed displays.

R1.justification: The main positioning within robust multi-objective alignment remains. v2 adds discussion of Transfer Q-star, Chehade et al.'s constrained inference-time alignment and Yoon et al.'s robust best-of-K work, and distinguishes objective robustness from MAXMIN-RLHF's user-group robustness. References supporting the removed preference-history motivation and no-regret discussion are dropped.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix D's alternative Hedge-BR treatment is removed, including payoff definitions, update derivations, an O(1/sqrt(I)) approximate-equilibrium guarantee and comparisons with gradient descent. The central RMOD proofs and KKT analysis remain in Appendices A-B. v2 additionally formalizes the MAXMIN-GRPO objective and updates in Appendix C.1.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily assesses alignment using the reward models driving optimization. v2 substantially strengthens validation through separate GPT-4o judging, direct investigation of reward overoptimization and a robust fine-tuning comparator. Distillation, latency and KL analyses also make practical tradeoffs more assessable, with fuller implementation and judging details. These gains outweigh removal of the optional Hedge-BR discussion and explicit concluding caveat, while the central proofs remain. The added judge comparisons still lack uncertainty estimates, and revised UltraFeedback results cannot establish gains over v1 under identical conditions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RMOD research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional distillation, GPT-4o evaluation, KL-divergence and latency results.

before.justification: v1 reports original RMOD experiments on HH, UltraFeedback and ValuePrism, including reward comparisons, ablations, latency measurements and generated examples.

results.title: Robust Multi-Objective Controlled Decoding of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central claim that semantic structural tokens and query-focused captions improve temporal localization is retained. V2's conclusion extends the effectiveness claim to dataset-wise fine-tuning, beyond v1's zero-shot evidence. Its introduction also drops v1's explicit claim to be the first framework eliminating all generated boundary-related information.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the brief account of unstable symmetric-loss training with an explanation based on fewer negative samples. Section 6 introduces a substantive tradeoff between semantic generalization and precise boundary modeling, explicitly declining to replace boundary-centric approaches entirely. Appendix B discusses temporal-position biases, while Appendix F identifies specific failure mechanisms absent from v1's general acknowledgment of room for improvement.

D1.justification: V2 adds stage-specific freezing details, hidden-state layer choices, overlap handling, QWen2VL integration instructions, and a statement describing supplementary code and generated data. The original hyperparameter table, hardware, and prompt templates are retained. Some specificity is lost: Table 1 omits per-model frame counts and numerical LoRA ranks, and Appendix D drops v1's explicit rank/alpha exception.

E1.justification: The datasets and nine E.T.Bench tasks are retained. However, v1 Table 2 and Section 5.3 evaluate standalone QVHighlights multi-segment moment retrieval; v2 drops that evaluation and retains highlight detection. Added dataset-wise fine-tuning uses existing datasets rather than expanding task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the reported comparator set. Table 1 adds Dispider, Tarsier, Tarsier2, and QWen2-VL; Table 2 adds Seq2Time, NumPro-FT, VideoChat-T, and specialist comparisons including M-DETR, UMT, QD-DETR, CG-DETR, and UniVTG. Table 7 adds the Interleaving strategy. Its Positional Embedding rows match v1's Timestamp Tokens rows and are not a new comparator.

E3.justification: V2 adds dataset-wise fine-tuning on Charades-STA and QVHighlights, a QWen2VL-7B configuration, and Charades-STA R@1 at IoU 0.3. These extend the evaluation design beyond v1's zero-shot comparisons. The highlight metric label changes from HIT@0.1 to HIT@1, but shared values remain identical, so an underlying recalculation is not established.

E4.justification: V2 Table 6 newly quantifies asymmetric versus symmetric grounding losses and frame-level versus segment-pooled features. Table 7 extends QFC compatibility testing to Interleaving. Appendix F and Figure 6 add four failure cases concerning incorrect attention, boundaries, event counts, and transition prediction. V1's existing component and backbone ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and averages across tasks. Neither reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests.

E6.justification: Shared MeCo ETChat results remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial result entries. For example, MeCo QWen2VL reports Charades-STA R@1 0.5 of 50.1 zero-shot and 68.5 after dataset-wise fine-tuning, plus fine-tuned QVHighlights mAP of 45.3. These concern new configurations or protocols, not improvements under unchanged settings. V1's QVHighlights moment-retrieval mAP results, including MeCo's 26.2 and 27.4, are removed.

M1.justification: The structural-token, query-focused-captioning, and contrastive-grounding framework remains intact. V2 Appendix B introduces a dataset-wise fine-tuning adaptation: one final transition token represents all background frames, replacing temporally interleaved transition tokens in that setting. MeCo is also implemented on QWen2VL-7B.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. V1's separate Preliminary section is absorbed into Method; captioning precedes grounding; training and inference receive a dedicated subsection. V2 also reorganizes the appendices and adds separate limitations, reproducibility, acknowledgments, and manuscript-assistance disclosures.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. Figures 1–2 are redrawn, new label-construction and failure-case figures are added, and Tables 1–2 are substantially restructured. Colored result highlighting becomes bold/italic emphasis. The inference algorithm moves to the appendix, while existing qualitative examples and prompt figures are largely retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 substantially refreshes the literature coverage, adding newer temporal methods such as Chrono, LLaVA-MR, and VideoChat-T, specialist comparisons, and additional contrastive-learning foundations. It removes v1's cognitive event-segmentation, visual-attention, and background-modeling literature. The semantic-versus-boundary positioning remains, but the supporting research context and explicit novelty framing are revised.

T1.justification: V1 Section 4.1 explicitly requires consecutive segments to tile the video; v2 removes those constraints and explicitly admits overlapping events in Figure 3 and Appendix E. V2 also defines segment-pooled features for the added loss variants. The central language-model and grounding equations remain equivalent, and no formal proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support and the account of applicability. The loss ablation quantifies a previously underexplained design choice; newer comparators, another backbone, and dataset-wise fine-tuning test broader practical validity. Specific failure cases and the boundary-precision limitation make the conclusions better qualified. These gains outweigh the loss of standalone QVHighlights moment-retrieval evidence and some baseline-setting detail.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MeCo by the same authors, despite the revised title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original MeCo evaluations and adds results for a QWen2VL implementation, dataset-wise fine-tuning, loss variants, and failure cases.

before.justification: V1 reports original MeCo evaluations on E.T.Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights, alongside controlled comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–6.

results.title: Measure Twice, Cut Once: A Semantic-Oriented Approach to Video Temporal Localization with Video LLMs

C1.justification: The central claim that hidden perturbations can destroy DNS output intelligibility remains. The abstract shifts from emphasizing near-term targeted-attack plausibility to describing targeted results as negative, qualifies imperceptibility through participant/sample variation, and focuses the deployment warning on open-source systems in safety-critical applications. The targeted-attack qualifications already present in v1 remain in the appendix.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability limits concerning offline, per-utterance attacks, streaming requirements, and playback nonlinearities, gain control, and codecs. It also interprets the new masking and transfer results, quantifies temporal masking's contribution, proposes possible RIR smoothing effects, and discusses inference-time model switching or ensembling as potential defenses. These extend v1's existing gradient-access and targeted-metric caveats.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, asset versions/commits and licenses in Table 4, fuller computing-resource and hyperparameter-selection disclosures, and detailed human-stimulus construction and assignment. It also explains MP-SENet's memory issue while retaining the original input truncation. Most model descriptions and STFT/Adam settings are relocated from v1 rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: Section 6 adds transcription and ABX discrimination tasks involving 15 audio/multimedia researchers, substantially extending evaluation beyond computational speech-quality measurements. The original DNS Challenge speech coverage remains; the recorded-RIR-only experiment isolates acoustic material that v2 describes as already represented in the original mixed-RIR evaluation.

E2.justification: Section 5.2.4 and Appendix D.4 introduce substantive comparisons against STFT-domain l-infinity and l2 constraints, calibrated frequency-only masking, and Qin et al.'s original masking constraint. These strategies are actually evaluated against the full pipeline, although only on one Demucs clip. The original four DNS target models and Gaussian defense remain.

E3.justification: The original computational budgets remain, but v2 introduces several new protocols: five-second human-study clips at 30/50 dB SNR with reverb and tighter masking; calibrated component comparisons on one clip; equal 5,000-iteration model comparisons; recorded-RIR-only evaluation; and leave-one-out transfer with relaxed masking. These additions substantially expand experimental controls and testing procedures.

E4.justification: Appendices D.3–D.6 add masking-offset sensitivity, component ablations isolating temporal masking and threshold reduction, robustness to recorded RIRs, and a fixed-iteration check of model rankings. Appendix D.2.2 also tests whether ensemble optimization improves transfer. These investigate distinct questions beyond v1's retained analyses.

E5.justification: v1 mainly reports standard errors across 20 seeds. v2 adds participant/item two-way bootstrap confidence intervals, an intersection–union test for transcription differences, an ABX test against chance, and standard deviations in Table 3. The new transfer experiment's run count is inconsistent: Figure 3 states 10 seeds, while Figure 8 states 20 for the same displayed reverb curves.

E6.justification: The original attack curves and performance entries in Tables 1–2 are retained. Added outcomes include near-zero attacked-output human word accuracy and 59% ABX accuracy, limited ensemble transfer under relaxed masking, and sensitivity and recorded-RIR results. New fixed-budget results include FSN+ at -0.338 ± 0.245 and MP-SENet at -1.258 ± 0.102 mean ± SD (Table 3); these are additional results under specified conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Appendix D.2.2 adds an attack variant trained against two Demucs checkpoints before evaluation on a held-out checkpoint. The core STOI-based PGD, temporal masking, and over-the-air projection procedures remain unchanged. The explicit loss equations clarify optimization already described in v1 rather than establish new losses.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, with an explicit contributions list and a question-by-question results summary. Related work is condensed; model descriptions, targeted attacks, and transfer discussion move into reorganized appendices. The human-study section and expanded appendix structure substantially change the narrative organization beyond simply appending results.

P2.justification: v2 adds human-study distribution plots, ensemble-transfer plots, masking-sensitivity figures, a recorded-RIR figure, and fixed-budget and asset-provenance tables. Existing targeted-attack and model-comparison displays move to the appendix, while captions and main-text figure arrangements are extensively revised. The original plotted attack values remain unchanged despite resizing and relocation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references covering emergency communications, mobile and air-traffic speech enhancement, recorded RIRs, bootstrap inference, and physical audio attacks. It removes the dedicated image-denoising discussion and its Yan/Ning references. The principal positioning against Dong et al. and earlier psychoacoustic audio attacks remains.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 adds formal statistical reasoning: participant/item bootstrap estimators, intersection–union hypotheses and rejection conditions, and the argument that this joint test needs no multiple-comparisons correction. The attack formulations and masking/deconvolution mathematics in Appendices A–C are retained, with no new attack-robustness theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked listener validation. v2's transcription study directly supports output unintelligibility for three models, while its crossed participant/item analysis, component comparisons, recorded-RIR tests, and fixed-budget check substantially strengthen the evidence. Code-access and asset-version disclosures also improve reproducibility. The human study covers narrower conditions with tighter masking, and nonsignificant ABX discrimination does not prove imperceptibility; the conclusion's validation language therefore remains too strong. Despite these limits and the transfer seed-count inconsistency, the overall evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same speech-denoising adversarial-attack study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains the original computational results and adds human transcription and ABX results, component comparisons, masking-sensitivity experiments, and additional robustness checks.

before.justification: v1 reports original computational experiments on four DNS models, including targeted and untargeted attacks, model transfer, Gaussian defenses, and simulated over-the-air attacks.

results.title: Are Deep Speech Denoising Models Robust to Adversarial Noise?

C1.justification: v2 expands CAVE's central applicability claim to training without ground-truth pose annotations and redefines its proposed representation around ellipsoid volumes. In v1, annotated poses and cuboid approximation were explicit limitations, with pose estimation only suggested as a workaround. The joint robustness, interpretability and NOV-aware attribution claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops applicability boundaries and mechanisms: pose-estimator errors, geometry-versus-scalability tradeoffs, missed instances from object-centric training, and concept ambiguity under symmetry or deformation. Appendix B additionally explains how canonical meshes can smooth fine details and miss intra-class shape variation. These replace or extend v1's largely prospective pose and cuboid limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a CAVE code link, a detailed training-hyperparameter table, H100 training times, Gaussian-visibility filtering details and mesh projection/rendering instructions. These greatly expand v1's sparse CAVE implementation documentation without establishing that every newly disclosed step changed. Conversely, v1's exact filtered Pascal-Part sample-count table is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on ImageNet3D, extending the original Pascal-based coverage to many additional object categories. It also evaluates orientation estimation and explicitly examines multi-object scenes in Appendices C and I. Pascal3D+, OccludedP3D+, OOD-CV and Pascal-Part remain represented.

E2.justification: v2 removes CRAFT, MCD, ICE and PCX from the classification-accuracy comparison, where they appeared in v1 Table 3, while retaining them for interpretability evaluation. Appendix G expands the original vanilla-LRP contrast with evaluated Guided Backpropagation, SmoothGrad, GradCAM and Integrated Gradients comparators.

E3.justification: Reported training budgets change from 100 to 200 epochs for ProtoPNet/TesNet and from 60 to 200 main-training epochs for PIP-Net; MCD's completeness threshold changes from 0.7 to 0.9. v2 drops the ConvNext PIP-Net configuration, introduces estimated-pose evaluation and revises 3D-C. Pureness is removed, while local coverage survives as spatial localisation. New pose-tolerance and controlled geometry experiments add further protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds estimated-versus-annotated pose comparisons, four-shape ablations, quantitative attribution comparisons and multi-object, symmetry and OOD failure analyses. Accuracy-versus-concept-count sweeps replace v1's reconstruction-quality-versus-count plot. The original concept-space separation and extraction-method analyses are retained in Appendix H, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 Figures J6–J9 newly specify seed 42 for randomly selecting concepts and example images; v1 gives no corresponding seed information. This is limited seed disclosure for qualitative sampling. Neither version reports repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial ImageNet3D, pose, geometry and attribution results. The reported OOD-CV ranking changes from LF-CBM 83.6% versus CAVE 81.4% in v1 Table 3 to CAVE 80.4% versus LF-CBM 73.5% in v2 Table 2. Method and training settings differ, so this is not a same-setting improvement. Pascal-Part accuracy and v1's complete class-wise 3D-C table are no longer reported.

M1.justification: v1 uses cuboid volumes trained with annotated poses. v2 Section 4.2 introduces training with Orient-Anything estimated poses and adopts ellipsoid volumes, also supporting more expressive CAD geometries. These materially change training inputs and object representations; the underlying K-Means concept extraction, concept matching and NOV-aware LRP remain.

P1.justification: The Plato's cave framing is removed from the title and narrative, and substantial introductory and explanatory passages are rewritten. v2 separates NOVUM preliminaries, CAVE and 3D consistency into dedicated sections, moves detailed LRP material to Appendix A, combines discussion and conclusion, and reorganises the supplement into indexed Appendices A–K.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. The opening illustration and method pipeline are redesigned, benchmark tables gain supervision and dataset groupings, and new geometry, pose, attribution and failure-case displays are added. Qualitative explanations receive extensive visual redesign; retained concept-space plots are relocated to Appendix H.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning around training without annotated poses and evaluating concepts without predefined part labels. New discussions cite Orient-Anything and concept-evaluation work by Huang, Behzadi-Khormouji and Oramas, and Zhu. This broadens the argument beyond v1's positioning around robust NOVUM classification and concept discovery, while retaining NOVUM as the foundation.

T1.justification: v2 Section 5 revises the existing 3D-C definition by explicitly normalising concept attributions and using the number of images containing a concept in its denominator, alongside converting dissimilarity to similarity. The 50% frequency filter and core dictionary-learning/LRP mathematics already existed in v1. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's suggested workaround for pose annotations into a tested method and substantially strengthens validation through ImageNet3D, controlled geometry experiments and quantitative attribution comparisons. Expanded implementation details and concrete failure analyses improve reproducibility and clarify applicability. Estimated poses incur accuracy losses, explicitly documented in Table C2, and some implementation descriptions remain inconsistent, including two versus three upsampling layers. Nevertheless, the demonstrated reduction in annotation dependence and stronger validation provide substantial overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CAVE, retaining identifiable concept-extraction, neural-volume classification and attribution foundations despite the changed title and substantial revision. The main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and interpretability results, plus pose-estimation, volume-shape and attribution experiments in Tables C1–C2, F1–F3 and G1.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification and interpretability results in Tables 2–3, alongside concept-extraction ablations and qualitative evaluations in its supplement.

results.title: Interpretable 3D Neural Object Volumes for Robust Conceptual Reasoning

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the four-role agent and efficient Chain-of-LoRA integration. v3 explicitly positions Chain-of-LoRA as a test-time scaling mechanism and extends the introduction's headline comparison to both GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro on long-video benchmarks. These refine the contribution claims without replacing the central research proposition.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's brief component explanations, v3 discusses why continuous timestamp regression helps, identifies grounding as the dominant failure source, and distinguishes grounding/QA correlations across datasets. It acknowledges sequential error accumulation and unmatched settings in imported API comparisons, interprets prompt-only transfer, and adds joint optimization and audio integration as future directions (Appendix B.2–B.3 and Section 5).

D1.justification: Most training hyperparameters and prompt templates are retained. v3 adds runtime hardware and controlled-API settings, and explicitly states that code, checkpoints, data, and training logs are released; v1 only supplies the project link. Conversely, v3 omits v1's general 2-FPS sampling specification with a 1-FPS grounder exception, and removes the explicit QVHighlights test-split label.

E1.justification: v3 adds MultiHop-EgoQA, requiring grounded reasoning across multiple relevant moments, and introduces egocentric training through 67K NaQ samples for VideoMind-Ego (Tables 10 and 12). These extend coverage within the existing video grounding and question-answering domains; the original 14 benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Comparison sets change substantially. v3 Table 5 adds Grounded-VideoLLM, TRACE, LLaVA-ST, and UniTime while dropping several earlier grounding comparators, including the fine-tuned specialist rows. Table 17 adds LongVILA-R1 and Video-R1. CG-Bench loses GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-Flash, Qwen-VL-Chat, and MiniCPM-v2.6; NExT-GQA loses VIOLETv2. These are comparator changes within corresponding experiments, beyond renamed methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces controlled 300-question MLVU/LVBench subsets with matched frame and decoding settings, an 80/20 held-out planner retraining experiment, and GPU latency evaluation. Additional configurations include Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, and the NaQ-trained variant. The Charades-STA VTimeLLM comparison also switches from 13B to 7B. These constitute substantial additions to evaluation design, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds alternative timestamp-modeling comparisons, planner input ablations, expanded verifier evaluation, error attribution, grounding-versus-answering correlation, runtime analysis, and transfer across backbones and prompted APIs (Appendix B.3). The original pyramid and verifier-style ablations remain, while v1's auxiliary decoding-loss ablation and its results are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The new random splits, sampled subsets, and error proportions do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Reported VideoMind-2B Video-MME All/Long scores change from 53.6/45.4 to 55.4/46.3; MVBench average changes from 61.9 to 62.5; QVHighlights R1@0.7 changes from 55.77 to 59.35. v3 also adds QVHighlights-7B, MultiHop-EgoQA, adapted-backbone, controlled-API, and diagnostic results. Main CG-Bench, ReXTime, and NExT-GQA scores remain unchanged. Results under newly introduced conditions are additional evidence, not same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: The principal four-role architecture, timestamp decoder, losses, and Algorithm 1 remain intact. Appendix B.3 adds a limited procedural adaptation: simulating the multi-role pipeline through successive prompts on closed-source models without role-specific architecture or training. The expanded Chain-of-LoRA section otherwise explains the existing mechanism.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method explanations are extensively rewritten. v3 creates a dedicated Chain-of-LoRA subsection, reorders the experimental questions, moves benchmark exposition into the appendix, places references before the appendix, and adds an appendix contents list plus ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to the single-column ICLR format. Figure 1 is substantially redrawn around a shared backbone; separate Charades-STA and ActivityNet tables are merged. New error-distribution and correlation plots accompany numerous new analysis tables, while retained figures and tables are resized, restyled, and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 substantially updates positioning through recent video reasoning, temporal grounding, and backbone literature, including explicit comparisons with LongVILA-R1 and Video-R1. It replaces v1's characterization of its own procedure as moment-level MCTS with moment-level searching, prunes older search references, and adds neuroscience references supporting the human-reasoning analogy. These exceed citation-style or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: v3 removes v1 Section 3.2's inconsistent pyramid-level shape expression T/n^2, retaining the explicitly specified lengths T, T/2, T/4, and T/8. This is a limited correction to the mathematical description. The numbered equations and inference algorithm otherwise remain, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central design and efficiency claims through alternative timestamp implementations, held-out planner evaluation, measured latency, failure analysis, and matched-setting API comparisons. These address important gaps in v1. The benefits outweigh the removed loss ablation and documentation omissions, although reporting inconsistencies remain: Table 5 gives UniTime higher Charades-STA mIoU despite blanket superiority language, and Figure 7 shows 6.6% planning errors despite the text claiming less than 5%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VideoMind research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the revised title, organization, and expanded experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds MultiHop-EgoQA results, controlled comparisons, planner tests, runtime measurements, and error analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original VideoMind evaluations across 14 benchmarks, component ablations, and qualitative analysis in the main text and appendix.

results.title: VideoMind: A Chain-of-LoRA Agent for Temporal-Grounded Video Reasoning

C1.justification: The core conflict-resolution contribution remains, but v3 adds a claim of using only 10% of VILA-U's tokenizer-pretraining data and elevates reciprocal benefits of pixel and semantic tokens to a main finding. Its conclusion claims state-of-the-art unified-model performance among discrete autoregressive approaches and a first demonstration of hierarchical conflict resolution. v1 presents the downstream model more cautiously as a baseline implementation with further task synergy left to explore.

C2.justification: v3 newly attributes dual-encoder degradation to incompatible representation spaces, explains pixel-token benefits as compensation for quantization-related semantic loss, and interprets semantic tokens as supervision for generation. Appendices B–D discuss layer-selection generality, complementarity with MCQ and computational overhead. Conversely, Section 3.2 softens v1's claim that semantic supervision improves reconstruction to saying it does not degrade reconstruction.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents four-stage MLLM training, learning rates, batch sizes and optimizers in Table 13, and stage-specific datasets in Table 14. Appendix F supplies projector architecture, image-boundary tokens, clustering/UMAP procedures and detailed dual-encoder implementation controls. It also adds a project-page link and states that clustering code accompanies supplementary material, without establishing availability from these PDFs alone. However, v1's EMA/codebook-restart description and CFG value of 3 are omitted.

E1.justification: v3 adds OCRBench, TextVQA and AI2D to understanding evaluation, including explicit OCR-related coverage. Generation evaluation expands from illustrative examples to GenAI-Bench, MJHQ-30K, GenEval and WISE. Tokenizer training is reported as using CC12M plus ImageNet-1K and 50M LAION-400M images, versus CC12M in v1. The newly disclosed MLLM dataset inventory alone does not establish that those training sources changed.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds comparisons with QLIP, UniTok, TokenFlow, Muse-VL and TokLIP, among others, while removing its VQGAN row. The unified-model comparison in Table 5 adds Liquid, TokenFlow, UniTok, UniToken and Show-o2, and removes DreamLLM and SEEDLLaMA. The combined SigLIP/MoVQGAN baseline already existed in v1 and is not a newly introduced comparator.

E3.justification: v1 specifies 384px inputs, SigLIP-SO400M and residual depth 8; v3 includes 256px/depth-4 and 384px/depth-8 configurations, additional backbones and 7B models. Table 4 switches from SigLIP-SO400M/384 to SigLIP-L/256 and normalizes MME scores. New generation experiments introduce VQAScore/FID protocols and a matched Qwen2.5-3B VILA-U reproduction. Appendix B adds controlled backbone/layer experiments with fixed quantization settings and 2M training samples.

E4.justification: v3 adds pixel-only generation ablations, inter-layer similarity and clustering analyses, UMAP comparisons, reconstruction-layer sensitivity across backbones and model sizes, RVQ-versus-MCQ experiments, and computational-cost analysis. It also quantifies the previously qualitative dual-encoder comparison on MJHQ-30K. These substantially extend the questions tested beyond v1's objective ablation and semantic-only understanding comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3's dataset-averaged similarities and computational measurements do not introduce uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the SigLIP-SO400M DualToken results, including rFID 0.54 to 0.25 and zero-shot accuracy 81.6 to 82.0, under changed training and loss settings. v3 newly reports GenAI-Bench scores of 0.68 versus 0.55 for pixel-only generation, and MJHQ-30K FID of 7.88 versus 17.55 for the dual encoder. Numerous configuration and appendix results are added. The original Table 5 score vector is retained but labeled 256px despite v1's stated 384px setup, preventing an unqualified same-setting comparison.

M1.justification: Equation 4 changes semantic supervision from squared L2 distance to squared L2 minus cosine similarity. Appendix C also introduces a variant replacing RVQ with UniTok's MCQ. The central shallow/deep dual-codebook design, separate prediction heads and autoregressive formulation remain intact; expanded projector and training descriptions do not establish additional procedural changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten around explicit findings and updated positioning. Experiments are reorganized into tokenizer and unified-model sections, while implementation material is expanded and partly relocated to dedicated appendices. Terminology is refined toward pixel/appearance and semantic vocabularies, and author, affiliation and conference-header information changes.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, expands Figure 1, and redraws v1's Figure 3 as Figure 4. The generation gallery becomes a structured comparison with VILA-U and pixel-only outputs. New similarity, clustering and UMAP figures accompany substantially expanded tables, including a two-part Table 5 and appendix Tables 7–14.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around newer unified tokenizers and dual-encoder systems, including FQGAN, UniTok, QLIP, TokLIP and ILLUME+. Appendix C explicitly positions DualToken's hierarchical design as complementary to UniTok's quantizer improvements. The v1 assertion that TokenFlow lacks a unified understanding-and-generation model disappears. These are substantive changes beyond reference-format and publication-status updates.

T1.justification: Equation 4 substantively revises the mathematical definition of the semantic loss by adding negative cosine similarity. The other central quantization and autoregressive equations remain equivalent. No theorem, proof or substantive theoretical derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's reliance on qualitative generation examples and sparse implementation reporting. Quantitative generation benchmarks, matched comparisons, token ablations, cross-backbone layer tests and detailed training documentation provide much stronger support for the central design. Lost EMA/CFG details, absent uncertainty estimates and inconsistent resolution labeling remain limitations, and higher cross-version scores cannot be attributed solely to the method. Nevertheless, the added controlled evidence and reproducibility information resolve important weaknesses and clearly improve overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DualToken and retain the same central dual-codebook architecture. All pages, equations, tables and figures are readable, including v3's Appendices A–G; v1 ends with references and contains no appendix. Changed experimental settings require qualification but do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original understanding and generation results, layer and backbone ablations, quantizer comparisons and computational measurements in the main text and Appendices B–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original tokenizer evaluations, objective ablations, controlled downstream understanding experiments and generated-image examples in Tables 1–5 and Figure 4.

results.title: DualToken: Towards Unifying Visual Understanding and Generation with Dual Visual Vocabularies

C1.justification: Video generation moves from future work in v1 to a central demonstrated contribution in v2, including joint spatial-temporal scaling and an approximately threefold same-step video speedup claim. v2 also explicitly claims that the MMD objective improves convergence. The original claims of efficient progressive generation and a useful standalone patch loss remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies the earlier low-resolution teacher discussion: DMD can inherit teacher failures, while MMD and GAN objectives enable recovery (Appendix B). It also explains conditional-information loss from batch averaging, acknowledges that spectral analysis cannot determine schedules by itself, and discusses the defect tradeoff of MMD-only training. These materially clarify mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Appendices A and C provide expanded model-specific feature layers, MMD noising intervals, adapter ranks, synthetic-data generation settings, and sampling schedules. Appendix G newly discloses TinyVAE use for runtime measurements. Conversely, v1's explicit 500K synthetic-sample count and fake-score guidance value are no longer specified. These are substantial documentation changes, including both gains and losses.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates image generation, whereas v2 additionally trains and evaluates text-to-video generation using Wan2.1-generated videos, MovieGenBench, and VBench-2.0. COCO2014, MJHQ, PartiPrompts, and GenEval image coverage remains. The earlier internal real-data training comparison is removed.

E2.justification: The image comparisons add Hyper-SD and SD3.5-M-Turbo, plus FLUX comparisons involving Schnell, Turbo-Alpha, and Hyper-FLUX (v2 Table 3). The new video comparison evaluates Wan2.1 and CausVid, with CausVid retrained on the authors' synthetic dataset (Table 2). These substantially expand the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Image evaluation replaces CLIP Score with HPSv3. Reported training changes from 5K iterations and batch size 80 to approximately 3K iterations and model-dependent batches of 64 or 24. The main SD3.5-Large configuration also changes its step and scale schedule. New protocols include video evaluation on 1003 MovieGenBench prompts and patch-based image-quality metrics.

E4.justification: v2 adds batch-averaging and noising ablations for MMD, human comparisons of MMD-only training, high-frequency detail tests, spatial-only versus spatiotemporal video scaling, and expanded spectral and upsampling-ratio analyses. Constant-scale tests are expanded. Conversely, v1's explicit time-shift, no-scale-wise-training, real-data, and naive token-wise loss ablations are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions average runtime measurements over 100 independent runs and collect three assessor responses per image pair with majority voting. Human preference plots contain error bars in both. No changed seed, confidence-interval, significance-testing, or uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial SDXL, FLUX, video, and supplementary-analysis results and revises existing image, runtime, and ablation entries. For example, Table 1's upscale-before-noising FID-5K at t=800 changes from 13.0 to 14.7. The new video Table 2 reports SWD at 1.8 seconds/video and VideoReward 6.27. Changed training and timing documentation prevents interpreting the revised tables as isolated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 extends spatial SWD to joint spatial and temporal generation, adding frame-count schedules and adjacent-frame blending during latent upsampling (Section 4.1, Appendix C). This extends the training and sampling procedure beyond images. The underlying per-image patch-mean loss is retained despite PDM being renamed MMD; newly documented feature noising does not alone establish a change to the earlier implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. PDM becomes MMD terminology; DMD2 implementation material moves to Appendix A, and the low-resolution teacher discussion moves from Section 5.1 to Appendix B. Experiments are reorganized to present main comparisons first, followed by full-resolution comparisons and focused MMD ablations.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format. Benchmark tables are regrouped by model family, timing information is split into separate tables, and spectral, video, and loss-analysis displays are added. Existing training/sampling diagrams are relocated, while the four assessor-interface screenshots are enlarged onto separate appendix pages.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around progressive diffusion and MMD, adding discussions of f-DM, Relay Diffusion, pyramidal flow matching, DMMD, IMM, and GAN feature matching. It presents SWD as extending an existing progressive-diffusion research line, replacing v1's broader differentiation from previous diffusion approaches. The earlier standalone discussion of dynamic token-routing methods is removed.

T1.justification: The kernel-based MMD expression in v2 restates the earlier mean-embedding definition, and the patch-mean loss remains mathematically equivalent. However, the explicit naive token-wise loss definition in v1 Appendix C, Equation 3, is removed with that comparison. Neither version supplies formal guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for generality and detail preservation through broader image/video validation and targeted loss, spectral, and upsampling analyses. Its explanation of low-resolution teacher failures and model-specific implementation guidance resolves important applicability gaps in v1. These gains outweigh the removed controls and dataset-size disclosure, although numerical consistency remains imperfect: spatial-only SWD's VBench score is 52.8 in Table 2 but 52.43 in Table 12.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SWD research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite extensive revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original image and video generation experiments, expanded spectral and loss analyses, runtime measurements, and human preference studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original spectral analyses, image-generation experiments, runtime measurements, ablations, and human preference studies in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Scale-wise Distillation of Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list shift the central innovation from multi-turn refinement using GRPO to the proposed 3D-SPO algorithm, emphasizing object-level physics modulation and temporal credit assignment during training. V2 also removes the conclusion's explicit claim of improved generation diversity over supervised approaches.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies the earlier increasing-depth interpretation with degradation at T=7, attributed to over-adjustment or reward saturation. It adds explanations of training efficiency and reasoning-trace benefits, and recognizes SFT as useful initialization despite its limitations as standalone training. Appendix C also explicitly identifies single-room and static-lighting boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents dataset construction, asset retrieval and filtering, collision processing, Blender settings, generation and evaluation prompts, and staged reward training. It clarifies initial empty-room inputs and single-turn testing. Conversely, v1's specification of four H100 GPUs disappears; the stated public repository remains unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds Open3DVQA evaluation covering qualitative and quantitative spatial questions in urban environments, extending beyond indoor layout generation to a distinct task and domain. Appendix C's description of 10,000 indoor scenes documents the training data; it does not establish that the indoor dataset changed.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds GPT-4o, I-Design, and LayoutGPT to the original Qwen comparisons. New comparisons also include GPT-4, LLaVA-7B, and Qwen-VL-7B-SFT on Open3DVQA, plus SFT and hybrid training strategies in Table 7. The existing PPO and GRPO comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Added protocols include zero-shot Open3DVQA evaluation using success rates and absolute relative errors, T=7 refinement settings, and pseudo-SFT selection above reward 0.8 followed by 100-step RL evaluations. Section 2.5 also revises the reported perceptual-scoring procedure to hold the color/material grade fixed. Single-turn final evaluation is newly explicit, without establishing that v1 used multi-turn testing.

E4.justification: V2 expands the depth study into matched GRPO/3D-SPO comparisons through T=7, adds reasoning-trace removal controls, and analyzes training efficiency and SFT warm starts. These test additional mechanisms and tradeoffs beyond v1's reward-component and refinement-depth ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. V2's group standard deviation is part of policy optimization, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V1's headline 7B results—GPT-4o score 0.58, collision 13.7%, and constraint violations 76.2%—remain as GRPO results in v2 Table 3. V2 Table 1 instead reports 3D-SPO results of 0.62, 11.5%, and 70.8%, so this is not an unchanged-method performance update. V2 also adds external-baseline, T=7, reasoning-trace, SFT, and Open3DVQA results.

M1.justification: Section 2.6 replaces the GRPO formulation with 3D-SPO, introducing object-specific physics modulation of coordinate-token advantages alongside trajectory-level rewards. This changes policy optimization rather than merely renaming GRPO. Section 3.5 also introduces an optional SFT warm-start procedure using high-reward layouts.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method descriptions, optimization section, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Related work moves from the main text to Appendix B, while a dedicated SFT section, acknowledgments, and organized appendices substantially restructure the document.

P2.justification: V2 adds GRPO/3D-SPO and coordinate-masking diagrams, expands Tables 1 and 3, and introduces Tables 4–7, prompt listings, and additional scene illustrations. The original before/after montage is retained as Figure 4 rather than new evidence. Typography, headings, captions, and page layout are also restyled.

R1.justification: The three-part related-work survey is largely retained in Appendix B. V2 adds focused references including DeepSeekMath, OpenShape, Open3DVQA, and VLM2-Bench, and explicitly distinguishes 3D-SPO from standard GRPO. The broader positioning as an RL framework for VLM-based 3D layout generation remains.

T1.justification: Section 2.6 substantively reformulates the mathematics: v1's per-layout discounted reward surrogate becomes a discounted trajectory aggregate with coordinate-dependent, group-normalized advantages and a token-level clipped objective. These are changed mathematical definitions and optimization expressions, although neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 materially addresses v1's lack of direct scene-generator and SFT comparisons, adds matched GRPO/3D-SPO ablations, and supplies substantial dataset, rendering, and prompt documentation. These additions strengthen empirical support and reproducibility beyond merely reporting higher scores. The gains outweigh the removed hardware detail and reporting weaknesses, including Table 7's inconsistent constraint-direction label; incomplete evaluation protocols and absent uncertainty estimates remain limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MetaSpatial by the same authors. All 11 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, references, and v2's appendices, are readable. V1 contains no appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original layout-generation experiments and additional spatial-question-answering, reasoning-trace, and SFT experiments in Section 3 and Appendices F–G.

before.justification: V1 reports original layout-generation experiments, reward ablations, refinement-depth comparisons, and qualitative examples in Section 3 and Tables 1–3.

results.title: MetaSpatial: Reinforcing 3D Spatial Reasoning in VLMs for the Metaverse

C1.justification: V2 broadens the central contribution from action recognition centered on EPIC-KITCHENS to fine-grained action understanding across domains and output formats. The introduction claims SOTA on four action-recognition datasets and improvements on ten MLLM benchmarks, versus v1's EPIC-focused SOTA and five additional benchmark improvements. Structured-action prediction is also promoted to a principal contribution.

C2.justification: V2 introduces interpretations linking stronger visual attention and action-token aggregation to improved recognition, argues robustness across semantic difficulty levels, and uses distribution and K analyses to support the OOD interpretation. It explicitly discusses the structured pipeline's first-stage recall ceiling and restriction to applications requiring structured actions. Earlier narration-bias and unsuccessful chain-of-thought discussions remain, largely in the appendices.

D1.justification: V2 adds the difficulty-assessment prompt, attention-computation instructions, KV-cache details for multi-round appending, and inference costs of approximately 820 versus 4.3 GPU hours. Its availability statement now includes data and the benchmark alongside code and models. Core training hardware, learning rates, epochs and existing task prompts are retained, while some earlier dataset and benchmark descriptions are removed.

E1.justification: V2 adds EPFL-Smart-Kitchen-30, MECCANO and Animal Kingdom, extending evaluation to another cooking population, assembly activities and simultaneous animal actions. Additional MLLM evaluation expands from six to thirteen benchmarks, adding captioning and open-ended tasks through VDC, VideoDC, VideoEval-Pro, ActNet-QA, VideoChatGPT, CVRR and TempCompass.

E2.justification: V2 adds IPL to the existing EPIC comparison and evaluates VideoMAE, multi-modal VideoMAE, SlowFast and InternVL3-8B variants in the new domain experiments. Appendix E.3 also introduces multi-round appending as a structured-output comparator. The comparator roster in the general video benchmark table otherwise remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include zero-shot second-stage and finetuned EPFL evaluations with shared top-five candidate filtering, one-epoch MECCANO finetuning, and Animal Kingdom evaluation using Jaccard accuracy and an InternVL3-8B configuration. V2 also introduces attention aggregation, GPT-4o difficulty grading and experiments varying K during both training and testing. These are additional evaluation designs, rather than demonstrated reruns of all retained experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds attention analysis and visualization, difficulty-stratified accuracy, AVION–TIM distribution comparisons and K sensitivity, action-token number and supervision-layer ablations, and structured-output accuracy and computational-cost comparisons. These test mechanisms and design choices beyond v1's additive and leave-one-out ablations. Existing benchmark subcategory analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly reports JSD as 0.674 ± 0.089, a 95% confidence interval, p < 0.001 and Cohen's d = 7.57 over 9,668 validation samples. This adds statistical reporting for one supporting analysis; the estimation and testing procedures are insufficiently specified. Neither version reports repeated-training-run or seed uncertainty for the principal accuracy results.

E6.justification: New results include EPFL accuracies of 36.2 zero-shot and 46.6 finetuned, MECCANO accuracy of 51.7, Animal Kingdom Jaccard scores of 61.0 and 58.7, and seven additional MLLM benchmark columns. Leave-one-out results change, including full-model 73.4 to 74.1 and without-AVION 68.2 to 69.7, without establishing identical settings. The 16-frame EPIC classification rows disappear; the 32-frame scores and original six additional benchmark results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The documented core procedure retains hard-distractor training, the supervised action token, temporal detection, direct prediction and prior-action conditioning. V2's named two-stage pipeline elaborates the specialist top-K refinement already described in v1 Sections 3.1.1 and 5.2 and used in Table 4. The additional backbone and dataset applications do not establish a redesigned algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. V2 separates data reformulation from model design, combines experimental setup and results, redistributes discussion into appendices, and adds distinct conclusion and ethics sections. Terminology also changes, including official keys to action labels and prior-action memory to temporal order learning.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, redraws the pipeline diagram and rearranges Figure 1. It adds an attention visualization and several experimental tables, and substantially expands and groups the general benchmark table by output format. Earlier qualitative figures and the verb/noun performance plot are retained with resizing, relabeling and renumbering.

R1.justification: The research positioning is substantially revised. V2 explicitly distinguishes fine-grained action contrastiveness from InsTALL's procedural assistance, HAIC's captioning and MotionLLM's motion understanding, and adds literature supporting new benchmarks, structured-action applications and attention analysis. V1's standalone vision-centric MLLM survey and several broader literature discussions are removed or condensed.

T1.justification: The distractor-sampling formulation, temporal-padding equations, action-token hidden-state notation and prior-action objective are mathematically retained, sometimes consolidated or moved inline. Neither version contains theoretical proofs, and v2's new attention and distribution analyses are empirical rather than new formal results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of generalization and design choices through independent cooking, assembly and animal evaluations, broader output-format testing, and token-design and structured-output ablations. These address important coverage and diagnostic gaps in v1 while retaining its principal results. Some new support remains weak: Appendix D changes training and testing K together when interpreting overfitting, statistical procedures are underspecified, and revised ablation settings are unclear. Nevertheless, the additional controlled comparisons and cross-domain evidence provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLaVAction research, and their main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. V2 substantially expands and reorganizes the work.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds cross-domain evaluations, attention analyses, difficulty-stratified results and further ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations, training experiments, ablations and qualitative analyses on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and additional video benchmarks.

results.title: LLaVAction: evaluating and training multi-modal large language models for action understanding

C1.justification: v3 retains the central target-aware generation, curated-dataset and two-application contributions. It reframes the loss contribution from proposing a novel cross-attention loss to utilizing cross-attention supervision, and adds an explicit introductory claim of robustness to mask quality. Motion-planning motivation receives greater emphasis but already existed in v1.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking noisy captions to preservation of pretrained priors and grounding to the target token rather than the object noun. It identifies channel-scaling, multi-object-mask and temporal-switching limitations, and explains the hand detector's inapplicability to non-human agents. Appendix C.3 also discusses false positives and undercounting under the original and extended metrics.

D1.justification: Most training and inference details are retained. v3 adds parameter-count and VRAM-saving information, evaluation-mask selection instructions, automatic-mask hardware/timing details and more precise inference timing. It adds a project-page pointer while omitting v1's future code/data-release statement; the PDFs do not establish actual release availability.

E1.justification: The 1,290-clip BEHAVE/Ego-Exo4D training collection remains. v3 adds EgoIT-99 training for egocentric generation, explicit outdoor human-interaction tests, corrupted or automatically generated conditioning inputs, and multiple-object and temporal target-switching scenarios. These substantially broaden viewpoint, environment and input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: The CogVideoX, data-fine-tuned CogVideoX and adapted Direct-a-video attention-modulation baselines remain, as do DragDiffusion, Go-with-the-Flow and inpainting comparisons. The CogVideoX-Ego experiment extends the existing backbone-versus-target-aware comparison through domain fine-tuning; it does not introduce a distinct competing method.

E3.justification: The principal benchmark grows from 50 to 80 images, yielding 250 versus 400 videos. v3 introduces stricter temporal/contact-plus-motion metrics, 50-image mask experiments, egocentric adaptation and additional ablation settings. Its Section 4.3 specifies every fifth supervised block, conflicting with Appendix A.1's retained every-third setting; the actual block schedule therefore remains unresolved.

E4.justification: v3 adds mask dilation, erosion, circular-mask and automatic-segmentation tests; caption-removal training ablations and corrupted-prompt inference tests; and explicit multiple-object and target-switching failures. It also expands loss-weight sensitivity and domain-transfer/action-diversity analyses. The original block-selection, attention-region and attention-modulation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies that the five videos per test image use random seeds; v1 already reported five videos per image. This adds seed information without establishing increased repetition. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original ablation tables contain revised scores: the proposed method's Contact Score changes from 0.896 to 0.878, and data-fine-tuned CogVideoX changes from 0.692 to 0.638. These concern different benchmark sizes, not demonstrated same-setting declines. New Table 9 reports 0.770, 0.693 and 0.783 for the proposed method's two-frame, three-frame and Interaction Scores. Numerous robustness and qualitative findings are added; user-study scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core mask-channel architecture, target token, attention loss and LoRA training remain. v3 adds an automated GPT-4o/Grounded-SAM mask-acquisition pipeline and an egocentric adaptation procedure that transfers the target-aware LoRA onto a separately fine-tuned backbone (Appendices B and C.1).

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around target awareness and motion planning. Application order is reversed, the video-creation account is condensed, attention-region and block discussions are reordered, and the main discussion becomes a conclusion. The appendix is reorganized into thematic discussions, including relocated and expanded limitations.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. The opening teaser is removed, method diagrams and attention visualizations are merged into paired figures, and the video-creation pipeline moves to the appendix. New robustness tables and extensive qualitative and failure-case figures substantially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly connects the planning motivation to World Models, Navigation World Models and Dexterous World Models, and adds references supporting new components, including Grounded-SAM, CoTracker and EgoLife. The established controllable-video and human-scene positioning remains. Publication-year and venue updates to retained works do not constitute additional research.

T1.justification: Appendix C.3 introduces precise definitions for consecutive-frame Contact Score and Interaction Score, which combines contact with a target-displacement threshold. The diffusion objectives and attention equations remain substantively equivalent; the downsampled-mask notation is clarified. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central claim. Unlike v1, it tests dependence on mask precision and caption quality, checks whether the advantage survives stricter temporal/contact-plus-motion criteria, and documents concrete failure boundaries (Tables 5–9 and Appendix C). These address important weaknesses in v1's reliance on single-frame contact and limited robustness evidence. The new block-selection inconsistency harms reproducibility, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential depth and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Target-Aware Video Diffusion Models work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds mask and caption robustness experiments, stricter interaction measurements, domain-transfer demonstrations and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation comparisons, two user studies, ablations, qualitative demonstrations and physics-based imitation results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Target-Aware Video Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's four contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: introduce the situated audiovisual benchmark, establish model-human performance gaps, demonstrate benefits from fine-tuning, and provide a streaming baseline. Additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Appendix A.1 newly identifies small classes, controlled recording conditions and possible demographic biases as limitations. Other additions interpret premature ASR responses, dependence on audio after multimodal fine-tuning, and QIVD's separation from other datasets in embedding space. These materially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability.

D1.justification: v1 largely refers to checkpoint defaults for fine-tuning. v2 specifies deterministic fold construction, hardware, trainable modules, frame counts, precision, optimizer, learning-rate schedule and gradient accumulation, and documents Stream-Qwen-Omni's training format. It also replaces the competition-release notice with an explicit dataset-page address. These are substantial documentation additions, not evidence that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: The core dataset remains 2,900 videos covering the same 13 categories. Appendix C.1 adds AVSD and Social-IQ to an empirical embedding-distribution comparison, without evaluating question answering on those datasets. The new facial-expression analysis uses 59 existing QIVD samples rather than newly collected coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds evaluated comparisons with VideoLLM-online, Flash-VStream, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Gemini-2.5-Flash. VideoLLM-online and Flash-VStream were only discussed in v1's related work. Appendix C.6 also introduces comparisons between alternative automatic judges and human ratings.

E3.justification: The main correctness judge changes from Llama3-8B to Qwen3-8B. v2 adds timestamp-source controls, separate early/late timing summaries, temporal sampling-window experiments, and a 300-sample human-rating study of GPT-4o answers. Newly specified settings for the retained VideoLLaMA experiment do not establish that its protocol changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained audio ablation and failure examples, v2 tests timestamp sources, temporal sampling windows, facial-expression performance, static versus temporal categories, judge sensitivity and metric correlations. It also analyzes ASR timing bias and cross-dataset embedding distributions. These substantially expand the questions investigated.

E5.justification: v1 reports standard deviations for dataset characteristics; v2 additionally reports ASR and model-score standard deviations in Tables C.8-C.10. This extends descriptive variability reporting, but supplies no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests despite the 'Statistical Significance' heading.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the new models and diagnostic experiments. Whisper-Streaming's reported timing MAE changes from 1.14 seconds to 0.83 seconds, and Stream-Qwen-Omni receives 0.52 seconds. Main correctness scores change under the new judge, including GPT-4o from 66.38% to 58.76%; this is not a same-protocol performance decline. Table C.7 largely preserves the earlier judge's results.

M1.justification: The original Whisper-Streaming pipeline remains, but v2 introduces Stream-Qwen-Omni (Section 5.2 and Appendix D.3). It processes one-second audiovisual chunks and learns to emit a listening token or an answer, training adapters and embeddings. This adds learned response timing and a new streaming inference procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing main-text prose and the main section sequence remain close to v1. Changes include standardizing the QIVD acronym, copyediting, moving the taxonomy to Appendix B.2, and regrouping supplementary material with a contents page. The extensive scientific additions do not amount to a wholesale rewrite of the original narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column conference layout, combines the streaming and offline comparison tables, redraws performance plots, and adds timing, distribution and architecture figures plus numerous analytical tables. Existing examples and refusal illustrations are relocated, while the combined judge-prompt table is split into two displays.

R1.justification: v2 Table 1 adds a structured comparison against 13 benchmarks, including AVSD, Social-IQ, LifeQA and TVQA. Appendix C.1 further positions QIVD through empirical comparisons with AVSD and Social-IQ. Together with references for newly evaluated models, this substantially expands research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1 describes timing error through aggregate MAE. v2 additionally defines signed error as the ASR timestamp minus the ground-truth timestamp in Figure B.3, supporting separate early and late error summaries. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition; no theoretical propositions or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens investigation of the benchmark's central timing requirement through a learned streaming baseline, timestamp-source controls and timing diagnostics. Detailed training specifications address v1's reliance on unspecified defaults, while broader comparisons and explicit limitations improve interpretability. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: Table C.6 compares aggregate correctness rates rather than per-answer judge agreement, and Section 5.3 retains numerical statements that do not match the updated Figure 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QIVD research, with readable text, tables, figures and complete appendices. Retained material can be matched across renaming, reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds streaming-model training, timing and sampling experiments, judge comparisons, and dataset-distribution analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ASR, streaming and offline question-answering evaluations, human comparisons, and VideoLLaMA fine-tuning experiments.

results.title: Can Vision-Language Models Answer Face to Face Questions in the Real-World?

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a perception benchmark, structured geometric training data, and evidence connecting perception with reasoning. v2 adds vertex-order insensitivity as a headline diagnostic finding and explicitly extends its transfer claims to generic 7B/32B models. Its abstract also makes the claim about improvements without additional chain-of-thought data more explicit.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning persistent textual reliance despite visual-priority prompts, failure to internalize vertex-order constraints, and possible reasoning-data overfitting.
