Appendix J substantially expands the limitations beyond v1's brief future-work remarks: synthetic geometry may not represent textbooks, handwriting, or scans; OCR and marker recognition remain uncovered; and visual grounding is not explicitly interleaved with reasoning. It also qualifies that better perception does not guarantee reliable reasoning.

D1.justification: v1 mainly supplies inference settings. v2 Appendix C adds trainable-module descriptions, batch sizes, learning rates, optimizer and schedule, precision, distributed-training setup, GPU configurations, and runtimes. It updates the project-page pointer and documents licensing and planned data/code release. However, v1's explicit 200K training-set composition and 512×512 evaluation-resolution statement disappear; this does not establish changes to the underlying data quantities or resolution.

E1.justification: The core 1,198-image, 1,609-question benchmark and its three domains remain unchanged. v2 adds actual MATH-V evaluation, previously only discussed, and substantially extends diagnostic coverage through overlapping-object counting, vertex-list grounding, and marker-referenced classification (Table 2; Appendix C). It also introduces MultiMath reasoning data into Qwen training.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 2, v2 Table 1 adds Vision-R1, MINT-CoT, GPT-o4-mini-high, Math-PUMA-DeepSeek-Math-VL, URSA, and an author-based human reference. The reasoning comparison also expands beyond the mathematical models in v1 Table 3 to include Qwen2.5-VL, Vision-R1, and MINT-CoT in v2 Table 2.

E3.justification: v2 introduces modality-priority prompting, randomized vertex ordering, reasoning-only SFT and frozen-encoder controls, and Qwen training configurations using additional MultiMath data. Appendix C specifies a new 200-image overlapping-counting evaluation with three annotators, alternative acceptable answers, and free-form matching, plus a separate 200-diagram marker experiment. These are substantial new evaluation designs, rather than merely disclosed settings for retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 retains the original noise, distractor, object-count, and alignment-data analyses while adding tests of explicit modality priority, vertex-order sensitivity, overlapping counting, symbolic versus coordinate grounding, and vertex-count shortcuts. Table 8 additionally isolates the effects of perception data and visual-encoder updating. Appendix Figure 18 adds Qwen/GPT-4o reasoning cases, and some earlier error examples are replaced.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, uncertainty bars, or significance tests. v2's three-author annotation procedure defines acceptable counting answers; it does not introduce statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new comparators, Qwen-trained variants, MATH-V, and diagnostic controls. It also revises retained entries: SVE-Math-DeepSeek+ plane relationship accuracy changes from 97.5 in v1 Table 2 to 96.5 in v2 Table 1; its conflicting-text score changes from 74.0 in v1 Table 5 to 82.5 in v2 Table 4. These are reported-value revisions, not established same-setting gains from rerunning experiments.

M1.justification: The structured diagram generator, caption/conversation representations, and two-stage training approach are retained. v2 adds a LoRA-based adaptation for Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B alongside SVE-Math training (Appendix C). This extends the training procedure without introducing a new perception architecture or loss; the dataset renaming itself is not a method change.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title and terminology, substantially rewrites the abstract and introduction, and reorganizes the benchmark section. Detailed construction moves from the main text to Appendix F, and dataset statistics move to Appendix B. The contribution-list presentation is replaced by a revised diagnostic narrative, with additional ethics, implementation, limitations, and disclosure sections.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a two-column layout to a predominantly single-column design with new headers and abstract styling. v2 expands comparison tables, adds six analysis tables and two figures, relocates the statistics display, restyles plots, and revises several illustrated examples. Many original figures remain with renumbering rather than representing new evidence.

R1.justification: The original related-work discussion is largely retained, but v2 substantially expands methodological positioning in Section 3.2 and Appendix C. It contrasts perception training with MINT-CoT's interleaved visual reasoning and Vision-R1's reinforcement-learning approach, discussing complementary scope and different data requirements. It also adds citations to texture-bias research, Math-PUMA, and URSA.

T1.justification: A local mathematical correction appears in the retained worked response: v1 Figure 16(b) says the central angle is half the inscribed angle, whereas v2 Figure 17(b) correctly states the reverse relationship. The displayed equation was already correct. Neither version develops a broader theoretical analysis or formal proof.

improvement.justification: v1's transfer evidence centers on one specialized 7B model and alignment-dataset comparisons. v2 adds reasoning-only SFT and frozen-encoder controls (Table 8), tests Qwen7B/32B, and supplies substantial training details and applicability limits (Appendices C and J). These address important weaknesses in attribution, validation breadth, and reproducibility. The abstract's claim about no additional chain-of-thought data needs qualification because Qwen training adds MultiMath samples, and some cross-table inconsistencies remain. These issues limit interpretation but do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, with readable main text, tables, figures, and complete appendices. MATHGLANCE becomes MATHEMETRIC and GeoPeP becomes GEOMETRIC. Retained content can be matched despite substantial restructuring and additional experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, training controls, alternative perception tasks, and diagnostic experiments in Tables 1–12 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, training experiments, robustness analyses, and model-response case studies, including Tables 2–6 and appendix figures.

results.title: Math Blind: Failures in Diagram Understanding Undermine Reasoning in MLLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add correction of advantage and gradient-estimation biases, AGE, and variance-reducing resampling as central contributions. The headline performance claim broadens from outperforming GRPO to achieving state-of-the-art results. The original claims of simplifying reinforcement learning by removing critic/reference models and distributional constraints remain.

C2.justification: V4 reinterprets standard-deviation normalization as introducing reward bias while incidentally providing gradient correction, replacing v1's straightforward variance-reduction justification. It adds discussion of high variance when valid samples are scarce, DAPO sampling inefficiency, and preservation of general capabilities. The limitation concerning unevaluated extremely large models is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies VERL, 144 prompts per batch, eight responses per prompt, AdamW, learning rate 1e−6, weight decay 0.1, threshold 0.6, 1,100 steps, and 48 NPUs for the added 7B experiment. V4 also supplies a dedicated 7B prompt and reproducibility statement. The project link already existed; v1's explicit 7,500-sample MATH-lighteval disclosure is no longer included.

E1.justification: V4 retains the original mathematics and multimodal coverage while adding MMLU, Chinese C-Eval, MBPP/MBPP+, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA evaluations. These extend coverage to general knowledge, Chinese disciplinary questions, coding, and general QA. It also adds training on the DAPO data source for the new 7B experiment.

E2.justification: DAPO moves from a discussed algorithm in v1 to an evaluated comparator in v4 Table 9. The expanded 7B comparison adds OpenReasoner-Zero and SimpleRL-Zero, among others. Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct disappears, while rStar-Math and Eurus are retained in the reorganized 7B table. Existing GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and multimodal comparisons remain.

E3.justification: V4 adds a 7B training protocol and DAPO comparison controlling the training dataset and 1,100 training steps, with GPG using accuracy-only rewards. It adds pass@3/pass@5 evaluation on four mathematics benchmarks, OpenCompass general-knowledge evaluation, and zero-shot coding/QA testing. The original 1.5B training budgets of 100 and 50 steps remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V4 adds ablations separating normalization, AGE, and resampling effects; threshold sensitivity tests; and diagnostics of reward dispersion and zero-gradient groups (Tables 1, 10, 15 and Figure 2). It also tests preservation of general capabilities. Original group-size results, training curves, and the case study are retained. Conversely, v1's numerical KL-penalty ablation disappears despite its discussion remaining.

E5.justification: V1 provides no explicit repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. V4 Table 16 reports accuracy and standard deviation, with its caption specifying four random seeds, and Table 19 reports standard errors for HellaSwag and TruthfulQA. This establishes substantially expanded uncertainty reporting, without establishing an increase from a known earlier run count or four independent retrainings.

E6.justification: Reported GPG results change from 69.11 to 76.15 on CV-Bench, 50.80 to 51.33 on GEOQA, and 86.0 to 89.0 average classification accuracy; LISA validation mIoU falls from 53.4 to 51.3. V4 adds general-task, repeated-evaluation, and resource-cost results. Its new GPG-Zero-7B average of 57.7 uses the DAPO-data setting and is not a same-setting gain over v1's 45.3. The 1.5B averages of 55.7 and 55.5 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V1 uses group-standard-deviation-normalized advantages and an unscaled policy-gradient loss. V4 makes normalization optional, uses unnormalized centered rewards in its final variant, and introduces AGE scaling by alpha = B/(B−M). Algorithm 1 additionally accumulates and resamples responses until a minimum valid-sample proportion is reached. These change the optimization and sampling procedure.

P1.justification: V4 moves Related Work after the experiments, reorganizes mathematical evaluation around distilled 1.5B and base 7B models, and transfers prompts, several ablations, training curves, and the case study into structured appendices. It adds a reproducibility section and substantially revises the introduction's motivation and method exposition, alongside widespread language editing.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned into separate mathematics and multimodal panels, and a new diagnostic Figure 2 is added. The original training curves and case illustration are reused in the appendix. Mathematical comparison tables are reorganized, and new component, resource, uncertainty, and general-benchmark tables are introduced. The conference layout also substantially compresses some tables, especially classification results.

R1.justification: V4 substantially develops its positioning against Dr. GRPO and DAPO: it disputes the benefit of removing normalization alone and argues that AGE avoids costs of constructing fully valid batches. This extends v1's primarily simplification-based positioning. References expand to OpenReasoner-Zero, SimpleRL, VERL, C-Eval, and recent reasoning-RL applications, while several older references are removed.

T1.justification: V4 introduces formal gradient-scaling definitions and derivations in Equations 7–8 and a new distributed-averaging analysis in Appendix A. The latter derives the relationship between averaging over all samples and averaging over nonzero-gradient samples. V1 has no corresponding analysis. Its existing PPO/GRPO derivations are retained in v4 Appendix C.

improvement.justification: V1 claims computational efficiency without quantitative resource comparisons and supplies no explicit uncertainty estimates. V4 adds a comparison controlling dataset and training steps with DAPO, measured resource costs, component ablations, broader evaluations, uncertainty reporting, and concrete training configurations. These substantially strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. There are material weaknesses: the KL-ablation evidence disappears, and Appendix A establishes a rescaling identity rather than proving unbiasedness for the original RL objective. Nevertheless, the gains in evaluability and supporting evidence constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GPG research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains original empirical results and reports additional method ablations, a DAPO comparison, general-capability evaluations, and results with uncertainty estimates.

before.justification: V1 reports original GPG training and evaluation results for mathematical reasoning and multimodal tasks, plus group-size and reward-normalization ablations in Tables 2–10.

results.title: GPG: A Simple and Strong Reinforcement Learning Baseline for Model Reasoning

C1.justification: The joint ID-noise/OOD-generalization objective and cross-domain DL4ND contribution remain central. v2 broadens the headline validation claim to seven datasets and three noise types and explicitly describes DL4ND as the first direct NAG method. These extend the claimed scope without replacing the paper's central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 Appendix C interprets VLCS noise mainly as missing annotations for co-occurring categories, whereas v1 Section 3.3 describes labels that do not match image content. v2 also qualifies v1's favorable interpretation of regularization combinations by attributing ELR+DG underperformance to excessive constraints. New discussion addresses erroneous relabeling of difficult domains, validation-based warmup selection, and multimodal-model applicability and contamination concerns.

D1.justification: v1 mentions an accompanying code archive and promises later public release; v2 supplies a project-code link and states that code, data and pretrained models are released. It adds DomainNet corruption mappings and warmup-selection guidance. Conversely, explicit disclosures about cleaning VLCS test sets and modifying the five-channel input layer disappear. Existing hardware details and six integration algorithms are retained.

E1.justification: The existing RotatedMNIST, VLCS, CHAMMI-CP, OfficeHome and TerraIncognita coverage remains. v2 adds real-noise PACS and synthetic-noise DomainNet evaluations, plus a symmetric-noise OfficeHome scenario beyond the earlier asymmetric corruption experiments. These substantially broaden the represented domains and noise conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds SAGM+SWAD+UNICON comparisons with and without per-domain sampling on VLCS and CHAMMI-CP (Tables 7, 9 and 10). The corresponding MIRO-based combinations and original standalone baselines remain. Newly discussed noisy-domain-adaptation methods are not directly benchmarked.

E3.justification: The leave-one-domain-out ID/OOD accuracy framework, retained backbones, batch size and stated VLCS/CHAMMI-CP training budget remain. Added experiments introduce a 20% TerraIncognita corruption condition, relabeling precision, component-removal controls and explicit warmup sweeps (Tables 4–6 and 12–13). These extend the evaluation design without replacing its basic protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct tests of relabeling versus discarding samples, cross-domain versus within-domain comparisons, and low-loss versus all-sample proxies (Table 5). Table 6 measures relabeling precision, and Tables 12–13 test warmup sensitivity. These substantially strengthen mechanism and robustness analyses. The earlier support-vector analysis and sample-selection tradeoff remain; v1 Figure 7 becomes v2 Figure 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or run-to-run variability for its performance results. The retained feature-distance boxplots describe sample distributions rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark, ablation, precision and sensitivity results. For example, Table 4 reports DomainNet OOD accuracy of 35.6 for SAGM+DL4ND versus 26.9 for SAGM in the newly evaluated setting. Most retained scores match after rounding, but the CHAMMI-CP ERM average is corrected from 58.18 in v1 Table 2 to 59.8 in v2 Table 8.

M1.justification: The warmup, GMM separation and low-loss proxy pipeline remains. However, v1 Section 4.2 selects the class with minimum average distance across other domains, whereas v2 Section 4.1 and Equation (3) select the nearest individual other-domain class proxy. This is a localized change to the procedure as specified; the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, challenge analysis, method exposition and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Section 3 adopts question-led subsections, real-world dataset discussion moves into Appendix C, and the appendices are reorganized into extended results, domain-adaptation comparisons, noise information and implementation details.

P2.justification: The two-column manuscript becomes a single-column conference layout, with redrawn conceptual illustrations and extensively reorganized displays. v1 Table 2 is redistributed across v2 Tables 8–10 and summarized by the new Figure 6 scatterplots. Existing figures move to the appendices, while new benchmark, ablation, precision and sensitivity tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v1 primarily surveys DG and LNL separately. v2 Section 2 and the new Appendix B substantially position NAG against noisy domain adaptation, discussing works including Shu et al., Han et al. and Yin et al. Additional recent pretraining and multimodal-model literature supports new positioning around benchmark contamination and backbone choice.

T1.justification: v1 introduces a sample-to-class versus sample-to-domain distance assumption and claims cross-domain separability as Theorem 1. v2 removes that theorem and its expectation-based formulation, replacing the earlier assumption with a class-domain-proxy distance-ordering condition in Equation (2), assessed empirically. This substantially revises the formal justification rather than merely changing notation.

improvement.justification: v1's benchmark comparisons and toy analysis did not directly isolate the proposed components on its main datasets. v2 Tables 5–6 address that important deficiency through component ablations and relabeling-precision tests, while Tables 12–13 examine warmup sensitivity. Broader dataset and noise coverage further strengthens empirical support. These gains outweigh documentation regressions, notably the unexplained averaging-versus-nearest-proxy discrepancy and omission of VLCS test-cleaning details. Run-to-run uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NAG/DL4ND research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds PACS and DomainNet evaluations, symmetric-noise experiments, component ablations, relabeling-precision measurements and warmup sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original RotatedMNIST experiments, VLCS and CHAMMI-CP comparisons, synthetic-noise experiments, and analyses of sample selection and manually identified label noise.

results.title: Noise-Aware Generalization: Robustness to In-Domain Noise and Out-of-Domain Generalization

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list shift emphasis from self-verification and cross-domain generalization toward candidate verification, the two-stage design, and mathematical benchmarks. The central claims about tool-assisted small-model verification and the 1B-versus-8B comparison remain. Knowledge-intensive applicability is still claimed in the conclusion and supported in the appendix.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly describes the theory as an idealized conceptual illustration, explains the complementary execution and reasoning signals of the two stages, and discusses memory and compute tradeoffs. It newly acknowledges that PRM alone can perform better at small budgets. Existing false-negative and parallel-scaling limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 describes GPT-4o trajectory distillation for the Themis adaptation and reports token usage by stage. Its new reproducibility statement promises scripts, prompts, configurations, instructions, and seeds, but supplies no package link. Existing Appendix D hyperparameters, hardware, prompts, and evaluation instructions are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic arithmetic, MATH500, GSM8K, and the Health, Economics, and History domains of MMLU-Pro. The MMLU-Pro experiments move to Appendix E.1 in v2; they are not removed. No new dataset or task coverage is introduced.

E2.justification: V2 substantially extends comparisons beyond majority voting and conventional GenRM/PRM baselines. Figure 9 evaluates a distilled 1B adaptation of the tool-integrated Themis method, while Tables 5–7 add two-stage GenRM without tools and ToolV-only comparisons. These directly test competing explanations for T1's advantages.

E3.justification: V2 introduces compute-budget comparisons using token-based rescaling: 1.14 times for GenRM and approximately twice the budget for PRM. It also adds stage-isolation controls and a 3B arithmetic-verification configuration. These extend the evaluation design; the retained experiments' splits, training hyperparameters, sampling temperatures, and 64-solution protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether both verification stages are needed, whether an additional GenRM stage can replace tool integration, and whether benefits survive accounting for computational overhead (Section 6.4 and Appendices E.5–E.7). Existing difficulty, category, model-size, data-efficiency, confusion-matrix, and case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, actual random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2 promises a future package containing seeds, but does not supply new statistical reporting for the results.

E6.justification: V2 adds 3B arithmetic and Themis results, token-cost measurements, budget-dependent findings, and component-control scores. At N=64, Table 5 reports 46.0% for two-stage GenRM versus 45.4% for one-stage GenRM and 50.6% with ToolV. Table 6 adds ToolV-only accuracy of 52.4% versus 53.2% with PRM. Original benchmark plots and diagnostic scores are retained; Tables 8–16 redisplay existing plotted results.

M1.justification: The tool-based filtering stage, subsequent reward-model scoring, distillation objectives, and task-specific procedures remain unchanged in Section 4 and Appendix B. Renaming self-verification to verification and evaluating additional control methods do not change the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 revises the title, abstract, introductory framing, and contribution bullets, and replaces much self-verification terminology. It moves the MMLU-Pro discussion into Appendix E, reorganizes appendix subsections, and adds ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements. Most method, theory, and existing experimental prose is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adopts conference typography and layout, redraws Figure 1, and adds Themis and compute-budget plots. It adds cost and ablation tables plus nine tables giving exact values for existing benchmark plots. MMLU-Pro figures move into the appendix, and several retained displays are repositioned and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to CRITIC, PAD, and Singhi et al. (2025). It also develops the distinction between T1's two-stage small-model verification and Themis's unified tool-augmented reward modeling; Li et al. (2024) was already cited in v1. The broader related-work organization remains.

T1.justification: Lemma 5.1, Theorems 5.2–5.3, their assumptions, and their appendix proofs retain the same mathematical substance. Relabeling Theorem C.1 as Lemma C.1 is editorial. The new discussion of idealized theory in Appendix C.1 qualifies interpretation without changing the formal results.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's support for the central design: comparison with a tool-integrated competitor, isolation of each stage's contribution, and assessment of additional computation. Figure 9, Figures 10–11, and Tables 5–7 substantially strengthen that evidence. The explicit small-budget tradeoff and qualification of the theory also improve interpretation. Compute accounting remains approximate and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same T1 framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across renaming, renumbering, and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds comparisons, component ablations, and computational-cost analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original arithmetic-verification experiments, MATH500, GSM8K, and MMLU-Pro evaluations, and additional diagnostic experiments in the appendices.

results.title: T1: Tool-integrated Verification for Test-time Compute Scaling in Small Language Models

C1.justification: The central training-free, data-free MASS contribution remains. V2's introduction extends the demonstrated scope to language and replaces v1's across-scale within-5% and batched below-1% claims with an 'up to 98%' statement. Automatic head selection becomes more prominent but was already explicitly claimed in v1.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking held-out performance to transferable subspaces, scalability to task composition, and weaker NLI results to potentially diffuse, higher-rank updates. It also explains threshold-related failures, qualifies orthogonalization's contribution as modest, and discusses why alternative distance and filtering choices underperform. These substantially extend v1's mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds baseline head-voting instructions, new dataset counts and fallback split instructions, and compute/storage accounting in Appendix B. The existing checkpoint sources, EMNIST preprocessing, shared classification head, MLP architecture, compression rate, hyperparameter searches and code address are retained.

E1.justification: V2 retains the 8/14/20-task vision benchmarks and adds 13 vision datasets for scaling to 33 tasks, eight GLUE language tasks, and evaluation on tasks excluded from merging. These substantially broaden the domains and generalization scenarios beyond v1's vision evaluations.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated WeMoE and SMILE-1/2 comparisons; v1 discussed these approaches without reporting corresponding experiments. V2 Table 2 also evaluates TIES-Merging on GLUE. The original fixed-merging baselines, TwinMerging comparison and alternative-router comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include Flan-T5-Base merging, majority-vote head selection for SMILE/WeMoE (Appendix B.6), oracle-head controls (Table 11), and merging seven experts before testing the excluded task (Appendix C.1). These are added protocols; unknown-task inference for MASS was already present in v1.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained layer, router and semantic analyses, v2 tests unseen-task transfer, scalability, residual-weighted merging, orthogonalization, oracle heads, routing/filtering sensitivity, Mahalanobis distance and principal-angle filtering. Tables 7–13 and Figures 6 and 10 substantially expand evidence about component choices, robustness and failure conditions.

E5.justification: V2 Table 14 newly reports means and standard deviations across tasks for the main MoErging comparisons. V1 already reports cross-task variability in routing-layer plots. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests; the added deviations describe task heterogeneity.

E6.justification: Main vision, router and batched-inference results are revised, alongside substantial new results. For example, v1 Table 2 reports MASS at 90.6% absolute/97.6% normalized accuracy for eight-task ViT-B-32; v2 Table 1 reports 87.0%/96.5%, with the fine-tuned reference also revised. V2 adds GLUE results and 33-task results of 0.83 versus Task Arithmetic's 0.64. The PDFs do not explain the revisions sufficiently to establish a controlled performance change.

M1.justification: The fixed and adaptive merging algorithms retain TSV compression, orthogonalization, redundancy filtering, residual routing and classification across selected heads. V1 Algorithms 1–2 correspond to v2 Algorithms 2–1. Unknown-task head selection already appears in v1 Section 3.3; the additional experimental variants do not replace the proposed method.

P1.justification: The introduction and results narrative are substantially rewritten, the background is condensed, and detailed related work and the fixed-merging algorithm move to appendices. Benchmark descriptions and batched-inference discussion are reorganized, alongside a new reproducibility statement and restructured appendices.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a single-column conference layout, combines routing-layer panels, rebuilds radar comparisons around MoErging baselines, and relocates algorithms and figures. New language, resource and ablation tables, plus scalability and sensitivity plots, substantially change the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 shifts the central positioning from fixed aggregation and task interference toward the absence of oracle task knowledge. It newly argues that known-task merging is effectively addressed by TSV-C compression and foregrounds this distinction from existing MoErging methods. New references support the probabilistic interpretation, language evaluation and added datasets; much of v1's related work survives in Appendix A.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.4 and Proposition D.2 add a conditional MAP interpretation and proof for residual-based selection, assuming common isotropic Gaussian residuals and uniform task priors. This extends the justification of an existing operation. V1's orthogonal-projection optimality theorem and proof are retained as Proposition D.1.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important weakness in v1's evaluation by adding direct MoErging competitors, documented head-routing adaptations and oracle-head controls. Component ablations, sensitivity tests and broader evaluations substantially strengthen the evidence for the method's usefulness and design choices. Unexplained score revisions and inconsistencies remain, including the retained 97.6% prose figure versus 96.5% in Table 1 and the miscounted GLUE wins, but the expanded comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MASS, with matching core algorithms and retained vision benchmarks. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original vision and language evaluations, scalability and held-out-task experiments, and component and sensitivity analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-merging experiments, router comparisons, layer analyses, batched-inference results and task-vector interpretations, including supplementary results.

results.title: MASS: MoErging through Adaptive Subspace Selection

C1.justification: v2 adds theoretical advantage over WAG and robustness to collusive backdoors as central abstract/introduction claims, and explicitly extends claimed applicability to CNNs. v1 primarily presents empirical module switching for Transformer models. Defense using few potentially compromised models was already claimed in v1 and is retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains collusion as reducing WAG to fewer-model behavior and interprets low strategy overlap as evidence of broadly distributed disruption. Appendix A newly limits demonstrated applicability to classification. Conversely, Section 5.2 replaces v1's explicit three-model exception with consistent-superiority wording, although Table 12 retains MSD's 13.0% versus WAG's 11.5% ASR in that case.

D1.justification: v2 provides a code-repository address and reproducibility statement, whereas v1 promises future switching-template release. It identifies the search CPU, reports 2.6/4.3-hour two-/four-model searches, and supplies selection/merging timings and dataset-license information. These refine disclosure; the earlier generic six-hour estimate does not establish a comparable runtime speedup.

E1.justification: v2 adds TinyImageNet's 200-class image-classification coverage while retaining the original datasets. It also evaluates distinct threat scenarios absent from v1: colluding models sharing backdoors, attackers adapting to a known switching strategy, Adaptive-Patch attacks, inconsistent target labels and identical triggers with different targets.

E2.justification: WAG becomes an evaluated comparator in the two-layer simulations in Section 3 and Appendix G; v1's corresponding simulations compared pretrained, fine-tuned and switched networks without WAG. The existing deep-model defense comparators—WAG, TIES, DARE, Z-Def, ONION, CutMix and ShrinkPad—remain.

E3.justification: Original benchmark splits, training schedules, CACC/ASR metrics and clean-data budgets are retained. Added experiments introduce four-model fusion, ResNet-18/50 configurations, adaptive retraining with unselected modules frozen, and simulations varying backdoor perturbation strength. New utility-loss and computational-efficiency measurements also expand the evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: The existing heuristic-rule, clean-data-budget and poisoning-rate studies remain. v2 adds second-order-interaction diagnostics, individual utility-loss analysis, overlap analysis across searched strategies, efficiency comparisons, and robustness tests for collusion, adaptation and label/trigger mismatches. These substantially expand the questions investigated beyond ordinary benchmark performance.

E5.justification: Both versions report defense results averaged over three seeds. v2 adds explicit mean±standard-deviation reporting for second-order ratios: across runs in Table 4 and across 24 layers in Table 5. Appendix F adds utility-loss distribution and tail summaries. Increased runs for retained defense experiments are not established.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and ablation values are largely retained, but substantial new results appear. For example, v2 Table 13 reports 20.5% MSD versus 31.9% WAG average ASR for collusive BadNet/InsertSent fusion. Table 11 reports TinyImageNet BadNet+WaNet ASR of 0.4% versus 8.6%, with CACC of 84.2% versus 88.2%. CNN, adaptive-attack and mechanism results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: The five-rule evolutionary switching framework remains. However, Algorithm 2 changes suspect-class identification from majority voting over model-specific choices to summing classwise cosine-distance scores. v2 also adapts switching to convolution–batch-normalization modules and uses pooled convolutional features for CNN candidate selection.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial method exposition are rewritten. Section 3 is reorganized into setup, theoretical analysis and empirical analysis; heuristic details move to the appendix, and the appendix structure is extensively reorganized. The shortened title and new reproducibility, limitations and disclosure sections accompany these narrative changes.

P2.justification: The two-column layout becomes a single-column conference format, and main tables are reorganized into paired blocks. Shallow-network bar charts become scatterplots; new distribution, overlap and CNN/four-model strategy figures appear. The original three-model Table 3 moves to appendix Table 12, alongside substantial new result tables.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through mixture-of-experts and one-shot federated-learning motivation, explicit discussion of WAG/DAM model-resource demands, and separation of detection from model repair. Related work adds substantial trigger-inversion, purification and unlearning coverage, including UNICORN, BaDExpert and UNIT. These citations are not additional evaluated defense baselines.

T1.justification: v1 provides simulation objectives and a weight-update decomposition without formal guarantees. v2 adds Definitions 1–4, a divergence bound against WAG, an existence proposition and proofs in Appendix D. Appendices E–F introduce a utility-loss identity and related definitions. The analysis assumes shared pretrained weights, identity activation and omission of second-order interactions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence about generality and deployment robustness through CNN, TinyImageNet, collusive, adaptive and target-mismatch evaluations, addressing important gaps in v1's deep-model testing. Mechanism diagnostics and code-access information also improve assessability and reproducibility. Material caveats remain: Section 4.4 extrapolates the approximate two-layer divergence bound into an unsupported deep-model defense guarantee, some new results incur accuracy costs, and the three-model superiority prose overlooks the retained Table 12 exception.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Module-Switching Defense (MSD) work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching content across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original TinyImageNet, CNN, collusion, adaptive-attack and mechanism-analysis results.

before.justification: v1 reports original two-layer-network simulations and backdoor-defense experiments on SST-2, MNLI, AG News and CIFAR-10, including appendix ablations.

results.title: Defending against Backdoor Attacks via Module Switching

C1.justification: The central claims about the 24,000-image dataset, two-branch adapter and improved real-world HDR fusion remain. The introduction revises the relative-scale claim from approximately six times existing datasets to 166 times typical datasets and explicitly distinguishes the contribution from GTA-HDR's single-image conversion task.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3 adds explanations for architecture-dependent gains over fine-tuning. Appendix A.12 acknowledges and interprets online adaptation costs, while A.9 and B.7 qualify reproducibility through purchased assets and describe applications beyond HDR as prospective. Earlier texture-domain-gap and knowledge-forgetting interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises future code/data availability; v2 states public availability and adds a reproducibility statement. It newly documents exposure triplets, approximately 30 supervised adaptation epochs, the rendering workflow, asset and motion provenance, auxiliary outputs, and runtime hardware and image resolution. The epoch and exposure specifications clarify previously unspecified settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds direct evaluation on Kalantari and adaptation tests on Sen and Tursun datasets. It also introduces HDR video reconstruction using Vimeo-90K, Sintel and Real-HDRV training data, with evaluation on DeepHDRVideo and the TOG HDR dynamic dataset (Appendices A.6–A.8). Kalantari already appeared as a training source in v1.

E2.justification: The original image-fusion comparator networks are retained. v2 introduces HDRFlow-based video comparisons, including Vimeo+Sintel-trained and Real-HDRV-trained baselines against S2R-HDR training (Table 14), and adds a Challenge123-pretrained S2R-Adapter comparison in Table 9.

E3.justification: v2 adds pooled SCT+Challenge123 training and fine-tuning controls, supervised and test-time Kalantari evaluation, MUSIQ scoring for Sen/Tursun, video reconstruction and flow-warping temporal evaluation, and timed adaptation (Tables 4, 8 and 11–17). The original SCT/Challenge123 splits and reconstruction metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original branch, teacher-student and forgetting ablations are retained. New analyses examine pooled real-data training and alternative pretraining (Tables 4, 8–9), temporal consistency (Table 15), motion-direction diversity (Figure 13), and adaptation efficiency (Table 17). The relocated t-SNE and difference-map figures reproduce existing analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. Both use augmentation variance within the adaptation algorithm; this is unchanged model behavior rather than uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: Tables 2, 3 and 5–7 retain their values, while v2 adds pooled-data, Kalantari, Sen/Tursun, video, temporal and runtime results. Table 14 newly reports 43.51 PSNR-µ for S2R-HDR pretraining followed by Real-HDRV fine-tuning. v1's Kalantari-trained SCT/Challenge123 results are replaced by different evaluations. Table 9 also reports 43.44 for adapted SAFNet on SCT, conflicting with 43.33 in retained Table 2.

M1.justification: The adapter architecture, scaling rules and teacher-student updates remain unchanged. Appendix B.7 explicitly extends the rendering pipeline to produce optical flow, depth, diffuse reflectance and surface normals alongside HDR frames, constituting a limited pipeline extension.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the original prose remain. v2 standardizes HDR fusion terminology, clarifies access to ground truth during adaptation, expands explanations, reorganizes appendix subsections, and adds reproducibility, acknowledgement and LLM-use statements. The retained narrative undergoes limited rewriting.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column conference layout, extensively repositioning figures and tables. The dataset t-SNE moves from v1 Figure 2 to appendix Figure 8, Table 1 gains a size column, and new experimental tables and pipeline, motion-direction and auxiliary-output figures substantially expand the displays. Figure 12's caption incorrectly describes optical-flow directions.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against GTA-HDR, discusses SelfHDR and UltraFusion, and adds references supporting video evaluation, quality metrics and test-time adaptation costs. These extend the literature context without substantially redefining the existing synthetic-data and adapter positioning.

T1.justification: The adapter definitions, rank assumptions and Equations 1–3 are unchanged. v2's Equation 4 supplies the adopted standard flow-warping metric for video evaluation; it introduces no new theoretical result, derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens generalization evidence through additional adaptation datasets, video evaluation and controls separating data-source and adaptation effects. Runtime measurements and expanded generation and implementation documentation address important omissions in v1. These gains outweigh localized reporting defects, particularly Table 9's unexplained 43.44 versus 43.33 discrepancy and Figure 12's incorrect caption. The improvement comes from stronger validation and transparency, while the original headline results remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe S2R-HDR and S2R-Adapter. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds further adaptation, video reconstruction, temporal consistency and runtime results.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset analyses, HDR reconstruction comparisons, adaptation experiments and ablations in Tables 1–7 and Appendix A.

results.title: S2R-HDR: A Large-Scale Rendered Dataset for HDR Fusion

C1.justification: The four central contributions and full-pipeline integration claim remain. V3 explicitly extends the claimed model family to fixed and dynamic resolution and emphasizes computational efficiency. V1's specific claim that the 3B model surpasses Cambrian-1 8B even at approximately 300 tokens is removed.

C2.justification: V3 newly attributes higher synthetic-data CLIPScores partly to filtering, acknowledges poorer generated-image quality, and discusses distribution gaps involving ScienceQA. It also adds interpretations of loss-weight and exchange-layer sensitivity. Conversely, v1's substantive discussion of initial-question encoding bias in multi-turn dialogue and its proposed compensation mechanism is removed.

D1.justification: V3 newly discloses one-epoch training on 64 A100 GPUs, exchange-layer insertion every three decoder layers, initialization details, and hardware for compute measurements. It specifies FLUX-dev and the description/QA generation model. V1's explicit 256-token text cap and 1024×1024 generation resolution are no longer documented. Most synthesis prompts and filtering thresholds are retained.

E1.justification: V3 removes ConvBench multi-turn evaluation and the HallusionBench, MME-RealWorld, and DocVQA benchmark results. DocVQA remains training data; VizWiz and LLaVA-Wild remain in appendix ablations. Appendix E.3 adds an image/text quality assessment task comparing synthetic and existing datasets. The extensive training-data mixture largely persists.

E2.justification: Within Table 1, v3 adds MiniCPM variants and Molmo-7B, removes InternVL2 and MM1.5, and replaces Qwen2VL-7B with Qwen2.5VL-7B. Molmo and Qwen2.5VL already appeared in v1's broader appendix comparison. V3 also expands controlled architectural comparisons beyond LLaVA-NeXT to Florence-VL, Cambrian-1, and Eagle.

E3.justification: V3 evaluates fixed-resolution FLARE-L and dynamic-resolution FLARE-X, adds NaViT/Qwen2.5 backbone experiments and matched-data comparisons, and changes latent-token sampling from {4,16,64,144,256} to {4,16,36,64,144}. New data-quality evaluations score 50 random examples per dataset on a 0–10 scale. Reported image-generation steps change from 60 to 50; this does not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds exchange-layer placement/count sweeps, reconstruction-loss weight sweeps, computational profiling, and synthetic-data quality and distribution analyses. V1's window-size study, latent-only versus interaction-layer control, inference-token compression studies, and ConvBench analysis disappear. Latent-sampling and parameter-freezing studies remain, while the snowboard/person attention visualization is relocated rather than newly added.

E5.justification: V3 Section 4 newly specifies seed 42 for training and evaluation. This is additional seed disclosure, not evidence of more runs. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing.

E6.justification: Main benchmark and component-ablation results are extensively revised, with additional controlled-comparison, compute, and data-quality results. For example, v1 Table 9 reports MMBench-EN 80.3 for FUSION-X 3B at 630 tokens; v3 Table 1 reports 79.6 for FLARE-L 3B at 630 and 81.4 for FLARE-X 3B at approximately 1400. These concern revised models/settings, not established same-setting gains or losses. ConvBench and compression result entries are removed.

M1.justification: V1 Section 3.2 constructs separately encoded, text-independent auxiliary image features and initializes latent tokens by interpolation. V3 uses the projected image tokens directly as attention keys/values and specifies randomly initialized latent tokens. It also introduces crop-wise processing for dynamic resolution. These revise the decoding procedure despite retaining the overall framework and reconstruction losses.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method explanations undergo extensive rewriting and condensation, alongside model/component renaming and revised notation. Data-collection material moves into the main paper, the experimental narrative is reorganized, and the appendices gain reproducibility and LLM-use statements. Most detailed synthesis prompts remain unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 changes the two-column presentation to a single-column conference format and consolidates the main benchmark table. It removes the opening performance plot and token-compression plots, adds loss curves, t-SNE plots, and comparison/compute tables, and relocates alignment and dataset-composition figures. Architecture diagrams are relabeled; synthetic-example Figures 10–19 retain their content.

R1.justification: V3 adds MiniCPM-V and newer data/reasoning references while removing substantial earlier citation coverage. More substantively, it removes Question Aware Vision Transformer for Multimodal Reasoning: v1 Section 3.1 explicitly credits this work as inspiration, whereas v3 presents the encoding contribution without that relationship. This changes attribution and positioning of a central component beyond bibliographic restyling.

T1.justification: The decoder's mathematical specification changes from square patches of an interpolated auxiliary representation to rectangular slices of projected image tokens, with window dimensions defined by w=m/l and h=n/l. Feature aggregation, reconstruction losses, and SSIM/CLIP filtering formulas remain substantively equivalent. Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens support for the central architecture and efficiency claims: Table 4 controls the LLM and training data across several baselines, Tables 5–6 measure computational cost directly, and Appendix E.3 evaluates synthetic-data quality and acknowledges weaknesses. These address important comparison and validation gaps in v1. Removing multi-turn/compression evidence, the associated limitation discussion, and the earlier encoder attribution weakens breadth and transparency, but the stronger controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, renamed from FUSION to FLARE. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison. Changed experimental configurations require care when comparing scores.

after.justification: V3 reports original benchmark evaluations, controlled model comparisons, computational measurements, parameter ablations, and human/GPT-4o evaluations of synthetic data.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component and training ablations, token-reduction experiments, and ConvBench multi-turn dialogue results.

results.title: FLARE: Fully Integration of Vision-Language Representations for Deep Cross-Modal Understanding

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes a challenging, decontaminated, verifiable dataset that improves mathematical reasoning. v2 adds explicit claims of substantial uniqueness relative to other datasets and demonstrated generalization to biology, physics, and chemistry. It also extends performance-superiority claims to additional model variants and comparisons with o1-mini and o3-mini.

C2.justification: v2 attributes science-task generalization to forum-derived diversity and rigorous curation, and interprets growing response lengths and cognitive behaviors as reproducing an 'aha moment.' Appendix E newly acknowledges difficulty-rating bias, topical imbalance, and guessable answers. v1's explicit caution that solution length does not directly measure quality is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds the verl framework, GRPO/DAPO and reward details, model-specific hyperparameters and training budgets (Appendix C), decoding settings, asset licenses, a direct dataset link, and a stated code/model-weight release. It clarifies the Math StackExchange source subsets. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit description of swapping question order during decontamination judgments.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on the English subset of PolyMath and on GPQA-Diamond, extending coverage beyond the original six mathematical benchmarks to biology, physics, and chemistry. GPQA appeared in v1's decontamination process, but science reasoning performance was not evaluated there.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Qwen-2.5-Math-7B and its SRL-Zoo comparator, Oat-Zero-7B (spelled Qat in the tables), Eurus-2-7B-PRIME, OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B, and o1-mini/o3-mini reference scores. Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct is removed. Figure 1a adds STILL-3-RL to the difficulty comparison; DSR-Preview is a shortened name for the retained DeepScaleR-Preview dataset.

E3.justification: The experimental design expands to training from Qwen-2.5-Math-7B and OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B with separate configurations. New analyses introduce embedding-similarity greater than 0.98 for identifying overlap and normalized indel similarity above 90% for contamination detection. Pass@1 with 16 samples is retained; newly disclosed decoding settings do not establish changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds cross-dataset uniqueness and t-SNE analyses (Figures 5–6), a MATH500 contamination audit (Appendix A), and response-length tracking during training (Figure 9a). The one-versus-three-solution SFT comparison is retained in Appendix B. Table 1 drops the MATH500 contamination example.

E5.justification: Both versions report pass@1 using 16 samples and average six GPT-4o difficulty ratings per problem. Neither provides training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Relabeling cognitive-behavior 'variance' as frequency change clarifies an existing quantity rather than changing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: New results include DeepMath-Omn-1.5B scoring 64.0/57.3 on AIME24/25 and DeepMath-Zero-7B scoring 41.7 overall on GPQA-Diamond. DeepMath-1.5B's reported MATH500/AIME24 scores change from 89.0/39.8 to 89.9/37.3; v1 lacks sufficient settings to establish a same-condition comparison. Original DeepMath-Zero-7B and SFT mathematics rows remain unchanged. v2 also introduces an inconsistency: Figure 1b gives SRL-Zoo 8.5 on AIME25 while Table 3 retains 8.7.

M1.justification: The dataset-construction stages, difficulty filtering, and multi-solution answer-consistency procedure are retained. v2 newly specifies GRPO with DAPO fixes and tests additional starting checkpoints, without establishing an algorithmic revision. Omission of v1's judge-order-swapping description does not establish that the underlying procedure changed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental discussion, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Section 4 becomes 'DeepMath Series Models' with separate setup, mathematics, generalization, and analysis subsections. SFT results move to Appendix B, other appendices are introduced, and the extended discussion of possible training applications is condensed.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned; new uniqueness, embedding, and contamination displays and several tables are added. Table 3 expands, with SFT rows moved to Table 5. Earlier reasoning plots are combined in Figure 9, replacing benchmark-specific lengths with aggregate bars and shortening the cognitive plot to 500 steps. Figure 9 introduces an incorrect caption describing difficulty and AIME25 instead of its actual panels.

R1.justification: Section 5 replaces broad coverage of chain-of-thought methods, inference scaling, and reasoning efficiency with a dataset taxonomy spanning continued pretraining, SFT, and RL. Added works include OpenWebMath, MathPile, InfiMM-WebMath, MegaMath, and OpenMathReasoning. The introduction newly emphasizes forum-derived problem novelty relative to datasets that reuse common competition sources.

T1.justification: No formal theoretical contribution, assumptions, or proofs are added or revised. Mathematical examples in Figure 2 and Table 2 are retained. The new similarity thresholds specify empirical analysis procedures.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited reproducibility information and empirical scope: Section 4.1 and Appendix C supply missing configurations, while additional checkpoints, science evaluations, and overlap audits make the dataset's usefulness and distinctiveness more assessable. These gains outweigh reporting problems, including Figure 9's incorrect caption and the overbroad claim that DeepMath-Omn-1.5B leads every benchmark, contradicted by its Minerva score of 28.3 versus DeepScaleR's 42.2 in Table 3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepMath-103K dataset and research work. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–E were included, and relocated material can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds model and benchmark results, dataset uniqueness analyses, and a contamination audit in Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset analyses, SFT and RL benchmark results in Table 3, and reasoning-length and cognitive-behavior analyses in Figures 7–8.

results.title: DeepMath-103K: A Large-Scale, Challenging, Decontaminated, and Verifiable Mathematical Dataset for Advancing Reasoning

C1.justification: V1 claims discovery and first proof-of-concept evidence of hidden semantic backdoors in deployed LLMs. V2 redefines the contribution as auditing concept-conditioned semantic divergence, explicitly treating flags as triage signals without causal or intent attribution. Controlled stance implantation and the twelve-topic screening remain central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 introduces benign explanations such as prescriptive pull and survey-like response tendencies, and states that flags establish neither malicious intent nor normative correctness. It explains that attribution requires independent provenance or mechanistic evidence. New appendix interpretations address judge-dependent misses, parameter sensitivity, and the effects of bias proportion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies the full question-generation prompt, topic-selection criteria, LLaMA-Factory identification, CPU/RAM information, judge-decoding settings, and supplementary-artifact instructions. The advertised repository changes from RAVEN to RAVEN-AI. Conversely, v1's detailed Algorithm 3 scoring pseudocode is removed, so reproducibility documentation gains substantial detail while losing one explicit procedural specification.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same twelve topics, conceptual relationships, and public-figure target/control task. Entity-X replaces the XXX XXX pseudonym. Added bias proportions, controls, and judge configurations operate within the retained data and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds a shuffled-label Null-adapter comparator in RQ1 and compares RAVEN implementations using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct judges against GPT-4o-mini in Table 9. These are controls and component variants; neither version benchmarks a competing backdoor detector.

E3.justification: The stated default alpha changes from 0.5 to 0.4. V2 distinguishes a 60% peer-disagreement gate from score-based reporting at 85, whereas v1 specifies divergence threshold 0.5 and Algorithm 3 filters scores above 50. New designs include shuffled-label controls, fixed-size 25%/75% biased training sets, parameter sweeps, and alternative judges. The original six samples, temperature 0.7, and 360-prompt audit remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's preliminary sampling check and brief examples, v2 adds threshold, weighting, and temperature sensitivity analyses in Appendix C.5, bias-proportion experiments in Appendix D, and judge ablations and manual cluster inspection in Appendix E. Appendix F expands the existing vaccination example with all five models' responses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run statistics, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. V2 adds point estimates and qualitative statements about reduced variance, without a new statistical uncertainty procedure. The ten-sample check was already mentioned in v1.

E6.justification: The main suspicion scores and implantation sentiment averages carry over, but v2 removes Table 2's contradiction-strength values and several individual LoRA example scores. New outcomes include control drift of at most two percentage points, 14–25 flags across entropy thresholds, and judge totals of 17, 15, 14, and 17 in Table 9. These are additional results under specified configurations, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The four-stage framework remains, but Algorithm 2 changes from all-pairs entailment-matrix cluster merging to sequential representative-based assignment. V2 also specifies low entropy plus majority disagreement for flagging, replacing the description of separate multiple-confident, confident-pair, and single-confident cases in v1's Algorithm 3. These materially revise the documented operational components, although v2's flagging descriptions are not fully consistent.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, threat-model exposition, research-question narratives, related work, discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Backdoor terminology is systematically replaced with divergence and triage language. Ethics material is moved and shortened, and reproducibility, acknowledgement, and expanded appendix sections reorganize the supporting narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 5–9 for sensitivity and judge comparisons, regroups Tables 1–2 by model, removes Table 2's Avg. Strength column, and reformats Tables 3–4. Figure 1's labeling and caption change, algorithm displays are revised or removed, and the document adopts the ICLR layout. These substantially alter evidence presentation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work as complementary behavioral triage rather than first-of-its-kind backdoor identification. It adds framing, agenda-setting, social-desirability, survey-response, and prescriptive-sampling literature, alongside BadChain and LLaMA-Factory, while removing several attack references. This changes the intellectual context beyond citation formatting.

T1.justification: Equation 1 replaces the qualitative large conditional-probability gap defining a semantic backdoor with an explicit probability-difference estimand over a paraphrase-controlled prompt distribution. V2 distinguishes this estimand from operational flagging. The entropy and bidirectional-entailment definitions remain, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves a central inferential overclaim by replacing asserted discovery of hidden backdoors with explicitly non-causal behavioral triage. Added controls and sensitivity analyses substantially strengthen validation. Reproducibility remains imperfect: detailed scoring pseudocode disappears, flagging descriptions conflict, and Table 9's 17-case baseline is not reconciled with Table 5's 14 cases at the default entropy threshold. These limitations qualify but do not outweigh the substantial gains in claim validity and supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAVEN framework, controlled LoRA study, and twelve-topic audit. All pages, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, are readable. The substantial reframing and appendix expansion do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds control outcomes, parameter sweeps, bias-proportion experiments, and entailment-judge comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original LoRA implantation experiments, sentiment measurements, and RAVEN audit results across five LLMs in Sections 3–4.

results.title: Propaganda AI: An Analysis of Semantic Divergence in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: accurate inversion, region-aware editing, model independence, and low inference cost. Added experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds an implicit-Euler interpretation and component-specific explanations of editing strength, background preservation, fusion benefits, and overexposure. Appendix G discusses broader plugin-based applicability, but Appendix J retains the earlier image-text-only limitation without reconciling it with the new image-conditioned demonstrations.

D1.justification: Appendices D.3 and G add concrete implementation information: baseline optimization settings, plugin checkpoints, application-specific hyperparameters, null-text conditioning, and Canny extraction from segmentation labels. Existing pseudocode, principal experimental settings, and the project-page link remain available.

E1.justification: v2 adds reference-image style transfer, reference-character face editing, and GTAV driving-scene environment editing constrained by segmentation-derived edges. These introduce new conditioning requirements and application coverage. Sketch/stroke generation and video editing already appeared in v1 and are retained.

E2.justification: The existing benchmark comparator sets remain intact. New Table D.3 adds GNRI and ReNoise to direct inversion/reconstruction comparisons; ReNoise previously appeared in the diffusion editing comparison, but not this inversion comparison.

E3.justification: Editing evaluation gains background LPIPS and MSE metrics. New protocols include controlled component ablations, inversion comparisons on 500 CC3M images using 50 diffusion or four SDXL-Turbo steps, and plugin-specific settings. The sketch/stroke delay setting also changes from '0.8 or 1' to 0.8, without establishing that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained delay/guidance sensitivity plots, v2 adds Table C.1 and Figures C.1/C.3 testing inversion, correction, velocity fusion, and regional masks. Figure 4 also adds Uni-Inv error curves. These directly examine component necessity, editing failures, background damage, and overexposure.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The signed parenthetical values in v2 Table C.1 are differences from the full method, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Matching earlier scores are retained, while v2 adds editing metrics, component-ablation results, inversion comparisons, error curves, and plugin demonstrations. For example, new Table D.3 reports unconditional SDXL-Turbo PSNR of 20.08 for Uni-Inv, 17.59 for ReNoise, and 13.46 for GNRI. These are new comparisons, not improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged, but Appendix G substantially extends the pipeline's inputs and components. IP-Adapter and InstantCharacter introduce source/reference-image conditioning, while ControlNet introduces spatial control through modified velocity functions in Equations G.20–G.21.

P1.justification: Section 4 receives explanatory and notation refinements, Applications moves from Section 5.4 to Appendix F, and the appendices gain a contents page and additional subsections. Author information, acknowledgements, and an LLM-use statement are updated or added, while most existing narrative is retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to the ICLR single-column format, with widespread repositioning of figures and tables. Figure 4 is expanded, Figure 5 is redrawn, editing tables gain metric columns, and new ablation tables, comparison tables, and application figures are added. Earlier qualitative galleries are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including FlowEdit, TweezeEdit, GNRI, InstantCharacter, and GTAV, and discusses connections to plugin-based conditioning. The main research-positioning argument remains intact; bibliographic updates and consolidated FLUX references do not constitute new positioning.

T1.justification: Proposition 4.1, its assumptions and Appendix A proof, the Appendix B guidance derivation, and the existing sampler formulations are retained. The expanded implicit-Euler explanation and plugin-conditioning formulas do not introduce a new theoretical result or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification of the central method: Table C.1 and Figure C.3 address v1's lack of direct component ablations, while Table D.3 adds relevant iterative-inversion comparisons and editing tables broaden quality measurement. The plugin experiments also substantiate wider applicability. These gains outweigh the unresolved inconsistency between Appendix G's image-conditioned demonstrations and Appendix J's retained limitation; the new applications remain supported primarily by qualitative examples.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniEdit-Flow, with matching core algorithms and identifiable retained experiments. The text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds component ablations, iterative-inversion comparisons, and experiments with image-conditioning and control plugins.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and editing evaluations, hyperparameter studies, and qualitative image/video results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: UniEdit-Flow: Unleashing Inversion and Editing in the Era of Flow Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary now acknowledge benefits from budget-aware TALE-EP, qualifying the earlier inference-time message centered on self-refinement and majority voting. Claims about model-family niches, temporal cost reductions and the importance of model-level innovation remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix D substantially expands applicability boundaries, covering provider variability, prompt sensitivity, benchmark contamination, model-selection bias, hybrid human-AI workflows and costly errors. C.6 interprets cheaper human labor as reducing the penalty for model failure, while C.8 identifies benchmark gaming and proposes mitigations. Existing verification, variance and human-reliability caveats are retained and developed.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents original-provider access for proprietary models and TogetherAI access for open models, supplementing provider links already present in v1. It clarifies averaging and supplies technical cost inputs for new analyses, including regional rates and the INR88:$1 conversion. The original prompt, decoding settings, token prices and repository link remain.

E1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds Tau-bench airline and retail tasks involving tool use and multi-turn agent-user interaction, substantially extending the original mathematical and question-answering coverage. All six original datasets remain. The India analysis changes labor-cost assumptions, not the evaluated problem population.

E2.justification: TALE-EP, previously only cited, joins the retained self-refinement and majority-voting comparisons in Table 2. Appendix C.8/Table 13 also compares a random-answer Llama-3.1-8B configuration against the original leading models. The original ten-model comparison panel remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include 16 Tau-bench tasks, costs aggregated across interaction rounds, a $2.06 human baseline, and a separate India labor-cost calibration. Section 3.4 also changes the essentialness denominator from the full-model frontier to the frontier excluding the tested family. Figure 3 retains its values, so this reported metric revision does not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test human-baseline essentialness (C.4), sensitivity to regional labor costs (C.6), ranking stability under bootstrap estimation (C.7), and exploitation by cheap random guessing (C.8). These directly examine assumptions and failure conditions previously untested. The earlier model-release and individual-model counterfactual analyses remain in C.3 and C.5.

E5.justification: v1 reports eight repetitions per model-instance pair without confidence intervals. v2 retains that sampling budget and adds 95% bootstrap percentile intervals for all Table 1 estimates using 10,000 resamples (C.7/Table 12). The new Tau-bench experiment separately reports four independent trials; this is not a reduction in the original experiments' repetitions.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include TALE-EP frontier-cost reductions of 66.6% on GSM8K and 50% on GPQA-Diamond, Tau-bench costs, regional estimates and human-essentialness findings. Table 13 reports random-guesser costs of $0.000079 on BBQ and $0.00021 on GPQA-Diamond. The original Table 1, accuracy/cost tables and Figures 2-5 retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: The proposed cost-of-pass calculation C/R, minimum frontier over model and human strategies, and estimation procedure remain intact. TALE-EP and random guessing are additional evaluated strategies. Richer cost functions and success criteria are discussed as extensions rather than implemented replacements.

P1.justification: The main five-section narrative remains, with localized rewrites to the introduction, economic setup and inference-time discussion. Appendix D reorganizes its explanations into modeling extensions, interpretability and limitations, while Appendix C accommodates additional analyses. Terminology, cross-references, acknowledgments and the author block are also edited.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format, extensively resizing and relocating existing displays. Table 2 gains a TALE-EP row, and Tables 7-13 introduce displays for Tau-bench, regional costs, confidence intervals and adversarial comparisons. All five original figures retain their plotted content.

R1.justification: Related work adds connections to inference-price studies by Cottier et al. and Gundlach et al., and economics research on automation, expertise, R&D and compute allocation. Additional references support Tau-bench, provider variability, hybrid workflows and revised labor-cost sources. The central positioning as an adaptation of production theory remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 revises the formal normalization of family essentialness. Section 2.5 replaces population-expectation equalities with explicit approximations using an i.i.d. empirical distribution. Appendix C.8 adds a short mathematical counterexample showing that random guessing among k options can achieve cost-of-pass approximately k times its inference cost. The foundational C/R and frontier definitions remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of assumptions left untested in v1: TALE-EP supplies a missing cost-oriented comparison, regional sensitivity tests the human-cost reference, and the random-guesser experiment exposes a fundamental failure mode. Expanded limitations make the conclusions better calibrated. Tau-bench remains small at 16 tasks, and bootstrap-midpoint ranking agreement does not establish the claimed statistical significance, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in critical validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cost-of-Pass framework. All 16 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including Appendices A-D, are readable. The original equations, experiments, tables and figures can be matched reliably despite additions and substantial layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds TALE-EP comparisons, Tau-bench evaluations, regional cost sensitivity, bootstrap intervals and a random-guessing experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of ten language models across six datasets, including accuracy, inference costs, temporal and counterfactual analyses, and inference-time technique comparisons.

results.title: Cost-of-Pass: An Economic Framework for Evaluating Language Models

C1.justification: The ViMo and STR novelty claims remain intact, but v2 broadens the introduction and conclusion to claim generalisation to unseen apps and successful online task completion. This extends v1's empirical contribution beyond offline action prediction and qualitative compositional generalisation; the contribution summary also adds a human-evaluation advantage.

C2.justification: v2 explains discrepancies between human and automatic ratings and discusses accumulated prediction errors at longer horizons. It also justifies one-step lookahead as an accuracy–cost tradeoff despite two steps scoring highest. The malformed-placeholder limitation is relocated into a dedicated section rather than newly discovered.

D1.justification: v2 specifies GPT-4o as the default LLM, explicitly documents IP2P fine-tuning, and supplies human-study instructions. It adds deployment information including 16 GB GPU memory, V100 timings, three-action requests, and API integration. Appendix F newly describes a user-commitment requirement for the planned checkpoint release; these disclosures do not establish changed training.

E1.justification: v2 adds online navigation on AndroidWorld's 116 tasks and zero-shot evaluation on Android Control apps excluded from training. These extend coverage beyond v1's offline evaluation on the retained 19-app dataset and qualitative examples of unusual action combinations.

E2.justification: SeeAct is newly included in the zero-shot and online comparisons in v2 Tables 4–5. Existing GUI, trajectory, and agent comparators remain present after matching appendix relocations. IP2P becomes IP2P* with explicit fine-tuning disclosure; its retained scores do not establish a new comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 70-participant study of 80 generated samples, including normalized 1–5 visual ratings, and online evaluation using task success. New Gemini-2.0-Flash experiments test rollout depths with only the final predicted state informing selection. The original data splits and 57-episode evaluation remain; Table 6 also clarifies the first control as no ViMo, without establishing a rerun.
