E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative unseen-app robustness testing, a one-/two-/three-step lookahead ablation in Table 7, and inference-time/accuracy analysis in Table 12. The original trajectory evaluation is retained as Table 10 and reframed as error analysis; the original component ablations and qualitative failure examples are also retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 11 adds standard deviations across the same three runs already listed in v1 Table 9. The run count and individual run results remain unchanged; no additional runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are established.

E6.justification: v2 adds human, unseen-app, online, rollout-depth, timing, and some category-level results. Its new online experiment reports 33.19% task success for Gemini-2.0-Flash T3A versus 40.95% with ViMo, not a cross-version performance gain. The retained full-test harmonic score changes from 0.7583 to 0.7578, while original trajectory and main agent scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed default STR construction, diffusion predictor, GUI-text predictor, and one-step action-selection pipeline remain unchanged. The expanded two-stage selector explanation already appears in v1 Appendix B. v2 tests deeper rollout variants as an ablation while retaining the original one-step default.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the experimental narrative around three evaluation settings, moves trajectory and qualitative analyses into Appendix B, and brings existing action-selection explanation into the main text. Earlier implementation appendices are consolidated under Experimental Details, with deployment and limitations separated. The title changes, although much method and related-work prose is retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout and substantially reorganizes its displays. v2 expands the introductory comparison and GUI-quality table, restructures agent-comparison tables, merges and relocates qualitative ablation figures, and adds rollout, deployment, and survey displays. Many original screenshots and numerical tables are retained through these moves.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the GPT-4o system card, Gemini 2.0, and a deepfake survey. The related-work discussion and positioning against language-based world models and pixel-based GUI generators otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, including the diffusion objective and prediction/selection formulations, retain their mathematical content. Neither version adds distinct theorems, proofs, formal assumptions, or derivations in its appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on offline proxies for practical usefulness by adding unseen-app and online task-completion evaluations, complemented by human assessment and horizon/cost analysis. These strengthen validation of the paper's central application claims. Reporting weaknesses remain: the unseen-app sample size is unspecified, and some human-study harmonic scores in Table 1 are inconsistent with their listed components. These issues limit precise quantitative claims but do not outweigh the broader validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViMo/STR research despite the revised title and formatting. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds human evaluation, unseen-app and online-navigation results, rollout-depth experiments, and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original GUI-generation evaluations, trajectory-synthesis results, agent comparisons, component ablations, and repeated-run experiments.

results.title: ViMo: A Generative Visual GUI World Model for App Agents

C1.justification: The training-free early-exit thesis remains, but v3 adds DEER-PRo's prompt-robust calibration as a core contribution and broadens its explicit effectiveness claim across model families and ten benchmarks. The abstract revises headline shortening and accuracy-gain ranges from 31-43% and 1.7-5.7 points to 19.1-80.1% and 0.3-5.0 points across the expanded evaluations.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations linking linguistic markers to high entropy and hidden-state discontinuities, and threshold robustness to polarized confidence scores. It interprets the different compression and accuracy benefits across task difficulties and identifies low intermediate-answer confidence as a limitation on Nemotron's efficiency gains. V1's performance-ceiling extrapolation is removed; its QwQ delimiter limitation is retained.

D1.justification: V3 adds a code-repository link, exact answer-inducing prompts, shared and variant-specific thresholds, DEER-PRo parameters, and an eight-H100 hardware specification. It documents the vLLM implementation, quantized DeepSeek-R1 evaluation through KTransformers, and confidence estimation from the first 50 code-answer tokens. These are substantial reproducibility disclosures; relocated pseudocode and the existing branch-parallel diagram are not new details.

E1.justification: V3 retains the six original benchmarks and adds GSM8K, AIME 2025, OlympiadBench, and LiveCodeBench, with results in Tables 1, 3, 8, and 13. This substantially extends elementary mathematics, advanced competition mathematics, and competitive programming coverage. Discussion of non-English applicability does not establish an added language evaluation.

E2.justification: V1 primarily compares DEER with Vanilla CoT and its own transition-marker variants. V3 Table 1 adds evaluated comparisons against TCC, CoD, NoThinking, Dynasor-CoT, and SEAL. SEAL results are limited to GSM8K and MATH-500 on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B; its participation should not be generalized to the other comparisons.

E3.justification: V3 changes the documented length measure from words to tokens and adds compression-rate reporting. It adds Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-671B, and Nemotron model configurations, token-budget sweeps, and a separate 32,768-token sampling evaluation with top-p 0.95 and temperature 0.6 (Table 8). These extend v1's documented 16,384-token greedy evaluation.

E4.justification: V3 substantially extends the threshold and trigger studies with token-budget and decoding sensitivity, entropy-trigger and arithmetic/geometric-mean comparisons, early-exit rate/accuracy diagnostics, hidden-state analysis, confidence-distribution analysis, and additional case comparisons. Conversely, v1 Figure 2's AIME pilot panels and Table 2's non-MATH Alternatively comparisons are absent from v3.

E5.justification: V1 documents single-sample greedy evaluation without confidence intervals. V3 reports four sampling rounds for small contest datasets and a separate uncertainty experiment using four independent runs on GSM8K, MATH, and GPQA and eight on AMC23 and AIME24, with 95% confidence intervals in Table 9. Seeds and interval-construction details are unspecified, and the relationship to retained single-sample greedy descriptions is unclear.

E6.justification: Many results are replaced or added. For example, v1 Table 1's R1-Distill-Qwen-7B MATH-500 accuracies of 86.0% for Vanilla and 87.4% for DEER are replaced by 87.4% and 89.8% in v3 Table 1 under revised method and evaluation conditions, not a demonstrated same-setting gain. V3 also adds comparator, DEER-PRo, additional-benchmark, and branch-parallel latency results.

M1.justification: V3 Section 3.2 adds entropy-based transition monitoring, replaces v1's arithmetic-mean answer confidence with a geometric mean, and introduces DEER-PRo, which combines multiple prompted answers using mean confidence minus a mean-absolute-deviation penalty. These change the inference procedure. Branch-parallel decoding itself was already proposed in v1.

P1.justification: V3 substantially reorganizes and rewrites the narrative: generation-pattern preliminaries move into Method, pilot setup and much experimental detail move to dedicated appendices, ablations receive a separate section, and related work is split between a concise main section and Appendix M. It also adds ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements and revises terminology from LRLM to LRM.

P2.justification: V3 redesigns Table 1 as a highlighted multi-baseline matrix with token and compression columns, adds numerous analysis tables and plots, and introduces a rotated comprehensive results table. Figure 2 is rearranged and loses its AIME panels; the branch-parallel diagram and pseudocode move to the appendix. The original three appendix case figures remain, renumbered and supplemented with additional comparisons.

R1.justification: V3 retains the original efficient-reasoning taxonomy but substantially expands the cited research and comparative positioning. Section 5 and Appendix M add Dynasor-CoT and SEAL and incorporate newer reinforcement-learning, confidence-guided compression, reasoning-path compression, distilled pruning, and manifold-steering work. This extends the discussion beyond v1's narrower concurrent-work comparisons.

T1.justification: V1 contains method equations but no comparable theoretical treatment. V3 Appendix B introduces an independent Gaussian prompt-noise model, false-positive probability derivations, a claimed exponential improvement theorem, and a MAD derivation. Appendix H adds attention-cost and KV-cache memory analyses under explicit assumptions about cached decoding and answer-induction overhead.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v1's limited comparative evidence through evaluated efficiency baselines, tests of important scoring and monitoring choices, and measured branch-parallel speedups that v1 deferred. Broader evaluation and explicit implementation details improve assessment and reproducibility. These gains outweigh important reporting weaknesses: sampling descriptions remain inconsistent, Table 9 does not by itself establish blanket statistical significance, and Appendix B overstates noise independence by treating a noise-independent probability bound as independence of the actual error probability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: V3 reports original benchmark comparisons, method ablations, latency measurements, repeated-run results with confidence intervals, and mechanistic analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, early-exit pilot experiments, threshold and transition-marker analyses, latency measurements, and generated case studies.

results.title: Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The central claim of a linear-response interpretability framework that separates functional structures in a 3M-parameter transformer remains. v3 adds a more specific headline contribution: attributing recovered circuits to data patterns and explaining their balance of expression and suppression. v1 framed the demonstrated structural inference primarily as preliminary validation.

C2.justification: v3 develops an explicit expression/suppression interpretation and associates per-token PCs with word segmentation, the induction circuit and, more tentatively, bracket matching. It links context-length effects to induction-pattern suppression and reports no simple correspondence with direct logit effects. New limitations address SGLD hyperparameter sensitivity, correlated samples, component-wise sampling costs and the uncertain adequacy of PCA for larger models.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents the 5,000-token tokenizer, BOS handling, detailed pattern-selection rules and additional data-mixing instructions. It replaces the TPU/runtime descriptions with A100 allocations and runtimes and adds scaling-cost formulas and Pythia cost measurements in Appendix C. These are substantial documentation changes; the underlying SGLD hyperparameters and dataset-access link are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions study next-token model structure using Pile subsets and the separate GitHub-code corpus. The new pattern and seed analyses use retained data. Philpapers remains in metric comparisons despite losing its dedicated catalogue subsection. The Pythia additions concern model scale and computational cost, without documenting a new corpus or task.

E2.justification: The comparisons with zero-ablation loss differences and original token losses are retained. v3 Appendix H adds an evaluated comparator: token-averaged direct logit effects calculated from the unembedding and head-output matrices, motivated by Gurnee et al. and Lad et al.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a substantial evaluation protocol for per-token PCA: 20,000 sampled tokens per dataset, separate analyses by layer, and pattern frequencies among the top positive and negative 1% and 10%. It also adds token aggregation for the direct-logit comparison and scaling measurements on Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B. The earlier checkpoint schedule, mixture ratio and core SGLD settings remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds circuit-recovery checks across training seeds, sensitivity to token sampling, all-token versus induction-token susceptibility distributions, and a test of the hypothesized connection to direct logit effects. It removes some earlier analyses, including the context-position variance plot, top-1,000 token-frequency analysis and Enron token-loss table. The original trajectory PCA is retained as supporting evidence.

E5.justification: v3 reports three additional independently trained models, giving four training seeds, and introduces means and standard deviations across ten independent draws of 20,000 tokens per dataset for PCA pattern percentages and head loadings (Appendices I–J). Both versions report four SGLD chains; the new variability estimates do not represent an increase in that chain count.

E6.justification: v3 adds per-token PCA, pattern-enrichment, cross-seed and direct-logit results and revises many retained measurements. The aggregate/per-token agreement diagnostic changes from r=0.817 and slope=15.992 to r=0.958 and slope=9.794. GitHub-all head 0:0's total susceptibility changes from 17,816 to 26,219 (v1 Table 1; v3 Table 2). The original trajectory-PCA variance percentages are retained in Appendix G.

M1.justification: v3 extends structural inference with separate per-layer PCA of per-token susceptibility matrices and associates their components with token patterns. v1 used dataset/checkpoint susceptibility matrices for PCA, which remain in v3 Appendix G. The covariance estimator, local SGLD sampling and mixture-probe procedure are retained.

P1.justification: The title, introduction, contribution statements and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. Much of v1's theory and main empirical discussion moves into reorganized appendices, while per-token structural inference becomes the main results narrative. v3 also adds an appendix guide and dedicated limitations, reproducibility and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: v3 adds pattern-enrichment heatmaps, per-token PCA loading plots, distribution comparisons, direct-logit plots and seed/variability displays. Existing token visualizations are redrawn with per-head z-score coloring, and many figures are relocated. Several earlier displays disappear, including trajectory projections, the trajectory scree plot and the context-position variance plot; these changes go well beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around suppression, self-repair, ensemble behavior and prediction/suppression neurons, adding discussion of work such as McGrath et al., McDougall et al., Gurnee et al. and Rushing and Nanda. It also adds Bayesian influence-function references, including Giordano and Broderick and Iba. This extends v1's narrower ablation and influence-function discussion.

T1.justification: v3 states the main covariance identity exactly for an h-independent observable, replacing v1's treatment of h-dependent observables with an O(1/n) term. It adds the population per-token integration identity and proof in Lemma A.1. Appendices D.4–D.5 replace the diagonal, mode-aligned expansion with a general mode-pair expansion, while v1's absolute-bigram derivation is removed.

improvement.justification: v1 left the data-pattern interpretation of its trajectory PCs substantially uncertain. v3 makes that interpretation more concrete through quantified pattern enrichment, circuit correspondence across four training seeds and sampling-variability checks (Section 4.2; Appendices I–J). These substantially strengthen the evidence for structural inference, alongside clearer organization and explicit limitations. Local reporting regressions remain: v3 Table 3 retains sums inconsistent with its revised positive and negative totals. Those errors do not outweigh the broader evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same susceptibility-based interpretability research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original empirical results, including per-token PCA, additional training seeds, sampling-variability analyses and comparisons with direct logit effects.

before.justification: v1 reports original susceptibility measurements, trajectory PCA, comparisons with ablation and loss, and token-level analyses on a small transformer.

results.title: Structural Inference: Interpreting Small Language Models with Susceptibilities

C1.justification: The parameter-free frequency-compression contribution remains, but the claimed empirical reach expands substantially. v3's abstract and introduction claim stable 256K extrapolation from 8K training, compared with v1's reported 64K extension, and explicitly claim improved long-generation capability alongside prefilling performance.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's energy-concentration rationale, v3 interprets low frequencies as global semantic context and high frequencies as local details. It sharpens the existing Proof-pile limitation by discussing symbol/index sensitivity, connects adaptation to the Frequency Principle, and explains retention-latency tradeoffs and progressive amplification without rescaling.

D1.justification: v3 adds a FreqKV repository link and states that supplementary material contains code. Its training-cost study specifies eight RTX6000 Ada-48GB GPUs, per-device batch size one, and eight accumulation steps, with time and memory measurements. Most previously documented training hyperparameters are retained; the PDFs do not independently verify the linked resources.

E1.justification: v3 adds RULER and LongGenBench, including extended generation from concatenated GSM8K/MMLU questions. It also introduces synonym-perturbed CNN/DailyMail inputs as a new test scenario. Existing training corpora and evaluations remain; Proof-pile moves into Appendix E rather than disappearing.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 2, v3 Table 3 removes LM-Infinite and LongHeads from LongBench and adds CaM, KVMerger, LaCache, D2O, GemFilter, FastKV, and ThinK. SnapKV also joins the LLaMA-3 comparison. The LLaMA-3 Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation gains multiple comparator methods.

E3.justification: v3 adds LLaMA-2-13B configurations, 1% retention on LongBench, and PG-19 evaluation through 256K rather than 64K. New protocols include cosine-similarity testing on 100 documents with 1% synonym replacement, a 4096-token generation limit on LongGenBench, and a controlled training-cost comparison. The established default training recipe remains substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix F add frequency-band perturbation tests, high-versus-low-frequency ablations on summarization and PG-19, mismatched training/evaluation retention ratios, sink-count ablations, and a rescaling ablation. Aggressive compression and longer extrapolation are also tested. Existing RoPE and Dropping analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v1 Section 6.2 and Table 3 report five-run latency means with standard deviations; that table is absent from v3. v3 Appendix F.2 specifies five-run averaging for retention-ratio latencies, but its main extrapolation table supplies no standard deviations or run count. This changes uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive benchmark, 13B-model, ablation, training-cost, and 256K results. For example, Table 5 reports LongGenBench scores of 54.2 and 31.2 for FreqKV on GSM8K and MMLU. Existing LLaMA-3 LongBench values also change: Qasper at 50% retention changes from 42.43 to 41.60. Original 7B PG-19/Proof-pile perplexities and FLOP results remain unchanged, while the earlier Dropping latency table is removed.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains DCT, low-frequency retention, rescaled IDCT, and iterative cache compression with protected sink tokens and RoPE applied afterward. v1 Sections 4.2–4.3 and v3 Sections 3.3–3.4 describe the same algorithm; the rescaling component was already present in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around prefilling and decoding. Preliminaries are reorganized into the method section, DCT formulas move to Appendix A, and Proof-pile, retention-ratio, Dropping, and overhead discussions move into expanded appendices. The title, author information, and conference statements also change.

P2.justification: The method diagram is redrawn to show DCT, filtering, IDCT, and iterative compression. LongBench gains retention-ratio groups and averages; the perplexity table is split and gains model-size groups. Needle-in-a-Haystack panels are reorganized, the retention plot gains latency bars and a second axis, and new diagnostic plots and tables accompany the conference layout.

R1.justification: The introductory and related-work coverage substantially expands to ALiBi, positional interpolation, LongRoPE, recent prefilling/compression methods, and the Frequency Principle. This broadens the positioning against alternative context-extension approaches. The claim of being the first frequency-domain KV compression method for decoder-only LLMs remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The DCT/IDCT, attention, rescaling, and compression equations remain mathematically equivalent despite relocation, consolidation, and notation changes. v3 adds conceptual explanations and references to the Frequency Principle, but no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central method and efficiency claims. Frequency-selection and rescaling ablations test previously underexamined design choices, Table 7 directly measures training costs, and LongGenBench evaluates generation beyond v1's perplexity and understanding evidence. Broader comparisons further strengthen the evaluation. Removing the earlier latency standard deviations weakens uncertainty reporting, but this limited loss does not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FreqKV. All 14 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v3, including their appendices, support comparison. Methods, equations, and retained experiments can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds RULER, LongGenBench, larger-model evaluations, training-cost measurements, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original FreqKV perplexity, LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, latency, and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: FreqKV: Key-Value Compression in Frequency Domain for Context Window Extension

C1.justification: The central contributions—adaptive reasoning modes for social agents and AMPO's performance/token advantages—remain. v5 refines the headline 15.6% comparison to explicitly name GPT-4o rather than broadly referring to state-of-the-art methods, and drops the abstract's explicit claim of more human-like reasoning than GRPO.

C2.justification: v5 adds substantive arguments connecting single-turn optimization to long-horizon consistency, interpretations of OOD transfer and efficient-reasoning tradeoffs, and expanded LRM failure explanations. It also discusses training/inference costs and explicitly qualifies alternative-judge results because those judges lack validation against human annotations (Appendices B, D, and K).

D1.justification: v5 newly specifies 4,000 BC examples and 2,057 RL queries, length-reward defaults, detailed BC/RL configurations (Tables 28–29), the SOTOPIA evaluation prompt (Tables 26–27), and adaptations of the new baselines (Appendix H.3). It adds an Apache-2.0 licensing statement. The repository link and eight-A100 hardware disclosure already existed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates SOTOPIA and SOTOPIA-Hard. v5 adds DEMO, including Chinese and English dialogue and more adversarial/non-cooperative scenarios, plus NegotiationArena's Sell&Buy and Ultimatum tasks (Appendix D.1, Tables 4–5). These extend evaluation coverage beyond the original benchmark family; training remains based on SOTOPIA-π.

E2.justification: v5 Table 7 newly compares AMPO against TALE-PT, DeGRPO, LS-Mix, and O1-Pruner on both backbones. In the corresponding main comparison, Table 1 replaces Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking with Gemini-2.5-Pro. The existing social-planning baselines and BC/GRPO comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v5 introduces OOD partner/role-swapping protocols, profit and winning-rate metrics, and evaluations with two alternative LLM judges. Human evaluation changes from 100 sampled dialogues to all episodes from both benchmarks. The reported Llama RL learning rate changes from 1e-7 in v1 Table 5 to 2e-7 in v5 Table 11; this documentation change does not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained single-mode and adaptive-behavior analyses, v5 adds answer-length-reward ablations, state-diversity and marginal-reward ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, and alternative-judge checks (Tables 3, 6, 8–9). It also adds OOD generalization tests and concrete LRM failure traces (Tables 15–18). The original AMPO dialogue case is retained and reformatted.

E5.justification: Both main-result tables report fourfold averaging and p < 0.05. v5 newly reports 73.39% pairwise agreement among human annotators in Appendix I.1. Its expanded ablation table no longer includes v1 Table 2's explicit four-evaluation and significance statement; no increase in main-experiment repetitions is established.

E6.justification: Matched main-table results, apart from the replaced Gemini comparator, and original single-mode ablations retain their numbers. v5 adds substantial results: for example, DEMO averages of 7.81/7.72 for Qwen AMPO/GRPO with GPT-4o (Table 4), and SOTOPIA-Hard GOAL of 7.12 without diverse states versus 7.85 for full AMPO (Table 6). Human win/lose percentages also change under the revised reported sampling, rather than demonstrating a same-setting performance change.

M1.justification: The four reasoning action sequences, behavioral cloning followed by single-turn RL, combined mode/sample advantages, and answer/format/length rewards are retained. The ASL renaming, explicit mode-prefix explanation, and revised notation do not establish a substantive change to the optimization or inference procedure.

P1.justification: The title, framework name, and thinking/reasoning terminology change alongside extensive rewriting of the abstract, introduction, method exposition, and research questions. Standalone preliminaries are removed, the method is reorganized around task formulation, modes, BC, and AMPO, and reward/pseudocode details move into substantially reorganized appendices.

P2.justification: v5 expands the original AMPO diagram into a three-stage framework overview, redraws and relocates the introductory scenario, and reformats the mode-distribution plots. It replaces the separate-benchmark human-results table with one set of bar charts, restructures the ablation table, adds experiment/configuration tables, and spreads the retained dialogue example across three tables.

R1.justification: v5 substantially expands positioning around efficient reasoning, overthinking, social-learning foundations, static versus interactive social benchmarks, and single-turn dialogue training. It explicitly distinguishes AMPO from compression, mixed-length training, and binary-reward approaches. This goes beyond bibliographic updates to retained works such as EPO, DSI, and DEMO.

T1.justification: v5 Section 2.1 adds an explicit POMDP formulation, defining observations, transitions, trajectories, and an expected terminal-reward objective where v1 provides a less formal interaction description. Existing AMPO and reward equations remain equivalent apart from notation and placement. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for transfer beyond SOTOPIA and efficiency relative to specialized reasoning methods. OOD evaluations, direct efficiency comparisons, targeted ablations, evaluator checks, and fuller implementation details strengthen validation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting shortcomings: human results lose their benchmark breakdown, and Table 7 overstates universal superiority—DeGRPO scores 3.72 versus AMPO's 3.68 on Llama SOTOPIA-Hard self-play OVERALL.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same four-mode social-agent framework and AMPO algorithm despite the retitling and AML-to-ASL renaming. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v5 retains original empirical results and adds out-of-distribution evaluations, efficient-reasoning comparisons, component ablations, and evaluator checks in Tables 4–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original SOTOPIA evaluations, mode ablations, training dynamics, and human comparisons in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–4.

results.title: Adaptive Social Learning via Mode Policy Optimization for Language Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: optimal convergence when p is known, the best-known centralized rate when p is unknown, topology independence and node-count speedup in the stated regime, and empirical robustness. The qualified Transformer interpretation appears in Section 5.2 without a corresponding revision of the broad main claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 replaces v1's interpretation that GT-NSGDm is the only successful Transformer optimizer with the finding that it nearly matches DSGD-GClip, emphasizing competitive performance together with theoretical guarantees. New Remarks 7–8 also explain required parameter knowledge, finite-horizon topology and node-count effects, and tradeoffs against bounded-variance theory. These substantially qualify the method's practical and theoretical advantages.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds update equations and Transformer hyperparameter-search ranges for the four new baselines, including GT-Adam's stabilization parameter and QG-DSGDm's momentum choices. Existing model architecture, hardware, reported runtime and original methods' search grids are retained. No new code or data access resource is supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions cover synthetic token-like regression and Multi30k language modeling, including the same noise families, graph topologies and node-count scenarios. The revised synthetic feature allocation changes the reported generation setting within existing coverage, rather than adding a dataset or task.

E2.justification: The Transformer comparison expands from four to eight baselines by adding DSGD-GClip, DSGD-CClip, GT-Adam and QG-DSGDm. All four have reported results in v2 Table 1; the original baselines remain. These additions substantially strengthen the comparison, while the synthetic comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 revises the synthetic feature specification: v1 states two frequent and eight rare features despite declaring d=20; v2 specifies four frequent and sixteen rare features. This is a reported data-generation correction, without evidence establishing a rerun. The retained Transformer experiments still use the same model, 12 epochs, batch size 64, validation metric and graph settings.

E4.justification: The gradient-noise investigation, comparisons across noise distributions, and sensitivity studies varying connectivity, noise level and node count are retained in Figures 1–3. No distinct ablation, robustness scenario or case study is added. The removed Transformer learning curves report the existing benchmark experiment rather than a separate supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report Transformer means and standard deviations over five independent runs. v2 presents this information in Table 1 and extends the same practice to additional baselines; it does not introduce a different run count, confidence interval or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for four Transformer comparators, changing the empirical ranking. DSGD-GClip reports losses of 0.253, 0.249 and 0.267 on ring, exponential and complete graphs, below GT-NSGDm's retained means of 0.258, 0.261 and 0.282. v1's validation and training trajectories are removed, including its reported training endpoints of 0.100, 0.096 and 0.091. The synthetic findings remain unchanged.

M1.justification: GT-NSGDm's momentum, gradient-tracking and normalized update equations remain unchanged. However, its theoretical step-size prescription in Equation (5) changes from min(1, max{three candidates}) to the minimum of all four quantities, and replaces 1+2.5L with 3.5L in one candidate. This changes parameter selection without introducing a new optimizer component.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammatical corrections, condenses the experimental prose, removes the paper-outline paragraph, and adds a proof roadmap and acknowledgments. The principal section organization is retained. A small new inconsistency remains: Section 5.2 says three additional baselines while listing four.

P2.justification: The Transformer evidence is substantially reformatted: v1 Figure 4's validation curves are replaced by a numerical table grouped by theoretical guarantees, and Figure 5's training curves are removed. Baseline-description and Transformer-search tables expand and move to separate appendix pages. Figures 1–3 retain their plotted content, with placement changes.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 adds discussion of adaptive federated optimization and earlier gradient tracking with normalization for deterministic max-margin learning. Additional references support the new baselines, spectral and bounded-variance comparisons, and related divergence examples in Appendix A; some general optimization references disappear. The overall research positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical support for both main theorems is materially revised. Equation (5) corrects the min/max step-size choice; the final derivation restores a missing smoothness factor L and propagates revised constants. Lemmas 6–8 separate unconditional martingale bounds from subsequent conditional-expectation calculations. Remarks 7–8 add parameter-selection and finite-horizon derivations. These changes affect the reasoning supporting the guarantees, although the assumptions and principal convergence exponents remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in both central forms of evidence: it repairs the step-size prescription and proof arguments supporting convergence, and introduces stronger Transformer baselines that produce a more credible, qualified empirical interpretation. These gains outweigh the loss of learning-curve detail. The unchanged broad superiority wording in the abstract remains a limitation, but the theoretical support and comparative evaluation are substantially improved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GT-NSGDm research, with matching algorithms, theoretical results and experimental tasks. Text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–C are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original synthetic experiments and gradient-noise measurements and reports Transformer validation results for an expanded comparator set in Table 1.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic regression experiments, empirical gradient-noise distributions and decentralized Transformer training results, including validation and training losses in Figures 1–5.

results.title: Decentralized Nonconvex Optimization under Heavy-Tailed Noise: Normalization and Optimal Convergence

C1.justification: The principal contribution remains two-stage RPCA decomposition followed by learned joint rank/sparsity allocation. v2's conclusion explicitly extends the superiority claim to modern reasoning and long-context tasks and low-rank baselines. The abstract and introduction also recast global optimization as global resource allocation.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly states that policy-gradient pruning has no global-optimum guarantee, explains why tuning RPCA lambda cannot replace budget-constrained selection, and attributes inference gains to the sparse component's high sparsity. It adds calibration-domain interpretations and qualifies the GLUE comparison as competitive or comparable rather than uniformly superior. The hardware-dependence limitation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the default lambda formula, mentions lm-eval-harness, identifies Wanda as the base pruner for OWL/AlphaPruning, and documents the inference benchmark's GPU capacity, batch size and sequence length. Most software versions and reproduction instructions are retained. v1's LoSparse float32, batch-size-64 and learning-rate-3e-5 disclosure is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds GSM8K reasoning, LongBench-v2 long-context evaluation, and Qwen evaluations on NarrativeQA, GovReport, Lcc code and TriviaQA. It also tests GitHub Code as a calibration domain. These extend task and input-domain coverage beyond v1; GLUE and OpenBookQA were already present in v1's appendices.

E2.justification: v2 Tables 1, 3 and 5 add evaluated comparisons with DSNoT, OATS, OWL, AlphaPruning, JSQ, L2QER, Naive-LoRA, SLiM-LoRA, SLiM-LoRAQ, SVD-LLM v2, Dobi-SVD and Basis Sharing. Original comparators, including BESA in Appendix I and the GLUE comparison methods, remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds Phi-3, OPT, LLaMA-3/3.1 and Qwen2.5 configurations, including LLaMA-3 70B, multiple compression budgets, quantized comparisons, eight-shot GSM8K evaluation and a batch-size-1, sequence-length-1024 inference benchmark. The LoSparse comparison changes its reported retention from 80% in v1 Table 4 to 20% in v2 Table 5; its scores therefore do not establish a matched-setting improvement.

E4.justification: v2 adds calibration-source robustness tests in Table 6 and an RPCA lambda sensitivity study in Appendix H/Table 7. The four CAP configurations in v1's LoSparse ablation are replaced by a simpler with/without-fine-tuning comparison. Earlier RPCA-iteration, threshold-pruning and layerwise analyses remain, reformatted or relocated to Figures 2 and 5.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's additional policy-gradient variance discussion concerns theoretical estimator behavior, not uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark, sensitivity and resource measurements; its new GSM8K comparison reports 56.8% for CAP versus 45.6% for Wanda. Existing CAP GLUE entries also change: RTE at 16% retention changes from 68.3 to 66.5, and SST-2 from 91.9 to 90.8. Conversely, v1 Tables 1, 6 and 7 retain their numerical results as v2 Tables 8, 9 and 10. v1's claimed 0.2 perplexity advantage for global over layerwise pruning is omitted.

M1.justification: The RPCA decomposition, Bernoulli policy-gradient updates and reconstruction remain. However, the stated final selection rule changes: v1 Section 5.2.2 ranks candidates by retention probability multiplied by parameter contribution, whereas v2 Section 2.3.2 ranks directly by retention probability. This is a localized procedural revision.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work and preliminaries move to appendices, earlier LLaMA experiments move to Appendix I, and the reproduction report becomes a separate statement. Method explanations are rewritten around the two stages' distinct objectives, experiments are reorganized into focused comparisons, and appendix navigation is added.

P2.justification: v2 introduces multiple benchmark and resource tables with grouped and side-by-side layouts. v1's RPCA and threshold-ablation tables become the two heatmaps in Figure 2, while the separate rank-distribution and layerwise-perplexity plots become Figure 5's panels. Existing figures and tables are extensively relocated within a redesigned conference layout.

R1.justification: Related-work positioning expands substantially in Appendices B and G to cover adaptive sparsity allocation, modern low-rank methods, quantization hybrids, distillation and structured pruning. Added discussions include SVD-LLM, MoDeGPT, MaskLLM, SpQR and CALDERA, while CAP's distinction from quantization-error reconstruction receives greater emphasis. This exceeds relocation or bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: The approximation theorem, parameter-efficiency lemma and performance-preservation corollary from v1 Appendix F remain in v2 Appendix E. New Appendix F adds Bernoulli mask variance, batch-averaging variance scaling and a conditional stationary-point convergence argument using Robbins-Monro step-size conditions. This extends the existing policy-gradient analysis without replacing its earlier theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's direct comparisons with alternative low-rank/joint compression methods and its largely qualitative deployment-efficiency discussion. New comparisons, challenging tasks, calibration/lambda analyses and measured throughput/memory substantially strengthen the empirical basis; explicitly limiting global-optimality claims improves interpretation. Reporting defects remain, including milliseconds versus seconds for identical latency values in Tables 6 and 11 and conflicting DSNoT descriptions in Appendices B and G. These limit confidence in some details but do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAP compression framework and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Matching methods and retained benchmark results support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds reasoning, long-context, calibration robustness, parameter sensitivity and inference-efficiency results.

before.justification: v1 reports original CAP perplexity, zero-shot accuracy, GLUE results and decomposition/pruning ablations in Section 6 and the appendices.

results.title: Large Language Model Compression with Global Rank and Sparsity Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the principal contribution to multi-shortcut mitigation. Bias partitions are now presented as modes capturing combinations of shortcuts or uninterpretable harmful cues, with correspondence to conventional annotated groups specifically qualified for single-shortcut settings. The original annotation-free and multiclass claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations involving causal covariate balance, stronger minority reweighting, tolerance of imperfect partitions, and convergence through progressive filtering. It explains the empirical basis of 50% selection and describes within-mode homogeneity as a practical approximation, supported by unsuccessful finer splitting. The earlier CelebA/CivilComments limitations remain, alongside stronger assertions about capturing harmful biases.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a code-repository pointer, identifies a single NVIDIA A40 GPU, and reports stage budgets and dataset-specific MST runtimes in Tables 10–11. Much of the training setup is relocated from v1's main text, and the original optimization table is retained. UrbanCars-specific architecture and optimization details remain incomplete.

E1.justification: v2 retains Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, and cCIFAR10, and adds UrbanCars with competing background and co-occurring-object shortcuts. Appendix D also evaluates UrbanCars(BG) and UrbanCars(CoObj), substantially expanding coverage of multiple-shortcut and controlled single-shortcut conditions.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds DaC, DebiAN, DDB, and GERNE; the multiclass comparison adds DaC and GERNE in Table 4. UrbanCars comparisons include ExMap. Figure 4(b) and Table 9 also newly compare MST's bias discovery against XRM and JTT, beyond their existing classification comparisons.

E3.justification: The retained benchmarks keep their stated splits, architectures, training budgets, and validation-selection rule. Added experiments introduce UrbanCars in-distribution accuracy and shortcut-gap evaluation, smallest-mode precision/F1 comparisons, controlled gamma and beta sweeps, and repetition counts extending through six. These substantially broaden the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Existing component ablations and sample-weight analyses remain. v2 adds selection-fraction sensitivity, adaptive selection, extended convergence tests, comparative bias-discovery diagnostics, and recall across UrbanCars minority groups. Appendix E also tests entropy-based within-mode splitting and reports degradation, adding evidence about failure conditions.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random seeds and use means with standard deviations. v2 introduces no new confidence-interval or significance-testing practice. Revised standard-deviation values in Table 3 are numerical result changes, without evidence of increased runs or a changed uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Shared classification rows in Table 1 and the multiclass table remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive results, including UrbanCars accuracy of 92.98% with a -4.9-point combined-shortcut gap, discovery comparisons, sensitivity results, and runtimes. Table 3 also revises uncertainty values: FG-CCDB's Waterbirds WGA changes from 90.56±0.006 to 90.56±0.24 while retaining its mean.

M1.justification: The default pipeline remains unchanged: BEO becomes MST, retaining confidence-based retraining, 50% selection, and the same closed-form weighting equations. Appendix E additionally introduces and tests an adaptive selection variant that assigns higher selection fractions to higher-confidence classes, a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The title changes, BEO becomes MST, and group terminology is extensively reframed around modes and confusion matrices. The introduction, related work, and method explanations are substantially rewritten; training details move into Appendix B. A hyperparameter section and lengthy question-and-answer discussions reorganize and expand the narrative.

P2.justification: Figures are substantially recomposed: the existing WGA curve moves into Figure 1, Figure 2 gains a numerical weighting example, and Figures 3–4 gain sensitivity and discovery-comparison panels. New UrbanCars, fairness, and convergence figures and multiple tables appear. The retained ablation table is compressed beside the new UrbanCars table; the sample-weight figure is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning around DDB, DaC, GERNE, ExMap, and multi-shortcut research. It explicitly relates MST's filtering principle to prior bias-amplification work by Lee et al. and DDB, and adds fairness and causal-inference connections. Earlier discussions and citations for methods including CSAD, SSA, and generative classifiers are removed.

T1.justification: The central reweighting equations remain equivalent. Appendix E adds the equal-opportunity fairness condition in Equation 5 and a confusion-matrix argument linking prediction-defined modes to true-positive-rate disparities whenever ERM accuracy is below 100%. This is a limited added theoretical rationale, without a rigorous robustness or convergence theorem.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of its central bias-discovery and debiasing claims through competing-shortcut evaluations, precision/recall/F1 comparisons, selection sensitivity, extended convergence, and a failed finer-partitioning experiment. These address important evidential gaps in v1; runtime disclosures and corrected internal consistency of Table 3 uncertainties also help assessment. The new fairness argument does not establish its broad bias-capture guarantee, and UrbanCars implementation details remain incomplete, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial empirical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FG-CCDB research despite the changed title and BEO-to-MST renaming. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds UrbanCars evaluations, bias-discovery comparisons, sensitivity and convergence experiments, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification results on five datasets, component ablations, bias-prediction experiments, and feature-correlation and sample-weight analyses.

results.title: Fine-Grained Class-Conditional Distribution Balancing for Debiased Learning

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged apart from formatting. The introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: the retrieve-and-rerank framework, SWELOC training data, state-of-the-art localization on the two main benchmarks, and favorable efficiency relative to agentic methods.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of retrieval and repair bottlenecks, failure on complex issues, semantic matching beyond lexical overlap, and transfer beyond Python. It attributes reranking gains to cross-function dependencies and discusses agents confusing symptom locations with underlying causes. These substantially extend v1's discussion of data quality, model choice, and cost.

D1.justification: V1 promises future code, data, and model releases; v2 reports code and models available through a repository. V2 also documents file/module score aggregation and latency hardware. Appendix A is unchanged, while the token-pricing footnote and agent-result provenance notes in Tables 1–2 are removed.

E1.justification: V2 adds downstream issue resolution using SWE-Fixer on SWE-Bench-Lite, extending evaluation beyond localization. Appendix F adds SWE-Bench Multilingual, covering 234 tasks across nine non-Python programming languages. The existing SWELOC training data and two main localization benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: New comparisons include Gemini-Embedding, Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B and 8B, and SWE-Fixer's native localization plus an oracle repair control. Appendix B also compares Llama reranker training variants. Conversely, both Agentless rows disappear from SWE-Bench-Lite Table 1, although Agentless remains in LocBench Table 2.

E3.justification: The existing 274-example SWE-Bench-Lite and 560-example LocBench evaluations and Appendix A training settings remain unchanged. New protocols include repair Pass@1 with an oracle control, complexity and lexical/semantic-overlap stratification, Acc@20/50/100 retrieval evaluation, controlled embedding-dimension experiments, and latency measurements over 50 instances with a matched GPT-4o comparison.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of downstream repair, issue complexity, lexical and semantic overlap, retrieval ceilings, encoder capacity and embedding dimension, iterative negative mining, latency and token use, and two qualitative localization cases. The original filtering and data-size studies remain, merged into Figure 5; the topic analysis moves from Appendix B to I.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new latency and token averages are point estimates and do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Retained numerical entries in Tables 1–5 are identical, with Agentless entries removed from Table 1. Substantial new results include repair Pass@1 of 24.5% for SweRank versus 22.6% for LocAgent (Table 6), multilingual retriever Acc@10 of 50.85% versus Gemini's 47.44% (Table 11), and matched GPT-4o latency of 30.2 versus 85.3 seconds (Table 12).

M1.justification: The main architecture and both training losses are unchanged. Appendix E adds an evaluated iterative mining variant: second-round negatives are selected using the first-round trained small encoder, extending v1's described mining with pretrained CodeRankEmbed. This is a limited procedural addition, without evidence that the retained main results changed.

P1.justification: Several introductory, related-work, analysis, and concluding passages are condensed or polished, and dataset and metric descriptions are combined. New result subsections and appendices are integrated, the old topic appendix is relocated, and acknowledgements are removed. The main section sequence and much existing wording remain intact.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to a single-column conference layout, substantially relocating and resizing displays. Original Figures 5 and 6 become Figure 5(a–b), Figure 3 gains a cumulative-distribution curve, and new Tables 6–13 and Figures 6–10 present added studies. The original topic plot is retained as Figure 11.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for Llama, Gemini-Embedding, Qwen3-Embedding, Matryoshka learning, SWE-Fixer, and SWE-smith. It removes the Böhme localization study, Wang's weakly supervised embeddings reference, and the Agentless reference. The related-work taxonomy and positioning of ranking against agentic localization remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The contrastive loss, positive-identifier reranker objective, and associated mathematical definitions are retained. V2 numbers the existing equations but adds no theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation; the new capacity and overlap studies are empirical.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked downstream repair, explicit non-Python transfer, and measured latency validation. V2 addresses these important gaps through repair comparisons with an oracle control, multilingual evaluation, and a matched-model latency experiment (Tables 6, 11, and 12). The added failure analyses also clarify practical boundaries. These gains outweigh the lost pricing and provenance details, although some new mechanism explanations remain inferential.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SweRank and SWELOC. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched reliably across the substantial additions and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds downstream repair, multilingual evaluation, capacity and mining studies, latency measurements, and error analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original retriever and reranker experiments on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, training-data ablations, and SWELOC topic analysis.

results.title: SWERank: Software Issue Localization with Code Ranking

C1.justification: The methodological contributions remain, but the flagship manipulation claim is materially narrowed. The abstract and introduction change SimplerEnv success from 54.1% to 40.6%, and the introduction attributes the 30% real-world advantage specifically to comparison with RoboPoint rather than mainstream VLAs. Section 6.2 also withdraws the blanket claim of outperforming fine-tuned VLAs.

C2.justification: Beyond v1’s brief limitations concerning 2D representations and data quality, Appendix J discusses explicit-instruction requirements, long-horizon decomposition, and execution bottlenecks in complex or dynamic environments. Section 6.2 qualifies controller readiness for the challenging tasks and adds explanations of MOKA failures and latency. Appendix I develops the object-centric versus agent-centric interpretation of generalization.

D1.justification: v3 supplies extensive previously unavailable documentation: data filtering and generation prompts, training-mixture counts, batch size 128, learning rate 2×10^-5, training epochs, eight A100 GPUs, training times, execution optimization, and baseline implementation details. It also provides code and dataset access information and states that datasets and checkpoints are publicly available.

E1.justification: Section 6.2 adds qualitative evaluation on whiteboard wiping and drawer opening, extending coverage to continuous-contact and articulated-object tasks. The original benchmarks and eight-task real-world evaluation remain. Appendix B details the previously summarized training mixture rather than establishing new training coverage.

E2.justification: Table 4 removes RT-1-X, RoboVLM, and SpatialVLA comparisons and adds π0, π0-fast, OpenVLA-OFT, MOKA, and RoboPoint. Table 3 adds RoboBrain to both VABench tasks and GPT-4o to VisualTrace. Figure 7 also adds MOKA to the real-world comparison, substantially revising the comparator set.

E3.justification: Section 5 changes the reported judge-score range from 0–10 to 1–10. Table 4 removes separate grasp-rate reporting while retaining 24 episodes per task, and Table 5 introduces execution-time evaluation on two retained tasks. Figure 4 corrects its 940k QA label to 300k, matching the existing body text; this does not establish actual dataset resizing.

E4.justification: The SrCoT and alignment ablations remain. v3 adds limited qualitative examinations of contact-rich and articulated manipulation, an execution-latency comparison, and the RoboBrain trajectory case studies now available in Appendix I. These extend supplementary analysis without introducing a broad sensitivity or robustness study.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports training seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Numerical comparisons and success-rate plots remain point estimates without uncertainty bars.

E6.justification: Table 4 changes FSD’s average from 54.1% to 40.6%, correctly averaging unchanged task scores of 41.6%, 50.0%, 33.3%, and 37.5%. Table 3 revises judge scores, including FSD’s 5.49 to 6.21, while retaining its RMSE and MAE; the revised scoring specification prevents interpreting this as a same-setting gain. Baseline results, latency measurements, and qualitative findings are added, while grasp-rate entries disappear. Tables 1–2 remain numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: Sections 3–4 retain the architecture, SrCoT reasoning, self-consistency mechanism, two-stage training, eight-point traces, and action-execution pipeline. The added coordinate-format and appendix implementation descriptions elaborate existing components without establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: Although the main section sequence remains, v3 substantially expands the exposition through structured appendices containing explanations, worked examples, and prompts. It also rewrites the decision-evaluation discussion, expands the SrCoT explanation, and adds acknowledgements, ethics, and reproducibility statements.

P2.justification: v3 changes typography and page layout, redistributes retained figures and tables, expands Table 3, redesigns Table 4 by method category, and updates Figure 7 with MOKA. It adds latency and training-data tables plus rollout, case-study, and appendix figures. Some benchmark examples are redisplayed rather than representing new experiments.

R1.justification: The three related-work themes and reasoning-based positioning largely remain. Selected references are added for MOKA, FAST, OpenVLA-OFT, InternVLA-M1, and technical resources, while RoboVLM and SpatialVLA references disappear. Appendix I adds a focused positioning comparison with RoboBrain.

T1.justification: The newly supplied Appendix C explicitly formulates intermediate-depth optimization by minimizing consecutive 3D path distances with endpoint depths fixed. This adds a mathematical specification beyond v1’s high-level optimization description. The visual-aid definitions and MAE/RMSE equations remain, and neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially reduces v1’s reproducibility gap by supplying the missing technical appendices, configurations, and prompts. It also corrects FSD’s inflated SimplerEnv average and narrows the associated superiority claim, while strengthening comparative evidence. These are substantial gains despite a new Table 4 inconsistency: π0-fast is assigned a 48.3% average although its listed task scores average 32.1%, leaving part of the ranking unreliable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe the same FSD work, and their main text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. However, v1 ends after the references without the appendices A–J that it cites; v3 includes them. This limits direct comparison of earlier supplementary details.

after.justification: v3 retains original FSD experiments and additionally reports execution times, further baseline comparisons, and qualitative whiteboard-wiping and drawer-opening experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original FSD benchmark results, component ablations, SimplerEnv experiments, and eight real-world manipulation tasks.

results.title: From Seeing to Doing: Bridging Reasoning and Decision for Robotic Manipulation

C1.justification: The abstract's framework, eight-method contribution, and optimality claims remain. Section 1.2 narrows coverage from 'virtually all' to 'a wide range' of distributed SGD methods and explicitly adds tighter time-complexity guarantees relative to canonical Local SGD/FedAvg as a contribution.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's homogeneous-data scope discussion, v3 identifies possible similarity assumptions needed for non-i.i.d. extensions and names preconditioning and non-Euclidean geometry as future extensions. Appendix I also makes the communication-family qualification of Dual-Process SGD's optimality more explicit.

D1.justification: The new experiments disclose selected learning rates and algorithm parameters in Figures 13–14, including Cycle SGD's group size. Existing hardware descriptions, Simpy setup, and Tables 2–6 remain unchanged. Neither version documents a code-release or access change.

E1.justification: The datasets and learning tasks remain MNIST, CIFAR10, and Wikitext-2. C.5 adds a distinct MNIST computing scenario where communication takes 1.5 times the number of synchronized workers in seconds, extending the earlier fixed and worker-dependent communication environments.

E2.justification: The existing experimental comparison methods are retained. New Figure 13 evaluates the already-proposed Cycle SGD against the existing set: Local SGD, Async-Local SGD, Rennala SGD, Ringmaster ASGD, and Synchronized SGD. Canonical FedAvg is added as an analytical comparison in Appendix H, without empirical results.

E3.justification: Existing settings and parameter grids in Tables 2–6 are unchanged. New C.5 uses 64 workers, computation time 10, synchronization-dependent communication, and Cycle groups of eight. C.6 uses 100 workers with computation/communication times 10/100 and B values 128, 256, 512, and 1024; its plotted learning rates are not all identical.

E4.justification: v3 adds two focused analyses absent from v1: C.5 tests whether Cycle SGD's reduced simultaneous synchronization benefits convergence under bandwidth pressure, and C.6 tests sensitivity to Rennala SGD's batch-size/tree-distance parameter. The earlier analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report selected grid-search convergence curves without repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. The additional experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark curves in Figures 6–12 are retained. New Figure 13 shows faster loss reduction for Cycle SGD in the added communication scenario. Figure 14 reports poorer convergence for B=512/1024 than B=128/256 under the displayed settings. These are additional findings, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The Birch SGD construction and proposed algorithms in Appendix E retain their procedures. Ringmaster's delay threshold is renamed from B to G without changing its update rule. Algorithm 20 newly documents canonical FedAvg for theoretical comparison; it is not a new proposed component.

P1.justification: v3 adds a Local SGD worked example and proof roadmap, splits Appendix D into explanation and proof, and places Insights and Guidelines before the experimental summary. Affiliations and acknowledgements also change. Most existing exposition and the overall organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 4 expands from one computation tree into a three-stage construction illustration. v3 adds Figures 13–14 and Algorithm 20, boxes the main theorem, and adopts conference headers and styling. Existing benchmark plots and table structures are largely retained, with placement and numbering changes.

R1.justification: New A.3 substantially expands positioning against other unifying SGD frameworks, including Cooperative SGD and the graph approaches of Even et al. and Huang et al., explaining differences in graph semantics and complexity measures. Appendix H adds a direct canonical FedAvg comparison using McMahan et al., Koloskova et al., and Luo et al.

T1.justification: Theorem 2.4's independence condition now includes the current iterates. Appendix D replaces a variance-decomposition step with Young's inequality, propagates factors of two, and corrects summation indices. New Appendix H derives a time-complexity comparison with canonical Local SGD/FedAvg, including an epsilon^-3/2 term in the comparison bound. These substantively revise the central proof and extend the theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is stronger theoretical reliability: v3 corrects the independence requirement and replaces v1's problematic variance-decomposition step with Young's inequality and consistent constants in the central proof supporting the framework. Appendix H and A.3 also address important gaps in comparison with canonical Local SGD and competing frameworks, while C.5–C.6 supply targeted empirical support. These gains substantially strengthen the paper despite remaining notation slips and the continued absence of empirical uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Birch SGD framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds MNIST experiments investigating Cycle SGD under synchronization-dependent communication costs and Rennala SGD batch-size sensitivity (C.5–C.6).

before.justification: v1 reports original optimization experiments using simulated distributed environments: MNIST logistic regression, CIFAR10 with ResNet18, and Wikitext-2 with GPT2 (Appendix C).

results.title: Birch SGD: A Tree Graph Framework for Local and Asynchronous SGD Methods

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adapting datamodels to offline robotic data selection through a differentiable surrogate, scaling to larger policies and heterogeneous datasets, and improving task success. The additional evidence supports these existing claims without redefining their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting reduced selection advantages at larger budgets to inclusion of more useful data, finer clusters to more precise selection, and excessive All-Data training to overfitting. It also interprets LIBERO retrieval through scene and object similarity. The computational, hyperparameter and target-scale limitations already existed in v1 and are consolidated into the conclusion.

D1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and Appendices G–H substantially expand reproducibility information: estimator pseudocode, gradient averaging, 10,000 regression fits, sampling probability, MLP dimensions, metagradient iteration counts, training steps, the final 100-step differentiation window, optimizers and schedules. Hardware and runtime estimates are newly documented across the experimental settings.

E1.justification: MetaWorld, LIBERO and the OXE subsets, robot embodiments and target tasks are retained. LIBERO-5 comprises five already evaluated LIBERO-10 tasks, and the extended proxy tests use tasks already covered by MetaWorld. These additions change analyses and experimental subsets rather than task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain the same retrieval methods and Target-Only, All-Data or Random controls. New ablations reuse existing comparators. CUPID and COLLAGE enter the related-work discussion but are not evaluated as baselines; longer All-Data training changes its budget rather than its identity.

E3.justification: Appendix C introduces controlled evaluations varying selection percentages from 5% to 30%, clustering at 15 steps, 30 steps or whole trajectories, co-training ratios of 0.3/0.5/0.7, and All-Data training budgets of 1×/2×/4×. Main benchmark protocols are retained. Regression sampling is also reported as p=0.1 in v2 Appendix H, versus Bernoulli(1/2) in v1 Appendix B.2; this documentation change does not establish reruns.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands tests of the method's design choices: proxy-versus-rollout selection extends from one to four MetaWorld tasks, Figure 13 tests selection budget, clustering and co-training sensitivity, and Appendix C.6 checks whether longer training helps All-Data. Appendix A.2 adds LIBERO selection case studies. The no-goal MetaWorld analysis already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report three MetaWorld seeds, five LIBERO seeds and one real-world seed. Figure 13 continues five-seed averaging. There is no new significance-testing or confidence-interval procedure; correction of an individual uncertainty value changes a result, not the reporting practice.

E6.justification: The LIBERO/OXE benchmark means in v1 Table 3 are retained in v2 Table 1, but v2 adds substantial sensitivity, proxy-comparison and qualitative results. Appendix C.6 reports All-Data success of 43.36, 44.13 and 38.40 at 1×, 2× and 4× training. The malformed STRAP Soup-Sauce uncertainty entry is also corrected to 15.7.

M1.justification: Both versions use clustered regression or metagradient datamodels, the behavior-cloning proxy, target-data splitting for OXE, ranked selection and downstream policy training. v2 provides operational details and pseudocode for the existing estimators; it does not establish a replacement algorithm, architecture or objective.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the metagradient explanation, tighten introductory and experimental prose, and improve appendix cross-references. The separate limitations section is merged into the conclusion, and existing appendix results are regrouped before implementation details. The overall narrative and most existing exposition remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with LIBERO selection plots, the extended proxy comparison, a three-panel ablation figure, two algorithm displays and a hyperparameter table. The real-world sample montage moves from v1 Figure 7 in the main text to v2 Figure 10 in the appendix. Existing benchmark tables and plots are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds COLLAGE, CUPID, DataRater and work on scale transfer and robot dataset factors, while pruning several broad background references. It replaces v1's statement that robotic data attribution was unknown with a comparison to concurrent CUPID, emphasizing offline selection from heterogeneous datasets. The broader datamodel-versus-heuristic positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix B.3 adds explicit definitions of training-count perturbations and stochastic metagradient updates in Equations 11–12. Appendix B.2 generalizes inclusion probability from 1/2 to p. The underlying datamodel objective and first-order influence approximation were already present; moving the Taylor expansion into the main text is not new theory, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 left important estimator settings undocumented and several design choices weakly tested. v2's algorithms, hyperparameters and compute costs substantially improve reproducibility and feasibility assessment, while Appendix C tests surrogate validity, sensitivity and baseline training budgets. These address important evidential gaps without changing the main benchmark results. Some interpretation remains overstated: Figure 11 shows roughly a 20-point proxy deficit on dial-turn despite describing all deficits as small. This limits that conclusion but does not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DataMIL work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds proxy comparisons, hyperparameter ablations, extended-training results and LIBERO selection analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original MetaWorld, LIBERO and real-robot OXE experiments, including benchmark comparisons, proxy-objective tests and qualitative analyses.

results.title: DataMIL: Selecting Data for Robot Imitation Learning with Datamodels

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the contribution from human animation to arbitrary-character animation explicitly including animals and objects, and add scalability across CogVideoX and Wan backbones. The benchmark claim expands from TikTok to TikTok and Fashion, while v1's specific 6.98 FID-VID and 65% advantage claim disappears. The central direct-4D-tokenization novelty claim remains.

C2.justification: v5 adds substantive explanations for neutral-shape and differential coordinates, their advantages over SMPL parameters, and the roles of motion representation and backbone capacity in generalization. v1's specific extreme-proportions/non-human-anatomy limitation becomes a general dependence on base-model capability in v5 Appendix D. Hand-control limitations and the inability to animate multiple people with independent poses remain.

D1.justification: v5 documents numerical precision, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, warm-up, augmentations, a 55-degree pose-estimation camera setting, and the 18B model's frozen/trainable components. Appendix J adds metric implementation details. Access information changes from an anonymous code link to a named project and commercial service. Conversely, v1's explicit TikTok sequence IDs, 512×512 evaluation crop, and approximately 90-second inference time are omitted.

E1.justification: v5 adds Fashion as an evaluated benchmark, whereas v1 only cites it. It also evaluates motion transfer to non-humanoid subjects such as birds, a chair, and a fire hydrant (Figures 1, 14, and 16), extending v1's predominantly real and stylized humanoid examples. Gymnastics reconstruction and earlier human galleries are retained.

E2.justification: The TikTok comparison in Table 1 substantially changes membership. Animate-X, RealisDance-DiT, and UniAnimate-DiT are added, while MRAA, DreamPose, MagicAnimate, Champ, and Human-DiT disappear from that table. MimicMotion and ControlNeXt remain. Several older comparators remain in qualitative figures, so they have not been removed from the entire paper.

E3.justification: The reported training corpus increases from 5K to 30K pairs. DiT training changes from 20K to 30K iterations, the learning rate from 1e-5 to 2e-5, fixed 49-frame clips to variable 33–129-frame sampling, and motion-condition dropout from 0.25 to 0.2. v5 evaluates 6B/18B configurations and specifies text conditioning. Evaluation is now described by reference to RealisDance-DiT without restating v1's explicit TikTok split and crop.

E4.justification: v5 adds differential-motion, 3D-quantization, and 2D-spatial-RoPE ablations, extends component testing to Fashion, and reports unsuccessful linear/MLP adapters and pretrained SMPL-parameter tokenization for the 18B model (Appendix H). Codebook, gymnastics, attention-map, and CFG analyses already existed in v1. The earlier visual component-ablation grid and extreme-proportions failure panel are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for benchmark results. The codebook-frequency analysis is retained. Pose-estimation uncertainty filtering concerns dataset curation and does not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting for the experimental findings.

E6.justification: TikTok and ablation values are substantially replaced: v1 reports FVD/FID-VID of 140.60/6.98, while v5 reports 317.21/8.56 for 6B and 276.65/7.31 for 18B. These use revised models and settings and do not establish a same-setting gain or loss. v5 adds Fashion results, non-humanoid animation outcomes, and negative findings from 18B design experiments.

M1.justification: v5 changes the motion representation from normalized joints using estimated body shapes to neutral-shape, first-frame-relative coordinates with root translation. Motion attention changes from every CogVideoX block to every second block, and vision queries receive 4D positional encoding. The new Wan-based 18B variant adds text/image conditioning, zero-padded motion embeddings, and masked reference latents (Sections 3.1–3.3; Appendices A and C).

P1.justification: v5 substantially rewrites method explanations and reorganizes the narrative around arbitrary characters and model scaling. It removes the latent-diffusion primer, subdivides implementation and tokenizer/RoPE discussions, separates qualitative comparisons from visualization appendices, and moves CFG analysis out of the main text. The title, terminology, authorship, and conference presentation also change.

P2.justification: The teaser is expanded, the 6B architecture diagram is revised, and an 18B schematic is added. TikTok tables are restructured and Fashion comparison/ablation tables are introduced. Qualitative comparisons are replaced or rearranged, new galleries are added, and the CFG plot moves to the appendix. The component-ablation grid and one failure panel disappear; captions, page layout, and appendix navigation are extensively revised.
