R1.justification: Related work is updated with AnimateDiff, UniAnimate-DiT, HyperMotion, RealisDance-DiT, Wan, and Wan-Animate, among others. v5 also makes the distinction between joint-coordinate and SMPL-parameter tokenization more explicit. The central research positioning against rendered 2D pose guidance remains intact, making this an update rather than a wholesale repositioning.

T1.justification: Local mathematical definitions change: motion M becomes first-frame-relative, vision-query positional encoding changes from 3D to 4D, and Appendix C defines the new zero-padded reference and masked input latents. The VQ loss and motion-RoPE algorithm remain essentially unchanged. No new theorems or proofs appear; Appendix J mainly explains existing evaluation metrics.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens validation through Fashion evaluation, newer DiT comparisons, and ablations isolating depth and differential-motion contributions. The second-backbone implementation and expanded technical documentation also make applicability more assessable. These gains address v1's narrower empirical support. Tradeoffs remain: explicit local evaluation details are lost, uncertainty is still unreported, and the Fashion claim of superiority across all metrics conflicts with Table 3's LPIPS ranking (RealisDance-DiT 0.053 versus MTVCraft-18B 0.057). These weaknesses temper but do not outweigh the stronger empirical and technical support.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same 4DMoT/MV-DiT research, renamed from MTVCrafter to MTVCraft. Both provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Changes in experimental settings limit direct performance comparisons but do not prevent reliable assessment of the revisions.

after.justification: v5 reports original 6B/18B results on TikTok and Fashion, component ablations in Tables 2 and 4, and additional qualitative and model-scaling experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original TikTok results and ablations in Tables 1–2, qualitative animation experiments, and appendix analyses of codebook usage and gymnastics reconstruction.

results.title: MTVCraft: Tokenizing 4D Motion for Arbitrary Character Animation

C1.justification: The stated empirical scope expands from Llama3 to Llama3 and Qwen3, and the introduction adds a geometry-of-LLM-quantization novelty claim. The earlier assertion that Qronos 'subsumes' existing approaches is removed. The core correction/diffusion, efficiency, and controlled-rounding contributions remain.

C2.justification: v3 interprets larger gains when multiple quantization-error sources interact and attributes declining relative calibration overhead on larger Qwen3 models to algorithmic cost. Appendix D adds an argument that grid tuning cannot close the OPTQ gap. These extend the existing activation-mismatch explanation rather than replace it.

D1.justification: v1 only promises a code release; v3 reports Brevitas integration and provides a repository link with reproduction instructions. Appendix C newly documents beginning-of-sequence token handling, transformation order, SmoothQuant gamma = 0.3, MagR theta = 0.01, SmoothRot strength = 0.6, and further SpinQuant details. Previously unspecified settings are disclosures, not established changes to earlier experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions use WikiText2 and C4 for calibration and evaluate WikiText2, ARC easy/challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and Winogrande. The Gaussian microbenchmark is retained. Additional model families, checkpoints, and precision configurations change experimental settings, without introducing new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: GPTAQ joins RTN, OPTQ, and GPFQ across the retained Llama3 weight-only and weight-activation comparisons in v3 Tables 1, 3, and 4. Adding this asymmetric-calibration competitor substantially strengthens the comparison set for Qronos's central contribution.

E3.justification: The main low-bit Llama3 experiments switch from an unscaled min-max grid to beta = 0.8, while beta = 1 remains in Appendix C.1. v3 adds Qwen3 and instruction-tuned checkpoints, models up to 32B, W3A3, SmoothRot configurations, and Qwen-specific grid selection. New calibration-runtime measurements use an AMD MI325X; the original microbenchmark settings remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds SmoothQuant and MagR parameter sweeps in Tables 9–10, a grid-scaling comparison in Appendix C.1, and token-averaged block-output error analysis in Appendix D/Figure 3. These provide substantial new evidence about parameter sensitivity and error accumulation beyond the retained runtime analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions average Figure 2's runtime measurements over three seeds. Neither supplies uncertainty intervals or significance tests for the model-quality tables, and v3 adds no explicit repeated-run counts or seed values for those results.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial GPTAQ, Qwen3, instruction-tuned, W3A3, sensitivity, and calibration-runtime results. Retained entries also change: matching v1 Table 1 to v3 Table 11, Qronos's 2-bit 1B perplexity remains 24.6, but zero-shot accuracy changes from 37.8 to 38.4. v3's main Table 1 uses a different grid, so its lower perplexities are not unchanged-setting improvements. Figure 2 is retained.

M1.justification: The objectives, alternating error-correction/diffusion updates, and efficient Cholesky formulation are retained. v3's pseudocode explicitly incorporates the memory-efficient initialization already derived in v1; this does not introduce a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraphs, and runtime discussion are revised. Qronos pseudocode moves to Appendix A, the existing OPTQ corollary moves into Section 3.2, and the ethics statement disappears. Much of the background, algorithm derivation, and proof wording is retained.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the displays with model, runtime, and ablation tables plus the new block-error Figure 3. Existing comparison tables gain GPTAQ rows and a SmoothRot block, and the W3/W4 column order reverses. Existing figures and pseudocode are relocated within the conference layout.

R1.justification: v3 adds positioning around GPTAQ, SmoothRot, gradient-based rounding work by Cheng et al., and concurrent quantization-geometry work by Birnick and Chen et al. QTIP and QLoRA discussion disappears. The organizing distinction between transformations and rounding methods remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds an explicit error decomposition and triangle-inequality bound separating activation mismatch from weight-rounding error. The central equivalence theorem, Cholesky lemmas, and proofs remain substantively unchanged. v1's Corollary D.1 becomes v3's Corollary 3.4, with its existing proof retained in Appendix H.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility through the missing GPTAQ comparison, broader model/precision evaluations, parameter and grid ablations, block-error diagnostics, and detailed reproduction information with a code link. These address important evidential and documentation gaps in v1. The new assertion that grid tuning cannot close the OPTQ gap is not established by Appendix D's error decomposition, but this overstatement does not outweigh the substantial empirical and reproducibility gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Qronos research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: v3 reports original quantization and runtime experiments, including additional model evaluations, parameter sweeps, and block-level error measurements in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Llama3 quantization experiments in Tables 1–3 and runtime measurements in Figure 2.

results.title: Qronos: Correcting the Past by Shaping the Future... in Post-Training Quantization

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution statements and conclusion retain the same central claims: unified adaptive reasoning and acting, synthetic vision-language co-training, and four demonstrated robot capabilities. The added methods and evidence do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: V2 reframes the annotation limitation around hand-selected reasoning-step heuristics and adds a potential action-inference bottleneck when scaling model size. It also interprets the new planning controls as showing limited generalization without VL co-training. Existing mechanism explanations and appendix failure cases remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies substantial annotation instructions: 32-frame sampling, midpoint selection, content assembly, recovery/dialogue handling and complete prompt templates with output schemas and visibility/gripper constraints. It also discloses baseline invocation scheduling, placement randomization and recovery-data subsets. The existing training hardware, budgets and deployment details are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds testing on 20 novel human-robot interaction scenarios in Hotpot and Cocktail and describes interaction content in synthetic planning data. The three long-horizon tasks, four generalizable-planning tasks, grounding environments and robot platforms already appear in v1, including its appendices.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 6 adds π0 and robot-only OneTwoVLA comparisons on the existing generalizable-planning tasks; Figure 2 includes Dual-System in task-time comparisons. The original long-horizon and grounding comparator sets remain unchanged. Changing the dual-system baseline's cited inspiration from ViLa to Hi Robot does not establish a different Gemini-plus-π0 implementation.

E3.justification: V2 adds quantitative evaluation designs for generalizable planning, recovery conditional on errors, subtask-level interaction, novel interaction scenarios and annotation quality, including a 50-instance synthetic-data audit. Existing training budgets and grounding protocols are retained. Newly specifying the placement range and recovery-demonstration subsets does not establish that those settings changed.

E4.justification: V2 adds a with/without-VL comparison for generalizable planning, examines interaction generalization, evaluates automatic robot-annotation quality and audits synthetic-image/text errors. These substantially extend the analysis of co-training and data quality beyond v1's examples. Existing multimodality, reasoning-action consistency and failure-case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional episode counts and audit frequencies in v2 provide sample sizes and results without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original long-horizon and grounding scores are retained. V2 newly reports generalizable-planning averages of 70% for OneTwoVLA-VL, 10% for OneTwoVLA and 6% for π0; quantitative recovery and interaction comparisons; 72.5% novel-interaction success; task timings; and annotation-quality findings, including 40 fully correct synthetic samples out of 50. These are added results, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under matched settings.

M1.justification: V1 describes manually annotated robot reasoning. V2 introduces a two-stage Gemini annotation pipeline using sampled demonstration frames, interval identification and reasoning-content assembly, with recovery and dialogue extensions in Appendix D. This adds a substantial data-curation component. The controller architecture, losses and adaptive inference algorithm remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main narrative sequence are retained, with localized method and experiment expansions. Co-training related work moves to Appendix B, conclusion and limitations are combined, and an LLM-usage statement is added. Author affiliations, acknowledgments, headings and citation style are also revised.

P2.justification: V1's long-horizon results table becomes a bar chart paired with new generalization results. V2 adds a timing chart, recovery and interaction tables, a quality-audit table and two annotation-prompt figures. It also adopts the ICLR layout and redistributes several appendix tables, environment illustrations and prompts across pages.

R1.justification: V2 adds ECoT-Lite and discusses its reasoning-efficiency and interaction tradeoffs, changes the baseline's cited inspiration to Hi Robot, and removes several background references concerning recovery, interaction and reinforcement learning. The broad positioning against separated reasoning/action systems remains unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.2 and Appendix D add formal specifications of ordered plans, reasoning intervals, history/next-step construction and dialogue-conditioned plan updates for automated annotation. The original policy formulation and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens capabilities supported mainly by examples in v1 through quantitative generalizable-planning, recovery and interaction comparisons. Annotation procedures and quality audits also address important documentation and evidence gaps while retaining the original benchmark results. Small recovery samples, absent uncertainty estimates and incomplete details behind the novel-interaction percentage limit the new evidence, but the overall improvement in empirical support and reproducibility is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OneTwoVLA. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations and prompts, support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and reports additional quantitative planning, recovery, interaction, timing and annotation-quality results.

before.justification: V1 reports original robot experiments, including long-horizon success rates, visual-grounding results, inference timings and appendix experiments on action multimodality.

results.title: OneTwoVLA: A Unified Vision-Language-Action Model with Adaptive Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about Markovian conditioning, O(Nk) attention, cache elimination, generation quality, and memory savings. Added appendix experiments provide broader support without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix D interprets the new results as evidence of generalization, scalability, and limited sensitivity to neighborhood size and larger training ratios. It also qualifies the new comparisons as constrained by available compute. The original mechanism explanations and limitations paragraph remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands workflow documentation: CUDA handling, mixed-training iteration cycles, attention-visualization sampling and averaging, and splits, budgets, and scale sequences for new experiments. It corrects the first-eight-scale token count from 256 to 255. Access instructions change from a direct code/model repository pointer to a project page and promised release; actual resource availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ImageNet at 256x256. v2 retains this coverage and adds ImageNet at 512x512, CelebA at 256x256 and 512x512, and FFHQ at 256x256 (Appendix D), substantially extending domain and resolution coverage.

E2.justification: The comparator membership in Tables 1–4 is retained. Added dataset and scalability experiments continue comparing MVAR with VAR; additional model depths and concatenated-versus-mixed training are configuration controls rather than new baseline methods.

E3.justification: Appendix D introduces 100-epoch ImageNet-512 training with a different scale sequence and grouping, 2B-model experiments, new dataset splits and batch sizes, and a d12 training-ratio study using 50 epochs and batch size 64. These are added protocols. The exact ImageNet-512 configuration remains somewhat ambiguous: D.1 references d20 settings while Table 6 labels the models d16.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining v1's component, conditioning-prefix, and neighborhood ablations, v2 tests neighborhood sensitivity across face datasets and resolutions (Table 9). Figure 9 adds concatenated-versus-mixed training comparisons and training-ratio sensitivity curves, directly examining the robustness of the memory-saving training strategy.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added curves compare training configurations over epochs, not uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: Tables 6–9, Figure 9, and additional qualitative comparisons substantially expand the results. Newly reported MVAR/VAR FIDs include 7.55/8.03 on ImageNet-512 and 1.33/2.65 for 2B models on CelebA; these are new settings, not improvements over matched v1 runs. Existing generation scores are retained, while Table 2 changes VAR-d16's KV-cache value from 5,440 to 5,704 MB.

M1.justification: The adjacent-scale factorization, spatial neighborhood attention, cross-entropy objective, and cache-free inference remain unchanged. Expanded explanations of mixed training and CUDA kernels document implementation; the additional training schedules are experimental variants rather than a replacement of the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. v2 converts contributions to bullets, introduces related-work subsections, incorporates the causal-mask discussion into the methodology, reorganizes appendices, and adds an appendix contents list and disclosure statements. These are limited narrative changes alongside the added scientific material.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 6–9, training-ratio plots, a higher-resolution comparison, and several comparative image galleries. It also changes the document template and table layouts and moves the causal-mask diagram into the main text. The original appendix figures are retained as Figures 10 and 15, rather than replaced.

R1.justification: v2 adds Liu et al. (2015) for CelebA and Karras et al. (2019) for FFHQ, and removes Salimans et al. (2016), Improved Techniques for Training GANs. Positioning relative to VAR and other generative approaches remains unchanged; most bibliography changes are formatting.

T1.justification: Equations 1–12, the Markov assumptions, and the computational-complexity derivations are retained. The complexity appendix moves from Appendix B to Appendix A without substantive mathematical changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's ImageNet-256 experiments. Appendix D tests higher resolution, additional data distributions, a 2B model, and sensitivity of the training strategy and neighborhood choice, addressing important gaps in evidence for scalability and robustness. Additional implementation documentation improves reproducibility. Some new configuration reporting remains ambiguous, particularly in D.1, but the broader controlled evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MVAR research, with matching authors, core methodology, and original experiments. The complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds experiments on higher-resolution ImageNet, CelebA, FFHQ, larger models, and training sensitivity.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation results, memory and timing measurements, component ablations, attention analyses, and generated examples.

results.title: MVAR: Visual Autoregressive Modeling with Scale and Spatial Markovian Conditioning

C1.justification: v1 explicitly presents RSD as extending Denoising Score Distillation beyond denoising. v2 presents a unified framework encompassing denoising and adds contribution-level claims about unknown-noise robustness, data-scale robustness, and conditional inverse solving. The central claim that one-step distillation improves upon corrupted-data teachers remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds a mode-covering versus mode-seeking explanation and distinguishes concentration from mode collapse. It identifies noise underestimation as harmful and qualifies loss rankings because hyperparameters were not tuned. The former conditional-sampling limitation becomes a demonstrated latent-optimization application, while more principled conditioning remains future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds denoising-specific budgets, normalization, dropout, Teacher-Consistency settings, optimizer settings, and an RSD repository URL. Reported hardware changes from A100 to A6000 configurations. Conversely, v1's explicit Gaussian blur kernel specifications and ESPIRiT sensitivity-map calibration details are omitted.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's CelebA-HQ restoration and FastMRI experiments, v2 adds CIFAR-10, FFHQ, AFHQ-v2, and a synthetic spiral dataset. Coverage expands to explicit denoising, conditional denoising and super-resolution, and heterogeneous or misspecified noise scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds comparisons involving SURE-Score, TweedieDiff, SFBD, Teacher-Consistency, clean-data diffusion models, and Rectified Flow. Conditional experiments introduce Noise2Self, DPS-based solvers, and a pseudoinverse baseline; SDS and DMD are now evaluated in a loss ablation. The renamed teacher rows in retained restoration experiments preserve v1's comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include 10%, 50%, and 100% training-data controls and dataset-specific denoising budgets. Evaluation expands beyond FID to IS, precision, recall, KID, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Conditional evaluations use 250 CIFAR-10 or 100 CelebA-HQ images with specified 1000-step optimization procedures.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's efficiency and Proximal FID analyses, v2 adds data-size, distillation-loss, noise-misspecification, and heterogeneous-noise ablations. Spiral visualizations and precision/recall analyses examine the proposed mechanism and mode coverage. Proximal FID validation also expands to denoising datasets.

E5.justification: v2 adds 95% confidence intervals from 100 noise-estimation trials in Table 14 and ± values for DMD and SiD in Table 18. These are selective additions: Table 18 does not define the uncertainty statistic or run count. v1's explicit generation-seed range is omitted.

E6.justification: The shared CelebA-HQ restoration scores remain unchanged, and MRI scores are only rounded. Substantial new results include CIFAR-10 denoising FID 4.77 at sigma 0.2 (v2 Table 2), conditional super-resolution PSNR 27.803 (Table 16), and numerous ablation results. New timing measurements use different settings and do not establish same-setting speed improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core corruption-aware pretraining and SiD distillation procedure remains intact. Limited extensions add calibration-based estimation of unknown noise, sample-dependent noise during distillation, and latent optimization for conditional reconstruction (v2 Section 4.7 and Appendices D.2–D.4).

P1.justification: v2 changes the title and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative, adopting consolidated teacher terminology. Theory moves into Appendix F, the RSD algorithm moves into the main text, and the appendices are reorganized with a contents list. Citation style and conference formatting also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show the corruption pipeline, Table 1 gains objectives and notation, and retained comparison tables are consolidated or rearranged. Numerous denoising, conditional, and ablation tables, toy plots, and image grids are added. The original restoration grids and MRI imagery are retained.

R1.justification: The DSD citation and dedicated comparison appendix disappear, removing v1's explicit predecessor relationship and changing novelty positioning. Citations and discussion expand substantially around SFBD, SURE-Score, Noise2Self, blind denoising, low-dimensional score theory, and scientific inverse problems.

T1.justification: v1's rank-one linear-corruption theorem and proof are retained as v2 Theorem 2. Appendix F adds a rank-r denoising/Wasserstein result, a strict-saddle analysis, variable-noise theory, and assumption-dependent Fisher-divergence bounds incorporating score-estimation and optimization errors, with accompanying proofs.

improvement.justification: The new noise-failure, data-size, loss-choice, and mode-coverage analyses address important untested aspects of v1, while conditional reconstruction is demonstrated instead of remaining future work. Expanded theory also goes beyond the original rank-one analysis. Removing explicit DSD positioning and some implementation details weakens transparency, but the added diagnostic evidence and demonstrated applicability provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe RSD and contain matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original RSD results and adds denoising benchmarks, controlled ablations, synthetic experiments, and conditional reconstruction results.

before.justification: v1 reports original RSD generation results on CelebA-HQ and FastMRI, alongside model-selection and efficiency analyses.

results.title: Score Distillation Beyond Acceleration: Generative Modeling from Corrupted Data

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: two pathological reasoning patterns, BARREL's boundary-aware SFT/GRPO framework, and the importance of intermediate refusal rewards. The headline reliability and accuracy claims are retained; the added experiments primarily provide supporting evidence.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of post-hoc miscalibration, GRPO-only failures, and overthinking as relative length imbalance rather than absolute verbosity. Appendices P and Q qualify domain generalization and discuss imperfect knowledge labels, sampling-sensitive abstention, reasoning-monitoring limits, and fixed rejection rewards restricting risk-tolerance flexibility. These substantially expand v1's limitations concerning model scale and verifiable questions.

D1.justification: V2 specifies numerical rewards, inference temperature and token limit, and confidence-filtering thresholds while retaining most training, hardware, and prompt details. It omits v1's public BARREL repository link and instead states that code and training data were submitted as supplementary material. Availability of those supplements cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: V2 extends the reasoning-length pilot from TruthfulQA to CommonsenseQA and GSM8K (Appendix A.2), and reports a preliminary instruction-following analysis referencing IFEval (Appendix P). This substantially broadens diagnostic task coverage. The original training and evaluation datasets remain; these additions do not establish BARREL transfer performance on the new domains.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Vanilla GRPO, Vanilla GRPO with Verbal Confidence, and Vanilla GRPO with Probing alongside the retained ICL, ICL-IDK, and Distill comparisons. These introduce direct reinforcement-learning and post-hoc abstention comparators absent from v1's main comparison.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen3-8B, confidence-threshold selection and calibration evaluation, controls crossing SFT initialization with rejection rewards, 50-response error audits per model, and four-sample stability tests. It also revises the stated Llama SFT known-sample count from approximately 2,500 to 2,400 and swaps the -1/+0.5 reward labels in the refusal ablation. These reported revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test construction versus rewriting, GRPO without prior BARREL SFT, response-length changes across training stages, failure-pattern prevalence, confidence-threshold sensitivity and calibration, and sampling stability. These substantially extend v1's reward/data-ratio ablations, qualitative examples, pass@k analyses, and out-of-distribution tests.

E5.justification: Appendix J first reports five-seed means and standard deviations for Llama-8B, including reliability of 61.44 ± 0.97, and discusses test-subset sampling variability. Appendix K reports consistency across four independent generations per question. V1 lacks comparable training-seed uncertainty reporting; its previous run count is not established.

E6.justification: The shared original Table 1 scores remain unchanged, but substantial new results are reported. Examples include Qwen3-8B reliability of 71.46 for BARREL versus 58.94 for Probing, and 63.17 for the rewriting variant versus 61.58 for default construction. New diagnostic and variability results are added. The refusal-ablation bars retain their values but are associated with corrected reward settings.

M1.justification: V2 introduces a tested alternative for constructing SFT data: GPT-4 rewrites failed student trajectories into BARREL format instead of generating traces from scratch (Section 4.3, Table 3). The default knowledge-labeling procedure, trace structure, SFT objective, and GRPO pipeline remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most retained prose and the main section sequence remain close to v1. V2 locally rewrites reward and baseline explanations, expands the metric explanation, reorganizes existing appendices, moves the mechanism discussion into Appendix O, and adds reproducibility and disclosure statements. Much of the expansion consists of new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains comparator rows, a Qwen3-8B block, and an abstention column. V2 adds multiple analysis tables and comparison, threshold, and calibration plots. The refusal-reward figure is redrawn with corrected axis labels and explanatory annotations. Existing figures and tables are also relocated and reformatted under the conference layout, with most original graphics retained.

R1.justification: V2 connects factual overthinking to Chen et al., expands discussion of uncertainty-training work by Stangel, Xu, and Damani, and adds calibration/probing references. It removes the Leng et al. reward-calibration discussion. These focused additions sharpen positioning around LRM reasoning pathologies while retaining the knowledge-boundary and factual-alignment framing.

T1.justification: Equation 5 corrects r_c > r_w > r_s to r_c > r_s > r_w, resolving its contradiction with v1's verbal reward design. Appendix K also introduces inconsistency definitions, using correctness fluctuations for vanilla models and answer/abstention fluctuations for BARREL. The remaining core mathematical formulation is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through direct GRPO and abstention baselines, quantitative checks of the proposed reasoning pathologies, training-stage ablations, and five-seed uncertainty reporting. These additions substantially strengthen evaluation of the mechanism and reliability claims; corrected reward reporting and expanded limitations improve clarity. The stability comparison uses different outcomes for vanilla models and BARREL, and the direct public code link disappears, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger empirical support and clearer applicability boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BARREL. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material across relocation and renumbering. No essential evidence gap was found.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds experiments with Qwen3-8B, additional baselines, trace-construction variants, calibration analyses, and training-seed variability.

before.justification: V1 reports original factual-QA training experiments, reward and data-ratio ablations, out-of-distribution refusal tests, pass@k analyses, and mathematical-reasoning evaluations.

results.title: BARREL: Boundary-Aware Reasoning for Factual and Reliable LRMs

C1.justification: The central claim of dynamic, self-extensible evaluation that exposes LLM value differences remains. Cross-value-system construction changes from future work in v1's conclusion to an achieved contribution in v2, while the introduction generalizes the dataset contribution beyond its original Schwartz-specific description.

C2.justification: New discussions operationalize LLM values as latent behavioral variables and distinguish inherent preferences from user-induced steering and context sensitivity. Appendix C.7 distinguishes factual memorization from value contamination and explains comparability within shared question sets. Failure-case analysis adds substantive explanations of unsuccessful question generation.

D1.justification: v2 provides a public repository address and states code/data release, whereas v1 mentions submission attachments. It adds detailed probability-based reward calculations, settings for new experiments, model-selection rationale, safeguard implementation, and annotator recruitment, consent, compensation and time accounting.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluation under Moral Foundations Theory, previously discussed only as a possible extension. Appendix J constructs AdAEM Bench-MFT with 589 questions covering five moral foundations, substantially extending the evaluation targets beyond the retained Schwartz-value benchmark.

E2.justification: The original SVS, ValueBench and ValueDCG comparison remains. v2 adds Moral Foundations Questionnaire as an evaluated comparator in Tables 14–15 and introduces ValueBench into the controlled-priming validation in Table 11.

E3.justification: The human study changes from 50 question pairs and two annotators to 300 pairs and five annotators. New protocols include a 100-seed-question approximation comparison, alternative model configurations, 200/500/1000-question evaluations, and a separately specified MFT construction budget and model pool.

E4.justification: v2 adds independent priming checks using ValueBench and GPT-5, approximate-versus-probability-based reward validation, sensitivity to participating models and question counts, explicit failure cases, and another convergence experiment. These examine validity and sensitivity questions beyond v1's existing topic, temporal, regional and five-partition analyses.

E5.justification: v2 extends statistical agreement assessment with Pearson correlation and intraclass correlation estimation for implementation, model-configuration and subset comparisons. Existing paired t-tests, effect sizes, Cohen's kappa and five-partition reliability reporting remain; no new seed counts, repeated-run counts or confidence intervals are specified.

E6.justification: The original 16-model scores and o3-mini priming table remain unchanged, but substantial new MFT, priming and robustness results appear. Table 9 replaces human value-elicitation scores of 1.87/2.46 with 1.47/2.24 for general/AdAEM questions under the expanded study, so this is not a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The core exploration/refinement procedure, opinion extraction and TrueSkill aggregation remain. However, v2's Ethics Statement reports integrating Llama-Guard-4-12B into the released iterative process to screen questions and responses and discard harmful questions, adding a procedural safeguard.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions and methodological exposition undergo broad rewriting and terminology clarification. Appendices are reorganized, limitations move into Appendix H, and the NeurIPS checklist is replaced by a different reporting structure including reproducibility and LLM-usage statements. Author information and citation style also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, the notation table expands, and Tables 11–18 and Figures 18–21 introduce new displays. Existing figures are resized or relocated, including the temporal-distribution plot moving to the appendix, alongside extensive conference-template reformatting.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands literature-supported positioning around latent value representations, value/persona steering, moral-foundation evaluation and approximation/convergence. Additions include Cahyawijaya et al. (2024), Jin et al. (2025) and Agakov (2005). The original distinction from static value benchmarks remains.

T1.justification: Most derivations are retained from v1 Appendix C in v2 Appendix D. v2 adds entropy-bound reasoning in Appendix I.1 and a claimed IM convergence justification in E.6. Equation (1) also presents as an equality the transition previously described as a lower-bound substitution.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of previously untested generality and sensitivity through MFT evaluation, independent priming checks, approximation comparisons and model/question-count robustness tests. Expanded human evaluation and implementation disclosures also improve scrutiny. The new convergence guarantee remains insufficiently established for the heuristic implementation, but this qualification does not outweigh the stronger empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AdAEM and retain matching core methods, experiments and results. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Moral Foundations evaluations, GPT-5 priming, approximation validation and robustness experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark construction, evaluations of 16 LLMs, human judgments, controlled value-priming experiments and reliability analyses.

results.title: AdAEM: An Adaptively and Automated Extensible Measurement of LLMs' Value Difference

C1.justification: The central claims about episodic spatial inference, emergent maps, adaptation, and navigation remain. V2 adds scalability to realistic continuous environments with high-dimensional inputs as an explicit main contribution. V1 presents only preliminary MiniGrid evidence and leaves more realistic sensory environments primarily to future work.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations for TEM-T's performance gap and the benefits of minimal-memory training, and revises the Open Arena failure discussion toward overfitting. It explicitly identifies ambiguity from duplicate states without historical context. The limitations discussion shifts from simplified sensory/action representations toward remaining challenges in physical robotic navigation.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's limited MiniGrid documentation, v2 specifies its object encoding and prediction heads. It also documents ProcThor sampling, DINOv3 processing, attention architecture, and training resources, including four A100 GPUs for 80,000 iterations over 19 days. Custom TEM-T implementation and sRSA/noise-analysis procedures provide substantial additional reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V2 adds ProcThor indoor scenes with first-person RGB observations and continuous displacement/rotation inputs, extending beyond v1's grid environments. It also evaluates duplicate-state environments and contradictory memories. MiniGrid was already evaluated in v1 Figure A9 and is not an entirely new benchmark.

E2.justification: V2 introduces TEM-T as an evaluated world-model comparator in Open Arena and Random Wall, including the non-minimal-memory comparison (Figures 2 and 9). This substantially expands the direct comparison with related spatial-memory models. EPN, EMWM, LSTM, and Mamba comparisons already existed in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include minimal spanning trajectories for TEM-T, ESWM controls trained on that trajectory distribution, and ProcThor evaluation using discretized action classes and state-feature cosine similarity. Figure 4c changes from a four-layer to a twelve-layer transformer and extends the memory-size sweep to partial-coverage settings. Figure 2 also revises evaluated model depths.

E4.justification: V2 adds attention-head and training-minimality ablations, controls separating TEM-T architecture from training distribution, trained-versus-untrained sRSA analysis, and noise and environment-size generalization tests. The EPN small-memory ablation in v1 Figure A6 is removed. Disconnected-memory and guided-planning analyses are retained after relocation to Appendix D.

E5.justification: V1 Figure A6 displays three individual EPN seeds; v2 Figure 15 reports four-seed means and standard deviations for both ESWM and EPN, with Welch tests. V2 also discloses best-seed selection for Figure 5 and identifies Figure 4a's uncertainty bands as 95% confidence intervals. These substantially change uncertainty reporting without establishing that every experiment received additional runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds ProcThor predictions, query-type accuracy tables, and numerous ablation and robustness outcomes, including trained/untrained sRSA of 0.78 ± 0.02 versus 0.50 ± 0.04. Exploration coverage is revised from 90% to 91 ± 2%. Figures 2 and 4c contain replaced results under revised model configurations, so they do not establish matched-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 adds a substantial ProcThor adaptation using DINOv3 features, 33 tokens per transition, alternating within-transition/global attention, and cosine-distance state loss (Appendix C.1.4–C.1.5). It also introduces trajectory-conditioned queries for duplicate states and changes the described LSTM/Mamba input from a terminal query token to query-conditioned memory tokens. The core episodic prediction and planning procedures remain.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract and substantial portions of related work, methods, and interpretation. It moves disconnected-memory analysis and guided imagination from the main text into Appendix D, restructures the experimental narrative around scalability, and reorganizes the appendices. These are substantial narrative changes beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adds four tables and Figures 7–9, expands MiniGrid into the combined MiniGrid/ProcThor Figure 6, and redraws Figures 2 and 4. Figure A6 becomes a redesigned four-seed comparison in Figure 15. Other appendix figures are largely retained and renumbered, alongside the document-wide conference-format change.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 and new Appendix A substantially expand positioning against GTM-SM, TEM, successor representations, and recurrent predictive models. New Appendix B develops the biological evidence for integrating disjoint experiences through additional cited studies. ProcThor, DINOv3, and VGGT references support the new extension; existing TEM citations are developed rather than newly introduced.

T1.justification: The core mathematical formulation, environment definitions, latent-distance heuristic construction, and admissibility discussion are retained. Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs. The added minimality experiments and standard sRSA metric concern empirical settings and analysis rather than new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for generalization and memory-based reasoning through ProcThor experiments, a relevant TEM-T comparison with distribution controls, and targeted robustness and ablation tests. Four-seed ESWM/EPN reporting and fuller implementation details address important validation and reproducibility gaps in v1. ProcThor remains preliminary simulation evidence, and the EPN memory-size ablation is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential strength.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ESWM research. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and rendered figures support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds ProcThor experiments, TEM-T comparisons, robustness tests, and additional quantitative analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original prediction, representation, exploration, navigation, and adaptation experiments in simulated environments, including MiniGrid results in Figure A9.

results.title: Building spatial world models from sparse transitional episodic memories

C1.justification: v2 makes greater effectiveness and efficiency than direct distillation a central claim in the abstract, contribution list, and conclusion. It also shifts the headline comparison from outperforming thinking-enabled Claude to outperforming the non-thinking teacher by approximately 10%, while describing thinking-Claude performance as comparable. The 141% improvement over the base model remains.

C2.justification: v2 explains the distillation gap through avoidance of accumulated rollout errors, attributes limited 7B gains to knowledge and grounding deficiencies, and qualifies test-time scaling through termination failures beyond the training horizon. These substantially expand mechanism and applicability discussions. v1's separate resource-limitations section and discussion of complementary RL/SFT development are removed.

D1.justification: v2 specifies previously vague decontamination cutoffs: zero 13-gram overlap, 3-gram overlap below 0.7, and cosine similarity below 0.85. It also reports synthesis runtimes, but omits v1's explicit random-subsampling description for smaller augmentation factors. Training hyperparameters, prompt content, tracker instructions, and the resource link are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 312 Windows training tasks and Windows/Linux evaluation coverage. v2 newly reports original-WindowsAgentArena scores, but v1 already explicitly describes evaluating that benchmark in Section 4. The smaller-model and longer-step experiments change configurations rather than represented tasks or domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-4o to the main benchmark comparison, direct distillation and human-plus-distillation training baselines, NAVI to the original-WindowsAgentArena comparison, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the smaller-model reference. The distillation controls substantially expand comparison of the proposed training strategy against alternatives.

E3.justification: New protocols include collecting ten end-to-end Claude trajectories per training task, a control combining one human trajectory with nine Claude trajectories per task, training a 7B backbone, and evaluating a 50-step limit. Existing 72B training settings and the main 30-step evaluation remain unchanged. The newly specified decontamination thresholds document an existing procedure.

E4.justification: Section 5.4 and Appendices C–E add tests of whether direct distillation or mixed human/teacher data can replace Trajectory Boost, whether the method benefits a smaller model, and whether scaling remains effective beyond 30 steps. The 50-step experiment adds a substantive termination-failure analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-evaluation counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The ten Claude trajectories per task in v2 describe training-data collection, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Shared benchmark scores and existing scaling points are unchanged. New results include direct and mixed distillation scores of 26.2% and 26.9% versus PC Agent-E's 36.0%, original-WindowsAgentArena scores of 27.9% versus NAVI's 19.5%, and 7B scores of 6.4% versus 5.0%. At 50 steps, PC Agent-E scores 31.4%, below its retained 30-step score of 36.0%. v2 also reports synthesis times of approximately 3 versus 900 hours.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline remains human trajectory collection, Claude thought completion, nine alternative decisions per human state, and supervised training with the same ReAct scaffold. The prompts are substantively unchanged. The additional 7B experiment applies the existing method, while direct distillation is a comparison method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, experimental narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the teacher-distillation comparison. Experiments are organized around explicit research questions, the standalone limitations section disappears, and the appendix structure expands while retaining the relocated prompts and tracker manual. An LLM writing-assistance disclosure is added.

P2.justification: v2 removes the example-trajectory figure, separates v1's two-panel scaling figure into individual figures, and adds a direct-distillation curve. It adds a trajectory-length table and four appendix result tables, expands the main comparison table, and reformats the document in the ICLR style. Most pipeline illustrations remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The native-agent and data-synthesis taxonomy remains largely intact. v2 adds GPT-4 and OmniParser references for the NAVI comparison, removes several earlier trajectory-collection, agent-framework, and reasoning/RL citations, and more explicitly distinguishes Trajectory Boost from direct distillation.

T1.justification: The environment-snapshot and trajectory-history formalization is unchanged. Replacing v1's scaling-factor notation s′ with v2's s preserves the same augmented-action ratio. Neither version contains substantive theoretical results or proofs that are added, removed, or revised.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct-distillation controls; v2 adds both direct and human-plus-distillation comparisons, materially strengthening evidence for the specific value of Trajectory Boost. The 7B experiment and the performance decline at 50 steps also establish useful limits to the method's applicability and scaling claims. Removing the earlier limitations discussion weakens transparency, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the new controls and better-qualified conclusions provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PC Agent-E research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, mathematical notation, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds distillation comparisons, a smaller-model experiment, original-WindowsAgentArena scores, and extended test-time evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original agent evaluations on WindowsAgentArena-V2 and OSWorld, training-data and test-time scaling experiments, and qualitative failure analysis.

results.title: Efficient Agent Training for Computer Use

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from a parameter-efficient block suppressing overfitting and spurious features to diagnosing low-dimensional feature-manifold degradation by linear layers and preserving geometry through a random anchor. This substantially changes the abstract, introduction, and conclusion's scientific emphasis. The earlier arbitrary-approximation/no-worse-performance claim remains in Section 3.2.3 and Appendix E.

C2.justification: V2 develops a substantially expanded geometric mechanism, including spectral sharpening and interpretations of differences between CONCH, UNI, and ResNet50 representations. It qualifies geometric statistics as diagnostics rather than predictors of performance gains. Appendix I adds limitations concerning the data-independent anchor and untested slide-level foundation models such as TITAN, alongside the retained rank and placement limitations.

D1.justification: V2 supplies project-code access information and a reproducibility statement, whereas v1 mainly promises later code-related details. It newly documents residual initialization, geometric-analysis procedures, treatment-response label construction, and insertion locations for additional backbones. Core optimizer and hardware information remains; v1's explicit batch-size statement is omitted. The PDFs establish the access disclosure, not the repository's contents or functionality.

E1.justification: V2 retains the three original datasets and adds two evaluated treatment-response cohorts: Boehmk ovarian cancer and Trastuzumab HER2-positive breast cancer (Table 9; Appendix G.1). These extend coverage beyond tumor detection and subtyping to clinical outcome prediction.

E2.justification: The main comparison adds FOCUS, DGRMIL, and RRTMIL, including MR-enhanced versions of the latter two, while removing CLAM/SR-CLAM. ABMIL, TransMIL, CATE, and ViLaMIL remain. The feature-extractor comparison also replaces TransMIL with CATE (v1 Tables 5/9; v2 Tables 6/12). FOCUS was cited in v1 but was not evaluated there.

E3.justification: The reported TCGA split changes from 60/15/25 to 60/20/20. V2 removes 1-shot evaluation, retains 2-shot results in Appendix Table 7, and adds 32/64-shot experiments. It adds AUPRC, specifies macro F1, and introduces geometric diagnostics, capacity-matched controls, and computation measurements under varying bag sizes. These are substantive evaluation changes, not just relocated settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds spectral, clustering, and tangent-space analyses; trainable-anchor and identity-skip ablations; a capacity-matched comparison; and analysis beyond extreme few-shot learning. It removes v1's activation-function comparison and revises initialization and rank-sensitivity studies using different backbones. The heatmap analysis is also revised and described as a 2-shot MR-CATE example, rather than the earlier SR-CLAM example.

E5.justification: V1 reports means and standard deviations from three training runs and states that methods share random seeds. V2 reports means and standard deviations across five sampled few-shot subsets/runs and mentions cross-validation folds without specifying their number. The shared-seed statement disappears; confidence intervals and significance tests are not introduced.

E6.justification: Many existing results are replaced. For example, Table 1 reports 8-shot Camelyon16 AUCs of 53.9%/88.5% for TransMIL/SR-TransMIL in v1, versus 57.5%/65.3% for TransMIL/MR-TransMIL in v2. Revised sampling protocols prevent treating this as a controlled performance decline. V2 also adds geometric measurements, AUPRC, treatment-response, capacity-matched, larger-shot, and runtime results.

M1.justification: The frozen random branch plus nonlinear low-rank residual mapping is retained under the MR name; GELU was already used in v1. The default ABMIL integration changes from replacing V alone to replacing both U and V (v1 Appendix D.3; v2 Appendix G.4), promoting a previously tested variant. Zero initialization of W1 is newly documented, not established as a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around geometry. SR/SP terminology becomes MR/LRP, related-work sections are reorganized, geometric preliminaries are inserted, and the main approximation proof moves to the appendix. Reproducibility, acknowledgements, an appendix contents page, and an LLM-usage statement are added.

P2.justification: V2 adds geometric Figures 1, 4, and 5, redraws the architecture schematic and rank-sensitivity plots, and restructures and expands the tables. The heatmap moves from main Figure 3 to appendix Figure 6 with revised heatmaps and layout. Its original biopsy images are reused, although the caption changes the model and slide attribution from SR-CLAM/tumor049 to MR-CATE/tumor058 without explanation.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated geometric deep learning and representation-analysis subsection, supported by manifold, effective-rank, and tangent-space literature. It newly positions MR relative to LoRA and prototype-based classifiers and discusses TITAN's applicability limits. Earlier boosting and extreme-learning-machine connections are removed, substantially changing the research positioning.

T1.justification: V2 introduces mathematical definitions for spectral entropy/effective rank and tangent-space drift in Sections 3.1.2–3.1.3. The approximation theorem and random-projection, full-rank, and low-rank-product arguments largely retain v1's substance after relocation to Appendices D–F. V1's explicit SR-specific forward/backward complexity bounds are no longer stated.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification: direct geometry diagnostics and capacity-matched controls address v1's lack of evidence separating the proposed mechanism from parameter reduction. Additional evaluated baselines, treatment-response tasks, and code-access information broaden validation and improve reproducibility. These gains are substantive despite remaining weaknesses: geometric diagnostics do not establish the full causal account, some blanket ablation claims exceed Table 2's results, and the retained approximation theorem does not resolve the fixed-low-rank no-loss guarantee.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and SR-to-MR renaming, both PDFs describe the same random-matrix-plus-low-rank MIL approach. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original classification, treatment-response, representation-geometry, ablation, and computational-cost results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification experiments on Camelyon16, TCGA-NSCLC, and TCGA-RCC, including component ablations, sensitivity studies, and attention heatmaps.

results.title: Exploiting Low-Dimensional Manifold of Features for Few-Shot Whole Slide Image Classification

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from evaluating multimodal reasoning with LENS to also enhancing it through SMEC. v2 additionally claims experimental confirmation that lower-level task information facilitates higher-level reasoning. The central benchmark design and reported difficulty of the original reasoning evaluations remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking counting and OCR through fine-grained localization, interpretations of auxiliary-context effects, and analyses of perceptual versus reasoning failures. It also discusses SMEC's proposed correction mechanisms. New limitations identify static-image and short-form coverage, demographic and scenario biases, and SMEC's potential redundancy and prompt sensitivity.

D1.justification: v2 supplies explicit synergy and SMEC prompt templates, pseudocode, and backbone specifications for additional evaluated models. It newly documents independent annotation verification, Qwen2.5-VL-72B-assisted checks, privacy screening, masking, and auditing procedures. These substantially expand reproducibility information, without establishing that the retained main-table experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 3.4K-image corpus, 60K+ questions, eight tasks, and 12 scenarios. However, OD coverage changes from 'more than 300' categories in v1 Section 3.1.2 to 'more than 500' in v2 Appendix A.2. The PDFs do not establish whether annotations expanded or the description was corrected. The added studies otherwise evaluate retained data and tasks.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains its comparator set. New comparisons substantially broaden it: Table 3 evaluates Self-Refine and majority voting against SMEC; Table 4 adds grounding comparators including TransVG, VLTVG, SimVG, G-DINO, Groma, Mova, and Ferret; Table 6 evaluates GLM-4.1V Base and Thinking models.

E3.justification: The main Table 2 metrics and evaluation strategy are retained. New protocols include a 3,500-question SKI subset and full-set SMEC evaluation, one to three expert-generation iterations, auxiliary-QA context controls, multiple grounding IoU thresholds and object-size groups, four input resolutions, publication-date partitions, and grading validation by ten independent human annotators.

E4.justification: v2 adds iteration-depth experiments, combinations of auxiliary task information for SKI, object-scale grounding analysis, resolution sensitivity, temporal generalization, qualitative failure cases, and human-versus-automatic grading checks. These substantially extend v1's correlation/regression analyses. The original annotation examples and low-level image analysis are retained in the appendix rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for model performance. The original correlation and regression procedures remain. Newly reported human-grader agreement percentages provide validation outcomes without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All 118 numerical scores in Table 2 are unchanged. v2 adds substantial results: Table 3 reports direct versus SMEC accuracy of 39.80% versus 43.24% for Qwen2.5-VL-7B on the sampled SKI subset, and 51.54% versus 54.66% for Qwen2.5-VL-32B on the full set. Tables 4–7 and Figures 9–11 add further quantitative and qualitative findings. Appendix grounding scores are newly reported results, not established same-setting improvements over Table 2.

M1.justification: v1 introduces a benchmark without SMEC. v2 adds the Self-Driven Multi-Expert Collaborative Framework: a base MLLM generates expert roles, screens redundant descriptions, adapts generation prompts, obtains expert responses, and integrates them into a final answer. Section 3 and Algorithm 1 specify a substantial new inference procedure.

P1.justification: The narrative is reorganized around a benchmark-plus-method contribution. Related work, detailed task definitions, quality control, and low-level feature analysis move into the appendix; the abstract, introduction, and conclusion are expanded or rewritten. Dedicated methodology, ethics, reproducibility, and limitations material changes the document's structure substantially.

P2.justification: v2 adds the SMEC workflow, failure cases, temporal-performance plots, qualitative comparisons, five experimental tables, an algorithm display, and prompt boxes. Existing figures are redistributed: v1 Figures 4 and 6 become appendix Figures 7 and 8. Retained plots are reformatted, and Table 1 loses its language column. These are substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: The existing benchmark and reasoning background is retained, largely in Appendix A.1. v2 substantially expands agentic reasoning and test-time computation coverage, citing work such as MetaGPT, AgentVerse, and Self-Refine. It positions SMEC against external-tool approaches and systems with manually specified roles and coordination rules.

T1.justification: Appendix A.10 adds a formal algorithmic specification of SMEC, defining expert-description and answer sets and their iterative generation, acceptance, update, and aggregation operations. This is a limited addition of formal definitions; v2 does not add theorems, proofs, or theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: v1 supports task synergy mainly through correlations. v2 adds direct auxiliary-context experiments, broader diagnostic evaluations, and independent human checks of automated grading, substantially strengthening the benchmark's empirical support. Detailed curation procedures and explicit SMEC prompts also improve transparency and reproducibility. Important limitations remain: uncertainty estimates and matched inference budgets are absent, and the grounding scores in Tables 2 and 4 are not reconciled. Nevertheless, the added validation addresses central evidential gaps in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LENS, with matching core tasks, dataset characteristics, and main benchmark results. Text, tables, figures, and algorithm material are readable. v1 ends with references; v2 includes a substantial Appendix A, which was included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds SMEC experiments, ablations, grounding and resolution evaluations, temporal analyses, and human validation of automated grading.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 16 multimodal models on LENS in Table 2, alongside dataset analyses and cross-task correlation and regression results.

results.title: LENS: Multi-level Evaluation of Multimodal Reasoning with Large Language Models

C1.justification: The hybrid solver and subspace-loss contributions remain, but v2 adds central claims of 3D applicability, resolution invariance and greater data efficiency. The introduction narrows v1's better-than-GMsFEM claim to comparable accuracy, while the conclusion extends demonstrated applicability to time-dependent and mixed-boundary problems.

C2.justification: v1 attributes marginal improvements over GMsFEM to more efficient learned subspaces; v2 instead suggests statistical variation. v2 also adds interpretations of data efficiency, size-dependent projection-regularization benefits and costs, inadequate four-basis accuracy, and amortization over repeated simulations. Limitations are updated to acknowledge the new heat and mixed-boundary tests.

D1.justification: v2 adds KLE field-generation instructions and correlation parameters, detailed new-baseline configurations, 3D Fourier-mode choices and training-cost information. Conversely, v1's selected GMsFEM-NO configuration tables and explicit regularization weight of 0.1 are removed; optimal configurations are deferred to a future code release. Neither PDF supplies access to released code.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only 2D steady diffusion and Richards equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundaries. v2 adds 3D versions of these problems, a time-dependent 2D heat equation, and diffusion with mixed Dirichlet–Robin boundaries, substantially extending the evaluated problem scope.

E2.justification: v2 adds GNOT and Transolver++ alongside F-FNO in Table 7. Appendix G adds evaluated PCA-Net, kernel, POD, DeepPOD and intrusive methods using DeepONet/F-FNO bases. The four-basis comparison against classical GMsFEM is dropped.

E3.justification: Reported GMsFEM-NO training changes from 800 epochs at 10^-4 to 600 at 10^-3. Standalone F-FNO changes from 10,000-epoch Lion training to 600-epoch AdamW training, with revised architecture and scheduling. Larger-grid, resolution-transfer and sample-size protocols are added, including a 150/50 train/test split for 100^3 problems. These reported changes do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss and forcing-shift experiments, v2 adds training-data sensitivity over 200–800 samples (Table 8), transfer from 100/250 to 500 grid resolution (Table 9), projection-vector-count sensitivity (Table 11), and training-cost amortization analysis (Appendix N). These address new questions about data efficiency, generalization, regularization and practical computational benefit.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run/seed counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v1 explicitly acknowledges this omission in its checklist; v2 removes that checklist but introduces no uncertainty-estimation practice. Its reference to statistical variation is an interpretation, not a statistical analysis.

E6.justification: The original loss scores are retained in v2 Tables 1 and 12, while extensive new benchmark and analysis results are added. Standalone comparisons move to 250×250 with revised training, so differing scores are not same-setting gains. The 100×100 Richards random-to-unit forcing error changes from 2311% to 6503% (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 13). Four-basis classical-GMsFEM and timing results disappear.

M1.justification: The subspace-learning losses and GMsFEM reconstruction procedure remain unchanged. Section 2.5.1 extends the geometry-specific operator procedure from three domain types in 2D to four in 3D, adding a quarter-domain operator; this is a limited adaptation of the existing method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The loss exposition is reordered, algorithm explanations are revised, and material is reorganized into topical Appendices A–N instead of two training appendices. The NeurIPS checklist is removed.

P2.justification: Figures 2–4 move into appendices, Figure 1's basis-count labels change, and Figure 5 adds accuracy-versus-basis-count curves. Results tables are split, restructured and expanded for new grids, comparators and analyses, while the original configuration tables disappear. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning beyond neural operators, GMsFEM and Spiridonov et al. It distinguishes learning solution spaces from learned homogenization/upscaling and discusses reduced-order approaches, adding relevant works by Bhattacharya, Kröpfl and others, plus literature supporting the new baselines and Grassmannian analysis.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix C introduces a projector-distance/Grassmannian derivation for SAL and a proposed solution-error bound, Equation 10, absent from v1. Appendix D adds a formal rotational-invariance argument. These substantially expand the mathematical justification, although the new error bound is not justified as written.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical scope and limited comparisons through 3D, time-dependent, mixed-boundary, resolution-transfer and broader baseline evaluations. Data-generation disclosure and narrower claims relative to GMsFEM also help. These empirical gains outweigh the lost configuration details and defects in the new supporting analyses: Appendix C's squared-norm bound is unjustified as written, and Table 16's negative break-even counts contradict its cost equation and positive count in the prose. The improvement is principally empirical, not an established theoretical guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GMsFEM-NO and share the core method and original experiments. All pages, including appendices, equations, figures, tables and v1's checklist, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional results for 3D problems, heat equations, mixed boundary conditions, new comparators and sensitivity studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original diffusion and Richards-equation experiments, including loss comparisons, solution errors, basis-generation timings and out-of-distribution results in Tables 1–5.

results.title: Locally Subspace-Informed Neural Operators for Efficient Multiscale PDE Solving

C1.justification: v2 withdraws the prominent first-benchmark/first-investigation claims and foregrounds the existing 11.4k evaluation benchmark and 46k thinking dataset instead of the full 77,646-pair pool. It emphasizes helpful responses and qualifies preservation of general capabilities as avoiding significant compromise. The central claims about video-induced safety degradation and the dual-stage defense remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds an attention-redistribution explanation for alarm tokens, distinguishes token load from harmful semantics more explicitly, and interprets cross-language safety gains as potentially conservative behavior with reduced helpfulness. It also distinguishes safety alignment from anomaly detection and adds limitations concerning long videos and evaluator reliability under complex attacks. Some interpretations overreach: Appendix N's universal non-English improvement claim has exceptions in Tables 19–20.

D1.justification: v2 discloses previously unspecified classification and reward weights, compute/latency measurements, baseline adaptation recipes, and additional sampling information. Appendix R.6 supplies the false-negative-check prompt missing from v1's duplicated prompt listing. A repository pointer replaces the supplementary-code statement, and release restrictions are documented. Dataset availability remains internally inconsistent: the abstract says available, while the reproducibility statement says release awaits verification.

E1.justification: v2 adds hallucination evaluation on VideoHallucer, anomaly detection on XD-Violence, and controlled evaluation with translated prompts across ten languages (Table 3 and Appendices N–O). These expand task and input-language coverage beyond v1's evaluations. The original multilingual video pool, 11.4k evaluation set, and 46k training set remain identifiable under revised names.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated defense comparators Self-Reminder, SPA-VL, VLGuard, and MM-RLHF, plus Holmes-VAD (Tables 2 and 21). The benchmark comparison expands from 14 to 21 video models, adding commercial models, InternVL3 variants, and larger Qwen2.5 VL variants. Conversely, VideoLLaMA2-7B and VideoChat2-7B disappear from the visual-attack comparison present in v1 Table 10.

E3.justification: The VLGuard-Video experiment changes from rotating images into videos to repeating static images and varying sampled frame counts from 1 to 60. v2 also introduces matched nine-frame video/thumbnail/middle-frame controls, training on Qwen2.5 VL-3B/7B, and new human-audit protocols involving 1,000 videos and 10,000 queries. Helpfulness itself already existed in v1; its human-score MSE validation is newly added.

E4.justification: Beyond retained FPS, visual-attack, and component ablations, v2 adds controlled semantic-richness tests, attention-sink analysis, video-length analysis, loss-weight sensitivity, Qwen2.5 VL ablations, reasoning-diversity measurements, and dataset-quality checks. Its case appendix replaces four examples with nineteen covering all subcategories, including a failure example and safe-query behavior. These substantially broaden the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's reported 0.81% standard deviation summarizes variation across frame-count conditions in a sensitivity experiment, rather than uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new defenses, backbones, audits, and diagnostic experiments. The original 18.4% baseline and 89.5% defended DSR remain, while their incorrectly reported 65.1-point difference becomes 71.1 points. The headline average safety drop changes from 42.3% across 14 models to 34.2% across 21, reflecting different comparator coverage. A retained Qwen2.5 VL-7B SH result changes from 65.7% to 66.7%; rotating-video results and detailed base-LLM category rows are removed.

M1.justification: The alarm tokens, multitask AT-SFT objective, cold-start stage, Safety-guided GRPO, and dynamic reward adaptation remain unchanged in Equations 1–6 and the training recipes. VideoSafetyThinking renames the existing VSB-R1-46k dataset. Applying the framework to Qwen2.5 VL and disclosing additional settings do not establish an algorithmic redesign.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, experimental narrative, and limitations. Dataset construction is condensed in the main text and moved into appendices, the training dataset becomes part of the method section, and helpfulness and robustness receive integrated main-text treatment. Terminology and appendix organization are extensively revised.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the main result tables to integrate safety, helpfulness, and false refusal; redisplays base-LLM comparisons as Figure 5; and redraws the dataset and framework diagrams. It adds frame-count and attention plots, multiple diagnostic tables, and an expanded case gallery with masked imagery. Existing taxonomy and helpfulness displays are relocated or consolidated, alongside the conference-format layout change.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive positioning against concurrent Video-SafetyBench, SafeVid, and Trust-VideoLLMs work, replacing v1's broad priority framing. A new video-anomaly-detection discussion distinguishes that objective from response safety. Additional attention-sink and SFT-versus-RL references support the expanded mechanism discussion; these exceed bibliographic or citation-style updates.

T1.justification: Equations 1–9 retain the same objectives, reward construction, GRPO update, and evaluation definitions. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced; the added mechanism arguments are empirical interpretations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's evidence: Table 2 adds competing safety defenses and validates the framework beyond its original backbone, while Appendix E adds human verification of benchmark labels. Controlled analyses and disclosed reward weights strengthen interpretation and reproducibility, and the headline improvement arithmetic is corrected. Overstated cross-language conclusions and conflicting dataset-release statements remain weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation of the paper's central contributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VideoSafety-R1 research, and their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison. The renamed evaluation and training datasets can be matched across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds defense comparisons, dataset audits, cross-language evaluations, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, training experiments, ablations, visual attacks, and human validation of its response evaluator in the main text and appendices.

results.title: From Evaluation to Defense: Advancing Safety in Video Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and overall classical-solver advantage remain. V2 narrows the conclusion from LLM 'novel strategy discovery' to better use of existing algorithms, and from neural excellence on structured problems to improving certain human heuristics. The introduction also drops the absolute claim that the hard set is immune to heuristic hacking.

C2.justification: V2 shifts the explanation of LLM variability from solver selection/integration toward a hypothesis about inability to assess generated algorithms, adding applicability concerns for hard-to-verify tasks. It expands memory and inference-bottleneck explanations and adds deployment-cost tradeoffs in Appendix G. V1's explicit reference-solution construction-cost limitation and interpretation of the unsuccessful DeepACO ablation are removed.

D1.justification: V1 provides hardware, data generators, and an example prompt but omits many solver-specific settings. V2's Appendix C supplies checkpoint sources, training sample counts, inference settings, and agent search parameters, including Self-Refine's o4-mini configuration, 64 iterations, and development timeout. It also adds a project code-repository link and discloses discarded route-length constraints in eight Golden instances.
