E1.justification: The original eight problem collections remain, but Appendix F adds a distinct non-Euclidean, non-metric asymmetric TSP benchmark from real-world applications: 31 easy and 33 hard instances. This substantively extends routing coverage beyond v1's symmetric two-dimensional Euclidean TSP.

E2.justification: V2 adds SIL to the existing TSP and CVRP comparisons and evaluates RRNCO on the added ATSP benchmark. Section 5.1 removes the CVRP ablation comparing DeepACO, ACO, and HGS; DeepACO and HGS remain in the main CVRP comparison. Most comparator membership is retained.

E3.justification: The principal one-hour budget, hardware, primal-gap metric, and aggregation rules remain. Appendix E adds fast TSP configurations: LKH-3 with POPMUSIC and 1,000 trials, greedy LEHD, DIFUSCO with 50 steps and greedy decoding, and SIL with 10 reconstruction steps. These are additional protocols; Appendix C's newly disclosed settings do not establish revisions to the retained experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantive analyses of efficiency across TSP instance sizes and difficulty on non-Euclidean ATSP instances in Appendices E–F. It removes the DeepACO–ACO neural-module ablation, including the case where the neural component did not improve quality. The STP learning-curve analysis and LLM algorithm word cloud are retained.

E5.justification: V1's detailed tables report point estimates. V2 adds ± dispersion values for primal gaps and geometric standard deviations for solving times throughout Tables 4–11. This substantially expands statistical reporting, although repeated-run counts, seeds, and the sampling basis of the gap dispersion remain unspecified; additional runs are not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds SIL results, aggregate LLM scores, fast TSP results, and ATSP results. SIL's TSP gaps are 2.51%/21.34% on easy/hard sets; the new ATSP hard-set gaps are 15.46% for RRNCO and 0.08% for LKH-3. Among matched entries, DiffUCO's easy-MIS gap changes from 9.57% to 9.54%, and IL-LNS/CL-LNS easy-CPMP times change from 3600s to 2636s/2649s. CVRP ablation entries are removed; most other retained means are unchanged.

M1.justification: No new proposed algorithmic component is introduced. The existing STP prediction-and-decoding procedure remains unchanged; SIL and RRNCO are additional evaluated baselines, while Appendix C documents implementation details.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the title, abstract, introduction, results narrative, and conclusion. It reorganizes the appendices around implementation details, moves the existing prompt into Appendix C.3, adds a reproducibility statement, and removes the acknowledgements and standalone impact/limitations paragraphs. The changes extend well beyond isolated wording edits.

P2.justification: V2 simplifies Figure 1, redraws Figure 2 with SIL and failure markers while removing numerical labels, and removes the classical-runtime chart. It splits the paired result tables into individual problem tables with dispersion reporting, reduces the ablation table, and adds aggregate, efficiency, and ATSP tables. Typography and page layout are extensively reformatted.

R1.justification: Section 6 extends benchmark positioning through RL4CO, Jumanji, ML4CO-bench-101, Routing Arena, and ML4TSPBench, and adds work such as AlphaEvolve and SPL-LNS. Further citations support the metric and new analyses. These are limited extensions of the retained neural/symbolic framing and realism/scalability motivation.

T1.justification: V2 removes v1's formal algorithm-search objective and associated search-space definitions in Equation 3. It explicitly formulates per-instance minimization and explains negating maximization objectives, including MIS. The primal-gap formula remains unchanged, and neither version contains substantial theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's missing reproducibility information through checkpoint provenance and detailed solver/agent settings. Dispersion reporting and the new efficiency and non-Euclidean evaluations strengthen evidence for the benchmark's central concerns. Removing the unfavorable DeepACO ablation reduces balance, and stronger explanations of LLM failures remain insufficiently tested, but the gains in reproducibility and empirical support outweigh these drawbacks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FrontierCO. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains those original benchmark evaluations and reports additional SIL, fast-configuration TSP, and asymmetric TSP results.

before.justification: V1 reports original solver evaluations across eight CO problems in Tables 3–6, plus neural-module ablations and STP training experiments in Section 5.

results.title: FrontierCO: Real-World and Large-Scale Evaluation of Machine Learning Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a benchmark with answer and reasoning annotations, and the claim that no evaluated MLLM exceeds 50% accuracy is retained. The introduction replaces v1's claim that open-source models remain below 40% with a claim that document-oriented models remain below 15%, consistent with the expanded comparisons.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation: it explains the single-image scope, attributes the error distribution primarily to higher-level reasoning, discusses guidance and input-length explanations for few-shot effects, and develops the official-prompt/CoT conflict hypothesis. Appendices A.5–A.6 extend the framework's stated applicability to training-data construction and outline future development. The original dataset-cost and LLM-judge limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the use of official RL-model prompts, additional few-shot demonstrations, and the generator, source datasets, and 5,000-image scale of synthetic training. However, v1's disclosure of eight A800 GPUs is removed, and fine-tuning hyperparameters remain unspecified. The existing repository link is retained; additional distribution channels are only planned.

E1.justification: The benchmark retains its reported 1,069 examples, six abilities, and 18 tasks. v2 adds direct model evaluation on conventional DocVQA, ChartQA, TextVQA, and OCRBench tasks in Table 6, plus synthetic training using DocVQA, InfoVQA, TextVQA, and ChartQA images. These extend dataset use within the existing text-rich domain; multilingual and multi-page expansion remains prospective.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Qwen2.5-32B with OCR, six additional multimodal models including GLM-4.1V-Thinking and DeepEyesV2, and a document-oriented group comprising mPLUG-DocOwl2, Docopilot, DocMark, and TokenVL. Table 4 expands its previously closed-source-only reasoning comparison to include 13 open-source and three document-oriented models.

E3.justification: The original zero-shot evaluation remains, but v2 introduces substantially different experimental designs: one- and three-shot prompting with additional demonstrations, synthetic-data fine-tuning, and a factorial comparison of official and generic CoT prompts. Section 3.3 also adds a 200-example answer-extraction check and human-versus-LLM scoring comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds scoring-pipeline validation, few-shot sensitivity analysis, a six-category DouBao error breakdown, a synthetic-training-data utility experiment, and an ablation testing the proposed VL-Rethinker prompt conflict. These address questions beyond v1's CoT comparison and illustrative cases. The earlier qualitative analyses are retained in Appendices A.2–A.4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The new human-versus-LLM score comparisons provide validation outcomes without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All original numerical entries in Tables 2–4 are retained, but substantial new results appear. The expanded model set raises the best reported open-source accuracy from Qwen2.5-VL-72B's 37.5% to GLM-4.1V-Thinking-9B's 44.1%. New Qwen2.5-VL-7B settings report 16.1% and 16.4% with few-shot prompting and 17.0% after fine-tuning, alongside the unchanged 15.7% zero-shot result. Additional reasoning scores, validation outcomes, benchmark comparisons, and diagnostic results are also reported.

M1.justification: The core benchmark construction and evaluation procedures remain. Appendix A.5 adds a limited methodological adaptation: replacing human annotators with DouBao-1.5-Vision-Pro to generate synthetic training data, then fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B. The proposed process-aware reward model is only future work.

P1.justification: v2 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, curation description, and conclusion, and reorganizes and consolidates the results narrative. Earlier qualitative discussion moves into separate appendix subsections, while the appendix gains a broader hierarchy. Author contribution notes, affiliations, acknowledgments, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with a different illustrative chart, Figure 2 is comprehensively redesigned, and Figure 3 is restyled. Tables 2 and 4 expand, four new tables and an error-distribution figure appear, and earlier qualitative figures move to the appendix, including v1 Figure 5 becoming v2 Figure 8. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: The related-work structure and positioning around reasoning versus text extraction remain largely unchanged. v2 adds references supporting newer model comparisons and scope discussion, including Docopilot, DocMark, Marten, Keye-VL, Thyme, DeepEyesV2, GLM, and MiMo-VL. Publication updates and the author-year citation format do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs about the benchmark or models. The mathematical worked examples retain their reasoning, and v2's new scope and mechanism explanations do not introduce formal assumptions, derivations, or guarantees.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's empirical foundation. It extends reasoning-process evaluation beyond the five closed-source models, adds human checks of scoring, and tests a previously speculative prompt-conflict explanation through ablation. The error analysis further supports the benchmark's focus on reasoning difficulties. These gains outweigh the loss of GPU information, although human-validation procedures and fine-tuning settings remain insufficiently documented and uncertainty reporting is still absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OCR-Reasoning benchmark, with matching authors, core dataset statistics, evaluation framework, and retained experiments. Their text, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds model evaluations, scoring validation, few-shot experiments, error analysis, synthetic-data fine-tuning, and a prompt ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original model accuracy, reasoning-process scores, CoT experiments, and qualitative error analyses in Tables 2–4 and Figures 5–6.

results.title: OCR-Reasoning Benchmark: Unveiling the True Capabilities of MLLMs in Complex Text-Rich Image Reasoning

C1.justification: Both versions claim a training-free, model-aware noise-selection framework using attention uncertainty, efficient Bernoulli approximation and layer truncation to improve video quality and alignment with modest overhead. V2's broader experiments support the existing generality claim; the abstract's generalized backbone and overhead wording does not materially redefine the central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly interprets seed quality as prompt-dependent and connects selection to attention stability, smoother latent trajectories and expressiveness. Appendices G-I add interpretations concerning attention type, CFG interaction and benefits beyond additional computation. The discussion adds compatibility with preference refinement and proposed Self-Forcing integration. Existing failure limitations remain, while v1's explicit caveat about possible BANSA-E bias is removed.

D1.justification: V2 supplies additional configuration details: 480p Wan2.1 and 360p HunyuanVideo evaluation, 50 sampling steps for the added backbones, and layer cutoffs of 10 for AnimateDiff and approximately 20 for HunyuanVideo/Wan2.1. Existing H100 hardware, noise-pool and masking settings, score-normalization instructions, project-page link and promised future prompt-list release are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds MSR-VTT test captions and corresponding real reference videos for motion evaluation (Table 6). This extends data coverage within the existing text-to-video task; VBench-long remains the principal benchmark. Additional model backbones primarily change experimental configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V1 explicitly omits quantitative noise-prior comparisons. V2 Table 4 evaluates FreqPrior on AnimateDiff alongside vanilla generation, ANSE and FreqPrior plus ANSE, introducing a substantive external-method comparison and combination test. The random, entropy and dropout acquisition comparisons are retained. FreeInit remains discussed without a reported evaluated comparison.

E3.justification: V2 adds AnimateDiff, HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1 and IPOC-2B configurations, quality-only evaluation for HunyuanVideo/Wan2.1, and FVMD evaluation using 200 MSR-VTT test prompts and real references. New controls compare CFG scales 5.0/7.5 and 50/60 sampling steps. Appendix K introduces a randomized, blinded human study with 30 prompts and 12 evaluators. The reported VBench video count changes from 4,730 to 4,750; the PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: New Section 4 tests cross-prompt seed transfer, attention-map consistency and latent trajectory behavior. Section 6 and Appendices G-I add masking-probability sensitivity, self- versus cross-attention analysis, CFG interaction and an equivalent-compute control; Figure 5 adds score-quality correlations. These substantially expand diagnostic evidence. The original ensemble-size, pool-size, reversed-selection, truncated-layer and temporal-scope analyses remain.

E5.justification: V1 provides point estimates without comparable confidence-interval reporting. V2 newly states five evaluation repetitions and reports 95% confidence intervals from ten runs using random subsets of 100 videos (Appendix J, Tables 17-19). This substantially changes uncertainty reporting, but does not establish an increase in independent full-generation runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive backbone, comparator, motion, human-preference and diagnostic results. For example, its new MSR-VTT comparison reports Wan2.1 FVMD of 16495.59 for vanilla generation versus 14306.19 with ANSE (Table 6). Original CogVideoX aggregate quality, semantic and total scores remain unchanged. However, main-table CogVideoX-5B inference times change from 1223.5/1392.1 to 667.3/754.1 seconds for vanilla/ANSE; these unexplained revisions should not be interpreted as demonstrated speedups under identical conditions.

M1.justification: The specified masking procedure changes from Softmax(QK^T multiplied by a mask) in v1 Equation 7 to masking attention probabilities and renormalizing rows in v2 Section 3.2. This locally revises stochastic attention construction while retaining seed minimization, single-step scoring and layer truncation. However, v2 Figure 3 still depicts the old construction, leaving implementation ambiguity. The score-sign correction alone does not establish changed selection behavior: v1's appendix already specifies the positive implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, preliminaries, methods, experiments and conclusion are rewritten or condensed. V2 introduces a dedicated noise-analysis section before experiments and reorganizes the appendix roadmap, removing the separate sign-convention discussion. Affiliation, acknowledgement and publication-header text also change. The editorial revision extends well beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: V2 adds numerous comparison, diagnostic and confidence-interval tables, a combined human-preference/correlation figure, and qualitative grids for additional backbones. Figure 4 replaces two CogVideoX examples with Wan2.1 examples. The original layer-correlation and noise-pool plots are retained but moved to appendix Figures 7-8; other original qualitative figures are also retained. The document adopts an ICLR layout with revised typography and headers.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for FVMD, MSR-VTT, iterative preference optimization and Self-Forcing, and discusses complementary relationships with noise priors and post-training refinement. The central positioning relative to BALD and prior noise-initialization methods remains. Switching from numbered to author-year citations is a presentation change.

T1.justification: V2 corrects the main BANSA and BANSA-E definitions to entropy of the mean minus mean entropy, matching v1's appendix implementation and proof. It removes v1's erroneous assertion that negating scores preserves their ordering. Proposition 1 and its Jensen-inequality proof are retained, so this is a localized mathematical correction rather than new theory. Figure 3 still contains the old sign.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's lack of an evaluated external noise-prior baseline and quantified uncertainty or human validation. Broader backbone tests, motion evaluation and compute/attention controls materially strengthen the evidence for generality and the proposed mechanism. Correcting the main score equations also improves mathematical clarity. Figure 3 still conflicts with the revised formulas, and the timing revisions and parts of the user-study protocol remain underexplained, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative and diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ANSE/BANSA research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds results for further backbones, FreqPrior comparisons, MSR-VTT motion evaluation, human preferences and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original CogVideoX generation experiments, VBench measurements, acquisition-function comparisons and ablations, including additional experiments in its appendices.

results.title: Model Already Knows the Best Noise: Bayesian Active Noise Selection via Attention  in Video Diffusion Model

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion shift the novelty claim from constructing a novel latent space to proposing refinement that exploits a latent space inherent in set propagation. The separate latent-space contribution is absorbed into the refinement contribution. The main claims of faster branch-and-bound verification and competitive performance remain.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly states that refinement preserves unsafe-input coverage rather than the full output enclosure. Appendix C explains why overhead can outweigh refinement benefits on low-dimensional benchmarks and how reduced batch sizes affect per-iteration costs. Appendices B and D add mechanism explanations for enclosure-gradient splitting and the practical adequacy of approximate bounds. These substantially qualify when and why acceleration occurs.

D1.justification: V3 newly discloses eight refinement iterations, at most four bounding iterations, aggregation over mutually solved instances for specified ablations, and the counterexample numerical-tolerance convention. It also updates hardware specifications. These disclosures do not establish that previously unspecified choices changed. V1's explicit main-result batch-size and automatic halving on out-of-memory errors are no longer stated.

E1.justification: Table 1 retains all seven original benchmarks and adds linearizenn, covering neural networks for autonomous aircraft taxiing. The expanded appendix experiments otherwise use tasks already represented in the main evaluation.

E2.justification: The five main comparators—alpha-beta-CROWN, NeuralSAT, PyRAT, Marabou and nnenum—remain unchanged. Within ablations, v3 removes the center-point falsifier and separate network-wise/layer-wise refinement comparison, while adding Local Gradient and exact constrained-zonotope bounds as comparators in Tables 4 and 6.

E3.justification: Appendix A changes the evaluation hardware from an EPYC/A100 server to an i7-13700H/RTX 4070 laptop. The GPU study replaces acasxu property-specific average times and matched CPU/GPU batch sizes with acasxu/safenlp maximum times at CPU batch 1 and GPU batches 128/1024. The revised falsification study specifies 50 iterations; the new exact-bounds experiment uses 45 acasxu instances with timeouts disabled.

E4.justification: The limited refinement-count ablation becomes an eight-benchmark analysis of solved instances, subproblem counts, runtime and per-iteration overhead (Tables 2 and 5). New studies examine enclosure-gradient versus local-gradient splitting and approximate versus exact bounds (Tables 4 and 6). Conversely, network-wise versus layer-wise refinement and several matched CPU/GPU batch controls disappear.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional averages and maxima in v3 summarize instance workloads and computational costs rather than uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes the proposed tool's solved rates from 98.9% to 99.5% on acasxu, 80.0% to 81.1% on cora, 96.0% to 97.0% on metaroom, and 84.3% to 89.2% on safenlp; linearizenn adds 100.0% (59 verified/1 falsified). These are revised results under changed settings, not isolated same-setting gains. Tables 4–6 add substantial heuristic, overhead and bounding results, including 823.3s versus 1.0s average time for exact versus approximate bounds.

M1.justification: The latent-space refinement, set-based falsification and branch-and-bound framework remain. Changes concern the reported splitting procedure: v1 refines before splitting and specifies sensitive input-dimension splits; v3 splits before refinement and ranks input dimensions or unstable ReLU neurons using gradients of the output enclosure's F-radius (Section 4, Appendix B).

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative remains recognizable, with targeted rewrites of the abstract, contributions, evaluation and conclusion. Section 3 is retitled, Section 4's numbered subsections become paragraph headings, and existing implementation/proof appendices move to D/F. Acknowledgements and an LLM-use disclosure are added; much foundational prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 adopts the ICLR template, revises legends in Figures 1–3 and adds Figure 4 illustrating approximate versus exact bounds. Table 1 gains a benchmark column, the ablation displays are substantially reorganized into Tables 2–3, and Tables 4–6 add heuristic, comprehensive refinement-cost and bounding comparisons. This materially expands and restructures the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V3 adds Combastel on the F-radius, Yang et al. on refinement, and Kotha et al. and Zhang et al. on neural network preimages. Section 6 adds a substantive comparison between its simultaneous constraint/dimension refinement and prior preimage approaches. Most existing related-work coverage remains.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds Proposition 4 and its proof, giving per-iteration complexity O(kappa q^3 + xi p q^2). Equation 13 corrects the positive/negative generator handling in v1's final interval-bound expression, Equation 10. The central unsafe-input enclosure proposition, bounding proposition and soundness corollary remain; relocating their proofs does not constitute new theory.

improvement.justification: V1's subproblem-count evidence left the practical cost of refinement and approximate bounding insufficiently tested. V3 substantially addresses these gaps through cross-benchmark runtime/overhead analyses, the exact-bounds comparison, and explicit discussion of slowdown cases, supported by complexity analysis and additional implementation details. These gains outweigh the loss of some earlier controls. Remaining weaknesses include unmatched CPU/GPU batch sizes and the incorrect claim of '60.3% more' falsifications despite Table 3b reporting 647 versus 257.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same latent-space approach to neural network verification. All 13 pages of v1.pdf and 18 pages of v3.pdf, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: Tables 1–6 report original verification results and ablations, including new splitting-heuristic and approximate-versus-exact bounding comparisons in the appendices.

before.justification: Tables 1–3 report original verification results and refinement, GPU/batch-size and falsification ablations, separately from results attributed to VNN-COMP.

results.title: Out of the Shadows: Exploring a Latent Space for Neural Network Verification

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion broaden the central contribution from one proposed negative-cosine schedule to a family of effective temperature schedules, explicitly including simple monotonic increases. The retained claims concern improved open- and closed-set recognition without additional computational overhead, particularly on harder semantic-shift benchmarks.

C2.justification: v2 adds a familiarity-hypothesis rationale and explains descending phases and periodic restarts as opportunities to refine instance-specific features and explore nearby solutions. Appendix F.6 adds a ceiling-effect explanation for small CIFAR gains. The earlier limitation concerning few training classes is largely retained there rather than removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds software versions, the ARPL loss weight, and ProtoCon implementation equations. However, v1's explicit project-code URL and statement that code is available are replaced by a future-release promise. The hardware, training-time range, and scheduler code example are largely retained or relocated; the PDFs alone do not establish actual external repository availability.

E1.justification: Reported dataset and task coverage remains CIFAR10, CIFAR+10, CIFAR+50, TinyImageNet, CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, and Stanford Cars, with closed-set classification and open-set recognition. CIFAR evaluations remain in Appendix F.6. The new TinyViT and ProtoCon experiments use existing benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands CE schedule comparisons with controls including random, linear-decrease, logarithmic-increase, and monotonic cosine schedules, and adds a ProtoCon baseline on TinyImageNet. It removes ConOSR comparisons, CE comparisons on CIFAR, and the SSB SupCon+CosSch comparison. The old TinyImageNet step-up and resetting Half-NegCosSch comparisons also disappear. ARPL was already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce a pretrained TinyViT backbone on CUB, CE without label smoothing and SupCon with label smoothing on TinyImageNet, and a TinyImageNet period comparison using P=100 and P=200. The established benchmark splits, evaluation metrics, CNN configurations, and 600-epoch training regime otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Table 1 systematically tests schedule shape and direction across CE experiments on TinyImageNet and all three SSBs, substantially extending v1's limited alternative-schedule analysis. Appendix F.4 adds period sensitivity tests, and F.2 tests applicability to TinyViT. Existing temperature-range, phase-shift, and training-class-count analyses remain rather than being entirely new.

E5.justification: v1 reports standard deviations across five regular-benchmark splits and error bars for the training-class study. v2 newly specifies five random seeds per split and supplies extensive seed-based standard-deviation tables for its main schedule and loss comparisons (Tables 3–4). Conversely, CIFAR standard deviations disappear from the retained results. The PDFs do not establish an explicit increase from a known previous seed count.

E6.justification: Many SSB values are revised: CUB CE-without-LS accuracy changes from 84.60/86.20 for baseline/periodic NegCosSch in v1 to 84.43/86.30 in v2. Numerous new schedule, TinyViT, ProtoCon, and period-sensitivity results appear, while ConOSR and other comparison results disappear. CIFAR accuracy and AUROC values are retained, with OSCR entries added. These are revised and expanded reported results, not demonstrated same-setting algorithmic gains between versions.

M1.justification: v2 retains periodic NegCosSch but expands the proposed method to include a single monotonic negative-cosine increase and linear and exponential increases over training (Section 4.3 and Appendix B). This materially broadens the scheduling procedures. v1's Half-NegCosSch ablation resets the temperature and is not equivalent to the new full-training monotonic schedule.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: temperature effects become a separate section, the method is divided into rationale and schedule choices, and the results emphasize schedule and loss comparisons. Regular-benchmark analyses and limitations move into expanded appendices. The introduction and related work are rewritten, and a reproducibility statement replaces the acknowledgments section.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn to include monotonic schedules; the main results tables are extensively restructured into dataset panels and separate loss/schedule columns. New variability, architecture, prototype-loss, and period tables are added. The regular-benchmark plot moves to the appendix with reordered panels, alongside document-wide typography, heading, and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds research connections and citations concerning the familiarity hypothesis, fine-grained OSR, TinyViT, and open-world prompt tuning. Most existing related-work discussion and positioning remain. Kukleva et al.'s updated publication information refers to the same work and is not a new citation.

T1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix C add explicit temperature-dependent gradient derivations for negative and positive SupCon pairs and CE, where v1 provided qualitative explanations. New schedule formulas are also defined. These are localized analytical additions; the OSR assumptions remain unchanged, and no new theorem or performance guarantee is established.

improvement.justification: v1 had limited alternative-schedule controls and no uncertainty estimates for its main SSB results. v2's broader schedule comparisons distinguish the benefits of increasing temperature from the particular periodic cosine shape, while Tables 3–4 make variability in the central results assessable. Together with architecture and loss checks, this substantially strengthens the empirical foundation. Removing some comparisons and replacing the available-code link with a future-release promise weakens completeness and reproducibility, but does not outweigh the improved validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same temperature-modulated open-set recognition research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments and expanded schedule, architecture, loss-function, and sensitivity evaluations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original recognition experiments, temperature-schedule comparisons, representation visualizations, and training-class ablations, including supplementary results.

results.title: Boosting Open Set Recognition Performance through Modulated Representation Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion now present three algorithms and claim that DB-MPA-LS preserves approximately DB-MPA-level alignment while eliminating inference cost that scales linearly with the number of rewards. This adds a central efficiency contribution to the retained inference-time reward and KL alignment claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains the small training set through RL-convergence considerations, excludes sampling-based KL blending when coefficients are negative, and suggests VAE noise sensitivity explains CoDe's SDXL behavior. It removes v1's explicit memory limitation and distillation/parameter-sharing future directions. The warning about very small KL regularization remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds sampling pseudocode, prompt-generation instructions and SDXL training-time information. It removes the printed train/test prompt lists and explicit GPU-count/capacity details, referring readers to code for prompt lists. Existing optimizer and LoRA hyperparameters and the underlying code link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on GenEval, extending coverage to counting, spatial relations and other compositional tasks. It also introduces JPEG compressibility objectives and four-reward alignment. Short-DrawBench is the retained DrawBench color subset under a new name; its larger test-set size is a protocol change.

E2.justification: The external comparator lineup remains Stable Diffusion, Rewarded Soup, CoDe, RGG and MORL. However, matched comparisons in Table 1 and Figure 2 now additionally evaluate DB-MPA-LS alongside DB-MPA, expanding the comparison lineup with the new proposed variant.

E3.justification: The main evaluation changes from 25 to 1,000 test prompts. New protocols include 550 GenEval training prompts with 700 held-out prompts, uniform-weight reward-count comparisons, and single-prompt SDXL fine-tuning with specified preference sweeps. These substantially expand evaluation design and model configurations.

E4.justification: Appendices C.3–C.7 add analyses of strongly conflicting rewards, scaling from two to four rewards, transfer to a larger SDXL backbone, and visual agreement between DB-MPA and its sampling approximation. These examine limitations and approximation quality beyond the earlier preference sweeps and qualitative examples.

E5.justification: v1 specifies 32 images per prompt with shared fixed seeds. v2 reports 30 seeds per prompt for retained training and three-reward evaluations, and 64 seeds per SDXL evaluation point, while omitting a general count for the expanded main tests. Neither version reports confidence intervals or significance tests; these disclosures do not establish additional training replications.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the earlier test results: DB-MPA at w=0.5 changes from reward pair (0.70, 0.32) to (0.27, 0.21), under different test sets, not a demonstrated performance decline. v2 adds extensive results for the new scenarios and reports DB-MPA-LS at 5.64 versus DB-MPA's 11.11 seconds per image.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 introduces DB-MPA-LS, which samples one reward-specific LoRA adapter per denoising step according to preference weights instead of evaluating and blending all models. This substantially changes inference computation. The original DB-MPA and DB-KLA procedures remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable. v2 condenses related work and original algorithm descriptions, reorganizes experimental appendix subsections, shortens captions, updates author/conference text and adds an LLM-use disclosure. Much of the original explanatory prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands tables and figures for GenEval, conflicting rewards, reward scaling, SDXL and DB-MPA-LS, and restructures Table 1 and Figure 2. The prompt table and original Figure 5 comparison grids disappear. Earlier Table 3 and Figures 7–11 survive as Table 2 and Figures 8 and 12–15.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds positioning against multi-LoRA composition, citing Zhong et al. (2024) and Zou et al. (2025) and contrasting heuristic scheduling with reward-aligned blending. Earlier diffusion-guidance, RL and LLM relationships are largely retained in condensed form.

T1.justification: v2 adds a marginal-distribution equivalence proposition for random drift selection and its proof in Appendix A.4. It also corrects Proposition 1 from f_pre + u to f_pre - beta(t)u, propagating the scaling and sign corrections through Lemma 2 and Appendix A.3. The earlier general Proposition 2 is retained as Proposition 3.

improvement.justification: The tested efficient variant, broader compositional evaluation and stress analyses substantially address v1's inference-cost and validation limitations, while corrected drift equations improve mathematical consistency. Reporting weaknesses temper these gains: prompt lists disappear, and some new aggregate scores are inconsistent—for example, Table 5's w=0.8 components imply 1.044 rather than the reported 0.88. These weaken exact effect-size claims but do not outweigh the substantial methodological and evidential improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Diffusion Blend, with matching core methods and substantial retained content. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations of DB-MPA-LS, GenEval, conflicting rewards, reward-count scaling and SDXL in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation experiments, reward measurements, inference timings and qualitative comparisons in Section 5 and Appendices C–D.

results.title: Diffusion Blend: Inference-Time Multi-Preference Alignment for Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion add a principal claim of 2.73–5.18 times higher throughput than the original 16-bit models. This expands the claimed contribution from accuracy under memory constraints to measured inference acceleration. The original methodological contributions and up-to-8% accuracy claim are retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of the accuracy–throughput tradeoff, memory-constrained comparisons, short-output applicability and sparse-attention compatibility. Appendix C.8 explains different benefits for short responses and long responses whose early tokens use higher precision. Section 4.4.3 explicitly qualifies aggressive interpolation scaling. The original limitations remain essentially unchanged in Appendix E.

D1.justification: v2 documents using KIVI's inference engine and 2/4-bit CUDA kernels, alongside newly implemented 8/16-bit and shrinking kernels. It also discloses BF16 model weights, OpenCompass scoring, KVTuner quantization settings, throughput configurations and preparation times. These substantially improve implementation documentation. Both versions advertise the same code repository.

E1.justification: v2 adds IFEval instruction following with short outputs, substantially extending coverage beyond competition mathematics and code generation (Appendix C.2, Table 6). Existing evaluation and calibration datasets are retained. Changing CMIMC-2025 to CMIMC-2024 in the setup prose aligns it with the existing Table 2 label rather than establishing a dataset replacement.

E2.justification: The original Table 2 comparators are retained. v2 additionally evaluates KVTuner for mixed-precision reasoning accuracy (Table 8), QuestAttention as the control for combined sparse attention and quantization (Table 10), and QServe for calibration time (Table 11). This substantially broadens the evaluated comparison methods and controls.

E3.justification: New protocols include A100-80G throughput measurements at 16K/24K/32K output lengths with different feasible batch sizes, memory-triggered truncation of higher-bit KIVI, and additional memory/bit-width configurations. IFEval introduces strict/loose prompt and instruction metrics with one response per prompt. MiKV's preserved cache is described as BF16 instead of FP16, a reported setting revision that does not establish rerunning the retained results.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of throughput versus output length, higher-bit KIVI under memory limits, hardware-memory sensitivity, sparse-attention compatibility, preparation overhead, and response-length distributions (Section 4.3; Appendices C.3 and C.5–C.8). The original shrinking and interpolation ablations and block-sensitivity analyses are retained; moving Figure 3 into the main text is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Table 2 retains its existing plus/minus reporting unchanged. Neither version supplies explicit seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or additional experiment-level repetition information. The new tables use point estimates, a practice already present in v1's ablations.

E6.justification: Table 2 and the original ablation tables retain identical numerical results. Substantial new results include throughput of 2.73–5.18 times the original 16-bit models, IFEval scores, and KVTuner comparisons: AIME-2024 pass@1 is 40.21 for PM-KVQ versus 34.17 for KVTuner. Tables 7 and 9–12 add memory-constrained accuracy, sparse-attention results, calibration timing and response-length counts.

M1.justification: v2 adds an evaluated PM-KVQ plus QuestAttention combination, extending inference to sparse attention (Appendix C.6, Table 10). The core progressive quantization schedule, Equivalent Right Shift, sensitivity-based allocation, positional-interpolation calibration and Section 3 pipeline remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains recognizable, with localized shortening, wording corrections and expanded explanations. Small-model sensitivity discussion moves into the main ablations; Broader Impacts becomes an Ethics Statement, and reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added. The conference header and author-role note also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a throughput table and seven appendix tables, substantially expanding the visual presentation of evidence. Existing ablation tables are renumbered, Figure 3 moves into the main text, and Figure 2 is relocated. The original figures retain their graphical content, while conference typography, headings and page layout replace the preprint styling.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to KVTuner, Quest, IFEval and OpenCompass and connects them to the additional evaluations. The original related-work coverage and central positioning remain largely intact. The switch from numbered to author–year citations does not itself change research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix D introduces Theorem D.1 and a detailed quotient-and-remainder proof of Equivalent Right Shift, whereas v1 states the equivalence without proof. This adds substantive formal reasoning for the existing formula. However, the new proof contains an incorrect inequality in Equation (25).

improvement.justification: v1 evaluates accuracy through fake quantization but lacks measured deployment efficiency. v2 substantially addresses that gap with CUDA-based throughput measurements and preparation costs, while KVTuner and memory-limited KIVI comparisons strengthen evaluation of the central memory-allocation approach. It also exposes the throughput cost relative to KIVI rather than presenting acceleration alone. The local proof error in Equation (25) and unchanged limitations text need correction, but do not outweigh these substantial empirical and reproducibility gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PM-KVQ research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched reliably across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds throughput measurements, instruction-following evaluations, additional comparisons, and implementation-cost analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning and coding evaluations, quantization ablations, and transformer-block sensitivity analyses in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: PM-KVQ: Progressive Mixed-precision KV Cache Quantization for Long-CoT LLMs

C1.justification: v1’s headline claims of over four AUROC points improvement for mortality prediction and nearly two points for CD are removed. v3 instead claims state-of-the-art ICU length-of-stay and CD prediction and explicitly promotes learning without information loss or imputation. The central interpretability and increased-expressivity contributions remain.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly interprets the existing perturbation analysis as a quantitative measure of faithfulness by construction, interprets the new ablations as evidence that the components are critical, and discusses calibration as reliability evidence. Its performance discussion also avoids v1’s blanket 'fully interpretable' description. The principal clinical interpretations and grouping-versus-interpretability trade-off remain.

D1.justification: v3 substantially revises reproducibility documentation: it replaces dataset-specific training recipes with a shared recipe, removes embedding-width ranges and separate GossipCop hardware details, and adds CD control-selection details, explicit alternative biomarker-group memberships, and Gaussian perturbation instructions. These include both added and lost information. The statement that code is provided in supplementary material is unchanged.

E1.justification: The reported P12 target changes from in-hospital mortality to whether ICU length of stay exceeds 72 hours. v3 also evaluates CD under additive measurement noise, multiplicative measurement noise, and temporal perturbations. The underlying P12, Danish CD, and GossipCop datasets remain; the stale mortality heading in Appendix F does not establish an additional retained mortality experiment.

E2.justification: For CD, v3 removes Random Forest, Naive Bayes, and Gradient Boosting, retains Transformer and Trans-mean, and adds GRU-D, SeFT, mTAND, DGM2, MTGNN, and Raindrop. The corresponding P12 comparison drops IP-Net. The four GossipCop comparators remain unchanged. This substantially revises comparator membership within the existing medical evaluations.

E3.justification: Medical evaluation switches from AUROC to AUPRC. Appendix F reports a shared 100-epoch setup instead of v1’s task-specific maxima of 300, 500, and 400 epochs, with revised batch sizes, regularization, and architecture search ranges. v3 also introduces calibration and clean-training/noisy-testing protocols. These are reported setting changes, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds five CD component ablations testing DeepSet aggregation, learned distance weighting, and alternatives to ExtGNAN, including standard GNAN. Appendix G adds calibration assessment and controlled additive, multiplicative, and temporal-noise robustness tests. These substantially extend v1’s node/subset attribution analyses, which are largely retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means and standard deviations over three seeds or runs. v3 additionally specifies that calibration ECE uncertainty is calculated over three data splits. This is limited additional repetition information, not evidence of increased benchmark run counts; no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v1’s medical AUROC results of 76.64 ± 1.2 for P12 and 83.64 ± 0.9 for CD are replaced by AUPRC results of 97.41 ± 0.38 for ICU length of stay and 83.93 ± 0.27 for CD. Different targets, metrics, and settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains. v3 Tables 3–8 add ablation, grouping, calibration, and robustness results. GossipCop accuracy remains 97.34 ± 0.2, with unchanged comparator scores.

M1.justification: The ExtGNAN, DeepSet aggregation, and additive prediction architecture remain substantially unchanged under renaming. v3 adds a reachability-conditioned distance definition in Section 3 and an optional sparse, adjacent-node masking adaptation in Appendix C. These are limited procedural additions; their use in the reported experiments is not established.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming GMAN to SuperMAN and changing the title, v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and conclusion, expands the graph-input explanation, combines the separate medical-task presentations into shared Data/Setup/Results passages, and reorganizes the appendices into lettered sections. These are substantial editorial and structural revisions.

P2.justification: The two medical result tables are merged into a two-task table. v3 adds the ablation, grouping, calibration, and robustness tables and a calibration plot, while Figure 1 gains explicit graph/subset labels and an expanded caption. Figures 2–4 are largely retained with caption and placement changes. The document also adopts the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: v3 adds related-work citations to Tipirneni and Reddy (2022) and Labach et al. (2023), while removing citations including Friedman, Ho, and the IP-Net paper. It more explicitly contrasts its multi-level interpretability and arbitrary-graph support with earlier temporal models. The overall positioning around GNAN and irregular-data learning remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: The XOR-based expressivity proofs and four-point recoverability argument are retained from v1 Section 6 in v3 Appendix B. v3 adds a reachability-conditioned distance definition and Appendix C’s computational scaling analysis, including O(m K n^2 d_psi) cost and a sparse-masking argument. These are bounded additions rather than replacements of the central theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its architectural choices mainly through overall scores and attribution examples. v3’s component ablations, including direct GNAN and aggregation controls, address the important missing evidence about which innovations contribute to performance. Quantified grouping comparisons and controlled noise tests further strengthen assessment of the central design. This constitutes a substantial evidential improvement, although lost dataset-specific implementation detail, inconsistent P12 descriptions, and unclear ECE scaling limit reproducibility and calibration claims. The changed medical scores themselves do not establish improvement across versions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ExtGNAN and graph-subset framework, renamed from GMAN to SuperMAN. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions to the medical evaluation.

after.justification: v3 reports medical and GossipCop experiments, component ablations, grouping comparisons, calibration, and noise-robustness results in Tables 1–8 and accompanying figures.

before.justification: v1 reports original P12, Crohn’s disease, and GossipCop experiments in Tables 1–3, together with attribution analyses in Figures 2–4.

results.title: SuperMAN: Interpretable and Expressive Networks over Temporally Sparse Heterogeneous Data

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the novelty claim from the first cross-domain pairwise creativity evaluator to being among the first. The principal claims about CreataSet, human alignment, domain generalization, and using CrEval to enhance creativity remain.

C2.justification: Appendices A.1–A.2 add substantive arguments about subjectivity, consensus versus conformity, and pairwise versus absolute assessment. Appendices A.4–A.5 add interpretations of creative attributes, subtle-preference failures, and preservation of reasoning and truthfulness. V2 explicitly identifies the dataset as predominantly Simplified Chinese and discusses linguistic applicability. The original limitations and societal-impact passages are retained.

D1.justification: V2 documents k=5, taxonomy construction, both Qwen backbones, and annotator recruitment, demographics, and compensation. Core hyperparameters, hardware, and prompt templates are retained, while the DPO evaluation's explicit three-rater count is omitted. The new Reproducibility Statement claims public code, data, and models, although Appendix A.3.2 retains future-release wording; actual availability is unresolved by the PDFs.

E1.justification: V2 adds WritingPrompts and the Alternative Uses Task to the retained creative-writing generalization evaluation (Section 4.4). Appendix A.4.5 additionally evaluates creativity-enhanced models on MATH, HumanEval, and TruthfulQA, extending coverage to mathematical reasoning, code generation, and truthfulness. CreataSet's original coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Creativity Index and replaces Gemini-2.0-Pro/Flash with Gemini-2.5-Pro/Flash. The retained creative-writing OOD comparison drops Qwen2.5-14B/72B, LLaMA3.1-70B, Gemma-3-12B/27B, and Prometheus-13B (v1 Figure 9; v2 Figure 8). Appendix A.4.2 adds a Bradley-Terry loss comparator. LitBench is discussed but is not evaluated as an evaluator baseline.

E3.justification: Section 3.3 replaces validation using 50 response pairs per model/prompt combination with a description specifying 150 groups and 1,050 pairs. New protocols select 213 WritingPrompts pairs using a like-count gap greater than 10 and 541 AUT pairs using a human-score gap greater than two. The appendices add defined pilot/diversity assessments and TruthfulQA metrics. These changes do not establish rerunning the retained main experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds a response-swapping ablation, classification-versus-Bradley-Terry loss comparison, absolute-scoring pilot, response-diversity assessment, analysis of attributes associated with CrEval choices, and success/failure cases. It also tests whether creativity tuning compromises reasoning or truthfulness. The original data-composition, data-scale, backbone, and DPO difficulty analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain deterministic evaluation and ICC-based annotation-reliability reporting. Neither documents repeated training runs, random seeds, confidence intervals, or a significance-testing procedure. V2 calls the newly reported reasoning differences statistically nonsignificant, but provides no test details; this is an added significance outcome rather than a documented statistical-method change.

E6.justification: Pseudo-label validation accuracies change from 90.4%/87% to 86.6%/81.4% under the revised sampling description. V2 newly reports CrEval-7B F1/agreement of 58.22%/45.54% on WritingPrompts and 92.46%/78.37% on AUT, plus diagnostic and capability-preservation results. Gemini results are replaced for newer model versions, and the CrEval-14B OOD result is removed. Main Table 2 CrEval scores and existing DPO results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The data-construction pipeline, pseudo-labeling heuristics, classification objective, response swapping, negative sampling, and three-way inference remain unchanged. Bradley-Terry training and omission of response swapping appear as new experimental comparisons. Explicitly documenting both Qwen backbones and k=5 does not establish a method revision.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites paragraphs in the introduction, related work, method overview, and results discussion. The separate A–G appendices are reorganized into one Appendix A with eleven subsections. Ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added, alongside revised headings and conference-status text.

P2.justification: The OOD mirrored bar chart becomes three heatmaps, Table 2 gains improvement rows and colored highlighting, and five appendix tables are added. The consistency plot gains an ablation bar. V1 Figure 5 moves to the appendix as v2 Figure 11, with other plots resized or repositioned. The conference template also changes title treatment, headers, typography, and layout.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of Creativity Index, LitBench's specialized reward models, and critical work on creativity evaluation, alongside additional psychological literature supporting its consensus-based framing. These refine comparisons and qualify novelty while preserving the central positioning as a cross-domain, text-level LLM evaluator.

T1.justification: Equation 1, the pairwise formulation, and the two pseudo-labeling assumptions are retained. The new Bradley-Terry discussion is explanatory and empirical; it introduces no formal derivation, theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens v1's narrow external validation, previously limited to 36 creative-writing pairs, and addresses its lack of checks on other capabilities after creativity tuning. The added AUT/WritingPrompts evaluations, loss and position ablations, reasoning/TruthfulQA checks, and failure examples provide substantial supporting and diagnostic evidence. These gains outweigh the removal of larger-model OOD comparisons, although popularity-based labels and underspecified statistical claims limit the strength of some conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CreataSet/CrEval study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, diagnostic analyses, and human assessments in Section 4 and Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original human-annotation results, evaluator comparisons, training ablations, out-of-distribution evaluation, and creativity-enhancement experiments in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Evaluating Text Creativity across Diverse Domains: a Dataset and Large Language Model Evaluator

C1.justification: The central weight-informed activation contribution remains, but v2's introduction and conclusion expand its claimed applicability to quantized inference and add long-context, social-bias and measured kernel-acceleration contributions. The introduction drops v1's explicit claim of guarantees extending under monotone activation assumptions. The abstract also removes the specific 2.94% performance headline.

C2.justification: v2 introduces implicit regularization or harmful-neuron suppression as possible explanations for HumanEval improvements, and bandwidth saturation as an explanation for declining speedups with larger batches. It interprets bias changes while explicitly limiting generalization beyond tested dimensions. Its limitations discuss preprocessing and gating overhead, replacing v1's main limitation concerning incomplete comparator coverage.

D1.justification: v2 adds transformation pseudocode and runtime estimates, offline norm precomputation, Triton-kernel details and hardware-benchmark settings. Resource reporting changes from two A100 GPUs for a couple of days to one A100 for several days plus A800 and Blackwell benchmarking. However, v1's Alpaca calibration description and explicit experimental top-K-versus-threshold rationale disappear; this does not establish an actual procedure change.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's six downstream benchmarks, v2 evaluates SciQ, OpenBookQA, BoolQ, ARC-Easy and HumanEval. LongBench adds long-context summarization, QA, code completion and other tasks; CrowS-Pairs adds gender, race and religion bias evaluation. These substantially broaden the represented tasks and test scenarios.

E2.justification: v1's numerical comparisons evaluate TEAL and TEAL-transform; CATS appears in discussion and a conceptual comparison but has no reported benchmark scores. v2 adds evaluated CATS and R-Sparse comparisons in Tables 3-5. TEAL-transform survives as a Llama-focused control in Table 8, while its Phi-4 comparisons are removed.

E3.justification: The model suite replaces Qwen-2.5-7B with Mistral-7B. New protocols include FP16/INT8/INT4 comparisons, synthetic network approximation-error evaluation, LongBench evaluations at 4K/8K/16K context windows, and GEMV latency measurements across matrix shapes, batch sizes and three GPU platforms. The existing 25%-65% sparsity settings and greedy allocation procedure remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds synthetic tests of the theoretical mechanism, quantization sensitivity, batch-size effects on acceleration and social-bias analysis. The orthogonalization control already existed through v1's TEAL-transform comparisons; v2 revises its benchmark scope and presents it separately in Table 8. These additions substantially extend the questions investigated beyond ordinary benchmark accuracy.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run counts or empirical uncertainty estimates. v2 Section 3.4 reports 20 random seeds and averaged results with plus/minus errors for synthetic experiments, without identifying the error statistic. LLM benchmark scores remain without error bars, justified in Section 4.1 by deterministic gating. This is a localized reporting addition, not evidence of increased repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark, synthetic-error, quantization, latency, LongBench and bias results, while removing Qwen results. Retained entries also change: WINA's Llama-3-8B GSM8K score at 65% sparsity is 7.05 in v1 Table 3 and 5.91 in v2 Table 10. Phi-4 MMLU and GSM8K scores carry over. Changed benchmark averages use different task sets and do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The weighted top-K gating rule in Equation 4, SVD-based orthogonal transformation and TEAL-derived greedy sparsity allocation are retained. Appendix A.2 expands the existing transformation into pseudocode. The Triton implementation and quantized evaluations do not establish a different activation-selection procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are substantially rewritten, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around commonsense reasoning, additional analyses, hardware acceleration and long-context tasks. The transformation discussion moves into an expanded appendix, and the former separate proof appendices become subsections within a broader appendix. Ethics and reproducibility statements also change the document structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with an added workflow and precision annotations; Figure 2 changes its panels, comparator curves and styling. v1's FLOP table becomes a percentage-reduction bar chart. Benchmark tables are reorganized by sparsity with highlighted WINA rows, and new latency plots, analysis tables and a pseudocode display substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to R-Sparse, TDA, SEAP and rotation/quantization research, while removing several pruning and distillation references. Appendix A.2 more explicitly attributes the transformation to SliceGPT. These update the surrounding literature and attribution while retaining WINA's central positioning as a training-free, weight-aware alternative to magnitude-based activation.

T1.justification: Lemma 3.1 replaces W-transpose-W equal to identity with a general diagonal matrix and states optimal-mask selection, already anticipated in v1's appendix. Theorem 3.2 replaces expected-error dominance over TEAL with upper-bound minimization. Appendix A.8 uses Young's inequality instead of assuming the cross-term vanishes. The monotone-activation definition, Lemma 3.4, Theorem 3.5 and their proofs are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical validation: measured GPU-kernel latency addresses v1's reliance on FLOP estimates, while broader comparator, quantization and long-context evaluations test important deployment claims. Transformation pseudocode also improves implementation transparency. These gains outweigh lost calibration documentation and remaining reporting problems, such as Table 5 giving R-Sparse 57.40 at 65% sparsity while its prose uses 59.91. The narrowed theory is useful, although Appendix A.8 still leaves its global separability argument insufficiently justified, and kernel measurements do not establish end-to-end inference speedups.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WINA framework and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be matched despite substantial revisions to the theory, experiments and organization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, synthetic experiments, quantization evaluations, GPU-kernel measurements, long-context evaluations and social-bias analyses, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original sparsity-performance evaluations on Qwen-2.5-7B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B and Phi-4-14B, including comparisons with TEAL and TEAL-transform.

results.title: WINA: Weight Informed Neuron Activation for Accelerating Large Language Model Inference

C1.justification: v3 withdraws the self-reparametrized KL as a principal contribution, reducing the introduction's contribution list from four items to three and revising the conclusion accordingly. The abstract newly claims priority for learning broken symmetries, and Section 4.2 extends the Hubbard performance claim to scalability at 18 × 100. The central symmetry-modulation contribution remains.

C2.justification: v3 attributes VMoNF's mode collapse to reverse-KL training rather than architectural inability, explicitly discusses ESS's dependence on mode coverage, and clarifies the data-free focus without restricting applicability to it. The existing limitations are largely retained, but their claimed applicability is narrowed from all presented methods to canonicalization and SESaMo.

D1.justification: Where v1 says code accompanies the supplement, v3 supplies a repository address, an archived implementation reference and MIT-license information. It adds training pseudocode, Python/PyTorch versions, VMoNF component counts and large-Hubbard hyperparameters. Existing GPU, optimizer and scheduler details remain. These are documented reproducibility improvements; external resource availability was not checked.

E1.justification: v3 adds an explicitly broken Z8 Gaussian-mixture target with alpha = 0.05 alongside the exact-symmetry case. Hubbard coverage expands from a 2 × 1 system to include an 18 × 100, temporally extended system with broken (Z2)^18 symmetry. The real and complex phi^4 scenarios already appear in v1.

E2.justification: The main comparisons add Flow Annealed Importance Sampling Bootstrap (FAB) and Variational Mixture of Normalizing Flows (VMoNF), replacing the standalone RealNVP column while retaining canonicalization. RealNVP remains in appendix comparisons. For the large Hubbard system, Table 1 reports FAB and canonicalization scores and no VMoNF score; the FAB entry conflicts with Section 4.2's statement that FAB is infeasible there.

E3.justification: v3 adds KL evaluation for targets with known normalization and changes the stated SESaMo training regime from gamma = 0.5 self-reparametrized KL to REINFORCE. The new large-Hubbard protocol uses ten coupling blocks, 100 neurons per layer and 20,000 steps. Appendix I introduces mixture-component choices and time-matched FAB training. These disclosures do not establish that retained appendix plots were regenerated.

E4.justification: The main density diagnostics now examine VMoNF's mode coverage, including collapse to three modes of the broken Gaussian mixture in v3 Figure 4; v1's corresponding figure examined RealNVP on the exact mixture. The temperature and symmetry-breaking sweeps, magnetization analysis and convergence plots in Appendix H are retained. There is no substantial new component-ablation study.

E5.justification: Both Table 1 captions report averages over ten models. Figures 9 and 14 retain means and standard deviations over ten independently seeded models, while Figures 10 and 12 retain three-model uncertainty estimates. Additional result rows and changed numerical uncertainties do not introduce a new statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes retained results and adds substantial new entries. Exact-GMM canonicalization ESS changes from 0.992(4) to 0.91(8), and SESaMo's exact complex-phi^4 ESS changes from 0.951(3) to 0.9472(8). v3 adds KL scores and large-Hubbard ESS values of 0.74(1) for SESaMo and 0.024(1) for canonicalization. Revised training and comparison settings preclude treating these as uniform same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces the self-reparametrized KL objective, including its importance-weighted partition-function term, with reverse KL plus the bijectivity penalty and a REINFORCE gradient estimator. Appendix E.3 also introduces a categorical modulation over product-symmetry sectors for larger Hubbard systems. These change the training procedure and its adaptation beyond the retained stochastic-modulation framework.

P1.justification: The overall narrative sequence and most background and appendix prose remain intact. Targeted revisions expand the modulation explanation, shorten the ELBO discussion and update the contribution narrative. Limitations move from Appendix A to Section 5; Appendix A becomes pseudocode, Appendix J disappears, and reproducibility and language-model-use statements are added.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially redesigned with volume and additional comparator columns, more scenarios, and separate ESS/KL blocks. The two main density comparisons are redrawn, an algorithm box is added, and the explanatory diagram moves from appendix Figure 5 to main-text Figure 3. The conference template and figure placement change throughout, while the appendix diagnostic plots are retained.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion largely persists, with a new comparison to Pires and Figueiredo's VMoNF for labelled data. References for FAB, stochastic-computation-graph gradient estimation, Adam and the implementation archive are added. v3 also makes the broken-symmetry priority claim explicit. Consolidated duplicate references do not represent removal of those works.

T1.justification: v1's Appendix J derivation claiming a vanishing reverse-KL gradient for the breaking parameter is removed; v3 Section 3.2 supplies a score-function gradient expression. Section 3.1 replaces the simple density-product expression with an explicit mixture density and modulation Jacobian. Appendix E.3 adds product-symmetry definitions and a categorical transformation. The canonicalization theorem and its Appendix C proof are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the training rationale by replacing the misleading zero-gradient argument with an explicit REINFORCE formulation. FAB/VMoNF comparisons, KL checks and the large-Hubbard experiment address important weaknesses in v1's empirical validation, while pseudocode and code/archive information improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting inconsistencies, including contradictory FAB-feasibility statements and Appendix G's retained claim that all systems have Nt = 1. The unchanged appendix plots nevertheless leave their relationship to the revised training procedure unclear.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SESaMo, with matching authors, methodological foundations and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original empirical results in Table 1 and Appendix H, including retained experiments and additional broken-symmetry Gaussian-mixture and large-volume Hubbard results.

before.justification: v1 reports original sampling experiments on Gaussian mixtures, real and complex phi^4 theories, and the Hubbard model, including ESS measurements, density plots and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: SESaMo: Symmetry-Enforcing Stochastic Modulation for Normalizing Flows

C1.justification: The central multi-view prediction and label-efficient pretraining contributions remain. v2 narrows the introduction's 'first predictive framework' claim to an 'underexplored problem' and the abstract's state-of-the-art comparison to several strong graph baselines. Headline improvements change from 12.12%/15.16% to explicitly averaged 6.90%/5.87% under expanded coverage.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of transfer to unseen agents/tools through structural and textual features, backbone robustness including the Mistral exception, and prompted LLM predictors' weaknesses. It qualifies zero search cost by excluding workflow-generation/update costs, adds amortization reasoning, and identifies independently curated benchmarks as a remaining evaluation need.

D1.justification: v2 documents node-aligned graph construction, attention/readout operations, the GCN backbone, embedding dimensions and token limits, and the 232,104-sample pretraining corpus with sampling and exclusion rules. It adds resource requirements and a source-code repository access statement. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's basic hyperparameters and embedding-model names.

E1.justification: v1's predictor benchmark uses only AFlow workflows; v2 adds the independently generated G-Designer workflow population and cross-system and disjoint-domain generalization scenarios (Tables 2–3 and 10–12). The original downstream datasets, including the appendix DROP and HotpotQA transfer evaluations, are retained.

E2.justification: Dir-GNN joins the main comparison, including the retained AFlow settings. Table 9 adds GPT-4.1, Claude 4 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.5 Flash as few-shot LLM performance predictors, substantially expanding comparator types. The original predictive and workflow-optimization comparators remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces cross-framework and six cross-domain train/test protocols, controlled GNN and controller-LLM substitutions, and five-shot LLM classification at temperature zero on up to 1,000 samples per task. It also adds training/inference resource profiling. The original split percentages, supervised training budget, accuracy metric, and utility metric remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to four controller LLMs and five GNN backbones, robustness under framework/domain shifts, and computational efficiency (Section 4.4 and Appendices B.1–B.4). The original input-view, graph-view, label-ratio, transfer, and case-study analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Tables 4 and 5 remove the standard deviations previously reported for the retained ablation means. Three-run averaging and Table 3 uncertainty reporting remain. The seed rule, 2^r, moves from a footnote to the Reproducibility Statement; no increase in runs is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial G-Designer, backbone, LLM, cost, and OOD results; Table 10 newly reports Agentic Predictor averages of 62.05 accuracy and 58.49 utility. Its original AFlow entries remain, while Table 3's average accuracy changes from 84.38 to 79.97 because coverage expands. Retained AFlow utility standard deviations change from 3.18 to 1.18 for GCN and 1.98 to 0.98 for GCN-II. v1 Table 6's optimization results are retained as v2 Table 13.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 substantially changes the reported pretraining procedure. v1 selects successful same-task workflows as contrastive positives and failed or mismatched workflows as negatives. v2 instead pairs different views of the same workflow, uses other batch configurations as negatives, and symmetrizes across three modality pairs without performance labels. The main multi-view predictor remains.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper and substantially rewrites contribution framing, related-work comparisons, and method explanations. Related-work subsections become paragraph headings, Algorithm 1 moves to a dedicated appendix, and the experimental appendices are reorganized. Acknowledgments, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: The paper adopts a different conference layout with changed typography, text width, and display placement. Tables 2–3 expand to distinguish G-Designer and AFlow, and seven new tables present cost, backbone, LLM, and OOD evidence. Existing figures are retained with resizing or relocation; the optimization table moves from Table 6 to Table 13.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LLM-PP, Dir-GNN, Sentence-BERT, and MONAQ, and removes DS-Agent. Section 2 describes FLORA-Bench as a released single-view benchmark and sharpens distinctions concerning representation, pretraining, and efficiency. The broader positioning around workflow prediction and NAS representation learning remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 redefines the positive and negative sets underlying the contrastive objective and specifies symmetric averaging across three modality pairs, changing its mathematical specification. The general optimization problem and loss templates remain; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the generalization and efficiency evidence beyond v1's AFlow-only predictor benchmark through G-Designer coverage, disjoint-system/domain tests, LLM comparisons, and resource measurements. It also makes the pretraining specification consistent with its label-free claim and clarifies previously unqualified search-cost reporting. Expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. Removing ablation standard deviations weakens reporting, but the gains address central weaknesses in methodological clarity and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Agentic Predictor. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, formatting, and expanded evaluation.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds workflow populations, backbone comparisons, LLM predictors, resource measurements, and out-of-distribution experiments in Section 4 and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original prediction experiments, component ablations, pretraining analyses, and workflow optimization and transfer results in Section 4 and Appendix A.

results.title: Multi-View Encoders for Performance Prediction in LLM-Based Agentic Workflows

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion update the headline token savings from 35% to 36%, consistent with the revised benchmark average. The central contributions—online sequential revision and reflection-aware rewards that reduce reasoning length while preserving performance—remain the same.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 changes the explanation of the component trade-off from overlapping encouragement of reflection to tension between penalizing overthinking and encouraging reflection.
