New appendix discussions interpret transfer across domains/model sizes, explain why reflection-token heuristics truncate useful reasoning, and distinguish local latency overhead from potential large-scale token-cost savings.

D1.justification: v2 adds checkpoint/prompt sourcing for new baselines, the NoThink prompt, QA data-construction and generation details, and per-batch token and timing measurements. Its reproducibility statement explicitly includes configuration files and evaluation scripts at the existing repository. Most core hyperparameters, prompts, hardware, and total training times were already disclosed in v1.

E1.justification: v2 removes OlympiadBench from the evaluated math suite, retaining the other five benchmarks and DeepScaleR training data. Appendix B.3 adds training and evaluation on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and SuperGPQA, substantially extending coverage from mathematical problem solving to general multiple-choice QA.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds evaluated NoThink, ShorterBetter, Light-R1, DAST, and Arora–Zanette baselines. Table 3 adds untrained Qwen-7B revision with and without gold answers; v1's trained '7B Revise' rows instead correspond to v2's MReflect rows. Table 9 adds first- and fifth-reflection heuristic truncation baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix B.3 introduces 1.5B policy and 4B reflection-model configurations, a mixed QA training set, shortest-path filtering, 5,000 test examples per QA dataset, and one generated path per test question. The reported main training budget also changes from 1,800 steps to one epoch with matched steps for other methods; this does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds untrained-detector comparisons, heuristic-cutoff tests, reflection-model size comparisons on QA, and token/latency analysis. Figure 3 replaces GSM8K-only training dynamics with averages over five test sets. The reward/quantile ablations and post-training overthinking analysis already existed in v1 and move to Appendices B.4 and B.6.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or independent training-run and seed counts. Sampling eight paths per AMC23/AIME24 question is retained. The new QA sampling protocol does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline, QA, smaller-model, heuristic, and cost results while removing Olympiad entries. Shared methods' per-dataset math scores remain unchanged. For example, the combined method's 16k average accuracy/token ratio changes from 77.13/65.11 to 80.74/63.51 because the average now excludes Olympiad, not because performance improved under the same benchmark coverage.

M1.justification: The GRPO procedure, learned overthinking detector, sequential revision, response filtering, and length/reflection rewards remain unchanged. Appendix B.3 applies the existing procedure with different model sizes and training data; it does not introduce a new algorithmic component. The all-incorrect-group filtering rule moves to Appendix B.2.

P1.justification: The six-section main narrative and much of the prose are retained. v2 edits related work and method explanations, moves dataset descriptions to Section 5.1 and common training settings to Appendix B.2, and adds ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements. The title, affiliations, and reward/advantage terminology also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to distinguish shared advantages from partial penalties/rewards, and Figure 3 changes its plotted summaries and scales. Tables gain baseline rows, lose the Olympiad column, and change highlighting conventions; four new tables present additional experiments. The conference template also changes typography, headers, and placement throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion or citations for NoThink, ShorterBetter, Light-R1, DeepCompress, QA benchmarks, and data filtering/synthesis work, while removing the general LRM-background paragraph. The main positioning against offline response revision and online length-reward methods remains intact. Publication and citation-style updates do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: The advantage decomposition and reward definitions are mathematically unchanged. v2 makes GRPO normalization explicit and writes the previously described refined length reward as Equation 4. Renaming 'partial reward' to 'partial advantage' clarifies terminology without changing the derivation; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method through relevant additional competitors, detector and heuristic comparisons, and experiments beyond a single 7B math policy. These address important comparative and generality gaps in v1; the measured cost breakdown also clarifies the known training overhead. The improvement concerns evidential support, not higher same-setting performance. Tradeoffs remain: Olympiad coverage is removed, uncertainty reporting is still absent, and the conclusion's retained claim of validation only on 7B models conflicts with the new 1.5B experiments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REA-RL research despite the shortened title in v2. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across renaming and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original math experiments and adds evaluated baselines, general-QA and smaller-model results, heuristic-truncation comparisons, and measured token consumption and latency.

before.justification: v1 reports original math-reasoning experiments, including accuracy and token consumption, reflection-model comparisons, reward ablations, and post-training overthinking analyses in Tables 1–6.

results.title: REA-RL: Reflection-Aware Online Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Reasoning

C1.justification: v3 adds the headline claim that PonderPythia-2.8B surpasses Pythia-6.9B and rivals Pythia-12B, extending v1's parameter-efficiency claims. The central contributions—self-supervised continuous pondering, compatibility across architectures, and scaling through additional pondering—remain, as does the TinyLlama comparison.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning mechanism-specific gains, the usefulness of token ranks 10–100, stabilization of embeddings and predictions, and the feasibility of continual pretraining. Figure 3 and Appendix H introduce a potentially interpretable account of intermediate predictions, which v1 left to future work. Existing limitations remain in Appendix C, with the tested scale boundary updated from 1.4B to 2.8B.

D1.justification: v3 adds a checkpoint URL and discloses 64GB GPU memory and training costs of 19,886, 31,680, and 109,570 GPU hours for the 1B, 1.4B, and 2.8B models. New experiments provide additional procedural details and a continual-pretraining learning-rate plot. The original scaling hyperparameter table is retained in Appendix B, not newly introduced.

E1.justification: Both versions use the Pile, Wikitext, both LAMBADA variants, the same nine downstream benchmarks, and Alpaca/MT-Bench. The added experiments change model configurations, training procedures, or analyses within this coverage; they do not establish a distinct new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 newly evaluates Looped Pythia, Pause Pythia, last-hidden-state feedback, and feedback with a linear projector. The main downstream comparison adds Pythia-6.9B and Pythia-12B while removing all GPT-Neo rows, OPT-125M, and Pythia-70M/160M rows. These substantially revise the actual comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 extends proposed-model evaluation to 2.8B parameters. The step sweep changes from 160M models with steps {0,1,3,5,10} to 70M models with {0,1,2,3,4,5,10}, retaining the 30B-token budget. New protocols include 3/6-step mechanism comparisons, 1B continual pretraining on 30B tokens, and embedding/distribution diagnostics on 64 sequences of length 2048. Existing zero/five-shot and MT-Bench evaluations remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's step-count sweep, v3 adds mechanism comparisons, randomized-step inference scaling, top-K sensitivity, LLaMA step-count scaling, continual-pretraining analysis, embedding and output-distribution diagnostics, gradient-norm analysis, and prediction case studies. Conversely, v1 Figure 2's explicit comparison of architectural-upgrade gains against pondering gains is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its results. Randomizing pondering depth in v3 is a training procedure, and its spectral variance analysis is not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 Table 1 adds PonderPythia-2.8B averages of 61.5/60.4 for five/zero-shot evaluation, versus 60.1/59.1 for Pythia-6.9B and 61.7/60.5 for Pythia-12B. Table 5 adds continual-pretraining averages of 51.5 versus 50.7/50.8. Numerous ablation and diagnostic findings are new; matched downstream rows and MT-Bench averages remain unchanged. Earlier small-model 300B-token result entries are omitted; new 70M/30B-token results are different-setting evidence.

M1.justification: The probability-weighted embedding recurrence, residual accumulation, final cross-entropy objective, and default three steps remain unchanged. Section 4.3 adds an optional variant that samples 1–10 pondering steps per training batch, enabling variable inference-time depth within one trained model.

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition, and conclusion largely retain their wording and narrative. v3 standardizes PonderLM/PonderPythia terminology, condenses Section 3.1, rewrites related work, groups ablations into a separate section, and moves scaling configurations and limitations to Appendices B and C.

P2.justification: v3 substantially redesigns the page template and opening page, relocates scaling plots to Figure 1, replaces the perplexity table with four bar-chart panels, and restructures the downstream table. It adds an inference diagram, comparison tables, diagnostic plots, and colored case-study tables. The architectural-gain subplot is removed, while the original hyperparameter table is relocated.

R1.justification: Section 5 retains the original test-time scaling and latent-thinking framing but adds discussion of pause tokens, block-recurrent transformers, additional looped-transformer work, and CoCoMix. New Table 3 compares training data, computation space, application level, and training method. The central distinction between probability-derived embeddings and hidden-state feedback is unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(7) retain the same mathematical content, with the pondering-step variable renamed from k to s. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. v3's cosine, KL, and spectral analyses use standard empirical diagnostics rather than new formal results.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct comparisons against alternative latent-computation mechanisms and evidence supporting several implementation choices. v3 Table 2 and Section 4 substantially address those gaps, while continual-pretraining, convergence, and stability analyses strengthen practical and mechanistic support. Larger-model results and resource disclosures further improve the paper. Removing small-model comparisons and replacing exact perplexity tables with plots reduces some detail, and uncertainty remains unreported, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pondering language-model research, with matching core equations and experiments despite renamed models. All material is readable, including v3 Appendices A–H; v1 ends with references and has no appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds larger-model evaluations, mechanism comparisons, ablations, continual pretraining, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining, perplexity, downstream benchmark, MT-Bench, and pondering-step experiments.

results.title: PonderLM: Pretraining Language Models to Ponder in Continuous Space

C1.justification: v1 frames its contributions around detecting, tracing and reversing ROME edits. v2 broadens the central claims to tracing and reversal across several editing methods, explicitly without the original edited weights, and adds recovery of the original output distribution as a claimed outcome. The original weight-pattern and relation-prediction contributions remain in the appendices.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes removing an edit from recovering the original behavior and discusses capability preservation. It adds explanations linking AlphaEdit's poor tracing performance and larger reversal thresholds to reduced overfitting and null-space projection. v1's single-edit limitation is replaced by experiments and discussion of model-dependent batch/sequential robustness and failures.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project repository link, online-editing and hypernetwork-source information, and matrix dimensions for additional models. However, v1 Appendix D.1's A100-80GB hardware disclosure and GPU-day breakdown disappear. Core tracing hyperparameters and dataset-construction details remain.

E1.justification: CounterFact, Yago and wikitext-103 are retained; Yago was already present in v1's appendix. v2 adds downstream evaluation on CoLA, MMLU, MRPC, NLI, RTE and SST, and extends reversal from isolated edits to batch and sequential editing scenarios in Appendices F–G.

E2.justification: The random relation-prediction baseline and k=0/no-reversal control are retained. The added r-ROME, MEMIT, MEND and AlphaEdit methods generate the edits being examined; they are not competing tracing or reversal methods evaluated against the proposed countermeasures.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B configurations, training the layer preceding multi-layer edits, KL-divergence and downstream F1 measurements, and much larger truncation sweeps. Batch experiments edit 1,000 facts, while sequential experiments use 1,000 facts in batches of 100. The original tracing splits and optimizer settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 Section 5.3 adds analyses asking whether reversal restores the output distribution and preserves downstream capabilities. Appendices E–G test generalization and failure conditions across editing mechanisms and batch/sequential settings. The original layer/rank sensitivity, weight-pattern and unique-prediction analyses remain present.

E5.justification: v2 first reports five-seed means and standard deviations for ROME/r-ROME object tracing and three-seed estimates for the additional editors. Conversely, it removes standard deviations from the retained CounterFact relation-prediction and CounterFact/Yago reversal tables. These additions and removals substantially change uncertainty reporting for central results.

E6.justification: The original three-model ROME reversal means are unchanged in Table 2. v2 adds results for other editors and models, batch/sequential reversal, KL divergence and downstream capabilities. For example, new Table 6 reports 99.45% tracing accuracy for MEND/GPT2-XL and 1.89% for AlphaEdit/GPT2-XL. These expand the reported findings rather than establish gains on the original experiments.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix E adapts reversal from intervention on one edited matrix to simultaneous bottom-rank approximation of all matrices affected by multi-layer editors. The fixed-token, cross-entropy tracing procedure and SVD truncation remain fundamentally unchanged; naming the tracing procedure EditScope does not itself introduce a new method.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around two principal tasks. A new Problem Statement replaces the main-text background, while ROME background, weight-pattern analysis and relation prediction move to Appendices B–D. The tracing method receives the name EditScope, and the appendix structure is extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: The overview diagram is revised, CounterFact and Yago tracing plots are combined in Figure 3, and diagnostic displays move to the appendices. Table 2 gains Qwen columns, several retained tables lose uncertainty columns, and new KL, capability and multi-edit displays are added. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for r-ROME, AlphaEdit, additional models and downstream benchmarks, and broadens the ROME-specific positioning. Its relationship to earlier prompt-dependent edit detection and in-context reversal remains substantially the same. Publication updates to already cited works do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: v1 Section 6 explicitly grants access to the original model, including the pre-edit matrix. v2 Section 2 revises the formal access assumption to exclude that matrix and defines tracing and reversal using post-edit parameters. The SVD construction and other mathematical derivations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's single-editor, single-edit setting. Distribution-recovery and downstream-capability checks, seeded tracing evaluation, and multi-editor/batch/sequential experiments address important gaps while exposing AlphaEdit tracing failures. Some older uncertainty and compute disclosures are lost, and capability checks cover only ROME on Llama3. Nevertheless, the new evidence materially improves understanding of both effectiveness and applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same weight-based tracing and reversal research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments across editing methods, downstream tasks, and batch and sequential editing scenarios.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on identifying ROME edits, predicting relations, extracting edited objects and reversing edits, including CounterFact and Yago results.

results.title: Tracing and Reversing Edits in LLMs

C1.justification: The principal claims about optimizer-level search, multi-task training, and strong cross-size performance remain. The novelty claim is modestly qualified: the introduction replaces discovering novel optimization strategies with discovering effective strategies, and Appendix A explicitly says that novelty of the generated meta-optimizers themselves is not emphasized.

C2.justification: Appendix A newly distinguishes cross-size generalization from direct cross-problem transfer and acknowledges difficulties using one meta-optimizer across structurally different problems. It also explains size weighting and the distinction from prompt optimization. New cost analyses argue that heuristic evaluation dominates runtime and discuss deployment tradeoffs. Some new superiority interpretations overreach: Table 14 includes settings where HSEvo outperforms MoH.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code repository address where v1 only promised future code and dataset release; the PDF establishes the access claim, not independently verified availability. It also specifies size-based task weights and discloses instance-wise selection among size-specific heuristics for TSPLIB, applied to baselines as well. Additional runtime, token, request, and evaluation-count measurements expand resource documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds QAP facility-layout optimization and Acrobot robotic control evaluations in Appendix C.7, substantially extending task and domain coverage. Appendix A also adds clustered-TSP evaluation after uniform-distribution training. CVRP and offline BPP were already evaluated in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: v2 adds ReEvo-GLS to Table 1, SIL to both TSPLIB comparisons, and LEHD to the larger-instance TSPLIB comparison. The new solver-time comparison includes NeuOpt and SIL, while Table 14 adds EoH and HSEvo to comparisons across LLMs that previously evaluated MoH alone. These materially broaden evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include joint training across TSP-GLS, TSP-KGLS, and online BPP; approximately matched solving-time comparisons, except for unconstrained Concorde; and evaluation over 100 Acrobot initial conditions and 128 QAP instances. A TSP100 cost experiment supplements the retained TSP200 experiment. The original main-experiment budgets remain unchanged; the newly explained TSPLIB selection procedure is a disclosure rather than an established protocol revision.

E4.justification: v2 adds uniform-to-cluster transfer testing, a mixed-problem training probe, comparative robustness analysis across four LLMs, and expanded computational-cost and solving-time analyses. These examine generalization boundaries, dependence on the LLM, and practical efficiency. The original population-size and idea-generation ablations and optimizer case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports best-of-three results and three-run averages without corresponding uncertainty estimates. v2 adds five-run means with standard errors in Table 6, five-run means with standard deviations in Table 14, further mean-and-standard-deviation results in Table 16, and one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests in Table 15. Existing three-run results remain alongside these additions.

E6.justification: Shared entries in Tables 1 and 2, the original TSPLIB comparisons, and the relocated CVRP/offline BPP table retain their values. Substantial new results include comparator scores, runtime measurements, repeated-run summaries, and additional tasks. For example, Table 7 reports clustered-TSP gaps of 0.268% for MoH versus 0.290% for ReEvo; Table 17 reports Acrobot steps of 88.76 versus 99.65. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The two-level optimization procedure, Algorithm 1, population management, prompt templates, and displayed heuristic and optimizer code retain their substantive operations. Renaming optimizers as heuristic-optimizers and specifying previously unspecified task weights clarify the method without establishing an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the narrative by moving main-text related work into Appendix B, bringing existing CVRP/offline BPP material forward, and adding an extensive FAQ and appendix contents page. Terminology is revised throughout to distinguish heuristic-optimizers from meta-optimizers, with expanded explanations of their roles. The title, author block, and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn with explicit populations, prompt examples, and illustrated utility aggregation. New evaluation and statistics tables expand the presentation; existing tables gain comparator rows or columns, and the CVRP/offline BPP table moves into the main text. The conference formatting also reorganizes figures, tables, and appendix code displays.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially develops positioning relative to evolutionary multitasking, multi-objective optimization, bilevel optimization, and meta-prompt optimization, adding references including Gupta, Osaba, Gunantara, and Xu. The related-work survey is also condensed: its separate heatmap-guided category and several citations disappear, while references supporting SIL and LLM4AD are added. These changes go beyond relocating related work or updating citation style.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 adds an explicit mathematical definition of the previously unspecified task weights: wi = si / sum_j sj, where si is task size. The two optimization objectives and existing problem constraints remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's best-of-three headline results through variability reporting, significance analyses, broader comparator coverage, and targeted generalization tests. Explicit cross-problem limitations and the disclosed TSPLIB selection procedure also improve interpretability and reproducibility. Some new claims remain overstated: Table 14 reports HSEvo beating MoH with Qwen-plus at TSP1000, contrary to its accompanying claim of consistently lower errors. Nevertheless, the added evidence and methodological transparency provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoH research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, figures, prompts, and code examples. Corresponding material can be matched despite reorganization and expanded evaluation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds distribution-shift evaluation, mixed-problem training, statistical analyses, and QAP and Acrobot results.

before.justification: v1 reports original TSP and online BPP experiments, ablations, and computational-cost measurements, with TSPLIB, CVRP, and offline BPP results in its appendices.

results.title: Generalizable Heuristic Generation Through LLMs with Meta-Optimization

C1.justification: The central boundary-guidance and transferability contributions remain. V2 explicitly qualifies comparable attack success as white-box performance and narrows the introduction/conclusion's natural-error alignment claim to comparison with adversarial classifier guidance, replacing v1's broader assertions of close resemblance to naturally occurring errors.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies v1's general advantage for untargeted attacks with a ViT-H exception and explicitly explains that artifacts inflate targeted ViT-H ASR. It adds substantive interpretations of augmentation quality tradeoffs, guidance strength, feature projections, Oxford Pets generalization and DiffPure failures, including increased NCF transferability. The human study also qualifies label preservation with observed failures. Appendix A nevertheless retains the now-inconsistent ImageNet-only limitation.

D1.justification: V2 adds a reproducibility section stating that code and configuration files accompany the supplementary material, expanded parameter tables for ImageNet and Oxford Pets, model-source information, and the human study's selected class list. Runtime documentation expands from approximately 90 seconds per sample to a comparison reporting 103.1 seconds for NatADiff. Conversely, v1's explicit corner-crop/horizontal-flip recipe and image/latent dimensions disappear. Actual supplementary code availability cannot be verified from these PDFs.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates ImageNet classification, using ImageNet-Val and ImageNet-A as reference distributions. V2 retains this coverage and adds Oxford Pets classification in Appendix I, testing finer distinctions between pet breeds that require subtler adversarial features. This materially extends evaluation beyond the original object-category setting.

E2.justification: V1 compares NatADiff with PGD, AutoAttack and adversarial classifier guidance, called AdvClass. V2 adds NCF, DiffAttack and ACA to both the main comparison and defence evaluation (Tables 1 and 10). AdvClass also gains comparisons using Inception-v3 and ViT-H surrogates, whereas v1 reports it only with ResNet-50.

E3.justification: ASR changes from matching the attack-selected adversarial label in v1 Section 4.1 to counting any misclassification in v2 Section 5.1, including randomly targeted attacks. The main evaluation expands from five to nine victim models, and the clean comparison baseline changes from SD1.5 samples to an ImageNet-compatible dataset. V2 also introduces NIQE, BRISQUE and TReS metrics and distinct protocols for prompt/guidance ablations, Oxford Pets and human evaluation.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's boundary-strength sweep and illustrative component comparison, v2 adds quantitative classifier-augmentation ablation, eight prompt variants, guidance-strength and gradient-trajectory analyses, UMAP/t-SNE feature probes, and human label-preservation and failure-case analyses. Defence testing is expanded. Conversely, v1 Appendix I's separate AutoAttack-implementation and model-family transferability investigation is removed; the original component illustration and boundary-strength examples are retained elsewhere.

E5.justification: V2 Figures 8–10 introduce mean gradient trajectories with bands representing plus/minus one standard deviation; v1 contains no corresponding dispersion reporting. This is a limited addition: principal performance tables remain point estimates, and the PDFs do not establish increased independent runs or multi-seed evaluation.

E6.justification: Main, ablation and defence results are revised and expanded. For targeted ResNet-50 NatADiff, reported IS/FID-Val/FID-A change from 37.2/42.8/53.8 in v1 Table 2 to 26.0/66.5/77.3 in v2 Table 1, without explaining the recalculation. New results include Oxford Pets and human judgments of 91% true class, 7% adversarial class and 2% neither. Revised ASR values cannot be interpreted as same-setting gains because its definition changes.

M1.justification: Equation 10 changes cosine-similarity target selection from argmin to argmax, correcting the formula toward the already-stated most-similar-class rule. Boundary guidance, normalized augmented gradients, time travel and adaptive retries remain unchanged. Algorithm 2 still uses argmin, so this documented correction does not establish a corresponding implementation change.

P1.justification: Preliminaries move from the methodology into a standalone section before related work, and the experimental setup and results narrative undergo substantial rewriting. V2 distinguishes surrogate from victim models and reorganizes the appendices, splitting parameter selection from ablations, moving proofs to the end and adding a contents page. These changes exceed simple renumbering or appended scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 redesigns the main table to combine ASR and image quality, group results by surrogate and victim architecture, and highlight rankings in color. Defence and boundary-ablation tables are also consolidated. It adds comparison images, gradient plots, manifold plots and failure examples. V1 Figure 2 moves to v2 Figure 5; v1 Figure 3 is simplified in the main text while its detailed version survives as v2 Figure 14.

R1.justification: V2 broadens positioning beyond the earlier emphasis on GANs and AdvClass by explaining NatADiff's relationship to NCF's color restrictions, DiffAttack's source-image constraints and ACA's semantic editing. It adds literature on these comparisons, additional architectures, perceptual metrics, manifold visualization and human annotation, while shortening the GAN discussion and removing several associated references. ACA was already cited in v1; its evaluated and discussed role expands.

T1.justification: V2 Section 2 adds formal definitions of unconstrained, constrained and natural adversarial sets using an oracle classifier, together with their inclusion relation. Equation 10 corrects the cosine-similarity extremum. The conditional-forward and score-model theorems and proofs are substantially retained, moving from v1 Appendix H to v2 Appendix P rather than constituting new theory.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central contribution through relevant unconstrained-attack baselines, component-specific ablations, Oxford Pets evaluation and direct human evidence of label preservation. Its explicit acknowledgment of artifact-inflated ViT-H results also improves interpretation. These gains outweigh the loss of target-specific ASR reporting and remaining reporting inconsistencies. The restricted human study and unexplained image-quality score revisions still limit conclusions, but the evidential basis is considerably stronger than v1's.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NatADiff work, with the same title and authors. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original ImageNet and Oxford Pets experiments, expanded ablations and defence evaluations, runtime measurements, and a human label-preservation study.

before.justification: V1 reports original ImageNet attack-generation experiments, transferability and image-quality results, boundary-guidance ablations, and defence evaluations.

results.title: NatADiff: Adversarial Boundary Guidance for Natural Adversarial Diffusion

C1.justification: v2 removes the conclusion's claim that TEMU-VTOFF is the first approach to effectively extend VTOFF to multiple categories. Its abstract shifts emphasis from competitors' single-category restriction toward visual ambiguity and detail degradation. The central multi-category, dual-DiT, multimodal-attention, alignment, and state-of-the-art contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of the CLIP bottleneck, multiscale feature conditioning, alignment-depth tradeoffs, and clean versus noisy conditioning. It adds interpretations of downstream utility and human preference, plus a dedicated discussion of LPIPS/DISTS disagreement. Existing limitations concerning small text, buttons, textures, and lower-body imbalance are retained rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes garment-image training captions from person-image test captions, documents the aligner's training-only role, and specifies the SigLIP 2 projection. These disclosures do not establish that the original experiments used different inputs. Existing hardware and optimization details are relocated unchanged, while projector zero-initialization detail is omitted. Code/models are newly advertised as available, although the reproducibility statement still promises future release.

E1.justification: Both versions use Dress Code and VITON-HD, but v2 extends evaluation beyond within-dataset VTOFF. Section 4.3 adds transfer between the datasets, introducing domain-shift scenarios. Section 4.4 adds downstream VTON evaluation using synthetic person-garment pairs, substantially expanding task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds MGT to Dress Code comparisons and adds published MGT, Voost, and One Model For All results to the VITON-HD comparison. Table 1 removes TryOffDiff's overall, lower-body, and dress comparisons while retaining upper-body results. Qualitative comparator membership also changes: Figure 4 replaces Any2AnyTryon with TryOffDiff.

E3.justification: v2 adds PSNR to the benchmark metrics and introduces cross-dataset testing, CatVTON training with versus without synthetic augmentation, and a randomized pairwise preference protocol involving 42 participants and 1,920 judgments. These substantially expand evaluation design. The original dataset splits and TEMU-VTOFF training budgets remain unchanged as reported.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained text, mask, and aligner ablations, v2 tests feature-extractor removal, alignment weights, alignment block depth, synchronous versus clean-feature timestep conditioning, and CLIP versus SigLIP 2. It also adds domain-shift robustness tests and per-image LPIPS/DISTS disagreement analysis in Figure 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The new user-study participant counts and randomized presentation describe evaluation design; its reported preference percentages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Shared numerical entries in Tables 1–3 are retained, but v2 adds PSNR, baseline scores, transfer and downstream results, sensitivity results, and preference rates of 75.77% against MGT and 77.74% against Any2AnyTryon. Expanded Table 2 changes the reported rankings: cited MGT and One Model For All results lead SSIM and LPIPS, respectively. TryOffDiff's non-upper-body Dress Code results are removed.

M1.justification: The main dual-DiT architecture, multimodal hybrid attention, and DINOv2 alignment procedure are retained. Appendix B/Table 7 adds an evaluated variant replacing CLIP with SigLIP 2 ViT-g/16 and introducing a 1536-to-2048-dimensional MLP projection, a limited architectural adaptation.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial methodology passages are rewritten, with feature extraction, modulation, and training explanations reorganized. Implementation details move to the appendix, caption extraction is integrated into its details section, and broader impact becomes an ethics statement. The experimental narrative and appendix organization are substantially revised.

P2.justification: v2 expands Tables 1–3 with metric columns and comparison or ablation rows, adds Tables 4–8, revises the architecture diagram, and replaces several qualitative panels. It adds an inference-caption illustration and a per-image metric figure, alongside conference-format layout changes. The original appendix component-ablation grid and both failure-case panels are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to cover MGT, Voost, One Model For All, and broader diffusion-conditioning approaches such as ControlNet, T2I-Adapter, and IP-Adapter. Additional discussion connects the design to CleanDIFT and ConceptAttention. Acknowledging existing multi-category and bidirectional systems revises the novelty positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The core flow-matching, attention, and alignment equations retain their mathematical substance after matching reordered equations and notation. Algorithm 1 retains the same objective while renaming the generator loss from Ldiff to LDiT. New explanations of feature alignment and timestep choices are conceptual, without new proofs or formal derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily supported its design through within-dataset comparisons and limited component ablations, while practical augmentation benefits remained untested. v2 adds direct transfer and downstream tests, isolates important architectural choices, supplies human-preference evidence, and clarifies test-time caption inputs. These address substantial validation and reproducibility gaps despite unchanged original scores. Uncertainty estimates remain absent and release-status wording is inconsistent, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TEMU-VTOFF, with matching research objectives and core architecture. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds cross-dataset evaluations, downstream augmentation experiments, additional ablations, and a human preference study.

before.justification: v1 reports original Dress Code and VITON-HD experiments, component ablations, and qualitative reconstructions in Tables 1–3 and the appendices.

results.title: Inverse Virtual Try-On: Generating Multi-Category Product-Style Images from Clothed Individuals

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list, and conclusion retain the same headline claims: optimizer-state alignment, full-rank AdamW recovery, removal of scaling-factor tuning, and improved adaptation without additional inference cost. The added experiments and variants do not redefine these summary contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the accuracy–efficiency interpretation: second-moment calibration is identified as the main memory and latency bottleneck, with little average accuracy benefit in the tested simplified variant. It removes the blanket statement about no additional overhead and adds interpretations concerning diminishing returns from larger coding ranks and stability across context lengths.

D1.justification: v2 adds an implementation-repository link, detailed Muon/Newton-Schulz pseudocode, and settings for the new 70B and coding experiments. It clarifies that PEFT's alpha/r scaling explains alpha=r in the tables and that Algorithm 1's full gradient is notation rather than an implementation requirement. These materially extend reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-100 image classification and Python code generation, using CodeFeedback for training and HumanEval/HumanEval+ for evaluation (Appendices E.1, G.3, and H). Earlier coverage, including Orca-Math and WikiText-2 experiments already present in v1's appendices, is retained.

E2.justification: LoRA-Pro is added to both retained GPT-2/WikiText-2 comparisons (v2 Tables 14–15 versus v1 Tables 10–11). v2 also evaluates VPT and Adapter, described as ViT-Adapter, on CIFAR-100 and Diabetic Retinopathy (Table 19), substantially broadening the evaluated comparator families.

E3.justification: New protocols include 70B-model fine-tuning with learning rate 0.005, coding rank sweeps through 256, and context lengths of 256 versus 512 tokens. Coding evaluation samples ten completions per problem at temperature 0.5 and reports pass@1/5/10. These extend the evaluation design; the existing main hyperparameter tables and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's synthetic and GPT-2 ablations, v2 tests component removal on LLaMA-7B and ViT-Base/CIFAR-100. It adds second-moment-specific accuracy and memory analysis, component-level latency measurements, and coding rank/context sensitivity studies (Tables 6–7, 10–13, and 20–21).

E5.justification: Both versions report the main vision results as mean and standard deviation over three runs. v2 adds no new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The ten coding completions define the new pass@k evaluation protocol rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main Tables 2–3 and the previously reported comparator scores are retained, but substantial new results appear. Examples include 70B average accuracy of 90.66 at rank 16 and 88.93 at rank 1 (Table 17), and HumanEval pass@1 of 0.460 for LoFT (simple) versus 0.421 for LoRA at rank 8 (Table 20). New ablation, latency, and vision-comparison results further expand the evidence.

M1.justification: v2 develops v1's proposed future Muon extension into LoFT-Muon with a factorized Newton-Schulz procedure (Appendix D.1). It also introduces LoFT (simple), which omits second-moment calibration. These are substantive procedural additions; the original LoFT-AdamW algorithm is retained.

P1.justification: The supplementary narrative is substantially reorganized: v1's combined experimental appendix becomes dedicated optimization/efficiency, language, vision, and coding appendices. v2 adds limitations and Muon sections and revises the contents and cross-references. Main-text language changes are comparatively limited.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for ablations, simplified LoFT, latency, 70B scaling, vision baselines, and coding analyses, plus four algorithm displays. WikiText-2 tables and plots gain LoRA-Pro entries, Figure 1's projection labels change, and retained displays are relocated or resized within the conference layout.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds a focused comparison with concurrent AltLoRA, distinguishing shared alternating updates from LoFT's AdamW moment alignment and asserting transformation-invariance novelty. References supporting the new vision and coding experiments are also added; the broader related-work narrative remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 replaces Eq. 8's intersection-projection interpretation with sequential projections and changes the full-fine-tuning recovery condition from r=min(m,n) to r=max(m,n). It also corrects algebra in the update equations and adds factorized Newton-Schulz mathematics and explicit optimizer-memory accounting. These revise central mathematical content, although the original matrix-factorization lemmas and proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves support for LoFT's mechanism and practical efficiency. Real-model ablations and Tables 10–13 address questions v1 left unresolved about component necessity and runtime cost, while demonstrating a cheaper variant with nearly unchanged average accuracy. Mathematical corrections and implementation information further strengthen the paper. The new Muon material has inconsistencies—Appendix A still calls it future work, and Algorithm 5 omits learning-rate multiplication of the update—but these do not outweigh the substantial improvements to the core AdamW evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoFT research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds component ablations, efficiency measurements, CIFAR-100 comparisons, 70B-model evaluation, and code-generation experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic optimization experiments and fine-tuning results for commonsense reasoning, image classification, mathematical reasoning, and language modeling.

results.title: LoFT: Low-Rank Adaptation That Behaves Like Full Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The central contribution—improving LLM optimization through adaptive partitioning and bandit-inspired selection—remains unchanged. The introduction and conclusion replace their emphasis on NAS with claims of applicability to real-world optimization tasks, and the abstract describes comparisons against leading global optimization methods more generally.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands explanations of variance-aware scoring, sampling collapse, global-history conditioning, surrogate behavior, and computational scaling. Its FCNet discussion emphasizes discrete-space and model-dependent effects instead of v1's Parkinsons outlier hypothesis. It also qualifies the retained three-run synthetic evidence as needing more repetitions and discusses differing benefits across continuous and discrete domains.

D1.justification: V2 adds simulator parameter ranges, surrogate prediction choices, and an approximate FCNet runtime and API cost of 330 seconds and $0.14 per 50-trial run. It clarifies global-history conditioning, updates prompt instructions, and changes the code pointer from automl/hollm to arberzela/mohollm. Much of the existing pseudocode, hyperparameter documentation, and prompt material is retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds Penicillin Production, Vehicle Safety, and Car Side Impact simulator tasks, plus a noisy Vehicle Safety scenario. The original six synthetic functions, four FCNet datasets, and NAS-Bench-201 tasks remain represented; Ackley and NAS results move to Appendix C.1 rather than disappearing.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds LA-MCTS variants, CMA-ES, HEBO, and SMAC comparisons; Appendix F adds TabPFN and a distinct GP ranking-surrogate comparison. RS + KD-Tree expands from a v1 component ablation into main benchmark comparisons. The new main synthetic plots omit TPE and TuRBO, whose earlier comparisons remain in Appendix C.1.

E3.justification: The default LLM changes from Gemini-1.5-Flash to Gemini-2.0-Flash, and the reported default budget changes from T=100 to T=50. V2 also introduces longer-budget baseline comparisons, Gaussian observation noise with standard deviation 1% of the objective range, and diversity and surrogate-evaluation protocols, including a reported 700-point calibration analysis. Earlier settings remain documented separately.

E4.justification: V2 adds Vehicle Safety scoring ablations, observation-noise robustness, comparisons across open-weight LLMs, and sampling-diversity analysis. Appendix F examines surrogate ranking and calibration while retaining the LLM candidate sampler, explicitly attributing those results to follow-up work. Earlier NAS component ablations and hyperparameter analyses are retained, with additional Gemini-2.0 exploration-weight results.

E5.justification: The revised main evaluation reports 10 runs instead of v1's default 3, while retained appendix experiments preserve their earlier counts. V2 adds a critical-difference rank diagram and reports five repetitions for Table 4. Mean and standard-error reporting continues; the diagram's statistical test and significance level are not specified.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive benchmark and analysis results while retaining earlier curves. Its new Gemini-2.0 Figure 3 shows the global LLM outperforming HOLLM on Rastrigin under the revised settings. New Table 4 reports Rosenbrock scores of -7.03 ± 0.01 for HOLLM and -4.66 ± 0.50 for the global LLM. These additions do not establish same-setting performance changes relative to v1.

M1.justification: The five-stage algorithm and scoring equations remain intact. Algorithm 3 revises the documented empty-cell branch from assigning mu=0 and expl=1 to assigning mu,V,E=0,1,1. Listing 3 also adds an explicit pre-output constraint-check instruction. These are localized procedural revisions.

P1.justification: The evaluation narrative and appendix organization are substantially reworked. NAS becomes Appendix C.1.3, the main text gains dedicated real-world and analysis sections, and prompts move from Appendix D to I around newly organized analyses. Several experimental interpretations are rewritten, alongside conference-format, affiliation, and acknowledgment edits.

P2.justification: V2 adds engineering-task plots, a critical-difference diagram, robustness and model-choice panels, diversity and calibration visualizations, and comparison and complexity tables. Main synthetic results change from a six-panel grid to a five-panel strip with a shared legend, while earlier plots are retained in the appendices. Figure arrangements and the document-wide conference layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting the new optimizers, simulator suite, Llama/Qwen models, TabPFN, and follow-up multi-objective HOLLM work. The main related-work discussion and positioning relative to hierarchical bandits, Bayesian optimization, and LLM optimizers remain largely unchanged. The citation-style conversion itself is presentational.

T1.justification: Appendix D introduces a mathematical definition of ICL Divergence as mean nearest-context-point distance. Appendix G adds an asymptotic complexity comparison between HOLLM, global LLM sampling, and exact GP methods. The original scoring mathematics is retained, and neither version supplies regret guarantees.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical validation through simulator tasks, competing partitioning methods, more main-evaluation repetitions, and tests of noise and LLM dependence, addressing important gaps in v1's evidence while retaining its experiments. Some claims remain too broad: Table 4 does not establish universal HOLLM superiority, and the critical-difference procedure is underspecified. These weaknesses temper the conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and understanding.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HOLLM and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Earlier experiments and analyses can be matched to their relocated counterparts in v2, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and reports additional simulator, observation-noise, and LLM-choice experiments. This judgment does not depend on the calibration results explicitly attributed to follow-up work in Appendix F.

before.justification: V1 reports original optimization experiments on synthetic functions, FCNet, and NAS-Bench-201, together with sampling demonstrations and component and hyperparameter ablations.

results.title: Improving LLM-based Global Optimization with Search Space Partitioning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the central contribution from structured-reference scientific reasoning to unstructured references and non-scientific translation. The abstract's reported average accuracy advantage changes from 11.3% to 12.3% alongside expanded comparisons, while the original benchmark scores remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning translation-rule organization, limitations of direct textbook training, reusable-tool cost amortization, and open-source creation for sensitive references. It removes v1 Appendix E's explicit discussion of general-code/web-agent applicability and foundational-domain requirements. A narrower warning about domain misunderstanding remains in the human-quality discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds category-generation and assignment prompts, translation settings and verification details, and training-data construction and hyperparameters, including two epochs and learning rate 1e-5. The access statement expands from code to code and data. Existing scientific model versions and hardware remain documented, but v1's explicit LaTeX-conversion step and original benchmark question counts are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 retains the scientific benchmarks, including the existing SciBench-fund transfer experiment, and adds bidirectional Zhuang–Chinese translation using ZHUANGRULES and 109 grammar rules. This introduces a non-scientific language task and evaluation with initially unstructured reference material, substantially broadening coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds LATM and TroVE, which v1 cited but explicitly excluded from evaluation. v2 also adds continued-pretraining and QA-fine-tuning comparators in Table 8, plus four translation baselines in Table 3: Whole Grammar Book, Retrieval from Whole Book, Rule-by-Rule Retrieval, and its code-augmented variant.

E3.justification: v2 adds BLEU/chrF++ translation evaluation using Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen-2.5-72B, dictionaries, and paired examples. New protocols reserve six test examples for LATM training/validation and use a 10% holdout and two training epochs for training-based comparisons. Human tool-quality sampling increases from 20 to 50 tools per domain; the tool-creation evaluation also adds Llama.

E4.justification: The component ablations, tool-selection consistency study, and case studies are retained. Appendix B.4 extends creator-model robustness from Gemini to include Llama, and Appendix B.6 broadens the existing cost analysis to more comparators. The tool-quality assessment is expanded through larger samples. These extend established analyses without substantially changing their questions.

E5.justification: v2 Section 3.2 newly claims that accuracy aggregated across four LLMs significantly exceeds all baselines in each scientific domain at alpha = 0.05. v1 makes no corresponding significance statement. The addition does not specify the test, exact p-values, confidence intervals, seeds, or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Existing Table 2 rows and Table 4 ablation scores remain unchanged. v2 adds substantial results for new baselines, translation, training alternatives, Llama-created tools, and costs. Translation averages are 54.0 BLEU/61.6 chrF++, versus 43.9/60.0 for code-augmented rule retrieval. Larger-sample human ratings replace earlier estimates, including chemistry faithfulness 90% to 96% and usefulness 95% to 90%; these are not same-sample changes.

M1.justification: v1 extracts an existing reference hierarchy and generates executable Python tools. v2 adds LLM-generated categories and segment assignment for unstructured references. Its translation adaptation uses pseudo-code tools, model-based verification against parallel examples, and refinement without discarding tools (Sections 2.1, 3.3 and Appendix A.4). These substantially extend the procedure.

P1.justification: The title and opening/concluding narrative are revised around knowledge-intensive reasoning. Baseline explanations move into Appendix A.3, Section 4 is reordered, and human tool-selection discussion moves to Appendix C. A dedicated generalizability subsection and reorganized implementation appendix are added, while Appendix E changes from limitations to an LLM-use disclosure. Together these substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds translation, training-comparison, and expanded-cost tables; enlarges several comparison tables; and splits v1's human-evaluation Table 3 between main-text Table 6 and appendix Table 14. It adds a knowledge-organization prompt figure, combines selection-prompt figures, relocates the overview figure, and changes the conference layout. Existing case-study graphics retain their substantive content.

R1.justification: v2 adds translation-related references by Tanzer et al. and Zhang et al., plus the Qwen2.5 report. Section 5 expands the comparison with embedding-based retrieval and distinguishes generated hierarchies from inherited API categories. The existing automatic-tool-creation positioning is largely retained; LATM and TroVE were already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The framework notation and Appendix C's selection-consistency formulas remain mathematically equivalent, with chapter renamed category. Reference equations in the example figures are retained. Neither version introduces new theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the framework's applicability: translation tests its extension beyond structured scientific references, while LATM/TroVE and training-based comparisons address important alternatives missing from v1. Open-source tool creation and larger human-quality samples further strengthen validation. Removing explicit limitations and adding an underspecified significance claim weaken transparency, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in testing the method's scope and comparative value.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RefTool, with matching authors, core framework, and retained scientific experiments. Their text, tables, figures, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the revised title and expanded scope.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds translation experiments, training-based comparisons, additional tool-creation evaluations, and revised human assessments.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, ablations, human tool-quality assessments, computational costs, and additional experiments in Appendix B.

results.title: RefTool: Reference-Guided Tool Creation for Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning

C1.justification: The efficient Hadamard feature-expansion objective remains, but v2's abstract and introduction make DySoft-based gradient stability, NAS-based integration and tailored GPU acceleration explicit central contributions. Hadaptive-Net is repositioned as a testbed for the operator, extending v1's emphasis on a manually designed lightweight backbone.

C2.justification: V2 presents DySoft as essential for stability, adds hardware-dependent explanations of kernel performance, and explicitly qualifies custom-CUDA timings as unsuitable for strict baseline speed comparisons. Appendix A.6 adds semantic interpretations of Grad-CAM and acknowledges that ACH underperforms standard BERT FFNs under the exploratory NLP setup.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code link, reproducibility statement, explicit temperature-update pseudocode, NAS optimization settings, a layer-level architecture table, CUDA indexing algorithms, CPU/mobile hardware specifications, and detailed detection/NLP configurations. These substantially expand v1's relatively brief implementation disclosure without establishing that every retained experiment was rerun.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates image classification on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K. V2 retains these and adds COCO object detection, SST-2 sentiment classification, and MNLI textual entailment, including a low-resource MNLI setting in Appendix A.6. These substantially broaden tasks and domains.

E2.justification: The main classification comparison adds GhostNet-1.0, GhostNetV3-1.0 and MobileOne-S0 through S3 in v2 Table 7, while retaining the earlier comparator families. Additional comparisons evaluate MobileViT variants and BERT with standard and fixed-width FFNs against ACH replacements.

E3.justification: V2 adds SSD evaluation at 320x320 for 120 epochs using COCO mAP, and randomly initialized BERT experiments trained for three epochs with a stratified 10% MNLI training subset. Latency evaluation expands to CPU and mobile hardware alongside GPU and kernel comparisons. The main classification table drops CIFAR-100 top-5 reporting.

E4.justification: V1's normalized-versus-unnormalized CrossHadaNorm study is replaced by comparisons of dynamic sigmoidal functions, and component ablations are revised. V2 adds NAS configuration studies, channel/expansion-ratio sweeps, kernel performance across tensor shapes, and Grad-CAM case studies. The earlier layer-placement and four-CNN replacement studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average latency over 500 inference iterations. Neither reports accuracy variability across repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's NAS selection confidences describe architectural preferences, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: From v1 Table 5 to v2 Table 7, Hadaptive-Net-S/M/L CIFAR-100 top-1 changes from 73.40/74.62/75.82% to 73.57/74.10/74.73%; their ImageNet scores remain unchanged. Parameter counts, FLOPs and several latencies also change. New detection, profiling, MobileViT and NLP results include a MobileViT-xx-small top-1 decline and ACH trailing standard BERT FFNs. The revised methods prevent interpreting these as matched-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 replaces the two-layer channel-scoring network with ECA and replaces covariance-based CrossHadaNorm with learnable dynamic softsign normalization. Section 3.4 introduces GDAS-based architecture search in place of v1's manual architectural design. These change substantive components and construction procedures; the underlying pairwise Hadamard expansion and Gumbel/STE selection remain.

P1.justification: Beyond retitling, v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work and methodological explanations. Complexity and acceleration receive a dedicated Implementation section, experiments are reorganized, and architecture discussion moves partly into appendices alongside expanded training and analytical material. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V2 changes from two-column to single-column presentation. Figure 1 becomes paired ImageNet accuracy-versus-FLOPs/latency plots; the ACH diagram is updated, the ablation diagram and table are combined, and the architecture figure moves to the appendix. The main comparison table gains hardware columns, while new NAS tables, profiling plots and Grad-CAM figures substantially expand the displays.

R1.justification: Section 2 broadens the Hadamard discussion into a four-category taxonomy grounded in Chrysos et al. (2025), adding bilinear pooling, MogaNet and Mamba/Vision Mamba positioning. DySoft is connected to Transformers without Normalization. Several earlier references, including MobileNeXt, DARTS and EfficientNetV2, are removed.

T1.justification: V1's covariance-based normalization derivation is removed. V2 Appendix A.2 introduces moment calculations and statistical-stability arguments for DySoft; Section 4 and Appendix A.5 add indexing formulas and complexity derivations comparing ACH, Ghost modules and pointwise convolution. This substantially changes the mathematical analysis, although some complexity expressions remain inconsistent.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens important weaknesses in v1: Table 7 evaluates the directly relevant GhostNet competitors, new tasks test applicability, and the appendices provide much fuller architecture, training and implementation details. The explicit qualification of custom-CUDA comparisons also improves evidential honesty. Conflicting complexity ratios and unreconciled FLOP counts between Tables 5 and 7 remain limitations, and accuracy uncertainty is still absent. Nevertheless, the gains substantially improve reproducibility and the basis for judging the method's capabilities and boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ACH/Hadaptive-Net research, despite the changed title and substantial revision. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable. All pages were inspected, including v2 Appendices A-B; v1 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original classification, architecture-search, detection, MobileViT, hardware-profiling and NLP results, including experiments in Appendix A.

before.justification: V1 reports original normalization and component ablations, network-replacement experiments, and CIFAR-100/ImageNet classification and latency results in Tables 1-5.

results.title: Expressive yet Efficient Feature Expansion with Adaptive Cross-Hadamard Products

C1.justification: The central contributions and claims of improved alignment, sample efficiency, and interpretability across three task domains remain. v2 adds an explicit conclusion that the gains transfer across model families, supported by the new Mistral evaluation in Section 4.7.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting moderate recall to label imbalance, dense-label failures to noisy rewards, and weighting failures to disrupted span coherence or increased variance. It interprets human disagreement by task subjectivity and discusses tokenization and annotation failures. Appendix G softens v1's scalability concerns using measured overhead and cost, while Appendix M adds the stronger assertion that residual annotation noise has no measurable downstream effect.

D1.justification: New disclosures cover character-span/tokenizer alignment, unmatched-span filtering, baseline preference construction and PRM segmentation, human-evaluation procedures, policy hardware, training times, and annotation budgets. However, the consolidated reward-model table drops v1's maximum prompt/sequence lengths and Adam beta/epsilon values. The code-access URL remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use SLF5K, KodCode, and UltraFeedback, with the same summarization, HumanEval/MBPP and enhanced variants, AlpacaEval, ARC-Challenge, and MT-Bench coverage. The Mistral evaluation and feedback-source ablations reuse existing data and tasks; they expand model configurations and analyses.

E2.justification: Tables 2–4 newly evaluate DPO and ILF across all three domains. PRM-PPO is added for summarization and code generation, and Dense Reward is added for summarization. These substantially broaden comparison beyond v1's PPO, SFT/reflection, and pretrained/proprietary references. PRM-PPO's stated exclusion from UltraFeedback is not a removal, since v1 did not evaluate it there.

E3.justification: v2 adds Mistral-7B configurations and controlled reward-granularity, feedback-source, and token-weighting experiments. Reported human-evaluation sampling changes from 50 to 100 instances per dataset, and reward-model training changes from three epochs to two. Appendix C replaces KodCode ROUGE-L with a 90%-overlap metric. These are substantive protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix I.1 adds dense-versus-span rewards, human-versus-GPT feedback, and uniform-versus-POS/positional weighting ablations. Appendices K–O add efficiency, span-grounding, failure-mode, and span-length analyses. Existing CoT ablations and training curves are retained and discussed further. The Prime Fibonacci case study from v1 Appendix F.2 is removed.

E5.justification: Figure 5's caption newly states that shaded regions, 'if present,' represent one standard deviation over three random seeds. v1 supplies no equivalent seed or uncertainty information. The plotted curves are retained without clearly visible uncertainty bands, so this is limited reporting rather than evidence that additional runs were performed.

E6.justification: Most original benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds extensive baseline, Mistral, ablation, efficiency, and grounding results. UltraFeedback predicted good/poor span counts change from 736/400 in v1 Table 5 to 932/528 in v2 Table 6; exact matches change from 292/101 to 394/167. KodCode ROUGE-L results of 0.64/0.59 are replaced by 90%-overlap results of 0.67/0.79, which are different-metric results, not directly comparable gains.

M1.justification: Critique/span annotation, the autoregressive reward model, uniform positive/negative token rewards, and PPO optimization remain unchanged; Algorithms 1–4 are retained. Replacing 'dual-headed' with 'unified' matches the model already specified in v1 Section 3.4. Expanded grounding and tokenization descriptions disclose implementation details without establishing a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, method explanations, and several results narratives receive extensive rewriting and terminology cleanup, including clarification that NL-Gradient does not mean literal differentiation through text. Reward-model hyperparameters move from Appendix I into consolidated Appendix D, and later appendices are reorganized. These changes extend beyond the addition of new scientific content.

P2.justification: Main comparison tables gain grouped baseline rows and revised highlighting; three separate PPO hyperparameter tables become one cross-dataset table. New tables display Mistral, reward-design, efficiency, fidelity, and span-length results. Figure 2 gains a fuller color legend and caption, while the existing training curves, preference plots, and coding illustration are largely retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Related work adds focused discussion and citations for PRMs, MA-RLHF, SCAR, Beyond Sparse Rewards, and Learning from Natural Language Feedback. Appendix N further discusses PRM applicability. This improves coverage of nearby approaches while retaining the original two-part framing and 'first complete framework' novelty claim.

T1.justification: The NL-Gradient definition, reward-model objective, PPO objective, and Appendix A derivation are retained. Section 3.5 now explicitly presents the GAE expression already included in v1 Algorithm 4. This expands the main-text explanation without adding a new theoretical result or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence against alternative learning approaches through DPO, PRM-PPO, and ILF comparisons, alongside Mistral generalization and reward-design ablations. Added timing, cost, and grounding analyses make practical feasibility more assessable. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including unexplained setting changes, omitted hyperparameters, and new numerical inconsistencies: Section 4.3 claims a 6.7-point ROUGE-L gain over PPO, while Table 2 implies 2.9 points. The stronger evaluation materially improves the paper despite these remaining problems.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Text2Grad, with matching authors, core methods, benchmarks, and substantial overlapping content. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including material moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, Mistral evaluations, reward-design ablations, and annotation quality and efficiency analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model evaluations, policy-training results across summarization, code generation, and question answering, human annotation agreement, and ablations.

results.title: Text2Grad: Reinforcement Learning from Natural Language Feedback

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: approximate KV caching, confidence-aware parallel decoding, and up to 27.6x acceleration with minimal accuracy loss. The added experiments and variants do not revise these headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds important applicability qualifications: small-block decoding does not transfer directly to LLaDA-V, and PrefixCache falls behind LLaMA at larger batch sizes, attributed to diffusion models' computational overhead. It also interprets factor decoding as a latency-versus-accuracy trade-off and explains changing parallelism and variability across decoding stages. These substantially extend v1's interpretation of practical deployment.

D1.justification: The new appendix documents reproducibility details for the added experiments, including 96-token multimodal blocks, refresh intervals of 2/4/8/16/32, and the precise prefill, output-length, and batch-size settings for throughput tests. The existing A100 80GB hardware disclosure, lm-eval usage, and code/project links remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 extends the retained GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP coverage to vision-language mathematical reasoning on MathVista and MathVerse using LLaDA-V. Appendix B.4 additionally evaluates image-description generation, introducing visual inputs and task requirements absent from v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds LLaDA-1.5 to a direct comparison with Fast-dLLM on original LLaDA (Table 12), and uses the original threshold strategy as the explicit comparator for factor decoding (Table 11). The original benchmark comparator columns remain. LLaMA already appeared in v1 Figure 1; it is not a newly introduced baseline.

E3.justification: The original benchmark settings remain, but v2 adds substantial experimental protocols. These include MathVista block-length tests at 48 decoding steps, refresh-interval sweeps, factor-value sweeps, and evaluations using LLaDA-1.5. Appendix C.5 introduces a caching-only throughput comparison with 256-token prefills, generation lengths of 16/32/64, and batch sizes from 1 to 32.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's cache, threshold, length, and arithmetic-case analyses, v2 tests why small blocks fail for LLaDA-V and how refresh frequency affects the trade-off. It also compares factor and threshold decoding, analyzes parallel token counts over decoding steps, examines batch-size scaling, and adds a visual-description case study (Appendices B.4 and C).

E5.justification: Figure 7 and Section C.4 newly report a 95% confidence band for average parallel token counts, described as cross-sample variability. v1 has no corresponding uncertainty reporting. This does not establish additional repeated runs; benchmark seed counts and repeated-run uncertainty remain unspecified.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and length-ablation tables retain their numerical values. v2 adds substantial results, including 9.9x and 8.5x multimodal speedups in Table 3. Table 11 reports factor decoding at 78.5 tokens/s and 77.5% accuracy versus threshold decoding at 54.4 tokens/s and 78.5% accuracy on GSM8K with length 256. Additional entries cover LLaDA-1.5, refresh sensitivity, token-count dynamics, and batch scaling; these are new comparisons rather than improvements to unchanged settings.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 and Algorithm 1 add factor-based decoding: sort token confidences and select the largest n satisfying (n+1)(1-c_(n)) < f, instead of using only a fixed confidence threshold. Section C.1 also introduces an LLaDA-V adaptation that retains a full block and refreshes its cache every r decoding steps. These change token selection and cache-update procedures.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains unchanged, including the abstract, introduction, conclusion, related work, and proof. Local additions explain factor decoding and the new results, while Appendix B.4 and Appendix C extend the document structure. This is an extension rather than extensive rewriting or reorganization.

P2.justification: v2 adds multimodal, refresh-sensitivity, strategy-comparison, and model-comparison tables (Tables 3 and 9-12). Figures 6-9 introduce an illustrated response comparison, a confidence-band plot, factor-decoding panels, and batch-scaling curves. Figure 4 is resized and repositioned, while retained tables are renumbered. These substantially expand the visual presentation of the evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to LLaDA-V and LLaDA 1.5 to support the expanded evaluations. The related-work discussion and positioning against earlier diffusion and acceleration approaches are otherwise retained; shifted reference numbers do not represent additional changes.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, its assumptions, tightness construction, distance and KL bounds, and the complete Appendix A proof are unchanged. The new factor-selection procedure draws on the existing bound without adding or revising a theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of applicability and deployment trade-offs beyond v1's predominantly single-batch, text-only evidence. It exposes multimodal small-block failures and large-batch disadvantages against autoregressive decoding, tests a cache-refresh adaptation, and evaluates the factor strategy's accuracy-throughput trade-off. These address important gaps behind the practical-deployment claims. Some added interpretation is overstated: Section C.3 claims consistent LLaDA-1.5 benefits although Table 12 shows worse MATH accuracy and throughput at length 512. That reporting weakness tempers, but does not outweigh, the substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fast-dLLM. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds multimodal evaluations, factor-decoding experiments, LLaDA-1.5 comparisons, and decoding-efficiency analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy and throughput experiments on LLaDA and Dream, component and parameter ablations, and generated-response case studies.

results.title: Fast-dLLM: Training-free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM by Enabling KV Cache and Parallel Decoding

C1.justification: V3 explicitly claims generalization to rare chemistries and out-of-distribution conformations and describes uncertainty as calibrated in the Introduction. These specific assertions extend v1's claims about transferable local representations and useful confidence scores. The central representation, likelihood and chemical-shift contributions remain.

C2.justification: V3 qualifies pKa comparisons by the mismatch between simulated and experimental supervision and by baseline training-set reuse, and attributes weaker histidine transfer to scarce training examples. It adds explanations for the radius/layer choices and interprets descriptor–RMSD correlations as approximate isometry (Appendices F, G.2 and J.1). Existing HA-prediction and side-chain reconstruction limitations remain.

D1.justification: V3 provides a repository location and states that code, trained models and processing scripts are public (Section 10), information absent from v1.
