It adds learned-baseline input construction, descriptor-layer/API details, altloc residue ranges and diffusion guidance parameters of eta = 0.5 and delta = 0.25. Existing GCN hyperparameters and hardware descriptions are largely retained.

E1.justification: V3 adds experimental-pKa evaluation using PKAD-R and crystallographic structures from PropKa's training cases, extending v1's evaluation against simulated PypKa targets. It also evaluates descriptor-conditioned generation from noise beyond the existing coordinate-inversion task. The original RefDB classification and chemical-shift coverage remains.

E2.justification: V3 adds ESM3 sequence/structure, ISM and ESMFold comparisons to classification, pKa and backbone chemical-shift experiments. Learned embeddings are added for pKa and backbone shifts, and Egret joins the pKa comparison. Conversely, the five side-chain ESM comparisons in v1 Table B.4 disappear from v3 Table B.6. V1's retained ESM comparator is identified as ESM2 in v3.

E3.justification: New protocols evaluate all PKAD-R entries and PropKa training cases, vary environment radii and descriptor layers, and compare guided/unguided generation using signed normalized distance. The original 823/225 RefDB split and training budgets remain. Appendix F.2 reports concatenated MACE layers rather than v1's final-layer setting, although v3 retains conflicting final-layer wording; this does not establish that original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds radius and layer ablations (Tables B.9–B.10), descriptor-distance versus structural-RMSD analysis (Fig. A.10), and inversion/guidance studies on four additional proteins. The original atom-set ablations and chemical-shift case studies remain. The paired relaxed-minus-unrelaxed likelihood distribution shown in v1 Fig. 5 is removed.

E5.justification: V3 adds Pearson and Spearman correlation estimation for descriptor distances versus structural RMSD (Fig. A.10), supplementing v1's qualitative PCA analysis. Existing chemical-shift quantile bands and likelihood-based confidence reporting remain unchanged. Neither version specifies training seeds or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark and atom-set ablation values remain unchanged; for example, MACE CA chemical-shift MAE remains 0.584 ppm. V3 adds extensive comparator, ablation and inversion results. Its new experimental-pKa comparison reports lysine MAE of 0.360 for MACE versus 0.648 for pKa-ANI, but histidine MAE of 0.925 versus 0.899 (Table B.8). Five side-chain ESM results and the paired-likelihood distribution are removed.

M1.justification: V1 inverts descriptors by optimizing coordinates of an existing structure. V3 retains this procedure and adds descriptor-gradient guidance inside AlphaFold3 reverse diffusion from Gaussian noise, using a new zeroth-order descriptor objective (Appendix J.2.2). This substantially extends inference capabilities; the core local-descriptor and GCN framework remains.

P1.justification: V3 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, background and discussion around MLFF representation reuse and transfer learning. It merges related work into the background, moves existing case studies into appendices, adds an experimental overview and reproducibility statement, and changes terminology, title, author information and citation style throughout.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to explain pretraining and transfer learning. Existing UMAP and ring-PCA figures move into the main text; comparison tables expand, and the chemical-shift table splits into backbone and side-chain tables. V3 adds overview, ablation and experimental-pKa tables plus correlation/guidance figures, removes the paired-likelihood panel and adopts conference formatting.

R1.justification: V3 adds literature on ESM3, structural distillation, experimental-pKa data and score-based generation. It also changes its characterization of pKa-ANI from a related AFM representation method to fixed symmetry-function descriptors, sharpening the novelty contrast with contextual MLFF features. The broader positioning against small-molecule descriptor applications remains.

T1.justification: Appendix J.2.2 adds a guided reverse-diffusion equation, a piecewise descriptor objective (Eq. 14) and a signed normalized conformer-distance definition (Eq. 15). The existing KDE, feature-construction, GCN and direct-inversion mathematics remains substantially unchanged. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation: broader ESM/learned controls and experimental-pKa tests address v1's limited comparisons and reliance on simulated pKa references. Radius/layer ablations and expanded inversion studies make important design and transfer claims more assessable, while new access information improves reproducibility. Training-set-based pKa comparisons, unresolved reporting inconsistencies and dropped side-chain ESM results limit the gains, but the added evidence provides a clear, substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same local-protein representation framework, renamed from AFMs to MLFFs in v3. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds experimental-pKa comparisons, radius/layer ablations and descriptor-guided AlphaFold3 generation results.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification, pKa and chemical-shift benchmarks, simulation-based analyses and descriptor-inversion results, including Tables B.1–B.4 and Appendix I.1.

results.title: Representing local protein environments with machine learning force fields

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain their original scope and headline findings. The conclusion additionally identifies two primary failure bottlenecks—fine-grained temporal perception and multi-hop reasoning—modestly expanding the explicitly stated diagnostic takeaway.

C2.justification: v2 develops the perception/reasoning diagnosis using text controls and failure cases, interprets judge stability and complexity resilience, and argues for broader applicability from LMArena alignment. Appendix E newly acknowledges that clean videos omit open-world difficulties such as blur and occlusion; the existing limitation about proposing no improvement method is retained.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 and Tables 20–22 newly explain that vid2txt inputs derive from ground-truth state transitions and illustrate their construction for all six demonstrations. Existing prompts, hardware descriptions, checkpoint and decoding configurations, and listed code/data links remain.

E1.justification: The core six demonstrations, six skills, and reported 240-video/1,440-question dataset remain. v2 adds ground-truth-text input scenarios and extends Number/Cup testing to 5×5 and 6×6 boards and sequences of 15–29 operations (Appendix A.3), beyond v1's smaller boards and 5–14 operations.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds vid2txt baseline variants for Qwen2.5-VL-7B/72B, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Seed1.5-VL, and Gemini-2.5-Flash. All original model and human comparators remain. The newly used Qwen3-235B-A22B serves as an alternative judge rather than an additional answering model.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation design through ground-truth-text controls, answer paraphrasing, alternative-judge evaluation, and extended complexity sweeps. The judge checks aggregate five directly graded skills (Tables 7–8). Original inference settings and human sampling remain unchanged, including v1 Table 14's configurations retained in v2 Table 23.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained analyses, v2 adds perception-versus-reasoning controls, a comparative failure case (Table 6), answer-format and judge sensitivity tests (Tables 7–8), alignment with five models' LMArena scores (Table 9), and larger-board/longer-sequence stress tests (Tables 10–11). These address several previously untested questions about validity and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: Neither version reports model run-count or seed protocols, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new judge and paraphrase comparisons report point accuracies; the LMArena comparison provides paired scores without a statistical correlation estimate or uncertainty analysis.

E6.justification: Original Table 2 scores and the existing quantitative analyses are retained. Substantial new results include vid2txt accuracies of 69.4% for Seed1.5-VL and 72.2% for Gemini-2.5-Flash, judge-check average differences below one percentage point, and extended-complexity results. These are additional conditions and findings, not improvements to the retained video-input scores.

M1.justification: The benchmark's state-transition design, video and question engines, reasoning skills, and default LLM-judging/simulation procedure remain unchanged. The additions concern auxiliary evaluation conditions and analyses.

P1.justification: Section 3.2 is locally rewritten around failure causes, a case-study subsection is added, and the appendices are reorganized with separate limitations and LLM-usage sections. Most original exposition and prompt wording remain, alongside conference-header, affiliation, and citation-style edits.

P2.justification: Table 2 is reordered and expanded with a vid2txt block. New displays include the response case study, five validation/scaling tables, and three illustrated video-to-text examples. Existing figures and prompt tables are largely retained, with relocation and conference-format layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 technical-report references and sharpens its comparison with VCR-Bench and MINERVA by naming their short-horizon tasks. The broader research positioning remains; switching to author-year citations is primarily presentational.

T1.justification: The state-transition formulation and formal task definitions are retained. Neither the new empirical analyses nor their interpretations introduce revised mathematical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation where v1 lacked controls separating perception from reasoning and checks of judge stability. The text controls, failure cases, and scoring-sensitivity experiments make the benchmark more diagnostically useful, while explicit clean-scene limitations better bound its applicability. The broad generalization claim based on only five LMArena models remains weakly supported, but this does not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoReasonBench and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, mathematical notation, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably despite reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds text-input controls, judge-robustness experiments, harder synthetic scenarios, and model-response case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 18 MLLMs, a human baseline, and experiments varying thinking budgets, visual inputs, video complexity, and state-reveal timing.

results.title: VideoReasonBench: Can MLLMs Perform Vision-Centric Complex Video Reasoning?

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims about biologically plausible bidirectional inference and combined generative/discriminative performance. The introduction refocuses the energy-landscape contribution from OOD detection toward capturing the training distribution and qualifies the multimodal contribution as learning in a bimodal architecture.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 refines the efficiency argument: bPC halves value neurons while retaining the same error-neuron count, with added discussion of dendritic error computation. Appendix H adds an interpretation of bottom-up learning as inversion supporting amortized inference. The central mutual-regularization explanation and max-pooling limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents stochastic updates, ancestral sampling, linear readouts, parameter-matched layer widths, and deep-model architectures, preprocessing, optimizers, schedules, and inference settings (Appendices A.5, G, and I). These substantially expand reproducibility information. The future code-release promise remains, but v1's GitHub organization link is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds Tiny-ImageNet and extends missing-pixel evaluation to CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet (Section 4.6). Section 4.2 additionally evaluates unsupervised distribution learning and unconditional sampling, extending v1's reconstruction and label-conditioned generation tasks.

E2.justification: A VAE is newly evaluated against the PC models for MNIST distribution learning (Section 4.2, Table 13). The existing comparison methods remain; arbitrary-graph PC, shared-weight bPC, and activity-decay discPC were already evaluated in v1 Appendix C.

E3.justification: New protocols include linear classifiers trained on representations, separate tuning for decoding and FID, stochastic training with 50 or 250 inference steps, and enlarged baselines matched to bPC's parameter count. The deep-network experiments introduce additional architectures, preprocessing, normalization, and a 1,000-plus-2,000-step inference schedule. These are additions alongside the retained original protocols.

E4.justification: New Appendix G tests whether the original advantages survive matching parameter counts. v2 also adds representation-decoding analysis, compares distribution learning at two inference budgets, and tests missing-input robustness in deeper networks. The earlier energy-weighting sensitivity study and max-pooling ablation remain.

E5.justification: v2 adds independent-samples t-tests with n=5 and p<0.05, marking comparisons significantly worse than bPC in Tables 10–12 and 14–15. Corresponding original results already reported five-seed means and SEMs. Figure captions now identify those error bars explicitly; this does not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: The numerical values in v1 Tables 10–16 are retained in v2 Tables 10, 11, and 14–18. Substantial new results appear for decoding, distribution learning, parameter-count controls, and deep-network robustness. Examples include bPC's MNIST FID of 3.34±0.53 with 250 activity updates (Table 13) and 73.4% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 50% missing pixels (Figure 8, Table 26), under newly introduced settings.

M1.justification: The original energy function and local weight updates remain, but v2 adds stochastic posterior inference and Monte Carlo learning for distribution estimation (Section 3 and Appendix A.5). Appendix I also introduces error-reparameterized optimization and staged generative/bidirectional inference for deep models. These extend the actual training and inference procedures.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and much of the experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Section headings become descriptive claims, Section 4.5 gains named subsections, and the hybridPC explanation moves into an expanded Appendix H. These changes reorganize and clarify existing material beyond simply appending new experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains explicit error-propagation arrows, Figure 4 expands with decoding and distribution-learning panels, and new Figures 8 and 13 display deep-network results and reconstructions. New result and implementation tables accompany these additions. Retained figures are resized or rearranged, captions are expanded, and the document's typography and layout are reformatted.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially broaden the biological and computational positioning. New discussion covers sampling-based perception, additional biologically motivated bidirectional models, and a machine-learning subsection addressing U-Net, VAVAE, VAR, and PredNet. The new scaling procedure is also positioned relative to error optimization.

T1.justification: v2 adds a mathematical specification of independent Gaussian inference noise and second-order Langevin updates (Equation 4 and Appendix A.5, Equations 7–8). The original energy and learning equations remain. The hybridPC objective in Appendix H is relocated from v1's main text, and no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: Appendix G directly addresses the parameter-count confound in the original MNIST/Fashion-MNIST comparisons. Expanded representation and distribution evaluations in Section 4.2 and deep-network tests in Section 4.6 materially strengthen the evidence for usefulness and generality. Added statistical tests and implementation details improve assessability. Remaining reporting weaknesses, including unlabeled paired accuracies in Tables 24–26 and removal of the planned code-location link, are limited relative to these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same bidirectional predictive coding work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched across reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds linear decoding, stochastic distribution learning, parameter-count controls, and deep-network experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, generation, representation-learning, XOR, bimodal-learning, and missing-input experiments, with numerical results in its appendices.

results.title: Bidirectional Predictive Coding

C1.justification: v1 emphasized a unified framework and efficient downstream search. v2 explicitly claims an improved BFS surpassing prior methods, the first adaptive DFS for diffusion inference scaling, and the first joint local/global scaling advancing the Pareto frontier (abstract and introduction). Expert iteration changes from a future direction into a demonstrated contribution.

C2.justification: v2 strengthens the central interpretation that global search is restricted to pretrained modes while local refinement can exceed base-model capabilities, and explains TFG saturation and DAS weaknesses through this distinction. It interprets higher MSP as reduced OOD generation. The hyperparameter-tuning limitation remains, but its proposed remedy changes from adaptive thresholds to evolutionary search.

D1.justification: Tables 6, 7 and 10 add BFS configurations, previously unspecified maze architecture/training parameters, and distillation settings; Appendix E.4.1 adds hardware and timing information. These maze disclosures do not establish an architecture change. Conversely, v2 omits v1's explicit ImageNet generator/resolution, complete class list, 100-step DDPM configuration and fixed local-search count.

E1.justification: v2 adds ImageReward prompt-based preference evaluation. Maze coverage contracts from Giant and Ultra to the retained 20-by-20 Ultra layout, now unnamed. The spatial/numeracy CompBench evaluations reported in v1 are absent from v2, which retains attribute-binding examples. D4RL locomotion and conditional ImageNet remain; the distillation study reuses D4RL.

E2.justification: v2 adds FK-steering, DAS, TreeG and SVDD to image-generation comparisons, TFG/DAS to maze and D4RL comparisons, and DPPO to the distillation comparison. CompBench additionally compares DFS with BFS. The D4RL table removes CQL and BCQ while retaining the other existing comparators (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 3).

E3.justification: New protocols include 100-step SD v1.5/SDXL evaluations, explicit TFG/DAS compute allowances, and five-epoch distillation followed by verifier-free evaluation. CompBench difficulty estimation changes from eight random samples to four. ImageNet adds MSP evaluation and replaces the reported class-specific BFS temperatures with a temperature sweep (Appendices E.1–E.5).

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled BFS resampling/scoring/tempering ablations (Table 1), maze temperature and DFS-threshold sensitivity analyses (Table 8; Figure 7), and expanded local-versus-global scaling comparisons (Figure 4). The existing double-verifier analysis is extended to BFS, MSP measurements and adversarial examples. Policy-distillation training curves provide another new supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix E.1 newly specifies four-trial mean and standard-deviation reporting for ImageReward experiments. CompBench Figure 3 adds uncertainty bands and error bars absent from v1 Figure 4, although their meaning is not specified there. The existing five-seed D4RL protocol remains unchanged; these additions do not establish increased runs for retained results.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial ImageReward, baseline, sensitivity and distillation results. New D4RL comparator averages are 82.1 for TFG and 80.2 for DAS; distillation scores are 51.6, 98.8 and 86.3 (Tables 3–4). Maze/CompBench curves are replaced and ImageNet results gain BFS and MSP entries. Existing TTS D4RL scores and four/eight-particle ImageNet BoN FID/accuracy values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 replaces rounded-allocation BFS-Resampling/BFS-Pruning with configurable tempering, path-based scoring and resampling, selecting Increase/Max/SSP (Section 4.1.1; Appendix D.1). It also revises DFS buffer selection and implements policy distillation through TTS-generated action labels and fine-tuning. Recurrent local search and the double-verifier principle already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction, contributions, related work and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Global search now precedes local search, and experiments are reorganized from domain-based sections into BFS design, DFS adaptivity, joint scaling and reward hacking. The appendices are substantially restructured, beyond merely accommodating new scientific content.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn, including removal of the pruning panel. Maze and CompBench plots are redesigned; v1's appendix Ultra examples move into v2 Figure 5. New ablation, distillation and parameter tables and sensitivity plots are added. ImageNet curves and uncurated image grids are replaced by an expanded table and adversarial examples, alongside a document-template change.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix B substantially refocus positioning around particle-based search, tree search and gradient guidance. Added discussions include DAS, SVDD, TreeG, ABCD and EvoSearch, while Appendix D maps prior designs into the BFS framework. Much of v1's broader LLM expert-iteration and diffusion-application review is removed.

T1.justification: Appendix C.3.3 adds Theorem 1 and a Wasserstein convergence-bound proof under bounded-support, strong-log-concavity, smoothness and Lipschitz-Hessian assumptions. Sections C.3.1–C.3.2 also revise recurrence coefficients and explicitly incorporate verifier tempering into the annealed target. The original continuous-limit Proposition 1 is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1's efficiency evidence, which relied mainly on Best-of-N comparisons: competitive search baselines and controlled BFS and joint-scaling experiments substantially strengthen support for the central claims (Tables 1–3; Figure 4). It also tests policy distillation previously left as future work. Narrower benchmark reporting and lost ImageNet implementation details are drawbacks, but the stronger comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a clear substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Content can be matched despite substantial restructuring and replacement of experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds BFS ablations and comparisons, policy-distillation outcomes, sensitivity analyses and reward-hacking evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original maze-planning, D4RL locomotion, CompBench and conditional ImageNet experiments, including search-efficiency and double-verifier results.

results.title: Inference-time scaling of diffusion models through classical search

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion redefine the contribution around masked guidance, semantic subject disentanglement and cross-pair data construction, explicitly targeting subject confusion and copy-paste artifacts. V1 centers its contributions on masking and channel concatenation. Its explicit claim of generalization from single-subject training is dropped.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking semantic injection to reduced subject interference and augmented reference pairs to reduced copying. Appendices E.2 and F expand v1's broad backbone-quality caveat into specific limitations involving complex interactions, physical behavior, reference-count scaling, T5 understanding and controllable long-video generation.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C add extensive processing and evaluation documentation, including baseline checkpoints, output resolutions/frame rates and identity-metric frame sampling. Conversely, v1's 22-million-to-0.5-million training-data counts, 32-H100/four-day budget and 480P/81-frame training settings disappear. V2 specifies H100 80GB GPUs and PyTorch but leaves its augmentation model and injection strength unspecified.

E1.justification: The benchmark retains 60 single-ID and 60 multi-subject cases. V2 adds background references to augmented training, whereas v1 explicitly describes training without background conditioning. Figures 9–11 extend qualitative coverage to clothing, eyewear and accessory transfer, including cluttered reference images, within the existing any-reference generation task.

E2.justification: The quantitative comparisons retain the same twelve single-ID and six multi-subject baselines. However, v2 Figure 6 reduces the single-ID qualitative comparison from v1 Figure 7, omitting HunyuanCustom, Concat-ID, EchoVideo, FantasyID, VACE and Vidu 2.0. These methods remain in the numerical evaluation.

E3.justification: V2 replaces optical-flow motion magnitude with Motion Smoothness, adds Subj-Sim and Bg-Sim, and introduces an averaged Total Score. New experiments include an ablation with matched training steps/resources and a 30-participant pairwise study with 60 questions per questionnaire and a tie option. Cross-pair augmentation also changes training preprocessing.

E4.justification: V1's qualitative masking/concatenation ablation is retained as v2 Figure 7. V2 additionally provides quantitative training-paradigm and pipeline ablations in Tables 3–4, semantic-alignment heatmaps and subject-disentanglement comparisons in Figures 4 and 8, and explicit failure cases in Figure 14. These substantially expand component validation and error analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's participant counts and preference percentages describe the new study but do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V1 reports MAGREF FaceSim scores of 0.567/0.581 for single-ID/multi-subject generation; v2's revised evaluation reports ID-Sim scores of 0.595/0.542. Numerous baseline entries change, and the reported single-ID identity leader changes from VACE to MAGREF. V2 adds subject/background scores, quantitative ablations, preference outcomes and qualitative findings. These are revised reports, not established same-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: V2 retains masked channel concatenation but adds subject disentanglement: text-derived cross-attention value embeddings are injected into corresponding subject regions at each layer. It also extends the three-stage data pipeline with generative cross-pair augmentation of face, object and background references. These change the procedure beyond expanded documentation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract and introduction around three challenges, extends the title, moves data curation after the generation mechanisms, combines qualitative and quantitative discussion into Main Results, and organizes detailed material into six appendices. This substantially changes the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column paper to a single-column report. V2 redraws and combines method diagrams, expands the pipeline illustration, splits the main results table, adds ablation tables, preference/radar plots, heatmaps and failure panels, and relocates retained qualitative material into new figure arrangements.

R1.justification: The related-work coverage remains broadly similar. V2 adds citations including CINEMA, OpenS2V-Nexus, Flow Matching, SDXL, SAM2 and Q-Align, while removing OpenCV and Open-Sora. These are localized updates supporting the revised method and evaluation.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.2 introduces the subject-specific mask and masked semantic-value update in Equations 5–6, a limited substantive mathematical extension. Most other added equations formalize previously described operations or standard background. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: Tables 3–4 address v1's lack of quantitative component validation, while subject/background metrics, human preference evidence and explicit failure analysis substantially strengthen evaluation of any-reference generation. These gains outweigh the loss of training-data counts and compute details. Reproducibility remains weakened by the unspecified augmentation model and injection strength, and neither version quantifies uncertainty, but v2 provides substantially stronger support and clearer boundaries for its contributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MAGREF, with matching masked-guidance components and single-ID/multi-subject evaluations. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–F were included in the comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and ablation results in Tables 1–4, a human preference study, and additional qualitative analyses and failure cases.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark results in Table 1, generated examples and qualitative component ablations in Figure 9.

results.title: MAGREF: Masked Guidance for Any-Reference Video Generation with Subject Disentanglement

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions and substantive conclusion retain the same central claims: SAM implicitly regularizes predictive entropy, improves calibration including under distribution shift, and CSAM further improves calibration while preserving generalization. The additional evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies the applicability of the Hessian assumption, distinguishing a potentially varying theoretical radius from the constant radius used in practice, and discusses the role of gradient magnitude. It adds explanations of rho–gamma overregularization and calibration–sharpness relationships, plus preliminary applicability beyond cross-entropy. The interpretation that using SAM only late in training suffices is removed with Appendix D.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly supplies a link described as providing reproduction code; v1 provides no code location. Its accessibility cannot be established from the PDFs. Existing disclosures of batch size, learning-rate and weight-decay searches, momentum, and the two-GPU/~1500-GPU-hour resource description are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100-C, ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-C and Tiny-ImageNet. V2 expands methods and analyses within the existing classification and distribution-shift coverage without introducing a distinct dataset, population or task.

E2.justification: V2 substantially broadens the evaluated alternatives. ACLS and BalCAL join the corresponding CIFAR comparisons in Table 3 and Table S5, formerly Table 4. New comparisons evaluate ASAM and VASSO in Tables S11–S12 and label smoothing, MBLS, CRL, CPC and MDCA in Tables S13–S14. These are reported evaluations, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: V2 adds diagnostic protocols measuring Hessian eigenvalues along ascent segments and across training epochs, a joint rho-by-gamma grid in Table S4, and largest-eigenvalue sharpness measurements in Table S16. The optimizer-switching design from v1 Appendix D is removed. These substantially expand and revise the diagnostic evaluation design; retained benchmark splits and training budgets are not reported as changed.

E4.justification: New analyses test the Hessian assumptions and entropy-weight behavior in Figures 2/S4, interactions between perturbation radius and regularization strength, compatibility with other losses, and the relationship between calibration and sharpness. Conversely, v1 Appendix D's SGD-to-SAM and SAM-to-SGD switching study disappears. The original separate rho and gamma sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly reports that the added ImageNet comparison in Table S14 uses only one run because of time limits. Retained CIFAR and appendix benchmarks continue reporting means and standard deviations over three runs. No increased replication or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: V2 adds CSAM results to Tables 1–2 and substantial new results in Tables S4 and S11–S16, while removing the switching-study results. Retained values also change: Table 1's vanilla SAM CIFAR10-C AUROC changes from 77.24 ± 0.54 to 63.32 ± 4.77, and Table 2's ViT-S/16 SAM TCE changes from 1.97 to 1.66. These are score revisions without an explained protocol change. V1 Tables S5–S9 remain numerically unchanged as v2 Tables S6–S10.

M1.justification: The main CSAM algorithm and piecewise loss are unchanged: v1 Equation 1 becomes v2 Equation 4, and Algorithm 1 is relocated. Table S15 introduces limited extensions combining SAM/CSAM with focal loss or ACLS, although the implementation of these combinations is not specified.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the six-section organization remain intact. Local revisions expand the theoretical discussion, move Algorithm 1 into Appendix A, consolidate gamma sensitivity into Appendix B, and remove Appendix D. V2 also adds affiliations, acknowledgments and a language-model-use disclosure. This is limited restructuring rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The conference template changes typography and text width throughout. Figure 2's analytical curve is replaced by three empirical panels, Figure 3 expands from two to four panels, and a new Hessian figure and several tables are added. Existing tables gain method rows, Table 4 moves to Appendix C as S5, and the switching figure disappears. The original rho and gamma plots are retained as Figures S5/S6.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting ACLS, BalCAL, MBLS, CPC, MDCA and CRL, and removes Zhou et al. (2025) alongside the switching study. The main related-work discussion and positioning of SAM's entropy interpretation remain substantially unchanged; bibliography formatting changes do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: Lemmas 1–2 replace the original curvature premise with nonzero-gradient and gradient-dependent Hessian conditions along the entire ascent segment. Lemma 1 changes its exponential bound from exp(-rho/2) to exp(-rho times gradient norm/2), and Appendix A restores the missing gradient factor in the Taylor argument. Theorem 3 explicitly invokes Lemma 1. These materially revise the theoretical justification, although the displayed Lemma 2 exponent still uses the loss norm rather than the gradient norm.

improvement.justification: Restoring gradient-norm dependence and requiring the Hessian condition along the full ascent segment repairs important defects in v1's Lemma 1 argument. Empirical assumption checks, broader baselines, CSAM ImageNet/OOD results and interaction studies substantially strengthen the paper's support. These gains outweigh removal of the switching study, although unexplained score revisions, the remaining Lemma 2 notation issue and single-run Table S14 limit confidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAM/CSAM calibration study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A–C retain original experiments and add empirical checks of theoretical assumptions, additional comparisons, and diagnostic studies.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendices B–D report original training experiments, calibration and accuracy measurements, distribution-shift evaluations, and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Towards Understanding The Calibration Benefits of Sharpness-Aware Minimization

C1.justification: V1 claims a first complete solution for exact volumetric Gaussian rendering. V2 narrows exactness to projective geometry and reframes the integral contribution as establishing the connection to an existing maximum-response heuristic. Its abstract and introduction also explicitly claim generalization to wider FoVs unseen during training. This substantially revises the scope and novelty of the central claims.

C2.justification: New Appendix A acknowledges ordering, overlap, self-attenuation, and occasional popping artifacts, explicitly disclaiming full physical volumetric exactness. V2 also adds substantive explanations of densification's limits, mismatched-culling artifacts, GOF instability, and why full-FoV perspective supervision can underperform central crops. These extend the original interpretation substantially.

D1.justification: V2 adds explicit CUDA numerical-stability implementation discussion, identifies H200 hardware for scaling experiments, and states that code/video/HTML accompany supplementary material, with training/evaluation scripts planned for release. Most initialization, hyperparameter, reprojection, and camera-pose details already existed in v1 and are relocated to Appendix G. The PDFs do not independently establish actual code availability.

E1.justification: V2 adds two Aria egocentric scenes with moderate-FoV, low-light imagery (Appendix J). It also adds ScanNet++ central-crop-to-full-FoV evaluation and unseen extreme-FoV scenarios, including 170-degree pinhole and 180-degree circular rendering. These materially extend the original datasets and cross-camera tests.

E2.justification: The main benchmark baseline sets largely persist. V2 adds 3DGS to the ScanNet++ comparison and evaluates GOF without filtering against GOF using 3DGEER formulas (Figure C.1); its revised BEAP table drops v1's separate 3DGS comparator. Newly discussed 2DGS and HTGS are conceptual comparisons, not added benchmark evaluations.

E3.justification: New protocols lower FisheyeGS's densification threshold and evaluate 4k–30k checkpoints, replace transmittance separately during inference and training, and expand supervision comparisons across central/full FoV and projection spaces. Gaussian-count, memory, and per-tile workload measurements are added. Table 4 also reverses GPU attribution for unchanged sourced FPS values, without establishing reruns; the original 30k benchmark protocol remains.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of whether increased Gaussian counts compensate for approximation, train/test-time transmittance substitutions, extreme-FoV robustness, GOF numerical degeneracy, and rendering the same pretrained scene with different engines (Sections 4.1, 4.4 and Appendices C.7, I). BEAP ablations expand substantially. The original PBF cross-association analysis is retained in Table K.6.

E5.justification: V2 Table K.6 newly reports means and standard deviations of Gaussian associations per tile, whereas v1 Table 7 reports only perceptual scores and their differences. This adds descriptive variability reporting, not repeated-run uncertainty. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores and most runtime results are retained, including 31.50 ScanNet++ and 27.76 MipNeRF360 PSNR. Substantial new entries cover Aria, central-crop generalization, scaling, transmittance replacement, memory, and numerical stability. Aria reports average PSNR of 33.5 versus FisheyeGS's 32.8. The original central-only BEAP result set is replaced under an expanded protocol, not shown to improve under identical settings.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same canonical ray integral, analytic gradients, PBF-CSF association with mirror handling, BEAP supervision, and training/rendering algorithms. V2's numerical-stability discussion explains the existing cross-product computation rather than introducing a changed core method.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries and the full rendering derivation move into Appendix B, ablations are integrated into Section 4, and implementation information is consolidated in Appendix G. A contents list and new limitations, ethics, reproducibility, and usage statements further reorganize the document.

P2.justification: The two-column ACM layout becomes a single-column ICLR layout. V1 Figures 3–4 are combined into v2 Figure 2, runtime tables and ScanNet++ visuals move to appendices, and the ZipNeRF qualitative display is redesigned. Expanded comparison tables and new scaling, extreme-FoV, stability, and Aria figures substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the contribution through Celarek et al.'s scaling argument, new comparisons with 2DGS and HTGS, and explicit recognition that its rendering expression matches prior maximum-response heuristics. Appendices A, D.3, and I expand comparisons of assumptions, exactness, and practical limitations. This goes beyond citation updates or EVER's publication-year change.

T1.justification: The ray-integral theorem, gradient derivations, and PBF solver are retained. V2 adds mathematical reasoning about numerical cancellation for nearly degenerate Gaussians (Appendix C.7, Equation C.14), states a condition for neglecting negative ray parameters (B.2), and identifies perspective-camera equivalences with earlier formulations (D.3). These are limited additions rather than a replacement of the theoretical framework.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves scientific qualification and empirical support. Appendix A addresses v1's overly broad exact-volumetric framing, while new scaling, transmittance-replacement, stability, and unseen-FoV tests directly examine the claimed advantages. These gains extend beyond additional benchmark scores. Some blanket performance claims remain overstated: Table 4 still gives EVER higher SSIM than 3DGEER, 0.825 versus 0.821, despite the all-metrics wording.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3DGEER work, with matching authors, algorithms, and benchmark results. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds Aria experiments, Gaussian-count scaling, extreme-FoV evaluations, and rendering and numerical-stability analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original ScanNet++, ZipNeRF, and MipNeRF360 experiments, runtime measurements, and PBF/BEAP ablations.

results.title: 3DGEER: 3D Gaussian Rendering Made Exact and Efficient for Generic Cameras

C1.justification: The central claims of robust experience-based planning and a 7B-model advantage remain. v2 narrows the 'from scratch' framing toward correcting flawed priors under binary feedback, makes superiority to LLM self-correction an explicit headline claim, and no longer presents DEX/sample efficiency as a principal contribution.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's brief Redstone explanation involving item-name ambiguity with a detailed account of missing analogous experience and controller resource limits. Standard-MineRL controls sharpen applicability boundaries. It also qualifies action correction's usefulness without accurate dependencies and explains the increasing exploration cost of larger action spaces, substantially expanding interpretation beyond v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, SC prompts, cycle-prevention instructions, environment versions/API mappings, and detailed perturbation and additional-goal specifications. Hardware and compute disclosures are retained. Documentation has drawbacks: Table 15 drops earlier error-analysis episode totals; x0 is 2 in the main text but -2 in Table 7; Algorithm 3 omits the counter increment described in prose.

E1.justification: v2 adds Mineflayer and the household TextWorld Cooking domain. Minecraft coverage also expands through additional leather, paper, flint, and other goal items, unmodified MineRL resource conditions, larger action spaces, and environments whose rules change during learning. The original 67-goal coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds an SC agent correcting both dependencies and actions to the dependency-learning comparisons; this is broader than v1's dependency-only self-correction ablation. Appendix K additionally evaluates DEPS† and OracleActionPlanner in controller comparisons, and Random+FAM, UCB, and an LLM without memory in action-selection experiments.

E3.justification: The reported MC-TextWorld horizon changes from 2,000 to 3,000 steps, and fixed rule modifications become graded randomized requirement/action perturbations, including combined perturbations. New protocols compare 4B/7B planners, one/three initial plans, and different action-set sizes. Cooking uses 50-step episodes with ingredients and tools supplied; dynamic-rule tests notify agents which items changed.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands mechanism testing through separated dependency/action-correction ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, controller and oracle-planner controls, dynamic-rule recovery, misleading external knowledge, goal/action scalability, and weaker-planner/initial-knowledge tests (Sections 5.5–5.6 and K.2–K.11). The earlier initial-graph and planning-error analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 reports MC-TextWorld means and standard deviations over 20 episodes; v2 specifies 15 runs and omission of negligible standard deviations. New experiments disclose three independent 100-episode cooking runs and 20 runs per goal for action selection. These refine repetition and uncertainty reporting without introducing a substantially different statistical framework.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include Mineflayer EGA near 0.9, cooking success rates of 1.00 versus SC's 0.75 and DECKARD's 0.09, and zero Diamond/Gold success under standard MineRL conditions (Table 14). Revised ablations and perturbation settings add further results. The original aggregate and per-goal MineRL scores remain unchanged after renaming, including overall learned/oracle success rates of 0.54/0.79.

M1.justification: The principal dependency-revision, action-memory, DEX, and CRe procedures survive the renaming. The reported revision trigger changes from aggregate net failures reaching d0 to all actions being classified invalid (Algorithms 1). Appendix A also adapts ADG to single-precondition cooking tasks. These are localized procedural changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. REPOA/ADL/FFOM become XENON/ADG/FAM, related work moves into the main text, and the overall algorithm and DEX move into appendices. The appendix organization is extensively rebuilt.

P2.justification: v2 adds failure-example, agent-overview, knowledge-correction, and perturbation diagrams, alongside numerous new experimental plots and tables. Existing displays are also reorganized: MineRL learning is paired with Mineflayer, the main success-rate table gains a planner-LLM column, and component ablations are restructured. These are substantial visual changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning against LLM self-correction, adding literature including Reflexion, CRITIC, and self-verification studies in Section 2.2. Much of v1's broader environmental-knowledge-learning discussion is replaced, while additional long-context and small-model literature supports the revised positioning. This exceeds merely moving related work into the main text.

T1.justification: The DAG formulation, requirement-set definitions, Ntrue objective in Equation 1, and DEX selection mathematics are retained. The added cycle-handling discussion explains implementation; it does not introduce a new formal theoretical result, proof, or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens evidence for why the method works and where it fails. Self-correction comparisons, separated mechanism ablations, sensitivity tests, and standard-MineRL/oracle-planner controls address important gaps in v1's validation and controller-limit analysis. Mineflayer and cooking broaden supporting evidence without relying on improved retained benchmark scores. Threshold, pseudocode, and some table inconsistencies limit reproducibility, but the stronger experimental controls and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite renaming REPOA to XENON and changing the title. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds Mineflayer, TextWorld Cooking, robustness, scalability, and controller-comparison results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MineRL and MC-TextWorld experiments, including dependency-learning curves, task success rates, ablations, and appendix error analyses.

results.title: Experience-based Knowledge Correction for Robust Planning in Minecraft

C1.justification: The central contribution—learning delay-robust policies solely from delay-free offline data through belief-constrained policy iteration—remains. V2 broadens the abstract's comparison claims to state-of-the-art delayed RL methods, explicitly includes goal-conditioned generalization, and calls joint belief-policy optimization essential. These extend the original headline claims without changing the central research objective.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations connecting Belief-IQL failures to exponentiated advantage errors, discusses prediction-accuracy versus computation tradeoffs, and interprets joint training as adapting beliefs to value-function errors. It also acknowledges that difficult AntMaze tasks may require goal-conditioned modifications and discusses transformer capacity and extreme-delay degradation. The earlier known-delay and vision-scaling limitations largely persist.

D1.justification: V2 adds a specific code repository URL, NVIDIA A5000/AMD EPYC hardware details, task-specific training-time examples, and ensemble/diffusion hyperparameter tables. The original transformer settings are retained, while the three-step setting disappears. Reproducibility documentation expands substantially, although the ensemble table repeats transformer settings and joint-training updates remain incompletely specified.

E1.justification: V2 expands beyond the three locomotion environments to four goal-conditioned AntMaze tasks and Adroit Pen, Door and Hammer manipulation tasks. It also adds 32- and 64-step delays and Gaussian, exponential and binomial delay scenarios beyond the original fixed and uniform 4/8/16-step settings.

E2.justification: The original Augmented-BC, Augmented-CQL and Belief-CQL comparisons are retained. V2 adds Belief-IQL across locomotion and unadapted IQL/CQL for Hopper in Table 2, plus Augmented-COMBO and DBPT-SAC for AntMaze in Table 1. Ensemble MLP and diffusion belief predictors are also evaluated against the transformer in Figure 2 and Table 3.

E3.justification: The original locomotion return metric and delay protocols remain. New evaluation designs compare predictors under a common 100-epoch budget using prediction MSE and inference latency, vary data availability from 25% to 100% at fixed HalfCheetah delay 8, and sweep transformer depth and width with convergence and memory measurements. These introduce substantial controlled evaluation settings.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's delay sweeps, v2 adds architecture and transformer-capacity ablations, joint versus separately pretrained belief comparisons, and data-availability experiments. It also adds longer-delay and alternative-distribution robustness tests and qualitative 16-step prediction rollouts. Section 5.3 and Appendix C therefore directly examine design choices and failure conditions previously untested.

E5.justification: V1 provides benchmark point estimates without seed counts or standard deviations. V2 Tables 7–8 report the retained locomotion results as mean ± standard deviation over three seeds; Tables 1 and 9 also specify three-seed averages, and new plots report uncertainty. This establishes substantially expanded reporting, not an explicit increase in runs.

E6.justification: All 288 numerical entries from v1 Tables 1–2 are retained as means in v2 Tables 7–8. V2 adds substantial task, baseline, ablation and robustness results. For example, Table 11 newly reports 105.20 for DT-CORL versus 0.22 for Belief-CQL on Hammer-expert-v1 with deterministic delay 16, while Table 1 exposes near-zero performance on large-play AntMaze.

M1.justification: The transformer belief model, policy-iteration objectives and deployment procedure are retained. However, v2 removes v1's n-step/Retrace description and 'Multi Steps = 3' hyperparameter without stating whether those updates were discontinued. Its stronger joint-training language also lacks an explicit revised update rule, leaving actual procedural changes unresolved.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, updates the byline, rewrites substantial introduction and related-work passages, moves related work from Section 6 to Section 2, and combines preliminaries with problem formulation. Experiments are reorganized from deterministic/stochastic subsections into task, baseline and ablation sections. Ethics, reproducibility and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: The original locomotion tables are relocated and expanded as compact Appendix Tables 7–8, while new main-text tables organize AntMaze and belief-baseline comparisons. V2 adds prediction-error, manipulation and long-delay plots, four rollout-image panels, and multiple ablation and implementation tables. Figure 1 and the document template/layout are also revised.

R1.justification: V2 adds a focused connection to classical delay compensation and Smith predictors, alongside references supporting differential-equation modeling, simulation, COMBO and dexterous manipulation. The three multi-step-return references disappear. The central positioning relative to offline RL and augmentation- versus belief-based delayed RL remains intact.

T1.justification: The Lipschitz definitions, delayed-MDP formulation, Lemmas 4.1–4.2, Proposition 4.3 and associated derivations and proof are substantively retained. V1 Appendix A becomes v2 Appendix B. Changes to indices, notation, wording and cross-references do not introduce new theoretical results or revise the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V1 supported its method mainly with locomotion return tables, without controlled component ablations or seed-level uncertainty. V2 substantially strengthens that evidence through architecture, joint-training and data-availability tests, broader task and delay evaluations, three-seed variability, and additional reproducibility information. These additions help assess design choices and expose applicability limits while preserving the original results. Overstated AntMaze comparisons and incomplete joint-training/ensemble specifications limit the gains, but the added diagnostic evidence establishes a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DT-CORL for learning from delay-free offline data and deployment under observation delays. Despite the changed title and expanded scope, matching methods, equations, proofs and experiments establish continuity. The main text, figures, tables and appendices are readable.

after.justification: V2 retains the original experiments and reports additional AntMaze, dexterous manipulation, belief-model ablation and robustness results in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original D4RL HalfCheetah, Hopper and Walker2d experiments under deterministic and stochastic delays in Tables 1–2.

results.title: Belief-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning for Delay-Robust Policy Optimization

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit abstract and introduction claim that CityLens is the largest or most extensive socioeconomic benchmark in geographic coverage, indicator diversity, and model scale. Its contribution summary also emphasizes model-architecture analysis. The central benchmark contribution and conclusion that current models struggle across indicators and regions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving perception errors, unsuitable reasoning strategies, and limitations of the extracted feature vectors, together with the conceptual mechanism in Appendix A.10. It newly discusses geographic underrepresentation, Mapillary quality and coverage limitations, and restrictions on operational use. These substantially broaden both interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed label mapping and aggregation rules, satellite pixel size and resolution, a complete CoT prompt, and available-case counts. Its Reproducibility Statement clarifies Google/Baidu redistribution restrictions, panorama IDs and retrieval scripts, and reported Mapillary and Hugging Face data access. Much of this information was absent from v1; it does not establish changes to the original processing procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation across all eleven indicators using CityLens-Mapillary, covering a different imagery distribution and the scenario where proprietary street-view APIs are unavailable (Appendix A.3). It also reports exploratory multiple-choice Population testing in A.8.1. The original geographic and indicator scope remains; the smaller Mapillary counts represent fewer cases, not removal of indicator categories.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated UrbanCLIP and UrbanVLP baselines, which v1 only cited. Additional comparisons introduce o4-mini, GLM-4.1v-Thinking, thinking-enabled Gemini, four vision-encoder variants, and Random Forest, XGBoost, and MLP regressors (Figure 7 and Table 5). The original 17-model comparison is retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds supervised fine-tuning on additional CityLens data with eight-task evaluation, a satellite-only control, controlled vision-encoder comparisons, and multiple-choice distractor construction. It also corrects the stated scatterplot exclusion threshold from R2 ≤ 0.5 to R2 ≤ −0.5. The scatterplot itself is unchanged, so this correction does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's city variation, satellite inclusion, and image-count analyses, v2 tests CoT, intrinsic reasoning, vision encoders, nonlinear regressors, and supervised adaptation. It adds perception/reasoning error cases and a Global North–South bias audit. These substantially expand investigation of input dependence, representation bottlenecks, adaptation potential, and geographic reliability.

E5.justification: Both versions report Mean and SD across tasks, without repeated-run or seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional result tables do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice, and descriptions of differences as significant are not accompanied by statistical tests.

E6.justification: All 17 shared rows in Table 1 retain identical numerical values. Substantial new results include UrbanVLP's mean R2 of 0.417, fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B's Building Height R2 of 0.872, and GDP group scores of 0.399 versus 0.168 for Global North and South cities (Tables 1, 2, and 9). Mapillary and diagnostic experiments add further results under their respective settings.

M1.justification: The original three paradigms remain, but v2 introduces substantive procedural extensions: four-stage CoT prompting, supervised adaptation for direct prediction, and Caption-Embed regression using generated captions encoded by BERT (Sections 3.4–3.5 and Appendices A.7.4 and A.8.2). These add training, inference, and representation pathways absent from v1.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: experimental settings and Discussion move to the appendix, numbered method subsections become paragraph headings, and detailed analysis is reorganized into geographic/input, reasoning/architecture, and error/adaptation sections. Related work is condensed and the appendix structure is extensively rebuilt. Title, authorship, affiliations, and LLVM-to-LVLM terminology also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview and construction diagrams, expands Table 1 with baseline groups, and adds a third modality condition to the existing ablation plot. New displays include prompt comparisons, reasoning/encoder results, error cases, fine-tuning, Mapillary, nonlinear regression, and bias-audit tables. Earlier appendix examples and comparison plots remain, renumbered and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 updates the literature context with works including CityRise, UrbanLLaVA, UrbanMLLM, Prismatic VLMs, and LLaVA-CoT, plus references concerning multiple-choice evaluation. Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench discussion and references are removed. The central positioning as a benchmark addressing an urban socioeconomic evaluation gap remains, with an added largest-benchmark claim.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results, proofs, or mathematical derivations. v2's low-level/high-level visual reasoning account in Appendix A.10 is explicitly an unvalidated conceptual hypothesis, rather than a new formal definition or theorem.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the benchmark's diagnostic value and usability. UrbanCLIP/UrbanVLP comparisons remedy v1's lack of evaluated domain-specific baselines, while targeted experiments investigate important sources of failure. Mapillary evaluation and clearer mapping, licensing, and access documentation strengthen reproducibility. Some additions remain underdocumented, and Appendix A.4 names Maverick while Table 5 names Scout, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CityLens, retaining the same core 17-city, 11-indicator benchmark and three evaluation paradigms. Text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renumbering, relocation, and additions.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds original fine-tuning, Mapillary, nonlinear-regression, reasoning, and geographic-bias results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original results for 17 models in Table 1, direct versus normalized prediction results in Figure 4, and city-level and input-composition experiments in Figure 5.

results.title: CityLens: Evaluating Large Vision-Language Models for Urban Socioeconomic Sensing

C1.justification: The title, abstract and conclusion narrow the framing from continuous ground-view video to multiview-consistent panoramic sequences. The contribution statement also specifies adaptation of epipolar attention to panoramic equirectangular projections and describes the triplane as adopted. The central framework, dataset contribution and superiority claims remain.

C2.justification: New discussions explain cross-batch inconsistency, the importance of vertical triplane information, dynamic sampling refinement and noise from distant frames. Appendix A.9 adds concrete limitations: road-network coverage, nearly identical outputs below 8 m pose separation associated with 15–20 m training spacing and limited triplane resolution, and slow inference. These materially qualify v1's broad continuity and applicability claims.

D1.justification: Appendices A.4–A.5 substantially expand implementation documentation with image-to-triplane attention, batch sizes, sequence lengths, warm-up and fine-tuning schedules, AdamW with learning rate 7e-5, and temporal-decoder training for 40 epochs. Section 3 clarifies feature summation and offset initialization. A new reproducibility statement promises code and dataset release, but supplies no release access.

E1.justification: CVUSA, VIGOR, VIGOR++ and downstream localization coverage are retained. Appendix A.4/Figure 9 adds an explicitly tested scenario involving different trajectories generated across batches, conditioning subsequent generation on previously generated images. This modestly extends the tested conditioning scenarios.

E2.justification: The quantitative baseline sets in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. Figure 4 adds ControlS2S to the qualitative comparison on retained trajectory examples; v1's corresponding comparison included EscherNet but not ControlS2S, although ControlS2S appeared elsewhere.

E3.justification: Section 4 adds LRCE for panorama-boundary consistency and a Pi3 reconstruction/rendering protocol evaluated with 3DPS and 3DSS. Appendices A.6–A.8 introduce controlled component comparisons and specified runtime/memory evaluations, including 10-, 20- and 30-frame sequences. Existing dataset splits and main training settings are retained; newly disclosed training details do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Tables 5–9 add dedicated tests of triplane versus BEV representations, ray-based versus standard attention, dynamic sampling refinement, and sparse versus dense interframe attention, including resource scaling. Figure 9 adds a cross-batch consistency case study. These substantially expand analysis beyond the retained full-cross-attention versus epipolar-attention comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional results retain single-point reporting.

E6.justification: Existing numerical entries in Tables 1–4 are retained. New results include SatDreamer360's 3DPS/3DSS of 13.31/0.5196, LRCE of 14.53 on CVUSA and 5.081 on VIGOR, and the ablation/resource outcomes in Tables 5–9. These are additional findings, not improved scores over v1. Table 6's CVUSA label conflicts with its proposed-method values matching the VIGOR row in Table 2, leaving that comparison's dataset attribution uncertain.

M1.justification: The loss, triplane representation, dynamic ray attention, epipolar constraint and sparse frame querying remain unchanged. However, Appendix A.5 newly describes temporal 3D-convolution modules in the decoder and their separate training. The PDFs do not establish whether these are an architectural addition or previously undocumented implementation details.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and model analysis receive extensive rewriting, with a pervasive shift from temporal/video terminology to multiview terminology. The title changes, and the document gains a reproducibility statement and a structured appendix covering explanations, experiments, limitations and disclosures.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain metric columns and Tables 5–9 are added. Figure 4 is reorganized and gains ControlS2S rows; retained satellite/trajectory panels move to Figure 10 with relabeling. Figures 8, 9 and 11 add a projection illustration, cross-batch demonstration and further comparisons. Typography, headings and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: The introduction, related work and method now explicitly credit prior epipolar-attention and view-synthesis research, including He et al., Tseng et al. and EpiDiff, positioning the contribution as an extension to panoramic imagery. Additional triplane, panorama-metric and reconstruction references broaden the discussion. This substantially revises the positioning of a central claimed contribution.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds a derivation of the existing epipolar constraint, using skew-symmetric products in Equations 9–15. The original constraint and main equations remain unchanged; Appendix A.2 restates the existing projection mapping. The added derivation leaves depth-scale factors implicit when identifying inverse projections with 3D points.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial gaps in component validation and reproducibility through dedicated ablations, geometry and boundary evaluations, detailed training documentation, and concrete failure conditions. These make the retained performance claims considerably easier to assess. Table 6's dataset inconsistency and the depth-scale ambiguity in the added proof weaken specific additions, but do not outweigh the broader gains in evidence, transparency and appropriately qualified claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SatDreamer360, the same VIGOR++ dataset construction, and matching core experiments. Text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 includes readable Appendices A.1–A.12.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, with additional reconstruction and panorama-boundary measurements, component ablations, resource measurements and qualitative experiments.

before.justification: Tables 1–4 report original generation experiments, an attention ablation, and downstream localization results using synthetic training data.

results.title: SatDreamer360: Multiview-Consistent Generation of Ground-Level Scenes from Satellite Imagery

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes feasibility, action-following evaluation metrics, decoding-design studies, and in-/out-of-distribution calibration behavior. v2's abstract, contributions, and conclusion instead emphasize agreement with real-world policy outcomes, rankings across policy versions and training stages, and evaluation of novel visual and language conditions. This substantially changes the main contribution claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning shape-versus-color discrimination, confusion between physical objects and displayed images, and pretraining/backbone explanations for policy generalization. v1's discussion of underestimating in-distribution policies, overestimating noisy policies, and sparse object-interaction training frames disappears. Brief realism qualifications remain, but the detailed world-model limitations analysis is reduced.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents percentile-based action normalization, a 20-frame context, rollout pseudocode, and graded reward prompts. Appendices C–D provide architecture, conditioning, losses, and training details for the video-based and diffusion policies. The core world-model hyperparameter table and project access link remain, while gridworld and segmentation/tracking implementation details are removed.

E1.justification: LIBERO and synthetic gridworld evaluations disappear. v2 adds evaluation on 17 held-out Bridge tasks and new scenarios involving edited objects, distractors, visual classification, and altered language instructions. Existing Open-X robot-video coverage and the Bridge dataset-size comparison remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated TinyLlama action-embedding alternative to raw-vector conditioning in v1 Section 3.2 and Figure 3 is removed. v2 expands the robot policies being assessed, but these are evaluation subjects rather than competing policy-evaluation methods. Cosmos, SIMPLER, and WorldEval are discussed without empirical comparisons against WorldGym.

E3.justification: v1's 32-rollout LIBERO evaluations and Gaussian-action-noise protocol are replaced by matched-initial-image evaluations of RT-1-X, Octo, and OpenVLA, using 10 trials per policy per Bridge task. v2 also introduces model-version/checkpoint evaluations, partial-credit scoring, and a 40-frame A100 timing experiment. These are new evaluation designs, not comparable reruns of v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic OOD robustness tests, policy-version and training-checkpoint ranking analyses, and horizon-dependent inference timing. It removes the action-representation study, context/horizon accuracy ablations, human–video-metric agreement analysis, reduced-frame reward-prompt analysis, and detailed simulator failure cases. The Bridge dataset-size ablation is retained in Appendix F.1.

E5.justification: v1 computes LIBERO uncertainty from four groups of eight rollouts. v2 explicitly reports standard errors across task success rates in Appendix E.3 and adds a correlation significance result, p < 0.001, in Figure 4a. The retained RT-1 reward table still reports four-run uncertainty; the PDFs do not establish increased seeded replication.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the LIBERO results with extensive new policy-evaluation results, including correlation r = 0.78 and OpenVLA scores of 67.4% in WorldGym versus 70.6% in the real-world reference trials. Its distractor evaluation reports 39.4% for OpenVLA, and Table 9 reports 93 versus 33 seconds for horizons 1 versus 4. RT-1 reward-validation entries and Bridge dataset-ablation values are retained. These additions do not establish performance gains over v1 under matching conditions.

M1.justification: The core DiT/Diffusion Forcing world model and Monte Carlo/VLM evaluation pipeline remain. v2 adds clip-level action dropout with classifier-free guidance and changes the reward procedure to support optional 0.5 partial credit. Matching the prediction horizon to policy action chunks refines the existing flexible blockwise inference scheme.

P1.justification: The title and framework name change, and the abstract, contributions, method narrative, and evaluation narrative are extensively rewritten. World-model construction and validation are combined in Section 3, policy evaluation is reorganized into Section 4, and reward validation and retained ablations move to appendices. The appendix organization and citation style also change substantially.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around interactive policy evaluation and OOD inputs. v2 adds correlation, ranking, training-progress, and distractor plots, numerous OOD illustrations, detailed task tables, and rollout pseudocode, while removing the gridworld, LIBERO, metric-analysis, and simulator-failure displays. Several robot-video panels are retained and relocated, and the document typography and headers change.

R1.justification: v2 substantively positions WorldGym against SIMPLER and WorldEval through its support for diverse morphologies and OOD inputs, and contrasts its flexible prediction horizon with Cosmos. It removes the video-generation-metrics related-work discussion and associated citations while adding literature supporting the expanded policy and implementation studies. This changes research positioning beyond citation-format updates.

T1.justification: v1's formal definition of arm-masked semantic MSE in Equation 3 is removed with that evaluation framework. The POMDP formulation and policy-value Equations 1–2 remain essentially unchanged, and neither version provides theoretical proofs. v2's standard-error formula documents statistical reporting rather than new theory.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrated LIBERO evaluation and real-video fidelity but lacked direct validation of learned robot-policy success estimates against physical trial outcomes. v2 substantially addresses this gap through matching initial images across three policies and 17 Bridge tasks, with detailed comparisons supporting the reported correlation of 0.78 (Figure 4 and Table 5). Removing useful calibration, ablation, and failure analyses weakens diagnostic transparency, and OOD conclusions remain dependent on simulator fidelity. Nevertheless, the direct real-outcome validation substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central purpose.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same video-world-model policy-evaluation framework, renamed from WPE to WorldGym. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original WorldGym rollouts, OOD evaluations, policy-checkpoint comparisons, and inference-time measurements. Table 5 distinguishes its original simulated results from real-world reference results taken from OpenVLA.

before.justification: v1 reports original gridworld experiments, LIBERO policy rollouts, robot-video evaluations, VLM reward validation, and ablations in Sections 3–5 and Appendices B–D.

results.title: WorldGym: World Model as An Environment for Policy Evaluation

C1.justification: v2's abstract and contributions explicitly claim quantitative convergence-time characterization and applicability to other energy-based architectures. The stationary-state solution emphasized in v1 is dropped as a contribution, with the conclusion now describing it as something one can consider. The central exact-GFA claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new comparisons as showing that retarded self-interaction increases capacity and discusses finite-size discrepancies near basin boundaries. It adds limitations concerning small systems and restricted interaction orders, qualifies the earlier categorical noise statement, and removes the Maxwell-construction interpretation accompanying the stationary-state result.

D1.justification: v2 identifies Monte Carlo as the numerical approach and documents concrete simulation settings, including N=512, n=3 and the 200-step basin evaluation. These are limited reproducibility additions: neither code access nor the Monte Carlo implementation, sample count or hardware is supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions study retrieval of independent, unbiased binary memory patterns from initial states with specified overlaps. The added simulations retain this task and population; network size and interaction-order changes concern experimental settings.

E2.justification: v1 Figure 1 evaluates approximate dynamics alone. v2 Figure 2 explicitly compares full-GFA and network results against the existing zero-retarded-interaction approximation, shown as a red reference curve. This adds a comparative evaluation without introducing an external baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Monte Carlo evaluation of the full GFA equations and finite-network simulations at N=512, n=3. It evaluates trajectories at loading rates 0.1–0.4 and attraction basins after 200 iterations. v1 instead evaluates approximate fixed points across several interaction orders up to n=20.

E4.justification: v2 adds trajectory analyses across initial overlaps and loading rates, and directly tests the effect of retaining versus neglecting retarded self-interaction through Figure 2.
