The earlier numerical sensitivity analysis across multiple interaction orders is removed, substantially changing the analytical evidence.

E5.justification: v2 first reports 100 simulation trials in Figures 1–2 and displays error bars in Figure 1. v1 has no repeated-run or uncertainty reporting. The later version does not define whether the bars represent standard deviations, standard errors or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v2 adds full-GFA and simulation trajectories, basin maps, convergence within several tens of iterations, and a reported n=3 capacity of 0.33. v1's approximate capacity list, including 0.252 for n=3, and higher-order basin curves disappear; the n=3 approximate boundary survives as a reference. The two capacity values come from different analyses, not an unchanged-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The polynomial-energy memory model, binary parallel update rule, GFA framework and approximation neglecting retarded self-interaction are retained. Numerically evaluating the existing exact equations does not introduce a new recall algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Notation moves into preliminaries, Analysis gains separate path-probability and generating-functional subsections, approximate dynamics and equilibrium comparisons move into Discussion, and derivations are redistributed into appendices.

P2.justification: The single monochrome, multi-order basin plot is replaced by eight trajectory panels and two color basin maps, adding error bars, color scales and an approximation overlay. The document also adopts different title, heading, equation and reference formatting. Neither version contains tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds GFA-related references by Düring et al. (1998), Coolen (2000), Mimura et al. (2004), and Mimura and Coolen (2009), while removing Amari and Maginu (1988). Its central positioning relative to Gardner, Abbott and equilibrium analyses remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendices A–B add combinatorial and saddle-point proof sketches. The pairing coefficient B(m) changes from the even-m indicator times (2m-1)!! to the indicator times (m-1)!!. Conversely, v1 Section 4.3's three stationary-state assumptions, derivation and Proposition 2 are removed. Appendix C largely relocates the earlier Gardner-model Lemma 2 rather than introducing a new result.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves its exact dynamics numerically untested. v2 directly compares full-GFA predictions with network simulations, examines the effect of retarded interaction, corrects the pairing coefficient and supplies substantial proof sketches. These changes strengthen the central dynamical argument enough to outweigh the removed stationary-state derivation and narrower interaction-order coverage. Remaining appendix notation problems and incomplete Monte Carlo/error-bar documentation limit the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dense-associative-memory study. Their complete text, equations and figures support comparison, including v2's Appendices A–C. v1 ends with references and has no appendices.

after.justification: Section 5.1 and Figures 1–2 report original network simulations with N=512 and 100 trials, comparing retrieval trajectories and attraction basins with numerical GFA predictions.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figure 1 give numerical illustrations of theoretical approximate fixed-point equations. v1 reports no experimental study, sampled network simulations or analysis of observed data.

results.title: Dynamical properties of dense associative memory

C1.justification: The contribution shifts from a multi-source dataset supporting detection and tracking toward a fully supervised detection resource comprising annotation tools, an evaluation toolkit, a benchmark and TDnet. v2 adds novelty claims for tailored annotation tools and instance-level distillation, while dropping tracking from its main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 attributes TDnet's gains to reduced class imbalance and cross-task interference, and adds interpretations of action/target confusions. This replaces v1's discussion of YOLO-Triplet's weak relational head and tracking perspectives. Appendix G.2 newly justifies per-frame detection with tracking deferred to future work; the long-tail limitation is largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds COCO-format information, preprocessing rules, exact fold assignments, training hyperparameters, annotation-tool JSON schemas and evaluation-toolkit instructions, plus repository README locations. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without proving that all previously unspecified settings changed. Appendix F.1 nevertheless gives conflicting auxiliary classification weights of 0.5 and 0.1.

E1.justification: Detection retains the same 21 prostatectomy videos, three sources and component vocabularies. However, v1 Table 3 includes aspirator–retract–catheter, whereas v2 Table 6 omits it and adds needle-driver–grasp–prostate. This modestly revises represented triplet coverage despite both versions reporting 89 categories; larger frame counts alone do not broaden coverage.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds Faster R-CNN, Cascade R-CNN, SSD, ViT-Det, TAPIR and MCIT-IG, while removing YOLOv5, YOLOv8 and YOLOv9. Table 5 also adds Deformable-DETR, TAPIR and MCIT-IG to the precision/recall comparison, substantially revising comparator membership.

E3.justification: The single 14/2/5-video training/validation/test split becomes five-fold cross-validation over all 21 videos. Dataset totals increase from 60,529 to 71,775 frames and 165,567 to 196,490 instances. v2 also introduces video-wise evaluation and an annotation-review protocol involving five independent surgeons and 1,000 sampled frames.

E4.justification: v2 supplies self-distillation and multitask ablations, video-wise assessment, confusion-matrix and per-class analyses (Appendix F), plus independent annotation agreement and source-specific distribution analyses. v1's tracking comparisons disappear. Although v1 mentions supplementary confusion analysis, that analysis is absent from the supplied PDF.

E5.justification: v1 reports single-split point estimates without evaluation uncertainty. v2 reports means and standard deviations across five folds in Tables 4, 5, 8 and 9, and Cohen's kappa for annotation agreement in Table 3. These introduce substantial statistical reporting; random-seed replication remains unspecified.

E6.justification: Benchmark scores, rankings, speeds and dataset frequencies change extensively. Table 4 replaces YOLO-Triplet's 36.02% triplet mAP50 and 77.4 FPS with TDnet's 36.1±3.4% and 126.6 FPS under changed data, architecture and evaluation, preventing a same-setting improvement claim. v2 adds agreement, ablation and per-class results, while v1's 204/953 tracking-ID counts disappear.

M1.justification: v1's YOLO-Triplet combines YOLOv12 instrument detection with cropped-region cross-attention and ResNet18-based action/target recognition. v2 replaces this with TDnet's teacher–student architecture, auxiliary component heads, shared positive assignments and instance-level self-distillation using mixed hard/soft targets (Appendix E). This changes architecture and training, beyond renaming.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, related work and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting. The tracking section disappears, limitations move to Appendix G, and triplet-frequency analysis moves to Appendix B. Dedicated agreement and reproducibility sections and organized appendices substantially restructure the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds architecture, software, instrument-variation and confusion-matrix figures, together with agreement, fold, ablation and per-class tables; tracking displays are removed. The frequency table is relocated and expanded by source, the precision/recall table is transposed, and benchmark tables gain uncertainty notation and colored rankings.

R1.justification: Research positioning is substantially revised around classification versus fully supervised detection, inaccessible challenge test annotations and limitations of original ESAD/PSI-AVA labels. New detector, metrics, RiT, SurgiTrack and ByteTrack references support the expanded benchmark and tools, while the earlier standalone tracking-literature discussion is removed.

T1.justification: The basic mathematical task definition is retained. Appendix E adds explicit definitions of shared foreground assignment and teacher/student loss objectives, while Appendix D defines video-wise aggregation. These are localized formal additions; neither version provides theorems, proofs or theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: Independent surgeon agreement, five-fold variability reporting, targeted ablations and detailed implementation documentation substantially strengthen validation and reproducibility beyond v1's single-split benchmark and descriptive annotation assurance. Tracking coverage is dropped, and v2 introduces reporting problems: Section 6.3 overstates TDnet's component rankings, and Appendix F.1 conflicts on loss weights. These shortcomings limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same ProstaTD study, with matching data sources, annotation definitions and corresponding detection benchmarks. v1 ends with references; v2's Appendices A–I were also inspected.

after.justification: v2 reports original cross-validation benchmarks, surgeon agreement measurements, detector ablations and per-class analyses in Tables 3–5 and 8–10.

before.justification: v1 reports original detector evaluations in Tables 4–5, alongside dataset and tracking annotation statistics.

results.title: ProstaTD: Bridging Surgical Triplet from Classification to Fully Supervised Detection

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: LLM-based time-series quality judgments, an efficient meta-learned rater, cross-domain adaptability, and downstream selection benefits. Additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of encoder and supervision contributions, distinguishes reusable evaluation costs from initial training costs, and clarifies why anomaly-sensitive tasks require criteria beyond normal-sequence quality. Appendix E interprets weighted fusion as offering no consistent advantage. The original averaging and segmentation limitations are retained in Appendix H.

D1.justification: v2 adds token accounting and separate judgment, meta-training, adaptation, and inference runtimes, plus implementation information for voting, fusion weights, and the lightweight encoder comparison. It omits v1's explicit per-token API prices. Core training hyperparameters and public repository access were already disclosed.

E1.justification: The original training domains and eleven benchmark datasets remain. Appendix F adds MSL binary anomaly detection, introducing a distinct task requiring preservation of meaningful irregularities. Appendix D.6 additionally evaluates multivariate-to-multivariate Electricity forecasting, extending the original univariate forecasting coverage.

E2.justification: The original Random, DataOob, DataShapley, KNNShapley, and TimeInf comparisons remain. New comparisons include direct numerical LLM scoring against pairwise judgments (Table 17), DeepSeek-V3 in synthetic judgment evaluation (Table 25), and Chronos/TimeGPT encoder alternatives (Table 5).

E3.justification: The main sampling, splits, and selection settings remain. New protocols evaluate full-pipeline runtime, alternative encoders, MOMENT fine-tuning, selection ratios, block sizes, and 4,000 synthetic comparison pairs. Anomaly detection introduces F1 evaluation. The forecasting configuration in D.6 is ambiguous: it labels 192/336/720 as horizons while stating that prediction length is fixed at 96.

E4.justification: v2 adds downstream same-/cross-dataset rater comparisons, encoder and direct-scoring ablations, selection/configuration sensitivity tests, ensemble and weighted-fusion analyses, and anomaly-aware examples. Appendix G adds single-expert alignment, inter-LLM agreement, prompt sensitivity, temperature sensitivity, and Bradley-Terry label-noise robustness tests. Existing pruning and adaptation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 20 newly reports mean RMSE and standard deviation over five random seeds for the added Traffic experiment. v1 provides no corresponding repeated-run uncertainty reporting. The twenty LLM judgments per pair were already documented in v1; retained benchmark results do not acquire uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values are retained, including Table 1 and the runtime table relocated from v1 Table 2 to v2 Table 15. Extensive new results include a 4,687-second full-pipeline runtime, component and robustness comparisons, and MOMENT fine-tuning. On the new MSL task, Table 24 reports PatchTST F1 of 0.8506 for extended TSRating versus 0.8140 for TimeInf and DataShapley.

M1.justification: The main Bradley-Terry, frozen-MOMENT/MLP, and SignSGD meta-learning pipeline remains unchanged. Supplementary variants introduce majority-voted multi-LLM supervision (D.8), fixed weighted criterion fusion (E), and an auxiliary Anomaly criterion with separate normal/anomalous sample scoring (F). These are localized extensions.

P1.justification: The core narrative largely survives. Local revisions update the title, authors, terminology, and prose; move baseline descriptions into D.2; separate data pruning into its own subsection; and reorganize the expanded appendices. Acknowledgments and an LLM writing-assistance disclosure are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn, Figure 3 gains a MOMENT panel, and new figures visualize combined criteria and anomaly-aware selection. Numerous new tables present controls and reliability analyses. Existing tables and figures are relocated and reformatted within the ICLR layout; these moves are distinct from added evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds recent domain-adaptation, time-series reasoning, and anomaly-detection references, including TimeOmni-1, TSAQA, CARLA, and DACAD, while removing some background references such as TimeGPT-1. Its central positioning against influence-function, Shapley-value, and text-quality approaches remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The scoring definitions, Bradley-Terry objective, training loss, Algorithm 1, and SignSGD derivation in Equations 1–16 are substantively unchanged. The added empirical variants introduce no new theoretical results or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of central design choices through encoder and supervision controls, expert alignment, and judgment-robustness tests. Its full-pipeline cost breakdown also addresses v1's emphasis on inference timing. These gains improve the assessability of the method and efficiency claims. Some additions remain weakened by Table 16's dataset mismatch, D.6's ambiguous horizon description, and unexplained amplitude-agreement inconsistencies in Table 27.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TSRating and are readable, including their equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained material can be matched across renumbering, relocation, and the revised title.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds component ablations, judgment-reliability evaluations, multivariate forecasting, and an MSL anomaly-detection case study.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting, classification, data-pruning, synthetic-judgment, and meta-learning experiments, including additional results in its appendices.

results.title: Rating Quality of Diverse Time Series Data by Meta-learning from LLM Judgment

C1.justification: The efficiency and random-sampling claims remain, but v2's abstract, contributions and conclusion explicitly extend demonstrated applicability to VLA-guided complex and physical-robot tasks. Identifying a fundamental blind-spot problem in importance-based selection also becomes a central contribution, beyond v1's comparative finding that random sampling performs competitively.

C2.justification: v2 develops a substantive blind-spot explanation involving static importance scores, lost action discrimination and unbiased coverage, extending v1's redundancy and grouped-training explanations. Limitations shift from simulation-only and DINO-focused validation toward encoder-quality dependence and task-dependent sparsity, with adaptive dropout presented as preliminary rather than universally superior.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds substantial reproduction information: new dataset sources and configurations, teleoperation procedures, physical-task evaluation positions, SmolVLA architecture and training hyperparameters, asynchronous execution settings, goal images and joint-state targets. LHS and cluster-retention calculations also receive implementation descriptions. Original world-model architecture and hardware disclosures largely remain.

E1.justification: The six original simulation environments are retained. v2 adds LIBERO training suites and LIBERO-10 evaluation, Meta-World's 50 manipulation tasks, and physical SO-101 PickPlace and Drawer tasks with newly collected demonstrations (Section 4.3; Appendix A.1), substantially expanding task and deployment coverage.

E2.justification: The existing Full/CLS and token-selection comparator roster is retained, with SmolVLA without planning added as VLA-only (Table 3; Figure 5). Within existing benchmarks, LHS gains Granular and Rope comparisons, while STAR and Attention-WM gain Granular comparisons previously absent from v1 Table 3 (v2 Table 4).

E3.justification: New protocols introduce 50-step action chunks, task-specific candidate counts, 100 LIBERO trials, 15 trials per Meta-World task, and 10 trials per physical task. Added experiments vary encoders, optimization steps, planning horizon and frame skipping, and introduce LPIPS, coverage-entropy and blind-spot measurements. Original CEM defaults largely persist; the longer horizon is an added ablation.

E4.justification: Beyond retained probing, grouped-attention and noise analyses, v2 tests alternative encoders, hyperparameter sensitivity, gradient-based planning, adaptive sparsity and prediction quality. Component-level latency profiling and controlled blind-spot studies investigate where acceleration originates and why importance-based selection fails (Section 5; Appendices B.1 and B.5–B.9).

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 masks for nHSIC and five-run means and standard deviations for probing and grouped-attention prediction errors; their corresponding plots are retained. No new seed-count, confidence-interval or significance-testing practice is introduced. The adaptive planner's rollout variance is a control signal, rather than added uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive policy-guided, physical-robot and ablation results, including 80% PickPlace and 70% Drawer success at 50% dropout (Figure 5). Existing results also change: Table 1's Wall Full/CLS scores move from 85.0/91.7% to 91.7/85.0%. Several Granular/Rope token-selection averages are revised between v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 4; these revisions do not establish same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The original grouped-attention world model and prediction/planning losses remain. v2 substantially extends inference through SmolVLA-guided action-chunk selection (Sections 3.2 and 4.3), gradient-descent trajectory optimization (B.5), and variance-driven Ada-Rand/Ada-Inc dropout adaptation (B.6).

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, experimental narrative, token-selection discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Experiments and analysis are separated into Sections 4 and 5, earlier explanations are reorganized, planning details move into Appendix A.3, and the appendices gain clearer subdivisions and disclosure statements.

P2.justification: v2 adds performance–latency plots, blind-spot illustrations, physical-task goal images and rollout panels, plus tables for new benchmarks and analyses. Existing tables gain average columns and additional rows, and the environment montage expands. Earlier probing, noise and simulation-rollout figures are retained and relocated; these are not new evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for SmolVLA, LeRobot, LIBERO, Meta-World, MoCo-v3, DINOv3 and LPIPS, while removing the Kaelbling and Chefer references. The core DINO-WM and token-efficiency positioning remains, with a refined argument about the mismatch between static importance metrics and dynamic planning.

T1.justification: v2 defines cluster-retention entropy through retained-token frequencies over spatial clusters (A.7) and corrects the token-cost description from exponential to quadratic (Section 3.2). Existing loss equations, nHSIC definitions and Gaussian-noise assumptions remain; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's explicit simulation-only and DINO-focused validation gaps through physical-robot experiments and alternative-encoder tests. Controlled failure analyses, hyperparameter checks and latency profiling also strengthen the explanations of robustness and efficiency. These gains outweigh reporting defects: physical evaluations use only 10 trials per task, Drawer test positions are described inconsistently in Section 4.3 and Appendix A.1, and Table 1's new Full/CLS averages do not reflect its revised Wall entries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sparse-imagination research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite substantial expansion and reorganization in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds LIBERO, Meta-World and physical-robot evaluations, together with new ablations and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation success rates, planning times, token-selection comparisons, probing experiments and robustness analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Sparse Imagination for Efficient Visual World Model Planning

C1.justification: The central zero-shot prompting and large-scale dataset contributions remain. V2 elevates MotionChat into the abstract and introduction, adding the claim that its 7B model achieves 48.3% FAVOR-Bench accuracy, comparable to Qwen2.5VL-72B's 48.1%. V1 discussed MotionChat's utility only in the appendix without this comparison.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations based on spotlight-like pretraining imagery, attention visualizations, coordinate-parsing difficulty and captioning's greater descriptive demands. Appendix D discusses runtime/performance tradeoffs. Appendix G replaces v1's inherited-bias and misuse limitations with detector-domain dependence and diminished benefits in object-free scenes, substantially revising applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V2 discloses the blur-weight implementation, the TempCompass evaluator identifier, conversion of SFT data into video-text pairs for generation, and an inference-overhead estimate below 75%. Existing hardware, batch size, detection thresholds, default prompting parameters and annotation instructions are retained. The project URL and code/data-release statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained MotionBench and FAVOR-Bench evaluations, v2 adds VideoMME general-video understanding, TempCompass including captioning, and text-to-video generation evaluated with VBench. This substantially broadens task coverage. MotionVid-QA's reported sources and 40K-video/87K-QA scale remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 removes GLM-4V-Plus, MiniCPM-V2.6, PLLaVA-34B and CogVLM2-Video. Table 3 reduces open-source baseline rows from fifteen to four, removing comparisons including Aria, Tarsier and Video-LLaVA. V2 also adds a direct-coordinate prompting comparator and the Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B generation baseline.

E3.justification: Existing MotionBench/FAVOR-Bench splits and retained models' frame budgets remain unchanged. New experimental designs include TempCompass grading with gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, VBench generation metrics, separate SFT and SFT+DPO controls, InternVL3 scaling from 1B to 78B, and controlled darkening/window/decay sweeps. These expand evaluation procedures substantially.

E4.justification: V2 adds training-stage ablation, background-darkening and blur-parameter sensitivity tests, model-size scaling, direct-coordinate prompting controls, and Grad-CAM analyses (Table 4, Tables 11–14, Figures 7, 11 and 14). The original visual-prompt ablation remains as Table 6; several qualitative examples are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's additional experiments continue reporting point estimates; its parameter sweeps do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Common MotionSight benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results, including VideoMME 76.0% versus its 73.7% baseline and TempCompass captioning 64.0 versus 54.6. V1 presents MotionChat's 45.8% FAVOR-Bench result as its full model; v2 labels that row SFT-only and adds 48.3% for SFT+DPO. This is revised stage/result reporting, not an established same-setting gain. MotionChat's MotionBench results and numerous baseline/category entries are omitted.

M1.justification: Equation (1) drops the optional object-motion response input from the specified camera-inference procedure. The core grounding/tracking, visual spotlight and motion-blur pipeline remains, as does the SFT/DPO training recipe already documented in v1. MotionChat is not a newly introduced architecture.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes existing material: benchmark descriptions and comparisons are merged, MotionChat moves into the main experimental narrative, and its former appendix material is redistributed. The standalone supplement becomes integrated appendices. Introduction and method passages are condensed or rewritten, with changed headings and citation style throughout.

P2.justification: V2 redraws pipeline Figures 2 and 4, compresses FAVOR-Bench Table 3, and adds attention, scaling and generation displays. Existing content is also redistributed: v1 Figure 5 becomes v2 Figures 5 and 15, while v1 Figure 7 is split across Figures 9 and 13 with an added baseline comparison. Wrapped tables, prompt boxes and document styling change substantially.

R1.justification: V2 adds VideoAgent and VideoTree to contextualize computational overhead and removes the Aria and Video-LLaVA references. The principal positioning against existing video models, motion datasets and image-derived visual prompting remains. The switch to author-year citations is stylistic.

T1.justification: V2 adds an explicit product-form temporal-weight definition in Equation (7), replacing v1's geometric-series characterization. It also corrects the zero-padding condition below Equation (5) from t-k <= 1 to s_t-k < 1. Existing aggregation, DPO and dataset-subset mathematics remains; no substantial theoretical framework or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1 largely leaves parameter sensitivity, scaling and transfer beyond motion QA untested. V2's controlled ablations and general-video, captioning and generation evaluations substantially strengthen evidence for robustness and utility, while detector and runtime discussions clarify practical constraints. Reduced baseline/detail reporting and the unexplained MotionChat result relabeling are drawbacks, but the added diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MotionSight, MotionVid-QA and MotionChat. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds general-video, captioning, video-generation, robustness and model-scaling results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original MotionSight benchmark results and ablations in Tables 2–4, plus MotionChat fine-tuning results in Appendix D and Table S3.

results.title: MotionSight: Boosting Fine-Grained Motion Understanding in Multimodal LLMs

C1.justification: The central contribution remains the largest fully open, multilingual pre-training corpus of approximately two trillion tokens. v2's abstract and introduction add the specific claim that models trained on it perform comparably to existing multilingual models, replacing the earlier emphasis on industry adoption without redefining the principal dataset contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting corpus distinctiveness to PDF versus HTML sourcing and explaining domain-specific quality profiles and benchmark performance. Appendix F newly identifies spurious OCRonos repetitions and limits Celadon's applicability to web text, while the explicit warning about shallow low-resource language coverage is removed. Appendix C's claim that only Gemma 3 outperforms the tokenizer is broader than Figure 5 supports.

D1.justification: v2 adds the full document schema, detailed tool architectures and annotation procedures, training sample counts, segmentation labels, and Celadon's classification-head and loss descriptions. Section 6 specifies model training schedules and 2,944/23,040 H100 hours. Deduplication and filtered PII categories are newly documented, although conflicting Celadon training descriptions limit reproducibility.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on MultiBLiMP, XStoryCloze, and XCOPA, tokenizer testing on six languages from FLORES200 devtest, and comparisons using C4 and FineWeb data. The underlying Common Corpus coverage remains substantially unchanged; expanding its language statistics from 10 to 50 languages does not establish additional training data.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 introduces evaluated comparisons with Gemma 3 270M/1B, XGLM 564M/1.7B, BLOOM 560M, and OLMo 1B. Figure 5 adds tokenizer comparisons with mBERT, GPT-2, SmolLM2, Llama 3.2, Qwen 3, and Gemma 3. Figure 3b also adds C4 and FineWeb to the embedding comparison; these comparisons are absent from v1.

E3.justification: The added evaluations introduce LM Evaluation Harness benchmarking, six document-level metrics on a 300,000-document sample, and tokenizer fertility measurement on FLORES200 devtest. These are substantial additions to the evaluation design. Newly specified training schedules for the previously described PleIAs models are documentation additions rather than evidence that their training changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of overlap with FineWeb's top 1,000 domains, embedding distributions relative to C4/FineWeb, document-quality distributions, and tokenizer fertility. These investigate corpus distinctiveness, composition, and tokenization efficiency beyond v1's descriptive statistics. The original segmentation and OCR case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed variation, confidence intervals, or formal significance-testing procedures. v2's statement that MultiBLiMP scores are 'significantly above random' is not accompanied by a statistical test or uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: v2 adds aggregate and per-language benchmark results, including MultiBLiMP scores of 0.774/0.797 for PleIAs 350M/1.2B versus 0.762/0.799 for Gemma 3 270M/1B; several baselines score higher on XStoryCloze and XCOPA. It also adds fertility, quality, overlap, and expanded language statistics. Table 3 incorporates v1's 'Other' totals into Open Government while preserving the overall corpus totals.

M1.justification: The same corpus pipeline and named curation tools are retained; expanded implementation descriptions do not establish redesigned methods. However, v2 Appendix F.5 describes Celadon as fine-tuned, while v2 Section 5 retains v1's statement that it was trained from scratch. The PDFs do not resolve whether this represents a procedural change or inconsistent documentation.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: composition tables move to an appendix, main-text curation descriptions are condensed while appendix explanations expand, and the Impact section and development-history appendix disappear. Dedicated Related Work and Evaluation sections replace the earlier emphasis on adoption, alongside extensive prose editing and revised author information.

P2.justification: v2 adds a treemap, quality-distribution plots, tokenizer panels, a dataset comparison table, and aggregate/per-language benchmark tables. The map is redrawn with a 10,000-document threshold instead of 1,000, and the t-SNE display gains external corpora. Composition tables are relocated, and the language table expands from 10 to 50 languages with document and word counts.

R1.justification: New Section 3 and Table 1 systematically position Common Corpus against seven datasets using domain coverage, multilinguality, sources beyond web crawls, and open licensing. ROOTS, DCAD-2000, FineWeb 2, and evaluation-related references expand the discussion. The earlier Impact section and associated adoption references are removed; bibliographic updates to retained works are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theory, propositions, or proofs. The added descriptions of standard empirical quality metrics in Appendix G do not introduce substantive mathematical results.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's lack of direct quantitative model validation through multilingual benchmarks, detailed language-level results, tokenizer comparisons, and corpus diagnostics. Expanded metadata and curation documentation also substantially improve assessability and reuse. Conflicting tool-training descriptions and the overstated tokenizer claim weaken precision, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Common Corpus research work. Their text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original corpus and curation results and adds multilingual model benchmarks, tokenizer evaluations, corpus-quality measurements, and overlap analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original corpus statistics, OCR detection and correction examples, and phone-number detection results improving from 55–60% to 85% with customized Presidio patterns.

results.title: Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training

C1.justification: v1's introduction and conclusion attribute the principal difficulty to perception rather than reasoning capacity. v2 explicitly recognizes complementary perception and reasoning bottlenecks while retaining perception as primary. It also elevates the two-stage PAVR model to a central contribution alongside the benchmark and synthesizer.

C2.justification: v2 interprets caption-only supervision as having limited generalization, CoT supervision as contributing reasoning capability, and GRPO as improving strategy selection and reasoning after perceptual grounding. It adds discussion of perceptual-strategy errors and self-correction, plus a specific limitation concerning restricted rule and icon resources. These substantially extend v1's predominantly perception-based explanation.

D1.justification: v2 documents the Gemini 2.5-Flash-Think annotation model, answer-validation filtering, named synthesis sub-rules, epoch counts, GPU memory, and an expanded model-version inventory. However, v1's learning rate, Adam optimizer, batch size, and per-category synthetic sample counts disappear. Much benchmark-construction text is merely relocated to Appendix A, and the promised code/data release remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on VisuLogic across six related visual-reasoning categories (Appendix D). The original eight-category VisuRiddles benchmark and seven synthetic reasoning categories remain. This extends dataset coverage within the existing abstract visual reasoning domain.

E2.justification: The main comparison adds Qwen3-VL Instruct and Thinking, Dots.vlm1, GPT-5, and Claude-3.7-Sonnet with CoT. It replaces the reported o1 and Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking rows with o3 and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking. Appendix D additionally compares against description-to-LLM pipelines and VisuLogic-trained SFT/RL methods, substantially expanding the comparator set.

E3.justification: Training changes from 80K fine-tuning examples in v1 Section 4.1 to 20K SFT examples for 20 epochs followed by 4K GRPO examples for 40 epochs in v2 Section 5.1. New component controls change the experimental design. Reported synthesis configurations also change, including spatial layouts from two to seven (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 5).

E4.justification: The training-data-volume ablation in v1 Table 5 is removed and replaced by Caption, CoT, GRPO, and combined-training comparisons in v2 Table 4. v2 adds a baseline/SFT/GRPO case study and revises the earlier case study to show PAVR self-correction. The visual-input versus perceptual-description ablation is retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. No new uncertainty-reporting practice is introduced.

E6.justification: Main-table results are extensively revised: the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline average changes from 20.9 to 24.6 and Gemini2.5-Pro from 26.8 to 33.9. PRS's 43.7 is replaced by PAVR-SFT at 39.5 and PAVR at 46.8 under changed training. New ablation results and PAVR's 30.6 on VisuLogic substantially expand the findings. These numbers do not establish controlled cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: v1 fine-tunes Qwen2.5-VL-7B on perceptually annotated synthetic data. v2 introduces PAVR, adding GRPO after supervised fine-tuning, with answer-correctness and output-format rewards. The synthesizer also introduces commercial-model CoT generation from perceptual descriptions and answer-based filtering (Section 4 and Appendix B.2). These change the training procedure substantially.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusion, and substantial experimental discussion are rewritten. The document separates VisuRiddles resources from a new PAVR section, renames PRS, and relocates construction, synthesis, and evaluation details into appendices. This is substantial narrative and structural reorganization.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is substantially redrawn to include API labeling; v2 adds Figure 4 and synthesis-example Figures 6–7, and expands the earlier case study as Figure 5. Tables are reorganized, the statistics table loses its image-count column, and new component-ablation, model-inventory, and VisuLogic tables change the presentation substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds eight references, including MARVEL, VisuLogic, VisualPuzzles, VisualSphinx, and PuzzleVQA, and updates the benchmark discussion accordingly. Section 3.1 newly contrasts VisuRiddles with RAVEN and PuzzleVQA. The broader positioning within multimodal perception and visual reasoning remains recognizable.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations. The added GRPO reward description and puzzle-rule illustrations specify procedures and examples rather than introducing a theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central argument by adding component controls that examine perception supervision, CoT, and GRPO separately, and by replacing v1's overly exclusive perception-based explanation with a more qualified account. VisuLogic adds evidence beyond the original benchmark. Removing the data-volume ablation and basic optimizer details reduces completeness, and model-list inconsistencies remain, but these costs are outweighed by the stronger diagnostic evidence and broader validation. The improvement concerns scientific support, not an established cross-version accuracy gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VisuRiddles research. All text, tables, figures, and v2 Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison. The supplied v1 ends after its references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original PAVR training and evaluation results, component ablations, and additional VisuLogic results in Tables 2–4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, synthetic-data fine-tuning results, and input-modality and training-data-volume ablations in Tables 3–5.

results.title: VisuRiddles: Fine-grained Perception is a Primary Bottleneck for Multimodal Large Language Models in Abstract Visual Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion add theoretical guarantees as a central contribution: greater expressivity than LoRA in the linear setting under parameter constraints, and claimed convergence to full-fine-tuning stationary points under low-rank conditions. v1 primarily claims empirical effectiveness, stable optimization, and efficiency, without these formal guarantees.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's geometric intuition and unresolved theoretical explanation with a low-rank sufficiency interpretation. It newly attributes quantized-model gains primarily to DiaBlo, explains diagonal sparsity advantages, and interprets block-count saturation and stronger early/middle-layer adaptability. The explicit v1 limitations section, including the acknowledgment that non-language modalities remain untested, is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds exact model-loading identifiers and non-instruction-tuned status (Table 11), explicit padding/truncation instructions, hyperparameters for MT-Bench, GLUE, and sparse GSM8K experiments (Tables 18–20), and retained-update scaling factors. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's original experiment settings. The code repository address is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds instruction-following training on WizardLM with first-turn MT-Bench evaluation, and natural-language-understanding evaluations on MRPC, CoLA, SST-2, QNLI, and MNLI from GLUE (Appendices A.3.2–A.3.3). These substantially broaden task coverage. The original reasoning, code-generation, and safety datasets remain; BF16 commonsense evaluation moves to the appendix.

E2.justification: v2 adds full-fine-tuning and zero-shot controls to existing benchmark comparisons, MagR-LoRA to the 2-bit comparison, and four random sparsity patterns in Table 5. LoRA-GA becomes an evaluated comparator on MT-Bench. The unquantized LoRA reference row from v1 Table 5 is removed from the corresponding quantization table. Renaming DiaBlo to MagR-DiaBlo does not constitute a new comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds model configurations including Llama-13B, Llama2-13B, Llama3.2-3B, and T5-base; GPTQ quantization controls; GPT-4 judging for MT-Bench; GLUE development-set evaluation; and controlled sparsity and sensitivity protocols. For existing Llama3-8B CodeAlpaca training at N=128, the reported learning rate changes from 5e-5 to 3e-5 and the scheduler from linear to constant (v1 Table 10; v2 Table 15). This establishes a reported setting revision, without establishing whether that experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct tests of diagonal versus random sparsity patterns, controls separating quantizer effects from adaptation effects, activation/output-gradient rank measurements, and gradient-norm diagnostics. Appendices A.3.4–A.3.7 add optimization-stability, block-count, learning-rate, module-selection, and layer-sensitivity analyses. These substantially expand the evidence explaining when and why DiaBlo works.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, benchmark confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 Table 9 measures gradient-norm variance across training steps as an optimization diagnostic, rather than uncertainty in performance estimates. The 95% effective-rank threshold likewise is not a confidence interval.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for larger models, quantization controls, diagnostic analyses, MT-Bench (6.26), and GLUE (87.8 average). Llama3-8B DiaBlo at N=64 changes its reported HumanEval Pass@1/5/10 from 41.8/56.4/62.9 to 43.2/57.4/63.5 (v1 Table 4; v2 Table 3), while v1's additional-epoch results disappear. Most original scores remain, including the relocated BF16 results; the 170/480-minute runtime findings are retained in prose.

M1.justification: The procedure remains zero-initialized, additive block-diagonal adaptation with frozen pretrained weights and batched block computations. v2 clarifies padding and truncation for nondivisible dimensions, an already stated capability. The additional quantizers, models, and restricted-update experiments do not introduce a new DiaBlo component.

P1.justification: v2 substantially revises the introduction, contribution list, and conclusion around theoretical sufficiency and sparse adaptation. It reorganizes Section 3.2, moves BF16 commonsense discussion into Appendix A.3.1, converts the runtime table discussion into prose, and restructures the appendix into proofs, validation, additional experiments, and implementation details. The limitations section is replaced by different end matter, including a reproducibility statement.

P2.justification: v2 adds a benchmark-summary chart and new rank, gradient, learning-rate, module, and layer plots (Figures 2–7), together with new benchmark and diagnostic tables. Existing tables gain model panels and control rows. The BF16 table moves to the appendix, while the runtime table is replaced by prose retaining its findings. Conference formatting also changes the page layout.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning beyond the existing LoRA and SMT discussion to random masking, sparse random adaptation, S2FT, and SparseLoRA, emphasizing structured sparsity and hardware efficiency. It also adds low-rank activation/gradient and mathematical references supporting the new theoretical comparison, plus sources for the added benchmarks. This is substantive positioning expansion rather than merely the switch to author-year citations.

T1.justification: v1 provides gradient identities and computational-complexity arguments but no sufficiency theorems. v2 Section 3.2 and Appendix A.1 add least-squares and full-objective stationarity results under generic low-rank assumptions, a supporting Kronecker-product rank lemma, and proofs. The general theorem establishes a conditional implication from block stationarity to full-weight stationarity.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly leaves diagonal adaptation's effectiveness theoretically unexplained and provides limited direct testing of the diagonal-block choice. v2 substantially strengthens that central argument through conditional proofs, matched sparsity comparisons, quantizer controls, and sensitivity studies. The broader benchmarks and implementation details add useful support. Qualifications remain: the general theorem assumes stationarity rather than proving training convergence, and the explicit limitations discussion disappears. These weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in justification and diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiaBlo research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original DiaBlo experiments and adds benchmark evaluations, sparsity comparisons, gradient measurements, and sensitivity analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original DiaBlo experiments on reasoning, code generation, safety alignment, quantized models, and training runtime, alongside explicitly attributed baseline results.

results.title: DiaBlo: Diagonal Blocks Are Sufficient For Finetuning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: hierarchical human-human/human-scene representations, coarse-to-fine spatial and frequency reasoning, and state-of-the-art forecasting across four datasets. Changes to dynamic-scene wording do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations of attention interpretability, holistic scene representation and close-interaction constraints. Appendices J-K qualify penetration scores and disclose abrupt-motion failures, limitations of distance-based modeling and the absence of explicit future-interaction coupling. Dynamic-object applicability is also discussed with qualifications about scarce training data.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly supplies layer widths, attention-head counts, GCN depth, sigma, dropout, optimizer settings, batch-sampling rules and rotation augmentation. V3 also identifies the FID feature extractor and supplies a planned code-repository location. Most architecture and training additions are newly disclosed details; the PDFs do not establish actual code availability.

E1.justification: The four core datasets are retained. V3 substantially expands tested scenarios to missing people and scene points, noisy inputs, interactions within 15 cm, moving objects and 10-second forecasting (Appendices D, G, H and M). These introduce distinct input conditions and forecasting requirements.

E2.justification: The forecasting comparator sets in the retained experiments are unchanged. V3 adds a random-chance comparator for attention-based interaction-object identification on HUMANISE: Table 9 reports 10.56% accuracy against HUMOF's 83.85%.

E3.justification: V3 adds NPSS, FID, penetration and object-identification evaluations, alongside long-horizon and input-corruption protocols and upsampling of rare moving-object examples. Appendix A also changes the reported HIK setting from 30 observed/60 predicted frames to 25/50. This is an explicit protocol-description revision, although the PDFs do not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations, v3 adds injection-schedule, point-count, Transformer-depth and SE(3) analyses; occlusion and noise robustness; attention interpretability; close-interaction and penetration analyses; and illustrated failure cases. These substantially expand the questions tested about effectiveness, robustness and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, run-to-run variability or significance tests. The added NPSS and FID evaluations are motion-quality metrics, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All 376 numerical entries in the original benchmark and ablation tables are retained. V3 adds substantial results, including 10-second path/pose errors of 747.8/188.7 mm and moving-object subset errors of 244.8/159.4 mm. Table 14 additionally finds MutualDistance best on human-to-scene penetration and HUMOF best on human-to-human penetration. These are new evaluations, not improvements to the retained scores.

M1.justification: The default HUMOF architecture, DCT rescaling, inference procedure and loss remain unchanged. Appendix L adds an implemented SE(3) interaction-encoding variant using body-local coordinate frames, 6D rotations and relative translation. This is a limited experimental variant.

P1.justification: Most introduction, methodology and conclusion prose is retained. V3 shortens the title, revises interaction terminology and author information, moves loss/setup/dataset material into appendices, separates comparisons from discussions, and adds publication statements. These are localized edits and reorganization around a stable main narrative.

P2.justification: V3 merges v1's GTA-IM and HUMANISE tables into Table 2 and renumbers the retained ablation table. It adds Tables 4-16 and Figures 6-10, including robustness plots, additional visual comparisons and failure cases. Colored result highlighting and the ICLR layout also change presentation substantially.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations supporting NPSS, T2M-based FID, SE(3) encoding and InterX examples. The main positioning relative to scene-aware, social-aware and SAST approaches remains unchanged. Citation-style changes and expanded bibliographic metadata are presentation edits.

T1.justification: Appendix J adds explicit mathematical definitions of penetration depth through summed negative-SDF magnitudes and penetration rate through the fraction of penetrating joints, followed by frame/sample averaging. The original model equations and loss are retained, with the loss relocated to Appendix A; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses important gaps in v1's robustness validation and reproducibility through extensive supplementary tests and implementation details. Penetration comparisons and explicit failure cases also make the method's capabilities and limitations more assessable. The unreconciled HIK frame specification and continued absence of run-to-run uncertainty remain weaknesses, but the overall evidential and documentation gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HUMOF work, with readable and matchable text, equations, figures and tables. V1 ends after its references despite mentioning an appendix; v3 includes Appendices A-M. Supplementary additions are assessed as newly documented in the supplied PDFs, without assuming when experiments were performed.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and reports additional sensitivity, robustness, interpretability, long-term forecasting and physical-penetration evaluations in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original HUMOF forecasting results on four datasets and component ablations in Tables 1-4.

results.title: HUMOF: Human Motion Forecasting in Interactive Social Scenes

C1.justification: The central claims about two algorithms for exact Wasserstein GPCA remain. v2 broadens the discussion's stated utility to classification, clustering and outlier detection, and highlights the existing univariate Gaussian result in the contribution list. This is a limited expansion and reframing of the contribution scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive arguments about comparator suitability, discretization artifacts and encoder geometry, interpretations of the regularization studies, and limitations of estimating Hessian extrema in high dimensions. One new interpretation overstates its evidence: Appendix E.2.2 says increasing lambda_I does not harm cost, although Table 3 increases from 5.76 at weight 1 to 5.91 at weight 100.

D1.justification: v2 documents access to two implementation repositories, identifies the pretrained PointNet source, supplies the POT-based outlier-scoring recipe and adds a reproducibility statement. It also revises learning-rate documentation. Most architecture, optimizer, hardware and training-budget information was already supplied in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds Weather CORGIS covariance analysis and an outlier-detection task using held-out chairs versus cars and planes. These extend the represented domain, object categories and task requirements beyond the retained Gaussian, MNIST, chair/lamp and landscape experiments.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates TPCA against GPCA in Gaussian examples. v2 additionally evaluates TPCA on the retained chair/lamp experiments and introduces pretrained PointNet embeddings followed by PCA as another comparator (Appendix A.2, Figures 15–17), substantially expanding comparisons for GPCAGEN.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes the projection-time learning rate from 0.001 to 0.005, and Appendix E revises its search grid. New evaluation designs include controlled regularization sweeps and held-out outlier scoring using 20 projection-time candidates and 2048 samples per candidate. The main network architectures and 120,000/200,000-step training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 provides informal regularization observations and a tuning-grid description. v2 adds controlled lamp experiments varying each regularization weight from 0.001 to 100 while fixing the other, measuring constraint satisfaction and component loss and displaying recovered geodesics (Tables 2–3, Figures 20–21). The new scalability sections discuss possible remedies rather than report scaling experiments.

E5.justification: Figure 4 changes from retaining the best of five runs to averaging ten runs with a standard-deviation band. Appendix E.2 introduces ± statistics and reports 100 runs for constraint measurement and five for cost measurement; these counts do not establish independent retraining runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds weather embeddings, baseline outputs, outlier-score histograms and numerical ablation results. For example, Table 2 newly reports orthogonality values of 0.909 at lambda_O=0.001 and 0.00031 at lambda_O=1. The reported chair modes also reverse order: chair-versus-armchair variation becomes the first component and seat height the second.

M1.justification: Section 4 replaces the Wasserstein intersection penalty between distributions with squared distance between lifted maps, enforcing a shared representative for the orthogonality calculation. Sections 3 and D.2 also fix redundant Gaussian rotation variables to the identity. These refine the existing algorithms while retaining their principal objectives and neural parameterization.

P1.justification: The six-section narrative and most proof text are retained. v2 rewrites introductory passages, adds a related-work paragraph, moves the distortion proposition into Section 3 and subdivides Appendices A and E. It also adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements, while accidentally repeating the title at the start of the abstract.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout, including narrower text blocks and text wrapped around several figures. It substantially expands the visual evidence with weather, baseline, outlier and ablation displays plus Tables 2–3. Existing plots are updated, Figure 4 gains an uncertainty band, and retained appendix figures are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning Sinkhorn methods, PointNet, LOBPCG and convex analysis, alongside targeted discussion of encoder-based PCA and alternative SPD geometries. The central positioning against tangent PCA and generalized-geodesic approximations remains; the switch to author-year citations is primarily presentational.

T1.justification: Section 5.1 repairs the SPD-cone inequality and its matching covariance parameterization, and the main distortion proposition gains a nonzero-rotation condition. The distortion expansion and univariate Gaussian preservation result, including their proofs, already appear in v1; their relocation and renumbering do not constitute new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the technical and empirical support for GPCAGEN. The revised intersection constraint aligns the lifted representatives used to assess orthogonality, while controlled ablations replace informal tuning assertions with measured constraint and loss tradeoffs. Baseline comparisons, averaged results with uncertainty and documented code access improve validation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh limited reporting inconsistencies such as the overstatement accompanying Table 3, although baseline comparisons remain chiefly qualitative.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GPCA work by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: Original empirical results include the retained applications, new weather and outlier-detection experiments, point-cloud baseline comparisons and quantitative regularization studies.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original Gaussian simulations and learned geodesic results for MNIST, ModelNet40 point clouds and landscape images.

results.title: On the Wasserstein Geodesic Principal Component Analysis of probability measures

C1.justification: The central dataset contribution expands from 206 objects across 26 types to 992 objects across 37 subcategories grouped into nine categories. V3 also explicitly claims compatibility through conversion to URDF or MJCF. The principal claims concerning visual realism, physical fidelity and embedded interactions remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations connecting annotation utility to consistent part modeling, FPS behavior to geometry and active joints, and generated-asset failures to camera estimation, training-domain restrictions and rendering incompatibilities. These extend v1's interpretations considerably. The limitation concerning labor-intensive asset creation is retained.

D1.justification: V3 adds an annotation-label catalog, per-subcategory modeling and physics-tuning labor estimates, simulator versions for profiling, and asset-conversion instructions. The abstract replaces the project-page pointer with a direct dataset-hosting link. Existing ACT, DP and EAGLE hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained four imitation-learning tasks, v3 evaluates door-pulling on an unseen real microwave using simulated microwave instances without an exact digital twin (Sec. 5.2). It also reports real-world CloseTrashcan deployment and evaluates SplArt reconstruction from real cabinet and refrigerator imagery, substantially extending the tested scenarios.

E2.justification: PartNet-Mobility becomes a downstream imitation-learning asset comparator in Table 2, whereas v1 compared it through geometry and appearance. V3 also adds vision-based PPO against EAGLE (Tables 3 and 12) and evaluates reproduced SplArt outputs against ArtVIP assets (Appendix L). ACT and DP remain unchanged comparison methods.

E3.justification: For the original imitation-learning tasks, evaluation changes from 10 rollouts to 60 per training seed, and mixed-data settings expand from 100 real plus 100 simulated trajectories to four simulation-data quantities. New protocols include 500 simulated trajectories per dataset for microwave transfer, simulation and real-world RL trials, and quantitative reconstruction-error evaluation.

E4.justification: V3 adds simulation-data quantity sensitivity experiments and generated-asset failure analysis covering collisions, geometry, joints and materials. It expands v1's profiling discussion into category-wise comparisons of triangle counts, active joints and isolated-object versus kitchen FPS (Table 7). The earlier physical-motion analyses remain present.

E5.justification: V1 provides imitation-learning point estimates without training-seed counts or confidence intervals. V3 specifies three training seeds and reports individual seed scores, means and 90% confidence intervals in Table 10. The existing five-seed RL curve and ten-trial physical evaluations are retained.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces many estimates: ACT PullDrawer success changes from 60% to 64% for real-only training and from 30% to 39% for simulation-only training, under the revised evaluation protocol. New results include DP microwave mixed-data success of 83% with ArtVIP versus 70% with PartNet-Mobility, EAGLE versus PPO checkpoint scores, and FPS and reconstruction-error tables.

M1.justification: V3's RL transfer application includes Visual Matching alongside RandomConv, adding a component to the procedure described in v1 (Sec. 5.3). The asset-construction pipeline, joint equations, EAGLE losses and reward remain unchanged. The expanded behavior-primitives description largely documents existing mechanisms.

P1.justification: V3 extensively polishes the prose and reorganizes the methodology: production becomes part of Visual Realism, modeling standards move to Appendix D, and Physical Fidelity precedes Modular Interaction. The appendices are reorganized from A.1–A.7 into thematic sections A–M, and the introduction and conclusion are revised.

P2.justification: V3 adds interaction-primitives, microwave-comparison, segmentation and generated-asset figures, substantially expands result tables, and replaces the earlier category chart with a detailed taxonomy table. The overview moves to page 2 and the unchanged RL training curve moves into the appendix. Conference formatting also changes the page layout.

R1.justification: The introduction and Appendix L substantially expand positioning against automated articulated-object pipelines, adding discussion of SplArt, Real2Code, Articulate-Anything, ArtGS and ArticulatedGS, among others. V3 develops the argument for manually authored fidelity through specific reconstruction and simulation-readiness limitations, beyond v1's broader criticism of generation methods.

T1.justification: The joint-drive, friction, target-position and stiffness equations, together with the learning losses and reward formulation, are retained. Appendix K adds the standard Pearson-correlation formula as evaluation explanation; no substantive theoretical result, assumption, proof or derivation changes.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v1's limited downstream validation through three-seed imitation-learning evaluation, more rollouts, uncertainty reporting, data-quantity analysis and a direct asset-dataset comparison. Expanded annotation and production documentation also improves usability. A material weakness remains: the claimed RL simulation-to-real correlation cannot be checked because its cited Table 3 contains EAGLE-versus-PPO scores rather than paired simulation and real-world outcomes. Despite that reporting gap, the gains in experimental support and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ArtVIP and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds microwave transfer comparisons, expanded imitation-learning measurements, computational profiling and generated-asset evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction and feature-distribution comparisons, measured physical trajectories, real-world imitation-learning results and simulated reinforcement-learning results.

results.title: ArtVIP: Articulated Digital Assets of Visual Realism, Modular Interaction, and Physical Fidelity for Robot Learning

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the claim of avoiding dependence on any teacher models or frozen priors and avoiding their bias to adversarial training without frozen priors that may alleviate bias. The abstract, principal contributions and conclusion retain the same one-step restoration, quality and speed claims.

C2.justification: Appendix A.2 extends the existing metric–perception discussion with an explanation of why reference misalignment can disadvantage generative restoration under warping error. It also elaborates the connection between distillation losses and oversmoothing. The VAE bottleneck, heavy-degradation failures and oversharpening limitations already appeared in v1.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the flow-matching target, noise schedule, Euler sampler/CFG and AdamW settings, including learning rate 1e-6 and weight decay 0.01. Section 7 adds PyTorch 2.4.0/CUDA 12.4 and promises code/checkpoints upon acceptance; v1 discussed releasing weights and validation sets. These disclosures do not establish changed training or an actual release.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same training-data coverage and evaluate SPMCS, UDM10, REDS30, YouHQ40, VideoLQ and AIGC28. The added comparisons remain within this restoration coverage; heavy degradations and large motions illustrated in v2 were already reported as encountered conditions in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct one-step competitors: DOVE-5B in Table 7 and Figures 6/9, and DLoRAL in Figure 11. It also introduces a distillation-only comparator in Table 5/Figure 8 and bicubic comparisons in Table 4. The original benchmark comparator set remains intact.

E3.justification: Appendix A.2 adds warping error and VMAF, and applies the existing no-reference metrics to synthetic benchmarks. Figure 10 introduces evaluations at 5, 10, 25 and 50 sampling steps, supplementing the retained fixed-50-step comparisons. The new distillation-only comparison explicitly matches training iterations.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled comparison of adversarial post-training against distillation alone, temporal-profile analysis, sampling-step sensitivity curves and challenging-condition case studies. These examine the benefit of adversarial training, temporal consistency and quality under reduced sampling budgets. The original attention and loss ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. The added tables and curves continue the existing practice of reporting point estimates without uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the inference-time results are retained; 24.185 becoming 24.19 is rounding. New results include VideoLQ MUSIQ of 45.57 for distillation alone versus 51.09 for Ours-3B in Table 5. Table 7 shows Ours-3B outperforming DOVE-5B on NIQE/MUSIQ but trailing on CLIP-IQA/DOVER on both VideoLQ and AIGC28.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 retain the adaptive window attention, progressive distillation, 3B/7B models and adversarial training losses. The additional optimizer, sampler and distillation-target specifications document the existing procedure without establishing a method change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main methodological narrative remain intact, with limited wording and author-note changes. Citations switch to author–year format, limitations and societal impacts move into main-text sections, and the appendices are reorganized around additional evaluations and comparisons.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual evidence through temporal profiles, challenging examples, distillation/concurrent-method comparisons, an eight-panel sampling-step figure and three new tables. Existing Figure 5 and Table 4 become Figure 7 and Table 6; the latter corrects the smaller model's header to Ours-3B. Retained displays and document typography are also reformatted.

R1.justification: Appendices A.4 and A.6 substantially extend positioning to direct concurrent one-step video-restoration methods. They distinguish SeedVR2 from DOVE's VAE adaptation and pixel-domain training, and DLoRAL's parameter-efficient tuning of a largely frozen prior. This materially supplements v1's emphasis on image-restoration acceleration and multi-step video methods.

T1.justification: The adaptive-window and loss equations (1)–(4) are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or mathematical derivation is introduced; the added metric and distillation discussions are empirical or explanatory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central one-step restoration claims. Sampling-step curves address questions left open by v1's fixed-50-step comparisons, while matched-iteration distillation and concurrent one-step comparisons directly test the approach's value. Temporal evaluations and additional implementation details improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Table 4 introduces inconsistent warping-error labeling, but this limited presentation defect does not outweigh the substantive evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SeedVR2. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds temporal evaluations, distillation comparisons, concurrent-method comparisons and sampling-step analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original restoration benchmarks, training ablations, inference timings and a three-expert user study involving 50 videos.

results.title: SeedVR2: One-Step Video Restoration via Diffusion Adversarial Post-Training

C1.justification: The four central contributions remain. However, the abstract and introduction replace broad off-the-shelf or seamless QD-integration language with explicit emphasis on CMA-MAE and black-box QD, qualifying the practical integration claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of premature convergence to stable, simple behaviors, possible drawbacks of fitness weighting, and quality-diversity trade-offs. It distinguishes adaptation by a successful subset from robustness of the entire population and discusses instability when combining changing descriptors with gradient-based QD.

D1.justification: The abstract newly supplies an AutoQD source-code link. v2 also documents procedures for the new diagnostics and qualitative selection, including filtering the top 20% of policies and selecting diverse candidates. Existing architecture, hyperparameter, hardware, and runtime disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six continuous-control tasks: Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Swimmer, Walker2d, and BipedalWalker. BipedalWalker friction and mass variations are also retained; the new analyses reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds PGA-ME with hand-crafted descriptors to the detailed six-environment comparison in Table 8. The original RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora, DvD-ES, and SMERL comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings are retained, but substantial new evaluation protocols appear. These include successful-policy counts at 70%/90% return thresholds, descriptor stability using up to 100 policies per archive and 32 rollouts per policy, and 2/5/10-rollout controls. Table 8 adds maximum-fitness and archive-coverage measurements; the new adaptation box plots exclude negative returns.

E4.justification: The original dimensionality ablations are retained in Appendix H. v2 adds weighting ablation (Appendix C), descriptor-stability and rollout-count tests (Appendix I), quality-diversity and failure analyses (Appendix F), population-level adaptation analyses (Appendix G), and visual behavior case studies (Appendix J).

E5.justification: The new weighting comparison reports means and standard errors over eight seeds and introduces a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, reporting p > 0.7. Existing three-seed benchmark/ablation reporting and Figure 3's 32 evaluation seeds remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–2 and the original dimensionality-ablation results are unchanged. v2 adds extensive results in Tables 3, 8, and 9 and new diagnostic figures. For example, Table 9 reports GT QD scores of 5.99, 6.09, and 6.12 × 10^4 for 2, 5, and 10 rollouts; these compare different settings, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The RFF trajectory embeddings, calibrated fitness-weighted PCA, affine descriptors, and alternating CMA-MAE procedure remain unchanged. The additional proofs and ablation variants do not replace the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain recognizable, with tightened prose, terminology edits, and author-year citations. The closing section becomes Conclusion, and acknowledgments and an AI-use statement are added. Existing appendices are renumbered around the new material.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual evidence: weighting and rollout tables, a detailed benchmark table, trade-off and adaptation-distribution plots, descriptor-variance plots, and behavior sequences. Existing Figures 1–3 and dimensionality plots are retained or relocated; the document also adopts the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against human-feedback QD through Ding et al. and references supporting extinction events, evolutionary optimization limitations, and the expanded concentration analysis. The overall positioning against unsupervised QD and skill-discovery methods remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A corrects RFF coordinate bounds and replaces part of the concentration argument with McDiarmid's inequality. New Appendix B develops lemmas and bounds for trajectory-averaged embeddings, including a finite-horizon error term of 2√2γ^T. The occupancy-measure correspondence is also qualified for Markovian policies in fully observable MDPs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through component ablations, descriptor-stability tests, population-level adaptation analysis, and inspectable behavior examples, addressing gaps in v1's mostly aggregate evidence. Expanded limitations and code-access information further improve transparency. These gains outweigh localized reporting errors, including Appendix F crediting SMERL with the five maximum-fitness wins that Table 8 shows for PGA-ME. The theoretical treatment improves but remains incomplete: the retained inequality in Eq. (36) does not justify the probability bound in Eq. (37).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoQD and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained content can be matched reliably despite additional appendices and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds weighting and rollout-count ablations, descriptor-stability measurements, additional comparisons, and qualitative behavior analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original six-task continuous-control experiments, BipedalWalker adaptation experiments, and embedding/descriptor dimensionality ablations.

results.title: AutoQD: Automatic Discovery of Diverse Behaviors with Quality-Diversity Optimization

C1.justification: V1 presents internet-video adaptation as critical to the improvement loop. V2 reframes the contribution around visual planning with optional internet priors and adds central claims of superior self-improvement and sample efficiency relative to behavior cloning and RL fine-tuning. Policy distillation for efficient deployment also becomes a claimed contribution.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies the importance of internet priors by environment and reports a stronger dependence on filtering in its revised simulation setting. It adds hypotheses about visual-planning generalization, saturation and exploration, task-dependent benefits of suboptimal data, and why both planning components require updating. Appendix G.5 distinguishes semantic and execution failures. The basic limitation concerning insufficient initial success already existed in v1.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds substantial implementation information for the diffusion IDM, including latent inputs, temporal conditioning, action chunks and training schedules. It also documents BCIL, DSRL and policy-distillation budgets, batch sizes and learning rates.
