V2 adds a reproducibility statement; much of the existing video-model, hardware and real-robot implementation information is retained.

E1.justification: Although MetaWorld and Panda remain the environments, task coverage changes substantially. V2 adds faucet, handle, plate and wall-constrained manipulation tasks, while tasks such as Assembly, Lever Pull, Coffee Push and ordinary Button Press disappear. Appendix G.4 adds ordered multi-cup sequences beyond the retained individual cup-pushing and drawer-opening tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated BCIL comparisons in simulation and on real robots, and DSRL comparisons on MetaWorld, including suboptimal initialization results (Table 1, Figure 3 and Table A10). The prior-versus-no-prior comparison remains under SILVR terminology. V1's PA alternative in Table A6 and relabeling comparison in Figure 4 are removed.

E3.justification: The MetaWorld design changes from seven training tasks and six evaluated tasks, including one seen task, to eight training tasks and twelve unseen evaluation tasks. Reported video fine-tuning learning rate changes from 1e-5 to 1e-6. Evaluation extends from iterations 0–2 to 0–4 and additionally 0–9. New policy comparisons and distillation introduce their own training protocols, including 120 teacher-collected demonstrations.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of ten-iteration saturation, GPT-5/Gemini filtering, joint versus individual component updates, and DSRL update budgets (Figure 4, Figure 5, Tables A7 and A11). It substantially revises the suboptimal-initialization analysis and adds prior-effect comparisons and explicit failure cases in Appendix G. V1's PA and relabeling ablations are dropped.

E5.justification: Both versions already report MetaWorld results over three seeds; there is no documented increase in that count. V2 explicitly identifies the reported dispersion as standard deviation and includes uncertainty for aggregate averages in Tables 1, A8 and A9. V1's Tables A5–A6 provide per-task ± values but leave average rows without uncertainty.

E6.justification: V1's six-task SAIL results, averaging 24.4% to 34.4% across iterations 0–2, are replaced by differently configured twelve-task results reaching 44.2% at iteration 4 and 53.1% at iteration 9. V2 adds baseline, VLM-filtering, distillation and component-ablation results. These are not same-setting gains over v1. Existing real-robot prior/no-prior results are largely retained, with the two cup colors averaged in Figure 3.

M1.justification: V2's main MetaWorld implementation replaces v1's frozen MLP inverse-dynamics model with a diffusion inverse-dynamics model predicting action chunks, jointly fine-tuned with the video model. Internet-video adaptation becomes optional, VLM-based success filtering is introduced, and Algorithm 1 adds optional distillation into a diffusion policy. These are substantive procedural changes beyond renaming.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and SAIL becomes SILVR. The abstract, introduction, contribution narrative and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Experiments are reorganized around filtered fine-tuning, internet priors, saturation/distillation, filtering signals and initialization quality. Appendices are reorganized and expanded, and a separate reproducibility section is introduced.

P2.justification: V2 revises the framework diagram, introduces a main comparison table, restructures the principal performance plots and combines the two cup-color panels. New saturation, distillation and initialization displays substantially change the visual presentation. Most earlier rollout montages are retained and relocated, alongside new comparative, sequential-task and failure-case figures. The document also adopts ICLR formatting.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the video-customization discussion, including DreamBooth and DreamVideo, with positioning against diffusion-policy RL fine-tuning. New references include Diffusion Policy, ResIP, DPPO and DSRL. The research argument shifts substantially toward visual planning versus direct action policies and their online sample efficiency. ResIP and DPPO are discussed rather than experimentally evaluated.

T1.justification: The IPA score-composition equation remains unchanged. However, v1 Appendix D.1's explicit PA sampling formulation, Equation 2, and its mathematical contrast with IPA are removed. Neither version presents theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1's principal comparisons were against variants of its own planner over iterations 0–2, leaving advantages over direct policy learning and longer-term behavior largely untested. V2 addresses these deficiencies with BCIL/DSRL comparisons, longer runs, component and update-budget ablations, and explicit failure analysis. Its more qualified discussion of internet priors also improves the account of applicability. Although earlier PA/relabeling analyses are removed and changed MetaWorld settings prevent direct version-to-version performance claims, the stronger validation and implementation documentation constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Despite the retitling and SAIL-to-SILVR renaming, both PDFs describe the same evolving research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison. Changes in experimental conditions require care when comparing results, but do not prevent comparison of the documents.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulation and real-robot results, including policy comparisons, distillation, component ablations and sequential-task demonstrations in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original MetaWorld simulations and Panda-arm experiments, including success rates, filtering and initialization ablations, and rollout visualizations in Section 4 and Appendices C–E.

results.title: Self-Improving Loops for Visual Robotic Planning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a parallelism-focused scheduling problem, X-DAPT, and a two-stage RoboPARA planner improving efficiency and reliability. The headline execution-time and success-rate claims remain unchanged; additional experiments broaden their supporting evidence.

C2.justification: New Appendices C–D explain the division between symbolic planning and low-level physical feasibility, collision avoidance, and hardware-specific control, and discuss global versus reactive planning. Appendix E adds interpretations concerning cross-dataset generalization and recovery. The existing cost, accuracy, and skill-library limitations in Section 5.5 remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2's abstract reports a public code repository where v1 promises release. Section 5.1 newly names ACT, DP, and pi0 as low-level action-model training algorithms, and the metric description explicitly includes planning time in TEI. A reproducibility statement consolidates resource information, while existing prompts, pseudocode, and retry limits are retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates four X-DAPT scenes despite describing a ten-scene dataset. v2 adds supermarket, hospital, disaster rescue, hotel, pet shop, and library evaluations, plus regrouped RoboTwin tasks (Appendix E.5). It also evaluates interrupted execution through deliberately introduced kitchen-task failures.

E2.justification: Corresponding original experiments retain the same seven named baselines and their participation, including the Franka comparison renumbered from Table 10 to Table 19. Additional X-DAPT scenes reuse this set; the new RoboTwin comparison uses six existing baselines, without introducing a new comparison method.

E3.justification: The original 60-unit evaluation protocol is retained. New protocols regroup atomic RoboTwin tasks into scene-level combinations and difficulty categories (Table 12), and introduce specified execution errors into nine kitchen tasks (Appendix E.6). The worked recovery case imposes an apple-dropping failure at 12 seconds. These are additional evaluation designs, not established reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: The four original component ablations are unchanged. Appendix E.6 adds a distinct investigation of recovery from execution failures, with original and repaired schedules in Tables 16–17 and nine error cases in Table 18, covering dropped objects and a slipping knife across three difficulty levels.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Averaging over five cumulative task groups is retained. The nine new recovery cases are different tasks, not documented repeated trials or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 10–11 add six-scene results, Table 13 adds RoboTwin results, and Table 18 reports successful replanning in all nine error cases. RoboTwin TEI values for RoboPARA are 10.6, 5.2, and 2.4 across easy, medium, and hard tasks. Original Tables 1–3 and 8–9, and the retained Franka comparison, have unchanged numerical results.

M1.justification: The two-stage planner, prompts, DAG validator, arm selector, and temporal scheduler remain unchanged, including Algorithms 1–4. Appendix E.6 newly describes and tests rerunning the existing planner with updated observations after execution errors; it does not establish a revision to the planning algorithm.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the detailed methodology appendix remain closely matched. Changes include localized wording edits, author and affiliation updates, new acknowledgements and reproducibility/LLM-use statements, and appendix restructuring: new Appendices C–D precede the experimental appendix, formerly C and now E.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout and substantially redistributes displays. Figure 1 moves off the title page, and the GPT-4o heatmap moves from main-text Figure 4 to appendix Figure 7. Nine tables are added, covering new results and tabulated task/plan examples. Existing robot photographs, framework diagrams, and benchmark plots are largely retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive System-1/System-2 positioning, locating RoboPARA within an established hierarchical architecture rather than retaining v1's broad final claim of a new planning class. Added references include dual-process foundations and hierarchical or constrained planning work by Holladay, Adu-Bredu, Vu, and Joublin. Other citations are added or removed beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The scheduling formulation, feasibility constraints, and metric formulas in Equations 1–12 are retained. The added architectural and global-planning discussions provide conceptual explanations, without new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation that was limited in v1: it evaluates the remaining six X-DAPT scenes, adds an external dataset adapted for high-level planning, and investigates execution-error recovery. These additions address important gaps in coverage and robustness evidence while preserving the original results. Clearer planning-versus-control boundaries also improve interpretation. Recovery evidence remains qualitative and lacks repeated-run uncertainty, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RoboPARA and X-DAPT. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained content to be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds evaluations on six additional X-DAPT scenes, reorganized RoboTwin tasks, and execution-error recovery cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original X-DAPT evaluations, component ablations, and physical-robot experiments, including Tables 1–3 and Appendix C.

results.title: RoboPARA: Dual-Arm Robot Planning with Parallel Allocation and Recomposition Across Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion broaden the mapper's claimed applicability from LLaVA v1.5 to any LMM architecture. v3 also extends superiority claims to parameter-efficient finetuning, reporting a 7.7-point average advantage over its best LoRA configuration, and adds claims about favorable scaling with test-time compute.

C2.justification: v3 adds attention-based explanations for ICL degradation and interprets component ablations as evidence for visual-feature distillation. Its compute discussion now distinguishes low-budget ICL advantages from higher-budget FT advantages and identifies context-length constraints. Appendix A.2.5 newly qualifies public-model comparisons by architecture, scale and training-data differences.

D1.justification: v3 adds training and evaluation meta-task counts and compositions, expanded hyperparameter-search tables, detailed instruction prompts, LoRA target matrices, ranks, scaling factors and learning rates, plus hardware requirements for smaller models. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. The MAPD code-access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The training mixture and four principal VL-ICL datasets remain unchanged. v3 Figure 2 adds text-to-text evaluation scenarios for Operator Induction and CLEVR Count Induction alongside their image-to-text versions, modestly extending input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds three LoRA configurations in Tables 2 and 12. Its Table 13 extends v1 Table 9 with Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and connector-finetuning variants of previously ICL-only public LLaVA comparators. The original prompt-distillation comparators remain.

E3.justification: New experiments vary language-model and vision-encoder configurations, LoRA placement and parameter budgets, and explicit task instructions. v3 also introduces normalized attention entropy and FLOPs-matched ICL-versus-FT evaluation. The original data splits and validation-based selection within 30 adaptation steps remain; newly disclosed meta-task counts do not establish changed sampling.

E4.justification: v3 adds modality comparisons, mapper-versus-MLP ablations with and without soft prompts, backbone-generalization tests, attention-entropy analysis and accuracy-versus-compute analysis. Its convergence plots also compare methods instead of only MAPD shot settings. The earlier perturbation and example-selection analyses are retained in Appendices A.2.7-A.2.8.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates, whereas v3 systematically adds 95% binomial confidence intervals to principal and model-comparison results in Tables 1-3 and 13. Neither PDF establishes repeated training runs or seed-based uncertainty; the intervals should not be interpreted as evidence of additional runs.

E6.justification: Original main scores are retained in v3 Table 11, while substantial new comparison and analysis results are added. In the retained high-shot FT experiment, In-ContextPD's Operator Induction scores change from 25.0/36.5/35.0 to 58.3/53.3/76.7 at 16/32/64 shots (v1 Table 6; v3 Table 16). These are revised reported values, not an established MAPD performance gain.

M1.justification: The attention mapper, learned soft prompts, frozen backbone components, two-stage training, first-order MAML updates and test-time adaptation procedure remain unchanged. Additional backbone configurations and component ablations test the existing method rather than introduce a revised MAPD algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract and substantial introductory and experimental discussion, adds a Related Work section, reorganizes analyses around explicit questions and extensively restructures the appendix. Standalone limitations become concluding qualifications, while the Broader Impact section is removed.

P2.justification: The dense main results table becomes a compact summary, with detailed scores retained as appendix Table 11. Earlier robustness and selection displays move to the appendix. New modality, component and architecture displays are added, convergence plots are redrawn, and the original FLOPs-overhead plot is replaced by latency and compute-matched accuracy panels.

R1.justification: A dedicated Related Work section substantially expands positioning around prompt learning and test-time adaptation, adding works including PromptSRC, TPT and LoRA. It explicitly distinguishes MAPD's use of full visual patch features from Najdenkoska et al.'s CLS-token approach, beyond v1's shorter attribution.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, MAPD objectives, first-order updates and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The added attention-analysis equations express standard probability normalization and Shannon entropy for an empirical metric; no substantive theoretical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through LoRA comparisons, direct component ablations, alternative-backbone tests and FLOPs-matched evaluation. Expanded sampling and hyperparameter documentation also makes the work substantially easier to assess and reproduce. Claims about applicability to any LMM and state-of-the-art performance remain broader than the demonstrated evidence, but the added controls and more qualified compute discussion provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MAPD study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained content to be matched despite substantial reorganization and added experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds LoRA comparisons, architecture experiments, attention analysis and compute-matched evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original few-shot VQA experiments, component analyses, image-perturbation tests and computational measurements in Section 3 and the appendices.

results.title: Meta-Adaptive Prompt Distillation for Few-Shot Visual Question Answering

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: learned null-space-constrained steering improves refusal while preserving benign utility. Additional experiments support this existing claim without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explains utility preservation through training/test activation-space coverage and identifies deterioration with insufficient benign data or excessive null-space ratios. It adds interpretations involving possible MLP overfitting, adaptive-attack geometry, and evaluator disagreement. Section 5 replaces the unexplored-MLP/model-size limitations with larger-model and reasoning-model boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds computational pseudocode, training-time information, stronger descriptions of attack-family exclusion, an additional implementation-access address, and an LLM-use disclosure. Existing hardware, software, decoding, and principal hyperparameter disclosures remain largely unchanged; the revised benign-data description contains an unresolved total.

E1.justification: v2 adds AdvPrompter, four FlipAttack variants, and WildGuard Test with 329 unseen harmful queries (Appendix E.5). It also introduces an adaptive white-box GCG scenario with access to the steering defense (E.6), substantially extending the original attack coverage.

E2.justification: Circuit Breaker, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator in Tables 1–2. Supervised refusal training is newly compared with AlphaSteer in Tables 7–9 and appears as Refusal SFT in Table 18. The original steering baselines remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include 1B/3B model configurations, data-matched refusal training, 200-step adaptive GCG, projection-energy coverage measurements, and Llama-Guard-3-8B evaluation. Appendix D.1 also adds 900 MATH training prompts to the previously stated composition while retaining the 14,000 total, an unresolved count inconsistency that does not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained activation and steering-strength analyses, v2 adds MLP substitution, math-data exclusion, benign-data-size and null-space-ratio ablations. It also examines adaptive robustness, CAST's math-trigger failure, training/test overlap, case-specific activation changes, and disagreement between evaluation models (Appendices D–G).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new coverage distributions describe activation variability, not uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Retained entries in Tables 1–2 have identical reported values, but v2 adds substantial new results. Examples include 95.5% DSR under adaptive GCG (Figure 7), 90 seconds versus 20 minutes for AlphaSteer and refusal training (Table 9), and utility scores falling from 67.30 to 39.43 when benign training data decrease from 14k to 1k (Table 14).

M1.justification: The principal null-space projection, regularized linear regression, and steering equations remain unchanged. Appendix E.3 adds an experimental AlphaSteer variant replacing linear regression with a two-layer MLP, a limited architectural adaptation rather than a replacement of the main method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable, with local condensation and terminology edits. Existing appendices are reorganized around new material, the broader-impacts discussion becomes an ethics statement, and reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 expands the main tables with Circuit Breaker rows and adds extensive appendix tables, an algorithm display, adaptive-attack plots, CAST condition distributions, coverage plots, and an evaluator-mismatch example. Most original figures survive under new numbering; the conference template also changes typography and layout.

R1.justification: Appendix A.2 now acknowledges learned steering in Guiding Giants, HyperSteer, and Activation Scaling, distinguishing AlphaSteer through principled guidance. Other safety, representation-learning, and attack references are updated, while the overall positioning around the safety–utility trade-off remains.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds a stepwise computational-cost derivation and training/inference complexity comparisons. The null-space equivalence lemma, projection proof, and closed-form regression derivation in Appendix B remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: Adaptive-attack testing, stronger comparators, and coverage/null-space ablations substantially address v1's limited evidence about robustness and when utility preservation fails. Evaluator comparisons further expose measurement sensitivity. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including the inconsistent training-data total and Table 15's 3k-data average of 98.71%, which conflicts with its displayed attack rates averaging 92.14%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AlphaSteer, with matching core equations, experiments, and identifiable appendix content. The text, tables, equations, and figures support a reliable comparison despite substantial appendix expansion and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, adaptive attacks, model-size experiments, ablations, and evaluator comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak-defense and utility experiments on three LLMs, alongside activation analyses and response case studies.

results.title: AlphaSteer: Learning Refusal Steering with Principled Null-Space Constraint

C1.justification: The broad first-video-unlearning positioning becomes a specific first training-free, closed-form weight-update claim, accompanied by explicit superiority claims over competing video methods. v2 also claims irreversible weight-level changes in its introduction, whereas v1 explicitly acknowledged adversarial reversibility. These revise novelty, comparative effectiveness, and protection claims.

C2.justification: v1's explicit misuse, governance, and vector-reversal limitations disappear. v2 adds substantive interpretations of prompt-selection stability, cPCA's benefits, neutral-concept overlap, UCE's fidelity tradeoff, and adversarial resistance. Appendix C.3 newly identifies substantial quality degradation when five vectors affect complex motion, extending the discussion of applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds ZeroScopeT2V injection locations, approximately 1,000 GPT-sampled neutral prompts, UCE retain-prompt lists and scales, and computational estimates including 0.4 GPU hours and ten forward passes. The detailed v1 layer-sweep rationale is removed. Original example prompt lists, project-page information, and code-folder availability statements are retained.

E1.justification: T2VSafetyBench coverage is retained, while SafeSora adds evaluated content including terrorism, racism, and animal abuse. v2 also introduces joint multi-category removal and targeted adversarial-prompt scenarios, substantially broadening the tested requirements and input conditions.

E2.justification: v1 compares the edited model with unmodified Open-Sora. v2 adds NullSCE to the T2VSafetyBench comparison, SAFREE to SafeSora, and an adapted UCE comparison in Appendix F. NullSCE has no Gore entry in Table 1; VideoEraser remains related work rather than an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The reported evaluator changes from GPT-4 to GPT-4o. FVD changes from XCLIP features and original-versus-censored comparisons to I3D features with real-video references; MM-Notox's printed definition also changes. v2 adds ZeroScopeT2V, FVMD, and new experimental protocols, including attacks on 100 previously fully censored prompts. The stated selected layers change from 17–19 to 17–18. These are reported setting changes, not proof that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original rank and suppression-strength studies remain. v2 adds safe/unsafe-pair similarity tests, neutral-set resampling, refusal-only versus PCA versus cPCA comparisons, alpha sensitivity, multi-vector interference and quality analysis, UCE hyperparameter sweeps, and targeted adversarial testing. These directly examine component necessity, sensitivity, and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v2 Table 4 newly reports five random neutral-set resamplings and their individual censorship rates, providing limited variability evidence absent from v1. This does not establish increased repeated runs for the main benchmarks. Neither version provides general benchmark confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The five original Open-Sora censorship pairs remain unchanged, but FVD and MM-Notox entries are replaced: for example, censored Pornography FVD changes from 144.0 to 151.24 and MM-Notox from 20.89 to 20.07. Revised metric definitions prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. v2 adds substantial comparator, SafeSora, FVMD, sensitivity, multi-vector, and attack results.

M1.justification: The core activation-difference averaging, cPCA refinement, and closed-form weight update remain. Appendix C.3 adds a multi-concept extension using several refusal directions, concept-specific suppression strengths, and sequential application; v1 explicitly restricted the method to one concept at a time.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method and evaluation passages are rewritten. Section 4.4 becomes an expanded Section 5 Discussion, the standalone Limitations section disappears, and new appendix sections surround retained qualitative material and prompt lists. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: The original results displays are reorganized into grouped comparison tables with censorship, FVD, MM-Notox, and averages, followed by numerous new analysis tables. Figure 1 moves to the first page and Figure 2 becomes a compact grid. ICLR formatting changes typography and placement throughout; the underlying images in Figures 1–12 are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around SAFREE, VideoEraser, and NullSCE, distinguishing filtering, fine-tuning, and training-free weight updates rather than asserting an unaddressed video-unlearning field. It also adds relevant benchmark, metric, model-editing, and attack references. The duplicated ModelScope entries represent the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: The main projection mathematics and Appendix B weight-update derivation are retained. Appendix C.3 adds a mathematical multi-concept extension summing projections across refusal directions. Equation 10 also changes the defined MM-Notox distance from an L2 norm to a squared norm. No substantial new proof framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked competing unlearning baselines and direct controls establishing cPCA's contribution. v2 substantially addresses these deficiencies through comparative evaluations, a second model and benchmark, component controls, and tests exposing multi-concept and adversarial behavior. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit limitations and reporting problems, including the mismatched-category NullSCE average and inconsistent UCE dataset label. The broader evidence improves assessment of effectiveness and boundaries, although it does not establish the claimed irreversibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same low-rank refusal-vector work and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The original derivation, qualitative figures, and prompt lists can be matched across restructuring. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ZeroScopeT2V/SafeSora evaluations, competing methods, component analyses, multi-concept experiments, and adversarial testing in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Open-Sora censorship, FVD, and MM-Notox results on T2VSafetyBench, qualitative generations, and rank and suppression-strength experiments in Section 4.

results.title: Video Unlearning via Low-Rank Refusal Vector

C1.justification: v2 removes the broad claim of being the first framework for learning high-speed flows and changes 'first steps' to 'takes steps.' It expands the stated dataset contribution from two to three primary datasets while retaining the central two-phase contribution and narrower adaptive-data novelty claim.

C2.justification: New interpretations connect fixed-mean timestep failures to mismatched state–timestep pairs and feature importance to vertical shock reflections. v2 also discusses dense MoE computational costs, hypersonic capacity difficulties and omitted transverse velocity, long-rollout behavior, and untested phenomena such as detonations and boundary layers.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed spherical-blast and airfoil generation procedures, graph construction and features, new architecture hyperparameters and resource measurements, hypersonic masking instructions, and runtime protocols. It also newly documents parameter sampling and evaluation-case selection for existing data. The code and dataset access pointers remain.

E1.justification: Beyond the original coal-dust and circular-blast settings, v2 evaluates shock–airfoil interactions with varying angles, three-dimensional spherical blasts, longer circular-blast trajectories, and Mach 5–6 hypersonic airfoil shocks. These substantially broaden geometry, dimensionality, temporal demands, and flow regimes.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated MGN and DGN backbones for airfoil shocks, oracle and constant-mean timestep controls for the retained benchmarks, and classical-solver runtime comparisons including a low-fidelity alternative. The original four-backbone comparisons remain; Base is renamed Affine.

E3.justification: Original benchmark splits, training budgets, and principal metrics remain. Added experiments introduce mesh-refinement sweeps, CPU/GPU timing against different CFD fidelities, feature-dropout tests, conservation measurements, and hypersonic evaluation on a 256×1024 grid using three output fields. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 extends the original component comparisons with grid-independence checks, mass-conservation analysis, long-rollout error trajectories, oracle/mean-timestep ablations, and feature-corruption sensitivity tests. Appendices E–I also examine hypersonic modeling difficulties and explain which inputs influence timestep predictions.

E5.justification: The original experiments retain three-run averaging, standard errors, and two-standard-error bars. Added runtime and rollout results continue standard-error reporting, including Figure 22's test-case mean and uncertainty band. No increased training-run count, new seed policy, or new inferential testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results, including DGN outperforming MGN in Figure 7b, runtime comparisons, conservation measurements, and timestep-control findings. All numerical entries in v1 Tables 3–11 match v2 Tables 8–16. However, Figure 2's coal-dust timestep errors become roughly fivefold smaller under the same stated normalization; the PDFs do not explain this change.

M1.justification: The two-phase framework and original conditioning formulas remain, but v2 adds graph-based solver and neural-CFL architectures for irregular geometry. Appendix E also introduces a hypersonic U-Net adaptation with grid interpolation, learned airfoil-interior embeddings, masked loss, and restricted output fields. These are substantive procedural adaptations.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence remain. Changes include Base-to-Affine terminology, a rewritten backbone overview, movement of the broader neural-solver survey into Appendix B, author-detail updates, and author–year citations. New analyses receive separate appendix sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material for new flow settings, runtime comparisons, conservation, sensitivity, and timestep ablations, plus new tables and expanded architecture tables. Original visualizations are retained and relocated. Figure 2's axis scale, conditioning legends, typography, and page layout also change.

R1.justification: v2 selectively adds literature on graph and hybrid solvers, CFD benchmarking, sampling, and variance reduction, including Valencia et al. and McGreivy and Hakim. Related work adds connections to adaptive optimizers and continuous-time generative models. The broader positioning remains recognizable, with narrower novelty wording.

T1.justification: Appendix F newly defines total mass and relative mass deviation and states the closed-domain conservation condition. The main mathematical framework remains unchanged, with no new theorem or proof. Appendix D's explicit interpolation formula elaborates a procedure already described in v1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the framework: Appendix H tests the timestep predictor's contribution, Appendix C.5 supplies previously absent runtime comparisons, and conservation and long-rollout analyses probe physical consistency and stability. Broader geometry coverage and implementation details improve applicability and reproducibility. The unexplained Figure 2 rescaling and restricted hypersonic outputs remain caveats, but the targeted validation gains clearly outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ShockCast and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained content can be matched despite substantial experimental additions and changes in layout.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and reports additional airfoil, spherical-blast, long-rollout, hypersonic, runtime, and diagnostic results.

before.justification: v1 reports original timestep-prediction and flow-modeling experiments on generated coal-dust explosion and circular-blast datasets, including Figures 2–6 and Appendix F.

results.title: A Two-Phase Deep Learning Framework for Adaptive Time-Stepping in High-Speed Flow Modeling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the claimed contribution from NAVSIM planning performance to state-of-the-art NAVSIM and Bench2Drive performance and quantitative driving-VQA capability. v2 also elevates the hierarchical cognitive-data pipeline and named DiffGRPO scheme as central innovations and emphasizes efficient trajectory generation. The underlying VLM-plus-diffusion proposition remains.

C2.justification: New discussion explains optional textual guidance, attributes its limited benefit to NAVSIM diversity, questions whether VQA scores demonstrate visual understanding, and motivates BC regularization over direct KL constraints. Failure analysis adds aggressive progress-seeking, perception weaknesses, unsafe following, and possible metric false negatives. The small-BC-weight interpretation changes from training collapse to greater progress. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation about non-interactive RL training is removed.

D1.justification: Most detailed training schedules, preprocessing, diffusion-step counts, and hardware information persist. v2 adds explicit code and model/data collection links, SGLang annotation tooling, and one-update/no-PPO-clipping implementation notes, while revising model specifications. Reproducibility remains imperfect: its ±5 noise-clipping prose conflicts with ±3 in Table 12, which also retains BC weight 0.01 despite Table 8 favoring 0.001.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from NAVSIM to CARLA Bench2Drive, adding interactive driving and safety-critical scenarios. DriveLM, previously included as training data, becomes an evaluation benchmark, and DriveBench adds quantitative driving VQA coverage under clean, corrupted-image, and text-only inputs. The existing NAVSIM and driving-QA training coverage largely persists.

E2.justification: New comparisons include TCP variants, ThinkTwice, DriveAdapter, and DriveTransformer on Bench2Drive; GPT-4o, LLaVA, InternVL2, and other VQA models; and alternative trajectory decoders. Within the corresponding NAVSIM Table 1, v2 removes Hydra-MDP-V8192, LTF, BevDrive, and ARTEMIS. ARTEMIS remains in the extended-metric comparison, so it is not removed from the paper entirely.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Bench2Drive route and multi-ability evaluation, GPT-Score VQA assessment, and latency and formatting-error measurements. It adds an InternVL3-2B configuration and changes the reported DiT hidden size/head size from 1536/32 to 384/8. NAVSIM splits and the 3/200/10-epoch training schedule remain. Noise-clipping prose changes from ±3 to ±5, although v2 Table 12 still specifies ±3.

E4.justification: v2 adds decoder and architectural ablations, high-level-command versus chain-of-thought guidance tests, visual-input robustness tests, comparisons of TransFuser and IL/RL trajectories, and categorized failure cases. It removes v1's QA-data scale/quality study and the discount-factor 0.5 condition. The BC-weight and sampling-noise sensitivity studies are retained with revised outcomes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. Diffusion-noise standard deviations and group-normalized advantages describe the algorithm rather than uncertainty in reported experimental results.

E6.justification: The main NAVSIM PDMS changes from 89.6 to 90.8, with revised component and sensitivity results; the best reported BC weight changes from 0.01 to 0.001. These accompany changed model settings and do not establish an isolated same-setting gain. New results include Bench2Drive Driving Score 71.36 and success rate 45.45%, DriveBench average 56.71, and decoder timing results. The extended NAVSIM results, including EPDMS 83.6, are unchanged.

M1.justification: The VLM-conditioned diffusion planner and three-stage training framework remain. v2 explicitly integrates SwiGLU, RMSNorm, RoPE, and QK normalization into the planner, supported by the incremental architectural comparison in Table 4. These are limited architectural refinements. Much of the hierarchical data pipeline and the RL procedure renamed DiffGRPO already appears in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, several sensitivity analyses move into the appendix, and data construction is reorganized around hierarchical stages. The appendices gain a nine-question discussion and separate failure-analysis and LLM-usage sections, substantially changing the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview and planner diagrams and replaces the appendix data-pipeline graphic with a hierarchical diagram in the main text. It adds benchmark, decoder, and guidance tables plus extensive trajectory comparisons and failure visualizations. Existing sensitivity tables are relocated, while the three dialogue figures are retained and renumbered. The document also adopts a different header and typography layout.

R1.justification: The related-work positioning is substantively revised through discussions of GoalFlow, Gen-Drive, R2SE, and Drive-R1, while earlier material such as HybridVLA and DAPO is removed. v2 introduces stronger priority claims for RL applied to driving VLAs and explicitly distinguishes NAVSIM simulator rewards from prior trajectory-distance rewards. These changes extend beyond the switch to author-year citations.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 11 corrects the full diffusion-chain log density by including log p(x_T), omitted from v1 Equation 13, and identifies this prior as independent of model parameters. This is a limited mathematical correction that leaves the policy-gradient objective effectively unchanged. No substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's broad planning and cognition claims relied mainly on non-reactive NAVSIM evaluation and illustrative dialogue. v2 substantially strengthens validation through interactive Bench2Drive testing, quantitative VQA evaluation, decoder and guidance ablations, and explicit failure analysis. These address important evidential gaps. The removed data-scaling study, weakened disclosure of non-interactive RL limitations, and new reporting inconsistencies temper the improvement: notably, the ablation prose disagrees with Table 3, and noise-clipping prose conflicts with Table 12. Nevertheless, the broader direct testing and more informative failure evidence provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReCogDrive and retain the same underlying research framework. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, references, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated analyses and retained dialogue examples.

after.justification: v2 reports original NAVSIM results and additional Bench2Drive, DriveLM, and DriveBench evaluations, alongside decoder comparisons, guidance ablations, robustness tests, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original ReCogDrive results on NAVSIM, component and hyperparameter ablations, QA-data scaling experiments, extended-metric evaluations, and qualitative examples.

results.title: ReCogDrive: A Reinforced Cognitive Framework for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

C1.justification: The central contribution remains GIQ as a benchmark exposing geometric-reasoning weaknesses. V3 qualifies its MRT conclusion by acknowledging that the strongest nonlinear configuration matches average human performance. Its conclusion also extends the diagnostic claim by presenting GIQ skills as necessary foundations for understanding complex scenes.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantial interpretations concerning nonlinear accessibility of representations, prompting limitations, and occlusion versus geometric reasoning. The conclusion introduces hypotheses about noisy training priors and texture-based approximations, while acknowledging that transfer to arbitrary organic shapes remains untested and future training requires broader real-world distributions. These go substantially beyond v1's largely descriptive account of failures.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies that non-reconstruction tasks retain complex backgrounds, explicitly identifies reconstruction evaluation as zero-shot, and documents synonym handling with manual verification for classification. These disclosures do not establish changes to the earlier experiments. Conversely, Section 3.3 omits v1's environment-emitter radiance of (0.3, 0.3, 0.3). The dataset access destination is unchanged.

E1.justification: The 224-polyhedron collection and four principal tasks remain. V3 substantially broadens evaluation scenarios through three-view classification inputs, classification from ground-truth point clouds, and a human MRT population of 42 participants. These introduce input conditions and a population absent from the reported v1 evaluations.

E2.justification: V3 Figure 3 adds VGGT, DUSt3R, and MASt3R to symmetry and MRT comparisons, plus a human MRT baseline. Figure 4 adds LLaVA-3D, ShapeLLM, and PointLLM to the four retained frontier classifiers. The reconstruction comparator set remains Shap-E, Stable Fast 3D, and OpenLRM.

E3.justification: Symmetry evaluation changes from a held-out set of 26 shapes to five-fold shape-disjoint cross-validation. For hard MRT, v1 describes mixed-pair training and testing, whereas v3 describes synthetic-only training followed by synthetic and synthetic-wild testing. V3 also introduces a timed human protocol: five easy and twenty hard questions, with 30 seconds per question.

E4.justification: V3 newly reports linear-versus-nonlinear probe comparisons and classification ablations testing Chain-of-Thought prompting and three-view inputs. It reports comparable average symmetry performance across probe types, minimal prompting gains, and marginal multiview gains concentrated on Johnson solids. These test additional explanations for failure, although their detailed results are deferred to the unavailable appendix.

E5.justification: V3 explicitly reports averaging symmetry accuracy across five cross-validation folds and gives a human hard-MRT standard deviation of 0.11. V1 reports single-split point estimates without these statistics. Statistical reporting expands, but fold-level variability, confidence intervals, and random-seed information remain absent from the supplied PDFs.

E6.justification: V3 reports revised cross-validated symmetry estimates and new comparator results. Its MRT results feature SigLIP at 69% and DINOv2 at 67%, replacing v1's headline ConvNeXt result of 60% under different probing and training conditions; these are not same-setting gains. New human results include 68.05% average hard-set accuracy and 90% for top performers. Geometry-native classification scores and prompting/multiview findings further expand the results.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 changes the principal MRT readout from linear probing of absolute embedding differences to a nonlinear probe. Section 4.2 also introduces nonlinear symmetry probes. These revise the probing component; the absolute-difference representation and stated symmetry loss remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten; geometry and reconstruction-model descriptions are condensed; the lengthy model-by-model error discussion becomes grouped error categories; and the conclusion is substantially expanded and reorganized. The principal section sequence remains, but the editorial revision extends well beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: V1's polyhedral-group table becomes compact Figure 2, while its symmetry table and MRT plots become the paired Figure 3. Reconstruction examples shrink from six displayed rows to four. The classification/results display is redesigned as Figure 4, showing two rather than four illustrated reasoning cases. Hard-pair examples and several detailed results are redirected to an appendix absent from the supplied v3.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations for the geometry-native comparators, model providers, and historical sources, while dropping some earlier geometry and representation references. Its central positioning against generic object datasets and earlier spatial-reasoning benchmarks remains largely unchanged. Citation-style and publication-metadata updates do not constitute additional scientific repositioning.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 drops the identical-vertex-configuration requirement from the definition of a regular polyhedron, making the stated definition less restrictive. It also omits the earlier discussion of constructing duals through face centroids and polar reciprocation. The weighted cross-entropy mathematics remains unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens benchmark validation through shape-disjoint cross-validation, nonlinear probes, geometry-native comparators, and a measured human baseline (Sections 4.2–4.4; Figures 3–4). These address important weaknesses in v1's reliance on one symmetry split, linear readouts, and assumed human superiority, while making the MRT conclusion more nuanced. The gains outweigh reduced visible detail and localized definition/presentation regressions. Missing referenced appendices and unsupported extrapolations to general spatial intelligence nevertheless limit verification and claim strength.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GIQ benchmark, and all supplied pages are readable. However, v1 ends at references on page 15 and v3 on page 14; neither includes the supplementary material or appendix repeatedly referenced in its text. This limits comparison of detailed results, ablations, and implementation information deferred there.

after.justification: V3 reports original results for the same four tasks, expanded model comparisons, and a new 42-participant mental-rotation study.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction examples, symmetry-detection accuracies, mental-rotation experiments, and zero-shot classification results in Section 4.

results.title: GIQ: Benchmarking 3D Geometric Reasoning of Vision Foundation Models with Simulated and Real Polyhedra

C1.justification: V2's introduction presents RULECOLLECTION-32K as a released dataset contribution and emphasizes training regularization for stable reasoning in small models. V1 instead emphasizes data curation and outcome-based verification. The central claims about generalizable rule reasoning, adaptive domain sampling, and improved efficiency remain, including the headline performance margins.

C2.justification: New Section 5.5 attributes generalization partly to meta-introspection, self-verification, and consistency checking. Appendix C adds interpretations concerning difficult-domain allocation, hyperparameter behavior, and the necessity of rule-centric training data. V2 also removes the explicit statement that extrapolation to long compositional reasoning chains remains unverified, while retaining noise, model-scaling, and possible BBH-contamination caveats.

D1.justification: Section 3.2 newly documents entropy-bonus removal and training-rule shuffling, and Appendix C.8 supplies curriculum implementation recipes. The hardware and main hyperparameter table remain. However, direct code/model links are replaced by a future-release statement, and the new o3-mini attribution for long-CoT distillation conflicts with the retained DeepSeek-R1 description in Appendix B.2.

E1.justification: V2 adds inference-only evaluations on AIME 2025, GPQA Diamond, and Coin Flip, extending coverage to mathematical, scientific, and symbolic reasoning. Appendix C.9 additionally uses AIME 1983–2024 for training experiments. The original eight-task collection is retained under the name RULECOLLECTION-32K with unchanged reported dataset counts.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 adds Data-balance RL, Easy-to-hard RL, and ADARFT to the existing ID comparison. Appendix comparisons additionally evaluate Easy-to-hard SFT and DAPO with dynamic sampling; v1 explicitly disabled DAPO's dynamic sampling. These substantially expand the evaluated alternatives to the proposed sampling strategy.

E3.justification: New protocols include eight difficulty partitions for progressive curricula, balanced resampling to 3,571 examples per domain, individual hyperparameter sweeps, and AR-LSAT evaluations every 50 steps in a dedicated ablation. V2 also introduces math-only, rule-only, and joint-data GRPO controls without DADS. The original main training and inference settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds sensitivity tests for alpha, tau, and epsilon; a DADS-versus-no-DADS learning comparison on difficult AR-LSAT examples; and training-data composition ablations. Table 15 adds before/after reasoning cases supporting the new mechanism discussion. V1's rule-noise, difficulty-level, and test-time-scaling analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 removes v1's statement that one-sided p-values are reported, while retaining five evaluation runs, mean/standard-deviation reporting, and seeds {21,42,84}. Figures 5–7 acquire shaded bands, but their statistical meaning is unspecified. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Substantial new results appear: Table 6 reports OOD averages of 81.7 for DADS, 78.1 for ADARFT, and 75.4 for dynamic-sampling DAPO; Table 8 adds DADS scores of 23.3, 44.9, and 95.1 on AIME 2025, GPQA Diamond, and Coin Flip. Original headline results remain. Figure 7 changes the GRPO/DAPO curve assignments and revises the reported efficiency comparison from approximately 100 fewer steps versus GRPO to 72 versus DAPO.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes the specified unnormalized sampling weight from exp((v+epsilon)/tau) to exp(v/tau)+epsilon, affecting normalized sampling probabilities. The reward function, GRPO objective, and historical-reward reweighting framework remain. Newly documented entropy removal and rule shuffling do not establish when those implementation choices were introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and data-curation prose are edited and condensed, and terminology is standardized around RULECOLLECTION-32K. Analyses become a standalone Section 5, ethics moves out of the appendix, and a reproducibility statement is added. Much of the existing technical prose and overall argument sequence is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a substantially different conference layout, expands the ID table with a curriculum block, and adds multiple comparison, ablation, and trajectory tables. The dataset-statistics table moves to the appendix and loses its Source column. Figures 5–7 gain shaded bands and a speedup annotation; Figure 10 uses tighter axes and adds pass@1 reference lines.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused positioning against loss-based and proxy-model data-mixture approaches, citing Velocitune, DIDS, and RegMix, alongside new curriculum-learning references. It also adds long-context motivation. The broader relationship to rule-based reasoning and RLVR literature remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The revised weighting definition in Algorithm 1 is mathematically substantive: epsilon cancels during normalization in v1, whereas v2's additive epsilon affects the resulting distribution. The GRPO equations remain unchanged, and neither version provides a theorem or proof establishing DADS guarantees.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central sampling contribution. V1 disabled DAPO's dynamic sampling and lacked direct curriculum comparisons; v2 evaluates these alternatives and adds DADS/no-DADS, hyperparameter, and training-data controls. These address important gaps in attribution and robustness despite unchanged headline scores. The gains outweigh weaker resource-access guidance and conflicting SFT-teacher documentation, although the new meta-introspection explanation remains supported mainly by illustrative cases.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RuleReasoner/DADS research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, with retained material identifiable despite reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 reports original model evaluations, curriculum comparisons, hyperparameter sensitivity experiments, additional reasoning benchmarks, and training-data ablations in the main text and Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original training and evaluation of 4B/8B models, including eight in-distribution tasks, three out-of-distribution benchmarks, sampling analyses, and appendix robustness and test-time-scaling results.

results.title: RuleReasoner: Reinforced Rule-based Reasoning via Domain-aware Dynamic Sampling

C1.justification: v2 drops v1's concluding assertion of generating outputs with higher complexity and focuses the stated benefits on controllability and fidelity. This is a limited narrowing; the central claims of training-free heterogeneous expert composition and efficient annealed/SMC sampling remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of character-insertion failures, including SDEdit's background changes from global noising, and interprets the layout results as reducing the need for application-specific attention interventions. Table 4 additionally interprets SMC as improving sampling efficiency with little overhead. Appendix B's limitations concerning computation, incompatible experts and small expert counts are retained.

D1.justification: v2 documents SAM2 segmentation, GPT o4-mini captions, character placement, SDEdit noise strength, layout-depth construction, regional rewards and new experiment hyperparameters (Appendices E.3–E.5), plus particle-dependent runtimes. Conversely, v1's detailed GPT-o1-mini text-to-layout recipe and specific video-checkpoint links disappear despite retention of those demonstrations. Reproducibility information changes substantially in both directions.

E1.justification: v2 adds character insertion using 80 background-character combinations from Magic Insert and explicit layout-conditioned generation on 50 MIG-Bench scenes. These expand the evaluated object population and control-input scenarios. The original graphics-engine, object-centric video, PhysGen3D and illustrative text-to-image evaluations remain.

E2.justification: The new character comparison evaluates Magic Insert, Add-it, FLUX-Fill and SDEdit (Table 1), while the layout comparison adds 3DIS-FLUX (Table 3). Original comparators remain. FramePack's appearance in the main text is a relabeling and relocation of the earlier autoregressive comparison, not a new baseline.

E3.justification: v2 introduces character-placement and preprocessing procedures, random selection of 50 of 800 MIG-Bench scenes, GroundingDINO bounding-box mIoU, global/regional VQA evaluation, and particle budgets extending to L=32. It also adds SAM2-based foreground IoU to the retained object-centric video evaluation. These are new evaluation protocols and metrics, rather than merely additional setting disclosures.

E4.justification: v1's conditional-sampling ablation and illustrative composition/particle comparisons are retained. v2 adds systematic quantitative particle scaling and SMC-on/off comparisons at matched particle counts, with runtime measurements (Tables 3 and 4). These directly examine whether intermediate resampling improves results beyond increasing the candidate budget.

E5.justification: v2 retains the mean-plus-minus reporting format but removes v1 Table 1's explicit statement that ± denotes standard deviation, without supplying an equivalent explanation. Neither version reports a repeated-run count or significance-testing protocol; additional result rows do not establish additional independent runs.

E6.justification: All retained numerical entries in Tables 1 and 2 are unchanged. v2 adds character-insertion scores, video foreground IoUs, and layout/SMC results. For example, Table 3 reports mIoU 0.728 and VQAScore 0.904 for L=32 versus 0.673 and 0.800 for 3DIS-FLUX. Table 4 shows semantic benefits from SMC but mixed small-budget mIoU effects. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance gains over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The core sampler in Algorithm 1 is retained. v2 adds a layout-control instantiation using regional FLUX-Depth experts conditioned on 3DIS-generated depth, with summed global and regional VQA rewards (Appendix E.5). This is a bounded procedural adaptation beyond v1's text-only regional composition. The autoregressive construction already existed in v1 Appendix C.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and sampling exposition are extensively rewritten. Implementation details move from the main text into Appendix E.1, autoregressive experiments move into Section 4.2, and the original text-to-image demonstration moves into Appendix D.5. The experimental narrative and appendix organization are substantially restructured.

P2.justification: v2 expands Tables 1 and 2, adds Tables 3 and 4 and character/layout comparison Figures 6 and 8, and redesigns the PhysGen3D gallery. Retained autoregressive and text-to-image figures are relocated and reformatted, while Figures 1 and 3 lose illustrative rows. Document-wide typography, headers and layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through historical product-distribution and MRF/CRF work and contemporary composition methods. Section 2 now specifically distinguishes its per-timestep MCMC approach from the path-wise importance weighting attributed to Skreta et al. and He et al. It also adds literature supporting the new benchmarks and comparators; these changes go beyond citation formatting.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix C.1 corrects the velocity-to-score conversion from v1 Appendix D.1 with an algebraically different expression, changing the schedule-dependent coefficients. The product-distribution definitions, conditional-independence assumption and conditional-sampling argument remain. The endpoint-prediction formula is relocated rather than newly derived.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its text-to-image composition and sampling-efficiency claims mainly through selected examples. v2 adds a 50-scene benchmark, matched particle/resampling controls and runtimes, making those claims substantially more assessable (Tables 3 and 4). The character-insertion comparison broadens validation against relevant methods, and the score-conversion correction improves mathematical accuracy. Lost reproduction details and the missing uncertainty definition are real regressions, but the stronger empirical support provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Product of Experts research. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds character-insertion, MIG-Bench layout-generation and quantitative sampling-ablation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-insertion and video-generation evaluations in Tables 1 and 2, plus text-to-image and autoregressive-video experiments.

results.title: Product of Experts for Visual Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add explicit claims of data efficiency with 25k–50k samples and scalability through 200k samples, extending v1's general fine-tuning-benefit claim. InterSyn, SEIR, and SynJudge remain the same principal contributions.

C2.justification: V2 interprets multi-turn training as improving context retention and reducing later-turn degradation, and presents understanding performance as preserved after fine-tuning. The latter requires qualification because Table 2 contains declines. The existing image-generation ceiling, single-image restrictions, and other appendix limitations remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: New Appendix D.6 explains generation and assignment of the 48,000 judge examples, the annotation period, and the 80/20 split. Table 16 details dataset composition. A reproducibility statement promises code, data, benchmarks, and weights, without establishing their availability. Existing generation models and judge-training hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on MME-P, MMBench, MMMU, and SEEDBench, plus explicit three-turn conversational testing (Tables 2–3). These extend the evaluated task requirements. InterSyn's eight domains and single-turn/multi-turn dataset composition remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The generator comparison expands from 11 to 13 models by adding BAGEL and VARGPT-v1.1; both also enter the fine-tuning study. The Gemini+FLUX comparator is identified as Gemini2.5 instead of Gemini1.5. The five model-based judge comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The generator benchmark expands from 500 to 4,000 questions, and the stated AR/IR evaluation sample changes from 500 to 7,000. V2 adds 25k–200k training-size protocols and fixed-50k single/multi-turn mixtures, and describes mandatory consensus for annotation disagreements. These are reported setting changes; identical retained AR/IR scores do not establish whether that experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds training-size sensitivity, understanding-retention analysis, and controlled dialogue-mixture ablations with turn-wise evaluation (Tables 1–3). Table 16 adds domain-distribution analysis. The earlier AR/IR and alternative-backbone analyses are retained, including the ablation relocated to Appendix D.5.

E5.justification: Both versions report variance across examples, judge score-gap distributions, and seed 42 for judge training. Neither introduces additional repeated-run information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures. The appendix score-gap distributions and one-point agreement values are unchanged.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial scaling, understanding, multi-turn, and new-generator results. Between v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5, Anole's human TCC changes from 2.86 to 3.06 and VILA-U's from 2.25 to 2.45; the revised benchmark prevents interpreting these as same-setting gains. Figure 7 corrects DDiT's TCC/ITS bars. Detailed per-generator RMSE entries are replaced by aggregate reporting.

M1.justification: The QR–AR–IR refinement pipeline, feedback and stopping logic, generation backbones, and SynJudge approach are retained. The generic refinement-operator notation and revised scoring labels do not establish a different algorithm or model.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and reorganized. SynJudge receives a dedicated methodological section, experiments are grouped around dataset utility, SEIR, and evaluator reliability, and the standalone ablation moves into the appendix. Template explanations and reproducibility statements are expanded.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, the fine-tuning table is expanded, and understanding, dialogue-mixture, and domain-distribution tables are added. Generator results switch to compact mean-with-variance cells, judge results become an aggregate table, and existing figures and ablations are repositioned within the conference layout.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for BAGEL, VARGPT-v1.1, Gemini2.5, and the understanding benchmarks, while removing the creative-industries review, SEED-Story, and Intelligent Grimm references. The central positioning against existing interleaved datasets and evaluators remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: V2's condensed SEIR formulation omits the explicit uniform topic and template sampling specifications in v1 Equations 2–3, a limited removal of formal assumptions. The remaining refinement mathematics is largely restated. The A@1 equation formalizes v1's existing one-point-tolerance accuracy definition rather than introducing a new metric.

improvement.justification: V1 claimed multi-turn benefits while validating dataset utility mainly through 50k fine-tuning on two models. V2's controlled dialogue-mixture study and three-turn evaluation directly strengthen that previously weak support, while four-model scaling experiments clarify practical data requirements. Clearer SEIR exposition and judge-data documentation also help. Reduced RMSE detail, unexplained sample-size revisions, and overstrong understanding-retention language remain drawbacks, but the added targeted validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InterSyn, SEIR, and SynJudge research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds data-scaling experiments, understanding-benchmark evaluations, and controlled multi-turn training comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original human evaluations, judge comparisons, SEIR ablations, and fine-tuning results for Anole and VILA-U.

results.title: A High Quality Dataset and Reliable Evaluation for Interleaved Image-Text Generation

C1.justification: The contributions of self-supervised Gaussian modeling, progressive part segmentation, and RS-Art remain. v2 explicitly claims superior consistency under continuous control in the abstract and adds an introduction claim about remaining within Gaussian parameterization without incompatible geometric or physics constraints. These refine the existing contribution claims rather than introduce a different research contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations contrasting generative plausibility with instance-specific reconstruction and explaining the computational cost of deformation-based inference. It also interprets the new component and robustness results. The pose discussion calls degradation slight, although Table 8 shows axis-angle error rising from 0.40 to 10.00 under stronger noise. Appendix E largely retains its limitations, adding diffusion priors as a possible completion direction.

D1.justification: v2 adds training/inference times and explains baseline interpolation timing in Appendix D.6. It documents visibility-threshold tuning but removes the fixed value, and deletes v1's disclosure that ArticulatedGS was reimplemented using official 3DGS and the paper's description. Both versions retain the same promise to release code and datasets upon publication.

E1.justification: The original PartNet-Mobility and RS-Art coverage remains. v2 adds evaluations with five movable parts (Table 6), cluttered real-scene RS-Art captures, and the PARIS real-scene benchmark (Figure 15 and Appendix D.3). These extend articulation complexity and capture conditions beyond v1's evaluations.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparator set remains unchanged. v2 adds D-NeRF, D2NeRF, Dynamic3DGS, 4D-GS, and ArtGS to the quantitative unseen-state comparison (Table 2), NAP and SINGAPO to the generative comparison (Table 9), and SAGD as an evaluated segmentation comparator (Table 14). DTArt also joins the qualitative interpolation comparison in Figure 5.

E3.justification: The four-state, 200-image main protocol already appeared in v1 Appendix C. v2 adds two-state controls across eight categories, PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS interpolation evaluation, Gaussian-noise and COLMAP pose protocols, timing procedures, and best-of-50 input-view selection for SINGAPO. Section 3.4 also replaces tau_vis=1.2 with tuning on one or two representative instances; this reports a setting revision without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original refinement and interaction-state ablations remain unchanged as v2 Tables 11-12. New analyses test VLM prompting alternatives, SAM segmentation against SAGD, and individual pipeline stages (Tables 13-15). Camera-pose robustness, broader two-state controls, and five-part scalability tests substantially expand the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions retain first-run reporting and qualitative assertions about run-to-run variation in Section 5.2. Neither adds repeated-run summaries, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new pose-noise standard deviations describe experimental perturbations, not uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: The numerical results in all six original tables are preserved: v1 Tables 1-6 correspond to v2 Tables 1, 4, 5, 7, 11, and 12. v2 adds substantial new results, including PD2GS's unseen-state PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS of 28.02/0.93/0.09 (Table 2), component-count accuracies of 100% versus 90% and 15% for alternative prompts (Table 13), and robustness, scalability, and timing results. These are newly reported evaluations, not performance gains over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The latent-conditioned Gaussian deformation, loss, trajectory clustering, VLM part counting, SAM prompting, recursive splitting, and mesh/joint estimation procedures remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix A. The renaming and revised visibility-threshold setting do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The title and method name change, and the abstract, introduction, and related work undergo extensive rewriting. Metric explanations and experimental narratives expand, Appendix D is reorganized from three subsections into seven, and terminology and author/header information are revised. Much of the method text and Appendices A-C remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 adds a teaser figure, new interpolation and real-scene comparison figures, and nine new tables. Existing displays are relocated, resized, and selectively trimmed or rearranged. Table 1 drops the Manual column and adds a depth-input clarification, while the conference format substantially reflows the document.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially expand positioning against dynamic rendering and conditional generative articulated models. Added works include D-NeRF, D2NeRF, NAP, SINGAPO, and additional dynamic Gaussian approaches; DGD and several background references disappear. Publication updates to retained works such as ArtGS and ArticulatedGS do not constitute new citations.

T1.justification: Equations 1-15 and Appendix A's projection, splitting, joint-classification rule, and joint-parameter derivations are retained. Changes to latent symbols and terminology are not substantive mathematical revisions; no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v1 supports unseen-state control mainly through qualitative examples. v2 adds quantitative comparisons with dynamic rendering methods (Table 2), broader two-state controls (Table 3), and targeted validation of prompting and segmentation (Tables 13-15), substantially strengthening evidence for central claims. These gains outweigh the limited loss of implementation disclosure and overstated pose-robustness interpretation. First-run reporting without uncertainty remains an unresolved weakness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework, renamed from DeGSS to PD2GS. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A-E support comparison, with clear correspondence between the original methods and experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds original interpolation, camera-pose robustness, five-part modeling, timing, and component-level evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and joint-estimation experiments on PartNet-Mobility and RS-Art, together with refinement and interaction-state ablations in Tables 1-6.

results.title: PD$^{2}$GS: Part-Level Decoupling and Continuous Deformation of Articulated Objects via Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: The abstract replaces the broad description of controllable multi-concept videos with the more specific capability of two-to-three-person dialogue generation or customization from multiple reference images. The main contributions and conclusion otherwise retain the same claims about layout-aligned conditioning and generation quality.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations linking cache removal to identity-assignment degradation and larger-person-count scalability to independent mask prediction. It also identifies overlapping subjects and coarse VAE resolution as sources of mask failure. Appendix A.4 somewhat overstates combined-mask superiority: layer 20 has higher final-step IoU in both Tables 9 and 10.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly specifies sliding-window continuation, the SAM2 confidence threshold of 0.5, focal-loss parameters, and the audio attention window. v2 also documents model overhead and reports providing a Wan2.1 reimplementation and data-processing code. Data provenance changes from an unspecified internal source to OpenHumanVid plus self-collected videos, without establishing that the underlying training corpus was replaced.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original evaluation coverage and adds single-person talking-head evaluations on CelebV-HQ and RAVDESS, explicit low/high-motion scenarios, and four-to-five-person generation tests (Tables 6–7 and 9–13). These substantially broaden the evaluated populations and operating conditions.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds MultiTalk to the existing multi-person comparison. New Tables 6–7 evaluate SadTalker, Hallo, VExpress, EchoMimic, Hallo-3, and Loopy alongside OmniHuman. HunyuanVideo-Avatar appears only in the capability matrix, rather than a reported generation benchmark.

E3.justification: The original protocols are retained, while new experiments introduce FID for talking-head evaluation, mask IoU across selected denoising steps and layers under two motion regimes, and cached-versus-uncached testing. Runtime is measured per forward pass at 720p and 109 frames on one A100 while varying reference count (Section 4.2 and Appendix A).

E4.justification: Beyond the unchanged global-audio, ID-embedding, and fixed-mask ablation, v2 tests mask refinement across steps and layers, sensitivity to motion, cache necessity, scaling beyond three people, and computational overhead. Figure 5 adds an overlapping-subject mask-failure case. These directly investigate previously untested aspects of the central mechanism.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new keypoint-motion variances in Table 11 describe motion regimes, rather than uncertainty in model performance.

E6.justification: Existing result entries in Tables 1–4 remain numerically unchanged. v2 adds MultiTalk results, including Sync-D 7.671 and FVD 35.472, and substantial new benchmark, runtime, mask-IoU, and scaling results. Table 12 reports Sync-D 6.921 with caching versus 11.046 without caching; these are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1's model.
