M1.justification: The reference-image injection, mask predictor, cached-mask audio conditioning, training objectives, and inference procedure remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. Appendix C newly documents implementation choices and long-video generation without establishing a change to the underlying method.

P1.justification: v2 polishes introduction and method prose, folds reference-image injection into the preliminaries, and reorganizes the appendices around a new experimental-results section. It also updates authorship and conference front matter and adds disclosure statements. The overall narrative and most existing passages remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–13 and a new mask-failure Figure 5, substantially expanding the experimental displays. The original Figure 5 is retained as Figure 6, Table 1 gains a comparator row, and the document adopts conference formatting with revised table sizing and placement.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ingredients, OpenHumanVid, HunyuanVideo-Avatar, and MultiTalk references. Section 2 distinguishes Ingredients' layout prediction from audio-conditioned generation, while Appendix A.3 and Table 8 position InterActHuman against concurrent multi-person systems. The broader literature review and positioning remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 adds a short analytical cost-scaling argument: increasing latent count from 28 to 28+n yields relative self-attention cost (1+n/28)^2. The existing flow-matching formulation, mask equations, and algorithmic mathematics are unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central cached-mask mechanism through direct mask-IoU measurements, a cache ablation, motion and population-scaling tests, and an explicit failure analysis. These address important gaps left by v1's alternative-conditioning comparisons, while added implementation details improve reproducibility. Missing uncertainty estimates and some overstated mask-refinement interpretations remain limitations, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InterActHuman. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across the revision, including relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds talking-head benchmarks, runtime measurements, mask analyses, a cache ablation, and evaluations with four to five people.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation benchmarks, user-study outcomes, and conditioning ablations in Tables 1–4 and Figures 3–5.

results.title: InterActHuman: Multi-Concept Human Animation with Layout-Aligned Audio Conditions

C1.justification: The first-framework claim, two complementary strategies and black-box copyright-tracing contribution remain. v2 explicitly extends the introduction’s robustness claim from common image transformations to regeneration attacks and broadens the stated experimental contribution beyond the original four named VLMs.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of filtering versus false-positive costs, watermark suppression versus utility loss, model scaling, deployment drift and provider collisions. It also explains dataset-specific reference calibration. Conversely, v1 Section 6’s explicit limitation about watermark quality increasing verification queries and its discussion of extensions beyond T2T are removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds filter prompts, caption templates, reference-calibration instructions, attack-training data composition and detailed LoRA/NEFTune hyperparameters in Table 13. It adds a supplemental-code availability statement while retaining the repository link. The original A40 GPU and CPU specifications disappear.

E1.justification: MMQA and WebQA remain the primary datasets. v2 additionally uses COCO and Alpaca-GPT4 samples for adversarial fine-tuning and evaluates substantially broader environments: VLM filtering, image regeneration, refusal-trained generators and MMQA corpora expanded with WebQA distractors.

E2.justification: Naive and Opt. remain the evaluated watermarking baselines. Their participation is unchanged in Table 1 and the retained diagnostic plots; v2 also includes both in the added Z-test comparison in Table 9.

E3.justification: v2 adds 2B–38B generator configurations, batch and single-image filtering protocols, adversarial fine-tuning with a 2,000-question utility evaluation, and retriever replacement/fine-tuning. Its image-attack evaluation uses WAVES strength 1 with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Rank/CGSR reporting, replacing the earlier specified transformation experiments and Rank/p-value reporting.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained PCA, relevant-query and watermark-count analyses, v2 adds adaptive filtering, regeneration and repeated-diffusion attacks, model-scale analysis, refusal and fine-tuning tests, retriever updates and corpus drift. The earlier four-generator transformation supplement is removed. These changes substantially broaden the robustness questions investigated.

E5.justification: v2 adds two-proportion Z-test results in Table 9 and system/dataset-specific reference means and variances in Table 8. It also reports five independent runs for the new basic filtering experiment and explains conservative reference-variance broadening. Both versions retain ten repetitions for the main effectiveness experiment; no increase there is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 is unchanged, but extensive new results cover filtering, model scales, attacks and deployment variations. Table 12 reports 100% acronym detection by stringent OCR filtering with 61.44–72.02% FPR. The new fine-tuning study reports utility falling from 27.25% to 24.90%. Acronym-replacement ranks change from 5.00 in v1 Table 7 to 10.00 in v2 Table 11; the old transformation p-values are removed.

M1.justification: The core acronym/OCR and spatial watermark procedures remain. Appendix A.4 adds an explicitly optional caption pipeline combining low-co-occurrence concepts with perplexity filtering, and Appendix B.2 proposes a centralized trigger registry. These extend the framework; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments used these extensions.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental prose are extensively rewritten, including correction of 'exact match' to 'substring match.' The standalone Discussion is removed, deployment material moves into an expanded appendix, and supplementary experiments are reorganized. Ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different conference layout, reformats tables and prompt boxes, merges v1 Figures 4–5 into v2 Figure 4, and relocates the unchanged watermark-count plot to the appendix. It adds numerous experimental tables and a 30-image gallery, and replaces several acronym examples with natural-scene variants.

R1.justification: v2 adds supporting references for WAVES, LoRA, NEFTune, SigLIP, newer VLMs and Xu et al.’s watermark verification work, while pruning several text-only RAG and future-work citations. Its substantive positioning relative to WARD, RAG-WM, RAG© and DMI-RAG remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1 newly states and argues statistical assumptions concerning unequal variances, normality and independence for the verification tests. This adds limited mathematical reasoning, without formal proofs. The numbered retrieval, verification, metric and optimization equations retain their substance apart from notation clarifications.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central security claims: v1 relied largely on PCA and simple transformations, whereas v2 measures adaptive filtering, regeneration, fine-tuning and deployment drift, including effects on benign data and QA utility. Added implementation details and the corrected rank inconsistency improve auditability. These gains outweigh the loss of the explicit limitations discussion and earlier cross-generator transformation results, although the added arguments that repetitions and retrieval separation establish statistical assumptions remain insufficiently justified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AQUA, with matching authors, core methods and original experiments. All 18 pages of v1 and 29 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and reports additional filtering, regeneration, fine-tuning, model-scale and deployment-drift results.

before.justification: v1 reports original watermark detection experiments on MMQA and WebQA, including effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness and image-transformation results.

results.title: Safeguarding Multimodal Knowledge Copyright in the RAG-as-a-Service Environment

C1.justification: The central claim that structured reasoning and reward optimization improve motion generation is retained. v4 adds specific leadership claims for KIT-ML retrieval/FID and BABEL, and changes the headline HumanML3D comparison to a 3.5% MM-Dist advantage already supported by the unchanged numbers. Renaming the method components does not itself introduce a new scientific contribution.

C2.justification: v4 corrects the HumanML3D Top-1 discussion from being on par with the best to near-top performance: Motion-R1 remains at 0.515 versus MoMask's 0.521. It adds a qualified KIT-ML tradeoff discussion acknowledging non-leading MM-Dist and interprets BABEL results as supporting complex-activity generalization. The limitations concerning noisy LLM plans and reward design are retained in Appendix A.6.

D1.justification: Appendices A.3–A.4 supply three prompt templates, metric sampling details, SFT batch size and learning rate, GRPO group size and coefficients, and compute costs: eight H20 GPUs, approximately two hours for SFT and four for RL. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. Conversely, v1's DeepSeek API version 250120 is omitted, and code availability remains a future promise.

E1.justification: v4 adds evaluation on BABEL's long, multi-label activity data, substantially extending the represented evaluation scenarios beyond HumanML3D and KIT-ML. KIT-ML was already explicitly evaluated in v1; its newly supplied quantitative table is additional evidence rather than new dataset coverage. The OOD examples are retained.

E2.justification: The HumanML3D comparator set is unchanged. v4 adds reported comparisons with AttT2M on KIT-ML and with TEACH, DoubleTake, DiffCollage and InfiniDreamer on BABEL, substantially expanding the comparison methods. TEACH was previously only cited; the newly discussed MotionCritic is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The added BABEL evaluation follows the separately cited InfiniDreamer setup and reports a single R-Precision column, FID, MM-Dist and Diversity, rather than the seven-column HumanML3D/KIT-ML panel. Changes to existing splits, backbone or training settings are not established. Appendix A.4 mainly discloses previously unspecified settings.

E4.justification: Table 2 retains the same seven component configurations and results. The circle-walking, noise-reaction and badminton comparisons are unchanged. Appendix A.2's purported additional visualizations reproduce v1 Figure 1 as v4 Figure 4. The BABEL table adds benchmark evidence, not a new ablation or robustness analysis.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports 20 evaluations except five for MModality. v4 retains 20-evaluation and 95% confidence-interval statements but omits the MModality exception, including in Appendix A.4.3's general 20-trial account. This changes repetition reporting without establishing that additional evaluations were performed.

E6.justification: All HumanML3D benchmark and ablation result entries are unchanged. v4 newly reports KIT-ML results, including Motion-R1 R-Precision@1 of 0.431 and FID of 0.287, and BABEL results including R-Precision of 0.536, FID of 0.53, MM-Dist of 6.16 and Diversity of 8.90. These substantially expand the reported evidence rather than demonstrate improvement over v1 under matched settings.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same VQ-VAE tokenizer, Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct backbone, LLM-generated action decomposition, supervised cold start and GRPO with format, motion-similarity and semantic-similarity rewards. 'Decomposed CoT Data Engine' and 'RL Binding' reframe existing components; the newly disclosed prompts and hyperparameters do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and contribution list are extensively rewritten around two named components. Framework and experimental discussions are revised or condensed, implementation details are merged into experimental settings, and limitations move to the appendix. Ethics, reproducibility and appendix sections are added, alongside document-wide terminology and citation-style changes.

P2.justification: v4 introduces a conceptual comparison diagram as Figure 1, combines v1's pipeline and Tai-chi example into Figure 2, and relocates the original OOD illustration to the appendix. Table 1 becomes a larger two-dataset display, Table 3 adds BABEL, and existing tables are reformatted. Headers, typography and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v4 develops a substantial additional motivation around MotionRL and newly cited MotionCritic being complex and annotation-dependent, positioning RL Binding as a simpler alternative. It drops v1's assertion that the relevant RL approach remained unexplored for 3D motion. References also expand to BABEL, long-motion comparators and recent motion-generation methods while removing several peripheral gesture and 3D-generation citations.

T1.justification: The tokenizer, loss, GRPO objective, normalized advantage and reward mathematics are unchanged. Appendix A.4 adds explanatory formulas for existing FID and Diversity metrics, not new theoretical results. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 closes important evidence and documentation gaps: KIT-ML claims gain quantitative support, BABEL broadens empirical validation, and actual prompts, hyperparameters and compute costs replace references to supplementary details absent from v1. These substantially improve assessability and reproducibility of the retained method. Reporting remains imperfect: the new MM-Dist description calls it cosine similarity despite values above one and lower-is-better rankings, and the MModality repetition exception disappears. Those defects do not outweigh the substantial evidence and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Motion-R1 and support reliable comparison of their text, equations, tables and figures. All 12 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v4 were inspected, including v4's appendix. The supplied v1 contains no appendix, although it references supplementary material.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds quantitative KIT-ML and BABEL comparisons in Table 1 and Appendix A.5, Table 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original HumanML3D benchmark results, component ablations and qualitative motion-generation comparisons in Tables 1–2 and Figures 1 and 4.

results.title: Motion-R1: Enhancing Motion Generation with Decomposed Chain-of-Thought and RL Binding

C1.justification: Both versions claim the same three principles, two-stage sampler, caching compatibility, headline speedups, and throughput advantage over LLaMA3 8B. v3 explicitly associates the 15.63× and 34.22× maxima with GPQA, clarifying the demonstration already identified in v1.

C2.justification: Appendices A.4 and A.6 add interpretations that unified hyperparameters transfer without extensive tuning and that dynamic scheduling handles separated stable blocks, including induced extreme cases. These extend the applicability discussion beyond v1's existing confidence and locality explanations.

D1.justification: Tables 5–6 newly provide benchmark-specific inference steps, generation lengths, few-shot counts, and LLaDA block lengths. Algorithm 1 supplies pseudocode, and the reproducibility statement reports supplementary experiment scripts. This substantially expands documentation beyond v1's hardware and sampler-parameter descriptions; the repository link is retained.

E1.justification: The same eight benchmark datasets remain. Appendix A.6 adds a targeted artificial test scenario involving manually induced, widely separated high-confidence blocks, extending the tested decoding conditions.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add Fast-dLLM's parallel and parallel-plus-cache variants as direct competitors across both models and all eight benchmarks. This substantially strengthens the comparator set beyond v1's vanilla models and basic sampling strategies; the existing Tables 3–4 comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v3 extends the experimental design with cache-enabled Dream evaluations and a controlled positional-jump intervention. Appendix A.3 newly documents benchmark-specific settings; this disclosure does not establish changes or reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 extends sensitivity analysis to MATH, MBPP, HumanEval, and Dream on GSM8K, and adds sentence-generation and non-contiguous-block case studies. These substantially expand tests of parameter transfer and positional robustness. v1's confidence-threshold study is retained as Appendix Figure 6.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and sensitivity curves without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The endpoint variance used by the algorithm is not uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive Fast-dLLM, cached Dream, and sensitivity results. Table 1 revises Dream HumanEval scores from 54.26/52.43 to 34.15/35.36 for vanilla/SlowFast, without explaining the cause; these are revised results, not established same-setting gains. Table 2 also corrects the LLaDA GSM8K cached speedup from 5.83× to 5.93×.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 retains the same exploratory top-k decoding, endpoint stability check, confidence-based parallel decoding, fallback refinement, and caching components. Appendix Algorithm 1 adds procedural documentation without establishing a revised method.

P1.justification: The main section order and most methodological prose remain intact. v3 shortens introductory explanations, edits captions and terminology, updates authors and headers, moves the confidence-threshold discussion into the appendix, and adds reproducibility, ethics, and appendix sections.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 are substantially expanded, Figures 1–2 are redrawn, and v3 adds case-study visualizations, sensitivity plots, settings tables, and an algorithm listing. The original threshold plot is relocated and renumbered; Figure 9 additionally redisplays existing GPQA results as a trade-off plot.

R1.justification: v3 adds Fast-dLLM, Sparse-dLLM, dKV-Cache, GtR, and a video-generation survey to its citations and discussion. It distinguishes SlowFast from confidence-only parallel decoding while retaining the existing research positioning around dynamic sampling and caching.

T1.justification: Equations 1–10 and the mathematical description of sampling remain unchanged. The three principles remain empirical observations, and v3 adds no theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important weaknesses in v1's competitive evaluation and reproducibility documentation. Direct Fast-dLLM comparisons, broader robustness tests, and benchmark-specific settings substantially improve the evidence supporting the efficiency claims and readers' ability to assess them. Unexplained Dream HumanEval revisions and the continued absence of uncertainty estimates remain limitations, but the overall gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SlowFast Sampling work, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends with references; v3 adds Appendix A.1–A.7. The complete supplied material supports comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds Fast-dLLM comparisons, cached Dream results, sensitivity studies, and decoding case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original throughput and task-performance experiments on LLaDA and Dream, sampling comparisons, and hyperparameter sensitivity studies.

results.title: Accelerating Diffusion Large Language Models with SlowFast Sampling: The Three Golden Principles

C1.justification: The central claims about joint generation-verification optimization and reasoning beyond the training horizon remain. V2 adds the explicit claim that ReVeal widens verification-generation asymmetry, conditions its general applicability on that asymmetry, and removes the headline claim of surpassing DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B.

C2.justification: V2 adds an asymmetry-based mechanism explanation and discusses how stronger code and tests reinforce each other. It also explains Figure 4's early accuracy dip through expanding format-valid evaluation coverage and qualifies critic comparisons by benchmark period. These refine the retained co-evolution and feedback-guided exploration interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the three-turn memory window and retained interaction contents, clarifies the critic results' source period, and documents format-dependent diagnostic coverage. Evaluation hyperparameter entries are revised. Hardware, training software, TACO preprocessing, prompt and feedback templates, and the promise of future project release remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates LiveCodeBench problems from August 2024–January 2025. V2 substantially expands evaluation coverage with CodeContests and LiveCodeBench V6 from February–May 2025, while retaining V5 Qwen evaluations in the appendices. TACO training coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: V2 adds an evaluated prompt-only ReVeal comparator without RL training (Table 9) and removes DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B from the reported comparisons. The base models, single-turn RL and Qwen2.5-Coder, GPT-4o and CTRL critic comparators remain.

E3.justification: Reported DAPO evaluation settings change from 51,200 to 32,768 maximum response tokens and from Pass@1 temperature 0.2/0.6 to 0.6 (v1 Table 4; v2 Table 3). Main evaluation budgets change from 6/19 to 8/25 turns, and Pass@k switches from Qwen with six turns to DAPO with ten. These are substantial protocol revisions; the training hyperparameter tables remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 extends reward ablations to DAPO on both main benchmarks and adds verification-accuracy training curves (Table 1, Figure 4). Appendix C tests truncated versus complete history, while Appendix E compares trained and untrained ReVeal using identical prompts and tools across one, three and six turns. These add substantive controls beyond v1's reward and scaling analyses.

E5.justification: V2 first reports eight repeated experiments and mean ± standard deviation for the Qwen reward comparison: 37.09 ± 0.33 versus 38.02 ± 0.31 (Table 8). V1 reports rollout counts without comparable variability estimates. V2 does not clarify whether training or evaluation is repeated, or specify a formal significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: V1's headline 42.4% after 19 turns on older LiveCodeBench is replaced by 38.7% on V6 and 33.6% on CodeContests after 25 turns; these are different-condition results, not a demonstrated performance decline. The retained Qwen outcome-only result changes from 37.5% to 37.1%, critic entries are revised, and new memory, prompt-only, repeated-experiment and DAPO diagnostic results are reported.

M1.justification: V2 introduces a short-term memory component retaining only the last three turns during inference, with a full-history comparison in Appendix C. The generation-verification loop, test filtering, rewards and credit-assignment equations remain equivalent; renaming TA-PPO to TAPO does not establish a new optimization algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial portions of the methods and analysis are rewritten around reliable self-verification. TA-PPO becomes TAPO, the main narrative focuses on DAPO, and the worked example and Qwen analyses move into a substantially reorganized appendix structure.

P2.justification: V2 adds the asymmetry schematic, redraws the framework with memory, introduces DAPO diagnostic plots, expands the main table to two benchmarks, and adds uncertainty and prompt-only tables. The worked example and Qwen displays move to the appendices; the Qwen last-turn training plot is extended, and table styling and page layout change extensively.

R1.justification: V2 adds Wei and Setlur for verification asymmetry and test-time scaling, discusses ReAct and Reflexion, and describes ReVeal as complementary to other tool-augmented approaches. It also adds the AlphaCode/CodeContests citation and removes the Qwen technical report and SRPO references. Most prior RL and self-verification positioning remains.

T1.justification: The reward definitions, GAE expression, token and turn return recurrences, and advantage construction match after renumbering (v1 Equations 1–9; v2 Equations 1–8). The new verification-generation asymmetry discussion is conceptual, without new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support by adding CodeContests and newer LiveCodeBench evaluations and a matched prompt/tool control that addresses whether prompting and tool access alone explain the gains. Memory ablation and repeated-experiment variability further improve assessment. These benefits outweigh remaining weaknesses: critic comparisons still mix benchmark periods, and the claimed statistical significance lacks a specified test.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReVeal research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite retitling, reorganization and expanded experiments.

after.justification: V2 reports original LiveCodeBench and CodeContests results, training diagnostics, and memory, repeated-experiment and prompt-only comparisons in the main text and Appendices C–E.

before.justification: V1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments, LiveCodeBench evaluations, reward ablations and training analyses in Table 2 and Figures 1 and 3.

results.title: ReVeal: Self-Evolving Code Agents via Reliable Self-Verification

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: aligned pose-free image/geometry synthesis through attention instillation and mesh conditioning, strong extrapolation, competitive interpolation and generalization. Rewording and additional supporting evaluations do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v3 refines the explanation of complementary image/geometry attention, qualifies that positional extrapolation may expose unseen regions, and adds interpretations concerning predictor-independent alignment and the geometry-versus-speed trade-off (Appendix A.2 and B.5). It removes the provisional depth-accuracy discussion. These extend the retained mechanism account rather than replace it.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.2 reports A6000 hardware, 9.81-second/28GB joint two-view generation and 4.3-second/14GB image-only operation. Most training and implementation details match v1. The abstract replaces the project-page link with a statement that code and weights will be publicly released, changing the documented access information without establishing an actual release.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual qualitative evaluation on NAVI and on previously untrained Cityscapes and MegaDepth data (Appendix B.1 and B.3). This substantially broadens evaluation to urban and in-the-wild scenes. The original training datasets and DTU, RealEstate10K and Co3D evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Figure 7 expands the LVSM comparison to include VGGT, ZeroNVS and both 16-frame and 25-frame ViewCrafter configurations. New Table 7 evaluates ViewCrafter and LVSM quantitatively on DTU. v1's dedicated LucidDreamer/GenWarp appendix comparison figure is removed, although both methods remain in Table 1.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs introduce Gaussian point perturbations at 3–15%, random masking at 30/50/80%, alternative geometry predictions from DepthAnything V3, runtime/memory measurements and a 1–7-reference-view Co3D sweep. The stated extrapolation definition also changes to camera positions only. Original training settings and described DTU/RealEstate10K view-sampling procedures remain; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds controlled geometry-noise and sparsity tests, greater-than-90-degree occlusion/shading examples, and cross-predictor alignment validation (Section 4.4; Appendix B.2, B.4–B.5). It adds a 1–7-view Co3D analysis alongside retained Table 4. Existing component and normalization ablations remain, while the provisional depth-accuracy comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for the experimental results. v3's Gaussian standard deviations specify input perturbations, not statistical uncertainty in measured performance.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical entries. New Table 7 reports DTU PSNR of 14.04 for ViewCrafter versus 15.56 for MoAI with one view, and 15.23 for LVSM versus 15.58 for MoAI with two views. Tables 5–6 add perturbation results, and Table 8 reports Co3D PSNR increasing from 14.62 to 23.45 across 1–7 views. New qualitative and runtime findings are also reported. v1's provisional depth-comparison Table 5 is removed; these changes do not demonstrate improved same-setting performance between versions.

M1.justification: The dual diffusion branches, aggregated attention, image-to-geometry attention instillation, mesh conditioning and camera-space normalization are retained. Equations (1)–(8) change notation rather than procedure. The newly described image-only operation and alternative-predictor evaluation do not establish a revision to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, mechanism explanations and results prose undergo broad rewriting and condensation. Related-work subsections become run-in headings, references move before the appendices, and appendix material is reorganized. A new Appendix C discloses LLM writing assistance. These constitute substantial editorial and structural revision beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 7 is rebuilt as a larger comparison with timing annotations; new figures and tables display robustness, domain, alignment and baseline evaluations. The reference-view illustration moves to Appendix Figure 18 and expands to 1–7 views. Existing normalization, component-ablation and scene-completion material is retained or rearranged, while v1 Figure 12 and its provisional depth table disappear. Typography, captions and table layouts also change throughout.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to ZeroNVS, ViewCrafter, DepthAnything 3, NAVI, Cityscapes and MegaDepth, with limited expansion of its positioning against large generative models. The broader relationship to feedforward, generative and warping-and-inpainting approaches remains unchanged. The switch to author-year citations is stylistic.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 replaces v1's convex-combination definition over SE(3) camera poses with a convex hull of camera positions, explicitly ignoring viewing direction. This substantively corrects and narrows the mathematical definition of extrapolation. The method equations otherwise remain equivalent, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical assessment of the unchanged method: modern baseline comparisons, controlled geometry-corruption tests and broader domain/predictor evaluations address important gaps in v1's evidence for competitiveness and robustness. Computational reporting and the corrected extrapolation definition also improve assessability. Trade-offs remain: the provisional depth comparison is removed without an equivalent quantitative replacement, and claims of minimal degradation overstate Tables 5–6, including a PSNR decline from 15.580 to 13.000 at 80% masking. Nevertheless, the added comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoAI framework and retain matching method equations and core experiments. Text, tables, figures and appendices support a reliable comparison. v1's explicitly unfinished depth-results table is a manuscript limitation, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds quantitative robustness tests, large-model comparisons and reference-view-count results, plus new qualitative evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative novel-view synthesis experiments, component ablations and geometry evaluations in Tables 1–4, alongside qualitative results in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Aligned Novel View Image and Geometry Synthesis via Cross-modal Attention Instillation

C1.justification: The central claims of the first action-level attack against TO models, low poisoning budget, and applicability to DT/GDT/DC remain. v2 explicitly adds a novel post-training attack paradigm to its contributions and emphasizes the computational impracticality of training-time attacks on larger models.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for defense failures, including destructive subspace projection and activation variation across input types masking trigger effects. It interprets repeated triggers as enabling policy-level disruption and explains the joint loss's role. The previous defense-research limitation is replaced by a limitation concerning image observations and physically plausible triggers; residual effects after fine-tuning are also discussed.

D1.justification: v2 documents defense implementations and explains that collection of ten attack trajectories is simulated by sampling the supplied dataset. It adds a supplementary-code statement, revises experiment-count accounting from 972 to 540, and removes the 3–8-hour training-time estimate. Core hyperparameters, hardware types, and the repository URL remain.

E1.justification: The same six D4RL datasets and task domains remain. Appendix E adds long-term return manipulation under periodic and sustained trigger activation, extending the tested scenario beyond the retained experiments on action persistence following a single trigger.

E2.justification: Baffle and IMC remain the main attack comparators. v2 adds an evaluated defense suite comprising activation-based and magnitude-based pruning, provable subspace defense, spectral analysis, activation clustering, and clean fine-tuning (Section 6.5 and Appendix B.1). These methods were not experimentally compared in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include pruning-rate and projection-dimension sweeps, detection thresholds, clean fine-tuning, trigger-interval/length tests, and a single-objective control. Appendix C.2 also introduces BTP clipping to [0,1], whereas v1 states an unclipped ratio. Some retained appendix values contradict this rule; the PDFs do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive defense analyses, an activation t-SNE visualization, repeated-trigger analysis of long-term damage, and a joint-versus-single-objective ablation in Appendix J.1. The earlier component, poisoning-budget, alternating-frequency, persistent-attack, and trigger-noise analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: The main experiments retain three-seed averaging and existing uncertainty displays. New Table 15 reports averages over five seeds, while Appendix B.1 explicitly restricts defense experiments to fixed seed 1. These are reporting practices for added experiments, not evidence of increased repetitions for retained results.

E6.justification: v2 adds defense outcomes, raw returns, activation-pattern results, and loss-ablation scores. For example, Table 18 reports ASR 0.474 for single-objective versus 0.667 for joint optimization. Main average ASR/BTP/CP remains 0.719/0.914/0.701. Table 4 changes TrojanTO's GDT/Walk BTP from 1.089 to 1.000, although Appendix Table 23 retains 1.089.

M1.justification: Trajectory filtering, single-transition batch poisoning, alternating trigger/model optimization, losses, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The post-training framing and new loss-formulation ablation clarify and evaluate the existing procedure rather than introduce a new TrojanTO component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, threat model, and attack explanations are substantially rewritten. Related work moves from near the conclusion to Section 2 and Appendix A; limitations and ethics are reorganized into Appendix B. A reproducibility statement and expanded explanatory sections materially change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds defense tables, raw-return and trigger-activation tables, a loss-formulation table, and t-SNE Figure 3. Existing plots and tables are retained with relocation, resizing, and revised highlighting. The conference template also changes headings, headers, typography, and page layout throughout.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A.1 substantially reposition TrojanTO within post-training and model-supply-chain attacks, distinguishing it from Baffle and training-loop poisoning. New citations cover weight poisoning, handcrafted backdoors, supply-chain security, defenses, and recent RL attacks. Existing material on other RL threats is largely relocated to Appendix A.2.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the RTG definition and indexing, replacing v1's target-return subtraction through the current reward with a future-reward sum and an explicit evaluation recurrence. v2 also specifies L2 distance and adds bounded BTP through clipping. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves mitigation largely as future work; v2 supplies direct evidence about defense effectiveness and benign-performance costs. Table 11 shows fine-tuning reducing ASR from 1.000 to 0.040 while BTP changes from 0.964 to 0.917. Repeated-trigger tests and the loss ablation further strengthen the security assessment and methodological support. These are substantial gains, although single-seed defenses and inconsistent application of BTP clipping limit the expanded conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TrojanTO work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the algorithms, experiments, tables, and figures can be matched despite reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds defense evaluations, repeated-trigger experiments, raw model returns, and a loss-formulation ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original D4RL attack experiments, baseline comparisons, component ablations, and persistent-attack and trigger-perturbation results.

results.title: TrojanTO: Action-Level Backdoor Attacks Against Trajectory Optimization Models

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims of training-free block-wise caching, optimal ACS scheduling, BUA-based error-propagation mitigation, and approximately threefold acceleration without performance degradation. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion preserve their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking FFN amplification to larger weight norms, physical failures to observation-action desynchronization, and DDIM results to complementary acceleration. It also interprets the new cache-behavior and homogeneity evidence. The limitations discussion retains weak-base-model accuracy but removes v1's explicit caveat about lacking real-world VLA experiments.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the physical robot, camera, and real-world n=3 setting, adds a project-page address, and states an intention to release implementation instructions. Existing checkpoint links remain. However, fast/fastest comparator labels replace explicit Uniform update budgets without equivalent configuration details.

E1.justification: v2 adds physical manipulation of a deformable bag using a Franka Research 3 arm and four ManiSkill tasks evaluated with RDT-1B. These substantially extend the earlier simulation coverage, while retaining Robomimic, Push-T, Block Pushing, and Kitchen.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares BAC with full-computation DP-T and Uniform caching. v2 adds evaluated TeaCache comparisons in Table 1 and DDIM comparisons in the physical experiment and Appendix A.16, substantially broadening the acceleration methods considered.

E3.justification: Table 1 replaces Uniform's explicit S=7/10 configurations with fast/fastest configurations having different reported FLOPs. New protocols include physical inference-frequency and latency measurements, DDIM with K=40 and BAC S=3/5/10 at n=3, and homogeneity analysis using 50 episodes per task across eight layers and ten timesteps.

E4.justification: v2 adds physical failure-case analysis, FFN-versus-attention weight-norm analysis, detailed cached-versus-ground-truth feature comparisons, expanded episode-homogeneity analysis, and DDIM compatibility tests. The earlier component, hyperparameter, similarity-metric, and error-propagation studies are largely retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.15 and Table 29 newly report inter-episode similarity standard deviations and fifth/ninety-fifth percentiles. This adds statistical characterization of feature variability; the original benchmark practice of averaging across three training seeds remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Original BAC entries in Table 1 remain unchanged, but v2 adds TeaCache results, replaces Uniform configuration results, and reports physical-robot, RDT-1B, homogeneity, and DDIM-plus-BAC outcomes. For example, the new physical experiment reports BAC achieving 71% success at 39.2 Hz. These are added or differently configured results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The cosine-similarity-based ACS optimization, dynamic programming solver, upstream-block selection, and BUA schedule union remain unchanged. Renaming k to n and applying BAC to additional models and samplers do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains recognizable. v2 condenses and relocates VLA background, moves and shortens limitations, reorganizes experiments into physical and simulation subsections, and adds ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements. It also changes k to n and updates authorship and conference formatting.

P2.justification: v2 splits the original framework figure, expands the main comparison table, replaces the detailed component-ablation table with a bar chart, and adds physical-robot, VLA, weight-norm, cache-feature, and homogeneity displays. These substantially change the visual presentation beyond renumbering and pagination.

R1.justification: v2 adds RDT-1B as a cited model and discusses compatibility with sampling-based acceleration. Most prior-work positioning is retained or relocated. TeaCache's underlying paper was already cited in v1, so its evaluation is not a newly introduced literature connection.

T1.justification: The ACS mathematical formulation, FFN perturbation propositions, regularity assumptions, and first-order derivation are retained. The proof moves from Appendix A.1 to A.4 without substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: Physical-robot validation, simulated VLA evaluation, additional acceleration baselines, and DDIM compatibility tests substantially address gaps in v1's practical and generalization evidence. Reporting weaknesses remain: new protocols are incompletely specified, the RDT-1B paragraph disagrees with Figure 7a about the lossless setting, and Table 29's Push-T mean of 0.9285 contradicts the claimed minimum of 0.96. These issues limit particular conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BAC research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds physical-robot experiments, RDT-1B evaluations, and further diagnostic and sampler-compatibility experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original robotic simulation evaluations, component ablations, caching-error experiments, and appendix sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Block-wise Adaptive Caching for Accelerating Diffusion Policy

C1.justification: The central bottleneck diagnosis, external-prefix contribution, and claimed average few-shot advantages remain. C2.justification: V3 connects its design to prompt-memory capacity limits and adds discussion of trainable-map initialization and stability. Appendix E explicitly qualifies extrapolation from 3B–7B downstream evaluations to larger models; the 72B experiment measures latency. D1.justification: V3 documents a code-repository address, explicitly states feature-map and memory dimensions, and supplies parameter counts in Table 8. E6.justification: The original classification, alignment, and CKA values are retained. V3 adds LoRA+, feature-map, rank, math, and efficiency results. P2.justification: V3 adds an architecture diagram, six new tables, and LoRA+ columns in Table 1. The original attention map moves from main-text Figure 2 to appendix Figure 10. Retained plots and tables are rearranged within a new conference layout, substantially changing the visual organization.

T1.justification: V3 omits v1's explicit ICL definition and Equation 9 describing an optional normalized memory term kept inside attention. The central prefix decomposition, kernel construction, and appendix covariance/CKA mathematics remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the practical case through open-ended math evaluation, a stronger LoRA+ comparison, feature-map and parameter-budget controls, and measured computational costs—important evidence missing from v1's proof of concept. These gains outweigh documentation weaknesses: Table 2 reports MLP results while surrounding text leaves MLPs to future work, Appendix A.4 overstates a monotonic rank–accuracy trend, and uncertainty reporting remains absent. The improvement is primarily in empirical support and research positioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, renamed from Prefix-Tuning+ to PrefixMemory-Tuning. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated diagnostics and retained results.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds math-reasoning results, feature-map and LoRA-rank comparisons, and computational-efficiency measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification, out-of-distribution generalization, representation-analysis, and preference-alignment experiments.

results.title: PrefixMemory-Tuning: Modernizing Prefix-Tuning by Decoupling the Prefix from Attention

C1.justification: The central claims remain automated, inexpensive generation of diverse computer-use tasks, controllable difficulty through subtask composition, and challenging agent evaluation. The three introduction contributions and central conclusion are retained; new experiments strengthen their support without redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning verifier reliability, partial-credit scoring, scaffolding, generation/evaluation asymmetry, and robustness to generator choice. It also links difficulty to memory and cross-application coordination. Conversely, it removes substantive discussion of intrinsic difficulty versus unfamiliarity, the coverage consequences of excluding authentication, and untested downstream training utility.

D1.justification: A new reproducibility statement describes supplementary anonymized code and a minimal dataset, while promising full public release after review. This conflicts with the retained abstract's availability statement; actual access cannot be established from the PDFs. Existing prompts, implementation parameters, cost accounting, and InSTA hardware/runtime details are retained.

E1.justification: OSWorld desktop tasks and InSTA web tasks remain the covered environments. Section 4.2 adds verification scenarios involving near-miss goal violations and benign UI perturbations, such as incorrect filenames, resized windows, and extra tabs. These modestly expand tested input conditions.

E2.justification: V2 adds a direct-instruction generation baseline and evaluates Agent S3 and Agent S2.5 configurations, including GPT-5 and GPT-5.1 backbones (Sections 5.4–5.5 and Figure C.2). These substantially expand comparisons beyond the retained bare-model evaluations.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce stratified human calibration with graded completion scores, trajectory perturbations, direct-instruction targets of 5–10, 10–20, and 20–30 actions with successful-generation filtering, and alternative generator configurations. Appendix C adds task-property metrics. The original 50 tasks per difficulty level and 20 hardest-level human tasks remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds verifier calibration and adversarial robustness tests, scaffold comparisons, an information-asymmetry ablation, generator-sensitivity experiments, and analysis of memory and application-switching demands. V1's domain-level performance analysis is removed. The worked case study and existing task examples are retained in Appendix D.

E5.justification: Section 4.1 newly reports human inter-rater agreement of 0.74 using Cohen's kappa. The InSTA 2-sigma error bars are retained in Figure F.1, formerly Figure D.1. This adds statistical reliability reporting without documenting an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Human-evaluation percentages change from 87% to 91% for feasibility, 91% to 90% for coherence, and 89% to 88% for verifier accuracy (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 1). Extensive new results include verifier stress tests and Tables 5–6; Table 6 reports GPT-5.1 + S3 at 62% and 14% on levels 1 and 6 with GPT-4.1-generated tasks. These are additional configurations, not improvements to the unchanged bare-model results. Domain-level scores and the topic-distribution display are removed.

M1.justification: The six-agent generation pipeline, two-stage executor, verification/revision process, and subtask summarization remain unchanged. The original prompt templates match after appendix renumbering. Additional generator models and agent scaffolds are experimental comparisons, not revisions to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the document: the worked case study moves to Appendix D, original statistics and action-space material move to appendices, and broader-impact content becomes an earlier ethics statement. The abstract, results discussion, and conclusion are shortened, with new reproducibility and LLM-usage statements. Much of the method prose remains intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds calibration, complexity, and scaffold plots plus several analysis tables. It relocates the original statistics to Figure C.1 and the action table to Table G.1, recombines the application-distribution graphic, and removes the topic-distribution graphic and domain-performance panel. Conference formatting also changes typography and placement throughout.

R1.justification: Related work adds distinctions from OS-Genesis, Learn-by-interact, and Evol-Instruct, alongside scaffold-related citations, and removes the PromptCoT discussion. Table 4 changes Explorer's long-horizon classification to positive, while the earlier explicit architectural contrast with Explorer is removed. The overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix C newly defines memory span quantitatively as the maximum step distance between reading information and subsequently using it within a trajectory. This is a limited mathematical definition accompanying a new empirical metric; no theorem, proof, or formal guarantee is added.

improvement.justification: V1 primarily establishes difficulty using bare agents and aggregate verifier agreement. V2 substantially strengthens the evidence through contemporary scaffolded agents, difficulty-dependent calibration, adversarial verifier tests, direct-generation comparisons, and generator-sensitivity analysis. These address important weaknesses in support for benchmark reliability and the generation rationale. Removed limitations and domain analysis, sparse details for some new experiments, and inconsistent release wording are drawbacks, but the empirical gains provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AgentSynth. Their text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material relocated between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds verifier calibration, adversarial tests, scaffolded-agent evaluations, generation ablations, and generator-sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original desktop-agent evaluations, human assessment of generated tasks and trajectories, and InSTA web-agent experiments in Appendix D.

results.title: AgentSynth: Scalable Task Generation for Generalist Computer-Use Agents

C1.justification: The central claim that RLVR incentivizes correct reasoning remains, but v2 explicitly claims demonstrated reasoning-boundary extension in both math and coding. Its introduction and conclusion also add SFT replication of post-RLVR capabilities from generated CoTs as a principal contribution, absent from v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for the contrasting effects of RLVR on distilled models in math and coding, and interprets the SFT results as evidence that even imperfect later-stage CoTs improve in quality. It explicitly connects DAPO reward saturation to an inability to correct remaining reasoning errors. The earlier response-length and overthinking explanation is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds an official LiveCodeBench evaluation-repository pointer and describes the SFT base model, training-question source, and answer filtering. Existing hardware, training duration, data sources, and verifier prompt are retained, largely through relocation. Detailed SFT hyperparameters are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 adds competitive code generation evaluated through execution on LiveCodeBench versions v1–v6. This substantially extends coverage beyond v1's mathematical-reasoning benchmarks. The five original math benchmarks and DAPO training questions are retained.

E2.justification: The Qwen2.5-32B versus DAPO comparison is retained. v2 additionally compares DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B with AceReason-Nemotron-7B, Skywork-OR1-7B, and Skywork-OR1-Math-7B in the relevant experiments, and introduces SFT-trained comparison models in Figure 6.

E3.justification: Added protocols include execution-based coding evaluation, LiveCodeBench difficulty subsets, and controlled SFT experiments starting from the same Qwen2.5-32B model with CoTs from different RL stages and correctness groups. These substantially expand the evaluation design; the original mathematical metrics and verification procedure are retained.

E4.justification: New Section 6 tests CoT quality through downstream SFT generalization, varying the generating checkpoint and using correct, incorrect, or all CoTs. Appendix A.4 adds difficulty-specific coding analysis identifying which problems sustain high-K gaps. The original manual case studies are retained as Appendix A.8.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three CoT verifications and the same voting strategies. New Figure 6(a) contains box-and-whisker marks for SFT performance, but their meaning and source of variation are unspecified. Consequently, whether they introduce a new uncertainty-estimation or repeated-run practice cannot be established reliably.

E6.justification: v2 adds coding Pass@K advantages in Figures 3 and 8, the absence of a distinct high-K advantage for the distilled-model AIME comparison in Figure 9, and improving SFT generalization with later-stage CoTs in Figure 6. The original benchmark and training plots are retained, so these are added findings rather than revised scores for the original comparisons.

M1.justification: The GRPO/DAPO procedure, answer-based reward, CoT-Pass@K definition, verifier prompt, and verification aggregation remain unchanged. SFT is introduced as an experimental probe of CoT quality, rather than a modification to the RL method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Empirical evaluation now precedes theory, while proofs, discussions, and much training detail move into the appendices. The verifier appendices are merged, case studies are renumbered, and author ordering changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds coding, SFT, and distilled-model comparison figures and substantially rearranges figure placement and surrounding layout. Original plots are retained: notably, v1 Figure 3(a) is redisplayed as v2 Figure 4, while the complete original training figure remains as Figure 10.

R1.justification: v2 positions its coding experiments as reproducing and extending AceReason results and comparing Skywork. It removes the long-CoT survey by Qiguang Chen and works by Jiang, Ouyang, and Yan from the bibliography. Most research positioning remains; AceReason's changed citation-year suffix does not denote a new reference.

T1.justification: The alpha > beta assumption, expected-advantage theorem, proof, variance and ideal-case derivations, and metric definitions are retained. Much of v1 Section 3 moves to v2 Section 4 and Appendix A.5; renaming Logical Coherence to Logic Prior does not change the assumption.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support concentrated on one 32B math-model comparison and judge-assessed reasoning. v2 substantially strengthens that foundation through execution-checked coding evaluations and SFT transfer experiments, while the distilled-model math results usefully qualify applicability. These additions address important limitations of the original evidence. Incomplete SFT implementation details and unexplained spread markers limit reproducibility, but do not outweigh the broader and more varied support for the central argument.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, and appendices. Matching relocated sections, original plots, and case studies supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds original LiveCodeBench evaluations, distilled-model comparisons, and supervised fine-tuning experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original math-benchmark evaluations, CoT verification results, and training-dynamics measurements from the authors' DAPO reproduction.

results.title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards Implicitly Incentivizes Correct Reasoning in Base LLMs

C1.justification: The introduction and Discussion broaden claimed generalization from unseen object categories and reconstruction backbones to varied lighting, camera distances, and realistic scenes. This materially expands claimed applicability beyond the original synthetic-object evaluation, while retaining the PUN/NUM contributions and headline efficiency and view-budget claims.

C2.justification: New Section 5.2 and Appendix E explain transfer through a shared notion of viewpoint difficulty associated with geometry and texture complexity. v2 also interprets anchor-count saturation, dataset-generation costs, and threshold sensitivity. The earlier symmetry explanation and image-metric/spherical-viewpoint limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future release; v2 supplies a repository address and reports code, model, and dataset availability. It also specifies mesh-distance units and the completion threshold, plus lighting and real-image selection details. Existing optimizer, preprocessing, hardware, and training-budget information is largely relocated to Appendix C.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained ShapeNet instance/category coverage, v2 evaluates four NeRFAssets objects and four real MIP360 scenes, plus changed-lighting and closer-camera scenarios. Renaming ID/OOD to NUM-inst/NUM-cat and labeling the existing 3DGS evaluation NUM-3DGS-recon do not themselves expand coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds the Fibonacci-sampling Uniform baseline to both original instance and category comparisons in Table S1. WD, A-NeRF, NVF, and Upper-bnd remain; WD's omission from parts of the main table is a presentation change, since its corresponding appendix results are retained.

E3.justification: v2 states that all methods resample 512 candidates each timestep, whereas v1 assigns fixed candidates to baselines. NUM-inst evaluation changes from ten to five instances per category, and the stated 40-view sampling changes from an 8-by-5 angular grid to uniform spherical sampling. New protocols include every-eighth-image MIP360 testing and alternative reconstruction backbones. These reported revisions do not establish that legacy experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds anchor-count and redundancy-threshold sensitivity tests, a small+add aggregation variant, alternative supervision and reconstruction backbones, environmental robustness tests, view-count curves, and uncertainty/complexity correlation analyses. The original uncertainty-metric, selection-policy, and dataset-diversity ablations remain. v1's training-loss analysis in Figure S2 is removed.

E5.justification: v2 introduces Pearson-correlation estimation and fitted linear trends for uncertainty prediction and viewpoint-complexity relationships in Figures S4–S5 and Table S7. Three-seed experiments and standard-deviation reporting already existed and are retained; no increase in replication or new significance-testing practice is reported.

E6.justification: Legacy reconstruction, resource, and ablation values are retained, while substantial new results cover Uniform, environmental changes, real scenes, additional backbones, and sensitivity analyses. For example, v2 Table 2 newly reports MIP360 PSNR of 17.49 for PUN versus 15.41 for NVF. These are additional comparisons, not performance improvements over v1 under matched conditions.

M1.justification: The proposed UPNet architecture, MSE training objective, anchor interpolation, redundancy filtering, and multiplicative uncertainty aggregation remain unchanged in Section 3. Alternative supervision generators and aggregation variants extend experimental checks of the existing framework without revising the default algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the experimental narrative: Section 4's numbered subsections become consolidated topical paragraphs, results are reordered, and training details move into a restructured appendix. Existing captions and discussion passages are condensed or rewritten, and ID/OOD terminology is replaced by dataset-specific names.

P2.justification: v2 combines the original NeRF and 3DGS comparisons into a redesigned Table 1, moves resource results to Table S4, and expands ablation displays. It adds dataset illustrations, view-count curves, and correlation plots, removes the training-loss plot, revises uncertainty-map coloring, and adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive comparison with pretrained occupancy-based active vision, including Smith et al. (2022), and citations supporting MIP360, Binocular3DGS, and mesh evaluation. Application references expand and the environmental-monitoring reference is removed. The central positioning around direct, efficient uncertainty prediction remains.

T1.justification: The interpolation and viewpoint-selection equations retain the same mathematical content, although their formatting changes. Neither version supplies formal guarantees or proofs. Added descriptions of existing mesh metrics and standard complexity measures support empirical evaluation rather than introduce new theoretical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow synthetic-object validation through real-scene and environmental tests, a Uniform baseline, backbone controls, and direct checks of uncertainty prediction and transfer. These address important gaps in evidence for applicability and design choices. Reporting weaknesses remain, including five versus ten NUM-inst examples in Section 4 and Figure S1, and geometry/coverage results favoring NVF in Table S5, but the added validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PUN/UPNet research and NUM dataset. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renaming and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds environmental robustness tests, real-scene evaluations, backbone experiments, and correlation analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction evaluations, resource measurements, uncertainty-map predictions, training curves, and ablations in Sections 4–5 and the appendix.

results.title: PEERING INTO THE UNKNOWN: ACTIVE VIEW SELECTION WITH NEURAL UNCERTAINTY MAPS FOR 3D RECONSTRUCTION

C1.justification: The principal abstract and conclusion claims about Pareto caching, acceleration and transfer remain. The introduction explicitly extends claimed applicability to class-conditioned and text-to-video tasks and strengthens the resource claim from low memory requirements to no memory overhead.

C2.justification: Section 4.4 replaces v1's diversity-based explanation of prompt sensitivity with an interpretation emphasizing prompt quantity, supported by A.4. New discussion also explains random-initialization failure and genetic-operator behavior. A.10 explicitly acknowledges substantial upfront search cost and discusses amortization and implementation limitations.

D1.justification: v3 supplies previously absent search-cost accounting, including approximately 700 A6000 GPU-hours for the full PixArt frontier. It also documents alternative-reward weights, synthetic-prompt instructions, first-step cache initialization, and TaylorSeer-specific batch sizes and MAC-accounting discrepancies (A.3-A.11). These substantially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v3 adds GenEval and DPG Bench evaluation, including object-focused text-image alignment coverage. Calibration coverage also expands beyond Image Reward and DrawBench200 to GPT-generated prompts, a painted-landscape-only domain and prompts restricted to five words (A.4). The original benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated DiCache and TaylorSeer comparators for FLUX at 256 resolution in Table 1, and TaylorSeer at 1024 resolution in Table 4. TaylorSeer was only cited in v1. Existing comparators, including DuCa, remain; SpeCa and ClusCa are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The original main evaluation settings remain. New protocols introduce CLIP-based fitness, controlled genetic-operator and initialization configurations, 10/20-step optimization-transfer experiments, and four generated images per prompt for GenEval/DPG Bench. TaylorSeer comparisons additionally use reduced batch sizes and the existing latency-normalization approach.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's population, prompt-count and DrawBench ablations, v3 tests reward choice, prompt source/domain/length, crossover and mutation settings, inference-step transfer, and heuristic versus random initialization (A.3-A.8). New qualitative comparisons examine artifacts from TaylorSeer and DuCa.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten fixed generation seeds per calibration prompt and average latency over measured batches. v3 adds no independent-search replication analysis, confidence intervals, error bars or significance testing; its new benchmark sampling counts are experimental sample sizes.

E6.justification: Shared rows in the main tables retain their numerical results, while v3 adds substantial comparator, benchmark and ablation outcomes. For example, new Table 13 reports GenEval scores of 0.5892 for ECAD Fast versus 0.5842 unaccelerated at 256 resolution and 20 steps. These are newly reported results, not improvements over v1 measurements.

M1.justification: The core binary-mask representation and NSGA-II search remain unchanged. v3 adds uniform-cost random initialization (A.8) and explicit schedule conversion between 10 and 20 inference steps (A.6), providing limited procedural extensions.

P1.justification: v3 condenses and edits prose, rewrites portions of related work, separates existing appendix ablations into topic-specific sections, and adds an LLM-use disclosure. Citation style, headers and FLUX terminology change, but the main section sequence and much original method/result prose remain.

P2.justification: v3 adds multiple ablation and benchmark tables, prompt illustrations, initialization plots and qualitative comparison panels. It expands existing comparison tables and calibration plots, transposes the Figure 5 schedule displays, relocates retained material and adopts the ICLR layout. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Related work adds coverage of pruning, quantization and newer caching methods. A.12 replaces the DuCa-focused concurrent-work discussion with SpeCa/ClusCa comparisons concerning inference steps, memory and manual tuning. ECAD's central positioning as an optimization alternative to handcrafted caching remains.

T1.justification: The original diffusion, caching, Pareto and NSGA-II mathematics is retained. v3 adds formal schedule up/downsampling definitions in A.6 and a cost-constrained initialization construction using a Diophantine equation and the Extended Euclidean Algorithm in A.8. No substantial theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves important evidentiary gaps by quantifying offline search cost, testing previously unexamined design choices, and revising the calibration-diversity explanation using controlled experiments. New comparators and GenEval/DPG evaluations strengthen validation without relying on changed original scores. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, and the stronger modality and memory claims receive limited direct support, but the diagnostic evidence and cost transparency substantially improve the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ECAD research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite additions and reorganization in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds comparator results, GenEval/DPG Bench evaluations and several controlled ablation studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original caching experiments on PixArt-α, PixArt-Σ and FLUX-1.dev, including benchmark results, transfer experiments and appendix ablations.

results.title: Evolutionary Caching to Accelerate Your Off-the-Shelf Diffusion Model

C1.justification: v2 adds central claims that position IDs use relative spatial coding, generalize to naturalistic images and are reused across tasks, alongside consistency across model families and scales. The unified three-stage presentation incorporates a retrieval stage already established in v1's appendix; that stage alone is not a new contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of relative coding, qualifies its weaker expression in LLaVA, and discusses possible positional-embedding or training explanations. It also relates recovery efficacy to source-prototype quality and introduces open questions about architectural versus training-driven emergence. v1's specific raster-order interpretation and single-model generality limitation are no longer presented.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands technical documentation with PUG's 200-image generation setup, COCO filtering and prototype-estimation procedures, counting/spatial prompts, and intervention strengths, head selection and parameter sweeps. The original 4x4 generation recipe disappears. A new reproducibility statement promises dataset and code release, but provides no release link.

E1.justification: v2 expands beyond colored-shape scenes and color retrieval to PUG photorealistic animal scenes, COCO real-world images, spatial-relation questions and counting tasks involving three to eight objects. These introduce substantive changes in image domains and task requirements, rather than merely additional scores on existing tasks.

E2.justification: v2 introduces bottom-K head ablation as an explicit comparator to top-K ablation on the counting task (Appendix C, Figure 46). v1's all-layer and early-layer key-swap comparison variants are no longer reported. The additional VLM families mainly expand the systems studied, rather than introduce competing algorithms.

E3.justification: The Qwen2-VL-7B-only evaluation expands to multiple Qwen and LLaVA families and sizes, with additional Idefics2 RSA results. Color-retrieval interventions now use alpha=2 and layers containing the top-20 feature-retrieval heads instead of fixed layer ranges. Binding-error recovery changes from replacing the layer-18 residual stream to replacing selected heads' outputs. New experiments also introduce parameter sweeps and separate COCO source/target sets.

E4.justification: v2 adds relative-versus-absolute-position tests, intervention-strength/head-count sensitivity sweeps, cross-task transfer tests and counting ablations. Conversely, v1's detailed attention-profile analyses, raster-order experiments, 4x4 binding-error analyses and key-swap layer-range comparisons are removed rather than merely relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly specifies three random source/target splits for the COCO experiment; this does not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments. v1's recovery table reports accuracies with plus/minus uncertainty values, whereas its replacement in v2 gives only point accuracies.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for naturalistic images, relative coding, spatial reasoning and counting. The recovery table is replaced: v1 reports Qwen2-VL 3x3 accuracy increasing from 89% to 94% under residual patching; v2 reports, for example, Qwen2.5-VL-3B increasing from 69.0% to 80.1% under head patching. These are different experiments, not same-setting gains between versions. Earlier raster-order results are removed.

M1.justification: The underlying three-stage mechanism is retained: v1's semantic matching heads in Appendix C correspond to v2's ID retrieval heads. Within the existing activation-intervention framework, v2 adds scaled head-output/query edits, cross-task ID injection and COCO prototypes estimated using model-generated object order, extending v1's key/value swaps and residual-stream replacement.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes and rewrites the narrative: Related Work moves earlier, task and architecture explanations receive dedicated subsections, mechanism identification is separated from property-testing results, and contribution and reproducibility statements are added. The conclusion is rewritten, and attention-head terminology is standardized across the main text.

P2.justification: v2 rebuilds Figure 1 as a combined architecture/PCA/RSA/CMA overview, redraws and relocates CMA schematics, and adds extensive model-comparison charts, position-coding illustrations, parameter-sweep panels and COCO/counting figures. Earlier attention maps and raster-order displays disappear, while the recovery table changes structure from grid-based to model-based rows.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for PUG, COCO and Griffiths et al., while dropping several architecture/pretraining references, including Löwe, Covert and Tschannen. Related Work adds an explicit distinction from Yang et al.'s text-only circuits based on computational function, distributed visual representations and practical relevance. The overall research positioning remains recognizable.

T1.justification: The CMA score and position/feature RSA definitions remain mathematically equivalent. Sections 4.2–4.4 extend the formal intervention definitions to scaled head-level edits and additive injection of scene-description-derived ID prototypes into spatial reasoning, beyond v1's pairwise key-swap equations. No new theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's explicit single-model generality limitation through tests across model families and scales, and examines the mechanism in photorealistic and real images and additional reasoning tasks. New causal comparisons and sensitivity analyses strengthen the evidence beyond simple grid scenes. Losing earlier attention/raster-order analyses and recovery-table uncertainties is a drawback, but the stronger support for the mechanism's generality constitutes a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on spatial indexing and visual binding in VLMs. Their complete main texts, figures, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments across multiple VLMs, including synthetic and naturalistic scenes, COCO interventions, spatial reasoning, counting and binding-error recovery.

before.justification: v1 reports original representational, causal-mediation, attention and intervention experiments on Qwen2-VL-7B, including binding-error recovery and appendix analyses of object ordering.

results.title: Visual symbolic mechanisms: Emergent symbol processing in Vision Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the central discovery and interpretability claims. The introduction adds an explicit claim of potential utility for data selection and learning-rate scheduling, modestly extending the claimed applications.

C2.justification: V3 qualifies the earlier favorable assessment of alternative bases: random orthonormal directions retain reasonable carry homogeneity but recover few late breakthroughs. Appendix A adds specific limitations concerning checkpoint sparsity and POS-based labeling missing interpretable skills. Appendix G also acknowledges comparable first- and second-order F1 scores.

D1.justification: V3 supplies a code-repository address, HDBSCAN hyperparameters, hyperparameter-selection rationale, filtering counts, and detailed POS-labeling rules, including the 70% threshold and two-tag restriction.
