Appendices D-E substantially improve documentation of the existing implementation, although the conflicting arithmetic checkpoint interval limits reproducibility.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate three-digit arithmetic addition and causal language modeling on March 2022 English Wikipedia. The additional approximation checks and language-cluster examples use these retained tasks; other modalities remain future work.

E2.justification: V1's decomposition comparison evaluates exact loss, Fisher information, and POLCA. V3 Tables 1 and 8 add change in exact loss, parameter-aligned LCA, and first-order POLCA to the clustering comparison. V1's first-versus-second-order trajectory similarity check did not evaluate first-order clustering quality.

E3.justification: V3 adds recall/F1 and quantitative hidden-breakthrough evaluation using delta=100 and tau=1000, plus approximation validation on 400 tokens, 10 checkpoints, and five basis vectors. Training budgets and datasets are retained. Table 3 lists an arithmetic POLCA interval of 5 iterations, conflicting with 20 in the retained prose, so an actual sampling change cannot be established.

E4.justification: V3 adds direct validation against the true second-order term in Appendix C, first-order clustering ablations, and analyses of hidden-breakthrough recovery across decomposition strategies and bases in Appendices G-H. Figures 10-11 also add language-cluster case studies for basis vectors 10 and 29.

E5.justification: The existing median/quartile reporting is retained. Neither version provides training-seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new RMSE measures approximation accuracy rather than uncertainty.

E6.justification: Original POLCA carry homogeneities of 0.973, 0.946, and 0.903 are retained. V3 adds recall/F1, comparator scores, and breakthrough fractions, including 0.355 for POLCA versus 0.019 for LCA in Table 9. Appendix C newly reports approximation RMSE of 0.145, substantially expanding the reported findings.

M1.justification: The Hessian-based basis construction, second-order POLCA allocation, trajectory filtering, and HDBSCAN clustering remain unchanged. V3 expands implementation explanations and introduces a breakthrough evaluation criterion, without establishing a change to the underlying POLCA procedure.

P1.justification: V3 expands motivation and methodological explanations, moves limitations and English experimental details into appendices, and adds reproducibility, ethics, and AI-use statements. The main section sequence and much of the original prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds comparison and hyperparameter tables, restructures homogeneity tables to include recall/F1, and expands the language-cluster panels. It redraws introductory schematics, crops arithmetic plots to 4000 iterations while retaining 10000-step training, relocates Figure 5 into the results, and adopts the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: V3 adds Saxe et al. on smooth aggregate learning curves and Foote et al. and Gao et al. when positioning automatic labeling. The introduction explicitly contrasts bottom-up discovery with predefined-skill analyses and relates POLCA to other unsupervised interpretability approaches; the existing research foundations remain.

T1.justification: New Section 3.4 formally defines breakthrough timing through finite differences and hidden breakthroughs through a thresholded average timing criterion. The POLCA decomposition and second-order derivation are otherwise retained; the new approximation validation is empirical, not a new proof.

improvement.justification: V1 supports hidden breakthroughs primarily through selected trajectories and carry homogeneity. V3 makes that central claim quantitatively testable and adds meaningful LCA/first-order controls, recall/F1, and direct approximation validation. Detailed clustering and labeling instructions also address important reproducibility gaps. The new 5-versus-20-iteration inconsistency is a defect, but the gains in evidential support and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same POLCA research, with matching authors, methods, and experimental tasks. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds quantitative breakthrough comparisons, additional clustering results, and empirical validation of the second-order approximation.

before.justification: V1 reports original arithmetic-addition and English Wikipedia experiments, including clustering results, carry-skill homogeneity measurements, and decomposition and basis ablations.

results.title: Hidden Breakthroughs in Language Model Training

C1.justification: The central contributions—RAA/RR formulations, decomposition results, and DOHJ-PPO—remain unchanged. V2's conclusion adds claims of rigorous justification for the stochastic-policy formulation and empirical robustness to certain stochastic dynamics, extending the stated contribution within the existing framework.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes stochastic-policy justification from unresolved guarantees under stochastic dynamics, discusses noncommuting expectations and extrema, and identifies high-noise limitations. It also develops applicability boundaries for larger logical compositions and explains why temporal-logic predicate algebra does not directly yield optimal-control decompositions.

D1.justification: V2 Tables 2–3 newly disclose parallel-environment counts, rollout lengths, total timesteps, scan steps, update epochs, and minibatches for retained experiments. Appendices J–K and Tables 4–5 document rewards, obstacles, initialization, and training settings for the added environments. These materially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V2 retains grid-world, Hopper, and F16 coverage while adding SafetyGym Point and HalfCheetah RAA/RR tasks. It also evaluates HalfCheetah under stochastic transition conditions absent from v1.

E2.justification: Compared with v1's CPPO, RA, and DSTL comparisons, v2 Figure 4 adds evaluated PPO, PPO-LAG, RCPPO, RESPO, MORL, SPARSE, P2BPO, and LOGBAR baselines on retained tasks. The RR figures show one C-PPO entry instead of separately displaying three CPPO variants, although their definitions remain in Appendix G.

E3.justification: V2 adds partial success as an evaluation metric and a controlled noise protocol: Gaussian perturbations to velocities/angular velocities at scales 0, 0.5, 1, and 2, with learning curves evaluated over 256 trajectories. The ordinary comparisons retain 1,000 evaluation trajectories. Newly disclosed budgets for retained experiments do not establish changed training settings.

E4.justification: Section 8.3 and Figure 5 add a dedicated noise-sensitivity study of both HalfCheetah tasks against three leading baselines per task, testing the stochastic approximation's robustness. V1 contains no corresponding sweep. The qualitative observation about removing coupled resets was already present in v1 Appendix F.

E5.justification: V2 Section 8.3 newly specifies three seeds and reports maximum learning curves over them; v1 states no seed count. This adds run-count and aggregation reporting without establishing increased runs for retained experiments. The new curves do not report across-seed uncertainty.

E6.justification: Figures 4–6 substantially expand success, partial-success, and achievement-time results across tasks and comparators. Figure 5 adds findings that the RAA advantage disappears at the highest noise level while RR performance remains stronger. New speed comparisons also show exceptions to universal superiority: SPARSE has fewer mean steps than DOHJ-PPO in Hopper-RAA.

M1.justification: The objectives, state augmentation, value decompositions, Bellman/GAE updates, and PPO procedure are retained. Concurrent training and coupled resets emphasized in v2 Section 7.2 already appear in v1 Appendix F; the DO-HJ-PPO to DOHJ-PPO renaming does not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: V2 adds a separate introduction and contribution list, substantially rewrites the motivation and related work, expands formulation explanations, and organizes experiments into dedicated subsections. Algorithm and policy-gradient material moves into the appendix, producing substantial narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, enlarging retained illustrations. V2 adds an environment montage and noise-learning curves, restructures success comparisons, separates achievement-time plots into Appendix Figure 6, and expands or adds hyperparameter tables.

R1.justification: V1's brief related-work discussion becomes an extensive treatment of constrained/MORL, goal-conditioned RL, temporal logic, generalized objectives, and HJ methods. V2 adds numerous substantive citations, including Wang et al. (2020), Cui and Yu (2023), and Tang et al. (2025), and sharpens its distinction from temporal-logic decomposition.

T1.justification: The original decomposition proofs are retained, but v2 adds Theorem 4 and its contraction/monotonicity proof relating stochastic-policy SRABE values to the optimal discounted RA value. Appendix A.1 adds a direct RAA Bellman derivation, and Appendix L adds formal temporal-logic semantics and counterexamples distinguishing predicate decomposition from optimal-value decomposition.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow empirical validation, supplies an explicit justification for the stochastic-policy surrogate, and fills important training-budget and rollout disclosures. These improve the paper's evidential basis and reproducibility. Maximum-over-three-seed noise curves and the blanket fewest-steps claim, contradicted by some Figure 6 comparisons, temper but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAA/RR formulations and DOHJ-PPO work. Their readable main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds SafetyGym, HalfCheetah, and stochastic-dynamics evaluations in Figures 4–6.

before.justification: V1 reports original grid-world simulations and Hopper/F16 experiments, including learned trajectories, success rates, and achievement times in Figures 1 and 3.

results.title: Dual-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Novel Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Formulations

C1.justification: The three principal contributions remain: explaining when chunking helps, showing weaker models can outperform stronger single-shot models, and improving coordination through prompts. However, the abstract and contribution list soften the empirical growth claim from superlinear noise/degradation to accelerated fidelity decay/degradation, and the conclusion adopts the revised fidelity-loss formulation.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly distinguishes empirical proxies from unobservable decomposition terms and explains task loss as an information bottleneck under a fixed output schema. New Appendices N–O substantially expand applicability discussions: efficiency depends on concurrency and short worker outputs, while fixed-length chunking controls confounding factors that adaptive segmentation would change.

D1.justification: V2 documents the existing sparse-search procedure more precisely, including its development set, sampling without replacement, score averaging, and selection rule. It also removes v1's opening footnote promising code release and providing a repository URL. The PDFs do not establish an actual change in repository availability.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate KV retrieval, Math, QA-IB, QA-LB, summarization, and character inference using the same modified InfiniteBench and LongBench-V2 coverage. V2 Appendix D relocates the existing task descriptions.

E2.justification: The evaluated model sets, single-shot comparisons, BM25/mpnet RAG baselines, and RoPE-extension comparisons are retained. LOGO, LongReward, and LongPO are newly cited as related work but are not added to the reported experimental comparisons.

E3.justification: The experiments retain their accuracy/F1/ROUGE metrics, context and chunk-size grids, model configurations, temperature-zero decoding, one planner refinement, and 3/5/10-document search budgets. V2 clarifies the existing sampling procedure and reframes the diagnostic curves without establishing changed experimental settings.

E4.justification: The prompt comparisons, sparse-search analysis, overlap tests, context-extension tests, and diverse-model evaluations already appear in v1. V2's new cost and segmentation appendices provide analytical arguments and explanations, without adding ablations, robustness tests, or empirical case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The retained 3/5/10-document sampling budgets concern chunk-size selection, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V1 Tables 1–8 retain their numerical entries in v2 Tables 2–9, and Figures 2–4 retain identical plot content. V2 Table 1 combines the existing sparse-search results from v1 Tables 3–4; it introduces no new outcomes.

M1.justification: The planner–worker–manager pipeline, chunk processing, prompts, and refinement procedure are retained. The sparse chunk-size selection described in v2 Sections 4 and 5.5 already appears in v1 Appendix F. The new fidelity losses reformulate the analysis without changing inference or training.

P1.justification: Section 3 and the conclusion are substantially rewritten, and terminology and experimental explanations are revised throughout. Task descriptions move to Appendix D, sparse-search material gains dedicated main-text treatment, and the appendices are reorganized and expanded with authorship disclosure, efficiency analysis, and segmentation rationale.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show planner connections to both workers and manager. V2 adds a combined main-text table displaying existing results, revises captions, relocates figures, and adopts conference headers and typography. The performance plots and existing table structures are largely preserved.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds LOGO, LongReward, and LongPO as complementary approaches based on preference or reward optimization. Section 2.3 removes the specific criticism that prior coordination mechanisms lack principled worker–manager balancing. The broader positioning against existing divide-and-conquer methods remains.

T1.justification: V2 replaces the product-of-outputs noise framework with score-ratio fidelity definitions and an exact additive logarithmic-loss decomposition. It introduces positivity and monotonicity assumptions, replaces Assumption 3.1/Theorem 3.2 and their appendices with a conditional linear-versus-superlinear loss argument, and derives the high-fidelity approximation. Appendix N also adds latency and monetary-cost equations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the central theoretical contribution. It replaces v1's unsupported growth-rate elimination and conflicting asymptotic chunk-count bounds with explicit fidelity definitions and a clearer conditional loss-scaling argument (Section 3 and Appendices B–C). The proxy qualifications and deployment caveats further improve interpretability. The unchanged experiments do not directly validate the new assumptions, and removing the code-release link modestly weakens reproducibility information, but these limitations do not outweigh the theoretical improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and are readable throughout, including their equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained methods and experiments can be matched reliably despite substantial theoretical rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experimental results in the main text and appendices. Results retained from v1 still constitute original empirical evidence.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on six long-context tasks, including model comparisons, chunk-size sweeps, prompt comparisons, and supplementary evaluations.

results.title: When Does Divide and Conquer Work for Long Context LLM? A Noise Decomposition Framework

C1.justification: The abstract shifts from emphasizing robust CNNs' greater human recognizability and biological fidelity to claiming that L2 adversarial training fails to improve high-level invariance interpretability. The introduction and discussion accordingly foreground depth-dependent perceptual misalignment. The central gradient-free, dual-objective SnS contribution remains.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1's model-capacity/accuracy–robustness explanation and develops interpretations involving stretching depth, ViT representations, robustness norms, and complementary metamer behavior. It explains the roles of individual loss components and adds substantive discussion of generator priors and practical constraints on biological applications.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 4096-dimensional codes, CMA-ES updates using the best 30% of the ranking, final Pareto-front output selection, and approximately 120 seconds per 500-iteration run. It also documents additional models' layer choices and desktop/laptop restrictions for participants. Core hyperparameters, hardware specifications, and code/data access were already supplied in v1.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds adversarial-generation tests using natural reference images, extending v1's MEI-referenced adversarial tests. Natural-image invariance experiments already existed in v1. The ImageNet domain, recognition task, and human population are otherwise retained.

E2.justification: v2 directly evaluates gradient-based metamers against SnS using the same 120 reference images, reporting interpretability and representational-distance comparisons in Tables S3–S4. v1 discussed metamers without evaluating this comparator. The affine-transformation and XDREAM-based controls remain.

E3.justification: The main observer evaluation changes from six standard and three L∞-robust models to six architectures with paired standard and L2-robust versions. Additional settings include ResNet18/VGG16_bn subjects, ViT and CLIP subjects, an L∞-robust ResNet50, and dedicated metamer and dimensionality protocols. The original human 12-alternative classification protocol is retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds four single-loss ablations, optimization trajectories, analysis of runs failing early stopping, diversity between invariant solutions, and PCA/2NN intrinsic-dimensionality analyses. These investigate component necessity, convergence, diversity, and manifold geometry. The hidden-layer and subsampling analyses from v1 are retained in renamed appendices.

E5.justification: Appendix H introduces repeated subsampling for dimensionality estimation: 50 repetitions per sample size, with SEM reporting. It also documents 100 SnS runs for each of five reference MEIs. AlexNet's GLMM and post-hoc significance reporting are removed; the human GLMM, planned contrasts, and multiple-comparison correction remain unchanged.

E6.justification: The original Figure 2 activation reductions of 111% for adversarial images and 34% for invariant images remain unchanged. v2 replaces the observer-network results and adds substantial new findings. For example, Table S3 reports late-layer standard-generator accuracy of 0.779 for SnS versus 0.310 for metamers under standard observers. These are new comparisons, not performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The SnS generator, CMA-ES optimization, stretch/squeeze objectives, Pareto ranking and tie-breaking, and stopping rules remain unchanged. The CLIP linear readout configures an additional target model; the expanded Pareto implementation description does not establish a change to SnS itself.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, results, and discussion are rewritten. Separability and representational-distance methods move into Appendix A, detailed human procedures move into Appendix B, and reproducibility and ethics sections are added. References move before the supplementary material.

P2.justification: v1 Figure 5 becomes a substantially revised Figure 4, removing the AlexNet panel and adding comparisons across subject architectures. v1 Figure 4 moves to Figure S3 and gains diversity panels. New figures cover Pareto fronts, convergence, natural-reference tests, ablations, ViTs, dimensionality, and L∞ robustness; tables add new comparisons and remove AlexNet statistical columns.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially to local manifold methods, CPPN-based neuronal invariance approaches, and perceptual-alignment methods such as controversial stimuli, maximum differentiation, EITs, and MIRCs. The discussion develops SnS's relationship to these approaches and to metamers beyond v1's narrower treatment.

T1.justification: v2 formally defines Pareto dominance and the nondominated solution set in Equations 2–4, making v1's informal vector-argmin formulation mathematically explicit. The underlying optimization objectives are retained, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: The loss ablations, direct metamer comparisons, convergence/diversity checks, and broader model tests address substantial validation gaps in v1, strengthening evidence for SnS's mechanism and applicability. Explicit Pareto definitions and implementation disclosures also improve clarity. The abstract's blanket claim about failed high-level improvement under L2 training overstates the mixed observer results in Table S3, but this weakness does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Stretch-and-Squeeze (SnS) study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplementary material are readable and support reliable matching across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds loss ablations, metamer comparisons, manifold-dimensionality analyses, and experiments with additional architectures and robustness settings.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-synthesis experiments, a 25-participant human classification study, and supplementary hidden-layer and representation-subsampling experiments.

results.title: Stretching Beyond the Obvious: A Gradient-Free Framework to Unveil the Hidden Landscape of Visual Invariance

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion explicitly extend the state-of-the-art claim from H2O and TACO to Assembly101 and Ego-Exo4D. The central contributions—single-image translation using geometric and semantic observations, diffusion reconstruction, and generalization to unseen scenarios—remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking hand visibility and global context to pose-modeling performance, and multimodal conditioning to the limited benefit of MANO representations. Its revised incorrect-text discussion emphasizes semantic control with preserved geometry, whereas v1 emphasized incorrect objects and VLM dependence. It also interprets estimated-input robustness and the temporal-consistency/image-quality tradeoff, while dropping the specific TACO head-visibility restriction.

D1.justification: v2 adds approximate reconstruction and pose-training times of 10 and 20 hours and specifies the video mixing ratio. Most architecture, hyperparameter, hardware, and project-access information is retained. However, it removes v1's explicit H2O/TACO ground-truth-input provisions, H2O-only pose-estimator training restriction, and identification of the checkpoint used for real-world examples.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained H2O, TACO, and smartphone examples, v2 actually evaluates Assembly101 and Ego-Exo4D, which v1 only cited. It also introduces a selected occluded/blurry H2O test scenario and evaluates sequential video generation.

E2.justification: The H2O comparator set is retained, but TACO expands from qualitative comparison with CFLD to quantitative comparisons also including pix2pixHD and pixelNeRF. Tables B-C add body-pose, camera-pose, and CNN-based hand-pose alternatives. The claimed 4Diff comparison reinterprets an existing no-pose/no-text ablation; it is not a separately implemented 4Diff baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds PA-MPJPE using HaMeR and CLIPScore to the original four image metrics. New protocols include pose-estimation MPJPE, manually selected noisy cases, predicted-versus-ground-truth component controls, and temporal evaluation using T-LPIPS and Flow-warp. The documented core training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Tables B-H add analyses of pose-modeling strategies, MANO versus keypoints, noisy inputs, component accuracy and removal, and temporal consistency versus image quality. The incorrect-text study is revised with new examples involving appearance attributes. Existing backbone and generation-consistency analyses are retained, while the TACO failure examples are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions show four generations per input in the qualitative consistency analysis. Neither reports quantitative uncertainty estimates, training-seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures; v2's additional tables retain point estimates.

E6.justification: The original four-metric H2O, conditioning, and backbone scores are retained. v2 adds metrics and substantial new results, including EgoWorld FIDs of 37.191, 50.232, and 61.231 on TACO, Assembly101, and Ego-Exo4D. Table H reports improved temporal consistency but worse FID with video extension, 35.455 versus 33.284. Several real-world outputs are also replaced; these additions do not establish same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The principal two-stage pipeline, architecture, and losses remain unchanged. Appendix A.2.7 adds an implemented video-generation adaptation: subsequent frames combine the previous generated latent with fresh noise at a 1:9 ratio. v1 only proposed temporal integration as future work.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the results narrative and reorganizes the paper: reconstruction implementation and backbone analysis move to the appendix, incorrect-text analysis moves into the main text, and limitations are consolidated. The appendix gains a broader subsection structure and an LLM-usage statement. Citation style and conference headers also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 2 and appendix Tables B-H, expands retained tables with metric columns, and substantially recomposes Figure 4. The incorrect-text figure gains sparse-map panels and changes examples; other figures are relocated or shortened, and the TACO failure figure disappears. Conference formatting also changes typography and page composition.

R1.justification: The main related-work discussion is largely retained. v2 adds references for HaMeR, CLIPScore, ResNet, Hand4Whole, OSX, Gemini, and AnimateDiff. It newly positions CFLD as an upper-bound reference for Exo2Ego and the existing unconditioned ablation as a proxy for 4Diff.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1-7 are substantively unchanged; changing the depth-stabilization symbol is not a mathematical revision. No new theorem, proof, or theoretical derivation appears. The added temporal measures concern empirical evaluation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central claims through two additional datasets, hand-pose and semantic metrics, and component analyses. Particularly valuable is Table F's quantitative evaluation with fully predicted inputs, addressing a gap left by v1's ground-truth-assisted benchmarks and qualitative full-pipeline examples. The revision loses some explicit setup disclosures and TACO failure evidence, and uncertainty reporting remains absent. Nevertheless, the new evidence substantially improves assessment of generalization, component dependence, and practical tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EgoWorld and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial reorganization, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds quantitative evaluations on additional datasets, pose-modeling comparisons, robustness tests, component analyses, and a video extension.

before.justification: v1 reports original H2O benchmark results, conditioning and backbone ablations, and qualitative TACO, real-world, and appendix experiments.

results.title: EgoWorld: Translating Exocentric View to Egocentric View using Rich Exocentric Observations

C1.justification: The central claims remain that adaptive partial supervision bridges SFT and RL, enables learning on the parity task, improves mathematical reasoning, and offers limited benefit when learning signals saturate. DeepScaleR expands supporting evidence. Although the separate pass@k contribution bullet disappears, its substantive claim remains in the experiments and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial interpretation of the mixed R3 results: clean step segmentation may favor R3 on GSM8k, while heterogeneous difficulty and longer solutions may favor adaptive supervision. It also discusses data and compute barriers to testing longer-horizon reasoning and explains threshold robustness and the variance-based motivation for choosing 0.5. These extend the existing saturation and large-dataset limitations.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the main threshold of 0.5, a simple boxed-answer prompt and decoding description, validation-based SFT tuning, and GRPO runs lasting at least as long as corresponding AdaBack runs. These clarify implementation and comparison practices without establishing changes to retained experiments. Hardware, token limits, and reported compute remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds DeepScaleR training and evaluation, extending coverage to another, harder mathematical-reasoning dataset. The parity task, MATH, GSM8k, Base-7 GSM8k, and Tensor-2 GSM8k remain; this extends the existing domain rather than introducing a substantially different task.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates R3 only in the synthetic parity comparison. v2 Table 2 adds this closely related comparator to GSM8k, MATH, and DeepScaleR evaluations with both 1B and 3B base models, substantially strengthening the mathematical-benchmark comparison set. The original GRPO and SFT comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The new sensitivity experiment evaluates nine thresholds from 0.1 to 0.9 over approximately 12,000 RL iterations using SFT-initialized Llama3.2-1B on GSM8k. The new R3 comparisons explicitly share ground-truth solutions and reward functions. Previously stated GRPO batch size, rollout count, learning rate, and checkpoint aggregation are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C introduces systematic evidence about sensitivity to the central reward threshold, examining training reward, test performance, and supervision trajectories in Figures 5–6. Figure 11 adds explicit Qwen base/instruct saturation curves where v1 offered only a qualitative observation. The existing MATH saturation analysis is retained as Figure 10, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-checkpoint averaging and the same shaded pass@k curves. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence-interval methodology, or significance tests. Its reference to inherent RL variance does not provide a new uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: All original Table 1 values are retained. New DeepScaleR accuracies include 9.0/10.6 for AdaBack and 9.5/12.5 for SFT+AdaBack at 1B/3B. Table 2 newly shows R3 ahead on GSM8k, 41.5/74.2 versus 39.2/73.3, and slightly ahead on 3B MATH, 19.2 versus 19.1; AdaBack leads on DeepScaleR. Threshold and Qwen trajectories add further results, rather than improving previously reported scores.

M1.justification: The reward-driven interval updates, partial-prefix conditioning, global-average initialization, and 10% supervision-free injection are already present in v1. v2 clarifies continuation-length notation and threshold selection without establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract opening, condenses the contribution list, revises selected experimental and R3 explanations, and changes citation style. It moves the scratchpad discussion into Appendix A and adds an LLM-usage appendix. The main section sequence and most existing technical prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout, expands Table 1 with DeepScaleR columns, adds Table 2 and Figures 5, 6, and 11, and substantially rearranges figure placement and sizing. v1 Figure 5 moves to appendix Figure 10; its appendix Figures 6–8 become Figures 7–9 with retained content.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops its positioning against R3, replacing the earlier infeasibility characterization with discussion of fallback segmentation and conditional strengths. Section 4 and Appendix A add relationships to curriculum-versus-mixture theory, recent batch-level curricula, symbolic solvers, and stronger mathematical-reasoning pipelines. The relocated scratchpad review and duplicate Pang reference do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: The parity construction, sample-complexity arguments, simplifying assumptions, and Appendix B reasoning are retained. The revised continuation-length notation is a clarification; v2 introduces no substantive new theorem, proof, or derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves an important validation gap by comparing AdaBack directly with the closely related R3 method on mathematical benchmarks under shared solutions and rewards, including acknowledging where R3 wins. DeepScaleR and the threshold-sensitivity study further strengthen evidence for applicability and robustness while preserving the original results. These additions substantially improve empirical credibility and clarify the method's boundaries, although run-to-run uncertainty remains unquantified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaBack research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports additional DeepScaleR results, mathematical-benchmark comparisons with R3, threshold-sensitivity experiments, and Qwen learning curves.

before.justification: v1 reports original chain-of-parities experiments, mathematical-reasoning accuracies, pass@k evaluations, and training-dynamics analyses.

results.title: RL for Reasoning by Adaptively Revealing Rationales

C1.justification: v1 centers PBB as a possible explanation for reasoning benefits from code training. v2 presents it as a general regime for acquiring behavior from declarative instructions across code and grammars. Its title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion make curriculum design and the new claim that one instruction can substitute for up to 100 demonstrations central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning delayed SFT generalization, reduced retroactive benefits in familiar domains, and grammar compliance as implicit syntactic computation. It qualifies sample efficiency by the amortized first-stage cost and discusses natural-language PBB as a scaling and representation problem (Appendix F.1). Conversely, v1's explicit limitations concerning synthetic tasks and extrapolation from finetuning to pretraining are omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data repository link and release statement, grammar-generation and parser details, explicit RL reward and KL settings, and clarification of the scaling experiment's fixed unpaired set. It removes v1's Adam parameters, gradient-clipping detail, precise cipher definitions, and several I/O split specifications. The MathInstruct mixture is no longer documented. These are substantial changes to reproducibility information, including both additions and losses.

E1.justification: v2 adds sentence generation under 200 synthetic context-free grammars with five vocabularies (Section 4.1), extending evaluation beyond algorithm execution to grammatical compliance. Random Arithmetic, Leetcode, and custom-cipher coverage remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds an algorithm-distillation comparison on Random Arithmetic with the same first-stage training, explicit in-context execution comparisons, a random-generation grammar baseline, and the combined instruction-plus-demonstration cipher condition (Figures 2, 3, 5, and 6). The earlier SFT, DPO, and GRPO comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 makes Qwen3 4B/8B/14B the primary models while retaining Llama evaluations. Stated settings change from one SFT epoch to five, from 90 Random Arithmetic SFT execution examples per training function to 30, and from GRPO group/batch sizes 6/6 to 8/32; learning rates and schedules also change. Grammar parsing and the demonstration-count sweep introduce additional protocols. These reported revisions do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds Random Arithmetic stage-isolation controls, execution-only retroactive training controls (Appendix H), instruction-versus-demonstration efficiency curves, and an analysis of combining instructions with biased cipher demonstrations. Representation analyses also cover more models. Earlier data-scaling, single-stage versus two-stage, and DPO/GRPO analyses remain in Appendices B-D.

E5.justification: Both versions report evaluation over 16 samples with 95% confidence intervals. v2 removes v1's explicit disclosure that training uses a single seed. It does not document an increase in independent training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive Qwen3 and grammar results, including reported 37% average Random Arithmetic execution accuracy for Qwen3-14B, approximately 47% proactive grammar compliance versus approximately 6% random compliance, and the comparison with up to 100 demonstrations. Figure 5 newly shows the hybrid cipher condition outperforming both individual training sources. Several older appendix plots remain unchanged; new scores under changed settings are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core proactive and retroactive two-stage curricula persist. v2 adds a cipher variant combining instruction modelling with skewed execution demonstrations during stage 2 (Section 5.2, Figure 5), whereas v1 compares code training and demonstration training separately. The broader formal description and grammar application do not establish a new core algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Results are reorganized around algorithmic execution, sample efficiency, and grammar compliance. The discussion-and-limitations section is replaced by a conclusion and reproducibility statement, with new natural-language discussion in Appendix F.1.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, introduces a six-panel main comparison, adds sample-efficiency and grammar figures, expands the cipher plot, and moves Llama results to Appendix A. Several earlier appendix plots are retained and renumbered. Conference formatting changes the layout throughout. The new Figure 3 caption incorrectly interchanges the descriptions of its upper-right and lower-right panels.

R1.justification: Research positioning is substantially rewritten around learning to execute, declarative knowledge, and curriculum design. Added connections include neural interpreters and execution engines, classical partial evaluation, latent learning, and continual pretraining. Several earlier references and contrasts disappear, including the discussion of Thomm et al.'s composition limits. v2 also more explicitly identifies proactive PBB with the earlier implicit-meta-learning pipeline.

T1.justification: Section 3 introduces explicit instruction denotations covering both functions and grammar-generated languages, context pointers, and specialization mappings. The accompanying loss and gradient expressions largely formalize the existing curricula. This is a limited extension of the mathematical definitions, without new theorems, proofs, or guarantees.

improvement.justification: The matched-first-stage demonstration comparison, additional stage-isolation controls, and non-code grammar experiments substantially strengthen the empirical case for PBB's efficiency and applicability beyond code. They address questions that v1's code-centered evidence left unresolved. The repository information also improves access documentation. Lost seed, implementation, and limitation disclosures, together with figure-labeling errors, reduce transparency and clarity, but the stronger experimental support provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Programming by Backprop (PBB), with identifiable continuity in curricula, datasets, and experiments despite substantial revision. Both complete documents, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original PBB experiments, including Qwen3 evaluations, grammar generation, sample-efficiency comparisons, and additional controls, alongside earlier analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Random Arithmetic, Leetcode, and custom ciphers, including composition, data-scaling, and training-algorithm analyses.

results.title: Programming by Backprop: An Instruction is Worth 100 Examples When Finetuning LLMs

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims of editable convex primitives at multiple scales, camera and object manipulation, texture preservation, and advantages over prior methods. The stronger emphasis on a 3D interaction paradigm and added supporting experiments do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit reasoning about shape constancy, contact consistency, and shape completion. New ablation interpretations explain the geometry–texture tradeoff and how dilation removes boundary misalignment. Existing limitations involving non-convex shapes, rotations, lighting, inversion, and video consistency largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a DragBench access link and describes interfaces and example prompts used for the commercial comparisons. Most architecture, hardware, timing, hyperparameter, and pseudocode details already appear in v1 and are retained or relocated to Appendices A.1–A.2.

E1.justification: v2 adds a reported DragBench evaluation for novel-view consistency in Table 4. LAION training, the original 48-image camera-move evaluation, and the overall camera/object-editing task coverage are retained.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 9 adds actual qualitative comparisons against Reve, ChatGPT, and Gemini, substantially extending comparison methods beyond the retained research baselines. GoodDrag, FlowDrag, and Editable Image Elements appear in the related-work matrix but are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The added evaluations introduce LPIPS, quantitative component controls, and systematic sweeps of hint timing, LoRA weight, and mask dilation. The original Table 1 protocol remains unchanged. Figures 18–19 recommend t_end=300, while Appendix A.2 retains the default 500; this does not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 4 quantitatively isolates texture-hint and StableFlow contributions. Figures 18–24 add timing sensitivity, depth-conditioning tradeoffs, dilation analyses, and additional DragDiffusion case studies. These substantially extend v1's predominantly qualitative component and parameter analyses; existing failure cases and vital-layer analysis are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 20 newly reports 95% confidence intervals, and Figure 23 displays additional error bars. v1 has no corresponding uncertainty reporting. The revision does not specify interval construction, seed counts, or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their numerical values. New DragBench results in Table 4 report PSNR 8.42 without hints versus 14.24 with hints; adding StableFlow gives 14.46 but reduces SSIM from 0.658 to 0.654. Parameter sweeps and additional comparative examples supply substantial new findings under their respective settings.

M1.justification: The convex-primitive extraction, depth-conditioned FLUX generation, correspondence-based texture hints, confidence masks, and inpainting procedure remain unchanged. Appendix Algorithms 1–2 match apart from formatting. The additional parameter studies do not establish a new algorithm or component.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten around 3D interaction and geometric consistency. Related work and discussion are condensed, generic diffusion exposition is removed, and technical details and hyperparameter selection move into structured appendix subsections. These are substantial narrative and organizational revisions.

P2.justification: v2 adds comparison and ablation tables, heatmaps, uncertainty plots, and qualitative grids; expands Figure 4; and redistributes existing figures between the main text and appendix. Figure labels and captions are revised, and the document adopts the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds FlowDrag, GoodDrag, and Editable Image Elements, removes several background citations, and introduces Table 3's capability comparison. It also acknowledges 3D aspects of prior dragging methods more explicitly. These refine the existing positioning around editable primitives rather than replace its research context.

T1.justification: v2 omits v1 Section 3.2's explicit forward-noising definition and reverse scheduler-update equation. The convex geometry, back-projection, nearest-neighbor inpainting mathematics, and appendix algorithms remain equivalent. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central texture-hint mechanism: Table 4 provides controlled quantitative ablations where v1 relied mainly on qualitative component comparisons. Figures 18–24 also test parameter choices and expose practical tradeoffs. These gains materially improve validation and guidance, despite unspecified confidence-interval construction and the unresolved t_end=500 versus 300 recommendation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Generative Blocks World. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, algorithms, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds DragBench ablations, parameter studies, confidence intervals, and comparisons with commercial editing systems.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative evaluations in Tables 1–2, qualitative editing comparisons, and appendix analyses of primitive density and vital layers.

results.title: Generative Blocks World: Moving Things Around in Pictures

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same symbolic-subroutine learning and adaptive fast-slow planning claims, including 49.3% cost savings with 3.2% quality degradation relative to CoSTA*. The additional experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: Appendices C, D, and J substantially expand interpretation through overhead amortization, explanations of fallback despite apparently applicable rules, attribution of gains to planning rather than tool access, and generalization versus memorization. Appendix C.1 also newly asserts no quality degradation, more strongly than its Table 7 decline from 0.93 to 0.91 supports.

D1.justification: New Appendix O explicitly assigns LLM roles, including GPT-4o for chain generation, and Appendix J specifies the cache's 5% matching tolerance. However, Appendix O names GPT-o1 for subroutine selection while Section 4.3 still names GPT-4o, creating an implementation ambiguity rather than establishing a model switch. The project link is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on a subset of the independent Complex-Edit benchmark (Table 4), extending the evaluated image data within the existing multi-turn editing domain and 1-8-subtask range. The CoSTA* benchmark, qualitative MagicBrush examples, and external induction data are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds a direct-cache comparator (Table 14) and GPT-4o image editing (Table 15), substantially extending comparisons beyond the original planners and editors. Gemini 2.0, already compared qualitatively in v1 Figure 13, also receives a quantitative comparison. The main Table 3 comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: New experiments restrict FaSTA* and CoSTA* to the baselines' toolsets and supported subtasks (Tables 10-11), introducing important comparison controls. Section 5.3 also tests Qwen 2.5VL 3B for subroutine selection. The original benchmark and human-scoring protocol are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds the smaller-selector ablation, cost-quality learning trajectory, amortized overhead analysis, fallback-reason and category breakdowns, and toolset-matched and caching analyses (Section 5.3; Appendices C, D, J). These substantially extend investigation of robustness, efficiency, and the source of the gains beyond v1's existing ablations.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix K newly reports evaluator-score variance of 0.07; v1 Appendix I supplies scoring rules and averaging formulas without this statistic. No additional seed, repeated-run, confidence-interval, or significance-testing information is reported.

E6.justification: The main Table 3 scores and original ablation values are retained, but substantial new results appear. Complex-Edit results report 55.12 seconds and 0.87 accuracy for FaSTA*, versus 78.27 seconds and 0.89 for CoSTA* (Table 4). Table 15 reports quality scores of 0.91, 0.78, and 0.74 for FaSTA*, Gemini 2.0, and GPT-4o. Further tables add learning, fallback, restricted-toolset, and caching outcomes.

M1.justification: The induction, verification, subroutine selection, and local A* fallback procedures remain unchanged. The new semantic-bucketing wording describes qualitative activation rules already present in v1 Table 7 and Appendix P; the corresponding rule table, algorithms, and prompts retain their substance.

P1.justification: Limited prose edits accompany expanded appendix subsections, updated affiliation and conference-header text, and changed citation and heading styles. Most existing exposition, section sequence, and prompt content remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds eight tables (Tables 4, 7-11, 14-15) and the learning-trajectory Figure 9. It also adopts conference formatting, relocates and resizes retained displays, and consolidates algorithm placement. These constitute substantial display and layout changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion and citations for BLIP-3o, BLIP3o-NEXT, and MuLan. The bibliography also drops references including DeblurGAN and Real-ESRGAN. The central positioning relative to CoSTA* and in-context reinforcement learning remains intact.

T1.justification: The A* cost and heuristic definitions, net-benefit acceptance criterion, and accuracy-aggregation formulas retain their mathematical substance. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: Quantitative external-benchmark validation and the toolset-matched and direct-cache comparisons address important gaps in v1's evidence for generalization and the source of efficiency gains. Learning-cost and fallback analyses also clarify practical tradeoffs. These validation gains substantially improve the paper, although underspecified new protocols, conflicting selector-model descriptions, and overstated quality-preservation language limit the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FaSTA* study. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering and formatting changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Complex-Edit evaluation, restricted-toolset comparisons, caching comparisons, and further analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original FaSTA* quality and execution-time measurements, component ablations, and appendix experiments, including Table 3, Figure 3, and Table 4.

results.title: FaSTA*: Fast-Slow Toolpath Agent with Subroutine Mining for Efficient Multi-turn Image Editing

C1.justification: The abstract's central empty-space confidence claim remains. However, the introduction now advertises end-to-end training with zero training hyperparameters and one inference hyperparameter, and broadens the stated contributions to street, robotics and drone applications. These add substantive capability and scope claims to the earlier two-stage, street-scene presentation.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning aleatoric versus epistemic uncertainty, the region-size dependence of multiplied pixel confidences, recalibration transfer, and ensemble variability. Its limitations replace the earlier two-stage training and efficiency concerns with problems caused by fixed peak patches for large objects and a proposed depth-dependent remedy. The non-interacting-point limitation remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds MMSegmentation integration, the joint output-channel specification, use of preset training settings, and model parameter counts and inference rates. The code-repository reference changes. The A100 hardware disclosure and most earlier UNet implementation details remain, with the latter relocated to Appendix A.5.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only Cityscapes. V2 retains it and adds VisDrone aerial imagery and TiROD robotics scenes covering indoor offices/labs and outdoor gardens with different illumination conditions. Table 2 reports empty-space calibration on both added datasets, substantially broadening the evaluated environments.

E2.justification: CenterNet joins Faster R-CNN in detection comparisons, and both detectors are newly evaluated for void-confidence calibration. V2 also adds a SegFormer semantic-segmentation comparator and evaluates temperature and Platt scaling for segmentation and detection baselines in Appendix A.3. These are actual reported comparisons, beyond the expanded citations.

E3.justification: The Cityscapes split and sampling of 50 test regions per image remain. New recalibration experiments fit on 20% of validation data and evaluate on the remaining 80%, with separate fits for region sizes and additional single-pixel evaluation. V2 adds SegFormer-B5 configurations, false-positive and runtime measurements, and uses a 32-by-32 main-model peak-suppression patch instead of v1's 20-by-20 patch.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's residual-distribution comparison and qualitative examples, v2 adds a peak-size sensitivity study reporting false positives and mAP, post-hoc recalibration experiments with discussion of failure across region sizes, and seed/ensemble robustness analyses. The original Laplace-versus-Gaussian experiment is retained in Appendix A.5 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 provides no repeated-run counts or result uncertainty estimates. V2 Appendix A.4 reports five random-seed trainings of DeepLabv3+ on Cityscapes, mAP of 51.46 ± 0.82, and visualizations of ensemble intensity variability. This introduces uncertainty reporting, but its coverage is limited to one model and dataset.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results for the end-to-end models, additional datasets, recalibration, sensitivity, runtime and ensembling. Main-model Cityscapes mAP is 49.43%, 55.49% and 51.04% for DeepLabv3+, HRNet and SegFormer. V1's two-stage 51.19% and 54.28% results and calibration tables remain in Appendix A.5; the new scores therefore are not same-setting improvements. Separately, Table 1's DeepLabv3+ segmentation ECE at s=1,000 changes from 0.2309 to 0.2245.

M1.justification: V1 implements a separately trained intensity network followed by a UNet-based mark predictor. V2 implements joint, end-to-end prediction of intensity, box dimensions and classes through one network, retaining the earlier architecture in Appendix A.5. Appendix A.4 also introduces ensemble inference by averaging intensity and mark feature maps. The underlying CMPPP framework remains.

P1.justification: The introduction and mathematical exposition are extensively rewritten, method subsections are consolidated, and model design and experimental settings are reorganized. Calibration-related work moves into the appendix, which gains distinct sections for sensitivity, recalibration, ensembling, alternative architectures and visual results. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adds intensity-landscape, ensemble-variability and VisDrone figures and new dataset, ablation and recalibration tables. The original architecture and qualitative figures become Figures 5 and 6; earlier calibration results are regrouped in Table 6, and the Gaussian table becomes Table 7. Figure 3 drops the CMPPP panel, while table formatting, highlighting and the conference layout are revised.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against object detectors, including CenterNet, FCOS, SSD, R-CNN variants, CenterNetv2 and probabilistic detection evaluation through PDQ. It develops distinctions between objectness, intensity and probabilistically derived regression losses. The earlier calibration literature review largely moves to Appendix A.3, where additional uncertainty-based calibration references are introduced.

T1.justification: The central Radon–Nikodym formula and characteristic-function proof are retained. Appendix A.1 corrects the negative-log-likelihood derivation from plus to minus the sum of log intensities and adds an explicit count-conditioning qualification. The marked configuration-space definition is revised, and Equation (7) replaces the incorrectly signed expanded classification term with a negative log-probability expression. These are localized formal revisions.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicitly identified end-to-end training limitation and substantially strengthens the Cityscapes-only study through additional environments, relevant recalibration controls, sensitivity checks, repeated seeds and runtime evidence. Earlier results remain available for comparison. Some interpretations overreach: Appendix A.3 reports fixed-size Platt-scaling ECE of 0.0023 despite broad claims that recalibration cannot repair void confidences. Nevertheless, the gains in methodological completeness and empirical validation constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CMPPP object-detection work, and their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison. Earlier experiments can be matched to v2 Appendix A.5 despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original experiments on Cityscapes, VisDrone and TiROD, plus sensitivity, recalibration, repeated-seed and ensemble results.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A.2 report original Cityscapes calibration and detection results, including experiments with Laplace and Gaussian residuals.

results.title: Towards Reliable Detection of Empty Space: Conditional Marked Point Processes for Object Detection

C1.justification: The corpus contribution and central research questions remain. v2 narrows the trained judge's standing from matching the best model to matching Gemini and approaching GPT-5. The headline informal/formal advantage changes from 11 times to 4 times with the updated comparator, and the best judge is now described as matching human performance.

C2.justification: v1's general contamination caveat and untested generalization warning become detailed, experiment-specific interpretations. v2 argues that contamination has limited impact while acknowledging it cannot be excluded, interprets undergraduate results as evidence of transfer, distinguishes agentic formal systems, and notes that GPT-5 and Grok-4 were evaluated only as judges. These materially expand applicability boundaries and qualifications.

D1.justification: New Appendix D specifies 1,733 training proofs, VERL, learning rate 10^-6, 14,000-token responses, 10 rollouts and batch size 16, alongside evaluation defaults. v2 also expands annotation-process documentation and discloses undergraduate training exclusion. Access instructions change from direct project, dataset and interface URLs to supplementary-material references, with explicit SMT release restrictions; actual external availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The corpus remains 5,062 proofs across 1,010 problems, with the same competition sources. v2 adds explicit undergraduate out-of-distribution judging and judging with supplied official solutions, extending the evaluated population and input conditions within the existing mathematical domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds GPT-5 and Grok-4 while removing Qwen3-30B-A3B and the length-based/random baseline. Section 5.3 replaces DeepSeek-Prover-V2 with Goedel-Prover-V2 as the formal comparator. These changes update both central comparison sets; Seed-Prover is discussed separately and explicitly excluded from direct comparison.

E3.justification: v1 describes the larger best-of-n evaluation as covering the entire subset; v2 specifies 134 problems and discloses 18 exclusions caused by a Swiss-selection bug. v2 also introduces a 560-proof undergraduate judging protocol and a with/without-reference-solution control. Newly supplied training hyperparameters document the existing experiment rather than establishing changed training.

E4.justification: v2 adds undergraduate generalization testing, a reference-solution contamination stress test, difficulty/category breakdowns, and standard-versus-nonstandard competition analysis (Section 5.6 and Appendix C). These substantially expand robustness and diagnostic evidence. The original self-evaluation analysis and qualitative error cases remain, with the latter relocated from Appendix C to E.

E5.justification: v1's main performance plots and judge tables report point estimates without confidence intervals. v2 adds error bars to existing plots and 95% intervals for aggregate and prover-specific judging results in Tables 7–8, specifying the large-sample normal approximation. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPT-5 results of 89.3% pass@1 and 90.8% maj@5, making it the reported leading judge, plus substantial new robustness results. The undergraduate test reports 77.0% maj@5 for OPC-R1-8B versus 72.4% for its base model. Its original 88.1% result remains unchanged. The larger-set discrete-selection value changes from 31.4% to 31.5% alongside the revised subset description, not an established same-setting gain.

M1.justification: The corpus-construction pipeline, GRPO-trained 8B judge and four best-of-n procedures remain unchanged. The original generation, grading and selection prompts match across v1 Appendix E and v2 Appendix I. The added reference-solution prompt supports a diagnostic experiment rather than a revision of the core method.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence and much retained prose remain recognizable. v2 revises the abstract and conclusion, expands explanations of the annotation process, adds Setup/Results-style signposts, and moves Future Work to Appendix F. Original prompts and qualitative examples are largely retained.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a predominantly single-column layout, with redesigned headings and table placement. v1 Figures 6–7 become panels of v2 Figure 6; Table 3 is transposed without changing matched results. New analysis figures and tables, error bars, revised axes and updated overview graphics substantially change the presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2 refocuses the general LLM-judge discussion on mathematical and educational grading, adding Chevalier et al. and Zhao et al. References also expand to Goedel-Prover-V2, Seed-Prover, contamination and the training framework, while several benchmark and self-correction references disappear. The broad positioning of OPC as a human-evaluated proof corpus remains.

T1.justification: The Bradley–Terry probability equation and fitting procedure, independent-judge noise calculation, and ranking-complexity statements remain unchanged. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its trained-judge contribution with sparse training details, point estimates and no out-of-distribution test. v2 addresses these important gaps through explicit training settings, confidence intervals and a 560-proof undergraduate evaluation showing a smaller retained advantage over the base model (77.0% versus 72.4% maj@5). These additions substantially strengthen reproducibility and evidential assessment. Contamination remains unresolved and direct resource links are removed, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Open Proof Corpus study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds undergraduate judging evaluations, reference-solution controls, and analyses of difficulty, problem category and potential contamination.

before.justification: v1 reports original human annotations, proof-generation and judging evaluations, best-of-n experiments, and results for an 8B model fine-tuned on the corpus.

results.title: The Open Proof Corpus: A Large-Scale Study of LLM-Generated Mathematical Proofs

C1.justification: The central claims of enabling SVLM thinking through dynamic SFT/RL switching and achieving cross-domain gains remain. V2 explicitly claims that switching alone provides a standalone stabilizing strategy, presents visual supervision as complementary, and qualifies the abstract's benefits around specialized tasks. This refines contribution attribution and applicability.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive discussion of computation versus annotation cost, helper-model capacity, structured templates and visual supervision as a denoising mechanism. It identifies limits involving abstract semantics, memes and dense scenes, suggesting Pure DyME as an alternative. It also corrects v1's reversed prose attribution of the memorization and exploration ablation drops to agree with Table 3.

D1.justification: V2 supplies visual-fact extraction, refiner and checker prompts, describes the dynamic example pool, and provides supervision-quality and complete training-data examples (S1 and S3). Table 4 adds runtime measurements and the new timing experiment's eight-H800 hardware context. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's brief descriptions; the code-access URL is unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds A-OKVQA for complex-scene/world-knowledge reasoning and GSM8K for text-only mathematical reasoning (Table S6), substantially extending v1's exclusively visual, three-domain coverage. SLAKE, ChartQA and Geo170K-to-MathVerse evaluation are retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds separately reported Two-stage variants with and without KL, reward-threshold switching, cosine SFT annealing and hard-mining SFT budgets (Table 1). Figure S2 also compares CHORD and LUFFY through off-policy influence trajectories, rather than accuracy. These substantially broaden the training-strategy comparisons. LLaVA-1.5's geometry comparison disappears from Table 2.

E3.justification: New protocols include controlled Low/Medium/High CoT supervision, switching-threshold and training-budget comparisons, epoch-based baseline selection, larger base/helper-model configurations, timing measurements and human assessment of 100 randomly sampled ChartQA cases. Original domain splits and sample counts are retained in Table S1. Fact acquisition is now described as automated, although the geometry source remains underspecified as 'Collected'.

E4.justification: V1's component ablation and training curves are retained. V2 adds analyses of supervision quality, switching rules, visual-fact supervision, output templates, training duration, helper size and off-policy influence, plus human evaluation of CoT validity (Tables 1, 4, S2–S5 and S7; Figure S2). Qualitative cases expand, although Figure S4 contains internally inconsistent traces.

E5.justification: V2 newly mentions repeated Two-stage trials and states that DyME achieves its tuning-comparison result in a single training run without epoch selection (S2.2). This is limited run-information disclosure, not evidence of increased repetitions. Neither version reports seed identities, repeated-run dispersion, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The main DyME averages of 55.6, 55.4 and 58.1 and the component-ablation accuracies remain unchanged. V2 adds extensive results, including A-OKVQA 73.0 versus Two-stage 54.2 and GSM8K 55.3 versus GRPO 49.5 (Table S6). Table 2 removes LLaVA-1.5's geometry score of 6.7 and average of 31.3. These are additions and removals, not improvements over matched v1 scores.

M1.justification: The binary SFT/GRPO switch and core losses remain. V2 adds an explicit Pure DyME variant using static supervision and a conventional trace reward, and expands the visual checker from visual-fact recall to include stylistic and structural alignment. V1 already allowed templates to adapt through exploration, so the dynamic example-pool description is largely additional detail.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized into algorithmic validation and full-system effectiveness, followed by efficiency and applicability discussion. Setup information moves into the new supplement. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments themselves.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 3 are redrawn; new main-text validation and efficiency tables and numerous supplementary tables and figures are added. V1's setup Table 1 becomes Table S1, Table 3 is relocated and compressed, and Table 2 loses its parameter-count column. The conference template also changes typography, headers and page composition.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated hybrid-training discussion and positions DyME against CHORD's annealing and LUFFY's off-policy shaping, developed further in S2.2 and Figure S2. This substantially expands the closest-method comparison beyond v1's focus on separate SFT/RL paradigms and two-stage training, alongside additional citations supporting the expanded coverage.

T1.justification: Equations 1–8 retain the SFT/GRPO objectives, gradient comparison, binary switching rule and combined loss. V2 restates the unit-advantage interpretation more briefly but supplies no substantive new derivation, theorem or proof. The appendix primarily adds implementation information and empirical analyses.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the evidence separating switching benefits from supervision quality through controlled Pure DyME experiments, stronger baseline checks and human evaluation of reasoning traces. Detailed prompts address v1's underdocumented visual supervision, while cost and applicability discussions make the claims easier to assess. Some new Figure S4 examples contain contradictory reasoning, and uncertainty estimates remain absent, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DyME by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 adds readable supplementary Sections S1–S3. Shared material can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds controlled training comparisons, additional benchmarks, efficiency measurements and human evaluation of reasoning traces.

before.justification: V1 reports original SVLM training and evaluation across medical VQA, chart understanding and geometry, including performance comparisons, training curves and component ablations.

results.title: Empowering Small VLMs to Think with Dynamic Memorization and Exploration

C1.justification: V2 removes v1's explicit claim to be the first to exploit VLM visual feedback for T2I prompt engineering. It emphasizes atomic semantic preservation more prominently, while retaining the central training-free optimization, semantic-alignment, state-of-the-art performance and broad compatibility claims.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's brief hallucination and latency limitations, v2 discusses multi-object failures, missed VLM errors, long-prompt constraints, evaluator bias, seed stability and multilingual applicability. It also changes the explanation of NeuroPrompts' poor CLIP scores from randomly selected keyword conflicts to restricted keyword diversity. These are substantive additions and revisions to interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies DSG construction details, prompt templates, invalid-output regeneration instructions, keyword examples and selection counts, model-size information, and a code-repository link. Appendix J documents the human-study interface, hidden optimized prompts and randomized image positions. These substantially improve documentation, although v1's explicit disclosure of random NeuroPrompts keyword selection disappears.

E1.justification: The DSG/TIFA benchmarks and existing online-generator demonstrations are retained. Appendices I and K extend coverage to skeleton-conditioned generation, additional complex-scene prompts and Chinese-language generation with Kolors. These introduce new input conditions and language coverage, although their evidence is qualitative.

E2.justification: V1's human study compares optimized prompts only against original prompts; v2 Table 11 additionally compares VisualPrompter against NeuroPrompts, Promptist and BeautifulPrompt. Tables 6 and 10 introduce Qwen3-32B as a comparator, distinct from the retained Qwen2 comparisons. The principal benchmark comparator set otherwise remains unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 adds Janus-Pro to the quantitative generator settings, reevaluates results with Llama-3.2-11B-Vision instead of the feedback VLM, and introduces end-to-end timing and competitor-based human evaluations. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The original benchmark sizes, core metrics and stated 10-annotator/50-sample study settings are retained.

E4.justification: The existing component and decorator ablations are retained. V2 adds seed sensitivity, independent-evaluator robustness, inference-time measurements, explicit failure cases and case studies of complex prompts, Chinese inputs and skeletal conditioning. These examine several limitations and robustness questions untested in the supplied v1.

E5.justification: Appendix H and Table 10 newly report five-seed means and standard deviations for three approaches using SD v1.5 and Flux-dev on DSG. V1 provides no corresponding repeated-run uncertainty reporting. This is a limited statistical addition; it does not establish an increase from a previously specified run count or provide uncertainty throughout the main results.

E6.justification: The retained three-generator semantic, CLIP, aesthetic and component-ablation scores remain unchanged. V2 adds substantial results, including Janus-Pro semantic scores of 82.6 on DSG and 93.7 on TIFA, independent-judge scores, timing and seed summaries. Table 11 newly shows semantic preference for VisualPrompter but frequent aesthetic preference for competitors. Changed CLIP averages reflect adding Janus-Pro, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The core SERE/TSPO procedure remains unchanged: identify missing concepts, expand them, reconstruct prompts and decorate them. Appendix I adds a limited adaptation using ControlNet, skeletal conditioning and VLM feedback on skeleton-image alignment. The newly supplied prompt templates primarily document the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The overview, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten, while related-work and metric explanations are condensed. Detailed result discussion and limitations are reorganized into appendices alongside expanded procedural explanations and explicit cross-references. The title also gains 'Semantic-Aware'.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a single-column conference layout, replaces Figure 1 examples, redraws the pipeline and shortens Figure 3. It introduces a combined benchmark summary and relocates retained detailed results to appendix tables. New procedural diagrams, case-study figures, and timing, uncertainty, human-comparison and evaluator tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting extensions such as Janus-Pro and ControlNet, removes several older references, and drops the first-use claim for VLM feedback. Related-work discussion is condensed, but its central positioning against aesthetic-focused prompt engineering remains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The appendix explanation of DSG construction elaborates the existing concept-question dependency mechanism, and its proportion-of-yes-responses score restates the definition already given in v1.

improvement.justification: The supplied v1 lacks its referenced procedural supplements and uses its feedback VLM for semantic benchmark evaluation. V2 adds concrete prompt templates, an independent Llama-Vision evaluation, direct human comparisons against competitors and five-seed summaries. These substantially strengthen reproducibility and evidential credibility. New human results reveal an aesthetic tradeoff, and some broad superiority language remains, but the validation and documentation gains clearly outweigh these limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisualPrompter, and their text, tables and figures support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A-M.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds generator evaluations, repeated-seed results, independent-evaluator checks and further human comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original DSG/TIFA evaluations, CLIP and aesthetic scores, component ablations, human preferences and generation examples.

results.title: VisualPrompter: Semantic-Aware Prompt Optimization with Visual Feedback for Text-to-Image Synthesis

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the broad claim of predicting unlabeled downstream accuracy with relative difficulty ranking and hard-slice discovery.
