Model selection is narrowed from reliably identifying better variants to coarse screening within a model family before full evaluation. The conclusion also drops its explicit unlabeled accuracy-estimation claim.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes relative hardness from calibrated accuracy, restricts model screening by family/tokenizer, and explains that calibration requires labeled, model- and domain-specific data. It interprets the perplexity comparison as evidence beyond next-token confidence and the squeeze ablation as causal evidence. Appendix C remains unchanged, including its caution that causality is not definitively established.

D1.justification: v2 documents calibration-batch construction, candidate regression models and validation selection, the OLMo checkpoint schedule and burn-in exclusion, and the squeeze weight λ = 0.1. These provide reproduction details for the additions. Existing hardware disclosures, training hyperparameters, search grids, and code-access link are retained.

E1.justification: v2 substantially extends evaluation coverage with HELLASWAG_CHAT, IF_EVAL, and QUAIL controlled-slice experiments in B.1.4, plus GSM8K in the OLMo training-trajectory study. Multilingual MMLU, WikiText, news, PubMed, MATH, and HumanEval were already represented in v1 and are retained.

E2.justification: B.1.2 adds query-text perplexity as a directly evaluated competing hardness signal on the same MMLU and ARC-Challenge correctness slices. v1 reported dispersion for this application without that comparator. Existing training-baseline and attention-versus-FFN comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 20%/10%/70% calibration/validation/test split with 2-percentage-point calibration increments, validation-selected regressors, and zero-shot evaluation of 30 OLMo-7B checkpoints sampled every 20,000 steps from 120,000 to 700,000. v2 also introduces held-out-split testing, Vendi Score measurement, and a reversed-loss control. Retained experiments largely preserve their settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantive tests of held-out generalization and metric robustness (A.4–A.5), calibration and distribution shift (B.1.3–B.1.4), model-selection robustness across training checkpoints (B.2.2), and the effect of deliberately suppressing dispersion (B.4.2). These investigate questions not tested by the corresponding v1 analyses.

E5.justification: The model-selection distance tables gain mean ± standard error reporting: v1 Tables 3–4 become v2 Tables 9–12. Figure 33 also introduces 95% confidence bands. v1 already reported seed-based errors and correlation significance elsewhere; the PDFs do not establish increased run counts for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: New results include calibration MAEs of 1.39, 1.75, and 2.15 percentage points (Table 5), OLMo rank correlations of 0.90 and 0.95, and squeeze perplexity of 101.7 versus baseline 83.0 at 1,000 steps with learning rate 5 × 10^-4 (Table 13). Existing distances also change beyond rounding: Qwen2.5-1.5B Euclidean D–NM changes from 1.54 to 1.4331. Original Tables 1–2 and listed MATH/HumanEval performance scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The dispersion statistic, dispersion-gap score, layer-selection rule, and push-away objectives are retained. Appendix B.1.3 adds a regression-based calibration procedure: fit and validate a mapping from dispersion to accuracy using labeled data, then apply it to unseen data. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 4; the accuracy-prediction application is retitled as hardness ranking. Selected application passages, interpretability discussion, and the conclusion are rewritten or condensed, and an LLM-usage statement and updated author information appear. Most existing prose and appendix explanations are preserved.

P2.justification: The ICLR format changes the title block, headings, running headers, and main-text layout. Table 1 is reorganized with sample sizes across columns, while v1 Tables 3–4 are split into v2 Tables 9–12. New generalization, metric-comparison, and trajectory figures and several new result tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Friedman and Dieng's Vendi Score reference. B.4.3 expands the relationship to already-cited supervised contrastive learning and ContraCLM, explicitly positioning the push-away loss as a simplified contrastive/repulsive regularizer rather than an entirely new idea. The remaining cited literature is retained despite bibliography-format changes.

T1.justification: The dispersion and dispersion-gap definitions, algebraic training objectives, Transformer equations, and uniform-binning algorithm are retained. v2 condenses equations and makes auxiliary-loss notation explicit, but adds no substantive mathematical derivation, formal assumption, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central diagnostic contribution. v1 inferred unlabeled accuracy prediction from controlled correctness mixtures; v2 narrows that claim, compares against perplexity, and separately evaluates calibration requiring labels on disjoint data. New robustness tests and the reverse-loss intervention address important gaps in the original evidence. Remaining perfect-ranking overstatements, strong causal wording, and the inconsistent Figure 22 caption limit the revision, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support and claim precision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same representation-dispersion research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds calibration, alternative-metric, distribution-shift, training-trajectory, and squeeze-ablation experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original dispersion–perplexity analyses, controlled correctness-slice experiments, model and layer comparisons, and auxiliary-loss training results.

results.title: On the Predictive Power of Representation Dispersion in Language Models

C1.justification: The central claims about transferable reasoning from self-play and RAE preventing thinking collapse remain. v3 shifts the headline from Kuhn-only Qwen3-4B results to multi-game gains of up to 10.5 percentage points, explicitly extending the stated applicability to base and instruction-tuned models across Qwen and Llama and to different training stages.

C2.justification: v1 explains random-opponent failure through difficulty producing valid multi-turn trajectories; v3 instead emphasizes the insufficiency of spurious rewards and the adaptive curriculum. v3 adds interpretations concerning SFT data volume and RLVR complementarity, plus limitations concerning environment-design bias, zero-shot evaluation, and reward hacking. The principal transfer and variance-reduction interpretations persist.

D1.justification: v3 adds model-specific training times, details of constructing the 52k-trajectory SFT dataset, and explicit GPQA-Diamond identification. Most implementation details and the GitHub code link remain. However, v1's 512-game evaluation count, randomized starting-player description, and Hugging Face access link are omitted, reducing some reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v3 adds distinct evaluation scenarios: 5x5 TicTacToe, 5-card Kuhn Poker, and 8-resource Negotiation (Table 8). It also introduces Math-12k training for the RLVR experiments in Appendix E.7. Liar's Dice and Connect Four results disappear, although their observation examples remain. Pig Dice and Truth and Deception were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v3 adds Random Policy and Instruct Model comparator rows to Table 5 and a math-RLVR comparator in Table 12. It also adds SFT comparisons for DeepSeek, where v1 compared only the base model and SPIRAL. The original random, Mistral, and Gemini opponent-training baselines remain.

E3.justification: The reported maximum response length changes from 4096 to 8192 tokens. v1 specifies four evaluation rollouts; v3 specifies AVG@32 for AIME24/25 and AMC23 and PASS@1 for other math benchmarks. Additional model configurations, a 52k-trajectory SFT control with one epoch, and pre/post-RLVR schedules expand the protocols. Table 5's stated opponent changes from Gemini-2.0-Flash-Lite to Gemini-2.0-Flash.

E4.justification: v3 adds harder-game generalization tests, an SFT data-volume control, trajectory diagnostics tracking game length, reasoning tokens and role-specific win rates, and a training-order study (Tables 8–12). These test new robustness and explanatory questions. The RAE analysis in v3 Figure 9 redisplays panels from v1 Figure 6 rather than constituting a new ablation.

E5.justification: v1 provides no training-seed comparison or between-run uncertainty reporting. v3 Appendix E.5 explicitly reports rerunning experiments with seeds 14, 42, and 100; Table 10 presents means with uncertainty for Qwen3-4B SFT and SPIRAL. The prose calls these confidence intervals, but their confidence level and construction are unspecified.

E6.justification: Many benchmark values change, alongside substantial new results. Table 9's Qwen3-4B three-game average changes from 42.3 to 44.5, and the two-game variant loses its lead over Kuhn-only training. Table 5 replaces game columns and reports 59.5 rather than 44.9 for the multi-game average. Changed evaluation protocols, game mix, and opponents prevent interpreting these as comparable performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the shared policy, alternating turns, terminal zero-sum rewards, and per-game/per-role exponential-moving-average baselines. Explicit full-response optimization and trajectory notation clarify the existing procedure. The new RLVR-stage experiments combine existing training procedures without changing SPIRAL itself.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites and condenses the narrative. Preliminaries move to Appendix C, experimental settings largely move to Appendix D, and the four research-question sections become a compact results section with an explanatory discussion. Limitations move into an expanded appendix; acknowledgements, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: The paper adopts ICLR formatting and removes v1's cover styling and boxed findings. Tables 1 and 9 expand into grouped model comparisons, Table 5 changes rows and columns, and new tables present the additional studies. The five-panel RAE figure is split between v3 Figures 6 and 9, with extensive resizing and relocation elsewhere.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands related work, including Foundation Model Self-Play, Prover-Verifier Games, Logic-RL, Code2Logic, and strategic agents for Diplomacy, Werewolf, and Avalon. v3 develops an explicit distinction between winning particular games and transferring reasoning beyond games, and incorporates spurious-reward research into its interpretation.

T1.justification: The formal MDP, zero-sum, policy-gradient, and RAE mathematics are retained or relocated. Table 2 makes a limited mathematical correction: v1 claims no solutions for all n >= 4, whereas v3 examines n = 4 and n = 5 separately and includes the valid n = 5 solutions m = 9 and 54.

improvement.justification: The broader model evaluations, larger SFT-data control, harder-game tests, and three-seed comparison address important gaps in v1's evidence for generalization, baseline fairness, and reliability. These substantially strengthen the central empirical case. Reporting defects limit some additions: Table 13 gives a SPIRAL average of 75.91, its prose gives 75.51, and its displayed scores average 75.26; some game-protocol details also disappear. These weaknesses constrain specific results but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in the main validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPIRAL framework and share substantial experimental material. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, allowing relocated material to be matched and substantive changes assessed.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds harder-game evaluations, additional model comparisons, repeated-seed experiments, and studies combining SPIRAL with math RLVR.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning benchmarks, game competitions, training curves, RAE ablations, and reasoning-trace analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: SPIRAL: Self-Play on Zero-Sum Games Incentivizes Reasoning via Multi-Agent Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and four introductory contributions retain their scientific scope. The conclusion now describes the annotations as expert-verified, replacing v1's explicit qualification that they usually lacked secondary review, and omits the explicit second-largest-overall dataset claim. The central dataset, performance, and generalization claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations for photo-based validation, interpretations of RF1 threshold behavior and crown-size differences, and practical model-selection boundaries in Section 5.4. It replaces the single-pass annotation limitation with systematic-review claims and residual-noise cautions. The conflicting annotation histories are not reconciled, so improved underlying annotation quality is not established.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.3 documents annotator preparation, systematic 60 × 60 m grid review, correction, and consensus procedures; Section 3 discloses DSM assistance. Tables 11 and 15 add training and inference settings for the expanded comparisons. The reproducibility statement adds access guidance for raster-level annotations and smaller model variants, while existing hardware and preprocessing details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same SelvaBox rasters and the same five external benchmark datasets, and retain ReforesTree qualitative examples. The additional experiments vary model training and evaluation within existing datasets and resolution levels; they introduce no additional geographic, biome, or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Tables 4–5 expand the corresponding six-row comparisons in v1 Tables 5–6 to fourteen rows. Faster R-CNN joins these cross-dataset comparisons, DeepForest gains SelvaBox-only and multi-dataset trained variants, and a NeonTreeEvaluation-only DINO control is added. The released Detectree2 and DeepForest comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds architecture-by-training-dataset controls with specified training budgets, evaluates fixed-resolution models at other resolutions, and sweeps RF1 matching IoU from 0.50 to 0.95 with independently tuned NMS. It also revises the annotation account from six biologists and usually single-pass annotation to five experts and systematic review. This establishes a reported protocol revision, not when or whether the released annotations were changed.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing resolution ablations and qualitative examples, v2 adds cross-resolution failure analyses in Figures 3 and 8, RF1 threshold sensitivity on four datasets in Figure 4 and Appendix E, and quantitative crown-size distribution comparisons in Appendix F.2. These test robustness and dataset distinctiveness that v1 did not analyze this way.

E5.justification: V1 already reports standard deviations and references multiple seeds without specifying their number. V2 Tables 4–5 explicitly identify three seeds for trained models and single released checkpoints for external models. Appendix F.2 additionally introduces two-sample KS tests, statistics, and p-values. The seed disclosure does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: The original resolution tables, Table 18, and retained benchmark scores are unchanged. V2 adds extensive results for additional training conditions: for example, SelvaBox-trained DeepForest and Faster R-CNN obtain SelvaBox RF1_75 scores of 38.00 and 36.37. It also adds cross-resolution curves, RF1 threshold curves, and distribution statistics in Table 20. These are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The detector architectures, crop-and-resize multi-resolution procedure, raster aggregation, and greedy RF1 computation remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 and Appendix D.1 retain the same procedures. Additional baseline training and annotation documentation do not introduce a new proposed detector.

P1.justification: The introduction, related-work discussion, benchmarking explanations, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and condensation. V2 separates ethical considerations from the conclusion, adds practical advice and a reproducibility statement, reorganizes the appendices, and includes an LLM-use disclosure. These changes substantially revise the narrative beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: V2 expands and groups the main comparison tables, adds relative-gain columns, four RF1 threshold plots, and Table 20. Resolution figures gain cross-resolution curves, and the cross-dataset crown-size histogram becomes a finer-binned line plot. The orthomosaic table moves to the appendix, and conference formatting changes headers, typography, caption placement, and layout.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces v1's assertion that previous research had not evaluated aggregated raster-level predictions with acknowledgment of OAM-TCD's raster-level keypoint recall, positioning RF1 as a detection-based extension. Background references are pruned and relevant satellite, annotation, and statistical sources are added, including Laliberté et al. (2025) and Marsaglia et al. (2003). The broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 adds the approximate KS p-value relationship p ≈ 2 exp(-2nD²) and a sample-size-based argument for extremely small p-values. This is a limited mathematical addition. The RF1 definition, aggregation equations, and matching algorithms remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical case through architecture comparisons using common training datasets, direct resolution-transfer tests, and RF1 threshold analyses. These reduce important gaps in v1's evidence about model versus training-data effects and robustness; expanded protocol and seed disclosures also improve reproducibility. The annotation-review history remains unreconciled, and the validation source for BCI50ha's new threshold sweeps is unclear, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger comparative evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SelvaBox dataset and benchmarking work. Their main text, tables, figures, algorithms, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds trained-baseline comparisons, resolution-transfer tests, RF1 threshold analyses, and statistical comparisons of crown-size distributions.

before.justification: V1 reports original detector benchmarks, resolution and spatial-extent experiments, multi-resolution training results, and cross-dataset evaluations, including supplementary results.

results.title: SelvaBox: A high‑resolution dataset for tropical tree crown detection

C1.justification: The principal dataset, curation-pipeline, eight-model release, and seven-benchmark leadership claims remain. v3 adds an explicit abstract-level claim of strong downstream performance. Its abstract's generative-reward-model comparison largely promotes a claim already present in v1 Section 4.2.

C2.justification: Section 2 replaces broad over-optimization interpretations with qualified statements about inconsistent cross-benchmark gains and limits the loss-modification critique to Gemma-2-27B variants. New appendices interpret intransitive preferences, filtering bias, privacy sensitivity, and differences between reward models and LLM ensembles. The original limitations are largely retained, moving from Appendix A to B.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands documentation of data allocation, composition and licensing, retrieval operations, annotator-model lists, and human annotation staffing, costs, and duration. It also adds budgeting guidance and a repository link. Core training hyperparameters and hardware remain, while complete annotation prompts are still deferred to supplementary material outside the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: The seven original reward-model benchmarks remain, while Appendix H.2 adds downstream policy optimization and evaluation on ArenaHard v1/v2, MT-Bench, and WildBench. Appendix D.3 adds test scenarios with personal information removed or replaced. Newly disclosed language and task distributions describe the existing mixture rather than establish changed training coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds an aggregated LLM-judge comparator, an LLM-plus-reward-model baseline without human guidance, alternative filtering combinations, and base/SFT/official-instruct policy controls in Tables 17 and 19-21. GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet also gain reported participation in PPE Correctness and RM-Bench comparisons previously left blank.

E3.justification: New protocols include policy training on selected hard prompts with two policy backbones, a 500-item human audit of preference attributes, and additional Gemma and Qwen2.5 backbone experiments. Table 3 also changes its metric description from best-of-N accuracy to pairwise accuracy on the best-of-N split, although surrounding prose remains inconsistent. This does not establish that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's retained data and first-iteration annotation ablations, v3 adds an eight-iteration control without human guidance, human verification of kept/flipped labels, broader decontamination checks, PII perturbation tests, attribute-quality audits, and backbone-generalization analysis. These directly examine annotation quality, filtering reliability, and robustness in Appendices D, E, and H.

E5.justification: Both versions primarily report point estimates and retain the single-run training curve. v3 adds no experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. New agreement percentages and self-consistency ensemble sampling do not constitute uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive outcomes, including downstream policy results, 86%/92% human agreement for kept/flipped pairs in Table 19, and an ensemble average of 86.0 versus 88.6 for the final reward model in Table 21. Retained values also change: Table 1 revises Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B-v0.2's RM-Bench score from 72.1 to 64.7, matching v1 Figure 5 rather than establishing a performance decline.

M1.justification: The Bradley-Terry objective, adaptive retrieval rule with k_max = 8, human-guided LLM labeling, dual-reward-model filtering, and flipped-label recycling remain. Section 3 expands the explanation of the two retrieval operations and filtering decisions; the unchanged Figure 3 supports treating these as clarifications rather than a new algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 moves related work from the main text to Appendix A, shortens the conclusion and removes the future-outlook passage, adds Section 4.5, and substantially reorganizes the appendices. It also rewrites the benchmark critique and expands method and ablation explanations, producing a substantial narrative revision beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: Main results are repacked into side-by-side displays, including v1 Figures 5 and 6 reformatted as v3 Tables 4 and 5. Numerous new appendix tables present dataset audits, annotation assessments, downstream results, and controls. The original pipeline diagram and plots are retained; their relocation or renumbering is not new scientific evidence.

R1.justification: The original related-work discussion is largely preserved in Appendix A. v3 adds references and connections concerning intransitive preferences, preference underspecification, mechanism design, and the new downstream/backbone experiments, while removing some earlier citations. Publication and bibliography corrections alone are not substantive positioning changes.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 adds an approximate mathematical cost model summing human-labeling, silver-labeling, and Stage 2 curation costs, together with budget-allocation constraints. This is a limited addition; the Bradley-Terry and adaptive-retrieval equations remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's predominantly offline evaluation with downstream policy results, human checks of filtering decisions, and a multi-iteration control isolating human guidance. Expanded implementation documentation also addresses important reproducibility gaps. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: several new studies omit sample sizes and uncertainty, some scores disagree across tables, and Appendix F.3's worked budget allocates funds inconsistently. The improvement comes from stronger practical validation and auditability, rather than increased length or higher headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Skywork-Reward-V2, SynPref-40M, and the same two-stage curation pipeline. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial appendix expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those results and adds original downstream policy evaluations, human-agreement studies, privacy tests, and filtering and annotation experiments in Appendices D, E, and H.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model evaluations, best-of-N experiments, and data-curation and annotation ablations in Sections 4.2-4.4 and Appendix B.

results.title: Skywork-Reward-V2: Scaling Preference Data Curation via Human-AI Synergy

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on eliminating redundant vertex encoding and improving geometric integrity. v3 explicitly broadens the contribution claims to lossless compression assessed in bits per face and online non-manifold processing plus resampling for scalable training without manual curation. Topology preservation becomes the central framing rather than primarily a beneficial property.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of preprocessing's role in data availability, vocabulary-aware compression efficiency, and the computational rationale for matrix-size filtering. Appendices H and L quantify coverage and attribute failures to the 10k-token ceiling and 7-bit quantization. These extend v1's narrower vocabulary-size and filtering limitations.

D1.justification: v3 adds tokenization pseudocode, implementation clarifications, a newly disclosed 200-layer limit, processing times of approximately 0.3-0.8 seconds per mesh, and details of component visualization using union-find. Core hardware, optimization, augmentation, and training schedules remain unchanged. The v1 checklist's promised code/checkpoint release statement disappears; the PDFs do not establish an actual availability change.

E1.justification: Both versions use Objaverse/gObjaverse, ShapeNetV2, 3D-FUTURE, and Toys4K, with point-cloud-conditioned generation and the same indirect text/image demonstrations. The added Objaverse subsets and ShapeNetV2 examples extend sampling and analyses within existing coverage, without introducing a distinct domain or conditioning task.

E2.justification: The main generation comparators remain EdgeRunner, TreeMeshGPT, and BPT, with DeepMesh compared qualitatively. The new bits-per-face comparison explicitly substitutes raw xyz coding for VQ-VAE vertex compression, adapting the compression comparators (Appendix D.4). v3 also explicitly compares preprocessing with Libigl in Figure 4.

E3.justification: v3 replaces face-number ratio with bits per face and specifies standardized 7-bit, lossless compression comparisons. It adds fine-tuning on approximately 50k meshes versus 13k manifold meshes, evaluated on 1,000 samples, and window-size studies on approximately 250k Objaverse items. EdgeRunner training now explicitly incorporates the proposed resampling strategy; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained resampling ablation, v3 adds the manifold-only versus mixed-data ablation, matrix-window sensitivity studies, quantization-induced topology statistics, and filtering-coverage analyses. Appendices J-L add real-mesh preprocessing comparisons, component-separation analysis against BPT, and generation failure cases.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v1's checklist asserts statistical reporting but cites only quality metrics. Its removal and v3's added descriptive frequency tables do not constitute a change in uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main comparison and resampling-ablation scores are replaced: for example, the proposed method's CD changes from 0.079 to 0.025 and NC from 0.708 to 0.792. FR results disappear. New results include 26.652 bits per face, non-manifold-data ablation scores, and Appendix G-H statistics. These are revised or additional reports, not demonstrated gains under verified identical settings.

M1.justification: The BFS vertex ordering, matrix compression schemes, component tokens, non-manifold partition rules, progressive resampling, and jointly trained transformer/Michelangelo architecture are retained. Comparing Appendices A-C confirms that the newly emphasized preprocessing and lossless coding are existing components; expanded explanations and pseudocode do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method explanations are rewritten. Vertex ordering moves ahead of preprocessing, geometric-property discussion moves into the method section, and experimental subsections are consolidated. The appendices are reorganized and extended, while the NeurIPS checklist is removed.

P2.justification: v3 substantially redraws the vertex-ordering and preprocessing diagrams, removes the earlier redundancy illustration, and adds a geometric-property summary, compression and sensitivity tables, and Figures 23-25. Main result tables are restructured. Earlier generation, resampling, and text/image illustrations are reused, while the conference layout relocates and reformats material throughout.

R1.justification: v3 adds Libigl as an explicit preprocessing reference and develops the distinction between lossless coding and VQ-VAE-based compression. It condenses broader 3D-generation background and removes references such as MVDream and Objaverse-XL. Most central mesh-generation references remain; publication-status updates alone do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: Appendix I.2 adds supporting time and space complexity derivations for vertex ordering and both matrix compressors. The existing stars-and-bars formulation and Euler-based derivation of approximately 2/9 compression are retained without substantive revision.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens areas weakly supported in v1: the vocabulary-aware compression comparison addresses compression fairness, while the preprocessing ablation and parameter studies better substantiate practical design choices. Pseudocode, filtering analyses, and concrete failure cases improve transparency and applicability assessment. Unexplained main-score revisions, absent uncertainty estimates, and an inconsistent frequency entry in Table 9 remain weaknesses, but the added validation and documentation provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mesh tokenization and generation work despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original generation experiments and adds non-manifold-data ablations, parameter studies, dataset statistics, and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original mesh-generation comparisons, a resampling ablation, compression statistics, and qualitative generation results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Topology-Preserved Auto-regressive Mesh Generation in the Manner of Weaving Silk

C1.justification: The introduction adds practical guidelines and application scenarios to the explicit contribution list. The central claims about concept-preserving adversarial generation, higher attack success, and consistency with probabilistic attacks remain substantively unchanged in the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: New Appendix H explains weak transferability through differing victim distributions and proposes an identity-preservation tradeoff. Appendices I and K–L add model-collapse considerations, application scenarios, and mitigation discussions. The new assertion of consistently best transferability is overbroad: Table 10 reports VGG19 top-1 success of 1.15% for OURS (AGGR), versus 1.67% for DiffAttack. The original limitations paragraph is relocated, not newly added.

D1.justification: V2 adds an explicit project URL and descriptions of reproducibility resources. Table 9 documents DDPM sampling with 250 steps and c = 30, alongside baseline sampling budgets, attack steps, and step sizes. Appendix I expands runtime reporting to baseline fine-tuning and per-image generation costs. These are substantive documentation additions, without evidence that the retained procedures changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate identity-preserving targeted attacks using the same 26 DreamBoothPlus concepts and 30 ImageNet target classes. Additional classifiers change model configurations, while the new advertising and physical-patch scenarios are discussed without corresponding experiments.

E2.justification: NCF is added to the existing MobileNet V2 and ViT-Base attack and image-quality comparisons in v2 Tables 11–12 and 16–17; it was absent from the corresponding v1 Tables 7–10. The main comparison set remains NCF, ACA, DiffAttack, and ProbAttack.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes the transfer-success criterion from top-100 to top-5. Appendix Q adds top-1/5/10 evaluations, ConvNeXT and adversarially trained ResNet-50 surrogate configurations, and a ResNet-50 Adv transfer target. The documented dataset sizes and fine-tuning budgets remain unchanged; Appendix P supplies previously unspecified settings.

E4.justification: Appendix Q extends robustness testing to direct white-box attacks on adversarially trained ResNet-50, beyond the earlier transfer evaluations against defended models. Appendix I adds comparative runtime analysis. The sample-selection sensitivity study and qualitative case studies are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: The common-random-number KL estimator and its mean/variance reporting are retained, including identical uncertainty values. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for attack performance.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive top-1/5/10, new-surrogate, image-quality, and runtime results, while omitting the former complete top-100 comparisons. Matched white-box values also change: MobileNet V2 OURS rises from 97.18% to 97.31%, and ViT-Base ProbAttack from 63.33% to 63.85%. The main ResNet-50 white-box results and Table 2 are unchanged. Top-5 and top-100 rates are not directly comparable.

M1.justification: The adversarial distribution in Equation 3, SDXL/LoRA augmentation, diffusion-model fitting, and conservative/aggressive sample selection remain unchanged. The expanded concept definition and newly disclosed sampling settings do not establish an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: The concept explanation is substantially rewritten into separate concept-distribution and distance-distribution subsections, and related work is restructured. Main-text limitations and usage guidelines move to Appendices O and K, while the former additional-experiments appendix becomes Appendix Q. New ethics and reproducibility statements further reorganize the document.

P2.justification: V2 adds the transferability schematic in Figure 6 and new positioning, runtime, and settings tables. Appendix results are reorganized into multi-metric tables with additional comparator columns and surrogate configurations. Existing qualitative image examples are retained, alongside extensive conference-template and layout changes.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially expands positioning through AdvGAN, AdvDiffuser, AdvDiff, NatADiff, and perceptual attacks. New Table 3 distinguishes single-image, identity-level, and class-level capabilities. Additional transferability literature supports Appendix H, extending the earlier discussion centered on Song et al. and ProbAttack.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 changes from a Gaussian variance result in v1 Section 3.2 to a general Gibbs-distribution result in v2 Section 3.4. Appendix A replaces the proof with a derivation showing that the KL derivative with respect to inverse temperature equals the difference in expected distances. Theorem 2 and the KL-estimation derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens justification and reproducibility through the broader conditional theorem and proof, explicit top-1 transfer results, stricter evaluation metrics, defended-surrogate tests, and previously missing sampling and baseline settings. These address important gaps in v1. There are shortcomings: Appendix Q promises top-100 results that its tables omit, and the new transferability discussion overstates consistent superiority. Nevertheless, the gains in theoretical scope, empirical transparency, and reproducibility documentation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and reports additional evaluations using ConvNeXT and adversarially trained ResNet-50 in Appendix Q.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack-success, image-quality, human-evaluation, KL-estimation, and sample-selection experiments in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: Concept-based Adversarial Attack: a Probabilistic Perspective

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: an eight-dataset generative DyTAG benchmark, TDGG/IDGG tasks, multifaceted metrics, GAG-General, and the importance of structural and textual information. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretations of practical utility and semantic quality: synthetic graphs are evaluated as substitutes and augmentation data, and semantic usefulness is distinguished from text length. Section F.14 newly identifies off-domain generation after approximately 5,000 edges and interprets prompt constraints as mitigation, adding a concrete applicability limitation absent from v1.

D1.justification: V2 supplies previously omitted evaluator prompts, detailed scoring rubrics, response formats, and dataset contexts in G.3, and specifies fixed evaluator hyperparameters in D.3/E.4. These substantially improve documentation of a central evaluation component. Most generation settings, hardware details, and generation templates were already present in v1.

E1.justification: The eight GDGB datasets remain unchanged. V2 extends TDGG/IDGG evaluation to all eight DTGB datasets, previously used for structural/text-feature comparisons, and adds generated-graph substitution and cold-start inductive link-prediction scenarios on Sephora, WikiLife, Cora, and WeiboTech (C.5, F.5, F.12).

E2.justification: V2 Tables 8 and 53 add TIGGER-I to the IDGG comparison against VRDAG and DG-Gen in v1 Tables 10 and 46. The existing LLM backbones and DGNN comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 introduces generated-versus-original graph controls, augmentation controls with Average Precision evaluation, intrinsic text-quality measurements, and a 10,000-edge semantic-drift protocol using ten snapshots. Human evaluation uses five annotators and 50 sampled nodes with interactions. The hub case changes from 5,000 to 2,000 edges; core generation budgets and splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Existing memory/reflection ablations, text-feature comparisons, and scalability analyses are retained. V2 adds substantial analyses of intrinsic textual quality, downstream synthetic-data utility, semantic drift with constrained-prompt controls, and human-perceived realism and contextual consistency (C.5, F.5, F.12–F.15).

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates only. V2 Tables 31, 32, and 54 introduce ± uncertainty terms for downstream results, but do not specify their statistical meaning, run counts, or seeds. This establishes a reporting change without establishing additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: Matched core result tables retain their values. V2 adds DTGB generation results, TIGGER-I scores, downstream utility results, drift curves, and human ratings. For example, Table 54 reports augmentation AP gains of 0.027–0.108, and Table 55 reports GPT-based Sephora node/edge human scores of 3.9/4.3. Hub examples are replaced under a different graph size.

M1.justification: The core pipeline, Algorithms 1–2, memory/reflection components, and base generation prompts are retained. V2 Section F.14 additionally evaluates guided generation with domain constraints inserted into node and edge prompts, a limited adaptation of the inference procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much technical prose remain intact. V2 revises introductory, results, and future-work passages, adds an appendix contents list and disclosure statements, and reorganizes appendix material, including moving Broader Impact to the opening Ethics Statement.

P2.justification: V2 adds the text-quality radar chart, hub visualizations, semantic-drift plots, and substantial new comparison, utility, human-evaluation, and evaluator-prompt tables. Earlier figures and discriminative result summaries are relocated or consolidated into appendices, alongside extensive conference-format layout changes.

R1.justification: V2 expands the targeted positioning against DTGB and explains GAG-General’s relationship to GAG in C.5/D.1. References to EvolveGCN, ROLAND, and Disentangled Dynamic Graph Deep Generation are removed. TIGGER was already cited in v1; its new experimental participation is separate from citation changes.

T1.justification: V2 Section F.14 introduces mathematical definitions for pooled snapshot semantic representations and consecutive-snapshot cosine similarity, Equations 1–2. Existing task definitions and structural/embedding metric formulations are retained; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1 largely left synthetic-data utility prospective and assessed generated text through an LLM evaluator. V2 adds direct utility and augmentation tests, human assessment, and semantic-drift diagnosis with mitigation controls, while disclosing the evaluator prompts. These substantially strengthen practical validation, failure characterization, and reproducibility. Underspecified downstream protocols and undefined ± statistics limit the new evidence but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GDGB benchmark, TDGG/IDGG tasks, and GAG-General framework. Their readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable matching across the reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains these experiments and adds downstream utility results, DTGB generation experiments, semantic-drift tests, and human evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original graph-generation experiments, comparisons with DGNNs and generative baselines, memory/reflection ablations, and scalability measurements.

results.title: GDGB: A Benchmark for Generative Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Learning

C1.justification: The central anchoring and few-step generation claims remain, but the abstract, introduction, and conclusion add Chain-JVP as a contribution and claim scalable 14B training with inference reduced from 2×40 to 2–8 steps. Large-model text-to-image generation moves from future work to a demonstrated central contribution, alongside stronger emphasis on trajectory fidelity.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving derivative dominance and catastrophic forgetting, interprets gradient traces and FM loss as evidence for stability and trajectory fidelity, and qualifies the required anchor weight by initialization. Limitations shift toward large-model minimal-step quality and remaining JVP overhead. The earlier explanation of two-step degradation through sampler trajectory mismatch is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds CFG implementation and condition-dropout details, attention differentiation considerations, teaser prompts, and substantial resource documentation. Appendix A.9 specifies 64 A100 GPUs, 5000 steps, batch size 512, and 73 hours for 14B distillation, plus accumulation/offloading options. These expand reproducibility information; the code/model link and promised baseline releases remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained CIFAR-10 and ImageNet tasks, v2 evaluates high-resolution text-to-image generation using Wan2.2 and an in-house image dataset. Section 5 additionally reports transfer to low-noise text-to-video acceleration, although without a dedicated quantitative evaluation.

E2.justification: The existing benchmark comparator sets remain. v2 adds actual qualitative comparisons against Wan2.2 A14B, FLUX.1-Schnell, and FLUX.1-Dev in Appendix A.10, fixed-r MeanFlow variants in Table 4, and a 250-step Euler latency comparison in A.9. These substantially extend the evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: Table 3 changes sCM's reported pretraining/distillation budgets from 800/250 to 600/30 epochs, and distilled MeanFlow/FACM budgets from 800/250 to 800/200. The hyperparameter table changes the CFG cutoff from 0.125 to 0.05, CIFAR-10 dropout from 0.1 to 0.2, and its AdamW beta2 from 0.995 to 0.99. New experiments introduce ten-epoch component comparisons and large-model evaluation protocols. These are reported setting revisions, not proof of reruns.

E4.justification: v2 adds cumulative component ablations, FM-loss-weight sensitivity with and without conditioning adaptation, gradient-norm diagnostics, large-model trajectory-fidelity comparisons, and cosine-loss removal tests (Tables 4–5, Figures 3–4, A.8). The earlier weighting-function comparison table is removed; teacher-quality and distillation-duration analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's sensitivity ranges summarize different settings, while its theoretical variance arguments do not add empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises ImageNet one-step FID from 1.76 to 1.70; two-step FID, CIFAR-10 scores, and Table 2 remain unchanged. Table 3 replaces auxiliary/expanded-conditioning FIDs of 1.93/1.76 with 1.97/1.81 under shorter training budgets, so these are not comparable performance losses. v2 also adds stability, sensitivity, large-model generation, and resource results, including approximately 72GB peak memory for 14B training and 70.2 versus 7062.9 ms image-generation latency (A.9).

M1.justification: The core FM-plus-CM objective and conditioning strategies remain, but v2 introduces module-wise Chain-JVP integrated with FSDP and an arbitrary-endpoint flow-mapping adaptation (Sections 3.3.3 and 4.4). It also adapts attention for large-model JVP computation. The stated norm-L2 denominator changes from sqrt(e+c) to sqrt(e+c^2) (v1 A.2; v2 A.3).

P1.justification: The abstract, background, instability discussion, experimental interpretation, and limitations are substantially rewritten. Method subsections are reorganized, and the from-scratch discussion and weighting explanation move into the appendix. The narrative is restructured around trajectory fidelity and scalability, although much of the original objective derivation remains.

P2.justification: v2 expands the opening teaser, revises the conditioning diagram, adds component/sensitivity tables and gradient plots, and reorganizes the earlier training curves alongside a new fidelity panel. Appendix visualizations add comparative and uncurated text-to-image grids while retaining the earlier ImageNet grids. The weighting-function table and plot are removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around flow mapping, including Align Your Flow, Transition Models, SplitMeanFlow, and flow-map matching. It develops relationships to FSDP, FlashAttention2, and derivative alternatives, and adds Wan/FLUX references supporting the new comparisons. The earlier sCM/MeanFlow discussion broadens into claims about trajectory fidelity and large-model applicability.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.1 presents stability and convergence arguments involving CM-gradient decomposition, network bounds, target variance, and shared-parameter alignment. Appendix A.6 derives the arbitrary-endpoint flow-mapping identity. These are substantial mathematical additions beyond v1's retained total-derivative explanation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's limited direct evidence for the anchoring mechanism through controlled ablations and gradient diagnostics, and addresses previously untested scalability through Chain-JVP, 14B generation, and concrete resource measurements. Reproducibility information also improves. These gains outweigh the removed weighting comparison, although large-model quality comparisons remain qualitative and Appendix A.1 does not justify its key inference that FM regression bounds network norms and parameter sensitivity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FACM and retain corresponding methods and benchmark experiments. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices, including image-only sample pages, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds component and sensitivity experiments, gradient analyses, large-model generation examples, and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 and ImageNet generation results, architecture and stabilization comparisons, weighting ablations, training curves, and generated samples.

results.title: FACM: Flow-Anchored Consistency Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions shift from parallel Bayesian/gradient-flow theories emphasizing elastic coupling to a gradient-flow framework distinguishing fixed-feature fine-tuning and jointly rich learning. New central claims concern multilayer networks, finite-source negative transfer and harmful feature collapse under ultra-rich pretraining. Bayesian theory remains but loses its central billing.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations involving finite-sample noise, crosstalk, representation overfitting and rank-one feature collapse. Hard-to-easy transfer failure is attributed to inherited unsuitable features rather than v1's elastic tethering mechanism. Limitations now emphasize isotropic-data assumptions and restricted quantitative applicability instead of the earlier absence of dataset averaging.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix D adds a 50K-sample Monte Carlo DMFT procedure, Gaussian-field initialization, Euler updates and kernel estimation. However, v1 Appendix B's Langevin temperature, step size and training budget, CIFAR preprocessing and class balancing, A100 hardware and approximately six-hour runtime disclosures are removed. These are documentation changes, not evidence that retained experiments used different implementations.

E1.justification: The main dataset families and linear/polynomial regression tasks remain. v2 adds anisotropic inputs with a power-law spectrum and CIFAR class-pair transfer from {0,1} to {0,9}. The within-Fashion-MNIST scenario and pooled animate/inanimate CIFAR task in v1 Figures 12-13 are absent.

E2.justification: The new fixed-feature analyses explicitly evaluate an uninformative linear-probe reference, L = 1 - ν2, in v2 Figures 1, 6 and 7. v1's displayed controls primarily use uncoupled or randomly initialized neural models. The nonlinear experiments retain their no-pretraining controls; no external transfer-learning algorithm is newly benchmarked.

E3.justification: v2 adds frozen-kernel fine-tuning protocols and replaces several elastic-coupling sweeps with training trajectories. Linear-to-quadratic regression changes from D=75, P2=20 to D=100, P2=100; the He5-to-He2 experiment changes P2 from 400 to 600. The matched CIFAR class-pair experiment changes P1/P2 from 1000/50 to 10000/200. These are different evaluation settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds sensitivity analyses separating signal, noise and crosstalk contributions, examines source richness under different source-data regimes, and tests anisotropic inputs (Figures 6-10). Several earlier gradient-flow coupling sweeps, the coupling-dependent activation analysis and CNN analysis are removed or replaced. Bayesian kernel-alignment analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix B specifies temporal averaging of linear Langevin losses and kernels after 50,000 steps; this estimation detail is omitted for the retained results in v2. The separate nonlinear Langevin averaging schedule survives in v2 Figure 11. Neither version reports independent-run uncertainty or confidence intervals; v2's 50K Monte Carlo samples describe solver particles, not repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds negative-transfer learning curves, source-data-dependent polynomial fine-tuning results and anisotropic-data results. Polynomial and CIFAR gradient-flow curves are replaced under changed settings, preventing direct performance-gain comparisons. Earlier CNN and within-Fashion-MNIST results disappear, whereas the Bayesian plots are largely retained and relocated.

M1.justification: v1's gradient-flow formulation resets the readout and elastically constrains target hidden weights to source weights. v2's stated sequential dynamics carries pretrained fields into target training without that elastic term and introduces general-depth MLP dynamics in Appendix B. The earlier CNN extension disappears, while Bayesian elastic coupling remains in Appendices E-F.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, theoretical exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The main text is reorganized around fine-tuning regimes, Bayesian material moves to later appendices, and a DMFT primer and solver explanation are added. Terminology and source/target richness notation are also revised throughout.

P2.justification: The main figures are substantially redesigned: new fine-tuning grids lead the results, polynomial comparisons are grouped into Figure 3, and CIFAR coupling sweeps become paired training trajectories. Bayesian figures move to Appendix F, new sensitivity plots appear, and several old displays disappear. The conference template, typography and captions are also reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 adds Aminian et al.'s mean-field transfer analysis and references supporting DMFT and dataset averaging. It sharpens the distinction from Tahir et al. around finite source data and revises the Bayesian comparison with prior work. The LoRA discussion and citation disappear, while the main related-work categories remain.

T1.justification: Results 2-4 and Appendix C introduce data-averaged fine-tuning analyses for population, finite-source and ultra-rich pretraining, including new limiting-loss expressions. The finite-source kernel uses an explicit ansatz with unresolved coefficients. Appendix B adds history-dependent deep-network DMFT equations. The Bayesian derivations remain, while the previous CNN derivation is removed.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's explicitly stated lack of dataset averaging through tractable linear transfer models, yielding clearer conditions for beneficial and harmful transfer. New fine-tuning experiments, deep-network equations and solver guidance substantially strengthen the paper's explanatory scope while retaining its Bayesian evidence. The finite-data kernel ansatz and loss of general experimental metadata limit completeness, but do not outweigh these analytical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same transfer-learning research. Their text, equations, figures and complete appendices are readable. Retained Bayesian material can be matched despite substantial restructuring and new gradient-flow analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original Bayesian simulations and reports revised neural-network experiments, additional fixed-feature fine-tuning experiments and anisotropic-data regression results.

before.justification: v1 reports original finite-width Langevin and gradient-descent simulations on synthetic regression tasks, CIFAR-10, MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, including appendix experiments.

results.title: Transfer Learning in Infinite Width Feature Learning Networks

C1.justification: The contribution list and central claims remain the same: per-step candidate sampling and judging improve planning, while click-reward reinforcement learning enables effective grounding without explicit reasoning. The added configurations and benchmarks mainly extend evidence for the retained grounding and agent-performance claims.

C2.justification: Section 5 newly acknowledges a concrete failure condition: difficulty selecting custom foregrounds and backgrounds during image editing. The explanations concerning objective alignment, reasoning in static versus dynamic environments, and cascading failures otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendices B–D substantially expand the short implementation description in v1. They disclose optimizer and rollout parameters, hardware and training times, image/bounding-box resizing, the 70K training sample description, evaluation serving arrangements, and exact grounding, planning, selection and ablation prompts. The linked code/model repository is unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 adds WindowsAgentArena evaluation, extending actual agent task execution to Windows applications beyond v1's OSWorld and AndroidWorld experiments. The three grounding benchmarks are retained. OSWorld-Verified is described as an environment/evaluator refinement, rather than clearly establishing another task domain.

E2.justification: OpenCUA-32B is added to all three grounding comparisons. The agent comparisons expand to include Agent S2.5 and CoAct-1 on OSWorld-Verified, while the new WindowsAgentArena comparison includes Kimi-VL, WAA and Jedi. These are reported comparators, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: The 32B configuration changes from Qwen2.5-VL-32B initialization, a 10^-6 learning rate and batch size 128 to OpenCUA-32B initialization, 10^-5 and batch size 256. v4 drops the proposed 72B configuration and adds GPT-5 planner configurations, OSWorld-Verified evaluation and original-instruction OSWorld-G evaluations alongside refined instructions. These materially change the reported experimental settings.

E4.justification: Table 3 adds paired OSWorld-G instruction-condition comparisons, providing limited evidence about sensitivity to instruction detail: GTA1-7B scores 55.1% with original instructions and 67.7% with refined instructions. The reward ablation, candidate-count/horizon study, AndroidWorld reasoning comparison and two trajectory case studies are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-evaluation run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its results. The rollout counts and newly disclosed parallel environment counts are training/infrastructure settings, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 replace the 32B results, including ScreenSpot-Pro 53.6% to 63.6%, under the changed initialization and training settings; these are not same-setting gains. The 72B results are removed. Table 1 also corrects GTA1-7B's Scientific Text/Icon entries from 31.8/76.4 to 76.4/31.8. New results include 62.0% on OSWorld-Verified for GTA1-32B with GPT-5 and 51.2% on WindowsAgentArena with o3.

M1.justification: Equation (4) changes the stated training loss from an unclipped probability-ratio-weighted advantage to a minimum of unclipped and clipped surrogates. The planning–judging–grounding procedure, annotation filtering and click reward remain unchanged. This establishes a limited revision to the reported objective, without establishing whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction and related work are rewritten and condensed. Implementation information is reorganized into a structured appendix with a contents page and training, evaluation and prompt subsections; the conclusion gains a limitations component. These changes extend beyond simply inserting new results.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with revised model series and an OSWorld-Verified panel. Table 3 expands and identifies instruction conditions, and Table 4 gains a second benchmark column. v4 adds WindowsAgentArena, training-parameter and extensive boxed prompt tables. Figures 5–6 are retained and relocated into the appendix, not new case studies.

R1.justification: v4 adds references supporting the expanded experiments and implementation, including OpenCUA, WindowsAgentArena, CoAct-1, Kimi-VL, additional training datasets and vLLM. The grounding/two-stage/native-agent taxonomy and the main positioning relative to previous reasoning-based grounding work remain intact.

T1.justification: Equation (4) substantively revises the mathematical objective by introducing the clipped surrogate and clipping parameter epsilon. Equations (1)–(3) retain equivalent filtering, reward and normalization definitions despite notation changes. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: Appendices B–D supply crucial training, preprocessing, deployment and prompt information missing from v1, substantially improving reproducibility. Table 3 also identifies instruction conditions previously left unmarked, making comparisons more interpretable. Windows evaluation and a concrete limitation strengthen validation. Stale prose in Section 4.2 and unresolved appendix references remain, but do not outweigh these gains; the higher 32B scores alone do not establish improvement because its configuration changed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GTA1. All pages, including v1's end-of-paper examples and v4's Appendices A–D, are readable, and the methods, equations, experiments and retained figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and reports additional 32B grounding, OSWorld-Verified and WindowsAgentArena results in Tables 1–5.

before.justification: v1 reports original grounding and OSWorld results in Tables 1–4, reward and scaling ablations, and an AndroidWorld experiment in Section 4.3.

results.title: GTA1: GUI Test-time Scaling Agent

C1.justification: The central contribution of perception-aware optimization remains. The abstract and conclusion extend explicit applicability from GRPO to both GRPO and DAPO. The abstract's claimed overall gains expand from approximately 4.4% to 4.4–17.5%, and vision-dependent gains from approximately 8.0% to 8.0–19.1%, reflecting the added comparisons.

C2.justification: v5 adds interpretations connecting PAPO to attention allocation, masking-dependent perception, compatibility with rollout modifications, and robustness to irrelevant images. Appendix N qualifies the perception argument by explaining that correcting perception need not eliminate other reasoning errors. The conclusion also identifies uniform application of the loss to all tokens as a direction for refinement.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly specifies rollout batch size 384, five responses per prompt, and 80 GB GPU memory, while documenting new DAPO and Qwen3 configurations. Section 8 reports a source-code supplement with training and evaluation instructions. Much of the learning-rate, epoch, masking, hardware-count, and timing information was already present; the new disclosures do not establish changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: ViRL39K training and the original eight reasoning benchmarks remain. v5 adds OCR-Bench-v2 for fine-grained visual-text perception and MMLU-Pro with irrelevant random-noise images, extending coverage to a distinct perception task and a strictly vision-independent reasoning scenario (Appendices K–L).

E2.justification: v5 adds evaluated DAPO baselines in Table 1, GRPO plus NoisyRollout in Table 2, and entropy-regularized DAPO in Table 10. These materially expand comparison beyond v1's GRPO-based controls; DAPO and NoisyRollout were previously discussed but not evaluated as these comparators.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce Qwen3-VL-2B-thinking, DAPO settings with an upper clipping threshold of 0.28 and up to 20 dynamic-sampling retries, and new analysis protocols using 100-instance attention samples, 30-instance error samples per dataset, and a stated 60-case follow-up. The retained GRPO experiments keep two training epochs and avg@8 evaluation at temperature 1.0.

E4.justification: v5 adds attention visualizations and entropy analysis, errors distinguishing random from semantic masking, entropy-coefficient sensitivity, regularized-DAPO controls, irrelevant-image robustness, and follow-up of perception-error outcomes. These investigate mechanisms and failure boundaries beyond v1's existing masking, KL-weighting, and collapse analyses, which are largely retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Collapse-comparison error bars and avg@8 accuracy reporting already appear in v1. v5 introduces no stated independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence-interval procedures, or significance tests. The added attention means and medians are descriptive results rather than new uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Original high-weight PAPO results remain as PAPO_G: overall accuracies are still 49.92 and 61.66 for Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 7B. New DAPO/PAPO_D comparisons report 52.40/55.24 and 55.01/63.16, alongside Qwen3, NoisyRollout, OCR, robustness, and analysis results. Detailed low-weight PAPO benchmark rows are omitted, although aggregate ablations remain. These are mostly added comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The perception KL loss, masking, and double-entropy regularizer remain, but v5 adds a substantive DAPO-based instantiation, PAPO_D. Its procedure uses token-level loss averaging and dynamic sampling that excludes all-correct or all-wrong rollout groups (Appendix B). v1 evaluated GRPO and reference-KL removal, explicitly leaving full DAPO integration to future work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method presentation, and results narrative are extensively reorganized around GRPO and DAPO instantiations. Implementation details, reference-KL experiments, computational overhead, and much collapse analysis move into an expanded appendix structure. v5 also adds an appendix contents page and reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: v5 switches from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format, revises the method schematic to display entropy regularization, and expands the main results table and training plots. It adds attention and error-outcome graphics and several comparison tables. Existing masking illustrations and collapse figures are relocated rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: The literature coverage is substantially revised: the standalone general-RLVR discussion is removed, while Appendix P adds comparisons including training-framework approaches such as Semi-off-Policy and Vision-SR1 and newer visual-reasoning systems. Appendix G additionally connects masking findings to masked autoencoders and masked visual modeling. The central positioning around optimization-level perception supervision remains.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds the formal token-normalized PAPO_D objective and its nondegenerate-reward sampling constraint. The original perception-KL formulation and masking mathematics remain substantively intact. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens evidence for portability and robustness beyond v1's GRPO-centered evaluation through DAPO controls, Qwen3, OCR, irrelevant-image testing, and targeted mechanism analyses. The entropy-regularized DAPO control is particularly useful: its 62.27 overall accuracy places PAPO_D's 63.16 in better context than the unstable baseline's 55.01. New reporting inconsistencies weaken Appendix N/Figure 15—the outcome counts total 59 despite a stated sample of 60—but do not outweigh the broader, more diagnostic validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PAPO and contain readable methods, experiments, figures, tables, and appendices. Shared results and analyses can be matched across renaming and relocation, supporting a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: v5 retains original empirical results and adds DAPO, Qwen3-VL, NoisyRollout, OCR, robustness, attention, and error-analysis experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original GRPO/PAPO benchmark experiments, masking and regularization ablations, training dynamics, and manual error analyses.

results.title: Perception-Aware Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list add theoretical guarantees of effectiveness as a central contribution, absent from v1. The stated main evaluation expands from 15 datasets against 15 baselines to 30 datasets against 17 baselines. The underlying claim of a universal detector requiring no target-dataset retraining remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of domain-exclusion robustness, difficulties transferring tuned hyperparameters, t-SNE distortions and the generalization bound's implications. It removes v1's dedicated limitations paragraph while acknowledging GPU-memory constraints in H.10. Its performance discussion shifts from acknowledging IF's AUPRC advantage to claiming best averages, although the full comparison in Table 9 still favors IF on AUPRC.

D1.justification: V2 supplies explicit per-method hyperparameter grids and MetaOD configuration information in Appendix G/Table 8, describes MLP+TF construction, and adds a UniOD code-repository link. These materially expand reproducibility information. Existing UniOD network dimensions, optimizer settings, training epochs and hardware disclosures are relocated to H.2 without substantive changes.

E1.justification: Appendix H.11 adds evaluation on 27 ADBench datasets beyond the original 30-dataset training/testing pool, including CIFAR10, MVTec-AD, agnews and 20news (Tables 18–19). This substantially expands represented data coverage. Reversing the original two groups is separately a protocol change.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparators MetaOD, MLP+TF and LODA, extending comparisons to model selection and another learned approach using historical datasets. ODIM is removed from the reported comparisons. IF, LOF and OC-SVM remain evaluated in Appendix Tables 9–10 despite their omission from the shortened main tables.

E3.justification: The main baseline comparison changes from recommended or published best-performing configurations to grid search on historical datasets, with default configurations retained separately. V2 adds reversed training/testing groups, a 6,000-sample cap for the reversed-group evaluation, domain-exclusion training conditions and partitioned large-dataset testing. UniOD's stated architecture and training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds baseline hyperparameter-sensitivity heatmaps, default-versus-tuned comparisons, historical-domain exclusion, representation visualizations and large-dataset analyses. The bandwidth, historical-dataset-count and subsampling ablation tables retain identical numerical entries after relocation. The separate SVD+MLP architecture ablation in v1 Appendix E.4 is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report means over five runs for the principal comparison. Neither provides seed identities, standard deviations, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's explicit five-run table captions do not establish additional repetitions or a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds tuned-baseline results, reversed-group results and extensive additional evaluations. Newly reported UniOD averages are 78.52/36.69 AUROC/AUPRC on Group II and 74.9/35.7 on the additional 27 datasets. The original main-comparison averages remain 78.93/45.43. Much of v1's default comparison reappears in Table 11, but with altered entries and misaligned labels; these are not evidence of same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The Gaussian similarity matrices, SVD features, parallel GIN/GT architecture, classifier, cross-entropy objective and training augmentation remain unchanged. Appendix H.10 adds a limited inference adaptation: randomly partitioning large datasets into disjoint subsets and applying UniOD independently to each partition.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract and portions of the introduction, methodology and experimental narrative, compresses numbered related-work subsections into shorter paragraphs, and establishes a separate theoretical-analysis section. Algorithm 1 and implementation details move to the appendices, whose organization is substantially expanded and revised.

P2.justification: V2 redraws and relocates Figure 1, adds eight hyperparameter-sensitivity panels and three t-SNE plots, and combines the earlier ablation figures into Figure 4. Benchmark tables are reorganized with colored ranking highlights, and numerous comparison and robustness tables are added. The framework diagram is retained with renumbering. Table 11 introduces malformed and misaligned rows.

R1.justification: The literature coverage is substantially revised: v2 adds heterogeneous-attribute meta-learning and tabular-foundation references, learning-theory sources supporting the new proofs, and recent missing-data, graph and fairness work. Numerous distinct normalizing-flow and ICA references are removed. The central positioning against dataset-specific detection and conventional transfer learning remains.

T1.justification: V1 provides complexity analysis but no generalization theorem. V2 introduces Theorem 4.1, a norm-dependent generalization bound under bounded Lipschitz-loss assumptions, with covering-number, Rademacher-complexity and attention-related arguments in Appendices A–B. The runtime complexity expressions are also revised.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central generalization claim through reversed training/testing groups, source-domain exclusion and 27 additional datasets, addressing v1's reliance on one test group. Historical-data tuning, relevant new comparators and explicit search spaces also improve comparison quality and reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting defects, but conclusions require qualification: Table 9 gives IF higher AUPRC than UniOD (47.59 versus 45.43), and Table 11 contains malformed and misaligned rows.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniOD work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison across renumbering and reorganization. Internal reporting inconsistencies in v2 are observable document issues, rather than extraction gaps.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix H report original detection experiments, reversed training/testing groups, domain-exclusion analyses, large-dataset evaluations and results on 27 additional datasets.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E report original UniOD detection results, runtime measurements and ablations. Some baseline results are borrowed, but UniOD's own empirical results clearly qualify.

results.title: UniOD: A Universal Model for Outlier Detection across Diverse Domains

C1.justification: Both retain the low-data, efficient two-stage RAG contribution. v3 makes difficulty-adaptive RL and zero-shot deep-research generalization central claims, including superiority over selected larger models on BrowseCompPlus. v1 foregrounds optimized ReAct's competitiveness and the argument that large-scale finetuning is unnecessary, without the deep-research contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds mechanism interpretations attributing benefits to stage separation and the stopping reward, interprets generator swaps as supporting modularity, and explains recall saturation through training-budget calibration. v1's explicit unseen-domain and joint-generator limitations disappear from the conclusion; v3 instead discusses transfer evidence and retains a large-scale-supervision caveat in Appendix A.

D1.justification: New Appendix H supplies reasoner prompt templates with and without FINISH, answer-extraction templates including an E5-specific variant, and MBE-judge instructions. These important implementation details are absent from v1. Most training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain. Public code release is still prospective, while v3 removes v1's statement that a code copy was attached for review.

E1.justification: v3 retains the three original multi-hop datasets and adds zero-shot evaluation on BrowseCompPlus, extending coverage to harder deep-research questions. Table 14 also introduces cross-dataset transfer scenarios, whereas v1 primarily trains and evaluates separately within each dataset.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's RAG/ReAct variants, LeReT, Search-R1, and CoRAG comparisons, v3 Table 2 reports IRCoT, Iter-RetGen, Ret-Robust, Self-RAG, O2 Searcher, SimpleDeepSearcher, and R1-Searcher. Table 3 adds BrowseCompPlus comparisons with DeepSeek-R1, Search-R1-32B, Qwen3-32B, and other models.

E3.justification: v3 replaces answer F1/EM/Match with Qwen3-32B-judged MBE and reports an answer-presence recall definition instead of v1's title-based definition. The E5-large/KILT comparison becomes E5-base-v2/FlashRAG Wikipedia evaluation, with revised model and generator configurations. Appendix F changes prompt-optimization examples from 50 to 100, although Algorithm 1 still specifies 50.

E4.justification: The SFT/Explore comparison remains, but v3 substantially extends v1's analyses with Stage-1 removal, alternative rewards, late-stop-penalty removal, and heuristic stopping tests (Tables 7–9). It also adds training-data and inference-budget sensitivity, cross-dataset transfer, tokens/FLOPs/latency analyses, difficulty-conditioned search analysis, and qualitative traces.
