E5.justification: v1 specifies no repeated-run or uncertainty-reporting protocol. v3 Appendix D adds a limited stability study with three independent Stage-2 runs trained on HotPotQA and reports ± values for recall and searches on all three datasets. Table 4 adds search-count dispersion; the precise interpretation of the ± statistics is not explicitly identified.

E6.justification: v1's answer-F1/EM/Match and Support-F1 grids, FrugalRAG-3B results, and E5-KILT results are replaced by substantially different result sets. v3 adds MBE comparisons and numerous transfer, ablation, and compute results. Its BrowseCompPlus Table 3 reports 20.46% accuracy and 7.95 searches for the HotPotQA-trained 7B system. Revised protocols prevent interpreting cross-version scores as matched performance gains.

M1.justification: The two-stage SFT/GRPO framework and 90/10 rollout mixture remain. Section 3.2 revises the reported stopping-reward calculation to use absolute normalized deviation, adds clipping and an unsuccessful-rollout convention, and changes format rewards from ±1 to ±0.5. These are limited reward-level revisions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative are extensively rewritten around RL frugality. Experiments are reorganized into separate main-results, comprehensive-comparison, deep-research, and analysis sections. The original training/metrics/index appendices become a substantially reorganized A–H appendix structure.

P2.justification: v1's dense colored multi-model tables are redesigned into MBE/recall comparisons, with new reward, transfer, compute, and qualitative tables. Its histogram and fixed-budget figure disappear; efficiency bars are redrawn around retrievers, and new budget/data-size plots appear. v3 also adds conference headers, a boxed problem statement, and formatted prompt listings.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands research positioning, adding discussion of question decomposition, Collab-RAG, SimpleDeepSearcher, R1-Searcher, and DRAGIN. It develops more specific contrasts with dynamic retrieval and search-RL methods and newly claims to be the first method jointly accounting for training and inference costs.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces Δ = (h_term − h)/B with Δ = |h_term − h*|/B and operationalizes h* as the first hop reaching the recall threshold. The separate answer and retrieval efficiency definitions become a joint (MBE + Recall)/(2 × Searches) metric. Neither version presents theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited direct evidence for stage separation, learned stopping, and generalization through Tables 7–9, transfer and BrowseCompPlus tests, broader common-retriever comparisons, stability results, and prompt documentation. These strengthen validation and reproducibility. Important weaknesses remain: Table 2 contradicts the claimed top-two MBE ranking on 2Wiki, Figure 3 contradicts consistently improving recall with more data, and prompt-example counts conflict. Despite these reporting problems and the loss of some original model/metric coverage, the new controlled tests resolve substantial evidential gaps.

A1.justification: Both complete PDFs describe the same FrugalRAG research, despite the changed title and expanded evaluation. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark, BrowseCompPlus, transfer, reward-ablation, efficiency, and repeated-run results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results and fixed-budget and SFT/RL analyses on HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue.

results.title: FrugalRAG: Less is More in RL Finetuning for Multi-hop Question Answering

C1.justification: The central claims about ATP-based constraints, generalization of earlier codes, and homeostatic flattening are retained. Section 3.2 adds an explicit claim that the solutions remain robust to differential correlations, including changes across metabolic states, extending their stated applicability beyond v1's independent-noise treatment.

C2.justification: v2 adds biological mechanism explanations in Section 2 and Appendix F. Appendix M substantially qualifies empirical fit because the two conditions contain different cells, and identifies unvalidated calibration stability and local minima. Appendix L.3 distinguishes Gabor homeostasis from still-unverified optimality. Appendix J replaces the earlier high-activity reliability warning with deviations concentrated at lower activity after refitting.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new noise-fitting formula and constraints, and specifies the correlated-noise optimizer's step size of 0.001, 3000 iterations, and penalty settings. Existing NEURON parameters, hardware, runtime information, and the reference to supplementary simulation code are retained.

E1.justification: The mouse visual-cortex data and natural-scene orientation prior are retained. Appendix N extends evaluated noise conditions to differential correlations, including differing correlation strengths across control and food-restricted states. The Gabor extension changes the model configuration within the retained orientation task.

E2.justification: The reference methods remain Ganguli and Simoncelli (2010) and Wang et al. (2016a), corresponding to references [5] and [30] in v1. Tables 2 and 5–7 and Figure 4 retain them; the new likelihood analysis reuses these comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds likelihood-based evaluation using responses summarized from 29 control and 32 food-restricted cells, Gabor-base evaluations, and a numerical correlated-noise protocol. Appendix N uses energy settings 1 and 0.76, correlation strengths up to 1000, and penalty weights 10, 100, and 1000. The original biophysical simulation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's objective, prior, and activity-level analyses, v2 tests homeostasis with Gabor base shapes in Appendix L.3 and robustness to differential correlations in Appendix N. Penalty-weight sensitivity and constraint-error analyses additionally check whether the new broadening results arise from numerical artifacts.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10,000 simulation trials per cell condition. v2 introduces no new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for the authors' results. The added likelihood scores measure fit; neuronal noise dispersion remains a modeled quantity.

E6.justification: Appendix J replaces fitted coefficients and adaptation results, including changing eta0 from order 10^9 to near 1. New results include Gabor firing-rate deviations from -0.45% to -0.31%, likelihoods of -155 for Ganguli and Simoncelli, -107 for Wang, -85 for the proposed model, and -47 with optimized dispersion. Appendix N reports approximately 4% additional correlation-related broadening versus 38% metabolic broadening in its new setting. Figure 9's values are unchanged; its accompanying 2% bound is corrected to 0.2%.

M1.justification: The central homeostasis and energy-constrained optimization remains intact. Appendix H.4 replaces the eighth-degree noise polynomial with a 17-parameter fourth-degree polynomial times an exponential, with nonnegative fitting parameters. Appendix J changes the b2 fit from quartic to quadratic. Appendix N also introduces a correlated-noise adaptation of the optimization.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing exposition remain. v2 moves motivation from the discussion into the introduction, expands Appendix F into a simulation overview, adds explanatory summaries, and consistently clarifies 'firing probability' as 'spike count.' These are targeted revisions rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 10–14 for Gabor responses, correlated-noise sensitivity, and penalty diagnostics. Existing noise-fit and adaptation plots are revised, including Figures 3 and 6–8. The ICLR format changes the title block, headers, table styling, and figure placement, while retained Figure 9 redisplays the same results.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of firing-rate energy proxies in Gutierrez and Deneve, Koren and Panzeri, Koren et al., and Tavoni, while retaining the original positioning. Moreno-Bote et al. (2014) is added to motivate differential correlations. These are localized extensions of related work.

T1.justification: The core propositions and analytical derivations in Appendices A–E are retained. Appendix M adds likelihood derivations and a parameter-calibration formulation; Appendix N introduces correlation-adjusted Fisher information and a penalized optimization formulation. These extend the mathematical treatment without replacing the central closed-form results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central flattening prediction by testing non-Gaussian base shapes, differential correlations, and numerical artifacts that v1 left unexamined. The revised Appendix J calibration also resolves the inconsistency between v1's enormous reported dispersion offset and its near-unit dispersion curves. Appendix M adds quantitative fit comparisons with explicit biological-data limitations. Gabor optimality and calibration stability remain incompletely validated, but the gains in assumption testing, numerical consistency, and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite reformatting and added appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds Gabor and correlated-noise analyses, plus likelihood comparisons using previously published biological data.

before.justification: v1 reports original NEURON simulations, fitted energy-noise relationships, and numerical analyses of tuning-curve adaptation and homeostasis, including in its appendices.

results.title: Homeostatic Adaptation of Optimal Population Codes under Metabolic Stress

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on reproducing existing operating-system interfaces and motivating future adaptive interfaces. v2 makes learning usable interfaces from fabricated demonstrations a central additional contribution, highlighted through the never-installed Doom application in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. This expands the claimed capability beyond reproducing the recorded operating environment.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new memory results as persistent recurrent representations that generalize beyond the training context, and contrasts this mechanism with fixed-context simulators. It adds interpretations of perceptual realism and synthetic demonstrations, plus substantive qualifications about Ubuntu-only coverage, redistribution constraints, and impractical H100 deployment costs. Earlier keyboard failures remain documented in the appendices.

D1.justification: v2 adds baseline adaptation and training details, synthetic-data construction, the DBSCAN clustering identification, extensive frontend/backend demo documentation, and explicit repository and checkpoint access instructions. The main training hyperparameter table is retained. Conversely, v1's 40K-video holdout size, distinct learnable initial states, and zero-valued keyboard-release embedding detail are no longer disclosed; their omission does not prove implementation changes.

E1.justification: v2 adds fabricated desktop interactions combined with VizDoom gameplay to train and demonstrate an application never installed in the underlying environment. It also introduces folder-state retention after delays beyond training and human real-versus-generated video discrimination. These substantially extend the tasks and test scenarios beyond v1's existing Ubuntu GUI evaluations.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares internal variants with random and majority-vote baselines. v2 adds an adapted DIAMOND model and DIAMOND with scheduled sampling to the generation comparison in Appendix A, Figures 7–8. It also adds an evaluated transformer encoder comparator for GPU-memory usage in Table 5.

E3.justification: New protocols include approximately 48-hour single-B200 baseline training, paired human judgments for 10–60-second clips with and without a 40-pixel crop, folder recall at 64/128/256-frame delays after 8-frame training delays, and 150 application-transition sequences with delayed scoring. Existing inference changes from 32 to 2 DDIM steps. The original 730-example evaluation is retained; omission of the earlier 40K-video holdout description does not establish a changed split.

E4.justification: v2 retains the original qualitative failures and training-stage ablations but adds quantitative scheduled-sampling rollout RMSE in Figure 4c, memory generalization beyond the training horizon in Table 2, and transformer-versus-RNN memory scaling in Table 5. Cropped versus uncropped human evaluation additionally tests sensitivity to visual artifacts, while Appendix H adds controlled application-transition diagnostics.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The added evaluations continue to report point estimates. Randomized human trials and additional test sequences change evaluation design rather than uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original 1.6/1.4-pixel cursor errors and 37.7% state-transition accuracy are retained. v2 adds human-identification rates, DIAMOND rollout errors, folder-recall matrices, GPU-memory measurements, and application RMSE/L1 scores; Table 2 reports 62% correct folder-present and 98% correct folder-absent predictions at 256 frames. Reported throughput changes from 1.8 to 18 fps alongside fewer DDIM steps, not under identical settings. The original cursor plot's radial-error series is removed.

M1.justification: The hierarchical LSTM architecture, attention, Gaussian cursor map, diffusion renderer, and four-stage training objectives remain unchanged. Section 6 changes the reported inference procedure from 32 to 2 DDIM denoising steps, a limited inference adjustment. The new demonstrations and evaluations do not establish a new NeuralOS architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially revised around synthetic interface learning. Main-text limitations and related work move into reorganized appendices, and reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-use statements are added. The demo explanation is extensively rewritten, although much of the architecture and training prose remains.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is replaced with a sequence including Doom, and the main evaluation figure drops the radial cursor-error series while adding a rollout-RMSE panel. New Doom, baseline-comparison, and human-interface figures and several substantive tables expand the visual evidence. The data-collection tree moves to the appendix, while existing qualitative examples and the full heatmap are retained and relocated within the conference layout.

R1.justification: The short related-work discussion becomes a substantially broader positioning section in Appendix P. Additions include Prompt-to-OS, Gemini OS, Lambda's NeuralOS, video-generation systems, and newer world models. v2 explicitly distinguishes pixel generation from code-generated interfaces and discusses differences in action conditioning and temporal-state representation, beyond merely moving existing citations.

T1.justification: The autoregressive factorization, recurrent-state equations, Gaussian cursor encoding, renderer conditioning, and pretraining loss are mathematically unchanged. Neither version contains theoretical proofs, and v2's additional memory arguments are conceptual explanations rather than new formal results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for properties that v1 supported mainly through internal variants and qualitative examples: competitiveness, perceptual realism, and persistent state. The DIAMOND comparison, human study, memory tests, and synthetic Doom demonstration directly address these important evidentiary gaps. These gains outweigh the loss of some implementation disclosures, although missing human-participant counts and uncertainty estimates, together with imperfect folder recall, still limit the strength of the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NeuralOS with the same authors, core architecture, and retained experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds human evaluation, synthetic Doom demonstrations, long-term memory tests, DIAMOND comparisons, and resource measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original cursor-localization measurements, state-transition accuracy, training-stage ablations, and qualitative generation results in Section 7 and the appendices.

results.title: NeuralOS: Towards Simulating Operating Systems via Neural Generative Models

C1.justification: The central contributions remain LLM-compatible video generation through MM-RoPE and AR-DF. The abstract strengthens the performance claim from comparability with EMU3, COSMOS-Video2World and OpenSoraPlan to surpassing Show-o2, COSMOS-Video2World and OpenSoraPlan, supported partly by newly reported fine-tuned results.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds an interpretation of AR-DF as mitigating drift and error accumulation, distinguishing this from FramePack's emphasis on forgetting. Appendix E.2 explains differences among RoPE alternatives and acknowledges possible gains from tuning VideoRoPE. Appendix F.1 adds a detailed roadmap and prerequisites for understanding-generation unification, while retaining the original limitations concerning data scale and complex motion.

D1.justification: v2 adds fine-tuning sample counts, controlled-experiment budgets, VideoRoPE's default-parameter disclosure and normalized training-cost information. Most architecture, tokenizer, sequence-formatting and memory-saving details are retained or relocated. A new reproducibility statement promises code, weights and evaluation scripts upon publication alongside the existing repository link; actual availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions cover text-to-image, image-to-video and text-to-video generation using GenEval and VBench, including the same aspect-ratio scenarios. The added small-scale image/video fine-tuning data have no stated distinct domain or population. The proposed understanding tasks in Appendix F.1 are future work, not evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: The GenEval comparison adds numerous methods, including Meissonic, Muddit, SANA 1.5, Fluid, Show-o2 and Lumina-mGPT variants, while removing SD v2.1 and LWM from that table. VBench-I2V adds VideoMAR and VBench-T2V adds NOVA. New controlled comparisons evaluate alternative loss-weighting strategies and U-RoPE, IL-RoPE, VideoRoPE and HoPE.

E3.justification: v2 adds fine-tuning experiments and 512×512 GenEval evaluations, plus controlled 1B-model studies trained for 10k steps on eight H20 GPUs. The reported T2V resolution changes from 448×256×25 to 672×384×25. Table D1 also changes the 3B model's 384p learning rate from 2.5e-5 to 5.0e-5; these reported revisions do not establish which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained validation-loss curves, v2 adds downstream generation comparisons of tube masking against random masking, loss reweighting and diffusion forcing, and quantitative MM-RoPE component and scaling ablations. It also tests alternative RoPE designs, decoding strategies and training efficiency in Tables 5–8 and E4. The earlier aspect-ratio and meta-group analyses are retained in Appendix E.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the experiments. The added tables retain point-estimate reporting, and the existing plotted analyses are unchanged.

E6.justification: The original GenEval scores of 0.601/0.664 remain, while v2 adds fine-tuned 512×512 results of 0.725/0.791. T2V adds fine-tuned totals of 78.17/78.90 and revises the non-fine-tuned 1.5B result under a changed resolution. Show-o's reported GenEval score changes from 0.53 to 0.68. New results also cover masking, RoPE alternatives, decoding speed and training costs; the changed settings preclude treating all differences as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The architecture, MM-RoPE and AR-DF algorithms remain intact, but Section 3.3 adds a final supervised fine-tuning stage using approximately 100k images and 20k videos. Section 3.2 also changes the stated loss targets from unmasked to masked tokens; this corrects the description without establishing that the earlier implementation differed.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and introduction around two challenges and adds an explicit contribution list. It reorganizes related work, mathematical preliminaries, implementation details and analyses between the main text and expanded appendices, moves references before the appendix, and adds ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements. The title also explicitly identifies discrete diffusion.

P2.justification: The two-column body becomes predominantly single-column with inset tables. Benchmark tables gain representation-type columns and fine-tuning annotations, and new design, ablation, comparison and cost tables are introduced. Existing figures and qualitative examples are retained but repositioned; v1 Figure 9 becomes Figure E1, and some new comparison tables are repeated in the appendix.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A substantially expand positioning against alternative RoPEs, LLM-based generators, Diffusion Forcing and FramePack. New citations include HoPE, UniViT, Mogao, Show-o2 and several discrete-diffusion generators. Architectural and RoPE design comparisons make the claimed distinctions more explicit; the earlier image-generation related work is relocated rather than removed.

T1.justification: The RoPE identities, MM-RoPE construction and AR-DF masking equations are retained. Appendix B in v2 reproduces the detailed RoPE preliminaries previously presented in the main text; it introduces no new proof, theorem or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central designs: Tables 5 and 7–8 extend v1's loss-curve evidence to downstream generation metrics and relevant alternatives, while Table 6 directly tests decoding efficiency. Broader comparisons and clearer positioning address important evidential gaps. Higher headline scores involve fine-tuning and changed resolutions, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the added controlled evidence materially improves the paper's overall support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Lumos-1, with matching core methods, experiments and qualitative examples. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds fine-tuned model results, controlled training-strategy and RoPE comparisons, and efficiency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original GenEval and VBench evaluations, masking and RoPE ablations, inference timings and generated examples.

results.title: Lumos-1: On Autoregressive Video Generation with Discrete Diffusion from a Unified Model Perspective

C1.justification: v2's abstract and introduction add wd1++ and the energy-guided diffusion/unlearning interpretation as central contributions. They claim state-of-the-art math performance after 20 training steps and tenfold fewer rollouts. The headline accuracy advantage changes from up to 16% to approximately 59%, although the conclusion retains the older 16% statement.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving energy guidance, unlearning, balanced positive/negative weights, and exponential weighting. Appendix D newly discusses identical-reward groups, text-only applicability, and biased likelihood approximation. Conversely, v1's explicit warning that the negative-weight term may alter the monotonic improvement guarantee is no longer retained.

D1.justification: The original wd1/d1 hyperparameters, reward descriptions, and code link are largely retained. v2 adds implementation disclosures for the extensions, including Math-Verify, 8×A800 hardware, wd1++/MDPO batching and rollout accounting in Table 8, and the 200-step AceCode training recipe. These supplement the existing reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The four original reasoning benchmarks remain. v2 adds code-generation coverage through AceCode-87K training and HumanEval/MBPP evaluation (Appendix C.3), plus OpenR1-derived training data for the wd1++ MATH500 experiments.

E2.justification: Beyond the original LLaDA, diffu-GRPO, and d1 comparisons, v2 Table 3 adds SDPO on GSM8K and TCR and MDPO on GSM8K/MATH500. MDPO is explicitly reproduced. These materially broaden the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 extends Sudoku training from 5,000 to 12,500 steps and adds that evaluation checkpoint. It introduces full-parameter wd1/wd1++/MDPO experiments alongside the original LoRA setting, with a different system prompt and Math-Verify parsing. New protocols also include verifier rewards for wd1++, its 20-step training result, and coding evaluations with specified generation lengths and diffusion steps.

E4.justification: The original SFT and positive-only ablations are retained in v2 Table 4. New analyses examine policy-ratio estimation versus Monte Carlo sample size, positive/negative weight balance, exponential-weight temperature, and a different-seed MATH training trajectory (Figures 1, 2, 4 and Table 9). These substantially extend the tested design and sensitivity questions.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports a MATH trajectory using a different random seed (Figure 4), without adding aggregate uncertainty estimates for benchmark accuracies. The main seed remains 42. v1's explicit description of reward-plot shading as standard deviation over a 50-step rolling window is no longer provided.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces wd1's 256/512-token Sudoku scores of 25.2/24.2 with 76.4/62.8 after longer training; diffu-GRPO's 512-token Sudoku score changes from 9.3 to 11.7. Table 2 changes wd1 runtime from 82.16 to 81.16 seconds per step. New results include full-tuned wd1++ at 84.5% GSM8K and 44.2% MATH500, additional sensitivity results, and coding scores. Most other original Table 1 scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 introduces wd1++ in Section 3.3. It uses clean completions from intermediate denoising steps, estimates advantages and weights over the expanded completion group, and optimizes a step-conditioned objective. v1's wd1 trains on final completions only.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, contribution bullets, likelihood-approximation discussion, and method exposition. It integrates a main-text theory section, moves training-dynamics discussion into Appendix C, reorganizes the appendices, and adds contents, ethics/reproducibility, and limitations sections.

P2.justification: The UCL report is reformatted into the ICLR layout. The opening benchmark bar chart is removed; new policy-ratio and sensitivity plots and a combined results/training-cost display are added. Existing reward and completion-length plots are retained or consolidated in the appendix, and tables are reorganized and expanded beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive ratio-free optimization discussion covering REINFORCE, RLOO, SPG, and d2, positioning wd1 as an off-policy approach. New energy-guidance and unlearning connections, together with SDPO/TCR/MDPO comparisons, significantly expand its relationship to prior and concurrent research.

T1.justification: The original reverse-KL derivation and monotonicity results remain, with renumbering. v2 adds approximation-error bounds, intermediate energy-guidance results, an advantage-weighted concrete-score matching theorem, and an unlearning derivation (Section 4; Appendices A.1, A.3, D.1). The latter contains a sign inconsistency between the log-likelihood penalty in Equation 67 and the DCE expression in Equation 68.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's d1-focused comparisons: it evaluates wd1++ against additional competitors, tests weighting choices, and demonstrates applicability to coding. These additions materially improve support for the method's usefulness and design. The gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent improvement percentages and the new unlearning derivation's sign inconsistency. Longer training and different fine-tuning settings limit direct performance comparisons between versions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same wd1 research, with readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. v2 substantially extends the work; retained content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds wd1++ evaluations, further ablations, and coding experiments in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original wd1 training and evaluation results, baseline reproductions, computational measurements, and ablations in Sections 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: wd1:  Weighted Policy Optimization for Reasoning in Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: v1's abstract, introduction and conclusion claim empirical benefits across multiple modalities; v2 confines the demonstrated benefits to 3D molecular generation. The central contribution remains Gaussian trajectory truncation that improves training and sampling efficiency while preserving trajectory granularity and generation quality.

C2.justification: v2 drops v1's explicit gradient-dilution and overregularization hypotheses, and adds explanations of premature truncation removing useful structure and solver behavior harming molecular diversity. It also interprets the new Gaussianity comparison as explaining earlier molecular cutoffs. The limitation concerning non-zero-mean-invariant images and videos remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, cutoff pseudocode, an MI threshold of 0.1, and Appendix G's backbone, hardware and distributed-training details. It newly explains proportional epoch reduction, including EDM's 3000-to-1650 example. Conversely, v1's explicit 25-step Gaussianity-check spacing is replaced by an unspecified frequency parameter.

E1.justification: Molecular-generation coverage remains QM9 and GEOM-Drugs. v2 Appendix D adds a population-level comparison using 10,000 CIFAR-10 test images and QM9 molecules; v1 contains only the illustrative image-noising comparison in Figure 2. This adds image-distribution evaluation, not image-generation experiments.

E2.justification: DDIM becomes an evaluated comparator and combined accelerator for EDM and GeoLDM in v2 Table 4; v1 only cites it. v2 also reports qualitative comparisons with higher-order DPM-Solver variants in Section 4.4's footnote. The main molecular-generator comparator roster is retained.

E3.justification: Reported trajectory settings change substantially: QM9 GeoLDM+GAGA uses 650 rather than 550 steps, EquiFM baseline/GAGA lengths change from 1000/550 to 200/160, and GEOM GeoLDM+GAGA changes from 650 to 800. New experiments vary cutoffs and apply 2× DDIM acceleration. Table 1 also changes stated baseline provenance from authors' implementations to original publications.

E4.justification: v2 adds cutoff sensitivity experiments testing premature versus delayed truncation (Table 3), a DDIM compatibility study (Table 4), and quantitative analysis of initial molecular versus image Gaussianity (Appendix D). These address cutoff selection, complementary acceleration and the proposed explanation for modality differences, beyond v1's retained qualitative Figure 2.

E5.justification: v1 reports single performance estimates without evaluation counts or uncertainty. v2 Tables 1–2 report GAGA quality means and standard deviations over three evaluations; Tables 3–4 report three-evaluation means. Table 5 additionally reports sample means and variances. These disclosures do not establish independent training repetitions or an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Numerous results change: QM9 EDM+GA/GAGA Valid * Uniq changes from 92.5% to 92.0% at the reported 550-step setting. GEOM GeoLDM's 99.2% atom stability at 650 steps is replaced by 85.9% at 800 steps, so this is not a same-setting performance comparison. The earlier QM9 GeoLDM 550-step 93.3% Valid * Uniq entry survives in Table 3; Tables 3–5 add further results.

M1.justification: The central Gaussian-prior truncation procedure remains. However, per-sample variance normalization changes from 1/d in v1 Equation 10 to 1/(d−1) in v2 Equation 5. As written, v2 Algorithm 1 also returns the second consecutive joint MI/KS passing step, whereas v1 Appendix C.2 selects the earlier of two KS-passing steps.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries and method exposition are extensively rewritten around Gaussian probability paths and Gaussianity rather than data identity. Section 3 is reorganized, experimental subsections are expanded, and the appendices are substantially restructured. The title, terminology, authorship and publication header also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds three substantive tables and an algorithm display, including text-wrapped layouts for Tables 3–4. Main tables are reformatted with shaded GAGA rows and uncertainty-bearing entries. Figures 1–2 retain their underlying illustrations but receive revised labels and captions; the expansion is more than pagination alone.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against adaptive priors, leapfrog initialization, noise-schedule design and alternative molecular generative paths. Its new Relation with Prior Works discussion emphasizes preserving the original probability path and complementing existing accelerators. The original general Gaussian-approximation discussion is largely retained.

T1.justification: v1 Proposition 3 concerns continued Gaussian convergence under VP noise. v2 Proposition 3.1 introduces a covariance/cumulant functional, prefix-dominance assumptions and a cross-distribution cutoff-ordering claim, with substantially new lemmas and derivations in Appendix C. Reverse-posterior formulas are also revised. The earlier zero-centering argument is largely retained in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: The cutoff ablations and DDIM experiments directly address important evidential gaps in v1, while repeated-evaluation reporting and training/hardware disclosures substantially improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh remaining problems: GeoLDM baseline values differ across Tables 1 and 3–4, cutoff definitions are inconsistent, and Appendix C's upper bounds do not establish its claimed MI/KS ordering. The improvement rests primarily on stronger empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Gaussian trajectory-truncation research, renamed GAGA in v2. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original GAGA results in Tables 1–2, truncation and DDIM experiments in Tables 3–4, and Gaussianity measurements in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original molecular-generation quality and computational-efficiency results on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs in Tables 1–2.

results.title: GAGA: Gaussianity-Aware Gaussian Approximation for Efficient 3D Molecular Generation

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on accelerated convergence for Lipschitz-smooth objectives. v2 adds near-optimal guarantees for (L0, L1)-smooth objectives and claims the first adaptive algorithm achieving them. The abstract and contribution list explicitly qualify optimality by additive terms.

C2.justification: v2 explains why geometric stepsize growth matters when curvature varies exponentially, discusses generalized-smooth initialization requirements and additive-complexity tradeoffs, and conjectures that AC-FGM and AdaNAG cannot achieve comparable near-optimal guarantees. v1 primarily discusses AC-FGM's difficulty recovering from small initial stepsizes.

D1.justification: Parameter guidance expands beyond v1's eta0 <= 1/L condition: v2 states eta0 L0 exp(L1||x0-x*||) <= 1 and gives the specific initialization used for Table 1's theoretical comparison. These are analytical prescriptions, not reported implementation settings; no code, hardware, or runtime information is added.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical evaluation tasks. The extension to (L0, L1)-smooth functions concerns theoretical applicability, not evaluated task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. The added AdaNAG discussion and Table 1 compare theoretical guarantees, without adding evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental protocols, data splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, or testing procedures. Revised mathematical parameter conditions do not establish an experimental setting change.

E4.justification: Neither version contains ablations, empirical sensitivity analyses, robustness tests, or case studies. The additional appendix develops convergence proofs.

E5.justification: Repeated runs, seeds, uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, and significance tests are absent from both versions.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance values or empirical findings. The new iteration bounds and theoretical comparison entries are changes to theory and research positioning.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains its update equations, but its required parameter condition changes: Eq. (19) doubles the gamma*theta^2/(1+theta)^2 term, tightening the admissible constants. No algorithm component is added.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and comparison discussion are revised; convergence-rate language is recast as iteration complexity, and B_f notation becomes D_f. The existing narrative and section sequence largely remain, while Section 4 and Appendix C principally introduce new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 with theoretical complexity, optimality, and adaptivity columns, colored checkmarks, and a highlighted proposed-result row. Algorithm 1 moves from page 4 to page 5 without display changes; the overall single-column layout remains.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through AdaNAG and generalized-smooth optimization literature, including Li et al., Gorbunov et al., Vankov et al., and Tyurin. Sections 1.4, 3.2, and 4.2 discuss their guarantees, adaptation restrictions, and novelty relationships. Li and Lan's 2023-to-2025 citation change is a publication update to the same work.

T1.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C add generalized smoothness assumptions, Lemmas 5–8, Theorem 3, and Corollary 3, establishing near-optimal complexity under (L0, L1)-smoothness with initialization-dependent additive terms. Theorem 1 gains explicit descent terms under tighter parameter conditions. Appendix A also expands the positivity proof and corrects the Corollary 1 derivation to retain its distance term.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central adaptivity claim by extending the analysis beyond globally Lipschitz gradients, with new curvature bounds, a near-optimal complexity guarantee, and Appendix C derivations. The strengthened descent analysis and expanded comparisons clarify both applicability and tradeoffs. These gains outweigh localized new errors, notably the reversed smoothness implication in Section 4 and the square-root error in Appendix C.5.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Accelerated GRAAL work, with matching algorithm updates and retained Sections 1–3 and Appendices A–B. The complete text, equations, and appendices support comparison; v2 adds Section 4, Table 1, and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical. Table 1 compares symbolic iteration complexities, and Appendix C supplies proofs. No original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes are reported.

before.justification: v1 contains algorithm development, convergence analysis, and mathematical proofs. References to experimental performance concern prior work; no original empirical results appear.

results.title: Nesterov Finds GRAAL: Optimal and Adaptive Gradient Method for Convex Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the central vulnerability and DIJA effectiveness claims. The introduction adds a preliminary refusal-aware alignment proposal, modestly extending the stated contribution toward mitigation while preserving the original central claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new defense as evidence that dLLMs can be aligned, while discussing capability costs. Appendices B.7 and C.6 explicitly condition applicability on access to edit or remask the assistant response. Limitations now emphasize unseen attack patterns and benign infilling utility, replacing earlier concerns about missing white-box comparisons and limited model coverage.

D1.justification: New documentation covers alignment-data composition, refusal-pair construction, and training inputs and targets (Appendix A), additional victim checkpoints, and model-specific mask syntax and access interfaces (Table 16). The reproducibility statement additionally promises alignment data, weights, and training resources; the PDFs do not establish that these new artifacts are already available.

E1.justification: v2 adds alignment training using 5,000 prompts each from WildGuard and Circuit Breaker, plus benign capability evaluation on GSM8K, GPQA, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, MMLU-Pro, and MMLU (Appendix A, Table 5). The original three jailbreak benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: GCG is newly evaluated in Tables 1-3, adding a white-box comparator that v1 cited but did not test. Zeroshot, AIM, PAIR, ReNeLLM, and the existing Self-reminder/RPO defense comparisons are retained; the comparator extension is concentrated in this additional attack method.

E3.justification: New settings include three code-oriented victim models, an aligned LLaDA variant, component-removal controls, a fixed 50-token mask budget with varying span counts, and auxiliary-model temperature variation. Appendix D.4 adds two human raters assessing 100 responses. Its binary threshold of HS >= 3 is separate from the retained HS=5 jailbreak criterion. Original baseline decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained generation-length and defense analyses, v2 adds prompt-diversity measurements, stability analysis, ablations removing the refinement LLM, masks, or separators, and mask-span constraint tests (Tables 9-12). Human validation of the judge and evaluation of the defense's capability costs add further substantive analyses.

E5.justification: v1 lacks comparable run-variability and human-agreement reporting. v2 newly reports three independent runs with different seeds and temperatures, including means and standard deviations (Table 10). It also adds descriptive distributions and human/GPT agreement, Cohen's kappa, and Pearson correlation (Tables 9 and 18). These runs vary temperature as well as seed.

E6.justification: Original rows in Tables 1-3 are numerically unchanged, while v2 adds GCG, alignment, code-model, and supplementary analysis results. Table 4 newly compares JailbreakBench ASR-e of 81.0% for unaligned LLaDA with 25.0% after alignment. GCG's added 6.7% ASR-e on Dream/HarmBench exceeds ReNeLLM's 6.5%, although the prose retains ReNeLLM's second-best designation.

M1.justification: The DIJA attack procedure remains substantively unchanged, but v2 introduces Refusal-Aware Denoising Alignment in Appendix A. This new defense fine-tunes LLaDA using adversarial prompt/refusal pairs and reconstruction of masked refusal tokens, adding a substantive training procedure absent from v1.

P1.justification: Existing main-text prose is largely retained, with localized language edits, clearer remasking explanations, revised algorithm labels, condensed related-work headings, and author/header updates. The appendix is reorganized, and ethics, reproducibility, acknowledgments, and LLM-use statements are added; the original narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: The original nine figures remain, with some relocated, and Tables 1-3 gain GCG rows. New tables present alignment and utility comparisons, code-model results, diversity, repeated runs, ablations, mask constraints, interface mappings, and human agreement (Tables 4-12, 16, and 18), substantially expanding the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Appendix B.7 substantively positions DIJA relative to autoregressive prefilling attacks, citing Vega and Andriushchenko, while Appendix A.1 frames the defense as an adaptation of Qi's deep alignment approach. References also expand to support new data and models, while LongLLaDA is removed. These additions extend research positioning beyond citation maintenance.

T1.justification: The substantive denoising equations, prompt construction, and probability factorization are retained. v1's separate infilling recurrence is replaced by an equivalent reference to the existing transition equation and clearer notation. The additions introduce empirical procedures rather than new theoretical results or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: The GCG comparison addresses an explicit v1 limitation, while component ablations, stability reporting, and human judge validation substantially strengthen previously unsupported aspects of the evidence. The trained defense, utility evaluation, and explicit access assumptions improve practical relevance and qualification of the claims. Defense generalization remains unresolved, and reporting errors persist, including Table 4 labeling the 96.3-to-33.8 reduction as 22.5 rather than 62.5 points. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same DIJA study. The methods, original experiments, figures, tables, and appendices can be matched despite substantial additions and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and reports additional alignment, ablation, stability, model evaluation, and human validation results in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak experiments across four diffusion models and three benchmarks, including defense evaluations and analyses of generation length and mask count.

results.title: The Devil behind the mask: An emergent safety vulnerability of Diffusion LLMs

C1.justification: The central compression, continuous-query, and tensor-differentiation contributions remain. V2 qualifies nine-digit precision as coordinate-dependent, explicitly limits advertised derivative advantages to single precision, and adds a claim of demonstrated applicability to realistic neutron-star simulation data.

C2.justification: V2 adds query latency as a downstream limitation and interprets the effects of removing overlapping refinement samples. Its stated accuracy floor changes from MAE 1e-8 to relative L2 1e-9, which are different criteria. V1's detailed explanation of SiLU versus periodic-activation stability is omitted.

D1.justification: Appendix G documents the numerical solver, ADM-variable reconstruction, refinement hierarchy, derivative computation, training hyperparameters, and finer-grid evaluation. A new reproducibility statement identifies scripts, configuration files, and environment instructions. The repository URL and hardware specifications were already present in v1.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates analytical Schwarzschild, Kerr, and linearized gravitational-wave solutions. V2 adds an oscillating neutron star evolved with coupled spacetime and hydrodynamics on refinement grids, extending evaluation to a time-dependent, matter-containing numerical solution without an analytical reference. Earlier coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator families remain finite differences, differentiation of analytical solutions, SIREN/WIRE, and ADAM within the corresponding comparisons. The neutron-star experiment extends finite-difference comparisons. Compression methods newly discussed in Appendix E are not experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: Appendix G adds medium-resolution FMR training and evaluation against a finer BSSN simulation over matching domains. It introduces large-batch training settings, ghost-zone and central-difference procedures, and overlap-removing SMR sampling. These substantially extend the evaluation design beyond the retained analytical-grid protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds focused analyses of query time versus network size (Figure 23), removing overlapping coarse-grid samples (Tables 3 and 14), and Bianchi-identity residuals (Table 2). The earlier optimizer, activation, Sobolev, coordinate-choice, tomography, and rollout-error analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: V1's point estimates in Tables 2–3 become estimates with ± terms in v2 Tables 1–2; Figure 3 gains error bars, and Figure 23 describes uncertainty bands. V2 does not define these summaries or report corresponding run counts, so additional runs cannot be established.

E6.justification: Central accuracy and storage entries change: metric-only Schwarzschild relative L2 error changes from 2.37e-7 in v1 Table 2 to (1.08±0.06)e-6 in v2 Table 1, without fully specified comparable run conditions. V2 removes Christoffel-Jacobian and metric-Lie-derivative result rows, adds Bianchi residuals, and reports new neutron-star results, including 2121-fold metric compression in Table 3.

M1.justification: The metric-distortion representation, Sobolev losses, and automatic-differentiation pipeline remain. Appendix G introduces a 256-dimensional Fourier input embedding with frequency scale 0.01 for the neutron-star experiment, constituting a limited architectural adaptation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and condenses the introduction, background, method exposition, experimental narrative, and conclusion. Detailed background and experiments move into reorganized Appendices D–F, while related work, reproducibility, and numerical-simulation material receive dedicated sections.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the differentiation diagram, combines v1's separate Schwarzschild and Kerr orbit figures into Figure 4, relocates many displays into appendices, and restructures the derivative-results table. It adds refinement-grid and query-time plots, numerical-simulation tables, and uncertainty displays.

R1.justification: New Appendix E substantially expands positioning around classical and neural scientific compression, gravitational-physics machine learning, PINNs, and neural operators. Added discussions include TTHRESH, COIN, climate compression, and DINGO, alongside a fuller explanation of field representation versus solving equations or learning solution operators.

T1.justification: Appendix G adds the explicit ADM-to-spacetime-metric reconstruction relation, a central-difference formula, and the nested refinement-box condition. Existing differential-geometric definitions and derivations remain substantially unchanged; the Kerr Kretschmann expression moves from B.2.2 to F.6.5.

improvement.justification: V1's numerical-relativity motivation was supported only by analytical examples. V2 substantially strengthens that foundation with a matter-coupled neutron-star benchmark, finer-simulation validation, compression measurements, and practical query-cost analysis while retaining the earlier diagnostic suite. Expanded positioning and implementation documentation also help. Undefined uncertainty summaries and inconsistent descriptions of overlapping FMR samples remain reproducibility weaknesses, but the added evidence materially improves the paper's empirical relevance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Einstein Fields. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated during v2's extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original analytical-benchmark results and adds neural reconstruction, compression, and timing results for an oscillating-neutron-star numerical simulation.

before.justification: V1 reports original neural-field fitting experiments, derivative-error measurements, geodesic simulations, gravitational-wave reconstructions, and ablations on analytical spacetime solutions.

results.title: Einstein Fields: A Neural Perspective To Computational General Relativity

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden the contribution from one dataset and zero-shot linker design to a dataset family and amortized pharmacophore-conditioned design. v2 claims superior conditional performance across diverse targets without external scoring functions or target-specific retraining, substantially extending v1's narrower demonstrated application claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of vocabulary scaling and its geometry-quality tradeoff. Figure 19 attributes part of docking performance to building-block curation and explicitly cautions that docking only proxies binding affinity. The conclusion calls for experimental synthesis and binding validation. Existing chemistry simplifications and the non-equivariance caveat are retained, although the latter moves to the appendix.

D1.justification: v2 documents pharmacophore preprocessing and conditioning, conditional-baseline inference settings, atom-count sampling, and fine-tuning details. Its new reproducibility statement describes pretrained checkpoints, configuration and evaluation scripts, and custom-dataset generation. The original code/data URLs and hardware information are retained; their relocation is not a new resource release.

E1.justification: v2 adds SynSpace-L, expanding represented chemistry from 93 building blocks and 19 reaction templates to 378 blocks and 26 templates. It also evaluates a distinct pharmacophore-conditioned task on ten targets, including seven from LIT-PCBA, while retaining v1's three fragment-linking targets.

E2.justification: The new conditional-generation comparison evaluates SynFormer, ShEPhERD, and CGFlow-ZS against SynCoGen (Figure 5). Figure 19 additionally compares random SynSpace and FDA-approved molecules as controls. The original Table 1 comparator set, including SynSpace-trained SemlaFlow, and the DiffLinker comparison are retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a ten-target protocol generating 100 molecules per method and target, with baseline-specific conditioning procedures. It adds five-epoch inpainting fine-tuning and controlled larger-vocabulary and edge-sampling evaluations. Section 5.1 also revises the stated diversity metric from Tanimoto similarity to dissimilarity; unchanged Table 1 values do not establish recomputation.

E4.justification: New analyses examine probabilistic versus argmax edge sampling, larger-vocabulary behavior, dataset physicochemical properties, fine-tuning, and hard-to-synthesize chemical features. Figure 19 tests how much docking performance reflects conditioning versus the curated chemical space. The original training and schedule ablations remain as v2 Tables 3–4 rather than being newly introduced.

E5.justification: The statement reporting averages over three random-seed runs for unconditional baselines is retained. v2 adds no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty estimates. Its new docking boxplots summarize variation across generated molecules.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original fragment-linking rows retain their numerical results. Substantial new results include SynCoGen's 86.3% validity and 61%/78% retrosynthesis solve rates in Figure 5, larger-vocabulary outcomes, and fine-tuned inpainting rows in Table 8. These are added experimental results, not same-setting improvements to the retained unconditional benchmark.

M1.justification: v2 adds a pharmacophore-conditioning backbone with a separate feature head, concatenated pharmacophore coordinates, and zero centering weight for pharmacophore features (Section 4.1). It also introduces an inpainting fine-tuning variant. These extend the procedure beyond v1's unconditional generator and zero-shot inpainting, while retaining the original joint diffusion/flow mechanism.

P1.justification: v2 substantially revises the abstract, conclusion, and coordinate-noising explanation, moves main-text pseudocode into Appendix B, and introduces a stepwise training and masking walkthrough. It reorganizes the experimental appendices and adds ethics and reproducibility statements. These are substantial explanatory and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds pharmacophore comparison plots, expanded-vocabulary illustrations, dataset-property plots, training/masking diagrams, and additional analysis tables. Figure 3 is condensed, with its omitted panels incorporated into appendix Figure 14. The original training-ablation table moves to the appendix, the inpainting table gains fine-tuning rows, and the document adopts the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to ShEPhERD, TacoGFN, and LIT-PCBA, and explicitly contrasts its amortized design with CGFlow's reward optimization and target-specific training. Most of the related-work discussion and cited literature remain unchanged; expanded author names and citation formatting are bibliographic presentation changes.

T1.justification: Sections 3.3 and 4.1 add mathematical definitions of pharmacophore feature and coordinate tensors and their mappings into augmented model inputs. The original diffusion objectives, posterior equations, losses, and equivariance qualification remain substantially unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for conditional molecular design and scaling beyond v1's small vocabulary through a new conditioning method, ten-target comparisons, larger-vocabulary tests, and controls separating conditioning benefits from library curation. The explanatory diagrams and reproducibility details also improve assessability. These gains are qualified by lower PoseBusters validity in the larger-vocabulary experiment and the continued absence of experimental synthesis or binding validation; v2 explicitly acknowledges the limits of docking evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SynCoGen, with matching authors, core methods, and retained experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices provide readable equations, tables, and figures, allowing additions to be distinguished from relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds larger-vocabulary experiments, pharmacophore-conditioned generation, fine-tuned fragment linking, and additional chemical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original molecule-generation experiments, training and sampling ablations, conformer evaluations, and fragment-linking results in Tables 1–6 and accompanying figures.

results.title: SynCoGen: Synthesizable 3D Molecule Generation via Joint Reaction and Coordinate Modeling

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: an IBE-derived spectral representation objective, structured exploration through learned features, Atari effectiveness, and extension to multi-step operators. The revised wording and additional evidence do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the automatic covariance-equality interpretation with a goal of orthogonal spectral alignment. Section 5.2 adds explanations based on reward-dependent versus reward-agnostic features, interprets distributional representation learning as important and orthogonality as secondary, and attributes Breakout failures to exploration noise while suggesting mitigation. These substantially expand mechanism discussion and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 adds details about online stochastic optimization, grid-search selection of the representation variance, Online PVN's Random Network Indicator tasks and matched architecture, and computational overhead. Most existing network descriptions and implementation information in Appendix E are retained; these disclosures do not establish a changed SBM implementation.

E1.justification: Section 5.1 changes the reported Atari coverage from 57 to 55 games; Appendix F enumerates the latter. Atari Explore remains, with its nine constituent games now explicitly listed instead of illustrated through examples. No new domain is introduced.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Online PVN with both epsilon-greedy and Thompson sampling. New Table 2 evaluates DQN-loss features with TS, naive-MSE features, and SBM without orthogonality regularization. These substantially extend the comparisons beyond v1's DQN/R2D2 and SBM variants.

E3.justification: New comparisons specify an online PVN protocol with matched architecture and latent dimension, and ablations using a fixed DQN backbone with TS. Appendix E.3 changes the reported setting from sigma_rep = 10^-2 to sigma_rep squared = 10^-2; whether this corrects notation or changes executed experiments is unstated. The 100M-step budget and HNS metrics remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained epsilon-greedy versus TS comparison, new Table 2 tests the spectral objective against naive MSE, learning across a value-function distribution against current-policy-only learning, and removing orthogonality regularization. These provide substantial new evidence about which components account for performance.

E5.justification: Appendix E.2 changes the reported seed count from five to ten. Unlike v1's point-estimate summaries, v2 introduces ± values throughout Tables 1–2 and Appendix F. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting, although the PDFs do not identify these quantities as standard deviations, standard errors, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises scores: SBM+DQN with TS changes from 1.91 to 2.23 overall mean HNS, while SBM+R2D2 with TS changes from 0.67 to 0.61 on Atari Explore. Changed coverage and seed reporting prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. v2 also adds PVN and ablation results, 55-game scores, and approximately 20% computational overhead.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2, the SBM loss, Thompson sampling, residual parameter network, and multi-step/Retrace integration are retained. The newly evaluated loss variants and Online PVN adaptation are experimental comparators, rather than changes to the proposed SBM procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, the method name is standardized, several explanations are expanded, and the main-text multi-step discussion and captions are condensed. Affiliations and publication headers change. Most prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable rather than undergoing wholesale reorganization.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation expands substantially through the new ablation table and 55-game appendix table, plus additional comparator rows and uncertainty displays in Table 1. Existing figures remain, with revised notation, captions, and benchmark labeling. Conference formatting also changes headings, headers, and table placement.

R1.justification: Sections 3.1 and 6 expand positioning against task-agnostic successor/Laplacian representations. New citations include Mahadevan, Touati and Ollivier, Farebrother et al., and Shribak et al. This is a focused extension within the retained IBE, representation-learning, and exploration positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A substantially revises Theorem 1 and its proof. v1 derives singular values from feature covariance alone; v2 explicitly assumes diagonal feature and parameter covariances and derives singular values sqrt(lambda_i * mu_i), with revised factorizations. Section 3.2 removes the covariance-equality assertion. Section 2 also restores the discount factor in the return definition.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects the central spectral relation by incorporating both covariances and making orthogonality assumptions explicit. The new comparator and ablations test the proposed representation objective's contribution, addressing important weaknesses in v1's empirical attribution. Per-game results also expose failures hidden by aggregate scores. The unexplained 57-to-55-game change and undefined ± statistic limit interpretation, but the gains in theoretical justification and empirical scrutiny are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Spectral Bellman Method work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including the revised theorem and added empirical material.

after.justification: v2 reports original Atari experiments, including revised benchmark results, Online PVN comparisons, component ablations, and per-game scores in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original Atari experiments comparing DQN and R2D2 with SBM variants, including aggregate scores and learning curves in Table 1 and Figure 3.

results.title: Spectral Bellman Method: Unifying Representation and Exploration in RL

C1.justification: The abstract narrows complete code-switching elimination from four cases in v1 to one in v2. The central contributions—SAE-based mechanistic analysis, SASFT, and reducing unwanted switching while preserving multilingual capabilities—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix K strengthens the interpretation to bidirectional causal evidence for language-feature control, while Appendix J newly argues that feature identification and SASFT are robust to SAE configuration choices. Conversely, Section 3.3.1 softens v1's Chinese-token interpretation into a predictive association with upcoming switching. The original limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V1 states that its private training data cannot be released and code release is planned. V2 supplies a public-data construction recipe, source/language counts, and a code/data availability statement. Appendices D–E substantially expand evaluation composition, software-stack, model-specific hyperparameter, optimization, and training-time information. External availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: V1 trains on proprietary instruction data; v2 replaces it with a mixture of public sources, including KULLM, Tulu3, WildChat, BelleGroup, Multialpaca, Flores, and GSM8KInstruct (Appendix C). This substantially replaces the training corpus, beyond changing sample counts. The three principal target languages and existing evaluation prompt families remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds SFT+Penalty to the principal comparisons and threshold ablation in Tables 1–3. Its variant experiment also adds SASFTReduce alongside SASFTEnhance in Table 9, enabling a direct comparison absent from v1 Table 4. These additions materially strengthen the comparison set.

E3.justification: Training sets change from 230k/130k to nominal 210k/110k samples. Appendix E replaces shared learning-rate and loss-weight settings with model-specific choices and changes GRPO batch size from 32 to 256. Table 2 switches from Chinese 230k to Chinese 110k training. V2 also adds MGSM accuracy scoring and protocols for the new SAE-configuration and induction experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds feature-consistency tests across SAE widths and sparsities at layers 19–25 (Appendix J), plus controlled feature enhancement on 100 originally non-code-switching samples (Appendix K). Existing layer, feature, threshold, and enhancement analyses receive revised evidence, including a direct reduction-versus-enhancement comparison.

E5.justification: V1's Appendix E and Table 5 report one-tailed two-proportion Z-tests; v2 removes this significance analysis without equivalent tests or confidence intervals. V2 newly discloses eight evaluations per prompt in Table 6. This establishes repeated evaluation reporting, not an increase in training runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced under revised settings. For example, Table 1's large-data Gemma-2-2B Chinese SFT/SASFT ratios change from 1.02/0.32% at 230k to 0.74/0.42% at 210k. These are not same-setting performance changes. V2 additionally reports MGSM accuracy, capability results for further training settings, and new robustness and induction findings.

M1.justification: SASFT retains the same language-feature identification procedure, thresholded pre-activation auxiliary loss, and combined training objective. SASFTEnhance moves from Appendix C to Appendix F without changing its definition. SFT+Penalty is an added comparator, not a modification of SASFT.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative is largely retained. Changes include the SASFT title prefix, localized rewrites, a separate language-feature background subsection, author/header and citation-style updates, and appendix reorganization. The submission checklist is removed and an LLM usage statement added; most substantive expansion consists of new experimental content.

P2.justification: V2 expands main tables with comparator rows and an MGSM column, adds detailed data/settings and capability tables, and introduces SAE-similarity heatmaps and an induction plot. It removes the significance table, redraws Figures 6–7, and adopts a different conference layout with substantially changed display placement.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds Wang et al. and Nie et al. on internal mechanisms of language mixing, and expands SAE references with Shi et al. and Fang et al. V2 also adds detection, data, and software references and removes the statistical-testing reference. The central research positioning remains largely intact.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a mathematical definition of the SFT+Penalty objective in Eq. (10). The existing task, SAE, SASFT, and enhancement-loss definitions remain substantively unchanged; the enhancement loss is merely renumbered. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses a major reproducibility weakness through a documented public-data training recipe and reported code/data access. The token-penalty baseline, direct reduction-versus-enhancement comparison, and new robustness and induction studies substantially strengthen evaluation and mechanistic support. Removing significance tests and retaining overly broad superiority claims despite GRPO wins in Table 1 weaken reporting, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SASFT research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison. Substantial changes to experimental settings can be distinguished from retained content.

after.justification: V2 reports revised original evaluations and additional benchmark results, SAE-configuration analyses, and controlled code-switching induction experiments in Appendices I–K.

before.justification: V1 reports original code-switching evaluations, multilingual benchmark results, and ablations across five models, including additional experiments and significance tests in its appendices.

results.title: SASFT: Sparse Autoencoder-guided Supervised Finetuning to Mitigate Unexpected Code-Switching in LLMs

C1.justification: The central denoising-alignment claim and original MAR improvement claims remain. v2 broadens the claimed applicability to text-conditioned and higher-resolution generation and explicitly claims benefits across 2D, 1D and VQ representations and CNN/Transformer architectures, including settings left untested in v1.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the ImageNet-only and untested-VQ limitations with moderate-scale evaluation and unresolved-theory limitations, while retaining the training/inference discrepancy. It adds interpretations of delayed 1D learning, denoising warm-up, distillation tradeoffs and potential teacher-coverage bottlenecks (Section 6 and Appendices A and D).

D1.justification: New appendices document distillation, 1D/VQ implementations, text conditioning and higher-resolution fine-tuning. v2 also newly documents QK-Norm stabilization and mixed-hardware compute accounting; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. Conversely, v1's explicit center-cropping and input-normalization instructions are omitted.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates class-conditioned generation only on ImageNet. v2 adds MS-COCO text-to-image training and evaluation, introducing a new dataset and caption-conditioning task (Section 5.4 and Appendix C).

E2.justification: v2 adds SD3-VAE to the six-generator tokenizer comparison. Conversely, the ImageNet-256 system comparison removes ADM, VDM++, MaskGIT, MAGVIT-v2, LDM-4, MDTv2-XL/2, MaskDiT and FlowAR-H (v1 Table 3 versus v2 Table 5), substantially changing comparator membership.

E3.justification: New protocols include ImageNet-512 tokenizer adaptation and generator training/fine-tuning, MS-COCO evaluation using FID-30k and CLIP scores, and model-size/token-count sweeps. Text-to-image MAR and SiT train for 800 and 1,000 epochs respectively. The original ImageNet-256 training protocols are largely retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained noise, masking and CFG analyses, v2 adds noise-schedule sensitivity, generator scaling, distillation and CNN experiments, higher-resolution encoder-versus-decoder fine-tuning, 1D training-failure/warm-up analysis, and reconstruction and convergence studies (Table 1, Table 3 and Appendices A–B).

E5.justification: Neither version specifies evaluation seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added training curves and approximate compute ranges do not introduce a stated uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Shared headline results remain unchanged, including MAR-B/L FIDs of 1.55/1.35. v2 adds extensive results for the new experiments: MS-COCO FIDs of 4.97/4.31 for MAR-B/SiT-B, for example, and VQ RandomAR FID improving from its new baseline's 8.48 to 7.03. These are additional comparisons, not improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The original interpolation and masking formulation remains, but v2 adds substantive variants: an auxiliary DINOv2 distillation projector and loss, a 1D latent-token architecture with delayed denoising, and a VQ bottleneck using masking-only denoising (Appendices A.4–A.7).

P1.justification: The title is shortened, related-work and conclusion prose are revised, and implementation, decoder-tuning and limitations material is reorganized into appendices. Much of the original introduction, method exposition and experimental narrative remains; the expansion primarily accompanies new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 adds multiple experimental tables, reconstruction/training plots and four text-to-image sample grids. Retained displays are relocated, comparison tables change structure, and Figure 5 shrinks from twelve samples to six. The document also adopts the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: v2 selectively updates research positioning, adding complementarity with epsilon-VAE and residual-VQ approaches and references supporting new experiments. It removes the explicit classical-DAE comparison and several earlier citations, while retaining the central positioning around downstream-aligned, teacher-independent tokenizer training.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 retain the same mathematical content. Neither version presents theoretical proofs or guarantees; v2's added training-dynamics analyses are empirical, and Appendix D explicitly leaves theoretical explanation open.

improvement.justification: v2 directly addresses two explicit v1 gaps: ImageNet-only validation and untested VQ tokenizers. Controlled extensions, documented training failures and substantially expanded implementation details strengthen evidence for generality and reproducibility. Comparator removals and some overbroad wording are drawbacks: Table 7 claims universal CLIP superiority although SiT scores 24.61 versus VA-VAE's 25.07. These localized weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe l-DeTok, with matching authors, core equations and retained experiments. Their complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite the shortened title and expanded scope.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds higher-resolution generation, MS-COCO text-to-image results, and evaluations of additional tokenizer variants.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation experiments, tokenizer ablations and decoder analyses in Section 5 and Appendices A–B.

results.title: Latent Denoising Makes Good Tokenizers

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds both co-improvement and co-degradation, including the inability of intrinsic metrics to distinguish them. v2 drops the co-degradation contribution and foregrounds systematic multi-model gap verification and stronger comparisons against externally rewarded systems. The central internal-supervision, co-improvement, and curriculum claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 removes the specific warning that unification can improve while both capabilities deteriorate. It adds substantive discussion of task-difficulty confounding, relative gaps versus absolute ability, Qwen's limitations on difficult tasks, and why larger-gap tasks supply more training data. Its mechanism discussion emphasizes shared eNTK dominance, while acknowledging that the origin of this sharing remains unresolved.

D1.justification: v2 adds a detailed hyperparameter table, the full scoring prompt, probability-based image selection details, image sizes, candidate counts, optimizer parameters, batch sizes, loss weights, implementation repositories, and VLMEvalKit usage. Appendix D documents similarity computation. v1's explicit checkpoint-selection rule is no longer stated, but implementation documentation is substantially expanded overall.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's compositional-image tasks, v2 adds GenEval, Science-T2I-S physics/chemistry/biology tasks, and POPE, MMB, SEED, GQA, and MMMU understanding evaluations. It also reports non-spatial relations and broadens training from spatial prompts to multiple compositional subtasks.

E2.justification: v1 Table 3 primarily compares Janus-Pro variants with T2I-R1. v2 retains T2I-R1, adds Hermesflow for Show-o, and reports eight generation-only comparators in Table 1, including SDv1.5, SD-XL-base-1.0, and FLUX.1. Appendix F.3 additionally compares self-improvement against Qwen-assisted SFT.
