E3.justification: v1 documents 700 spatial training samples and 120 training epochs; v2 describes about 6000 candidate prompts and 20 SFT or 30 DPO epochs. Curriculum replay moves from epoch 60 to epoch 10. v2 adds Show-o training settings, difficulty-stratified evaluation, human checking, and exact-match understanding evaluations; v1's spatial-training ID/OOD design is no longer retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds human-versus-Qwen checks, similarity controls supporting the eNTK explanation, single-branch versus joint curriculum-data expansion, and component, replay-timing, and external-reward ablations. Conversely, v1's corrupted-supervision co-degradation experiments and Top-K generation-proxy sensitivity plots are removed, rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Statistical displays change: v1 Figure 8 presents sample-level dynamics with boxplots, while v2 adds error-bar summaries for similarity analyses in Figures 7, 13, 15, and 16. The new bars are not defined. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or benchmark confidence intervals, so additional experimental replication is not established.

E6.justification: Numerous benchmark, human-check, and ablation results are added, while co-degradation results are removed. Janus-Pro SFT's reported texture generation score changes from 44.90 in v1 Table 3 to 53.93 in v2 Table 5; these belong to different training settings and are not a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The operative framework remains internal image scoring, generation-side SFT or DPO with auxiliary NLL, and curriculum replay of previously unusable prompts. v2's algorithms and probability-based selection details expand documentation without establishing a different underlying method. CLO-SFT/CLO-DPO become C-SFT/C-DPO.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, terminology, and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten. Related work moves near the beginning; phenomenon verification, method evaluation, mechanism analysis, and curriculum learning receive separate sections. The takeaway-box structure is replaced, and the appendices are reorganized into six thematic sections with a contents page.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redesigns the visual presentation: the opening example is simplified, multi-model difficulty plots and algorithm blocks are added, and comparison tables gain model groups and supervision indicators. Expanded appendix tables, similarity plots, and qualitative examples replace or supplement earlier displays. v1's corruption figures, curriculum rings, and pipeline diagram are removed.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially reorganized around gap measurement, mitigation, and co-improvement, with stronger positioning against external-assessment and external-supervision approaches. v2 adds works such as Yan et al. on joint understanding/generation benefits and Xie et al. on reconstruction alignment, alongside broader architecture and benchmark literature. References supporting v1's self-correction failure discussion are removed.

T1.justification: v1's single-token dynamics and linear-network case study are substantially revised into multi-token SFT analysis with explicit causal-masking and shared-tokenizer assumptions. v2 adds a DPO proposition and corresponding proofs in Appendices D–E, addressing extensions explicitly left for future work in v1. It also introduces a threshold rule connecting likelihoods to binary understanding decisions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical support through multiple architectures, independent understanding benchmarks, human checking, and targeted ablations. Expanded multi-token/DPO derivations and implementation details also make the central argument more assessable. Removing the co-degradation experiments and intrinsic-metric warning weakens coverage of failure conditions, but the stronger validation of the central self-improvement claims provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same internal-supervision and curriculum-based self-improvement study, despite the revised title. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original multi-model gap measurements, Janus-Pro and Show-o fine-tuning experiments, human evaluations, understanding benchmarks, and ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Janus-Pro experiments on generation, understanding, curriculum learning, learning dynamics, and corrupted-label co-degradation.

results.title: Turning Internal Gap into Self-Improvement: Promoting the Generation-Understanding Unification in MLLMs

C1.justification: The abstract relaxes the blanket claim of calibration improvement 'with no loss in accuracy' to improvement 'while maintaining strong accuracy.' The central contributions concerning joint incentives, calibration generalization, and confidence-based test-time scaling remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix J qualifies v1's forgetting hypothesis by attributing much of the SFT accuracy loss to reversible answer-formatting bias. v2 also distinguishes reward-learning benefits from prompting benefits, qualifies log-score reward hacking as dependent on the setting, explains modest ensemble gains, and discusses misleadingly favorable calibration on high-accuracy datasets.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents learning rates, a 0.1 warmup ratio, one training epoch, and A100/H100 hardware. These are disclosures about retained experiments, not evidence of changed original settings. The abstract adds access information for code, models, and demonstrations, while new experiments document baseline masking, initialization, and prompt interventions.

E1.justification: The original QA and mathematics coverage is retained. Appendix E.2 adds a synthetic five-arm next-draw prediction task with short observation sequences and an optional invalid answer, extending coverage to a controlled stochastic prediction environment. This is a limited diagnostic extension.

E2.justification: v2 adds generation-likelihood selection and weighted-voting baselines to the scaling comparison, RLCR-Log to the scoring-rule comparisons, and full-sequence calibration RL, masked calibration RL, and Abstention-RL in Appendix I. These substantially expand evaluated alternatives; the original Table 1 comparator set remains despite naming refinements.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce OLMo-2-7B-Instruct and Qwen-3-8B configurations, synthetic training on 10,000 examples with zero to five observations, controlled analysis-prompt variants with token-cost measurement, and an SFT prompt intervention. Appendix I specifies distinct baseline initialization, loss masking, and abstention evaluation procedures. Existing benchmark splits and primary evaluation metrics remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct ablations separating calibrated rewards from uncertainty prompting, Brier-versus-log reward-hacking experiments, confidence-distribution analyses, and an investigation of SFT answer-formatting failures. These address mechanisms and failure conditions absent from v1. The earlier classifier-capacity study is retained in Appendix G rather than removed.

E5.justification: The detailed benchmark tables change from point estimates to reporting 95% bootstrap confidence-interval half-widths for accuracy, AUROC, and Brier score in Tables 8–15. ECE remains without intervals. v1 already contains classifier-plot error bars, but v2 substantially broadens explicit uncertainty reporting; this does not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 remains unchanged, but numerous new results cover ablations, baselines, model families, and confidence distributions. The synthetic task reports 34.4% accuracy for RLCR-Brier versus 0% for RLCR-Log. The changed SFT prompt yields 49.8% OOD accuracy versus 43.8%, although Table 7's caption inconsistently says 48%. Some retained appendix estimates also change, including base CommonsenseQA accuracy from 88.9% to 88.6%.

M1.justification: The core RLCR reward, training procedure, SFT warmup, and confidence-based scaling methods remain. Section 4.6 adds a recommended inference variant that omits uncertainty analysis, while Appendix J introduces an answer-formatting instruction for SFT+RLCR. These are limited inference adaptations using existing trained models.

P1.justification: v2 tightens experimental and related-work prose, moves the classifier study from Section 4.5 to Appendix G, relocates training discussion to Appendix K, and reorganizes detailed results into Appendices L and M. Front matter and disclosures are updated. Much of the core exposition, conclusion, proof, and prompts remains intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds reward and synthetic-task displays, reliability histograms, confidence-variability plots, and ablation, baseline, and model-comparison tables. The scaling plot gains two comparator curves and an expanded legend. Existing tables merge shared accuracy cells and accommodate confidence intervals, while training and classifier figures move to the appendices.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references on confidence-weighted self-consistency, abstention rewards, forgetting, GRPO, and OLMo. Appendix I also acknowledges and evaluates an accuracy-preserving masked calibration approach. These refine comparison with prior research while retaining the original four-part related-work organization and central novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Section 2 corrects the logarithmic-loss sign, the spherical score's outcome dependence, and the minimization convention. The consistency formulation is generalized from equality for exhaustive answer sets to a confidence sum at most one, with equality when exhaustive. The central theorem and Appendix A proof are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence supporting RLCR. Direct reward-versus-analysis ablations and relevant RL-calibration baselines address important attribution and comparison gaps in v1, while additional model families test broader applicability. Bootstrap intervals, essential training details, and the SFT formatting investigation improve transparency and interpretation. The Table 7 caption discrepancy limits precision for that result but does not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RLCR study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained material across substantial additions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original ablations, synthetic prediction experiments, additional model evaluations, and calibration-baseline comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL training and evaluation on question answering and mathematics, alongside test-time scaling, classifier, and confidence-consistency experiments in Section 4 and Appendix D.

results.title: Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty

C1.justification: The central claim that reflective prompt evolution can outperform RL with fewer rollouts is retained. The abstract revises the average GRPO advantage from 10% over four tasks to 6% over six tasks, and the introduction expands the stated applications to adversarial prompt search.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of cross-model transfer and distractor-induced literal answer-formatting failures. It removes v1's dedicated limitations discussion, including qualifications about data-rich regimes, omitted exemplar optimization, and possible prompt/weight integration. Some existing caveats, particularly Merge budget allocation and preliminary kernel results, remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-release URL, monetary costs in Appendix E.3, reflection-model call counts in Table 4, and implementation details for Trace/TextGrad and full-parameter GRPO. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Much of the original setup is simply relocated to Appendix E.

E1.justification: The main evaluation expands from four benchmarks to six by adding AIME-2025, with earlier AIME questions for optimization, and LiveBench-Math. v2 also introduces an adversarial distractor scenario on AIME. The original four benchmarks and both kernel-generation benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds evaluated comparisons with Trace/OptoPrime, TextGrad, and MIPROv2-No-Demos. Table 3 adds BeamSearch to the candidate-selection comparison, and Figure 11 adds full-parameter GRPO. These substantially broaden v1's comparisons with MIPROv2, LoRA-GRPO, and greedy candidate selection.

E3.justification: New protocols include math-specific splits and single-step ChainOfThought systems, Qwen-to-GPT prompt transfer, and GPT-5 Mini adversarial evaluation. The full-parameter GRPO experiment uses a separately specified two-hop HoVer system and new training settings, including eight GPUs and FSDP2; it does not replace the original three-hop comparison.

E4.justification: v2 adds a beam-search ablation testing Pareto selection, cross-model transfer analysis, and a full-parameter GRPO comparison probing the LoRA restriction. Adversarial search adds robustness testing and manual analysis of formatting failures. Existing generalization-gap, prompt-length, search-tree, and intermediate-prompt analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 reports five evaluations per AIME-2025 problem, including five generations per problem in the adversarial study, and specifies LiveBench's shuffle seed as 0. These are new reporting details and evaluation repetitions, not evidence of increased optimizer-run counts. Neither version provides confidence intervals or statistical significance tests.

E6.justification: The original four-task scores and kernel results are retained, while substantial new results appear. Qwen3-8B GEPA scores 32.00 on AIME versus GRPO's 38.00; transferred prompts achieve a 62.03 aggregate on GPT-4.1 Mini; adversarial prompts reduce GPT-5 Mini AIME pass@1 from 76% to 10%. Revised six-task aggregates are not same-coverage performance changes.

M1.justification: The core GEPA algorithms, reflection meta-prompt, Pareto selection, and Merge procedure are retained. Section 5.2 adds a limited adversarial adaptation: reversing the reward to minimize pass@1 while constraining prompt edits to preserve the task and necessary information.

P1.justification: v2 substantially condenses and rewrites the introduction, method exposition, and related work. Evaluation setup and results are consolidated, detailed settings move to Appendix E, applications are regrouped, and appendices are reordered with an outline. The limitations section is removed and an LLM-usage disclosure is added.

P2.justification: The original combined results table becomes expanded model-specific Tables 1–2; the ablation table is extended, and Figure 11 and Table 4 are added. Figure 1 replaces HoVer with an already reported IFBench panel. Revised margins, extensive figure relocation, and regrouped appendix displays substantially change presentation.

R1.justification: Related-work positioning expands to verbal reflection and self-refinement, adversarial evolutionary search, and agent-policy evolution through works including Reflexion, Self-Refine, Trace, Rainbow Teaming, and Agent-Pro. APO, math-benchmark, and SkyRL references are also added; FrugalRAG and Search Wisely are removed.

T1.justification: The compound-system formalization, optimization objectives in Equations 1–2, and mathematical content of Algorithms 1–4 remain equivalent. Explicitly describing GEPA's weights as frozen clarifies the existing method. No substantive new theorem, proof, or derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for GEPA's comparative advantages through relevant competing optimizers, a beam-search control, cross-model transfer, and math results that expose an AIME exception. Figure 11 addresses v1's untested full-finetuning comparison, although on a separately specified two-hop HoVer system. New cost, code-access, and reflection-call disclosures improve auditability. These gains outweigh the loss of the dedicated limitations discussion, which weakens qualification of the broader claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GEPA research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds math benchmarks, additional optimizer comparisons, cross-model transfer, full-parameter GRPO evaluation, and adversarial prompt-search results.

before.justification: v1 reports original optimizer comparisons on four benchmarks, candidate-selection ablations, and NPUEval and KernelBench experiments.

results.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The benchmark, longitudinal data, two-track novelty, and benefits of user-oriented fine-tuning remain the central contributions. v2's abstract and introduction additionally claim a substantial human–agent capability gap, supported by its newly reported human study.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning generalization, negative cross-track transfer, the importance of history and time, agreement between Sim2 and user preferences, and possible reuse of identical tasks. Its limitations no longer state that generalization was untested or training used only 1,000 episodes. Appendix A.3 also discusses realistic interaction noise and regional applicability.

D1.justification: v2 documents participant demographics, quality and privacy checks, training-set selection, and construction of the new experimental variants and human studies. It directs code and data access to GitHub instead of the anonymous-code and Kaggle links. Conversely, v1's Qwen-VL-Max/PaddleOCR action-repair recipe disappears. These are documentation changes; the PDFs do not establish when the underlying collection procedures changed.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the Chinese Android benchmark with 21,437 episodes, 506 apps, and two principal tracks. v2 adds a cold-start scenario without historical intents and a multiple-suggestion probability task. The unseen-user/app/intent experiments partition existing coverage rather than introduce external datasets.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen-2.5-VL-72B and Qwen-QVQ-Max to both tracks, a human reference for suggestion, and GPT-4.1-based AutoDroid and AppAgent for execution. Qwen-QVQ-Max also replaces GPT-4.1 in the fine-tuning comparison table. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds rank-64 and 16,000-episode fine-tuning settings, held-out evaluations with retraining on 14,706 episodes, a 20-annotator/400-episode human baseline, and five-point preference ratings over 200 episodes. Its probability experiment changes success to top-three matching and revises similarity scoring. Reported collection settings also change from 91 participants and one-to-two months per participant to 95 and one month.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained screenshot-count and action-length analyses, v2 adds training-size/rank sensitivity, unseen-user/app/intent tests, cross-track and joint-training comparisons, history/context ablations, probability-output analysis, human validation of Sim2, and a control excluding identical historical tasks. These address several previously untested mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The added user-rating averages and predicted intent distributions do not introduce uncertainty estimates for experimental results.

E6.justification: Matched original baseline and 1,000-episode/rank-4 fine-tuning scores remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive results, including Qwen-QVQ-Max's 12.8% suggestion success and the 16,000-episode/rank-64 model's 26.0% suggestion and 15.5% execution success; these are new configurations, not same-setting gains. Tables 8–14 add supplementary outcomes, and the validation category count changes from 0 to 27.

M1.justification: The core task formulations and separately fine-tuned agents remain. Appendix A.6 adds limited procedural variants: joint training across tracks, DeepSeek-V3 summarization of relevant intents from the full history, and prediction of intent distributions instead of a single intent.

P1.justification: v2 revises the abstract and selected explanatory passages, standardizes terminology, adds affiliation and conference information, and introduces ethics and reproducibility statements. Data splits move from Section 4.5 to Appendix A.5. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are substantially redesigned, Table 1 is reorganized around user-defined tasks, contextual information, and historical data, and the main result tables expand. Seven supplementary result tables are added. Figures and tables are resized or relocated throughout the new conference layout; the original quantitative plots are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds AppAgent and AutoDroid references and includes AndroidWorld in the related-work comparison table, while removing SmartAgent and several peripheral references. The central positioning around longitudinal user context and proactive/personalized mobile interaction remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The principal task equations and metric definitions remain unchanged. Appendix A.6.5 introduces a time-conditioned distributional target constructed from clustered intents and redefines success and similarity for that target. This is a limited mathematical-definition extension, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential foundation. Appendix A.6 addresses v1's explicitly untested generalization, adds human evidence for the personalization metric, and tests context dependence and possible reuse of identical tasks. Expanded baselines and training-scale experiments further improve assessment of the benchmark. These gains outweigh the loss of the action-repair documentation, although uncertainty remains unreported and the human–model comparison uses different test-set sizes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FingerTip 20K and its two benchmark tracks. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds model comparisons, fine-tuning configurations, human studies, and generalization and ablation experiments in Appendix A.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset analyses, model evaluations, task-difficulty experiments, and fine-tuning results in Sections 4–5, Tables 4–6, and Figure 6.

results.title: FingerTip 20K: A Benchmark for Proactive and Personalized Mobile LLM Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory findings and conclusion retain the same central contributions: classification-oriented GP/SCM generation, sample-efficient synthetic-only pretraining, and clearer scaling behavior than with the studied real datasets. The added applications support these claims without redefining them. Removing 'only' from the title does not remove the synthetic-only claim from the paper.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of kernel diversity and failure modes, embedding coverage, domain-specific gains and deficits, attention localization, and transfer to forecasting and supervised adaptation. It also discusses possible multivariate applicability while specifying univariate pretraining. v1's separate comparison with forecasting scaling laws, including its sub-exponential-growth qualification, is removed. The original in-distribution caveat for official checkpoints is retained and emphasized.

D1.justification: v1's pseudocode subsection contains only prose; v3 supplies Algorithm 1 with sampling, graph traversal and output construction details. v3 also adds a CauKer source-code link and documents procedures for the new forecasting, alignment and visualization experiments. These substantially improve documented reproducibility, although some implementation choices remain ambiguous and repository availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained UCR evaluation and pretraining corpora, v3 evaluates 17 WOODS datasets, irregular multivariate clinical classification on P12/P19, and forecasting on 27 chronos-zero-shot subsets. These substantially extend the represented domains, input conditions and prediction tasks.

E2.justification: The original SCM, FPFN, KernelSynth and Mean-KernelSynth comparison is retained. v3 adds raw-series Logistic Regression, XGBoost and Random Forest comparisons, the supervised WOODS ERM baseline, and official Chronos checkpoints plus Seasonal Naive in forecasting. These are reported comparisons, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: The original frozen-encoder UCR protocol and training budgets are retained. New protocols include supervised downstream fine-tuning, clinical evaluation with AUROC/AUPRC, Chronos forecasting with MASE, controlled generation timing for 1,000 length-512 series, and distribution alignment using 512 random projections. These substantially expand evaluation procedures rather than establish reruns of existing experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds kernel/parent and DAG-size sensitivity sweeps, single-kernel failure tests, SWD/CKNNA alignment analysis, domain-wise UCR results, PCA coverage plots, and ECG/Fish attention-rollout case studies. The earlier DTW clustering, nonlinearity/CKA and UMAP analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly reports means and standard deviations across five independent synthetic draws. Section 4.4 adds a two-sided Wilcoxon forecasting comparison with p=0.84 at significance level 0.05. These are localized additions; repeated-training uncertainty is still not reported for the headline UCR accuracies.

E6.justification: The original generator comparison and data/model scaling tables retain their values. Numerous results are newly reported: Table 10 gives WOODS averages of 0.820 for CauKer100K, 0.810 for original Mantis and 0.800 for ERM; Table 12 gives fine-tuning accuracies of 0.8291/0.8457 for CauKer100K/1M versus 0.8496 for original Mantis. Table 13 shows CauKer1M outperforming the baseline on P12 but trailing on P19. Runtime, sensitivity, alignment and forecasting results are also added.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the stated causal propagation rule: v1 applies edge activations before linear aggregation, whereas v3 applies an activation after aggregating parents. The GP construction, function banks and pretraining losses remain unchanged. Edge-based descriptions elsewhere remain inconsistent, so the implemented behavior is not fully resolved.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable. v3 locally rewrites protocol and motivation passages, removes the forecasting-scaling subsection, adds an appendix roadmap and disclosures, and updates the title, authors and affiliations. The additional scientific sections do not amount to a wholesale rewrite of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adds the algorithm display, numerous experimental tables, PCA figures and attention-rollout panels. Figure 3's staggered plot groups become a single row, and existing kernel, mean-function and embedding illustrations are resized or relocated. The document template, headings and figure placement also change substantially.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to newer TSFMs, vision-based approaches, synthetic-data research, and the new benchmarks and analysis tools. Edwards et al. (2025) and Shi et al. (2024) disappear with the forecasting-scaling discussion. The added positioning paragraph largely reinforces the existing distinction from forecasting generators and tabular SCMs rather than changing the novelty claim.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the formal activation map from edges to vertices and reverses the order of nonlinear activation and linear aggregation. This is a local, mathematically non-equivalent specification change. Neither version develops new theorems or proofs; the added standard metric formulas mainly document evaluation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's UCR-centered evidence through WOODS, irregular clinical, forecasting and fine-tuning evaluations, including mixed outcomes that expose applicability limits. Sensitivity and failure analyses address previously untested generator choices, while Algorithm 1 and code-access information address documentation gaps. These gains outweigh localized weaknesses, including unresolved activation descriptions, limited training uncertainty reporting, and the WOODS discrepancy of 11 wins in Table 10 versus 12 in the prose.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CauKer and retain corresponding methods, experiments and appendices. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the equations, tables and figures, including the expanded v3 appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds runtime, sensitivity, WOODS, forecasting, fine-tuning and irregular clinical-data experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original UCR classification experiments, data/model/training-time scaling results, and analyses of synthetic data and learned representations.

results.title: CauKer: Classification Time Series Foundation Models Can Be Pretrained on Synthetic Data

C1.justification: The core contribution remains an orchestrated hybrid of coding and GUI actions. v3 broadens the abstract, introduction, and conclusion's state-of-the-art claim to include 52.5% on WindowsAgentArena alongside the retained OSWorld result. The central architectural and efficiency claims otherwise remain.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the new ablation as evidence that coding offers efficiency but insufficient task coverage alone, while GUI execution supplies complementary capabilities. It revises the backbone discussion around role-specific model strengths and adds explanations of hidden intermediate errors and hallucinated planning in Appendix D. Appendix C also acknowledges that alternative open-source GUI operators were not tested.

D1.justification: v1 provides model families, AG2 implementation information, and round limits but no full prompts. v3 Appendix C supplies dated model identifiers, initialization guidance including a recommended 60-second VM wait, and complete agent and summarizer prompts in Tables 5-9. The front page adds a code-repository link. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing that all newly disclosed settings changed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only OSWorld. v3 adds WindowsAgentArena with 154 tasks, extending evaluation to Windows and applications such as Edge, Settings, File Explorer, and Windows utilities. This substantially broadens the tested operating environments and task coverage.

E2.justification: The OSWorld comparison adds OpenCUA and removes UI-TARS-72B-DPO, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude 4 Sonnet, and Agent S2 with Gemini-2.5-Pro. The new WindowsAgentArena comparison includes Agent S, NAVI, and Agent S2. These are substantive changes to evaluated comparator membership, beyond updated citations or scores.

E3.justification: v3 adds Programmer-only and GUI-only control configurations for the component ablation in Table 4 and reports Windows evaluation at 15, 50, and 100 steps. The existing Programmer/GUI/Orchestrator limits remain 20/25/15, and rule-based success evaluation is retained. The OSWorld label changes from 100+ to 150 steps, with an early-termination explanation rather than evidence of a changed internal execution limit.

E4.justification: New Table 4 directly tests whether combining coding and GUI execution improves on either modality alone, addressing a central architectural question absent from v1. Appendix D retains the two original VSCode cases and adds reflection-error and hallucination analyses. The backbone comparison and Figure 3 efficiency analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Additional point estimates and changed scores in v3 do not change this reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds Windows results reaching 52.5% and component-ablation results of 35.73% for coding only and 50.68% for GUI only. Table 3 revises the two alternative-backbone scores from 47.41% to 43.43% and from 53.12% to 58.72%. The reported 15-step Jedi score changes from 26.80% to 42.37%, exceeding CoAct-1's retained 39.81%. CoAct-1's headline OSWorld 60.76% and Figure 3's 10.15-step result remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The three-agent architecture is retained, but the feedback procedure is ambiguous. v1 Section 3.2 and Figure 2 return a Programmer summary plus screenshot. v3 Figure 2 omits that screenshot and Table 6 explicitly says none is provided, while Section 3.3 still describes returning screenshots. This conflict prevents determining whether the procedure changed or its documentation was corrected inconsistently.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites the retained method exposition around formal policies and separate workflow/memory descriptions, reorganizes baseline descriptions into model categories, and rewrites the results discussion. The original main-text case study moves into an expanded Appendix D, alongside new disclosure and reproducibility appendices. The title and terminology are also revised.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the ICLR layout, redraws Figure 1, revises Figure 2 annotations, and updates Figure 3 labels and captions. The original overall and application-level OSWorld tables are reorganized into a grouped-domain table across step budgets. New Windows, component-ablation, and boxed prompt tables substantially change the document's visual organization.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to OpenCUA, UI-TARS-2, Beyond Browsing, WindowsAgentArena, and prompt-formatting research, while removing the Anthropic system-card and DeepSeek-R1 references. It more explicitly distinguishes free-form coding from application-specific APIs or SDKs, but retains the overall positioning among GUI, modular, and hybrid agent systems.

T1.justification: New Section 3.1 mathematically defines observations, interaction history, a goal-conditioned policy, the union of GUI and coding action spaces, and hierarchical executor policies. v1 describes the system informally. This adds a limited formal problem definition, without new theorems, proofs, or theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: Table 4 addresses v1's important lack of direct component-level evidence for the hybrid design, while Windows evaluation broadens empirical support. Exact model identifiers and full prompts resolve substantial reproducibility omissions. Expanded failure analysis also improves understanding of limitations. These gains outweigh the unresolved screenshot-return inconsistency and unexplained revisions to existing scores; the improvement does not depend on a higher headline OSWorld result.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoAct-1 and support comparison of the text, equations, tables, and figures. All 12 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v3 were readable, including v3 Appendices A-D; v1 ends with references.

after.justification: v3 reports original OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena results, backbone and component ablations, efficiency analyses, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original OSWorld experiments, backbone comparisons, efficiency analyses, and failure cases in Tables 1-3, Figure 3, and Section 4.6.

results.title: CoAct-1: Computer-using Multi-agent System with Coding Actions

C1.justification: The central ACM claim remains, but RL changes from a future direction into a principal contribution. v2's abstract and contribution list claim effective dynamic-context training, learned context-management strategies, and reduced context consumption supported by broader analyses, extending v1's preliminary zero-shot evaluation claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of prompting failures, attention dilution, and the disadvantages of irreversible filtering in its RAG and MemAgent comparisons. It identifies limited benefits on LongBenchV2 and FRAMES. The computational trade-off is reinterpreted: v1 warns of increased costs from cache invalidation, whereas v2 argues that context reduction compensates for those costs.

D1.justification: Appendices C–F add exact system prompts, baseline preprocessing and retrieval settings, trajectory-collection pseudocode, reward specifications, and complete tool schemas. Table 4 supplies GSPO hyperparameters and hardware, including 200 iterations, a 1e-6 learning rate, and 128 H800 GPUs. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's brief descriptions.

E1.justification: Beyond PI-LLM and NeedleBench, v2 evaluates ACM on MRCR, LongBenchV2, and FRAMES, adding conversational reference resolution and broader long-context reasoning requirements. BABILong and GSM-Infinite are used for training. Appendix B additionally evaluates the M3 base model on coding, tool-use, mathematics, and general-knowledge tasks.

E2.justification: The original three-model comparisons remain. v2 Table 2 adds controlled comparisons against M3 alone and M3 implementations of BM25 RAG and MemAgent, alongside the supervised and RL Sculptor variants. Appendix B also adds Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B comparisons.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 13B M3 training and evaluation, a 20-step training limit, prompt comparisons using 50 samples per benchmark, and 128K filtering or truncation for MRCR and LongBenchV2. The retained PI-LLM table drops the two-update condition and averages over 4–256 updates, although the prose still states 2–256. Newly disclosed prompts alone do not establish changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparisons of generic versus task-specific prompting and tool-use patterns, supervised versus RL training stages, folded versus complete-context attention for 46 key-value pairs, and context-reduction analysis. These investigate guidance, training, mechanisms, and efficiency beyond v1's benchmark and context-length comparisons.

E5.justification: v2 adds attention-distribution statistics and a one-sample t-test reporting p < 0.001 in Section 4.3. NeedleBench's ten-run statement is retained in Appendix C.3, but v1's five-repeat PI-LLM statement disappears. Benchmark tables still lack uncertainty intervals; the statistical additions are localized.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including Sculptor-M3-RL accuracies of 99.4% on PI-LLM and 84.8% on NeedleBench in Table 2, plus prompt, attention, and context-reduction findings. Original NeedleBench table values and retained PI-LLM condition scores are unchanged. Claude's reported PI-LLM gain changes from 2.62 to 5.90 points because the two-update condition is excluded, not because retained scores improve.

M1.justification: v1 leaves RL training as unfinished future work. v2 introduces supervised fine-tuning followed by dynamic context-aware GSPO, with conditional trajectory collection and incremental loss assignment. Its method section and Appendix F also replace embedding-based semantic search with exact matching and consolidate restoration operations into a six-tool suite.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes existing material extensively: related work moves to an appendix, teaching tools becomes a separate main section, and experiments are restructured around prompting, RL, attention, and cost. The contribution list, tool explanations, and limitations are substantially rewritten, with additional terminology and author-list edits.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn; v1's two result tables merge into v2 Table 1 with difference rows; and v1 Figures 2–3 are combined and restyled as v2 Figure 4. New training, prompting, attention, and context-reduction diagrams accompany additional result/configuration tables, pseudocode, and formatted prompt and schema displays.

R1.justification: The original related work moves to Appendix A and expands substantially. New discussions position ACM relative to sparse attention, external prompt compression, KV-cache methods, and revisable generation, including LLMLingua-2, SnapKV, and Self-Refine. GSPO also becomes an explicit methodological foundation.

T1.justification: v1 provides no formal training formulation. v2 Section 3.2 introduces the GSPO objective, sequence-level importance ratio, group-normalized advantage, and non-prefix context condition; Appendix E defines the reward function. These substantially formalize the newly implemented learning framework, although no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's unfinished RL direction into a specified and evaluated training procedure, adds meaningful alternative-method comparisons, and tests applicability beyond the original narrow benchmarks. Its diagnostic analyses and reproducibility appendices substantially strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh material weaknesses: PI-LLM averages omit a previously reported failure condition without explanation, and the stronger speed claims lack timing measurements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sculptor and retain identifiable methods and experiments. All supplied pages, figures, tables, and equations support comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–F are included in this assessment.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds trained M3 results, baseline comparisons, prompt experiments, attention analysis, and context-reduction measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original PI-LLM and NeedleBench experiments comparing three language models with and without ACM tools.

results.title: Sculptor: Empowering LLMs with Cognitive Agency via Active Context Management

C1.justification: The abstract replaces v1's ReLU claim for any initialization with a claim for a dense set, and changes the linear necessity claim from intrinsic dynamics to the intrinsic metric property. These correct the scope of retained central claims; the overall research objective and principal contributions remain.

C2.justification: V2 more explicitly positions intrinsic dynamics as a preliminary step toward mirror or warped-mirror implicit-bias analyses. It also adds discussion of dimensional restrictions motivating square weight matrices for nonzero relaxed balance. The open regime r > max(n,m) remains.

D1.justification: The same numerical-illustration repository is linked in v1 Appendix A and v2 Appendix B. No implementation, hardware, data-processing or experimental replication settings are added.

E1.justification: Neither version evaluates datasets or empirical tasks. V2's additional analysis of graphs and initialization domains changes theoretical scope rather than evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version reports evaluated baseline comparisons. Additional citations support mathematical arguments rather than introduce experimental comparators.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, metrics, budgets or testing protocols. The piecewise C2 losses introduced in Appendix I define a theoretical property, not an experimental setting.

E4.justification: The worked mathematical examples and perturbation analysis are retained. Added graph and reachability arguments are proofs, not new ablations, robustness evaluations or empirical case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or empirical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: No empirical result entries are added or revised. Table 1 retains the same theoretical summary; the new formal conclusions and proofs are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Gradient-flow training, ReLU path lifting and weight-product parameterizations are retained. The new prunability and strong-dynamics concepts are theoretical criteria, not changes to a training or inference procedure.

P1.justification: V2 revises the introductory motivation, moves recoverability into Section 2.4, and groups network applications under Section 3. It also copyedits retained prose and adds Appendix N's LLM-use disclosure. Much of the existing exposition and proof text remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The existing Table 1 moves from the main text to Appendix A without changing its entries. V2 adopts conference formatting, including running headers, revised headings and author-block layout; it does not add new figures or result tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds Le and Jegelka on DAG conservation laws, Gleiss et al. on graph ranks, Isidori on involutivity, and Jurdjevic on controllability. These support the expanded theory without replacing the main research positioning. Gonon and Marcotte publication updates refer to already cited works.

T1.justification: V2 adds Theorem 3.2 and Appendix F's prunable-DAG and rank arguments, extending the Frobenius result to parameters with at most one zero under stated architectural conditions. Corollaries 3.3–3.4 specify initialization domains and establish conservation-law completeness that v1 explicitly left unproved. Theorem 3.9 and Appendix I also add a strong intrinsic dynamic property for piecewise C2 losses and a reachability argument extending the earlier metric impossibility result.

improvement.justification: For this theoretical paper, Appendix F substantially strengthens the foundation by supplying rank and completeness arguments expressly absent from v1 and specifying admissible initialization domains. Appendix I further develops the linear impossibility analysis, while the abstract states the scope more accurately. Table 1 and the conclusion still retain overbroad universal initialization wording, but the added theoretical support provides a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, Table 1 and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 likewise reports theoretical results without original experiments, simulations or data analyses. The added appendices contain proofs, and Appendix B retains the external illustration link without reporting outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical results and proofs, not original empirical outcomes. Symbolic-computation evidence is attributed to earlier work; Appendix A only links externally to numerical illustrations.

results.title: Intrinsic training dynamics of deep neural networks

C1.justification: The central contribution remains theoretically motivated PD selection for efficient alignment. v2 replaces the abstract's specific claim of over 10% relative improvement against holistic and oracle preferences with a nonquantified claim of consistent improvement over full-data alignment using as little as 30% of the data.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets conflicts as primarily data-quality problems among compatible criteria, qualifying v1's broader discussion of quality trade-offs. It adds explanations of the rating comparator's discretization and annotation costs, proxy-model sensitivity, and why filtering can help even with consistent labels. Appendix D substantially expands limitations concerning reward-model dependence, distribution shift and the offline setting, alongside possible iterative, alternative-objective and distillation extensions.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset counts, Qwen's SFT-data assignment, HelpSteer reward prompts and Taobao annotation details while retaining most of the training recipe. It revises the DPO learning rate and removes the explicit count of 16 H20 GPUs. A new statement claims supplementary processing/training code, whose availability cannot be verified from the PDFs; its assertion that all datasets are public conflicts with the proprietary Taobao experiment.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's UltraFeedback experiments, v2 adds HelpSteer with five preference aspects, UltraChat for Qwen supervised fine-tuning, and a proprietary Taobao Live task generating product-specific sales scripts. The original conflict scenarios, five public evaluation sets and AlpacaEval 2 remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds PD (rati.), which selects using ground-truth discrete aspect ratings, to the reported comparisons. Other apparent additions are matched renamings: RAF corresponds to A1, PD (nl) to A2, OVA. to Overall, and AVG. to Oracle. HIGH and MID remain as PD (high) and PD (mid).

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen2.5-7B policy experiments, additional proxy-model configurations, a 50% main selection budget for HelpSteer, and Taobao evaluations against the SFT model. The reported DPO learning rate changes from 5e-7 in v1 Appendix B.3 to 1e-6 in v2 Appendix C.5; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. The existing public evaluation judges and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds sensitivity studies of proxy-model size, family and training-data fraction in Figure 5, plus length-penalty and quantile-normalization sweeps in Tables C.3–C.5. Existing conflict, selection-budget, reward-prediction and length-distribution analyses are substantially retained under renamed methods. The former generated-response-length ablation table is no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same mean-plus/minus presentation for average win scores. Neither supplies new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures. Changed plus/minus values and additional rows are result changes, not changes in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive HelpSteer, Qwen, Taobao and sensitivity results. Retained UltraFeedback entries also change: OURS at 10% conflict and 30% selection changes from AW 1.26 to 1.24, while A2/PD (nl) at 30% conflict and 50% selection changes from 1.29 to 1.21 (v1 Tables B.3/B.1; v2 Tables E.6/E.8). Generated-response-length results and detailed 10% selection rows are removed. The revised learning-rate disclosure prevents interpreting these revisions as established same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains cross-aspect proxy reward estimation, quantile normalization, length-balanced sampling, the length penalty, selection of the most negative PD values and subsequent DPO training. DMPO is renamed DFPO, and Algorithm 1 moves into Appendix B; these do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, terminology is revised throughout, and the experimental narrative is reorganized into six result subsections. Detailed setup and the algorithm move into appendices, while the derivation receives a four-step explanatory structure. These are substantial editorial and organizational changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from two-column to single-column formatting. Main comparison tables are rebuilt, budget plots are reorganized, the ablation table is replaced by plots, and new sensitivity and downstream-result displays are added. Detailed appendix tables are restructured, while the existing heatmaps and distribution figures are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for UltraChat, scaling laws, HelpSteer and HelpSteer2, and removes the Stiennon and Ziegler references. Related work expands the discussion of alignment-data quality versus pre-training scale, while retaining the central positioning against single-preference filtering and multi-objective alignment.

T1.justification: The loss-bound theorems, selection condition and supporting lemmas remain substantively the same. However, v2 Appendix A.1.1 adds an inconsistent identity: Equation 36 defines the loss as negative expected preference probability, before Equation 37 uses negative expected log probability. v1 Equation 39 directly gives the log-probability loss. The expanded derivation otherwise mainly adds explanation.

improvement.justification: HelpSteer and Qwen experiments substantially address v1's reliance on one preference dataset and one policy-model family. Proxy-model and hyperparameter sensitivity tests also strengthen support for the method's practical reliability, and the expanded limitations clarify its scope. These gains outweigh localized reporting defects, including the new missing-log identity, inconsistent Qwen AW summaries between Tables C.2 and E.10, and the public-data claim contradicting the proprietary experiment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same preference-divergence data-selection work. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, terminology and organization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds HelpSteer, Qwen2.5, Taobao Live and sensitivity experiments, reported in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Llama alignment experiments on UltraFeedback, including conflict-level comparisons, selection-budget studies, ablations and detailed benchmark scores in Appendix B.

results.title: Data Selection for LLM Alignment Using Fine-Grained Preferences

C1.justification: Both versions make the same central claim: retrospective updates mitigate accumulated attention errors without increasing the KV budget and with negligible overhead. The headline claims of up to 1.6-fold effective exposure and 21.9% accuracy improvement remain; the contribution bullets reorganize existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains saturation through diminishing supplementary attention mass and limited LongBench benefits through short generation lengths. It also distinguishes agreement with full attention from correctness, provides window-selection guidance, and explicitly identifies full-KV GPU residency and batch-size limits. These materially clarify mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link and a reproducibility statement describing source code, documentation and evaluation scripts. It explicitly discloses greedy LongGenBench decoding and its prompt-construction source. These improve documented reproducibility without establishing changes to the retained implementation or decoding procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on 12 LongBench tasks spanning single-document and multi-document QA, summarization, code completion and few-shot QA. This substantially extends coverage to long-input, generally short-output scenarios while retaining the original long-generation, reasoning and language-modeling benchmarks.

E2.justification: The original Full Attention, StreamingLLM, TOVA and Quest comparisons remain. V2 additionally evaluates Quest with top-k selection reuse in Table 4 and ArkVale with and without RetroAttention in Table 9; ArkVale was only discussed in v1.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen2.5-14B/32B evaluations, a selection-reuse control refreshing every two steps, throughput profiling across batch sizes 1–16 and contexts 32k–128k, and token-level normalized Levenshtein similarity. These are substantial additional evaluation configurations; the original main-table settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 extends the existing window/budget analyses with tests of selection-reuse failure, attention mass recovered by successive updates, batch-dependent throughput and memory exhaustion, and page overlap across additional datasets. Tables 4–6 and Figure 8 substantially strengthen investigation of the mechanism and practical operating limits.

E5.justification: Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests or new seed-based uncertainty estimates. The reasoning evaluations retain the same 8, 2 and 1 samples per question documented in v1 Appendix D and v2 Appendix F.1.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 and reasoning table are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results for larger models, ArkVale, reuse, throughput and LongBench. For example, Table 2 reports Qwen2.5-14B mean GSM8K accuracy of 77.6 versus Quest's 73.2. V2 Table 4 also inconsistently prints a CSQA mean of 63.0 for scores whose unchanged Table 1 mean is 60.3.

M1.justification: The supplementary-attention computation, output cache, retrospective mask and deeper-layer KV updates remain unchanged, including Algorithms 1–2. The ArkVale experiments exercise the existing generic page-selector interface without documenting a new RetroAttention procedure.

P1.justification: Most original prose remains. V2 revises the contribution list and motivational narrative, moves Related Works after the experiments, subdivides experimental and appendix sections, and adds acknowledgment, ethics and reproducibility statements.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column conference format, rearranges Figure 1, and adds a prompt-example panel to Figure 2. It introduces numerous evaluation tables and the expanded overlap Figure 8. The original linear-layer Figure 8 is retained as Figure 9.

R1.justification: V2 adds the LongBench and LServe references and explicitly contrasts retrospective correction with cache-selection reuse in Section 2.2 and Appendix B. Most prior-work discussion, including the comparison with Rectified Sparse Attention, is retained.

T1.justification: The attention and output-merging equations, smooth-QKV approximation assumption, and arithmetic-intensity and memory derivations are retained. Their renumbering and relocation introduce no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation across model families and cache selectors through Qwen14B/32B and ArkVale experiments. New throughput measurements and LongBench evaluations clarify deployment limits and where benefits diminish, while code-access information supports reproducibility. New reporting errors temper this improvement: Table 4's CSQA mean conflicts with Table 1, and Table 5's 0.650 entry contradicts the stated 4–7% range. These localized inconsistencies do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and applicability guidance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RetroAttention work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and algorithms, equations, figures and results can be matched despite reformatting and expansion.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, LongBench results, ArkVale comparisons and further diagnostic measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original accuracy, perplexity, attention-overlap and latency experiments, including supplementary measurements in the appendices.

results.title: Retrospective Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: training-free color editing, structural/material preservation, word-level control, superior editing consistency, and generalization across image, video, and instruction-based models. The expanded appendix supports these retained headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of threshold robustness, synthetic-data utility, and broader editing enabled by weaker preservation. B.5 distinguishes semantic success from perceptual naturalness and extends the CLIP critique to attribute binding. The existing backbone/localization and inversion limitations are retained, moving from v1 B.3 to v3 B.10.

D1.justification: v3 discloses 40,000 generated training pairs and 2,300 H800 GPU-hours, additional metric implementation details, GPT-4o's evaluation access date, and the user-study interface. It also adds LLM/manual-review disclosure and a future code-release commitment. Most inference and baseline implementation details in Appendix A remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The original image/video benchmark coverage remains. v3 adds a synthetic paired-image corpus actually used for downstream training, Chinese-instruction evaluation of the fine-tuned editor (B.1), and style, material, texture, and transparency editing demonstrations beyond the original color-editing task (B.9).

E2.justification: v3 adds PnP-Inversion and FlowEdit comparisons on real images (Table 12), plus an original-versus-fine-tuned Step1X-Edit-v1.1 comparison (Figure 10). FlowEdit's unchanged score row moves from v1's video Table 3 to v3's image Table 1, correcting its placement to match both versions' stated exclusion of FlowEdit from video evaluation.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a randomized, blinded study with 24 experts and 34 cases, Y-GCS/Y-GMS structural metrics, and GPT-4o SC/PQ scoring with three sampled frames per video (B.2, B.5). It also adds downstream fine-tuning and quantitative real-image evaluation protocols. The original benchmark's inference settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original component ablation and failure examples are retained. v3 adds threshold sensitivity tests at epsilon 0, 0.05, 0.1, and 0.2 (Figure 14), crowded/overlapping-object and reflection case studies (Figure 13), and before/after fine-tuning evidence testing the usefulness of generated training data (Figure 10). These substantially broaden the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Both versions retain benchmark seed 42. v3 newly reports preference scores with uncertainty terms in Table 7, including 64.71 ± 9.90% for ColorCtrl. It does not define these terms as standard deviations, standard errors, or confidence intervals, or explain their calculation.

E6.justification: The original ColorCtrl benchmark and component-ablation values are retained. v3 adds user preferences, four additional image/video metrics, real-image comparisons, and fine-tuning/application findings. For example, the new real-image Table 12 reports Canny-SSIM of 0.7683 for ColorCtrl, 0.6524 for FlowEdit, and 0.6178 for PnP-Inversion; these are newly reported comparisons under that evaluation.

M1.justification: The core attention-map transfer, masked value replacement, and attribute reweighting remain unchanged. B.9 adds an inference variant using fewer structure-preservation timesteps for broader edits; B.1 separately fine-tunes Step1X-Edit-v1.1 on ColorCtrl-generated data.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose, section order, and Appendix A remain close to v1. Changes include local wording and cross-reference edits, expanded appendix organization, and new Ethics, Reproducibility, and LLM Usage statements; the core explanatory narrative is retained.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the dense two-column format with a single-column ICLR layout, extensively resizes and relocates displays, and adds several experimental figures and tables. v1's video Table 3 is split across v3 Tables 3 and 8. Existing qualitative galleries and failure examples are retained and redistributed, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v3 adds related-work citations including TextCrafter and ConsistEdit, and explicitly associates TextCrafter with DiTCtrl's attention-consistency problem. Additional references support VIEScore, gradient-based assessment, and CLIP limitations. The overall positioning as training-free MM-DiT color editing remains stable.

T1.justification: The rendering/editing formulation in Equations (1)–(2), constraints C1–C3, and attention reasoning are retained. The added standard evaluation measures introduce empirical procedures, without new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation: B.5 evaluates edit success and perceptual quality separately, addressing v1's reliance on CLIP scores and qualitative explanations, while B.6 adds quantitative real-image evidence previously limited to examples. Sensitivity and downstream fine-tuning tests provide further support. The user study has documentation weaknesses—pairwise wording versus a nine-choice interface and undefined uncertainty terms—but the other empirical additions provide a clear substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same ColorCtrl work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added material.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds a user study, downstream fine-tuning, additional metrics, quantitative real-image comparisons, and sensitivity tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original image/video editing experiments on PIE-Bench and ColorCtrl-Bench, component ablations, and qualitative real-image and instruction-based editing results.

results.title: Training-Free Text-Guided Color Editing with Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: temporal oscillation, temporal self-consistency voting, and TSE-based reinforcement. The headline numerical claims are unchanged; the additional experiments support existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the misleading calibration explanation with an interpretation of the composite reward as correctness plus temporal consistency. It also fixes the contradictory description of correctness groups in the TSE discussion and adds a multi-task generalization interpretation. Existing Sudoku limitations are retained in Appendix E.

D1.justification: v2 documents the adapter/backbone loading correction and equal-per-task subsampling for joint training. A new reproducibility statement promises release of models and training/inference code upon acceptance. Existing hardware, LoRA settings, training details, and evaluation schedule are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions cover GSM8K, MATH500, SVAMP, Countdown, and Sudoku, with s1K used for supervised fine-tuning. The new joint-training experiment combines existing tasks without adding datasets or task requirements. Sudoku results are relocated, not newly introduced.

E2.justification: The base/SFT baselines and accuracy-reward comparator d1 are retained. The new joint-training experiment uses the same RFT comparator set. Corrected scores and backbone loading do not introduce a different comparison method.

E3.justification: Appendix G reports correcting evaluation of LLaDA-1.5-trained LoRA adapters, previously loaded into LLaDA, by using the proper LLaDA-1.5 backbone. This affects central RFT comparisons and scoring-rule ablations. Appendix F.1 also introduces joint training on equally sized subsamples from four tasks.

E4.justification: Appendix F.1 adds a focused generalization analysis testing whether one jointly trained model retains benefits across four tasks. Existing voting-weight, entropy, post-RFT voting, and Sudoku failure analyses remain. The scoring-rule ablation is updated under the corrected evaluation backbone.

E5.justification: No run-count, seed, uncertainty-estimation, or significance-testing information is added or revised. New and corrected tables retain point-accuracy reporting, and existing graphical uncertainty displays are unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces LLaDA-1.5 RFT results after the backbone correction: combined-reward GSM8K/128 changes from 70.2 to 73.2, while MATH500/128 changes from 30.8 to 29.6. These are corrected evaluations, not same-setting gains or losses. Scoring-rule results also change, and v2 Table S2 adds joint-training results. Voting and Sudoku results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 and Equation 5 change the stated GRPO rollout distribution from the current policy to the old policy. This is a limited correction to the specified training procedure; temporal voting, TSE, and the composite reward formula remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether the training implementation changed.

P1.justification: Related work, analyses, methods, and experimental discussion undergo extensive compression and rewriting. Limitations move from the main text into a reorganized appendix. New LLM-usage and reproducibility disclosures and a changelog further revise the document structure.

P2.justification: v2 adds the joint-training table, relocates and renumbers existing appendix tables, shortens captions, and reflows figures within the condensed text. Existing figure graphics and established table formats are retained.

R1.justification: The bibliography contains the same works. Section 2 is condensed while preserving the research positioning relative to diffusion models, self-consistency, semantic entropy, and GRPO-based post-training.

T1.justification: Equation 5 corrects the sampling distribution to the old policy. Section 4.2 and Appendix F.2 also correct the mathematical characterization of the spherical reward: it encourages consistency without penalizing overconfidence in incorrect predictions. The reward formula and other principal definitions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Correcting the adapter/backbone mismatch repairs an important validity problem in the central LLaDA-1.5 comparisons and scoring-rule ablations. v2 also corrects the GRPO formulation and misleading reward-calibration explanation, substantially improving reliability. The new multi-task discussion overstates uniform improvement—Table S2 includes 28.2 versus a 29.0 baseline on LLaDA-1.5 MATH500/128—but this limited overstatement does not outweigh the substantive corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 23-page versions of the same work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results, reports corrected LLaDA-1.5 evaluations, and adds joint multi-task training results in Table S2.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, reinforcement fine-tuning experiments, ablations, and analyses of intermediate diffusion predictions, including appendix results.

results.title: Time Is a Feature: Exploiting Temporal Dynamics in Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The main feedback-regulation, residual-connection, and speedup contributions remain. v2 removes the abstract's explicit large-scale-AI applicability assertion, changes 'fully restoring' classification performance to 'partly restoring,' and qualifies BP comparability as applying to shallow architectures.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving numerical precision, distorted random feedback, and noise accumulation. Its Discussion explicitly identifies deep/asymmetric CIFAR-10 performance gaps, untested deep-CNN applicability, empirical hyperparameter selection, and unresolved sequence-task extensions. These qualifications substantially sharpen the applicability boundaries compared with v1.

D1.justification: Appendix D expands reproducibility information with residual-network pseudocode (Algorithm S3), architecture diagrams (S14–S15), CIFAR-10 normalization, additional optimizer and scheduling settings, and default numerical precision. A new reproducibility statement describes supplementary Jupyter notebooks. The repository link and hardware descriptions were already present in v1.

E1.justification: MNIST is retained, but Fashion-MNIST evaluation is removed and CIFAR-10 natural-image classification is added. Appendix C.6 also introduces noisy-weight and noisy-state training/testing scenarios, substantially extending the evaluated environmental conditions.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds BP with tanh and Adam to the two-hidden-layer comparison; v1 compares only P-EP and Ours there. The broader comparator families remain P-EP, BP, and FA.

E3.justification: v2 revises the alpha/beta sweep grid, adds 20-layer and additional convolutional configurations, and introduces gradient comparisons with float32/float64 and distinct noise-training/testing protocols. The stated convolutional nudging default becomes 0.25 rather than v1's general 0.1. These are reported settings and added protocols, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained dynamics and gradient-flow analyses, v2 adds before/after-training spectral-radius and convergence comparisons (Figure 5), an AGT connection-probability sweep (Figure S8), BP gradient/state alignment and precision tests (S10), frozen-layer controls (S11), and noise-robustness analyses (S12–S13). These directly investigate mechanisms and failure conditions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Five-run reporting remains for the main comparisons, but v2 omits the training-accuracy standard deviations reported in v1 Tables 1–2 while retaining test deviations. The newly added Figure S13 is explicitly described as a single experiment; other new analyses report five repetitions.

E6.justification: v2 replaces Fashion-MNIST scores with CIFAR-10 results and adds deeper-network, topology, gradient, freezing, and noise results. Existing Table 2 MNIST entries also change: residual accuracy moves from 97.52%±0.09% to 97.49%±0.05%, and AGT from 96.71%±0.14% to 96.87%±0.11%. Most existing Table 1 and Table S1 scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core feedback-regulation and residual-connection method remains. Algorithm S2 corrects the specified convolutional clamped-phase recurrence to use clamped states, whereas v1 prints free-phase states in those updates. This is a limited algorithmic correction; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: The original introduction–background–method–experiments–discussion progression and much prose remain. v2 polishes language, subdivides the method discussion, labels appendices A–D, improves cross-references, and adds acknowledgements and reproducibility/disclosure statements.

P2.justification: The paper is extensively retypeset from a two-column main text into a single-column ICLR layout. Tables combine testing and training values, scaling heatmaps are reorganized, and v1 Figure 5 becomes logarithmic-error Figure 6. New analytical and architecture figures are added, while retained appendix plots are resized and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds Sacramento et al., Haider et al., and Meulemans et al. to weak-feedback positioning, Veit et al. for residual-path interpretation, and Shadden et al. for finite-time Lyapunov analysis. The existing research positioning largely remains; Liu's preprint-to-publication update concerns the same cited work.

T1.justification: The MLE/FTMLE definitions and first-order Taylor derivations relating EP, LRA, and BP are substantively retained in Appendices A and C.1–C.3. Renumbering and explanatory edits do not introduce new theoretical results; the added gradient-similarity evidence is empirical.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the mechanism and its practical limits. CIFAR-10 and deeper-network tests expose performance boundaries, while gradient-precision, frozen-layer, topology, and noise controls investigate credit assignment and robustness directly. More qualified performance claims and explicit limitations improve scientific calibration. These gains outweigh the loss of Fashion-MNIST coverage and training-accuracy uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FRE-RNN work. All 23 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison. Text extraction and visual inspection allow figures, tables, equations, and relocated content to be matched.

after.justification: v2 reports original MNIST and CIFAR-10 experiments, including retained results and additional topology, gradient-similarity, frozen-layer, numerical-precision, and noise-robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST and Fashion-MNIST experiments, including accuracy, training time, convergence dynamics, feedback-scaling studies, and residual-connection comparisons.

results.title: Toward Practical Equilibrium Propagation: Brain-inspired Recurrent Neural Network with Feedback Regulation and Residual Connections

C1.justification: The contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: complementary Hindsight/Foresight modules, reusable knowledge, adaptive search control, superior AHD performance, and query efficiency. The revised abstract and symbolic-meta-optimizer framing do not materially change those claims.

C2.justification: New discussion attributes performance to adaptive regime switching, knowledge management rather than seed quality alone, balanced utility components, and compatibility between framework and LLM. Existing controller and cross-task-transfer limitations remain. One new interpretation is incorrect: Table 13 shows MCTS-AHD improving with seeds in all five cases, although the prose cites it as deteriorating.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository pointer, CPU specification, text preprocessing and recency-window details, and four generated-heuristic code listings. Appendix B.1 clarifies offline synthesis versus heuristic execution. Conversely, v1's framework and selection pseudocode disappears, along with its explicit API and temperature disclosure. These substantially alter the available reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The four problem families and existing benchmark collections remain. TSP-GLS evaluation changes from 50/100/200-node instances to 100/200/500-node instances. Small construction cases are retained in v2 Table 7 rather than removed; the additional LLM and parameter configurations do not introduce new task families.

E2.justification: Comparator membership changes within retained experiments: POMO and LEHD move from the GLS comparison into construction comparisons, while GLS gains ReEvo and an explicit LKH3 row. The appendix BPP table drops Funsearch, although main Table 3 retains it. The cost comparison replaces HSEvo with MCTS-AHD.

E3.justification: Section 4 changes the stated population size from 4 to 8. New protocols evaluate five underlying LLMs and systematically vary search and memory parameters. Evaluation also adds heuristic execution times and input/output token consumption, substantially extending the experimental design beyond the original benchmark and component comparisons.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component-removal ablations, Appendices C.5-C.7 add cross-LLM robustness tests, eight-parameter sensitivity analysis, seed-insight controls for baselines, adaptive versus fixed-Balance comparisons, regime-frequency analysis, and utility/reward ablations. These directly investigate portability, architectural necessity, and internal mechanisms.

E5.justification: v1 already labels its efficiency figure as averaged over five runs. v2 newly specifies three-run averages for main benchmark tables and additional studies, and Table 18 reports individual runs and standard deviations across representative tasks and methods.
