This broadens statistical reporting without establishing a general increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Many benchmark and ablation entries change: HiFo-Prompt's TSP50 construction gap changes from 5.808% to 6.625%, and BPP 5k_C100 from 0.66% to 0.69%. Extensive new robustness, ablation, runtime, and token results appear. TSPLib and BO scores remain unchanged. Revised settings and aggregation preclude interpreting updated scores as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The architecture and prompt operators remain. However, Section 3.3 replaces fitness-standard-deviation diversity with the fraction of algorithm-description pairs having unequal text. Section 3.2 also revises credit-assignment inequalities and introduces numerical stabilization and clipping. These change parts of the documented procedure without replacing the framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method passages are rewritten. Appendix B.1 receives a significant explanatory correction, comparative discussion moves into expanded appendices, and appendix organization changes. Author information, acknowledgments, and an LLM writing-assistance disclosure are also revised or added.

P2.justification: Benchmark tables are split or restructured and gain runtime or objective columns. The retained convergence plot moves to the appendix; v1's efficiency plot is replaced by v2's cost table, while a new sensitivity figure and numerous analysis tables appear. Figures 1-2 largely retain their artwork.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially reposition HiFo-Prompt against model fine-tuning approaches such as EvoTune and CALM, and distinguish MoH and RedAHD as addressing other dimensions. Numerous earlier background citations are removed, while new discussion connects recency management to sliding-window bandit methods.

T1.justification: The formal diversity definition changes, normalization gains an epsilon term, and Eq. 3 reverses its inequalities to agree with the maximized-fitness formulation in Appendix A.1. Credit clipping and a sliding-window recency formula are also specified. These are operational mathematical revisions; no theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for robustness and the proposed mechanisms through cross-LLM tests, parameter and controlled ablations, and explicit run-level variability. Runtime/token reporting and generated code make costs and outputs more inspectable. Removal of framework pseudocode and the incorrect Table 13 interpretation are meaningful drawbacks, but the broader, more diagnostic validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HiFo-Prompt. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds experiments across LLMs, parameter sensitivity studies, mechanism ablations, and statistical summaries.

before.justification: v1 reports original heuristic evaluations on TSP, online bin packing, flow-shop scheduling, and Bayesian optimization, alongside component ablations and efficiency measurements.

results.title: HiFo-Prompt: Prompting with Hindsight and Foresight for LLM-based Automatic Heuristic Design

C1.justification: The central claims about the SFT plateau, the large training corpus, multimodal rewards and benchmark improvements are retained. V2 narrowly softens novelty by dropping the abstract's claim that competitiveness with advanced closed-source models is achieved 'for the first time'.

C2.justification: V2 reframes the two-stage strategy around computational efficiency rather than primarily training stability and best performance. It interprets visual rewards as effective but expensive, discusses evaluator agreement and alternative optimizers, and adds concrete limitations: invented chart details and imperfect subplot layouts in Appendix D.

D1.justification: V2 newly supplies exact generation, filtering and visual-scoring prompts, chart-type counts and exclusions, the pre-2024 source-paper cutoff, and additional computational-cost information. Its reproducibility statement reports supplementary training and reward code. The existing hyperparameter and hardware description is relocated almost unchanged from Section 4.2 to Appendix B.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on Seaborn- and Plotly-style chart images, extending testing beyond the retained ChartMimic and ReachQA benchmarks to unseen visual styles. Appendix C also introduces actual SFT and RL experiments using ChartCoder training data.

E2.justification: The headline benchmark comparator sets are unchanged, but v2 substantially expands controlled comparisons: DPO is evaluated against GRPO, and InternViT and DINOv2-L become alternative visual-reward evaluators. Appendix C also compares five scoring models against human judgments, including GPT-4.1 and InternVL3-38B.

E3.justification: V2 introduces budget-dependent training comparisons, a 200-sample human-scoring evaluation, a 100-sample filtering audit, and DPO preference pairs generated by perturbing 2–3 code attributes. Table 5 selects 5.5k second-stage samples instead of v1's stated 11k, although Appendix B retains 11k, leaving the final training setting inconsistent. The original benchmark splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds RL saturation curves, computational-cost analysis, evaluator validation, optimizer and training-data ablations, distribution-shift tests, and explicit failure cases. It replaces v1's Figure 4 reward-training traces and removes the single-stage hybrid and textual-then-visual comparisons, changing the evidence used to justify the curriculum.

E5.justification: Appendix C and Figure A newly estimate Pearson correlations between evaluator scores and human judgments, adding statistical agreement analysis absent from v1. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: The headline benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results, including MSRL high-level scores of 30.5 and 35.9 on Seaborn and Plotly images, and DPO versus GRPO comparisons. V1's visual-only scores of 77.8/81.9 survive in Appendix Table B; v2 Table 5 separately reports 79.13/84.01 for a 22k-sample configuration, without establishing a like-for-like performance gain.

M1.justification: The backbone, GRPO optimization, textual and visual reward components, and textual-then-hybrid training sequence remain unchanged. V2 clarifies that execution reward is separate from textual accuracy, consistent with the reward equation and weights already reported in v1; this does not establish a new method component.

P1.justification: V2 polishes the abstract, introductory motivation and conclusion, clarifies reward terminology, consolidates reward/stage-ablation discussion, and moves implementation details into the appendix. It adds a reproducibility statement and organized appendices, while retaining most of the main method and results exposition.

P2.justification: V2 adds dataset and generalization tables, evaluator scatter plots, prompt panels, and detailed code-image examples. Figure 4 changes from reward-training traces to data-scaling curves, and the reward/stage tables are reorganized into a comparison containing sample budgets and GPU hours. Most other original main figures are retained.

R1.justification: V2 broadens citations to work including StructChart, ChartEdit, ChartM3, rendering-aware vector-graphics RL and DINOv2, and adds an explicit dataset comparison. The related-work organization and central positioning remain stable. Publication and author-list updates for existing references do not represent new works.

T1.justification: V1's Equations 2–3 explicitly define the clipped GRPO objective and normalized advantage. V2 removes these formulations and substitutes a short verbal description, while retaining the weighted reward equation. Neither version supplies original theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of the central visual-reward design through human agreement checks and alternative evaluator, optimizer and dataset comparisons. Exact prompts, cost analysis, generalization tests and explicit failure cases address important validation and reproducibility gaps in v1. These gains outweigh the removed ablation controls, although the unresolved 5.5k-versus-11k second-stage setting limits reproducibility of the final configuration.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MSRL research. All text, tables, equations and figures support comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A–F and their associated figures.

after.justification: V2 retains these benchmark results and adds original generalization tests, evaluator validation, optimizer and dataset comparisons, and qualitative error analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original ChartMimic and ReachQA evaluations, SFT scaling experiments, reward and training-stage ablations, and qualitative comparisons.

results.title: Breaking the SFT Plateau: Multimodal Structured Reinforcement Learning for Chart-to-Code Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: inferring interpretable constitutive laws and material parameters through bilevel optimization, improving search through decoupled evolution, and supporting generalizable physical interaction. Consolidating the contribution bullets and adding supporting experiments do not materially change these claims.

C2.justification: v2 extends the physical-inductive-bias interpretation to viewpoint overfitting and transfer instability, and argues for applicability to non-differentiable simulation through gradient-free optimization while acknowledging its computational overhead. Appendix F newly identifies extensive simulation and parameter optimization as a practical limitation and proposes preliminary screening as future work.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantial details missing from the supplied v1: Particle-GS binding, parent/offspring counts, the default evolution schedule, lower-level iteration counts, simulation resolutions, and frame subsampling. Appendices G and H provide full prompts and inferred Python constitutive laws for all eight original scenes. The abstract also adds an implementation repository address.

E1.justification: The original six synthetic and two real-world scenes remain. v2 adds image-to-4D and 3D-to-4D generation on new assets, transfers inferred laws between scenes, and tests initial velocities of 0.5 and 1.5 times the original velocity (Figures 6, 12, and 13). These substantially broaden coverage beyond reconstruction and temporal extrapolation.

E2.justification: NCLaw, previously discussed only as related work, becomes an evaluated comparator in Table 1 and the trajectory comparisons in Figure 10. PAC-NeRF, NeuMA, and Spring-Gaus remain in their corresponding original comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled optimizer comparisons using differential-evolution populations of 5 and 10 with 10 lower-level iterations, gravity-only transfer evaluations, velocity perturbations, and viewwise PSNR/variance evaluation. It also reports linear-isotropic initialization in Section 4.1.1 and Appendix A.1 instead of v1's fixed-corotated initialization, although Appendix E contradictorily retains the old setting. The original temporal split and five-iteration decoupling ablation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The temporal generalization experiment and original decoupling curves are retained, with v1 Figure 6 becoming v2 Figure 7. Added analyses examine viewpoint overfitting, time-resolved trajectory errors, cross-scene and velocity robustness, NeuMA's numerical divergence during transfer, gradient-free optimization, and decoupling's runtime-versus-accuracy tradeoff.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1 newly specifies seed IDs 0–4, and Figure 11(b) adds PSNR variance across viewpoints. Both versions already report five independent seeded runs and mean curves with minimum–maximum shading for the decoupling ablation. The additions disclose seeds and quantify viewpoint variability; they do not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains every original entry, including VisionLaw's average Chamfer distance of 1.65, and adds NCLaw's average of 12.86. v2 adds extensive transfer, trajectory, optimizer, and runtime results; Table 2 reports RGB losses of 10.73 versus 7.14 at 11,343 versus 11,405 seconds without versus with decoupling. Visual-fidelity summaries also change, with v2 explicitly reporting non-training-view averages; these should not be interpreted as established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core bilevel framework, alternating-then-joint constitutive evolution, and visual loss remain unchanged. Section 4.3.4 adds a tested adaptation replacing gradient-based lower-level parameter optimization with differential evolution. Newly documented prompts and Particle-GS binding do not independently establish changes to the original method.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: Related Work moves to Appendix C, four contribution bullets become two, the MPM explanation expands, and the experimental discussion separates dynamics consistency, visual fidelity, and several generalization analyses into numbered subsections. Much of the core method description remains recognizable despite this structural revision.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. Figure 1 becomes a comparative overview, Figure 4 gains a constitutive-code panel, and the original visual-metric figure is reorganized across Figures 3 and 11. Existing ablation plots are rearranged, and numerous transfer, diagnostic, and runtime displays are added, including Table 2.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including differential evolution by Storn and Price, Blickhan's spring-mass model, and recent scientific-discovery and simulation work; the Mip-NeRF reference is removed. Related-work discussion receives limited expansion, while the central positioning relative to predefined laws, neural constitutive models, and SGA remains.

T1.justification: Equation 3 corrects the transmittance product's upper limit from i to i−1. Appendices D and E additionally formalize standard MPM updates and classical elastic/plastic constitutive laws. The main bilevel optimization formulation remains essentially intact, without new theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's gaps in reproducibility, inspectability, and support for cross-scene transfer. Appendices A, G, and H disclose settings, prompts, and inferred laws, while Figures 6, 12, and 13 provide concrete transfer evidence beyond the original temporal tests. Added baseline, viewpoint, and runtime analyses strengthen assessment without relying on improved headline scores. The conflicting initialization descriptions remain a reproducibility weakness, but the substantive evidence and documentation gains outweigh it.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisionLaw, with matching methods and substantial shared results. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–H, which provide newly available documentation and evidence.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds transfer experiments, optimizer comparisons, and supplementary quantitative and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on six synthetic scenes and two real-world scenes, including quantitative comparisons, temporal generalization, and a decoupling ablation.

results.title: VisionLaw: Inferring Interpretable Intrinsic Dynamics from Visual Observations via Bilevel Optimization

C1.justification: The abstract, main contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: unified embodiment-agnostic pointing, four capabilities, Embodied-Points-200K, a 3B model trained through RFT, and strong zero-shot manipulation. The headline benchmark coverage and success rates are unchanged; revised wording emphasizes ideas already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking policy improvements to dense trajectory constraints and execution efficiency to single-pass inference, alongside MOKA failure mechanisms. Learned-policy integration changes from untested future work to preliminary demonstrated capability, and physical common-sense hallucinations become an explicit limitation. The RGB-D discussion becomes more positive, although Appendix G retains an earlier deficit description inconsistent with the updated Table 13.

D1.justification: v2 identifies EasyR1 and CleanDiffuser, provides specific model and dataset links, and documents new alignment stages, planner/controller choices, demonstration counts, and replanning intervals. Core hardware and training hyperparameters remain unchanged. Conversely, v2 removes details explaining construction of the SFT/RL reasoning ablation and the six-trial count for visual-disturbance testing.

E1.justification: LIBERO expands from qualitative trace examples in v1 to executed policy evaluations across 40 Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long tasks in v2 Appendix F. v2 also uses RefSpatial alignment data and adds real-world sorting, multistep organization, mathematically grounded placement, wiping, and bottle pressing. Open6DOR coverage is retained in the appendix.

E2.justification: The SIMPLEREnv comparison replaces RT-1-X, RoboVLM, and SpatialVLA entries with π0, π0-fast, OpenVLA-OFT, ThinkAct, and Magma. v2 also adds MOKA to the eight-task real-world comparison, evaluates A0 trajectories, introduces a Diffusion Policy baseline, and includes OpenVLA (FT) in execution-time comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50 demonstrations per LIBERO task, trace updates every 15 steps on LIBERO-Long, and a bottle-pressing policy trained on 50 demonstrations. SIMPLEREnv reporting changes to 24 episodes per task, removes the grasp-success metric, and changes baseline-result provenance. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds complex-task case studies in Figure 8, A0 trajectory comparisons in Figure 10, and execution-time and failure analyses in Appendix D. Table 12 tests the benefit of trace conditioning for Diffusion Policy. Existing common-sense, SFT/RFT reasoning, mixed-training, and trajectory-point-count ablations remain substantially unchanged.

E5.justification: v1 Table 5 explicitly averages Embodied-R1 and SoFar results over three rounds of 24 runs. v2 Table 4 states 24 episodes per task but omits the three-round aggregation information. This changes statistical reporting without establishing an actual reduction in runs. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or variability estimates for these results.

E6.justification: New results include LIBERO averages of 64.4% for Diffusion Policy and 79.4% with Embodied-R1, MOKA's 9.2% real-world average, and execution-time measurements. RGB-D Level0/Level1/overall scores change from 99.8/50.9/90.2 to 99.2/74.5/94.3 under the revised model and training account. SIMPLEREnv baseline scores are replaced, including OpenVLA's 1.0% versus 5.2% average, and grasp results are removed. The headline 56.2% and 87.5% results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core pointing model and RFT curriculum remain, but v2 implements extensions that v1 left as future work: visual-trace-conditioned Diffusion Policy, periodic replanning, Gemini-based task decomposition, and contact-sensitive controllers. Appendix F also presents a dual-encoder RGB-D architecture with RefSpatial alignment through SFT before 3D RFT, extending the earlier RGB-D fine-tuning account.

P1.justification: The introduction, architecture description, training explanation, and experimental discussion undergo extensive condensation and rewriting. Related Work moves before the method, analysis and ablations are merged, and RGB-D evaluation moves into the appendix. The appendices are reorganized and expanded, with additional authorship, funding, and LLM-use disclosures.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is rearranged into a compact four-panel display, and existing generalization examples are incorporated into the composite Figure 5. v2 adds complex-task and A0 comparison figures and tables for latency, LIBERO, and method positioning. The SIMPLEREnv table is redesigned without grasp columns, while the Open6DOR table moves to the appendix. Typography and captions also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial discussion of VLM reasoning through RFT, including Seg-Zero, VisionReasoner, and Reason-RFT. Appendix H and Table 14 systematically position Embodied-R1 against RoboPoint, RoboBrain, A0, and FSD across representations, capabilities, and reasoning. Additional policy-learning and RGB-D references, alongside removed older citations, materially revise the research positioning.

T1.justification: v1 Equations 1–2 explicitly define the normalized GRPO advantage and clipped objective; v2 replaces these equations with a verbal summary. This reduces formal mathematical specification without establishing a changed optimization rule. The pointing definitions and principal reward equations remain, and neither version develops theorem or proof results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for pointing as a general manipulation interface: v1 left learned-policy integration untested, whereas v2 evaluates it across 40 LIBERO tasks and demonstrates long-horizon and contact-rich execution. The RGB-D design and expanded comparisons further improve assessability. These gains outweigh reporting regressions: Table 4's π0-fast scores average 32.1%, not the stated 48.3%; repeated-round information is lost; and Appendix G retains an RGB-D limitation contradicted by Table 13.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Embodied-R1 and retain matching core methods, datasets, and experiments. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds LIBERO policy evaluations, complex real-world demonstrations, execution-time comparisons, and updated RGB-D results.

before.justification: v1 reports original spatial and pointing evaluations, SIMPLEREnv and real-world robot experiments, and training and reward ablations.

results.title: Embodied-R1: Reinforced Embodied Reasoning for General Robotic Manipulation

C1.justification: The central API-GUI, scalable infrastructure, and Entropulse contribution claims remain. v2 adds an explicit resource contribution in the abstract by introducing OfficeWorld and announcing code and benchmark availability.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly explains how active-application API filtering reduces selection complexity and how omitting historical GUI observations preserves useful interaction history within context limits. Existing interpretations of Entropulse and limitations concerning robustness, long-horizon autonomy, and safety are largely retained.

D1.justification: New Appendices B–E document action definitions, 103 application APIs, prompt and observation formats, history handling, training hyperparameters, computing resources, and annotation procedures. The abstract also adds a code/OfficeWorld repository link. Appendix A largely relocates the previously described API construction workflow.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained OSWorld and OSWorld-Verified evaluations, v2 introduces OfficeWorld: 180 office tasks drawn from SpreadsheetBench, PPTC, and internally developed Writer tasks. This substantially expands the evaluated data within spreadsheet, presentation, and document manipulation.

E2.justification: v2 adds an eight-baseline OfficeWorld comparison, including DeepSeek-V3.1, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4.1, and standalone OpenAI o3 under a common tool framework. This substantially expands the evaluated comparator set. The original OSWorld Table 1 baseline membership is unchanged.

E3.justification: The new OfficeWorld comparison specifies shared tools, framework, and testing conditions. The added multimodal configuration uses screenshots resized from 1920×1080 to 1280×720. Existing ablation settings are retained; Appendix D's newly documented training settings do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: The framework and training ablations match across v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3. Figure 5's Entropulse comparison, the error analysis, and all six demonstrations are retained. Redrawing the error distribution and relocating demonstrations introduce no new analysis.

E5.justification: v2 Table 6 newly discloses training seed 42. Both versions already report ± values in Table 1 and 95% confidence intervals in training plots. Neither specifies repeated-run counts, and no increase in statistical replication is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds GLM-4.1V results of 48.9±0.5 on OSWorld and 48.0 on OSWorld-Verified; retained GLM-4 results remain 48.1±1.0 and 47.3. New OfficeWorld averages are 41.1 and 43.3 for the two proposed variants, versus 33.9 for OpenAI o3. Qwen's Table 1 row disappears, but its 45.8 result remains in the ablation. The headline increase reflects a different backbone.

M1.justification: v2 adds a multimodal GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking variant whose observations use screenshots instead of the accessibility tree (Appendix C). The API-GUI framework, step-level GRPO objective, reward assignment, and Entropulse procedure remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: Sections 2–3 are extensively condensed and rewritten. Detailed API construction moves to Appendix A, Future Direction moves from Section 5 to Appendix F, demonstrations move from Appendix A to G, and a new related-work section and technical appendices substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds OfficeWorld, action-space, API-count, and training-configuration tables, plus two annotation-guideline figures. The error table becomes a pie chart with unchanged proportions, and retained displays are repositioned. The demonstration images remain identical despite renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated related-work section covering language and vision-language models, computer agents, benchmarks, and RL frameworks. New discussion includes CogAgent, OS-Atlas, ZeroGUI, WebArena, SWE-bench, PPO, and Verl, substantially expanding research positioning beyond v1's introductory citations.

T1.justification: The step-level GRPO objective and normalized reward advantage remain mathematically equivalent. Changing conditioning notation from q to q_i,j clarifies the step context without changing the derivation. Neither version adds formal guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing reproducibility information through explicit observation and prompt formats, action definitions, training configurations, and annotation instructions in Appendices B–E. OfficeWorld also supplies additional empirical comparisons under shared tools and settings. Repeated-run reporting remains underspecified, and the higher headline score uses a different backbone, but the substantial gains in technical transparency and empirical support clearly improve overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ComputerRL and retain the same central framework and training approach. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds OfficeWorld evaluations and results for GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking.

before.justification: v1 reports original OSWorld evaluations, framework and training ablations, training curves, error analysis, and execution demonstrations.

results.title: ComputerRL: Scaling End-to-End Online Reinforcement Learning for Computer Use Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: expert-inspired multi-agent IR structure elucidation, complementary expert reasoning, improved baseline performance and flexible incorporation of chemical information.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations and applicability boundaries concerning mixture failures, latency constraints, dependence on translator quality and ReAct tool-selection failures. These extend v1's limitations concerning peak shapes/intensities and translator retraining, and qualify the framework's practical scope.

D1.justification: V2 adds dataset composition/filtering details, pretrained-translator input encoding, measured runtimes and setup information for new comparisons. Core hyperparameters, hardware, software versions, prompt templates and the code link remain. V1's explicit 790k simulated-pretraining sample count is no longer stated.

E1.justification: V2 adds an evaluated incomplete-information scenario using carbon-count ranges rather than exact counts (Appendix C.4). The 9,052-spectrum NIST dataset remains; newly documented phase diversity and mixture composition describe retained data rather than a new dataset.

E2.justification: V2 substantially broadens comparison beyond the retained translator and agent variants by evaluating the Patch-Based Self-Attention Transformer, a GPT-4o ReAct workflow, and zero-shot/QLoRA Llama attempts. The Llama version is inconsistently named Llama-3-8B in prose and LLaMA-3.1-8B in Table 6.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols add MACCS/RDKit/Morgan Tanimoto similarity, two paraphrased prompt sets, carbon-count ranges, zero-shot versus QLoRA Llama evaluation, and a ReAct comparison capped at five tool calls. These substantially expand evaluation design; the existing 80/10/10 split and core training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds prompt robustness, ambiguous-information robustness, ReAct tool-selection failure analysis, single-compound/mixture analysis and a new TI reasoning case study (Figure 4; Appendix C.3–C.6). Existing expert ablations, candidate-count sensitivity, beam-width tests and earlier case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages across three independent experiments and parenthesized uncertainty values. Additional accuracy tables follow the existing practice; no changed run counts, new seed information, confidence intervals or formal significance tests are specified.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results, but v2 adds substantial new findings. Table 6 reports patch-attention versus IR-Agent Top-1 accuracy of 0.129 versus 0.103 and Top-10 accuracy of 0.181 versus 0.216. Table 10 reveals zero exact-match accuracy for 20 mixture test cases. Robustness, ReAct, similarity and runtime results are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The translator, TI/Ret/SE expert pipeline, training objective, retrieval procedure and substantive prompt instructions remain unchanged. Expanded translator explanations and the ReAct comparator do not establish a modification to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify related work, the task and translator roles. V2 adds a dataset appendix and reproducibility statement, moves Broader Impacts into an Ethics Statement, and updates author/header and citation formatting. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the displays with a new TI case-study figure, five new results tables and timing rows in Table 5. It also revises Figure 1 and adopts conference formatting. The earlier beam-width and supplementary case-study figures are retained as Figures 5–6, rather than newly added.

R1.justification: V2 adds references on IR-only reinforcement learning, Llama and mass-spectrometry/formula inference, removes the shift-robust molecular-learning citation, and more explicitly contrasts its setting with formula-conditioned IR models. The central novelty positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–8, including the agent definitions, absorbance conversion, positional embeddings and cross-entropy objective, retain their mathematical substance. V2 adds explanatory motivation rather than new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's narrow comparative validation through external-model and ReAct comparisons, robustness tests and clearer applicability evidence (Tables 6–10). Reporting the patch-attention baseline's Top-1 advantage and complete mixture exact-match failure makes the paper more informative and balanced. Added dataset and latency documentation further strengthens assessment, although Llama naming and some new baseline implementation details remain unclear.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IR-Agent research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures and prompts, support reliable comparison despite reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds baseline comparisons, robustness tests, runtime measurements and single-compound versus mixture results.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on NIST IR spectra, including accuracy comparisons, agent ablations, sensitivity analyses and case studies.

results.title: IR-Agent: Expert-Inspired LLM Agents for Structure Elucidation from Infrared Spectra

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and contribution list extend the performance claim to Mikasa-Robo, reporting 41.2% success and an 11.8-point advantage. The central methodological contributions and previous headline claims remain unchanged. The abstract also corrects the real-world aggregate's description from success rate to success score.

C2.justification: New appendix discussions substantially expand mechanism interpretation: attention to historical frames is interpreted as resolving current-frame ambiguity; episode lengths motivate larger temporal-task memory; cognitive-token results motivate a single-token capacity explanation; and compression/consolidation explain limited inference overhead. Appendix L further explains real-task memory dependence. The existing camera-view limitation and future-work discussion are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reproducibility statement with explicit code, model, and log access links beyond v1's project-page pointer. It clarifies sequential and grouped dataloading, documents Mikasa-Robo data and training/evaluation settings, and specifies inference hardware, precision, and action-chunk configuration. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to retained implementations.

E1.justification: v2 adds five memory-dependent Mikasa-Robo tasks and zero-shot tests on three unseen object/target combinations relative to Apple To Basket. These extend evaluation beyond the retained SimplerEnv, LIBERO, real-robot, and visual-OOD coverage. LIBERO Long and LIBERO-90 becoming Long-10 and Long-90 is renaming, not additional coverage.

E2.justification: CronusVLA is added to the Bridge and LIBERO comparisons in Tables 1 and 3. The new Mikasa-Robo comparison includes OpenVLA-OFT and reproduced CronusVLA alongside existing comparator families. Appendix J additionally evaluates TTF-VLA and MAP-VLA on LIBERO, substantially broadening comparisons with temporal-context methods. TraceVLA, RoboVLMs, and 4D-VLA were already compared in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include joint Mikasa-Robo training for 20k steps using 250 demonstrations per task and 128×128 observations, with 100 evaluation episodes per task. v2 also introduces five-trial zero-shot tests and inference benchmarking on RTX 4090 and HGX H20 in bfloat16. Section 4.2 changes Fractal's reported trial total from 2,352 to 2,856, but Appendix K.2 retains 2,352; an actual increase or rerun cannot be established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Bridge ablations and OOD tests, Appendices E–I add retrieval-attention case studies, episode-length analysis, memory-length/fusion/consolidation ablations on LIBERO-90 and Clean Table & Count, a one-versus-four cognitive-token ablation, inference-overhead analysis, and zero-shot task generalization tests. These directly examine memory behavior and design choices beyond v1's ablation coverage.

E5.justification: Appendix H and Table 15 newly specify that inference measurements are averaged over 300 runs. Neither version reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests for task-success comparisons. This is a limited addition of repeated-measurement information.

E6.justification: Original MemoryVLA headline scores are retained, while v2 adds Mikasa-Robo results (41.2% versus PI-0's 29.4%), further ablation outcomes, runtime measurements, and zero-shot scores. Table 3 changes 4D-VLA's LIBERO average from 88.6 to 92.2, but v2 Table 17 retains 88.6 and gives CronusVLA 92.2 rather than Table 3's 86.2. The new claim of winning every Mikasa task conflicts with Table 4: MemoryVLA scores 24 versus PI-0's 42 on Intercept and 44 versus OpenVLA-OFT's 59 on Remember Color3.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same VLM, perceptual-cognitive memory bank, temporal retrieval, gated fusion, adjacent-entry consolidation, and diffusion action expert. Additional dataloader explanations and experimental component variants do not establish a change to the proposed default method.

P1.justification: Most existing introduction, method, and conclusion prose is retained. Local revisions standardize LIBERO terminology, expand dataloader explanations, update the publication header, and add acknowledgments, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements. The appendices are reorganized and the qualitative sections combined, without a pervasive rewrite of retained content.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 4 are expanded for Mikasa-Robo; new Figures 10–12 visualize retrieval attention and memory-dependent ambiguities. Nine additional tables present benchmark comparisons, statistics, ablations, efficiency, and transfer results. Retained rollout figures are relocated and resized, including combining the SimplerEnv displays on one page. Figure 1 incorrectly labels Table 4's 28.4 OpenVLA-OFT result as π0-FAST.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Mikasa-Robo, CronusVLA, TTF-VLA, MAP-VLA, and several recent VLA works. Appendix J explicitly positions the results against contemporary temporal-context approaches. The original related-work narrative, cognitive-science motivation, and claimed perceptual/cognitive-memory distinction remain largely intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–9 for actions, memory, retrieval, fusion, and consolidation are substantively unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central memory design: component testing extends beyond v1's Bridge tasks to temporal real-world and LIBERO tasks, complemented by a memory-focused benchmark, retrieval evidence, measured overhead, and explicit reproducibility links. These address important gaps in demonstrating where and how memory helps. New baseline inconsistencies, conflicting Fractal trial totals, and overstated Mikasa superiority reduce reporting reliability and require correction, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in direct validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MemoryVLA, with matching methods and identifiable corresponding experiments. All 30 pages of v1 and 36 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not constitute missing material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Mikasa-Robo experiments, further ablations, retrieval-attention analyses, inference measurements, and zero-shot task evaluations.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original simulation and real-robot evaluations, component ablations, and robustness experiments.

results.title: MemoryVLA: Perceptual-Cognitive Memory in Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: unified feedforward avatar reconstruction from variable-length observations, incremental quality improvement, and a favorable quality–speed trade-off. The added methods and experiments support these existing claims. Removing 'High-Fidelity' from the title does not remove the retained high-quality reconstruction claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of pruning, complementary information from compressed frames and tolerance to FLAME tracking errors. Appendix D explicitly connects failures in wrinkles, gaze and tongue reconstruction to LBS and FLAME topology. Conversely, v1's discussion of tracking-head instability, weak tracking-metric gains and anisotropic-fusion limitations is omitted, substantially changing the account of mechanisms and limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents 521 clips sampled at 15 FPS, camera filtering, background processing, image/token dimensions, attention depth and compression implementation. Reported training duration changes from 12 to 14 days; v1's explicit 10,000-step ablation budget is omitted. Access disclosures also change: v1 advertises code, while v2 advertises code and models but elsewhere promises code after acceptance, leaving availability internally inconsistent.

E1.justification: NeRSemble training and Ava256 evaluation remain. v2 adds INSTA evaluation, explicit testing beyond the training camera viewpoints, and reconstruction under streaming arrival of observations (Figures 7, 11–13). These broaden the evaluated data and observation conditions; additional frame counts alone are not treated as new task coverage.

E2.justification: Figures 7–8 add evaluated comparisons with Arc2Avatar and SynShot on INSTA, and Arc2Avatar and HeadGap on NeRSemble, alongside LAM. The earlier main comparator set and Ava256 comparisons remain. LAM* corresponds to v1's already modified multi-frame LAM renderer rather than an additional comparator.

E3.justification: Reported training changes from 124K iterations with a constant learning rate to 150K with cosine scheduling, and sampled input subsets change from 2–16 to 1–16 frames. v2 adds ArcFace-based identity and Gaussian-count metrics, separates ablations across four input counts, and introduces landmark-perturbation and long-sequence evaluation protocols. These are explicit setting changes and new protocols.

E4.justification: Table 2 expands the two-loss ablation into tests of sliced fusion loss, tracking loss, global attention, Gaussian fusion and pruning across multiple input counts. v2 also adds controlled landmark perturbations (Table 4), frame-packing comparisons (Figure 5), wider-viewpoint tests and concrete failure cases (Figures 10, 12–13), substantially extending analysis of mechanisms and robustness.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 4 includes error bars on its PSNR-versus-input-count curve, although their statistical meaning is unspecified. That curve is removed in v2, whose new long-sequence plot has no uncertainty bars. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces many values: FastAvatar's one-frame PSNR changes from 25.24 to 20.08, and its 16-frame rendering speed from 53 to 17.65 FPS. Revised model and training settings prevent a controlled performance comparison between versions. LAM's one-to-16-frame PSNR trend changes from 17.30–19.42 to 17.30–16.49. v2 also adds identity scores, expanded ablation results, perturbation measurements and long-sequence/streaming outcomes.

M1.justification: v2 adds Gaussian importance scores, differentiable Gumbel-Softmax pruning and mask regularization, and reweights the existing losses. It also introduces FramePack-style token compression for long inputs and a streaming procedure using 16-frame windows with four-frame overlap (Section 4.5, Appendices C.3 and D). These extend the retained LGRT architecture and its training and inference procedures.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the introduction and methodology wording remain. Changes include title and author-information edits, terminology and citation-style revisions, targeted rewrites of experimental discussions, and relocation of training details into newly organized appendices. The revision does not extensively rewrite the retained narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout. The teaser and qualitative comparison grids are redesigned; the Ava256 and ablation displays are revised and renumbered. Table 1 gains an identity column and reorganized input-count blocks, Table 2 expands substantially, and new implementation, robustness, long-sequence, viewpoint and failure-case displays are added. v1's error-bar plot is removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens cited research to identity-preserving avatars, additional human-avatar methods and feedforward reconstruction. It explicitly grounds new components in LP-3DGS, MaskGaussian and FramePack, and discusses identity-focused work corresponding to the added comparators. These additions extend research positioning beyond the change from numerical to author-year citations; the original VGGT/LAM relationship remains.

T1.justification: v2 extends the Gaussian representation with an importance score, defines binary pruning masks and an L1 mask regularizer, and adds that regularizer to Equation 10. These are limited additions to the mathematical formulation; the existing reconstruction equations remain, and neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central incremental-reconstruction mechanism: Table 2 isolates additional components across input counts, Table 4 tests dependence on tracking accuracy, and Figures 5 and 11 demonstrate long and streaming inputs. Implementation disclosures and concrete failure cases address v1's limited reproducibility information and narrow validation. Removing unexplained error bars, omitting the ablation budget and giving conflicting code-release statements weaken reporting, but the targeted evidence and technical detail provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FastAvatar and retain matching core sections and experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, expanded component ablations, landmark-perturbation measurements, and long-sequence and streaming reconstruction outcomes in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction-quality and runtime measurements in Table 1, loss ablations in Table 2, and qualitative reconstruction experiments.

results.title: FastAvatar: Towards Unified and Fast 3D Avatar Reconstruction with Large Gaussian Reconstruction Transformers

C1.justification: Integration with other offline RL algorithms changes from future work in v1's conclusion to a central generality claim in v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The abstract also adds an explicit 35% improvement claim over the baseline, based on the retained D4RL results.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking AntMaze/Adroit limitations to sparse rewards and indiscriminate imitation, interprets the roles of L3's factors and increasing BC loss, and discusses sensitivity to initialization and learning rate. Its conclusion acknowledges smaller gains from other algorithm integrations and the possible need for method-specific adaptations.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future repository release; v2's reproducibility statement reports that implementation code is included in supplementary material. Hardware, software versions, and retained hyperparameter tables match. However, v2 removes v1's explicit explanation that the alpha learning rate was scaled proportionally to its update interval in the runtime study.

E1.justification: v2 retains the 39 D4RL datasets and adds ten OGBench AntMaze navigation settings covering large and giant layouts with five tasks each (Section 5.7, Table 4). These extend environment and goal coverage. The additional MuJoCo integration experiments reuse existing dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparator set is retained. Table 3 adds performance comparisons involving CQL and Diffusion-QL and their ASPC adaptations; CQL previously appeared only in runtime comparisons. Table 4 introduces FQL and FQL+ASPC alongside TD3+BC, IQL, ReBRAC, and ASPC.

E3.justification: New sensitivity experiments explicitly test initial alpha values of 0.1, 2.5, and 10 and learning rates of 0.02, 0.002, and 0.0002. Appendix E.2 adds controlled comparisons of five L3 formulations. These add experimental settings, while the retained Appendix B network and training hyperparameters match.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained critic, loss-component, dynamic-alpha, and runtime analyses, v2 adds advantage-weighted imitation tests on sparse-reward tasks, ablations of individual L3 factors and supremum versus expectation formulations, a Q-value/BC-loss training case study, and initialization and learning-rate sensitivity analyses (Appendices E–F).

E5.justification: Table 1 still reports means and standard deviations across four random seeds, and Appendix C retains mean ± one-standard-deviation curves over four seeds. No new repeated-run count, confidence-interval procedure, significance test, or uncertainty-estimation method is described. Several added comparisons report point estimates only, a practice already present in v1.

E6.justification: Table 1 is numerically unchanged, including ASPC's 77.9 overall average. New comparisons include CQL averaging 75.7 versus 81.6 with ASPC (Table 3), and OGBench averages of 68.4 for ASPC, 53.5 for ReBRAC, and 43.6 versus 49.5 for FQL without/with ASPC (Table 4). Appendices E–F add further ablation and sensitivity findings, including task-dependent regressions.

M1.justification: v1 instantiates ASPC on TD3+BC. v2 introduces algorithm-specific adaptations for IQL, CQL, Diffusion-QL, and FQL, including actor-temperature, critic-conservatism, and student-policy updates. Appendix D specifies their inner objectives and L1+L2 outer objectives. Appendix E.1 also introduces an advantage-weighted BC variant.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and method exposition are substantially rewritten. Theory now precedes practical implementation, theorem statements and pseudocode are streamlined, and the conclusion is recast around algorithm generality. Ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements add further document structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column conference formatting. Figure 1 is rearranged, v1 Figures 6–7 become panels of v2 Figure 6, and Tables 1–2 are reformatted. New Tables 3, 4, and 13 and Figures 9–12 add substantial displays; existing appendix learning curves are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for OGBench, Flow Q-learning, Diffusion-QL, and the D4RL dataset paper, while removing the model-based RL discussion and references such as MOPO, MOReL, and COMBO. The central positioning around global constraint scaling without per-dataset tuning remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 corrects the lower bound from |x - 2c sqrt(x)| to max{x - 2c sqrt(x), 0}, revising the resulting mutual-bound argument. v1's Theorem 4.5 asserted that the outer loss guarantees non-decreasing performance under a small-change assumption; v2's Theorem 4.4 instead conditions this conclusion on an idealized update satisfying Delta Q ≥ Phi.

improvement.justification: Correcting the Appendix A.1 bound and qualifying the main guarantee improve mathematical credibility. The integration experiments and Appendices E–F substantially strengthen evidence about applicability, mechanisms, and sensitivity beyond v1's evaluation. Some new comparisons lack uncertainty or detailed settings, broad improvement language overlooks task-level regressions, and Appendix A.3 retains stronger guarantee language. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ASPC and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably despite substantial reformatting and additional sections.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds algorithm-integration experiments, OGBench evaluations, and analyses in Appendices E–F.

before.justification: v1 reports original D4RL evaluations, runtime measurements, ablations, and training curves in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: Adaptive Scaling of Policy Constraints for Offline Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: v2 adds medical-model protection as an explicit contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. Its headline ImageNet-100-Typo accuracy gain changes from 19.6 to 22.06 percentage points. The central claim of defending CLIP through causal head interventions without fine-tuning remains.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses OCR unsuitability, trade-offs against the stronger blurring baseline, and possible effects of training-data typography on medical models. It also newly asserts that non-differentiability prevents adaptive-attack evaluation. The existing spatial-token limitation remains. Figure 10's medical-probe interpretation conflicts with its plotted ordering.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit project/code links, a reproducibility statement, attack fonts, a two-token-row attention mask description, and precise blurring settings (kernel 51, sigma 25). It documents H200 timing conditions and Titan RTX memory feasibility. Conversely, v1's explicit statement that interventions use Prisma is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds typographic Food-101 and Aircraft evaluations, IIIT5K word recognition, and medical skin-lesion classification with clean and attacked inputs, including ISIC2019, HAM10k and BCN20k. The original general-vision and real typographic-attack benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Defense-Prefix and unmodified-model comparisons are retained. v2 Appendix J adds an evaluated PaddleOCR-plus-Gaussian-blur defense and its combination with Dyslexify across five model sizes, substantially expanding the defense comparison.

E3.justification: Circuit construction changes from v1's class-balanced 5% ImageNet-100 training subset to the full training split, with an additional typographic accuracy criterion and k=10 skip limit. New protocols include IIIT5K small/medium-lexicon classification and runtime comparisons on an H200 using matched pipelines and batch sizes.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of OCR capability loss, runtime and memory costs, medical-model probes, and combined blurring/circuit interventions. Circuit-ablation curves are revised and extended to WhyLesionCLIP. The original PCA and attention-sink studies remain, rather than being new appendix additions.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. Existing graphical error bars receive no new uncertainty explanation. The new mean-plus-two-standard-deviations head-score cutoff is an analysis threshold, not a repeated-run uncertainty procedure.

E6.justification: Many scores, circuit sizes and plotted results change. For example, ViT-L RTA-100 accuracy changes from 61.60% to 71.00%; the Defense-Prefix ranking reverses on RTA-100 and PAINT, while clean Food-101 now favors Defense-Prefix. New medical, OCR, runtime and blurring results appear. Construction settings and base-model scores also change, preventing attribution to an isolated same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: v1 Algorithm 1 adds ranked heads until clean accuracy breaches its tolerance. v2 additionally requires each ablation to improve typographic accuracy, skips unsuccessful candidates, and stops after a consecutive-skip limit. This substantially changes circuit selection, while retaining CLS-only head ablation.

P1.justification: v2 renames the paper and method, shifts terminology from training-free to gradient-free, and edits explanatory prose. It reframes probing as motivation, redistributes the standalone dataset section, folds Discussion into Conclusion, and adds backmatter and appendix contents. Much of the existing exposition remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redesigns the head-score/probe figures using thresholded masks and different axis arrangements, redistributes ablation plots, and moves the circuit-size table into the appendix. New medical figures and OCR, runtime and blurring tables materially expand the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: The main related-work argument is largely retained. v2 adds references supporting medical datasets, IIIT5K, PaddleOCR/OpenCV and adaptive-attack evaluation, while removing Prisma and several broad VLM/generative-model references. Appendix J additionally positions mechanistic intervention relative to image-level preprocessing.

T1.justification: The written attention-score definition changes substantively: v1 Equation 6 divides each attention entry by itself, whereas v2 Equation 7 divides summed typographic attention by summed spatial attention. This corrects the formula's attention dependence. The PCA definition and attention-intervention equation remain; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves assessment of the defense's practical value: Appendices H–J quantify OCR losses, computational costs, and a stronger blurring alternative, addressing important gaps in v1's robustness–utility evidence. Medical experiments, the corrected score formula and explicit implementation/access information further strengthen the paper. New reporting problems remain, particularly Figure 10's reversed interpretation and the unsupported dismissal of adaptive evaluation, but these do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mechanistic CLIP defense, renamed Dyslexify in v2. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 reports revised original experiments and adds medical evaluations, OCR results, runtime measurements and comparisons with image blurring.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification results, linear-probe experiments, circuit interventions, and appendix analyses of intrinsic dimensionality and attention sinks.

results.title: Dyslexify: A Mechanistic Defense Against Typographic Attacks in CLIP

C1.justification: The three headline contributions—dimensional limitations, free-embedding experiments, and LIMIT—remain. However, v2's introduction removes the explicit attribution of state-of-the-art LIMIT failures to 'the theoretical underpinnings.' The broad abstract and conclusion claims otherwise persist despite the substantially revised formal assumptions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises the explanation of the limitation: Appendix D distinguishes the k-dependent margin-free result from the new margin-dependent bound, and Appendix C introduces learnability and loss-function qualifications. Section 5.2 adds evidence-based qualifications of BM25's lexical advantage and discusses architectural weaknesses beyond dimensional capacity. The alternatives discussion also allows more expressive similarity functions and future single-vector approaches.

D1.justification: v2 documents how Gemini 2.5 Pro generated synonym replacements, including avoiding collisions with existing items and using scientific names, similar meanings, or hypernyms. It also acknowledges remaining lexical overlap. The existing learning rate, epochs, sampling, hardware, inference framework, and code/data access information are unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds LIMIT-small with corpus attributes replaced by synonyms, introducing retrieval with reduced lexical overlap within the existing synthetic preference task. The random, cycle, and disjoint qrel variants disappear with their ablation. Standard full/small LIMIT and the external-dataset qrel analyses remain.

E2.justification: Corresponding retained experiments use the same comparison methods. The synonym panel reuses existing models, including GTE-ModernColBERT under the shortened GTE-ColBERT label. Newly cited methods such as Reason-ModernColBERT and Hypencoder are discussed without reported evaluations.

E3.justification: v2 adds synonym substitution followed by evaluation against the original LIMIT-small condition, and removes the controlled comparison of four qrel-generation patterns. Retained experiments preserve corpus/query counts, embedding-dimension sweeps, optimization stopping rules, and fine-tuning budgets. The new margin parameter belongs to the theorem, not a documented change to training.

E4.justification: v1's Section 5.4, Figure 6, and Table 3 test whether qrel connectivity explains difficulty; this entire ablation is removed. v2 instead adds a lexical-overlap robustness analysis showing how synonym substitution changes model performance. These address substantially different explanatory questions. The domain-shift experiment remains, and the BEIR correlation analysis moves to Appendix D.4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports explicit seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for these experiments. The new synonym results use the existing point-estimate reporting practice, and the polynomial fit's reported R-squared remains unchanged.

E6.justification: All matched numerical tables retain their values, but the qrel-pattern results are removed and a substantively different finding is added. v2 Figure 6 reports synonym-condition Recall@2 of 10.6 for BM25 and 25.6 for GTE-ColBERT, versus 97.8 and 83.5 on original LIMIT-small; BM25 consequently falls below most tested neural models. These compare different input conditions, not improved or degraded same-setting performance. Table 1 also adds numerical instances of the new theoretical bound.

M1.justification: The retrieval models and free-embedding optimization procedure remain unchanged: Adam, InfoNCE, and unit-vector normalization are retained. Describing normalization as projected gradient descent does not establish a procedural change. Appendix C discusses other researchers' sigmoid-loss findings without introducing an implemented method.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: the original theoretical development moves to Appendix D, the BEIR discussion moves to D.4, and the domain-shift subsection is folded into Section 5.2. Theoretical related work and implications are rewritten, new appendix sections are introduced, and language is edited throughout.

P2.justification: The document is reformatted from the DeepMind template to the ICLR layout, changing the title/abstract presentation, text width, typography, table scaling, and float placement. v2 adds the dimension-bound table and synonym bar chart, removes the qrel-pattern plot and table, and relocates the BEIR scatter plot to the appendix.

R1.justification: The main theoretical positioning shifts from communication complexity and sign-rank to sphere packing, Johnson–Lindenstrauss, and margin-based capacity arguments. New discussions of Alon et al. (1985), Bangachev et al. (2025), and related sigmoid-bottleneck work qualify the original argument. Several earlier sign-rank references disappear; this is a substantive repositioning rather than a bibliography-format change.

T1.justification: v2 adds a unit-norm, positive-margin definition and Theorem 1, proving d ≥ log binom(n,k)/log(1+1/γ) through sphere packing, with asymptotic consequences. The original sign-rank definitions and proofs are retained in Appendix D rather than deleted. That appendix newly explains the k-dependent no-margin bound and its normalization and precision qualifications.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is a more defensible theoretical foundation: v2 explicitly acknowledges the k-dependent no-margin bound and supplies a proved corpus-size-dependent bound under stated margin assumptions, addressing an important gap in v1's theoretical interpretation. The synonym experiment also provides a useful check on BM25's apparent advantage. These gains outweigh the loss of the qrel-pattern ablation, although broad claims equating optimization failure with representational impossibility remain insufficiently qualified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LIMIT and embedding-capacity study. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, allowing the substantial theoretical revision and relocated material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original optimization and retrieval results and adds a LIMIT-small synonym evaluation in Section 5.2 and Figure 6.

before.justification: v1 reports original free-embedding optimization, LIMIT evaluations, fine-tuning experiments, qrel-pattern ablations, and dataset graph analyses.

results.title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval

C1.justification: The headline dataset, two-stage method and OOD-generalization contributions remain unchanged. The limited narrowing is that Section 2.2 removes v1's explicit 'first attempt' priority claim for introducing human-like reasoning into deepfake detection. Additional experiments principally support the retained contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of individual reasoning patterns, MiPO rejection types, exploration strength, group size and inference-cost tradeoffs. It explains its disagreement with BusterX++ about cold-start training and adds an explicit image-only benchmark limitation and discussion of video detection challenges. Failure analysis extends the discussion beyond v1's existing low-resolution caveat.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly documents GPU resources, stage-specific training times, software frameworks, baseline preprocessing, augmentation, training budgets and validation selection. Appendices A.4/A.6 add real-image annotation procedures, expanded artifact definitions, valid output formats and training/inference prompts. These substantially improve documentation, although Figure 40's displayed system prompt conflicts with its caption's default-system description.

E1.justification: v2 Tables 14–15 add AIGIBench facial subsets, LOKI, FakeClue, Forensics-Bench and Nano-banana-150K evaluations. Coverage expands beyond HydraFake facial images to general synthetic imagery, including animals, documents, satellite images and scenes illustrated in Figures 23–27. AIGIBench also supplies data for an additional P-GRPO training experiment.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds evaluated specialized MLLM detectors: M2F2-Det, FakeShield, SIDA-7B, SIDA-13B, FFAA and FakeVLM. These constitute a substantial new comparator category; the original ten vision detectors and six generic MLLMs remain. New qualitative comparisons also examine these specialized detectors.

E3.justification: New protocols include restricted-source VERITAS-MINI with OOD-only averaging, equal-sized 48K FF++ versus HydraFake training comparisons, AIGIBench facial evaluation using VFHQ real images, F1 reporting and batched latency measurements. The reported IC-Light sample count changes from 1,676 in v1 Table 7 to 2,082 in v2 Table 9. MiMo prompting is now explicitly described as omitting prior knowledge. These reporting changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds individual reasoning-pattern removals, separate MiPO rejection-type ablations, data-selection experiments, KL-penalty and rollout-count sensitivity, and reward-model comparisons (Tables 5–6 and 17–19; Figure 10). It also adds efficiency analyses and explicit failure and comparative case studies. The original training-stage, reasoning-quality and JPEG/blur analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 19 newly identifies two random data-sampling settings with seeds 42 and 100. This adds limited seed-specific reporting, without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests or aggregated training-run variability, or establishing an increased repeated-run budget.

E6.justification: Original performance-table entries remain unchanged, including Veritas's 90.7% average in Table 1. Substantial new results include VERITAS-MINI's 85.8% OOD average, 88.9% accuracy on the AIGIBench evaluation and 72.1% on LOKI, alongside new ablation, timing and qualitative findings. These are additional results under newly reported conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The pattern-aware SFT, MiPO cold-start and P-GRPO pipeline, including its losses and reward components, remains unchanged in Section 4. Additional annotation and prompt descriptions document the existing method; restricted-data and reward-model experiments do not establish a revised proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section ordering are retained. v2 makes localized edits to the abstract, related work and conclusion, shortens HydraFake-100K to HydraFake in the narrative, updates author/header information, and adds an appendix contents guide and subsections. The scientific additions do not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 is expanded and grouped by model category. v2 adds numerous ablation, benchmark and efficiency displays, comparative reasoning panels, failure examples and prompt panels. v1 Figure 4 is relocated and expanded as v2 Figure 9; the original training-stage charts and reasoning-quality/robustness tables are retained under new numbers.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including DFBench, BusterX/BusterX++, LOKI, SophiaVL-R1, DeepfakeBench and Swift, and explicitly contrasts its cold-start findings with BusterX++. It also removes the 'first attempt' wording. The main related-work organization and positioning around pattern-aware reasoning versus post-hoc explanations remain intact.

T1.justification: The objectives and reward definitions in Equations 1–6 and the explanation-versus-reasoning formulations in Equations 7–8 are retained. v2 adds conceptual explanations but no new or substantively revised formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's HydraFake-centered evidence: specialized MLLM comparisons with a restricted-training control, external benchmark testing, and targeted component ablations address important gaps in assessing generalization and the proposed mechanisms. Detailed implementation information and explicit failure and modality limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. The original scores remain unchanged, and Figure 40 introduces a prompt-documentation inconsistency, but this localized ambiguity does not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HydraFake dataset and Veritas research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds specialized-detector comparisons, external benchmark evaluations, component ablations, efficiency measurements and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original HydraFake evaluations, training-stage and reward ablations, reasoning-quality assessments and robustness experiments in Section 5 and Appendix A.4.

results.title: Veritas: Generalizable Deepfake Detection via Pattern-Aware Reasoning

C1.justification: v3 makes SoM-assisted zoom-and-retrieve a headline contribution and claims consistent accuracy gains and improved multistep robustness. v1 emphasizes the benchmark and general browsing framework while acknowledging that full-scale cropping experiments were not conducted. The benchmark's central difficulty and Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 attributes o3's easy-split failures primarily to skipping image search, distinguishes OCR-driven text search from visual retrieval, and explains different uses of zooming across models. It adds interpretations concerning internal-knowledge dependence and temporal benchmark drift. Appendix F also clarifies that human boxes bypass unreliable localization rather than demonstrate autonomous grounding. The original general limitations are retained within the Ethics Statement.

D1.justification: v3 provides SoM annotation and tool-interface details, the full system prompt, and executed tool traces (Appendices F, K, and L). It identifies Gemini as the webpage summarizer and reports an anonymized dataset-use archive and a 30-example supplement, replacing v1's project-page disclosure. The judge-consistency information is retained in Appendix G rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same benchmark coverage: 311 image-based questions across eight primary categories, with identical primary-category counts. MMSearch+lite selects 239 existing tasks rather than introducing another domain or task. Its filtering belongs to evaluation protocol, while SoM changes the agent's assistance and tools.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds an evaluated human/browser baseline and an o3 text-search-only comparator. GPT-5 also participates in the agentic Full Rollout + SoM comparison, whereas v1 evaluates it only without search and with image search. The underlying four-model roster remains unchanged; v1's human row contains only placeholders.

E3.justification: v3 adds the 239-task evaluation excluding questions answered without search by any tested model, a human protocol using Chrome for 10–20 minutes per task, text-only rollout, and marked-image SoM evaluation with a stated 20-tool-call limit. These are additional evaluation designs. The text-only budget is internally inconsistent: Section 3 states 20 rounds, while Section 5.1 states 10.

E4.justification: v3 adds SoM ablations, the internal-knowledge filtering analysis, inspection of 10 of 23 o3 easy-split failures, scene-text/OCR analyses, tool-transition and zoom-behavior diagnostics, and two detailed successful trajectories. The original trajectory plot survives as Figure 15. Conversely, v1's detailed o3 trajectory tables and its video-dependent failure case are removed.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies seed 42 for selecting 30 supplementary task examples. This is a limited seed disclosure, not evidence of additional evaluation runs. Neither version reports repeated-run accuracy estimates, significance tests, or confidence intervals for the benchmark scores.

E6.justification: All 11 corresponding Table 1 rows are unchanged, including Full Rollout accuracies of 36.0/23.8/6.1 for o3/Gemini/Qwen. v3 adds SoM results of 37.6/27.7/7.1, GPT-5 + SoM at 35.4, humans at 22.8, o3 text-only search at 37.0, and the lite results in Table 4. These are additional conditions, not same-setting performance improvements. Detailed secondary-category counts and numerical trajectory summaries are removed.

M1.justification: v1 supports cropping in principle but explicitly excludes it from the main experiments because models cannot reliably localize regions. v3 introduces an operational Set-of-Mark pathway: human-curated indexed boxes, raw and annotated image inputs, indexed zooming, and crop-seeded image retrieval (Section 2.5 and Appendix F). This substantially changes the agent's inputs and available procedure, without changing the underlying MLLMs.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, framework description, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Contributions move earlier, the analysis section is reorganized, detailed related work and judge information move into appendices, and ethics and reproducibility statements are added. This constitutes substantial narrative restructuring beyond the insertion of new experiments.

P2.justification: v3 introduces a new opening paradigm diagram, relocates the original concert example to Figure 8, redesigns dataset statistics and accuracy tables, and adds performance comparisons, tool heatmaps, raster plots, zoom histograms, and annotated-image examples. Error cases are reformatted and reduced from four to three. The original trajectory figure moves to Appendix J, while several numerical appendix tables disappear.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion or citations for GQA, OK-VQA, InfoSeek, LiveVQA, SoM, and evaluated model reports. Table 2 now includes BrowseComp-VL and MM-BrowseComp, already discussed in v1. Most of the original literature review survives in Appendix D, and the central positioning around sustained reasoning from sparse visual cues remains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems, proofs, or guarantees. Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation remains a conceptual curation procedure; the new conditional tool-transition frequencies are empirical analyses rather than new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v1 emphasizes fine-grained visual reasoning but omits full-scale cropping evaluation. v3 substantially addresses that evidential gap through documented human-mark-assisted experiments, a text-only control, human comparison, and analyses of memory and tool-choice confounds. The prompt and tool specifications also materially improve reproducibility. Conflicting text-search budgets, Sports gains that do not match Table 4, and removal of detailed trajectory tables limit precision, but do not outweigh the stronger experimental support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MMSearch-Plus, its 311-task benchmark, Spatial-Temporal Extrapolation, and browsing-agent framework. All 18 pages of v1 and 38 pages of v3, including figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds human performance, SoM-assisted browsing, text-only search, filtered-subset results, and tool-behavior analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on MMSearch-Plus in Table 1, together with trajectory statistics and manually annotated failure analyses.

results.title: MMSearch-Plus: Benchmarking Provenance-Aware Search for Multimodal Browsing Agents

C1.justification: The central claims about universal functional sparsity, scaling, and the first diffusion-LLM sparsity study remain. v2 extends its stated contributions to reasoning models and temporal mask dynamics.
