The conclusion also narrows input sparsification from the 'most efficient approach' to the 'most practical training-free approach.'

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations and boundaries: effective rank alone cannot explain sparsification tolerance; generation limits confound reasoning-model degradation; diffusion masks generally lack sufficient stability for reuse; and MoE task variation can average out across experts. Section 5 also explicitly discusses the FFN-only scope and its dependence on context length and attention costs.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reproducibility statement reporting a public code repository and A100/GH200 hardware, explicitly lists the retained evaluation suite, and documents batchwise effective-rank computation and MoE configurations. These substantially expand reproducibility information. The repository's availability is asserted by the PDF, and the hardware disclosure does not establish a change to retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds generative reasoning evaluations on MMLU-Redux, GSM8K, and TruthfulQA. Diffusion evaluation expands to additional knowledge/science tasks, HumanEval and MBPP coding, and CMMLU and C-Eval Chinese benchmarks. This substantially broadens task and language coverage beyond v1; explicitly naming the retained nine-task suite is additional documentation.

E2.justification: The original top-k and max-p comparisons remain in v2 Figure 8, corresponding to v1 Figure 4. v2 Figure 9 additionally compares standard top-p with generalized variants using L=0.5 and L=2, expanding the evaluated sparsification-rule comparators.

E3.justification: The original zero-shot evaluation and 99%-performance-retention criterion remain. New protocols include Qwen3-4B Instruct/Thinking generative evaluation with a generation limit, expert-level testing of Qwen3-30B-A3B and OLMoE-7B-A1B, normalized effective-rank measurements, and consecutive/drift Jaccard measurements across diffusion steps. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of effective rank and critical thresholds versus model size, generalized-rule sensitivity, sparsity variation across MoE experts and tasks, and diffusion-mask stability across steps and layers. These investigate redundancy, operator choice, expert heterogeneity, and mask-reuse feasibility beyond v1's retained rule comparisons and transferability heatmaps.

E5.justification: v2 adds expert-level dispersion reporting, including explicitly labeled standard-deviation shading in Figure 17, and error bars in Figure 3c. The latter bars are not clearly defined. Neither version reports repeated-run counts or seed-based confidence intervals; expert variation should not be interpreted as uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: The original critical-sparsity entries are unchanged between v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2. v2 adds all-inputs results, including 66.26% for pretrained Gemma3-27B, and extensive reasoning, rank, MoE, and temporal-mask findings. Its new diffusion table reports HumanEval critical sparsities of 81.25% for intermediate and 77.89% for all-inputs sparsification. These are added results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core top-p procedure remains unchanged. v2 adds simultaneous input-and-intermediate sparsification, called all-inputs, and an optional generalized top-p^L operator using powered activation magnitudes (Section 2.2 and Appendix A.2). These are limited procedural extensions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and background are extensively rewritten. The compact question-led experimental narrative becomes a structured set of subsections, the sparsification framework receives a separate section, and appendices are reordered and expanded. Reproducibility, ethics, contribution, and acknowledgement statements are also added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn as three full GLU diagrams, Figure 2 gains all-inputs displays, and the task-density plot is replaced by explicit per-task plots. v2 adds rank, reasoning, MoE, and diffusion-stability figures, introduces a diffusion-results table, and expands the original critical-sparsity table with all-inputs columns. The visual organization changes substantially.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning around sparsity's origins, activation functions, scaling, and acceleration, adding works such as Andriushchenko et al., Peng et al., Luo et al., and ShadowLLM. Conversely, v1's detailed diffusion pruning/caching survey in Appendix C is reduced, with several associated references removed. This exceeds bibliographic or citation-style editing.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 introduces a formal generalized top-p^L mask-selection definition and identifies L=1 as the original rule. The existing sparsification definitions remain, with no new theorems or proofs. The effective-rank and Jaccard formulas primarily document standard evaluation metrics.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 by directly testing reasoning models, extending universality evidence to MoE and coding/Chinese diffusion tasks, and investigating mask stability rather than assuming reuse is practical. The added reproducibility information and clearer organization make the evidence substantially easier to assess. Generation-limit confounding and incomplete uncertainty reporting remain, but the stronger empirical grounding and explicit applicability boundaries provide a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same activation-sparsity study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds reasoning-model evaluations, expanded diffusion benchmarks, MoE experiments, effective-rank measurements, and temporal sparsity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original sparsification experiments across model families, sizes, tasks, and training variants, including LLaDA comparisons, numerical critical sparsities, and appendix analyses.

results.title: Universal Properties of Activation Sparsity in Modern Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions now claim additional gains from GC verification, superiority to standard few-shot and self-consistency, and effectiveness on open-source VLMs, including cross-model transfer approaching GPT-4o mini. Open-source integration changes from future work in v1 to a claimed demonstrated contribution in v3.

C2.justification: V3 explains strict filtering's failure on Qwen through rejection of otherwise acceptable traces, interprets cross-model notebooks as reasoning transfer, and argues for retrieval-score robustness and manageable overhead. Its latency explanation invokes improved coherence and reduced internal search as possibilities. V1's interpretation that Gemini 2.5 better aligns with human preferences is removed.

D1.justification: V3 discloses character-level retrieval scoring, open-source hardware/runtimes, baseline generation settings and token/API costs. It also identifies GPT-4o and prompt tailoring for the retained image-only ablation. Original prompts and core API details remain. Conversely, v1's reproducibility statement and promise to release code are removed; neither PDF supplies a code-access link.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate specification-driven part retrieval using the same Fusion 360 archive and its self-generated and human-preference datasets. New model configurations, retrieval variants and smaller evaluation subsets do not introduce another dataset domain or task.

E2.justification: V3 adds evaluated standard few-shot and self-consistency baselines in Table 3, substantially extending comparison beyond notebook removal and image-only reasoning. It also adds with/without-notebook comparisons for Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and Aya-Vision-8B. The original proprietary-model comparators and image-only comparison remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include recall/F1 evaluation, self-consistency with five samples at temperature 0.7, and a 100-sample latency study using one endpoint, one worker and no batching. V3 also introduces 2B/8B model configurations and Aya evaluations on 666/370 cases. These supplement the retained original evaluation rather than establish changed settings for its unchanged results.

E4.justification: V3 tests strict versus relaxed filtering, notebook transfer from GPT-4o to Qwen, character versus token-based retrieval, and computational overhead. These address filter failure, exemplar quality, retrieval sensitivity and practicality. The original CoT/exemplar ablation, image-only comparison and twelve case studies remain; their relocation is not new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports seeds, confidence intervals or variability estimates. V3 mentions an additional Aya-Vision run on different hardware, but does not clarify whether it repeats the evaluation or covers additional computation. Thus, a change in repeated-evaluation reporting is ambiguous. Self-consistency's five samples are part of inference, not an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: All original rows in Tables 1 and 2 are retained unchanged. V3 adds substantial results for filtering, baselines, open-source models, recall/F1, retrieval scoring and efficiency. For example, GPT-4o human-preference accuracy is 66.8% with sGC and 68.1% with token-level retrieval, versus the retained 65.1% notebook result. These are new variant results, not corrections to the original setting.

M1.justification: The two-stage pipeline, reasoning correction and RAG procedure remain. V3 adds strict/relaxed notebook filtering based on answer markers and valid filenames (Section 2.4), a token-Jaccard retrieval alternative, and GPT-4o-generated notebooks for Qwen inference. These are bounded extensions to filtering, retrieval and exemplar sourcing.

P1.justification: V3 rewrites the abstract and contribution narrative, places problem formulation before dataset construction, expands the explanation of the two stages, and reorganizes the appendices around supplementary results and prompts. The LLM-use, ethics and reproducibility sections are removed. This is substantial structural revision beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: V3 adds a front-page scope diagram, combines the dataset and inference diagrams, redraws notebook construction to include GC, expands Table 1 and introduces several result tables. Original Figures 4–5 move unchanged to Figures A.1–A.2; engineering and case-study images are retained with relocation and layout changes.

R1.justification: V3 adds references for Qwen2-VL and Aya-Vision and explicitly positions the approach against alternative training-free inference strategies. The CAD survey and CAD-automation references have corrected author attributions but identify the same works. The broader CAD and self-correction positioning remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds an elementary API-call cost derivation: notebook construction requires the sum of each assembly's part count plus two calls per assembly (Equation 7). The original reasoning-trajectory and retrieval mathematics remain substantively unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the empirical case by addressing v1's lack of alternative training-free baselines, testing filter and retriever choices, and measuring engineering costs. Open-source evaluations also replace a proposed extension with evidence. These gains outweigh reporting drawbacks: the abstract's roughly four-point GPT-4o-mini gap applies only to the fewer-than-ten-part human-preference subset against the unaugmented comparator, and the code-release commitment is dropped.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Error Notebook-guided CAD part-retrieval work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains those experiments and adds grammar-filter evaluations, alternative baselines, open-source model results, retrieval metrics, retriever sensitivity and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original retrieval experiments across several VLMs, CoT/exemplar ablations, an image-only comparison and qualitative retrieval cases.

results.title: Error Notebook-Guided, Training-Free Part Retrieval in 3D CAD Assemblies via Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: v1's abstract emphasizes separating persona effects from persistent model dispositions. v4 instead foregrounds claims of agreement with human evaluators and recovery of objective GPQA rankings without labels. Its conclusion incorporates these validation claims into the justification for meaningful value rankings. The original disposition finding and proposed applications remain in the paper.

C2.justification: v4 qualifies the premise that models aligned with a trait are better judges of it, distinguishing kindness from plainspokenness. It adds interpretations of human agreement, constitution-wording robustness, and Deep Ecology's larger uncertainty from frequent ties. The dimension analysis now emphasizes the usefulness of larger embeddings for diverse populations. The conclusion newly discusses collection inefficiency and possible active-learning remedies; the Greenbeard limitation is retained.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-access link and explicit model identifiers for the main, GPQA, and 37-model experiments. It supplies the Loving criteria, revised constitution-generation information, and human-data collection details. The old Claude/OpenAI constitution lists disappear with their experiment. Adam settings and the generic persona and judge-scaffold prompts are retained. The PDFs establish the new access information, not whether the linked repository is operational.

E1.justification: v4 adds graduate-level scientific question answering through GPQA and a human-judgment study. Deep Ecology progresses from a documented constitution in v1 to reported evaluation in v4. The Claude-constitution/OpenAI-spec evaluation is replaced by evaluation using the Loving constitution. AskReddit, OpenAssistant, and AIRiskDilemmas remain in use.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained self-rating surveys, v4 adds human-derived scalar-BTD trust vectors as references for LM judgments and GPQA accuracy rankings as references for EigenBench rankings. These substantially broaden the comparison evidence. The scaffold-versus-no-scaffold comparator and its five judges are retained; additional evaluated LMs are not themselves new ranking-method baselines.

E3.justification: The main ranking experiment expands from five to eight models and from 24,000 to approximately 30,000 comparisons over 1,000 scenarios. Conservatism changes from eleven Gemini-assisted criteria to ten GPT-4.1-generated criteria. New designs include seven human judges, 448 GPQA questions, and a 37-model run with 140,000 comparisons over 2,000 scenarios. Character-training evaluation now compares base, prompted, and fine-tuned versions of the same Llama model.

E4.justification: v4 adds constitution-generation sensitivity testing and analyses of human judge embeddings and human-teleportation weights. It replaces the five-model confidence-width analysis with split-sample score stability on 37 models and replaces the 25-persona embedding-dimension experiment with a 37-model analysis. The original judge-quality and Greenbeard tests remain, with the latter moved to Appendix L.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix F uses 100 bootstrap resamples per confidence-interval estimate with adaptive repetitions. Its replacement in v4 Appendix K.1 uses 20 disjoint-subsample comparisons per sample size and reports Monte Carlo means and standard errors. GPQA validation adds a random-ranking probability calculation. The existing practice of displaying 95% percentile-bootstrap intervals for model rankings continues.

E6.justification: v4 replaces the main rankings and Claude/OpenAI-spec results and adds Loving scores of 1426, 1579, and 1573 for base, prompted, and fine-tuned Llama 3.1. New findings include human-human versus human-LM distances of 0.3133 versus 0.3130, GPQA Kendall tau approximately 0.77, and the 37-model leaderboard. Changed populations and constitutions prevent interpreting revised scores as same-setting gains. The 21%/79% variance decomposition, scenario-distribution scores, and judge-bias rates remain; the population-sensitivity table reorders existing values.

M1.justification: The original judge scaffold, low-rank Bradley–Terry–Davidson model, and LM-only EigenTrust procedure remain. However, Appendix H adds joint human/LM judge modeling and hybrid aggregation through teleportation toward human trust vectors. Section 5.3 also introduces a constitution-free GPQA adaptation using answer-choice comparisons and ties for identical answers. These extend the procedure beyond simply evaluating the unchanged method on additional data.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are rewritten around validation, and the introduction expands its explanation of eigenvector weighting. Character-training background moves into related work; survey details, variance calculations, and Greenbeard analysis move into appendices. References and appendix organization are substantially reorganized. These changes alter the narrative structure beyond merely inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a single-column ICLR layout and redraws Figure 3 from two stacked horizontal-ranking panels into three side-by-side panels. It adds human-embedding, teleportation, and 37-model displays and restructures the stability/dimension plots. The causal data-collection diagram and separate tie-propensity heatmap are removed, while several retained figures and tables are relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: v4 adds Maiya et al. on Open Character Training and Rein et al. on GPQA, while removing the Sharma et al. sycophancy reference. Existing Constitutional AI and deliberative-alignment discussion moves into related work. The principal positioning against LMArena, Prompt-to-Leaderboard, and LitmusValues remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v4 adds formal definitions for human-guided teleportation and expected split-sample score instability, and changes the stated minimum model population from three to two. The original BTD likelihood, EigenTrust construction, and identifiability argument remain substantively unchanged. The variance decomposition is relocated to Appendix F, rather than newly derived.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation of what EigenBench scores measure. Human-judgment comparison, GPQA rank recovery, and the same-base-model character-training comparison address a central weakness of v1's predominantly internal evidence. Constitution sensitivity testing, larger-population analysis, and model identifiers further improve credibility and reproducibility. Some earlier diagnostics are removed, and the seven-person, single-constitution human study and extrapolation from GPQA still limit generalization. Nevertheless, the added validation provides a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EigenBench and retain the same core research framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, allowing additions, replacements, and relocated material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds human judgments, GPQA ranking experiments, character-training evaluation, constitution sensitivity tests, and a 37-model study.

before.justification: v1 reports original model rankings, persona experiments, model surveys, robustness tests, and judge-quality and confidence analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: EigenBench: A Comparative Behavioral Measure of Value Alignment

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes trade-offs among three propagators. v4 adds central claims about coherent physical timescales, performance across protein scales and superiority relative to external simulators. The introduction also claims the first learned all-atom rollout recovering a GPCR activation surface and explicitly scopes GLDP as a system-specific surrogate. These exceed the significance of simply naming the framework.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly excludes NVE energy conservation and exact physical kinetics and describes timescale comparisons as diagnostic. It adds interpretations of uncertainty, data scarcity, temporal-stride effects and latent-capacity trade-offs. The alanine Langevin failure explanation also replaces v1's reused-GPCR-hyperparameter account with an account based on system-specific RMSD calibration.

D1.justification: Appendices A.2–A.5 newly document architectures, training budgets, the 80/20 split, noise scales, diffusion settings and pseudocode; A.9.4 identifies timing hardware. v4 reports an integrated GLDP repository with seeds, an environment file and latent data, replacing two earlier code links. Conversely, GPCR provenance becomes less precise because v1's explicit dataset DOIs are replaced by study-level references.

E1.justification: v4 adds actual evaluations on ATLAS proteins 7JFL and HIV-1 protease 1R6W, extending coverage to intermediate-size globular proteins and mixed alpha/beta topology. Alanine dipeptide, A1AR and A2AR remain represented. A2AR activation analysis already appeared in v1 and is not a newly introduced task.

E2.justification: v1's evaluated external comparator was EGNO on alanine dipeptide. v4 removes that comparison and evaluates LSS and GeoTDM on alanine dipeptide, plus LSS and MD-Gen on 7JFL, 1R6W and A1AR (Table 1). GeoTDM has no reported scores on the larger proteins, and MD-Gen is omitted from the alanine comparison.

E3.justification: v4 adds coordinate-distribution JSD, contact-map correlation and TICA/autocorrelation-based kinetic evaluation, with procedures in Appendices A.6–A.7. New experiments vary training-data fractions and prediction strides and measure runtime across rollout lengths. These substantially expand evaluation design; the existing lDDT failure threshold and main Langevin timestep/sampling-stride specifications are retained.

E4.justification: v1 mainly supplies descriptive rollout and ensemble analyses. v4 adds controlled A1AR studies of encoder width, pooling size, diffusion schedules, score-query level, clipping and integration step size. Appendix A.9 additionally tests data efficiency, temporal stride, residual versus direct prediction, and computational scaling on 7JFL.

E5.justification: v1 presents point estimates without run-count or uncertainty reporting. v4 Table 2 first reports means and standard deviations over five independent runs; Table 10 reports three-run means, and the reproducibility statement mentions fixed seeds. This establishes substantially richer statistical reporting, without establishing an explicit increase over v1's undisclosed run budget.

E6.justification: v4 adds baseline, kinetic, ablation and runtime outcomes and revises retained summaries: alanine NN backbone JSD changes from 0.0056 to 0.061 ± 0.003. Its reported failure changes from 3,176 frames to no failure within 10,000, aligning the text with unchanged Figure 2. v1's A2AR numerical summary and average-RMSF summary disappear. These are revised reports, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The fixed LD-FPG backbone and three primary propagator families remain. However, v4 revises the stated denoiser-to-score normalization from -epsilon/sigma^2 to -epsilon/sigma and introduces an evaluated residual-prediction NN variant in Appendix A.9.3. Direct prediction remains the main NN formulation; expanded architecture documentation alone does not establish further method changes.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, methods and discussion are extensively rewritten and reorganized. v4 introduces GLDP terminology, an explicit contributions list, a four-step workflow, a standalone Outlook and a reproducibility statement. The supplement is reorganized into detailed methods, evaluation and ablation subsections, substantially changing the narrative beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: v4 replaces the combined quantitative summary with separate benchmark and uncertainty tables, adds numerous appendix tables and algorithm displays, and introduces baseline landscape Figures 6–8. The earlier A2AR supplementary activation surface is redesigned as main Figure 4; the A1AR activation figure and A2AR dihedral figure are omitted. Figures 1–2 remain unchanged, while typography, headers and figure placement change throughout.

R1.justification: v4 substantially revises positioning around system-specific surrogates and introduces an explicit first-GPCR-activation novelty claim. Related work adds ITO, an LSS extension, diffusion/flow-matching foundations and ATLAS references, while removing discussions such as Hamiltonian and Lagrangian networks. These are substantive changes beyond renumbering or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: Section 3.4 revises the mathematical score normalization and explicitly defines the target latent distribution as the encoder pushforward of the coordinate equilibrium, with an exact-score stationary-density qualification. The DMD least-squares construction and NN prediction objective remain essentially unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially improves the assessability of v1's comparison through repeated-run uncertainty, controlled sensitivity studies, broader external comparisons and detailed implementation documentation. It also fixes the alanine stability text/figure inconsistency and revises the score formula. These gains address important evidential and reproducibility gaps. Material problems remain: the claim of uniquely stable GPCR kinetics exceeds Table 1, and Table 9's A1AR budget permits only 5,000 sampled Langevin outputs despite a reported failure at 7,476. Those inconsistencies limit the new kinetic conclusions without outweighing the broader improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LD-FPG-based latent dynamics study. All 16 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v4, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison. The substantial expansion does not prevent matching retained material.

after.justification: v4 reports original baseline comparisons, kinetic measurements, propagator evaluations, ablations and runtime results in Section 4 and Appendices A.8–A.9.

before.justification: v1 reports original propagator rollouts, stability measurements, dihedral statistics and GPCR free-energy analyses in Sections 4 and S1.

results.title: Beyond Ensembles: Simulating All-Atom Protein Dynamics in a Learned Latent Space

C1.justification: Both versions claim user-defined policy moderation, the DynaBench dataset, small dual-mode guardian models, strong safety/compliance performance, and actionable explanations. V3's abstract emphasizes surpassing static guardians, but that claim already appears in v1's introduction. The central contributions and conclusion retain their scope.

C2.justification: V3 qualifies cross-domain generalization by explaining that DynaBench-only training does not achieve state-of-the-art safety performance. Appendix A.9 describes the safety/compliance tradeoff beyond 11k GRPO samples, and A.10 discusses missing response-safety fields in NemoGuard outputs. The original limitations and societal-impact discussion are otherwise retained.

D1.justification: V3 adds the five baseline guardian prompts, identifies VERL, and documents validation-based hyperparameter selection, search ranges, optimizer settings, generation controls, and scaling schedules. It also details rule-writing categories and iterative label-validation procedures. These substantially extend v1's brief hyperparameter list and general prompting description; model/data and code access links remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The named training datasets, safety benchmarks, DynaBench task, and IFEval scenario are retained. However, DynaBench's test inventory changes from eight business-impact categories and fifteen failure modes to twelve and sixteen. The overlapping descriptions and retained examples do not establish whether this represents changed scenario coverage or recategorization of existing examples.

E2.justification: The corresponding benchmark, IFEval, ablation, and model-family comparisons retain their comparator sets. GuardReasoner and DynaGuard CoT/non-CoT rows are relabeled, not added. NemoGuard's revised score concerns its reported results, not a different comparison method.

E3.justification: The training-label audit changes from 50 examples reviewed by two annotators to 743 deliberately harder examples divided among three annotators, with one annotation per example. Appendix A.9 also revises stated settings: GRPO batch size changes from 64 to 48, with model-specific learning rates replacing the previous common rates. V3 adds a training-scaling evaluation protocol and replaces ablation score deltas with relative error-rate reduction. These reported revisions do not establish that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V3 substantially expands validation and diagnostics through the larger label audit, detailed accuracy breakdowns by business impact, failure mode, policy length, dialogue length, tokens, and logical hops, plus a training-scaling analysis. Existing ablations gain separate WildGuard and DynaBench scores. The original ablations, model-family comparisons, error-summary tables, and IFEval analysis were already present in v1's appendix.

E5.justification: V1 states only that evaluations use three to six seeds. V3 Table 17 supplies dataset-specific run counts and F1 standard deviations across the benchmark comparison, including two runs for BeaverTails. The label audit adds Cohen's kappa of 0.85; training inter-rater agreement is no longer reported because examples receive single human annotations. These changes concern reporting and audit design, not an established increase in evaluation runs.

E6.justification: V1 Table 2 becomes v3 Table 3: NemoGuard's WildGuard F1 changes from a self-reported 77.5 to a measured 64.5; DynaGuard-1.7B and 4B DynaBench F1 change from 63.5/68.2 to 65.2/72.0, with revised averages. V3 adds dataset-specific ablation results and extensive failure profiles. Human-label agreement changes from 76% to 92.6% under a different audit design, not a matched improvement comparison. DynaGuard-8B's 73.1 DynaBench F1 and the 63.8% IFEval result remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same policy/dialogue inputs, dual reasoning and direct-answer modes, mixed safety/DynaBench supervised fine-tuning, and subsequent GRPO. The training equations and principal algorithmic components are retained. Expanded implementation disclosures and revised hyperparameters do not establish a new method.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten and condensed, and dataset construction is reorganized into explicit subsections. Training mathematics, ablations, and model-family results move into the main text, while the taxonomy, synthetic example, and distribution figure move into the appendix. Terminology is standardized from Compliance to DynaBench, alongside the title's Guardrail-to-Guardian edit.

P2.justification: V3 adds a multi-panel failure-analysis figure, category-distribution charts, and extensive appendix performance plots. Tables gain grouped rows, shading, separate ablation dataset columns, and new validation, hyperparameter, and uncertainty displays. Existing IFEval statistics become three tables. The original distribution figure is retained as Figure 6, rather than removed.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion adds controllable safety configurations, Guardformer, and CantTalkAboutThis, acknowledging nearby work on customization, efficiency, and topic control. Additional references support already-used models, benchmarks, statistics, and training software. The overall positioning around arbitrary application-specific policies remains stable.

T1.justification: The classification-SFT, reasoning-SFT, and GRPO objectives, including the advantage expression, move from v1 Appendix A.5 to v3 Section 3.5 without substantive mathematical changes. No new theorem, proof, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses v1's limited dataset validation and missing uncertainty and reproduction information through the 743-example audit, benchmark standard deviations, explicit prompts/settings, and detailed failure analyses. These strengthen assessment of the central dataset and model evidence despite mostly stable headline findings. The audit loses training inter-rater measurement, and conflicting policy-length maxima of 86 and 103 remain unresolved, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical transparency and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DynaGuard/DynaBench work. All 22 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison. Extensive relocation and terminology changes can be matched.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and reports additional human validation, detailed failure analyses, evaluation variability, and training-scaling findings.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, training ablations, human label validation, failure analyses, and an IFEval correction experiment in the main text and appendix.

results.title: DynaGuard: A Dynamic Guardian Model With User-Defined Policies

C1.justification: The main upper-bound, lower-bound, and near-optimality contributions remain. V2 corrects the abstract's complexity expression to match the existing Theorem 3.1 and explicitly presents the finite-difference contribution as extending Chayti and Jaggi's meta-learning results and addressing their broader-applicability conjecture.

C2.justification: V2 removes the experimental explanation favoring p=2 because higher orders require more lower-level solves, and drops the broad dismissal of variance reduction. It instead proposes combining variance reduction or momentum with the method. New discussion connects high smoothness to logistic regression and presents the MLP experiment as evidence of potential beyond the theoretical assumptions.

D1.justification: V2 newly discloses K=10 inner iterations and T=1000 outer iterations for the main experiment, identifies the unregularized baseline as SGD, specifies the MLP's depth, ReLU activation, and width 500, and supplies a reproduction-code link. The iteration counts are newly documented, not established increases over v1.

E1.justification: The empirical coverage remains the 20 Newsgroup learn-to-regularize task; no additional dataset is identified. The added MLP changes the evaluation model within that task. Data hyper-cleaning and reinforcement learning appear as illustrative applications, without reported experiments.

E2.justification: Figure 1 retains F2SA, stocBiO, MRBO, VRBO, and the unregularized baseline. Figure 2 uses the same comparator set. Additional F2SA-p orders are variants of the proposed method, while newly cited methods are not added empirical baselines.

E3.justification: The evaluated orders change from p=1,...,5 to F2SA plus p=2,3,5,8,10, and Appendix G introduces a five-layer ReLU MLP evaluation. The stated regularizer also changes from ||W_x y||^2 to y^T W_x y while retaining W_x=diag(exp(x)), changing its parameterization. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1 reports tuning p=1,...,5 but displays only F2SA and F2SA-2. V2 supplies explicit higher-order sensitivity curves and adds an MLP experiment testing behavior on a nonsmooth, nonconvex objective outside the main theoretical setting. This substantially expands the supplementary empirical analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bands. Changes to stochastic algorithm sampling and theoretical expectations do not constitute experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figure 1 adds results for p=3,5,8,10 and changes retained trajectories, including F2SA-2. V1 reports p=2 as optimal, whereas v2's p=10 curve has the best final plotted loss and accuracy. Figure 2 adds MLP outcomes. These are revised or new iteration-based results, not established gains under identical settings or equal computational work.

M1.justification: For odd p, Algorithm 2 replaces the forward-difference stencil j=0,...,p with j=-(p-1)/2,...,(p+1)/2 and different coefficients. This substantively changes the hyper-gradient estimator. Algorithms 1–3 also move stochastic sampling inside the inner iteration, specifying fresh samples at each step instead of sampling before the loop.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and Appendices A–F remain recognizable. V2 locally rewrites introductory, methodological, and experimental passages, adds illustrative examples, acknowledgments, and Appendices G–H, and updates authorship. Much of the existing narrative is retained rather than comprehensively reorganized.

P2.justification: V2 adopts an ICLR conference layout throughout, changing typography, text width, headings, author blocks, and running headers. Figure 1 is redrawn with additional curves, revised colors, legend, axes, and caption; Figure 2 adds another two-panel display. Table 1 retains its basic structure.

R1.justification: V2 acknowledges Chayti and Jaggi's earlier finite-difference connection and substantially revises the novelty positioning around extending that work. It also adds concurrent condition-number lower bounds by Ji and Chen and Zhang, cites finite-difference coefficient literature, and changes Table 1's lower-bound attribution from Theorem 4.1 to Arjevani et al.

T1.justification: Lemma 3.1 and Appendix B replace the earlier coefficient-existence argument with explicit formulas and coefficient bounds, including an extended derivation for odd p. V2 corrects the even-order antisymmetry sign and states the lemma directly for vector-valued functions. Definition 2.1 adopts expected-gradient stationarity, and Lemma D.2 corrects its SGD update. The headline complexity rates remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the strengthened finite-difference construction: v2 replaces odd-order forward coefficients, whose exponential growth it identifies, with an explicitly bounded alternative and develops the supporting derivation. Corrected sampling pseudocode and formal statements improve consistency, while prior-work attribution and expanded experimental evidence improve assessability. The plots still lack uncertainty reporting and equal-work comparisons, but the central mathematical and methodological repairs provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same F2SA-p research, retaining the main complexity theorems and experimental benchmark. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 and Figure 1 report expanded original experiments, and Appendix G adds MLP results in Figure 2.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figure 1 report original test-loss and accuracy results for learning regularization on 20 Newsgroup.

results.title: Faster Gradient Methods for Highly-smooth Stochastic Bilevel Optimization

C1.justification: The central claims about comprehensive, complex evaluation and reasoning as a bottleneck remain. However, v1's contribution statement proposes an automatic checklist-based evaluation protocol, whereas v3 emphasizes human-verified prompt/checklist pairs and explicitly follows earlier VQA evaluation paradigms. This modestly narrows the methodological novelty claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations about native reasoning, unified-model advantages, and visual biases that persist after textual rewriting. Appendix C.2 interprets performance through negation, inference depth, and rule variation. Appendix E newly acknowledges limited human-centric and face-related coverage. These substantially extend v1's aggregate performance discussion, although some architectural and generality claims exceed the direct experimental controls.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 newly documents a detailed generation instruction, checklist tags, JSON format, candidate counts, and filtering/refinement stages for the retained benchmark. v3 also supplies the rewriting instruction, generator parameter counts, and direct code, benchmark, dataset, and leaderboard links. These materially expand reproducibility information, although the hardware description loses v1's explicit NVIDIA A800 specification.

E1.justification: Both retain the English benchmark with 12 dimensions, 1,080 prompts, and 13,536 checklist questions. Rewriting and subgroup analyses reuse retained task coverage. Additional benchmarks in v3 Table 1 are literature comparisons, not newly evaluated datasets.

E2.justification: v3 Table 3 retains all 27 original generators and adds 11, including FLUX.2 variants, Qwen-Image-2512, HunyuanImage-3.0, Seedream 4.0/4.5, Nano Banana Pro, and GPT-Image-1.5. The human-alignment comparison also expands from 10 to 16 evaluators through six Qwen3-VL Instruct/Thinking variants.

E3.justification: Existing evaluations retain default model configurations, four images per prompt, binary checklist scoring, and balanced accuracy for human alignment. v3 adds original-versus-rewritten prompt comparisons across eight reasoning dimensions for four generators, plus scoring stratified by question labels. These are extensions of the evaluation design rather than documented changes to the original settings.

E4.justification: v1 describes fine-grained analyses and case studies as forthcoming. v3 supplies prompt-rewriting controls (Table 4/Figure 5), analyses of negation, affected versus unaffected objects, reasoning hops, and invariant versus variant rules (Table 6), and cross-model examples across all dimensions (Figures 9–12). These substantially deepen the investigation of failure modes.

E5.justification: Both specify fixed random seeds where supported and four generated images per prompt. Neither reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. Added result rows and subgroup means do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds results for 11 generators, rewriting conditions, six evaluators, and numerous question subgroups. Most retained main-table scores are identical, but Nano Banana's MI/MA values change from 77.9/85.7 to 85.7/77.9, and Qwen2.5-VL's human-alignment mean changes from 71.1 to 70.6. Nano Banana Pro becomes the reported overall leader at 85.0. v1's complete Qwen-evaluated benchmark matrix is absent from v3, which instead references an external leaderboard.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction and binary checklist evaluator remain intact. v3 adds an experimental inference variant that uses OpenAI o3 to resolve reasoning prompts into explicit scene descriptions before image generation (Section 4.3 and Figure 8), extending beyond v1's existing BAGEL thinking comparison.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: detailed dimension definitions and human verification move into Appendix A, human alignment moves from Section 4.3 to Appendix C.1, prompt rewriting becomes Section 4.3, and discussion moves into Appendix E. The introduction and construction explanation are rewritten, alongside author, affiliation, and publication-header updates.

P2.justification: v3 combines the taxonomy and scored examples in a redesigned opening figure, adds a pipeline diagram and dimension-summary table, and redraws the statistics display. It also adds rewriting and subgroup tables, instructional figures, and extensive cross-model image panels. Existing result tables expand and gain structural changes, including a parameter-count column; the former Qwen benchmark table is removed.

R1.justification: v3 broadens benchmark positioning through PRISM-Bench and UniGenBench comparisons and additional related benchmarks. More substantively, Section 3.2 explicitly situates checklist evaluation within earlier VQA, Davidsonian scene graph, and visual-programming work; Section 4.3 relates rewriting to prior approaches and interleaved reasoning. This expands methodological attribution beyond routine bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The conceptual composition/reasoning taxonomy is retained, with detailed definitions moved to Appendix A.1 and summarized in Table 2. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs, and v3 introduces no substantive mathematical derivation or formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged lack of diagnostic analyses: rewriting controls and question-level breakdowns provide evidence about specific reasoning failures, while detailed construction instructions improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of the self-contained Qwen benchmark matrix and remaining reporting inconsistencies. For example, Section 4.2 calls Qwen-Image-2512 the overall leader despite Table 3 placing FLUX.2-dev higher. The improvement rests on stronger diagnostic evidence and documentation, not simply the larger model count.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe T2I-COREBench, with the same 12-dimensional taxonomy and benchmark totals. Their text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports evaluations of 38 generators, prompt-rewriting experiments, an expanded human-alignment study, and fine-grained performance analyses (Tables 3–6).

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 27 image generators, a human-alignment study, and additional benchmark results using Qwen2.5-VL-72B (Tables 2–4).

results.title: Easier Painting Than Thinking: Can Text-to-Image Models Set the Stage, but Not Direct the Play?

C1.justification: The introduction expands the contribution list to include latent guidance and distillation and explicitly claims application to four tasks. The abstract and introduction add the open-source, approximately 100M-parameter Pocket TTS contribution and faster-than-real-time laptop CPU operation. The earlier claim of being the first application across both speech and music is removed; the general efficiency/fidelity thesis remains.

C2.justification: v3 adds a localized explanation attributing poor automatic TTS speaker similarity partly to the VAE and uses human evaluation to qualify that metric. It also discusses guidance-related quality/similarity tradeoffs and LSD's suitability at the tested smaller scale. The original explanations concerning error accumulation, noisy long-term context, clean local detail, and incomplete scaling evaluation remain substantially intact.

D1.justification: v3 documents the 88k-hour TTS dataset mixture, SentencePiece vocabulary, LSD loss-batch allocation, guidance settings, and TTS architecture/training hyperparameters in Table 14. It provides Pocket TTS distillation details and tested CPU models, reports a model release with repository and enhanced evaluation-data links, and promises CALM training code. Existing continuation and VAE hyperparameters are largely unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates speech and music continuation. v3 additionally evaluates text-to-speech on LibriSpeech test-clean and conditioned music generation using CLAP, including text-to-music evaluation on MusicCaps. These introduce different conditioning requirements and benchmark coverage. The original French/English speech continuation and LAION-Disco music coverage are retained.

E2.justification: New TTS comparisons include F5-TTS, DSM, DiTAR, and SALAD; Pocket TTS additionally includes Chatterbox Turbo and Kokoro. MusicCaps comparisons add MusicLM, AudioLDM2, Noise2Music, Jen-1, MusicFlow, and the original text-conditioned MusicGen. DiTAR/SALAD and several MusicCaps baseline scores are explicitly borrowed from publications. Comparator membership in the original continuation experiments remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 introduces TTS training/evaluation settings, WER/CER and speaker-similarity measurements, MUSHRA evaluations, and PANN-based KLD/CLAP music metrics. Speech compression gains PESQ, STOI, and human evaluation. Pocket TTS uses enhanced 24 kHz inputs for all its baselines, separating that comparison from Table 3. The runtime table also reverses the RTF convention while retaining the measured generation times.

E4.justification: Appendix E.5 adds substantive TTS ablations comparing LSD with consistency and varying absent, text-only, and text-plus-audio guidance. Table 3 adds a reference-through-VAE diagnostic investigating low speaker-similarity scores. The original component, context-window, scaling, sampling-step, temperature, and head-batch analyses are retained; their relocation does not constitute new evidence.

E5.justification: v3 removes the PPX and VERT confidence intervals from Table 2 while retaining their point estimates. It also removes v1's general statement that all reported intervals use 95% confidence. The Bayesian Elo estimation procedure and its 95% posterior intervals remain unchanged. Neither version establishes additional repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for compression, conditioned generation, TTS ablations, and Pocket TTS: examples include CALM's 1.81 WER in Table 3, 2.14 MusicCaps FAD in Table 11, and Pocket TTS's 1.84 WER, tied with DSM, in Table 12. These are newly reported experiments, not gains over v1 under identical settings. Original continuation point estimates and plots remain; changed RTF values reflect the inverted convention.

M1.justification: v3 adds text/CLAP conditioning, latent classifier-free guidance, and backbone latent distillation (Sections 4.6–4.7), and adopts Lagrangian Self-Distillation for TTS sampling. Pocket TTS distills a 24-layer teacher backbone into six layers while retaining its sampling head. These substantially extend the procedure. The original continuation architecture remains; explicitly adding WavLM distillation to Equation 2 documents a component already described in v1.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized around four task evaluations. Music VAE details, the temperature study, and several efficiency analyses move from the main text into dedicated appendices. Noise-injection exposition moves within the method section, temperature sampling is rewritten, and the appendix structure is expanded and reorganized. Much original prose and the conclusion remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 adds TTS, conditioned-music, MusicCaps, Pocket TTS, and TTS-ablation tables, expands speech-compression metric columns, and adds a TTS hyperparameter column. Several existing tables are relocated or reformatted. All three original figures are retained; the two analysis plots move to the appendix and exchange numbering. Title, headings, running headers, and page layout also change.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens positioning through continuous word-sized and spectral speech representations, IMPACT, MingUni-Audio, and other newer work. It connects temperature sampling to GAN truncation, credits latent guidance to SoundReactor, and incorporates Boffi et al.'s LSD framework. It also drops v1's first-across-both-domains assertion and its near-exclusivity statement about accelerating continuous autoregressive sampling.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds the two-time LSD flow-map definition and combined flow-matching/self-distillation objectives. Section 4.6 formalizes latent guidance. Section 4.5 replaces v1's Jacobian-based temperature argument and stated variance 1/sqrt(tau) with standard-deviation scaling by sqrt(tau), correcting the mathematical description without establishing that experiments were rerun. Existing consistency and Bayesian Elo formulations are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens practical validation beyond v1's continuation experiments: conditioned-generation benchmarks and TTS ablations test the new mechanisms, while the distilled Pocket TTS model provides small-model CPU evidence relevant to the original edge-device motivation. Expanded technical documentation and the corrected temperature explanation also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting regressions: PPX/VERT intervals disappear, and Appendix F overstates Table 12, which also marks Kokoro as real-time on CPU and contains no ground-truth row supporting its ground-truth comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CALM research, with matching authors, architecture, and retained continuation experiments. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original empirical results and adds original text-to-speech, conditioned music generation, TTS ablation, and Pocket TTS evaluations, alongside explicitly attributed baseline results.

before.justification: v1 reports original speech and music compression and continuation experiments, human evaluations, component ablations, and supplementary context-window and scaling studies.

results.title: Continuous Audio Language Models

C1.justification: v3 refines the novelty framing by explicitly crediting SG-Splatting's earlier hybrid SH/SG approach and identifying MEGS2's contribution as fully standalone, arbitrarily oriented and prunable SG color modeling. The central joint-pruning contribution and headline 50% static and 40% rendering VRAM reduction claims remain.

C2.justification: The limitations concerning unoptimized dynamic VRAM and complex highlights are retained within the conclusion. v3 adds concrete applicability qualifications for highly specular surfaces and dense transparency (Figure 8), and attributes Playroom speckles to ground-truth shadows and image roughness (Figure 14). Figure 1 also qualifies 3DGS's mobile failure claim to some platforms.

D1.justification: A.2 newly specifies 10,000 memory-constrained optimization iterations, a 50-iteration interval, penalty 0.0005, sharpness threshold 1 and the opacity importance calculation. v3 also documents LocoGS initialization, the WebGL viewer's origin and GPU-specific training times. Its reproducibility statement promises a future release of renderer, training and evaluation code; it does not establish current availability.

E1.justification: v3 adds the Shiny Blender Real evaluation on Garden, Sedan and Toycar (Table 11), plus explicit highly specular and dense-transparency test cases (Figure 8). These substantially extend the tested material conditions. The original Mip-NeRF360, Tanks & Temples and DeepBlending coverage remains; its new per-scene breakdowns are not additional datasets.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds LightGaussian, LocoGS and MaskGaussian while retaining the earlier comparators. Table 11 introduces comparisons with Ref-NeRF, ENVIDR, 2DGS, GShader, R3DG, 3DGS-DR and Ref-Gaussian. The expanded WebGL comparison includes GaussianSpa. The earlier Scaffold-GS/HAC++ comparison is retained as v3 Table 4.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs cover storage size, training duration on RTX 3090/4090, expanded WebGL device configurations and rendering-failure categories, and a controlled primitive/lobe-budget sweep (Tables 9–12; Figure 6). The original image-quality metrics and static/rendering VRAM measurement definitions remain. Newly disclosed pruning settings do not establish changes to the original training protocol.

E4.justification: The original pruning ablations remain unchanged numerically in v3 Table 2, formerly Table 4. v3 adds scene-wise lobe-allocation analysis, pruning-budget sensitivity, challenging-material success/failure cases, visual ablations and a Playroom texture case study (Figures 5, 6, 8, 9 and 14). These test additional questions about allocation, sensitivity and failure behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new mean columns summarize scenes rather than introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive per-scene, reflective-scene, device, storage, training-time and sensitivity results. Existing entries also change: the first Ours row, now labeled HQ, changes on Tanks & Temples from 23.57 to 23.45 PSNR, 0.855 to 0.853 SSIM, 59 to 51 MB static VRAM and 209 to 211 MB rendering VRAM. Figure 1 replaces 3DGS's Dimensity 9400+ N/A with 6.6 FPS. Most original aggregate and ablation values remain.

M1.justification: The SG representation, joint pruning objective and color compensation remain. v3 retains only dynamic-range-based lobe selection from v1's two alternatives and specifies importance-based opacity selection across all scenes in A.2. Algorithm 1 also replaces the shared penalty coefficient with weighted opacity and sharpness coefficients. These refine the reported procedure without introducing a new framework.

P1.justification: The main text is substantially condensed and reorganized: the method overview and preliminaries are shortened, experimental setup and analyses are rewritten, detailed evaluation information moves to A.2, and limitations merge into the conclusion. v3 introduces a structured appendix and reproducibility, ethics and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: v3 expands and reformats Table 1 with explicit HQ/LM labels, relocates the parameter-cost and HAC++ tables to the appendix, wraps the ablation table beside text, and redraws the color-model plot. It adds lobe-distribution and sensitivity charts, per-scene tables, failure-case panels, visual ablations and extensive device-image grids.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly positions its standalone representation relative to SG-Splatting's hybrid design. It adds references for ADMM, LightGaussian, MaskGaussian, LocoGS and the WebGL viewer, and removes the end-to-end rate-distortion Gaussian representation reference. Most related-work discussion and the rendering-memory-versus-storage positioning remain.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds an augmented-Lagrangian derivation of the optimization updates and a spherical-integral derivation of the color-compensation solution, whereas v1 largely states the updates and final solution. It also explicitly derives delta_o = delta times rho_o and delta_s = delta times rho_s, matching the revised pseudocode. This substantially expands the mathematical support for existing components.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central memory-efficiency and edge-rendering claims through broader comparisons, practical cost measurements, sensitivity tests and explicit failure cases. The derivations and pruning details also address important gaps in v1's methodological transparency. Some new reporting needs reconciliation: for example, Table 6's 3DGS static VRAM values of 397 and 752 MB do not average to Table 1's 370 MB. These inconsistencies limit confidence in individual entries, but the overall gains in inspectability and validation remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MEGS2 with the same authors, core framework and principal experiments. All pages are readable, including v3's Appendix A.1–A.5; v1 ends with references and has no appendix. Renumbered and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark and ablation results and adds reflective-scene evaluations, device comparisons, training-time measurements, sensitivity analyses and qualitative case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction, rendering-memory and ablation results on three benchmark datasets, alongside WebGL device demonstrations.

results.title: MEGS^{2}: Memory-Efficient Gaussian Splatting via Spherical Gaussians and Unified Pruning

C1.justification: The central claims about PINN-based CT-MARL, VGI-enhanced value learning, and superior continuous-time benchmark performance remain. v3 explicitly qualifies its first contribution as addressing cooperative deterministic systems, making the claimed applicability more restricted and explicit.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations connecting noise sensitivity to absent diffusion/uncertainty modeling and large-step degradation to linearization and claimed contraction conditions. These qualify the earlier robustness narrative. The conclusion replaces v1's discussion of competitive-value discontinuities and state constraints with an HJI-based extension, while the anchor-loss explanation is adapted to absent terminal supervision.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code link, specifies coverage up to six agents and 113 state dimensions, and revises Table 2's network input dimensions. Hardware, hidden-layer architectures, learning rates, and other Table 1 settings remain documented as before. Some implementation prose still mentions time inputs despite the revised table.

E1.justification: The eight MPE/MuJoCo tasks and coupled oscillator are retained; Cheetah/HalfCheetah naming does not establish a new task. Appendix C.3 adds stochastic-dynamics variants of the two existing MPE tasks. The newly specified agent counts and state dimensionality clarify existing coverage rather than demonstrate additional benchmarks.

E2.justification: v3 adds HJBPPO to the MPE and MuJoCo comparisons in Figures 2 and 4; v1 only discussed it as related work. New Figure 9 evaluates MATD3, MAPPO, and MADDPG against VIP on four MuJoCo tasks. MADDPG previously participated only in the oscillator comparison.

E3.justification: Figure 6 drops the boundary-loss control, and Figure 7 substitutes anchor-weight variation for boundary-weight variation. Added protocols use Gaussian noise variances 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0 with average target distance, and a VIP-only oscillator sweep extending to Δt = 0.20. Existing simulator timing rules and Table 1 hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices C.3–C.4 test robustness to stochastic dynamics and failure under larger time steps, substantially expanding the investigation of applicability limits. Loss-removal and loss-weight analyses are revised for the terminal-loss-free method. Earlier gradient-surface and ReLU/Tanh analyses remain, with their appendix figures renumbered.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed mean benchmark curves, retain the seed range 111–120 in Table 1, and display graphical dispersion. v3 does not specify a changed run count, confidence-interval procedure, or significance test. Additional uncertainty-bearing plots accompany new results without establishing a different statistical practice.

E6.justification: Benchmark and loss-analysis results in Figures 2, 4, 6, and 7 change, alongside added comparator and robustness results. Revised Figure 6 shows a much larger penalty for removing anchor loss than v1. New appendix results show deterioration under stronger noise and large Δt. These are revised or additional findings, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Algorithm 1 replace time-conditioned value/policy learning with a stationary formulation and remove terminal loss from the critic objective. Table 2 reduces network inputs, and dynamics/reward equations drop explicit time-interval conditioning. Although PINN and VGI remain central, the documented inputs and optimization procedure materially change.

P1.justification: The introduction and VGI motivation are substantially rewritten, related-work discussion is reorganized, and methodology gains an explanatory roadmap and lemma introductions. Results discussion and the conclusion are reworked. Author-year citations, acknowledgments, an ethics statement, and an LLM-use disclosure further change the document's presentation.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 9, 12, and 13, redraws benchmark and loss-analysis displays with revised legends, axes, and categories, and adopts a conference layout with compact author information and running headers. Earlier appendix gradient and activation figures are retained as Figures 10–11, rather than newly added.

R1.justification: v3 adds focused references and discussion on stochastic CTRL, PINN convergence, time-discretization robustness, and MATD3, while removing several broader citations. The central positioning around PINN-plus-VGI cooperative CT-MARL remains. HJBPPO's bibliographic update refers to the same work already cited in v1.

T1.justification: v1 mixes an infinite-horizon value definition with finite-horizon HJB equations, terminal conditions, and proofs. v3 removes the time derivative and terminal boundary and revises the HJB and advantage derivations toward a stationary infinite-horizon formulation. Appendix A.5 also adds a time-invariance argument for a fixed contraction map; this changes the reasoning without resolving all justification gaps.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evaluation by adding the closely related HJBPPO and standard MARL comparators, while new noise and time-step tests expose failure regimes absent from v1. The stationary formulation also reduces the mismatch between the original value definition and HJB treatment. These address important weaknesses in validation and scope calibration. The theoretical cleanup remains incomplete: Appendix A.5 still does not establish contraction from bounded Jacobians and small Δt alone, and some input descriptions remain inconsistent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VIP/PINN/VGI research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark and ablation results, including additional baseline comparisons and appendix experiments on dynamics noise and time-step sensitivity.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on continuous-time MPE, multi-agent MuJoCo, and a coupled oscillator, including value-gradient, activation-function, and loss ablations.

results.title: Continuous-Time Value Iteration for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: Both versions claim task-adaptive 3D grounding, embodiment-aware reasoning, four primitive benchmarks, leading performance on seven of eight public benchmarks, and strong downstream planning. v3 makes the abstract more explicit but does not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving positional-encoding amplitude and cross-attention learning difficulties, plus explicit limitations concerning scene-level gating and unmodeled physical parameters. It also interprets unseen-embodiment and dynamic-obstruction results. Conversely, v1's specific explanation that grasp-controller limitations constrain Mobile Pickup gains is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands implementation disclosure with mixed RGB/RGB-D preprocessing, depth masking, forward-pass listings, reward-computation pseudocode, temperature scheduling and eight-candidate GRPO groups. v3 also specifies backbone resetting after router pretraining and promises code/data release. However, v1's explicit KL weight of 0.01 is omitted; actual resource availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: The training corpus and established benchmarks are retained. v3 substantially extends embodied test scenarios through unseen physical configurations, two real robot platforms instead of single-platform demonstrations, explicit cluttered-picking and constrained-navigation evaluations, and moving-pedestrian occlusion cases (Section 4.3 and Appendix B.3).

E2.justification: Table 1 adds separate-token cross-attention, interleaved-token cross-attention, and continuous soft gating to the existing hard-coded and no-3D comparisons. These substantially broaden the alternatives evaluated against the central routing mechanism. Comparator membership in Tables 2–4 is unchanged.

E3.justification: New experiments train on 75, 88 and 110 cm arms and evaluate seven held-out lengths, while real-robot comparisons report ten attempts per model/task/embodiment. Gate analysis changes from frequent-word statistics to whole-prompt semantic categorization with specified similarity thresholds (Appendix C.2). Retained benchmark settings are largely unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of alternative fusion mechanisms, generalization to unseen embodiments, and robustness to moving occluders. It replaces word-level gate analysis with semantic-category analysis. Existing reward ablations and several qualitative cases are retained or relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports multi-seed variability, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new ten-attempt robot evaluations specify sample sizes, rather than introducing uncertainty estimation or repeated-training-run reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds fusion-comparator scores, semantic gate-activation results, and Tables 5–6: ER achieves 80.52% success on unseen arm lengths and 9/10 placement successes on both robots. Navigation is 8/10 versus Base's 9/10 and 8/10, so improvements are not universal. Tables 2–4 and the original reward-ablation scores remain unchanged. Table 1's reported dynamic-fusion average changes from 58.56 to 58.7, beyond equivalent rounding.

M1.justification: The hard TAGR gate, additive 3D fusion, training losses and TE-GRPO reward curriculum remain unchanged. The explicitly named three-stage pipeline was already represented in v1's pretraining description and Table 5; additional implementation details and Base/ER checkpoint names do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, training exposition and experimental narrative are extensively revised. Training receives explicit stage and checkpoint labels; benchmark descriptions and case studies are reorganized into appendices. Dedicated limitations, reproducibility and LLM-use sections are added.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes from word-level activation bars to a semantic-category chart, and Table 1 gains grouped fusion comparisons. New embodiment and robot-result tables, dynamic-obstruction and fusion diagrams, algorithms and code listings substantially expand the presentation. Existing case studies and benchmark illustrations are also relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds the DeepSeek-R1 reference for its language-editing disclosure in Appendix H. The substantive related-work coverage and positioning against embodied-reasoning and 3D-language-model research remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation of TAGR, reward composition, normalized advantages and GRPO optimization is retained; the latter equations move to Appendix A.3. Added implementation and analysis pseudocode does not introduce a new theoretical result or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of both central contributions: Table 1 tests meaningful fusion alternatives, while Tables 5–6 supplement v1's qualitative physical demonstrations with held-out-embodiment and comparative real-robot results. Expanded implementation disclosure also improves assessability. These gains outweigh the removed grasp-controller caveat and numerical inconsistencies, although ten-attempt robot tests without uncertainty estimates still limit the strength of deployment conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniEVA. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison of methods, equations, experiments, tables and figures despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds fusion comparisons, embodiment-generalization experiments, quantitative real-robot evaluations, and dynamic-occlusion cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, simulated navigation and manipulation results, reward ablations, and qualitative robot deployments.

results.title: OmniEVA: Embodied Versatile Planner via Task-Adaptive 3D-Grounded and Embodiment-aware Reasoning

C1.justification: The central claims about weakly supervised, interpretable localization and scale recovery remain. V3 adds specific headline claims that correspondence inliers and ground-layout alignment indicate localization reliability and support error detection. The introduction's explicit 26% KITTI improvement claim is removed.

C2.justification: V3 replaces v1's characterization of aerial imagery as often not orthorectified with a standard-DOM versus true-DOM discussion, proposing contextual features and confidence sampling as mitigation mechanisms. It adds explanations for homography, resolution and non-road results and interprets inliers/layout alignment as reliability signals. Conversely, v1's explicit depth-error limitation and warning that an incorrect symmetric pose can still align convincingly are omitted.

D1.justification: V3 adds a repository link and a reproducibility statement promising code, configurations and evaluation scripts; actual availability cannot be established from the PDFs. Newly disclosed details include 630×630 aerial inputs, 45×45 DINO features and three correspondences per RANSAC trial. Core optimizer, hardware, batch-size and loss settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V3 retains KITTI and VIGOR and adds direct VIGOR-to-CVACT transfer, evaluated qualitatively on Australian scenes. It also adds fully unknown-orientation KITTI testing with ±180° noise and a non-road-facing KITTI subset. These extend geographical coverage and viewing conditions beyond v1.

E2.justification: SliceMatch, already compared on VIGOR in v1, is newly included in KITTI's ±180° comparisons in v3 Table 1. Table 12 adds BEV-matching and homography-estimation alternatives. The original KITTI comparator set remains in the ±10° block, and VIGOR's external baseline membership is unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include uniform ±180° orientation noise during KITTI training/testing, manually selected non-road-facing evaluation, and qualitative CVACT transfer without retraining. Appendix A separately varies training and inference settings, including 256–2048 correspondences, aerial grids, image/feature resolution and temperature. These substantially extend evaluation design while retaining the original splits and core metrics.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained topmost-point, scale and depth-robustness studies, v3 tests correspondence density, resolution, temperature and RANSAC sensitivity. It directly tests BEV matching and homography alternatives, adds inlier-versus-error diagnostics, investigates road-alignment bias, and expands failure analysis with building-occlusion examples. These address substantially more robustness and design questions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V3's inlier-quantile/error curves add a diagnostic analysis, without introducing uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive numerical and qualitative results, including KITTI ±180° mean localization errors of 11.71 m cross-area and 1.85 m same-area. Existing KITTI entries also change: the proposed method's cross-area mean becomes 5.60 m instead of 5.51 m, and FG2's becomes 7.31 m instead of 7.45 m. The updates are unexplained, and v1 does not specify orientation noise, so controlled performance changes cannot be inferred. Most VIGOR scores persist, although the unknown-orientation Ours-Unik3Drel row is removed.

M1.justification: The adopted pipeline retains frozen DINOv2 features, projection heads, dustbin/dual-softmax matching, depth lifting, scale-aware Procrustes alignment and VCE/InfoNCE supervision. RANSAC was already used in v1. The newly evaluated BEV-matching and homography variants are ablation controls; the proposed method itself is unchanged.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming the method Loc², v3 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion, separates local matching from pose estimation, and recasts the qualitative narrative around interpretability. The appendices are extensively reorganized, references move before them, and dedicated limitations/broader-impact sections give way to different discussion and disclosure sections.

P2.justification: V3 redraws Figures 1–2, reorganizes qualitative panels, restructures KITTI Table 1 by orientation setting and reverses area/orientation ordering in VIGOR Table 2. It adds inlier-error and CVACT figures, ablation tables and a runtime/memory table. Earlier initial-versus-recovered-scale grids are replaced by selected layout-alignment displays.

R1.justification: V3 removes the standalone monocular-depth survey and much of the visual-grounding and LiDAR context, substantially narrowing the related-work coverage. It introduces positioning against MAST3R/VGGT-style image matching and references for CVACT and GeoCalib. The central comparison with FG2 remains; its publication metadata update does not constitute a new work.

T1.justification: V3 explicitly assumes that the camera viewing direction is orthogonal to gravity in Section 3.2, adding a stated geometric condition absent from v1. The Procrustes derivations and loss formulas remain substantively unchanged. V1's separate assumptions paragraph is removed, while similarity-transform applicability is discussed in v3 Appendix I.

improvement.justification: V3's controlled BEV-matching and homography comparisons directly test central design advantages that v1 largely motivated conceptually. The broader orientation tests, sensitivity studies and inlier-error analysis substantially strengthen the empirical support for the method. CVACT evidence remains qualitative, and removing useful symmetry/depth-error caveats weakens qualification, but the added controls and diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite the new Loc² title, both PDFs describe the same research, authors, matching pipeline and core experiments. Both main texts and complete appendices are readable, including equations, tables and figures, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds KITTI orientation scenarios, CVACT transfer examples, extensive ablations and correspondence-inlier analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original KITTI and VIGOR localization experiments, design ablations, depth-robustness tests, relative-depth training results and runtime measurements.

results.title: Loc$^{2}$: Interpretable Cross-View Localization via Depth-Lifted Local Feature Matching

C1.justification: The central contributions remain uncertainty-aware floorplan depth and pretrained monodepth encoders.
