V2 extends the claimed role of uncertainty to post-processing optimization and strengthens the abstract's 15-frame HGE improvement from 16.7-fold to 42.2-fold. The 100-frame 2.7-fold claim remains.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly identifies the modeled uncertainty as aleatoric and leaves epistemic uncertainty for future work. It qualifies the ground-truth-depth upper bound when refinement is applied and acknowledges the absence of independent 2D pose ground truth in Appendix A.1.2. Existing generalization and fine-tuning interpretations largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1.2 newly documents affine alignment using four doorways, pose conversion, split-selection rationale, and test-session conditions. V2 supplies a code/model access link and availability statement, plus the refinement window and runtime. The original training recipe remains, although the brief Structured3D setup description is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Gibson, full and cropped LaMAR HGE, LaMAR CAB generalization/fine-tuning, and Structured3D single-frame localization. Structured3D and the single-frame analysis move to the appendix in v2; they are not removed. Newly described lighting and occlusion conditions clarify existing test sessions.

E2.justification: Appendix Table 11 adds a Gaussian-uncertainty UnLoc comparator motivated by Roessle et al. (2022). Existing localization comparators, including F3Loc mono/fusion, LASER, and PF-Net, are retained. The '+Depth Anything v2' rows match v1's uncertainty-free variant.

E3.justification: V2 Table 4 extends CAB evaluation at the 1 m threshold to shorter sequences; v1 reports that threshold only for length 100, with shorter CAB sequences evaluated at 2 m in the appendix. The new distribution comparison specifies Depth Anything v2 Small without post-processing. Existing training settings, splits, and main Gibson/HGE metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds with/without-refinement comparisons across Gibson, full/cropped HGE, and CAB, and directly tests Laplace versus Gaussian uncertainty in Appendix A.2.4. These substantially expand component validation. Existing encoder, single-frame, fine-tuning, update-frequency, and grid-resolution studies remain; the separate qualitative example in v1 Figure 5 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed experiments, confidence intervals, or significance tests for localization results. The expanded discussion and comparison of predicted depth uncertainty concern model outputs, not statistical uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add refined-method results: 15-frame success reaches 81.3% on Gibson and 50.6% on full HGE, alongside retained unrefined scores of 65.3% and 20.0%. CAB sequential results are revised and Gaussian-comparison results are added. These concern changed method variants. V2 also contains an unresolved discrepancy: the apparently matching Small-encoder Laplace setting scores 5.9% at T=15 in Table 5 but 4.7% in Table 11.

M1.justification: Section 3.8 adds an inference stage absent from v1: reconstructing the last ten poses from the final estimate and optimizing a global SE(2) correction using uncertainty-weighted depth residuals. The existing encoder, masked attention, Laplace matching, histogram filter, and training loss remain.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites selected contribution and results paragraphs, renames variants, moves single-frame analysis from Section 4.2 to Appendix A.2.1, and adds reproducibility and acknowledgment sections. The main section sequence and much of the existing prose remain.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from two-column to single-column layout, with resized and repositioned displays. Tables gain refinement rows, the main CAB table changes structure, and Table 11 is added. Figure 2 is redrawn, v1 Figure 5 is removed, and the remaining qualitative figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: Related work gains a substantial discussion of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, positioning UnLoc against prior uncertainty-estimation approaches, including Gaussian depth models. It also adds language/scene-graph localization and OrienterNet. This expands substantive research positioning beyond citation-format changes.

T1.justification: New Equations 6–8 formally define backward trajectory reconstruction, the SE(2) correction, and its uncertainty-weighted L1 objective. This is a limited mathematical extension; the existing matching, motion, filtering, and training formulations are retained, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens methodological support and reproducibility: it defines and ablates trajectory refinement, tests the uncertainty-distribution choice, and addresses v1's missing explanation of LaMAR pose alignment and split selection. Retaining unrefined results makes the added component's benefits assessable. The reported 0.96-second refinement cost and the isolated Tables 5/11 discrepancy limit the gains, but do not outweigh the stronger validation and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UnLoc and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched despite substantial changes in formatting and content placement.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations of trajectory refinement and alternative uncertainty distributions.

before.justification: V1 reports original localization, depth-prediction, runtime, ablation, and generalization results on Gibson, Structured3D, and LaMAR, including supplementary experiments.

results.title: UnLoc: Leveraging Depth Uncertainties for Floorplan Localization

C1.justification: v2 adds adaptive efficiency and RL-based summary safety as contributions in the introduction and conclusion, and explicitly claims in the abstract that inference-time strategies alone are insufficient. The original claims about the 80K dataset, safety versus over-refusal tradeoff, safe completion and effectiveness with 500 examples remain.

C2.justification: v1 treats making internal summaries safe through RL as future work; v2 interprets its RL results as supporting disclosure of reasoning and claims elimination of the exposure risk. New discussions attribute some failures to evaluator bias or ambiguity, assess safety-check reliability and explain inference-time defenses' limitations through insufficient safety-policy knowledge.

D1.justification: v2 adds RL reward coefficients, framework and training settings, attack budgets and prefilling text, safeguard prompts, runtime hardware information and an explicit over-refusal judge. It also supplies dataset-curation pseudocode and directly reports a public ReSA dataset location in the abstract and Appendix B. Existing curation and baseline templates largely remain.

E1.justification: The original safety and capability benchmarks remain. v2 adds ordinary instruction-tuning examples from Tulu-3 and extends evaluation to white-box GCG, AutoDAN-Turbo and prompts containing prefilled safety-check sequences. In particular, gradient-access attacks and prefilling broaden the tested threat conditions beyond v1's evaluation.

E2.justification: The established defense comparators are retained. v2 adds an evaluated post-hoc gpt-oss-safeguard-20b comparator alongside LlamaGuard, the base model and ReSA-SFT in Table 17, constituting a limited extension of the baseline set.

E3.justification: Alongside retained SFT settings, v2 introduces GRPO training with 10 epochs, batch size 512 and eight rollouts per prompt, plus a Gemma-3-4b-it configuration. New attack protocols include GCG on 50 prompts and AutoDAN-Turbo on 100 prompts with a fixed learned strategy library. Separate summary-safety evaluation and runtime measurements also expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: The original training-size and WJ-only ablations are retained. v2 adds robustness tests for GCG, AutoDAN-Turbo and prefilling; analyses of adaptive checking's efficiency and capability tradeoffs; intended-summary safety tests; and measurements of safety-check failures. Appendix I also adds evaluator-error and STAIR-DPO comparison case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new GRPO rollout count specifies training sampling, not repeated evaluation or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Original principal safety scores and WJ-only ablation results are retained after reorganization. v2 adds extensive RL, adaptive, Gemma, attack, runtime and summary-safety results; Table 2 adds Llama ReSA-RL at 0.9932 average LlamaGuard DSR alongside unchanged ReSA-SFT at 0.9046. A retained value also changes incorrectly: the Llama base over-refusal average becomes 93.27% rather than 92.60%, despite unchanged component scores.

M1.justification: v2 retains the original SFT method but introduces adaptive bypass of safety reasoning for ordinary queries and GRPO-based ReSA-RL. The latter rewards intended-summary safety, final-answer safety, benign-query compliance and output format. These additions materially change training objectives and inference behavior (Sections 3.5-3.6).

P1.justification: v2 extensively condenses and rewrites existing method, experimental-setup, results and discussion prose. It reorganizes implementation details and case studies into Appendices F and J, separates full results and additional discussions into G and I, and restructures the narrative around the original method and its variants.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn. The original safety tables are reorganized by benchmark into v2 Tables 2, 7 and 8, while the original over-refusal and reasoning tables are merged into Table 3. Numerous new experimental tables and case panels are added, and retained examples gain clearer highlighting of user-visible output.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting its extensions, including Tulu-3, DeepSeekMath/GRPO, HybridFlow, Gemma 3, AutoDAN-Turbo, SafeChain and gpt-oss-safeguard. Related work gives STAIR-DPO and Realsafe-r1 more explicit discussion, while retaining the central distinction from Deliberative Alignment.

T1.justification: Section 3.6 newly defines sequential rollout variables and a piecewise reward for harmful, benign and normal queries. This is a limited addition of mathematical definitions accompanying RL, without new theorems or proofs. Algorithm 1 primarily restates the existing dataset-curation procedure.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves safer internal summaries to future RL work and assesses efficiency through token length. v2 implements and evaluates RL and adaptive variants, separately tests summary safety, measures runtime and broadens threat testing, substantially strengthening evidence about practical risks and costs. Added settings and dataset-access information improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized problems: lower Llama reasoning accuracy under RL, the inconsistent baseline average in Table 3, and assurances of harmless reasoning exposure that exceed Table 16's benchmark evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReSA and Answer-Then-Check research. The main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching experiments and examples moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds RL, adaptive checking, additional attack evaluations, summary-safety measurements and failure analyses, particularly in Appendices G-I.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, jailbreak-defense and general-capability scores, safe-completion evaluations, efficiency measurements and ablations in Sections 4-5 and the appendices.

results.title: Reasoned Safety Alignment: Ensuring Jailbreak Defense via Answer-Then-Check

C1.justification: The abstract's central RAC claim remains unchanged. v2's introduction adds explicit headline claims about pruning to 50% sparsity, retaining up to 95% of dense accuracy, and improving accuracy by up to 17% over existing pruning approaches. These quantify the contribution without replacing its central thesis.

C2.justification: v2 interprets Qwen3 results as evidence of broader applicability, AIME-25 results as supporting calibration alignment on harder problems, and the alternative-pruner results as showing algorithm-independent benefits and sometimes stronger ALPS performance. Existing mechanism explanations and limitations remain. The decoding-budget mitigation added to the limitations paragraph was already discussed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 newly states that all one-shot pruning experiments use a single H100 GPU and changes the printed code-repository address from RAC to Reasoning-Aware-Compression. These are documentation/access-information changes; the PDFs do not establish a hardware change or repository availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds AIME-25 competition-math evaluation in Tables 4 and 10. MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and the C4, Open-R1-Math-220K, and Codeforces calibration sources remain. This extends mathematical difficulty coverage within the existing math-and-coding scope.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates SparseGPT; ALPS and WANDA appear only as references or examples. v2 evaluates ALPS and WANDA on MATH500 in Table 9, compares them with SparseGPT results, and reports ALPS on AIME-25 in Table 10. The C4, prompt-only, and RAC calibration comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluated model configurations to Qwen3-1.7B/8B/14B and DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B/70B, with new comparisons at 30–50% sparsity. The retained experiments still specify 1M calibration tokens, up to 8192 generated calibration tokens, and zero-shot evaluation with a 32k output budget.

E4.justification: The new 'Varying the pruning algorithm' analysis tests whether RAC's benefits depend on SparseGPT, using ALPS/WANDA on MATH500 and ALPS on AIME-25. This adds a substantive generality check. The original on/off-policy, structured-pruning/FP8, decoding-budget, and reconstruction-error analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report accuracy with standard errors. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure. Additional rows follow the existing reporting practice; changing some SE notation to parentheses is presentational.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new model configurations, AIME-25, and alternative pruners. New entries include Qwen3-8B MATH500 accuracy at 50% sparsity of 0.862 with SparseGPT+RAC and 0.940 with ALPS+RAC. All five original tables retain their numerical values after renumbering. Figure 1 changes the displayed 70%-sparsity runtime from approximately 9 hours to 8.4 hours.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same collection of prompt and dense-model-generated CoT activations, concatenation, and layer-wise pruning. The empirical RAC reconstruction loss is unchanged. Testing ALPS and WANDA exercises the existing pruning interface without introducing a new RAC component.

P1.justification: The introduction and pruning background receive targeted rewrites, the method gains a short overview, and the results discussion expands. Section 5.2 changes from 'Ablations' to 'Additional Experiments' and reorders analyses. The main section sequence and most method and retained-analysis prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different conference layout, adds Tables 2–4 and 9–10, rearranges and reformats retained tables, and adds highlighting to appendix results. Figure 1 is redrawn with colored axes and revised scaling. Figure 2 retains the identical heatmap image but moves within the document.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive comparison with Williams et al.'s self-calibration, distinguishing task-conditioned reasoning traces from unconditional generated text. It also adds pruning, C4, and sparse-hardware references while removing GPTQ, Liu's quantization study, and Zhu's compression survey. The existing positioning against calibration-selection and CoT-distillation work remains.

T1.justification: v2 removes the explicit expected-loss minimization over dense-policy rollouts and layers presented in v1 Section 4. It retains the empirical RAC reconstruction identity, now Equation 7, and the decoding equations. This is a limited removal of formal exposition; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 supports RAC's broad applicability primarily through SparseGPT on DeepSeek-R1-Qwen models. v2 directly tests additional pruners, Qwen3 and Llama models, and harder AIME-25 problems, substantially addressing uncertainty about generality. The self-calibration comparison also clarifies novelty. Although added experiment settings remain briefly documented and statistical reporting does not improve, the broader validation materially strengthens the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAC research, with matching algorithms, experiments, and figures. All 10 pages of v1 and 13 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-Llama, AIME-25, and alternative-pruner results.

before.justification: v1 reports original pruning accuracy, runtime, reconstruction-error, calibration, and throughput experiments in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Reasoning Models Can be Accurately Pruned Via Chain-of-Thought Reconstruction

C1.justification: The central contribution remains training-free block-wise caching with similarity-based decisions and periodic recomputation. The abstract increases the reported maximum speedup from 2.24× to 2.6×, and the introduction adds explicit memory-efficiency positioning. These refine the performance and practicality claims without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds frequency/noise-schedule explanations for feature trajectories, a prompt-adaptivity explanation for block-level caching, and substantive discussion of memory constraints. Appendix E distinguishes image/class-conditional feature patterns from the video U-shape and explains why latent drift cannot be controlled through L1 monitoring alone. These materially expand mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 adds scheduler/encoder settings for the new backbones, explicit ProfilingDiT and TaylorSeer parameters, uniformly spaced block-selection details, NVLink information and model-specific threshold guidance. The existing hardware/software disclosures, default threshold and reuse interval, and code-access link remain unchanged. These are useful additions rather than a comprehensive reproducibility overhaul.

E1.justification: The main video-generation task and prompt sources remain Open-Sora gallery, VBench and T2V-CompBench. v3 Appendix E.2 adds limited diagnostic coverage of text-to-image and class-conditional generation. The high-motion evaluation selects from already represented videos; adding video backbones alone does not establish new task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds FasterCache on all three original backbones and Skip-DiT on Latte. Appendix D.1 evaluates ProfilingDiT and TaylorSeer against BWCache on shortened Wan 2.1 and HunyuanVideo sequences. Table 2 also adds TeaCache to the existing multi-GPU comparisons, substantially expanding the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 adds FlowMatch-based backbone configurations, 9-frame and 17-frame comparisons accommodating baseline memory limits, block-fraction sweeps, and memory and indicator-time measurements. FLOPs are removed from the evaluation metrics. Figure 7 replaces several original Open-Sora resolution/length configurations with Open-Sora-Plan and Wan configurations. The original models' schedules and default threshold/reuse interval remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds cross-model feature trajectories, block-versus-timestep feature comparisons, memory/OOM analysis, indicator-overhead measurements, block-fraction sensitivity, high-motion evaluation and latent-drift analysis. These substantially extend the questions investigated. The reduced-inference-step comparison already appeared in v1 Appendix C.3 and is relocated to Section 4.4; existing reuse-interval and final-step ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 Table 9 and v3 Table 10 use the same paired t-tests, means, standard deviations, p-values and confidence intervals. v3 extends this reporting to additional model rows without changing the statistical procedure. Neither version supplies changed repeated-run counts or seed information.

E6.justification: The shared Table 1 scores for the original three backbones remain unchanged, but v3 adds substantial results for new comparators, backbones and supplementary analyses. Newly reported BWCache results include 81.99% VBench with 2.00× speedup on Wan 2.1 and 82.48% with 2.60× on HunyuanVideo; these are new-setting results, not matched-run gains. FLOPs entries and several Open-Sora scaling configurations are removed.

M1.justification: v1 computes the similarity indicator across all blocks. v3 Appendix D.5 introduces an adaptation using uniformly spaced subsets, defaulting to 50% of blocks for Wan 2.1 and HunyuanVideo. The threshold trigger, final-step recomputation and periodic reuse procedure remain unchanged. Pooling and compression are suggested options rather than demonstrated additions.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Targeted edits clarify terminology, move the reduced-step experiment from the appendix into Section 4.4, and organize added material into feature-reuse and discussion appendices. Acknowledgements, an LLM-use statement and conference-header/affiliation edits are added; the original narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the caching overview, adds a model diagram, reorganizes and expands the qualitative comparison grid, changes scaling-plot panels, and adds multiple feature-analysis and resource tables/figures. Table 1 gains comparison rows and loses its FLOPs column. Existing reduced-step displays move into the main text, and the document adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against closely related caching methods: it distinguishes BWCache from Skip-DiT's architectural changes/retraining and ProfilingDiT/TaylorSeer's feature-storage demands. It also introduces cited frequency-domain and noise-schedule explanations. FasterCache was already cited in v1; its publication update alone is not new related work.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(11) retain the diffusion formulation, block operations, relative-L1 definitions, caching criterion, reuse schedule and metric formulas, with notation changes only. The added frequency-domain and noise-schedule explanations are conceptual interpretations, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 established quality/latency benefits but did not quantify memory or indicator overhead and lacked several relevant evaluated comparators. v3's expanded comparisons and Appendices D–E substantially strengthen evidence about practical costs, motion sensitivity and applicability limits. These address important weaknesses in an inference-acceleration paper. Dropped FLOPs reporting and some overbroad summaries remain drawbacks—for example, Section 4.3 claims superiority over TeaCache despite its lower Open-Sora-Plan latencies in Table 2—but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BWCache and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. The shared method and experiments can be matched reliably despite added material, renumbering and layout changes.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds experiments on Wan 2.1 and HunyuanVideo, additional comparators, memory measurements and feature-dynamics analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation quality, latency, multi-GPU scaling and ablation results on Open-Sora, Open-Sora-Plan and Latte, including statistical comparisons in Appendix C.

results.title: BWCache: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers through Block-Wise Caching

C1.justification: v1 claims that its proposed alphabet estimator matches or exceeds all nine comparators. v2 reframes this central contribution around two alphabet estimators, including the existing U_EigV, performing competitively with most alternatives, and acknowledges U_EigV's leading strength estimate. It also extends the hybrid entropy estimator's incorrectness-detection claim to comparison with white-box SE.

C2.justification: v2 explains how early sampling of rare categories can exaggerate tail mass and cause hybrid entropy overshooting, qualifying v1's predominantly downward-bias interpretation. It argues that sequence probabilities help white-box SE down-weight these events and interprets the otherwise similar SE/DSE distributions (Appendices D–E). Appendix C supplies an empirical rationale for the retained reference assumption.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds the embedding model identifier and access link, cosine-distance specification, and DBSCAN radii 0.05, 0.075, 0.1 and 0.15. Section 6.3 adds reproducibility pointers. Existing generation limits, prompts, temperatures, NLI model and core estimator settings are largely retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use HotpotQA, SQuAD 2.0, BioASQ and POTATO for the same QA uncertainty and semantic-clustering tasks. The additional model, larger HotpotQA sample and new diagnostics remain within this existing data and task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds white-box SE to the incorrectness comparison and sample-size plots; v1 used it as the entropy reference but omitted it from these comparator sets. Table 2 also expands beyond LLM and NLI-NQ clustering to include embedding-based HDBSCAN and DBSCAN at four radii. These substantially broaden two comparison sets.

E3.justification: v2 adds Gemma-3-12B. The reported HotpotQA setting changes from 1,852 examples to all 7,405 for incorrectness detection, while entropy-estimation experiments use the first 25%. Table 2 replaces the combined |S| >= 1 evaluation with a separate |S| = 1 stratum. New diagnostics introduce ten-sample batches, KL/TVD/MAE comparisons and an SE* < 0.005 exclusion sensitivity check.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing sample-size and regularization analyses, v2 adds information-gain evidence for the 100-sample reference (Appendix C), diagnosis and filtering of extreme entropy-ratio cases (D), empirical-frequency versus RBMCI distribution comparisons (E), and direct alphabet-size underestimation analysis (G). Appendix A.3 also expands clustering diagnostics against human annotations.

E5.justification: Both versions report MSE confidence intervals using standard errors, DeLong AUROC intervals, 100 simulated matches per method pair and model-dataset setting, and Bradley–Terry strength/rank intervals. v2 retains these procedures; changed interval values and additional result entries do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds Gemma-3-12B and revises existing values, such as Llama-3.1/SQuAD plugin MSE from 0.84 to 0.78. Under the revised comparison suite, the hybrid alphabet estimator's rank interval changes from [1, 2] to [1, 4], while U_EigV changes from [3, 4] to [1, 3] and has the highest strength estimate. These are revised results, not established same-setting gains. New diagnostics also report overshooting cases and close SE/DSE probability distributions.

M1.justification: The proposed hybrid alphabet-size and coverage-adjusted entropy estimators remain unchanged in Equations 9–10. Both versions use NLI-NQ bidirectional entailment clustering for the main experiments. Newly evaluated embedding-based clustering methods are comparators.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and method exposition are retained. v2 refines SE/DSE terminology, locally rewrites the results and conclusion, moves the n=10 explanation from Appendix A.1 to Section 4.1, adds a reproducibility subsection, relabels the LLM-use disclosure and reorganizes the expanded appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds diagnostic Figures 6, 8, 9 and 11 and Table 4. Existing displays expand to accommodate five models and eleven uncertainty methods, while Table 2 gains grouped embedding-comparator rows and revised evaluation columns. The ranking plot and heatmap exchange figure numbers and the heatmap moves to the following page. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Gemma 3, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, KL divergence and total variation distance. Appendix A.5 clarifies why the evaluated SNNE and KLE configurations are not classified as explicit SE estimators. The broader related-work framework in Section 5 remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical substance of Equations 1–14, the Zipfian argument in Appendix B and the rank-interval construction in Appendix A.6 is retained. The added empirical-frequency expression after Equation 8 spells out an existing quantity. The new empirical diagnostics introduce no substantive theorem, proof or derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification through reference-sample diagnostics, white-box and clustering comparisons, and explicit analysis of an estimator failure case. It also recalibrates v1's superiority claim to acknowledge U_EigV's stronger showing. The 100-sample reference remains a proxy, and minor presentation errors persist, including Figure 3's ten-method caption despite eleven plotted methods. Nevertheless, the added diagnostics and better-qualified conclusions substantially improve the paper's evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same semantic alphabet-size and entropy estimators. All 18 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable; equations, tables, figures and relocated content support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for Gemma-3-12B, clustering comparators, sampling diagnostics and semantic probability-distribution comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original entropy-estimation, incorrectness-detection and human-annotated semantic-clustering results, including Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–7.

results.title: Estimating Semantic Alphabet Size for LLM Uncertainty Quantification

C1.justification: V1 advertises general minimax-optimal CAMDP guarantees. V2's abstract and conclusion qualify the upper bounds by a variance condition and an external-mixture benchmark, and restrict the full B+H lower bound to balanced algorithms while retaining an adaptive H-scale lower bound. Cross-signal concentration also becomes an explicit main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 materially narrows the stated applicability of the results and explains why concentration covers the finite oracle-policy family rather than the entire policy class. It also distinguishes adaptive from balanced lower bounds and explains their worst-case combination. These replace v1's broader interpretation that the general minimax complexity had been resolved without those qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 specifies external-mixture execution, lexicographic oracle selection, grid and rounding conventions, and the distinction between n samples per transition row and Ntot = SAn. It explicitly requires supplied structural bounds and a positive Slater lower bound, replacing v1's suggestion that an estimated Slater constant could be used. Neither version supplies code or implementation benchmarks.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or tasks for empirical training or evaluation. Revisions to mathematical hard-instance families belong to the theoretical analysis.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods against the proposed algorithm. Cited algorithms provide theoretical context or proof ingredients, not experimental baselines.

E3.justification: Neither version contains an experimental evaluation protocol. The new balanced-sampling restriction concerns the lower-bound theorem, rather than a changed experimental procedure.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, empirical robustness tests, sensitivity experiments or case studies. The expanded appendices contain mathematical proofs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical uncertainty intervals or significance tests. Changes to concentration inequalities and theorem success probabilities are theoretical revisions.

E6.justification: Neither version contains empirical result entries, measured performance or experimental rankings. Revised sample-complexity guarantees and analytic optimization values are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Although v1 mentions discounted reductions, Algorithm 1 and its reference optimization use average-reward/Blackwell-optimal updates. V2 explicitly uses statewise discounted-optimal policies and normalized discounted constraint values in the dual update. Sections 4–5 also substantially revise the discount, perturbation, threshold and optimization parameter schedules; mixture output itself already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, problem formulation, methodology, proof sketches and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The appendices replace substantial prose and reorganize the lower-bound arguments into explicit construction, separation, testing and calibration subsections. This is a broad expository revision beyond adding new theorems.

P2.justification: The existing diagram artwork is retained. V1's Figures 1–2 are combined into v2's Figure 1, and appendix Figures 5–6 become Figure 4; the six-state diagram is retained with new numbering and placement. Captions, figure sizing and the algorithm box change, while the overall visual template remains.

R1.justification: The related-work framework centered on Vaswani et al. (2022) and Zurek and Chen (2024) remains. V2 adds Li et al. (2020) for concentration analysis and removes references including Bartlett and Tewari, Paternain et al., and Wang et al. (2022). Its concluding novelty statement is qualified to balanced B+H rates and adaptive H-scale lower bounds.

T1.justification: V2 changes the benchmark to external mixtures, introduces the policy-wise discounted variance assumption, and develops a new cross-signal concentration theorem with row-independent candidates and a Bernstein hierarchy. It revises primal–dual and sensitivity proofs and removes v1's bias-span/transient-time estimation lemmas. Appendices F–G rebuild the lower bounds using exact occupancy separations, balanced-sampling and adaptive testing arguments, and an actual H = Θ(D) calibration instead of relying only on H ≤ D.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the coherence and checkability of the central theory. Its discounted formulation and new Appendix D remove reliance on v1's empirical-span estimation argument, whose stated and derived sample bounds disagree; Appendices F–G add exact occupancy separations and explicit testing reductions. The guarantees are less general—external-mixture benchmarks, a variance assumption, and balanced sampling for the full lower bound—but stating these limits addresses material overclaiming in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAMDP research work. The complete main texts, Appendices A–G, equations and diagrams are readable and support comparison despite substantial theoretical revisions.

after.justification: V2 remains entirely theoretical. Its expanded concentration proofs, linear-program calculations and hard-instance constructions are not experimental, simulation or data-analysis results.

before.justification: V1 reports algorithms, mathematical guarantees and analytic lower-bound constructions. Neither the main text nor the appendices report original empirical results.

results.title: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity Bounds for Constrained Average-Reward MDPs

C1.justification: The abstract, two stated contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about annotation-free denoising and self-distillation, efficient RoI inference and data-efficient generalization. Additional model applications support these existing claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds explanations concerning feature reuse versus external grounders, attention noise from clutter and abstract queries, and dependence on base-model capability. Appendix E newly discusses incomplete activation, incorrect localization and spatial-reasoning failures, including cases where SD-RPN turns a correct baseline answer into an incorrect one.

D1.justification: V3 documents Qwen-specific attention and frozen-backbone layers in Table 7, visual-token budgets in Section 4.1, and Grounding-DINO box-selection rules in Table 10. Existing optimizer settings, hardware, training time, pseudocode, prompt templates and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Table 11 adds an OCR-assisted TextVQA condition, whereas v1 explicitly evaluates without external OCR annotations. This adds a limited input-information scenario. Training datasets and benchmark domains otherwise remain unchanged; additional model configurations and DocVQA splits are protocol changes.

E2.justification: V3 retains S2 and ViCrop while substantially expanding comparisons. Table 2 adds Thyme and DeepEyes using published scores; Table 10 evaluates Grounding-DINO-B with one or two boxes; Table 11 adds reported comparisons with Monkey, LLaVA-NeXT, Mini-Gemini-HD and LLaVA-TokenPacker-HD.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 adopts a background threshold of 0.05 instead of 0.10, although Section 4.1 still states 0.10. New protocols include Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B configurations, 576/up-to-4096 visual-token budgets, a resolution sweep, one/two-box grounding controls, OCR-assisted TextVQA and DocVQA test-split comparisons.

E4.justification: V3 adds foreground/background threshold sensitivity tests (Table 5), native-resolution versus SD-RPN throughput analysis (Figure 6), attention-noise examples (Figure 7), and explicit failure cases (Figure 9). Existing component, backbone-depth, data-size, RPN-depth and smoothing ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The retained conditional-variance argument is theoretical reasoning, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise numerous SD-RPN scores: LLaVA-1.5-7B's document/OCR average changes from 34.3 to 34.6, V* from 67.5 to 70.7, and HR-Bench 4K from 48.0 to 47.3. Qwen results, threshold sweeps, timing comparisons and failure examples add substantial outcomes. Changed settings prevent treating all revisions as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same sink-token removal, selective pseudo-label assignment, frozen-backbone RPN, BCE training and two-stage inference. Threshold retuning and additional backbone configurations do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: V3 makes local wording edits, updates experimental descriptions and the publication header, adds acknowledgements, and inserts a comparison appendix with subsequent renumbering. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 expands Tables 1–2, adds Tables 5, 10 and 11, redraws Figure 1, and introduces success, resolution-throughput, attention-noise and failure displays in Figures 5, 6, 7 and 9. V1's qualitative Figure 5 is retained as Figure 8, rather than replaced.

R1.justification: Appendix C substantially broadens positioning against external grounding and high-resolution/token-compression approaches, explaining claimed efficiency and data-efficiency advantages. Added references include Honeybee, TokenPacker, Mini-Gemini, Monkey, Thyme and training-free open-vocabulary segmentation; this extends beyond bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: The method equations and conditional-expectation, class-conditional-noise and variance arguments remain substantively identical. The theoretical discussion moves from Appendix E to Appendix F without new assumptions, derivations or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 left important questions about stronger dynamic-resolution models and alternatives to its RoI mechanism unresolved. V3's Qwen evaluations, resolution-scaling analysis and Grounding-DINO comparison substantially strengthen validation of applicability and efficiency. Concrete failure cases also qualify the method's benefits. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses introduced or left unresolved in v3, particularly inconsistent threshold descriptions and mixed OCRBench score scales in Table 11.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SD-RPN research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds Qwen2.5-VL evaluations, threshold sensitivity results, resolution-scaling experiments, grounding comparisons and failure cases.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, throughput measurements, component and training-data ablations, attention analysis and qualitative examples.

results.title: Catching the Details: Self-Distilled RoI Predictors for Fine-Grained MLLM Perception

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three verification findings and the same TTS conclusions about generator convergence and limited advantages from stronger verifiers. The added experiments support these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 strengthens the case-based explanation of false negatives through solving-mistake attribution and expands explanations of difficulty-dependent capability regimes (C.4). It adds cost-aware selection guidance and drops v1's categorical assertion that the bottleneck is not model capacity, while retaining the principal verification limitations.

D1.justification: v2 supplies additional verification and error-analysis prompt templates, judge identities, sampling details, and computational-cost assumptions. It also specifies the Qwen3-235B checkpoint and decoding settings and newly documents reasoning-model sampling parameters. The original RQ2 sampling description is relocated to B.4, rather than newly disclosed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 12 benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, knowledge, and natural-language reasoning, with 2,347, 1,196, and 901 problems respectively. The added analyses change procedures and model configurations within this coverage.

E2.justification: The original model comparisons and reasoning-model variants are retained. v2 adds Qwen3-235B verification results and evaluates solve-then-verify and step-by-step prompt alternatives (D.3–D.4). Its new TTS selection experiments also use Qwen3-32B as a fixed verifier alongside GPT-4o.

E3.justification: The original 64-response pools and eight-response verification subsampling remain. New experiments introduce 50/50 validation/test splits for model selection, majority-vote accuracy, FLOPs and token-cost evaluation, and difficulty stratification estimated from eight Qwen2.5-3B responses (D.1–D.2, D.5). These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative analyses of verifier solving mistakes and generator surface-level errors (Figures 3 and 5), robustness checks using estimated difficulty, larger models and alternative prompts, and model-selection/cost analyses (Appendix D). The earlier reasoning-model analyses and illustrative cases are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 introduces 10,000 bootstrap resamples and 95% confidence intervals for the two added error analyses. This uncertainty reporting is confined to those analyses; the original RQ2 procedure of averaging eight random-subsampling repetitions remains unchanged.

E6.justification: New results quantify solving mistakes, surface-level errors, robustness, and held-out model-selection outcomes. Table 2 adds token measurements, including 193 GPT-4o tokens per prompt for verification versus 482 for generation. Existing principal heatmap values are retained, while the abstract's reported Gemma performance-gap closure changes from 75.5% to 75.7%.

M1.justification: The core generative-verification and response-filtering procedures remain unchanged. Appendix D adds auxiliary procedures for entropy-based difficulty estimation and generator/verifier selection using validation-set balanced accuracy, making earlier deployment suggestions more operational.

P1.justification: Related work and preliminaries are substantially condensed, results and TTS discussions are rewritten, and detailed RQ2 procedures move to the appendix. The appendices are reorganized into expanded setup, separate generator/verifier analyses, extended studies, and relocated case studies, with a contents list and new statements.

P2.justification: v2 adds mechanism-analysis plots, robustness and efficiency figures, and two tables. Main-text TTS figures are reorganized into mathematics-focused displays, with the earlier multi-domain material retained in the appendix. Several existing figures are resized, relocated, or reduced to selected panels, substantially changing the visual organization.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly positions the study alongside concurrent work by Lu et al. on cross-family verification, adds sources supporting difficulty estimation and error analysis, and removes the earlier self-preference-bias discussion and associated citations. The central positioning relative to capability–verification research remains intact; publication-year updates alone are not substantive changes.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds the mathematical definition of normalized answer-entropy difficulty, H/log K, including its bounds and endpoint interpretation. Existing pass-rate, difficulty, verification, and TTS definitions are otherwise retained or expressed more compactly; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens two weaknesses in v1: mechanisms supported mainly by illustrative cases, and efficiency implications inferred from accuracy alone. Quantitative error analyses with confidence intervals, difficulty/prompt/model robustness checks, and held-out selection and cost experiments provide substantial additional support. Cost conclusions remain qualified by the assumed GPT-4o parameter count and model-specific token accounting, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence and practical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original error analyses, robustness evaluations, model-selection experiments, and computational-cost results.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original verification and test-time-scaling experiments. Appendix C includes additional difficulty-stratified results and reasoning-model evaluations.

results.title: Variation in Verification: Understanding Verification Dynamics in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The framework, algorithm, and state-of-the-art claims remain, with revised headline results. v2 removes the claim that MobileRL is deployed in AutoGLM products. It also changes the claimed 7B AndroidWorld margin from +7.8% to +16%, although Table 1 still shows 72.0 versus 64.2, a 7.8-point difference.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's brief future-work discussion and reward-model caveat, Appendix E explicitly identifies absent out-of-domain public-app evaluation, incomplete XML coverage, reward-model bias, and substantial rollout resource constraints. Appendix B.3 adds explanations for resolution sensitivity. The limitations also connect reward-model problems to selecting AndroidWorld-only RL for the strongest 9B model.

D1.justification: v2 adds SFT learning-rate schedules, Llama-Factory packing details, dataset composition and construction, sanitization procedures, AndroidControl input/action conversions, and hardware/runtime information. The implementation is described as Verl-based instead of AgentRL-based. Existing XML preprocessing and reward-model instructions are retained through relocation; the stated code-access URL remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds AndroidControl to SFT training and evaluates its Low and High settings on 8,444 test samples. This extends evaluation from interactive task completion to static action prediction using step instructions or overall goals and interaction history. AndroidWorld and AndroidLab coverage remains.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same interactive comparators. The new AndroidControl comparison in Table 2 evaluates 7B and 72B UI-Tars and UI-Genie variants, including the previously unevaluated UI-Genie-7B, providing a limited extension of the comparator set.

E3.justification: Reported SFT corpus sizes change from 500k and approximately 71.4k steps to 97.9k and 23.6k. v2 replaces compressed-image experiments with full-resolution results and raises the maximum pixel setting from 500,000 to 5,000,000. The fixed 4:1 RL mixture becomes backbone-dependent training, with AndroidWorld-only RL selected for 9B. AndroidControl also introduces distinct Low/High evaluation procedures and action-matching rules.

E4.justification: Table 6 adds image-resolution sensitivity across training stages, Appendix D.1 reports backbone-dependent effects of mixed training, and Table 2 compares offline performance before and after RL. Existing component, complexity, step-efficiency, pruning, and case-study analyses remain; the pruning analysis is moved to the appendix.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run ablation averages, eight trials for the complexity-based pass@k analysis, and training curves with 95% confidence intervals. No changed run counts, seed reporting, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are specified.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces MobileRL-9B's 75.8/46.8 success rates with 80.2/53.6 under revised settings; Table 6 retains the earlier values as compressed-image results. The 7B scores remain 72.0/42.5. New AndroidControl results include 9B Low/High success rates of 95.9/77.5 before RL and 94.3/73.9 after RL. Figure 1 also adds train/test learning curves.

M1.justification: The three-stage framework and SPA, AdaPR, and FCF components remain. However, v2 adds Home and Wait actions to the action space and changes the stated reasoning-refinement scoring criterion from conciseness and log-probability to correctness. Negative-trajectory pruning remains, relocated to Appendix B.3.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the narrative remain. Edits add contribution bullets, rewrite the problem and GRPO exposition, shorten the conclusion, and reorganize supporting material: pruning moves to Appendix B.3, XML preprocessing becomes Appendix C, and reward-model material is nested within the expanded data-collection appendix.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains a train/test panel, and new tables present AndroidControl results, resolution comparisons, data composition, and action mappings. Complexity plots are rearranged with common vertical scales, and case-study composites are substantially enlarged and reformatted. Existing pruning and reward curves are relocated. The reasoning-free SFT plot is also relabeled as Table 3.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly connects AdaPR to experience replay and FCF to curriculum learning, adding Mnih, Zha, Matiisen, and Narvekar citations. It also adds A3 and UI-Agile references and replaces the AgentRL implementation citation with HybridFlow/Verl. The broader mobile-agent research positioning remains.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 revises the GRPO formulation from state-conditioned action groups to complete trajectories sharing an initial state and instruction, with a trajectory-level advantage. v1's separate time-averaged SPA advantage equation is removed. The SPA reward expression is algebraically equivalent, and neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves reproducibility and assessment of applicability through detailed data/evaluation documentation, the resolution comparison explaining revised scores, and concrete limitations. AndroidControl results also reveal an offline performance tradeoff after RL. These gains address important documentation and validation gaps in v1. The erroneous +16% 7B claim, understated offline declines, and some cross-reference problems temper but do not outweigh the improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MobileRL framework, model backbones, and core experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds AndroidControl results and an image-resolution comparison, alongside revised MobileRL-9B results.

before.justification: v1 reports original AndroidWorld and AndroidLab results, component ablations, trajectory analyses, and reward-model evaluation.

results.title: MobileRL: Online Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Mobile GUI Agents

C1.justification: The central claims remain the log-barrier LP reformulation, approximation errors scaling linearly with the barrier parameter, gradient-descent convergence, and extensions to DQN/DDPG. The new introductory contribution summary and rewritten conclusion largely restate these claims rather than redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes tabular guarantees from nonlinear deep-RL behavior and substantially expands discussion of barrier sensitivity, feasibility failures, coupled parameter tuning, and speed–bias tradeoffs. Appendix R explains underestimation and overestimation under different enforcement strengths; Appendix T.2 explains identical robotics returns as shared manipulation failures.

D1.justification: v2 adds complete toy-MDP reward and transition matrices, the feature matrix, least-squares initialization, update pseudocode, and Table 3's training and barrier settings. Table 1 gains settings for the two added DQN tasks, and Appendices T–U document sweep ranges and bias-experiment parameters. This substantially expands reproducibility information.

E1.justification: DQN coverage expands from three environments to five, adding MountainCar-v0 with shaped rewards and Pendulum-v1 with discretized actions. Appendix T.2 adds twelve robotics environments, while Appendices R and U introduce a four-state stochastic MDP and a maximization-bias scenario. Original benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained DQN/DDPG comparisons, v2 evaluates standard Q-learning, double Q-learning, and Lee and He's stochastic primal-dual Q-learning. Value iteration becomes a direct convergence comparator in Figure 6; in v1 it supplied the reference optimal Q-function. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce reward shaping, action discretization, 100,000-step toy-MDP training with linear or tabular representations, greedy versus reverse-greedy sampling, and controlled learning-rate and barrier-parameter sweeps. Figure 18 adds robotics evaluations extending to one million steps. The stated settings for the original DQN/DDPG benchmarks remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's FrozenLake barrier-coefficient study is retained and supplemented by learning-rate sweeps, off-policy sampling comparisons, enforcement-parameter ablations with underestimation/overestimation analyses, deep-RL barrier-coefficient sweeps, and a maximization-bias case study. These directly examine stability and mechanisms previously supported mainly by discussion.

E5.justification: Appendix T.2 newly specifies five random seeds per algorithm for robotics experiments. Table 4 supplies ± values without explicitly defining their statistic. Figures 1–2 retain the original ten-seed DQN and eight-seed DDPG mean/standard-deviation reporting; increased replication of those experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include faster value-iteration convergence in Figure 6, standard DQN outperforming the barrier variant on the added MountainCar and Pendulum tasks, and mixed robotics outcomes. Table 4 reports HandReach returns of -5.1 versus -3.2, but AdroitHandPen returns of -519.1 versus -635.9, for DDPG versus log-barrier DDPG. Figure 20 adds action-selection bias findings. These are newly reported comparisons, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: The main LP objective and DQN/DDPG algorithms are retained. Appendix R adds stochastic linear and tabular Q-learning adaptations using a maximized next-state target and a single Bellman-gap penalty, with explicit updates in Algorithms 3–4. These are limited procedural extensions of the existing barrier framework.

P1.justification: The introduction gains motivation and a contribution summary, the conclusion is shortened and rewritten, and local explanations and title capitalization change. New appendices Q–U organize the added material, while the original section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from three panels to five and is replotted. Figures 4–20 add convergence plots, sensitivity displays, value comparisons, robotics curves, and MDP diagrams; Tables 3–4 and Algorithms 3–4 are new. Existing figures, algorithms, and hyperparameter tables are also resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Applegate et al. (2021), Jaakkola et al. (1993), Munos and Szepesvari (2008), and Tsitsiklis (1994), supporting optimization and off-policy discussions. The introduction expands motivation concerning primal-dual methods, but the central positioning of barrier-based LP optimization remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds Theorem 5, deriving an explicit maximum-norm convergence bound and iteration requirement under an additional initialization bound. Appendix J adds Lemma 9 bounding the barrier minimizer's norm. These extend existing results; the central approximation-error, convexity, convergence, and policy-evaluation arguments are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 supported practical claims mainly through benchmark curves and one tabular sensitivity study. v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through targeted ablations, additional classical comparators, broader environments, and direct bias testing. Its explicit tuning limitations and reported failures make applicability clearer. Some supplementary protocols and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete, and favorable main-text summaries do not fully reflect the added negative results, but the gains in evidence and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same log-barrier approach to LP formulations of MDPs. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds toy-MDP, robotics, sensitivity, baseline-comparison, and maximization-bias results in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original DQN and DDPG benchmark experiments in Section 7 and a FrozenLake gradient-descent experiment in Appendix I.

results.title: Analysis of approximate linear programming solution to Markov decision problem with log barrier function

C1.justification: v3 adds an introductory claim of state-of-the-art performance in specialized DeepH scenarios. It also explicitly credits the established delta-learning paradigm while emphasizing H(0) as an informative input. The central contributions—NextHAM, joint real/reciprocal-space supervision, Materials-HAM-SOC, and accurate efficient prediction—remain intact.

C2.justification: v3 attributes the neon result to transfer through physically informed descriptors and acknowledges that broader element-level OOD evaluation remains future work. It interprets the conductivity comparison as evidence of improved wavefunction-dependent observables and expands explanations of embedding sparsity and DeepH-E3's generalization difficulties. The original ghost-state mechanism and large-system efficiency qualifications are retained.

D1.justification: A new reproducibility statement supplies access links and extraction codes for code, pretrained models, and data. Appendix E specifies initial node/edge construction through inverse Wigner–Eckart conversion, tensor products, and distance-dependent decomposition. Appendix M documents baseline adaptation and the reduced model. One tradeoff is that Appendix I replaces v1's exact irrep multiplicity/parity list with a less specific channel-count description.

E1.justification: v3 adds material-specific prediction tasks on Monolayer Graphene and Monolayer MoS2, extending evaluation beyond the original cross-material benchmark. Section 4.3 also evaluates optical conductivity. Materials-HAM-SOC itself is retained: changing '68 elements' to 'more than 60' does not establish changed coverage, and the neon example already appears in v1's figures.

E2.justification: v1 compares against DFT, zeroth-step Hamiltonians, and internal ablations without external neural-baseline result tables. v3 adds an evaluated DeepH-E3 baseline on Materials-HAM-SOC in Table 5 and comparisons with DeepH-E3 and original TraceGrad on graphene and MoS2 in Table 7. The latter baseline scores are explicitly taken from Yin et al. (2025), rather than newly rerun.

E3.justification: The added specialized experiments use ordinary MAE, training without pretraining, and DeepH-E3's splits: 270/90/90 samples for graphene and 300/100/100 for MoS2. The main benchmark's split, Gauge MAE, and 100-epoch budget remain unchanged. Appendix I replaces v1's explicit feature-irrep specification with 392 channels in the first three blocks and a final-block representation expansion; this revises the reported configuration without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The six original component ablations, Table 4, and their appendix band plots are retained. Section 4.3 and Figure 4 extend the k-space-loss analysis to optical conductivity and report closely matched real-space errors for the compared models. Section 4.2 adds an OOD interpretation of the existing neon example, rather than a newly constructed held-out-element experiment.

E5.justification: Both implementation sections specify random seed 1 throughout training and inference. Neither version reports repeated-seed accuracy estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The runtime minimum/maximum/mean reporting practice is also unchanged.

E6.justification: The original accuracy, runtime, and ablation results remain unchanged, including the 1.417 meV overall Gauge MAE. New Table 5 reports DeepH-E3 at 12.605 meV versus NextHAM at 1.417. Table 7 adds graphene/MoS2 MAEs of 0.102/0.163 for NextHAMcut-down, versus 0.175/0.285 for TraceGrad and 0.251/0.406 for DeepH-E3. The optical case adds 0.53 versus 0.49 meV real-space errors and improved conductivity agreement with k-space supervision.

M1.justification: Appendix M introduces NextHAMcut-down: learned embeddings replace H(0) inputs, the output directly predicts H(T), and training omits the k-space loss. Figure 2 also revises the reported block order, placing TraceGrad after the feed-forward update rather than before it. The full framework retains its Hamiltonian correction approach, distance-based ensemble, and joint loss.

P1.justification: v3 reorganizes the narrative by moving related work out of the main text, dividing the empirical section into statistical results and two case studies, and restructuring Appendix A.1–A.8 into appendices A–M. Extensive new background explanations, revised method prose, and reproducibility and other statements substantially change document organization.

P2.justification: v3 adds the four-panel band/conductivity Figure 4 and Tables 5–7, and revises Figures 1–2, including the architecture flow and explicit output converter. Existing result tables and appendix band plots are retained, with relocation and renumbering. The visual changes are targeted additions and revisions within the established presentation.

R1.justification: Beyond relocating related work to Appendix C, v3 substantially expands equivariant-model coverage, adds delta-learning and QH9 references, and develops detailed positioning against DeepH-E3 and TraceGrad. It also strengthens distinctions from molecular Hamiltonian methods around periodic-system subspace coupling and gauge ambiguity. These are substantive changes in attribution and research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendices B and D add formal group and representation definitions and explicit mathematical treatment of TraceGrad's O(3)-invariant and equivariant constructions. These expand supporting formal material without introducing a new central theorem. The eigenvalue/eigenspace perturbation bounds and analytical gauge-parameter derivation from v1 are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 chiefly validates against DFT, H(0), and its own ablations. v3 addresses an important validation gap through external neural comparisons and specialized-dataset tests, while optical conductivity provides additional evidence for downstream physical accuracy. Initial-feature formulas and resource-access instructions also substantially improve reproducibility. The less explicit irrep specification and limited single-example OOD evidence temper these gains, but the added validation and documentation provide a clear substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NextHAM research and Materials-HAM-SOC benchmark. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds its own specialized-dataset predictions, a DeepH-E3 evaluation on Materials-HAM-SOC, and optical-conductivity comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original Hamiltonian prediction experiments, band-structure comparisons, runtime measurements, and component ablations on Materials-HAM-SOC.

results.title: Advancing Universal Deep Learning for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction of Materials

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: synthesis-constrained genetic search, ML-guided block filtering, SynGBO, and competitive or state-of-the-art molecular optimization. The expanded evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: Appendix B.5 adds substantive applicability qualifications, explaining SynFormer's advantage through reconstruction training and distinguishing exact reconstruction from smoother analog projection. It hypothesizes different behavior on reachable versus out-of-distribution queries. Appendix C.6 newly attributes late-stage diversity deficits to GA exploitation versus reward-proportional sampling, substantially extending the interpretation of strengths and limitations.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the anonymous code location with a named GitHub repository and removes the promise of a future MLP-checkpoint release; checkpoint availability is not established by the PDFs. It documents catalog downsampling and the top-10k block filter used with the 1.2M catalog. Existing architecture, training and hardware details are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds analog-search evaluations on DDS-10 and ZINC; v1 used ZINC only to check oracle-version consistency. Docking expands from ALDH1, ESR_ant and TP53 to all 15 LIT-PCBA receptors. Appendix C.6 also evaluates additional Enamine building-block catalogs, substantially broadening the chemical search environments.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained analog-search, PMO and docking experiments is unchanged. Added datasets and controls reuse existing comparators, including SynFormer, ChemProjector and 3DSynthFlow. The corrected name RGFN denotes the comparator called RFGN in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 3.3k-call SynGA run with proportionally reduced initialization for approximate runtime matching, top-five analog diversity reporting, and search-space controls using 38 bimolecular templates, two reaction steps and 40 atoms. The ALDH1 mode-count caption also changes its docking threshold from <10 to <-10; unchanged result values do not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: Appendix B.5 adds a runtime-budget study testing whether analog quality survives reduced computation. Appendix C.6/Table 13 adds catalog and reaction-space ablations addressing search-space confounding. These introduce important controls beyond the retained mutation, filtering, random-search and NAM ablations.

E5.justification: The existing reporting practices remain: means and standard deviations over five seeds for PMO and related ablations, and four seeds for docking, with the same stated baseline exceptions. Added docking results follow that practice. No new uncertainty estimator, significance test or increase in repeated-run counts is reported.

E6.justification: Shared ChEMBL, PMO and three-receptor docking scores are retained, but substantial results are added. Table 9 reports SynFormer/SynGA reconstruction rates of 0.858/0.707 on DDS-10 and 0.558/0.459 on ZINC. V2 also adds reduced-budget results, search-space ablation outcomes, docking and ligand-efficiency results for twelve more receptors, and PMO optimization trajectories.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 change their stated return value from P to H, the archive of evaluated molecules and fitnesses. This is a limited pseudocode/output correction; the genetic operators, filtering models, losses and Bayesian optimization steps remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and section ordering are retained. V2 adds a separate Section 3.4 heading for the existing SynGBO description, introduces Appendix B.5, expands C.6, corrects grammar and terminology, and updates the publication header. These are localized narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: V2 adds comparison/control tables and PMO optimization curves, gives Table 5 a mean column, adds full receptor-wise docking displays and expands the ligand-efficiency table. The ligand figures are reorganized from per-seed examples for three receptors into separate 15-receptor grids for SynGA and SynGBO, substantially changing the empirical presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds the Enamine diversity-libraries citation and refines its positioning against amortized projection methods through the SynFormer discussion in Appendix B.5. The background literature and central novelty positioning otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The synthesis-tree definitions and assumptions, NAM Equation 1, inverse-rank sampling derivation in Appendix A.3 and ranking-loss formulation remain unchanged. V2 introduces no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evaluation of the existing method. The three-target docking study expands to all fifteen receptors, while runtime and search-space controls address important comparison confounds. DDS-10/ZINC results favoring SynFormer also establish clearer limits to SynGA's advantages. Runtime and catalog matching remain approximate, but the broader evidence, added controls and more balanced interpretation materially improve the support for the paper's conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SynGA/SynGBO research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–E support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds analog-search datasets, broader docking evaluations, runtime controls and search-space ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original analog-search, molecular-property optimization and computational docking results, together with mutation, filtering and neural additive model ablations.

results.title: A Genetic Algorithm for Navigating Synthesizable Molecular Spaces

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same principal claims: conditional whitening with JMCE, sufficient conditions supporting informative Gaussian priors, CW-Diff/CW-Flow, and forecasting benefits across five datasets and six principal models.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix D newly discuss when small conditional means, inaccurate estimators or near-singular covariance estimates can invalidate the sufficient condition and potentially harm performance. The appendices also add substantive interpretations of prior components, window sensitivity and joint estimation, and acknowledge substantial computational costs at high dimensionality.

D1.justification: V2 supplies previously missing training and sampling pseudocode, dataset and metric details, and implementation specifications. Appendix F documents architecture sizes, AdamW settings, learning rates, batch sizes, epochs and the 48 GB NVIDIA A6000. Section 7 adds a code link, and Appendix G reports computational costs. These disclosures do not establish that existing settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate forecasting on ETTh1, ETTh2, ILI, Weather and Solar Energy. V2 supplies detailed results for coverage already reported in v1; its additional comparisons and ablations use these retained datasets and forecasting tasks.

E2.justification: The six principal baselines remain unchanged. Appendix E.8 and Table 17 add an ETTh1 comparison with DSPD and TsFlow, which were not evaluated in v1's supplied results. TsFlow's existing citation in v1 does not constitute an earlier empirical comparison.

E3.justification: The main splits, forecasting horizons, sampling steps and generated-sample counts remain unchanged. Newly reported experiments introduce controlled variations of prior components, JMCE backbones, eigenvalue regularization and window lengths, plus sequential versus end-to-end training and runtime comparisons. DSPD/TsFlow are evaluated per variable before aggregating samples. Appendix F's newly disclosed training settings do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: V1 mentions ablations without supplying them. Appendices E.4–E.10 now provide evidence on eigenvalue stability, joint versus separate estimation, alternative backbones, individual prior components, window-length sensitivity and end-to-end training. Figure 4 examines JMCE predictions against targets, and Appendix G analyzes computational costs.

E5.justification: Both versions report forecasting means and standard deviations over ten differently seeded runs; additional result tables retain that practice. Appendix G newly specifies single-run timing measurements, asserting negligible variability without reporting timing uncertainty. There is no documented increase in forecasting repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 2 extensively revises scores: for example, CW-SSSD conditional FID changes from 35.645 to 9.265, and CW-TMDM QICE from 3.205 to 4.555. Table 1 changes ILI wins from 21/24 to 20/24. Tables 3–21 supply previously absent detailed results and new comparisons. The causes of score revisions are unexplained. Section 5 also changes the claimed ProbMAE win rate from 73.33% to 80.00%, although v2's Table 8 entries yield 22/30 wins, or 73.33%.

M1.justification: The default JMCE and CW-Diff/CW-Flow formulations remain. However, Appendices E.9–E.10 add triangular-factor whitening and an end-to-end variant that jointly updates JMCE and the generator using combined losses, explicitly specified in Algorithms 6–7. These extend the procedure beyond v1's sequential training.

P1.justification: The main section order and most abstract, introduction, method and conclusion wording remain intact. V2 adds a reproducibility statement, acknowledgments and appendix organization, updates cross-references and author/header information, and makes limited explanatory edits. The scientific additions do not constitute extensive rewriting of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the displays with detailed benchmark, ablation and timing tables, algorithm boxes, multi-dataset forecast panels and JMCE diagnostic plots. Figure 1 gains explicit history/future annotations; Figure 2 is redrawn and compressed alongside Table 2. These are substantial visual additions and layout changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: The central positioning relative to prior-informed generative forecasting remains. Appendix A expands the TMDM/NsDiff discussion, while Appendix E.8 adds DSPD and elaborates the TsFlow comparison. Additional references support the proofs, metrics, implementation and alternative backbones without redefining the main novelty claim.

T1.justification: The main Theorem 1 remains unchanged. Appendix C newly supplies the previously referenced Theorem 2, its covariance-dependent comparison conditions, proofs of both theorems and the terminal-distribution derivation. Appendix E.9 also derives whitening using the triangular factor.

improvement.justification: V1 references essential proofs, detailed results, ablations and implementation information that its supplied PDF omits. V2 supplies this material, substantially improving the assessability of the central claims and reproducibility of the method, while adding explicit failure conditions. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including unexplained Table 2 revisions and the incorrect 80.00% ProbMAE summary. The improvement rests on stronger documentation and supporting evidence, not higher reported scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same CW-Gen/JMCE work. Corresponding methods, experiments and displays can be matched. The supplied v1 ends after its references despite citing appendices; v2 includes Appendices A–H.

after.justification: Section 5 and the appendices report original forecasting results, ablations, additional baseline comparisons, end-to-end training experiments and computational measurements.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original forecasting experiments, including numerical ETTh1 comparisons in Table 2, dataset-level win rates and generated forecasts in Figure 2.

results.title: Conditionally Whitened Generative Models for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
