C1.justification: Both versions claim integration of omics, text and biological graphs through GPRM-guided subgraph construction without intermediate reasoning labels, and introduce Target-QA. v2 foregrounds existing schema rules and rephrases the conclusion without materially changing these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning transfer to unseen cancers, external generalization, missing-input robustness and immediate versus delayed rewards. Appendix D.2 newly explains four existing components as defenses against reward hacking. Appendix D.3 qualifies the added baselines' supervision as noisy and biologically incomplete, while E.2 interprets expert/LLM plausibility judgments.

D1.justification: v2 documents ChatGPT-5.1-generated training paths for the added retrieval baselines and explicitly describes the reward classifier as frozen. Existing training hyperparameters and hardware are largely unchanged. The reproducibility statement now points to supplementary source code, while GitHub and Hugging Face links remain in the abstract.

E1.justification: v2 adds external evaluation on 31 PedDep pediatric cancer cell lines and scenarios with missing omic modalities or depleted graph structure. The original Target-QA cancer coverage remains. Holding out existing cancer types changes the evaluation split rather than adding cancer categories.

E2.justification: RoG, SubgraphRAG and GNN-RAG become evaluated comparators in Tables 1–2 and the corresponding appendix cohort tables. RoG was previously cited but not evaluated. Existing comparators remain after matching expanded Omics and pre-GAT labels.

E3.justification: The original Target-QA split and metrics are retained, but v2 introduces three cancer-type holdout designs, zero-shot PedDep evaluation, a Qwen2.5-7B backbone, graph/input perturbation controls and varied reward intervals. Appendix E.2 also introduces a five-point biological-relevance assessment of ten examples by three bioinformaticians and two LLMs.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component comparisons and enrichment cases, v2 tests graph node/edge deletion, individual and complete omics removal, reward density, and removal of the graph supervisor, rules, rollouts and gating. Backbone and cancer-transfer analyses and expert/LLM plausibility assessments substantially broaden validation. The existing enrichment cases are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Table 15 newly reports individual judge scores and per-example mean ± standard deviation across human and LLM raters. The existing four-seed experimental statement and five-trial training analyses remain unchanged; additional benchmark error bars do not establish increased run counts.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive comparator, Qwen, robustness, holdout, PedDep and rating results. Original overall GALAX precision/recall remain 0.5472/0.5332; newly reported held-out average F1 is 0.4862 and PedDep LLaMA-GALAX F1 is 0.2901 under different settings. Some existing baseline values also change: ESCA L3-FT(Med) precision rises from 0.0047 to 0.0143, while L3+KG becomes zero.

M1.justification: The initial/final answering pipeline, pretrained GNN, edge-generation policy, rollout and rule rewards, acceptance gating and training objectives are retained. The schema rules emphasized in v2 already appear in v1. Qwen and reward-interval experiments evaluate variants of the existing procedure rather than introduce a new core method.

P1.justification: Section 3 reorganizes its explanation into feature, textual and topological spaces and separates Target-QA input components. Introduction, related-work and conclusion passages receive localized rewrites, and appendices gain subdivisions. Most existing method, pretraining and enrichment prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds dedicated tables for perturbations, reward analyses, holdout assignments/results, PedDep, judge ratings and cancer-code definitions. Existing performance tables gain grouped comparator and Qwen rows, and Figures 4a and 11 are redrawn with additional model series. These substantially expand the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical edits.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for SubgraphRAG, GNN-RAG and PedDep and sharpens its positioning against methods dependent on reliable retrieved subgraphs and reasoning-path supervision. The broader related-work organization and claimed integration novelty remain intact.

T1.justification: Section 5 extends the asymptotic complexity analysis to RoG, SubgraphRAG and GNN-RAG. It also corrects the static-KG baseline's prose cost from O(κ + M²ε) to O(κ + M²), matching Table 3. Core mathematical objectives remain unchanged, and neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 directly tests transferability and reward-component contributions that v1 supported mainly through the standard Target-QA evaluation and enrichment examples. Additional graph baselines, held-out cancers, PedDep, targeted ablations and expert ratings substantially strengthen the empirical basis. Some interpretations overreach: reward-hacking prevention is not directly tested, and LLaMA-GALAX trails GNN-RAG on PedDep Hit@10 (0.5179 versus 0.5333). Despite these qualifications and the ten-case rating sample, the targeted validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GALAX framework and Target-QA study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite expanded experiments and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds comparator evaluations, robustness experiments, held-out cancer tests, PedDep evaluation and human/LLM assessments.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on Target-QA, component comparisons, pretraining results and biological enrichment analyses.

results.title: GALAX: Graph-Augmented Language Model for Explainable Reinforcement-Guided Subgraph Reasoning in Precision Medicine

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and central conclusion retain the same claims about knowledge-informed conditional optimization without LLM fine-tuning. The headline comparison against ten baselines on five tasks, including average rank 1.2, is unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning whether knowledge alone explains LEON's advantage, the value of iterative feedback, and demographic bias in evaluated subgroups. It also discusses multi-objective applicability and explicitly notes that a scalarized critic constraint need not preserve individual constraints. The original clinical-use and surrogate-model limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: D.11 specifies how the new knowledge-augmented baselines are constructed: run Algorithm 2 with each backbone and append the generated knowledge to its task context. E.13–E.14 document the fixed-class-count and noniterative configurations. Existing implementation details, hardware, code access, and data-access instructions remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Warfarin, HIV, Breast, Lung, and ADR using the same datasets and distribution shifts. The new subgroup analyses partition existing patients, and NSCLC denotes the existing Lung task. The multi-objective discussion adds no evaluated task.

E2.justification: v2 Table S4 adds knowledge-augmented versions of LLAMBO, OPRO, and Eureka, which v1 evaluates without external knowledge. Table S11 also adds a noniterative, knowledge-conditioned LLM comparator. These substantially strengthen the relevant comparisons, while Table 1's comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs standardize knowledge generation across LLM methods, stratify outcomes by gender and race, fix equivalence-class counts at 2–64, and compare iterative optimization with a single proposal made without surrogate feedback. The original splits, metrics, 100-patient evaluations, and 2,048-evaluation surrogate budget are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds source-critic weight trajectories (D.6), subgroup fairness analysis (D.10), controls separating knowledge access from optimizer design (D.11), equivalence-class count sensitivity (E.13), and iterative-feedback ablation (E.14). These address substantive questions beyond v1's retained analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix D.10 adds two-sample, unpaired, two-tailed t-tests with a 0.05 significance threshold, subgroup sample sizes, and test statistics and p-values. Existing mean ± SEM reporting and other statistical analyses remain unchanged; no increase in repeated runs or seeds is reported.

E6.justification: Existing results are retained, but substantial new results appear in Figure S7 and Tables S3, S4, S10, and S11. For example, Table S4 reports Lung TTNTD of 38.90 ± 0.44 for knowledge-augmented OPRO and 38.93 ± 0.38 for knowledge-augmented Eureka, versus LEON's 32.71 ± 0.32. Table S11 reports Breast TTNTD of 29.35 ± 4.98 without iteration versus 72.43 ± 2.86 with iteration. These are new comparisons, not changes to Table 1 performance.

M1.justification: Appendix D.12 newly sketches multi-objective adaptations using weighted scalarization or additional objective constraints, with corresponding combinations of objectives and source critics. These are prospective, unevaluated adaptations; the original single-objective LEON procedure and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The original narrative and most wording remain intact. v2 expands Section 5's appendix roadmap, inserts new appendix subsections, updates cross-references and publication headers, and shortens the ethics and reproducibility statements. There is no extensive rewrite or restructuring of the existing argument.

P2.justification: v2 adds the five-panel source-critic trajectory Figure S7 and four substantive tables: S3, S4, S10, and S11. Existing figures and tables are retained, with renumbering and page reflow rather than redrawn results. The additions substantially expand the displayed evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and contextual discussion concerning Lipschitz-constant estimation, subgroup fairness, and multi-objective optimization. The main related-work section and Appendix B retain the original positioning of LEON relative to prior optimization and medical research.

T1.justification: Appendix D.12 substantially extends the formal scope through a multi-objective problem, scalarization, epsilon constraints, generalized Lagrangians, and an associated sampling expression (Equations 14–16 and subsequent derivation). Several extension claims are explicitly stated without proof. The original lemmas, proofs, and empirical-risk theorem are unchanged.

improvement.justification: Table S4 addresses an important weakness in v1 by giving competing LLM optimizers the same knowledge-generation procedure, distinguishing optimizer benefits from unequal knowledge access and revealing stronger baseline results on Lung. Tables S10–S11 further test class-count sensitivity and the need for iterative feedback. These controls substantially improve the empirical argument. The fairness interpretation remains stronger than nonsignificant tests with small subgroups support, and the multi-objective extension remains unproved, but these limitations do not outweigh the improved comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEON study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched across the added sections and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds knowledge-augmented baseline comparisons, subgroup analyses, and further ablation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original optimization experiments on five clinical tasks in Table 1, with additional experiments, ablations, and analyses in Appendices D and E.

results.title: Knowledgeable Language Models as Black-Box Optimizers for Personalized Medicine

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list now explicitly claim no additional training data or inference computation, refining v1's general negligible-overhead claim. The central trajectory-drift, SVR, radius-modeling and performance contributions retain their scope.

C2.justification: v1 explains declining radius through preserving hard-negative information later in training. v2 links it to decreasing negative-pair similarity and argues that harder batches require larger radii (Appendix E.8). It also adds substantive interpretations of transfer, noisy-encoder robustness and why SVR differs from scalar gradient reweighting.

D1.justification: v2 supplies implementation information for added experiments, including reproducing ATRI's CACL objective, scaling P+ with a learnable scalar for Simple Reweight, and the hard-negative sampling procedure. Core SVR hyperparameters, optimizer, hardware and inference details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix E.2 adds WavCaps training and evaluation, plus AudioCaps-to-Clotho and Clotho-to-AudioCaps transfer scenarios. This substantially broadens coverage beyond the retained within-dataset retrieval, multilingual retrieval and classification evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 adds Cacophony to Table 1, a Simple Reweight control in Appendix E.4, and ATRI-CACL with SVR variants in the multilingual comparison. Table 2 drops the separately reported Elizalde et al. (2023) row; most other changes from author names to model names preserve existing comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 5,000-sample WavCaps test holdout, cross-dataset transfer, random initialization of both encoders with text-encoder depth reduced from 24 to 12 layers, and selecting 6, 12 or 18 hard negatives from 720 candidates. The original main training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds distribution-shift tests, positive-pair similarity distributions, a gradient-reweighting control, convergence curves, weak-encoder robustness tests and hard-negative sensitivity analysis. These investigate generalization and the proposed mechanism beyond v1's retained component, batch-size, weight and radius analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports retrieval point estimates without seed counts or uncertainty. Appendix E.1 and Table 4 first report five independent random-seed runs and means with standard deviations. The accompanying significance claim refers to confidence intervals, although no interval construction or formal test is specified.

E6.justification: Existing SupCLAP headline scores and retained ablation and overhead values are unchanged. v2 adds seed aggregates, comparator entries, WavCaps, transfer, reweighting and weak-encoder results, plus new plotted findings. For example, Table 5 newly reports DynamicSVR WavCaps R@1 of 21.30 for A2T and 8.30 for T2A; these are additional results, not improvements over a v1 WavCaps experiment.

M1.justification: The support-vector construction, SVR loss, static and dynamic radius modeling, constraint term and inference procedure are retained. Applying the existing regularizer to ATRI-CACL adds an evaluation without introducing a new SVR component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order remain intact. v2 shortens the conclusion and Figure 1 caption, revises the radius interpretation, changes baseline naming, adds the conference header and reorganizes appendix numbering around the new material.

P2.justification: v2 adds five tables and Figures 4–7, including a four-panel convergence display. It expands the multilingual table, changes comparator rows and labels in the main tables, enlarges Figure 2 and relocates retained appendix displays. Figures 1–3 retain their underlying graphics.

R1.justification: Appendix A's related-work discussion is retained. v2 newly emphasizes compatibility with ATRI-CACL, which was already cited, and removes bibliography entries for Deshmukh et al. (2022), Mei et al. (2022) and Oncescu et al. (2021), while retaining corresponding model-level comparison rows.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.1 derives the one-step change in squared positive-pair distance, isolating the perpendicular component's eta-squared norm term as a penalty. This adds a formal connection between drift and alignment progress. The original SVR Jacobian and force-decomposition derivation is retained in Appendix D.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for repeatability, transfer and predictor robustness through five-seed reporting, cross-dataset tests and targeted mechanism analyses—important gaps in v1's support for SVR. The added one-step derivation also clarifies the alignment argument. These gains outweigh the statistical overstatement in Appendix E.1, where standard-deviation ranges are discussed as confidence intervals. Test-set checkpoint selection in Section 4.1.2 remains an unresolved limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SupCLAP work and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Existing content can be reliably matched across the expanded and renumbered appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds repeated-run statistics, transfer evaluations, new comparisons and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval, zero-shot classification, ablation, trajectory-drift, semantic-radius and computational-overhead results.

results.title: SupCLAP: Controlling Optimization Trajectory Drift in Audio-Text Contrastive Learning with Support Vector Regularization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about conditional diffusion, adaptive MGD-inspired guidance, diversity, and applicability across three optimization settings. Added experiments support or qualify these claims without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds qualifications about costly sample-wise adaptation needed for positive-diversity descent guarantees, the lack of a directly transferable guarantee for explicit conditioning, and transfer learning's requirement for compatible decision spaces and objective counts. It also interprets the new component and sensitivity results, while retaining the original overall conclusions.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly specifies the batch-dependent positive shift, its fallback value, and setting- and problem-specific perturbation defaults and their selection rationale. v2 also documents new variant/evaluation details and replaces v1's future code-release promise with repository access statements in the abstract, Section 8, and Appendix C. These materially improve documented reproducibility without establishing changes to the original settings.

E1.justification: v2 extends online DTLZ2, DTLZ4, and DTLZ7 evaluation to ten objectives (Figure 14), adding many-objective task coverage. The original benchmark families and offline and Bayesian task suites are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds MGD+RBF and SPREAD without guidance as comparison methods across online, offline, and Bayesian settings (Tables 9–10 and Figure 6). Existing external-baseline comparisons remain; the new ten-objective comparison explicitly excludes HVGrad while including MOO-SVGD, STCH, and PMGDA.

E3.justification: The original evaluation budgets and sample counts are retained, but v2 substantially extends experimental designs: diffusion/guidance controls, DTLZ4 dimensionality sweeps over 10–40 variables, inner-step sweeps over 5–50 steps, grouped-model training, and pygmo/hvwfg hypervolume evaluation for ten objectives. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct unguided-dominance visualization, diffusion-versus-guidance controls, explicit-conditioning ablation, decision-dimensionality and inner-optimization sensitivity analyses, and transfer-learning feasibility tests. These substantially expand the diagnostic evidence beyond v1's diversity-component, parameter, architecture-depth, and SBX ablations, which are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds, 1000 through 5000, mean and standard deviation reporting, and seed 1000 for ablations without uncertainty summaries. The new single-seed results follow that existing practice; no new statistical estimation procedure or increased run count is reported.

E6.justification: Original main-table values and offline Tables 9–12, renumbered 14–17, remain unchanged. Substantial new results include mixed component findings: in v2 Table 10, single-seed offline RE61 hypervolume is 2004.69 for MGD+RBF versus 201.43 for SPREAD. New conditioning, transfer, sensitivity, and ten-objective results further expand the evidence without establishing a same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The default SPREAD procedure and Algorithms 1–4 remain unchanged. Appendix D adds an evaluated explicit-conditioning variant with separate objective and shift embeddings, changing the attention context from (n,2,e) to (n,3,e) and sampling with condition (F(x),0), plus shared-model training across related problems.

P1.justification: v2 adds ethics and reproducibility sections, an appendix contents list, a conference header, and targeted explanatory passages, while standardizing guidance-direction notation. The original main narrative and most existing prose remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: New Figures 4, 6, 8, 12, and 14 and Tables 9–13 substantially expand the visual presentation of dominance, component controls, scaling, conditioning, and transfer results. Existing graphics are retained and renumbered, while the original offline result tables are regrouped in the expanded appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds Peitz and Dellnitz's gradient-uncertainty work, Biscani and Izzo's pagmo reference, and While and Bradstreet's WFG reference. The earlier Peitz–Dellnitz survey is retained as 2018b; Section 2 and Appendix E otherwise preserve the research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds Appendix A.3's attempted extension of descent reasoning to positive diversity weight and Appendix A.5's computational and memory complexity derivations, Equations 36–38. The original theorems and proofs are retained. The extension remains a sketch and contains inconsistencies, including a displayed maximum where the surrounding argument requires a minimum.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially reduces two important weaknesses in v1: missing direct evidence separating diffusion from guidance, and insufficient disclosure of key implementation choices. The new controls across all three settings expose both benefits and exceptions, while parameter specifications and reported code access improve reproducibility. Most additions use one seed, and the inconsistent positive-diversity proof sketch does not close the theoretical gap; nevertheless, the empirical diagnostic and reproducibility gains provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPREAD, retaining the same core algorithms and headline experiments. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component comparisons, conditioning and transfer experiments, sensitivity analyses, and ten-objective evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original SPREAD experiments in online, offline, and Bayesian multi-objective optimization, including performance, scalability, and ablation results.

results.title: SPREAD: Sampling-based Pareto front Refinement via Efficient Adaptive Diffusion

C1.justification: Introduction contribution 3 newly claims that GraphUniverse datasets can serve as effective real-world proxies through correlated model rankings. The conclusion also narrows foundation-model applications to potential extensions requiring further development. The original claims about inductive evaluation and context-dependent robustness remain.

C2.justification: New Appendices B and D explicitly discuss unvalidated foundation-model applications, realistic feature fitting, community-identification difficulties, inability to control motifs or geometry, and possible bias toward community-structured models. New interpretations address synthetic-to-real transfer and why heterophily-specific advantages may diminish inductively.

D1.justification: v1 promises release upon acceptance; v2 reports available PyPI/GitHub resources, TopoBench integration, and local demo deployment. It adds dataset-to-generator extraction instructions, specialized-model search grids, and default sum pooling. Conversely, the default-parameter table removes the degree-heterogeneity and Use DCCC-SBM rows; this does not establish an underlying implementation change.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic community detection and triangle counting. v2 adds native-task evaluation on OGBG-MolHIV, AQSOL, NCI1, IMDB-MULTI, and ZINC, together with corresponding synthetic datasets. Section 5.5, Table 4, and the alignment figures establish substantial new molecular and social-network coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix L and Figure 12 add FAGCN, H2GCN, and ChebNet as evaluated comparators, substantially extending the architectural comparison to heterophily-specialized approaches. Figure 12 omits TopoTune, although the original nine-model comparisons remain in Figures 3 and 4.

E3.justification: The new real-world comparison matches GraphUniverse property ranges to dataset percentiles and GraphWorld parameters to means, using 1000-node GraphWorld graphs. Models solve native tasks on real data and community detection on synthetic data. Appendix L adds a five-point transductive homophily sweep. Table 1 also expands the graph-size timing sweep and removes R-squared reporting.

E4.justification: v2 adds synthetic-to-real performance and ranking alignment analyses, including comparisons with and without DeepSet and GraphMLP to examine correlation inflation. Appendix L tests whether specialized heterophily advantages persist inductively. These are substantive additions beyond the retained parameter-sensitivity, distribution-shift, and size-generalization analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix K adds 1000-iteration bootstrap rank estimation, bootstrap standard-deviation error bars, and rank-correlation p-values. The existing three-data-seed performance reporting remains; bootstrap iterations are not additional training runs. The reported timing average changes from 500 graphs in v1 to 100 in v2.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive real-world alignment and specialized-model results. For example, Figure 10 reports OGBG-MolHIV rank correlations of 0.771 for GraphUniverse and -0.143 for GraphWorld after excluding non-message-passing baselines. Table 1 replaces timing estimates, including 0.020 to 0.023 seconds for 100-node graphs, under changed averaging conditions; this is not a controlled performance deterioration.

M1.justification: The implemented hierarchical generator is retained. Appendix D.1.1 newly specifies a prospective overlapping-community variant using co-occurrence distributions, a mixing matrix, weighted edge probabilities, and mixed feature centroids. This is a limited proposed extension, explicitly not established as implemented or evaluated.

P1.justification: The title and publication header change, model descriptions are compressed, and selected introductory, validation, and concluding passages are revised. New research-question, discussion, reproducibility, and acknowledgment sections are inserted, but the original narrative order and much of the existing prose remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds alignment and heterophily displays, extracted-parameter and specialized-model tables, and reorganizes legends, colors, and appendix layouts. Table 1 gains size rows and loses its R-squared column. Figure 11 visibly duplicates Figure 10 despite a caption claiming inclusion of additional baselines, introducing a substantive presentation error.

R1.justification: Related work and Appendix B substantially broaden positioning through CGT, metadata-driven synthetic evaluation, GraphFM, OpenGraph, and synthetic-data precedents in vision and language. These additions develop relationships to dataset matching and foundation-model augmentation beyond v1's principal comparisons with GraphWorld and static benchmarks. Publication updates to existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1.1 adds formal membership-vector definitions and equations for overlapping-community edge probabilities, degree-factor selection, and feature generation. The earlier Bernoulli–Poisson correspondence, scaling derivations, and validation-metric definitions are retained after renumbering. No new proof establishes the proposed extension's claimed properties.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens a central weakness of v1: its validation was entirely synthetic. The five-dataset alignment study, specialized-architecture checks, explicit applicability limits, and reported code availability improve evidential support and reproducibility. Reporting problems qualify these gains: Figure 11 duplicates Figure 10, and uniformly superior alignment is overstated, since IMDB-MULTI rank correlation without baselines is 0.543 versus GraphWorld's 0.600. These localized weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial new validation and clearer boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GraphUniverse and are readable throughout, including equations, figures, tables, and all appendices. The shared methodology and experiments can be matched despite the revised title, added sections, and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds real-world dataset alignment experiments and evaluations of heterophily-specialized architectures.

before.justification: v1 reports original graph-generation validation, timing measurements, architecture benchmarks, distribution-shift experiments, and graph-size generalization results.

results.title: GraphUniverse: Synthetic Graph Generation for Evaluating Inductive Generalization

C1.justification: The abstract extends the study's stated scope from mathematical to mathematical and code domains, and the introduction explicitly confines RL to practical policy-gradient methods. The central claims that RL compresses trajectories and concentrates graph functionality while SFT expands them, supporting SFT followed by RL, remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets Pass@1/Pass@k associations as evidence of efficient single-attempt exploration and suggests graph metrics as process rewards. It adds the caveat that sparsification can disconnect graphs and produce zero betweenness values. The earlier coding-domain limitation is superseded by experiments, while the limitation concerning uncontrolled training-dataset differences remains.

D1.justification: v2 announces code availability and documents HumanEval prompts and settings, the s1k-1.1 training recipe, and implementation choices for the new graph variants. The SFT recipe specifies Adam, learning rate, weight decay, cosine scheduling, five epochs, and a 20000-token block size. Existing inference and clustering documentation is largely retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates mathematical reasoning on AIME24, AIME25, and AMC23. v2 adds HumanEval Python-function completion for the existing 7B model family at both analysis levels (Sections C.8 and D.7), substantially extending domain and task coverage. It also uses s1k-1.1 to train an additional SFT model.

E2.justification: The model sets in Tables 1 and 2 are retained. v2 adds Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B fine-tuned on s1k-1.1 as an alternative SFT comparator against the corresponding Base and Oat-Zero RL models (Figures 19, 35, and 36). HumanEval uses the existing four-model 7B comparison set.

E3.justification: Existing mathematical evaluation settings are retained, but v2 adds several experimental designs: single-response SFT training, graph-construction and sparsification controls, and the Pass@1/Pass@k metric. The HumanEval appendices specify 128 responses and a chrF threshold of 70, versus the main text's general statements of 256 and 60; this inconsistency leaves the exact code protocol ambiguous without obscuring the substantial additions.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's trajectory-similarity checks and examples, v2 tests cluster counts of 1000 and 3000, cosine distance, an alternative GTE encoder, and top-10/top-20 graph sparsification (Sections D.4–D.5). It also tests whether the findings persist with single-response SFT and examines associations between graph topology and Pass@1/Pass@k. These directly investigate previously untested explanations and sensitivities.

E5.justification: Both versions report per-problem distributions through boxplots and disclose the same 10 K-means restarts. v2 introduces no new repeated-evaluation counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests; its additional plots reuse existing reporting practices.

E6.justification: The original mathematical result plots are retained, while substantial new results cover HumanEval, single-response SFT, graph ablations, sparsification, and the performance-ratio analysis. For example, v2 Figure 21 reports HumanEval correct/incorrect cluster counts of 23.6/54.4 for Base, 5.8/4.6 for RL, 48.9/8.4 for SFT, and 26.6/3.5 for SFT+RL. These are new evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core chrF/UPGMA trajectory analysis and sentence-embedding/K-means graph framework remain unchanged. v2 adds an optional graph-processing variant that retains each node's 10 or 20 closest edges before recomputing graph statistics (Section D.5), a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 adds local explanations and cross-references, an explicit graph-construction subsection, acknowledgments, and an LLM-use appendix, while updating the publication header. These are limited editorial and organizational changes rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with code-domain, SFT-control, performance-ratio, ablation, and sparsification plots. It adds a HumanEval row to the main decay-rate figure, merges v1's separate graphlet illustrations and proportions into Figure 9, and extensively resizes and relocates appendix displays. Existing mathematical plots are reused rather than replaced.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Liu et al.'s 'try again' reasoning work, Shao et al.'s DeepSeekMath, and Zhang et al.'s mGTE. It also changes the description of Oertell et al.'s policy gradients from 'unbiased' to 'biased.' The broader positioning beyond accuracy-based reasoning evaluation remains intact.

T1.justification: The trajectory probability model, SFT/RL objectives, exponential-decay formulation, and graph-metric mathematics are substantively retained. Appendix C.1 repairs an omitted normalization summand and adds an equivalent expected-reward expression for Pass@1; these are notation and restatement changes, with no new proof or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument by testing sensitivity to graph construction and sparsification, checking single-response SFT, and extending evaluation beyond mathematics. These address important robustness and generalization gaps in v1, rather than merely adding benchmark scores. The code pointer also improves reproducibility information. Conflicting HumanEval settings and the unspecified k in the new Pass@1/Pass@k analysis limit reproducibility, and training-data confounding remains unresolved, but these limitations do not outweigh the added evidence supporting the central findings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same trajectory- and step-level study of RL and SFT. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite renumbering and layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds HumanEval evaluations, an independently trained SFT comparison, and graph-construction robustness experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations and analyses, including Pass@k curves, trajectory-cluster counts, reasoning-graph statistics, sensitivity checks, and qualitative examples.

results.title: RL Squeezes, SFT Expands: A Comparative Study of Reasoning LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: the first VGGT-specific PTQ framework, DSFQ and NFDS contributions, strong low-bit accuracy, and approximately 3.7x memory reduction and 2.5x acceleration. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: V3 adds specific interpretations concerning transfer across architectures and quantization formats, complementarity with token merging, and robustness to inconsistent first frames through filtering and relative-frame geometry. It also discusses QAT's accuracy–cost tradeoff. These extend applicability and mechanism discussion while retaining the original explanations of DSFQ and NFDS.

D1.justification: V3 specifies RTX 4090 24GB hardware, CUDA 12.4, and CUTLASS/PyTorch for efficiency measurements, and explains CUDA Hadamard execution, LayerNorm fusion, and static versus dynamic activation quantization. V1 already supplied calibration counts, learning rates, and blockwise calibration details. The code URL and release statements are unchanged.

E1.justification: CO3Dv2 camera-pose and DTU point-map coverage is retained. V3 adds point-cloud reconstruction on 7-Scenes and NRGBD (Table 3), substantially extending dataset coverage. Appendix E also introduces a calibration scenario restricted to sequences whose first frame has very low similarity to subsequent frames.

E2.justification: V3 adds RepQ-ViT and AWQ to the W4A4 CO3Dv2 comparison in Table 1 and introduces a comparison against token-compression method FastVGGT in Table 7. Figures 11–13 additionally compare reconstructions against RTN and QuaRot. The original DTU comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include Fast3R evaluation, mixed-precision/asymmetric settings, one-epoch QAT, Table 5's first 200 sequences per class, calibration-size and hyperparameter sweeps, FLOPs comparison, and timing over 10–80 frames. Appendix B also changes the stated filtering parameter from T = 0.2 to p = 0.2; whether this corrects notation or reflects an executed change is unspecified.

E4.justification: V3 adds quantization-format/QAT comparisons, Hadamard and smoothing-factor sensitivity, NFDS threshold/cluster/sample-size sweeps, an inconsistent-first-frame stress test, preprocessing overhead measurements, sequence-length scaling, and qualitative baseline comparisons. The smoothing-order ablation is retained from v1 Table 6 and merged into v3 Table 4, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V3 Table 10 reports Hadamard sensitivity using three labeled random seeds, adding information about a separate source of variability. The five-seed sampling experiments and their reported means and variances in Figures 5 and 8 remain unchanged. No new confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Matched original CO3Dv2 and DTU scores remain unchanged; W6A6 results move into Table 1. Substantial new results cover additional datasets, models, baselines, configurations, and robustness tests. For example, Table 6 reports Fast3R mean accuracy of 0.049 for both full precision and QuantVGGT, while Table 15 reports speedups from 2.47x to 2.55x across sequence lengths. These are additions, not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: V3 adds experimental mixed-precision/asymmetric variants and a QAT variant that fine-tunes the quantized model for one epoch on calibration data (Appendix C, Table 5). The principal DSFQ/NFDS procedure remains unchanged. Random Hadamard rotation was already specified in v1 Appendix B; its expanded construction does not establish a new core algorithm.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization are retained. V3 expands selected mathematical and implementation explanations, moves the smoothing-order discussion into the main text, updates affiliations and publication headers, and adds acknowledgements. This is localized editing and expansion rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the experimental displays with new benchmark, sensitivity, robustness, and efficiency tables and Figures 11–13. Table 1 incorporates the former appendix W6A6 table, and Table 4 consolidates architecture ablations. Figure 4 gains clearer labels and captions, while Figure 6 changes its latency axis from normalized units to seconds.

R1.justification: V3 adds references including RepQ-ViT, AWQ, FastVGGT, CUTLASS, and additional quantization and 3D research. Appendix C newly positions quantization as complementary to token compression. The main related-work narrative and VGGT-specific novelty claim remain intact; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces v1's unnormalized sign-matrix description, which nevertheless asserted orthogonality, with an explicitly normalized recursive Hadamard construction and randomized diagonal signs. This corrects a mathematical-definition inconsistency. Theorem 3.2 gains symbol explanations, but its substantive statement and Appendix A proof remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1's evidence centered on one backbone and lacked direct hyperparameter and first-frame stress tests. V3 adds indoor-dataset and Fast3R transfer results plus targeted sensitivity and robustness checks (Tables 3, 6, and 10–12), substantially strengthening the empirical basis for generalization and calibration stability. Deployment details also improve reproducibility. Some new settings, particularly the mixed-precision policy and evaluation subsets for Tables 11–12, remain insufficiently specified, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QuantVGGT study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–H are readable and support reliable matching, including material moved between the appendices and main text.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds reconstruction benchmarks, Fast3R evaluation, sensitivity and robustness tests, and additional efficiency measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original CO3Dv2 camera-pose and DTU point-map experiments, quantization and sampling ablations, and calibration and inference measurements.

results.title: Quantized Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer

C1.justification: The abstract, numbered introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims about stochastic dense trajectory forecasting, advantages over prior predictors, and the overhead of RGB generation. The added experiments do not revise these statements.

C2.justification: v2 explains how observing velocity reduces predictive diversity while occlusions preserve ambiguity, discusses conditioning-related failures on Cityscapes, and interprets joint generation as improving RGB motion rigidity. The earlier mechanism explanations and limitations section remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplies targeted implementation details for the additions: Cityscapes preprocessing and CoTracker3 labeling, joint VAE resolution and latent channels, multi-frame temporal embeddings, and density-study training and checkpoint rules. The existing architecture, hyperparameter and hardware tables remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds Cityscapes urban driving, including camera turns, traffic and pedestrians, beyond the earlier controlled physical and robotics scenes. It also evaluates forecasting with two conditioning frames on Kubric, changing the information available about initial motion. Earlier coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds the SD3.5 + Tracks joint-generation configuration to the existing RGB-only and trajectory-only comparison. External baseline membership in retained experiments is unchanged; the new Cityscapes evaluation uses the already evaluated Track2Act and WAN.

E3.justification: New protocols include approximately 3,000 training and 500 validation Cityscapes clips from separate locations, with 28×56 trajectory grids; matched one-frame/two-frame Kubric evaluations; and density comparisons on a common 8×8 subgrid. The density study reports best scores across checkpoints at epochs 350, 375 and 400. Existing protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 directly tests whether denser grids improve forecasting (Table 17), additional input frames reduce ambiguity (Table 12 and Figures 4–5), and joint trajectory generation improves motion in generated RGB video (Table 6). These add substantial controlled analyses while retaining the earlier ablations and robustness tests.

E5.justification: v2 adds explicit sampling information for new evaluations: eight differently seeded predictions per Cityscapes clip and three predictions per multi-frame input configuration. These are generation samples, not repeated training runs. Existing standard-deviation reporting is retained, without new confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing scores are retained, while substantial new results appear. Cityscapes mean MSE is 1565.06 for the proposed model, 3495.43 for WAN and 9305.63 for Track2Act (Table 9). Joint generation achieves in-distribution LRTL 28.2 versus 33.7 for RGB-only SD3.5 (Table 6). Tables 12 and 17 add context-length and density findings under new experimental conditions.

M1.justification: The original trajectory VAE and flow-matching core remains. However, v2 adds trained multi-frame conditioning with temporal embeddings and variable context (Appendix A.2), plus joint RGB/trajectory generation through concatenated latent channels (Section 4.3). These substantially extend the model's inputs and outputs.

P1.justification: v2 expands selected experimental and related-work passages, subdivides real-world evaluation and adds appendix subsections. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence remain intact. Publication headers and author formatting change, and the acknowledgements are removed.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual evidence with multi-frame comparisons, additional Physics101 examples, Cityscapes panels and new evaluation tables, while extending Table 6. The original Physics101 Figure 4 is retained as appendix Figure 8. Existing visual material is preserved despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Walker et al. (2016), Li et al. (2018) and AllTracker, explaining distinctions in trajectory compression, temporal consistency, VAE usage and evaluation. This improves positioning against relevant earlier approaches without substantially reorganizing the existing literature discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 extends the formal target from p(X|I) to a family of distributions conditioned on a variable number of images. The original VAE and flow objectives, rigidity metric and variance definition are unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a direct density control and confined quantitative real-world evaluation to controlled Physics101 scenes. v2 adds a common-subgrid density experiment (Table 17) and urban driving evaluation across held-out locations (Table 9), substantially strengthening support for dense scene modeling and its applicability. Multi-frame and joint-generation experiments provide further targeted evidence. These gains materially improve the paper despite continued limited statistical uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be matched across additions, relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Cityscapes evaluation, multi-frame conditioning, joint video/trajectory generation and sampling-density experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on Kubric, LIBERO and Physics101, alongside ablations, qualitative evaluations and a user study.

results.title: What Happens Next? Anticipating Future Motion by Generating Point Trajectories

C1.justification: The abstract and Section 1.1 retain the same principal contributions: the manifold reformulation, Newton subproblems linear in sample size, second-order convergence complexity, and faster empirical convergence with comparable statistical accuracy. The added experiments support these claims without redefining the headline contribution.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies the earlier rank-insensitivity recommendation: larger rank may help when the penalty is large or clusters are imbalanced. It adds an explanation linking imbalance to harmonic-mean cluster sizes and separation requirements, interprets the new misspecification results, and explicitly limits the linear-time guarantee for kernel inputs. These materially expand the applicability boundaries and practical guidance.

D1.justification: V2 newly provides a repository link described as containing a Python demonstration and GMM/CyTOF scripts, while acknowledging incomplete experiment coverage. It adds feature-processing and kernel settings, joint penalty/rank tuning guidance, and revised derivative and pseudocode instructions. These substantially expand reproduction resources; hardware and license disclosures were already present in v1.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual CIFAR-10 image-clustering evaluation, previously mentioned only through prior work, and RBF-kernel clustering on Circles and Moon datasets. It also adds GMM scenarios with incorrect supplied cluster counts and controlled unequal cluster proportions, substantially broadening coverage beyond the retained GMM and CyTOF experiments.

E2.justification: The corresponding original comparisons retain their comparator membership, including NLR, SC, NMF, KM++, Carson's method, RTR, and I-AManPG. Added scenarios reuse subsets of these methods. The newly cited hybrid SDP methods are discussed but not evaluated as new baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include CIFAR-10 ViT-B-16 features reduced from 768 to 50 dimensions and 1,000-image subsamples; NMI evaluation with supplied cluster counts 3 or 5 when the truth is 4; and RBF bandwidths 3 and 15. The imbalance experiment uses r = K + 3, and new runtime sweeps vary r and d at n = 1000. These are additions, not documented changes to retained experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds explicit tests of robustness to incorrect cluster counts and controlled GMM imbalance, kernel-clustering case studies, and runtime sensitivity to rank and feature dimension. Earlier initialization and convergence analyses remain. The claimed additional large-penalty rank analysis is not visibly supplied: Figure 6 retains its original two panels.

E5.justification: Retained experiments preserve their 50-initialization or 50-repetition reporting and distribution plots. CIFAR-10 also uses 50 trials, continuing the existing practice. No increased repetition count for retained experiments or new confidence-interval, significance-testing, or seed-reporting procedure is documented.

E6.justification: V2 adds CIFAR-10 error distributions, misspecified-cluster-count NMI and convergence results, kernel-clustering outcomes, imbalance results, and approximately cubic-in-r and linear-in-d runtime trends. Figure 3's runtime measurements change, with the stated per-step cost revised from approximately 30–100 to 25–100 NLR steps. The 152-versus-80k iteration comparison and most original plotted results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The product-manifold formulation and cubic-regularized Newton procedure remain intact. Although v1 already discusses kernelization conceptually in Appendix A, v2 Appendix G explicitly implements kernel-matrix input; this variant cannot use the original factor-based linear-time subproblem solver.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. V2 makes localized explanatory and terminology edits, moves the formulation appendix after the proofs, adds a tightness subsection, and introduces acknowledgments, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements. This is a limited reorganization rather than a comprehensive rewrite.

P2.justification: Five new figures provide substantial multi-panel displays for misspecification, CIFAR-10, kernel clustering, imbalance, and runtime scaling. All fourteen original figures remain, with relocation, resizing, renumbering, and some caption changes. Figure 3's runtime panel is updated. Figure 6 introduces a presentation defect: its revised caption describes three panels although only two are displayed.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 adds a focused comparison with four hybrid low-rank SDP works, distinguishing their augmented-Lagrangian treatment from the proposed feasibility-preserving approach. V2 also adds the Cartis et al. cubic-regularization reference and the Vision Transformer reference. The broader positioning and existing cited works remain.

T1.justification: V2 corrects the missing one-half coefficient in Equation (11), repairs the completing-square argument in the LICQ proof (v1 Lemma 4; v2 Lemma 3), and corrects derivative expressions in Appendix F, including a missing commutation factor. Appendix B adds an explicit tightness argument. These are localized mathematical additions and repairs; the central assumptions and theorem guarantees remain.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens practical validation by testing incorrect cluster counts, controlled imbalance, image embeddings, and nonlinear clustering, while examining rank and dimension costs. It also repairs mathematical and implementation formulas and supplies code-access guidance. These address important gaps in applicability evidence and reproducibility in v1. The missing panel described by Figure 6 and incomplete code coverage limit the gains, but do not outweigh them; benign nonconvexity still remains an assumption.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across reordering and renumbering.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix G retain original experiments and add CIFAR-10, kernel clustering, cluster-number misspecification, imbalance, and runtime-scaling results.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F report original GMM simulations and CyTOF experiments, including clustering accuracy, convergence, runtime, and baseline comparisons.

results.title: Scalable Second-order Riemannian Optimization for $K$-means Clustering

C1.justification: The central LLR-BC, CaEW, and DsBC contributions remain. The conclusion narrows applicability claims: lifelong learning across problem variants becomes future work potentially requiring task-specific components, and removing reliance on task identity becomes a possible reduction in that reliance.

C2.justification: v3 explains the Li baselines' lower forgetting through their allocation of training to past tasks, adds explanations for low-confidence decisions and alternative confidence measures, and interprets buffer imbalance as potentially appropriate for larger tasks. It also specifies how fixed replay sizes can impair small-task plasticity and large-task stability. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices C.1 and C.3 substantially expand implementation documentation: 200-instance task buffers and alpha = 0.5 for the new baselines, removal of Feng's fixed-size parameter, confidence normalization, and instance-buffering budgets. v1's EWC/LiBOG parameter-search description is dropped. The new reproducibility statement expands the promised materials, but code availability remains conditional on acceptance.

E1.justification: Both versions use CVRP and TSP with the same six synthetic distributions, scales 20/50/100, five task orders, and 42 CVRPLIB/TSPLIB benchmark instances. The added comparisons and analyses reuse this evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds adapted Li (inter), Li (intra), and Feng baselines to the lifelong-learning and benchmark comparisons, retaining Restart, Fine-tuning, EWC, and LiBOG. New Tables 6–7 also compare POMO-MT-BL, POMO-MT-EL, and pretrained INViT. INViT previously appeared as a base solver in the applicability experiment; its standalone comparator role is new.

E3.justification: The original training budgets, test sets, and five lifelong-learning metrics remain. Added evaluations introduce batch-level and epoch-level multitask training, pretrained INViT testing, and task-specific Restart checkpoints. Tables 6–7 additionally report absolute distances and optimality gaps using HGS/Gurobi reference solutions. Appendix C.3 specifies new buffering and confidence-measure controls.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and hyperparameter sweeps, v3 tests buffering every epoch, entropy and top-two-margin confidence measures, rebalanced reservoir sampling, and whole-instance buffering. Table 3 and Appendix C.3 also add variance–entropy correlation and per-task buffer-composition analyses, substantially expanding tests of the design choices.

E5.justification: Appendix C.3 introduces Pearson correlation estimation between variance and negative entropy over buffered experiences from one task-order-1 run, reporting 0.972367. The existing one-run-per-order design and mean/standard-deviation reporting remain unchanged; no additional seed replication or uncertainty intervals are documented.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive baseline, ablation, distance/gap, and buffer-analysis results. Original Table 1 values remain unchanged, but the added Li variants achieve lower forgetting than LLR-BC. The instance-buffering ablation reports CVRP AP 35.4 versus 4.9 for the default, in Table 3's units. The new Li TSPLIB averages have conflicting method labels between Tables 2 and 10.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains final-epoch reservoir buffering, state-behavior experiences, variance-based CaEW weighting, reverse-KL consolidation, and the combined training loss. Algorithms 1–2 and Equations 1–2 are unchanged. The additional variants serve as ablation controls.

P1.justification: v3 locally rewrites the introduction, replay explanation, and conclusion; redistributes the former novelty discussion; and adds reproducibility and LLM-usage statements. It also corrects wording and affiliation/contact details. The main narrative and section sequence remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: The comparison and ablation tables expand, Table 2 becomes two blocks, and new Tables 6–7 display distances and optimality gaps. Figures 3–4 and 12–15 are redrawn with additional methods, revised axes, and expanded legends. Figure 2 gains explanatory caption definitions, and several appendix displays are relocated.

R1.justification: Five new references support confidence measurement, KL behavior, and cross-variant models. Comparisons with Li and Feng are elaborated, although much of this positioning already appeared in v1 Appendix A.5. Li's updated bibliographic entry refers to the same work.

T1.justification: The computational-cost discussion corrects the ideal overhead estimate for |E| = 4 and problem scale 100 from 2% in v1 Appendix A.4 to 4% in v3 Appendix A.5, consistent with 4/100. Mathematical definitions, losses, and assumptions otherwise remain; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 by evaluating the closest lifelong-routing comparators and testing buffering time, replay granularity, and confidence-measure choices. Absolute distances and optimality gaps also make solution quality more assessable. These additions substantially strengthen the paper, although arbitrary baseline settings and removal of Feng's parameter limit comparative conclusions. Reporting still needs care: Tables 2 and 10 conflict on Li labels, and blanket stability-superiority statements remain despite the newly reported Li advantage in forgetting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLR-BC research, with matching authors, method, and core experiments. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds evaluated comparators, ablations, non-lifelong comparisons, and analyses of confidence measures and buffer composition.

before.justification: v1 reports original CVRP and TSP lifelong-learning experiments, benchmark evaluations, component ablations, hyperparameter studies, and experiments with multiple base solvers.

results.title: Lifelong Learning with Behavior Consolidation for Vehicle Routing

C1.justification: The central claims of invariant diffraction-based crystal representation and strong predictive performance remain. v2's first contribution additionally claims to clarify the previously omitted premise of complete reciprocal-space information, while the introduction emphasizes modality-level fusion as a distinguishing requirement.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the physical interpretation of reciprocal-space information, arguing that global diffraction requires modality-level fusion and distinguishing it from generic Fourier processing. It interprets the new backbone-transfer results and their exceptions. The conclusion replaces the earlier inversion difficulty explanation with an invariance-breaking argument for structure generation and removes the explicit limitation concerning non-periodic structures.

D1.justification: v1 promises code after acceptance; v2 supplies a repository link and a reproducibility statement describing its documentation. v2 also reports model parameter counts, detailed configurations for EwaldMP, PotNet and ReGNet, and hardware allocations for Table 4. It explicitly identifies ReGNet as an independent implementation using 304 hidden dimensions. These are substantial disclosures, not evidence that retained model configurations changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds JARVIS total-energy and energy-above-hull prediction, plus an MBJ band-gap target. Existing MP and Matbench tasks remain. The additional JARVIS-DFT-3D-2021 and MP (MEGNet) collections retain the crystal-property domain; the clear task-coverage expansion concerns the additional prediction targets.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add EwaldMP, PotNet and ReGNet to the eight retained baselines across MP, JARVIS and Matbench. This substantially strengthens comparison with directly relevant long-range methods. ReGNet was discussed but not evaluated in v1; its alternative name ReciNet does not constitute another comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds independently retrained comparisons on the 55,723-entry JARVIS-DFT-3D-2021 collection using an 8:1:1 split, alongside separate comparisons with published baseline scores in Tables 9–10. It also introduces diffraction-augmented backbone controls and settings for three new baselines. These extend the evaluation design without establishing changes to the retained experiments' protocols.

E4.justification: The new Table 4 tests whether the diffraction module benefits eight alternative backbones across six MP targets, substantially extending analysis of its generality and revealing exceptions. Existing component ablations and the CaF2 walkthrough remain unchanged. The X-ray comparison and Miller-index sensitivity analysis are retained and relocated, not newly added.

E5.justification: v2 Table 8 specifies random seed 123 for dataset splitting; v1 provides no seed information. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or comparable uncertainty estimates. The added split seed does not establish additional training runs.

E6.justification: Matching original benchmark and ablation scores are unchanged, but new comparator rows, target columns, backbone-transfer outcomes and Tables 8–10 substantially expand the results. For example, v2 reports JARVIS total-energy MAE of 0.032 eV/atom and Ehull MAE of 0.041 eV, versus 0.034 eV for Matformer and eComFormer on Ehull. Alternate-dataset results are new evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: PRDNet's core architecture, loss, diffraction computation and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. However, Section 5.1 introduces architectural adaptations that attach its diffraction and fusion modules to eight existing graph backbones, evaluated in the new Table 4.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most technical exposition remain intact. Localized rewrites expand the motivation and related-work explanations, replace 'long-term' with 'long-range', consolidate limitations and future work into the conclusion, and move the sensitivity discussion to Appendix B. Reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds a diffraction-analogy figure and four result tables, expands Tables 1–2 with comparator rows and parameter-count or target columns, and adds hardware and directional annotations to the transfer comparison. The original X-ray table becomes Appendix Table 7, and the unchanged sensitivity plot becomes an enlarged Appendix Figure 5. These substantially reorganize the empirical displays.

R1.justification: The brief ReGNet comparison becomes a broader account of reciprocal-space research, including EwaldMP, PotNet and earlier reciprocal-space networks. Sections 2–3 and Appendix A.3 expand distinctions concerning form-factor dependencies, invariance, fusion and generic Fourier-learning methods, substantially revising the research positioning and cited literature.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, Equations 1–88, invariance argument and appendix derivations are retained. Added discussion of physical diffraction and modality-level fusion supplies conceptual reasoning without introducing or correcting a formal proof.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidential gap by directly evaluating relevant reciprocal-space competitors and testing whether its diffraction module transfers across backbones. Separate retrained and literature-based comparisons expose both strengths and exceptions. Code-access disclosure, parameter counts and implementation details substantially improve transparency. These gains outweigh the removed non-periodic limitation and a new discussion error: Section 5.1 attributes bulk-modulus degradation to Crystalformer, whereas Table 4 shows Crystalframer. The theoretical argument remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PRDNet research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline evaluations, diffraction-module transfer experiments and additional dataset-version comparisons. Some appendix baseline scores are explicitly attributed to earlier publications.

before.justification: v1 reports original PRDNet benchmark results, component ablations, a pseudo-particle versus X-ray comparison and Miller-index sensitivity experiments.

results.title: Beyond Structure: Invariant Crystal Property Prediction with Pseudo-Particle Ray Diffraction

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements and conclusion retain the same central claims about hallucination propagation, declining visual attention and mitigation through unimodal visual relays. Replacing 'plug-and-play' with 'model-agnostic' does not otherwise redefine the scientific contribution.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations concerning compression loss, recovery through renewed visual grounding and the source of computational overhead. It also calls for better combinations with other mitigators and improved token selection. These extend the discussion while retaining the central attention-degradation explanation and existing model-coverage limitations.

D1.justification: V3 identifies GPT-5-20250807 as the HS judge and supplies its complete scoring prompt, addressing a consequential omission in v1. Appendix C.1 expands the actor/critic collaboration description, and the abstract reports code as publicly available rather than forthcoming. These are documentation and access-statement changes; the training recipe and hardware disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: V3 extends the original eight benchmarks to multi-image understanding with MMIU and MuirBench and video understanding with MVBench and Video-MME (Table 4). Appendix D.2 also introduces masked and mismatched-image scenarios, substantially broadening evaluated input conditions.

E2.justification: The original MemVR, VISTA, FarSight, DeCo and TAME comparisons remain. V3 Table 11 adds pooling, MLP and transformer compression and SAM2-based object-level relays as substantive alternatives. Figure 11 additionally compares combinations of ViF with the five existing mitigators against standalone methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include injecting corrupted images at turns 2–4 and evaluating subsequent recovery, measuring latency and FLOPs, bilinearly downsampling CHAIR images, checking another hallucination judge, and inspecting three-turn linear trajectories. The existing training settings and original benchmark metrics are retained; these additions do not establish reruns of earlier experiments.

E4.justification: V3 adds tests of relay representation and token mixtures, corrupted-input recovery, compatibility with other mitigators, judge sensitivity, efficiency scaling and generated-answer case studies (Tables 8, 11 and 15; Figures 10–12). The original component ablations and hyperparameter sweeps remain and should not be counted as new.

E5.justification: No repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are added or revised. The new cross-judge discrepancy result is a sensitivity analysis, rather than uncertainty estimation for the reported benchmark scores.

E6.justification: Original table values are retained, but substantial new benchmark, efficiency, robustness and combination results appear. For example, new Table 4 reports LLaVA-NeXT-7B MMIU scores of 31.6 without ViF and 33.9 with it. Figure 11 also reports a negative combination result: VISTA falls from 91.2 alone to 87.9 with ViF. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under matched conditions.

M1.justification: Unimodal token selection, instruction contextualization, attention reallocation, the Key-Norm alternative and two-stage training are retained. Expanded mask and MAS descriptions document the existing procedure; the new relay alternatives are comparison experiments rather than changes to ViF.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. V3 expands the MAS explanation into Appendix C.1, moves limitations into the conclusion, reorders additional analyses, abbreviates OneVision as OV and revises terminology and cross-references. This is limited reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: V3 adds four tables, three figures and a formatted judge-prompt box, substantially expanding the visual presentation. Existing displays are rearranged and renumbered, sensitivity-table metric arrows are corrected, and the Qwen2.5 layer-attention panel has a revised horizontal range. Most original displays are otherwise reused.

R1.justification: V3 adds references for the new benchmarks, Gemini, a MAS survey and object-level visual processing, among other bibliography additions. Appendix A and the central positioning against single-agent hallucination mitigation remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7, including attention allocation, reallocation and the hallucination snowballing score, retain their mathematical content. No new theorem, proof or formal assumption is introduced; the additional mask explanation clarifies existing operations.

improvement.justification: V1 left the HS judge unspecified and lacked comparisons against compressed/object-level relays and measurements of inference cost. V3 addresses these gaps with judge documentation, direct controls, efficiency measurements and robustness checks, substantially strengthening reproducibility and evidential support. Broader visual-task evaluations further support applicability. Minor reporting overstatements remain, including the under-3% 34B FLOPs-overhead claim despite Table 8 reaching about 3.3%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViF research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds multi-image/video evaluations, alternative-relay comparisons, robustness tests and efficiency measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original attention analyses, token-dropping experiments, benchmark evaluations and ablations in Sections 2 and 4 and Appendices B and D.

results.title: Visual Multi-Agent System: Mitigating Hallucination Snowballing via Visual Flow

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the central claim that capacity-adaptive band retrieval balances coverage and distraction, improving accuracy with fewer tokens. Added experiments support this existing contribution without redefining it.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving similarity-scale/rank alignment, task-structure alignment, mid-ranked informative passages and cost-penalty-induced collapse. It also interprets deployment volume as determining training-cost amortization. These substantially expand applicability conditions and mechanism explanations; the original limitations paragraph is merely relocated to Appendix B.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents 600-token chunks with 100-token overlap, RankZephyr's top-50-to-top-5 procedure, and per-document caching for CAG. The anonymous code-access link is replaced by the named GitHub repository. Core LDAR hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds Ada-LEval's BestAnswer task, requiring selection of the most helpful answer among StackOverflow candidates (D.7, Table 8). The existing LaRA tasks and HELMET HotpotQA/NQ coverage are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds RankZephyr to the main LaRA comparisons and all nine per-model tables, and adds cache-augmented generation, CAG, to efficiency comparisons. These substantively broaden evaluated alternatives to include listwise reranking and document-cache reuse while retaining the previous comparator suite.

E3.justification: New protocols measure end-to-end latency and cumulative training/inference costs at 10K, 100K and 500K inference calls. Additional designs include embedding-model swaps, misaligned task transfers, clustering 100 similarity distributions and sliding windows of 20, 50 and 100 passages. The original split and correctness judging remain unchanged; newly disclosed chunking details do not establish changed preprocessing.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained band-versus-Bernoulli and hallucination-training analyses, v2 adds cost-objective and architecture ablations, cross-embedder generalization and task-alignment tests. New case studies, clustering and sliding-window experiments investigate when broader or non-top-ranked retrieval helps (D.2–D.10).

E5.justification: Figure 11 newly specifies standard-deviation bands across examples for similarity distributions. Existing standard-error reporting across LLMs is retained. Neither version provides explicit seed or repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Original LDAR accuracy results are retained, while v2 adds substantial baseline, efficiency, ablation and transfer results. New Table 3 reports open-source LDAR/LC latency of 3.9/15.4 seconds, and Table 8 adds BestAnswer results. A retained entry also changes: GPT-4o Top-5's 128K overall token ratio goes from 0.082 to 0.025 (v1 Table 10; v2 Table 16).

M1.justification: The core architecture, band-selection procedure and policy-gradient update are retained. Appendices D.5 and D.9 add evaluated variants with token-cost regularization, standard learnable embeddings and a pooled MLP encoder. These extend the studied procedures without replacing the main LDAR method.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main narrative are preserved. Local revisions clarify baseline descriptions and task alignment, move limitations into Appendix B, reorganize the appendices, and update author, affiliation and publication information. Added scientific sections do not constitute extensive rewriting of the existing text.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual presentation with efficiency plots, an annotated case study, rank-agreement and clustering figures, sliding-window plots and ablation tables. Existing comparison tables gain RankZephyr rows. v1 Figures 5–6 are retained as v2 Figures 6–7, while new Table 3 is redisplayed as Table 6.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion for CAG, RankZephyr, Ada-LEval, C-pack and Deep Sets. These support added comparisons and analyses; the main related-work organization and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4's equations and Algorithm 1 retain the same mathematical content. The added mechanism and transfer discussions are empirical; no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 supported efficiency mainly through token ratios and offered limited controlled evidence for architectural and transfer assumptions. v2 adds measured latency, training-cost analyses and targeted ablations that substantially strengthen those arguments and expose transfer boundaries. Localized reporting errors temper the gains—for example, Table 15 reports RankZephyr's 128K overall score as 73.3 although its component scores average 48.35—but do not outweigh the stronger empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LDAR research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching material across appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds efficiency measurements, baseline comparisons, ablations, transfer experiments and Ada-LEval evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original multi-model LaRA experiments, zero-shot HotpotQA/NQ evaluations, and retrieval-strategy analyses.

results.title: Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: native-3D promptable segmentation, a scalable dual-branch encoder, millions of curated shape-part pairs, and strong interactive and automatic performance.
