The added experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v1's limitations discussion focuses on the absence of semantic labels. v3 retains that limitation and adds explanations involving rare parts, engraved details, ambiguous part hierarchies and irregular generated or scanned geometry. It acknowledges SAMesh's fine surface-detail strengths and adds interpretations of initialization, scaling and correspondence results, substantially refining the account of applicability and failure.

D1.justification: Expanded A.1 documents voxel and channel dimensions, encoder processing, decoder token handling, the IoU head, previous-mask embeddings and additional curation safeguards. A.2.5 explains the existing graph-cut refinement in greater detail. These are mainly disclosures about retained components. v3 also replaces the promised future code/model release with a project-page pointer; the PDFs do not establish what resources are actually available there.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartNet-E and generated-shape evaluations, v3 adds coarse and fine-grained semantic-label evaluation on five 3DCoMPAT++ categories (A.3, Table 6), qualitative real-world scan evaluation (Figure 18), and cross-shape correspondence testing (A.2.7). These broaden annotation requirements, input domains and evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: Table 3 replaces the PartSAM variant using Point-SAM's encoder with the complete Point-SAM model trained on the curated dataset, as explained in A.2.1. This changes the comparator within that experiment. The external comparator sets in the main interactive and automatic benchmarks remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Added experimental designs include training-data sweeps from 40k to 500k shapes, a training-from-scratch control, automatic prompt-budget sweeps from 256 to 1024 points, functional-map correspondence testing, and coarse/fine semantic-label evaluation. Table 3 also replaces an encoder-swap control with whole-model Point-SAM training. The original main benchmark protocols and stated training budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 substantially extends the existing encoder, data and connectivity analyses. It adds a pretrained-initialization ablation, direct data-scaling curves, prompt-density sensitivity, native-versus-lifted label comparisons, cross-shape consistency examples, and explicit failure analyses with randomly sampled galleries. These investigate scalability, initialization dependence, efficiency tradeoffs and failure conditions beyond v1's analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added scaling plot and result tables continue to report point estimates without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2 and 4 and the retained Table 3 rows are unchanged. Table 3 replaces the encoder-swap results of 45.1 IoU@1 and 56.4 automatic IoU with 38.9 and 48.6 for retrained Point-SAM; these concern different comparators. New results include the scratch variant, scaling curves, prompt-budget tradeoffs, correspondence/failure examples and Table 6—for example, plane coarse/fine-average IoU of 53.5 for PartSAM versus 38.9 for PartField.

M1.justification: Equation (3) revises the stated objective by explicitly including IoU-MSE supervision and weighting Dice loss by alpha, specified as 2 in A.1.4, instead of the unweighted Dice term in v1. The architecture and segmentation pipeline remain substantially unchanged. Since v1 already describes training the IoU head, its explicit supervision is partly clarification; the PDFs do not establish whether the loss revision reflects retraining or corrected documentation.

P1.justification: Although the main narrative is largely retained, appendix exposition is substantially expanded and reorganized. The short implementation section becomes four subsections covering the pipeline, previous prompts, curation and training; the architecture-ablation discussion is rewritten into separate comparisons, and limitations become an extended failure discussion. There are also localized wording corrections, updated headers and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 9–11, 13–14 and 17–18, covering interior comparisons, labels, scaling, correspondences and failures. It expands Tables 3 and 5 and adds Table 6. Existing v1 Figures 9–11 are retained as v3 Figures 12, 15 and 16. These additions and revised displays substantially change visual presentation beyond pagination or renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for functional maps, 3DCoMPAT++, object scans and OmniObject3D, and removes Dosovitskiy et al. when replacing the encoder-specific ablation description. The main related-work organization and novelty positioning against lifting, clustering and existing promptable methods remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (3)'s mathematical definition of total loss changes through the explicit IoU term and non-unit Dice coefficient. This is a limited formal-definition revision. The remaining mathematics is retained or elaborated through tensor-shape descriptions, without new theorems, proofs or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for scalability through direct data-size experiments and initialization controls, broadens evaluation, and makes previously narrow limitations concrete through failure cases. Expanded implementation explanations also improve reproducibility. Replacing the encoder-only Point-SAM ablation sacrifices one isolated control, while some new evaluation details and the relationship between the revised loss and unchanged main scores remain unclear. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support, transparency and assessment of applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PartSAM work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds benchmark results, scaling experiments, initialization and prompt-density analyses, correspondence examples and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original interactive and automatic segmentation experiments, architecture and training-data ablations, mesh-connectivity tests and runtime measurements.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: WeatherPEFT combines TADP and SFAS for efficient weather-model adaptation, approaches full-tuning performance with fewer parameters, and surpasses full tuning on regional precipitation forecasting. The added evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of limited-budget performance saturation, TADP's value beyond generic adapters combined with SFAS, and the training-time tradeoff. Appendix B.7 newly qualifies performance outside weather and attributes weaker VTAB results to frozen RGB embeddings making prompts effectively static. The original Discussion limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 supplies a repository link and reports that source code and a README cover setup, data preparation, and execution. Table 11 adds method-specific training times. Existing implementation and hyperparameter tables are largely unchanged, and the reported external resources cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: Appendix B.7 adds coverage beyond the retained weather tasks: Cityscapes-to-ACDC semantic segmentation across night, snow, fog, and rain conditions, and VTAB-1K classification across natural, specialized, and structured tasks. These introduce substantially different data domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds nine precipitation comparators: ConvPass, FacT-TT, RepAdapter, SCT, Child-TuningD, MoA, HydraLoRA, VeRA, and SAM. New Table 10 also evaluates AdaptFormer+SFAS, LoRA+SFAS, and VPT+SFAS, substantially expanding comparisons with task-selective methods and alternative component combinations.

E3.justification: New vision experiments introduce DINOv2-L segmentation evaluated by mIoU and ImageNet-21k-pretrained ViT-B/16 classification evaluated by accuracy. Table 8 extends component ablations to an increased parameter budget. The original weather splits, training schedules, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged; these are added evaluation designs.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing ablations and extreme-weather case study, v2 adds larger-budget component ablations, tests whether generic adapters combined with SFAS can replace TADP, measures computational overhead, and investigates domain specificity through vision experiments. Appendices B.3 and B.5–B.7 substantially broaden the questions tested.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The new experiments retain point-estimate reporting; references to significant performance differences do not introduce statistical testing.

E6.justification: Matched original weather results remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 3, 8, and 10–13. Examples include Child-TuningD's 12-hour SEEPS of 0.407 versus the retained WeatherPEFT value of 0.368, and WeatherPEFT's newly reported 70.7% ACDC mean mIoU and 74.0% VTAB-1K accuracy. These are additional comparisons and settings, not improved scores for the original experiments.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 retain the same TADP adapters, attention-based prompt generation, and SFAS Fisher-guided selection with annealed randomness. The new SFAS-plus-adapter combinations are experimental comparators, not revisions to WeatherPEFT.

P1.justification: Selected introduction, related-work, and results passages are expanded, while most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 adds acknowledgments, ethics and reproducibility statements, an LLM-use appendix, and publication-status headers; the former implementation and task appendices become E and F.

P2.justification: The tabular presentation expands substantially: Table 3 gains comparator rows, Table 8 gains separate parameter-budget blocks, and new Tables 10–13 display hybrid comparisons, training times, segmentation results, and a wide VTAB task matrix. Existing figures are retained, with Figure 2 relocated and surrounding material reflowed.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work add a focused distinction between WeatherPEFT's dynamic selection and existing task-selective approaches, including SAM and SCT. References also expand for the added PEFT comparators, vision benchmarks, and weather studies. The overall positioning within weather foundation models and PEFT remains intact.

T1.justification: The task definitions, TADP equations, Fisher-information derivation, stochastic selection formula, and existing metric definitions are retained. The metric appendix moves from E.5 to F.5. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical revision appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central contribution by addressing v1's missing comparisons with close task-selective alternatives and generic adapters equipped with SFAS (Tables 3 and 10). Larger-budget ablations improve component evidence, while training times and vision results expose practical costs and applicability limits. New experiment settings remain incompletely documented, statistical uncertainty is still absent, and the domain-specific mechanism explanation remains inferential, but the stronger comparative validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WeatherPEFT and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite additions, relocation, and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds comparator results, component-combination studies, training-time measurements, and vision benchmark evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original downscaling, ensemble forecast post-processing, and regional precipitation experiments, plus hyperparameter ablations, backbone comparisons, and an extreme-weather case study.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution bullets retain the same central claims: distribution-independent mechanistic identifiability, multidimensional factors and non-invertible generators, a hierarchy of criteria, and graph-based characterization. The conclusion's emphasis on the coherence–interaction tradeoff restates an interpretation already present in v1.

C2.justification: New Section 4.3 explains criterion-specific limitations involving shadows, reflections, transparency, occlusion, and higher-order derivatives. Appendices C and D.2 expand the distinction between decoder identifiability and encoder ambiguity or discontinuity. Conversely, v1's specific discussion of compositional-contrast failure from a large shared Jacobian row is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds extensive reproducibility information: image construction and filtering, resolution and pixel range, dataset splits, the ResNet-18 encoder and additive subdecoder layers, and AdamW hyperparameters. The original synthetic experiment's details are retained in Appendix D.1; they are not replaced by these new settings.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained invertible-MLP synthetic observations, v2 evaluates non-invertible generation of two-ball RGB images with position and color factors. This introduces image-domain disentanglement under permutation ambiguity. Occluded scenes are excluded from this experiment; their discussion is theoretical.

E2.justification: No competing-method baselines are added or removed. The original autoencoder configuration comparisons remain, and the new image experiment reports one additive autoencoder without comparative baseline results.

E3.justification: The new image experiment introduces a permutation-aware evaluation procedure: center-of-mass matching selects latent permutations before computing SIS*. It also specifies 300,000/10,000/50,000 training/validation/test images and a 1,000-epoch training protocol. The original overlap experiment's configuration grid and normalization remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix D.2 adds a focused diagnostic case study using individual-slot reconstructions and position/color traversals to examine factor separation and encoder discontinuities. The existing sensitivity analysis over support overlap is retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports five seeds per overlap configuration. v2 additionally presents five-seed RMSE and SIS* summaries with ± values in Table 1, but does not identify the uncertainty statistic. This adds uncertainty reporting without establishing increased repetition of the original experiments.

E6.justification: The original overlap scatter plot and findings are retained. New Table 1 reports RMSE 1.30 ± 0.18 and SIS* 99.6 ± 0.05; Figures 4–6 add image reconstructions and evidence of a latent discontinuity despite accurate decoding. These are additional results under new conditions, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The independence framework and original compositional-contrast training remain. Appendix D.2 adds an experimental autoencoder with separately parameterized additive slot decoders and MSE-only training, structurally enforcing Type H2 independence.

P1.justification: v2 moves the overlap experiment into a dedicated Experiments section, adds a limitations subsection, reorganizes the appendices, and clarifies full versus partial disentanglement terminology. It also updates affiliations and publication headers. Much of the existing narrative remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 and Figures 4–6, introducing quantitative summaries, slot-reconstruction grids, latent-code curves, and traversal reconstructions. The original scatter plot is relocated with a revised caption and redrawn support schematic; the hierarchy and slice-connectedness diagrams are retained.

R1.justification: The introduction expands its structural-identifiability taxonomy with citations including Jutten and Karhunen, Kivva et al., Lyu and Fu, and Nguyen and Fu. An AdamW reference is added and Reizinger et al. (2022) is removed. The central positioning relative to prior mechanistic-identifiability work remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 strengthens path-connectedness to simple connectedness, explicitly requires continuity of the generator and a covering-map decoder, and receives a replacement lifting-based proof and relaxation conditions. Appendix A.2 revises the equivalence propositions and proofs. Appendix B adds a proof characterizing compositional-contrast minimizers for a constructed generator under a determinant constraint.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the precision of the central global-identifiability argument through explicit lifting conditions, a rewritten proof, and revised equivalence assumptions. The new non-invertible image experiment and detailed applicability discussion provide support absent from v1's invertible-vector experiments. The guarantee is narrower, and Appendix C still does not verify all newly required lifting conditions, but the gains in theoretical qualification and empirical support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mechanistic-independence framework. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, proofs, figures, and results, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the overlap experiments and adds original two-ball image experiments, quantitative results, reconstructions, and latent traversals in Appendix D.2.

before.justification: Figure 1 and Appendix C report original autoencoder experiments across support-overlap levels, comprising 120 trained models.

results.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and central conclusion retain the same reconstruction-threshold claim, theoretical scope and projection-based reconstruction proposal. The expanded experiments support these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly separates fitting the parameter vector from satisfying the full feature-span hypothesis, explains the obstacle to extending Theorem 2 beyond n = 2, and clarifies that whole-dataset reconstruction limits do not prevent individual-sample memorization. Appendix E.3 additionally interprets failures and applicability under size uncertainty, learning-rate variation, regularization and pruning.

D1.justification: Documentation adds classification training settings, Tiny-ImageNet class selection and preprocessing, its reconstruction step size of 8000, and ablation ranges and budgets. Transformer and pruning configurations are also described. The core optimizer implementation, hardware disclosure and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained spherical-data and CIFAR-10 experiments, v2 adds higher-resolution Tiny-ImageNet reconstruction, synthetic classification with sign-generated labels, and reconstruction without the exact training-set size. These broaden both the represented data and the information requirements of the reconstruction task.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing reconstruction algorithms against the proposed method. Optimal Brain Surgeon is newly used to produce pruned target models in v2, not as a competing reconstruction method.

E3.justification: v2 adds classification training with logistic/cross-entropy losses, full-batch gradient descent at step size 0.001 for one million steps, transformer embedding-size sweeps, and regularization/pruning settings. Appendix E.3 also introduces candidate-count variations and a learning-rate experiment capped at 60,000 reconstruction iterations. These are additional protocols; the original experiments' settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.3 tests sensitivity to reconstruction learning rate, incorrect candidate-set size, ridge regularization and pruning (Figures 11–12 and 15–16). These directly examine optimization failures and reconstruction robustness beyond v1's retained span-inclusion and activation-sign analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly explains that seeds independently initialize network parameters and reconstruction variables. Existing four-seed and ten-seed results retain their run counts and mean/standard-deviation reporting. The additional ten-seed experiments do not establish increased replication of earlier results.

E6.justification: The original plotted results and reconstruction images are retained. New results cover classification, Tiny-ImageNet and transformers, plus findings that excessive learning rates prevent convergence, underestimated dataset size produces mixed images, excess candidates produce duplicates, fixed ridge penalties preserve similar thresholds, and pruning increases reconstruction difficulty.

M1.justification: The projection loss in Eq. (11) and its optimization remain unchanged. Appendix E.3 adds a limited procedural suggestion for unknown dataset size: increase the number of reconstructed candidates until duplicates appear to estimate n. This is proposed as a practical heuristic, rather than an established new algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 expands the theory-to-algorithm explanation, adds Remark 2 and experimental paragraphs, broadens the natural-image heading, and introduces Appendix E.3. Most existing prose and the main section order remain intact, so this is an extension with localized rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial new plots and image montages for classification, Tiny-ImageNet, transformers and robustness studies (Figures 5, 8 and 11–17). Original Figures 5–8 survive as Figures 6, 7, 9 and 10. The Tiny-ImageNet images are redisplayed in Figures 5 and 14; this is not two independent results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for vision transformers, Tiny-ImageNet, Optimal Brain Surgeon and Vardi–Yehudai–Shamir's memorization result. Section 2 adds a brief discussion of sublinear-parameter label memorization under separability. The broader positioning against prior reconstruction work is retained.

T1.justification: The assumptions, main theorems and proofs in Appendices A–C are unchanged. Appendix E.3 adds the ridge objective, its closed-form solution and a spectral scaling argument explaining why fixed regularization becomes negligible as p grows (Eqs. 168–170). The expanded main proof sketch restates reasoning already present in v1's appendix.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support concentrated on square-loss models and left important practical dependencies untested. v2 substantially strengthens that support through classification experiments and controlled tests of optimization, dataset-size knowledge, regularization and pruning, while explaining relevant failure conditions and theoretical limits. Small evaluation subsets and the unresolved general-n and optimization guarantees remain, but the broader evidence materially improves the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching core methods, theorems and original experiments. Text, equations, figures and appendices support a reliable comparison; the expanded material in v2 is identifiable.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original classification, Tiny-ImageNet, transformer and robustness results in Section 5 and Appendix E.3.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data and CIFAR-10 reconstruction experiments with random features, two-layer networks and ResNets in Section 5 and Appendix E.

results.title: A Law of Data Reconstruction for Random Features (And Beyond)

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central findings: explanations help detect biased predictions and supervise mitigation but do not reliably select fair models. The claims about detection after explanation-based debiasing and superiority to LLM judgments also remain; v2 principally expands their supporting evidence.

C2.justification: Appendix M adds specific qualifications concerning alternative model-selection metrics, validation strategies, limited group-fairness analysis and the absence of a universally best explanation method. New interpretations distinguish human auditing effectiveness from automatic detection and interpretability, and discuss vocabulary robustness and complementary hybrid mitigation.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the promised future code release with a repository link and states that code and preprocessing scripts are available. It also documents the DecompX implementation source, single-pass Progressive Inference, and efficiency-measurement settings including GPU allocation, batch size and gradient checkpointing. These materially extend the available reproducibility information.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates automated fairness on Civil Comments and Jigsaw. V2 adds sentiment analysis using Twitter Sentiment and human fairness auditing involving 48 examples and six annotators, substantially extending task coverage. Appendix H also tests incomplete sensitive-token coverage as an additional deployment scenario.

E2.justification: V2 adds DecompX and Progressive Inference to the explanation comparisons and GPT-OSS-120B to the LLM-judge comparison in Table 2. Integrated Gradients also enters the bias-mitigation comparison in Table 7 after being explicitly excluded from that experiment in v1. These extend several substantive comparator sets.

E3.justification: V2 adds an answer-only instruction to the decoder prompt template and reports an Occlusion-specific regularization grid of 0.002-0.01 instead of v1's general 0.01-100 grid. New settings include Qwen3-8B, additional alignment configurations, a human rating protocol and a 200-example efficiency benchmark. These are revised reported settings and new protocols; they do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test transfer across tasks and alignment settings, sensitivity to incomplete sensitive vocabularies, human auditing under different conditions, and whether preprocessing complements explanation-based debiasing. V2 also measures explanation efficiency. These substantially expand the questions examined beyond v1's existing faithfulness and post-debiasing analyses.

E5.justification: V2 Table 4 newly specifies three-run averaging for the efficiency measurements. Retained experiments still use three-run debiasing averages, six/three random validation selections and the same p < 0.05 correlation-significance convention. The addition documents repetition for the new analysis without establishing increased repetitions for existing experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for the new comparators, configurations and appendix studies. Table 1 replaces Qwen3-4B few-shot accuracies of 63.00/76.40/74.30 with 70.15/80.73/79.53 alongside the revised prompt, so these are not established same-setting gains. MRR@1 plots and the associated below-random interpretation are revised, and Occlusion mitigation results also change.

M1.justification: The central attribution-based framework and regularized training objective remain unchanged. Appendix K introduces a limited procedural extension combining group balancing, group-class balancing or counterfactual data augmentation with IxG L1/L2 regularization.

P1.justification: The main section order and much existing prose remain intact. V2 makes localized rewrites, clarifies model names and LLM-judge terminology, expands background and limitations explanations, and reorganizes appendix headings around the additional studies.

P2.justification: V2 adds a workflow diagram, generalization plots, and efficiency, Integrated Gradients, human-auditing and hybrid-debiasing tables. Existing comparison plots gain methods or model panels, and appendix model-selection figures are regrouped by architecture. Legends, axes and the overall conference layout are also revised.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands positioning within hate-speech fairness and explainability research, covering mitigation stages, rationale supervision and human evaluation. It adds works such as Park et al. (2018), Garg et al. (2019) and Nirmal et al. (2024), while explaining the study's relationship to these research lines.

T1.justification: The sensitive-token reliance, group disparity, individual unfairness and regularized-loss formulations are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs or theorems. Appendix A's new definitions of hate speech and social bias are conceptual background rather than new formal mathematical content.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens practical applicability by testing assumptions left unexamined in v1, especially task transfer and incomplete sensitive vocabularies, and by expanding the LLM-judge comparison beyond Qwen3-4B. Computational-cost reporting, stated code access and specific limitations further improve assessability and reproducibility. The human study remains preliminary and lacks a no-explanation control, and Figure 27 has a race/gender caption inconsistency, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in directly relevant validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with the same title, authors and three research questions. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on sentiment analysis, vocabulary coverage, model alignment, computational efficiency, human auditing and hybrid debiasing.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on bias detection, fair model selection and bias mitigation using Civil Comments and Jigsaw, with additional results and analyses in its appendices.

C1.justification: The three contribution bullets and central claims remain unchanged: a black-box narrative attack whose scene combinations constrain generation toward harmful outputs and bypass T2V safety filters. The abstract and conclusion incorporate additional target-specific results and baseline support for these retained claims.

C2.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 newly distinguish attacks on text preprocessing filters from video postprocessing defenses. Added discussions explain initialization and component-model robustness, retrieval sensitivity, claimed four-to-five-scene optimality, runtime overhead, and the attack-success/semantic-fidelity tradeoff. The original identity-preservation limitation is retained, moving from Appendix E to G.

D1.justification: v2 documents RPG-RT's Veo2 fine-tuning, detector/evaluator handling, and modification budget, and supplies runtime information in Tables 7 and 10. Existing SceneSplit defaults and appendix implementation listings remain unchanged; no new code or data access resource is specified.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same stated T2VSafetyBench coverage: 220 prompts across the same 11 safety categories. The added target models and ablations extend model settings and analyses without introducing a new dataset, domain, or generation task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds RPG-RT as a competing attack on all five commercial targets, including the three evaluated in v1. Previously, the main comparison included only the T2VSafetyBench prompt baseline. This substantially strengthens the scope of direct method comparison; the LTX-Video comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds Kling/Sora2 settings and an RPG-RT protocol specifying Veo2 fine-tuning, detector/evaluator handling, and a 15-modification limit. New experiments vary initialization, component models, retrieval thresholds, and paraphrasing intensity, and introduce attempt-count and runtime metrics. The original sampling, default iteration budgets, and success threshold remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds efficiency analyses in Tables 7 and 10; initialization, component-model, and threshold robustness in Appendix C; successful-attack scene-count distributions and a paraphrasing–fidelity comparison in Appendix D; and additional qualitative cases in Appendix I. The original ablations and semantic/output-space analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The semantic-similarity variance reporting in v1 Table 10 is retained in v2 Table 12. No new repeated-run counts, seeds, ASR uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The fixed/non-fixed initialization comparison changes experimental conditions rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 scores and matched ablation and LTX-Video results remain unchanged. New results include SceneSplit ASRs of 78.6% on Kling and 68.6% on Sora2, plus RPG-RT comparisons. Added analyses report 77.3% ASR with non-fixed initialization and 80.9% ASR/0.5051 semantic similarity under over-paraphrasing versus 78.2%/0.5308 under the standard setting, alongside new runtime and attempt-count results.

M1.justification: The Scene Splitting, Scene Manipulation, and Strategy Update procedure, Algorithm 1, and appendix prompt/code implementations remain unchanged. Alternative component models and stronger paraphrasing are experimental variants; the proposed default procedure is retained.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized method/result explanations, acknowledgements and an ethics statement, inserted appendix sections, updated cross-references, and author affiliation/contact and publication-header edits. There is no extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands to five targets and three methods per target, using numbered categories and substantially smaller text. Figure 3 adds Kling/Sora2 examples; Figure 2 corrects its strategy illustration and expands its caption. New analysis tables and Figures 8–9 substantially expand the displays, while older figures and tables are redistributed.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for RPG-RT, its detector discussion, Kling, and Sora2. Section 2.1 explicitly acknowledges conceptual similarity to T2VSafetyBench's temporal risks. The broader related-work discussion and attribution of the strategy-library concept to AutoDAN-Turbo remain intact.

T1.justification: Appendix A retains the same divergence definition in Equation 1 and its mathematical explanation. No new or revised formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations appear; the additions are empirical analyses and interpretations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1's competitive validation by adding RPG-RT with a reported matched modification budget. Broader target-model tests and controlled robustness, efficiency, and semantic-fidelity analyses substantially strengthen the evidence and expose practical tradeoffs. ASR uncertainty remains unreported, successful-attack counts alone do not establish optimal scene depth, and Table 1 becomes harder to read, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SceneSplit research, with matching core methodology and retained experiments. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds evaluations on Kling v1.0 and Sora2, RPG-RT comparisons, and robustness and efficiency experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack evaluations on three commercial T2V models, component ablations, semantic analyses, and an appendix evaluation on LTX-Video.

C1.justification: The abstract newly claims to characterize when collapse is inevitable and when synthetic data helps across three additional data-generation settings. This substantially broadens the contribution beyond v1's fresh-label, fixed-covariate framework, while retaining its golden-ratio and ridge-regression claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains that synthetic augmentation cannot improve the studied fixed-label procedure, that refreshed covariates make both bias and variance weight-dependent, and that pooling can produce collapse despite fresh real labels. These findings materially qualify the applicability of the original collapse-prevention conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 documents the added simulations' sample sizes, iteration counts, SNRs, and covariate-generation assumptions—for example, n=1500, SNR=5, and 20 iterations in Figure 4(b). Existing experimental details are retained; no code-release, hardware, or runtime information is added.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond fixed covariates with fresh labels to three distinct scenarios: reused original labels, independently refreshed covariates, and separate real/synthetic covariate batches with partial real-label availability. Figures 3(c), 4(b), and 5 evaluate these scenarios; the original synthetic regression coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Figure 3(b) adds an empirical comparison of dynamic weighting, fixed golden-ratio weighting, and real-only weighting w=1. v1's iteration plot evaluates fixed golden-ratio weighting, while dynamic mixing appears only in its theoretical analysis. No external benchmark method is added.

E3.justification: The original risk metric and Figures 1–2 settings are retained. Added simulations introduce configurations including n=500 and 50 iterations for reused labels, n=1500 and 20 iterations for refreshed covariates, and n=100 with 100 plotted iterations for pooled data. These are settings for new experiments, not revisions to the earlier runs.

E4.justification: v2 adds empirical fixed-versus-dynamic mixing analysis, optimal-weight sensitivity to aspect ratio, and tests of whether fresh labels and shared covariates are essential. Figures 3–5 substantially extend the analysis of applicability and failure conditions beyond v1's covariance, noise, and regularization studies.

E5.justification: The 100-run averaging information is retained for the original plots, now described as the 'first two plots.' No changed replication count is reported for matched experiments, and the added simulations introduce no run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 1–2 retain identical plot content. New findings include near-overlap of dynamic and fixed golden-ratio risks after two iterations, optimal w=1 when labels are reused, aspect-ratio-dependent optimal weights with refreshed covariates, and exponentially growing pooled-data risk at gamma=2.1, 2.2, and 2.5. These are additional outcomes under distinct conditions.

M1.justification: Section 5 and Algorithms 2–4 introduce interpolation procedures that reuse original labels, refresh covariates each iteration, or fit concatenated real/synthetic datasets. Pooling replaces the original shared-covariate weighted-label update with a combined-data estimator. Algorithm 1 and the previously defined dynamic-weight recursion remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction gains motivation and related-work explanations, some theorem statements are streamlined, and Section 5 plus Appendix E are inserted. Most existing exposition and section order remain intact. The expanded introduction also contains two substantially duplicated motivation paragraphs.

P2.justification: Figures 3–5 add substantial visual evidence on mixing dynamics, aspect-ratio sensitivity, label reuse, and collapse; Algorithms 2–4 add corresponding procedure displays. Figures 1–2 preserve their plot content but move with the document reflow and receive edited captions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Li et al. (2021), Gneiting et al. (2005), and Rezaei et al. (2025), supporting label-reuse motivation and synthetic-data positioning. Its introduction broadens the description of He et al. (2025) from Gaussian ordinary least squares to low-dimensional GLMs and nonparametric estimation, although the abstract retains the narrower description.

T1.justification: Theorems 5.1, E.1, and E.2 add risk characterizations, an optimal-weight formula, and a pooled-data divergence condition, with proofs in Appendix E. Remark E.1 specifies the different limit order for refreshed covariates. Existing proofs also receive corrections, including removal of the extra covariance factor in equation (C.3) and restoration of a factor of two in its base-case identity.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially clarifies how collapse prevention depends on data-refresh assumptions, an important boundary left unexplored in v1. Section 5 and Appendix E supply theoretical results and supporting simulations showing when synthetic augmentation helps, fails to help, or causes collapse; existing algebraic corrections also improve reliability. These gains outweigh the duplicated introductory text, inconsistent prior-work wording, and unspecified replication counts for the new simulations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core framework, and retained results. Their text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable; v1 Appendices A–D correspond to v2 Appendices A–D, with Appendix E added.

after.justification: v2 retains the original simulations and adds empirical studies of dynamic mixing, reused labels, refreshed covariates, and pooled real/synthetic data in Figures 3–5.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original linear-regression simulations, including empirical risks averaged over 100 runs and comparisons with theoretical predictions in Figures 1–2.
