C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: joint continuous–discrete generation, WPG/text controllability through CrossGuid, a textual sports benchmark, and strong scene-level performance. The rewritten contribution list emphasizes capabilities already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 explains the absorbing comparator's weaker consistency through irreversible unmasking and links generation quality to consistency. It also interprets guidance-strength results and tentatively attributes T5-Large's weaker performance to embedding compression. Existing limitations concerning sparse events, limited text data, and NFL actor-assignment heuristics remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies zero-tensor conditioning dropout and RTX A6000 training hardware, documents the absorbing comparator's implementation source and parameter, and adds a project-page link. Most architecture, preprocessing, and training details were already present. The PDFs retain the prospective code/data release commitment.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2.4 adds an evaluation named NBA12/13, but the PDFs do not explain its underlying data relationship to the existing NBA and Basketball-U datasets. Thus, expanded represented data or task coverage cannot be reliably distinguished from an additional forecasting protocol. The established sports datasets and tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds NRI, dNRI, FQA, Social-GAN, and GRIN to the reported NBA12/13 comparison in Table 6. It also introduces an absorbing-state JointDiff comparator across the existing sports generation settings in Tables 3 and 11. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives; previous comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include NBA12/13 minimum errors over 100 modes, consistency accuracy comparing generated events with possession inferred from generated trajectories, guidance-weight sweeps, and three T5 sizes. The absorbing comparison specifies an absorption rate of 0.01. Existing benchmark splits, training budgets, and 20-mode evaluations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendices D.3.3–D.3.5 add direct trajectory–event consistency analysis, multinomial-versus-absorbing tests, guidance-strength sensitivity, and text-encoder-size ablations. Existing scheduler, loss-weight, architectural, attention-entropy, and failure-case analyses remain. The human evaluation is relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The human-study participant and comparison counts are unchanged. The new 100-mode evaluation is a sampling-budget choice, not additional uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All seven original tables retain their numerical results after matching renumbered tables. v2 adds substantial results in Tables 3, 6, and 9–11: for example, NBA12/13 minimum SADE/SFDE is 1.36/2.52 feet versus GRIN's 1.72/3.59, and unconditioned NFL average consistency is 0.86 versus 0.80 for absorbing diffusion. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The proposed Gaussian–multinomial diffusion model, joint loss, CrossGuid conditioning, and hybrid sampler remain unchanged. Two residual blocks were already documented in v1's Appendix B. The absorbing-state and alternative T5 configurations are experimental variants rather than replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted rewrites to contributions, related work, and the human-evaluation narrative, moves the human study into Section 5.1, and adds consistency and ablation subsections. Terminology, grammar, and publication headers are updated, while most existing methodological and appendix prose remains.

P2.justification: v2 adds five experimental tables, redraws the overview and architecture diagrams, enlarges and crops qualitative panels, and revises plot labeling. The unchanged human-evaluation histogram moves from the appendix into the main text. These substantially revise the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: Related work adds trajectory-modeling and robotics references and sharpens distinctions from Zeng et al.'s sequential event forecasting and absorbing-state diffusion. This refines the rationale for simultaneous, controllable multinomial generation while retaining the original research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 corrects the posterior-transition condition accompanying Equation 17 from s ≥ 1 to s ≥ 2, separating it from the final-step categorical prediction. The main factorization assumptions, loss derivation, and remaining mathematical development are retained.

improvement.justification: Section 5.3 and Tables 3 and 11 address an important validation gap in v1 by directly testing agreement between generated trajectories and events and comparing multinomial with absorbing diffusion. Guidance and encoder ablations further substantiate design choices. Together, these substantially strengthen the evidence for coherent joint generation while preserving existing results. Repeated-run uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JointDiff study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–F are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds trajectory–event consistency measurements, further ablations, and an NBA12/13 forecasting comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original trajectory-generation experiments, ablations, attention analyses, and a 15-participant NBA human evaluation in Appendix D.2.1.

results.title: JointDiff: Bridging Continuous and Discrete in Multi-Agent Trajectory Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: unsupervised behavioral compression, dimensionality governed primarily by environment complexity, compression up to five orders of magnitude, and efficient latent-space fine-tuning. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.1 adds interpretation of beyond-dataset generalization, task-dependent recovery, and variance obscuring Hopper's dimensionality trend. Appendix B connects the new representation-range findings to network expressivity while explicitly limiting that evidence to random weight sampling in one environment. Existing dataset-coverage and fine-tuning limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a GitHub code link alongside the supplementary-material reference, specifies autoencoder ELU activation placement, and explains PGPE evaluation and curve aggregation. Appendix B also supplies the new environments' reward conditions, state bounds, horizons, and configuration details. Much of the original implementation documentation is retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds compression evaluation in Hopper and HalfCheetah. Hopper introduces forward, backward, standstill, and jump tasks; HalfCheetah introduces forward, backward, frontflip, and backflip tasks. This substantially extends the represented dynamics and behaviors beyond Mountain Car and Reacher; fine-tuning coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: The existing PPO, DDPG, TD3, SAC, and Parameter PGPE comparisons are retained. Figures 4–5 newly include a Best in Dataset policy-performance reference alongside the learning algorithms, adding a comparator within those reported comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix B replaces the stated 5D/8D latent-space grids with 10,000 random samples for dimensions above three and changes Reacher's reported PGPE center learning rate from 0.01 to 0.1. New Hopper/HalfCheetah experiments use 10k-policy datasets and 5D/8D/16D representations. These reported settings do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds the Policy Representation Range analysis and Figure 6, comparing reward distributions from randomly sampled Small and Large Mountain Car policies. This directly examines whether larger networks represent richer behaviors. Existing baseline-size ablations and appendix manifold visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly documents interpolation and terminal-value extension when aggregating PGPE runs, plus 10-episode intermediate and 100-episode final evaluations. New compression results report 10-seed confidence intervals, and the representation-range analysis reports five-seed intervals. Existing reported run counts remain unchanged; an increase in repetitions of retained experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds Hopper/HalfCheetah recovery results, including HalfCheetah forward recovery of 1.84 with 95% CI [1.41, 2.39] at 16D. Figure 6 adds reward-distribution findings, including broader height-task coverage for Large policies. Mountain Car recovery values in Table 1 and v1 Table 2/v2 Table 3 are unchanged; the additions are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The novelty-filtered policy dataset, autoencoder with behavioral reconstruction loss, frozen decoder, and latent-space policy optimization remain unchanged. Newly specified activation functions and evaluation details do not establish an algorithmic or architectural change.

P1.justification: v2 corrects grammar and terminology, rewrites selected explanatory passages, adds an ethics statement, and updates publication and acknowledgment text. The main section sequence and narrative remain recognizable; new scientific content does not amount to a wholesale structural rewrite.

P2.justification: Figures 4–5 are substantially enlarged and reorganized from four-panel rows into 2-by-2 grids, with revised colors, legends, and dataset-reference lines. Table 1 gains bolding and shading; a new recovery table and reward-distribution figure are added. The appendix manifold plots are retained, resized, and relocated rather than replaced with new results.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds substantial positioning within Weight Space Learning, discussing goal-conditioned generators, checkpoint models, hyper-representations, parameter symmetries, and policy fingerprinting. It explains how behavioral reconstruction differs from these approaches. Additional expressivity references support the new analysis, extending the original positioning beyond policy manifolds, quality diversity, and policy optimization.

T1.justification: Section 2 adds the missing 1/(T+1) normalization to the state-occupancy distribution and distinguishes continuous probability measures from finite probability simplices. Appendix B corrects the latent-policy trajectory probability factorization. These are limited mathematical corrections; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for behavioral compression beyond v1's two environments. Hopper/HalfCheetah results with ten-seed confidence intervals support recovery beyond the training dataset on several tasks, addressing v1's tentative attribution of such recovery to generalization or evaluation variance. The new diagnostic, clearer implementation reporting, and expanded research positioning improve assessability. Fine-tuning evidence still covers only Mountain Car and Reacher, so the broader validation principally strengthens the compression contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same framework and research questions. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–B are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: The original empirical studies remain, with additional compression experiments in Hopper and HalfCheetah and a policy-representation analysis.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original policy-compression experiments, latent-manifold analyses, and fine-tuning comparisons in Mountain Car and Reacher.

results.title: From Parameters to Behaviors: Unsupervised Compression of the Policy Space

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same claims about RS limitations, similarity-guided extreme sequences, and improved distributional evaluation. The expanded conclusion restates these claims rather than changing their scientific scope.

C2.justification: New discussion explains why technical medical labels can fail as visual-similarity proxies and how captions mitigate this limitation. Sections D.2–D.5 also develop deployment-dependent model-selection tradeoffs, alternative samplers' cost and transferability limitations, and circumstances in which larger RS budgets narrow EDGE's advantage.

D1.justification: New Appendix E documents PILOT/PyCIL integration, dependencies, execution commands, configuration controls, and registration of additional datasets. Section D.3.2 supplies the caption-generation model and prompt. These substantially extend v1's code link and general hyperparameter disclosure, although D.5 references an absent Appendix E.5.

E1.justification: Section D.3.2 adds EyePACS retinal images and HAM10000 skin-lesion images, substantially extending domain coverage beyond the retained natural-image benchmarks. These datasets support text-image similarity analyses, not end-to-end medical CIL evaluations. ImageNet-A is mentioned only as supported software coverage.

E2.justification: v1 compares EDGE against RS. New Table A10 additionally evaluates Adversarial Sampling, Max-cover Sampling, single-round LLM generation, and five-round LLM refinement across six CIL learners, substantially broadening the sequence-generation comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include ranking evaluations using a randomly selected six-class subset, text-image alignment metrics, sampling-budget sweeps from 3 to 40 sequences, and extensive CUB random-order evaluations. These extend the evaluation design; the previously documented training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds class-subset robustness checks for model rankings, text-versus-image similarity analyses, a medical-label caption ablation, and sampling-budget and tail-coverage studies in Sections D.1.3 and D.3–D.5. These investigate limitations and robustness questions beyond v1's encoder-configuration analysis.

E5.justification: v2 adds Spearman correlation p-values for the medical analyses and specifies seed 42 for the class-subset replication. Figure A7 reports 600 L2P and 400 EASE random-order evaluations. These concern new studies; the existing normality tests and original three order seeds are retained.

E6.justification: Tables A5–A10 and Figures A6–A7 add rankings, benchmark statistics, alignment results, sampler comparisons, and sampling-budget findings. For example, Table A10 reports L2P hard/easy accuracies of 58.35/72.13 for EDGE versus 62.58/66.21 for RS. Figure 2a–b also changes plotted accuracies, while Tables 1–2 and A3–A4 retain their values.

M1.justification: Section D.3.2 introduces a tested input-processing adaptation: GPT-5 expands medical class names into visual captions before CLIP encoding. The core EDGE sequence-generation algorithms and easy/random/hard evaluation procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most retained exposition remains substantially verbatim. v2 expands the conclusion, adds acknowledgments, ethics and reproducibility statements, introduces an appendix roadmap, and organizes the new appendix material into dedicated subsections. This is a limited revision of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables A5–A10 and Figures A4–A7, including fitted-distribution overlays, sampling-budget curves, and histograms. Figure 2 changes axis limits and legend placement, while the conference template reformats tables and page layout. Some new plots redisplay existing distributions with additional estimates.

R1.justification: v2 adds Li et al. (2025), Exploring Open-world Continual Learning with Knowns-Unknowns Knowledge Transfer, to the introduction and references. The related-work taxonomy and central research positioning remain substantially unchanged; citation-style conversion is presentational.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, Lemmas 1–2, Theorems 1–4, and their proofs are retained across the main text and Appendices B–C. Reformatting and relocation do not introduce new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1's comparison against three random orders by testing alternative samplers, larger sampling budgets, and the CLIP similarity assumption. The medical-domain qualifications and practical reproduction guide substantially improve applicability assessment and usability. Some new experimental details remain incomplete, including the reference to nonexistent Appendix E.5, but the added scrutiny of central assumptions provides a clear net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EDGE study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original model-ranking, alternative-sampler, sampling-budget, and medical-image similarity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original exhaustive class-order evaluations, RS-versus-EDGE experiments on CIL benchmarks, and encoder-configuration analyses in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: The Lie of the Average: How Class Incremental Learning Evaluation Deceives You?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: unified reasoning modes, context-adaptive selection through AdaVaR/AdaGRPO, and broad benchmark improvements. The claims that AdaVaR-3B approaches Qwen2.5-VL-7B and AdaVaR-7B surpasses GPT-4o on average are retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of text-dominated mode-selection attention, sample-level complementarity, selection errors, prompt sensitivity, SFT dependence, and computational cost. It expands future-work discussion into width/depth extensions and identifies limited multilingual training/evaluation data as an applicability constraint. These go substantially beyond v1's existing mode-complementarity and future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promised artifact release with a repository link and a statement that code, data, and weights are available. It adds preprocessing, licensing and data-quality checks, the 8192-token mode-switching threshold, benchmark averaging rules, checkpoint/evaluation instructions, vLLM hardware details, and KV-cache sharing information. These expand reproducibility disclosure without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: The training corpora and eight benchmark tasks are retained. Appendix C.7.5 adds evaluation with Gaussian-blurred images, introducing a limited degraded-input scenario. New MMStar subgroup analyses and examples use existing task coverage.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparator set is unchanged. v2 Table 6 adds Expert Pick and Max(GRD, TXT), two dataset-level mode-selection strategies compared against AdaVaR's adaptive selection.

E3.justification: v2 adds substantial controlled evaluation protocols: fixed-total SFT mixtures at 1:1, 3:1, and 1:3 ratios; alternate prefixes and training/evaluation prompts; omission of SFT; reversed curriculum order; and Gaussian blur with radius 0.5. It also specifies attention aggregation and computational profiling protocols, including timing averaged over 100 training steps. Existing benchmark splits and principal training settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing ablations, v2 tests dependence on data balance, prefix semantics, SFT, prompt descriptions, curriculum order, and image quality. It adds attention and image-type analyses, selection-versus-reasoning error breakdowns, efficiency comparisons, supplementary training curves, and two MMStar cases. These substantially broaden scrutiny of the method.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, significance tests, or evaluation seed information. v2's 100-step timing average is a new measurement protocol, without accompanying uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and ablation values are retained, including v1 Table 5 as v2 Table 7. Substantial new results include average accuracies of 49.8 for Expert Pick and 50.1 for Max(GRD, TXT), 46.5 without SFT, 50.0 with reversed curriculum, and 50.5 under blur, compared with the retained AdaVaR-3B average of 50.8. New attention, error, efficiency, and qualitative findings further expand the results.

M1.justification: The two-stage SFT/AdaGRPO procedure, reasoning modes, prefix-guided exploration, advantages, rewards, and curriculum remain unchanged. The expanded scalability discussion concerns prospective extensions; newly documented implementation details do not establish a changed implemented method.

P1.justification: v2 adds an appendix roadmap, finer subsection organization, and expanded implementation and future-work explanations. Affiliations, publication headers, acknowledgments, and cross-references are updated. The main narrative and much of the retained appendix prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with comparison, error, efficiency, and sensitivity tables; attention distributions and heatmaps; training curves; an extension diagram; and additional qualitative cases. Existing displays are retained, including v1 Table 5 becoming Table 7 and Figures 7–11 becoming Figures 11–15. New Table 6 incorrectly reverses the POPE and V* headings relative to the retained results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting implementation and analysis, including R1-V, VLM-R1, Open R1, Kaduri et al.'s attention analysis, and Kwon et al.'s serving framework. The main related-work positioning is retained. Changing the DeepSeek-R1 citation from DeepSeek-AI to Guo et al. identifies the same work.

T1.justification: The probability factorization, Gaussian reward assumptions, mode-advantage derivation, and optimization objectives are unchanged. Algorithm 1 clarifies the reward-array inputs without changing its calculation. No new formal theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method: Appendix C.7 directly tests whether its behavior depends on prompt wording, prefix semantics, SFT, and data balance, while the error and efficiency analyses clarify practical strengths and weaknesses. Expanded reproducibility information further improves auditability. These gains outweigh localized new reporting errors, notably Table 6's swapped POPE/V* headings and Table 11's overhead wording contradicting its timing values.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoVT/AdaVaR research. The text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments on sensitivity, robustness, computational efficiency, and mode-selection behavior.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of AdaVaR-3B and AdaVaR-7B, ablation experiments, training dynamics, and qualitative analyses.

results.title: Mixture-of-Visual-Thoughts: Exploring Context-Adaptive Reasoning Mode Selection for General Visual Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same scientific contribution: efficient, self-evaluation-free improvement through semantic consensus, with broadly competitive performance against self-evaluation methods. Additional experiments support that existing claim rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of diversity loss, its relationship to model collapse, and implications for creativity-focused applications. It also proposes a format-compliance explanation for hard-negative results and discusses multilingual embeddings and cross-encoder cost/applicability tradeoffs. These materially expand the account of mechanisms and limitations beyond v1.

D1.justification: v1 refers to code and data in supplementary materials; v2 explicitly reports a public code release and supplies a repository address. It also identifies the cross-encoder checkpoint and the multilingual embedding choice for reverse translation. Existing Appendix B prompts, model versions, optimization settings, and sample counts are retained.

E1.justification: v2 substantially broadens task coverage through AlpacaEval general instruction following and English-to-German/French/Russian/Spanish translation in Appendices E–F. v1 evaluated translation into English and English summarization. The original WMT24++, CNN/DailyMail, PubMed, and WMT14/WMT19 coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The main SJ, EM, EMPO, and EMRL-seq comparators are retained. Table 2 adds BGE-M3 and a TinyBERT cross-encoder to the similarity-method comparison, while Appendix J introduces a random-ranking control. BGE in v1 matches BGE-en in v2 and is not a new comparator.

E3.justification: v2 introduces substantially different evaluation procedures: DeepSeek-V3 judging with win/tie/loss reporting for instruction following, TTR and embedding RMSD for diversity, and Kendall's tau against MetricX rankings. Reverse translation uses BGE-M3 instead of SimCSE. These are additional experimental protocols; the original training settings, decoding, metrics, and summarization sample counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations and robustness studies, v2 tests whether reward discretization reduces GRPO instability, whether malformed-output negatives change learning, whether SVSI reduces linguistic diversity, and whether voting rankings agree with quality rankings. It also extends clustering sensitivity analysis to CNN/DailyMail and expands the existing embedding study with multilingual and cross-encoder alternatives.

E5.justification: Both versions already discuss multiple GRPO runs and display error bars. Figure 13 applies that reporting practice to the new discretized variant, without newly specifying run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimators, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Kendall's tau is introduced as an agreement metric, without inferential uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original results in Tables 1, 3, and 4 and Figures 2–8 are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in expanded Table 2, Tables 5–8, and Figures 12–14. For example, new English-to-German Qwen-7B results report BLEU 12.18 for the base model and 15.22 for SVSI. AlpacaEval averages 38.2% wins versus 36.5% losses, with Llama-8B losing more often than winning. New analyses also report reduced diversity and reduced fluctuations with discretized GRPO rewards.

M1.justification: The main SVSI pipeline and DPO objective remain unchanged. v2 adds limited variants: five-level quantile rewards for SVSI-G in Appendix G, malformed responses as hard negatives in Appendix I, and cross-encoder similarity scoring in Section 4.8. These modify particular components without replacing the core method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. The embedding study moves from Appendix C to Section 4.8 with some rewriting, subsequent appendices are renumbered, and new appendix sections are appended. Conference, affiliation, correspondence, acknowledgment, and reproducibility text also receive limited updates.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with instruction-following, discretized-GRPO, and summarization-sensitivity plots and new tables for reverse translation, diversity, hard negatives, and ranking agreement. Table 2 gains rows and moves into the main text; original displays otherwise retain their content. Table 7 apparently mislabels its Llama-1B reference row as 'base', although its values match retained SVSI results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting multilingual embeddings, cross-encoders, AlpacaEval and its judge model, translation asymmetry, and linguistic-diversity/model-collapse discussion. The original related-work organization and positioning against majority voting, self-judging, and entropy minimization remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The original voting definitions and DPO equations are retained. Neither version provides original theorems or proofs, and v2's additional metrics and procedural explanations do not introduce substantive formal derivations or assumptions.

improvement.justification: v1 did not quantify diversity costs or directly examine quality-ranking alignment, and its explanation of GRPO instability remained largely conjectural. v2's Appendices G–J provide targeted evidence on these important issues, substantially improving assessment of the method's mechanism and tradeoffs. Broader task evaluations and explicit code-access information also help. The small, mixed AlpacaEval advantage, limited uncertainty documentation, and Table 7 labeling defect constrain individual conclusions but do not outweigh the stronger empirical grounding.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Semantic Voting/SVSI research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds instruction-following, reverse-translation, reward-discretization, diversity, hard-negative, and ranking analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original translation and summarization experiments, computational-cost measurements, GRPO comparisons, ablations, sensitivity studies, and out-of-distribution evaluations.

results.title: Semantic Voting: A Self-Evaluation-Free Approach for Efficient LLM Self-Improvement on Unverifiable Open-ended Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: training-free acceleration through two-stage adaptive caching, more reliable certainty-guided decoding, and improved generation quality. Additional experiments broaden the supporting evidence without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix D discusses memory costs, why quasi-left-to-right decoding retains diffusion-model flexibility, and limitations involving larger models, rollout approximations, and Gaussian contextual weighting. v2 also removes v1's interpretation that poor Fast-dLLM Base-model results demonstrate restricted applicability. Its new long-generation interpretation claims no performance loss, although Table 7 shows lower GSM8K and Math-500 scores than Vanilla.

D1.justification: v2 documents refresh intervals for the added benchmarks in Table 3, the parallel-decoding threshold, rollout-depth configurations, and LLM assistance with writing and coding. The hardware, evaluation framework, default sigma/k/p values, and code-access URL remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds GPQA and MMLU-Pro evaluations for both Base and Instruct model variants, expanding coverage from mathematical reasoning and code generation to scientific question answering and broader knowledge tasks. The original four benchmarks remain. Longer generation lengths are additional settings within retained tasks.

E2.justification: Vanilla, dLLM-Cache, and Fast-dLLM remain the principal baselines. v2 adds an uncached Parallel comparator in Table 6 and includes Semi-AR (Vanilla) in the decoding comparison in Table 2, where v1 compared only NAR configurations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces comparisons using semi-AR parallel decoding with a 0.9 threshold, Dream-Inst evaluations at generation length 1024, peak-memory measurements, and sensitivity sweeps across lengths 256, 512, and 1024. The baseline decoding settings moved into Section 5.1 were already documented in v1 Appendix B and do not establish a changed protocol for the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds a five-layer versus full-rollout ablation, parallel-decoding compatibility comparisons, and analyses of longer-generation efficiency and memory. The existing hyperparameter analysis in v1 Appendix C.4 is expanded across three generation lengths and moved to Section 5.3. The original attention, KV-trajectory, and update-phase analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or uncertainty bars for the empirical results. The Gaussian standard deviation is a method hyperparameter, not an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: Beyond substantial new result entries, v2 revises retained results: Table 1 changes LLaDA-Inst MBPP scores from 14.4 to 38.0 for Vanilla and 12.4 to 39.4 for d2Cache, and d2Cache GSM8K throughput from 8.56 to 11.39. Fast-dLLM's Dream-Base MBPP score changes from 31.2 in v1 Table 4 to 52.6 in v2 Table 5. These are reported-value revisions; their cause is not explained. New parallel-decoding speedups, including 48.3x, use a different protocol and are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The default two-stage algorithm and Equations (3)-(9) remain unchanged; the revised certainty-prior terminology does not alter the selection formula. Appendix D.3 adds a lightweight Rollout-5 variant that computes attention rollout using the first five Dream layers instead of all 28, a limited procedural variant rather than a replacement for the default method.

P1.justification: Most main-text wording and the section sequence remain intact. v2 refines certainty-prior terminology, removes the Key Observations and Takeaways box, moves and condenses the hyperparameter discussion, and reorganizes the appendices around added disclosure and discussion sections. It also adds the conference-publication header.

P2.justification: v2 expands the benchmark and configuration tables, adds decoding rows to Table 2, and introduces separate rollout-depth, parallel-decoding, and long-generation/memory tables. The two-panel hyperparameter Figure 9 in v1 becomes a four-panel main-text Figure 6. Existing attention and trajectory figures are retained with renumbering and relocation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for GPQA and MMLU-Pro, two Li et al. diffusion-model works, and Zhu et al. on attentive feature regularization. It drops the specific argument that Fast-dLLM's Base-model performance restricts its applicability, while retaining the principal positioning of token-level adaptive caching against segment-level approaches.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds an analytical storage calculation: 2LNd floating-point values for the KV cache plus an L-by-L attention-rollout matrix. The core mathematical definitions and Equations (1)-(9) remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The added common-protocol parallel-decoding comparisons and rollout-depth and memory analyses address important gaps in v1's evidence about practical acceleration and its costs. Broader task coverage and explicit limitations substantially strengthen the evaluation. Reporting problems temper this improvement: substantial score revisions are unexplained, LLaDA-Inst Vanilla MBPP is 38.0 in Table 1 but 14.4 in Table 6, and the long-generation discussion overlooks math-score losses. These issues limit specific conclusions but do not negate the substantial gains from the added controls and analyses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe d2Cache and retain matching methods, experiments, and figures. All 17 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, parallel-decoding comparisons, rollout-depth ablations, and memory measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, decoding and caching ablations, and analyses of attention and KV-state dynamics on LLaDA and Dream.

results.title: d$^2$Cache: Accelerating Diffusion-Based LLMs via Dual Adaptive Caching

C1.justification: The central feasibility, replication, independence-testing, and minimal-training-impact claims remain. The abstract and contribution list extend validation from one 1.5B model to models up to 2.7B parameters, and the introduction adds release of an OLMo-2/OLMo-3 experimentation package as a contribution.

C2.justification: V2 removes v1's explanation that weaker joint CPDT effects reflect harder simultaneous learning. It adds explanations involving stronger baseline reasoning in larger models, intervention-strength versus training-stability tradeoffs, and explicit uncertainty about applicability beyond language and unsupervised learning. The principal applicability restrictions remain.

D1.justification: V1 provides model/data links and upstream training-code references. V2 documents a project-specific Python package, links models at four sizes, adds a reproducibility statement, and consolidates resources in Appendix H. New appendices specify larger-model checkpoints and canary-comparison sample counts. These substantially expand documented reproducibility resources; external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: Appendix B.5 adds supplementary evaluation on NQ, DROP, AGIEval, GSM8K, MMLU Pro, and TQA alongside the retained OLMES benchmarks. The original training-data mix and ten intervention tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: V2 adds OLMo-2-1B controls to the watermark and contamination plots, directly compares Gaussian watermarks, rare-token canaries, and non-canary membership inference in Figure 4, and introduces the full 4T-token model comparison in Table 4. The original comparator families are otherwise retained.

New protocols vary intervention intensity and compare 50, 100, and 500 training steps while holding inserted data constant. Appendix G also specifies a single-inclusion canary comparison. These extend the evaluation design substantially; the original 1.5B training protocol remains.

E4.justification: Sections 4.3–4.4 add a comparative canary case study and model-size analyses. Appendices F.3–F.5 investigate larger-model dependence, intervention-strength sensitivity, and training-duration sensitivity. These substantially expand robustness testing beyond v1's retained alternative-checkpoint analysis.

E5.justification: V1 already reports bootstrap intervals for canary results. V2 additionally develops range-based '2000-Step Confidence Intervals' from 20 checkpoint measurements without intervention, adds significance markings to the main dependence matrix, and explicitly identifies 99% reasoning and 90% contamination intervals. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting without establishing additional independent pretraining runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds scaling, canary ROC, general-benchmark, and CPDT sensitivity results. Existing results also change: Figure 2c's watermark curve is revised, and the ALL/GW matrix entry changes from 1.6 in v1 Figure 4b to 6.9 in v2 Figure 6b. Figure 25 fills the previously missing IID row and GW entry in v1 Figure 22. The original mathematical-reasoning table remains unchanged.

M1.justification: The simultaneous-training framework, ten interventions, knowledge-control Algorithm 1, Gaussian-watermark construction, and CPDT matrix procedure remain unchanged. Additional model sizes and statistical analyses extend their evaluation rather than revise these core procedures.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion receive localized rewrites. V2 adds subsections for new analyses, organizes Appendix F into named subsections, moves the data-mixtures paragraph, and adds reproducibility and resource sections. Most existing methodological and experimental prose is preserved.

P2.justification: V2 adds eleven figures and a general-capability table, including canary ROC curves, scaling plots, sensitivity panels, and interval illustrations. Existing plots gain controls, revised legends, and significance highlighting. The document also adopts ICLR formatting and substantially rearranges figure placement, beyond simple renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds limited references supporting practical combined interventions, evaluation noise, scaling, standard membership inference, and OLMo-3, including Heineman et al. and Shokri et al. It removes the Hayes et al. citation. The main research positioning is retained; the data-mixtures discussion moves to Appendix A.

V2 directly strengthens that evidence through multiple trained model sizes, larger-model dependence tests, and intervention-strength and duration ablations. Added controls and documented code resources further improve interpretability and reproducibility. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same simultaneous-pretraining study and retain the ten original interventions. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds model-scaling experiments, canary comparisons, general-capability evaluations, and dependence-testing analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original results from training a 1.5B-parameter model on 210B tokens, including reasoning, memorization, poisoning, training-dynamics, and continual-pretraining dependence experiments.

results.title: Train Once, Answer All: Many Pretraining Experiments for the Cost of One

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the stated empirical scope from mathematics to two datasets covering multiple domains. The principal claims about future-proofing, backward compatibility, continual learning, and question generalization remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets smaller MMLU-Pro degradations as evidence of domain dependence, explains why the generator grouping is insensitive to thresholds within the observed gaps, and acknowledges a medium-difficulty selection bias from response filtering. These qualify the interpretation without replacing the central conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 adds code/data and project-page links, dataset identifiers, explicit question matching across weak/strong splits, and Appendix G with six prompt templates, temperature/sample allocations, top-p, prompt randomization, and greedy judge decoding. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the linked resources' availability is not verified by the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates mathematics through DeepScaleR. v2 adds training and evaluation on MMLU-Pro, extending coverage to knowledge-intensive multiple-choice questions across 14 domains, including humanities, social sciences, and law. Continual-training experiments remain confined to DeepScaleR.

E2.justification: The zero-shot, SFT, DPO, SFT+DPO, and existing continual-training comparisons are retained. MMLU-Pro extends the existing comparator set to another dataset; no comparator is added or removed from a corresponding DeepScaleR experiment.

E3.justification: The added MMLU-Pro experiments use 10K training samples and 10 epochs/1,500 steps, while DeepScaleR retains 70K samples and 3 epochs/2,800 steps. Both use the existing split design, consistent accuracy, and 2.5K evaluation pairs before order reversal. The newly stated matching of questions across weak/strong splits is a disclosure, not an established alteration of the earlier protocol.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix C adds a focused selection-bias diagnostic: Table 3 and Figure 9 measure question retention by generator and relate it to generator strength. This examines the consequences of requiring both correct and incorrect sampled responses. Existing continual-training and preference-strength comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The 20 generator responses per question were already specified in v1; v2 supplies sampling details without establishing additional repetitions.

E6.justification: v2 adds MMLU-Pro generator strengths and judge results, plus retention percentages for both datasets. For example, Table 4 reports MMLU-Pro strong/unseen accuracy of 52.92% versus 57.31% for weak- versus strong-trained Mistral-24B with SFT+DPO. These are newly reported comparisons; all DeepScaleR accuracy entries from v1 Table 3 are preserved in v2 Table 4.

M1.justification: The pairwise judging procedure, GPT-4o supervision, SFT/DPO/SFT+DPO objectives, backbones, and continual-training procedure are retained. Added prompt and split descriptions document the setup without establishing changes to the existing method.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes terminology and hyphenation, updates author notes and the publication header, expands setup explanations, and adds appendix contents and Sections F–G. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact, rather than undergoing extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 moves the existing DeepScaleR generator-strength plot into the main text, adds Figures 8–12 and a retention table, and redesigns the accuracy table into side-by-side dataset blocks. It also adds six boxed prompts. Captions for Figures 7 and 12 incorrectly describe weak/strong bar patterns as seen/unseen questions.

R1.justification: v2 adds the MMLU-Pro reference, Wang et al. (2024c), to support the new dataset. The existing related-work discussion and positioning relative to judge training and distribution-shift research remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The dual-distribution formulation, judge mapping, generalization metrics, and consistent-accuracy definition in Equations (1)–(10) are unchanged. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added.

improvement.justification: The MMLU-Pro experiments substantially strengthen evidence beyond v1's mathematics-only setting. The selection-bias audit and detailed prompt, sampling, and data-construction disclosures also address important transparency and reproducibility gaps. Different training budgets limit the domain-dependence interpretation, and some new captions are misleading, but these issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scope and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same judge-generalization study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite expanded content and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original MMLU-Pro evaluations with Ministral-8B and Mistral-24B, plus generator-level question-retention measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original DeepScaleR experiments with three judge backbones, multiple training recipes, continual training, and seen-versus-unseen question evaluations.

results.title: On the Shelf Life of Fine-Tuned LLM-Judges: Future-Proofing, Backward-Compatibility, and Question Generalization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and main conclusion retain the same contributions: discrete dual-path visual encoding, a single-iteration GLA separator, and improved separation–efficiency trade-offs. The new experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific limitations concerning synchronized, clean lip videos, difficult visual conditions, extremely constrained edge devices, and lost articulatory detail. It also discusses the synthetic-to-natural speech gap through the Lombard effect and expands the proposed interpretation of VQ as a semantic anchor and regularizer.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents unshared encoder parameters, from-scratch retraining with frozen DP-LipCoder in Table 2, and which Table 3 baseline results were reproduced versus taken from papers. The reproducibility statement replaces its direct GitHub reference with the project homepage; an actual change in resource availability is not established.

E1.justification: The original datasets and multi-speaker tasks remain. v2 Appendix I adds VoxCeleb2 scenarios combining FSD50K environmental noise or FMA music with one or three speakers. Appendix J adds naturally overlapping speech from debate recordings, substantially extending evaluation beyond artificially constructed speech mixtures.

E2.justification: v2 Table 7 introduces a VQ-free DP-LipCoder control, distinct from the earlier AE and LipCoder comparators. External baseline membership in matched comparisons is unchanged; the added noise and listening evaluations reuse IIANet and AV-Mossformer2.
