Existing benchmark settings remain unchanged; Table 2's added retraining description is a disclosure rather than evidence of a revised protocol.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix G directly tests VQ's contribution by removing the quantizer and commitment loss while retaining reconstruction and distillation objectives. Appendix I adds systematic environmental-noise, music, and interfering-speaker robustness tests. Earlier component, iteration, depth, output-formulation, and fusion-location ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 10 introduces MOS averages with ± values, whereas v1 has no corresponding uncertainty reporting. The PDF does not define whether these values represent standard deviations, standard errors, or confidence intervals. No additional training-run or seed reporting is provided.

E6.justification: Retained tables preserve their scores. New Table 7 reports SI-SNRi of 16.3 without VQ versus 16.8 with VQ. Table 9 adds four noisy-scenario comparisons, with Dolphin leading all reported metrics. Table 10 reports MOS of 3.86 ± 0.25 for Dolphin, 2.24 ± 0.15 for IIANet, and 2.85 ± 0.27 for AV-Mossformer2. These are additional results, not improvements over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The proposed DP-LipCoder, fusion module, GLA separator, losses, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Section 3.2 newly clarifies that the encoder paths do not share parameters; VQ removal is an experimental control, not a revision of the proposed model.

P1.justification: v2 removes the Dolphin prefix from the title, updates affiliation and publication-header text, adds limitations and acknowledgments, and inserts three appendix sections. Clarifications and cross-references change locally, while the existing narrative and section organization are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds the VQ, four-panel noise, and MOS tables as Tables 7, 9, and 10. It enlarges Figure 4, expands Tables 2–3 captions, and relocates several displays. All nine scientific figures and the earlier tabular content are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for FMA (Defferrard et al., 2017) and FSD50K (Fonseca et al., 2022), supporting the new noise evaluations. The related-work sections and positioning against existing AVSS architectures remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The DCT/heat-diffusion formulation and equations 1–28, including the appendix architecture and loss definitions, are retained. No new formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or mathematical corrections are introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its central discretization claim through comparisons that also differed architecturally, and its reported separation evaluations used artificial mixtures. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence with a controlled VQ ablation, systematic acoustic stress tests, and a blinded listening study on natural overlap. Explicit limitations and clearer experimental provenance further improve assessability. Undefined MOS ± values and unspecified noise-mixing levels still limit interpretation and reproducibility, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Dolphin research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds a VQ-removal experiment, acoustic robustness tests, and a human listening study.

before.justification: v1 reports original speech-separation experiments, visual reconstruction results, efficiency measurements, and architectural ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Efficient Audio-Visual Speech Separation with Discrete Lip Semantics and Multi-Scale Global-Local Attention

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the explicitly demonstrated scope from continuous control to both discrete and continuous control. The principal two-component contribution, SNN-specific normalization positioning, unchanged inference claim, and headline 22.6% and 5.9% performance claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix D.4.6 adds discussion of performance dependence on simulation length and explains retaining five steps for consistency with prior studies despite stronger eight-step results. Section 4.2 expands the rationale for estimating confidence from minibatch deviations. The main exploration-feedback explanation and interpretation of limited ANN benefits remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies architecture and surrogate-gradient details, neuron parameters, preprocessing, hardware and extensive RL hyperparameter tables absent from the supplied v1. Table 4 specifies momentum 0.8, recalibration every 5000 steps and 100 calibration batches. It also adds code-access information. These substantially improve documentation without establishing that retained experiments changed implementation.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from MuJoCo continuous control to RAM-based Atari discrete control. Figure 7 reports Pong, Breakout, Freeway, Seaquest and SpaceInvaders. The original five MuJoCo environments remain.

E2.justification: The main CLIF/TD3 comparator set in Table 1 is unchanged. However, v2 Table 16 adds tdBN, BNTT, TEBN and TABN to the LIF/TD3 comparison, where v1 Figure 4 compared CaRe-BN with vanilla LIF. This extends comparator participation within an existing experimental configuration.

E3.justification: v2 adds DQN and SAC experimental setups, Dynamic Neuron configurations, simulation lengths of 2, 3 and 8 steps, a Wasserstein-distance evaluation, and timing, memory and energy-estimation protocols. The retained main experiments still use five simulation steps and ten evaluation trials. Newly supplied settings for existing experiments are documentation rather than established protocol revisions.

E4.justification: New analyses directly quantify layerwise BN distribution mismatch (Figure 3), test sensitivity to simulation length (Table 17), and assess training overhead and estimated inference energy (Tables 20–21). The original Ca-BN/Re-BN component ablation is retained as Figure 6(c). These additions substantially broaden mechanistic, sensitivity and efficiency analysis.

E5.justification: v1 states that each algorithm uses five random seeds. v2 retains five-seed reporting for MuJoCo but specifies three seeds for the added Atari experiments in Figure 7. Half-standard-deviation shading and mean-plus-or-minus-standard-deviation tables remain the reporting conventions; no increased run count is established for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 scores, including the 5.90% APG, and the original component-ablation values are unchanged. v2 adds Atari, SAC and Dynamic Neuron results, distribution-error measurements, detailed appendix results and cost estimates. Table 17 newly reports APGs of -23.80% at two simulation steps and 6.32% at eight steps; these are additional settings, not improvements to the unchanged five-step result.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same adaptive updates and recalibration procedure. However, v1 Equation 10 uses previous moving estimates for prediction, whereas v2 Section 4.2 footnote 2 specifies previous minibatch statistics, conflicting with its unchanged pseudocode. The PDFs do not resolve whether this is an intended procedural change or a notation error.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section order are retained. Local revisions expand the motivation, confidence-estimation explanation and experimental setup, while new appendix organization, acknowledgments, disclosure statements and conference/contact text improve navigation and documentation. The main narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, expands the learning-curve figure with Dynamic Neuron rows, and adds distribution-error, Atari, SAC and detailed ANN plots. Numerous settings, results and cost tables create a substantial new appendix presentation. Existing exploration and component-ablation figures are largely retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting Atari evaluation, RL normalization context and energy estimation, and discusses Xu et al. (2026) on continuous-control ANN-to-SNN conversion. It also explicitly acknowledges the already-cited Proxy Target framework's ability to surpass ANNs. The central positioning around SNN-RL normalization remains.

T1.justification: The central optimal-weight theorem, proof and Gaussian assumption remain. Section 4.2 adds a mathematical assertion that squared minibatch deviations provide unbiased variance probes, while Appendix D.1.2 adds encoder-gradient derivations with an explicit surrogate-derivative assumption. These are limited additions to the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves reproducibility by supplying the implementation details and hyperparameters that v1 referred to but did not include. Direct distribution-error measurements, Atari/SAC evaluation, simulation-length sensitivity and cost analyses materially strengthen empirical support beyond the unchanged headline scores. The conflicting prediction footnote and some labeling errors limit precision, but do not outweigh these substantial gains in documentation and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CaRe-BN work, with matching core equations, pseudocode and main comparison table. Their text and visual material support comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 includes substantial appendix material.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and reports additional Atari, SAC, distribution-error, simulation-step and computational-cost results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MuJoCo experiments, including learning curves, exploration results, component ablations and comparisons in Table 1.

results.title: CaRe-BN: Precise Moving Statistics for Stabilizing Spiking Neural Networks in Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central claims about structured domain knowledge, adaptive planning, diagnostic optimization, benchmark performance, and genetics discoveries remain. v2 condenses numerical examples in the abstract and contribution list without materially changing the claims retained in Sections 4–5.

C2.justification: The new Discussion explicitly identifies dependence on fast, representative validation experiments; limitations when methods span multiple functions; inherited weaknesses of existing evaluators; and heuristic components lacking theoretical justification. v2 also develops the interpretation of diversity in search and warm-start complementarity with expert models, substantially expanding the account of applicability and limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix U newly provides prompts for implementation, instruction-based optimization, diagnostic generation and use, feedback, and debugging. v2 also expands expert-baseline specifications, identifies API access routes, supplies task-construction examples, clarifies pgBoost discovery thresholds, and reports runtime and cost information. These materially improve documentation of retained procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six single-cell tasks, five scientific deep-learning tasks, and two genetics applications. Warm-start NinaPro changes initialization within an existing task. The generic classification example in v2 Appendix V is illustrative, not an additional evaluated task.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is retained in Tables 1–3 and the genetics comparisons. Appendix F supplies names, descriptions, and citations for existing expert baselines rather than establishing replacements. The new warm-start NinaPro comparison reuses the existing NinaPro comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the experimental design with controls for 0, 10, and 50 retrieved papers, filtered versus unfiltered summaries, and 5-, 15-, and 30-point summaries. Appendix T adds an eight-hour NinaPro optimization initialized from the expert model. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, and standard optimization budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to literature quantity, filtering, and summary length; relate diversity persistence to optimization convergence; report broader TusoAI and AIDE trajectories; and examine runtime and cost. Appendix T adds a warm-start case study with identified optimization steps. These substantially extend v1's component, backbone, and genetics analyses.

E5.justification: v1 already reports three-seed confidence intervals and replicate stability. v2 adds five-replicate score distributions for the component ablations and reports five replicates for literature-sensitivity tests. Table 2 also supplies the previously missing AMBER/DeepSEA uncertainty term. This does not establish that the original three-seed benchmarks were expanded to five runs.

E6.justification: The point estimates and rankings in Tables 1–3 and the principal genetics findings are retained. Substantial new results include warm-start NinaPro scoring 0.94 versus the expert model's 0.91, a diversity-persistence/convergence correlation of 0.519, and literature-sensitivity, runtime, cost, and trajectory results. The NinaPro finding uses a different initialization, not an improved score under the original cold-start setting.

M1.justification: The core TusoAI procedure remains unchanged, but Appendix O introduces an evaluated variant with optional paper-summary filtering, a limited addition to literature processing whose filtering rule is unspecified. Algorithm 1 also corrects diagnostic initialization to match the predefined instructions already described in v1; this is not a new diagnostic mechanism.

P1.justification: v2 shortens the abstract and contribution list, adds a Discussion and acknowledgments, clarifies terminology and cross-references, and rewrites prompt listings into more readable templates. Most existing main-text prose and its narrative sequence remain intact; much of the expansion is additional scientific or technical content.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material for trajectories, efficiency, literature sensitivity, diversity/convergence, and warm-start performance, plus a symbol table and example tables. Existing figures receive revised labels, legends, captions, and positioning; Figure 2 replaces connected candidate scores with scatter points. Prompt and code appendices are extensively reformatted into styled boxes and lists.

R1.justification: New Appendix H substantially develops novelty positioning against ALRA and DenoiseIt, coordinate- and graph-based spatial-gene methods, and restricted NAS search spaces. Numerous supporting references and expert-method citations are added. Section 1.1 also sharpens the distinction from prior systems through function-level optimization without requiring existing models.

T1.justification: The optimization formulation and multiplicative category-update rule are unchanged. The new symbol glossary and Bayesian-style interpretation explain existing mathematics; neither version adds theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves scrutiny and reproducibility by supplying previously missing optimization-loop prompts, testing literature-use choices, and reporting replicated ablations and efficiency evidence. Its explicit limitations also better delimit the retained claims. These address important documentation and validation gaps in v1, although the new summary-filtering procedure remains underspecified and the headline benchmark scores are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TusoAI, with matching methods, benchmarks, and genetics applications. Text, tables, figures, and all appendices are readable, allowing retained material to be matched despite extensive appendix additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds literature-sensitivity experiments, efficiency analyses, and a warm-start NinaPro experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component and backbone ablations, and simulation and real-data results for scDRS and pgBoost.

results.title: TusoAI: Agentic Optimization for Scientific Methods

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the dual reasoning/retrieval account, the same dominance factors, and FARL's claimed contribution. The headline improvements of 47.8%, 22.8%, and 5.8% are unchanged. Added experiments support the existing core claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets activation patching as causal evidence of head-level control and logit trajectories as competition throughout reasoning. Appendix D adds arguments about editing locality, applicability beyond multiple-choice QA, and limited positional confounding. Section 4.1 also qualifies retrieval interference as a potential risk. The original limitations concerning longer traces and untested larger models remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and a reproducibility statement describing training/evaluation code, preprocessing scripts, and dataset-version information. It discloses 1,353 training and 147 validation samples, grid-search use, and procedural details for the new analyses, including head selection, step segmentation, and GPT-5-mini usage. Repository contents are not verified by the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates multiple-choice QA on MMLU, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and GPQA. v2 extends evaluation to 400 GeneralThought free-form questions requiring numerical, noun, or short-phrase answers, substantially broadening the answer-generation requirements. Appendix D.1 also evaluates paraphrased questions within the retained domains.

E2.justification: The new activation-patching experiment compares AUC-selected attention heads against randomly selected heads. FARL's base-model, SFT, and GRPO comparators remain unchanged in Tables 1–2. ROME and MEMIT are discussed in Appendix D.1 but are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds bidirectional activation patching of the top 5% of heads, stepwise answer-logit probing, 400-question free-form evaluation, paraphrase testing on 50 selected examples per domain, locality checks with and without CoT, and beginning-versus-end cue insertion. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Original training budgets and settings are retained; the newly stated training/validation counts are disclosures rather than established split changes.

E4.justification: Section 3.4 adds causal tests of attention-head involvement and four reasoning-step logit case studies. Appendix D adds analyses of editing efficacy, paraphrase robustness, unrelated-domain locality, and sensitivity to cue position. These test important attribution assumptions beyond v1's correlational probes and existing supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: No repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests are added or revised. Existing five-fold probing and reasoning-trajectory distribution displays are retained; the new experiments report point estimates without additional uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and all original plotted results are retained. Newly reported activation-patching success rates are 87.2% versus 5.3% for restoring answers and 89.5% versus 2.1% for inducing perturbed answers, comparing selected with random heads. Figure 6 and Tables 3–7 add logit trajectories, editing-validation results, free-form QA scores, and cue-position outcomes. These are additional results, not improved scores under the original FARL settings.

M1.justification: FARL's training procedure and GRPO/NPO objectives are unchanged. Appendix D.2 makes a limited adaptation to the diagnostic perturbation procedure: GPT-5-mini generates misleading free-form answers, whereas the original multiple-choice procedure selects retrieval targets using incorrect-answer logits.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 adds analysis subsections, Appendix D, an appendix contents list, ethics/reproducibility statements, and acknowledgements; it also refines appendix headings, makes local language edits, and updates affiliations and publication headers. There is no extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds a four-panel logit-trajectory figure and five tables displaying editing validity, free-form QA, and cue-position results, substantially extending the visual evidence. All ten original figures and Tables 1–2 are retained, with relocation and figure renumbering rather than substantive redraws.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds focused comparisons with concurrent memorization-attribution and latent-CoT studies, plus newer faithfulness and RL citations. Appendix D.1 positions SFT editing against fact-editing methods such as ROME and MEMIT, while Appendix B.2 adds grid-search citations. These expand the context without replacing the paper's central research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 introduces mathematical success conditions for the newly evaluated editing efficacy, paraphrase generalization, and locality metrics. Existing perturbation/PER definitions and FARL equations (1)–(4) remain unchanged. There are no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central mechanistic argument by supplementing v1's correlational head probes with bidirectional activation patching and random-head controls. Free-form evaluation and locality/position checks address previously untested assumptions, while code-access and split disclosures improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting concerns in the new appendix: Tables 3–4 contain identical values, and rates such as 0.975 are unexplained for the stated 50 paraphrase examples per domain. Those issues limit confidence in part of the added evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same answer-attribution study and FARL framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds activation-patching experiments, logit trajectories, memory-editing validation, free-form QA evaluation, and cue-position tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original perturbation experiments, attention-head probing, and FARL training evaluations, including Tables 1–2 and the additional results in Appendix C.

results.title: Reasoning or Retrieval? A Study of Answer Attribution on Large Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same central claims: TSLA localizes separable TR/TL functions, TR promotes task-subspace alignment, TL promotes within-subspace discrimination, and the framework explains induction heads and task vectors. The new contribution list summarizes existing claims rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 explains the earlier occurrence of TL heads through the distinction between within-task discrimination and task-versus-nontask separation. It adds interpretations of query-versus-label attention and shared TR versus specialized TL mechanisms in composite tasks. It also discusses task vectors' single-token scope and explicitly motivates broader generation tests by acknowledging the synthetic movie task's simplicity.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the promised future code release with a code-implementation repository link. It documents the new semantic-token set, threshold sweep, composite prompts and intervention positions, and SubjQA book split and rating procedure. Existing hardware, quantization, sample limits, prompt templates, and steering recipes remain unchanged; repository contents were not inspected.

E1.justification: V2 adds Country–Capital plus Antonym composite ICL in Appendix H.4 and book-review generation using SubjQA with human-written reviews and a richer sentiment-label space in Appendix I.3. These extend v1's seven classification datasets and synthetic binary movie reviews to sequential constituent tasks and more varied generation.

E2.justification: DLA-based head identification, induction heads, random heads, and the relevant ICL and zero-shot reference conditions remain in their corresponding comparisons. SubjQA extends the existing task-vector comparison set. The new random-subspace contrast tests an assumption rather than introducing a competing head-identification method.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a 1–10% head-selection sweep, equal-sized random-vocabulary subspace controls, attention-mass and layerwise logit-margin measurements, and position-specific composite-task ablations using 10% of heads in one direction and 3% in the other. These supplement rather than replace the retained eight-shot experiments and default 3% threshold.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct tests of the shared semantic-subspace premise, sensitivity of ablation and steering to head-selection thresholds, aggregate attention distributions and individual prompt traces, and analyses explaining why TL heads occur earlier than TR heads. Composite-task cross-ablation also tests whether TR transfers across subtasks while TL remains specialized.

E5.justification: Appendix F and Table 5 introduce Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for paired semantic-versus-random projection norms. V1 already reported Mann–Whitney tests for layer distributions and means with standard deviations for generation ratings. V2 does not state an increase in repeated runs or introduce seed counts.

E6.justification: The earlier figure results and layer-statistics table values are retained, while substantial new results are added. Table 4 reports cross-subtask Spearman correlations of 0.8365 for TR heads versus 0.2980 for TL heads; Figure 53 shows TR-vector accuracy increasing up to roughly 7% head selection. Figures 100–105 add SubjQA ratings, although Figures 100 and 102 repeat an identical plot under different model captions.

M1.justification: The TR projection-norm score, normalized TL logit-gap score, head-ranking procedure, and task-vector construction and injection remain unchanged. The added tasks apply the existing procedure; expanded explanations and revised notation do not establish an algorithm change.

P1.justification: V2 adds an explicit contribution list, organizes related work with thematic paragraph headings, and revises method explanations and experimental transitions. Appendix organization expands, and publication headers and affiliations change. The overall main-section sequence and much of the existing prose remain.

P2.justification: V2 adds main-text attention-distribution and token-attention figures, extensive appendix plots for the new analyses and tasks, and two new results tables. Existing figures are retained and reflowed, while the layer-statistics tables are grouped near the end. These are substantial additions to the visual evidence, beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds Bjerva et al. (2020) for SubjQA and Li et al. (2025), whose findings motivate the composite-task discussion in Appendix H.4. It removes Li et al. (2024) and Marks and Tegmark (2024). Related work more explicitly connects prior approaches to individual experiments, while the overarching research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: V2 removes the unsupported assertion that Equation 3's TL score lies in [-1,1] and qualifies the random-set Jaccard expression as asymptotic. Theorem 1 and its Appendix B proof are unchanged. The revised row-oriented unembedding dimensions also introduce an inconsistency with the unchanged projector formula near Equation 2.

improvement.justification: V1 offered limited direct checks of the semantic-subspace premise and fixed 3% selection threshold, and its generation evidence used synthetic binary movie reviews. V2 adds targeted controls, threshold sweeps, layer-order explanations, and composite and human-written review tasks, substantially strengthening support for the retained framework. These gains outweigh localized problems: the unexplained duplicate SubjQA plots in Figures 100 and 102 and the matrix-dimension inconsistency near Equation 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TSLA study. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched despite renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds semantic-subspace tests, threshold sensitivity analyses, attention and layer-dynamics analyses, composite-task experiments, and SubjQA generation results.

before.justification: V1 reports original attention-head analyses, ablations, input perturbations, steering experiments, and generation results across six language models, including extensive appendix results.

results.title: Localizing Task Recognition and Task Learning in In-Context Learning via Attention Head Analysis

C1.justification: v1's central claim concerns negative differentiation as a mechanism supporting syntax. v2 retains the functional importance claim but adds a prominent double-dissociation claim: targeted Wasserstein-neuron ablation preferentially harms grammar, whereas broad perplexity-matched ablation preferentially harms other capabilities. This becomes a central contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: Appendix A.6 newly acknowledges that negative clamping preferentially collapses negative-negative pairs, making their association with grammatical vulnerability suggestive rather than causal. v2 also introduces sign-versus-magnitude and syntax-versus-general-capacity interpretations, discusses TruthfulQA and Qwen exceptions, and moderates the categorical contrast with ReLU models.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link on the first page, identifies the Language Model Evaluation Harness and zero-shot setup, and clarifies that perplexity matching uses one percentage applied uniformly across layers. These improve access and procedural documentation; the PDFs do not establish changes to the implementation of retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 retains WikiText 2, BLiMP, and TSE and adds ARC Challenge, ARC Easy, BoolQ, HellaSwag, PIQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA, and WinoGrande for Llama, Mistral, and Qwen (Tables A3-A5). This substantially extends evaluation beyond grammatical judgments to science, commonsense reasoning, comprehension, and truthfulness.

E2.justification: The original random and low-WD perplexity-matched controls remain. Appendix A.1 adds comparisons with MD, skewness, and kurtosis rankings, including a causal replication using MD-selected controls. Appendix A.4 compares negative zeroing with positive-branch ReLU substitution, positive zeroing, and negative post-activation sign reversal. These substantially broaden the alternative selection rules and interventions evaluated.

E3.justification: Retained experiments preserve their stated splits and principal ablation settings. New designs include zero-shot multiple-choice evaluation, top-1% ranking-overlap comparisons across Llama layers, a top-1% MD ablation with a bottom-30% MD perplexity-matched control, and POS enrichment using 50 token pairs per neuron. These are added protocols, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix A.1 tests the WD proxy against distributional confounds and repeats causal ablations using MD. Appendix A.4 separates effects of activation sign, magnitude, and positive-branch curvature. Appendix A.5 extends the single-neuron illustration to six additional neurons with quantitative POS enrichment. The Llama layerwise analysis in A.6 is retained from v1, not newly added.

E5.justification: Table A2 newly gives explicit ± uncertainties for absolute baseline and ablated grammatical accuracies, including targeted and perplexity-matched conditions; v1 principally presents error increases with random-control error bars. Ten random-control trials and one-standard-error figure reporting remain. No increased run count or new significance testing is documented, and the tables' referenced confidence intervals lack a specified confidence level.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark, proxy-validation, activation-control, and POS-enrichment results. Existing Figure 3c also changes: Llama's rounded targeted TSE error increase changes from 28 to 29 percentage points; perplexity-matched TSE changes switch from +1 to -1 for Llama and +2 to -3 for Mistral. Table A2 supplies revised absolute accuracies. Separately, the new 2% negative-sign-flip condition raises perplexity from 6.50 to 2277 (A.4).

M1.justification: The primary procedure remains identifying high-Wasserstein-distance neurons and zeroing their negative pre-activations while retaining model weights and nonlinearities. WD and MD computation remain substantively unchanged. Direct-MD selection and alternative activation interventions are introduced as validation experiments, without replacing the primary method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten to foreground negative-activation computation and the double dissociation. Related-work subsections are reordered and revised, and the former main-text Llama section moves into a structured appendix. These constitute substantial narrative reorganization beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds nine figures and five numbered tables covering general-task comparisons, metric validation, activation controls, and neuron examples. Original figures are matched across renumbering, including Figure 7 becoming Figure A9. Figure 3c is redrawn with a negative error range, and Figure 1's caption is revised despite an unchanged image.

R1.justification: v2 adds benchmark and evaluation-harness references, contemporaneous work by Gerstner and Schuetze, and the preliminary workshop version. It acknowledges sparse autoencoders' potential sensitivity to negative activations and sharpens the distinction between its MLP mechanism and earlier syntactic representations. References to activation-sparsification work by Mirzadeh and Lee are removed, while the main relationship to prior Wasserstein-neuron research remains.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions underlying WD, MD, and the primary negative-clamping intervention are retained. The additions specify empirical controls and standard overlap/enrichment statistics; they introduce no substantive theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence for syntax specificity relied largely on grammatical benchmarks and perplexity matching. v2 directly tests general capabilities, validates neuron selection, and adds sign controls, substantially strengthening that inference. Raw scores, uncertainty values, code-access information, and explicit acknowledgment of the negative-negative-pair confound improve transparency. The broad double-dissociation wording remains stronger than the Qwen and TruthfulQA results warrant, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable text, equations, figures, and references. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendix A. Retained experiments can be matched, including v1 Section 7 and Figure 7, relocated to v2 Appendix A.6 and Figure A9.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds non-grammatical benchmark evaluations, neuron-selection validation, activation-function controls, and additional token-pair analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original neuron-distribution measurements, training-checkpoint analyses, and controlled activation ablations evaluated using WikiText 2, BLiMP, and TSE.

results.title: Negative Pre-activations Differentiate Syntax

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction strengthen specific mechanistic claims: spatial embeddings now purportedly reconstruct unified functional geometry, while expert routing prevents or relieves interference between tasks. These extend the earlier spatial-prior and specialized-routing claims, while the core contribution, model scale, and nine-task performance claims remain.

C2.justification: New discussions interpret regional-embedding failures, spatial compensation under channel loss, augmentation benefits, capacity–compute tradeoffs, label efficiency, and routing patterns as expert specialization. These substantially extend v1's interpretations. Section 3.3 also replaces the characterization of linear probing as zero-shot transfer with transferability and representation quality.

D1.justification: V2 adds named brain-region and montage-identity details, specifies Top-2 gating for the efficiency comparison, and describes the STFT baseline's magnitude/phase inputs and compute matching. Existing model hyperparameters, computing environment, dataset information, and code-access address are retained.

E1.justification: The pre-training corpus and nine downstream datasets/tasks are retained. Appendix L adds bounded evaluation scenarios involving missing channels on BCIC-IV-2a and SEED, plus transfer from a 62-channel training montage to a 19-channel inference montage on SEED.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged, but Appendix J adds Dense-Small and Dense-Large controls matched approximately for inference compute and total capacity. Appendix M adds an evaluated STFT-MoE comparator. These substantially expand the comparisons testing the architectural choices.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce compute/capacity matching, inference-time masking of 1, 3, 5, or 7 channels, 62-to-19-channel montage transfer, and fine-tuning with 1%, 10%, 30%, 50%, or 70% labeled data. The retained main evaluation procedures and hyperparameter tables are unchanged; these are added protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations, scaling studies, and t-SNE analysis, Appendices J–O investigate MoE efficiency, augmentation dependence, individual topology embeddings, missing-channel robustness, montage transfer, the STFT alternative, label efficiency, and expert specialization. The new ablation Figure 3 merely redisplays existing results.

E5.justification: Section 3.3 newly identifies the reported values as means and standard deviations over five independent trials. V1 already displayed plus/minus values without this explanation. This discloses the reporting procedure rather than demonstrating increased runs; the new appendix result tables generally omit uncertainty.

E6.justification: The original benchmark, component-ablation, and scaling values are unchanged after percentage conversion. Substantial new results appear in Tables 5 and 14–21 and Figures 6–8. For example, Table 20 reports TUEV balanced accuracy of 66.94% for Uni-NTFMsmall versus 52.37% for STFT-MoE. These are added comparisons, not improvements over v1's original scores.

M1.justification: The HFPM paths, cross-domain attention, three-part topological embedding, RoPE, sparse MoE, and reconstruction objectives remain unchanged. Expanded electrode descriptions and newly specified Top-2 gating document the existing method; the PDFs do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The abstract, architectural-challenge discussion, and contribution statements are substantially rewritten, and Section 2.3 receives an extensive explanatory expansion. Appendix organization is extended while retained sections are renumbered. Publication headers, affiliations, acknowledgments, and localized language corrections also change.

P2.justification: V2 merges the two original component-ablation tables and adds Figure 3 to visualize them. It introduces Tables 5 and 14–21 and three expert-analysis figures. Retained result tables switch to percentage presentation, while the unchanged scaling and t-SNE figures are renumbered and repositioned.

R1.justification: The bibliography and Appendix A are unchanged. However, the introduction refines the research positioning around biological transient/sustained coding, functional topography, and sparse modularity, including task interference as a limitation of dense architectures. This is a limited positioning change rather than an expansion of cited literature.

T1.justification: The mathematical method, metric definitions, and pseudocode equations are retained. Equation 7 is restated using electrode-specific notation, without changing the embedding operation. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's efficiency and montage-unification claims relied mainly on architectural descriptions and coarse ablations. V2's matched dense/STFT controls and missing-channel/cross-montage tests substantially strengthen their empirical support, while five-trial standard-deviation disclosure improves transparency. New analyses often omit uncertainty, Table 17's small-model scores match Table 1's tiny-model row, and biological interpretations exceed what the diagnostics establish. These weaknesses limit confidence in details but do not outweigh the substantial validation gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Uni-NTFM. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across appendix renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds controlled efficiency comparisons, augmentation and topology ablations, robustness tests, label-efficiency experiments, and expert-routing analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original Uni-NTFM evaluations on nine downstream EEG datasets, component ablations, model/data scaling experiments, and feature visualizations.

results.title: Uni-NTFM: A Unified Foundation Model for EEG Signal Representation Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion extend the claimed empirical generality to robot manipulation. The central contributions—two-phase flow matching, finite-time CBF certification, efficiency and mitigation of distributional drift and local traps—retain their earlier meaning.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications about prediction-error bias and heavy tails, limits assumption validation to Maze2D, and discusses compatibility with learned CBFs. It explains when relaxation is necessary, interprets localized versus propagated drift, and distinguishes mild short-horizon oscillations from incomplete trapped paths. The block-stacking example also exposes the limits of single-step prediction.

D1.justification: v3 supplies previously missing CBF parameter values, the relaxation schedule, conditioning information and CPU/GPU specifications. It adds block-stacking training and inference settings, consolidates experimental configuration tables, and announces project-page and supplementary-code access. These substantially improve documentation beyond v1's training hyperparameter tables; actual code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v3 adds robot block stacking with joint-limit constraints, extending evaluation beyond Maze2D and locomotion. Appendix F.1 also adds a six-constraint narrow-corridor maze scenario beyond the original two-constraint setting. These substantially broaden task and environmental coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds explicit comparison rows for DDIM with both randomness settings, FM and FlowMatcher, which already appeared in v1's sampling-horizon plots. It also adds SafeFlowMatcher without relaxation. The existing safe-baseline families are retained; extending them to block stacking does not introduce another comparator family.

E3.justification: The reported Maze2D planning horizon changes from 256 to 384 and the episode limit from 1000 to 800. The locomotion constraint changes from z + φv_z ≤ h_r to z ≤ h_r, and curvature is described as Menger curvature instead of angular deviation. v3 also introduces total-generation timing and protocols for solver comparisons, prediction-error estimation and distributional drift. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Existing prediction-horizon and scaling ablations gain additional measurements. New analyses test the prediction-error assumption, removal of relaxation, block-stacking prediction/correction allocation, six-constraint robustness, CBF-parameter sensitivity, solver-dependent behavior and distributional drift (Appendix B.1, Figure 12 and Appendix F). This substantially expands scrutiny of assumptions, mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v1 specifies 100 independent trials for Table 1 but leaves the meaning of its ± notation implicit. v3 explicitly identifies means and standard deviations and states a 100-trial protocol covering Table 4 as well. This improves statistical disclosure without establishing an increase in runs or introducing seed lists, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds block-stacking scores of 0.76, 0.73 and 0.72 for SafeFlowMatcher, SafeFM and SafeDiffuser, plus extensive timing, sensitivity and drift results. Existing entries also change: SafeDiffuser's Walker2D/Hopper scores become 0.283/0.435 from 0.321/0.464 in Table 4, and the prediction-horizon-8 score becomes 1.404±0.538 from 1.362±0.480 in Table 2. These are revised reports, not demonstrated same-setting performance changes, given the accompanying protocol revisions.

M1.justification: The flow-matching objective, prediction–correction procedure, vanishing time-scaled dynamics and relaxed waypoint-wise CBF quadratic program remain the same. The explicit velocity calculation added to Algorithm 1 and the waypoint-level equation clarify operations already specified in v1; they do not establish a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the introduction and theory remain intact. v3 refines terminology and prose, clarifies planning versus sampling horizons and waypoint-wise control, revises experimental explanations, and reorganizes the appendices around added material. A reproducibility statement and updated author/header text are also added.

P2.justification: v3 adds prediction-error distributions, locomotion and manipulation illustrations, multi-constraint and drift plots, and detailed generation sequences. Existing tables gain comparison rows, additional metrics and task categories; training/evaluation tables are consolidated. Retained figures are also relocated or relabeled, and the vanishing-scale illustration gains magnified annotations.

R1.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands positioning around discrete-time, nonconvex, measurement-robust, dynamic-obstacle and learned/perception-based CBFs, including their potential compatibility with SafeFlowMatcher. The earlier reachability/MPC/shielding survey is trimmed. The SafeDiffuser citation change from Wei to Xiao is a bibliographic correction, not a different prior method.

T1.justification: The central lemmas, safety theorem, convergence bound and proofs are retained, with v1 Appendices A–B corresponding to v3 Appendices B.2–C. Limited formal changes include broadening the stated scaling condition from α≥1 to α>0 and defining trajectory-level and waypoint-level energy-distance quantities in Appendix F.4. The empirical assumption check is not a new proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support and reproducibility for the existing contribution. Qualitative drift arguments and limited timing evidence gain direct distributional measurements, solver-specific total runtimes, multi-constraint stress tests and an empirical check of the prediction-error assumption. Detailed CBF settings and documented failure cases make the method easier to reproduce and assess. Revised evaluation definitions and unexplained changes to retained scores still limit cross-version performance comparisons, but the gains address important evidential and documentation gaps in v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SafeFlowMatcher work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated proofs and experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds block-stacking evaluation, prediction-error measurements, multi-constraint experiments, sensitivity tests, timing comparisons and distributional-drift analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original Maze2D, Walker2D and Hopper experiments, alongside prediction-horizon, scaling and batch-size ablations in Tables 1–5.

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged, including the headline ASR reduction from 47.9% to 14.7%. The introduction and conclusion retain the same intra-step/inter-step findings, two-component training-free defense, and claims of preserved utility and efficiency.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 clarifies attacker and defender access and operational constraints. New Appendix F.3 acknowledges similarities with AR safety phenomena while explaining distinctions involving remasking, parallel decoding, and path dependence. Added experiments receive robustness and evaluator-agreement interpretations; the existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 specifies implementation details for the added experiments, including sampling temperatures, o3-mini, Llama-Guard-3-8B, HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls, and manual-evaluation sample counts. Existing checkpoints, hardware, precision, and principal hyperparameters remain unchanged. The new reproducibility statement repeats the code access already supplied in v1.

E1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds defense-aware adversaries that optimize prompts to evade Safety Divergence detection, substantially extending the tested threat conditions. Table 11 also adds PAD evaluations on HarmBench prompts. The original datasets and four evaluated models remain; StrongREJECT is introduced as an assessment method.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds random-remasking and alpha=0.3 comparison rows for both LLaDA and Dream alongside the retained component ablations. Table 1 retains PPL-Filter and Self-reminder. The additional safety judges are evaluators, rather than new defense baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include success across five temperature-varied attempts, SD-minimizing adversarial optimization, human assessment of 200 samples per dataset, additional classifier judges, and StrongREJECT scoring. Original settings in Tables 3–6 remain unchanged. V2's corrected description of transferred GCG agrees with v1 Appendix A.3 and does not establish a changed experiment.

E4.justification: Table 2 expands the ablation to remasking controls, AutoDAN, and GSM8K. Appendices D.3–D.5 add adaptive robustness tests, extend the motivating randomness and token-injection analyses beyond LLaDA, and examine evaluator dependence. Figure 4 additionally tests a compliance-token intervention on jailbreak queries. Existing sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D.3 newly specifies five generation attempts per prompt at different temperatures, aggregated by whether any attempt succeeds. This adds repeated-sampling information for an attack protocol, without adding confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-seed uncertainty estimates for the existing results.

E6.justification: Table 1 remains unchanged, while expanded ablations and Tables 9–11 add substantial results. Table 9 reports threshold-probing ASRs of 65.58% and 84.62% for defended LLaDA and Dream. A new Table 2 AutoDAN entry is ambiguous: LLaDA+DiffuGuard scores 16.73%, whereas Table 1 reports 31.54% alone and 16.73% with Self-reminder. The unexplained configuration difference prevents interpreting this as a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The stochastic annealing remasking and block-level audit-and-repair procedures remain unchanged. Equations 7–10 and Algorithm 1 retain the same randomness schedule, Safety Divergence calculation, remasking, token suppression, and first-block repair.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are largely retained. Local revisions clarify background notation, the threat model, and GCG categorization. V2 updates author and publication information, adds acknowledgments, reproducibility and LLM-usage statements, and renumbers appendices around the additions.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn, replacing its detailed method schematic with enlarged outcome displays. Figure 4 gains a bar, Figure 6 corrects swapped PAD/WildJailbreak labels, and Table 2 gains rows and columns. Three new tables and two multi-panel appendix figures present expanded evidence. The existing judge prompt is retained as Figure 11.

R1.justification: Appendix F.3 adds targeted positioning against prior AR decoding and shallow-alignment studies, including Huang et al., Zhang et al., and Qi et al. HarmBench, StrongREJECT, and several other references are added. The main related-work taxonomy and overall contribution positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: The numbered equations and algorithmic mathematical definitions are retained. V2 adds explanatory threat-model and autoregressive-model discussion, but no new mathematical derivations, propositions, proofs, or formal guarantees.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation by testing defense-aware attacks, checking the primary evaluator against human and alternative assessments, and extending the motivating analyses beyond LLaDA. These address important gaps in v1, while expanded ablations better establish component contributions and utility costs. The high adaptive ASRs warrant more cautious robustness claims, and some defense configurations remain unclear, but the added validation and evidence of failure conditions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiffuGuard study. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across appendix renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds adaptive-attack experiments, analyses across additional models, and human and alternative-evaluator assessments in Appendix D.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on dLLM safety, defense effectiveness, utility, inference speed, component ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity in Sections 3–5 and Appendix C.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking convergence efficiency to dense autoregressive supervision and inference cost to the diffusion head. Appendix I newly discusses facial artifacts, illegible text and fine-detail failures, hypothesizes a dataset-related cause, and explicitly identifies ImageNet-only evaluation as a generalization limitation.

D1.justification: V2 documents settings for the added experiments, including the higher-resolution KL coefficient and conditioning-token count, eight-A100 training timing, and single-A100 inference measurements with specified batch sizes and sampling steps. The original posterior, normalization and backbone ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify evaluation on 50,000 samples drawn with a fixed random seed. Neither reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests; the added plots continue to present point estimates.

E6.justification: The retained 256×256 results, including SphereAR-B/L/H FIDs of 1.92/1.54/1.34 and Tables 2–4, are unchanged. V2 adds 512×512 SphereAR-L results of FID 1.67 and IS 292.5, plus checkpoint, throughput, high-CFG and failure-case findings. Table 1 drops the XXL baseline entries with FIDs 2.34 and 2.15.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same hyperspherical VAE, Power Spherical posterior, hybrid backbone, causal Transformer, Rectified Flow head and final normalization after guided sampling. The added resolution and sampling-step configurations are evaluation settings, not new method components.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. Limited edits clarify the component ablation with numbered-row references, expand the appendix organization, add an LLM-use disclosure, update author/publication information and remove the acknowledgments.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 5 and Figures 6–9 for higher-resolution results, convergence, inference speed, robustness and failures. Table 2 becomes a standalone display with numbered rows, and the conference template reflows existing material. The original sample images are retained and renumbered from Figures 6–17 to Figures 10–21.

T1.justification: The mathematical method exposition and Appendices A–B retain the same assumptions, projection lemmas, linearized refeeding bound and radial-KL derivation. No substantive definition, theorem or proof changes were found.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical assessment of SphereAR by addressing v1's missing evidence about autoregressive training and inference costs, higher-resolution behavior and practical failure boundaries. Removing two XXL baseline rows modestly reduces comparison coverage, but the retained main results and added evidence support a clear net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same SphereAR research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and matchable, including the relocated sample gallery.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds higher-resolution generation, timing measurements, high-CFG experiments and qualitative failure comparisons in Appendices E–I.

before.justification: V1 reports original ImageNet generation results, posterior and normalization ablations, and VAE-backbone experiments in Tables 1–4 and Figure 4.

results.title: Hyperspherical Latents Improve Continuous-Token Autoregressive Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: the first tailored DLM watermark, its constrained-optimization formulation and ARLM connection, high detectability with minimal quality impact, and robustness. Additional evidence and qualifications elsewhere do not revise these headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges potentially non-negligible accuracy losses depending on model and watermark settings in Section 4.1 and Appendix C.5. It adds an explanation of fixed-key Unigram miscalibration and qualifies runtime comparisons because hardware conditions were uncontrolled. These materially extend v1's discussion of practical reliability and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds keyed green-matrix row generation, bisection bounds and a 16-iteration implementation, GaussMark weight-selection details, benchmark evaluation libraries, and the optimized implementation's restrictions. Hardware disclosures and the abstract's code link remain. E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluations on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-C, GPQA, MBPP, and GSM8K, substantially extending coverage to knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, and code-generation utility. The WATERBENCH instruction tasks and C4 infilling evaluation from v1 remain.
