E3.justification: New protocols include benchmark accuracy at temperature 0.1, with random remasking and an additional LLADA-8B entropy-remasking configuration. Appendix B.2 introduces calibration on 10,000 unwatermarked, 200-token C4 passages. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original 600-prompt, temperature-0.5 instruction-generation protocol is retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of Unigram detector implementation sensitivity, false-positive calibration across keys, the SelfHash variant, and equivalence between standard and optimized implementations. These test detector reliability and implementation choices beyond v1's retained component ablations, text-edit robustness tests, and examples.

E5.justification: Appendix B.2 introduces a substantial assessment of variation across 100 watermark keys, reporting calibration curves and standard deviations of false-positive rates. Runtime reporting changes from 300 repetitions to five nonconsecutive batches of 300 and adds error bars. Existing shaded detection curves are retained, so uncertainty visualization itself is not entirely new.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 detection, perplexity, and judge scores remain unchanged, but substantial results are added. Table 2 reports maximum false-positive rates at nominal 1% of 17.0% for Unigram versus 1.7% and 1.1% for the proposed contexts. Table 3 reports LLADA-8B average accuracy of 59.42% unwatermarked versus 55.97% with C={-1}, delta=4. New comparison curves and replaced runtime estimates further expand the results.

M1.justification: The core optimization, expectation boost, predictive bias, and detector remain unchanged. Appendix H adds a SelfHash variant with H_t(omega)=omega_t and a diagonal-G token boost. Appendix I.1 implements the previously suggested optimization of computing watermark distributions only for tokens being unmasked, described as functionally equivalent.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains intact. The order-agnostic comparison moves from Appendix B into Section 4.4, Appendix B gains descriptive and limitations subsections, and implementation material gains additional organization. Local explanations, cross-references, and the publication header are revised without a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains accuracy columns, Tables 2-4 are added, and new Figures 6, 7, 16, 20, and 22 display additional evaluations. The runtime chart is redrawn with optimized variants and error bars. Figure 5 moves into the main text, and new or simplified algorithm blocks substantially alter method presentation. Most original plots are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds GaussMark, benchmark and evaluation-framework references, and citations supporting the discussion of fixed-key reliability and zero-shot detection. These extend the comparison with prior work, while the central positioning as a DLM adaptation of Red-Green watermarking remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly requires no self-hashing for the factorization in Equation 2; v1 states this assumption only in the appendix's component decomposition. New Appendix H derives the joint token/hash objective and SelfHash solution, while Appendix G.2 adds Theorem G.1 and a KL expansion proof. The original principal theorem remains. The new KL derivation has a normalization omission in Equation 36 as printed.

improvement.justification: The six-task utility evaluation and 100-key false-positive study address important gaps in v1's evidence for practical quality and reliable detection. v2 exposes model-dependent accuracy losses and qualifies runtime measurements, substantially improving the paper's empirical grounding. These gains outweigh localized regressions in Algorithm 2's completeness and normalization omissions in the new epsilon-parameterization material. The unchanged headline claim of minimal quality impact still needs qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core method, and retained experiments. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and relocated sections, figures, and proofs can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds benchmark accuracies, key-dependent false-positive measurements, additional comparisons, and implementation evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original watermark-detection, text-quality, robustness, and ablation experiments, plus infilling experiments and detector simulations in the appendices.

results.title: Watermarking Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: prioritizing reasoning safety, using corrective interventions for preference learning, reducing overall harmfulness by over 30% relative to leading baselines, and preserving reasoning capabilities. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix B adds substantive interpretations concerning truthfulness, generalization beyond attack templates, model capacity and over-refusal, and differences from TARS and BackTrack. Section 4.2 qualifies 'lowest' response harmfulness to 'one of the lowest.' However, the new broad-utility preservation interpretation overstates Table 5's mixed results.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds reproduction details for TARS's benign-task reward and BackTrack's RESET-based data construction and evaluation. v2 also supplies separate access pointers for the existing benign STAR data and the added paraphrased benchmark. Original IPO hyperparameters, hardware, and implementation frameworks remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds TruthfulQA, SimpleQA, IF-Eval, MMLU, DROP, and SuperGPQA, broadening evaluation to truthfulness, factual knowledge, instruction following, and paragraph reasoning. It also adds JailbreakV-28K obfuscation, paraphrased JailbreakBench, and an adaptive-prompt attack scenario. Original training data and benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: v2 retains SafeChain, RealSafe, STAR, SafeKey, and GRPO, and adds reproduced TARS and BackTrack comparisons on DS-8B across the three original safety benchmarks and XsTest. Table 9 materially expands comparison with alternative safety-alignment procedures.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings remain unchanged. Added evaluations introduce 1.5B and 14B backbones and BackTrack scoring restricted to reasoning after its RESET token. Reporting also adds relative harmfulness reductions and replaces Table 2's combined safety average with separate reasoning and response averages.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds attack-family and harm-category breakdowns, robustness tests under obfuscation, paraphrasing and adaptive prompting, model-scale analysis, and replication of CSR dynamics on Qwen3-8B. Existing detector and training-algorithm ablations remain; the three qualitative examples are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions state that evaluation metrics are averaged over multiple runs without specifying counts or seeds. The added Qwen3 CSR figure follows the existing mean and ±1 standard-deviation convention. No new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Tables 5–10 and Figure 10 add substantial utility, robustness, comparator, scaling, and mechanism results. For example, the new adaptive-attack evaluation reports harmful reasoning of 20.0% for IPO versus 74.0% for the base model. Table 2's original per-benchmark scores are unchanged; its revised averages are reaggregations.

M1.justification: IPO's cue replacement, preference-pair construction, partial DPO objective, and over-refusal mitigation remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. The auxiliary SFT loss newly discussed in Section 4.1 was already documented with coefficient 0.2 in v1 Appendix A.2.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely retained, with localized wording changes and expanded explanations. v2 updates affiliations and headers, adds acknowledgements and cross-references, and inserts an experimental Appendix B, moving the previous qualitative-example and LLM-use appendices to C and D.

P2.justification: v2 adds six result tables, Tables 5–10, and a two-panel Qwen3 dynamics figure. Table 2 is redesigned with separate safety averages and revised labels and highlighting. Original figures are retained; the qualitative examples move from Figures 10–12 to Figures 11–13.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds a substantial discussion of process supervision for safety, covering reasoning interventions, unlearning, step-level supervision, backtracking, internal classification, and CoT monitoring risks. New citations and explicit comparisons materially broaden IPO's positioning beyond v1's emphasis on LRMs and existing safety-alignment methods.

T1.justification: v1 gives an informal reward-shaping analogy. v2 Section 3.4 additionally identifies CSR with a policy value function and introduces a potential function and the shaped reward r_t = gamma Phi(s_{t+1}) - Phi(s_t). This adds limited formal reasoning, without changing the existing equations or supplying a theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing gaps in attack robustness, model-scale generalization, comparison with alternative alignment methods, and replication of the proposed safety dynamics. Broader utility testing also makes tradeoffs more assessable. These gains outweigh interpretive weaknesses: Appendix B.1 claims preservation too broadly despite IPO scoring 56.2% versus the base model's 63.7% on IF-Eval and 31.5% versus 33.5% on SuperGPQA. The improvement comes from stronger validation and positioning, not higher scores on the unchanged main experiments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IPO study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated, and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds broader utility, attack robustness, baseline, model-scale, and reasoning-dynamics results in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original LRM safety evaluations, corrective-intervention experiments, capability measurements, and ablations in Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–7.

results.title: Towards Safe Reasoning in Large Reasoning Models via Corrective Intervention

C1.justification: The central claim of selective reading impairment is retained. However, v3's abstract adds two substantive contributions: identified units predict human VWFA responses, and the ablated model mirrors dyslexic font sensitivity. These extend the claimed achievements beyond v1's behavioral impairment simulation.

C2.justification: v3 introduces a feature-redundancy explanation for the subset-size-dependent neural results and suggests unreported comorbidities may explain human orthographic deficits. It develops font-intervention implications and removes the now-addressed lack-of-neural-data limitation. It also drops v1's explicit qualification that the model captures end-state deficits rather than developmental trajectories.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.3 supplies exact activation-extraction, lexical-decision, Kempler, and RAVEN prompts, materially improving documentation of experimental inputs. Appendix A.5 specifies two 80GB NVIDIA A100 GPUs and negligible ablation overhead. The code reference changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original experiments.

E1.justification: v3 adds human VWFA response prediction using the Marvi et al. (2025) fMRI dataset, substantially extending evaluation beyond behavioral tasks. It also tests retained ROAR items under alternative fonts and orange backgrounds, adding distinct visual input conditions. The original behavioral benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: The comparison strategies remain intact versus ablated models and VWF-selected versus randomly selected units; the new analyses extend these controls. LLaVA-NeXT is replaced by Molmo as a backbone for applying the same procedure, rather than as a competing method evaluated against it.

E3.justification: The new neural evaluation introduces voxelwise ridge regression, five-fold cross-validation, noise-ceiling-normalized Pearson correlations, and subset sizes from 0.25% to 5%. Font experiments vary typography and backgrounds while approximately matching font size. Appendix A.1 replaces LLaVA-NeXT-13B with Molmo-72B. The original ROAR split and twelve-item RAVEN setting remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial analyses of whether selected units predict human brain activity better than random subsets across subset sizes, and whether ablated models respond selectively to font and background changes. Existing mask-size, perturbation-strength, layer-choice, and qualitative error analyses are retained, including their appendix material.

E5.justification: v3 specifies five localizer-resampling seeds for neural alignment and ten seeds for font experiments, with 95% confidence intervals across seeds. The retained main experiments still report twenty seeds and the same Student's t-test framework; supplementary model evaluations still use five seeds. These are additional experiment-specific disclosures, not evidence of increased runs for existing results.

E6.justification: New Figure 5 shows selective-unit alignment exceeding random subsets at 0.25–1.25%, no significant difference at 2.5%, and a reversed advantage at 3.75–5%. Figure 7 adds font-specific improvements and deterioration, including improved OpenDyslexic performance and worse Papyrus performance. Molmo results replace LLaVA-NeXT results. The original reported ROAR and phonological effects remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains functional localization by word-versus-control t-statistics, ranking units, and ablating the smallest subset that crosses the ROAR dyslexia threshold. The principal Qwen2-VL-72B implementation still targets approximately 6.89% of language-decoder MLP units. The additions evaluate this approach rather than change it.

P1.justification: Most introductory, benchmark, methodological, and original-results prose is retained. The abstract is revised, the discussion is shortened and reorganized, and appendix subsections for prompts, resources, and writing assistance are added. Author information and reference metadata also change, but the main section sequence and overall narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual evidence with new neural-alignment and font-comparison charts, and redraws the supplementary model comparison around Molmo. Existing figures are resized or relocated, and the document adopts conference headers and revised spacing. The unchanged error-example tables are reordered: v1 Tables 2 and 3 become v3 Tables 3 and 2.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted references for neural encoding and data, fonts, comorbidity, and nonverbal abilities, including Naselaris, Marvi, Gonzalez, and Chalikia. Molmo's reference replaces LLaVA-NeXT's, and Du et al. is added to related work. The overall novelty positioning remains largely unchanged; bibliographic updates to existing works are not new research coverage.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs, and the localization statistic and threshold-based selection reasoning remain unchanged. The added ridge-regression and correlation procedures are empirical evaluation methods, without new formal assumptions, derivations, or theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's explicit inability to test neural alignment: controlled fMRI prediction now supports correspondence between small selective subsets and human VWFA activity. Font experiments extend practical evaluation, while exact prompts and hardware improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removal of developmental caveats and the inconclusive LLaVA experiment. The neural advantage remains limited to small subsets, and claimed human font correspondence relies on indirect evidence rather than a new matched human study.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dyslexia-modeling study. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains original behavioral experiments and adds original analyses of human fMRI prediction, font sensitivity, and ablation effects in Molmo.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM ablation experiments on reading, phonological and orthographic processing, RAVEN, and Kempler, including sensitivity analyses and supplementary model evaluations.

results.title: Inducing Dyslexia in Vision Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract removes the specific claim of a 20% ImageNet FID improvement. The introduction more prominently highlights expressive robot control, whose demonstration already existed in v1. The central contributions—discrete VAE training through policy search without reparameterization and strong reconstruction performance—remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of architecture, entropy and computational tradeoffs. It attributes Gumbel-NA's advantage over Gumbel to autoregressive gradient-estimation difficulty and connects broad code utilization to entropy regularization. Appendix H acknowledges computational costs and confines efficiency advantages to appropriate comparators. Appendix F qualifies scaling findings by noting different optimization objectives and no advantage at the tiny CIFAR bottleneck.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository pointer, a full MNIST architecture configuration, explicit GR-MCK sampling counts, method- and beta-specific hyperparameter Tables 3–6, and GPU, memory and throughput details in Appendix H. However, v1's explicit FSQ level lists and online Welford-normalization statement are omitted. Documentation therefore expands substantially but loses some reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions use MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-256 and retargeted LAFAN motions, including latent-space image generation and goal-conditioned robot control. The added capacity sweeps, architecture variants and utilization measurements concern retained data and tasks rather than new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Tables 1–2 add Gumbel-NA and GRMCK-NA comparisons alongside the retained autoregressive methods, FSQ, VQ-VAE and PPO. Gumbel-NA also supplies an ImageNet reconstruction comparator where autoregressive Gumbel remains excluded. These additions substantially broaden the comparison beyond autoregressive gradient estimators.

E3.justification: v2 adds PSNR and SSIM evaluation, bottleneck-size sweeps and resource profiling, and enlarges VQ networks to better match parameter budgets. Reported MNIST decoder and beta/ESS settings change. LAFAN inputs change from 127 to 121 features in Section 4 and Appendix J.1, although Appendix J retains 127. These are reported setting revisions, not evidence of performance gains under unchanged conditions.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained beta/ESS and baseline-sample ablations, v2 tests autoregressive versus non-autoregressive architectures, reconstruction scaling with bottleneck capacity, empirical vocabulary utilization, and memory/speed tradeoffs. Appendices F–H provide substantial new evidence about capacity sensitivity, representation behavior and computational scalability.

E5.justification: Appendix F specifies five seeds for the new tiny, small and medium bottleneck experiments and reuse of ten-seed main experiments for large bottlenecks. Main benchmark repetition counts remain ten seeds, or five for ImageNet, and summary curves retain the mean plus/minus one standard error convention. There is no stated increase in existing benchmark repetitions.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive non-autoregressive, PSNR/SSIM, scaling, utilization and computational results. Existing entries also change: MNIST DAPS beta=0.01 ELBO changes from -49.49 to -46.54, and ImageNet VQ-VAE FID from 76.78 to 65.01, alongside revised settings. These are replaced results rather than established same-setting improvements. DAPS ImageNet FID remains 48.65; newly evaluated Gumbel-NA obtains 51.66.

M1.justification: v2 introduces DAPS-NA, replacing autoregressive latent generation with a decoder-only transformer that produces all logits in one forward pass. This is a concrete architectural adaptation, while the central nonparametric target, weighted-likelihood encoder objective, decoder objective and ESS adaptation remain.

P1.justification: Section 3 is substantially rewritten around episode-based policy search and a separate variance-reduction explanation, and Algorithm 1 is reorganized into weight-computation and update procedures. The results narrative is reworked around separate beta settings, ablations move into the experiments section, and model-specific hyperparameters are integrated into dataset architecture appendices. These changes extend beyond inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: The original combined results table becomes two reorganized tables, and the hyperparameter summary figure becomes Tables 3–6. v2 adds utilization heatmaps, capacity-scaling plots and computational bar charts, redraws metric summaries, and revises Figure 1. Existing reconstruction and robotics images are retained and relocated rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds Higgins et al. on beta-VAE, Greensmith et al. on variance reduction, and Ziebart on maximum causal entropy, while removing Kober et al. The exposition more explicitly positions DAPS within episode-based policy search. Its principal relationship to REPS, V-MPO, SPU and LBPS remains.

T1.justification: The constrained optimum and ESS/Renyi-2 theoretical development are retained. Appendix A's derivation, lemma, corollary and proofs are unchanged apart from notation. Section 3 expands the return/baseline explanation and makes the Monte Carlo expression more explicit, without a substantive new derivation or theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the support for its central performance and scalability claims through non-autoregressive comparators, parameter-budget controls, capacity sweeps and direct computational measurements. The new ImageNet Gumbel-NA result, FID 51.66 against DAPS's 48.65, exposes a closer competitor, while the abstract drops its 20% headline claim and the discussion better qualifies efficiency. Expanded implementation documentation also helps reproducibility. Missing FSQ settings and inconsistent LAFAN feature counts are drawbacks, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparison quality, validation and interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DAPS research. Their full main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, plots and qualitative examples, support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched despite substantial renumbering and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds non-autoregressive comparisons, bottleneck-scaling experiments, latent-code utilization analyses and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-256 and LAFAN, hyperparameter ablations, generated samples and simulated robot-control demonstrations.

results.title: Discrete Variational Autoencoding via Policy Search

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same substantive contributions: the four-task reasoning suite, unified two-stage model, joint-training benefits and headline GPT-4.1 comparisons. The added resource-availability statement does not redefine the scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking prompt robustness to internalized priors, reward design to training stability, and external transfer to contextual alignment. Appendix F.3 newly qualifies text serialization as suitable for modest sequence lengths and dimensionality, while discussing encoder data requirements and possible advantages for longer or higher-dimensional inputs. Appendix J adds interpretations of data scaling.

D1.justification: v1 already supplied detailed prompts and training configurations. v2 adds explicit public code/checkpoint availability statements and access links, sequence-length and tokenizer-budget statistics, serialization details, and the response cap used for training-dynamics evaluation. These materially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing a change to the original training configuration.

E1.justification: Appendix K adds MTBench, TimeSeriesExam and CaTS-Bench, covering 13 tasks and 3,406 samples. These extend evaluation to financial/weather QA, synthetic anomaly/noise/pattern/similarity questions, retrieval and amplitude/mean comparisons. The original TSR-SUITE coverage remains intact.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparators are retained. Appendix F.3 adds a newly trained ChatTS-style embedding comparator with a matched Qwen2.5-Instruct-14B backbone. Tables 10–12 additionally compare against source-reported GPT-4o, Phi-3.5 and LLaVA v1.6 Mistral scores; these are identified as published reference results, not fresh baseline runs.

E3.justification: Original evaluation settings are retained, while new experiments introduce matched 14B encoding comparisons, a 100-sample efficiency test, one-epoch reward sweeps and training-data fractions of 25–100%. The no-system-prompt experiment changes answer parsing to handle free-form responses and omits SR, distinguishing its protocol from the original evaluation.

E4.justification: Appendices E.3, F.3, G.1, I and J add substantial analyses of prompt dependence, text versus learned embeddings, reward-component sensitivity, RL optimization dynamics and training-data scaling. These supplement the retained training-stage, joint-training and case-study analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random-seed specifications, confidence intervals or formal significance tests for the reported comparisons. The new training curves and sensitivity sweeps do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–2 and the retained appendix results are numerically unchanged. v2 adds extensive robustness, encoding, efficiency, scaling and external benchmark results. In Tables 10–12, newly reported TimeOmni-1/base-model averages are respectively 58.1/49.2, 47.8/46.9 and 63.5/65.0, showing mixed external transfer rather than uniform gains.

M1.justification: The proposed hierarchical annotation pipeline, supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO, joint training and task-grounded rewards remain unchanged. Appendix F newly explains text serialization and evaluates an embedding-based comparator; it does not replace the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained. Changes include localized related-work wording, the conference header, ethics and reproducibility statements, an LLM-use appendix, and additional appendix subsections. Existing appendices are renumbered with limited reordering.

P2.justification: v2 adds eight tables covering input statistics, prompt robustness, encoding/efficiency and external benchmarks, plus Figures 11–14 for sensitivity, dynamics and scaling. Existing displays are retained with reflow and renumbering: v1 Table 4 becomes Table 6, and case-study Tables 5–8 become Tables 13–16.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including ChatTime, ITFormer, OpenTSLM, ViT and the three external benchmarks, and discusses serialization relative to encoder-based approaches. The broader distinction between time-series language and reasoning models, and the paper's central novelty positioning, remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The reasoning formulation, context-sufficiency principle, SFT/GRPO objectives and reward definitions in Equations 1–9 remain unchanged. Appendix K repeats the existing probabilistic formulation; no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses gaps in v1's validation of robustness, encoding choices and external time-series QA transfer, while adding useful applicability limits and code/checkpoint access information. These gains strengthen the paper beyond merely adding scores. Some new interpretations overreach: Table 12 shows lower CaTS-Bench performance than the base model, and Figures 13–14 contain exceptions to claimed monotonic scaling. Those localized weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in empirical scrutiny and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TSR-SUITE and TimeOmni-1 work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds prompt robustness, encoding comparisons, reward sensitivity, training dynamics, data scaling and external benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ID/OOD evaluations, training ablations, general-reasoning benchmark results and appendix analyses, including Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–9.

results.title: TimeOmni-1: Incentivizing Complex Reasoning with Time Series in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central architectural contribution and headline claims of 7%-54% lower Navier-Stokes error and approximately 15% fewer parameters remain. The conclusion adds an explicit claim that accuracy benefits extend to elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic PDEs and describes DRIFT-Net as an integral-kernel backbone.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning image-branch importance, optimization robustness, approximate mesh independence under the tested interpolation setup, and manageable resolution scaling. The abstract softens the locality-to-drift statement from causation to association; substantive limitations remain unchanged. The new characterization of scOT as typically strongest is misleading: Table 1 contains stronger baselines on every Navier-Stokes task.

D1.justification: New Appendix F substantially expands reproducibility information: dataset shapes and splits, physical simulation parameters, model configurations and implementation links, from-scratch training, AdamW settings, batch size, checkpoint selection, and H200/FP32 hardware details. These are largely newly documented details; the main DRIFT-Net code-access statement is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 retains the four Navier-Stokes tasks and two ApeBench flow variants, while adding Poisson-Gauss, Allen-Cahn, and Wave-Gauss evaluations. This substantially broadens coverage to stationary elliptic, reaction-diffusion, and wave-propagation problems (Section 5, Table 1).

E2.justification: Table 1 adds U-NO, U-Net-ConvNeXt, and a Refiner U-Net adapted from PDE-Refiner alongside scOT and FNO, including comparisons on all four retained Navier-Stokes tasks. Refiner U-Net has no reported Poisson-Gauss result. The ApeBench comparisons remain against scOT.

E3.justification: v1 states approximately 20,000 trajectories and 40 epochs; v2 specifies task-dependent budgets, including 39,640 training trajectories and 20 epochs for NS-SL (Appendix F). This revises the reported settings without establishing that retained results were rerun. New experiments vary width, learning rate, schedule, sample count, and resolution, and introduce instantaneous error growth and training memory/time measurements.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds separate ablations of the depth-wise convolution and pointwise linear layer. Appendix G adds capacity, optimization sensitivity, sample-efficiency, cross-resolution, and computational-scaling analyses. Figure 3 replaces the NS-Tracer-PwC rollout-error analysis with instantaneous error growth on smoother ApeBench Kolmogorov flow. Existing spectral ablations and the qualitative visualization are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix F.4 newly states that random seeds are fixed for each run. Neither version supplies seed values, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or variability estimates. This is a limited addition of seed information, not evidence of increased replication.

E6.justification: Shared headline error values and base-model throughput values are retained. New Table 1 results include DRIFT-Net/scOT errors of 0.86/0.87 on Poisson-Gauss, 1.03/1.10 on Allen-Cahn, and 12.15/12.34 on Wave-Gauss. Additional comparator, ablation, resource, and Appendix G results substantially expand the findings. The NS-Tracer rollout means and growth slopes reported in v1 are removed.

M1.justification: The architecture, low-frequency mixing, radial gating, frequency-weighted loss, spectral pipeline, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix F supplies configurations and task-specific input details without introducing a new DRIFT component or revising the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Related work and the conclusion are extensively rewritten. Section 5 reorganizes baseline descriptions, main results, long-horizon analyses, and efficiency discussion, removing the redundant additional-final-time subsection. New structured setup and supplementary-experiment appendices expand the document organization, alongside terminology cleanup and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains task rows and comparator columns; Tables 3 and 4 expand; six new appendix tables appear. ApeBench rows move from Table 1 into a dedicated Table 2, replacing the earlier duplicate-results table. Figure 3 changes its dataset, quantity, axes, and caption. Other figures are retained or relocated, including Figure 5 from Appendix F to H.

R1.justification: Section 2 is reframed around a neural-operator taxonomy and explicitly positions DRIFT-Net within integral-kernel operators. It adds a survey, localized-kernel research, and discussion of MPP, DPOT, ICON, and CoDA-NO. The AFNO and Subramanian et al. references are removed, substantially changing the surrounding research context.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, method equations, Lipschitz and cumulative bounds, gating lemma, Sobolev defect theorem, and accompanying reasoning remain unchanged. Appendix F's added benchmark equations document experimental dynamics rather than introduce new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation and sparse reproducibility documentation. Broader PDE coverage, additional competing architectures, targeted ablations, and controlled sensitivity studies make the retained method's strengths and applicability more assessable; Appendix F supplies important missing experimental details. These gains outweigh the loss of NS-Tracer rollout diagnostics and reporting weaknesses, including absent repeated-run uncertainty, unexplained budget revisions, and misleading baseline-ranking prose.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DRIFT-Net research. All 14 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable. Methods, equations, tables, and figures can be reliably matched despite substantial experimental additions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations on three other PDE tasks, additional baselines and ablations, and the capacity, optimization, sample-efficiency, and resolution studies in Appendix G.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original benchmark evaluations, rollout analyses, component ablations, and efficiency measurements on four Navier-Stokes tasks and two ApeBench Kolmogorov-flow variants.

results.title: DRIFT-Net: A Spectral-Coupled Neural Operator for PDEs Learning

C1.justification: The abstract qualifies v1's categorical claim of outperforming the teacher and GPT-2 with 64× acceleration to comparable or superior performance with up to 64× acceleration. The central distribution-matching novelty, few-step generation contribution, and headline OpenWebText results remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of adversarial optimization stability, an exploration–exploitation mechanism, and difficulties transferring DiMO from image tokens to text. It interprets the new sensitivity results as guidance for tuning h versus M and explicitly discusses reduced protein diversity at large NFE budgets. These extend the earlier regularization and scaling-limit discussions.

D1.justification: v3 adds baseline reproduction and score-provenance details, stabilization practices, and implementation settings for the new evaluations. Teacher training is documented as approximately 200,000/350,000 steps instead of 5/7 epochs, without establishing whether the underlying runs changed. The front matter replaces the release promise with Code and Project Page links. Conversely, the software-version table and teacher pretraining GPU-hour estimates are removed.

E1.justification: v3 adds MMLU domain adaptation and GLUE MRPC paraphrase classification, substantially extending evaluation beyond generation and likelihood. PubMed also gains a fine-tuning evaluation, whereas v1 used it for zero-shot likelihood. Existing OpenWebText, seven-corpus zero-shot, and protein-generation coverage remains.

E2.justification: The core benchmark comparators remain. The latency comparison changes from GPT-2, teacher, AS, and RGAS in v1 Figure 3 to AR, MDLM, SDTT, and DiDi-Instruct in v3 Table 7. Appendix A.3 additionally reports a preliminary adapted-DiMO text experiment with entropy 4.0; v1 discussed DiMO without reporting this comparison.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a separate 1,024-sample MAUVE/Self-BLEU evaluation, downstream fine-tuning and classification protocols, protein clustering metrics, and a latency benchmark using H100, bfloat16, and batch size 16. The reported early-stage RGAS guidance ramp changes from 0–30 in v1 Appendix F.3 to 30–40 in v3 Appendix E.5. This documents a setting revision without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds RGAS parameter landscapes and global sensitivity analysis, text fidelity/diversity analysis, and protein clustering to investigate mode collapse. These examine robustness and diversity beyond v1's component ablations and structural-confidence measurements. The original cumulative and leave-one-out studies remain, while the AS–RGAS quality–latency curve is removed.

E5.justification: v3 adds fANOVA variance estimation using 1,000 sampled hyperparameter pairs at each of three NFE budgets. Appendix D.1 newly acknowledges variation across baseline training runs and explains reporting published scores matching the strongest reproductions. These disclosures do not provide run counts, seeds, or repeated-run uncertainty intervals for the headline comparisons.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results in Tables 6–7 and 9–13, including 2366.604 tokens/sec at 16 NFEs, PubMed post-adaptation perplexity 24.894, and MRPC accuracy/F1 of 62.3%/73.3%. These are newly reported evaluations, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical settings. Tables 1–2, the seven-corpus zero-shot values, and the scaling and pLDDT results remain; the earlier latency curve and many text excerpts are omitted or replaced.

M1.justification: The IKL objective, discriminator-based rewards, grouped normalization, score decomposition, model architectures, and two-phase RGAS algorithm remain. Remark 3.3 adds stabilization details without establishing a newly introduced component; the changed guidance ramp is an experimental parameter revision.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and background receive extensive rewriting. Related work is consolidated into Appendix A, the experimental narrative gains a downstream-task section, and the separate language showcase is removed while the long example appendix is heavily condensed. These are substantial editorial and structural changes beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a different document template, redraws the pipeline in Figure 2, replaces the latency plot with a new comparison table, and introduces sensitivity heatmaps and several result tables. It removes the software-version table, rearranges retained protein illustrations, and substantially changes the text-example displays. Retained plots and tables are also resized and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for the new evaluations and newer diffusion-language work, including MAUVE, fANOVA, MMseqs2, Dream, Mercury, Block Diffusion, and Fast-dLLM, while removing Luo's 2023 distillation survey. It expands comparisons with DiMO and trajectory-matching methods, but retains the central positioning relative to Diff-Instruct, SDTT, and DUO. Publication-metadata updates are not substantive additions.

T1.justification: The reward definition accompanying Theorem 4.1 in v1, renumbered Theorem 3.1 in v3, changes from log pν minus log pθ to log qν minus log qθ. This corrects the statement to use forward marginals, consistent with the IKL objective and existing appendix derivation. The principal assumptions, proofs, and density-ratio lemma otherwise retain their substance.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical support for preserved diversity, downstream utility, and practical efficiency. MAUVE/Self-BLEU, protein clustering, downstream tasks, and specified latency and sensitivity experiments address important gaps in v1's reliance on perplexity, token entropy, and pLDDT. These gains outweigh the loss of software versions and the AS–RGAS latency curve. Limitations remain: Table 6 contradicts the claim of highest MAUVE at every budget, and the nominally frozen MRPC evaluation unfreezes the final encoder block.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiDi-Instruct research. The text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained content across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds downstream evaluations, diversity measurements, practical speed benchmarks, and sampler sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-generation experiments, component ablations, model-scaling results, zero-shot evaluations, and protein-generation experiments.

results.title: Ultra-Fast Language Generation via Discrete Diffusion Divergence Instruct

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same three-part framework and broad claims of diverse, predictive alphas and superior cross-market portfolio performance. The additional experiments do not redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations of reward compatibility, capacity and scheduling tradeoffs, computational overhead and the distinction between IC and realized returns. Appendix E.8 explicitly qualifies short-window return dominance under market shocks, adding applicability limits absent from v1's discussion.

D1.justification: V3 newly discloses baseline repository pointers and default-setting instructions in D.3, plus caching details and training times in E.6. The original pseudocode, relation types, feature/operator inventory, default hyperparameters and AlphaSAGE code-access information are retained.

Tables 9–10 also introduce a Transformer encoder comparator and an RL configuration augmented with the proposed structural components, substantially expanding the comparisons used to assess AlphaSAGE's advantages.

E3.justification: The retained benchmarks keep their stated splits, metrics, portfolio rules and default settings. V3 adds protocols varying maximum expression length, encoder depth, hidden dimension and reward schedules, alongside a similar-parameter-budget Transformer comparison and crossed RL/GFlowNet component controls.

E4.justification: V3 retains the original ablations and sensitivity plots, then adds expression-length, encoder-depth, hidden-size and reward-schedule studies, encoder comparisons, framework/component disentanglement and runtime analysis in Appendix E.2–E.6. The regime discussion in E.8 supplies interpretation, not additional subperiod-test results.

E5.justification: V1 lacks explicit repeated-run counts and uncertainty summaries. V3 Appendix E.7/Table 12 reports means and standard deviations over five seeds for AlphaGen, AlphaQCM, AlphaForge and AlphaSAGE on CSI300. This is newly documented uncertainty, not evidence of an increase from a previously specified run count.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 entries and Table 2 are numerically unchanged. V3 adds AlphaAgent/CSI1000 outcomes and extensive diagnostic, runtime and repeated-run results. New comparisons include AlphaAgent exceeding AlphaSAGE on CSI500 ICIR, 0.396 versus 0.379, and AlphaQCM exceeding it on CSI1000 RIC, 0.107 versus 0.096.

M1.justification: The RGCN encoder, GFlowNet objective, early stopping, reward components, entropy regularization and dynamic combiner are retained. Algorithm 1 is unchanged apart from references; alternative encoders and schedules are experimental comparisons, not revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: V3 adds a finance-background subsection and targeted explanatory passages, edits citation and author/header presentation, and reorders the implementation, experiment, results and proof appendices. Most original prose and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains dataset and comparator rows, Figure 3 gains an AlphaAgent curve and revised legend, and Tables 5–12 add several distinct analytical displays. Existing figures and tables are relocated, Figure 2 receives a revised caption, and Table 13 redisplays selected CSI300 results rather than new evidence.

R1.justification: The reference lists and existing literature survey are unchanged. V3 gives the already-cited AlphaAgent an explicit role as an LLM comparator and adds a description of its multi-agent workflow, modestly extending comparative positioning.

T1.justification: The diversity proposition, proof and ridge corollary are unchanged, moving from Appendix E to F. The added standard portfolio-return formula in Section 2.1 explains existing financial concepts rather than introducing new theoretical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens experimental attribution and reliability: the similar-budget Transformer comparison and RL/component controls address alternatives unresolved by v1's ablations, while five-seed summaries quantify previously unreported variability. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including the retained all-correlation-metrics superiority claim contradicted by Table 1 and Table 13's repetition of CSI300 results without a new subperiod analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AlphaSAGE, with readable text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices. Retained content can be matched across appendix moves and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds CSI1000 evaluation, additional comparisons, diagnostic experiments, runtimes and five-seed summaries.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on CSI300, CSI500 and S&P500, including backtests, component ablations and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: AlphaSAGE: Structure-Aware Alpha Mining via GFlowNets for Robust Exploration

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same core contributions: the DATAMIND pipeline, DATAMIND-12K, the 7B/14B agents, and their benchmark-superiority claims. Additional experiments support these claims without substantively redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly attributes most performance gains to training data and adds interpretations concerning evaluator reliability, transfer across model families, scaffolding, and QRData's knowledge demands. It adds a tabular-data/text-only limitation and removes v1's conjecture about a cold-start strength beyond which RL provides no improvement. Appendix H also newly claims absence of contamination from header overlap.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents a ten-round interaction limit, eight 80GB A100 GPUs, training within two days, and baseline input-format reproduction details. The abstract changes the resource-release statement to completed release, but the reproducibility statement still promises future release, leaving availability internally inconsistent.

E1.justification: Appendix G.3 adds QRData evaluation, extending the retained tabular-analysis coverage to additional challenging causal-reasoning questions requiring domain knowledge. DABench, TableBench, and BIRD remain. The unexplained DATAMIND-14K reference in Appendix G.1 does not establish a distinct training corpus.

E2.justification: Data Interpreter changes from cited related work to an evaluated comparator across four backbones on DABench and TableBench (Table 5). Table 2 also introduces a direct comparison with pure SFT, zero-RL, and SFT-then-RL. These substantially expand the comparisons beyond the unchanged Table 1 comparator set.

E3.justification: The reported RL batch and minibatch sizes change from 16/2 to 32/4; this does not establish that the retained results were rerun. New experiments introduce training-data subsets, a Llama-3.1-8B backbone, 14B cold-start tests, external Qwen-2.5-72B judging, and Rouge-L evaluation of descriptive TableBench tasks.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's filtering and training-stability analyses, v2 tests data-volume scaling, training-strategy contributions, and dependence on evaluator choice and metric (Section 5.3 and Appendix G.4). It also adds header-overlap contamination analysis and extends the cold-start study from 7B to 14B.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three evaluation trials and the same pass@1/pass@3 aggregation. V2 newly discloses 'many trials' for zero-RL and SFT-then-RL, with validation-based checkpoint selection, and introduces Pearson correlation for judge agreement. Exact training-run counts, seeds, and uncertainty intervals are not supplied.

E6.justification: Table 1 is unchanged, including average pass@1 scores of 68.10% and 71.16%. Added results include zero-RL at 58.03% and SFT-then-RL at 63.42% average pass@1, Llama-8B at 65.56%, and DATAMIND-14B on QRData at 62.04%/77.62% pass@1/pass@3. Further additions report Data Interpreter, scaling, evaluator-agreement, and header-overlap findings.

M1.justification: The synthesis pipeline, trajectory filtering, hybrid SFT–DAPO objective, rewards, and rollout procedure remain unchanged in Sections 3–4. The prompt appendix is unchanged after renumbering. The Llama experiment applies the existing procedure without introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. V2 inserts an ablation subsection and two experimental appendices, renumbers Analysis and the prompt appendix, adds acknowledgments, and updates the publication header. These are localized structural changes rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 adds data-volume and judge-agreement plots and six comparison or analysis tables. It expands the cold-start plot with 14B series, updates Figure 1's display and caption, and relocates retained figures and tables. This substantially expands the visual presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Gandhi et al., OctoThinker, Llama 3.1, and DataWiseAgent to contextualize model selection and reproduction findings. Appendix G.2 strengthens the argument for agent training over scaffolding, while Section 6 and the detailed related-work appendix remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The task and trajectory definitions and Equations 1–8 are retained. The added scaling, evaluator, and contamination analyses introduce no new theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked direct full-benchmark training-strategy controls and an external check of its training/evaluation judge. V2 supplies both (Table 2 and Figure 5), alongside cross-family and QRData evaluations, substantially strengthening support for the training and generalization claims. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the undefined DATAMIND-14K reference, stale Qwen-only limitation, and overstrong no-contamination conclusion from header overlap.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DATAMIND work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison; retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds training ablations, evaluator comparisons, additional model and benchmark evaluations, and a contamination analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations in Table 1 and experiments on trajectory filtering, training stability, and cold-start training in Figures 3–6.

results.title: Scaling Generalist Data-Analytic Agents

C1.justification: The introduction refocuses the headline effectiveness claim from up to 34.2% improvement for the approaches collectively, citing Figure 4(b), to up to 20% for ReasoningBank, citing Table 1. The central contributions concerning reasoning memory, learning from failures, and memory-aware scaling remain intact.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning judge-noise tolerance, token-cost tradeoffs, and applicability to smaller models. Section 4.4 changes its explanation from weaker memories being harmed by scaling to receiving smaller benefits, although it inconsistently retains a statement that their performance decreases. Appendix D expands modular-memory possibilities; the substantive limitations in Appendix E remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a project code location, identifies and links the Gemma checkpoint, and newly states that baselines share retrieval and consolidation mechanisms. It also clarifies step counting. These improve documentation; the PDFs do not establish that baseline implementations changed, and the existing prompts, temperatures, and retrieval defaults are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same WebArena domains, Mind2Web generalization settings, and SWE-Bench-Verified tasks. The added experiments reuse existing task coverage; smaller backbones and simulated judge errors change configurations and controls.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator sets remain No Memory, Synapse, and AWM for web tasks, with AWM excluded from software engineering in both versions. Figure 5 retains the same memory comparisons, and the added Gemma evaluation uses the existing comparator set.

E3.justification: Figure 5 changes from three rollouts and Best-of-3 to five rollouts and Best-of-5. V2 also adds controlled ground-truth label flipping across simulated judge accuracies of 50–100%, a Gemma-3-12B-Instruct configuration, token-consumption evaluation, and five-rollout MaTTS pass@1 reporting across WebArena backbones. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: V2 adds a judge-accuracy assessment and controlled verification-noise study in Section 5, a token-cost breakdown in Appendix C.2, and a third case study diagnosing search-query failure in Appendix C.5. Existing failure-trajectory, retrieval-count, and pass@k analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, or reports confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. V2's probabilistic label flipping is an experimental control rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Existing entries in Tables 1–4 remain unchanged, but Table 1 adds MaTTS overall success rates of 51.8, 56.3, and 48.8 for the three backbones. New results include 72.7% judge accuracy, the noise-sensitivity scores, token totals, and Gemma success rates of 24.1% for ReasoningBank versus 17.1% without memory. Figure 5 replaces three-rollout results with five-rollout results; its changed values do not establish same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: The memory schema, success/failure extraction, embedding retrieval, append-only consolidation, and parallel/sequential MaTTS procedures remain unchanged. Figure 2 newly depicts the judge explicitly, but that component was already described in v1.

P1.justification: Revisions include localized introduction and related-work rewrites, expanded metric explanations, consistent use of memory extraction terminology, and replacing numbered analysis subsections with descriptive headings. V2 also adds an appendix contents page and an LLM-writing-assistance statement. The overall narrative structure is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds the judge-noise plot and failure-diagnosis illustration as Figures 8 and 17, plus cost and smaller-model Tables 5 and 6. It expands Table 1, redraws Figure 2 to show judge-mediated extraction, and updates Figure 5's legend and axis range for Best-of-5. Other displays are retained with relocation, renumbering, or limited formatting changes.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning against instance-level memory approaches and adds works including AutoGuide, Dynamic Cheatsheet, MobileSteward, Skill Set Optimization, and recent memory surveys. It removes the explicit sentence claiming to be first to explore memory-aware scaling. The broader positioning remains similar; publication updates and consolidation of duplicate references are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: The formal agent and streaming-task formulation is unchanged. V2 adds standard formulas for the existing success-rate and average-step metrics, without introducing new mathematical reasoning, assumptions, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of central claims: MaTTS evidence expands beyond one backbone/subset, Figure 8 directly investigates previously untested judge reliability, and Table 5 exposes inference overhead beyond v1's interaction-step accounting. The smaller-model experiment and added code-access information further improve applicability evidence and reproducibility. The revised Figure 5 discussion contains a contradictory claim of baseline deterioration, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReasoningBank and MaTTS research. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds broader MaTTS evaluations, judge-noise experiments, token-consumption measurements, and Gemma-3-12B-Instruct results.

before.justification: V1 reports original WebArena, Mind2Web, and SWE-Bench-Verified experiments, scaling evaluations, ablations, and case studies.

results.title: ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the principal claims about automatic generation, transferability, image quality, and mitigation. The conclusion narrows its novelty claim by removing v1's assertion that the exposed failure modes are 'not detectable by prior works.'

C2.justification: New Section 7 explicitly limits generator compatibility to models supporting image-embedding conditioning. Appendix B clarifies that naturalness is assessed relative to the diffusion baseline rather than perfect photorealism, while Appendix H treats attribute/relation generalization as preliminary. These add focused qualifications without replacing the central interpretation of misleading cues and shared model vulnerabilities.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands implementation disclosure: a 3,000-sample fine-tuning dataset, BitsAndBytes/TRL usage, quantization and module settings, GPU hardware, seed, and new attribute/relation templates and hyperparameters. It also states that code was submitted as supplementary material; public availability is not established. However, v1's explicit POPE training-split checkpoint procedure is replaced by less specific model-selection wording.

E1.justification: v2 expands beyond COCO object-presence failures to ten ObjectNet categories and five attribute/relation queries, including material, transparency, holding, and spatial relationships (Appendices G–H). These introduce a different visual distribution and substantively broader task requirements.

E2.justification: The DASH-LLM/DASH-OPT and Stable Diffusion v2.1/unCLIP comparison methods are retained. Added image-quality evaluations reuse existing diffusion baselines. GroundingDINO, YOLO-World, and YOLOv8 participate as filtering controls in a robustness experiment, not as competing hallucination-generation methods.

E3.justification: Reported fine-tuning settings change substantially: LoRA rank/alpha change from 8/32 to 2/2, epochs from 15 to 6, batch size from 16 to 8, and the optimizer and learning rate also change. POPE evaluation narrows from Random/Popular/Adversarial to Random. New protocols include CHAIR evaluation on 1,000 COCO validation images, paired 1–5 naturalness ratings, SSIM, detector-ensemble filtering, and a 756×756 resolution experiment.

E4.justification: v2 adds a four-detector ensemble experiment addressing dependence on OWLv2, human naturalness and SSIM analyses addressing image preservation, runtime/resolution scalability tests, and ObjectNet distribution-shift evaluation. Existing mapper and hyperparameter ablations remain. Conversely, the fine-tuned model's robustness results on GHOST-LLaVA and GHOST-GLM images disappear from Table 4.

E5.justification: Appendix F.9 newly reports SSIM means and standard deviations, and Table 23 specifies fine-tuning seed 42. The SSIM deviations describe variation across image outputs; the PDFs do not establish additional repeated training runs or new significance testing.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and matched original appendix results are retained. New reported outcomes include 28% ObjectNet success, 32.2% average attribute/relation success, 22.7% success with ensemble filtering, and naturalness ratings of 3.55 versus 3.56 for unCLIP. Table 4 replaces POPE baseline/fine-tuned scores of 88.5/90.7 with 88.7/93.2, adds CHAIRs 3.8/2.9 and CHAIRi 3.0/2.6, removes cross-model mitigation entries, and changes VQAv2 and captioning scores. Revised mitigation settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The original mapper, optimization losses, and diffusion-generation procedure remain unchanged. The new attribute/relation variant changes the query templates and explicitly omits object-detector filtering because its targets are not object-presence questions (Section 6.3 and Appendix H). This is a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: Most original exposition remains intact. Changes include localized wording edits, a rewritten fine-tuning appendix, reordered supplementary sections, and new extension, limitations, reproducibility, and AI-usage headings. The document also changes from preprint to ICLR conference presentation; this is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds qualitative figures for attribute/relation failures and ObjectNet, plus tables covering naturalness, runtime, resolution scaling, new tasks, and ensemble filtering. Table 4 changes its column structure, and the fine-tuning configuration table expands substantially. Original figure images are retained, with appendix displays relocated and the document reformatted into the conference layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting ObjectNet, CHAIR, SSIM, additional detectors, and training tools. Removing the original fine-tuning literature paragraph also removes references such as HaloQuest, ANTIDOTE, and CF-VLM. The main related-work discussion remains substantially unchanged, while the conclusion softens its exclusivity relative to prior work.

T1.justification: The optimization equations, mapper construction, compositional text embedding, and diffusion mathematics are retained. Notational edits do not change their substance, and v2 adds no theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: The ObjectNet evaluation, four-detector filtering study, and naturalness/SSIM checks substantially strengthen validation of generalization, object absence, and image preservation beyond v1's evidence. Expanded implementation details and explicit generator limitations also improve reproducibility and scope clarity. Removing cross-model mitigation results and weakening disclosure of POPE selection/test separation are drawbacks, and the higher-resolution sample counts conflict with the accompanying prose. Nevertheless, the added checks address important validity concerns and provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GHOST, with matching authors, core methodology, and retained experiments. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ObjectNet evaluation, attribute/relation experiments, detector-ensemble testing, naturalness ratings, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original hallucination-generation experiments, cross-model transfer results, human evaluation, ablations, and fine-tuning outcomes in Tables 1–4 and the appendices.

results.title: GHOST: Hallucination-Inducing Image Generation for Multimodal LLMs

C1.justification: The introduction and contribution summary add formal distribution-level sensitivity, covering-map structure for polynomial neural networks, and empirical chaos in deep ReLU training. These substantially broaden the claimed contributions while retaining the original critical-step-size and fractal-boundary claims.

C2.justification: Section 4 reframes the mechanism around invariant boundaries and folding, adds a transient-chaos explanation for initializations outside the orthogonal set, and explicitly states what the polynomial-network covering result does not establish. The new experiments introduce interpretations of EoS versus chaotic regimes and deviations from predicted momentum sharpness.

D1.justification: Appendix J adds architecture widths, data-subset sizes, momentum and weight-decay parameters, stopping criteria, and initialization-grid construction for the new neural experiments. The reproducibility statement also replaces the anonymous code-access link with a named GitHub repository. These are documented access instructions, not externally verified availability.

E1.justification: v3 extends the empirical coverage from synthetic scalar and matrix factorization to image-classification training with deep ReLU networks on a two-class CIFAR-10 subset containing 25 images per class. The earlier factorization coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Figures 4 and 12 add comparisons between plain GD and GD with Polyak momentum, which v1 did not evaluate. The Wang et al. (2022) convergence bound newly visualized in Figure 7 was already compared analytically in v1.

E3.justification: The new neural experiments introduce fixed-initialization learning-rate sweeps, MSE and cross-entropy losses, two hidden layers of width 100 or 25, and 5000- or 3000-iteration budgets. Initialization studies use a 300 × 300 grid, step size 0.05, and weight decay of 0 or 10^-3. These are new protocols; Appendix H retains the earlier experiment settings.

E4.justification: v3 adds learning-rate and initialization sensitivity analyses and tests whether the observed phenomena persist with momentum, cross-entropy, and removal of weight decay (Figures 4–5 and 12–13). The earlier regularization sweep and general-initialization/depth analyses remain as Figures 8–11.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed aggregation, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing histogram and box-counting regression reporting is retained; the added initialization grids and fixed-initialization sweeps do not introduce statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: New neural-network results show smooth small-step-size behavior transitioning to sensitive, scattered final norms and sharpness at larger step sizes, including with momentum and cross-entropy. New plots also show fractal-like loss and sharpness basins with and without weight decay. The earlier factorization findings, including the dimension estimate of 1.249, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The work continues to analyze constant-step gradient descent on the same matrix-factorization objectives. The neural-network architectures, momentum, and alternative losses appear as experimental settings or comparators, not as a revised proposed optimization method.

P1.justification: The contribution summary and mechanism discussion are substantially rewritten, and Section 4 is reorganized into orthogonal initialization, general mechanism, and neural-network experiments. The matrix decomposition proposition moves to Appendix G, several proof passages are extensively rewritten, and the experimental appendices are reorganized with a new Appendix J.

P2.justification: v3 adds multi-panel neural training and basin plots in Figures 4–5 and 12–13, a folding-map illustration in Figure 6, and a convergence-region comparison in Figure 7. Earlier appendix figures are retained as Figures 8–11; existing figures also receive caption, axis-label, and sizing edits.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Kalra et al. (2025), Marion and Chizat (2024), Krizhevsky et al. (2009), and Polyak (1964), and expands the comparison with Wang et al. (2022)'s proof techniques and convergence region. The main related-work framing remains; publication updates to existing references are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: v3 adds Theorem 2 and its positive-measure sensitivity argument, and generalizes v1's matrix-factorization covering-map proposition to polynomial neural networks in Proposition 6. Appendices D–G substantially revise proofs, including the regularized convergence correspondence, algebraic inequalities, and periodic-orbit lifting. Theorem 2 nevertheless states a norm bound where its proof tracks squared norm.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens mathematical support through corrected convergence arguments and explicit periodic-orbit lifting, while adding a positive-measure sensitivity argument. The documented CIFAR-10 studies provide evidence beyond v1's factorization experiments. These gains outweigh the remaining norm-versus-squared-norm inconsistency in Theorem 2 and the limited experimental scale; general neural-network chaos still is not proved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, and appendices. The earlier results can be matched across the later version's renumbering, relocation, and substantive additions.

after.justification: The earlier empirical results remain, and Section 4.3 and Appendix J add original neural-network training experiments on a two-class CIFAR-10 subset.

before.justification: Figures 1–3 report original gradient-descent simulations, convergence distributions, and a box-counting dimension estimate. Appendix I adds experiments with general initializations and deep matrix factorization.

results.title: Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes: Chaos and Fractal Convergence Region

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims: imitation-based CDCL branching, compact expert KeyTraces, reduced propagation, favorable runtime and generalization beyond random 3-SAT. The additional experiments support or qualify these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of applicability and failure conditions. It discusses diminishing returns from additional queries, difficulty-dependent runtime benefits over MiniSAT, overhead and underperformance of naive GNN integration, and low confidence as a possible explanation for Top-K failures. Appendix R explains why Kissat preprocessing can solve instances before learned branching is invoked.

D1.justification: Appendix P specifies the GNN configuration source, positive and negative edge sampling, and embedding substitution procedure. Appendix R identifies the PySAT interface and solver configuration choices. These add reproducibility information for new experiments; the original architecture and hardware disclosures, code/model link and release statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates planted random 3-SAT and five structured SATLIB families. Appendix M adds a distinct competition-derived, industrial-style SATCOMP domain. This materially broadens evaluation coverage, although the subset remains restricted to at most 100 variables and formulas fitting the model context.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add GQSAT* and SATformer* trained on the authors' data, plus explicit KeyTrace comparator rows. KeyTrace previously appeared only in the replay analysis. Appendix O adds MiniSAT to a direct runtime comparison, while Appendix R compares ImitSAT integrations against CaDiCaL and Kissat baselines. The original learned comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include matched-training controls, expanded query budgets and schedules, a 10-second MiniSAT cap and 30-instance runtime groups for SATCOMP, and runtime comparisons on the 50 hardest instances per range. CaDiCaL evaluation excludes preprocessing-solved instances; Kissat also receives a probing-disabled condition, with propagation normalized to the respective host solver. Figure 4 additionally changes PRET from four to five plotted instances.

E4.justification: The original augmentation, curriculum and single-query timing analyses remain. Appendix E adds delayed versus distributed versus immediate three-call schedules on the 100-variable and AIM sets. New analyses examine budget saturation, GNN input substitution, Top-K masking versus fallback, and how Kissat preprocessing affects opportunities for learned branching.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bars. v2 continues point-estimate reporting; its SATCOMP batch means aggregate instances rather than quantify repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: Shared rows in Tables 1–2 and the retained ablations preserve their values, but v2 adds extensive comparator, SATCOMP, variant and modern-solver results. Table 12 newly reports 6.11 seconds for ImitSAT versus 6.44 for MiniSAT on 50 hard 61–100-variable instances; Table 16 also shows worse-than-baseline JNH propagation ratios of 1.15 and 1.46. Figure 4 adds five-call curves and revises PRET timings alongside its changed plotted instance count, preventing a same-setting speedup interpretation.

M1.justification: The main KeyTrace construction, Perceiver AR learner, behavior-cloning objective and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendices P and Q introduce experimental alternatives: a self-supervised GNN encoder replacing CNF tokens with variable embeddings, and Top-K legal-action selection instead of immediate heuristic fallback. These supplement the retained method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local changes include an expanded related-work paragraph, an experimental roadmap, rewriting Appendix E, and adding Appendices M–R. Author contact information, conference headers and acknowledgments are also added; the established narrative is not extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain expert and retrained-baseline blocks, and Figure 4 is redrawn with additional curves and revised axes, legends and caption. New Figures 6–7 and Tables 9 and 12–17 substantially expand the visual evidence. The former Tables 9–10 become Tables 10–11 without substantive content changes.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds He et al. (2014) and Khalil et al. (2016), explicitly distinguishing MIP branching from SAT CDCL in search dynamics and learning formulation. Additional references support SATCOMP, modern solvers, PySAT and GNN efficiency discussion. This is a focused expansion of the existing positioning.

T1.justification: The SAT definitions, KeyTrace extraction equations, autoregressive formulation, loss, metric formulas and mathematical example in Appendix H are retained. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation through matched-training baselines, direct MiniSAT runtime comparisons, modern-solver integrations, and tests explaining design choices and failure conditions. These address important gaps in v1's evidence for practical usefulness and transfer. Limitations remain: industrial coverage is small-scale, uncertainty is unreported, and Section 5.3 retains a best-or-tied claim contradicted by the new PHOLE comparison (GQSAT*-5calls 0.77 versus ImitSAT-5calls 0.82). These issues temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in validation and understanding of applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ImitSAT research. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching despite added material and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds SATCOMP evaluation, retrained baselines, additional ablations, and CaDiCaL/Kissat integration results.

before.justification: v1 reports original propagation and runtime comparisons, KeyTrace replay measurements, and query-timing, augmentation and curriculum experiments.

results.title: Boolean Satisfiability via Imitation Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central suggestibility, calibration, saturation, and sampling-efficiency claims. The introduction narrows the reported TriviaQA advantage from 0.099 to 0.077 ECE, consistent with Section 3.2's corrected identification of MSP as the best average-ECE baseline.

C2.justification: Appendix C.1 substantially expands the reasoning about model-relative distractor plausibility, potentially factual distractors, and NLI reliability in specialized domains. Section 4 qualifies budget matching by acknowledging 32% greater FLOP cost. Appendix D.7 explains API restrictions on the cheaper variant, while smaller-model distractor generation is explicitly presented as untested.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the one-step validation prompt, additional NLI checkpoint identifiers and parameter counts, and FLOP accounting. It identifies the human evaluator as one author and updates the code pointer from dubai03nsr/dinco to victorwang37/dinco. Existing prompts and implementation descriptions largely remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix D.6 adds BioASQ14 factoid evaluation requiring biomedical expertise, substantially extending coverage beyond general factual questions and biographies.
