TriviaQA, SimpleQA, and biography generation remain; the additional analyses on those datasets do not themselves introduce new task coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding benchmark comparisons retain VC, K-VC, MSP, SC-VC, and SC, with the same applicable subset for biography generation. The added Qwen3-32B and BioASQ comparisons reuse these methods. Correcting K-VC's citation and identifying MSP as the strongest average-ECE baseline do not change comparator membership.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce Qwen3-32B, comparisons across four NLI checkpoints, and budgets of 8, 12, and 16 with varied self-consistency/distractor allocations (Appendices D.3–D.6). BioASQ uses 1,000 factoid questions from its Task B training set. The original experiments retain their splits, metrics, and default budget.

E4.justification: v2 adds distractor case studies and attribute analyses (C.1), extends the suggestibility analysis to SimpleQA and biographies (D.1), tests NLI-checkpoint and budget-allocation sensitivity (D.3–D.4), and compares one-step versus two-step execution (D.7). These substantially expand validation of the method's components and practical tradeoffs beyond v1's existing ablations.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly uses kernel density estimation for joint distractor-attribute distributions, a limited addition to statistical estimation. The existing 10,000-resample ECE/BS procedures and one-sided DeLong test remain unchanged in the renumbered significance-testing appendix; no new repeated-run uncertainty reporting is introduced.

E6.justification: The retained result tables have unchanged numerical entries, but v2 adds substantial results for distractor properties, sensitivity, efficiency, Qwen3-32B, and BioASQ. Newly reported DINCO ECE is 0.065 on Qwen3-32B TriviaQA and 0.071 on BioASQ (Tables 13 and 15). The TriviaQA summary changes from a 0.099 advantage over SC to 0.077 over MSP, correcting the comparison rather than demonstrating a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: Appendix D.7 introduces a one-step variant that validates each distractor through a follow-up correctness turn in the same conversation, replacing separate generation and validation calls. The original normalization, NLI weighting, and equal combination of self-consistency and normalized confidence remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact. v2 refines explanations and result summaries, expands and subdivides the appendices, updates cross-references, and adds a conference header and acknowledgments. This is targeted editing and organizational expansion rather than a comprehensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds distractor-example tables, correlation and density displays, sensitivity plots, and benchmark and efficiency tables. Figure 3 gains cumulative distributions and mean markers; Figure 4 gains FLOP annotations and an expanded caption. Existing tables are redistributed, and the numerical-confidence tables are retained as Tables 10–11.

R1.justification: v2 adds the BioASQ citation and connects possible smaller-model distractor generation to Li et al.'s contrastive decoding. K-VC is reattributed to the already-cited Tian et al. (2023), and the Tian et al. (2024) reference is removed. The broader positioning against joint confidence prompting and prior coherence methods is retained.

T1.justification: Section 2.3 adds an idealized invariance argument: with fully equivalent or contradictory claims, uniqueness weights become reciprocal equivalence-class sizes, yielding duplication invariance, while contradiction weights neutralize inclusion of the original claim. The original bias assumptions, normalization derivation, and equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for DINCO by examining previously untested distractor quality, NLI-checkpoint sensitivity, and budget allocation. It also corrects the strongest-baseline comparison and replaces an implication of equal compute with explicit FLOP accounting. These changes improve experimental credibility and practical interpretability. One qualification remains: Table 16's claim of calibration parity is too broad because the cheaper variant has worse Brier scores and AUC, but this does not outweigh the stronger validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DINCO research and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained experiments can be matched reliably, including v1 Tables 7–8, which become v2 Tables 10–11.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds biomedical QA experiments, larger-model evaluation, sensitivity analyses, distractor statistics, and an efficiency-variant comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original calibration experiments on TriviaQA, SimpleQA, and biography generation, together with suggestibility, sampling-budget, saturation, and NLI-ablation results.

results.title: Calibrating Verbalized Confidence with Self-Generated Distractors

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the demonstrated transferability claim from molecules of up to 60 atoms to approximately 900-atom polymers and polypeptides without retraining. The central method and dataset contributions remain. Although the title drops 'Universally', the abstract retains the aspiration of a universally transferable accelerator.

C2.justification: New appendices explain retaining SCF for orbital-based observables, restoration of electron number through orbital occupation, and the initialization bottleneck from XC grid evaluation. They distinguish chemical-accuracy energy predictions from precise SCF convergence. Appendix L also qualifies the largest-system evidence: the tested chains contain repetitive units, leaving chemically diverse large systems unverified.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the coming-soon project notice with a SCFbench dataset link and reports release. It additionally specifies DIIS space size 8, no level shifting or damping, the V100/GPU4PySCF timing setup, Python integration implementation, and use of QHFlow's QH9 defaults. Existing architecture and training hyperparameter tables are unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 Section 6.2 extends evaluation beyond SCFbench's molecules of up to 60 atoms to 110 QMugs molecules containing 100–200 atoms, a 703-atom Glycine-100 polypeptide, and a 905-atom polypropylene chain. This substantially broadens molecular-size coverage and introduces polymer/polypeptide scenarios.

E2.justification: QHFlow, previously only discussed as related work, is trained and evaluated on SCFbench in v3 Appendix K/Table 10. Existing QHNet Hamiltonian, density-matrix, and WALoss comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the stated ID evaluation subset from 1,000 molecules to 1% of the test set, although retained result tables have identical values; the PDFs do not establish whether experiments were rerun. Added protocols include end-to-end GPU timing, single-diagonalization energy/orbital-error evaluation, and the larger-system tests, whose Table 2 explicitly averages RIC over converged molecules only.

E4.justification: v3 adds a density-normalization ablation, initialization-cost decomposition, direct-to-solution error analysis, and two large-system case studies. Appendix B reports OOD RIC changing from 66.68% to 67.81% with normalization. The original D-Glucose auxiliary-basis analysis and WALoss sweep remain, under new appendix/table numbers.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported. Figure 1's shaded bands are retained, and the added timing and accuracy results introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained tables preserve their numerical entries, but substantial new results appear. Table 2 reports 73.42–81.77% RIC with 100% convergence on QMugs; the 703/905-atom cases require 10/8 iterations versus minao's 17/12. Figure 4 reports approximately 1.3× end-to-end speedup, Table 9 reports NequIP-L OOD energy MAE of 7.5e-4 Hartree, and Table 10 reports QHFlow ID/OOD RICs of 56.80%/146.97%.

M1.justification: The auxiliary-density representation, modified NequIP/QHNet prediction heads, MAE-plus-RMSE training loss, and density-to-Fock construction remain unchanged. The hybrid/meta-GGA approximations already appeared in v1 Appendix C. Normalization and direct-to-solution evaluations do not establish changes to the proposed initializer.

P1.justification: The title and parts of the abstract/introduction are revised, related-work attribution is clarified, and explanatory subsections are added. A large-system subsection and additional appendices extend the structure, but most existing prose, the main section sequence, and the conclusion remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the displayed evidence with a QMugs scalability table, a two-panel runtime and initialization-breakdown figure, and direct-to-solution and QHFlow tables. Figure 2 changes from a small text-wrapped inset to a large full-width display. Retained tables are relocated or renumbered, and the extended-results caption clarifies metric units.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for QMugs, another electron-density prediction study, GPU4PySCF, and efficient equivariant computations. Section 3.2 revises attribution of kernel-based versus equivariant density-matrix methods. Appendix K positions QHFlow as potentially complementary while retaining the paper's central transferability argument.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(17), including density-projection and Fock-construction derivations, are retained. The added normalization and SCF-consistency discussions explain standard physical requirements and existing operations without introducing a new proof or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central scalability and practical-acceleration claims: v1 stopped at 60 atoms and iteration ratios, whereas v3 adds larger-system tests and end-to-end timing that includes initialization overhead. The normalization analysis, QHFlow comparison, and explicit limitations further improve evaluation and interpretation. The unexplained ID sample change despite identical retained tables remains a reproducibility concern, but the new evidence addresses important gaps and provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same electron-density-based SCF acceleration method and SCFbench study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison despite the title change and expanded experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds larger-molecule evaluations, normalization experiments, runtime measurements, direct-to-solution accuracy results, and QHFlow experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original SCFbench experiments, functional and basis-set transfer tests, auxiliary-basis analysis, and WALoss experiments in Section 6 and the appendices.

results.title: Towards a Transferable Acceleration Method for Density Functional Theory

C1.justification: The claimed validation expands from tense-jailbreak mitigation on three models to four models and explicit mitigation of GCG and LogiBreak in the introduction's contribution list. Tense manipulation becomes an example of broader targeted-jailbreak applicability. The central circuit-guided scaling and safety–utility claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning cross-attack generalization and why circuit-selected heads outperform arbitrary-head interventions in safety–utility balance. It also explains why its unified evaluation pipeline can produce ASRs different from cited papers. The original mechanistic explanation and architecture-related limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds RepE steering settings, OLMo training configurations and refusal prompts, and attack-specific learning rates. Tables 3–4 document additional vulnerable and random head lists. A new reproducibility statement describes supplementary code and instructions; the public repository disclosure and two-H100 hardware specification already existed.

E1.justification: v2 expands beyond tense jailbreaks to GCG adversarial suffixes and LogiBreak logical reformulations. Appendix A.2.1 adds HarmBench behaviors for GCG training/evaluation and English LogiBreak data. The original JBB-Behaviors, chat-training datasets, OR-Bench, and MMLU coverage remains.

E2.justification: Representation Engineering (RepE) becomes an evaluated comparator in the retained tense benchmark, rather than merely cited background. New Table 4 adds Random Scaling and Random PFT controls. The existing SFT, DPO, Circuit Breaker, RepBend, and head-ablation comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds OLMo configurations, attack-specific training, separate out-of-domain testing, and a control applying the pipeline to 10 non-circuit heads. Appendix A.2.2 specifies a 7e-6 preventative-fine-tuning learning rate for GCG/LogiBreak versus 9e-6 for Llama tense experiments. Table 2 introduces zero-clipping of negative R-Scores. The reported judge prompt also drops its opening sentence; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's brief random-ablation comparison, v2 Appendix A.3 tests learned scaling and preventative fine-tuning on non-circuit heads and reports Temporal Head intervention controls. Section 5.3 adds cross-attack generalization testing. New OLMo probe and circuit figures extend the mechanistic analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed-based variability, repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing prompt-reformulation counts and distribution-plot reporting practices are retained; additional results do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: All 27 original main-table rows retain their numerical values. v2 adds RepE and OLMo results, including OLMo ASGuard ASR of 9% versus 28% for its base model. New Table 2 reports ASGuard ASRs of 1% on GCG and 13% on LogiBreak; the separate out-of-domain experiment reports 1% and 15%. Table 4 adds Random Scaling/PFT ASRs of 25%/5%, with Random PFT over-refusal of 89%.

M1.justification: The three-stage procedure remains circuit-based head identification, channel-wise scaling, and preventative fine-tuning with fixed scaling vectors subsequently removed. Sections 2–3 retain the same components and objectives; application to additional attacks and models does not establish an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the section sequence remain intact. Local additions include the out-of-domain subsection, random-head appendix, and reproducibility statement, alongside terminology, acknowledgments, and conference-header edits. The revision does not extensively rewrite the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The main results table expands, Figure 2 gains an OLMo panel and RepE markers, and new tables display additional attacks and random-head controls. The vulnerable-head table moves to the appendix and expands. New OLMo probe/circuit figures are added, while Figures 5–6 receive corrected model/head captions without changing their plotted data.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gradient Cuff, Mehrbod et al.'s circuit-discovery work, and the OLMo reference, with explicit positioning against detection and single-token ablation in Appendix A.3. LogiBreak receives expanded discussion, but its underlying paper was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The circuit definitions, scaling derivation, training objectives, and numbered equations remain unchanged. However, v2 Table 2 adds an effective max(0, R) definition for negative robustness scores and uses the clipped values in Overall scores. This is a limited mathematical metric-definition change, without new theoretical results or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for both the method's design and applicability. Table 4 tests the full intervention pipeline on non-circuit heads, addressing a question v1's simple ablation comparison left open. Additional attack and transfer experiments test applicability beyond tense manipulation, supported by another model and RepE comparisons. The new attack protocols remain briefly documented and uncertainty reporting is unchanged, but the added controls and broader tests materially strengthen the empirical case.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ASGuard research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds OLMo experiments, additional jailbreak evaluations, and random-head controls.

before.justification: v1 reports original three-model benchmark results, attention-head interventions, linear probes, and circuit analyses.

results.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack

C1.justification: Both versions retain the dual-nature diagnosis, visual forgetting explanation, VAPO contribution, and benchmark-superiority claims. v3 explicitly emphasizes growing reasoning length, but v1 already attributes deterioration to prolonged reasoning. The added appendix evidence does not redefine the main contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations involving training-data bias and autoregressive objectives, arguments about gate normalization and anchor placement, and interpretations supporting independence from GPT-5 and applicability beyond single-image tasks. It also argues that gains are not merely attributable to longer outputs. However, B.10 retains the single-image-only limitation despite the new multi-image study in B.23.

D1.justification: A.6 newly documents filtering and resampling, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B similarity filtering above 0.95, and claim-diversity constraints. B.9 adds the one-time claim-generation cost of 38 minutes. These are focused reproducibility additions; the main training configuration remains unchanged. The project-page link provided in v1's abstract is omitted from v3.

E1.justification: v3 adds V* and RealWorldQA evaluations for fine-grained perception and spatial reasoning (B.14). More substantially, B.23 introduces explicit multi-image training on a ViRL39K subset and evaluation on BLINK and MuirBench, extending coverage to relationships across images. The original ten benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: v3 Table 24 adds actual comparisons against MM-Eureka, PAPO, and VL-Rethinker, which were cited but not evaluated as comparators in v1. Conversely, v1 Table 15's dedicated comparison against Qwen2.5-VL-3B, InternVL2.5-2B, R1-OneVision-3B, and VLAA-Thinker-3B is removed. The main-table comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The existing main experimental settings are retained, but new studies substantially expand the evaluation design: audits of 500 failures and 250/2000 examples, Qwen3-VL-8B experiments, single-cut recovery at four reasoning depths, difficulty and 300-token length stratification, and a roughly 2500-example multi-image training setting. These are additional protocols, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, v3 adds error co-occurrence and claim-quality audits, sensitivity to alternative claim generators, self-supervision tests, single-cut recovery, training/evaluation overlap checks, gate activation and curriculum analyses, anchor-placement comparisons, and reasoning-length analyses (A.3 and B.11-B.22). These test substantial new questions about reliability, mechanisms, and robustness.

E5.justification: No repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing practice is added or revised. The new audit percentages and inter-generator differences are descriptive results; the differences written with plus/minus notation in B.12 are not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1-3 and the matched supplementary main results and K/beta ablations retain their values. Substantial new results include Qwen3-VL averages of 68.8 for VAPO versus 64.9 for GRPO (Table 16), and multi-image averages of 61.2 versus 58.7 (Table 27), alongside new audit and control findings. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under unchanged conditions. v1's dedicated 3B comparison is deleted.

M1.justification: The default VAPO objective, anchor scoring, late-emphasis weighting, and accuracy gate remain unchanged. v3 adds limited procedural variants: iterative self-generated claims during rollout (B.15), a relaxed-gate curriculum (B.18), and cross-image claim generation (B.23). The expanded filtering description does not establish that the original method was changed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion receive localized edits, and the header changes from preprint to ICLR 2026 publication. The appendix gains B.11-B.23 and loses D.5. Most existing exposition and section ordering remain intact; the expansion primarily reflects added scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial tabular presentation for audits, generation costs, new evaluations, and diagnostic controls (Table 4 and Tables 12-27), removes v1 Table 15, and reflows the appendix. Added appendix prose is displayed in blue. Existing main figures and Tables 1-3 retain their displays, while surviving supplementary tables are renumbered and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for selective reasoning, visual instruction tuning, V*, MuirBench, Qwen3 embeddings, and other VLM research, and updates citation placement in related work. The central positioning around visual forgetting and training-based mitigation remains intact. Bibliographic venue updates do not constitute additional research-positioning changes.

T1.justification: The GRPO and VAPO mathematical definitions and Equations 1-5 are unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. The new gate discussion is qualitative interpretation, while the single-cut recovery analysis extends an empirical testing procedure.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical validation by auditing the supervision whose quality v1 identified as a limitation, testing alternative and self-generated claims, probing recovery and gating mechanisms, and demonstrating multi-image applicability. These additions address important uncertainties about reliability and generality, outweighing the loss of dedicated 3B comparisons. Reporting remains imperfect: B.10 still claims exclusively single-image coverage, and B.15's stated average gap disagrees with Table 18's 51.9 versus 52.5. The main benchmark scores themselves are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VAPO study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds claim-quality audits, controlled analyses, additional model comparisons, and new task evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM experiments, visual-forgetting analyses, VAPO training results, ablations, and computational measurements in the main text and appendices.

results.title: More Thought, Less Accuracy? On the Dual Nature of Reasoning in Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the mode-overlap hypothesis, Tweedie-mean framework, hybrid resampling/correction contribution, and claims of improved alignment without training or gradients. The additional experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of rare-concept benefits, corrector-only attribute binding, and sparse backgrounds as adherence to specified concepts. It expands discussion of solver applicability and memory/runtime tradeoffs while retaining the original limitations. Its new assertion of matching or beating every Table 2 category overstates the evidence: RareBench Relations ImageReward is 0.2588 for CO3 versus 0.3620 for R2F.

D1.justification: V2 adds an explicit code-repository address, documents the Tweediemix adaptation and human-rating procedure, and supplies memory and reduced-budget timing information. The existing Stanza parsing procedure, core hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds rare and novel concept generation through RareBench's Concat, Relations and Complex categories, plus explicit-background prompt variants. T2ICompbench Complex and PixArt were already evaluated qualitatively in v1; their new quantitative results are not new coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Magnet and Tweediemix, with Tweediemix evaluated without its LoRA customization stage. Complex-prompt comparisons introduce R2F. Conversely, the efficiency comparison changes from v1 Table 3 to v2 Table 8 by dropping SynGen and Composable Diffusion.

E3.justification: V2 adds DINOv2 scoring and an 11-participant human evaluation using anonymized, randomly ordered images and normalized 0–5 ratings. It also introduces 10- and 20-step DDIM/DPM++ evaluations and a 20-step CO3 efficiency comparison. The original 50-step SDXL setup remains documented unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds corrector-only ablations with and without weight modulation, a controlled background-prompt comparison, robustness tests across solvers and reduced sampling budgets, and memory/runtime tradeoff analysis. The original hyperparameter sweeps and failure cases are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests, and retain the same generic reproducible-seed statement. The new participant count describes evaluation design rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V2 retains the original Table 1 BLIP-VQA/ImageReward values and hyperparameter sweeps while adding substantial quantitative and qualitative results. For example, new Table 2 reports T2ICompbench Complex ImageReward of 0.4406 for CO3 versus 0.3083 for SDXL. The resampling ablation average changes from 0.9407 to 0.9437 despite unchanged component scores. Table 8 also reports Table 7's 10-step SDXL scores under a 50-step label.

M1.justification: The contrastive corrector, zero-sum resampler, unit-sum correction, normalization and closeness-aware weight modulation remain unchanged in Algorithms 1–3. Additional solver experiments and explicit algorithm input declarations do not document a revised CO3 mechanism.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, changes CO3's expansion to Concept Contrasting Corrector, edits prose and notation, and reorganizes experimental discussion and appendix sections. Most introductory, methodological and retained analytical text remains close to v1.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands and reformats tables, adds evaluation and analysis displays, annotates Figure 2 with sampling thresholds, replaces the complex-prompt grid, and reduces the PixArt grid. New ablation, background and rare-concept figures accompany relocated material; the original SDXL example grid and failure cases survive as Figures 9 and 8.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations and limited positioning for Magnet, R2F/RareBench, DINOv2 and Skreta et al.'s density-based composition. The related-work organization and relationship to Composable Diffusion and the already-cited Tweediemix remain largely intact.

T1.justification: Equation 9 changes the compositional distribution from a product of conditional image distributions to an image prior multiplied by concept likelihoods, a substantive formula revision. The unit-sum and zero-sum propositions and appendix proofs otherwise retain their substance, with notation and numbering changes.

improvement.justification: V1's complex-prompt and PixArt generalization evidence was largely qualitative. V2 adds quantitative comparisons, human ratings, relevant baselines and targeted component/sampler tests, substantially strengthening support for its alignment and generalization claims. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, although Table 2's sweeping superiority statement and Table 8's conflicting SDXL step label weaken confidence in those comparisons.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same CO3 research, with matching authors, algorithms and retained experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds human evaluations, rare-concept results, quantitative PixArt comparisons, and sampler, sampling-budget and memory measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark measurements, component and hyperparameter ablations, runtime measurements, and generated-image comparisons, including appendix results.

results.title: STEER AWAY FROM MODE COLLISIONS: IMPROVING COMPOSITION IN DIFFUSION MODELS

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same claims: a unified continuous Fourier video representation, arbitrary spatial/temporal sampling, improved reconstruction and greater computational efficiency. Added experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets learned frequency concentrations as adaptation to video structure and fine-detail reconstruction. Appendix B.3 explains fixed-basis weakness through sparse frequency allocation and motivates 512 functions as a capacity compromise. The existing limitations concerning oversmoothing, finite representational capacity and broader degradations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the L1 reconstruction loss, describes the 256-dimensional encoder-output mapping used in ablations, and documents corruption generation through normalization, noise addition, 8-bit rounding and compression. Figure 14 explains the unavailable B-AVSR checkpoint. Existing hardware, optimizer and project-access information is retained.

E1.justification: Adobe240, GoPro, Vid4 and REDS remain the datasets, with the same principal super-resolution tasks. v2 extends input conditions through Gaussian-noise and noise-plus-H.264 tests on Vid4 (Appendix B.4), alongside a selected camera-motion-blur example in Figure 13.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds RDN-HIIF to the image-super-resolution comparators. Appendix B.2 and Table 7 introduce a separate comparison against BasicVSR, TTVSR and FTVSR, substantially broadening the evaluated competitor families. The V2.5 comparison against SAVSR, B-AVSR and ST-AVSR already existed in v1.

E3.justification: New controlled experiments vary basis size from 128 to 768, compare learned and fixed frequencies, and evaluate 25% and 50% training budgets. Appendix B.4 adds five noise levels, with and without H.264 compression, evaluated against clean ground truth at Vid4 spatial ×4 and temporal ×2. The retained main benchmark protocols are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds learned-frequency analysis (Section 4.4/Figure 6), controlled basis-capacity, frequency-learning and training-duration ablations (Table 8), and corruption robustness tests (Table 9). Figure 13 also examines a motion-blurred example. These substantially extend v1's model-scaling and temporal-consistency analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new frequency histograms and corruption-noise standard deviations do not represent experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial baseline, ablation, corruption and qualitative results. Existing values also change under the same reported settings: V3's Adobe240 Average becomes 32.29/0.917 from 32.24/0.916 in Table 1; its VFI result becomes 33.43/0.936 from 33.31/0.935 in Table 3; and tOF becomes 0.254 from 0.257. Table 2's V3 scores and Table 3's VideoINR scores also change. These revisions are not explained as a documented method or protocol change.

M1.justification: The RVRT-conditioned local Fourier representation, globally learned frequencies and PSF-aware sampling remain unchanged. V3-Large and V2.5 already appear in v1. Specifying the L1 reconstruction loss in v2 documents an existing training objective rather than establishing a method change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. v2 expands selected PSF and baseline explanations, subdivides Appendix B, moves computational complexity into Section 4.5, and updates the conference header. These are limited editorial and organizational changes rather than a pervasive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds the frequency-analysis visualization, two qualitative comparison figures and three substantive tables covering VSR comparisons, ablations and corruptions. Table 2 gains the HIIF row, and the existing computational table moves into the main text. Most earlier qualitative figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for CLIT, HIIF, BasicVSR, TTVSR, FTVSR and the signal-processing textbook, and expands discussion of AISR generations and specialized VSR competitors. The central novelty positioning and related-work section remain largely unchanged. Thera's publication update is bibliographic maintenance.

T1.justification: The mathematical representation and Equations 1–4 are retained, apart from notation and punctuation corrections. Additional Nyquist/PSF explanations and discussion of fixed-basis capacity introduce no substantive new formal definition, derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification: Table 8 directly tests basis design and training-budget choices that v1 mainly supported through benchmark performance and intuition, while Table 9 establishes behavior under input corruption. Broader comparisons and loss disclosure further improve evaluation and reproducibility. Table 7's unspecified evaluation dataset and missing H.264 settings limit some additions, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VFF/V3 research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, basis analyses, ablations and input-corruption experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original super-resolution experiments, including PSNR/SSIM, temporal consistency, computational requirements and appendix evaluations of V2.5.

results.title: Continuous Space-Time Video Super-Resolution with 3D Fourier Fields

C1.justification: The central novelty claim and four-pathway contributions remain unchanged. However, the introduction revises its quantified risk claims: the memory-related refusal-rate reduction changes from 55% to 45%, and failure to reject malicious external tools changes from approximately 84% to 93%. These refine the claimed empirical magnitude without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes cumulative model-safety decay from incident-triggered memory collapse, develops optimization-pressure and domain-sensitivity explanations, and discusses interactions between memory and tool-failure risks. Appendix B adds substantive deployment guidance. Additional qualifications address DPO's supervision/computational costs and the limitations of post-hoc workflow patches; the earlier general limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies temperatures for AgentNet/tool experiments, DPO's 1,000 preference pairs, and the ensemble mitigation prompt. Many details emphasized in the revised main text, including three SE-Agent rounds and 20 AFlow iterations, already appeared in v1's appendices. The abstract changes its availability statement from 'code and data' to 'code' while retaining the same repository link.

E1.justification: V2 adds a nonfunctional-tool scenario using 30 GAIA-inspired cases and approximately 1,300 Memento memories from DeepResearcher (Appendix D.10), plus PKU-RLHF-10K preference data for mitigation training (E.1). The original benchmark and domain coverage largely remains. The additional code/math and OSWorld scores in Tables 16–17 are attributed to prior papers.

E2.justification: The model sets in the original main comparisons are retained. Appendix D.8 newly compares supervised fine-tuning with RL-based self-play, and D.9 directly compares AgentNet memory evolution with AFlow workflow evolution using Qwen2.5-72B on HumanEval.

E3.justification: SALAD-Bench evaluation changes from 1,000 sampled instances to all 21.3k instances. External-tool evaluation changes from 814 to 371 samples, adds filtering for concrete security consequences, and changes the judge from Llama3.1-70B-Instruct to Gemini-2.5-Flash. New longitudinal protocols evaluate 200 training steps and 100 interaction rounds at ten-step or ten-round intervals.

E4.justification: V2 adds longitudinal safety analyses, data-quality and SFT/RL ablations, domain-level case analysis, cross-pathway susceptibility comparisons, nonfunctional-tool confabulation tests, and human validation of tool judgments (Figures 5–6; Appendix D.6–D.11). It also tests model/workflow mitigations and the utility cost of memory mitigation. V1's existing dynamic-memory simulation and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average static AgentNet results over three runs with error bars. V2 clarifies that the retained human-comparison table covers one run, adds Cohen's kappa for tool judgments—0.72 for GPT-4o and 0.82 for Qwen3-235B—and introduces LOWESS trend fitting. No increase in repeated-run counts is established.

E6.justification: Table 6 revises SALAD-Bench and RedCode results; the 7B Coder's initial/evolved RedCode refusal rates change from 100.0%/27.5% to 31.3%/0.6%. AFlow's reported refusal rates change from 46.3%/6.3% to 36.3%/5.6%. Table 3's highest refusal rate changes from GPT-4o-mini's 15.9% to Qwen3-235B's 7.28%, under changed samples and judging conditions. Numerous temporal, utility, ablation, confabulation, and mitigation results are newly reported.

M1.justification: The underlying evolution frameworks remain unchanged. V2 specifies DPO-based post-evolution alignment and adds a safety instruction inside AFlow's ensemble node, whereas v1 discussed generic safety post-training and inserting guardrail nodes. These are limited adaptations to the mitigation procedures.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites setup and mitigation passages, expands explanatory transitions, renames Sections 2 and 4, and moves the standalone Discussion to Appendix A. The appendices are reorganized around deployment guidance, experimental settings, combined results/showcases, and mitigations. This materially changes narrative organization beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: V2 adds temporal plots in Figures 5 and 6(b), a medical-case graphic in Figure 6(a), and a visual summary of the existing deidentification case in Figure 8. It adds the deployment checklist and performance Tables 16–19, relocates the original judge-comparison table to Table 20, updates Figure 3's plotted scales, and adopts conference formatting with widespread figure, table, and code-box reflow.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands positioning relative to safe open-ended systems, episodic-memory risks, and multi-agent risks, explicitly presenting this study as an empirical complement to conceptual work. Appendix B additionally connects deployment recommendations to monitoring, tool-security, and memory-defense research. These additions extend the research context beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Section 2 retains the same agent-component formalization, evolution function, iterative update, and cumulative-utility objective. The new mechanism discussions and experiments introduce no formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V1 relied largely on endpoint safety comparisons and left model/workflow mitigation conceptual. V2 substantially strengthens the study with temporal evidence, mechanism ablations, tool-judge validation, implemented mitigations, and a check that memory mitigation preserves task performance. These address important gaps in empirical support and practical interpretation. Large unexplained RedCode/AFlow revisions and preliminary causal controls limit confidence in some findings, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same misevolution study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original evaluations and adds longitudinal measurements, ablations, confabulation tests, judge validation, and mitigation experiments. Tables 16–17 explicitly reproduce earlier papers' results, but numerous other results are original.

before.justification: Sections 3–4 and the appendices report original safety evaluations, agent trajectories, and memory/tool mitigation experiments across four evolutionary pathways.

results.title: Your Agent May Misevolve: Emergent Risks in Self-evolving LLM Agents

C1.justification: The central claims remain that initialization creates seed-specific fingerprints, these persist through training and distribution shifts, and SeedPrints supports birth-to-lifecycle attribution with strong deployment performance. The emphasis on large-scale pretraining and new empirical examples supports these existing claims rather than introducing a different core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds a representation-contraction explanation for initialization bias and interpretations of hyperparameter sensitivity and null approximation. It explicitly discusses restricted-API limitations and qualifies merger robustness: interpolation with unrelated weights can dilute the fingerprint, explaining the reported merge failure. These are substantive additions to applicability and mechanism discussions.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, states that both null implementations are provided, and documents softmax temperature 10 and detector defaults n=2000, length=1024 and m=0.1dout for Sections 5.2–5.3, plus separate ablation defaults. These materially improve implementation guidance; their disclosure alone does not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

E1.justification: The principal coverage addition is OLMo-2-7B's heterogeneous-corpus pretraining trajectory, extending the existing controlled-pretraining scenario. The lineage-identification task, OpenWebText/TinyStories/The Stack experiments and six deployment transformations remain. Additional model sizes and catalog entries primarily expand experimental configurations.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain Intrinsic, REEF, PCS and ICS, with Gradient additionally evaluated on LeaFBench. The new experiments reuse these methods. HuRef in v2's cross-size comparison is already identified with PCS/ICS in v1, rather than establishing a new comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds comparisons of OLMo checkpoints against the final checkpoint, controlled sweeps of input count, sequence length and fingerprint size with accuracy/FPR metrics, and targeted cross-size Qwen comparisons. The reported LeaFBench pool expands from 58 to 65 models, and fine-tuning evaluation extends to Llemma at 700B tokens. These substantially expand evaluation protocols and configurations.

E4.justification: New analyses test the null approximation against approximately 2,500 independent-model pairs and Gaussian simulations (Appendix B), sensitivity to three hyperparameters (Table 8), and whether fingerprints collapse across model sizes within Qwen (Appendix D.3). The original continual-training and checkpoint analyses remain, largely relocated into Appendix D.

E5.justification: v2 adds analytical variance-based z-scores and one-sided Gaussian p-values, together with empirical assessment of the null approximation and dependence assumptions. The original ten-trial averaging remains documented for simulation-based results in Appendix D.2; an increase in repeated-run counts is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial trajectory, ablation, null-validation, cross-size and pairwise results. Main-table p-values now use the analytical test, so their smaller magnitudes are not comparable performance gains. Table 7 reports Merge AUC 0.959 versus 1.000 under the revised detector/pool. Retained empirical-null results also change: Qwen s2000 versus s42 hidden-state t/U p-values change from 0.130/0.095 to 0.230/0.295 (v1 Table 9; v2 Table 9b).

M1.justification: v1 uses simulated Gaussian reference correlations with t-tests or Mann–Whitney U-tests. v2 introduces an analytical Gaussian z-test on mean Kendall correlation and adopts it for the main results. Its simulated-null procedure also now includes identity-dimension selection and intersection. These change inference, while the underlying mean-based fingerprint extraction remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, bias explanation and algorithm section are extensively rewritten. Contributions become an explicit list, lifecycle evaluation receives a separate subsection, and the appendices are reorganized with a contents page. Much existing experimental material moves into a consolidated simulation-based-results appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adds the OLMo trajectory and null-validation figures, substantially redraws the initialization-bias figure, and simplifies main experimental tables around analytical p-values. Earlier checkpoint plots are combined into Figure 5, while new ablation, cross-size and pairwise-results tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations connecting initialization bias to representation contraction (Li et al., 2026), Gaussian approximations to earlier work (Carlini et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2019), and the new OLMo/Llemma evaluations. The active/passive fingerprinting taxonomy and principal contrast with post-hoc methods remain.

T1.justification: v1 contains algorithmic definitions but no comparable theoretical development. v2 adds analytical-null derivations, formal noise and margin assumptions, stability and instability lemmas, and proofs of bottom-m recovery and sample-complexity bounds in Appendices B–C.

improvement.justification: v1's all-stage claim relied on controlled pretraining experiments with little null-model or hyperparameter validation. v2 adds a realistic OLMo trajectory, independent-model/null checks, ablations, implementation defaults and explicit deployment limitations, substantially strengthening empirical support and reproducibility. Gains are tempered by new inconsistencies: Lemma C.2 uses stronger noise assumptions than stated, and Table 5 incorrectly flags Intrinsic's 0.9470 Llemma score despite the stated 0.8 threshold.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SeedPrints and retain identifiable corresponding methods and experiments. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds OLMo pretraining evaluations, null-distribution validation, hyperparameter ablations and cross-size analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original initialization-bias, training-lineage, distribution-shift and fingerprinting benchmark experiments, including additional Qwen results in Appendix B.

results.title: SeedPrints: Fingerprints Can Even Tell Which Seed Your Large Language Model Was Trained From

C1.justification: The abstract, three contribution bullets and conclusion retain the central claims about feedforward, pose-free, generalizable and view-consistent stylization. The introduction makes a limited narrowing: global attention now preserves fine visual details in Gaussian renderings, replacing the earlier claim about preserving geometric details.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive applicability limits involving thin or cluttered structures, extreme palettes, lighting changes, invented colors and oversmoothing. Appendix A.5 attributes increasing-view degradation primarily to VGGT reconstruction instability, extending v1's discussion of training-view mismatch and unstable Gaussians. Appendix A.3 also develops the explanation of why independent frame conditioning harms reconstruction.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 supplies previously missing layer counts, initialization, voxel size, optimizer, 15k-iteration training schedules, learning rates, augmentation and input sampling details. V2 also documents comparison hardware and displays the evaluation styles. Image/scene-loss pseudocode is removed and 3D-loss pseudocode revised. Code availability changes from promised to announced, although the reproducibility statement still says release will follow acceptance.

E1.justification: V2 reports DELAUNAY as an additional style-image source and evaluates two-style blending and adjustable stylization strength. CO3D, DL3DV-10K, Tanks and Temples, and WikiArt remain the principal content/style coverage. Displaying the 50 held-out styles adds documentation rather than establishing a new test set.

E2.justification: V1 compares against StyleRF and StyleGS. V2 retains StyleGS under its full name, StyleGaussian, removes StyleRF from the reported comparisons, and adds G-Style, SGSST and Styl3R. StylizedGS participates in Figure 5 and appendix Tables 5–6, although excluded from the main quantitative tables.

E3.justification: V2 substantially broadens evaluation with ArtFID, supplementary FID, LPIPS-gray, CFSD and color-matching metrics, plus comparative stylization timing. The added timing protocol specifies common GH200 hardware, method-specific resolutions and inclusion of per-scene fitting costs. Appendix A.4 also introduces failure-case filtering for StylizedGS, although its application is not fully clear.

E4.justification: V2 expands loss ablations across additional styles in Figures 8–10, adds blending and strength-control experiments in Figure 6, and presents explicit reconstruction, unwanted-color and oversmoothing failure studies in Figures 11–13. These substantially extend the diagnostic evidence beyond v1's attention/loss ablations and retained view-count analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 newly specifies comparative timing averages over 112 samples after 48 warm-up samples. This is distinct from the unchanged efficiency-scaling experiment averaged over 100 iterations in both versions. No seed-based performance uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the consistency values and adds ArtScores of 4.78, 9.12 and 9.15 for image, scene and 3D losses. For example, 3D-loss long-range LPIPS changes from 0.140 to 0.153; matching evaluation sampling is not established, so this is not a demonstrated performance regression. Tables 3–6 add substantial comparator, quality and timing results, while corresponding Stylos and StyleGaussian entries in Tables 3–4 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V2 introduces embedding interpolation for style blending and stylization-strength control in Section 4.3. Section 3.2.2 also changes the specified hybrid variant from concatenating separate frame/global outputs to sequential frame-then-global processing. The principal global-only architecture and training objectives remain; expanded CrossBlock details alone do not establish a replaced core model.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the related-work discussion, attention-module explanation and experimental narratives. It reorganizes the appendix around implementation, scaling, ablations, reproducibility, limitations and visual results, replacing the earlier pseudocode-led organization. The 3D-loss algorithm moves into the main text, and acknowledgements and conference/author information are added or revised.

P2.justification: V2 revises the architecture diagram, rebuilds Figure 5 for the expanded comparisons, adds blending, ablation, failure and evaluation-style figures, and expands tables with metrics, timings and comparison highlighting. Tables 5–6 are new. The original appendix gallery is retained as Figures 16–25, and the unchanged scaling plots move from Figure 6 to Figure 7.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for StyTr2, G-Style, DELAUNAY, ArtFID and StyleID, and refines positioning against per-scene fitting methods and the closest feedforward competitor, Styl3R. The overall research lineage remains. Publication-year and venue updates for existing references do not represent additional works.

T1.justification: The hybrid-attention definition changes substantively from channel concatenation in v1 Equation 3 to sequential composition in v2 Section 3.2.2. The 3D-loss pseudocode also corrects per-view voxel statistics to joint multi-view fusion, aligning it with the existing mathematical objective. The principal style-loss equations remain equivalent; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses substantial evidential and reproducibility gaps: v1 lacked a direct comparison with the closest feedforward competitor and supplied few training details. The expanded comparisons, implementation information and explicit failure studies substantially improve assessment of practical tradeoffs and applicability. Ambiguities remain around StylizedGS failure exclusions and code-release wording, but these do not outweigh the gains in empirical support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Stylos, with matching authors, core architecture, objectives and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, artistic-quality and timing measurements, interpolation experiments, expanded ablation examples and failure cases.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction and stylization experiments, baseline comparisons, attention and loss ablations, and inference-scaling measurements in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Stylos: Multi-View 3D Stylization with Single-Forward Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: v1 primarily claims floorplan reconstruction and presents blind inverse problems as future work. v2 reframes the abstract around a broader class of partially specified, nonsmooth operators and claims demonstrated applicability beyond spatial mapping through blind audio restoration; the introduction and conclusion adopt this broader contribution.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 newly attributes CFG’s real-world failures to the shift from synthetic A* trajectories to sparse human trajectories. v2 also explains conditional-prior complementarity and defines its audio setting as requiring neither an analytical degradation operator nor operator estimation at inference. Existing furniture and ill-posedness discussions remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantial CFG architecture/training details, audio preprocessing and encoder hyperparameters, and UWB collection procedures. It newly states that all baselines receive the intersection penalty and that DiPPeR was reimplemented because official code was unavailable; these disclosures do not establish changed implementations. Direct DiffPIR/DMPlug URLs are removed, while the project access statement remains.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic HouseExpo trajectories, v2 evaluates UWB-measured human trajectories from two apartments. Appendix D introduces piano-audio restoration, with MAESTRO training data and degraded recordings, substantially extending both input conditions and task coverage.

E2.justification: The six original floorplan baselines remain unchanged. The new audio comparison evaluates LTAS equalization and an unprocessed-recording control against CoGuide (Table 4). BABE2 is discussed but is not an evaluated comparator in that table.

E3.justification: The original 64×64 HouseExpo setup, 80/10/10 split, and F1/IoU metrics remain. New protocols include UWB trajectory acquisition and projection, 22,050-Hz audio with 8.35-second crops, FAD evaluation using VGG/PANN, and RMSE/MAE-based CFG tuning. Newly disclosed CFG training settings do not establish changes to earlier runs.

E4.justification: v2 adds a CFG guidance-scale sensitivity plot (Appendix C.2), a conditional-prior comparison through CFG+CoGuide, and two qualitative cases examining synthetic-to-real generalization. These are bounded additions; the existing intersection-weight, optimizer, noise, embedding, uncertainty, and planner analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The original floorplan tables retain mean±standard-deviation reporting, and Appendix B retains distance-transform variance across five seeds. No new repeated-run, confidence-interval, or significance-testing procedure is introduced. The added audio table reports point estimates only.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 scores and Tables 2–3 are unchanged. The added CFG+CoGuide row reports sparse/moderate/dense F1 of 0.93/0.97/0.99 and IoU of 0.87/0.93/0.97. New apartment reconstructions, guidance-sweep results, and audio results substantially expand the evidence. Table 4 reports FAD-VGG 0.84 versus LTAS 2.88 and scaled FAD-PANN 0.19 versus 0.27.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds CFG+CoGuide, replacing the unconditional diffusion prior with a trajectory-conditioned CFG model. Appendix D adds an audio adaptation using a shared CQT-based CNN/ResNet encoder and continuous-time contrastive guidance. These extend the procedure substantially while retaining the original floorplan method.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, local grammar and terminology are edited, and new experimental and implementation subsections are inserted. Conference headers, acknowledgments, and the conclusion heading change. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds apartment comparisons (Figure 5), a CFG sweep (Figure 10), audio spectrograms (Figure 11), and the FAD table. Table 1 gains a hybrid-method row and moves; Figure 4 is redrawn. Existing qualitative, uncertainty, retrieval, and planner images are retained and renumbered, with planner figures placed beside their discussions.

R1.justification: v2 adds audio-restoration, MAESTRO, FAD, CQT, and UWB references, and contrasts its audio guidance with Moliner et al.’s operator-estimation approach. CFG attribution changes to Ho and Salimans, and related work adds Amballa et al. The established floorplan research positioning is largely retained.

T1.justification: The central InfoNCE likelihood-ratio argument and Appendix A derivation remain unchanged. Appendix D adds a limited formal extension through the audio probability-flow ODE and contrastive posterior update. Algorithm 1 also inserts the previously missing gradient on the intersection-penalty term.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1’s exclusively synthetic empirical foundation through measured apartment trajectories and a worked audio-restoration application, while documenting the important CFG baseline and testing its integration with CoGuide. These additions address significant validation and reproducibility gaps. The gains remain qualified: apartment evidence is limited to two qualitative cases, audio evaluation lacks a clear test-set size, and Figure 10 does not display the stated selected guidance scale of 1.5.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoGuide work, and their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison. Retained material can be matched, including v1 Appendix D becoming v2 Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds CFG+CoGuide results, measurements from two apartments, a CFG guidance sweep, and audio-restoration results.

before.justification: v1 reports original HouseExpo reconstruction experiments, intersection-penalty and optimizer ablations, measurement-noise tests, and posterior-sampling analyses.

results.title: Contrastive Diffusion Guidance for Spatial Inverse Problems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about conditional process-outcome modeling, credit assignment, cross-sample comparability, and resistance to reward hacking. The expanded experiments provide additional support without redefining these central claims.

C2.justification: Appendix I newly attributes differing Best-of-N scaling behavior to generator-dependent availability of correct candidates. Appendix J explains data efficiency through supervision propagating to earlier steps, while Section 4.5.4 interprets the new results as evidence of applicability beyond mathematics. These extend the interpretation without changing the central mechanism explanation.

D1.justification: Appendix A.4 specifies that CRM rewards every step and VR is added only at the final step. V2 also adds a project-site address and removes v1's promise to release code and checkpoints upon acceptance; the PDFs do not establish actual artifact availability. Existing hardware and training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates mathematical reasoning only. V2 adds training on MMLU-Pro-CoT-Train and evaluation on MMLU-Pro-CoT-Eval across biology, business, health, history, and physics (Section 4.5.4, Table 5), substantially broadening domain coverage while retaining the mathematical datasets.

E2.justification: V2 adds Major@N and oracle Pass@N comparisons to Table 1, R-PRM and GenPRM in Appendix H, and PRM to the data-efficiency comparison in Appendix J. It also adds verifier-only RL to Table 3 across six benchmarks, although VR already appeared in v1's Figure 1. These materially expand the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: The original experimental protocols remain largely intact. Added settings include MetaMath-Mistral-7B generation, Pass@N evaluation, released-checkpoint comparisons, and PRM process-data subsampling. Section 4.5.3 corrects the stated ablation fractions from 0/25/50/75% to 0/10/25/50%, matching the unchanged Table 4; this does not establish rerunning the experiment.

E4.justification: Appendix I adds a substantive investigation of generator-dependent Best-of-N scaling using two generators and oracle candidate availability. Appendix J extends the CRM supervision ablation into a comparative data-efficiency study against PRM. The original reward-hacking, self-reflection, case-study, and reward-formulation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that beam-search results average three random seeds and retain the same plus/minus reporting in Appendix B. The added experiments introduce no new run-count disclosures, uncertainty estimates, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Matched original scores and empirical plots remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial new results. For example, Table 5 reports physics Best-of-64 accuracy of 66.4 for CRM versus 62.3 for PQM; Table 11 adds Best-of-16 scores of 51.2 for R-PRM and 55.2 for GenPRM alongside CRM's retained 56.4. Further additions cover verifier-only RL, majority/oracle selection, alternate generation, and PRM data budgets.

M1.justification: The conditional probability model, process reward log(1-h(t)), three training losses, and inference procedures remain unchanged. Appendix A.4 newly explains the already evaluated CRM+VR combination; it does not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely intact. V2 makes local grammatical edits, expands the potential-function explanation, adds Section 4.5.4 and Appendices H–J, introduces acknowledgments, and updates affiliation and conference text. The revision extends rather than extensively rewrites the document.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial tabular displays for domain coverage, reasoning-enhanced baselines, generator behavior, oracle performance, and paired supervision budgets (Tables 5 and 11–14), and expands Tables 1 and 3. Figure 1a replaces probability-curve sketches with conditional-probability bars and a new legend. Existing empirical plots are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix H add focused positioning against reasoning-enhanced reward models, including R-PRM and GenPRM, and discuss their training and inference costs. Additional citations support potential-based shaping and introduce VersaPRM. The original novelty framing relative to PRM, PQM, and IPRM remains intact.

T1.justification: The probability definitions, assumptions, chain-rule decomposition, reward-shaping derivation, and loss equations are unchanged. The revised potential-function discussion is explanatory, and new Equation 17 documents the existing CRM+VR implementation rather than introducing a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's mathematics-only experiments and original comparator set. Five additional domains, reasoning-enhanced PRM comparisons, and quantitative verifier-only results address important gaps in applicability and comparative evidence. Generator-sensitivity and data-efficiency analyses further examine performance dependencies, while implementation clarification and corrected ablation percentages improve reproducibility. The added comparisons still lack uncertainty estimates and exact checkpoint identifiers, but the overall evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CRM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds multi-domain evaluation, additional baseline comparisons, generator-sensitivity results, and comparative data-efficiency experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original Best-of-N, beam-search, reinforcement-learning, and ablation results in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Linking Process to Outcome: Conditional Reward Modeling for LLM Reasoning

C1.justification: The headline TTT perspective, training-free gate, approximately twofold pose improvement, and 20-FPS/6-GB claims remain. Section 5 adds the optional reset remedy, while Figure 1 now qualifies the extreme-length demonstration as using reset. This limits attribution of that success to the confidence gate alone.

C2.justification: v1 acknowledges residual forgetting generally. v4 documents failures beyond 1000 frames, connects them to unexplored state distributions, and explains the reset remedy and its use in long-sequence demonstrations. It also interprets learned gates' training-length limitations and the finetuning tradeoff between global alignment and per-view depth accuracy.

D1.justification: v4 supplies consequential missing details: mean aggregation in Equation 7, resetting every 100 frames, chunk alignment through metric camera poses without optimization, and which demonstrations use reset. It also documents frozen components, training sequence lengths, and baseline hyperparameter choices. These materially improve reproducibility; the stated code-access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Evaluation coverage remains ScanNet, TUM-dynamics, Sintel, KITTI, Bonn, 7-scene, and in-the-wild reconstruction, including thousands-frame sequences already shown in v1. Added studies change procedures within these tasks. Finetuning uses CUT3R's existing training dataset; no distinct new data domain is identified.

E2.justification: v4 adds STream3R to the retained short-sequence pose and depth comparisons. New controlled comparisons evaluate CUT3R with ScalarLR, ConditionLR, TokenLR, Reset, EMA, and BurnIn. Reset-enabled CUT3R also becomes a comparator for the extreme-length visualizations. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: Appendix A introduces gate-only training with the encoder, decoder, and output heads frozen, plus TTT3R finetuning on 4–64-view sequences. It sweeps reset/keyframe intervals and EMA shrinkage rates. Appendix B adds matched reset comparisons and long-sequence metric-depth evaluation on Bonn. Original benchmark protocols are otherwise retained.

E4.justification: v1 lacks the systematic design tests added in v4: learned-gate comparisons, finetuning tradeoffs, reset-period and EMA-rate sensitivity, and keyframe-interval ablations. Appendix B additionally examines failures beyond 1000 frames and whether resetting alleviates them, substantially extending mechanism and robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for the experiments. The added results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Original benchmark curves and shared entries in v1 Tables 1–2, now v4 Tables 6–7, are unchanged. New results establish substantial additional findings: v4 Table 5 reports 1000-frame TUM ATE of 0.093 with reset versus 0.106 without it; Table 1 shows finetuning lowers ATE but worsens KITTI depth. STream3R also changes short-sequence rankings, achieving TUM ATE 0.026 versus TTT3R's 0.028.

M1.justification: The core confidence-gated inference rule remains. Appendix A.2 adds a finetuned variant that applies this rule during training. v4 also explicitly specifies TTT3R + State Reset, but several v1 reconstructions reappear labeled as reset-enabled; this disclosure alone does not establish that reset was newly implemented.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v4 adds local associative-memory explanations, expands the discussion, and inserts analysis/reset appendices before the retained results and LLM-use sections. Affiliations and the publication header also change; this is not a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Five new analysis tables and several gating/reset plots substantially expand the visual presentation. Figure 1 replaces the CUT3R reconstruction with a reset-enabled comparison; v1 Figure 11 is reworked into v4 Figures 14–15 with additional controls. Retained tables gain STream3R rows, and several captions are expanded.

R1.justification: Related work expands to learned/dynamic SLAM systems such as VIPE, VGGT-SLAM, and VGGT-Long, and to scene-specific test-time adaptation through CVD and Test3R. STream3R is also added. These refine the existing positioning rather than replace the paper's central research framing.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 explicitly defines the summation in Equation 7 as a normalized mean, whereas v1 leaves it as an unqualified sum. This is a limited mathematical specification/correction. The central TTT reformulation and derivations remain, with no new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important validation and transparency gaps: Appendices A–B test the gate against learned and simple retention alternatives, expose extreme-length failures, and explain reset behind the strongest demonstrations. Adding reset-enabled CUT3R comparisons makes attribution fairer. These substantially strengthen the paper beyond its largely unchanged benchmark results. Some superiority wording remains too broad: Table 5 gives CUT3R + Reset lower rotation error and KITTI Abs Rel than unreset TTT3R, but this qualification does not outweigh the gains in evidence and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TTT3R and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite renumbering and the expanded appendix.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds gating, finetuning, and state-reset experiments in Appendices A–B.

before.justification: v1 reports original camera-pose, video-depth, and 3D-reconstruction experiments, including benchmark curves, qualitative reconstructions, and appendix Tables 1–2.

results.title: TTT3R: 3D Reconstruction as Test-Time Training

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the claimed benchmark contribution from 15 tasks and 114 groundtruth insights to 100 tasks and 1093 insights. This substantially enlarges the claimed deliverable. The central enterprise-research positioning and conclusions about agents missing important insights remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning novel insights excluded by the cutoff, coarse attribution, restricted task families, and residual judge bias. Sections 5.2–5.6 expand explanations involving contextual binding, missing-knowledge detection, query formulation, and interaction complexity. The new scope discussion explicitly frames the benchmark as document-centric and diagnostic.

D1.justification: The abstract now advertises code and data rather than code alone, and a new reproducibility statement describes release contents and a permissive license. V2 clarifies structured evaluation inputs and supplies additional task metadata. The detailed implementation, hardware, hyperparameters, container setup, and cost information largely remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond increasing task counts, Tables 29–34 add substantive scenarios absent from v1's Table 7, including retail knowledge management, healthcare medication-safety knowledge management, and EV asset management using digital twins. The same three industries remain, but their represented research requirements broaden substantially.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same planning variants, backbone models, browser agent, and commercial comparators, including Perplexity, OpenAI Deep Research, and Gemini. Simple and Complex planning are renamed SRP and CRP. The new judge comparison tests evaluation sensitivity rather than adding a competing research agent.

E3.justification: The reported FullBenchmark expands from 15 to 100 tasks and MinEval from five retail tasks to 15 tasks. Backbone comparisons move from MinEval to FullBenchmark. Section 5.6 changes the local-setting description from files in an accessible folder to files passed directly to agents. New human-validation and paraphrase experiments introduce additional evaluation designs.

E4.justification: V2 adds GPT-4o versus Llama-3.1-405B judge sensitivity in Appendix L, paraphrase robustness in Appendix S, and direct human validation of insight judgments in Section 6. Appendix T newly reports near-perfect recall from copying documents without the cutoff. Existing planning, iteration, and source-type analyses remain.

E5.justification: Three-run averaging and standard-error reporting already existed. V2 adds a four-run paraphrase-variance estimate and Cohen's kappa for human–judge agreement. Table 19's uncertainty values change, but the PDFs do not establish an increased repetition count or a changed estimation procedure for that table.

E6.justification: Major performance tables receive replacement scores under expanded settings: Table 2's base-DRBA recall changes from 16.92 to 13.18, which is not a same-setting decline. Table 5's report-quality leader changes from OpenAI Deep Research to DRBA (GPT-5). V2 also adds judge-agreement and paraphrase results and revises Table 19's error bars beyond percentage conversion.

M1.justification: The five-stage data-generation pipeline and DRBA's planning, adaptive research loop, retrieval, and report-generation procedures are retained. V2 clarifies structured versus narrative reports without establishing a new algorithmic component or an actual change to the agent.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. V2 makes focused explanatory expansions, adds validation appendices and ethics/reproducibility/limitations statements, shortens the conclusion, standardizes terminology, and updates authorship and conference headers. These changes do not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands task and validation displays through Table 20 and Tables 29–34. Figures 1 and 3 clarify report formats, Figure 4 is redrawn, and v1's source-type Figure 8 becomes v2's Table 22 with retained values. Several tables also receive revised labels, units, and formatting.

R1.justification: V2 adds Choubey et al. (2025), distinguishing its closed-form enterprise fact retrieval from DRBench's research tasks. Cohen (1960) and Gwet (2001) support the added agreement analysis. The broader related-work taxonomy and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The task and insight definitions, distractor-avoidance formula, and human-preference scoring formula are retained. The latter moves from Appendix Q to R. No new formal assumptions, proofs, theorems, or substantive mathematical derivations appear.

improvement.justification: Broader task scenarios and expanded evaluations substantially strengthen v1's limited benchmark coverage. Direct human validation on 264 insights, reporting over 91.3% agreement, plus judge-sensitivity and paraphrase checks strengthen confidence in the central metric. These gains outweigh reporting problems, including duplicate task entries and stale inventory counts. Section 5.6 also retains an inaccurate all-metrics leadership claim: v2 Table 5 gives DRBA higher report quality than OpenAI Deep Research.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DRBench and DRBA. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material across renumbering and changes in presentation.

after.justification: V2 reports expanded agent evaluations and adds human validation of insight judgments, judge-sensitivity results, and paraphrase-robustness experiments.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and the appendices report original agent evaluations, planning and backbone comparisons, iteration ablations, and human evaluations.

results.title: DRBench: A Realistic Benchmark for Enterprise Deep Research

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes integrating heterogeneous and dynamic physics-informed graphs. V2 makes hard causal topology, prevention of spurious correlations and physical-operator decoupling central contributions. Its abstract and conclusion replace the 17% FLOPs headline with 73.8% fewer FLOPs and 21% lower training time relative to LRGCN, while framing applicability around dynamics governed by known physical equations.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving operator decoupling, reduced over-smoothing, Markovian transport as motivation for LSTM, and negative transfer in multitask learning. It interprets the new validations as evidence of broader robustness. The limitations retain concerns about predefined physics but replace generic adaptive graph learning with a proposed physical topology plus learnable residual graph.
