D1.justification: V2 clarifies feature contents, source-map resolution and spatial holdout, and documents sensor forcing, city-validation aggregation, OpenFOAM/RANS configuration, geometry, inflow, mesh sizes and fluid-edge construction. The scalability test specifies 16 CPU workers. These substantially expand technical documentation; the original hyperparameter table and code/data availability disclosure remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 retains UMC4/12 and its six targets but adds NUS sensor measurements for simulator validation, Singapore-wide comparison against HiGTS, and UWF3D velocity-component prediction. These extend evaluation beyond the original simulated microclimate blocks to observational references and a distinct vector-field task.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the original comparators and adds Pix2Pix+PINN, STGCN, ASTGCN and LRGCN. Appendix G additionally evaluates a Grid-GCN control against the adapted UrbanGraph. These are reported comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: New protocols include five-station simulator validation, aggregated HiGTS comparison for May 3, 2023, a 64x64 Grid-GCN control, physics-injection controls, shared-encoder multitask evaluation and a 36-window scalability test. The original 70/20/10 split and main training settings remain; the spatially unseen-block description newly clarifies the split without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds a comparison of data-only, soft-physics and structural-physics approaches, single-task versus multitask learning, and reconstruction timing for approximately 90,000 nodes. Appendix B.2 adds external validation analyses. The original temporal, fusion, initialization, feature, edge and sensitivity ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Figure A3 newly reports station-wise Pearson correlations and significance thresholds. Existing three-trial reporting, standard deviations and confidence bands remain; no increase in the stated repeated-run count is established.

E6.justification: The retained main UrbanGraph scores remain R²=0.8542 and RMSE=1.0535, and the five auxiliary-target scores persist in expanded Table A13. V2 adds MAE values, comparator and control results, city-scale correlation r=0.842, and velocity-component R² values of 0.8886, 0.8474 and 0.7937 in Table A14. The convergence plot also replaces training/validation results with test-set results.

M1.justification: The original five-relation microclimate graph and RGCN-LSTM predictor remain substantially unchanged. Appendix G.2 adds a fluid-specific adaptation using directed advection edges and building-to-wake edges, focusing graph construction on fluid mechanisms.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, results discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the causal-topology framing. Dynamic and static edge descriptions are reordered, appendix subsections are expanded, and author and publication headers are reformatted.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, replaces the convergence panel, adds input/prediction and validation figures, and introduces the vector-field illustration. Figure A1 expands from two displayed sites to ten. Table 1 gains category grouping, comparator rows and an MAE column, while new control and vector-result tables are added. Many original appendix heatmaps are simply relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: Related work substantially repositions UrbanGraph as a structural inductive bias relative to observational inputs, soft PDE losses and implicit graph learning. New references support STGCN/ASTGCN comparisons, HiGTS validation and physical threshold choices; Banerjee et al. and Yan et al. are removed. The LRGCN paper was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Appendix G and Figure A12 add formal inlet, symmetry, wall and outlet boundary conditions for the CFD benchmark. Existing graph, network, ENVI-met and edge-weight equations (1)-(17) remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for applicability beyond the original UMC4/12 experiments through broader comparisons, field checks of the simulator, HiGTS validation and a distinct vector-field task. Added controls also make architectural choices more assessable. Reporting problems temper these gains: LRGCN is mislabeled as the strongest baseline despite Table 1, and the field-validation text overstates several wind correlations shown in Figure A3. These problems limit the stronger claims but do not outweigh the substantial expansion of relevant empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UrbanGraph and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. The original model and experiments can be matched across versions, including relocated appendix material.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds simulator validation against measurements, city-scale validation, additional controls and wind-vector prediction results.

before.justification: Tables 1-2 and Appendices E-F report original microclimate prediction experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: UrbanGraph: Physics-Informed Spatio-Temporal Dynamic Heterogeneous Graphs for Urban Microclimate Prediction

C1.justification: Both versions claim that high-copying prompting and preference training improve contextual faithfulness with 365 training examples, and attribute effectiveness to recalibrated parametric reliance. v2 distinguishes the Copy-Paste paradigm from its CopyPasteLLM implementation more explicitly, but this clarifies ideas already present in v1. The headline performance and efficiency claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds attention-anchoring and entropy explanations, interprets copying as selective evidence use rather than indiscriminate reproduction, and explains answer stamping as enforcing a final commitment. It also connects weak or negative Negotiation-subset gains to ambiguous evidence lacking decisive copyable fragments. The original incomplete-context and future-work limitations are retained through relocation.

D1.justification: v2 discloses previously unspecified prompting details, including extraction validation at 0.95 similarity, LangGraph implementation, five refinement iterations, a 0.99 copying threshold, score coefficients, and temperature 0.1. Table 4 clarifies training-example allocation and PubMedQA sampling. Section 8 now states that implementation is available, replacing its future-release wording; the repository address already appeared in v1's abstract.

E1.justification: Both versions use RAGTruth, FaithEval, PubMedQA, and ConFiQA with the same underlying task coverage. The 20,000-example PubMedQA evaluation already appears in v1 Table 3. v2's knowledge-type, ambiguity, and MeSH breakdowns partition existing coverage; ARC supplies a classification taxonomy, not an additional evaluated benchmark.

E2.justification: External comparator membership in the retained benchmark tables is unchanged. Appendix G and Figure 12 add two evaluated comparison variants, w/o Copying and w/o Stamping, alongside the full model and Base; these are limited additions of ablation controls.

E3.justification: v2 introduces substantial protocols for added analyses: knowledge-type classification and subgroup evaluation, fragment-length relevance analysis, and checkpoint ablations on Llama-3.1-8B over two epochs and 218 steps. The ablations evaluate every 10 steps and introduce JSON-formatted Accuracy after CoT with temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.95. These supplement rather than replace the retained main evaluation and training settings.

E4.justification: New Appendices E–G test performance across knowledge types, biomedical ambiguity and MeSH categories, analyze response length and copied-fragment relevance, and isolate high-copying preference data and answer stamping through ablations. Figure 12 additionally examines convergence and generation stability. v1 lacks these component tests and detailed diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds 95% t-distribution confidence intervals across eight evaluation seeds in Figure 12, five-run majority voting for knowledge-type annotation, and median-plus-standard-deviation reporting in Table 5. These substantially expand statistical reporting beyond v1's point performance estimates and representation visualizations. The eight seeds concern evaluation randomness, not eight independently trained models.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and v1 Table 5, now Table 6, retain their numerical results. v2 nevertheless adds substantial subgroup, response-statistics, and ablation results. For example, its new PubMedQA-Labeled analysis reports Llama-3.1-8B Consensus accuracy of 84.58% versus Attributed's 76.79%, but Negotiation accuracy of 44.93% versus 46.38%. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over corresponding v1 scores.

M1.justification: The three prompting procedures, preference construction, answer stamping, DPO objective, and knowledge-capturing procedure are unchanged. All four algorithm bodies match after renumbering. New implementation disclosures and experimental ablation variants do not revise the proposed full method.

P1.justification: The appendix organization is substantially revised: the standalone formalization section is redistributed into implementation and analysis sections, prompting results receive structured copying and relevance discussions, and limitations and LLM-use disclosures move. Terminology is standardized around Copy-Paste, with revised abstract and conclusion framing. The main section sequence remains stable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 7–12 and a new Table 5, introducing subgroup charts, fragment-relevance plots, response statistics, and learning curves with confidence bands. Table 4 gains explicit sample allocations. Existing figures are retained with relocation or legend changes, while prompt boxes are substantially compressed through smaller typography.

R1.justification: v2 adds Clark et al. (2018) for the ARC knowledge taxonomy and Olsson et al. (2022) for induction heads. These support the new analyses and mechanistic interpretation. The main related-work discussion and positioning against existing faithfulness methods remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: New Appendix A introduces mathematical arguments connecting copying to contextual attention concentration and conditional-entropy reduction, including Equations 2–7. v1 contains no corresponding derivation. This is substantive new mathematical reasoning, although the asserted attention and entropy relationships are not established through rigorous proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing component validation through copying and stamping ablations, while subgroup results expose an important boundary on ambiguous evidence. Added implementation details and uncertainty reporting make the evidence more assessable and reproducible despite unchanged headline scores. These gains outweigh weaknesses in the additions: Appendix A asserts unproved attention and entropy relationships, and Appendix E.2's claim of matching or beating baselines in every category overstates Figure 7.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CopyPasteLLM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds component ablations, subgroup evaluations, response analyses, and training dynamics.

before.justification: v1 reports original prompting and trained-model evaluations in Tables 1–3, plus copying, relevance, logits, and hidden-state analyses.

results.title: Copy-Paste to Mitigate Large Language Model Hallucinations

C1.justification: The introduction adds systematic analysis of visual-prompt integration and resulting guidance as an explicit contribution. The central VIRTUE and SCaR novelty claims and the abstract/conclusion performance claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations that SCaR finetuning increases bounding-box dependence, random prompts demonstrate meaningful prompt use, and finetuning SAM-2 on uniform-point inputs biases it toward noninteractive settings. It also discusses accuracy–latency tradeoffs. The existing limitations and broader applicability discussion remain intact.

D1.justification: v2 replaces future-release and supplementary-material statements with explicit repository/project links and stated availability of code, models, and SCaR material. It also specifies 64 queries for attention pooling and hardware, precision, and batch size for profiling. Core training configurations are unchanged; external availability was not independently verified.

E1.justification: The 36 MMEB tasks and five SCaR datasets remain unchanged. Section 5.4 extends evaluated input conditions to jittered, partially masked, and shifted visual prompts, centroid points, and random bounding boxes.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparator sets in Tables 2–3 are unchanged. Appendix E.1 newly evaluates cross-attention and attention-pooling connector alternatives against Conv-MLP in Table 9, providing a limited expansion of comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the evaluation design with controlled prompt perturbations, substitutions, inference-only versus training-and-inference point removal, and SAM-2 freezing/finetuning comparisons. Appendix E.6 adds latency and memory measurements using batch size one on a single H100, with matched bf16 precision for I2T. Existing benchmark splits and primary training settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.4 adds systematic robustness and prompt-dependence tests absent from v1. Appendix E.1 adds connector and SAM-2 finetuning ablations, while Appendices D.4 and E.6 add annotation-reliability and efficiency analyses. These materially expand scrutiny of component necessity, robustness, and practical cost.

E5.justification: v1 describes two independent inspectors without quantifying agreement. v2 first reports average Cohen’s kappa of 0.89 in Table 7 for that inspection process. Neither version reports performance uncertainty across repeated training runs.

E6.justification: The original benchmark scores are retained, but substantial new results appear. Table 4 reports random-box SCaR scores of 9.2 and 13.0 versus 27.8 and 56.9 with correct boxes; Table 5 reports a 68.6-to-24.1 MMEB drop when uniform points are removed only at inference. Tables 7, 9, and 11 add agreement, ablation, and efficiency results.

M1.justification: The proposed SAM-2/VLM architecture, convolution-plus-MLP connector, embedding concatenation, InfoNCE objective, and training procedure remain unchanged. Newly tested connector alternatives and SAM-2 finetuning are ablation variants, not changes to the adopted method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section ordering are retained. Changes include local introduction edits, a clarifying task-instruction footnote, acknowledgements and publication-header updates, and insertion of Sections 5.4 and E.6. This is a localized expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds a three-panel robustness figure and tables for prompt substitutions, point removal, annotator agreement, and efficiency. The ablation display expands from seven to nine panels. Several existing diagrams are redrawn, and retained qualitative figures are resized and relocated, substantially expanding the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds You Mostly Walk Alone (Makansi et al., 2022) and ShuttleSHAP (Wang et al., 2025) to motivate prompt-dependence tests. The related-work discussion and principal research positioning otherwise remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal retrieval task, representation definitions, connector equation, and InfoNCE objective are unchanged. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs that are added or revised in v2.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked systematic tests of imperfect or irrelevant user prompts and an inference-cost assessment. Section 5.4 and Appendices E.1/E.6 add controls that test actual prompt dependence, justify design choices, and expose accuracy–cost tradeoffs. Appendix D.4 also quantifies annotation reliability. Together these substantially strengthen validation of the central interactive-embedding claim and assessment of its practical usefulness, while preserving the original benchmark evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VIRTUE/SCaR research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds prompt-robustness experiments, further ablations, annotation-agreement statistics, and inference-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original VIRTUE evaluations on MMEB and SCaR, component ablations, hyperparameter studies, and qualitative retrieval and correction results.

results.title: VIRTUE: Visual-Interactive Text-Image Universal Embedder

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: discovering reward-assignment functions through LLM-guided evolution, introducing DAIL as the first meta-learned AIL algorithm, and demonstrating generalization and improved training behavior.

C2.justification: v2 interprets similar repeated discoveries as search stability and suggests that OpenES reward-function irregularity contributes to weaker performance. It adds computational limits on broader benchmark testing and drops the explicit statistical-significance assertion for probability of improvement. The original mechanism explanation and static-function limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies the rliable library and documents settings for added comparisons, including WGAIL’s selected learning rate. It removes the abstract’s explicit public code link while retaining the supplementary-code statement. Original prompts, hyperparameter tables, hardware information, and runtime values remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same five Brax tasks and three MinAtar games. The additional Breakout discovery experiment reuses an existing task. Atari-57, Procgen, and larger discovery suites appear only as future directions.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons against OpenES, Pearson chi-squared, squared-Hellinger, total-variation, and Wasserstein-GAIL methods in Tables 10–11. The original GAIL, AIRL, FAIRL, GAIL-heuristic, BC, and IQ-Learn comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The evaluation design expands to five discriminator-regularization regimes, a matched budget of 200 inner-loop evaluations for OpenES, an additional Breakout discovery experiment, and a WGAIL learning-rate sweep selecting 0.003. Original demonstration sampling, PPO/A2C settings, training budgets, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 tests sensitivity to discriminator regularization, repeatability across independent searches, discovery on another retained task, and the contribution of LLM guidance through OpenES. These substantially extend the original entropy, density-ratio, and reward-component analyses.

E5.justification: Section 6.4 explicitly adds a second independent SpaceInvaders evolutionary run. The existing 16-seed policy evaluations, SEM reporting, and four-seed 95% confidence intervals for the non-adversarial comparison are retained.

E6.justification: New results show DAIL leading GAIL overall under three of five regularization regimes and leading the additional divergence baselines on five of seven tasks. Table 10 reports DAIL/OpenES returns of 0.90/0.73 on SpaceInvaders but 0.66/1.27 on Asterix. Table 8 adds discoveries from two further searches. Original plotted results and the BC/IQ-Learn table remain unchanged.

M1.justification: DAIL retains the reward function in Equation 4, the meta-learning objective, and Algorithms 1–2. The prompts and evolutionary procedure are unchanged; additional discovered functions are experimental outputs.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized language and citation edits, updates author affiliations and publication headers, and adds acknowledgments, Section 6.4, and two comparison appendices. The overall narrative and most existing explanations retain their structure.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with regularization, divergence-definition, OpenES, and additional-baseline tables, plus two new figures. The discovered-function table gains environment/run groupings and ten functions. All eight original figures are retained, with some relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds acknowledgment of Ke et al. (2021), Zhang et al. (2020), and Teoh et al. (2025). New future-work citations cover larger benchmarks and discovery efforts. The central research positioning remains stable; removal of bibliography URLs does not remove the cited works.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 instantiates the existing variational derivation for additional divergences, including squared Hellinger, Pearson chi-squared, and total variation in Table 3. Appendix I adds the Lipschitz-constrained Wasserstein discriminator objective in Equation 38. Existing lemmas and proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked independent search repetitions and a non-LLM search control. v2 addresses these important evidential gaps and adds regularization and broader baseline comparisons, strengthening the central empirical case while revealing conditions where DAIL loses. The removed public code link and limited OpenES implementation detail weaken reproducibility, but the new controls provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DAIL research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, moves, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds regularization tests, evolutionary-search repetitions, OpenES comparisons, and additional divergence-based comparisons.

before.justification: Section 6 and the appendices report original Brax and MinAtar experiments, reward-function ablations, and comparisons with adversarial and non-adversarial imitation methods.

results.title: On Discovering Algorithms for Adversarial Imitation Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: sparse mapping features enable feed-forward localization with minimal map preparation, and scene/scale normalization supports generalization. Benchmark-specific ranking revisions do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies practical applicability. Section 4.5 discusses amortizing mapping costs over repeated queries; Appendix B.1 explains storage disadvantages relative to SCR. The benchmark discussion and Appendix C.6 explain when geometric matching excels or fails. Appendix B.2 also interprets existing results in terms of imperfect SLAM poses and retrieval failures, without adding dedicated tests of those conditions.

D1.justification: V2 adds ALIKED-LightGlue resolution/keypoint settings, E5+1 RANSAC budgets, storage requirements, and Wayspots pose-provenance details. Core training hyperparameters and hardware remain unchanged. V1's supplementary-video access instructions are omitted, although the project link remains; this does not establish that the videos became unavailable.

E1.justification: The training dataset mixture and evaluation coverage remain unchanged: Cambridge, Wayspots, Indoor6, RIO10, 7-Scenes, and Map-free validation analyses. Additional baseline configurations and acceptance thresholds do not introduce new datasets or task scenarios.

E2.justification: V2 adds E5+1 with ALIKED-LightGlue to comparisons on all five localization benchmarks and E5+1 with RoMa on Wayspots. These introduce a substantive geometric comparator family absent from v1's evaluations; existing benchmark competitors are retained.

E3.justification: Section 4 changes the stated PnP correspondence maximum from 100,000 to 5,000. Figures 4–5 add a 25cm/5° acceptance threshold, and Appendix C.6 introduces keypoint-count and RANSAC-budget sweeps. Existing training budgets and dataset splits remain unchanged. V2 Appendix A's 'at least 5,000' wording leaves the precise subsampling rule unclear.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.6 and Table 10 systematically test the strongest added comparator's accuracy–latency trade-off on Cambridge and Wayspots by varying keypoints and RANSAC iterations. This adds a substantive comparative sensitivity analysis. Existing scale, retrieval, feature-count, and MASt3R analyses remain, with Figures 4–5 extended to another acceptance threshold.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for the empirical results. The model's predicted confidence scores and confidence-based loss are unchanged.

E6.justification: New comparator results alter rankings: v2 Table 4 reports Cambridge errors of 0.18m/0.3° for E5+1 versus FastForward's retained 0.27m/0.4°. Existing FastForward accuracies are revised, including Wayspots 51.0% to 51.4% and RIO10 44.6% to 40.6% at 10cm/10°. Appendix C.3 changes reported network/PnP times from 0.6/2.2 seconds to 0.4/0.1 seconds. These revisions accompany a changed correspondence budget and do not establish controlled same-setting gains. V1's per-scene Cambridge threshold-accuracy breakdown is removed.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same encoder, decoders, prediction heads, feature sampling, ray encoding, scale normalization, and training loss. The changed PnP correspondence budget is an experimental setting revision, without a new model component or localization algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 tightens introductory prose, moves Cambridge from Section 4.1 to 4.4, adds focused discussion and Appendix C.6, and changes the publication header. Most method exposition, the abstract, and the conclusion remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are substantially reorganized: Wayspots accuracies move from appendix Table 6 into main-text Table 2, replacing the Cambridge accuracy table. Several tables gain comparator rows and latency/storage columns, and Table 10 is new. Figures 4–5 have expanded curves, axes, and legends; the architecture and qualitative figures are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantive positioning against semi-generalized relative-pose methods, including their ability to recover absolute scale from posed mapping images. It also discusses retrieval-based local triangulation and Viewformer, with supporting citations. This expands the relevant research context beyond v1's emphasis on regression and foundation-model approaches.

T1.justification: The normalization definitions, ray encoding, decoder equations, and confidence-weighted loss are unchanged. The added E5+1 discussion explains an existing geometric solver without introducing new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important comparison gap by evaluating relevant multi-view geometric baselines, acknowledging their wins on Cambridge and the strict 7-Scenes threshold, and examining their accuracy–latency trade-offs. The added amortization and storage discussion makes the central efficiency argument more credible and useful. These gains outweigh the loss of Cambridge's per-scene threshold breakdown and remaining ambiguity in the 5,000-correspondence wording.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FastForward research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across reordered sections.

after.justification: V2 retains original FastForward experiments and reports additional comparator evaluations and an E5+1 accuracy–latency study.

before.justification: V1 reports original FastForward localization results, scale-normalization and map-representation ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative examples.

results.title: A Scene is Worth a Thousand Features: Feed-Forward Camera Localization from a Collection of Image Features

C1.justification: The introduction replaces v1's first-work claim for dynamic low-frame-rate codecs with more specific novelty claims about reconstructible audio below 10 Hz and ASR-guided allocation. The abstract adds insufficient semantic decoupling and temporal resolution as proposed causes of low-rate degradation. The central performance and TTS claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 develops component-attribution arguments and interprets English domain robustness, poor multilingual semantic transfer and Chinese adaptation. It also discusses limitations of heuristic merging and possible syllable-guided or learnable alternatives. However, Appendix J retains v1's now-obsolete statement that multilingual evaluation and adaptation have not been performed.

D1.justification: v3 states that code is available, replacing v1's future public-release promise, and explains straight-through gradients, duration-bit overhead and new experiment settings. Transformer bypass during the first 10% of training changes from a reported practice to an example recommendation; this does not establish that training actually changed.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds codec reconstruction evaluation on Emilia's spontaneous/conversational English and on Chinese, Korean, Japanese, French and German, plus Chinese adaptation training. This substantially extends the previous reconstruction coverage beyond English audiobooks; existing TTS, TIMIT and audio-understanding evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Table 5 substantially expands its low-bitrate comparison by adding TAAE/Stable-Codec at 700 and 400 bps and SemantiCodec at 50 and 25 Hz. These methods were discussed in v1 but were not evaluated in that comparison. Existing comparator rows are retained.

E3.justification: New Emilia evaluations use 1,140 English samples, 200 samples per other language, Whisper-large-v3 scoring and language-specific threshold calibration. Chinese adaptation runs for 250,000 steps with nonoverlapping test data. The new codec timing benchmark specifies V100, FP32 and batch size one. Existing LibriSpeech and TTS protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds substantial domain-shift, multilingual generalization and adaptation tests. Appendix D.2 adds a fixed-rate ASR-plus-transformer configuration without FSQ to examine component contributions. Its factorial table otherwise consolidates five previously reported results, rather than introducing six new ablations.

E5.justification: The MOS plus/minus reporting, six-expert listening evaluation and Figure 4 statistical summaries are unchanged. v3 introduces no repeated-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results are retained, but substantial new entries appear in Tables 5 and 9–12. Examples include the new F3 ablation's 5.40% WER, encoding/decoding RTFs of 0.018/0.006, and Chinese RVQ1 WER of 100% before versus 8.51% after fine-tuning at 12.5 Hz. These are additional experimental conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The dual-stream architecture, ASR-guided merging, FSQ/RVQ quantization, losses and TTS procedure remain unchanged. Straight-through gradients are newly documented. Chinese fine-tuning uses the existing codec, while learnable merging is proposed only as future work.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the abstract and introduction, Appendix D gains subsections, and new appendices are inserted. The reproducibility statement is replaced by acknowledgements, with author and publication-header edits. Most existing methodological and experimental prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 5 is expanded and reordered, and new Tables 9–12 present component combinations, timings, English domain-shift results and multilingual results. These substantially expand the visual evidence. Figures 1–6 are retained with placement changes, while v1 Tables 9–12 survive as v3 Tables 13–16.

R1.justification: v3 adds Sylber and supporting citations for gradient estimation, Emilia and speech-text pretraining, and replaces the MaskGCT citation with Seed-TTS. It expands the comparison with XY-Tokenizer's supervision and disentanglement, acknowledges residual FSQ, and refines novelty positioning without changing the overall research context.

T1.justification: The merging, quantization, loss and TTS formulations are retained, with no new theorem, proof or substantive derivation. The corrected projection symbol, straight-through explanation and standard bitrate formula do not change the mathematical substance.

improvement.justification: The Emilia experiments substantially strengthen the previously limited reconstruction-generalization evidence by documenting English robustness, multilingual semantic failures and adaptation (Tables 11–12). Added low-bitrate competitors and codec-specific timings improve assessment of competitiveness and practical cost. These gains outweigh the stale multilingual limitation in Appendix J and acoustic-superiority wording in Section 4.4 that was not qualified despite the new TAAE results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FlexiCodec. Their main texts, appendices, figures, tables and equations are readable, and retained material can be matched despite expanded and renumbered appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds codec timing, out-of-domain and multilingual evaluations, Chinese fine-tuning results and an additional ablation configuration (Tables 9–12).

before.justification: v1 reports original codec benchmarks, ablations, ASR probing, TTS evaluations and audio-understanding experiments, including subjective listening scores (Figure 3 and Tables 2–8).

results.title: FlexiCodec: A Dynamic Neural Audio Codec for Low Frame Rates

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are unchanged in substance, as are the introduction's contribution statements: commit-history-based episodic and semantic memory improves LocAgent localization. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds a specific limitation concerning missing or noisy commit–issue links and reduced retrieval recall. It also discusses better history filtering, repository-specific memory sizes, diminishing returns, and downstream repair usefulness. Existing explanations of memory complementarity, sparse-history failures, and variable costs remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly specifies dependency-aware summary generation through LocAgent, explicit commit–issue linking, per-file summary cost, and construction/runtime details. Appendix D supplies the existing agent task prompt in full. The reproducibility statement also promises code release, but provides no repository link.

E1.justification: The SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live dataset selections remain unchanged. Appendix B.2 adds actual end-to-end issue resolution on SWE-bench-verified, substantially extending evaluated task coverage beyond file localization.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 4 retain their main baselines and retrieval comparators. The new repair evaluation reuses CodeRankEmbed, Agentless, and LocAgent, while Table 8 extends the existing tokenizer comparison. CoRNStack in related work refers to the same Suresh et al. work, not a new baseline.

E3.justification: The original localization protocol is retained. Added experiments introduce an Agentless repair pipeline generating ten patches per issue, regression/reproduction-test reranking, and resolution-rate evaluation; a K sweep over 50, 100, 200, 300, and 400 files; and latency measurement on a random 50-instance subset.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds target-file coverage and localization sensitivity analyses for semantic-memory size, and extends the tokenizer ablation beyond Django to all repository groups. Appendix A adds construction-time, tool-latency, and response-length analyses. The original component ablations and failure analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new random 50-instance timing sample changes evaluation design, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain identical results. New results include 40.4% issue resolution for RepoMem versus 37.0% for LocAgent (Table 7), Django Acc@5 ranging from 74.4% to 81.0% across memory sizes (Table 6), additional standard-BM25 repository scores, and construction/latency measurements. These are added outcomes, not improvements over v1 under the original settings.

M1.justification: The episodic and semantic memories, four memory tools, BM25 retrieval, and LocAgent integration remain unchanged. Appendix A clarifies summary generation through LocAgent and dependency exploration; this is presented as further implementation detail, not a revised algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely preserved, with localized wording edits. v2 adds related-work and disclosure sections plus supplementary appendices; the original tool-documentation Appendix A becomes Appendix C with unchanged content.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to the single-column ICLR format, with extensive resizing and relocation of figures and tables and changed caption placement. Four new tables and the prompt Figure 9 are added; the original Figures 1–8 are retained.

R1.justification: A new Just-in-Time Software Defect Prediction subsection substantially broadens research positioning, distinguishing defect prediction from localization and grounding hotspot selection and historical linking in that literature. Relevant citations are added throughout the method and appendix discussions, while the Gutiérrez et al. memory citation is removed.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The existing Accuracy@k definition is retained; the new memory-size investigations are empirical.

improvement.justification: v1 establishes localization gains but leaves their downstream repair benefit and memory-construction overhead unmeasured. v2 addresses both with the common repair-pipeline comparison in Table 7 and operational measurements in Appendix A. Together with sensitivity tests, broader retrieval checks, and explicit construction and prompt details, these additions substantially strengthen practical validation and reproducibility. Statistical uncertainty and concrete code-access information remain unprovided.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RepoMem research. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds issue-resolution results, sensitivity tests, and operational measurements in Appendices A and B.

before.justification: v1 reports original RepoMem localization experiments, memory and retrieval ablations, and cost and behavior analyses in Section 4.

results.title: Improving Code Localization with Repository Memory

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add contributions concerning downstream preference optimization and human-validated reasoning and rubrics, explicitly including languages unseen during MR3 training. The original claims about broad language coverage and competitive, compact reward models remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking teacher quality and SFT supervision to rubric adherence, and suggests that weaker target-language benchmark performance may partly reflect evaluation bias despite favorable human ratings. Human feedback and case studies introduce specific translation, code-switching, and reasoning failures. The original limitations section is largely unchanged.

D1.justification: New disclosures include alignment-data composition and deduplication, annotation instructions and sampling, GRPO rewards, and SFT/RLVR hardware and training-time comparisons. Core SFT/inference settings and the access link remain. However, v1's identification of the Qwen-235B translation model disappears even though translated-reasoning comparisons are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds policy-alignment training using Aya, m-RewardBench, and PolyMath, and evaluates generated responses on m-ArenaHard-v2.0, MCLM, and INCLUDE. This extends coverage beyond reward-model judgments. Human assessment expands from English/Chinese rubrics to a study across 12 languages; the original reward benchmarks and 72-language training corpus remain.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 add DeepSeek-R1-14B and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct comparisons while retaining the earlier reward baselines. New comparisons include Nemotron-based DPO alignment in Table 4 and GRPO-based RLVR against SFT in Table 28, substantially broadening the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: New protocols cover additional backbones, DPO evaluation with GPT-4.1-mini and fixed reference position, and a 50K SFT plus 50K RLVR comparison against 100K SFT. The earlier GPT-5-mini reasoning assessment sampled only correct outputs; v2's human assessment includes correct and incorrect outputs, with 15 questions per annotator.

E4.justification: Appendices G–I add data-size and teacher-strength ablations, quantitative curriculum comparisons, SFT-versus-RLVR analysis, unseen-language subgroup analysis, and human reasoning case studies. The earlier language/translation comparisons remain, while the automated reasoning-quality assessment is removed. Table 27 explicitly reproduces prior R3 ablations rather than reporting newly performed MR3 experiments.

E5.justification: v2 first reports five-run means and standard deviations in the main benchmark tables, five-seed information for ablations, and 95% confidence intervals for DPO win rates. v1 reported variability for rubric and reasoning ratings but did not specify equivalent repeated-run reporting for its main benchmarks.

E6.justification: Main-table estimates change: MR3-Qwen3-14B's RewardBench entry becomes 90.79 ± 0.25 instead of 91.12. New alignment, ablation, and human results substantially expand the findings. Table 4 reports overall m-ArenaHard win rates of 39.1% before alignment, 45.2% with MR3-based DPO, and 47.0% with Nemotron-based DPO. The legacy detailed benchmark tables retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a downstream procedure using MR3 for DPO post-training of Qwen3-30B-A3B. This extends the workflow, while MR3's dataset construction, filtering, SFT objective, and language-forcing procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in the abstract, contributions, curriculum description, baseline presentation, and language-strategy discussion. Alignment, human-evaluation, and ablation subsections are inserted, with terminology and header updates. The six-section main outline and most existing method and prompt text remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are restyled or redrawn, including revised colors, legends, and caption placement. Main tables gain model rows and uncertainty displays, and Table 2 loses its average column. New alignment, subgroup, ablation, human-evaluation, and case-study tables substantially expand the displays; earlier detailed Tables 7–20 become Tables 9–22.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting DPO, additional models and benchmarks, position bias, and ensemble metrics. Related work now explicitly identifies R3 as the underlying rubric-based framework extended to multilingual settings. The broader literature organization and positioning remain similar.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the SFT loss, and Appendix C.1's task definitions are unchanged. The additional experiments introduce no substantive formal derivations, theoretical assumptions, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 assessed reasoning automatically only on correct outputs and supplied little quantitative support for several training choices. v2 adds human assessment including failures, substantive training ablations, downstream alignment tests, and repeated-run uncertainty, substantially strengthening the empirical support. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including small human samples, removal of the translator identification, and apparently swapped MM-Eval/IndoPref headings in new ablation tables. The DPO results support downstream usefulness without establishing superiority over Nemotron on every benchmark.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MR3 research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison and matching across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds policy-alignment results, training ablations, and expanded human evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual benchmark experiments, language-strategy comparisons, automated reasoning assessments, and human rubric ratings.

results.title: mR3: Multilingual Rubric-Agnostic Reward Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same four contributions and headline claims: thought-adaptive hybrid compression, efficient memory-slot reuse, near-lossless accuracy below 5% of the original cache, and throughput improvements up to 5.8×. The additions primarily provide further support.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking K/V sensitivity to precision assignments and component performance to generation-length inflation. It discusses compatibility with prefill compression and removes the serving-framework integration limitation from Appendix F following the vLLM experiments. The limitation concerning predominantly long-input workloads remains.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's Transformers proof of concept, v2 documents vLLM v1 integration, identifying modified block-table and attention files and environment flags for switching methods (E.2). It also clarifies that dequantization overhead is included in attention timing. Core hyperparameters, pseudocode, quantization formats, and hardware disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds LongBench v2's Code Repo QA subtask, covering long-input/long-output reasoning with 16K–32K-token inputs and outputs up to 8K tokens (E.16). Existing mathematics, code-generation, GSM8K, and LongWriter coverage is retained. The added Qwen3 experiments reuse LiveCodeBench.

E2.justification: v2 introduces a non-thinking FullKV comparator for Qwen3-8B (Table 13) and adds TBE to the generation-length comparison (Figure 10(d), formerly Figure 9(d)). The principal eviction and quantization baseline sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled vLLM and concurrent-request evaluations, fixed-batch component measurements, additional cache-budget sweeps, Qwen3 thinking-mode comparisons, and request-latency and Intelligence/Watt metrics. It also reattributes the retained LiveCodeBench precision-ablation plot from R1-Llama-8B to R1-Llama-70B; this reported setting revision does not establish that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The accuracy-only component ablation in v1 Table 3 becomes a broader accuracy/throughput/latency analysis with additional TBE budgets in v2 Table 4. New analyses examine separate K/V quantization sensitivity by thought type, accuracy–memory frontiers, overhead across batch sizes, thinking versus non-thinking behavior, and compatibility with SnapKV (E.9 and E.11–E.16).

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies eight independent responses per question for pass@1 estimation and averaging throughput and latency over three independent runs (6.1). This is newly reported sampling information, not evidence of increased run counts. The existing 50-rollout thought-importance analysis is retained; confidence intervals and significance tests are not added.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 8 retain their numerical results, but substantial additional results appear. Examples include vLLM throughput of 6622.4 for ThinKV versus 4883.3 for R-KV (ovl) at batch 256 (Table 12), and Code Repo QA accuracy of 28 versus FullKV's 30 with the 4096-token SnapKV prefill budget (Table 15). Further additions cover Qwen3, component performance, sensitivity, generation length, and request latency.

M1.justification: Appendix E.16 adds an optional composite procedure using SnapKV eviction of quantized prefill tokens before ThinKV decoding. This extends the compression pipeline for long inputs. The core thought decomposition, TBQ, TBE, calibration algorithm, and Continuous Thinking procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The central exposition is substantially reorganized: v1 interleaves observations and procedures within Section 3, whereas v2 groups motivating analyses in Section 3 and methodology in Section 4. Formulations are renamed, evaluation discussions are rewritten and expanded, and navigation and cross-references are updated.

P2.justification: v2 adds serving, sensitivity, Pareto-front, and latency-breakdown figures and five tables, while expanding the component-ablation table with performance columns. Existing sparsity plots are exchanged between Figure 3 and the appendix, captions identify settings more explicitly, and Figure 1(c)'s axes are redrawn. These changes substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting quantization sensitivity, Qwen3, serving evaluation, Intelligence/Watt, and vLLM integration, alongside additional quantization and sparsity citations. The research positioning in Section 1.1 and Appendix B remains essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The thought-decomposition and compression formulations, calibration mathematics, and Appendix C permutation-invariance theorem and proof are retained. Renaming Definitions 2–3 as Problem Formulations 1–2 does not alter their mathematics. The added standard pass@1 formula introduces no new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's explicit gap in optimized-serving validation through documented vLLM integration and controlled throughput/concurrent-request measurements (E.2, E.12, Figure 9). This substantially strengthens the central systems contribution. Expanded component, sensitivity, and long-context tests also improve its evidential support. Uncertainty intervals remain absent and Intelligence/Watt is underexplained, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ThinKV and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices A–H. Content can be matched across the section reorganization, renumbering, and moves between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds serving measurements, sensitivity analyses, Qwen3 experiments, and LongBench v2 evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy, throughput, attention-pattern, and ablation results, including Figure 8, Tables 1–4, and Appendix E.

results.title: ThinKV: Thought-Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Efficient Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: a first VCM-based zero-shot/PnP solver for high-definition video restoration, combining temporal coherence and spatial detail with few evaluations and no automatic differentiation. Added experiments support these retained contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of runtime-memory tradeoffs, nonlinear applicability conditional on evaluating the likelihood proximal operator, and robustness inferred from the new analyses. It also identifies restricted pretrained timesteps as a limitation on tuning eta and discusses error accumulation in long-video generation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/project-access statement, changes video links from Streamable to GitHub, identifies the A100 timing hardware, specifies bicubic ×8 upsampling for VIDUE, and documents additional scheduling configurations. The hyperparameter table is revised, while the existing forward-operator and proximal-solver implementation descriptions are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on 239 GoPRO240 test clips, supplementing Adobe240. Appendix A.7 also adds a higher-noise scenario and a nonlinear task combining Gaussian noise with JPEG compression. GoPRO240 appeared in v1 only as the initialization network's training source.

E2.justification: VIDUE becomes an explicit Problem C comparator in v2 Tables 1, 2 and 6, whereas v1 used its network only for initialization. VISION-XL and ADMM-TV remain. BiM-VFI appears in a separate diagnostic comparison against VIDUE in Figure 7, rather than a direct LVTINO benchmark.

E3.justification: v1 Table 2 becomes v2 Table 4 with revised settings for all three problems: A's temporal TV weight changes from 0.005 to 2.8e-4 and both proximal coefficients from 1e5 to 1e6; B's coefficients change from (1e5, 2e3) to (3e3, 1.5e5); C's spatial TV weights change from 1e-4 to 1e-6. New experiments introduce timing and parameter-sweep protocols. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original TV and ICM ablations are retained as v2 Table 5. New Appendix A.7 adds noise robustness testing, step-size/regularization sensitivity heatmaps, VCM/ICM scheduling ablations, residual error maps, and a BiM-VFI-versus-VIDUE case study examining motion-blur handling.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed information, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added tables and sensitivity heatmaps do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original Adobe240 and component-ablation numerical entries are retained, while v2 adds substantial results for GoPRO240, noise, computational cost, scheduling and JPEG restoration. The new VIDUE entry achieves FVMD 142.5 versus LVTINO's 602.5 on Adobe240 Problem C. Table 3 reports LVTINO at 132 seconds and 35.15 GB versus VISION-XL at 176 seconds and 15.64 GB.

M1.justification: The VCM/ICM/TV splitting, CausVid and DMD2 backbones, and LVTINO/LVTINO-V update procedures are retained. Flow-LVTINO is discussed as a future extension; the nonlinear experiments do not document a new solver component.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence remain. Changes include conference headers, limited wording edits, condensation of the numerical-stability discussion into a footnote, and insertion of new appendix subsections with updated cross-references.

P2.justification: v2 adds four tables covering GoPRO240, computational costs, noise and scheduling, plus four figures showing baseline diagnostics, JPEG restoration, sensitivity heatmaps and error maps. Table 1 gains a VIDUE row, and main qualitative figures are consolidated. Original appendix Figures 7–12 are retained as Figures 11–16.

R1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds an extended relationship to Martin et al.'s PnP-Flow and supporting flow-matching/PnP literature. v2 also positions the work relative to concurrent zero-shot restoration, task-specific video restorers, DiffIR2VR and recent long-video generation research, substantially expanding the prior-work discussion.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.5 adds a formal flow-matching setup, derives the flow-induced denoiser's MMSE identity in Equations 11–12, states straight-flow exact-recovery conditions, and develops the PnP-Flow iteration in Equations 13–14. This substantially expands the mathematical treatment, drawing on prior work; the original Langevin derivation remains and no new LVTINO convergence proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method: the second benchmark, VIDUE comparison, noise/compression tests and sensitivity analyses address v1's limited evidence of generalization and robustness. Actual runtime and memory measurements make efficiency claims assessable beyond NFE counts. Unexplained hyperparameter revisions alongside unchanged scores and Table 7's inconsistent task label limit reproducibility, but the gains in validation and transparency clearly outweigh these caveats.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LVTINO research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original GoPRO240 results, runtime and memory measurements, noise tests, scheduling ablations and nonlinear restoration examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original Adobe240 restoration experiments, quantitative comparisons in Table 1, component ablations in Table 3, and qualitative reconstruction examples.

results.title: LVTINO: LAtent Video consisTency INverse sOlver for High Definition Video Restoration

C1.justification: The central diagnostic, dataset-bias and invariant-regression contributions remain. The abstract now identifies label-predictive symmetry bias as particularly relevant to equivariance's failures, and the contributions highlight the auxiliary task-dependent diagnostic. The conclusion narrows the salient augmentation failure from MNIST and ModelNet40 to primarily ModelNet40.

C2.justification: v1 describes the task-dependent metric as largely inconclusive beyond Swiss Roll. v2 interprets controlled direct-prediction results as supporting task relevance, adds practical recommendations conditioned on distribution shift and label correlation (Figure 6), and discusses improved architectural robustness. It also qualifies molecular augmentation benefits and explicitly leaves a reliable decision threshold for future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds a public-code address and Reproducibility Statement, plus implementation settings for selective augmentation and the new simulation classifier. It removes v1's detailed empirical-MMD and kernel implementations, Algorithms 3–6, replacing them with brief descriptions. This substantially changes the available reproduction guidance, although most original training and hardware details remain.

E1.justification: The benchmark roster, local point-cloud datasets and dipole-canonicalized QM7b scenario are retained. v2 D.2.4 adds a class-dependent MNIST rotation scenario, where only digits 3, 4 and 5 are rotated, alongside original and fully rotated variants.

E2.justification: The main Table 1 comparator set is retained. However, v1 C.9 compares the classifier with Chamfer, Hausdorff and Mean/Covar MMD on OC20; v2 drops that comparison while retaining these comparators for QM9 and rMD17.

E3.justification: v2 adds original-versus-rotated controls and relative loss/accuracy evaluation for the task-dependent diagnostic, selective-augmentation testing on 1,000 MNIST images, and joint sample-size, learning-rate and architecture sweeps (D.5). These substantially extend evaluation design; existing benchmark splits and training descriptions are largely retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test sample efficiency and hyperparameter sensitivity on MNIST/QM9, direct-metric sensitivity to canonicalizer and predictor architectures, selective augmentation, and diagnostic behavior across covariance strengths. Conversely, v1's QM9 and rMD17 moments-of-inertia analyses are removed.

E5.justification: Tables 1 and 4 in v2 specify three-seed means and standard deviations where v1 reported unqualified point estimates. Table 2 reports five-seed results, and Figure 17 specifies four trials with fresh splits and detectors. v1 already included uncertainty in selected appendix analyses; the main expansion is systematic reporting for central comparisons.

E6.justification: Main benchmark estimates change extensively. For example, Table 1's QM9 heat-capacity FF/TF values change from 0.158/0.154 to 0.143/0.146 cal/mol K, reversing their point-estimate ordering in the new three-seed summaries. Task-dependent ratios, selective-augmentation and sensitivity results are added; OC20 MMD results and QM7b's ten-rotation group-averaging entries disappear.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1's core classifier diagnostic is unchanged. v2 adds selective augmentation using a 0.45 classifier-probability threshold (D.2.4). Direct task-dependent prediction already existed in v1 Appendix B; v2 refines it into a loss/accuracy ratio against a rotated-input control.

P1.justification: The task-dependent definition moves from the experiments discussion into Section 2.1, its results are rewritten and redistributed, Swiss Roll discussion moves into the appendix, and statistical comparisons are consolidated in D.10. Terminology and experimental narrative are revised throughout, constituting substantial structural editing beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 adds a practical flowchart, task-dependent summary table, selective-augmentation and sensitivity plots, and a QM9 results visualization. The ridge simulation figure moves into the main text and gains a diagnostic panel; other displays are relocated, expanded or simplified. Inertia and OC20 comparison figures are removed, alongside comprehensive conference-format reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds supporting references on invariance and learning theory, including Lyle et al., Sriperumbudur et al., Nguyen et al. and Cohen et al. (2019), and removes the workshop-version citation. The main related-work organization and positioning against existing symmetry tests remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 A.1 adds proofs of loss/gradient invariance and identical optimization trajectories under per-example group transformations. Appendix B adds a population-risk formulation, connections to distributional distances, and a Rademacher-complexity generalization bound. The original ridge-regression theory is retained; v1 Theorem 2 becoming v2 Fact 1 is principally relabeling.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central practical argument: rotated-input controls and architecture checks address v1's inconclusive task-dependent diagnostic, while seed-based uncertainty makes the main comparisons more assessable. Additional formal analysis strengthens the explanation. These gains outweigh reduced self-contained kernel implementation detail and removed OC20 comparisons, although the practical flowchart remains heuristic without a validated decision threshold.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same symmetry-breaking diagnostic and invariant-regression study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds controlled task-dependent evaluations, selective-augmentation experiments and broader sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark experiments in Table 1, ridge-regression simulations, and extensive diagnostic and ablation results in the appendices.

results.title: To Augment or Not to Augment? Diagnosing Distributional Symmetry Breaking

C1.justification: V2 expands the headline empirical scope from approximately 80–90% sparsity to effectiveness at 95–99%. Its abstract, introduction, and discussion newly claim realized deployment benefits, including up to 3.98-fold throughput improvement and 7.80-fold memory compression. The central surrogate-free ADMM contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking deployment gains to decoding dominated by sparse matrix-vector operations and arguing that ELSA converts pruning compute into quality more effectively. It also narrows the ELSA-L memory-saving statement to optimizer and auxiliary states. The original surrogate-objective explanation and memory discussion largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 substantially revises the hyperparameter specification, adds a model/sparsity-specific batch-and-step table, and explicitly states 32,768 training sequences of length 2,048. It documents matched-data baseline retraining, MACKO/RTX 3090 inference, and A100-80GB timing. Appendix B.1 changes environment/script availability from promised to stated available, although the PDFs cannot verify repository access.

E1.justification: C4, WikiText2, and the seven zero-shot tasks are retained. V2 adds an end-to-end text-generation deployment scenario in Section 5.3, beyond v1's perplexity and task-accuracy evaluations. The additional sparsity percentages are configuration changes rather than new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: V2 introduces Wanda+LoRA and Wanda+Full as evaluated retraining baselines in Tables 2–3, with training-data counts and sequence lengths matched to ELSA. These provide substantive controls absent from v1's comparisons. The original pruners and the relocated OWL/EvoPress comparison are retained.

E3.justification: V1 specifies batch size 8 and 4,096 steps universally. V2 instead reports 16/2,048 for OPT-125M and 32/1,024 for larger models at 50–60% sparsity, retaining 8/4,096 at 70–90%. Table 5 revises learning rates, penalties, and scheduling. V2 also introduces 95–99% configurations and inference/pruning timing protocols. These reported setting revisions do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Sections 5.2 and 5.5 add extreme-compression stress tests and a pruning-cost versus quality analysis, examining performance after baseline retraining and under tighter sparsity constraints. The original data-efficiency/objective and projection ablations remain unchanged, moving from Section 5.4 to Appendix C.2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2 reports mean inference latency but supplies no repetition count or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds efficiency, pruning-time, and retraining-comparison results; ELSA's new 99% sparsity result is 55.94/40.10 WikiText2/C4 perplexity. Tables 10–12 replace ELSA's 50–60% scores alongside revised settings, including LLaMA-2-7B's 50% average accuracy changing from 53.35 to 56.39. ELSA-L's reported memory reduction changes from 66% to 55%, now specifically referring to optimizer and auxiliary states. Existing 70–90% tabulated quality results are retained.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same sparsity-constrained objective, ADMM updates, Fisher-weighted projection, and ELSA-L quantization procedure. Appendix Algorithm 1 is also unchanged. The added MACKO benchmarking backend does not revise the proposed pruning algorithm.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: v1's main-text sections on other sparsity patterns and ablations become Appendix C.1–C.2, while the main text prioritizes extreme sparsity, deployment, and computational cost. The abstract, introduction, and discussion are revised around this emphasis; method and proof prose remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adds dedicated inference-efficiency, extreme-sparsity, and compute-quality Tables 1–3, adds batch/step Table 6, and restructures hyperparameter Table 5. V1's Tables 1–3 become Tables 8, 7, and 9 in Appendix C, and Figure 6 moves there as well. This substantially redistributes the empirical displays while retaining the original plots.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) and MACKO (Macko and Boža, 2025), and removes the bfloat16 reference by Kalamkar et al. The broader positioning against layer-wise surrogate-based pruning remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations, Assumptions 4.1–4.3, stationarity definition, convergence statements, and Appendix A proof are unchanged. Theorem 4.6 moves across a page boundary without a substantive revision.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked explicit matched-data pruning-plus-retraining controls and measured inference performance. V2 addresses these important gaps through Wanda retraining comparisons, pruning-cost measurements, and actual speed/memory benchmarks (Tables 1–3), substantially strengthening comparative validity and practical relevance. New benchmark details remain incomplete, and Section 5.5 incorrectly groups SparseGPT with perplexities of at least 10,000 despite Table 3 reporting 1430/864.5. These reporting weaknesses limit, but do not outweigh, the added validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ELSA/ELSA-L research and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–C. Relocated experiments and renumbered tables can be reliably matched.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds extreme-sparsity comparisons, inference measurements, and pruning-cost results in Sections 5.2, 5.3, and 5.5.

before.justification: V1 reports original pruning experiments, perplexity and zero-shot accuracy measurements, scalability results, and objective/projection ablations in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: The Unseen Frontier: Pushing the Limits of LLM Sparsity with Surrogate-Free ADMM

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions and superiority claims: DiT-based drag editing through region supervision, background constraints, adapter-enhanced inversion, and ReD Bench. The abstract's revised wording clarifies the existing rationale without materially changing these claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations of prompt conflicts, compositional affine editing, cross-backbone applicability, and LoRA specialization, plus substantive limitations concerning mask precision and computational cost. The inversion-drift limitation remains. Separately, the introduction reverses its cited distortion comparison from SD outperforming GAN priors to GAN outperforming SD priors.

D1.justification: V3 replaces a future-release promise with reported code/dataset access, adds adapter resource links, and documents H100 hardware, qint8 quantization, and CPU offloading. Table 3 now identifies ReD Bench. Conversely, Appendix C.5 removes the exact KV-injection layer lists and caching instructions; this is lost documentation, not evidence that KV injection was removed.

E1.justification: ReD Bench and DragBench-DR remain the evaluation datasets. V3 adds targeted scenarios involving absent or misleading prompts, inaccurate masks, intricate hair/clothing structures, and bending or sequential composite edits (Appendices D.4 and H.2-H.3), extending coverage within the existing editing task.

E2.justification: The nine external editing baselines remain unchanged. V3 adds an augmented point-based DiT comparator with background preservation and adapter enhancement (Table 4), unlike v1's unaugmented point-based ablation baseline. It also evaluates QWen-VL prompting and subject-specific LoRA alternatives in Tables 5 and 8.

E3.justification: The original metrics and editing schedule are retained. Added experiments introduce matched auxiliary-module controls, a feature-layer sweep, prompt manipulations, SD3.5 and LoRA configurations, and preparation-plus-edit time and peak-memory measurements on DragBench-DR using one H100 (Appendices C.5-C.6, D.4, I-J). These are new protocols, not demonstrated reruns of the original comparisons.

E4.justification: V1's cumulative component ablation and PCA visualizations are substantially extended by quantitative layer selection, controlled point-versus-region supervision, prompt ablations, mask-failure cases, complex-edit robustness examples, and backbone/identity-module analyses. These directly test several previously unexamined design choices and applicability boundaries.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V3's additional dataset averages and layer sweep do not introduce uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1-3 retain their numerical results. V3 adds Tables 4-8 and qualitative findings: matched-module point/region MD1 scores are 37.02/31.59; SD3.5 and LoRA variants report MD1 of 35.21 and 30.98; runtime and memory are 158.7 seconds and 23.5 GB. These concern added conditions, not improvements to the original benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The standard DragFlow pipeline, losses, and optimization procedure remain unchanged. Appendix J.2 adds a procedural variant that first trains a subject-specific LoRA and then uses it instead of the pretrained identity adapter, constituting a limited method extension.

P1.justification: V3 lightly revises the abstract and selected passages, adds acknowledgments and conference headers, and expands the appendix hierarchy with new analysis subsections. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain intact; the scientific additions do not constitute wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: V3 adds five experimental tables, a three-panel layer-performance chart, failure/success comparisons, and a substantial challenging-scenario image grid. Existing figures are retained and sometimes relocated or renumbered. It also corrects PCA layer labels in Figures 7-8 and the dataset-example caption's row/column descriptions.

R1.justification: Appendix A updates a limited citation set, adding works such as Target-aware Image Editing and LUVE while dropping AddSR and 3DIS-FLUX. The explicit FreeFlux implementation attribution in C.5 disappears. The main related-work taxonomy and positioning against RegionDrag remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical content in Equations 1-31 is retained, including supervision losses, affine transformations, region weighting, gradient masking, and metric definitions. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the central supervision rationale through the controlled comparison in Table 4 and quantitative layer sweep in Figure 9. Prompt tests, portability checks, and explicit failure and computational-cost analyses make the paper's effectiveness and practical boundaries considerably easier to assess. These gains outweigh the loss of exact KV-injection documentation, although uncertainty reporting and details for reproducing some new variants remain limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DragFlow, with matching authors, methodology, benchmarks, and retained results. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds controlled comparisons, robustness analyses, runtime measurements, and backbone and identity-module experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original inversion experiments, evaluations on ReD Bench and DragBench-DR, component ablations, and qualitative editing results.

results.title: DragFlow: Unleashing DiT Priors with Region-Based Supervision for Drag Editing

C1.justification: The headline empirical claim changes from a reported 85.3% average ASR and 25.9-point advantage across ten targets to 81.5% and 44.2 points across twelve. The introduction also explicitly claims actionable defense insights. The central claims of tree-based RL, transferable attacks, and discovery of new strategies remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking trajectory diversity to attack success, attributing stronger-target gains to RL beyond SFT, and explaining robustness against external defenses. New Appendix F discusses reward hacking, held-out evaluation, possible ensemble or human verification, and the boundary between attack discovery and defense development. These substantially broaden the interpretation and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies that pruned trajectories are not replenished and explicitly identifies the default single-attempt metric. It adds conditional access instructions for models, code, and data through author-approved requests, while retaining the earlier release promise. Core hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are unchanged; the PDFs do not establish actual resource availability.

E1.justification: The training datasets, HarmBench attack task, and guardrail-classification benchmarks are retained. Appendix D.12 adds a distinct evaluation scenario: attacking systems protected by external prompt and response guardrails, rather than relying solely on the target models' internal safety alignment.

E2.justification: ActorAttack and X-Teaming become evaluated comparators in Table 1, whereas v1 only cited them. SFT-only comparisons expand to the full target suite and new analyses. Conversely, the attacker-backbone comparison drops its SFT controls and improvement columns (v1 Table 8 versus v2 Table 10), although SFT comparisons remain elsewhere.

E3.justification: New protocols include one-, three-, and five-attempt evaluations, Self-BLEU over the first 100 training steps with branching factors through eight, and success criteria requiring both external guardrails to accept an attack. Claude-4-Sonnet and GPT-oss-20B extend the target configurations. ASR@1 is newly explicit, but v1's attempt count is unspecified, so a change to the earlier main evaluation protocol cannot be established.

E4.justification: v2 adds trajectory-diversity analysis, broader SFT-versus-RL ablations, DAPO generalization, test-time scaling, and external-defense robustness studies (Table 3; Appendix D.3 and D.8-D.12). Earlier pruning, tree-depth, group-size, training-data-size, and backbone analyses largely remain. The no-tree-rollout results omitted from Table 2 are retained in Appendix Table 8.

E5.justification: v1 reports human-judge agreement but no across-training uncertainty. v2 Appendix D.9 and Table 12 report five independent training runs with different seeds and mean plus standard deviation across ten targets. This newly documents repeated-run variability; it does not establish an increase from any specified v1 run count.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces many baseline scores, including PAIR against GPT-4o changing from 61% to 18%, while retaining DIALTREE's scores on the original ten targets. It adds DIALTREE results of 71% on Claude-4-Sonnet and 53.5% on GPT-oss-20B, plus extensive supplementary results. Because earlier attempt budgets are unclear, the replaced baseline scores do not establish comparable-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: v2 adds a DAPO-based training variant alongside GRPO (Appendix D.8, Table 11). The default SFT initialization, dialogue-tree rollout, pruning, reward, and adaptive masking remain unchanged. Renaming the framework and explicitly writing the existing masking rule do not establish additional method changes.

P1.justification: v2 renames the method, updates affiliations and publication headers, revises selected introduction and related-work passages, and places adaptive masking before the GRPO objective.
