It adds a limitations appendix and moves the retained case studies from Appendix F to G. Most existing exposition and all dialogue examples remain.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes an expanded red heatmap, Table 2 gains component-indicator columns, and the backbone comparison is simplified. Seven new tables display diversity, SFT comparisons, optimizer variants, uncertainty, scaling, Claude results, and guardrail robustness. The six existing figures are largely retained and repositioned rather than replaced.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds multi-turn defense work, particularly distinguishing Hu et al.'s sequential decision-making defense from attack-policy learning. References also add sources for new models and diversity measurement, while removing works including Crescendo and TreePO. The main novelty positioning remains; publication updates and duplicate-reference removal are bibliographic edits.

T1.justification: v2 expresses adaptive masking with an indicator and incorporates it into the displayed GRPO objective (Equations 3-4). This formalizes the masking rule already specified in v1 Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1, rather than introducing different mathematical content. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation: direct comparisons with two additional multi-turn attackers, five-run uncertainty reporting, broader SFT controls, and guarded-system tests address important comparison, stability, and applicability gaps in v1. These gains go beyond higher claimed performance. They are tempered by unexplained revisions to older baseline scores, an efficiency plot retaining earlier results without clearly reconciling settings, and conditional resource access. Overall, the added validation provides a substantial quality improvement despite these reporting weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. DIALTREE-RPO in v1 matches DIALTREE in v2; renamed and relocated material can be reliably aligned.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, repeated-training statistics, attack-budget scaling, and external-guardrail experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-success experiments, training ablations, guardrail evaluations, and human validation of the automated judge.

results.title: Tree-based Dialogue Reinforced Policy Optimization for Red-Teaming Attacks

C1.justification: The abstract changes the relative-performance claim from 'improved' to 'competitive' against compression and training-free sparse baselines. This modestly qualifies that comparison; the introduction's contribution statements and the conclusion's main claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: New appendices attribute context-length behavior to backbone limitations and RoPE geometry, explain attention-budget sensitivity through routing disruption, and interpret gating as content-dependent and modality-specific. They also distinguish ideal computational savings from padding and kernel overheads, substantially expanding the mechanism and limitation discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix Q newly discloses padding 28 query heads to 64 for the Triton kernel and reports the dense baseline's 5280 H100 GPU hours alongside the retained 4600-hour VideoNSA figure. Implementation-specific discussion is expanded, while the existing training hyperparameters and project, code, and model access links are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds evaluations on LSDBench and VideoEvalPro, including the latter's holistic/local perception and reasoning categories. This extends evaluation within the existing video-understanding domain; the training data and original six benchmarks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Tables 12–13 introduce reported comparisons with LongVA, LongVila, and Video-XL, distinct from the retained Video-XL-2. Appendix K adds Qwen2.5-VL as a comparator in context-scaling analysis, and Table 37 introduces flash-nsa versus nsa-impl. These substantially expand supplementary comparisons while preserving the original benchmark comparator sets.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include static gates averaged over a 1K training subset, dense-versus-sparse comparisons at 32K/64K/128K context, FLOPs and prefill profiling, and CMP block-size sweeps over 4K–128K contexts. Kernel forward/backward timing is compared at 8K. The original training and benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a direct static-gate ablation and benchmark-level PCA analysis of routing, dense-backbone context-scaling controls, and block-size/kernel investigations of the latency bottleneck. Appendix T also compares video and text-only NSA gating patterns. These test questions beyond v1's retained branch-removal, allocation, and sink analyses.

E5.justification: The existing gate-distribution means and interquartile summaries are retained. v2 adds no reported seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures; additional plots and point estimates do not change these reporting practices.

E6.justification: The original numerical table entries are retained, but substantial results are added: VideoNSA scores 55.2 on LSDBench and 29.4 overall on VideoEvalPro; static gating scores 31.8 versus dynamic gating's 36.1 on VSIBench. New context-scaling, training-cost, FLOPs, and kernel-latency results extend the evidence rather than establish improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.3 retain the Qwen2.5-VL backbone, dense text attention, three sparse vision branches, learned gates, and training recipe. Static gates and alternative kernels appear as experimental comparisons, without replacing the proposed method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and existing appendix prose are largely preserved. Changes include the conference header, the abstract qualification, updated cross-references, and an expanded appendix roadmap with inserted analytical sections. The added scientific content does not amount to a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The appendix adds benchmark and diagnostic tables, context-scaling curves, PCA plots, efficiency charts, and text-only NSA visualizations. Existing inter-head heatmaps gain numbered captions and are regrouped, while dense-attention sink panels are consolidated. These substantially change the appendix's visual organization; the main displays are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands citations covering video modeling and efficiency, and connects its scaling analysis to routing generalization, RoPE, LM-Infinite, and positional-encoding research. New kernel comparisons and the detailed contrast with text-only NSA broaden research positioning, while the original distinction from token-compression methods remains.

T1.justification: New Appendix M introduces a routing-stability deviation definition, mask-based mathematical reasoning about attention-budget changes, and RoPE-based extrapolation arguments incorporating a cited logit-growth bound. This substantially expands the mathematical treatment beyond v1's method and budget equations, although it supplies theoretical interpretations rather than a proved VideoNSA performance guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidentiary gaps: the static-gate control directly tests dynamic routing beyond v1's branch-removal ablations, and Appendices Q–R quantify comparative efficiency and disclose implementation overheads. These substantially strengthen validation and transparency. The gains are qualified by heuristic theoretical arguments and Appendix K's overstated 128K stability: Table 27 shows declines from 64K on three benchmarks. Those weaknesses limit interpretation but do not outweigh the stronger empirical controls and cost analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoNSA with matching architecture and main experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds benchmark evaluations, a static-gate ablation, context-scaling comparisons, and efficiency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-understanding evaluations, branch ablations, scaling experiments, latency measurements, and analyses of learned gates and attention sinks.

results.title: VideoNSA: Native Sparse Attention Scales Video Understanding

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same claims about compressed-cache self-distillation, natural-language robustness, scaling and efficiency. The revised second contribution emphasizes existing compressors and direct cache generation, both already described in v1, without substantively changing the overall claim scope.

C2.justification: Appendix G introduces explanations for weak fully latent MetaMathQA performance, including limited latent capacity and fewer unique training questions, and discusses instability and hybrid reasoning as a remedy. Appendices H–I interpret data dependence and trace-length/source effects. Section 7 adds interpretability qualifications and a speculative safety argument about distilled reasoners.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C add MetaMathQA's dataset identifier, size, trace length and hyperparameter column. Appendix I documents prompting, generation modes, answer filtering, retries, fallback to GPT-4 traces and deduplication. These substantially extend reproducibility information for the new experiments; existing pseudocode and GSM8k hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: v1 trains on GSM8k-Aug and GSM8k-Aug-NL and evaluates GSM8k, GSM8k-Hard and SVAMP. v2 adds MetaMathQA training, including MATH-derived problems and longer traces, plus MATH500, multiArith and DeepMind-Mathematics evaluation. This broadens the represented mathematical problems beyond the original arithmetic coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 fills previously missing Llama-1B comparisons: PCCoT appears on GSM8k-Hard and SVAMP under both training datasets, and CODI appears on those benchmarks after GSM8k-Aug-NL training. The baseline families otherwise remain unchanged; Table 2's grouped method labels primarily reflect shared inference behavior.

E3.justification: New MetaMathQA experiments vary replacement ratios and latent placement, use five epochs and batch size 64, and disable KaVa's CODI loss. Only non-diverged CODI/PCCoT runs are reported. Appendix H adds dataset-fraction and training-budget controls; Appendix I adds trace-generation and filtering protocols. The original GSM8k settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of hybrid replacement ratio and placement, training-data quantity versus matched training steps, and alternative trace generators (Appendices G–I). Existing component, loss, eviction and iteration ablations, decoded examples and cache-similarity analyses are retained. Appendix F primarily redisplays benchmark results rather than introducing a separate robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions already specify three seeds and standard-error reporting. v2 extends uncertainty reporting to Llama-1B CODI comparisons previously represented by cited point estimates, such as 53.9 ± 0.5 on GSM8k after GSM8k-Aug training. No explicit increase in run counts is stated; changing parentheses to ± alone is cosmetic.

E6.justification: v2 adds MetaMathQA and data-sensitivity outcomes and revises several Llama-1B baseline results. For GSM8k-Aug training and GSM8k testing, Full CoT accuracy changes from 61.6 to 63.4 and forward passes from 65 to 31.9. KaVa remains at 56.5 accuracy and 6.9 passes, changing its reported reduction from 89% to 78%. These are baseline revisions, not improved KaVa scores.

M1.justification: v1's student replaces the entire reasoning trace with latent tokens. v2 additionally introduces hybrid reasoning, retaining explicit tokens before or after the latent sequence and incorporating them into the student loss (Section 4.1; Appendix G). This substantially extends training and inference behavior, although the underlying KV-cache compression and matching mechanism remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes comprise localized contribution and related-work edits, added experimental explanations, an ethics/reproducibility section, new appendix sections and the publication header. The existing narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds multi-panel MetaMathQA, accuracy-efficiency, data-size and teacher-trace displays; expands dataset and hyperparameter tables; and regroups Table 2. Existing key/value heatmaps exchange main-text and appendix placement without new underlying analyses. A layout regression causes Figures 5–6 to obscure part of Table 3's last row.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds System1.5 and clarifies the use of existing cache-compression methods. Additional citations support the new datasets, teacher models and safety discussion. The principal positioning against CODI, PCCoT and KV-Distill remains intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7, the formal cache definitions and Appendix A's eviction pseudocode retain their mathematical content. No theorem, proof or substantive derivation is added or revised.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical support for scalability through longer-trace mathematics evaluations, hybrid reasoning experiments and controlled studies of data quantity and supervision source. These additions reveal failure conditions as well as strengths, while filling missing baseline comparisons. Some Figure 14 points retain older baseline values inconsistent with Tables 1–2, Table 3 suffers overlap, and MetaMathQA comparisons exclude diverged baseline runs. These limitations reduce clarity and comparison strength but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and understanding.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KaVa research, with matching methods and identifiable retained experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison. A table overlap in v2 is recoverable through text extraction.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds MetaMathQA experiments, training-data-size ablations and evaluations using alternative teacher-generated traces.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and the appendices report original benchmark results, efficiency measurements, ablations, decoded latent traces and KV-cache analyses, alongside attributed baseline results.

results.title: KaVa: Latent Reasoning via Compressed KV-Cache Distillation

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are unchanged. Both versions claim that RL can conceal earlier SFT contamination, final-stage CoT contamination can evade existing detectors, and PPO-style importance sampling/clipping helps explain concealment.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies weak RL performance gains as a consequence of short training, argues that response length is not the main concealment driver, and distinguishes coding from general QA, where detection remains stronger (Appendices E.3, E.7, E.11). Quantitative embedding results also qualify v1's visual-only inference about indistinguishability. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability boundaries, although Appendix A itself is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents the Llama-specific training-data recipe and adds UMAP parameters, embedding inputs, classifier splitting, and layer-selection details. The original SFT/RL hyperparameter tables, hardware disclosure, and code repository remain unchanged; the new reproducibility statement mainly points to existing material.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, v2 evaluates LiveCodeBench v2 for coding and six selected MMLU-Pro domains for general QA. Appendix E.11 reports both pre-LRM and post-LRM contamination experiments on this substantially broader task coverage.

E2.justification: The original ten detectors and training-objective controls are retained. v2 adds an evaluated embedding-based MLP detector following Liu et al. (2024), with AUROCs in Table 19; v1 only cited embedding methods and presented embedding visualizations.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 30K clean SFT samples and ninefold member duplication, Qwen 3B/14B configurations, and a 14B distilled reasoning model. v2 also adds a 280-step RL experiment and an embedding-classifier protocol using an 80/20 train/test split and hidden-layer selection. These extend the experimental design; the original shared settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analysis of response length as a possible confound (Figure 6), model-size sensitivity (Appendix E.6), and longer RL training testing whether task improvement coexists with concealment (E.7). It also supplements embedding visualizations with quantitative detection analysis (E.8). The original clipping and token-selection ablations remain.

E5.justification: The documented detection averaging over eight responses and pass@1 rollout counts are unchanged. Neither version reports training-seed replications, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new response-length boxplots describe variation across questions rather than uncertainty in experimental effects.

E6.justification: Original numerical table rows are retained, while substantial results are added for model families, sizes, longer training, embeddings, and non-math tasks. Newly reported examples include DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B pass@1 increasing from 59.83% to 69.24% after contamination (Table 4), and embedding-detector average AUROC decreasing from 66.31% to 50.66% after clean RL (Table 19). These are new experimental results, not cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The two contamination procedures and the SFT, GRPO, RAFT, and RAFT++ objectives remain unchanged. Additional model configurations and the embedding-based comparator extend evaluation without revising the contamination method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section structure are retained. v2 makes localized rewrites, reorders related-work paragraphs and appendix material, adds an appendix contents page and stage labels, and introduces acknowledgements, reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: Tables 1, 4, and 5 expand to include additional models. v2 adds a Llama detection-trend chart, response-length boxplots, and substantial new tables for model-size, training-duration, embedding, and domain experiments. Existing figures are retained and relocated, with some revised captions; these are distinguishable from the genuinely new displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds Dominguez-Olmedo et al. (2024) to the contamination-concealment discussion and Dubey et al. (2024) for Llama 3. The main literature positioning and claim of investigating concealment at the algorithmic level remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1, the membership-gap definitions, algorithm-specific derivations, and the full proof in Appendix C are unchanged. The additional experiments introduce no new formal result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis by addressing v1's reliance on one pre-LRM base model, math/science evaluation, and visual-only embedding evidence. Model-family and size checks, non-math evaluations, response-length analysis, longer-training controls, and quantitative embedding detection address important generality and validity gaps. Some broad near-random-detection wording remains insufficiently qualified by the stronger general-QA results in Table 22, but the added evidence and applicability distinctions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same contamination-detection study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results for additional models, model sizes, detection methods, and task domains.

before.justification: v1 reports original contamination experiments, benchmark pass@1 scores, detector AUROCs, and training-objective ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: On The Fragility of Benchmark Contamination Detection in Reasoning Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: minimum-based online/target bootstrapping mitigates overestimation, supports faster stable learning, and applies broadly with negligible overhead. Added experiments support these existing claims rather than redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific interpretations: conservative ensemble updates can be advantageous offline because exploration is less consequential, and incorporating online estimates can increase variance. Appendix B discusses alternative critic-specific targets and leaves their systematic comparison open. The original concerns about underestimation and exploration remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 states that code is released and supplies a MINTO repository link plus implementation provenance for the discrete online and offline experiments. Appendix E adds detailed network, optimizer, replay, exploration and reference-value construction settings. This substantially expands reproducibility information, although repository availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v2 adds the deterministic Car-on-the-Hill task, with continuous states and discrete actions, in Appendix E. The original Atari and continuous-control task sets remain. Offline appendix captions change from 15 to 14 games, correcting the description of existing coverage rather than documenting a removed game.

E2.justification: v1's offline experiments compare CQL with CQL+MINTO; v2 adds Double CQL, FR-CQL, ScCQL and Maxmin CQL in Figure 6 and Appendix D. It also adds CrossQ+WN and FR-SimbaV1/V2 comparisons in Appendix D.6. These substantially expand comparator membership. Maxmin DQN was already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces a distinct evaluation protocol: 3,000 training episodes, a 10-by-10 state grid evaluated under both actions, depth-50 search for reference values, and measurements of value error, bias and training loss. Section 5.2 additionally tests IQN with IMPALA and LayerNorm. These are substantial protocol additions; the existing settings in Tables 1–6 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's operator ablations and selection-frequency analysis are retained. New Appendix E directly investigates estimation bias, value error and learning instability, including an Online Only comparison, addressing the proposed mechanism beyond return measurements. Figure 4 also extends selection-frequency monitoring to the IMPALA configuration.

E5.justification: The SimbaV2 MuJoCo caption changes from 5 seeds in v1 Figure 13 to 10 in v2 Figure 18, matching the existing main-text reporting. This does not establish additional runs. New Figures 35–36 specify 100 seeds with IQM or mean estimates and 95% confidence intervals; the general uncertainty-reporting practice is retained.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for offline comparators, CrossQ+WN, functional regularization and value-estimation diagnostics. Figure 6 shows Maxmin CQL outperforming CQL+MINTO, with further improvement from Maxmin CQL+MINTO. Figure 4 adds an approximately 10% IQN AUC advantage with IMPALA. The reported DQN AUC advantages in Section 5.1 also change from approximately 18%/24% to 17%/22% for CNN/IMPALA.

M1.justification: The core MINTO update remains unchanged. However, Algorithm 2 changes the specified IQN target from target-network quantiles alone to the minimum of online and target quantiles at the selected action. Appendix B also introduces a critic-specific integration for CrossQ+WN. These are limited procedural changes; the PDFs do not establish whether the IQN revision reflects changed code or corrected pseudocode.

P1.justification: Most core prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 consolidates paragraphs, edits terminology and grammar, updates publication and affiliation text, and reorganizes Appendix D with additional subsections. The scientific additions do not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is expanded to display both CNN and IMPALA results. v2 adds an offline comparison figure, extensive per-task comparison plots, and the multi-panel bias/error/loss Figures 35–36. Existing figures are largely retained or relocated, with some caption, legend and axis refinements; the six hyperparameter tables remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work adds explicit positioning against clipped Double Q-learning and Kapturowski et al.'s trust-region approach. Additional citations support the new diagnostics and implementation provenance. These extend the existing discussion without substantially changing MINTO's positioning relative to target-free methods and ensembles.

T1.justification: Section 3 changes the formal reward model from a real-valued reward function to a reward distribution. Corollary 1, its assumptions and the complete non-expansion proof in Appendix A are otherwise unchanged; no new convergence theorem is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly supports its bias and stability explanation through return comparisons; v2 adds direct value-error, bias and loss diagnostics in Appendix E. New offline and actor–critic comparator checks address important gaps, while code-access information improves reproducibility documentation. Together these substantially strengthen the paper's empirical support, including evidence of a stronger ensemble baseline. The diagnostic remains limited to a small deterministic task, and some broad performance claims remain insufficiently qualified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MINTO research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds further algorithm comparisons, IQN architecture experiments, and Car-on-the-Hill value-estimation diagnostics in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original Atari experiments in online, offline and distributional RL, continuous-control experiments, and operator ablations, with additional results in Appendix D.

results.title: Use the Online Network If You Can: Towards Fast and Stable Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction drop the explicit assertion that learned interactions are biologically consistent, emphasizing interpretability and TRRUST validation instead. This modestly qualifies the headline biological claim. The five stated contributions and the main interpolation, scalability, and amortization claims remain.

C2.justification: Appendix E newly scopes the contribution as improving dynamics given a standard embedding. Appendix F.1 qualifies the global GRN evaluation because averaging discards context and signs, and restricting GRNBoost2's regulators supplies prior information. Appendix G.1 explains the memory benefit of fewer analytical decoding points. The existing local-linearity and TRRUST-context limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated reproducibility statement with repository and data-access information, environment.yml, and README reproduction instructions, beyond v1's existing hyperparameter disclosures. Appendix G.1 documents normalization, an L40S GPU, dimensionality-specific settings, runtimes, and memory use; Appendix F.1 specifies operator aggregation for the new evaluation.

E1.justification: EB, Cite, Multi, and TRRUST remain the data sources. Appendix F.1 adds prediction of interaction existence beyond classifying the signs of known interactions, while Appendix E adds cell-type classification diagnostics. These provide a focused task expansion; the higher PCA dimensions change settings rather than biological dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v1's gene-interaction evaluation compared Cell-MNN variants with guessing. v2 adds SCODE and OT-CFM Jacobians to the signed-interaction comparison in Table 2, and GRNBoost2, SCODE, and OT-CFM Jacobians to the new existence evaluation in Table 9. Table 11 also introduces WLF-SB and WLF-OT comparisons. This substantially strengthens comparator coverage.

E3.justification: The original experimental protocols remain, but v2 adds substantial new settings: 10D interpolation and 50D/100D experiments with unwhitened PCA, global rescaling, different learning rates, batch size 1028, and revised stopping patience. Appendix F.1 introduces a 70-regulator candidate set with 447 reference interactions and AUROC/Enrichment@500 evaluation; Appendix E adds k-nearest-neighbor classification with k=15.

E4.justification: v2 adds explained-variance analysis, cell-type UMAPs, and classification diagnostics to assess information retained by 5D PCA, plus experiments testing sensitivity to 10, 50, and 100 dimensions. These substantially broaden validation of the representation choice. The earlier zero-eigenvalue ablations and appendix operator visualizations are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Table 1 removes standard deviations from the across-dataset Average column; for example, Cell-MNN's 0.741 ± 0.050 becomes 0.741. Per-dataset uncertainty remains. Both versions already specify three random seeds, so the new reproducibility statement and seed-based result tables do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: The retained interpolation, scaling, amortization, and eigenvalue-ablation means are unchanged. New Table 2 reports average signed-interaction F1 of 69% for Cell-MNN versus 46% for SCODE and 48% for OT-CFM(J). Table 9 adds Cell-MNN AUROC 0.659 and Enrichment@500 18.572, without leading both metrics. Tables 10–11 add mixed-ranking higher-dimensional results, and Appendix E reports cell-type accuracies of 87% for Multi and 90% for Cite.

M1.justification: The PCA projection, MLP-predicted local operator, eigendecomposition, analytical decoding, loss terms, and optional zero-eigenvalue variant are retained. The additional evaluation procedures and dimensional configurations do not establish a change to the proposed Cell-MNN algorithm.

P1.justification: Most methodological prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 makes targeted abstract and results rewrites, expands related work, adds a reproducibility section and appendix subsections, and reorganizes the closing statements. These are localized narrative changes rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds the multipanel PCA Figure 7 and Tables 2 and 9–11, revises Figure 1's labels, and adopts ICLR typography, headers, and substantially reflowed figure/table placement. Table 1 explicitly labels the 5D settings. The original appendix UMAP panels remain, renumbered as Figures 8–11, rather than constituting new visual analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds SCODE and discusses time-resolved GRN methods Dynamo, SCENIC+, Marlene, and Dictys, distinguishing their input requirements from Cell-MNN's use of standard expression counts. This is a focused expansion of GRN positioning. The broader interpolation and ODE-discovery positioning remains, while bibliographic and citation-style updates do not represent new research.

T1.justification: The main equations and Appendix D's ODE-factorization proposition and proof are unchanged. v2 adds the normalized definition of Enrichment@K in Appendix F.1 and an EMD homogeneity argument justifying conversion of rescaled evaluation scores back to original PCA units in Appendix G.1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two weaknesses in v1: biological validation without learned GRN comparators and evaluation restricted to 5D embeddings. Tables 2 and 9–11 and Appendix E provide meaningful comparative and representation checks, including mixed outcomes that better establish applicability boundaries. Added reproduction instructions improve transparency. The loss of Table 1's average-column uncertainty is a limited reporting drawback, outweighed by the stronger validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cell-MNN work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including the rasterized appendix figures in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds GRN comparisons, interaction-existence evaluation, PCA diagnostics, and higher-dimensional interpolation experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original single-cell interpolation, amortized training, scaling, TRRUST validation, and eigenvalue-ablation results in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Learning Explicit Single-Cell Dynamics Using ODE Representations

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion now explicitly claim scalability to complex long-horizon 3D assembly and multi-robot planning under partial observability and visual variation. This substantially broadens the demonstrated applicability claimed in v1. The original autonomous dual-file generation and grid-world performance claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of simulator correctness without an external oracle, backbone independence, and perception failures in cluttered or visually unfamiliar scenes (Appendices B.2–B.3 and C.2). Appendix C.3 explains how an unconverged instance may still produce a reusable domain file. New discussion also proposes targeted error mitigation and temporal-image extensions, while retaining the earlier failure on entirely novel freezing dynamics.

D1.justification: Appendix C.3 supplies the previously omitted refinement prompt, a four-round refinement cap, numerical EW stopping tolerance, and behavior on nonconvergence. v2 also adds 3D input/output examples and states that code accompanies supplementary material, with public release planned. Existing fine-tuning hardware, hyperparameters, and the separate five-round prescreening limit are retained; these disclosures do not establish changes to those settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds Assembly and MultiRob to the six retained grid-world domains. These introduce 3D assembly dependencies, image-specified goals, multiple robots, reachability constraints, occlusions, and multiple viewpoints (Section 5.6; Appendix A.1). The original appearance and FrozenLake rule-variation coverage remains.

E2.justification: Appendix B.1 adds systematic SimVLM comparisons with GPT4o-Direct and GPT4o-InContext across four output tasks. Appendix B.2 additionally compares LLaVA-NeXT-7B and PaliGemma2-10B simulator backbones. These substantially expand component-level comparisons; the end-to-end Direct, CoT, and CodePDDL comparator set in Table 2 is unchanged.

E3.justification: New 3D protocols collect 100k examples per domain and evaluate 1,000 simulator examples and 1,500 planning trials per appearance condition, with specified visual randomization and unseen color distributions. New backbone experiments vary model configurations. Appendix B.1 uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2 semantic similarity for GPT-4o execution reasoning while retaining exact matching for SimVLM, limiting direct comparability. The original grid-world protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds simulator-backbone sensitivity studies, quantified perception-versus-generation failure distributions, and refinement convergence measurements across six domains (Tables 7–8 and 12–13). These investigate dependencies and failure mechanisms beyond v1's component ablations and qualitative examples. The original component ablations and unseen-rule tests are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 newly reports means and standard deviations across three random seeds for all four SimVLM outputs, six domains, and both appearance settings (Tables 9–10). v1 reports averages over evaluation cases without seed-level uncertainty. The PDFs do not establish an increase from a specified earlier seed count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 are unchanged, including VLMFP's 70.0%/54.1% grid-world success rates. New Table 5 reports Assembly success of 92.4%/85.9% and MultiRob success of 80.3%/73.6% for seen/unseen appearances. Further tables add simulator comparisons, backbone and seed results, error counts, and convergence rates. Table 13's reported averages, 77.1%/64.8%, conflict with its domain entries, which average approximately 73.3%/58.9%.

M1.justification: The dual-VLM architecture and generation, prescreening, consistency-checking, and refinement procedure remain intact. The 3D applications make a limited input adaptation: Assembly supplies initial and goal images, while MultiRob uses multiple views, enabling SimVLM to extract dependencies and occluded spatial relationships (Section 5.6; Appendix B.7).

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, tightens several explanatory passages, separates implementation details into Section 4, and reorganizes the appendix into parts A–E. It moves the unseen-rule descriptions and writing disclosure, and adds ethics, reproducibility, and acknowledgment sections. Most existing method and experimental prose remains recognizable and in the same narrative order.

P2.justification: v2 adds the 3D visualization in Figure 4 and eight tables covering 3D results, simulator comparisons, backbone tests, seed statistics, errors, and convergence. Original Tables 1–4 remain, and the old dataset-statistics Table 5 becomes Table 11. Existing figures are largely retained, with a corrected ice-hole precondition in Figure 2.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the two 3D task sources and Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-NeXT, and PaliGemma2. The related-work positioning against methods requiring predefined domain files, human corrections, or environment interaction, and the central novelty claim, remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, generation and refinement equations, and Exploration Walk score in Equations 1–3 remain unchanged. v2 adds empirical convergence measurements and implementation thresholds, but no new theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's grid-world evidence through 3D tasks, simulator comparisons, backbone sensitivity, seed statistics, and quantified failure analysis. The complete refinement prompt and stopping details also resolve important reproducibility omissions. These gains outweigh weaknesses in the additions: 3D results lack baseline comparisons, reasoning metrics differ between simulator comparators, and Table 13 contains inconsistent averages. The improvement comes from addressing validation and documentation gaps, while the original headline results remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VLMFP study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite reorganization and substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original 3D planning results, simulator comparisons, backbone evaluations, seed statistics, and failure and convergence analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original six-domain SimVLM and VLMFP experiments, component ablations, and unseen-rule evaluations in Tables 1–4.

results.title: Simulation to Rules: A Dual-VLM Framework for Formal Visual Planning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the annotation-resource, harmful-association, SAE-analysis, and 60–70% linear-fit claims. Replacing 'linearly explained' with 'predicted by a linear fit' preserves the statistical meaning already specified through R-squared in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of classifier-conditioned human sampling, subjective demographic judgments, contextual gender-label errors, and possible Black/unclear confusion. It also interprets nonlinear patterns, qualifies transfer for specific word groups, argues for CC12M generalizability, and discusses possible sources of caption bias. Its new conclusion that captions are 'overall safe' extends beyond the earlier discussion; Appendix A's existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The reproducibility statement replaces the promised code release with a specific GitHub link and reports data availability. Appendix F supplies the complete caption-judging prompt and GPT-5.1 reasoning setting, while Appendix D adds consensus-pool counts. Existing classifier training details remain.

E1.justification: Coverage expands through an external demographic-composition audit of CC12M (G.4) and sentiment/crime-word evaluation of generated person captions (F). These extend the existing web-image/text bias-auditing domain; earlier datasets and tasks remain.

E2.justification: G.3 adds cubic Chebyshev fits for comparison with the retained linear bias-transfer fits. The caption-model comparison still evaluates InternVL3-2B/8B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B; GPT-5.1 is introduced as their evaluator, not as another captioning baseline.

E3.justification: Caption evaluation changes from qualitative inspection of 4,939 bounding boxes to pairwise GPT-5.1 judgments on 500. Section 3 adds a 200-image detection check by one annotator and a stratified 648-image demographic-label study with two annotators. G.3 and G.5 introduce polynomial-fit and focused word-group evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds human-label error analysis, race/ethnicity logit correlations, generated-caption bias diagnostics, nonlinear-fit sensitivity analysis, and crime/personality subgroup analyses. These examine annotation validity, possible classifier bias, and limits of linear transfer. The small LAION detection case-study panel from v1 Figure 13b is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figures 8–9 add 95% confidence intervals to the previously reported correlation and R-squared estimates, such as R-squared 0.71 with interval [0.69, 0.72]. The PDFs do not document the interval-construction procedure or establish additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: New results include 82.5% fully correct detection images and race/ethnicity agreement of kappa 0.638 for human–classifier versus 0.654 between humans. InternVL3-8B wins 75.6%, 63.0%, and 58.2% against Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL3-2B, respectively. New polynomial CLIP fits yield R-squared 0.61, 0.67, and 0.73; crime/personality linear fits yield 0.12 and 0.10. CC12M and caption-bias results are also added, while the original headline linear-fit values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The YOLO detection and filtering procedure, consensus-based SigLIP classifiers, InternVL3-8B caption generation, and SAE/PMI pipeline are retained. The additions evaluate and diagnose these methods without changing the annotation procedure.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and section organization are retained. Local changes include a human-validation block, a discussion paragraph, new G.3–G.5 subsections, revised caption-evaluation prose, predictive wording, and conference-header and acknowledgement edits. There is no extensive rewriting of retained material.

P2.justification: v2 adds human-agreement matrices, a logit-correlation heatmap, caption-bias bars, nonlinear-fit plots, CC12M distributions, and subgroup plots. Existing transfer plots gain interval annotations and shaded bands. Example faces are blurred or regenerated, the LAION detection panel is removed, and several retained displays are relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds Changpinyo et al. (2021) for CC12M and Rudman et al. (2012) for personality traits. The main related-work discussion and Appendix H retain their prior research positioning.

T1.justification: The SAE/PMI definitions, conditional-independence assumption, probability decomposition, and CLIP bias equation are unchanged. Moving the main-text PMI equation inline and renumbering equations do not alter the mathematics. The polynomial addition supplies empirical fits without new proofs or formal derivations.

improvement.justification: The direct human checks address an important validation gap: v1's in-domain race/ethnicity evaluation relied on model-consensus labels. This substantially strengthens the central annotation resource, while quantitative caption assessment and subgroup analyses improve support and clarify applicability. Undocumented confidence-interval construction and an overly broad caption-safety conclusion remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same annotation and bias-auditing study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds human validation, quantitative caption comparisons, CC12M statistics, and additional bias-transfer analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotation-model evaluations, LAION-400M demographic and association analyses, and CLIP and Stable Diffusion bias-transfer experiments.

results.title: Person-Centric Annotations of LAION-400M: Auditing Bias and Its Transfer to Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: separating concept exploration from solution generation, improving sampling diversity and performance, and using these trajectories for post-training. Their headline numerical claims are also unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 develops an applicability boundary around whether useful concepts can be formulated, supported by the CommonsenseQA failure. It adds interpretations of concept-order effects and sparse late-concept coverage, discusses sequential exploration overhead, and introduces explicit limitations concerning model/domain coverage and selecting correct minority answers. Appendix F also adds a tentative no-collapse interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 supplies CommonsenseQA prompts, discloses best-K selection in Figure 4, and identifies the finish-reason diagnostic used in Appendix F. Figure 4 additionally labels the math benchmark MATH-500; the PDFs do not establish that retained results were rerun. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware, and code/data access remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds CommonsenseQA evaluation with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, extending coverage to commonsense questions without well-defined task-specific concepts. The original four evaluation benchmarks and OpenMathInstruct-2 training coverage remain. Additional Gemma experiments use retained tasks.

E2.justification: Tree-of-Thought is added to the primary inference pass@k comparisons in Figure 4 and participates in the new voting and call-cost comparisons. v1 already evaluated ToT for fine-tuning and diversity, but its main inference-performance comparison used only RS. The fine-tuning comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation of Gemma-3-27b-it, majority-vote accuracy, analysis conditional on reaching each concept index, a ten-candidate HumanEval stopping diagnostic, and average LLM-call measurements. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original sampling budgets and fine-tuning settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine earlier versus later concepts and their declining coverage, failure on CommonsenseQA, possible CAA model collapse through stopping behavior, and performance versus LLM calls. Figure 5 also extends the existing exploration-budget sensitivity analysis to Gemma. The original examples and irrelevant-concept case study remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical error bars. The training-split seed remains 21. v2 adds qualitative variability cautions and concept-index sample counts, but no new statistical uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Original results in Tables 1 and 6 and the existing Figure 4–5 series are retained, while extensive new results are added. Examples include Gemma GPQA pass@50 of 92.42% for GuidedSampling versus 70.20% for RS, CommonsenseQA scores of 95.66% versus 98.94%, and majority-vote averages of 35.87%, 32.80%, and 26.26% for GuidedSampling, RS, and ToT. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under changed settings.

M1.justification: The two-phase sampling algorithm, Algorithm 1, and FA/CAA training objectives remain unchanged. Section 5 and Appendix E.3 add majority-vote final-answer selection on top of sampled candidates, a limited inference-pipeline extension applied to all compared samplers.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 adds discussion and limitations statements, subdivides Appendices A and E, appends I and J, corrects IAA to CAA in prompt headings, and updates publication and author information. These are localized expansions and organizational edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figures 4 and 5 expand to three model rows, with Figure 4 adding ToT curves and revised axes, legends, and captions. New Tables 7–10 and Figures 6–7 display additional evaluations, concept-order behavior, and call costs. Existing tables and examples are retained but reflowed or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 updates agentic and reinforcement-learning citations, adds references for Gemma, CommonsenseQA, and model collapse, and removes Estornell and Liu. The central positioning against repeated sampling, tree search, and RandIdeaInjection remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Assumption 1 now explicitly applies to relevant concepts in Cr rather than informative concepts in Cinf, and its amplification equation changes from equality to a lower bound. Appendix A.1 adapts the derivation previously shown in the main text. The theorem and principal proof remain essentially unchanged; this is not a new proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation beyond v1's main RS comparison: it adds direct ToT comparisons, a larger model, final-answer voting tests, cost evidence, and an informative commonsense failure. These additions clarify practical benefits and applicability limits. Important weaknesses remain: Theorem 1 still claims equivalence from a sufficient lower-bound argument, and Appendix J's stated all-model averages match only the original two-model results. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and explicit failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GuidedSampling work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite added material and changed pagination.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds Gemma results, CommonsenseQA evaluation, majority-vote accuracy, concept-order analysis, and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original inference and fine-tuning experiments, diversity measurements, exploration-budget analyses, and additional model results in Appendix E.

results.title: GuidedSampling: Steering LLMs Towards Diverse Candidate Solutions at Inference-Time

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central diversity–fidelity claims. The rewritten introduction explicitly extends the contributions to accelerated few-step sampling, naming FLUX and SDXL-Lightning and claiming effectiveness where repeated inference-time interventions have limited opportunities. The underlying contribution remains initial-noise optimization.

C2.justification: v3 adds a substantive compositional-grounding limitation and explains how lower gamma can recover alignment (C.8). It develops interpretations of extreme attraction, spatial pooling, variance inflation and batch size, attributes accelerated-model effectiveness to sharper initial Tweedie estimates, and invokes personalization-related forgetting to explain TweedieMix failures. These substantially expand the mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: The main pseudocode and hyperparameter table are retained. v3 adds practical batch-size guidance, memory and timing measurements at B=3 and B=5, and human-study procedural details. Conversely, the explicit statement that the retained sample gallery uses SDXL is dropped between v1 C.4 and v3 D.4. No new code or data access instructions appear.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's MS-COCO evaluation and selected illustrative prompts, v3 uses GenEval and T2I-CompBench prompt sets (C.4 and D.3) and compositions derived from TweedieMix's personalized concepts (C.6). This substantially broadens the represented prompt domains, although the new benchmark prompts are evaluated using the paper's existing quality and diversity metrics.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets remain. v3 adds TweedieMix in Table 7/Figure 8 and variance-scaled Gaussian sampling controls in Table 6. Table 1 relabels the SD3 reference row from DDIM to FM-ODE while retaining every score; this does not establish a newly evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The original prompt counts and Table 2 settings remain, but v3 adds four-step SDXL-Lightning and FLUX-1-Schnell evaluations and a study with 32 participants, 30 randomized image pairs and two preference criteria. New experiments introduce extreme-gamma, pooling, noise-variance and batch-size controls, plus peak-memory measurement. The SD3 reference sampler is now identified as FM-ODE, without evidence of a rerun.

E4.justification: v3 substantially extends the retained ablations with extreme gamma values, pooling across prompt types, initial-noise variance and batch-size scaling. It also adds initial Tweedie-estimate visualizations across backbones and a compositional failure case with a lower-gamma remedy (Figure 9). These investigate mechanisms and failure boundaries absent from v1.

E5.justification: The new human study explicitly reports matching prompts and seeds between compared methods (D.2), adding seed-control information for that experiment. The original learning-rate sample-variance analysis in Table 3 is unchanged. No additional repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: All Table 1 numbers and the original computational table's numbers are retained. Substantial new results appear in v3 Tables 4–7 and 9–13. For example, four-step SDXL-Lightning gives CNO versus CADS Vendi scores of 2.8258 versus 2.7749, but PickScores of 22.5659 versus 22.5767. The human study reports 78.71% quality and 83.55% diversity preference over CADS. These are new experimental results, not version-to-version gains under the original settings.

M1.justification: The contrastive objective, fixed Tweedie anchors, gamma weighting, pooling, stop-gradient and optional KL regularization are retained. Algorithms 1–2 mainly change notation, and Table 2 still specifies three optimization iterations. The accelerated-model experiments do not document a new method component.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution bullets are extensively rewritten around initial-noise selection and preprocessing. v3 standardizes latent and loss notation, adds a substantial stepwise explanation, reorganizes the appendices into analyses/discussions and experimental results, and moves the existing future-work paragraph out of the conclusion. Affiliations and publication headers are also updated.

P2.justification: v3 redraws Figure 2, rearranges and renumbers the retained Pareto/window plots, and preserves old Figure 8 as Figure 11. New sensitivity, resource, benchmark and preference tables accompany concept-fusion comparisons, a failure-case figure, initial-estimate visualizations and another sample grid. These substantially expand the visual presentation beyond relocation or numerical edits.

R1.justification: New C.6 substantially expands positioning beyond zero-shot diversity samplers, contrasting CNO with TweedieMix and discussing complementarity to DiffSplat, CoT-lized Diffusion and counterfactual image editing. C.1 connects stop-gradient to Score Distillation Sampling. Additional citations support contrastive learning, the new prompt benchmarks and accelerated backbones; most original related-work discussion remains.

T1.justification: The mutual-information propositions, gamma selection rule and central proof arguments remain. New Appendix C.1 explicitly derives the noise gradient through the Tweedie estimate and the Jacobian approximation induced by stop-gradient. Appendix A also clarifies exponentiated-similarity and temperature notation without changing the claimed bounds.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's evidence through broader prompt domains, accelerated-model tests, direct human preferences and controls probing alternative explanations. The explicit compositional failure and mitigation in Figure 9 also make applicability boundaries clearer. These additions address important gaps in validation despite the unchanged core method and original scores. Uncertainty reporting and some implementation details remain limited, and the new results still show quality–diversity tradeoffs, so the evidence does not establish every broad fidelity claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Contrastive Noise Optimization with the same authors, core method and principal experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds prompt-domain evaluations, accelerated-model results, further analyses and a human preference study.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments on three Stable Diffusion backbones, quantitative comparisons, ablations and computational measurements.

results.title: Diverse Text-to-Image Generation via Contrastive Noise Optimization

C1.justification: The central contributions remain differentiable categorical trust-region projections, scalable sparsification, and improved training relative to clipping. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now explicitly extend the demonstrated benefits to code generation, including a new quantitative code-performance claim. Code generation was previously future work.

C2.justification: v2 interprets batch-size results as evidence that projection tolerates older rollout data and explains GPG stabilization through constraining policy outputs without requiring importance ratios. It also connects code-generation performance with entropy preservation. Code generation leaves the future-work discussion; limitations concerning larger models, mixture-of-experts architectures, and other modalities remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds the overall training pseudocode and documents Eurus-Code filtering, sample counts, reward execution, PRIME reward management, and SandboxFusion. The project-link footnote now advertises datasets as well as code. However, the unchanged reproducibility statement still promises future release, leaving actual availability unresolved. Existing solver listings, checkpoints, default hyperparameters, and hardware information are retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates mathematical reasoning and lists code generation as future work. v2 adds training and evaluation on Eurus-Code, comprising programming tasks from APPS, CodeContests, TACO, and Codeforces. This introduces a distinct task domain requiring executable solutions. Existing math coverage is retained; Eurus-Math is a clarified name for the previous math subset.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 4 and their associated curves add REINFORCE++ comparisons for Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Appendix D.4 and Figure 14 additionally evaluate adaptive clipping through BAPO and clipping-free GPG, including GPG with TROLL. These substantially broaden the comparator set beyond the retained GRPO, Dr.GRPO, PPO, and GSPO comparisons.

E3.justification: New code experiments introduce test-execution rewards, a ten-second timeout, up to ten test cases, and evaluation averaging pass@1 across four benchmarks. Appendix E.2 adds batch sizes from 256 to 2048, increasing updates between data collections. Existing default hyperparameters remain unchanged. The sensitivity caption changes from 8B to 1.7B, but Section 6 still says 8B, so a rerun is not established.

E4.justification: Appendix E.2 and Figure 16 add a controlled batch-size study testing robustness to increasingly stale rollout data. Figure 17 adds entropy-versus-success analysis across Qwen3 sizes on code generation. These extend the stability and behavioral analyses substantially. Earlier KL/sparsity sensitivity, overhead, response-length analyses, and example generations remain present after relocation.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 32-response averaging for AMC and AIME evaluations and the same sliding-window smoothing with unsmoothed curves displayed. Neither reports training-seed counts, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new plots do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds code-generation results, reporting 7–18 percentage-point advantages over Clip, plus REINFORCE++, BAPO/GPG, batch-size, and entropy findings. For example, new Qwen3-8B REINFORCE++ DAPO-Eval entries are 0.626 for Clip and 0.728 for TROLL. These are newly reported comparisons. All retained numerical entries in Tables 1, 4, and 5 match v1.

M1.justification: The KL projection, dual optimization and differentiation, regression objective, and sparsification procedure are retained. Algorithm 1 and Figure 6 explain the existing procedure. Additional training algorithms use the same projection; the PDFs do not establish a revised TROLL component.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, and the method explanation gains named stages and reordered discussion of optimization and differentiation. Analysis becomes a separate main section, while appendix analyses are reorganized into Appendix E and unchanged example generations move to Appendix F. Terminology, notation, and publication headers are also revised.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 3 gain code-generation panels; Tables 1 and 4 and associated plots gain REINFORCE++ comparisons. v2 adds Algorithm 1, the computation graph in Figure 6, and Figures 14, 16, and 17 for new comparisons and analyses. Multiple retained displays are resized, relocated, or given revised captions and legends.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially broadens positioning against adaptive clipping, expected-KL regularization, clipping-free policy gradients, Q-learning, and contrastive/off-policy approaches. New references include BAPO, GPG, REINFORCE++, MPO, and several alternative LLM reinforcement-learning methods. This expands the comparison landscape beyond the earlier emphasis on PPO-style algorithms and Gaussian trust-region projections.

T1.justification: Equation 4 restores a missing logarithm on the current-policy probability, Equation 8 corrects the Lagrangian expansion, and Appendix A.3 revises multiplier signs around the KKT expressions. These are local mathematical corrections. The sparsification theorems, assumptions, and bounds are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for TROLL's generality and stability: code generation moves from future work to experiments across model sizes, while BAPO/GPG comparisons and the batch-size study test alternatives and operating conditions absent from v1. Training pseudocode, the computation graph, and local mathematical corrections improve clarity. Seed-level uncertainty remains unreported, but the additions address important limits of the earlier empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TROLL by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds code-generation experiments, additional algorithm comparisons, batch-size experiments, and code-generation entropy analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical-reasoning experiments, comparisons across models and training algorithms, hyperparameter analyses, and computational-overhead measurements.

results.title: TROLL: Trust Regions Improve Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: LLMs act as algorithmists, generate reusable detector-specific synthesis code without accessing raw data, and improve anomaly detection across 36 benchmarks. Additional evidence and optional variants do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of local boundary refinement, detector-specific anomaly-type alignment and failures caused by overly hard synthetic anomalies. It qualifies the theory's applicability to non-smooth tree models and discusses lowering hardness to recover performance. Sections 6.14 and 6.19 also add stronger preservation and non-degradation assertions that exceed the conditional proof and conflict with reported failures.

D1.justification: The appendix supplies dataset properties, workflow pseudocode, complete example prompts, generated IForest synthesis code, and PyOD/DeepOD implementation information. The abstract adds a source-code repository link. These substantially improve documentation of the existing pipeline, although v1's explicit RTX 4090 hardware disclosure is removed.

E1.justification: Both versions report the 36-dataset ODDS/ADBench benchmark. Section 6.15 adds four controlled Hepatitis-derived test scenarios containing local, global, dependency and clustered anomalies. This extends the evaluated distributions without introducing a broad new application domain.

E2.justification: The main comparison methods remain those already shown in v1 Figure 3, and Gaussian, random and SMOTE synthesis comparisons are retained. Table 19 newly compares LOF with LOF enhanced by LLM-DAS; v1 evaluated LOF only as a standalone comparator, outside its five source-detector enhancement pairings.

E3.justification: The main normal-data split and AUC metrics remain unchanged. Added studies introduce alternative LLM backbones and classifiers, synthesis ratios from 0.1 to 1.0, controlled anomaly-generation procedures, and Wasserstein-based diagnostic metrics (Sections 6.9, 6.12 and 6.15–6.16). These substantially expand evaluation protocols without establishing that the original benchmark was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds backbone and query sensitivity, synthesis-ratio tests, classifier-choice and score-fusion ablations, anomaly-type alignment analysis, hardness-related failure analysis and multi-weakness synthesis comparisons. These investigate robustness and mechanisms beyond v1's retained component ablations, cross-detector experiment and Thyroid visualization.

E5.justification: Tables 4–5 introduce per-dataset ± quantities absent from v1, but do not define their statistical meaning or specify repetition counts and seeds. The paired one-tailed t-test and Table 1 p-values are retained. Added uncertainty reporting does not establish increased experimental repetitions.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their numerical results. V2 supplies detailed benchmark results and new backbone, runtime, sensitivity, anomaly-type and hardness outcomes. For example, Table 20 reports IForest–Cardio AUC-PR of 0.718 with low-hardness synthesis versus 0.622 with original LLM-DAS. Some new reporting is inconsistent: PCA+LLM-DAS on Breastw has AUC-ROC 0.996 in Table 5 but 0.6196 in Table 7.

M1.justification: The two-stage synthesis pipeline and normalized score fusion remain intact. Sections 6.16–6.18 add optional hardness-controlled synthesis, a mixture targeting multiple detector weaknesses, and a prompt-based proposal for generating detector-specific auxiliary classifiers. These are localized extensions of the retained framework.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose are preserved. Editorial changes include affiliations and conference headers, precise appendix cross-references, ethics and reproducibility statements, and a table of contents organizing the added appendix. Most expansion comes from added technical content rather than rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 preserves the main figures and tables while adding Tables 3–22, Figures 6–13, workflow pseudocode, and prompt/code displays. These substantially expand visual presentation of detailed results and diagnostics. Figure 6 redisplays the existing Thyroid visualization alongside a new Vertebral analysis.

R1.justification: V2 adds an isolation-method survey and references supporting already evaluated baselines and implementation libraries, including LOF, KNN, ICL, DTE and PyOD. The related-work narrative and positioning of the LLM as an algorithmist remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 6.14 adds Proposition 1 and its proof, transferring a synthetic-anomaly margin under Lipschitz continuity and epsilon-coverage assumptions. This is a limited conditional formalization of v1's intuitive boundary-refinement explanation, not a general guarantee for the complete framework. Section 6.16 also defines the Relative Hardness Ratio.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important documentation gap: v1 references an absent appendix, whereas v2 supplies prompts, example programs, dataset details and detailed results. Controlled anomaly-type tests, sensitivity checks and explicit failure analyses substantially improve assessment of the mechanism and its limits. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the Tables 5/7 inconsistency, undefined ± quantities and unsupported non-degradation assertions. The substantial improvement is in auditability and diagnostic evidence; headline performance remains essentially unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLM-DAS work, and their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. The supplied v1 ends after its references despite referring to an appendix; v2 supplies Appendix 6.1–6.20. Newly supplied documentation can be distinguished from explicitly introduced extensions.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds sensitivity experiments, controlled anomaly-type evaluations, hardness analysis and multi-weakness synthesis results.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original evaluations across 36 datasets, component ablations, cross-detector experiments and synthetic-anomaly visualizations.

results.title: LLM as an Algorithmist: Enhancing Anomaly Detectors via Programmatic Synthesis

C1.justification: The environment, agent-family, and benchmark contributions remain central. V2 adds climatology to the stated environment contribution, updates the headline advantage from up to 35 to 44 percentage points, and replaces the claim of hard-task parity with text-only baselines with the broader statement that hard tasks remain challenging even for frontier LLMs.

C2.justification: V2 develops specific explanations beyond v1's general discussion of difficult meteorological reasoning: fixation on the deepest global pressure minimum, inappropriate simulator use for short-term forecasting, and failure to invoke the simulator for counterfactuals. It interprets the ground-truth forecaster experiment as showing that accurate forecasts alone do not resolve hard-task reasoning and domain-knowledge limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds code and benchmark access information, the text-only baseline prompt, the generation model and source-report details, and the high reasoning-effort setting. It documents the climatology reference period and aggregation timescales. These are useful disclosures, although the retained Direct and Reflective prompt listings still omit the new climatology argument.

E1.justification: Table 2 adds explicit standard-deviation and percentile anomaly queries, an exceedance query, and targeted disaster localization, corresponding to v2 tasks 6, 7, 10, and 48. These extend existing anomaly and disaster task families within the same meteorological data sources; most earlier tasks remain under different numbers.

E2.justification: The main comparisons remove GPT-5-Nano and add GPT-5.2 and Qwen3-30B, including their evaluated text-only baselines. Appendix A.4 additionally evaluates a Geolocator-and-Climatology-only baseline and a ground-truth forecaster comparator. These introduce substantive information-access controls beyond v1's text-only, Direct, and Reflective comparisons.

E3.justification: The reported evaluation changes from LLM validity checking followed by extraction to structured extraction followed by programmatic validation and up to three extraction retries. Direct's execution budget increases from 5 to 20 attempts, and benchmark composition changes from 2,158 to 2,230 samples. V2 also revises some synthetic-task thresholds, adds IoU reporting, and introduces tool-removal and ground-truth forecasting protocols on 50% subsamples.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's difficulty and task breakdowns, v2 adds a four-turn storm-detection failure case, tool-use and runtime-error analysis, leave-one-tool-out ablations, a climatology-only control, and a ground-truth forecaster experiment. Appendices A.4.1–A.4.5 substantially expand evidence about component utility, tool selection, failure causes, and stability.

E5.justification: V1 reports error quantiles but no repeated-run variability. V2's Appendix A.4.5 and Table 8 report three identical-setting runs of Reflective with gpt-oss-120b on a 50% subsample, including per-run values and means with standard deviations. Numerical task tables also add error-standard-deviation columns. Cross-run uncertainty reporting remains limited to one configuration.

E6.justification: Results are broadly revised and expanded. Figure 4 changes GPT-5-Mini's Reflective/Direct/text-only correctness from 54.7/48.5/19.9% to 61.2/58.5/17.0%; Gemini's Direct-versus-Reflective ranking reverses. V2 adds ablation outcomes, human-versus-synthetic breakdowns, and previously unreported per-template results. These are results under revised benchmark and experimental conditions, not controlled same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 adds a Climatology tool providing historical summary statistics across multiple timescales and increases Direct's error-correction limit from 5 to 20 attempts. The core Direct and Reflective workflows remain intact. The JAX-GCM/JCM naming change retains the same described simulator configuration and does not establish a simulator redesign.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted edits to the abstract, evaluation description, results, and conclusion, reorders related-work paragraphs, and adds a Section 5.1 guide to supplementary analyses. The appendix moves prompts from A.7 to A.3 and groups results beneath A.4. Much of the original introduction, method exposition, and task descriptions remains unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adopts conference formatting, redraws the framework diagrams, restyles the performance plots, and combines the three difficulty plots into one figure. It adds failure-case and tool-use figures, ablation and variance tables, separate human/synthetic result displays, and extensively expanded per-task tables with additional metric columns. These are substantial visual and structural changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for JCM, Gemini 2.5, the gpt-oss model card, MathVista, and MMMU. It explicitly attributes the simulator to JCM and supports the discussion of quantitative VLM weaknesses with additional references. The broader positioning relative to scientific agents, weather models, and multimodal weather datasets remains stable.

T1.justification: The discussion-score precision, recall, and F1 definitions and the task-correctness formulas and thresholds are retained. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs. V2's additional empirical metrics and reformatted equations do not introduce new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V1 mainly established benchmark performance without directly testing tool contributions or explaining failures. V2 substantially addresses that deficiency through tool ablations, a ground-truth forecaster comparison, execution traces, and a repeated-run check. Expanded task-level reporting and access information also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. The narrow scope of the variance study and outdated agent prompt listings remain limitations, but the added diagnostic evidence substantially strengthens the paper's scientific support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Zephyrus, ZephyrusWorld, and ZephyrusBench. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching renumbered tasks and relocated material.

after.justification: V2 reports original evaluations using five LLM backbones, plus tool ablations, a ground-truth forecaster comparison, failure analysis, and repeated-run results in Appendix A.4.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations of Direct, Reflective, and text-only systems using four LLM backbones, with aggregate and task-level results in Section 5 and Appendices A.4–A.6.

results.title: Zephyrus: An Agentic Framework for Weather Science

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add a SOTA and robust-generalization claim for refined C-STS and extend named superiority claims to GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1. The first-RL-for-C-STS claim, two-stage curriculum, PSRR contribution and original 48.18 headline result remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning transfer across domains and label scales, exploration–cost tradeoffs, reasoning optimization versus scalar regression, and resistance to label-noise overfitting. It also recasts the unchanged reward-weight results from a delicate balance toward broad robustness. These substantially expand the scientific interpretation, although the causal explanations are not directly isolated experimentally.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies Stage I reward weights, R_base=0.5 and G=8; the preferred Stage II weights and N=24 were already identifiable in v1. V2 also advertises checkpoints alongside code. The added disclosure is inconsistent about format-reward weight: Table 6 gives 1, whereas Table 7 uses 0.1.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only the original C-STS task. V2 adds WMT-QE 2020 English–Chinese translation-quality estimation, involving continuous 0–100 labels and independent samples, plus evaluation on refined C-STS data with corrected annotations and conditions.
