E2.justification: The matched Table 1 comparison adds DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-4o while retaining earlier comparators. Appendix A.4 adds a Qwen3-8B regression baseline trained with Pearson correlation loss, and Table 11 introduces QA-SimCSE_LARGE. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen3-0.6B and 4B configurations alongside 8B, a 30% validation holdout for refined C-STS, adapted WMT prompts, and additional hyperparameter sweeps. These are added evaluation designs; the original Spearman/Pearson metrics remain unchanged, and newly disclosed defaults do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 adds sensitivity studies of Stage I binary-reward weight, generation multiplicity G and pairwise base reward, testing stability and exploration tradeoffs. Appendix A.5 adds a check against annotation-quality concerns. The original component, Stage II weight and slice-size ablations, error analysis and case study are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its performance results. V2 continues the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original 8B result remains 48.18/48.27 Spearman/Pearson, and Tables 2–4 retain their values. V2 adds 0.6B and 4B PoLi-RL Spearman scores of 44.34 and 46.23, WMT results of 54.33 versus SFT's 50.90, regression results of 46.44, and refined C-STS results of 76.08 versus SFT's 72.09, alongside new sensitivity results.

M1.justification: Equation 7 revises the specified pairwise reward through graded handling of tied labels and a normalization denominator of 4 instead of 3. Section 3.4 also introduces a WMT configuration disabling the C-STS-specific binary and pairwise rewards. The underlying two-stage curriculum and PSRR mechanism remain intact.

P1.justification: V2 copyedits existing prose, clarifies input and prompt notation, reorganizes the main-results discussion into labeled observations, and removes the standalone contact section. The principal section order and existing appendix narrative remain recognizable; new experimental appendices and an LLM writing-assistance statement are appended.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the branded report design with an ICLR template, changing typography, headers, spacing and figure placement. Table 1 gains model-size blocks, Tables 5–11 are added, Figure 2 relabels the policy model as Qwen, and the unchanged prompt is consolidated onto one page.

R1.justification: V2 adds references and targeted positioning around Pearson-loss training, translation-quality estimation, C-STS annotation quality and sentence embeddings, while dropping Agirre et al. (2013) and Tay et al. (2022). The related-work narrative and claimed novelty of applying RL to C-STS remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 7 substantively changes the mathematical reward definition: tied ground-truth labels receive 1 minus the absolute predicted difference divided by 4, rather than requiring an exact predicted tie for positive reward. The normalization bound also changes from 3 to 4. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation through a competitive Pearson-loss regression baseline, additional model scales, translation-quality experiments and refined-label evaluation. These test important alternatives and applicability claims while retaining the original headline result. Conflicting reward-weight disclosures, absent uncertainty estimates and overly strong causal interpretations limit the gains, but the expanded and more diagnostic evidence clearly improves overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PoLi-RL research. All pages, including appendices, equations, figures and tables, are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reformatting and added experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds model-scale experiments, translation-quality evaluation, refined C-STS results, regression comparisons and further sensitivity studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original Qwen3-8B experiments, reward and slice-size ablations, prediction-error analysis and a qualitative case study.

results.title: PoLi-RL: A Point-to-List Reinforcement Learning Framework for Conditional Semantic Textual Similarity

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list replace the claim of human-preferred dialogue with a claim of expert-validated clinical capability and patient-centric performance. The central contributions—unified inquiry and decision-making, experiential RL, and parameter-efficient benchmark performance—remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning action-bearing retrieval, irrelevant-experience interference, GRPO optimization and backbone transferability. It documents specific omission and hallucination failures, observed reward-hacking behavior, and a computational cost-benefit argument. These considerably extend v1's component explanations and general limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code/model release statement and model-weight link, training/inference timing details, and disclosure of approximately 50 manually reviewed high-reward trajectories per day. Most hardware, prompts and hyperparameters remain unchanged; the previously stated reward-model/critic learning rate is removed, without establishing that the underlying training changed.

E1.justification: The training and evaluation coverage remains KaMed-derived dialogue data, HealthBench Main/Hard, MAQuE, MedQA and medical MMLU questions. Physician judging, additional backbone experiments and examples from existing trajectories change evaluation or analysis, without establishing new clinical datasets, populations or task environments.

E2.justification: GPT-5 replaces GPT-o3 in the HealthBench Main, HealthBench Hard and MAQuE comparisons. v2 also adds evaluated SFT and PPO baselines and retrieval/reward variants, substantially expanding the comparisons used to isolate component contributions. Figure 3 no longer reports DeepSeek-V3 in the pairwise human comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces physician scoring of 80 sampled trajectories, categorical retrieval-utility assessment, and a 40-case cross-evaluator study (Appendix E). Additional protocols include Llama-3.1-8B experiments, safety-violation and empathy measurements, and a 200-case inference-cost evaluation. The existing benchmark sampling and deterministic decoding settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component-removal, similarity-retrieval and scaling studies, v2 tests SFT/PPO versus GRPO, state-only versus random/full retrieval, backbone transferability, and removal of safety vetoes or soft-skill rewards. It also adds evaluator validation, retrieval examples, concrete failure and simulation-fidelity analyses, and computational-overhead studies (Appendices D–I).

E5.justification: Appendix E.3 newly reports Spearman rank correlations between the Qwen3-8B evaluator and GPT-4.1/human judgments. This adds statistical agreement assessment beyond v1's win-rate aggregation. Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Doctor-R1's headline scores remain 36.29 on HealthBench Main, 18.73 on Hard and 60.00 accuracy on MAQuE. v2 adds GPT-5 results of 46.38, 29.57 and 67.00 respectively, plus optimization, transfer, physician, safety, retrieval-utility and runtime results. An existing result also changes: similarity-only retrieval's Health Data Tasks score is 26.96 in v1 Table 6 and 24.96 in v2 Table 8.

M1.justification: The multi-agent environment, GRPO training, two-tier reward architecture and experience retrieval/storage procedure remain unchanged. The Llama experiment applies the existing framework to another backbone; additional component tests and explanations do not introduce a revised proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, human-evaluation discussion and related work receive localized revisions. Appendices gain dedicated ablation and human-evaluation subsections, alongside LLM-usage and reproducibility statements. The main section sequence and most existing method prose remain stable; much of the expansion is new scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised, and Figure 3 becomes a combined patient-preference and physician-rating display. v2 expands the retrieval table's columns and adds optimization, transfer, reward, evaluator and overhead tables plus boxed case studies. Existing scaling plots and the original clinical case table are retained, with relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds a feature comparison matrix and distinguishes single-turn RL, test-time adaptation and interactive agents, incorporating FineMedLM-o1, Med-PRM and MedAdapter. It revises the positioning against DoctorAgent-RL: v1 characterizes it as focused on static answering, whereas v2 acknowledges interaction and emphasizes differential diagnosis and experiential learning as distinguishing capabilities.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation and numbered equations remain unchanged. Appendix D.1 adds a qualitative explanation of GRPO's purported advantages over SFT and PPO, but supplies no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence missing from v1: physician assessment supplements lay preferences, while optimization, retrieval and reward controls directly test central component claims. Concrete failure examples and cost measurements also make limitations and practical tradeoffs clearer. Some new summaries overstate the evidence: Appendix E.3 claims Doctor-R1 ranks first among open models under every judge, although Tables 14–15 give Baichuan-M2 a higher human mean, 4.31 versus 4.30. This reporting weakness limits the conclusions but does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Doctor-R1 research, with matching core methods and benchmark results. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds physician assessments, further ablations, evaluator comparisons, failure analyses and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, scaling experiments and a human preference study in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: Doctor-R1: Mastering Clinical Inquiry with Experiential Agentic Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The central non-monotonic effective-noise claim remains. v2 extends the introduction's claimed validation to permutation symmetries and adds the conclusion that noise-based tuning may reduce hyperparameter-search dimensions. The conclusion also narrows the low-noise characterization from incompatible solutions to low merging benefits.

C2.justification: v2 adds a representation-level interpretation: intermediate noise encourages complementary features while facilitating permutation alignment. It also interprets TIES as partially counteracting noise and distinguishes SWA's within-trajectory averaging from merging across trajectories. The WikiText-103 failure to achieve loss-reducing interpolation and the SGD distribution-shift findings qualify applicability beyond v1's discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial implementation information for the new analyses: GPT-2 dimensions, tokenizer and training budget; TIES retention of 70% of values with mean aggregation; CKA layer and sample selection; SWA checkpoint counts; and the TinyImageNet sweep's training and branching schedule. It also newly states SGD and momentum 0.9 for retained vision experiments. Appendix A's original schedules remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds WikiText-103 language modeling beyond the retained TinyStories experiments and a three-task merging scenario combining RESISC45, FMoW, and CIFAR10. The earlier vision datasets and distribution-shift evaluations remain; the additional TinyImageNet noise sweep uses already represented data and tasks.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evaluated comparison methods: TIES is compared with task arithmetic in Section 4.2, vanilla averaging is compared with weight matching and learned matching in Appendix D.1, and SWA-based endpoints are compared with ordinary endpoints in Appendix G. These comparisons were absent from v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include momentum sweeps, independent-initialization rebasing, CKA on 2,048 test samples, six-layer GPT-2 evaluation, scheduler controls, and averaging the last three or ten checkpoints. Figure 8 extends the interpolation range and introduces method-specific coefficient selection. Section 4.1 also changes the reported transfer architecture from CLIP ViT-B/16 to ConvNext-Tiny; this establishes a documentation revision, not that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial tests of the noise explanation: momentum sensitivity, a joint noise sweep on TinyImageNet, permutation connectivity, feature diversity, scheduler dependence, optimizer-dependent distribution-shift behavior, and complementarity with SWA. Earlier augmentation, excessive-noise, convergence, Hessian, and branching-time analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 14 newly specifies two independent fine-tuning seeds per checkpoint, and Figure 28 displays error bars for the new peak-loss-barrier results without defining their statistical meaning. Existing three-seed averaging remains. These are limited reporting additions, not evidence of increased replication for retained experiments or new significance testing.

E6.justification: v2 adds momentum gains, feature-alignment correlations, permutation and WikiText-103 loss barriers, and scheduler, optimizer, TIES, and SWA outcomes. Section 4.2 reports 88.0% normalized accuracy for TIES versus the retained 85.9% task-arithmetic result at learning rate 3e-5, using different interpolation coefficients. This is a new comparison, not a same-method improvement; the TIES coefficient labels conflict between Figures 8 and 25.

M1.justification: The linear-interpolation and task-arithmetic rules in Equations (1)–(2), and the core branching-and-merging procedure, remain unchanged. TIES, permutation matching, and SWA are established methods added for evaluation rather than newly proposed algorithmic components.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, experimental explanations, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. v2 standardizes terminology and notation, recasts the pretraining distinction as transfer versus non-transfer learning, adds a dedicated permutation/feature-alignment section, and reorganizes the appendices with a contents page. Author-contribution and equal-contribution statements are also added.

P2.justification: Figure 4 becomes a larger three-component display including momentum, Figure 5 is rearranged vertically, and Figure 8 expands to paired task-arithmetic/TIES curves and heatmaps. Numerous new diagnostic figures are added. The earlier ConvNext transfer figure is retained within Figure 34's optimizer comparison, while many other appendix figures are simply renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting TIES, SWA, CKA, momentum, and contemporary model merging, including Yadav et al. (2023), Izmailov et al. (2018), and Kornblith et al. (2019), while removing the CutMix citation. The dedicated related-work discussion and the main positioning relative to optimization and mode-connectivity research remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (3) changes the effective-noise scaling and its proxy from η/[B(1−μ)^2] to η/[B(1−μ)]. v2 also explicitly assumes approximately constant gradient-noise covariance when augmentation is fixed. These are substantive but localized mathematical revisions; neither version develops new theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support for the noise explanation through direct momentum testing, independent-initialization and feature-alignment analyses, stronger merging comparisons, and scheduler/optimizer controls. The revised noise definition and newly reported failure conditions also improve precision and scope. Reporting problems remain: notably, the same TIES heatmap is labeled α=1.0 in Figure 8 and α=0.8 in Figure 25. This limits confidence in that comparison, but the broader gains in validation and interpretation outweigh the localized ambiguity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same optimizer-noise and model-merging study. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original momentum, permutation-alignment, feature-similarity, WikiText-103, scheduler, TIES, and SWA experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy and loss measurements from vision, language-modeling, transfer-learning, and task-arithmetic experiments, including extensive appendix analyses.

results.title: How does the optimizer implicitly bias the model merging loss landscape?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: theoretical limits from token dependencies, the 17-task ParallelBench benchmark, severe parallel-decoding degradation, and inadequate adaptation of parallelism. The added experiments primarily extend support for these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning capacity bottlenecks in longer outputs and the correspondence between tokens per step and measured latency. Appendix I extends the applicability discussion to modified autoregressive decoding. The limitations now acknowledge preliminary longer-output evidence while retaining the need for a thorough study; the central dependency-based explanation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds direct GitHub and leaderboard links, specifies the latency setup as one A100 80GB GPU with batch size 1, and documents configurations for the added experiments. Existing LoRA training details were already present in v1. Table 3 corrects the Latin-square example from size 3 to 4, consistent with the existing 4×4 specification.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on MATH and IFEval beyond the previously included GSM8K and HumanEval comparisons. Appendix D.5 also introduces XSum-based paraphrasing and changes the added Words-to-Sentence scenario to ten sentences using seven words. These broaden represented data and task requirements while retaining the original 17-task benchmark.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 19 adds evaluated comparisons with SlowFast Sampling, DUS, and WINO on LLaDA 1.5, and APD on Dream 7B. SlowFast and DUS were previously discussed without these evaluations. Appendix I additionally evaluates modified Medusa with Vicuna-1.5-7B. The original model-comparison tables retain their comparator membership.

E3.justification: Figure 7 changes from v1's stated 10-task aggregation to all 17 tasks. Added experiments use Waiting Line lengths 21–24 with a 128-token limit, longer text generation with 256-token limits, fine-tuned puzzle models, and wall-clock latency evaluation. The short-output evaluations remain, and the aggregation change prevents interpreting the revised curve as a same-setting performance change.

E4.justification: v2 adds length sensitivity and capacity-confounding analyses in D.5, metric sensitivity across parallelism in D.6, and fine-tuning analysis for Sudoku and Latin Square in E.2. F.4 tests whether token-based speed comparisons correspond to measured latency, while Appendix I probes applicability to an autoregressive parallel-prediction setting.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for the experimental results. v2 introduces no new statistical uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Substantial new results cover longer outputs, metric sensitivity, fine-tuned puzzles, additional decoders, latency, and modified Medusa. Figure 19 shows WINO improving on the confidence-threshold trade-off on LLaDA 1.5, while DUS and SlowFast perform worse; APD's relative performance on Dream depends on parallelism. Figure 7 is replaced under revised aggregation. Original Tables 5–7 retain their numerical values as v2 Tables 7–9.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix I introduces an experimental adaptation of Medusa that bypasses dynamic verification and forces generation of 1–5 tokens per step. This changes that inference procedure; the core benchmark design and previously evaluated diffusion procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main-section sequence are retained. Changes include localized rewrites, additional appendix subsections, moving Discrete Diffusion Strategies into B.3, updated cross-references, conference and affiliation text, and an LLM usage disclosure. The experimental expansion does not constitute wholesale narrative rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds dedicated figures for longer outputs, metric sensitivity, additional decoders, fine-tuned puzzles, existing benchmarks, latency, and Medusa, plus two dependency-taxonomy tables. Figures 6 and 7 are revised, including added benchmark points and changed axes or legends. Most original displays are retained and relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references covering APD, WINO, Medusa/Vicuna, consistency and corrective diffusion, MATH, and IFEval, alongside brief discussion of trained remasking. These update the surrounding literature and applicability discussion without substantially replacing the original research positioning.

T1.justification: The conditional-total-correlation bounds, list-operation derivations, Theorems 1–3, and Appendix A proofs are retained unchanged. The new dependency taxonomy is qualitative and introduces no new formal result.

improvement.justification: The new length and metric-sensitivity studies, advanced-decoder comparisons, existing-benchmark analyses, and wall-clock measurements address important gaps in v1's validation of benchmark utility and practical speed-quality trade-offs. They substantially strengthen the empirical case while preserving the theory. Longer-output evaluation remains preliminary, and disabling Medusa verification limits conclusions about its normal operation, but these limitations do not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ParallelBench and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. The retained material can be reliably matched despite appendix reorganization and substantial experimental additions.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds longer-output evaluations, additional decoding comparisons, metric analyses, latency measurements, and a modified Medusa experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-task validation, ParallelBench evaluations, fine-tuning experiments, and decoding analyses, including Figures 2–8 and appendix results.

results.title: ParallelBench: Understanding the Trade-offs of Parallel Decoding in Diffusion LLMs

C1.justification: v1 explicitly describes the model variants as vanilla instances rather than new methods; v2 removes that qualification and calls BAM novel. The principal benchmark, multitask-performance, transfer and targeted-descriptor-benefit claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of late adapter integration and shared behavioral features, plus interpretations concerning descriptor complementarity, adapter capacity, stream selection, imbalance, generation retention and judge reliability. The revised ethics statement also newly asserts that discrimination, bias and fairness issues should not arise, without corresponding analyses.

D1.justification: Where v1 promises release after review, v2 supplies a repository address for the benchmark, models and code. It also adds fresh-session judging instructions, generation-quality and paraphrased judging prompts, timing hardware/precision/batch-size details, and the revised RL learning rate. These substantially expand access and reproduction information.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds IEMOCAP as an external emotion-recognition dataset for transfer evaluation. The original 13-dataset, 10-task benchmark remains intact; the other supplementary evaluations principally reuse its datasets.

E2.justification: Table 16 expands transfer comparisons with Gemma-3-4B, HumanOmniV2-7B and untuned Qwen Omni/VL models. Table 20 newly compares RLOO against GRPO, while Table 18 adds Qwen3-30B and human judge comparisons. Table 5's renamed Qwen SFT control was already classifier-equipped in v1 Appendix C.1.

E3.justification: v2 adds zero-shot transfer, adapter and RL configuration sweeps, 500-sample timing and judge-validation protocols, generation-quality metrics and seven-class sentiment reporting. Appendix C.2 changes the reported RL learning rate from 1×10⁻⁶ to 5×10⁻⁷. Main splits remain unchanged; the learning-rate revision does not establish that the main experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's taskwise BAM comparison and qualitative examples, Appendix D adds raw-input removal, descriptor-stream and adapter-width ablations; RL rollout, learning-rate and algorithm comparisons; computational-cost, dataset-imbalance and generation-retention analyses; and judge validation with prompt perturbations.

E5.justification: v2 introduces latency standard deviations across 500 inputs, Spearman correlations and Cohen's kappa estimates in Tables 13, 15 and 18. These expand statistical reporting for supplementary analyses, but neither version reports repeated-training-run counts or confidence intervals for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: Tables 4–6 retain their numerical entries, while Appendix D adds substantial results from new evaluations and ablations. Examples include IEMOCAP scores of 0.6213 versus 0.5625 in Table 9 and GPT-5-nano–human agreement of κ=0.78, falling to 0.75 with altered prompts, in Table 18. These are newly reported results rather than same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The SFT classifier/decoder architecture, pooled-descriptor residual BAM, and GRPO-based generative model remain unchanged in Sections 3.5–3.7 and Appendix B. Added architectural explanations and experimental ablations do not establish a revised proposed method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain. v2 changes much 'unified model' terminology to 'foundation model,' expands selected model and transfer explanations, revises contributions and ethics text, updates the conference header, and appends an organized additional-experiments section.

P2.justification: Appendix D substantially expands the visual presentation with Tables 8–20 and two additional judging-prompt boxes; some tables reorganize existing scores alongside new comparisons. Figures 1–4 are retained with layout shifts, Table 1 gains a DEP column, and the former appendix Tables 8–9 become Tables 21–22.

R1.justification: Five references are added, covering Qwen3-Omni, emotion labeling, language modeling and LLM-based evaluation. BAM's novelty positioning changes from explicitly non-novel supporting variant to novel adapter, while the main related-work discussion and benchmark positioning remain largely intact.

T1.justification: The BAM equations, SFT objectives, GRPO derivation and reward formulation are retained. Added design explanations and empirical statistical measures introduce no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked controlled adapter ablations and empirical validation of its LLM judge. v2 adds both, alongside external-dataset and zero-shot transfer evidence, substantially strengthening the empirical foundation. Some new interpretations overreach, particularly claims about negligible imbalance and preserved general generation ability, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the important validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Human Behavior Atlas benchmark and OmniSapiens models. The text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching v1 Tables 8–9 to v2 Tables 21–22.

after.justification: The original empirical results remain, and Appendix D adds transfer experiments, controlled ablations, computational measurements and human–LLM judge agreement results.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 report original multitask evaluations, held-out transfer experiments and behavioral-descriptor results, including Tables 4–6 and qualitative examples.

results.title: Human Behavior Atlas: Benchmarking Unified Psychological And Social Behavior Understanding

C1.justification: The central claim that spectral normalization accelerates grokking is retained. v2 extends the stated empirical contribution to practical computational efficiency, robustness, and broader datasets and architectures, and strengthens the conclusion's practical-efficiency language.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about rank tuning, wall-clock versus iteration efficiency, and exact-SVD instability on transformers. It also interprets nonstationarity recovery and divergent parameter trajectories, while explicitly leaving convergence theory for complex models unresolved. These substantially expand v1's interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, three pseudocode algorithms, RSVD ranks and two inner iterations, the omission of oversampling, Tesla T4 timing conditions, and architecture-specific EGD application details. These provide substantially more implementation information; the linked repository itself was not inspected.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST digit classification, CIFAR-10 learning under repeated label changes, and an empirical toy experiment with identical training and testing distributions. These substantially extend the represented data and scenarios beyond v1's retained arithmetic, parity, and distribution-shift toy experiments.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's vanilla SGD and column-normalization comparisons, Appendix D evaluates EMA-based Grokfast and AdamW/Adam controls. Appendix E compares Adam, RAdam, and RMSprop with and without EGD. Muon receives discussion but is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The original Table 1 hyperparameters are retained. New experiments introduce a three-layer MLP with AdamW, a two-layer transformer with Adam, CNN configurations, accuracy-threshold and runtime metrics, and CIFAR-10 label-shuffling schedules evaluated through training-accuracy area under the curve.

E4.justification: Appendices C–F add RSVD rank-sensitivity experiments, computational-cost tradeoffs, exact-versus-randomized SVD stability comparisons, nonstationarity recovery tests, and parameter-trajectory analyses. These investigate efficiency, failure conditions, adaptation, and whether EGD reaches different parameter regions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, specified experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The seed argument in v2's RSVD pseudocode and averages across tasks do not establish repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 2–8 add extensive timing, accuracy, and adaptation results absent from v1. On MNIST, rank-4 RSVD reaches 85% in 500 steps and 9.2 seconds versus Grokfast's 1800 steps and 28.7 seconds. Conversely, the new transformer comparison favors Grokfast: 910 steps and 114.0 seconds to 95%, versus rank-36 RSVD's 980 steps and 129.3 seconds.

M1.justification: The defining gradient transformation G -> UV^T remains unchanged. v1 already discusses randomized approximations and switching off EGD after grokking; v2 documents and evaluates these options more extensively without establishing a distinct new optimization rule.

P1.justification: The retained narrative largely preserves its wording and section order, with local language corrections and clarifications. New subsections, appendix contents, and cross-references improve navigation; the scientific expansion does not amount to a wholesale rewrite of the existing exposition.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figures 1–3 with revised axes and shared legends, adds Figures 7–22, Tables 2–8, and three algorithm displays, and adopts conference formatting. These substantially expand and revise visual presentation; the original hyperparameter table remains present.

R1.justification: New Section 4.3 positions EGD relative to Muon's similar update geometry, distinguishing raw-gradient SVD normalization from Newton–Schulz momentum updates. v2 also adds literature on linear-model grokking, randomized linear algebra, adaptive optimizers, and nonstationary learning, substantially expanding research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds population-moment derivations, dynamics, test-error expressions, plateau bounds, and Theorem 2 for equal training/testing distributions. Corollary 1 and its proof are also revised. Some new notation is inconsistent: Equation (6) defines r_k as mu_k/nu_k, while Equation (7) retains mu_k/L_k.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's practical validation through runtime measurements, direct Grokfast comparisons, broader tasks, and documented failure conditions. Implementation documentation and Muon positioning also materially improve assessability. These gains outweigh local notation and reporting inconsistencies, including Table 6's blanket final-accuracy claim despite rank-8 RSVD scoring 89.6% versus Grokfast's 91.0%. Experimental uncertainty reporting remains absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EGD research, retaining the central update, theoretical setup, and original experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable throughout, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds empirical results for MNIST, CIFAR-10 nonstationarity, randomized-SVD variants, runtime, and parameter trajectories.

before.justification: v1 reports original modular-arithmetic, sparse-parity, gradient-spectrum, and toy-model experiments in Figures 1–6.

results.title: Egalitarian Gradient Descent: A Simple Approach to Accelerated Grokking

C1.justification: The abstract and four principal FLOP contributions remain. Section 6 now explicitly conditions successful graph recovery on the true graph being Gaussian-BIC-optimal and emphasizes developing suitable scoring criteria. This refines the earlier conclusion that BIC optimization on standard benchmarks is largely solved.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops v1's distinction between optimization and causal recovery through nonlinear and causalAssembly failure analyses and stronger applicability qualifications. Appendix C.12 explains the mismatch between standardized data and DAGMA's assumptions and motivates the unequal-variance GOLEM comparison. The discussion more clearly attributes poor recovery to score misspecification or insufficient samples despite successful optimization.

D1.justification: v2 adds a concrete pip installation command, replacing the earlier Python/R availability wording. It documents the nonlinear generator's 100-unit sigmoid hidden layer, the GP kernel, GOLEM's gCastle version and defaults, and the software's fixed perturbation setting. Core hardware and implementation information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's simulated linear ANMs, v2 adds nonlinear MLP and Gaussian-process mechanisms, semi-synthetic manufacturing data from causalAssembly, and real protein-signaling data from Sachs (Appendices C.7–C.9). These substantially broaden the represented data and assumption-violation scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds nonlinear DAGMA to the MLP/GP comparisons in Figure 12 and unequal-noise-variance GOLEM to the standard ER comparison in Appendix C.12. These introduce substantive comparators addressing nonlinear modeling and the suitability of continuous-method assumptions. The earlier comparator sets are otherwise retained; DirectLiNGAM is not new.

E3.justification: New protocols include 25-node, degree-4 nonlinear graphs, 5000-observation causalAssembly resamples, Sachs bootstraps from 853 observations, and penalty/perturbation sweeps. Nonlinear evaluations compare SHD with distance from the exact BIC optimum. Existing core settings remain; corrections from 50 to 25 nodes in Figure 3's caption and from degree 8 to 16 in the dense-ER appendix resolve inconsistent descriptions without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v2 adds sensitivity analyses for the BIC penalty and ILS perturbation strength (Appendix C.10, Figure 14), plus substantial score-versus-recovery diagnostics under standard and misspecified settings (Figures 5, 12 and 13). Earlier runtime, initialization and restart ablations remain; the pre-FLOP labels rename existing ablations.

E5.justification: v2 introduces explicit resampling procedures: 50 samples with replacement for causalAssembly and 50 bootstrap samples for Sachs. The original 50-instance simulation practice and Figure 2's standard-deviation bars remain. There is no reported increase in repetitions for retained experiments or new confidence-interval/significance-testing framework.

E6.justification: Substantial results are added: Figure 12 reports FLOP100 reaching the BIC optimum in 44% of MLP and 72% of GP cases, versus BOSS at 12% and 16%. Sachs results report mean SHD 12.58 for FLOP20/BOSS/GES and 11.7 for DAGMA. The retained uniform-noise comparison also revises DirectLiNGAM's plotted SHD sharply downward, from approximately 200 to near zero (v1 Figure 5; v2 Figure 7), without explaining the revision.

M1.justification: Sections 2 and 3.2 correct the specified local score from n times conditional variance to n times its logarithm, retaining the penalty. Warm-start grow-shrink, Cholesky updates, initialization and ILS remain unchanged. This is a scoring-formula correction; the PDFs do not establish a corresponding implementation change.

P1.justification: Most introductory and methodological prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Changes are concentrated in the rewritten discussion, a new high-level algorithm overview, numbered benchmark subsections, acknowledgments and localized clarifications. Author and conference-header text also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds BIC comparisons, an algorithm flowchart, nonlinear and causalAssembly plots, and sensitivity panels (Figures 5, 6 and 12–14). Earlier figures are retained and renumbered, with revised captions, labels and conference formatting. Some labels introduce errors: Figure 11 displays BICtrue minus BICtrue, while Figure 12's difference label has the opposite sign from the plotted optimality gaps.

R1.justification: v2 credits earlier causal-search uses of ILS by Liu et al. and Nazaret and Blei, adds recent order-based work, GOLEM and equal-variance theory, and dataset references. Its principal positioning relative to BOSS and continuous optimization remains. The Benchpress preprint-to-journal update concerns the same work.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the Gaussian BIC expression, explicitly states faithfulness for asymptotic consistency, and adds an empirical-covariance validity qualification. Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3 and their proofs are retained, as is the Cholesky derivation moved from Appendix A to B.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the distinction central to the paper: efficient BIC optimization does not guarantee accurate causal recovery. New misspecification and real-data evaluations, more suitable continuous comparators, and sensitivity checks make that boundary assessable rather than mainly cautionary. Correcting the BIC formula and stating assumptions also improve precision. Erroneous BIC-axis labels and the unexplained DirectLiNGAM revision detract from reporting quality, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and applicability analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FLOP research, with matching authors, methods and retained experiments. Text, equations, algorithms, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulations and adds nonlinear experiments, causalAssembly and Sachs evaluations, parameter sensitivity tests and a GOLEM comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations measuring graph recovery, runtime and ablation effects on random graphs, paths and bnlearn network structures, including appendix results.

results.title: Embracing Discrete Search: A Reasonable Approach to Causal Structure Learning

C1.justification: The central orchestration, model-selection, and two-SLM-versus-Qwen-72B claims remain. The abstract adds an explicit generalization claim covering open-ended HumanEval generation, frontier LLMs, and domain-specific fine-tuned models.

C2.justification: v2 adds an upper/lower-bound rationale for the search objective, interprets prompt-optimization results as evidence of inherent aggregation limitations, argues that search improves an already robust architecture, and attributes limited frontier gains to overlapping correct predictions. These substantially expand the scientific interpretation. The existing limitations concerning static model sets and confidently incorrect outputs remain.

D1.justification: Appendix E specifies the CodeT5+ embedding checkpoint, similarity-matrix computation, alternative Qwen2.5-7B judge, model pairings, and sampling settings for the extensions. Figure 5 newly discloses temperature-zero decoding for discussion baselines. These additions improve documentation without establishing that previously reported experiments changed settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds HumanEval code generation to the retained MATH, GPQA, and GSM8K evaluations. This substantially extends task coverage from discrete-answer reasoning to open-ended executable-code generation; the additional frontier and specialist model configurations largely reuse these tasks.

E2.justification: The original orchestration comparators remain, including Single-Best-SC, which was already reported in v1 Table 1. v2 adds evaluated prompt-optimized MoA variants in Appendix C.2/Table 9 and constituent-model comparisons involving Gemini-2.5-Flash and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B in Appendix E.

E3.justification: New protocols include HumanEval Pass@1 evaluation with five samples per model at temperature 0.3, varying search-set sizes, random model subsets, and test-set scaling across K=1–5. Appendix C.2 also evaluates ten generated MoA prompts and six rounds of optimization directly on the test set. These are added evaluation designs; the original experiments' stated sampling settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether the baseline gap depends on prompts, whether consistency predicts correctness, whether model rankings withstand smaller search sets, whether gains persist without optimized model selection, and whether scaling trends transfer to test data. These appear in Appendices C.2 and D.1–D.4. The original groupthink analysis is retained in C.1.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3/Table 7 newly reports Bernoulli standard errors for Figure 5, although it calls them standard deviations, and Figure 15 reports Pearson correlations. Existing three-run descriptions and uncertainty reporting in Tables 1–4 remain; the PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include HumanEval Pass@1 of 0.506 and 0.939 (Table 14), frontier-model GPQA accuracy of 60.1% (Table 15), and random-selection and test-set scaling outcomes (Tables 10–12). Original Tables 1–4 retain their values. Figure 5 changes MoA's MATH accuracy from 51.4% to 46.2%, creating an unresolved disagreement with the retained 51.4% in Table 1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the model-selection procedure are retained. Appendix E.1 adds a code-generation adaptation that replaces exact-answer frequency with CodeT5+ embeddings, pairwise cosine similarities, and a coherent-cluster fraction for estimating confidence. This changes one inference component for the extension.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. Local rewrites clarify self-consistency and search, while the appendix is regrouped: original single-model results move from D to B.2, and the original mathematical discussion moves from Section 5 to D.2. Author notes and several explanations are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 15–17 for consistency, ranking stability, and test-set scaling, plus Tables 7 and 9–16 for uncertainty, sensitivity, selection, and generalization results. Existing appendix tables are relocated and several captions expanded. This substantially expands the evidentiary displays while retaining most original figures and tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds Chen et al. (2021), Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code, and Fu et al. (2025), Cache-to-Cache. The broader positioning relative to discussion-based orchestration, model selection, and test-time scaling remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 5 adds answer-distribution and positive model-margin assumptions, then derives a Hoeffding/union-bound guarantee for selecting the strongest model, with error decreasing exponentially in sample count. v1 had no corresponding selection guarantee. Its binomial comparison of self-consistency, SLM-MUX, and Agent Forest is retained in v2 Appendix D.2.

improvement.justification: The new prompt controls, random-selection analyses, direct consistency validation, and held-out scaling results address important untested assumptions in v1. HumanEval and additional model-class experiments further strengthen empirical support for applicability. These are substantial evidential gains, despite the new MoA discrepancy between Figure 5 and Table 1 and incomplete specification of the semantic-clustering procedure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SLM-MUX. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and newly added material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds prompt-sensitivity, design-validation, HumanEval, frontier-model, and specialist-model experiments in Appendices C–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark experiments, model-selection and compute-scaling results in Section 4, and debate-failure analysis in Appendix C.

results.title: SLM-MUX: Orchestrating Small Language Models for Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain DIT and its two proof-of-concept demonstrations, including rank generalization. v4 foregrounds failed cross-behavior transfer in the introduction, but this limitation was already established in v1 Section 6.1. The added evidence does not redefine the core contribution.

C2.justification: Section 6.1 adds architectural limitations involving unavailable original-model internals and possible adapter interference, plus proposed reasoning-based training. New appendices interpret capacity saturation, data scaling, agent failures, and lexical versus conceptual scoring biases. Appendix H also adds broader mechanistic and generalization interpretations to the retained weight visualizations.

D1.justification: v4 adds training-data and agent-transcript access links, the agent's versioned model identifier and query interface, and monetary compute estimates with pricing assumptions and data-generation costs. Existing code and weight links, training times, hardware, and core implementation descriptions are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic hidden-topic and news-summary tasks, including the existing zero-width-space trigger scenarios. The added experiments vary comparators, adapter configurations, training-set sizes, and scoring within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix C.6 adds a GPT-5.1 adaptive probing agent and its trigger-informed oracle variant to the hidden-topic comparison. Unlike the retained fixed-question baselines, this agent queries both original and finetuned models and chooses subsequent questions interactively. Figures C.3–C.4 report its evaluated performance.

E3.justification: New protocols include agent budgets of 20 queries and 100 for Qwen3-4B, DIT-adapter ranks from 1 to 128, and OOD training-data scaling with fixed training steps. Appendix K adds text-embedding-3-small cosine similarity, min-max scaled to 1–5. The original splits and primary LLM-judge evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds interpreter-rank sensitivity, OOD data-scaling analysis, agent query-budget sensitivity, and metric robustness with individual scoring disagreements. These address new questions beyond v1's retained inspected-weight-rank sweep, in-distribution data scaling, and generalization tests.

E5.justification: The original score-distribution tables and error-barred figures are retained. Additional plots do not establish a new uncertainty-reporting practice, and v4 adds no explicit repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence-interval methodology, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1 Tables F.1–F.6 retain their numerical results as v4 Tables G.1–G.6. Substantial new findings include weak agent recovery even with 100 queries, limited gains beyond adapter rank 16, improving OOD recovery with more training data, and preserved advantages over non-oracle probes under embedding scoring. Table K.2 adds concrete scoring disagreements.

M1.justification: The synthetic labeled-weight-diff training scheme, supervised objective, LoRA interpreter, and inference procedure are retained. Appendix E relocates the original method motivation. Varying interpreter rank is an experimental ablation, not a new method component.

P1.justification: v4 standardizes WEIGHTDIFFQA and DIT-adapter terminology, edits existing prose, and relocates method motivation and mechanistic visualization discussion to Appendices E and H. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 revises Figure 3.1, adds agent, rank, scaling, and metric-comparison figures plus Table K.2, and adds cost columns to the compute tables. Figure K.1 partly redisplays the original evaluation. Weight visualizations are relocated and reordered, and the ICLR layout changes figure sizing and placement throughout.

R1.justification: Section 7 adds substantive positioning relative to model diffing, including sparse crosscoders, stage-wise dictionary updates, and mechanistic finetuning studies. It also addresses privileged-information critiques of activation verbalization and connects the work to latent-knowledge elicitation. Appendix H adds supporting finetuning and representation literature.

T1.justification: WEIGHTDIFFQA renames the existing problem without changing its mathematical content. The training losses, adapter-commutativity argument, and parallel-LoRA formula are retained; Equation 3 moves to Appendix E. No substantive formal assumptions, proofs, or theoretical results are added.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens empirical validation beyond v1's fixed-question comparisons and single scoring approach. The adaptive-agent evaluation and alternative-metric check address important weaknesses in assessing DIT's advantage, while rank and controlled data-scaling analyses test explanations for its performance. Added resource information and research positioning further improve assessability. Applicability remains limited by synthetic tasks and failed cross-behavior transfer, and some mechanistic interpretations remain speculative, but these limits do not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DIT research, with matching methods and original evaluations. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material relocated in v4.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds adaptive-agent comparisons, adapter-rank ablations, OOD data-scaling experiments, and evaluation-metric analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original hidden-topic recovery, news-summary reconstruction, rank and trigger generalization, cross-behavior transfer, and trigger-recovery experiments.

results.title: Learning to Interpret Weight Differences in Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the claimed applicability from hardware-oriented 2:4 pruning to improvements under general N:M patterns and unstructured sparsity. This substantially expands the claimed methodological scope, although the original 2:4 contribution and conclusion remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of calibration efficiency and MoE applicability, and explains the accuracy–latency tradeoff against rotation methods. Section 4.4 quantifies the wrappers' theoretical throughput cost. Section 4.5 acknowledges intractable general unstructured mask updates and characterizes its reduced-budget extension results as lower bounds. These refine the existing interpretation without replacing it.

D1.justification: Section 6 changes from promising a future code release to reporting available code with a specific GitHub repository, materially expanding documented reproducibility support. V2 also identifies the inference implementation as a PyTorch-only proof of concept and specifies settings for the added experiments. Repository contents are not verifiable from the PDFs; the original implementation appendix is otherwise retained.

E1.justification: The calibration datasets, evaluation datasets, and downstream tasks are retained. New sparsity-pattern and MoE experiments reuse Wikitext2/C4 or MMLU, changing compression and model settings rather than represented data or downstream task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds RotPruner, Wanda+DenoiseRotator, and SparseGPT+DenoiseRotator as evaluated comparators in Table 5, substantially extending comparison to learnable pruning methods. The original SparseGPT, Wanda, and NoWag-P comparisons remain. MaskLLM and Targeted Low-Rank Refinement are discussed but explicitly excluded from evaluation.

E3.justification: Original protocols remain, but substantial additional protocols appear: 2048-token evaluation for Table 5; 5000 iterations for unstructured and 2000 for other N:M experiments; a 16–128-sample calibration sweep; and Qwen3-30B-A3B evaluation using block size 32, 1000 iterations, and 512 calibration samples. These are additional settings, not replacements for the main experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix E.3 adds a calibration-size sensitivity analysis using 16, 32, 64, and 128 samples, finding less than 1% perplexity variation. Existing optimization-progress, block-size, selection-heuristic, and calibration-source analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added results retain the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original table values and plotted results remain unchanged, while Tables 5, 6, 9, and 10 add substantial results. New results also cover other sparsity patterns, calibration sensitivity, and MoE MMLU accuracy of 72.50 versus NoWag-P's 66.67. Table 5 is a separate protocol, not a performance change from Table 3.

M1.justification: The factorization, loss, and main alternating optimizer remain. Section 4.5 adds an unstructured variant using only continuous updates. Equation 3 revises the stated initialization from selecting weights directly to selecting normalized squared weights multiplied by activation squared norms. These are limited procedural changes; they do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized language corrections, revises related-work and efficiency paragraphs, adds results subsections and appendix material, and updates affiliations and publication headers. The overall narrative and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds four compact tables, including side-by-side Tables 5–6, and relocates Figure 3 while clarifying its caption. Original appendix tables are renumbered. All three figure images and the existing table structures are retained; there is no broad visual redesign.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands positioning against learnable, rotation-based, and low-rank approaches, adding RotPruner, DenoiseRotator, MaskLLM, LoSparse, Targeted Low-Rank Refinement, and OWL. Equation 3 also corrects the initialization score underlying its optimality statement. The convergence theorem and existing proofs in Appendices C–D otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important validation gaps through relevant learnable baselines under an explicitly matched context length, calibration-size testing, and additional applicability experiments. The corrected initialization formula and reported code access also strengthen reproducibility. These are substantial gains over v1's narrower evidence. Remaining weaknesses include blanket superiority wording despite losses in Table 5 and a stale statement excluding MoE models, but these do not outweigh the improved evidence and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ARMOR. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, other sparsity patterns, calibration-size experiments, and MoE evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original pruning experiments, downstream accuracy, perplexity, inference benchmarks, and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix E.

results.title: ARMOR: High-Performance Semi-Structured Pruning via Adaptive Matrix Factorization

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the assertion that masking ensures maximum uncertainty to providing action uncertainty. The abstract replaces numerical highlights with a broader statement about reliable selection and benchmark improvements, while those numerical claims remain in the introduction. The principal verifier-free selection and joint-training contributions are retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains how unnecessary stochasticity can harm simple LIBERO tasks, proposes reasons for poor performance at low and high dropout ratios, and discusses domain-dependent aggregation spans. New KL visualizations and reconstruction analysis support interpretations of task-sensitive confidence and token truncation. It also explicitly weighs marginal gains beyond four candidates against computational cost.

D1.justification: v2 provides targeted implementation details for MiniVLA and CALVIN, specifies RoboMonkey's LLaVA-7B verifier and comparison modifications, and identifies the RTX A6000 used for that latency comparison. Table 10 newly identifies an A100 for existing latency measurements. The original training configurations and deployment search ranges remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds CALVIN with training environments A/B/C and zero-shot testing in environment D, evaluating chains of up to five instructions across its manipulation tasks. This substantially extends coverage to another environment-transfer and sequential-instruction setting. RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and the original real-world tasks are retained.

Table 5 also expands candidate-count and aggregation-span sweeps. These investigate several previously untested design choices and failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly reports means, medians, and interquartile ranges of KL scores across four candidate actions. This is descriptive statistical reporting, not benchmark confidence intervals. The existing three-seed success-rate averaging and five-seed latency protocol remain, with no stated increase in repeated runs or new significance testing.

E6.justification: Table 6 revises OpenVLA's average from 69.2 to 69.1 and its MG-Select counterpart from 70.8 to 71.7 without explaining the changes. New results include MiniVLA averages of 54.1 versus 60.5, CALVIN average chain lengths of 3.69 versus 3.86, and modified RoboMonkey versus MG-Select success rates of 50.7 versus 50.3. Numerous ablation, latency, and diagnostic findings are also added; the original RoboCasa, SIMPLER, and real-world headline scores remain.

M1.justification: The proposed sampling procedure, masked-reference KL scoring, token aggregation, joint-training objective, and single-prefill deployment remain unchanged. MiniVLA evaluation applies existing text-masking and aggregation choices; the additional explanations and experiments do not establish a revised MG-Select algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative receives limited abstract, conclusion, terminology, heading, and cross-reference edits, alongside an updated publication header and acknowledgments. New appendices organize the added material, and the unchanged LLM disclosure moves from Appendix D to I. Existing sections are not extensively rewritten or reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 11–15 and Figures 4–6, introducing additional comparison tables, failure rollouts, KL box plots, and a reconstruction-error scatter plot. Tables 5 and 10 gain rows. Figure 3 is relocated and redrawn with candidate counts through 64 and an expanded latency axis; Figures 1–2 are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to MiniVLA and CALVIN and develops its empirical positioning against the already-cited RoboMonkey. The main related-work discussion and distinction between intrinsic confidence and external verifiers are otherwise retained.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a theorem and complete derivation establishing that masked-reference entropy increases with temperature, with derivative Var(z)/tau^3 >= 0. v1 supplied an empirical temperature rationale but no corresponding theorem or proof. This establishes the entropy property, not a guarantee of improved action selection.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a direct external-verifier comparison and substantive failure analysis despite their importance to its motivation. v2 addresses these gaps through Table 14 and Figure 4, while sensitivity studies, model-scale evaluation, and CALVIN results substantially strengthen the evidence and clarify applicability. These limitations constrain particular conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in comparative support and diagnostic understanding.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds CALVIN evaluation, MiniVLA experiments, a RoboMonkey comparison, and further diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation and Franka robot experiments, including benchmark success rates, component ablations, and inference-latency measurements.

results.title: Verifier-free Test-Time Sampling for Vision-Language-Action Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and concluding contribution statement retain the central claims: learn unmasking policies for frozen MDMs through a regularized MDP, provide convergence and KL-tightening guarantees, and outperform strong heuristics across the four principal benchmarks. C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and applicability discussion. It explains smaller mathematical-reasoning gains through weaker ordering regularity, vocabulary size and training-data limitations; interprets the theorem's reward conditions; and frames general-purpose policy learning as preliminary. Appendix F adds distinct explanations of confidence-sampling failures, while Appendix D discusses reward-density and exploration tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v2 adds a stated code-access link and Appendix E with optimizer settings, group size, learning-rate schedules, regularization coefficients, GPU allocations, quantization, checkpoint selection and prompt templates. These fill substantial omissions in v1's reproducibility information without proving those settings were newly adopted.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates logic puzzles and mathematical reasoning on four benchmarks. v2 retains these and adds Natural Questions in Appendix D.2, substantially extending the represented domain to open-domain question answering and unconstrained natural-language answers.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 retain their numerical results. Appendix D.2 reports 70.5% GSM8K accuracy against its stated 68.2% confidence baseline, and new figures report likelihood trends, Pass@N behavior and qualitative trajectories. These are additional results, not demonstrated same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The frozen-MDM architecture, UPO loss and reference-policy realizations remain intact. Appendices D.2–D.3 introduce limited adaptations: training with Qwen-3 32B log-likelihood rewards and noise-perturbed position selection for multi-shot generation. Newly disclosed details of the retained experiments do not establish that their underlying implementation changed.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 adds localized explanations, an expanded conclusion discussion, a contents page, conference statements and new appendix sections, while polishing cross-references and proof exposition. The header changes from preprint to ICLR 2026 publication status.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 4 and Figures 6–10, introducing reward-comparison plots, likelihood curves, learned-policy Pass@N visualization and detailed Sudoku trajectories. It also adds boxed prompt templates and colored proof parentheses, and relocates existing displays. The original figures and tables retain their substantive content.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Qwen3, Natural Questions, Gumbel-Softmax, planted constraint-satisfaction hardness and Seed Diffusion, with localized discussion connecting them to the additions. Its principal positioning relative to MDM post-training and DCOLT remains unchanged. Publication and bibliographic updates otherwise concern the same cited works.

Theorem 2 changes non-strict KL tightening to strict tightening with explicit binary-reward and nondegeneracy conditions. Appendix C adds terminal-support and trajectory absolute-continuity arguments, corrects Proposition 2's strict inequality to a non-strict bound, and repairs local algebra and indexing.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves reproducibility and validation: Appendix E supplies previously missing reward construction, training settings and prompts, while Table 4 tests the binary-reward regime assumed by the theory. Appendix C corrects and strengthens mathematical justification, and the trajectory analyses explain concrete failures. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UPO research, with matching authors, architecture, principal experiments and theoretical framework. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds reward ablations, Natural Questions experiments, learned-policy Pass@N results and Sudoku case studies.

These test component utility and robustness beyond v1's retained round-wise plots, uncertainty probes and qualitative examples.

The retained toxicity-reduction comparison still reports mean ± standard deviation over five runs (v1 Figure 5; v3 Figure 7). No increase in runs or new confidence intervals or significance tests is documented.

E6.justification: New results include helpfulness pairwise accuracies of 0.725/0.729 for 1B/8B models (Table 1), 8B toxicity AUROC of 0.916 (Table 2), and single-round/sequential log-determinants of -196/-897 (Table 3). P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Changes include targeted explanatory rewrites, standardized model names and spelling, conference-header and author-format edits, and moving limitations into Appendix A. The appendices are reorganized around the additional experiments and positioning discussion.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 4, 6 and 12–14 and Tables 1–4, expands Figure 3 with an 8B row, and relocates the framework overview into the introduction. Original qualitative Tables 1–5 become Tables 5–9, with some spanning pages. This substantially expands and reorganizes the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds the HH-RLHF dataset citation and Appendix F's feature comparison against already-cited RLHF, Bayesian IRL, ensemble and reward-model approaches. It makes the claimed novelty of integrating sequential auditing and policy validation more explicit, while largely retaining the original related-work discussion.

T1.justification: The contextual-bandit formulation, linear reward definition, Bayesian likelihood and posterior, ELBO and uncertainty decomposition are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs. The new expert-noise explanation does not revise the mathematical likelihood or introduce a formal result.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's toxicity-only, at-most-1B evidence through helpfulness and 8B experiments, a targeted inference ablation and direct auditor comparisons. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Alignment Auditor framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, with retained material identifiable despite relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original detoxification experiments, sequential posterior analyses, uncertainty diagnostics, PPO validation and qualitative model outputs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evaluation of cross-model generality and practical usefulness through newer backbones, a relevant CoT control, and explicit accuracy–latency comparisons, addressing important gaps in v1. results.title: ChainMPQ: Interleaved Text-Image Reasoning Chains for Mitigating Relation Hallucinations

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: zero-shot resolution generalization is unreliable, physics constraints and band-limited learning do not reliably solve it, and inexpensive mixed-resolution training improves generalization. The additions primarily support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations distinguishing architecture-driven from data-driven aliasing, a hypothesis connecting DeepONet's mixture sensitivity to its fixed-resolution input, and interpretation of hardware-dependent errors. It also introduces substantive limitations concerning Darcy-only seed replication, unavailable or unsupported hardware, and suspected Apple M2 software incompatibility.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 specifies strided sampling and FFT filtering; Appendix H expands implementation links into explicit architecture configurations. The new reproducibility statement and Appendix N disclose hardware, software versions, and dedicated replication-script links. These are substantial documentation additions, without establishing changes to the retained experiments' implementations.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Darcy, Burgers, and Navier–Stokes datasets and resolution-generalization tasks. The additions primarily revisit Darcy with different models, preprocessing, seeds, and computing platforms.

Appendix K additionally compares anti-aliasing FNO with ordinary GELU FNO, substantially extending the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: New protocols compare striding, average pooling, and bilinear downsampling (Appendix M), and six hardware/software stacks using normalized-residual-spectrum AUC (Appendix N). Section 5 also changes the stated pairwise fractions from 0.05/0.95 to 0.5/0.1, although Figures 28–30 retain 5%/95% rows; this inconsistency does not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained physics-weight and Fourier-mode ablations, v2 tests activation-driven aliasing, sensitivity to downsampling and initialization, and reproducibility across computing platforms. Appendix J also examines whether multi-resolution training transfers to DeepONet and how its performance depends on resolution mixtures.

E5.justification: v1 provides no random-seed variability estimates. Appendix L first reports three-seed Darcy experiments, mean and standard deviation in Table 5, shaded uncertainty bands in Figures 44–45, and individual-seed heatmaps. It explicitly states that computational cost prevented equivalent repeated-seed studies for Burgers and Navier–Stokes.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical and spectral results for the new comparisons and robustness studies, while retaining the original loss heatmaps and mode-ablation plots. For example, Table 5 newly reports Darcy train-16/test-128 MSE of 2.0e-3 ± 3e-4. Tables 3–4 add storage and training-time comparisons, including 0.33 versus 0.05 hours for single-maximum-resolution versus mixed-resolution Darcy training.

M1.justification: The proposed multi-resolution training procedure remains unchanged. DeepONet and anti-aliasing FNO are added as evaluated alternatives and ablations; the expanded architecture descriptions document implementations rather than revise the proposed remedy.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and narrative are retained with local sentence and caption editing. v2 adds a reproducibility statement, subdivides Appendix C, expands implementation explanations, and extends the appendix structure without substantially rewriting the central argument.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive spectral plots, heatmaps, uncertainty displays, and hardware prediction examples in Figures 35–57, plus Tables 3–5 and an expanded Table 2. It changes Figure 9's Burgers display and adopts conference formatting. The old mode plots are renumbered, while the existing timing plot is duplicated as Figures 31 and 32.

improvement.justification: The activation and downsampling controls, DeepONet comparisons, seed estimates, and hardware replication address important untested alternatives behind v1's broad empirical conclusions. Expanded implementation documentation also substantially improves reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including the inconsistent Section 5 ratio list and reversed axis descriptions in Figure 51; repeated-seed evidence remains limited to Darcy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds DeepONet, activation, seed-sensitivity, downsampling, resource-cost, and hardware experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Darcy, Burgers, and Navier–Stokes, including resolution generalization, corrective approaches, and multi-resolution training.

results.title: The False Promise of Zero-Shot Super-Resolution in Machine-Learned Operators

C1.justification: V2 narrows the headline priority claim from the first fine-grained bounds for model-free RL generally to the first such UCB-based bound plus rigorous non-UCB counterparts. It explicitly credits AMB with the earlier fine-grained bound while retaining the same substantive algorithmic contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix C discusses horizon dependence versus state-space and memory costs, explains the historical-versus-current value-estimate mismatch that obstructs transferring model-based analyses, and suggests possible extensions. Section 3.1 also revises the ideal-case illustration to an MDP with only one suboptimal triple at the final step. Empirical interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 explicitly preserve visit counts for unvisited pairs, and Algorithm 2 corrects its lower-bound learning-rate index to t. These are limited specification improvements. The new reproducibility statement repeats the existing processor, 12-hour runtime and statement that code accompanies supplementary materials.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic episodic tabular MDPs at four scales: (H,S,A) = (2,3,3), (5,5,5), (7,8,6) and (10,15,10). No additional dataset, task or test scenario is evaluated.

E2.justification: All four experiments retain AMB, Refined AMB, UCB-Hoeffding and ULCB-Hoeffding. The added model-based comparisons in Appendix C concern theoretical guarantees, not additional evaluated baselines.

E4.justification: Neither version reports additional experimental ablations, sensitivity tests, robustness studies or case studies. V2's new appendices supply theoretical comparisons and proofs; Appendix B redisplays the existing experiments.

E5.justification: Both report 10 sample trajectories per algorithm under the same MDP instance, median curves and 10th–90th percentile bands. No run-count, seed or statistical reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: The four Figure 1 plot images are identical across versions. Both retain the finding that UCB-Hoeffding performs best overall, while ULCB-Hoeffding and Refined AMB perform comparably and outperform AMB.

M1.justification: ULCB-Hoeffding and Refined AMB retain their action selection, updates, bonuses and truncation rules. Explicit counter bookkeeping and a corrected learning-rate index clarify the pseudocode without establishing a different algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the main narrative around the analytical framework and two AMB refinements, rewrites the abstract and contribution summary, and moves related work to Appendix A. It adds a technical-novelty discussion and acknowledgment, ethics, reproducibility and language-model-use statements.

P2.justification: The document adopts substantially different typography, margins, title and heading styles, and denser equation and pseudocode layouts. Figure 1 is reduced and relocated from the main experiments section to Appendix B; its panels remain unchanged. Algorithm blocks are also repositioned and repacked.

R1.justification: Appendix C substantially expands positioning against model-based research through explicit regret, memory and surplus-analysis comparisons. V2 also qualifies its novelty relative to AMB and adds Papini et al. (2021), Zhang et al. (2024a) and Zhang et al. (2026) to the linear-function-approximation discussion. Most earlier references are retained.

T1.justification: V2 adds the analytical framework in Section 3.2, weight lemmas in Appendix D, and proofs of the UCB-Hoeffding and ULCB-Hoeffding guarantees in Appendices E–F, which v1 lacked. Although the main UCB bound is retained, its simplified optimal-triple term changes from H^6 to H^5.
