Refined AMB's stated multiple-optimal-action term likewise changes from H^6 to H^5, and new Appendix G.4 derives absorption of the additive SAH^2 term. The earlier AMB optimism proof is largely retained.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is theoretical completeness and assessability: v1 states the central UCB-based guarantees without their derivations, whereas v2 supplies an explicit framework and extensive supporting analysis in Section 3.2 and Appendices D–F. The added comparison with model-based methods and more precise novelty claims further strengthen the paper. These substantially improve support for its central contribution while preserving the empirical evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, algorithms and experiments. Their text, equations, algorithm boxes, figures and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 Section 5 and Appendix B retain these original simulations and their regret curves.

before.justification: V1 Section 6 and Figure 1 report original simulations comparing four algorithms on synthetic tabular MDPs.

results.title: Q-Learning with Fine-Grained Gap-Dependent Regret

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: training-free weight fingerprinting, robustness across six post-training categories, perfect classification on the 150-pair testbed, and computation within 30 seconds on an NVIDIA 3090. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix F newly interprets the method as requiring little vocabulary overlap and argues that unbiased estimation is important. It also explains retaining the linear kernel for efficiency despite stronger RBF separation. Appendix I connects its manipulation results to the theoretical analysis; the main interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The expanded model table adds training-corpus descriptions and direct checkpoint links to previously listed models. V2 also adds a supplementary-code statement and consolidates implementation choices in Appendix H. The existing GitHub link remains; these are documentation and access-information additions, not evidence of implementation changes.

E1.justification: Appendix I adds explicit permutation, sign-flip, constant-scaling and orthogonal-transformation test scenarios across five existing model families. The original model collection and six post-training categories remain unchanged; the newly listed training corpora document existing models rather than expand coverage.

E2.justification: Section 6.4 and Table 3 add PCS, identified as another HuRef measure, and Intrinsic Fingerprint as evaluated comparators. HuRef, now clarified as ICS, and REEF remain. This substantially broadens the principal comparison, although Figures 1–2 and Table 2 retain their original comparator sets.

E3.justification: New supplementary protocols vary shared-token counts from 10 to 10,000, compare linear/RBF kernels with biased/unbiased CKA, and apply four transformations to five models. The original 150-pair evaluation and its metrics are retained; no revision of its existing settings is established.

E4.justification: V2 introduces systematic vocabulary-overlap sensitivity analysis in Figure 3, kernel/estimator ablations in Table 4, and explicit manipulation-robustness tests in Table 6. These directly investigate alignment requirements, CKA design choices and transformation invariance, questions without corresponding empirical analyses in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same negative-pair-based Z-score reporting. Neither reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional averages and CKA comparisons do not introduce uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: Table 3 adds Intrinsic Fingerprint and PCS results, including overall AUCs of 0.957 and 0.860. Figure 3 and Table 4 add sensitivity and CKA-variant outcomes; Table 6 reports 100% similarity in every model–manipulation cell. Existing AWM, HuRef and REEF results remain unchanged, so these are added findings rather than improved same-setting scores.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains shared-vocabulary embedding alignment through LAP, permutation/sign recovery, and aggregation of unbiased CKA similarities for Q/K weights. Appendix H elaborates existing choices, including layer matching; the CKA alternatives are ablations, not changes to the proposed method.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites and subdivides the fingerprinting discussion, adds explanatory transitions in Section 4, and expands the appendix organization with disclosure, ablation and implementation sections. Affiliation/contact text changes and the acknowledgement is removed. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the six-panel Figure 3 and result Tables 4 and 6, expands Table 3 with two comparator blocks, and redesigns the original model-mapping table as Table 5 with a training-corpus column and checkpoint links. The existing ROC and heatmap figures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands fingerprinting coverage into white-box and black-box approaches, discussing static weights, activations, gradients, output distributions and trigger queries. Added works include DeepJudge, EasyDetector, TensorGuard and LLMmap, alongside a broader discussion of black-box robustness limitations.

T1.justification: Equation 6 replaces the RMSNorm expression involving XX^T 1_m with the per-row squared-sum expression (X ⊙ X)1_n. Appendix E.3 updates the corresponding derivation and explicitly states row-norm invariance under orthogonal transformations. This is a localized mathematical correction; the theorem statements and remaining theory are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important validation gaps by testing vocabulary dependence, CKA design choices and explicit weight manipulations, while broadening baseline comparisons. These additions substantially strengthen support for the retained method; the RMSNorm correction and checkpoint documentation also improve technical reliability and reproducibility. Manipulation settings remain sparse, and Table 4's linear/unbiased averages are not reconciled with Table 3, but these qualifications do not outweigh the added direct evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AWM research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and reports additional baseline results, vocabulary-overlap and CKA ablations, and explicit weight-manipulation tests.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-lineage experiments on 60 positive and 90 negative model pairs, including comparisons with HuRef and REEF.

results.title: AWM: Accurate Weight-Matrix Fingerprint for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and concluding discussion retain the same central claims: offline vision computation, learned token compression, efficient joint encoding, and competitive retrieval. The headline 50k pairs/second and 49 kB/image claims are unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations linking compression to semantic redundancy removal and preserved alignment, negative-miner strength to retrieval quality, and limited BERT gains to adequate MiniLM capacity at the studied training scale. Appendix C qualifies deployment claims through storage-I/O costs and advises against networked storage. Appendix I develops previously unelaborated video-extension possibilities.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the forthcoming implementation/checkpoint promise with a stated public code link and adds offline indexing and online retrieval pseudocode. New documentation specifies SSD access layouts, token precision and quantization procedures, caption preprocessing, and compression-baseline construction. The original hyperparameter table is retained; these additions substantially improve documented implementation and deployment guidance.

E1.justification: The training corpora and evaluated image-text retrieval tasks remain unchanged. Flickr Full and COCO Full expand candidate pools using existing dataset splits, constituting protocol changes rather than new dataset or task coverage. Appendix I proposes video extensions but reports no video evaluation.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets in Tables 1-2 are retained. v2 adds LightningDOT comparisons in Tables 8-9 and matched compression comparisons against striding, k-means++ clustering, and attention pruning in Table 10. Table 11 additionally compares BERT-Base with MiniLM, substantially expanding comparative evidence.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings are retained, while new experiments introduce full-dataset candidate pools, k=100, and Recall@5/10/20; controlled 64-token compression comparisons; alternative negative miners and text encoders; and BF16/FP8/FP4 storage conditions. Appendices C-D also introduce contiguous versus random-access SSD timing and caption-preprocessed token-alignment evaluation.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained token-count, pool-size, objective, and distillation ablations, v2 investigates token semantics and caption alignment, cross-model negative mining, alternative compression mechanisms, quantization robustness, and text-encoder capacity. The new I/O analysis also tests a deployment cost omitted from v1's compute-focused efficiency evaluation.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without comparable uncertainty reporting. Appendix C.1 newly reports I/O timing variability and explicitly identifies 10 runs for contiguous loading. Appendix D.2 reports alignment means with plus/minus spreads, a paired two-sided t-test, and effect size. These additions are limited to supplementary measurements; retrieval tables still lack repeated-training uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1-2 and the original ablation results in Tables 4-5 are unchanged. Substantial new results include Flickr Full text-to-image R@5 of 78.32 versus LightningDOT's 60.1 in Table 8, and 64-token Flickr text-to-image R@1 of 86.9 for EDJE versus 85.66 for clustering in Table 10. Further additions cover I/O, alignment, mining, quantization, and BERT. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements to retained v1 scores.

M1.justification: The core adapter, joint encoder, training objectives, and distillation procedure remain unchanged. Appendix H adds an evaluated deployment variant that quantizes cached tokens to FP8 or FP4 and dequantizes them before inference, without further fine-tuning. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence are retained. v2 standardizes 're-ranking', updates publication and citation formatting, adds cross-references and Section 5.4, renames Appendix B, and organizes new appendices. The expansion does not constitute extensive rewriting of the original exposition.

P2.justification: v2 adds semantic word-cloud displays, an alignment histogram, a quantization/storage plot, Tables 6-11, and two pseudocode algorithms. Figures 4-5 move from vertically stacked, text-wrapped placement to a side-by-side arrangement. Figure 6's example is repeated within Figure 7. These substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Related work adds a focused discussion distinguishing EDJE from LightningDOT's cached region representations. References to LightningDOT, BERT, and two video-related works support the new comparisons and proposed extensions. The broader positioning among embedding models, joint encoders, and generative VLMs remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D.2 newly defines the diagnostic image-caption alignment score as the average, over caption tokens, of maximum cosine similarity to visual tokens. The original adapter equations and training losses remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central efficiency and compression argument: v1 lacked matched alternative-compression baselines and measurements of token-fetch costs, both now addressed in Appendices G and C. Larger-candidate retrieval tests, failure-sensitive ablations, and practical implementation guidance further improve validation and usability. Localized editing problems remain: Figure 9's caption describes lower alignment despite higher reported compressed-token means, and Appendix J quotes R@10=97.98 where Table 11 shows 97.9. These weaken particular statements but do not outweigh the substantial gains in supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EDJE research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds original storage-I/O measurements, semantic analyses, larger-candidate retrieval evaluations, and compression, quantization, negative-mining, and text-encoder experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original EDJE retrieval results on Flickr30k and COCO, efficiency measurements, and token-count, training-objective, and distillation ablations.

results.title: Efficient Discriminative Joint Encoders for Large Scale Vision-Language Reranking

C1.justification: The architecture, theoretical contributions, and million-step retention claims are retained. The abstract and introduction expand the robotics claim to approximately 70% aggregate improvement and wins on 21 of 23 tasks. The aggregate comparison is supported, but Table 8 shows only 18 highest means among the 23 tasks with nonzero scores.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial interpretations concerning conditioning robustness, navigation applicability, stable color representations, slot allocation, and layer/head specialization. Appendices A.9–A.11 further attribute performance causally to functional memory rather than parameter count, exceeding what the post-hoc analyses alone establish. The original limitations paragraph is retained in A.12.

D1.justification: v2 documents the probes' three-layer, 512-hidden-unit MLP, Adam optimization, and 200 training epochs. A new reproducibility statement reports supplementary implementation, training scripts, and configuration files. The original policy hyperparameters, demonstration counts, hardware disclosure, and project address are retained.

E1.justification: v2 expands MIKASA-Robo evaluation from four tasks to 32, adding ShellGame, interception, rotation, shape-recall, and multi-color task families. It also adds high-dimensional D4RL locomotion tasks and ViZDoom-Two-Colors navigation with visual cue recall. The original benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Trajectory Transformer becomes an additional reported comparator in v2 Table 4. The original comparison sets remain intact. RATE, RMT, TrXL, and the other ViZDoom comparators already appeared in v1 experiments; their use on an added benchmark does not independently establish new baseline methods.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings and the shared hyperparameter table are retained. New protocols include normalized D4RL evaluation under two conditioning modes and post-hoc memory probing: collecting 1,000 episodes, retaining successful episodes, training separate probes by layer and timestep, and using an 80/20 training-validation split. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: The original component and hyperparameter ablations remain unchanged. v2 adds conditioning comparisons and extensive analyses of memory content and operation: color decoding, slot updates, cosine similarity, embedding variance, PCA trajectories, and read/write attention maps (Appendices A.5 and A.9–A.11).

E5.justification: The original three-run protocol, four-run T-Maze exception, SEM reporting, and Figure 5 confidence intervals are retained. v2 additionally specifies six runs with SEM for ViZDoom and averaging across 20 batches with standard-deviation shading in Figure 11. These are new reporting details for added analyses, not increases established for existing experiments.

E6.justification: Shared main results and the full POPGym table remain unchanged. Added results include D4RL averages of 76.4 and 74.7 under different conditioning modes, ViZDoom returns of 55.28±0.94 for ELMUR versus 59.21±1.19 for RATE, and 32-task robotics sums of 9.24 versus 5.42. Memory probes also add evidence of target-color decodability.

M1.justification: The architecture, memory updates, cross-attention, MoE components, and supervised losses remain unchanged. Appendix A.5 adds a tested input adaptation conditioning ELMUR on returns-to-go, observations, and actions, alongside its original observation-only mode.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are preserved. v2 updates the title, affiliations, and conference header, adds a reproducibility statement, and inserts new appendix sections while renumbering retained material. The revision primarily adds scientific content rather than extensively rewriting the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds three substantive result tables for D4RL, ViZDoom, and the full robotics suite, plus Figures 8–15 showing the navigation environment and memory analyses. Existing tables are renumbered and repositioned, with revised highlighting and page flow; the original main figures are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Trajectory Transformer, ViZDoom, MuJoCo, and PCA, and removes the RozumFormer/Staroverov reference. The broad positioning against recurrent models, external-memory architectures, and robotic transformers remains stable. The updated Cherepanov conference references correspond to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A.1–A.3 retain the exponential-forgetting result, half-life and retention-horizon expressions, boundedness assumptions and proof, and memory-intensive-environment definition. No substantive mathematical revision is evident.

improvement.justification: v1's robotics evidence covered four tasks, and its fully observable check saturated CartPole. v2 substantially strengthens validation through the full robotics suite, harder control and visual-navigation tasks, and probes demonstrating stored target-color information. The added results expose failures as well as successes, making applicability more assessable. These gains outweigh the new reporting and interpretation weaknesses, although the unsupported 21/23 win count and causal claims based on observational probing need correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ELMUR, with clearly matching architecture, theory, experiments, and authors. The text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds D4RL control, ViZDoom navigation, broader robotics evaluation, and memory-probing results.

before.justification: v1 reports original T-Maze, POPGym, MIKASA-Robo, and CartPole experiments, including memory-component and hyperparameter ablations.

results.title: ELMUR: External Layer Memory with Update/Rewrite for Long-Horizon RL Problems

C1.justification: The abstract expands the demonstrated Pythia range from 160M–1.4B to 160M–6.9B. The central diagnostic and architectural contributions, the specific 1.4B accuracy/parameter-efficiency claim, and the conclusion remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 2 develops information overload into an explicit stability–plasticity tradeoff. New appendices interpret shared-subspace collapse, token-specific routing, and historical-state recombination, and explain MeSH's complementarity with MoE routing. The limitations update the validated scale ceiling to 6.9B while retaining uncertainty about larger scales and other training regimes.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository access link, OLMoE implementation settings including expert dimensions and learning rate, and fvcore/input-shape details for FLOP measurement. Existing training hyperparameters, evaluation hardware disclosure, and pseudocode remain. The PDFs establish the new access information, not the repository's contents.

E1.justification: Both versions use deduplicated Pile training, the same four perplexity datasets, and the same nine downstream tasks. The larger-model, MoE, and expanded buffer-ablation experiments reuse this coverage; the new illustrative sentence introduces no distinct task or domain.

E2.justification: Appendix E.7 and Table 9 add evaluated OLMoE-based vanilla and naive-recursive controls. The original Pythia comparator sets, including residual, anchor, anchor*, and fixed or learnable combinations, remain unchanged. The additional large-Pythia experiments reuse the naive-recursive comparison.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 2.8B/6.9B models with 6+10R2+6 configurations and an OLMoE setup using two of sixteen experts. New evaluation procedures include forward-pass FLOP measurement for a [1, 4096] input and shared-subspace projections. Appendix B's settings for the original experiments are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a shared-subspace SVD analysis of loop collapse (Appendix E.8, Figure 10) and a token-level router/state-composition case study (Appendix F, Figure 11). The buffer-length ablation expands from Pile results to four existing evaluation datasets. Earlier heuristic-combination, training-dynamics, and non-recursive analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report diagnostic means and standard deviations across 500 samples. New Figure 10 follows that existing practice. Neither version supplies training-seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty estimates, or formal significance tests for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: Table 3 reports 6.9B base/MeSH Pile perplexities of 6.29/6.09 and 0-shot averages of 56.67/58.83; Table 9 adds MoE results, with MeSH improving over recursion but remaining below vanilla. It also adds FLOP and diagnostic findings and expands buffer-ablation scores. Table 1 corrects the existing 410M MeSH 5-shot average from 45.60 to 45.56, matching Table 2.

M1.justification: The buffer initialization, iteration-specific read/write routers, memory-update equations, and Algorithm 2 remain unchanged. The MoE experiment applies the existing MeSH procedure to another backbone.

P1.justification: The introduction and diagnostic explanation receive targeted clarifications, while most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. New appendix subsections and an LLM-use statement are added, and the affiliation and conference header are updated. This is an extension rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds shared-subspace plots and multipart router/state-composition heatmaps in Figures 10–11, plus larger-model, FLOP, and MoE tables. The buffer-ablation table gains dataset columns, and Figure 8 becomes a larger full-width display. Existing figures and tables are also relocated without removing their underlying analyses.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds substantial positioning within memory-augmented models, covering LSTMs, Neural Turing Machines, Transformer-XL, RMT, LONGMEM, and related approaches. It explicitly distinguishes managing iterations over one input from long-context or persistent-memory objectives. Additional MoE references support the newly discussed complementary architecture.

T1.justification: Appendix D corrects Equation 7's summation start from i=0 to i=-1, including the prelude contribution already present in Algorithm 2. Appendix E.4 adds Equation 8 for MeSH's additional FLOPs. Proposition 2.1 and its main argument otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that was limited to dense Pythia models through 1.4B: Tables 3 and 9 test larger scales and a MoE backbone, while Figures 10–11 and Table 7 make internal routing and computational overhead more assessable. Expanded memory-related positioning and code-access information also improve the paper. Largest-scale vanilla controls and run-to-run uncertainty remain absent, but the additions materially strengthen support for scalability, applicability, and efficiency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MeSH research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds larger-model and MoE experiments, computational-cost measurements, and internal-state analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, downstream evaluations, representation diagnostics, and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix E.

results.title: MeSH: Memory-as-State-Highways for Recursive Transformers

C1.justification: The two central failure-mode contributions remain. V2 qualifies the abstract from 'cannot be reliably inferred' to 'cannot always be inferred' and frames the cluster contribution around strong versus weak distance separation. Its discussion adds a preliminary extension to other force-based visualization methods.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly distinguishes weakened metric separation from preserved neighbor ordering, qualifying v1's 'unclustered impostor' interpretation. It replaces the poison-point distance-gap explanation with affinity redistribution and perplexity dependence. New qualifications explain that PCA preprocessing breaks exact additive invariance and that UMAP differs in poisoning sensitivity and outlier placement.

D1.justification: V2 documents the financial input's 30 dimensions, the revised Ward-based clustering, and construction details and projection dimensions for the new preprocessing experiments. Algorithm 1, the BBC injection recipe, and the supplied code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 Figure 11 adds a controlled synthetic test contrasting the exactly equidistant X0 and two-block clustered X1 constructions under insertion of a shared center point. The real datasets and broader tasks remain unchanged; larger samples and PCA variations primarily change evaluation settings.

E2.justification: UMAP changes from cited background to an evaluated comparator across impostor, near-simplex, poison-point, and outlier experiments (v2 Appendices A.3 and B.2). PCA is removed from the corresponding single-cell impostor comparison, although retained in other experiments.

E3.justification: The single-cell comparison changes from DBSCAN labels derived from the t-SNE output to a partition from the input's Ward dendrogram. New protocols vary PCA preprocessing, dataset size, and injection counts, and explicitly test perplexity 1. The BBC outlier setting is also revised from alpha > 1 to alpha in (0.8, 1), despite retaining the plotted results; this does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of whether cluster exaggeration survives PCA preprocessing, whether single-point poisoning persists at larger sample sizes, and whether the constructed Theorem 7 example behaves as predicted (Figures 7–11). New UMAP analyses examine shared failure modes and differences in responses to poison points and outliers.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional plots do not introduce an uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial preprocessing, robustness, and UMAP results and removes v1 Table 1's three-index numerical comparison. Single-cell t-SNE silhouette scores change from 0.514/0.619 to 0.429/0.462 for original/impostor inputs, under changed clustering labels, so these are not comparable performance changes. The BBC t-SNE scores remain 0.399/0.196/0.418; new UMAP scores are 0.528/0.314/0.377.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1's impostor construction, the t-SNE objective, and the existing poison-point procedures are retained. The new poison-point theorem formalizes an existing attack; preprocessing and UMAP experiments do not revise the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The overall six-section narrative remains. V2 rewrites the introductory illustration and poison-point explanation, consistently emphasizes cluster salience, and subdivides Section 4 into distinct input/output and instability cases. Much of the surrounding exposition is retained.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the introductory table and small illustrations with a three-scenario overview figure, redesigns the single-cell figure around distance matrices and dendrograms, and adds extensive preprocessing, robustness, and UMAP displays. Several original empirical figures are retained with renumbering and revised captions.

R1.justification: V1's assertion that additive invariance had not been studied is replaced by attribution to Lee and Verleysen (2011; 2014). V2 also credits Schubert and Gertz (2017) for empirical outlier observations and adds prior work on noise robustness. These changes substantively revise the positioning of central mechanisms, beyond the bibliographic update to the existing Snoeck work.

T1.justification: V2 adds Theorem 7 and its proof establishing identical poisoned loss landscapes for differently clustered inputs, supported by a new nearest-neighbor affinity lemma. It replaces Lemma 6's construction proof with a continuity argument and corrects the deformation formula. The outlier derivation changes substantially, replacing the stated 3 + o(1) bound with 3.266 + o_n(1); several statements also expand their stated perplexity domain to include endpoints.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the support and interpretation of the central conclusions: it corrects mathematical derivations, formally supports the poison-point example, tests common PCA preprocessing, and distinguishes weak distance separation from preserved neighbor ordering. Corrected attribution and UMAP comparisons improve scientific context. The outlier bound becomes weaker but better supported; Section 5's inconsistent approximation of 3.6 remains a limited defect alongside Theorem 9's 3.266.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same t-SNE study. Their main text, figures, equations, and complete Appendices A–B support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical demonstrations and adds PCA preprocessing, poison-point robustness, and UMAP experiments in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic experiments and t-SNE/PCA analyses of PBMC3k, credit-card fraud, and BBC news data, including appendix experiments.

results.title: t-SNE Exaggerates Clusters, Provably

C1.justification: The central contributions remain geometry-preserving post-pruning compensation combined with variance-aware scoring, requiring no additional architectural changes and modest computation. The broad claims of better perplexity and task accuracy remain; additional model evaluations provide supporting evidence without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 develops a calibration-dependent interpretation of Ridge compensation: improved perplexity with more samples need not imply better downstream generalization (Sections 4.2 and 7.4). It adds arguments involving effective degrees of freedom and tuning cost, explains scaling benefits through more stable norm estimates, and proposes accumulated distribution mismatch as an explanation for SliceGPT results.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link in Section 4.1 and documents the Ridge search grid and calibration-based selection rule. The original projection-pruning details, evaluation harness, and A100 80GB hardware disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use WikiText-2 for calibration and perplexity, and BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-easy, ARC-challenge, and OpenBookQA for downstream evaluation. The additional models are evaluated on these retained tasks; no new dataset or task coverage is established.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated SliceGPT comparisons on Llama-2-13B (Tables 3 and 7); v1 only discussed SliceGPT. It also replaces the unconstrained output-map LS comparator with Ridge-regularized fitting of retained weights and adds this comparator to downstream accuracy tables, including the retained Llama-7B experiment in Table 2.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from Llama-7B with 128 calibration samples to include Llama-2-13B and Vicuna-7B with 128 and 512 samples. Figure 2 introduces an 8–512-sample sweep. The Ridge comparison searches λ from 10⁻⁶ to 10⁶, selecting by perplexity on the fitting calibration data (Sections 4.2 and 7.1).

E4.justification: v2 adds calibration-size sensitivity analysis (Figure 2) and extensive Ridge regularization sensitivity analyses (Figures 5–6), and expands score-by-compensation comparisons across calibration sizes and models (Figures 3–4). The original projection-target ablation is retained unchanged as Table 4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added calibration sample counts and hyperparameter sweeps do not introduce run-to-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original Llama-7B/128 table results are retained, while v2 adds substantial results for new model, calibration, and comparator settings. New findings distinguish perplexity from downstream accuracy: at 30% pruning on Vicuna-7B with 512 samples, Ridge has lower PPL than rotation-only RCPU (20.52 versus 21.55), but lower mean accuracy (57.32 versus 57.56; Tables 8 and 10).

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains variance-aware column selection, the Procrustes solution Q = UVᵀ, rotation of retained weights, and optional isotropic scaling. The revised least-squares procedure is a comparison baseline; no operational change to RCPU is established.

P1.justification: The six main sections retain their order and much of their wording. v2 locally revises the least-squares discussion, experimental interpretation, and conclusion, converts some numbered subsections into paragraph headings, and adds an ethics/reproducibility statement and appendix structure. Title, affiliation, and publication-header text also change.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains model and calibration-size columns, and the original two-panel compensation figure becomes the four-panel Figure 3. v2 adds calibration-size and regularization plots, a second-model comparison figure, and multiple benchmark tables. The original projection-ablation and efficiency tables are retained and renumbered, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 adds RotPruner and DenoiseRotator and distinguishes their learned pruning-oriented rotations from RCPU's analytic compensation after removal. It also adds references supporting Ridge regression, effective degrees of freedom, and Llama 2. The broader compression literature and positioning relative to FLAP remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2 replaces the unconstrained output-map objective and pseudoinverse solution with a regularized retained-weight objective and its closed-form solution. Section 4.2 adds effective-degrees-of-freedom formulas and comparisons. The core Procrustes mathematics remains intact, although Equation 8 changes the scale constraint from s ≥ 0 to s > 0.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation on one model and one calibration budget, and its reliance on an unconstrained LS comparator. Additional models, evaluated SliceGPT and tuned Ridge comparisons, and calibration/regularization sensitivity analyses make the central robustness argument much better supported and its boundaries more visible. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, and superiority wording remains too broad: Table 7 favors WANDA-sp over both RCPU variants at 10% and 20% pruning. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RCPU research. Their text, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 adds readable Appendices 7.1–7.4.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original experiments on Llama-7B, Llama-2-13B, and Vicuna-7B, including additional comparisons and sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original Llama-7B pruning experiments, including perplexity, downstream accuracy, compensation ablations, and resource measurements.

results.title: RCPU: Rotation-Constrained Error Compensation for Structured Pruning of Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions and principal claims: retrieval plus C-GRPO preserves approximately baseline mean accuracy with about 95% fewer visual tokens and reduced memory and latency.

C2.justification: Appendix A.4 expands the existing acknowledgment of VideoMME degradation into a specific explanation: top-3 retrieval can discard essential temporal information in long videos that distillation cannot recover. It qualifies applicability by video duration and proposes a temporal Q-Former as future mitigation.

D1.justification: v2 supplies previously absent Appendices A–B with evaluation prompts, resolution and output limits, baseline implementation details, training-data composition, optimizer settings, KL weight, DeepSpeed configurations and SFT hardware. It also adds code and model links. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changed experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same six evaluation benchmarks and Video-R1 training sources. Appendix B names constituent datasets within the existing training mixture; it does not establish expanded data or task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 1–2 is identical, including the model baselines, ByteVideoLLM, MovieChat, VidCom and SFT variants. Appendix A.2 documents implementations of existing comparators.

E3.justification: Previously specified sampling, frame budgets, model configurations and training sample counts remain unchanged. The appendices disclose additional prompts, resolution limits and optimization settings without reporting revisions to existing protocols. The 16-frame condition already appeared in v1 Table 1.

E4.justification: Tables 2–3 retain identical SFT/VMR comparisons and threshold ablations. Appendix A.4 explains failures using existing results; it provides no separately documented new robustness test, parameter sweep or case-level experiment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added appendices introduce no statistical reporting procedure.

E6.justification: New Table 4 reports the previously unreported 16-frame token-count breakdown, with mean 858.53, and tabulates the 64-frame and compressed counts already represented in v1's plot. Accuracy entries in Tables 1–3 and the efficiency measurements are unchanged.

M1.justification: The method text and objectives remain unchanged, but v2 Figure 1 adds VMR to the uncompressed branch that bypassed retrieval in v1 Figure 1. Both versions already describe VMR preprocessing of training data. The PDFs do not resolve whether this corrects the schematic or changes teacher inputs.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains almost verbatim. v2 adds ethics and reproducibility statements, organized appendices and an LLM-use disclosure, updates the publication header, and repairs the unresolved appendix reference.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 1–2 are combined and redrawn as a two-panel Figure 1 with explicit policy-model and input-group labels. v2 also adds Table 4 and clarifies Table 1's frame-column caption. The remaining result displays are essentially retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: The reference list and related-work discussion are unchanged. Appendix citations reuse existing references without materially revising novelty or positioning against prior research.

T1.justification: Equations 1–10 retain the same token definitions, merging rules, retention reward, advantage normalization and optimization objective. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation appears in the appendices.

improvement.justification: v1 repeatedly directs readers to absent appendices for essential experimental details. v2 supplies prompts, preprocessing and training settings, comparator implementations and resource links, substantially reducing this reproducibility gap. Its long-video discussion also improves interpretation. These are substantial reporting gains despite unchanged accuracy evidence and residual ambiguity about the revised teacher-branch diagram.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MARC work, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. v1 ends after its references despite citing appendices; v2 supplies Appendices A–C. This addition can be compared reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experimental results and additionally tabulates benchmark token counts in Appendix A.1.

before.justification: v1 reports original six-benchmark evaluations, SFT/VMR and threshold ablations, and GPU-memory and latency measurements in Tables 1–3 and Figures 5–6.

results.title: MARC: Memory-Augmented RL Token Compression for Efficient Video Understanding

C1.justification: The central claims remain disagreement-based selection, simple signature-based prediction, information-theoretic motivation, and over 99% evaluation-cost reduction with strong prediction accuracy. The added experiments primarily support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning calibration, source-model heterogeneity, and reduced benefits under large performance gaps. It explicitly excludes open-ended generation without predefined answer choices and explains amortization of offline costs through a reported 389-evaluation break-even point. Appendix F also newly argues that large performance gaps are unrealistic.

D1.justification: Appendix I supplies previously missing hardware, output-generation tools, predictor hyperparameters, training durations and source-model subsampling details, including kNN k=1 and random-forest defaults. Appendices B and J.2 document resource requirements and vision-baseline implementations. The project and code links are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MMLU, HellaSwag, Winogrande, ARC and ImageNet. Winogrande and ARC already appear in v1 Table 1 despite its narrower dataset-description paragraph. Additional experiments change splits and analyses within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds Lifelong Benchmark and SSEPY to the ImageNet comparison, where v1 included only random evaluation and model-signature controls alongside DISCO. These provide substantive comparisons against dedicated vision evaluation methods. The language comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds bootstrapped chronological evaluation using 346 source and 36 target models, performance-sorted splits with and without a gap, calibration measurements, and computational profiling on an H100. The stated LLM size ceiling also changes from 32B to 72B. Section 5.1 primarily documents the existing pipeline rather than establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained factor ablations, Appendices D–F test sensitivity to resampled model splits, calibration and confidence, and source–target performance gaps. Appendix B adds computational overhead and break-even analysis. These address stability, extrapolation failure and practical efficiency questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: v2 first discloses five-run averaging and reports standard deviations for fixed-split MMLU results, bootstrapped splits and computational costs. v1 lacks equivalent uncertainty reporting. The headings call these confidence intervals, but the tables report mean plus/minus standard deviation; an increase over the earlier run count is not established.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original Table 3 rows retain their values, while substantial new results are added. ImageNet comparators obtain MAE/rank of 2.06/0.838 for Lifelong Benchmark and 3.05/0.762 for SSEPY. Under the newly tested large performance gap, Table 10 reports rank correlations of 89.2% for DISCO and 87.4% for direct evaluation. Computational, bootstrap and calibration results are also new.

M1.justification: Both versions use top-k PDS/JSD selection and model signatures with dimensionality reduction and kNN or regression prediction. Appendix I newly documents a 100-source-model subset for MMLU disagreement scoring, but does not establish that the procedure underlying the retained results changed.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. Changes include wording corrections, standardized mathematical notation, an explicit stepwise evaluation protocol, separate experimental-setup subsections, and reorganized appendices. The revision mainly expands documentation rather than extensively rewriting the existing account.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4–10 and three diagnostic figures, expands Table 3 with vision-baseline rows, and revises compression-plot sizing, axes and legends. The original vision figures are retained as Figures 9–10, rather than being new results displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds Fogliato et al./SSEPY and develops the relationship to Prabhu et al.'s existing vision work. It also repositions Metabench within benchmark compression and adds dataset and implementation citations. The central novelty positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mutual-information identity, JSD–PDS bounds and underlying proofs are retained, largely with equivalent notation in Appendices G–H. Appendix G.0.2 adds a mathematical argument for representing nonuniform model priors through proportional model replication, a limited addition to the treatment of assumptions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's missing uncertainty reporting, limited vision comparisons, undocumented implementation choices and unquantified setup costs. The added robustness analyses also expose conditions where DISCO's advantage weakens. Confidence-interval labels actually denote standard deviations, and dismissing large performance gaps as unrealistic is weakly supported, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence, reproducibility and practical interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DISCO work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching the relocated theory and vision appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original baseline comparisons, uncertainty estimates, computational measurements and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original DISCO experiments on four language benchmarks and ImageNet, including performance comparisons and ablations.

results.title: DISCO: Diversifying Sample Condensation for Efficient Model Evaluation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: the first pruning-activated LLM attack, benign behavior before pruning, malicious activation afterward, and a deployment-time security gap. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining their stated scope.

C2.justification: Section 6.4 adds a substantive qualification: security-data fine-tuning can mitigate the attack, but requires identifying the compromise and curating appropriate data. Appendix B.1 interprets calibration-domain shifts as insufficient for reliable protection despite reduced SparseGPT ASR. Existing mechanism explanations and limitations are retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.4 documents the existing security-aware calibration experiment: 512 sequences, approximately 2048 tokens each, formed by concatenating five query/refusal pairs from roughly 2.5k LLM-LAT entries, with an example in Figure 9. V3 also specifies settings for the new transformation experiments. These additions improve documentation; the original attack hyperparameters and code-access information remain.

E1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds reasoning-domain calibration scenarios using GSM8K question-answer/reasoning pairs and OpenPlatypus, extending the original C4-to-WikiText calibration mismatch. The three attack tasks and five utility benchmarks remain unchanged; GSM8K's new role is calibration rather than an additional utility benchmark.

E2.justification: Figure 4 adds evaluated mitigation comparisons using sparse fine-tuning on general instruction data alone versus general plus security data. The base-model comparisons in Table 2 and the existing security-aware calibration and patching comparisons in Tables 3–4 are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include Qwen2.5-14B/32B evaluation, sparsity-preserving fine-tuning with a 1:1 general/security-data mixture, and FP8 or 4-bit GPTQ after pruning. Figure 10 varies injection fractions across 20%, 50%, and 80%, while Figure 2 extends the repair sweep to 0.1%. These substantially expand experimental settings without changing the retained main attack setup.

E4.justification: Section 6.4 newly tests whether attacks survive subsequent fine-tuning and quantization, including targeted security fine-tuning as mitigation. Appendix B.1 adds injection-fraction sensitivity and reasoning-calibration distribution-shift analyses, while Figure 2 extends the existing repair-fraction ablation. These address several previously untested robustness questions.

E5.justification: Table 1 newly reports mean benchmark-score changes with standard deviations across the five benchmarks, replacing absolute averages. This adds descriptive variability reporting, not repeated-run uncertainty. Neither version reports additional seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 5–7 and Figures 4 and 10 add substantial ASR and utility results, including suppression through security fine-tuning and persistence after quantization. Table 2 is unchanged. Table 1 corrects summaries, including Llama's benign-refusal rate from 0.8% to 3.9%, and v3 Table 11 corrects the model assignments of result blocks in v1 Table 8; these corrections do not establish rerun performance changes.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 and Algorithm 1 retain Wanda-based score estimation, injection into high-scoring parameters, repair through low-scoring parameters, and the same losses. Correcting percentage-complement expressions does not change the already specified freezing procedure; the new experiments do not introduce an attack component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative order remain intact. V3 adds Sections 6.4, A.4, and B.1, moves the full-results subsection to B.2, makes localized wording corrections, updates publication headers and bibliography formatting, and removes the acknowledgements containing a drafting note. This is a bounded structural expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with clearer pruning options and illustrative responses, Table 1 is redesigned around score changes and standard deviations, and Figure 2 gains an extended axis and additional points. New Figures 4, 9, and 10 and Tables 5–7 substantially expand the visual presentation beyond renumbering or relocation.

R1.justification: V3 adds references to GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) and Platypus (Lee et al., 2023) for the new experiments. Section 2's research positioning remains essentially unchanged. Numerous other reference edits change metadata or publication versions of already cited works.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 corrects the frozen-parameter complements from (1 − alpha)% to (100 − alpha)% for injection and repair, resolving an arithmetic inconsistency with percentage-valued alpha. The pruning-score derivation and algorithmic update equations remain unchanged; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V3 resolves important reporting inconsistencies in the utility summary and model attribution of content-injection results, improving the reliability of the evidence. The added transformation and calibration-shift tests strengthen its practical assessment, while Figure 4 provides an empirically supported, explicitly qualified mitigation. Together these substantially improve trustworthiness and usefulness. Several new tests remain limited to Qwen, and the added standard deviations do not establish repeated-run uncertainty.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pruning-activated attack, with matching authors, method, and core experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, and equations, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on larger models, post-pruning transformations, injection-size sensitivity, and calibration-domain shifts.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack-success and utility measurements across five language models, three attack scenarios, and multiple pruning configurations, plus ablations and defense experiments.

results.title: Fewer Weights, More Problems: A Practical Attack on LLM Pruning

C1.justification: Both versions claim distribution-preserving reduction to arbitrary sub-vocabularies, an efficient approximation, and efficient ensemble cooperation through the maximal common vocabulary. The revised abstract explicitly names ensemble as the empirical application, which v1 already claimed and demonstrated.

C2.justification: New captions explain why top-1 dominance can make small K sufficient for greedy accuracy, while larger K is needed to approximate behavior under random sampling. Figure 4 adds an interpretation of overhead relative to K, with an initial-step qualification. Existing greedy-decoding caveats remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds tokenizer and vocabulary information for additional model families, and Table 10 documents common-vocabulary sizes. Conversely, Table 3 removes the specification that throughput was measured on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU. This is lost hardware disclosure, not evidence of changed hardware.

E1.justification: Appendix D.5.2 adds English–French translation in both directions on WMT14 and English–German translation in both directions on WMT16. This substantially broadens task and language coverage beyond the retained GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, and MMLU-Pro evaluations.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the original-model references, Naive Restriction, byte-level reduction, Union, and Naive MCV comparisons. New evaluations reuse existing comparison approaches; the additional constituent models and LVR-to-K-LVR renaming do not introduce new comparison methods.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce temperature-1.0 random sampling, BLEU scoring for translation, four additional ensemble pairs, and K sweeps over 1, 2, 10, 50, 250, and 1250. Figure 4 measures summand counts across token positions, averaged over 100 generations. Existing benchmark settings and the default K=300 are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices D.6–D.7 add substantial scrutiny of the approximation: random sampling tests preservation beyond greedy decoding, Tables 12–14 examine K sensitivity for reduction and ensemble accuracy, and Figure 4 examines computational overhead. The previous PoE/MoE comparison and qualitative failure example remain.

E5.justification: Table 3 retains the same plus/minus uncertainty reporting. The added accuracy tables and overhead curves introduce no seed counts, repeated-evaluation uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Figure 4's 100 generations specify the sample size for its average rather than a documented repeated-run uncertainty analysis.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 4 revise the at-most-two-byte GSM8K accuracy from 68.31 to 70.43 for Qwen2.5-3B and from 67.17 to 79.38 for Falcon3-7B, without explaining the revisions or stating changed settings. Tables 8–14 and Figure 4 add extensive results for model pairs, translation, vocabulary sizes, sampling, K sensitivity, and overhead.

M1.justification: Nested tokenization, the reduction procedure, Algorithms 1–2, and maximal-common-vocabulary ensembling remain unchanged. Algorithm 2 is renamed from Efficient LVR to Top-K Approximation (K-LVR); its top-K step already existed in v1.

P1.justification: Limited abstract and algorithm-prose edits clarify the exact-versus-approximate distinction and introduce K-LVR terminology. Appendix D.3 is retitled, new experimental subsections are appended, and the header changes from Preprint to ICLR 2026 publication status. The existing narrative and main-section order are retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with an explanatory calculation diagram, Tables 8–14 covering the new evaluations and vocabulary summaries, and a six-panel overhead plot. The original generation example is retained as Figure 3, formerly Figure 2, and existing tables are redistributed across pages.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for WMT14, WMT16, Phi-2, Llama 3.1, and Yi to support its expanded experiments. Section 6 and the positioning relative to byte-level reduction and heuristic ensemble methods remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The definitions, validity assumption, lemmas, theorems, derivations, and Appendix A proofs are retained. New Figure 2 visualizes the existing binary worked example; it adds no mathematical result or revised reasoning.

improvement.justification: v1 evaluated the practical approximation mainly through greedy decoding at a fixed K. v2's sampling experiments and K sweeps address an important validation gap by exposing how approximation behavior depends on decoding and truncation; translation and additional model pairs also strengthen the evidence for applicability. These gains outweigh the removed GPU disclosure, although unexplained numerical revisions and absent uncertainty estimates remain weaknesses, and accuracy agreement alone does not establish distributional equivalence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same lossless vocabulary reduction work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be reliably matched across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds translation evaluations, additional model pairs, random-sampling experiments, and top-K analyses in Appendices D.5–D.7.

before.justification: v1 reports original vocabulary-reduction and ensemble evaluations, inference-speed measurements, and generated examples in Section 5 and Appendix D.

results.title: Lossless Vocabulary Reduction for Auto-Regressive Language Models

C1.justification: v1's headline empirical claims emphasize MRQA QA and the 5× compression improvement. v4 broadens the abstract and conclusion to performance across model sizes and long-context summarization, including cross-task generalization. It retains the autoencoding-free contribution while softening the abstract's fundamental reconstruction mismatch into a potential conflict with downstream requirements.

C2.justification: v4 adds an explanation of AE harm through gradient orthogonality and competition for representation capacity. Appendix B.5 acknowledges AE's benefit on QMSum and proposes training-data size and contextual redundancy as explanations. It also adds an encoder–decoder semantic-gap caveat and replaces the earlier anti-diagonal attention explanation with more explicitly hypothetical interpretations of focused attention.

D1.justification: The existing hyperparameter table remains unchanged. v4 newly specifies 8 A100 GPUs for larger-model training, clarifies LLMLingua-2's 5× ratio and full encoder bidirectionality, and documents the timing setup. Its reproducibility statement replaces the anonymous source-code link with a reported public release of data, models, and code.

E1.justification: v4 retains SlimPajama and MRQA coverage but adds QMSum and GovReport long-context summarization. It also evaluates 24K-context single- and multi-document QA on MultiFieldQA, NarrativeQA, Qasper, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue, and HotpotQA, substantially extending task and input-context coverage beyond v1.

E2.justification: v4 adds Activation Beacon, labeled Beacon, and DAST to the 15× in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA comparisons in Tables 1–2. These are additional evaluated compression methods, while the original comparators remain represented.

E3.justification: The original 1B training settings and MRQA compression ratios remain unchanged. New protocols evaluate Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, train summarization models with 32K inputs at 15× compression, and test checkpoints trained on 2K contexts on 24K QA. v4 also introduces reconstruction metrics and compression timing over 1,000 sequences with batch size 10.

E4.justification: v4 adds AE–LM gradient alignment analysis, reconstruction-versus-LM diagnostics, AE-on/off comparisons on long-context tasks, length-extrapolation tests, and computational-efficiency analysis. Existing component ablations, compression-ratio analyses, attention maps, representation plots, and training curves are largely retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new gradient plot shows per-step observations and smoothing, not uncertainty across independent runs.

E6.justification: The original MRQA benchmark rows are preserved in v4 Tables 11 and 15, while new baseline, scaling, long-context, reconstruction, and latency results substantially extend the evidence. Separately, SAC(Random) changes from 55.75/39.85 to 59.54/43.58 ID F1/EM and from 39.82/26.45 to 45.35/30.44 OOD F1/EM between v1 Tables 8–9 and v4 Tables 16–17. The PDFs do not explain these ablation-value revisions.

M1.justification: Both versions use uniformly selected context anchors, additive anchor embeddings, a bidirectional LoRA encoder, per-layer KV compression, a frozen decoder, and LM-only pretraining followed by downstream fine-tuning. v4 clarifies that bidirectional attention covers all encoder tokens; it does not establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory motivation, method explanations, AE discussion, attention interpretation, and conclusion receive substantial rewriting. Existing multi-ratio results discussion moves into Appendix B.2, and attention discussion is consolidated in the main analysis. The experimental narrative is reorganized into dedicated scaling, ratio-sensitivity, and summarization sections.

P2.justification: Main Tables 1–2 now focus on 15× compression, with the original full tables retained in the appendix and ratio averages summarized separately. Table 4 changes from selected-task columns to overall averages. Numerous new evaluation and analysis tables and a gradient plot are added; original visualization images are reused and rearranged, while Figure 10 newly plots existing compression-ratio results.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to recent compression work, including DAST, Activation Beacon, PerceptionCompressor, and GMSA, and discusses encoder–decoder alignment using Lv et al. It explicitly describes SAC as building upon EPL's position layout. The existing related-work taxonomy and positioning between token selection and learned compression remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: v4 Appendix B.6 and Table 12 add module-wise FLOP expressions and summed computational-cost formulas for SAC versus 500xCompressor. This is a limited new analytical derivation; the original loss definitions and anchor-embedding equation remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's single-model MRQA setting through larger models, long-context summarization and QA, additional baselines, and direct efficiency measurements. These additions address important gaps in assessing SAC's generality and computational benefits. Some interpretations overreach: near-zero gradient cosine does not establish interference, and Table 18 shows only a 0.01 F1 advantage at 8B in-domain despite the broad scaling claim. Unexplained random-ablation revisions also reduce transparency, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Semantic-Anchor Compression (SAC). Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds larger-model evaluations, long-context summarization and QA, gradient diagnostics, reconstruction measurements, and compression latency.

before.justification: v1 reports original MRQA evaluations, component and training-objective ablations, perplexity, training times, and attention and representation analyses.

results.title: Autoencoding-Free Context Compression for LLMs via Contextual Semantic Anchors

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: differentiable projection during training and inference enables physically valid two-step predictions with competitive accuracy and approximately tenfold speedups over 200-step baselines. The additional evaluations do not redefine that contribution.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 narrows improvement over Protenix-Mini from all to most benchmarks, replaces outperformance language with comparability, and removes the ligand-interface leadership explanation. New appendices discuss penalty-dependent failure, projection stability and structural preservation, attribute the remaining Boltz-2 accuracy gap to the base model and training data, and explain docking-score discrepancies through evaluation tools.

D1.justification: V2 adds a ProteinGS repository address and states that code is available. It newly identifies OpenStructure as the primary docking evaluator and documents A100 hardware and CUDA kernels for the added profiling study. Existing training hardware, training duration, solver settings, and pseudocode are largely retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use RCSB training data and evaluate CASP15, Test, PoseBusters, AF3-AB, dsDNA, and RNA-Protein. The added analyses use retained biomolecular tasks and datasets; different step budgets, solver parameters, and individual examples do not establish expanded task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds AlphaFold3 comparisons on CASP15, Test, and PoseBusters in Table 1. Figure 7 adds the Boltz-2-plus-GS variant, while Figure 5 now separately reports Protenix and Protenix-Mini runtimes. These materially extend the comparisons beyond v1's reported comparator configurations.

E3.justification: V2 adds TM-score, removes Mean LDDT-PLI reporting, and adds protein-protein interface scores for AF3-AB. It introduces ten-step Protenix-Mini evaluations, comparisons at 2/5/10/200 denoising steps, and a separate PXMeter docking evaluation. New profiling uses token-count bins on an A100. Section 4.1 also expands the reported penalty choice from 10^-7 to 10^-7 or 10^-6; this does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices B–G examine projection repeatability, penalty sensitivity, accuracy and validity across step budgets, Boltz-2 post-processing, module runtime and memory, docking-tool dependence, and structural perturbations. These address distinct questions beyond v1's convergence comparison, qualitative examples, and finetuning ablation.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly specifies five independent projection runs per denoised PoseBusters structure and reports pairwise RMSD of 0.0000 ± 0.0000 Å. Both versions already report uncertainty using ± values; changed error magnitudes do not establish a different estimator or increased repetition of the main benchmarks.

E6.justification: Many benchmark and ablation values are revised, alongside substantial new result entries. For example, Table 1 changes Protenix's CASP15 Complex LDDT from 0.54 ± 0.04 to 0.65 ± 0.06. Section 5.4 changes the reported Protenix-Mini speedup from about 9.5× to 2.3×, assigning 9.5× to Protenix. New results include projection perturbation RMSD of 0.1865 ± 0.0219 Å and PXMeter scores. The PDFs do not explain the cause of every numerical revision.

M1.justification: The projection objective, Gauss-Seidel updates, implicit differentiation, and Algorithms 1–4 are retained. The Boltz-2 experiment applies the already-described post-processing capability without documenting a new algorithmic component or procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition and the main section sequence are retained. V2 makes local grammar and terminology edits, updates the publication header and author formatting, adds a related-work paragraph, and reorganizes the appendices around the new analyses. This is not an extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain rows and metric columns, and Table 2 moves into the main text. V2 adds Figures 6–8 and Table 3, revises the runtime chart and its legend, and expands Figure 4's caption. The earlier qualitative and constraint figures remain as Figures 9–11 rather than being removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a paragraph positioning the method against diffusion finetuning approaches DRaFT, DPPO, DPOK, and DiffPPO. References to OpenStructure and Matrix Computations are also added. The existing positioning relative to biomolecular predictors, diffusion steering, and position-based dynamics remains.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, constraint definitions, and convergence proofs are retained; v1 Appendices D–G correspond to v2 Appendices I–L. The new uniqueness discussion restates the linearized-system uniqueness property already established in v1, while its repeated-projection evidence is empirical.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through matched-budget comparisons, solver sensitivity tests, structural perturbation measurements, and isolated training overhead analysis, addressing important gaps in v1's practical validation. It also corrects the overstated Protenix-Mini speed comparison and moderates the accuracy discussion. These gains improve support and calibration of the central claims, although many revised benchmark values remain unexplained and the formal guarantees are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Gauss-Seidel projection method. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds empirical studies of projection stability, penalty sensitivity, denoising budgets, computational overhead, and structural perturbations.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations on six biomolecular benchmarks, runtime and convergence measurements, qualitative predictions, and a finetuning/projection ablation.

results.title: Physically Valid Biomolecular Interaction Modeling with Gauss-Seidel Projection

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same token-perception findings, hierarchical VPPO contribution, performance claims, and 7B/32B scalability claims. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking binary filtering to stronger noise rejection, advantage shaping to greater stability, VQA transfer to visual grounding, and equal-budget performance to learning efficiency. These refine the existing interpretation; the substantive limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendices I–J add soft-mask implementation details and runtime/throughput information. Hardware reporting changes from eight H800 GPUs for 7B and 32 for 32B to Appendix B's claim that all models used eight; Table 14 still specifies 32 for 32B, leaving an internal inconsistency. Core hyperparameters and the repository address remain unchanged.

E1.justification: ViRL39K training and the eight original reasoning benchmarks remain. Section 5.3 and Table 8 add A-OKVQA-val and SimpleVQA-EN, substantially extending evaluation to unseen, out-of-domain knowledge and factual VQA tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds GRPO and DAPO to the 32B comparison, which previously included the base model, MM-Eureka, and NoisyRollout. Tables 6–7 also introduce soft-mask and reward-shaping comparators, expanding direct tests of VPPO's advantages and design choices.

E3.justification: The retained reasoning experiments keep the original training and exact-match avg@8 settings. New controls include extending 7B DAPO training from 15.5 to 17 hours to match VPPO's time budget, and calibrating the soft mask to mean weight 0.4 to control update magnitude.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of VPPO on GRPO, binary versus soft filtering, advantage versus reward shaping, out-of-domain transfer, and equal-time efficiency. These substantially strengthen mechanism and generalization analyses. The original entropy, perturbation, dependency-metric, rollout-size, and qualitative studies remain.

E5.justification: The avg@8 reporting practice is retained. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests; the new experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original VPPO averages remain 57.5 at 7B and 64.6 at 32B. New results include 32B GRPO/DAPO averages of 62.6/63.5, GRPO-based VPPO at 54.8, soft-mask and reward-shaping variants at 56.2/56.8, and VQA results. Appendix J adds runtime, throughput, and equal-budget results.

M1.justification: The proposed VPPO procedure retains KL-based visual dependency, trajectory advantage shaping, binary token filtering, and the same objective and algorithm steps. Soft-mask and reward-shaping alternatives are evaluated as ablations rather than adopted into the main method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization are retained. Changes include expanded entropy-selection explanations, consistent dependency terminology in Algorithm 1, ethics/reproducibility/LLM-use statements, and updated author and conference-header text.

P2.justification: Six new tables present the added ablations, VQA results, computational overhead, and equal-budget comparison. Table 1 gains comparison rows, and several main tables are reformatted. Existing figures and qualitative displays retain their content, with some relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for the VQA benchmarks and several video-grounding/localization works, while removing works including Intern-S1, FrameThinker, and OpenThinkImg. The central positioning against data-centric, reward-centric, and entropy-based approaches remains.

T1.justification: Appendix I newly defines the calibrated soft mask mathematically, including standardized scores and a sigmoid-offset constraint enforcing mean weight 0.4. The central dependency definition, Theorem 3.1, four assumptions, and variance-reduction proof remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through direct 32B GRPO/DAPO comparisons, controlled design ablations, and an equal-17-hour experiment showing VPPO at 57.5 versus DAPO at 55.0. Together with out-of-domain VQA testing, these materially strengthen attribution, efficiency, and generalization evidence. The conflicting 32B hardware disclosures weaken reproducibility, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VPPO research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, proofs, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, design ablations, out-of-domain VQA evaluation, and computational-efficiency experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original VPPO training and evaluation results at 7B and 32B scales, component ablations, training dynamics, and qualitative analyses.

results.title: Spotlight on Token Perception for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The introduction extends the empirical contribution from four reasoning benchmarks to include two coding benchmarks, claiming gains of 1.9 percentage points on HumanEval and 4.7 on MBPP. The central SPG and block-wise masking claims, abstract, and conclusion otherwise retain their earlier substance.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds substantive discussion of unresolved KL/trust-region stabilization, remaining group-relative advantage bias, and proposed exploration disadvantages of reward shifting. Appendices H.2–H.3 add interpretations of prompt masking, sampling cost and stability, and possible test-set overfitting from checkpoint selection. These go substantially beyond v1's bound-mixture explanations.

D1.justification: v3 adds the coding dataset link, formatting and unit-test reward rules, blocked-module handling, and a 6,000-update coding budget. It also specifies full-fine-tuning learning rates, measured runtimes with hardware context, and a project-page link. The existing code link and core implementation settings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 covers mathematical and logical reasoning through GSM8K, MATH500, Countdown, and Sudoku. v3 adds coding training on KodCode-Light-RL-10K and evaluation on HumanEval and MBPP, substantially extending coverage to executable program generation.

E2.justification: v3 adds StepWise, a reimplementation of LLaDOU's trajectory-level RL component, reward-shifted REINFORCE and GRPO, and UniGRPO with block-wise masking (Tables 6, 7, and 22). These expand the evaluated alternatives beyond v1's retained comparators. The complete LLaDOU system, including learned decoding order, is not evaluated.

E3.justification: The original main evaluation protocol remains. v3 adds an evaluation splitting each original reasoning test set equally into validation and test subsets, selecting checkpoints on validation accuracy (Table 23). New experiments also introduce full fine-tuning with smaller learning rates, removal of prompt masking, and four rather than two Monte Carlo samples.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained bound, masking, hyperparameter, inference, and diversity analyses, v3 tests dependence on LoRA, prompt masking, and Monte Carlo sample count. Reward shifting and block-wise UniGRPO probe alternative explanations for SPG's advantages; checkpoint-selection and computational-cost analyses further strengthen the supplementary evidence.
