E5.justification: Both versions report rolling-window means and standard deviations over 50 training steps in Figures 3, 7, and 9. Neither introduces independent-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new Monte Carlo sample-count ablation concerns training estimation, not repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original results are retained, but substantial new results appear. At length 256, Table 2 reports HumanEval accuracy of 41.5 for SPG/EUBO versus 39.6 for UniGRPO, and MBPP accuracy of 50.6 for SPG/Mixture versus 45.9 for WD1. Further tables add comparator, ablation, timing, and validation-selected results; the latter use different splits and are not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the SPG objectives remain unchanged: ELBO for positive advantages, EUBO or its ELBO mixture for negative advantages, and block-wise masking. Coding experiments apply the existing method; the additional training variants are experimental controls.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Related work moves from the main text to Appendix A, while new overview, discussion, and evaluation sections organize the additions. Local explanatory expansions, acknowledgements, and front-matter edits do not amount to extensive rewriting of the original narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adopts an ICLR layout with different title treatment, typography, margins, running headers, and figure/table placement. It adds tables for coding, algorithm comparison, new baselines, and supplementary tests. The original nine figures are retained and resized or relocated; retained inference-table groups are reordered.

R1.justification: New Appendix C and Table 5 substantially expand comparison of RL objectives, likelihood estimators, and masking strategies. v3 positions LLaDOU's learned decoding order as complementary to SPG while contrasting its costly trajectory-level updates. It also adds literature supporting the RLOO discussion, coding evaluation, and LoRA analysis; the original related-work section is largely retained.

T1.justification: The EUBO theorem, mixture-variance proposition, proofs, and toy-example derivations are retained. Appendix F adds theoretical assertions about reward-shift invariance under termination and terminal-reward assumptions, and about RLOO unbiasedness, without supplying new proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical credibility and scope. The validation-selected evaluation addresses sensitivity to v1's test-based checkpoint selection, while StepWise, reward-shifting, and block-wise UniGRPO comparisons better test competing explanations for SPG's advantages. Coding results and implementation-sensitivity studies provide evidence beyond the original reasoning setup, and measured runtimes substantiate efficiency discussion. These are consequential improvements in validation, although the main results still use the original selection protocol and independent-run uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPG research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite reformatting and section relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds coding evaluations, comparator experiments, sensitivity studies, computational measurements, and validation-based checkpoint evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original RL fine-tuning results on four reasoning benchmarks, component ablations, training dynamics, and qualitative examples.

results.title: SPG: Sandwiched Policy Gradient for Masked Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add improved multi-task and multi-source model merging as an explicit contribution, extending the paper's main claim beyond individual task-vector transport. The existing claims about few-shot transfer, avoiding additional fine-tuning, and first-order descent remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations connecting magnitude-mask failure to basin-specific scales, randomized-vector failure to missing source knowledge, and merging-order effects to complementary or misaligned coordinates. It also interprets ImageNet-R results as preserving general robustness. That last interpretation is stronger than some displayed results, including the DTD support-accuracy decrease from 79.78 to 79.27.

D1.justification: V3 adds an explicit code-repository link beyond v1's supplementary-code statement and documents operation-level FLOP assumptions in Appendix F. Table 5 corrects the ViT-B/16 target-checkpoint identifier to match the main text already present in v1. The original hyperparameter values and one-step fine-tuning description are retained; no measured runtime or detailed hardware specification is added.

E1.justification: The original five vision and five language benchmarks remain. V3 adds multi-task transport and transport from five independently pre-trained sources, extending the evaluated scenarios beyond single-source, single-task transfer. Appendix C.4 additionally evaluates held-out ImageNet-R generalization.

E2.justification: V3 evaluates TIES-Merging alongside Task Arithmetic in the new merging comparisons; TIES was only cited in v1. It also adds magnitude-scaled masking and a randomized source-task-vector comparator, distinct from the existing random-sign mask. The original single-task comparators, including TransFusion, remain.

E3.justification: V3 introduces protocols comparing masking before versus after merging, five-source aggregation, random vectors matched to source-vector statistics, and paired downstream/ImageNet-R testing. These substantially expand the evaluation design. The original training budgets, per-class supervision budgets, optimizer settings, and validation-based scaling selection are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test magnitude information in masking, whether source-task structure is necessary, which merging order works in each setting, and whether transport preserves held-out generalization. The existing subset-selection study moves largely to Appendix C.2; the scaling sensitivity and layerwise sign-agreement analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging over random seeds, standard deviations in Tables 5–6, and uncertainty bands for random subset selection. V3 adds no explicit run counts, seed lists, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures; the retained tables' uncertainty values are unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, 5, and 6 retain their numerical results. Substantial new results include multi-task TIES accuracy of 66.02 with Merge-then-Mask versus 54.67 without GradFix, and randomized-vector accuracy of 54.79 versus GradFix's 64.45 at one example per class. Table 8 adds ImageNet-R accuracies of 79.27–80.17 versus the target's 79.78 zero-shot baseline. These are newly reported comparisons, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: Equations (4)–(5) and Algorithm 1 change from retaining coordinates aligned with the gradient and subtracting them to retaining coordinates aligned with the negative gradient and adding them. With the gradient and source vector defined identically, this changes which coordinates survive, not merely notation. Section 5.2 also introduces merging pipelines with a multi-task consensus-sign mask. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V3 extensively revises explanatory prose across the abstract, introduction, method, and experimental discussion, consistently distinguishing gradients from negative gradients. It also reorganizes the experimental narrative, moves detailed subset selection to the appendix, and separates additional results, ablations, datasets, hyperparameters, and computational analysis into dedicated appendix sections.

P2.justification: V3 adds substantial tables for merging, randomized-vector controls, and paired task/support performance, and expands the masking table. It relocates the subset-selection figure to the appendix, regroups the supplementary tables, and redraws the scaling-sensitivity plot with revised markers and axis ticks. The masking illustration and heatmap values are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations to Gargiulo et al. (2025), Hendrycks et al. (2020), Kaplan et al. (2020), and Porrello et al. (2026), while removing Zhou et al. (2024) and Zeng et al. (2024). The central positioning relative to model merging, rebasing, and gradient-sign methods remains similar. Bibliographic metadata changes do not constitute additional research-positioning changes.

T1.justification: Section 4 substantively corrects the central mathematical account: the Taylor expansion removes duplicated scaling, the inner-product derivation matches the revised update, and Equation (10) bounds estimated-sign agreement with the negative true gradient instead of v1's gradient/oracle-task-vector event. Appendix A is aligned with this formulation. Appendix F also adds an analytical computational-cost derivation.

improvement.justification: V3 resolves important sign, scaling, and estimator-statement inconsistencies in the central method and theory, while adding meaningful controls and merging/generalization tests that address validation gaps in v1. These substantially improve mathematical coherence and empirical support. Qualifications remain: unchanged legacy scores do not establish reruns of the revised algorithm, the ImageNet-R preservation claim overstates some results, and computational savings are approximate analytical estimates. These limitations do not outweigh the documented gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GradFix research, with matching titles, authors, and core experiments. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains these empirical results and adds model-merging experiments, randomized-vector and magnitude-based controls, and ImageNet-R generalization results.

before.justification: V1 reports original CLIP and T5 transport experiments, masking and subset-selection ablations, and additional vision results in its appendix.

results.title: Gradient-Sign Masking for Task Vector Transport Across Pre-Trained Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same claims about adaptive rollout, multi-interval modeling, spatial encoding and state-of-the-art forecasting with approximately 10% improvements. The added evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting expert specialization to load balance, interval selection to horizon-dependent error accumulation, and seasonal scheduler behavior to severe-weather episodes. It also interprets comparative forecast artifacts and broadens downstream application arguments. Section 4.2 revises the discussion of graph methods to recognize GraphCast's stronger performance.

D1.justification: v1 provides software and hardware information but few concrete implementation settings. Appendix G.2 adds architecture dimensions, expert counts, optimizer settings, learning rates, warm-up, early stopping, replay-buffer sizes and update schedules. The abstract also adds a code-access URL, substantially improving reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same WeatherBench/ERA5 data and multivariate global forecasting task. Table 4 and Appendix J report additional pressure-level outputs already included in v1's modeled weather state. The scheduler analyses examine the retained 2018 test population; no new dataset or downstream task is evaluated.

E2.justification: GraphCast, previously cited but not evaluated, becomes an additional comparator across the original variables and horizons in Table 1. All earlier comparators remain; Pangu becoming Pangu-weather is a naming clarification.

E3.justification: Appendix I introduces diagnostic procedures comparing 120h and 354h trajectories through interval frequencies, trajectory lengths and weekly aggregation. The original data splits, resolution, forecast metrics and ablation settings remain unchanged. Appendix G.2's newly disclosed hyperparameters do not establish changed training settings.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations and two weather examples, v2 adds training stability and convergence diagnostics, expert-routing analysis, scheduler behavior across horizons and seasons, and comparative forecast case studies. Appendices D.2 and H–J substantially expand the evidence about optimization, component behavior and forecast errors.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bars for forecast performance. The new training curves and routing-frequency distributions are descriptive analyses rather than additions to uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All retained numerical entries in Table 1 are unchanged, and Table 2 changes only equivalent rounding. v2 adds GraphCast scores, Table 4 results for T500, Z850, U500, V500, U1000 and V1000, and findings in Figures 7–16. For example, new Figure 9 reports 6h interval shares of 36.5% at 120h and 12.5% at 354h.

M1.justification: The forecasting architecture, RPE, shared/private experts, losses, DQN and alternating fine-tuning procedure are retained. Algorithm 1 makes existing inputs and outputs explicit and changes the counter wording to 'global step'; this does not establish a different learning procedure. Appendix G.2 supplies previously unstated implementation choices.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the overall narrative remain intact. Changes include targeted introduction and MoE wording edits, an acknowledgement, conference headers, and restructuring the former A.1–A.7 appendix headings into separate appendices. Much of the expansion consists of new technical and analytical content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figures 7–16 introduce training curves, routing distributions, scheduler diagnostics and extensive comparative forecast maps. Table 4 is new, and Table 1 gains GraphCast columns. Existing figures are retained with some relocation, while Figure 2 receives an expanded caption and Table 2 revises highlighting.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands cited literature on air quality, traffic and navigation, and multimodal time-series forecasting, with new downstream positioning in Appendix K and GraphCast discussion in Appendix E.4. Several earlier contextual references are removed. The central adaptive-rollout novelty claim remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, RPE derivation and metric formulas are retained, with notation and formatting adjustments only. Appendix D.2 adds empirical convergence curves, not a convergence theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves assessability by filling important architecture and training-documentation gaps in Appendix G.2 and providing a code-access pointer. The GraphCast comparison and new convergence and routing analyses strengthen empirical support beyond v1's ablations and two examples. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including Section 4.2's incorrect Table 4 references and Figure 13's 234h/222h mismatch; the new storm-association arguments remain correlational.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ARROW research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, figures and tables, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds GraphCast comparisons, additional forecast scores, training diagnostics, routing analyses and comparative forecast maps.

before.justification: v1 reports original WeatherBench forecasting results, component and rollout ablations, and weather-event case studies in Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–5.

results.title: ARROW: An Adaptive Rollout and Routing Method for Global Weather Forecasting

C1.justification: The introduction replaces the broad 'unique skill' contribution statement with an explicit contribution about WARC-Bench tracking long-horizon performance better than ScreenSpot V2 and MiniWoB++. This refines the main contribution framing around a finding already discussed in v1. The abstract's scientific claims and conclusion remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about planner quality, the model-dependent benefit of hierarchical decomposition, and potentially cheaper execution with trained specialists. It also discusses human reading/formatting failures and explains the desktop/mobile restriction through uncertain ScreenSpot web-source overlap. Existing archive limitations and frontier-model failure explanations remain.

D1.justification: The reproducibility statement replaces future release plans with stated repository locations for benchmark execution and training recipes. v2 also supplies the complete planner prompt, additional task examples, and explicit training-site exclusion information. Existing hyperparameters and hardware details are retained. Repository contents or availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: The reported task and domain coverage is retained. WebArena-Lite is introduced as a filtered subset of WebArena, and the desktop/mobile ScreenSpot analysis selects previously covered domains. Humans evaluate existing Dev-Real tasks; Appendix A illustrates existing tasks rather than adding coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparator sets in Tables 2 and 3 remain unchanged. v2 adds a human reference and focused hierarchical comparisons using Qwen and Claude planners with base-model, Claude, or trained SVA executors, alongside single-loop controls in new Table 4.

E3.justification: v2 adds distinct evaluation designs: planner/executor comparisons on 165 evaluator-correctness-filtered WebArena-Lite tasks, human evaluation involving three participants on 60 Dev-Real tasks, and ScreenSpot scoring restricted to desktop/mobile screenshots. Existing training budgets, WARC-Bench splits, and original benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: New Table 4 tests the effects of hierarchical decomposition and planner/executor selection. Appendix L adds an out-of-domain grounding check, and the human evaluation discusses reading and output-format errors. Existing behavioral, latency, offline-training, and frontier-model failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes from reporting means alone to adding ± values for Dev-Total and Test results of repeatedly evaluated models. New hierarchical and human results also include ± values. The original three-run convention and OpenCUA single-run exceptions remain; additional runs are not established, and the ± statistic is not defined.

E6.justification: New results include WA-Lite success rates of 16.17% for single-loop Qwen versus 24.63% for Qwen planner/Ours executor, human accuracy of 87.11%, and desktop/mobile ScreenSpot scores in Table 7. These are additional settings, not same-setting improvements over v1. Table 2 also changes Ours-72B-RLVR Dev-Real from 78.33% to 76.67%, with the stated SFT-to-RLVR gain revised from 9.43 to 7.78 points. Original test means and Table 3 results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix J add a hierarchical inference procedure: a planner delegates subtasks to an SVA executor, receives completion/status feedback, and controls overall termination. This substantially extends the single-loop agent design evaluated in v1. The underlying SVA, SFT, and PPO procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized contribution-list edits, additional analysis paragraphs, and new appendices for task examples, the planner prompt, and OOD evaluation. Conference headers, contact information, and cross-references are updated. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence are preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4 and 7 and boxed task examples, adjusts Table 2 spacing, and adds syntax highlighting to prompt listings. Existing tables are renumbered or relocated, and figures move with pagination. The seven existing figures retain their content; there is no substantial visual redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds VisualAgentBench by Liu et al. (2024b) as the source associated with WebArena-Lite. The related-work discussion and broader positioning are largely unchanged; VisualWebBench becoming Liu et al. (2024a) is citation disambiguation.

T1.justification: The subtask definition, agent formulation, and PPO objective in Equation 1 are unchanged after matching appendix renumbering. Changing the contribution wording to 'formally define' introduces no new mathematical definition, derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens benchmark validation: beyond v1's cross-benchmark comparisons, it directly tests planner/executor contributions, adds a human reference, and checks transfer on non-web screenshots. These additions address important questions about subtask usefulness, difficulty, and generalization. Repository pointers and the complete planner prompt also make reproduction more actionable. The undefined ± statistic and unmeasured inference-cost benefit limit some conclusions, but the overall evidential and reproducibility gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WARC-Bench study. Their main text, tables, figures, equation, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds planner–executor experiments, a human baseline, and desktop/mobile-only ScreenSpot evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, SFT/RLVR experiments, cross-benchmark results, behavioral analyses, and offline-training comparisons in the main text and appendices.

results.title: WARC-Bench: Web Archive based Benchmark for GUI Subtask Executions

C1.justification: v2 materially narrows the performance claims: the abstract claims state of the art among generative retrievers, and the introduction describes narrowing the gap to leading dense systems rather than broadly surpassing them. OpenAI performance becomes 'on par.' The existing training collection, renamed OpenInstIR, is also elevated to an explicit dataset contribution in the abstract and contribution list.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges underperformance against leading dense retrievers and offers explanations involving training-data overlap and mature dense-retrieval optimization (Appendix C). It adds limitations concerning untested large corpora and larger models, discusses indexing-cost amortization, and interprets docid branching and query-generator effects. These substantially extend and qualify v1's predominantly favorable interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 adds task-resampling thresholds, evaluation sample totals, development-task/query counts and model assignments, beam-size information, baseline checkpoints and configurations, and cost-estimation hardware/runtime details. Figure 6 supplies sigmoid code with default k=10 and m=0.5. These materially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that previously reported experiments changed.

E1.justification: OpenInstIR corresponds to the existing ZeroGR-Train collection, retaining its six domains and source datasets. Main MAIR and BEIR coverage is unchanged. Additional appendix analyses reuse represented task coverage; newly disclosed development-task lists and query/document types do not establish a coverage expansion. Conflicting task totals do not identify actual dataset additions or removals.

E2.justification: The main MAIR/BEIR comparator sets are unchanged, including GTE-Qwen2-1.5B already present in v1's appendix. v2 adds a doc2query-versus-instructed-query comparison within TIGER (Table 13) and a separate cost comparison using Dense-3B, GENRET-3B and Summary-3B configurations (Table 10).

E3.justification: Retained benchmark metrics and stated generator-training settings remain unchanged. Added protocols include docid-prefix-length analysis, controlled query-generator replacement within TIGER, and cost estimation for a 100K-document corpus with top-1 retrieval, Llama-3B and a single A100 using vLLM. Newly disclosed development-set details do not establish changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands component analysis: Figure 4 examines docid collisions versus prefix length and trie branching; Table 13 isolates the query generator's contribution across 25 tasks; Appendix D analyzes computational costs. Tables 5 and 7 add train/evaluation type comparisons and qualitative docid examples. Existing scaling, docid-design and decoding ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. Existing boxplots and per-task curves describe task variation; v2 does not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The main benchmark values are identical in Table 2 and the corresponding appendix tables, as are retained ablation scores. Substantial new results include a 0.45% eight-word docid conflict rate, estimated indexing/retrieval costs, and Table 13's TIGER comparison: averages of 16.95 with doc2query and 23.35 with the proposed generator, alongside losses such as NFCorpus falling from 41.00 to 6.50. These are additional findings, not improvements over v1's benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The docid generator, instructed query generator, cross-entropy training objective and reverse-annealed retrieval procedure remain unchanged. Expanded Algorithm 1 makes explicit the trie masking and leaf removal already described in v1 Section 4.3; it does not introduce a new procedure.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: research questions move into experimental design, ablations precede a separate benchmark-evaluation section, and the appendices are reorganized into seven sections. The abstract, introduction, contribution list and conclusion are revised, related-work subsection headings become paragraph headings, and ZeroGR-Train is renamed throughout.

P2.justification: The unchanged framework diagram moves into the introduction; the BEIR radar chart is replaced by a numerical comparison table; the unseen-MAIR scatterplot and training-data overview graphic are removed. The decoding chart is redrawn horizontally, dataset tables are restructured, and new diagnostic plots, analysis tables and a code display substantially alter the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The related-work framework largely remains intact. v2 adds source-dataset citations, citations for retained GLEN/TIGER baselines, and Wu et al. (2025) on decoding limitations, while removing the instruction-distillation citation by Sun et al. It also explicitly positions OpenInstIR against single-domain or closed training resources. Publication and citation-label updates alone are not substantive changes.

T1.justification: The retrieval definitions, docid formulation, training loss, masked sampling distribution and normalized sigmoid schedule are mathematically unchanged. Moving the sampling equation inline and expanding pseudocode introduce no new assumptions, derivations, propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's claims and supporting evidence. It aligns the performance narrative with the unchanged gaps to leading dense retrievers, adds controlled evidence for the query generator and diagnostics for docid design, and substantially improves experimental documentation. These strengthen the paper's validity and reproducibility without relying on higher benchmark scores. Dataset-count inconsistencies remain, and the new efficiency numbers are estimates, so the revision does not establish large-scale scalability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ZeroGR study and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Renamed datasets and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds docid diagnostics and a controlled query-generator ablation, including results in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original MAIR and BEIR retrieval results and experiments on task diversity, docid design, query volume, model size and decoding.

results.title: ZeroGR: A Generalizable and Scalable Framework for Zero-Shot Generative Retrieval

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: the Vlaser model and dataset, analysis of data effectiveness for VLA transfer, leading embodied-reasoning/WidowX performance, and competitive Google Robot performance. The added experiments provide further support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges the absence of real-robot experiments in its new limitations section. It also interprets combined in-domain data as beneficial for transfer and the new hyperparameter experiments as evidence of robustness. The central explanation based on visual observation domain shift is retained.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's generation instructions, v2 supplies the filtering judge, three scoring rubrics, rejection rule, complete filtering prompts, and human-check procedure. It also expands action-expert implementation explanations and documents RoboTwin's training budget. Existing hyperparameter tables largely remain. The new declaration that AI generated no research data conflicts with the LLM-based data generation described in Appendix A.2.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on 12 RoboTwin tasks using the bimanual Aloha-AgileX embodiment and explicitly includes RoboTwin in its training-data sources. This substantially extends the previous SimplerEnv robot evaluations. v1 already contained an illustrative RoboTwin grounding sample in Figure 4, but no corresponding benchmark evaluation.

E2.justification: v2 adds RDT-1B as an evaluated comparator in RoboTwin Table 4. It also adds Spatial and Grounding variants to the WidowX comparison and Vlaser-All to both SimplerEnv tables. Existing external comparator sets in Tables 1–3 are retained; Vlaser-OOD matches the earlier Vlaser variant.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled prediction/execution-length and 10-versus-20 sampling-step experiments, plus a RoboTwin comparison with aligned 30k-step training. Section 2.3 corrects the integration step from 10 to 0.1, consistent with the previously documented ten inference steps. Reporting remains inconsistent: Section 3.3 and Table 5 use four executed actions by default, while Appendix A.1/A.3 still specify two.

E4.justification: v2 expands data-source ablations with WidowX Spatial/Grounding results and combined-data Vlaser-All experiments. New Section 3.3 tests sensitivity to action prediction length, execution length, and sampling steps. Appendix A.2 adds human validation of automated data-quality scores. The earlier qualitative rollout demonstrations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports benchmark confidence intervals, repeated-training seed statistics, or significance tests. The new human–judge agreement percentage is an additional validation result, without an accompanying uncertainty estimate or changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial RoboTwin, data-mixture, and sensitivity results. Vlaser-All reports 65.1% on WidowX, 76.2%/59.0% on Google Robot visual matching/variant aggregation, and 67.5% on RoboTwin. These are new configurations, not same-setting improvements over v1. Table 2 corrects Vlaser-QA's average from 64.6% to 62.6% while retaining its task scores. Table 1's results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an explicit judge-and-filter stage to the described in-domain data pipeline: Qwen2.5VL-32B scores QA pairs, and score-1 samples are rejected. The InternVL3 backbone, flow-matching action expert, and two-stage training remain. The PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun with this filtering.

P1.justification: Editing is concentrated in the action-expert explanation and experimental discussion, including clearer Vlaser-OOD terminology. Ablation, limitations, ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use sections are added, and the conference header changes. The abstract, introduction, conclusion, and substantial portions of the body remain essentially unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to explain token flow and robot outputs. Figure 1 revises the radar display and corrects robot labels. New RoboTwin and ablation tables accompany expanded Tables 2–3; Figures 3 and 5 gain RoboTwin examples. Appendix examples are rearranged, while Figures 6–7 retain their original demonstrations.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references for RoboTwin, RDT-1B, mixture-of-experts architecture, synthetic-data construction, and LLM judging, while retaining its central research positioning. It trims some broad criticism of existing VLAs. The revised open-pi-zero attribution and duplicate Shazeer entry do not represent distinct new prior works.

T1.justification: The explicit expectation added to Equation 2 and expanded observation/noise notation formalize the existing sampled flow-matching objective. They introduce no substantive new mathematical argument, theorem, proof, or formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central transfer argument through an additional bimanual embodiment, fuller data-mixture comparisons, and controlled action/sampling ablations, reducing reliance on one simulator and one configuration. The filtering documentation and explicit real-robot limitation also improve assessability. These gains outweigh the execution-length inconsistency and contradictory AI-use declaration, which remain material reporting weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Vlaser study and contain readable methods, results, figures, equations, and appendices. Renamed models and relocated appendix material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds RoboTwin evaluations, controlled ablations, and human reassessment of generated-data quality.

before.justification: v1 reports original embodied-reasoning evaluations and downstream WidowX and Google Robot experiments in Tables 1–3, with qualitative demonstrations in the appendix.

results.title: Vlaser: Vision-Language-Action Model with Synergistic Embodied Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same dataset–benchmark–model contribution, dataset-scale claims, unified-modeling benefits, and broad performance claims. The new experiments principally support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations connecting primitive diversity and concise SVG structure to editability and inference efficiency (B.6), external and zero-shot results to broader generalization (B.5/B.8), and human judgments to synthetic-data reliability and practical usability (B.10). These extend v1's interpretation beyond visual fidelity and cross-task transfer.

D1.justification: Section 3.1.2 newly specifies training/test annotator assignments, template-based editing verification, a 147-color palette, and CLIP similarity above 0.8 for style-transfer pairing. v3 also provides human-study instruments and discloses assistive LLM use. These improve documentation without demonstrating changed data construction; existing training hyperparameters, hardware, prompt templates, and project link remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on SVG-Stack for image-to-SVG and UniSVG for understanding and generation, previously only discussed as related resources. Appendix B.10 also introduces human assessment involving researchers, PhD students, and UI designers. The original SAgoge and SArena domains and dataset sizes are retained.

E2.justification: Six InternVL3.5 sizes are added to SArena-Icon generation comparisons in v3 Table 12, although several already appeared in v1's illustration or editing tables. The new external comparisons also include GPT-4V, StarVector 1B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, and fine-tuned LLaMA/Qwen baselines, substantially extending the evaluated comparator configurations.

E3.justification: New protocols include component ablations using 50% of selected stage-two data, icon-only training followed by chemistry evaluation, and structural-count and inference-time measurements. v3 also adds success-rate metrics and a 42-participant study with blinded caption comparisons, randomized output ordering, and 1–5 ratings. These additions substantially extend evaluation design; the original training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.4 extends the existing token-length and training-loss illustrations with task-level Raw/T/T+E component ablations. Appendices B.6, B.8, and B.10 add analyses of code structure and efficiency, zero-shot icon-to-chemistry transfer, synthetic-data quality, and human judgments of generated outputs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance-testing procedures. The new human-study ratings and success percentages are point estimates; participant counts and sampling procedures change evaluation design rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive benchmark, ablation, transfer, code-quality, success-rate, and human-evaluation results, including a UniSVG Final Score of 0.826. Reported FVDs also change: Table 4's InternSVG value becomes 99.474 instead of 207.935, matching v1's appendix, while the one-stage ablation changes from 237.524 to 101.433. These reporting changes do not establish improvements from retraining the same model.

M1.justification: The architecture, SVG-specific vocabulary, subword-averaged embedding initialization, and two-stage training procedure remain unchanged in Section 4 and Appendix A. New ablation variants test existing components; expanded annotation descriptions do not establish a changed method.

P1.justification: v3 expands the annotation explanation and experimental discussion, adds appendix subsections and reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-use statements, and standardizes some model names. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained; this is a localized expansion rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial visual reporting through component-ablation, external-benchmark, transfer, code-quality, and human-evaluation tables, questionnaire screenshots, and eight rating plots. Existing generation tables gain success-rate columns and baseline rows. Qualitative panels are redistributed or resized, while their underlying examples are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds the InternVL3.5 reference and relates its new code-quality analysis to SVGenius's complexity metrics and StarVector's primitive representations. The main related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The embedding-initialization equation and associated mathematical content are unchanged. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs; v3's new metrics and analyses are empirical.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged proposal. Table 7 directly tests the tokenization and initialization components; external generation benchmarks and cross-domain transfer address generalization beyond SArena; and Appendix B.10 supplies human evidence for synthetic-data reliability and practical output quality. These address important evidential gaps in v1, while numerical reconciliations improve consistency. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported and some numerical prose inconsistencies persist, but the additions materially improve the paper's empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InternSVG–SAgoge–SArena work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds external benchmark evaluations, component ablations, cross-domain transfer, code-quality analysis, and a human study.

before.justification: v1 reports original InternSVG evaluations on SArena and SGP-Bench, multitask and training-strategy ablations, and qualitative results in Section 5 and Appendix B.

results.title: InternSVG: Towards Unified SVG Tasks with Multimodal Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: the ten-task ODI benchmark, evaluation of 20 MLLMs revealing immersive-understanding weaknesses, and a training-free Omni-CoT framework that improves performance. Additional validation does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation: Appendix D.5 explains resolution sensitivity through fine-detail loss versus global spatial layout; D.6–D.7 discuss benchmark stability and the insufficiency of more explicit prompts; D.8 assesses the accuracy–latency tradeoff. Section 5.2.3 interprets limitations of alternative input pipelines. Appendix F also newly asserts pre-training and post-training utility, without corresponding training experiments.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a specific repository address for the planned code/data release and adds CC BY 4.0 release terms in Appendix G. It also documents the new view/video construction settings and reports inference times. Core annotation procedures and prompts are retained. The release statements remain prospective rather than establishing resource availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 2,000 indoor/outdoor ODIs and 4,254 QA pairs across ten tasks. The added multi-view, synthetic-video, resizing, and prompt experiments reuse these scenes and questions through different evaluation procedures. No additional dataset, population, or underlying task is evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 adds multi-view input comparisons for GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0-flash, and InternVL2.5-8B, plus video-input comparisons for the latter two models in Table 7. Table 14 also extends Zero-shot CoT comparisons to InternVL2.5-8B and o3. These substantially broaden the inference alternatives evaluated against Omni-CoT; the original 20-model benchmark remains intact.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 12 oriented perspective views, 12-second videos at 60 FPS, 80/90/100-degree FoV comparisons, 512×1024 downsampling, alternative GPT-4o prompt prefixes, and latency evaluation. These substantially extend the experimental controls. The original benchmark metrics and primary evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Table 5 expands the sequential crop-refinement ablation with additional component combinations. New analyses test FoV selection, crop-filtering rates, resolution sensitivity, prompt sensitivity, and accuracy versus inference time (Tables 6 and 10–14). Existing error cases, qualitative comparisons, and open-ended Omni-CoT evaluation are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run uncertainty analysis. v2 adds three-run results, means, and standard deviations for GPT-4o and InternVL2.5-8B in Table 12, a limited addition without uncertainty estimates for Omni-CoT gains. Some summaries are inconsistent: InternVL's reported human-attribute mean/SD of 70.28/0.18 do not match its displayed runs.

E6.justification: Primary scores in Tables 2–4 and the former appendix Tables 6–7, now Tables 8–9, are retained. Numerous new results cover component variants, input formats, sensitivity, filtering, repetitions, and latency. For example, Table 11 reports downsampled overall scores of 54.08 for GPT-4o and 55.52 for InternVL3-78B; Table 14 reports InternVL2.5-8B latency of 3.44 seconds for direct answering versus 13.81 seconds for full Omni-CoT. These are additional results under specified conditions, not improved headline scores between versions.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline retains six-view captioning, viewpoint-guided answering, crop grounding and relevance filtering, and response refinement. Its equations and prompts are unchanged. The additional component and FoV experiments test the existing framework rather than introduce a revised method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall section order are retained. v2 subdivides Section 5.2, extends Appendix D, adds acknowledgements and a licensing appendix, and updates affiliations and conference headers. Local edits clarify terminology and correct the Table 1 name from 360Bench to ODI-Bench; there is no pervasive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven tables (6, 7, and 10–14) and transforms Table 5 from a compact sequential ablation into a larger component-checkmark matrix. Figure 1 gains explicit panel labels and a revised caption. Existing appendix tables and figures are largely retained, with renumbering and reflow around the substantial new tabular material.

R1.justification: v2 adds Liao et al.'s visual-token-compression evaluation work and Yang et al.'s VisionThink, using them to motivate the resizing experiment in Appendix D.5. The main related-work discussion and positioning against existing ODI benchmarks remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The spherical-coordinate and crop-FoV equations (1)–(3) are unchanged. Neither version contains additional theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 introduces no substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked multi-view/video comparators and direct tests of resolution and prompt sensitivity. v2 adds these controls, expands component ablations, and exposes inference costs, substantially strengthening the evidence for both Omni-CoT and the benchmark's design. Table 12's inconsistent summary statistics and limited uncertainty coverage weaken the new stability evidence, but do not outweigh the broader gains in experimental validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ODI-Bench and Omni-CoT. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite added experiments, reflow, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds input-format comparisons, sensitivity analyses, repeated-run results, and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 20 MLLMs, Omni-CoT experiments, component ablations, and additional quantitative and qualitative results in Appendix D.

results.title: ODI-Bench: Can MLLMs Understand Immersive Omnidirectional Environments?

C1.justification: The central claims about tutorial grounding and longer-horizon world modeling remain. v2 narrows the abstract's empirical claim to relative improvements on benchmark subsets and revises the maximum claimed gains from 25.3%/18.1% to 23.4%/16.3% for OSWorld/WebArena.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of generation-dominated cost, adaptive efficiency, filtering and fallback under irrelevant retrieval, and difficulties with ambiguous goals and content modification. It removes v1's domain-specific interpretation and the conclusion's explicit caveats about tutorial availability, outdated documentation and remaining cost. Applicability and failure mechanisms receive substantially different treatment.

D1.justification: Appendices A.2–A.3 provide new synthesis, consolidation, adaptive-branching and deduplication prompts, skill-format requirements, trajectory provenance and a test-task nonoverlap statement. Action/output specifications are revised. Cost documentation changes from the earlier cross-benchmark call-count/runtime table to retrieval latency, trigger reductions and token accounting.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates tutorial-covered subsets and leaves tutorial-scarce environments to future work. v2 evaluates OSWorld tasks lacking existing tutorials, supported by approximately 1.3k tutorials synthesized from 2k AgentNet trajectories (Section 5.5, Table 3). This substantially extends the tested conditions while retaining the original benchmark families.

E2.justification: v1's main world-model comparator is WoM, explicitly a LongCoT adaptation of WebDreamer; v2 instead specifies iterative WebDreamer in Section 5.1 and Table 2. v1's cost table lists these as separate methods, establishing a substantive change in the reported comparator. Identical retained comparator scores and residual WoM labels leave implementation consistency and rerunning unresolved.

E3.justification: v2 introduces retrieval-conditioned planning evaluation, Claude-4/4.5 backbones, alternative LLM judges, adaptive/full-rollout controls, absolute reward scoring and candidate counts of 2, 3 and 5. Oracle annotation changes from one or two chunks to one, and the reported OSWorld action space changes. Section 5.1 now states 87 OSWorld tasks, but Appendix A.2 retains 85, so an actual subset-size revision is not established.

E4.justification: Appendices A.4–A.6 add adaptive efficiency analysis, retrieval-failure examples and counts, failure categorization, cross-judge checks, and reward-design/candidate-size ablations. The earlier domain-level success analysis and full call-count/runtime comparison are removed or replaced. Existing grounding, horizon and retrieval-strategy analyses are retained; the retrieval plot is moved into the main text.

E5.justification: Table 2 continues to report three runs with the same uncertainty notation and uncertainty values. No new seed information, repeated-run policy, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is introduced. Additional ablations report point estimates, as earlier ablations did.

E6.justification: All six Table 2 R-WoM means are revised downward; for example, Qwen's OSWorld/WebArena values change from 38.05/28.92 to 37.48/28.49, while its leading rank remains. Table 1 adds planning-with-retrieval results, and new tables report tutorial-scarce, efficiency, failure and ablation outcomes. v1's domain and detailed runtime results disappear. Changed reported methods/settings prevent treating the revised means as controlled performance regressions.

M1.justification: v2 adds adaptive action branching and semantic deduplication that can bypass world-model rollouts, plus a two-stage trajectory-to-tutorial synthesis/consolidation procedure. The reported OSWorld action interface also changes from higher-level operations such as opening applications and setting spreadsheet cells to explicit clicks and keys. Retrieval grounding, LongCoT simulation and listwise ranking already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The main narrative and much background/probing prose are retained. v2 revises method, setup and retrieval explanations, adds RQ4 and an ethics/reproducibility section, and reorganizes the empirical appendix around cost, failures and ablations. The LLM-use disclosure moves from A.5 to A.7, and publication headers change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn to show synthetic tutorials and adaptive rollout paths; Table 1 gains a retrieval column, and numerous new tables replace the former domain/runtime displays. The retrieval plot moves from v1 Figure 8 to v2 Figure 3 and is restyled. Existing grounding, horizon and probing illustrations are retained and renumbered; prompt boxes and table formatting also change.

R1.justification: v2 adds WorldGPT, WALL-E, LiteCUA, OpenCUA/AgentNet and procedural-memory/skill-induction references. The introduction distinguishes computer-use grounding from prior video and simulated-environment grounding, while synthesis is linked to procedural memory. The established positioning of inference-time tutorial grounding relative to offline trajectory generation remains.

T1.justification: The background, probing definitions and core rollout/reward equations remain substantively unchanged. Retrieval-equation notation is edited, but no new formal assumptions, theoretical properties, derivations or proofs are supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical and empirical support by testing tutorial-scarce operation and adaptive cost reduction, both explicit future-work concerns in v1. Reward-design, candidate-size and judge ablations, failure analyses and implementation prompts also address previously untested explanations and reproducibility needs. These gains outweigh the loss of domain/runtime breakdowns. However, conflicting subset counts and insufficiently reconciled comparator and main-versus-appendix results remain material reporting weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe R-WoM, with matching authors, core framework, probing tasks and benchmarks. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds tutorial-scarce experiments, efficiency measurements, failure analyses and ablations in Section 5.5 and Appendices A.4–A.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original probing results, OSWorld/WebArena evaluations, grounding and horizon experiments, and retrieval/cost analyses in Tables 1–2 and Appendix A.4.

results.title: R-WoM: Retrieval-augmented World Model For Computer-use Agents

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction contributions remain unchanged. The discussion now includes demonstrated compatibility with learned CVs as an achieved capability, extending what v1 presented primarily as a prospective application.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits exact bias reweighting to a perfectly trained sampler and discusses refinement and path-weight alternatives. It explains why tetrapeptide free-energy error does not beat WTMetaD, connects buffer-refresh failures to inadequate sampler adaptation, and qualifies learned-CV performance through known-state requirements and poor psi resolution. These substantially expand the practical interpretation and limitations.

D1.justification: v2 replaces Code: TBA with a repository link, adds convergence-based guidance for selecting training duration, and documents the learned-CV inputs, 24/12-unit hidden layers, target distributions, and training data. Existing implementation documentation is largely retained, with several reported hyperparameters revised.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate alanine dipeptide, alanine tetrapeptide, nucleophilic substitution, and post-transition-state bifurcation. The new ablations and learned-CV experiment retain the alanine-dipeptide equilibrium-sampling task; they change configurations and procedures rather than molecular or task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain WTMetaD, ASBS, and MD, while Table 2 retains PIS, DDS, AS, NAAS, and ASBS. The added experiments introduce ablated configurations and reference-distribution comparisons, not additional external baseline methods.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation design with controlled bias-parameter sweeps, AM-update and pretraining comparisons, and a learned-CV setup using 5,000 configurations per state. Table 1 changes dipeptide h from 1e-4 to 5e-4 eV, SN2 stages from 4 to 2, and bifurcation stages from 2 to 4. D.4 changes the bifurcation WTMetaD bias factor from 20 to 30. These reported revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix E systematically tests Gaussian height, width, bias factor, AM updates between buffer refreshes, and pretraining, tracking both convergence and intermediate sampling distributions. F.4 adds a learned-CV case study examining recovered free energies and residual distortion along an insufficiently resolved coordinate.

E5.justification: The four-repeat WTMetaD descriptions and Table 2 uncertainty reporting are retained. The additions do not introduce new seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Figures 7–13 add substantial convergence and sampling results: excessive Gaussian height impairs final convergence, too few AM updates slow adaptation, and pretraining accelerates convergence. Figure 18 adds learned-CV free-energy agreement alongside broadened psi-direction modes. Original Table 2 scores, benchmark plots, and reaction timing figures are retained; these additions do not demonstrate improved performance in the original settings.

M1.justification: v2 adds an implemented variant using a separately trained Deep-TDA network to supply a one-dimensional collective variable (F.4), whereas v1 only suggested learned CVs. The WT-ASBS update rules, losses, replay-buffer algorithm, and main sampler architecture remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and methods structure remain largely intact. v2 rewrites the discussion, expands selected explanations, inserts an extended related-work subsection and an ablation appendix, and moves the former Additional Results appendix from E to F.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive convergence plots and bias/sample grids in Figures 7–13, plus the learned-CV panels in Figure 18. Original supplementary Figures 7–10 become Figures 14–17. Main figure captions are expanded and retained figures and tables are repositioned.

R1.justification: New A.3 substantially broadens positioning relative to learned transition-path sampling and data-trained thermodynamic generators, discussing works by Holdijk, Du, Seong, Wang, Herron, Qiu, and Benayad and Stirnemann. It distinguishes equilibrium configuration sampling from trajectory generation and data-based approaches; the discussion also adds connections beyond molecular sampling.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, Proposition 3.1, and its Appendix B proof are retained. The new discussion of imperfect-sampler reweighting qualifies practical applicability without changing the formal results or derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 left the practical bias-update and replay-buffer choices largely unsupported by sensitivity analysis. v2 directly tests these choices, identifies failure regimes, and explains their relationship to the idealized algorithm, substantially strengthening methodological validation. The learned-CV demonstration and more candid exactness and accuracy qualifications further improve the paper. The gains remain bounded: new analyses concentrate on alanine dipeptide, add no uncertainty procedures, and do not establish improved original benchmark performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WT-ASBS and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original hyperparameter and training ablations plus a learned-CV experiment on alanine dipeptide.

before.justification: v1 reports original peptide and reaction sampling experiments, including free-energy estimates, convergence comparisons, computational timings, and distributional metrics.

results.title: Enhancing Diffusion-Based Sampling with Molecular Collective Variables

C1.justification: The headline claim changes from a 160-fold inference speedup to approximately 89-fold lower computational cost relative specifically to the DiT classifier. The abstract replaces its broad contrast with diffusion models with a contrast against discriminative classifiers and emphasizes replay-free incremental adaptation. The central efficient, explainable VAR-classifier contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 proposes a velocity-training mismatch as a possible explanation for MeanFlow's poor classification results. It also interprets reduced smoothing gains after CCA and explains how excessive noise can average semantically dissimilar samples. Existing interpretations of distribution-shift weaknesses, model-size tradeoffs, and failure cases are retained.

D1.justification: V2 supplies an author-implementation repository link and documents Kernel SHAP, 5,000 attribution perturbations, and masking of precomputed token likelihoods. The earlier A6000 runtime-estimation disclosure disappears with runtime reporting. Existing subset-selection recipes, class lists, and classifier pseudocode remain unchanged. Repository availability is stated in the PDF, not independently verified.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-100, the same five distribution-shift datasets, and the first ten ImageNet classes for incremental learning. The appendix class lists are identical. New attribution tests and sensitivity studies extend analysis of existing coverage rather than introduce a new dataset, population, or task.

E2.justification: V2 adds MeanFlow-based DC-MF(25) to Table 1, LIME and SHAP to the new quantitative explanation comparison in Table 3, and a DiT diffusion classifier to the incremental-learning comparison in Table 4. These substantially broaden comparator coverage; the earlier comparators remain.

E3.justification: Efficiency evaluation changes from runtime, including diffusion times estimated for an A6000, to per-image GFLOPs. New attribution evaluation uses insertion/deletion AUC, masked token likelihoods, and 5,000 perturbations for LIME and SHAP. The added incremental-learning diffusion baseline uses DiT-S/2 trained for 2,000 epochs; existing ResNet and VAR training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests smoothing sample counts, noise magnitude, and smoothing during partial-scale pruning. Section 6.1 and Appendix C add quantitative attribution comparisons and insertion/deletion curves, while Figure 8 adds visual cases. The earlier component ablation, model-size analysis, and failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added smoothing sample counts and attribution perturbation budgets concern computation and evaluation design, rather than uncertainty estimation across repeated experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds DC-MF's 50.30% ImageNet accuracy, attribution AUCs, a 76.0% incremental-learning average for DC, and smoothing sensitivity results. TMI achieves insertion/deletion AUCs of 0.944/0.605 for A-VARC+. Runtime entries are replaced by GFLOPs. Existing classification accuracies remain unchanged, including A-VARC+'s 89.32% versus DC's 90.30%; the revised efficiency ratio is not a same-metric performance change.

M1.justification: The proposed classifier retains likelihood smoothing, partial-scale candidate pruning, CCA finetuning, and the same three-stage inference configuration. Token-wise mutual information is renamed TMI without changing its definition. The added attribution-evaluation machinery and comparator implementations do not revise A-VARC itself.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraphs, conclusion, and incremental-learning discussion receive targeted rewrites. V2 standardizes TMI terminology, renames Section 6.2, reorganizes the appendices, and adds acknowledgements. The main section sequence and most methodological and related-work prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds attribution and sensitivity tables, pruning and insertion/deletion plots, and another visual-explanation panel. Figure 2 replaces its runtime axis with GFLOPs; Tables 1–2 replace time columns, and the incremental-learning table gains a DC comparison. Earlier heatmaps and confusion matrices are retained and relocated, while appendix tables and surrounding text are substantially rearranged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to MeanFlow, LIME, SHAP, and RISE to position the new comparisons and attribution metrics. These are focused extensions; the dedicated related-work discussion and its account of earlier generative classifiers remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds Equations 13–14 defining the mask-weighted token log-likelihood and associated normalized class posterior used for attribution evaluation. The original classifier equations and token-wise mutual-information definition remain substantively unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1 supports its central explainability claim primarily through visual examples; v2 adds a documented quantitative evaluation against LIME and SHAP. New sensitivity studies strengthen support for the inference choices, and added generative comparators better establish the scope of the findings. Implementation access information also improves reproducibility. Attribution evaluation remains a masked-likelihood approximation, and removing runtimes sacrifices direct latency evidence, but the added validation substantially strengthens the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same A-VARC research. Their main text and appendices are readable, and retained methods, equations, tables, and figures can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds quantitative attribution evaluation, comparator results, and smoothing/pruning sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification and distribution-shift results, component ablations, class-incremental learning experiments, and model-size analyses.

results.title: Your VAR Model is Secretly an Efficient and Explainable Generative Classifier

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: neighborhood-based improvement and convergence, world-model and representation guarantees, and a PPO-based algorithm competitive with PPO and DeepMDP. The additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 connects the maze's return differences to representation collapse or separation and interprets the transition-loss statistics as evidence against sampling noise. It also discusses the measured runtime overhead and explains computational advantages of architectural Lipschitz constraints. The existing discussion of DreamSPI's planning limitations is largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 discloses NVIDIA A40 hardware, per-algorithm runtime means and standard deviations, transition-density and loss-coefficient search ranges, and maze implementation details. These expand reproducibility information; the selected Atari hyperparameters were already present in v1 and remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on a raw-pixel, two-branch maze designed to expose confounding policy updates (Section 6.1 and Appendix G). The existing stochastic Atari coverage is retained; the maze is a focused additional task.

E2.justification: PPO and PPO augmented with DeepMDP losses remain the Atari baselines, with DreamSPI retained as the planning variant. The new maze comparison reuses PPO. Added related-work citations and externally attributed runtime comparisons do not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds IQM, mean and optimality-gap summaries alongside medians. Its new maze protocol uses 84-by-84 observations, a 256-state discrete representation and tighter DeepSPI clipping. Existing Atari preprocessing, collection settings and the hyperparameters in Tables 1–2 remain substantively unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 6.1 adds a focused diagnostic case study tracking whether PPO and DeepSPI merge or separate the two critical maze states. Appendix H.2 extends the existing model-quality analysis with aggregate loss comparisons and statistical assessment. v1 already contained Atari loss curves and DreamSPI examples.

E5.justification: The reported Atari seed count increases from three to eight, and the stated per-environment bands change from 40–60% to the proper 25–75% interquartile range. v2 adds 95% stratified-bootstrap intervals, a paired bootstrap and Wilcoxon signed-rank test, plus ten-seed maze summaries.

E6.justification: Atari performance and loss curves are revised alongside the expanded seed count, and new aggregate results are reported. The maze yields returns around 8 for DeepSPI versus 4.8 for PPO. Appendix H.2 newly reports a DeepSPI-minus-DeepMDP mean transition-loss difference of -0.1381, a 95% interval of [-0.2226, -0.05907], and p = 0.00066.

M1.justification: The neighborhood operator, DeepSPI's PPO-style clipped utility incorporating reward and transition losses, and DreamSPI's imagined-trajectory procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 2 corrects gradient subscripts to match the parameter groups already specified in v1.

P1.justification: v2 adds a theoretical roadmap, changes much baseline-policy terminology to behavioral policy, makes the episodic assumption more explicit, and reorganizes the experimental appendices. It also updates affiliations and the publication header. Most existing prose and proof structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation is substantially expanded with maze diagrams, observation examples, representation curves and aggregate confidence-interval plots. The score learning curve switches to IQM, existing plots are redrawn, and v1's main-text relative-improvement chart moves to Appendix H as Figure 11. Tables 1–2 retain their structure.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 adds positioning relative to offline model-based methods including MOPO and COMBO, and connects the representation guarantees to state abstraction and bisimulation. Additional references support these connections and the statistical analyses, while the central online, representation-aware positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Theorems 1–5 and their existing proofs remain substantively unchanged. New Appendix G formally defines the maze MDP and derives values for three policies. Numbering the previously stated episodic assumption does not itself introduce a new assumption.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical claims relied on three-seed plots with narrow 40–60% bands. v2 substantially strengthens their support through eight-seed results, corrected interquartile reporting, bootstrap confidence intervals and a paired transition-loss analysis. The maze supplies direct evidence of representation behavior in a specified setting, while runtime and search disclosures improve reproducibility. These changes address an important weakness in empirical reliability without relying on higher scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepSPI work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renumbering and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original Atari results and statistical analyses, plus a new trained-agent maze experiment measuring returns and learned representation separation.

before.justification: v1 reports original stochastic Atari experiments comparing DeepSPI, PPO, DeepMDP and DreamSPI, including learning curves and model-prediction losses.

results.title: Deep SPI: Safe Policy Improvement via World Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: self-contained, parameter-free layer alignment, faster diffusion training, improved representations, and multimodal applicability. The headline 8.75-fold acceleration and 23.6% image-quality improvement also remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 develops a three-group block-structure explanation and interprets LayerSync as inducing that structure earlier in training. It adds arguments distinguishing the effect from increased learning rates and presents internal alignment and external REPA guidance as complementary. The existing recursive-refinement hypothesis is expanded, while the principal long-term regularization and pruning qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies GPU, batch-size, iteration, and learning-rate settings for added studies and specifies SRA profiling hardware. Replacement video details include LoRA, alignment of layers 8 and 16, and weight 0.02; the earlier TRD and preprocessing description disappears. Core hyperparameter tables and code-access statements remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix A replaces SSv2 video fine-tuning with MixKit. ImageNet, Tiny ImageNet, PASCAL VOC, MTG-Jamendo, HumanML3D, and CLEVRER coverage remains. The additional image-generation and representation analyses largely reuse existing datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds VAR-d20, D-JEPA-L, and SRA, while Appendix F adds a direct SRA computational comparison. Dispersive is removed from the video comparison and randomized-layer summary, although retained in the main image experiments. These changes substantially broaden image comparisons while narrowing video comparisons.

E3.justification: The replacement video experiment uses Wan2.1 with LoRA, 81-frame clips, and 1,000 evaluation videos, versus CogVideoX/Wan2.1, 33-frame clips, and 5,000 evaluation videos in v1. New image protocols include scheduled CFG, 100K-step ablations with batch size 1024, and REPA-combination evaluations at 50K and 200K steps. These are additional or replacement settings, not revisions to all retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds timestep-restricted alignment, extensive block-pair sweeps, global and early-layer learning-rate controls, gradient-norm analysis, representation trajectories, REPA-placement tests, and block-correlation analyses. The original coefficient ablation, pruning experiments, and noise-dependent PCA visualizations remain. The SiT-B randomized-pair summary is removed.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly specifies ten independent runs for randomized layer selection; v2's Section 5 and Table 6 omit that count. The SiT-XL FID standard deviation remains, IS mean/standard deviation is added, and the SiT-B uncertainty summary disappears. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Most original main results remain, but substantial new results appear. Table 2 adds scheduled-CFG LayerSync FID 1.49 while retaining the original 1.89 result. Table 5 reports REPA FID 7.88 versus 7.01 with LayerSync. New diagnostic and computational results accompany replacement MixKit FVD scores of 321.84 for vanilla and 304.68 for LayerSync; these cannot be compared directly with the removed SSv2 scores.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 adds exclusion of the earliest blocks to the layer-selection heuristic. Section 4.5 introduces joint REPA and LayerSync training. The core self-alignment objective, stop-gradient formulation, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes local grammar and terminology corrections, adds publication headers and author emails, reorganizes the representation rationale, and introduces Section 4.5 and additional appendix sections. Much of the existing prose and overall narrative structure remains; the scientific expansion does not amount to a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds correlation heatmaps, gradient-norm plots, representation-evolution plots, and numerous comparison and ablation tables. Table 2 gains an autoregressive comparison group, and the randomized-layer and video tables change structure. Existing qualitative examples, pruning illustrations, and PCA galleries are retained and relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: The main literature framing remains, with added connections to transformer block structure, generalization, and LLM pruning, plus discussion of VAR, D-JEPA, and SRA as a direct concurrent comparator. SSv2 and CogVideoX references disappear. Revelio's changed author citation and several publication-year updates concern retained works rather than newly added research.

T1.justification: v1 Appendix A's spatial similarity, temporal similarity, and combined TRD-loss definitions, Equations 4–6, are removed with the earlier video setup. The main mathematical formulation, stochastic-interpolant derivation, and computational-complexity analysis remain unchanged apart from renumbering. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: The new learning-rate controls, representation analyses, and direct SRA computational comparison substantially strengthen evidence for LayerSync's distinctive effects and practical efficiency. REPA-combination experiments also establish a useful extension. These gains outweigh the reduced video-comparator coverage and loss of explicit run-count disclosure. Reporting remains imperfect: Appendix F says FID is higher, contradicting Table 15's lower LayerSync value of 1.49 versus SRA's 1.58.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LayerSync and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite additions, renumbering, and replacement of the video fine-tuning experiment.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and reports additional controlled experiments, representation analyses, computational measurements, and replacement video fine-tuning results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LayerSync experiments on image, audio, motion, and video generation, alongside representation probing, ablations, and pruning analyses.

results.title: LayerSync: Self-aligning Intermediate Layers

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: generalizable grasping from four primitive shapes, DetPool as the key representation mechanism, data-efficient scaling, and approximately 67% real-world YCB success. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: V2 newly interprets performance as weakly dependent on geometric similarity, attributes mask-error tolerance to patch-level pooling, and argues that longer conditioning and absolute control provide more stable prediction. It also extends the applicability discussion to contact-rich pushing and interprets the new baseline and robustness results. The existing limitations section is unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 revises OpenVLA-OFT batch-size documentation and specifies ground-truth simulator depth for GROOT and bounding-box perturbations supplied to SAM in the new robustness test. Existing LEGO hyperparameters, hardware, teleoperation procedures, printing instructions, and project-access information remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds push-to-target manipulation, requiring sustained contact rather than grasp-and-lift behavior, while retaining toy training and YCB evaluation. Appendix B also adds controlled evaluation scenarios involving reduced illumination, multiple clutter objects, random or lookalike distractors, and inaccurate segmentation inputs. The original robot embodiments and grasping object sets remain.

E2.justification: Appendix C.1 and Table 12 add GROOT (Zhu et al., 2023) and DexGraspVLA (Zhong et al., 2025) to the simulation comparisons at 250 and 2,500 demonstrations. These materially extend comparisons against other object-centric approaches. Existing VLA, pooling, and ShapeGrasp comparisons are retained.
