E3.justification: New protocols include Chamfer-distance grouping at the 33rd/66th percentiles, specified lighting reductions, 2–5 clutter objects, bounding-box IoU perturbations, and condition/prediction-length variations. The scaling study adds 5- and 15-toy subsets. OpenVLA-OFT documentation changes from batch size 2 to global batch size 16 across three setups; this is revised reporting, without establishing whether experiments were rerun or the earlier number was per-device.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of dependence on training-object geometry, lighting/clutter/distractor robustness, mask-error sensitivity, temporal conditioning and prediction horizons, and absolute versus delta control. Figure 4 further probes low-diversity training with 5 and 15 toys. The existing primitive, complexity, model-size, and color ablations remain; the color analysis moves from Appendix B to C.2.

E5.justification: New Table 6 reports success rates with 95% confidence intervals for geometric-similarity groups, whereas v1 reports point estimates. It also includes Chamfer-distance dispersion statistics. The confidence-interval calculation is not explained, and no increase in independent training runs or new seed protocol is documented.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–5 and the color-ablation values are retained, but substantial new results appear. At 2,500 demonstrations, v2 reports 67.21% success with clutter, 77.98% at 60% bounding-box IoU, and pushing success of 81.83% versus 75.77% for OpenVLA-OFT (Tables 9, 11, 14). Table 16 adds 37.02% for delta control versus 80.00% for absolute control. Figure 4 changes the stated sufficient toy count from 25 to 15. These are added findings, not improved scores on the retained evaluations.

M1.justification: The MVP vision encoder, segmentation-based attention restriction, object-token pooling, transformer policy, L1 loss, and default absolute-joint control remain unchanged. New horizon and control-mode experiments are ablations; the pushing experiment does not document a new method component.

P1.justification: Related Work moves after Experiments, and the expanded appendices receive new subdivisions. V2 also edits the humanoid π0-FAST implementation prose and updates authorship, affiliations, and conference headers. Most existing prose, including the abstract, method, conclusion, and limitations, remains unchanged.

P2.justification: V2 adds nine result tables covering geometry, robustness, baselines, pushing, horizons, and control modes. Figure 4 is redrawn with additional curves and legend entries and without its former zoomed inset. Table 2 reorders and groups rows, and figures and tables are redistributed through the document. Existing overview and hardware illustrations are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Emukpere et al.'s object-centric representation work, GROOT, and DexGraspVLA, and expands its contrast with large pretrained object-centric VLAs. Most research positioning is retained, including the comparison with OTTER. Moving Related Work from Section 2 to Section 5 is structural rather than a positioning change.

T1.justification: The observation/action definitions, policy mapping, and training-loss mathematics are retained. Neither version presents a theorem or proof contribution. The new Chamfer-distance stratification is an empirical analysis, without a new mathematical derivation or formal property.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central generalization argument: geometric-similarity analysis and mask/scene perturbations address important untested explanations and sensitivities in v1, while direct object-centric comparisons and pushing evaluation broaden the evidence. Some new interpretations overstate their tables—for example, DexGraspVLA does not outperform OpenVLA-OFT at 250 demonstrations in Table 12—and uncertainty reporting remains limited. These shortcomings qualify the conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEGO/DetPool grasping study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison; relocated sections and renumbered tables can be matched.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds geometric-similarity analysis, robustness experiments, additional baselines, pushing results, and further ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation and physical-robot grasping results in Tables 1–3, alongside scaling studies and ablations.

results.title: Learning to Grasp Anything By Playing with Random Toys

C1.justification: The abstract, five stated contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about transferability, geometry-free self-supervision, XFactor, and its advantage over prior models. The new geometry-free footnote clarifies terminology, while the appendix additions supply supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning rendering's role in learning geometry, sensitivity to imperfect pose correspondence, and the reliability of TPS oracles. It qualifies masked-transfer comparisons, explains RayZer reproduction discrepancies, and uses LVSM artifacts to support the existing rendering limitation. Its assertion that corrupted variants outperform all earlier ablations is not consistently supported by Tables 3 and 7.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the 5% probability of omitting masks and AdamW weight decay of 0.005; neither establishes a changed setting. It also documents new experiments' temporal-mixing probabilities and SSL implementation choices, including InfoNCE temperature 0.1. Existing architecture, hardware, training budgets, and project access information remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, and CO3Dv2. Appendix B adds visually corrupted-video oracle tests and masked-input transfer evaluation, extending evaluated input conditions without adding datasets or domains.

E2.justification: RayZer and RUST remain the main NVS comparators. Table 6 adds trained SimCLR and VICReg objective baselines, Figure 3 adds LVSM as a qualitative artifact comparator, and Tables 8–9 evaluate COLMAP as an alternative TPS oracle. Less3Depend is newly discussed but not benchmarked.

E3.justification: The main evaluation retains 4,000 sequence pairs per dataset and five target frames. New experiments introduce pose swapping between augmented sequences, encoder-only SSL training, probabilistic mixtures of one- and two-frame temporal offsets, and oracle evaluation under visual corruption with registration success reporting. These substantially extend experimental procedures.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds tests of whether rendering-based training outperforms standard SSL objectives, robustness to imperfect pose correspondence, TPS oracle sensitivity and registration failures, masked-transfer fidelity, and LVSM reconstruction artifacts. These investigate several methodological and evaluation weaknesses beyond the retained design ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added tables retain point-estimate reporting; VICReg's batch variance and covariance describe its training objective, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Every numerical entry in Tables 1–4 is unchanged. Tables 5–9 add substantial results under new experimental conditions. For example, Table 6 reports RE10K probe AUC at 20 degrees of 54.8 for XFactor versus 3.8 for SimCLR and 0.8 for VICReg; Table 8 reports 100% VGGT registration success versus 21.4–52.3% for COLMAP across datasets.

M1.justification: The stereo-monocular model, transferability objective, pose-preserving augmentation, and multi-view fine-tuning remain unchanged. The loss and masking descriptions move into Section 3.5. Augmented inference and corrupted training are additional experimental interventions, not revisions to the default method.

P1.justification: Most prose and the section hierarchy are retained. Loss and masking explanations move from the appendices into Section 3.5; terminology, grammar, author information, acknowledgments, and publication headers receive limited edits. Appendix B gains subsections, rather than the paper undergoing extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds five tables and two figures, including oracle-corruption trajectory panels and LVSM reconstruction grids, substantially expanding visual reporting. The original illustrations and Tables 1–4 retain their content and display structure, with surrounding text reflow and a small caption correction.

R1.justification: Related work expands to additional explicit-3D approaches and Less3Depend, while new experiments and discussion cite SimCLR, VICReg, and camera-controlled generative models. These broaden contextual coverage without changing the central research positioning. Duplicate publication entries for existing works do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Equations 1–12, including the transferability definition, TPS metric, and training objective, remain unchanged. Explicitly discussing single-scene oracle models clarifies the existing formulation without adding mathematical assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for two central elements that v1 left less tested: the learning objective and the oracle underlying TPS comparisons. Tables 6–9 add alternative-objective comparisons, correspondence-corruption tests, and direct oracle robustness checks; Table 5 adds a qualified fidelity evaluation. Reproducibility also improves. The robustness discussion overstates superiority—for example, shifted DL3DV AUC is 36.2 versus the earlier bottleneck's 41.4—but this local weakness does not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same XFactor study. Text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–B are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds objective comparisons, robustness tests, perceptual evaluations, and qualitative analyses in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original transferability, pose-probing, ablation, and reconstruction experiments across four datasets in Tables 1–4.

results.title: True Self-Supervised Novel View Synthesis is Transferable

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: J-TTL, gradient-free whole-system evolution, superiority over adaptation baselines and unique wins on Detective and Library. The introduction still states 38% improvement over prompt evolution and 57% over online RL. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendix A substantially qualifies applicability: frozen-backbone capability limits, task-specific overfitting and brittle transfer, dependence on a powerful Evolver, and possible local optima. v2 also adds interpretations attributing gains to structured evolution, adaptive temperature and stronger backbones, plus expanded explanations of baseline failures.

D1.justification: The reproducibility statement and implementation appendix replace anonymous-review repository instructions with the public GitHub destination already footnoted in v1. This updates access instructions rather than establishing a first code release. Hardware, master prompts and promises to release exact seeds, configurations and hyperparameters otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate repeated learning on Detective, Library, Zork1, Zork3, Balances and Temple. The added experiments reuse these games, especially the Detective/Zork1/Balances subset; newer backbones do not introduce new tasks or environmental conditions.

E2.justification: The main benchmark retains its comparator set. v2 Table 5 adds the explicitly evaluated Simple Mutation comparator, which replaces the structured Evolver instruction with a generic prompt-improvement instruction, alongside EvoPrompt and existing EvoTest variants.

E3.justification: v2 adds a control using Qwen3-32B for both Actor and Evolver, beyond v1's matched-Actor control, and evaluates GPT-5.1 and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview backbones. The 50-episode, 110-step protocol, preprocessing and metrics remain unchanged. Appendix G.2 newly describes positive-reward-only SFT filtering, contradicting the full-trajectory description retained in Appendix D; an actual implementation change or rerun cannot be established.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends analyses of mechanism and model dependence: structured versus generic prompt evolution in Table 5, the all-Qwen control in Table 6, temperature adaptation in Figure 9/Appendix M, and backbone scaling in Appendix N. Existing component ablations and Library/Detective case studies remain. Figure 9 adds temperature evidence alongside a score trajectory already shown in v1 Figure 3.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repeated-run counts or dispersion. v2 Appendix F/Table 8 explicitly reports AUC means and standard deviations over five random seeds across the benchmark comparison. This introduces substantial uncertainty reporting, but does not establish an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their values, and v1's Qwen/o3 results survive in v2 Tables 6 and 9. Added results include Simple Mutation AUCs of 0.65/0.07/0.20, an all-Qwen three-game average of 0.35, newer-backbone results and five-seed summaries. Figure 3 changes the prompt, UCB, memory and tool-use ablation trajectories despite retaining Table 3's AUC values.

M1.justification: The Actor/Evolver loop, four-part agent configuration, transcript-based updates, UCB selection, Algorithm 1 and master prompt retain the same procedure. Expanded explanations, ablation variants and additional backbone configurations do not change the proposed method.

P1.justification: v2 expands the introduction's task explanation and navigation example, clarifies UCB operation, brings an expanded controlled comparison into the main text, and inserts new appendix sections. Publication headers, contact information and acknowledgements also change. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation expands substantially through new ablation, uncertainty and backbone tables, a main-text control table separating Actor and Evolver identities, and the dual-axis temperature figure. Figures 2 and 3 receive clearer labels and revised legends. The original Qwen comparison remains as Table 9, and Figure 9 partly reuses an existing score curve.

R1.justification: v2 adds seven cited works, including EvoClinician, Just-in-Time Reinforcement Learning, Zombie Agents and Klong. These are mostly brief citation additions and a future-work reference; the central positioning of whole-system evolution relative to prompt optimization, memory and reflection remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, learning update, AUC definition, UCB equation and computational-cost derivations remain unchanged. v1 Appendix D becomes v2 Appendix E. Additional explanations of UCB symbols and operation do not introduce new mathematical reasoning, assumptions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked reported across-seed variability, and its matched-Actor comparison still used an o3 Evolver. v2's five-seed summaries and all-Qwen control substantially strengthen the central empirical comparison; the prompt-structure ablation and explicit capability and generalization limits further improve support and scope. These gains outweigh introduced reporting weaknesses: Table 8's Memory average of 0.13 conflicts with its displayed game values, which average about 0.18, and Appendices D and G.2 give contradictory SFT training descriptions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EvoTest/J-TTL research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds a prompt-structure ablation, an all-Qwen control, five-seed summaries, temperature observations and additional backbone evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on six Jericho games, component and Evolver-model ablations, learning trajectories, computational costs and a controlled Qwen3-32B actor comparison.

results.title: EvoTest: Evolutionary Test-Time Learning for Self-Improving Agentic Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same four central claims: early-to-middle cross-frame interaction, temporal-keyword integration, middle-to-late answer generation, and performance retention through effective pathways. The 58% attention-edge suppression example is unchanged. Added experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning spatial concepts stabilizing before temporal concepts occupy remaining tokens, dynamically emerging response checkpoints, erroneous temporal signals versus static-bias failures, and weaker visual dependence in some tasks. Section 4 and Appendix G.7 also add proposed applications and an explanation of late-layer probability increases.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the spaCy model used for verb extraction and adds a reproducibility statement describing the implementation's codebase and explicitly reporting model availability through the existing project page. Training hyperparameters, hardware, vocabulary lists and effective-layer selection details are retained from v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds VCGBench Temporal QA for multi-token open-ended responses and Video-MME action-recognition and spatial-perception tasks. These substantially broaden the evaluated question and response requirements. TVBench, TOMATO and LongVideoBench were already evaluated in v1; long-video coverage itself is not new.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same ImageLLM counterparts and VideoLLMs. Table 3 still compares full causal attention, effective pathways and random blocking for the same four models. The added analyses introduce no new baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: New protocols include successive verb-generation probes, separate incorrect-answer tracing on failure samples, VideoLLaMA3-7B evaluation with 8 versus 24 frames on LongVideoBench, and progressively expanding prefix/suffix layer knockouts (Appendices B.2 and G.2–G.4). The original training recipes and principal evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds concept-localization analysis, attention-map case studies across additional tasks, multi-token routing analysis, frame-count sensitivity, spatial-versus-temporal comparisons, failure diagnostics and a cumulative signal-leakage check. These test substantially more questions about mechanisms and robustness. The original half-layer and window-size ablations remain.

E5.justification: Shaded bands already appear in v1's plots and are retained in v2. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence-interval procedures or significance tests. The added plots and discussion of sample variance do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: The original tabulated values remain unchanged: for example, Table 3 retains TVBench scores of 51.5 and 51.2 for LLaVA-NeXT-7B-Video-FT with full and effective attention. Substantial new results show increasing reliance on generated-response anchors, task-dependent cross-frame sensitivity, two failure profiles, concept localization and robustness under cumulative knockouts (Figures D, V–AB, 5 and 10).

M1.justification: The models, basic Attention Knockout and Logit Lens operations, and effective-pathway selection rule remain unchanged. Appendix B.2 adds a limited adaptation of the analysis procedure: identifying verb anchors and tracing successive generation stages through previously generated response tokens.

P1.justification: Substantial portions of the main exposition are rewritten. Related Work moves to Appendix A, a new Discussion occupies Section 4, and the appendices are reordered and subdivided, including separate single-token and multi-token analyses. Reproducibility, acknowledgments and LLM-use statements are also added.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual material for concept localization, multi-token generation, additional attention maps, failures, long-video and spatial analyses, and signal leakage. Existing plot images are retained but regrouped and relocated, including consolidated model-specific appendix pages. Several tables also receive revised widths and spacing.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds a VideoQA-benchmark discussion, including TempCompass, Vinoground, TemporalBench and MotionBench. Section 4 adds references connecting the findings to regularization and early exit. The core positioning relative to existing multimodal mechanistic-interpretability research remains unchanged; bibliography corrections and relocation are not new research relationships.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 corrects the dimensional specification of standard attention: v1 groups the output projection with d × d_H projections, whereas v2 specifies per-head query/key/value projections and a d × d output projection. This is a limited mathematical correction; no new theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is added.

improvement.justification: v1 concentrated on successful cases and constrained single-token completion, leaving important questions about generation, failures and knockout validity. v2 substantially strengthens the evidence through multi-token analysis, failure diagnostics, spatial-task comparisons and cumulative interventions (Appendix B.2, Section 4 and Appendices G.2–G.4), while preserving the original experiments. Some mechanistic explanations remain conjectural and statistical reporting is unchanged, but the added controls and diagnostics provide a substantial net improvement in the support and applicability of the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original multi-token generation, spatial-task, failure-case and cumulative-knockout analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original attention-knockout experiments, layer-wise representation probes and VideoQA evaluations in Sections 3.2–3.5 and Appendices A–D.

results.title: Map the Flow: Revealing Hidden Pathways of Information in VideoLLMs

C1.justification: v1 claims improved sample efficiency with negligible computational overhead. The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion in v3 claim simultaneous state-of-the-art sample and computational efficiency across Bayesian optimization, reinforcement learning, and evolutionary search. This adds a central comparative computational-efficiency claim; the algorithmic and regret-bound contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of why larger models benefit FAQ refinement more than discovery tasks and how FIBO's growing context limits memory and runtime. Appendix A.3 newly connects objective nonstationarity to the choice of SGD and asserts a distinction between policy and surrogate overfitting. These substantially expand the interpretation, although Section 7.1's limitations remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds substantial comparator implementation information: tournament selection, population size, mutation rates, initial candidates, and explicit prompts. Larger-model learning rates and configuration-file information are also added. Conversely, v1's 512-token generation limit and selected task-specific SAC coefficients disappear; this is a documentation loss, not evidence that those settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate password-reset FAQ refinement, protein thermal-instability optimization, and quantum circuit energy minimization. Weakened prompt context and batched protein evaluation already appear in v1. Larger models and additional comparators do not introduce new task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator set expands from four to seven by adding Evolutionary Search (Character), Evolutionary Search (LLM), and a prompt-based FIBO implementation in Figure 4. FIBO was only discussed as related work in v1; v3 also evaluates top-10 context variants in Figure 4d and the runtime comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds Qwen3-8B FAQ and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B circuit configurations, instruction-following models for the new baselines, and a longer fully batched runtime comparison. Figure 7 introduces a c = 1, 2, 4, 8 gradient-step sweep, while new diagnostics track generation entropy and the VBOS objective. Appendix B.3 also adds 2.0E-7 to the reported learning-rate search grid.

E4.justification: New analyses test generation diversity and collapse against actor-critic methods (Figures 5 and 10), changing objective trajectories (Figure 11), and computational versus sample efficiency (Figure 7). These substantially extend v1's initialization, learning-rate, batching, and per-step timing analyses, which are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 25 random seeds, numbered 0 through 24, and report means with standard errors. v3 extends this reporting to more results without documenting a changed repeated-run design or a new significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 4 adds results for three comparators and larger model configurations. Figure 7 newly reports reward versus runtime and improved sample efficiency with additional gradient steps; Figures 10–11 add diversity and objective trajectories. Table 2 adds a fine-tuning time of 0.21 ± 0.01 seconds while retaining the 1.29 ± 0.05-second total. These are added results, not evidence of same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same sampling, GP posterior updates, marginal likelihood maximization, VBOS objective, and standardized RLOO gradient procedure. Larger backbones and additional gradient-step settings evaluate existing components rather than introduce a new method.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: settings precede baselines, computational efficiency receives its own subsection, and prior-related analyses move later. Experimental results and implementation details now precede the RLOO and GP appendices, with implementation prose relocated from the main text and proof sketches separated from formal proofs.

P2.justification: Figure 4 expands from three to six panels with additional legends and revised axes. v3 adds a method-property table and plots for runtime, gradient-step sensitivity, diversity, and objective trajectories, while expanding the timing table. Existing initialization, learning-rate, and batching figures are relocated and renumbered rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v3 adds Holland (1975) and expands positioning against evolutionary search. FIBO shifts from a related-work discussion emphasizing specialized pretraining to a comparison emphasizing in-context operation and resource limitations. Most other related-work relationships and cited works are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix E's Lemma 4 corrects predictive-variance indexing to use the sampled location x_t and the pre-observation posterior at t−1 consistently in the bound and derivation. The central theorem and other proofs remain substantively unchanged. The optimism inequality added to Section 2.3 restates the existing Corollary 2.

improvement.justification: v3 materially strengthens the practical evidence: reward-versus-time comparisons and the gradient-step sweep directly test efficiency claims that v1 supported mainly with per-step timings. Diversity diagnostics, larger-model evaluations, and broader comparisons also make the empirical argument more assessable. These gains outweigh the loss of some generation and tuning details, although broad superiority claims remain limited by the tested configurations and the prompt-based, sometimes truncated FIBO implementation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ToSFiT, retaining the same algorithm, central regret analysis, and three optimization tasks. Text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original optimization results, expanded baseline and model comparisons, runtime measurements, and diversity and objective diagnostics.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original optimization experiments, initialization and learning-rate ablations, batched evaluations, and GPU timing measurements.

results.title: Thompson Sampling via Fine-Tuning of LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and discussion retain the central contribution: lightweight simplicial representations improve actor-critic sample efficiency and final performance while preserving runtime efficiency. The abstract adds a code link but no new scientific claim; additional experiments do not redefine the headline contribution.

C2.justification: Section 4 replaces v1's interpretation that excessive L harms returns with a capacity-driven improvement-and-saturation account of the same Figure 7 curves. New discussion identifies inconsistent benefits for PQN and possible game-specific dependencies. Appendix L adds evidence-based reasoning that a penultimate-layer intervention captures most benefits of modifying every layer.

D1.justification: v2 adds a source-code link, specifies L=2 for Figure 3 and L=128, V=4 for PPO's 512-dimensional Atari representation, and explicitly depicts LayerNorm. Appendix H supplies implementation details and parameter values for the added comparators. Reproducibility documentation expands substantially, although Shrink-and-Perturb settings in the prose conflict with Figure 16's labels.

E1.justification: Atari coverage increases from 27 to 28 games: Asteroids is added in v2 Figure 30, compared with v1 Figure 19. The other benchmark and task coverage is retained. The new PQN evaluation uses the same Atari tasks rather than introducing a new domain.

E2.justification: Appendix H substantially expands evaluated comparators with ReGen, Shrink-and-Perturb, weight clipping, resets, spectral and feature normalization, GELU, Dropout, SoftMoE/Top1-MoE, ReDo and magnitude pruning. Appendix M also adds PQN versus PQN+SEM. The original actor-critic and discrete-representation comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce extensive controlled settings, including one versus four MoE experts, 50% versus 95% pruning, and individual-layer versus all-layer interventions at dimensions 64 and 128. Figure 33 extends the walk/critic-rank diagnostic horizon. These additions do not establish reruns of retained experiments. The PQN aggregation scope is inconsistent: Appendix M specifies 28 games, whereas Figure 38 says 18.

E4.justification: v2 adds regularizer-strength sensitivity studies in Appendix H, a single-simplex control in Figure 34, layer-placement ablations in Figures 35–36, and an extended return/effective-rank diagnostic in Figure 33. These investigate alternative regularization mechanisms, grouping and intervention location beyond the original SEM-parameter and FastTD3-design ablations.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies three CIFAR-10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals, identifies shaded intervals in Sections 4–5, and reports stratified-bootstrap confidence intervals for PQN in Figure 38. Existing six-seed continuous-control, three-seed Atari and five-seed OGBench counts remain unchanged; additional runs for retained experiments are not established.

E6.justification: Substantial new results accompany the regularizer comparisons, single-simplex and layer-placement tests, extended diagnostics, Asteroids evaluation and PQN experiments. Reported findings include Layer-3 performing comparably to all-layer intervention, single-simplex performance plateauing, and no consistent aggregate PQN benefit. Most earlier learning curves and all runtime values in Table 2 are retained.

M1.justification: The grouped-softmax mapping, objectives and recommended penultimate-layer placement remain unchanged. However, v2 Figure 2 newly depicts LayerNorm before softmax. Neither the method text nor Appendix E establishes whether this operation was introduced or merely omitted from the earlier diagram, leaving an actual procedural change unresolved.

P1.justification: The main six-section narrative is retained, with localized rewrites of the capacity discussion, Atari description and discussion, plus a value-based evaluation paragraph. New appendix sections organize additional comparisons and analyses. Headers change from preprint to conference publication, and minor wording and reference corrections appear throughout.

P2.justification: The visual evidence expands substantially through new regularizer, diagnostic, single-simplex, layer-placement and PQN plots. The Atari grid gains an Asteroids panel, Figure 2 gains LayerNorm, and several captions are expanded. Existing figures and tables are largely preserved, with relocation and renumbering distinguished from these additions.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting regularization baselines, non-stationary learning and Atari evaluation, including regenerative regularization, spectral normalization, resets and statistical evaluation. Appendix A and the original positioning relative to model-based and discrete-latent approaches remain largely unchanged. Numerous publication-year and venue updates refer to existing works.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and its proof in Appendix B, the FastTD3 derivations in Appendix C, and diagnostic definitions in Appendix G are unchanged. Moving the expected-return expression inline and renumbering equations do not alter the mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation by testing plausible alternative regularizers and directly examining the chosen SEM insertion layer, important gaps in v1. Negative PQN results provide a useful applicability boundary, while additional SEM settings and a code-access link improve reproducibility documentation. These gains outweigh the added reporting inconsistencies, particularly conflicting Shrink-and-Perturb settings and the 18-versus-28-game PQN aggregation description.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEM research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds regularizer comparisons, layer-placement experiments, an additional Atari game and PQN evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 non-stationarity experiments and reinforcement-learning evaluations, including learning curves, representation diagnostics, ablations and runtime measurements.

results.title: Simplicial Embeddings Improve Sample Efficiency in Actor–Critic Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same three contributions and the same claims of fully open state-of-the-art performance, competitiveness with semi-open models and the importance of data quality. The additional validation supports these existing claims rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: New Appendix E explains false rejection of valid enriched responses, the precision–recall–cost tradeoff in verification, and evaluator subjectivity and possible self-preference. Appendices A.2–A.6 add interpretations concerning judge robustness, human alignment, limited contamination and verifier consistency. These substantially expand the qualifications and explanations surrounding the unchanged method.

D1.justification: v4 supplies the exact answer-grading prompt, clarifies classification using approximately five examples per source, and explicitly promises intermediate checkpoints and stage-specific training subsets. Appendix G adds a licensing framework, source-specific restrictions in Tables 13–19, and a takedown policy. These substantially improve documentation; the PDFs establish release commitments, not verified resource availability.

E1.justification: The training-source domains and 29 downstream benchmarks remain unchanged, matching v1 Tables 7–8 to v4 Tables 12 and 20. The new human ratings and diagnostic checks examine existing responses, corpus samples and evaluation sets; they expand assessment procedures rather than represented domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: The model baselines in Table 2 remain unchanged. However, v4 Appendix A.6 adds Qwen2.5-VL-32B and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct as alternative verifiers compared with the pipeline's Qwen2.5-VL-72B. The GLM evaluator in A.2 is a judging-protocol comparison, not an additional competing Bee-8B baseline.

E3.justification: v4 introduces substantial diagnostic protocols: cross-family GLM judging, blind assessment by 14 evaluators of 38 questions, overlap checks across 66,682 evaluation samples at several Hamming-distance thresholds, and three-verifier assessment of approximately 83,800 samples. The original benchmark settings remain unchanged. Reported short/long-CoT counts change from 12.2M/2.7M to 12.1M/2.9M, without establishing that training was rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices A.2–A.6 add analyses of evaluator sensitivity, inference stability, human-perceived data quality, training–evaluation overlap and verifier agreement. These address several previously untested reliability questions. The original curation ablations, training-stage comparisons and qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without run-level uncertainty. v4 Appendix A.3 and Table 8 first report five independent inference runs for both SFT and RL across all 29 benchmarks, including individual scores, means and standard deviations. These are repeated evaluations, not independently repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 2–6 and Figures 4–5 retain their results, while new Tables 7–11 add substantial findings: RL averages of 70.2 versus 69.9 under Qwen and GLM judges, 72.74% preference for enriched reasoning, 29 potential overlaps among 66,682 evaluation samples, and 63,203 samples accepted by all three verifiers. New Tables 7–8 also report SFT CountBench/MMMU-Pro scores of 90.6/50.5, differing from the retained 90.5/50.4 in Table 2.

M1.justification: The dual-level curation pipeline, Bee-8B architecture, five-stage training recipe and GRPO rewards remain unchanged. The expanded source-labeling description clarifies the existing manual classification procedure; alternative verifiers are evaluated diagnostically without replacing the proposed verifier.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain nearly verbatim. Changes include localized wording and explanation edits, updated affiliations and author notes, a new Availability section, and additional appendix headings. The substantial scientific additions do not involve extensive rewriting of the retained argument.

P2.justification: v4 substantially expands the tabular presentation with five diagnostic-results tables and seven licensing tables, including a detailed matrix of repeated-run scores. It also adds a boxed grading prompt. Original figures and tables are retained, with Figure 3 relocated and the source and benchmark inventories renumbered.

R1.justification: v4 adds seven references, including GLM-4.5 and six works supporting a new sentence about multimodal applications in Section 5. The central positioning around transparent data curation, rather than architectural novelty, remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces a theoretical contribution with formal propositions or proofs. The mathematics in the retained qualitative examples is unchanged; the new overlap thresholds and agreement calculations are empirical analysis procedures.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked quantified inference variability and direct checks of evaluator sensitivity, human-perceived data quality and contamination. v4 Appendices A.2–A.6 substantially strengthen evidence for the central claims, while the new limitations and reproducibility documentation improve transparency. The human study remains small, two appendix scores disagree slightly with Table 2, and the new ethics statement's claim of no human subjects conflicts with the reported 14-person evaluation. These reporting defects temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in validation and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Honey-Data-15M, HoneyPipe/DataStudio and Bee-8B research. Their text, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds evaluator sensitivity, repeated inference evaluations, human response-quality assessments, contamination checks and verifier-agreement results.

before.justification: v1 reports original Bee-8B benchmark results, data-curation ablations and comparisons of training stages and reasoning modes in Tables 2–6 and Figures 4–5.

results.title: Bee: A High-Quality Corpus and Full-Stack Suite to Unlock Advanced Fully Open MLLMs

C1.justification: The principal ADL findings and four stated contributions remain intact. Section 7 adds an explicit conditional recommendation to maximize unrelated-data mixing while preserving the target behavior, whereas v1 presented mitigation as a possibility requiring further investigation.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies general representational disruption as a confound for Gemma3 causal inference, qualifies grader reliability using imperfect agreement, and discusses the unknown training data behind the chat comparisons. It also explains why mixture-model ablation can harm pretraining performance. These additions materially refine the mechanism and applicability arguments.

D1.justification: v2 documents construction of the revised causal controls, Claude's default non-reasoning setting, and the generic chat-finetuning description in Prompt 14. Appendix F.8 newly states that the existing 1:2 mixture models use three times the training steps. Appendix C's implementation details and the code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds direct base-to-chat/instruct comparisons for Qwen3 1.7B, Llama3.2 1B, and Llama3.1 8B, substantially extending coverage to broad post-training itself. This differs from v1's base-to-chat-plus-SDF comparison. The biomedical, food, and remote-sensing evaluations already existed in v1 Appendix D.5.

E2.justification: Section 5 and Figure 7 replace the displayed random-vector causal control with differences between base-model activations at randomly sampled chat-token positions. The blackbox agents and principal token-relevance and steering comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces evaluation designs varying graders across pipeline stages, a four-depth layer sweep, and chat-finetuning evaluation using a proxy corpus and generic objective description. The causal comparison now averages 64 sampled activation differences instead of 50 random vectors, and Figure 7 reports positions 0–8 instead of the earlier extended positional range.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to token-relevance, Patchscope-scale, coherence, and hypothesis graders, including agent–grader interactions (Appendix D). Appendix F.1 adds layer sensitivity, and F.8 tests causal effects after data mixing. The earlier full-finetuning, sample-count, CAFT, and emergent-misalignment analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 substantially expands statistical assessment through grader-effect and interaction models, Krippendorff agreement measures, and Pearson correlations with significance reporting. It newly reports three grading repetitions per agent hypothesis. Five agent runs and Bayesian intervals were already reported in v1.

E6.justification: New results establish grader-dependent absolute scores with persistent ADL advantages, limited detectable chat-finetuning traces, a layer-dependent relevance/steering tradeoff, and reduced causal effects in mixture models. Figure 7 reports revised causal results under changed controls and positional coverage. The headline broad-objective identification rates remain 91% for ADL versus 39% for the strongest blackbox baseline.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix C retain the same activation averaging, Patchscope calibration and filtering, steering search, and interpretability-agent procedures. The revised main-text explanation describes components already documented in v1; the added experiments do not alter ADL.

P1.justification: The main narrative and much existing appendix prose are retained, with localized explanatory rewrites. v2 adds an appendix contents page, reorganizes generalization and additional results, changes the publication header, and removes the author-contribution and acknowledgment paragraphs.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual evidence with grader diagnostics, chat-finetuning plots and two token tables, layer comparisons, and mixture-model causal plots. Figure 4 adds grader terms, and Figure 7 changes curves, controls, axes, and caption. Existing qualitative example images are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Added references support middle-layer selection, alternative grader models, and agreement measurement, including Skean et al., Ali et al., Comanici et al., Anthropic, and Krippendorff. Section 2 and the paper's substantive positioning relative to prior interpretability work remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds a formal hierarchical Gaussian model for log steering strength and its prior assumptions in Equations 3–4. The existing ADL definitions and causal-intervention equations are unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: The grader ablations and agreement analyses substantially address v1's untested dependence on particular graders. The more informative causal control, layer analysis, and direct chat-finetuning comparison strengthen central mechanism and applicability arguments. Proxy chat data and reporting inconsistencies remain—for example, Figure 12 describes an ordered-logistic likelihood while Appendix D.3 specifies a Gaussian model—but the gains in empirical validation are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Activation Difference Lens (ADL) study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds grader-reliability experiments, direct chat-finetuning evaluations, layer ablations, and causal analysis of mixture models.

before.justification: v1 reports original activation, steering, interpretability-agent, causal-ablation, and data-mixing experiments across multiple model organisms.

results.title: Narrow Finetuning Leaves Clearly Readable Traces in Activation Differences

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contributions remain substantially unchanged, but Section 6 adds a stronger, quantified central claim. Proposition 6.1 states that exact parity at logarithmic depth requires 2^{Ω(N^c)} majority-voting agents, whereas Prefix Sum uses N agents. V1 discussed advantages over voting without this depth-matched separation claim.

C2.justification: Appendix D explains how persistent independent errors can drive parity accuracy toward chance as problem size grows. Appendix H explicitly restricts the voting separation to zero-error computation and leaves approximate computation open. Appendix I specifies finite precision, finite width, and bounded absolute positional encodings for transferring lower bounds.

D1.justification: V2 discloses additional tuning ranges for voting, parity, permutations, and k-hop reasoning. It also documents the needle query and answer, essay-corpus repetition, selected configurations, and tuning subset. Existing prompts and code-access information remain; these disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: V2 adds long-document needle-in-a-haystack retrieval using Paul Graham essays, varying context length and needle position. This substantially extends the input environment beyond synthetic key-value recall. The original recall experiment moves to Appendix F.1; parity, permutation tracking, and k-hop coverage remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is retained in the corresponding experiments: Majority Voting versus CoA for recall, Majority Voting versus Iterative Query for k-hop reasoning, and the existing three-way state-tracking comparisons. Needle-in-a-haystack uses the existing recall comparator pair. Appendix H's theoretical voting model does not introduce a new empirical baseline.

E3.justification: The new needle experiment introduces a context-length and placement grid, Llama-8B evaluation, eight voters, 2,000-word CoA chunks, and tuning on a specified subset of the grid. Existing experiment settings are retained. The expanded 100/200/500-fact description documents k-hop conditions already represented in v1's figures.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds an analytical study of parity-error accumulation under independent node errors. Figure 3(c) adds recall computation-depth sensitivity to chunk size. Appendix E newly reports voting-count and task-specific tuning analyses, although their outcomes are mostly summarized rather than presented as full ablation curves.

E5.justification: Appendix E.5 specifies ten repetitions and mean accuracy for the new needle experiment. The existing 100-run, seed-42 prescription and standard-error displays remain. No new formal significance-testing procedure is documented; the added phrase 'no significant improvement' alone does not establish one.

E6.justification: Figure 3 adds needle-retrieval accuracy grids and approximately constant CoA computation-depth results across chunk sizes. For example, at 100,000 words and 50% needle depth, CoA scores 1.00 versus Majority Voting's 0.00. Newly reported tuning findings include little benefit beyond eight voters. Original experimental curves are retained; these are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The Transformer framework, recall protocol, Prefix Sum, Iterative Query, and existing task prompts are retained. The new benchmark applies existing protocols; the additional communication and voting formalizations develop their analysis rather than establish an implemented method change.

P1.justification: The recall presentation and parts of Appendix B are rewritten, Section 6 is expanded, and the original recall discussion moves to Appendix F.1. Experimental appendices are renumbered around new sections, with scattered wording and bibliographic capitalization edits. Most existing prose and the main section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds a three-panel needle figure, relocates v1's recall bar chart as Figure 6, and reflows existing appendix plots. The summary table and other experimental displays are retained. Figure 1(b)'s final inter-agent message changes from 1 to 0, introducing an inconsistency with the sender's displayed parity of 1.

R1.justification: V2 adds Aspnes et al. (1991), Kamradt (2024), Jerad et al. (2025b), and Li and Cotterell (2025), while removing Bhattamishra et al. (2020). Appendix H sharpens the comparison with Mirtaheri et al. by contrasting their setting with depth-matched communicating protocols. The broader research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: V2 adds the parity-tree error formula and proof in Lemma D.1, a formal majority-voting definition and super-polynomial separation proof in Appendix H, and a fixed-precision soft-attention simulation proposition and proof in Appendix I. Appendix G also develops the argument for representing multi-token messages as sequential token transmissions.

improvement.justification: The depth-matched voting separation and proof substantially strengthen a central comparison that v1 treated largely qualitatively. The error-propagation analysis and explicit transfer conditions improve understanding of the theory's practical limits, while the long-document experiment and tuning disclosures strengthen empirical support. These gains retain the original evidence and outweigh the small new Figure 1(b) inconsistency. The voting theorem remains restricted to exact computation, and the new retrieval evaluation is narrow.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F retain the original empirical results and add needle-in-a-haystack accuracy and computation-depth measurements.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix E report original LLM experiments on associative recall, parity, permutation tracking, and k-hop reasoning, including accuracy and computation-depth results.

results.title: Benefits and Limitations of Communication in Multi-Agent Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: MAP-derived weighted aggregation, model-dependent negative weights, practical calibration, and improved test-time efficiency. The headline 37.1% and 21.3% computation claims are unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning applicability beyond mathematics, cross-domain transfer, and self-verification signals. Appendix B strengthens the attribution of KDE's weakness to estimation difficulties and question-dependent score distributions. New Appendix C argues that calibration costs amortize after approximately 127 queries. The original limitations paragraph remains, including its now-outdated math-focused evaluation description.

D1.justification: Section 4.2 newly identifies held-out calibration accuracy as the grid-search objective. Appendix B specifies the P(True) implementation used for self-verification and normalization to (-0.5, 0.5) before weighting-function MSE calculation. These are limited additions to implementation and reproduction guidance.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates mathematical reasoning on MATH and MATH500. V2 adds MMLU-Pro-CoT-Eval across 11 subjects, including health, law, history, philosophy, and engineering, together with cross-subject calibration-transfer scenarios in Sections 5.2–5.3.

E2.justification: The main Majority Vote, Best-of-N, and Vanilla Weighted Vote comparators remain. Appendix B.2 and Table 4 add two diagnostic comparators, KDE WV with an optimal PRM term and KDE WV with an optimal LLM term. The CISC experiment reuses the existing aggregation comparator set.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the reported MATH split from 1,000 calibration and 6,500 test questions to calibration sampling within a 2,000-question pool and 5,500 held-out test questions; MATH500 similarly changes from 100/400 to a 200-question pool and 300 test questions. New protocols include Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with VersaPRM at n=16, cross-subject testing, oracle-component controls, normalized weighting-function MSE, and synthetic verification scores.

E4.justification: V1 already analyzes weighting offsets, calibration-set size, question-specific weighting functions, and reliability-estimation error. V2 adds component-oracle ablations in Table 4, quantitative global-versus-question-specific function comparisons in Table 7, a controlled pseudo-PRM experiment in Table 8, and cross-domain calibration robustness in Table 3. These substantially expand the diagnosis of estimation failures and transferability.

E5.justification: V1's accuracy tables contain point values without a stated repeated-run count. V2 first specifies three runs with different seeds and adds ± quantities throughout Tables 1 and 5. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting, although the statistic represented by ± is undefined and the PDFs do not establish an increase from any particular previous run count.

E6.justification: MATH and MATH500 accuracy entries change, and substantial new results appear. For example, Table 1's Llama3.1-Mistral-8B averages change from 61.2 to 62.6 for Logit WV and from 58.2 to 59.4 for Vanilla WV; revised protocols prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains. New Table 2 reports multidomain averages of 58.8 versus 57.7, while Table 8 reports KDE WV at 57.1 versus Logit WV at 55.8 under synthetic scores.

M1.justification: The KDE, linear, and logit calibration procedures and weighted-voting rules remain unchanged. Appendix B.3 evaluates the same aggregators using CISC confidence scores without specifying a new aggregation component or modified algorithm. The newly stated grid-search objective clarifies the existing procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the six-section main narrative remain intact. V2 adds localized experimental discussion, Appendix B subsections, a calibration-cost appendix, and acknowledgments, alongside conference-header and wording edits. The original limitations appendix moves from C to D without substantive rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 adds substantial table displays for multidomain evaluation, transfer, oracle ablations, self-verification, function discrepancy, and synthetic scores. Existing benchmark tables incorporate ± entries, and v1's MATH500 Table 2 becomes Table 5. Conference formatting changes typography, headers, spacing, and placement throughout; the four existing figures are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2's positioning is largely retained, but Appendix B.3 newly presents calibration as applicable to CISC's self-confidence signals. The additional Taubenfeld reference duplicates the already cited CISC work rather than introducing a distinct paper; the substantive change is the newly articulated relationship.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the likelihood simplification from P(s_i|alpha_k,M), concerning the generated answer, to P(c_i|alpha_k,M), concerning binary correctness. Appendix A still uses s_i, leaving a localized mathematical inconsistency. The assumptions, optimal-weight theorem, and substantive proof otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical scope and limited controlled diagnosis through multidomain and transfer tests, oracle-component ablations, and the pseudo-PRM experiment. Three-seed reporting also improves assessment of calibration stability. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including undefined ± quantities, outdated limitations wording, and Section 5.2 retaining the 61.2/58.2 example although Table 1 now reports 62.6/59.4.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same aggregation framework and research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original mathematical-reasoning experiments and adds multidomain evaluation, calibration-transfer tests, oracle-component ablations, self-verification experiments, and a pseudo-PRM simulation.

before.justification: V1 reports original MATH and MATH500 experiments, aggregation accuracies, calibration sensitivity analyses, and estimation-error analyses in Section 5 and Appendix B.

results.title: Optimal Aggregation of LLM and PRM Signals for Efficient Test-Time Scaling

C1.justification: The central claims about distributional fidelity, reduced noise fitting and compatibility with regularization remain. v2 adds real 3D PET applicability as an explicit contribution and narrows the abstract's framing to unsupervised, noise-dominated inverse problems without paired training data.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly excludes problems dominated by large null spaces, such as inpainting, from its intended scope. It interprets PnP stability through reduced conflict between fidelity and the learned prior, and qualifies the clinical example as an initial feasibility demonstration. The earlier nonuniqueness and need-for-priors limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promise of a future anonymous repository with an explicit source-code address. It adds clinical scanner geometry, corrections, voxel dimensions, initialization, optimization and runtime details; noise-mismatch generation instructions; and PnP kernel, denoiser and optimization specifications. These substantially expand the documented reproduction information.

E1.justification: v2 adds a real clinical 3D PET scan, grayscale image deblurring with a learned prior, and denoising under outlier-contaminated, spatially correlated and intensity-dependent noise. These extend the represented data and inverse-problem conditions beyond the retained synthetic PET, denoising and 1D deconvolution experiments.

E2.justification: Appendix G introduces PnP-MSE with the same fixed DnCNN prior as the comparator for PnP-DC. The clinical comparison includes a vendor MLEM reconstruction. Existing DIP-MSE, NLL-Adam and synthetic MLEM comparisons remain; newly discussed robust losses and SURE are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include clinical PET reconstruction with 21 subsets, positivity projection and learning rate 10^-4, and PnP reconstruction with 2,500 ADMM iterations and five inner Adam steps. Appendix E.5 introduces controlled noise-mismatch sweeps. These are additional evaluation designs; the earlier experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.5 directly tests violations of the assumed noise model through outliers, spatial correlation and heteroscedasticity. Appendix G adds sensitivity analysis over the ADMM penalty. These substantially extend the earlier noise-level, measurement-count, voxel-size and TV-regularization analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-initialization DIP reporting, error bars described as 1.96 times standard deviation, 100-evaluation distribution checks and timing statistics over 1,000 runs. The added studies introduce no stated new replication, confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Appendix G newly reports peak PnP PSNR of 27.5 dB for DC versus 26.9 dB for MSE. Figures E14–E16 add mismatch results, including a substantially reduced advantage under correlated noise. Figure 9 adds clinical reconstructions, and Appendix F.5 reports 0.057 versus 0.037 seconds per iteration for DC-Adam and NLL-Adam. Earlier results are retained.

M1.justification: The core CDF–logit–Wasserstein loss and Algorithms 1–4 remain unchanged. Appendix G adds a concrete PnP-DC inference procedure that alternates Adam data updates, fixed DnCNN denoising and ADMM dual updates, extending the method beyond its previous implementations.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction and Sections 3.1–3.2 around a clearer percentile/PIT explanation. Related work moves into the background with a different narrative, the DIP comparison explains peak-PSNR early stopping more explicitly, and the appendix guide is reorganized. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial visual evidence: clinical PET images in Figure 9, robustness curves with reconstruction panels in Figures E14–E16, and PnP sensitivity and reconstruction comparisons in Figures F8–F9. Retained figures are reflowed and some captions revised; Tables 1–2 retain their structure and values.

R1.justification: The brief v1 discussion linking DC to method noise and likelihood scheduling is replaced by expanded background positioning against robust losses, SURE, Noise2Noise, goodness-of-fit tests and early stopping. Section 2.2 particularly frames DC as an optimization-oriented analogue of classical goodness-of-fit criteria, substantially changing its relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: The displayed PET likelihood drops the unexplained additive background b: v1 Equation 8 uses Ax+b, whereas v2 Equation 7 uses Aθ, matching the stated synthetic forward model. This is a limited formula correction. The PIT proofs, error propositions, counterexample and tail derivations in Appendices A–C remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on synthetic corruption and correctly specified noise models. Controlled mismatch tests expose an important weakness under correlation, while clinical PET and learned-prior experiments test previously unverified applicability. Clearer scope, stronger research positioning and concrete reproduction details further improve the paper. The new clinical and PnP demonstrations remain single cases without broad uncertainty assessment, so they establish feasibility rather than general superiority, but the combined gains materially strengthen the paper's evidential foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DC-loss research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, allowing retained material to be matched reliably despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds noise-misspecification experiments, a clinical 3D PET reconstruction and learned-prior image deblurring.

before.justification: v1 reports original DIP denoising, simulated PET reconstruction, 1D deconvolution, sensitivity analyses and computational timing results.

results.title: Distributional Consistency Loss: Beyond Pointwise Data Terms in Inverse Problems

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged. The central contributions remain exploratory treatment-effect discovery through foundation models and SAEs, the significance-collapse paradox, NES recovery, and validation on simulated and ecological trials. The expanded experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: V2 develops concrete applicability limits: representation assumptions cannot be checked without outcome supervision, DINOv2 has weaker hat alignment, and JumpReLU can invalidate principal-neuron ground truth. It also revises the interpretation of the unchanged testing-rule curves, recognizing similar high-power performance rather than v1's claimed exact stopping advantage, and qualifies the ecological neurons' semantic interpretations.

D1.justification: V2 documents additional configuration grids and the stability-selection threshold of 0.6. Its reproducibility statement removes v1's submitted-code assertion and planned standalone-code release while retaining the Python snippet. A new inconsistency limits reproducibility: Table 1 specifies top-k = 5, whereas Appendix E describes 20 as the main setting.

E1.justification: CelebA, its selected attributes, and ISTAnt remain unchanged. Appendix E.2.3 adds a limited simulation scenario with unequal outcome effects, testing recovery of weaker effects alongside stronger ones. Despite the heading 'Opposite effects,' the specified grid contains positive effects with differing magnitudes, not opposite signs.

E2.justification: V1 compares NES with Bonferroni, FDR, uncorrected t-tests and top-k selection. V2 retains these and evaluates sparse logistic regression and stability-selected LASSO, displayed as CFL (Lasso) and CFL (Lasso+) in Figure 37. This substantially broadens comparison to multivariate treatment-prediction methods.

E3.justification: V2 introduces controlled evaluations across foundation models, SAE widths from 3,072 to 12,288, top-k activation settings and JumpReLU, and residualization choices. It also tests treatment-assignment probabilities of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 at specified sample sizes. These extend the experimental design while retaining the original dataset splits and evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: V1's alignment checks, null-effect test, testing-rule ablation and AD/AIPW comparison are retained. V2 adds foundation-model probes, encoder-width and sparsity sensitivity, separate SAE-seed replications, a JumpReLU failure analysis, residualization comparisons, and unequal-effect and treatment-imbalance stress tests. Appendix E substantially expands examination of why and when NES works.

E5.justification: V1 describes ten seeds combining trial redraws and SAE initializations. V2 specifies ten trial resamples per trained representation and reporting of mean plus or minus standard deviation, with two additional SAE initializations reported separately. This changes the description and attribution of variability; it does not establish an increased run count for the retained plots.

E6.justification: The original main benchmark plot is retained as Figure 5, and grooming F1 remains 0.398. V2 adds substantial condition-specific results for representation quality, robustness and new baselines, including near-zero NES precision with JumpReLU in Figure 24. It also newly reports background-code F1 of 0.568. These are added outcomes, not improvements to the retained main scores.

M1.justification: The foundation-model/SAE pipeline and recursive NES selection and stratification procedure are retained. V2 explicitly marks residualization as optional, but v1 Appendix A.3 already documented that option. Alternative encoders and activations are evaluated as ablations.

P1.justification: Appendix E is substantially reorganized around assumption validation, method consistency and additional baselines, redistributing v1's separate full-results and ablation sections. V2 adds an appendix contents page and rewrites substantial motivating, problem-formulation and interpretation passages. This structural revision extends beyond simply appending experiments.

P2.justification: V2 updates the pipeline illustration, adds a boxed motivating example and a recursive NES diagram, and introduces numerous representation galleries and experimental panels. Existing benchmark, ecological, testing-rule and AIPW graphics are largely reused and relocated, with revised numbering and captions; the training tables are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds Cremer et al. (2007) for the social-immunity motivation and develops the connection to previously cited Causal Feature Learning through the new heuristic baselines. The main related-work positioning is retained. The renamed Cadei et al. (2025) reference identifies the same preprint.

T1.justification: Section 2 replaces independence of T and W given Y and minimal I(Y;X) with a minimal sufficient (Y,W) representation satisfying independence of T and X given (Y,W). Appendix A.3 adds asymptotic FWER/FDR and O(n^-1/2) detectability remarks. The principal NES assumptions, theorems and proofs remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses the limited testing of representation dependence in v1 through encoder, sparsity, width and residualization studies, additional multivariate comparators, and a concrete JumpReLU failure case. These additions make the central assumptions and applicability limits much more assessable. Correcting the interpretation of retained testing-rule curves also improves accuracy. These gains outweigh the limited reproducibility setbacks from conflicting top-k settings and removed code-release statements; they do not establish stronger main performance or resolve the largely unchanged theoretical arguments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same exploratory causal inference study and NES algorithm. Their full text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched reliably across the expanded revision.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds representation diagnostics, robustness experiments, additional baseline comparisons and further quantitative analysis of ISTAnt.

before.justification: V1 reports original CelebA-based simulated trials, comparative experiments and ablations, together with the authors' analysis of the ISTAnt ecological trial.

results.title: Exploratory Causal Inference in SAEnce

C1.justification: v2 removes the abstract's claim that ICA is equivalent to a first-order update toward the holdout optimum under local linearization. The introduction instead describes approximating the effects of parameter updates. The central claims of efficient, reference-free scoring and improved SFT/DPO/SimPO alignment remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting excessive demonstrations to lower relevance and diminishing benefits of score updates to stabilizing weights. It interprets the new noise and holdout controls and changes the limitation from ICA being inherently off-policy to the experiments using off-policy paradigms. The existing concern about unrepresentative holdouts remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents the GSM8K holdout size, corruption fraction and example corruption operations, and describes reimplementing LESS/GREATS from their public code with specified selection fractions. The original hyperparameter table, hardware and prompts are retained. The exact corruption recipe and weaker model are unspecified, and both versions still promise a future code release.

E1.justification: v2 retains Alpaca, Yahoo_Answers_Topics, UltraFeedback and SHP-2, and adds GSM8K mathematical reasoning. Experiments use both original training data and data with intentionally corrupted chain-of-thought annotations, substantially extending coverage beyond the original instruction and preference-alignment tasks.

E2.justification: LESS and GREATS, previously cited but not evaluated, become actual SFT comparators on Yahoo_Answers_Topics and GSM8K in Tables 14–16. The original comparisons against standard training, RHO-Loss and One-shot remain.

E3.justification: New protocols introduce PPL/BERTScore, zero-shot CoT Pass@1, matched top-5% and per-batch 50% selection, and holdout-exclusion and holdout-only controls. Appendix B.1 also changes Yahoo training counts from 1,000 examples per other domain and 12,000 total to 10,000 and a stated 100,300 total. This is a reported setting revision, without evidence that retained experiments were rerun; the new total does not reconcile with the stated sampling recipe.

E4.justification: v2 adds corrupted-CoT robustness experiments, controls testing whether gains depend on training on holdout examples or on the broader training set, and an analysis of ICA-weight dynamics across updates (Section 5.5 and Appendices C.4–C.6). The original k, update-frequency, filtering and embedding ablations remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports repeated GPT-evaluation variability for one trained model. v2 specifies that these were three evaluations and adds means and standard deviations across three independent training seeds for both LLaMA-8B and Qwen-8B on Yahoo (Appendix B.2, Table 5). This extends uncertainty assessment to training randomness; the main experiments remain single runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain every numerical result, while v2 adds seed aggregates, absolute metrics, baseline comparisons, runtime measurements and holdout-control outcomes. For example, new Table 15 reports corrupted-GSM8K accuracy of 79.95%/83.04% for ICA reweighting versus 52.75%/62.40% for unweighted SFT on LLaMA/Qwen-8B. These are newly reported experiments, not performance improvements between versions under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The ICA loss difference, min-max weights, weighted gradients, nearest-neighbor demonstrations and periodic scoring remain unchanged in Equations 6–9 and Algorithms 1–2. v1 already permits hard selection and evaluates percentile filtering; v2's matched subset-selection comparisons use that existing scoring framework.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the abstract, methodological explanation and experimental discussion, plus an added author. Experimental-setup paragraphs are reordered, and existing LoRA results, prompts and examples are regrouped into Appendices C and D. The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial tabular displays for training variability, absolute metrics, additional baselines, GSM8K and holdout controls. It reformats evaluation uncertainty as mean ± standard deviation, revises captions and headers, and rearranges appendix tables. The top-k labels change from 1/3/5 to 1/5/10, matching the existing prose. Figure 1 and the qualitative examples are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for GSM8K, an in-context-learning survey and BERTScore. Section 5.2 also contrasts ICA's Bayesian scoring with the first-order approximations and computational requirements of LESS/GREATS. The related-work section and positioning relative to RHO-Loss otherwise remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 3 changes from an approximate relation to an asserted equality, and the accompanying optimal-selection statement loses its approximation qualifier. Appendix A explicitly formulates the existing conditional-independence assumption but otherwise retains the derivation. No new theorem or ICA approximation-error proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: The new non-GPT metrics, GSM8K accuracy, independent training seeds and holdout controls address important weaknesses in v1's reliance on single trained models and judge-based target matching. LESS/GREATS comparisons also strengthen the evidence against relevant alternatives. The inconsistent Yahoo sample-count revision and stronger equality assertion in Equation 3 remain concerns, but the added controls and independent measurements provide a substantial net improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICA data-selection framework. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and retained equations, algorithms, tables and examples can be matched across revisions. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds GSM8K results, additional baseline comparisons, training-seed variability and holdout-use controls.

before.justification: v1 reports original SFT, DPO and SimPO experiments across LLaMA and Qwen models, together with ablations, runtime measurements and LoRA results.

results.title: Holdout-Loss-Based Data Selection for LLM Finetuning via In-Context Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: end-to-end agentic FL synthesis, the 16-task AgentFL-Bench, and competitiveness with handcrafted FL baselines. The additional experiments do not redefine these stated contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces the explicit computational-cost and 62.5%-automation limitation discussion with a claim of 100% full automation and presents human expertise as optional assistance.
