New interpretations attribute success to system components and coordination, and treat consistent folder structures as evidence of reproducibility. The general non-convergence caveat in Section 3.3 remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds concrete API-cost, token-use, and walltime disclosures for the generation experiments and identifies additional backbone configurations. The extensive implementation prompts remain unchanged. The 80/20 split now mentioned in the main text was already specified, with seed 42, in v1's task-coder appendix.

E1.justification: The original 16 tasks and their underlying datasets are retained. Appendix A.3 adds limited coverage of different input conditions by testing paraphrased, incomplete, and out-of-schema versions of the Q1 research query.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated code-generation competitors: Codex with GPT-5.1-Codex and Claude Code with Claude-Sonnet-4.5 across all 16 tasks (Tables 7–11). Table 6 also introduces single-agent ReAct comparators. These substantially extend v1's comparisons against FL strategies.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include six configurations on seven queries, additional Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-5.1 backbones, and generation success, API cost, token consumption, and walltime measurements. Section 4.2 also states 10 cross-device clients, conflicting with the retained 15-client specification in Table 17; an actual change in client count cannot be established.

E4.justification: v2 adds component and HITL ablations (Table 6), backbone comparisons, a Q1 code-structure stability comparison (Appendix A.2), and input-schema robustness cases (Appendix A.3). It removes v1's Figure 4 analysis of evaluation attempts and human intervention. The extended continual-learning comparison in Table 5 is retained.

E5.justification: Tables 2–4 change from point estimates to means with standard deviations over three independent runs, substantially expanding uncertainty reporting for the central benchmark. Appendix A.2 also specifies three independent generation runs. v1 already averaged its evaluation-attempt figure over three runs; the PDFs do not establish an increase in the earlier benchmark's run count.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 replace the reported values: for example, Helmsman's Q1 accuracy changes from 76.26 to 76.71 ± 0.43 and Q16 from 51.04 to 50.95 ± 1.09. Table 5 is unchanged. New Table 11 reports 100% success for Helmsman with Sonnet-4.5 or GPT-5.1, versus 37.5% for Codex and 43.75% for Claude Code. These additions and the removal of v1's intervention results do not establish a same-setting improvement in autonomy.

M1.justification: The planning, supervised modular coding, and sandboxed evaluation/refinement procedure remains unchanged, including the detailed agent prompts. Additional LLM backbones and component-removal experiments are evaluation configurations rather than revisions to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Multi-Agent Collaboration' to 'Collaborative LLM Agents,' and the implementation and discussion passages receive localized revisions. Three new appendix sections precede the renumbered original appendices; most existing prose and document organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven tables, a code-structure comparison figure, and four dialogue figures. The original evaluation-attempt Figure 4 is removed, while the new Figure 4 presents different content. Tables 2–4 gain uncertainty formatting, Table 3 moves to page 7, and Figure 2 is reduced in size.

R1.justification: The related-work section and reference list are unchanged. Appendix A.1 adds focused positioning against Codex and Claude Code, arguing advantages in generation effectiveness and cost efficiency beyond the earlier emphasis on handcrafted FL strategies.

T1.justification: The simulation, diagnosis, code-correction equations, and termination reasoning in Section 3 are unchanged. The added appendices contain empirical evaluations and explanations, without new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: The agent-level comparisons and component ablations address an important gap in v1: FL accuracy comparisons alone did not establish the value of the proposed agent system against alternative code-generation approaches. Reporting variability across three runs also strengthens the central empirical evidence. These gains substantially improve the paper, although removal of the intervention/cost limitation analysis, stronger autonomy wording, and conflicting client-count specifications weaken transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Helmsman system and AgentFL-Bench study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison. The original appendix content is retained after renumbering.

after.justification: v2 reports original FL benchmark results and adds code-generation comparisons, component ablations, generation-stability results, and input-schema case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on 16 FL tasks, additional continual-learning comparisons, and evaluation-attempt and human-intervention results.

results.title: Helmsman: Autonomous Synthesis of Federated Learning Systems via Collaborative LLM Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: future-summary auxiliary supervision, handcrafted and reverse-LM variants, and improved reasoning/coding performance at 3B/8B scale. The added experiments support these claims without replacing or materially broadening them.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses roughly doubled training compute and argues for its value under data constraints. It adds interpretations concerning overfitting under data reuse, structure preservation in reverse-LM attention, and possible post-training benefits from solution diversity. These substantially extend v1's explanations of long-horizon supervision and irrelevant future tokens.

D1.justification: Appendix D.1 and Table 5 newly specify the LLaMA-3-based architectures, widths/layers, attention configuration, RoPE, normalization, initialization, BF16, FSDP, AdamW, and warmup. Section 4.1 also discloses matching forward/reverse model sizes and training steps. These substantially expand v1's comparatively brief hardware and hyperparameter recipe.

E1.justification: v2 adds held-out Dolci-Think and Dolmino evaluations of next-token predictive performance. The original synthetic tasks, reasoning/coding benchmarks, and pretraining sources remain. Reducing unique-token counts within the retained training coverage changes the protocol, not the domains.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain NTP, MTP, DS-MTP, MTP-Skip, and the existing auxiliary-head variants. New language-modeling and data-constrained comparisons reuse NTP/MTP/DS-MTP. Newly discussed methods such as Twin Networks and SemFormer are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds fixed training-token-budget studies: 8B training on 50B unique tokens for 20 epochs, and 3B training with 250B down to 5B unique tokens over increasing repetitions. It also adds NLL/NTA evaluation over approximately 4M held-out tokens and task-averaged scores. Existing benchmark protocols remain; ARC's accuracy-to-pass@1 wording is equivalent.

E4.justification: Existing head-count, summary-window, tf-idf, and teacher-layer analyses are retained. Figures 6 and 8 add substantial sensitivity studies of data availability and reuse. Figure 7 adds a final-layer attention analysis testing whether reverse-LM summaries preserve component structure in sibling discovery.

E5.justification: Existing seed counts and mean/standard-error reporting remain. However, new Tables 6–7 report three-seed means without standard errors, and the new data-constrained plots lack uncertainty bars. This introduces less complete uncertainty reporting for the added evidence; no increase in run counts is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds language-modeling results, data-reuse curves, and attention findings. In the new 8B 50B-token/20-epoch setting, Figure 6 reports average scores of 39.90% for FSP-RevLM, 37.84% for NTP, and 39.78% for MTP. Tables 1–3 and the relocated 3B ablation table retain their values. Table 4 changes MTP on G(2,8) from 0.49 to 0.48, and Figure 4 revises error-bar values.

M1.justification: The single auxiliary head, bag-of-words BCE objective, reverse-LM summary targets, L2 alignment, and inference procedure remain unchanged. FSP-BCE becomes FSP-BoW; the newly documented architecture and teacher configuration do not establish a method change.

P1.justification: The core exposition remains largely intact. Changes include consistent FSP-BoW terminology, affiliation/venue edits, expanded explanatory passages, merging former Section 4.3 into 4.2, and organizing the appendices into related work, MTP variants, synthetic experiments, and real-world pretraining with a contents page.

P2.justification: v2 adds data-constrained plots, attention heatmaps, an architecture table, and two language-modeling tables. Figures 1 and 3–5 are restyled, including revised labels, colors, sizing, and captions. The original 3B ablation table is retained as Table 8; Figure 6's standard-training panel aggregates existing Table 1 results.

R1.justification: Section 5 and new Appendix A substantially expand research positioning. They acknowledge Twin Networks as a close reverse-state-matching antecedent, discuss related unordered-future objectives from SemFormer and Frydenlund, and distinguish FSP's framework, diagnostic insights, and transformer-scale validation. Additional discussion covers latent prediction and data-constrained training.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives and parameterizations in Equations 1–15 are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs. Additional architectural formulas and explanations of prior methods do not introduce substantive theoretical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important omissions through substantially fuller implementation details, explicit compute-cost discussion, recognition of close prior work, and new language-modeling/data-reuse evidence. These improve reproducibility and scientific positioning beyond the unchanged headline results. Reporting weaknesses remain: new results lack consistent uncertainty, and Figure 8's universal-superiority claim conflicts with Dolci-Think accuracy at 12.5B tokens. Those weaknesses limit the new conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FSP research. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching across renaming and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original language-modeling evaluations, data-constrained pretraining studies, and attention analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original path-star and sibling-discovery experiments, plus 3B/8B pretraining evaluations and ablations.

results.title: Beyond Multi-Token Prediction: Pretraining LLMs with Future Summaries

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add a claim of demonstrated downstream trajectory-prediction performance, extending v1's mapping-focused contribution and proposed downstream usefulness. The introduction also replaces its specific nearly-two-orders-of-magnitude speedup claim with broader computational-efficiency language. The central continuous-MoD novelty claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits applicability to abrupt spatial or temporal changes, such as temporary barriers, and states that adaptation requires additional observations. It also interprets the new ablations as accuracy–resource tradeoffs and links prediction gains to continuous motion fields. The existing continuity and topology explanations remain.

D1.justification: Most implementation details move unchanged from Section 4.3 to Appendix C. v2 adds dataset-specific time preprocessing and prediction implementation details. Section 7 newly states that supplementary code, instructions, visualization scripts and per-sample NLL results are provided; their actual availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates NeMo-map on indoor ATC motion mapping. v2 adds outdoor ETH, HOTEL, UNIV and ZARA scenes, including nonperiodic temporal variation, and directly evaluates NeMo-map in long-term trajectory prediction on ATC. This substantially expands both environmental and task coverage.

E2.justification: The mapping comparators remain CLiFF-map, Online CLiFF-map and STeF-map. v2 adds quantitative NeMo prediction comparisons against CLiFF-LHMP, STeF-LHMP, TUTR and MID in Table 4. Some predictors already appeared in v1's illustrative Figure 1; its Social LSTM comparator is omitted from v2's revised example.

E3.justification: The existing ATC mapping split, sampling rate and training settings are retained. The new prediction protocol uses 3-second observations, 10–60-second horizons, five predicted trajectories and ADE/FDE, selecting the most likely trajectory where available and averaging MID predictions. Appendix E additionally varies mixture count and spatial-grid resolution.

E4.justification: The temporal-encoding ablation is retained unchanged. Appendix E adds sensitivity studies of SWGMM component count and spatial-grid resolution. Figures 3–5 introduce comparative crossing-flow and changing-flow case studies, including spatial NLL heatmaps that expose baseline representation failures beyond v1's whole-map visualization.

E5.justification: Both versions use means, standard deviations, paired t-tests and 95% confidence intervals for NLL comparisons. v2 applies the existing standard-deviation and paired-test practices to prediction errors. Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, and no new uncertainty-estimation procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 1–3 are numerically retained as v2 Tables 1, 3 and 5. New results include four-scene ETH/UCY NLLs and 60-second prediction mean ADE/FDE of 5.08/10.97, versus 5.45/11.45 for CLiFF-LHMP (Table 4). Figures 3–8 add qualitative findings, horizon-dependent errors and hyperparameter trends.

M1.justification: Temporal input is broadened from periodic time-of-day to general continuous time. Appendix C uses frame indices for nonperiodic ETH/UCY sequences while retaining time-of-day for ATC. The spatial-grid/SIREN architecture, SWGMM outputs and negative-log-likelihood training remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 adds NeMo-map to the title and a publication header, shortens introductory prose, and rewrites the qualitative discussion. Dataset and implementation sections move to Appendices B/C, with new validation and disclosure sections added. The main section sequence and most methodological exposition are retained.

P2.justification: v1's whole-map all-component/dominant-component panels are replaced by extensive comparative flow and NLL-heatmap displays. v2 adds ETH/UCY and prediction tables, horizon plots and hyperparameter plots. The ATC layout moves to Appendix Figure 7, while the original planning illustration is removed and the trajectory illustration is revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds the ETH/UCY dataset references by Pellegrini et al. (2009) and Lerner et al. (2007), removes Alahi et al. (2016), and expands descriptions of the already-cited TUTR and MID predictors. Its positioning against discretized MoDs and its distinction between motion priors and trajectory predictors remain.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces normalized time-of-day t in [0,1] and the stated daily-periodicity assumption with a general continuous temporal variable t in R. The SWGMM definitions, parameter constraints and likelihood objective are retained; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's single-environment mapping study and illustrative downstream motivation: it directly tests additional environments and NeMo-guided trajectory prediction, examines spatial errors and parameter sensitivity, and states concrete failure conditions. ETH/UCY splits and the trajectory-generation procedure remain insufficiently specified, but the added evidence materially improves support for the method's applicability and usefulness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NeMo-map research, with matching authors, core methodology and retained experiments. All pages, equations, tables and figures were readable, including v2's Appendices A–E; v1 has no appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains the ATC experiments and adds ETH/UCY evaluation, quantitative trajectory-prediction results, and hyperparameter experiments in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original ATC experiments measuring motion-model accuracy, training and inference times, and alternative temporal encodings in Tables 1–3.

results.title: NeMo-map: Neural Implicit Flow Fields for Spatio-Temporal Motion Mapping

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contribution: static 3D scene memory and dual spatio-temporal conditioning enable camera-controlled continuations from arbitrary-length context while preserving scene consistency and motion. Revised wording and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations separating spatial prompts' camera-control role from temporal context's motion-continuity role, explains soft geometric guidance versus inpainting, and discusses replaceable reconstruction components. Appendices A and D introduce substantive limitations concerning autoregressive error accumulation, reconstruction overhead and dependence on mask quality.

D1.justification: v2 specifies approximately 30K RealEstate10K and 20K OpenVid-1M training videos, filtering criteria, geometry tools, SEA-RAFT usage, 49-frame chunk accounting and component-level runtimes. Appendix E adds a future code-release commitment. However, v1 Section 3.5's explicit last-T-frame target and preceding-context construction is omitted; existing optimizer, hardware and training-budget details remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds DAVIS evaluation of iterative long-video generation, extending coverage beyond the next-chunk evaluations in v1 to generation with accumulated autoregressive history. RealEstate10K and OpenVid-1M training sources and RealEstate10K/DynPose-100K evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds CameraCtrl with latent interpolation and CameraCtrl with FreeLong as evaluated long-video comparators. Existing main-table comparator sets remain unchanged. CameraCtrl2, APT2 and SPMem receive new discussion but are not added as experimentally evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include autoregressive DAVIS evaluation with RMSE, MSE and ATE reporting; temporal-window and zero-spatial-conditioning controls; masking-stage experiments on a DynPose-100K subset; and component/runtime comparisons. Appendix B also changes the stated static-training reconstruction tool from MegaSAM to VGGT. This establishes a reported setting revision, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v1 tests masking on/off and spatial-frame counts. v2 retains these and adds cumulative masking-stage ablations, temporal windows w=1/5/9, an n=0 spatial-prompt control, and reconstruction-component and runtime analyses in Tables 6–10. These directly examine previously untested component roles and practical costs.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without seed counts, repeated-run information, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. Additional result rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 3 and 4 and existing Table 2 scores are retained. v2 adds the w=1 result, Tables 5–10 and qualitative outputs: examples include DAVIS PSNR 17.28 for the proposed method and DynPose-100K PSNR 13.4534 for its DepthAnything v3 variant versus 13.0468 with MegaSAM. These are new experiments or variants, not improvements to retained same-setting results. Table 7 also reports w=9 VBench values differing from unchanged Table 3 without explaining the discrepancy.

M1.justification: Appendix A explicitly extends inference through iterative autoregressive generation and introduces a DepthAnything v3 variant replacing MegaSAM at inference. These are limited procedural extensions; the CogVideoX backbone, dual conditioning and three-stage dynamic masking remain.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introductory/method paragraphs are rewritten, related-work headings are refined, and the main-text training-data section is replaced by a shorter appendix account. A notation guide and appendices organize the additions, while most existing exposition and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds six experimental tables, a notation table and five figures, including qualitative comparison grids and long-video timelines. Table 2 gains a conditioning variant. Existing figures are retained with resizing, label/caption adjustments and reflow; the substantial change is the expanded visual evidence and display structure.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds multi-frame conditioning work, including CameraCtrl2 and Seaweed-APT2. Appendix C substantially expands positioning against persistent embodied world models, WorldMem, SPMem and video inpainting. References for new experiments and tools are added, while several earlier supporting citations, including RAFT and Direct2V, are removed.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 revises the conditional-latent definition from concatenating separately encoded conditions to encoding their concatenation. This changes the displayed mathematical composition, although v1 Figure 3 already depicts a shared encoder and an implementation change is not established. The core numbered equations remain; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidential gap in v1 by adding a zero-spatial-prompt control, temporal-window comparisons and stage-wise masking tests, substantially improving attribution of the framework's benefits. Long-video evaluation, runtime breakdowns, curation details and explicit limitations also improve practical assessability. These gains outweigh the omitted target/context construction details and reporting weaknesses: Tables 3 and 7 contain unreconciled VBench values, and the latency discussion overstates comparability with CameraCtrl and MotionCtrl relative to Table 10.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe 3DScenePrompt with the same authors, framework and retained experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes a readable appendix with sections A–F.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds DAVIS evaluations, further ablations, reconstruction-component comparisons, runtime measurements and qualitative outputs in Appendix A.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original video-generation evaluations on RealEstate10K and DynPose-100K, baseline comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–4.

results.title: 3D Scene Prompting for Scene-Consistent Camera-Controllable Video Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same principal claims: a VAE-free SVG representation supports efficient diffusion training, few-step generation and preserved downstream capabilities. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix E newly explains the layer experiment through shallow texture features versus deeper semantic abstraction. Appendix F interprets tokenizer costs as supporting batch scalability despite latency differences, and Appendix H extends the stated applicability to higher resolutions without architectural changes. The original limitations paragraph remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 specifies the alignment normalization, adds project-page and code-repository links, and documents checkpoints and fine-tuning schedules for the higher-resolution experiments. The existing hyperparameter table, training hardware and downstream implementation details are retained. The PDFs establish the added access information, but not the external resources' contents or availability.

E1.justification: Appendix H extends demonstrated generation coverage from 256×256 to 512×512 and 1024×1024, supported by Figures 15–18; v1 left higher-resolution generation to future work. The datasets, semantic domains, and downstream tasks otherwise remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The main generation comparator roster is unchanged, including the already-present REPA-XL row. Comparator participation expands in diagnostic evaluations: Figure 4 supplies VA-VAE, SD-VAE and MAR-VAE linear-probe comparisons, while Table 7 directly compares SVG tokenizer modules with SD-VAE, VA-VAE and DINOv3.

E3.justification: Substantial additional protocols accompany the new analyses: intermediate-layer evaluation using SVG-B at 200K steps with 5/20-epoch autoencoders; tokenizer latency at batch size 1 and throughput at 64; guidance sweeps comparing constant CFG and zero initialization; and staged fine-tuning at 512×512 and 1024×1024. These supplement the retained experimental settings rather than establish reruns of existing results.

E4.justification: v4 adds intermediate-layer reconstruction/generation experiments and alignment-related latent visualizations (Appendix E), tokenizer cost analysis (Appendix F), guidance sensitivity comparisons (Figure 13), and convergence curves across model sizes (Figure 14). These investigate feature semantics, efficiency, sampling sensitivity and training stability beyond v1's retained component ablations, interpolation tests and PCA visualizations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. The added curves and tables do not introduce such reporting; references to random image or noise sampling are not repeated-run statistics.

E6.justification: The headline SVG scores remain unchanged. Table 1 fills the 80-epoch REPA-XL row with unguided IS 118.6, guided gFID 2.65 and guided IS 268.62. v4 also adds VAE linear-probe accuracies, layer-specific gFIDs of 73.45, 36.63 and 27.00 in Table 6, tokenizer measurements, guidance/convergence curves and higher-resolution samples. These are additional results, not matched-setting improvements over v1's SVG scores.

M1.justification: The frozen DINOv3 encoder, residual encoder, distribution alignment, decoder, and flow-matching pipeline are retained. Equation (6) specifies the existing alignment component rather than establishing a changed algorithm. Appendix H explicitly reports higher-resolution adaptation without architectural modifications.

P1.justification: Editing is localized: abstract and introduction wording is refined, related work is expanded, Section 3.3 is renamed, and acknowledgments and additional appendix sections appear. Publication and corresponding-author information are updated. Most existing method, experimental and conclusion prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned with a representation legend, expanded caption and corrected training/inference panel descriptions. Figure 4 gains accuracy annotations. Two new tables and new latent-space, guidance, convergence and higher-resolution figures substantially expand the visual evidence. Existing main-text displays are redistributed; the retained interpolation, PCA and sample-gallery figures are matched across renumbering.

R1.justification: The visual-generation related-work passage expands to latent-space regularization, diffusion autoencoders and joint image-feature generation, adding works including EQ-VAE, Preechakul et al., Pandey et al. and Wu et al. The introduction also replaces its criticism about unchanged VAE training objectives with a narrower semantic-discriminability criticism. The overall novelty positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Equation (6) newly gives an explicit mathematical definition of residual-feature alignment through DINO mean and standard-deviation matching, previously described verbally. The diffusion, flow-matching and interpolation mathematics otherwise remain substantively unchanged, with no added theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the central semantic-structure and efficiency arguments. Quantitative linear probes and the controlled encoder-layer study supplement v1's qualitative embeddings and toy example, while Table 7 makes tokenizer costs assessable and exposes the throughput versus single-image latency tradeoff. The alignment formula improves methodological clarity, and guidance analyses test an acknowledged weakness. These gains improve the support and assessability of the paper despite unchanged headline SVG scores. Higher-resolution evidence remains qualitative, and statistical uncertainty is still unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SVG work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds encoder-layer experiments, tokenizer efficiency measurements, guidance analyses, and higher-resolution generation demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original image reconstruction and generation experiments, encoder ablations, downstream classification, segmentation and depth results, and editing and interpolation demonstrations.

results.title: Latent Diffusion Model without Variational Autoencoder

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from learning primarily from optimal demonstrations to matching arbitrary demonstrators' value under bounded rewards with optimistic rates. The abstract also qualifies the novelty claim through explicit similarity to Syed and Schapire, emphasizing rate and online-processing distinctions. Adaptive optimal demonstrations were already covered in v1.

C2.justification: v2 addresses v1 Section 6's open general-reward limitation and adds a substantive explanation of iterative reward discrimination and planning, distinguishing it from cloning and reward recovery. It newly discusses deterministic-transition MDP applicability and the unresolved suboptimal-demonstrator pass@k extension. Continuous-class and computational-tractability limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds guidance that action maximization may be solved to 1/m accuracy when an exact maximizer is unavailable, and specifies a gamma schedule using sample size, confidence, and demonstrator suboptimality. These extend v1's technical prescriptions without adding an implemented system or empirical reproducibility package.

E1.justification: Neither version actually trains or evaluates on datasets or benchmarks. The broader theoretical reward and demonstrator assumptions do not constitute added empirical task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates experimental baselines. v2's comparisons with Syed and Schapire and Moulin et al. are analytical comparisons, assessed under T1 and R1.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, preprocessing, training budgets, or testing protocols. Revised theoretical assumptions and sample-complexity formulas are not experimental setting changes.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, or error studies. The counterexamples and lower-bound constructions are theoretical analyses.

E5.justification: Neither reports repeated runs, seeds, empirical confidence intervals, or significance tests. Changes to high-probability mathematical guarantees belong to T1.

E6.justification: There are no empirical result entries in either version. The changed regret and sample-complexity bounds are theoretical results assessed under T1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 generalizes support-membership voting to maximizing weighted reward values, with updates depending on prediction and demonstration reward gaps. This enables general bounded rewards with suboptimal demonstrators, beyond v1's indicator-based updates. The optimal binary special case and greedy pass@k procedure are retained.

P1.justification: The introduction, definitions, algorithm narrative, and interpretation sections are extensively rewritten around reward values. Former separate extensions are integrated into Section 4, pass@k moves to Section 6 and Appendix E, and properness discussion moves into Appendix D.3. Appendix C.2 also acquires a duplicated proof of Theorem 2.

P2.justification: Table 1 is expanded with rate formulas and explanatory shading; v2 adds Table 2 and an unnumbered comparison of apprenticeship approaches. Figures 1–2 receive revised descriptions or labels, and online-to-batch pseudocode is consolidated. The overall visual format remains similar.

R1.justification: New Section 5 develops a detailed correspondence with Syed and Schapire (2007) and discusses Moulin et al. (2025). Section 7 situates the method within reward-hedging apprenticeship approaches, including Swamy et al. This substantially revises contribution positioning; the earlier Kleinberg–Mullainathan comparison is removed.

T1.justification: v2 replaces v1's fixed-factor suboptimal-demonstrator loss guarantees with general-reward regret and optimistic excess-value bounds in Theorems 5–6. It expands Proposition 1 and revises concentration arguments, removing log-log sample-size terms from reported optimal-demonstrator and pass@k bounds. The new proofs contain local errors: Appendix D.1 overstates a logarithmic inequality's gamma range, D.2 incorrectly simplifies a coefficient, and E.2 introduces an extra eta factor.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the treatment of the important limitation explicitly left open in v1: competing with suboptimal demonstrators under general bounded rewards. Its revised algorithm and convergence analysis, together with much clearer attribution and technical comparison to prior apprenticeship methods, are substantial quality gains. The new proofs still require local range and constant-factor corrections, and a duplicated proof reduces polish, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the broader theoretical treatment and improved research positioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including alignment of reorganized and renamed material.

after.justification: v2 remains theoretical throughout. Its additional comparisons concern analytical convergence rates, not original empirical evaluations.

before.justification: v1 contains algorithms, mathematical constructions, learning guarantees, and proofs, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis results, including in its appendices.

results.title: Learning to Answer from Correct Demonstrations

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and central conclusion retain the same contributions: almost-sure injectivity preserved under training and training-free exact reconstruction through SIPIT with a linear verifier-step bound. The expanded evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: Section 3 explicitly distinguishes SIPIT's access to all per-position states from the unresolved problem of efficient inversion using only the final embedding. New discussions interpret quantization, vocabulary scaling, faster random-sequence inversion, and geometric structure. Section 6 also distinguishes inference-time representations from training data encoded in weights, refining the privacy argument.

D1.justification: v4 adds a named SIPIT implementation link and documents gradient clipping at norm 1 and coordinatewise torch.allclose tolerances of 1e-5 relative and 1e-8 absolute. v1 instead claimed an anonymous supplementary repository. The hardware/software description, periodic projection every 50 proposals, and HARDPROMPTS implementation remain.

E1.justification: v4 retains the Wikipedia, C4, Pile, and Python-code coverage, while adding WebText-based inversion evaluation and English–French translation and arithmetic collision tests using google/smol and ProCreations/SimpleMath. Appendix E.3 also introduces delimiter variations and variable-prefix/fixed-suffix scenarios designed to produce identical next-token predictions.

E2.justification: The corresponding GPT-2 inversion comparison retains HARDPROMPTS and BRUTEFORCE, including the same HARDPROMPTS adaptation. BRUTEFORCE is clarified as the random candidate policy. Newly discussed Thomas et al. (2025) is not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Added protocols include FP4/INT8 weight quantization, 14B/70B model evaluations, inversion of 50 ten-token prompts, and separate groups of 50 hundred-token WebText, Wikipedia, and random prompts. Appendix E adds matched-tokenization controls, approximately 140K delimiter-pair comparisons, 10K fixed-suffix prompts, and geometry measurements using 100 prompts with 1,000 continuations each. The original principal evaluations remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained policy, depth, scale, and length analyses, v4 tests quantization robustness, vocabulary-size scaling, and inversion across training-source, unseen, and random sequences. Appendices E.3–E.5 add identical-next-token stress tests, closest-prompt case studies, and analyses relating separation margins to anisotropy and intrinsic dimension.

E5.justification: Appendix E.5 adds Pearson and Spearman correlation estimation across layers. The existing runtime ± reporting is retained without newly specified confidence intervals, significance tests, or increased repeated-run counts. The reproducibility statement drops v1's claim that fixed seeds are supplied.

E6.justification: The original inversion results remain unchanged in v4 Table 5, including SIPIT's 28.01 ± 35.87 seconds and 100% accuracy. New Table 4 reports 100% FP4-model recovery with times of 111.78 ± 46.50 seconds for Mistral-7B-v0.1 and 549.48 ± 265.75 seconds for Llama-3.1-8B. Additional tables report quantized-model separation, targeted collision searches, distribution-specific timings, and geometric correlations. These are added results under new conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: SIPIT's sequential reconstruction, local verifier, gradient-guided candidate ranking, and Algorithms 1–3 are retained. Appendix E.1 newly documents gradient clipping, but does not establish a change to the previously used procedure; this is additional implementation disclosure.

P1.justification: The main narrative and ordering of the existing theoretical appendices are retained. v4 adds an appendix overview and explanatory roadmaps, standardizes SIPIT terminology, revises selected related-work and reproducibility paragraphs, and updates author affiliations and publication headers. Existing content is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v4 adds Tables 2–4 and 6–12, covering new experiments and the activation survey, plus boxed translation, arithmetic, and code examples. Existing figures are largely retained, but Figures 7–8 move out of the inversion-proof discussion into the experimental appendix, and the main experimental tables and figures are rearranged.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds Thomas et al. (2025) as a closely related sequential hidden-state inversion method and distinguishes its guarantees. Appendices E.5 and F substantially expand positioning relative to anisotropy, intrinsic dimension, information-bottleneck accounts, universal approximation, and Turing completeness, beyond the earlier related-work discussion.

T1.justification: New Appendix F supplies supporting analyticity proofs for sigmoid, SiLU, the error function, GELU, and gated/vector-valued constructions. The central injectivity and training-preservation arguments remain substantively unchanged. Theorem 3.2 brings robustness into the main text, but its margin-based recovery guarantee was already established in v1 Appendix D.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's narrow inversion validation, extending exact recovery beyond GPT-2 to quantized Mistral and Llama models and adding targeted collision and distribution tests. Clearer access limitations, supporting activation proofs, and discussion of the closest prior inverter also improve assessability. Some new interpretations overreach: Table 2 does not support the claim that quantization more than doubles separation in every case, and comparisons between different models do not isolate vocabulary-size effects. These weaknesses limit individual conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains in practical evidence and scope clarification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same injectivity and SIPIT research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds quantized-model evaluations, targeted collision tests, distribution-specific inversion results, and representation-geometry analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original collision-search experiments, GPT-2 prompt-inversion accuracy and timing, and appendix analyses of depth, model scale, and sequence length.

results.title: Language Models are Injective and Hence Invertible

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and central conclusion retain the same claims about full personalization, adaptive affinity-based speedup, independent-learning-level worst-case rates, and agent-specific gains. Additional experiments and expanded future directions do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly discusses the communication/computation overhead accompanying personalization and possible ways to reduce it in Appendix C.1. Figure 3 also introduces the interpretation that density estimation is relatively inexpensive compared with policy optimization, based on the similar learning curves with and without estimated ratios.

D1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands implementation information: fine-tuning uses 30 federated plus 30 local steps, pFedMe and Ditto use regularization 15, and clustered FL uses 10 clusters. It also documents FEMNIST feature and label construction, batching and communication settings, and SARSA hyperparameters, reference computation, and density estimation.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic linear systems only. V2 additionally evaluates personalized digit/curved-letter regression on FEMNIST and SARSA control with heterogeneous rewards and transition kernels. V1 already discussed reinforcement learning theoretically in Appendix C.6, but did not report these experiments.

E2.justification: The synthetic comparison expands from independent learning and FedAvg to also include fine-tuning, pFedMe, Ditto, and clustered FL, all appearing in v2 Figure 1. These additions substantially broaden the comparison to personalized-learning alternatives.

E3.justification: V2 adds distinct FEMNIST and SARSA protocols, including test-label MSE and MSE against optimal Q-functions obtained by value iteration, with new feature dimensions, budgets, and controls. Section 7 also changes the synthetic medium/high heterogeneity levels from 0.2/0.5 to 0.3/0.8, although Appendix B retains the earlier values, leaving those settings inconsistent.

E4.justification: V2 Figure 3 adds a targeted comparison of AffPCL with and without estimated density ratios across heterogeneity levels, testing whether asynchronous estimation harms learning. The earlier heterogeneity heatmaps, agent-count contours, and agent-specific analysis remain unchanged as Figures 4–6.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 10 runs and 90% confidence regions in Appendix B. V2 retains shaded uncertainty displays without documenting a changed repetition count, confidence level, seed protocol, or statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 1 contains revised curves and results for four additional baselines. New Figures 2–3 report FEMNIST test MSE and SARSA Q-function MSE, including similar performance with and without estimated density ratios. The synthetic medium/high cases cannot support direct same-setting improvement claims because their reported settings differ and are inconsistent within v2.

M1.justification: The core AffPCL updates and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V2 adds limited task-specific adaptations: the FEMNIST implementation omits importance correction, while the SARSA implementation uses evolving softmax policies and a density-ratio estimator based on state visitation frequencies.

P1.justification: The progressive method exposition and section organization remain intact. Local revisions organize Section 7 into synthetic, real-world, and reinforcement-learning paragraphs, enumerate baselines in Appendix B, and add the cost discussion. Author affiliation, publication headers, and bibliography presentation are also edited.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation substantially expands: Figure 1 is rebuilt with additional comparator curves and a larger legend, and two new four-panel figures present FEMNIST and SARSA results on a consolidated results page. Earlier appendix Figures 2–4 are retained as Figures 4–6, rather than replaced.

R1.justification: V2 adds Zhang, Chen, and Di (2025) to the density-ratio discussion. The principal related-work positioning remains unchanged. Numerous other author, year, and venue edits, including FedBR and FedDC, refer to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: New Remark 1 in Appendix C.1 adds mathematical communication and computation cost accounting relative to FedAvg, reporting up to fourfold communication and sixfold per-agent computation overhead. The convergence theorems, density-ratio lower bound, assumptions, and existing proofs remain unchanged; no nonlinear SARSA convergence proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support that v1 limited to synthetic systems and two basic baselines. Personalized FL comparators, FEMNIST, SARSA, and the density-estimation comparison address important gaps in comparative and practical validation; the cost analysis adds transparency. These gains outweigh the reporting weaknesses, although conflicting synthetic heterogeneity settings and omitted FEMNIST importance correction limit reproducibility and how directly the new experiments validate the complete method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AffPCL research and contain readable main texts and Appendices A–G. Equations, algorithms, references, and retained figures can be matched across the revision, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic, FEMNIST, and SARSA experiments in Figures 1–6 and Appendix B, including a comparison involving estimated density ratios.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic multi-agent simulations, including baseline comparisons, heterogeneity sweeps, and agent-specific results in Figures 1–4 and Appendix B.

results.title: Personalized Collaborative Learning with Affinity-Based Variance Reduction

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims that RL improves visual representations relative to SFT and that PIVOT efficiently improves existing encoders, including against larger counterparts. The additional algorithm comparisons support the existing broad RL claim without redefining the principal contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning unequal supervision per update and preference-data bias (D.4 and Section 7), and identifies reward-model confounding in the PPO comparison. It also introduces explanations based on response length and training-data overlap for the filtered-data and text-only results, plus qualifications about hyperparameter retuning at larger data scales.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a direct PIVOT code link and implementation details for the added experiments, including GRPO training steps and image resolutions, PPO checkpoint provenance, and response-filtering rules. Most existing hardware, data-access, and probing details remain intact. Conversely, Table 2 omits several encoder patch-size and resolution details previously present in v1 Table 1.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained VQA and visual-probing coverage, v2 adds HallusionBench and POPE; MS COCO and DetailCaps-4870 captioning; NaturalBench, MME-RealWorld, and VL-RewardBench; and text-only MMLU, HellaSwag, and GSM8K evaluations. Sections B.5–B.6 substantially broaden the evaluated task requirements and domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated GRPO-versus-SFT, PPO-versus-SFT, and MPO-versus-DPO-versus-SFT comparisons (Table 1 and Tables C–D). Tables K and P additionally compare PIVOT-based models with BLIP-2, SPHINX, SPHINX-Tiny, LLaVA-Next variants, and LLaVA-OneVision; these were not evaluated comparators in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces GRPO/PPO training protocols, a learning-rate sweep, response-filtered 20K-sample controls, and post-training data scales up to 150K. It also revises the existing SFT learning rate from 1e-5 to 5e-6 (v1 F.1; v2 E.1) and changes the distribution-shift filter threshold from 100 tokens to 100 words. These reported setting revisions do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test learning-rate sensitivity (Figure A), whether preference-data formatting favors DPO using NoThink/Under30 controls (Table E), behavior beyond the original 40K data limit (Table L), and robustness on additional benchmarks (Table F). The earlier projector-reuse, downstream-data-scale, and full-parameter-training ablations are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report six random seeds for segmentation probing and three-seed averages for representation alignment. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated-run counts, or uncertainty-reporting practice for its added comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results, including GRPO versus SFT average scores of 65.9 versus 62.8 (Table 1), and a 150K-sample result where SFT exceeds DPO, 55.7 versus 54.7 (Table L). Main PIVOT aggregate scores remain unchanged. The retained full-training ablation also corrects misplaced category values in the 0.5B PIVOT row, from v1 Table D to v2 Table J.

M1.justification: The PIVOT recipe, SFT/DPO objectives, encoder transfer procedure, and projector-reuse configuration remain unchanged. GRPO, PPO, and MPO are added experimental comparisons; they do not replace or introduce a new component into the default PIVOT procedure.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the narrative sequence remain intact, with localized copyediting. v2 inserts a section on generalization beyond DPO, separates the existing PIVOT contribution discussion into Section 6.3, and regroups appendix explanations, discussions, and experimental details. These changes do not amount to an extensive rewrite of the retained material.

P2.justification: v2 adds numerous comparison and diagnostic tables and a learning-rate plot. Figure 11 is expanded to include downstream evaluation, incorporating material previously illustrated in appendix Figure D. The main PIVOT table gains a separate size column, and benchmark-table headers are revised; Table R unfortunately changes metric labels without correspondingly rearranging the retained values.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the new benchmarks and RL implementations, cites BRAVE and SPHINX, and surveys GRPO/PPO implementations in Table B. Section D.3 elaborates the comparison with MPO and RLAIF-V, while retaining the established positioning around controlled post-training comparisons and underexplored vision-encoder effects.

T1.justification: Equation (1), the SFT/DPO objectives, and their mathematical definitions are retained. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2's additional algorithm descriptions and mechanism discussions introduce no substantive formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's broad RL conclusions rested on DPO experiments. v2 substantially strengthens their basis through other RL algorithms, learning-rate sensitivity, SFT-friendly controls, broader evaluations, and explicit supervision/data-bias limitations. These address important generality and experimental-control weaknesses. The gains outweigh new reporting problems, including Table R's mismatched metric labels and claims of persistent DPO superiority contradicted by exceptions in Tables F and L.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PIVOT study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across renumbering and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds RL algorithm comparisons, sensitivity tests, filtered-data controls, and evaluations on additional visual and text-only benchmarks.

before.justification: v1 reports original SFT-versus-DPO experiments, model and data scaling, ImageNet and segmentation probing, gradient visualizations, and PIVOT evaluations and ablations.

results.title: RL makes MLLMs see better than SFT

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same encoder-focused novelty claim, three-part training-free framework, hallucination-reduction claim and broader perception benefits. Added experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations attributing overhead to caption generation and adversarial optimization, arguing that plausible caption hallucinations usually have weak visual grounding, and motivating learned perturbations over fixed-step attacks. Existing qualifications concerning Q-Former and reduced reliance on prior knowledge remain. These are targeted extensions of the original interpretation.

D1.justification: The abstract supplies a code-repository link where v1 only promised release. V2 also documents attack-step settings and module-specific resource requirements, while retaining the main hyperparameters and GPU specification. Disclosure remains imperfect: the reproducibility statement still promises future release, and the MMHal evaluator is identified only as the latest GPT-4.

E1.justification: V2 adds AMBER's generative and discriminative hallucination evaluation and MMHal-Bench's eight open-ended categories, including environment and holistic descriptions. It also adds noise-token replacement and corrupted-caption test conditions. The earlier benchmark coverage remains.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's vanilla, VCD and OPERA comparisons, v2 Table 16 evaluates DoLa, ICD, TAME, SID, LLaVA-RLHF, CCA-LLaVA, Less is More and MCA-LLaVA on CHAIR. This substantially expands comparison methods, including training-based approaches. HALC, MARINE and VTI are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: Added protocols include AMBER metrics, GPT-4 judging for MMHal-Bench, and Qwen2-VL/2.5-VL 7B and Qwen3-VL 8B configurations. Efficiency evaluation changes from POPE latency to CHAIR latency and peak memory. New controls specify ten questions per object and attack-step/strategy sweeps. Existing experiments retain their stated settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds attack-step sensitivity testing, noise-image versus noise-token controls for encoder bias, robustness testing with hallucinated naive captions, FGSM/PGD comparisons, and module-level computational-cost analysis. These test substantive questions beyond v1's analyses. Existing module and hyperparameter ablations and the two original case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated benchmark-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new ten-question-per-category control specifies evaluation sample size. Averaging K noise inputs was already part of SHIELD and is not newly introduced uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original matched performance tables retain their values, but v2 adds substantial results: AMBER scores of 88.0 for SHIELD versus 86.5 for OPERA, MMHal overall scores of 2.65 versus vanilla's 2.21, and newer-model, baseline and controlled-analysis results. V1's POPE timing entries are removed and CHAIR profiling is added, preventing direct speed comparisons. New Table 16 gives OPERA CS as 44.8, inconsistent with 44.6 in retained Table 1.

M1.justification: SHIELD retains caption-guided token reweighting, averaged noise-token subtraction, learned adversarial perturbations, contrastive decoding and plausibility filtering. Equations 1–16 are unchanged. FGSM and PGD are tested as ablation alternatives; they do not replace the proposed method.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized wording and heading revisions, updates affiliations, and adds ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements. Appendices gain several subsections, while the main narrative remains largely unchanged. The original case-study section moves from Appendix D to E rather than becoming a new study.

P2.justification: V2 adopts an ICLR layout with narrower text, revised headings and recurring headers, substantially reflowing figures and tables. It adds benchmark, comparison, efficiency and control tables plus a new caption-example figure. The original case-study figure is reformatted and relabeled from CCD to SHIELD; the POPE timing table is removed.

R1.justification: Related work adds descriptions of HALC, MARINE and VTI, with further references supporting the expanded comparisons, benchmarks and adversarial-attack analysis. These broaden the literature context, but the training-required/training-free organization and encoder-focused novelty positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: The inference equations and CHAIR definitions are unchanged. The added appendix explanations are empirical or conceptual; they introduce no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical validation. Table 16 addresses v1's narrow baseline comparison, Appendix D adds controls for encoder attribution and misleading captions, and new benchmarks and models test broader applicability. Module-level profiling also clarifies computational tradeoffs. These additions materially improve support for the central claims despite remaining weaknesses, including the OPERA discrepancy, unspecified MMHal evaluator version and absent uncertainty estimates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SHIELD with the same authors, core method and shared experiments. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical evaluations and adds benchmark results, newer-model evaluations, expanded comparisons and controlled analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations on CHAIR, POPE, MME and LLaVA-Bench, together with module ablations, sensitivity studies and inference measurements.

results.title: SHIELD: Suppressing Hallucinations In LVLM Encoders via Bias and Vulnerability Defense

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same SA-MoE contribution, full-duplex multimodal novelty claim, advanced interaction capabilities, and competitive-performance claims. Replacing several AGI references with human-like intelligence changes framing without redefining the claimed capabilities.

C2.justification: Appendix G adds explanations linking shorter action sequences to reduced temporal coherence, favoring two experts for efficiency, and attributing concurrent-task degradation primarily to model capacity following the SPEAR experiment. Appendix H interprets CALVIN results as supporting adaptation through task-specific experts. The original limitations are unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents token/action counts for the shorter-block variant, initialization of separated experts, the SPEAR encoder, and hardware for latency measurements. The abstract also supplies a repository destination for promised code, data, and checkpoints. Release remains prospective; the PDFs do not establish actual availability.

E1.justification: Appendix H adds CALVIN's simulated environments and five-task manipulation sequences to the retained LIBERO and speech-task coverage. This extends coverage within simulated robot manipulation; the other new ablations reuse existing tasks.

E2.justification: The original comparator sets are retained. The new CALVIN comparison in Table 12 substantially expands evaluated comparators with MCIL, RT-1, Robo-Flamingo, GR-1, UP-VLA, and RoboVLMs. Its speech comparison retains Moshi and Freeze-Omni.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands experimental settings through block-duration, expert-count, and encoder comparisons plus A100 per-block latency measurements. The 0.48-second variant generates four text tokens and five action frames per block. E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Existing evaluation episode counts are retained; the new tables continue reporting point estimates without uncertainty.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main narrative structure remain intact. v2 makes localized terminology edits and inserts Appendices G and H, shifting the former G-I to I-K. P2.justification: New multipart Tables 9-12 substantially expand the displayed evidence with block-duration/latency comparisons, expert-count ablations, independent-versus-concurrent encoder results, and CALVIN chain-success results. Figures 1-8 and existing table content are retained; main-text tables shift position, and former Tables 9-11 become Tables 13-15.

Table 9 supplies measured inference times within both block budgets; Tables 10-11 test architectural choices and concurrent-task degradation; Table 12 extends validation beyond LIBERO. These additions materially strengthen the empirical foundation of the central claims while preserving the original evidence. after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds model ablations, inference-latency measurements, and CALVIN experiments in Appendices G and H.

before.justification: v1 reports original speech-interaction, simulated robot-manipulation, full-duplex, and context-grounded VQA results, together with dense-model and individual-expert comparisons.

results.title: End-to-end Listen, Look, Speak and Act

The introduction strengthens the biological subclaim: v1 asks whether the KC-to-MBON pathway supports decorrelation, while v2 claims a theoretical connection through consistency between Hebbian learning and ridge classification.

C2.justification: Section 6 adds a substantive mechanism explanation connecting Hebbian strengthening, anti-Hebbian error correction, and homeostatic decay to the ridge classifier. New appendix discussions interpret geometric preservation and backbone scalability. Appendix F expands prospective applicability to LLM-informed representations, reinforcement learning, and adaptive sampling without reporting experiments in those domains.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 explicitly documents ImageNet-21K pretraining followed by ImageNet-1K fine-tuning for ViT; the checkpoint link itself is unchanged. Appendix B.1 specifies sampling and projection normalization for the new diagnostic. Existing code/data links, implementation settings, and hardware disclosures remain, while details for the added baselines and Qwen experiments are limited.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate image classification on CIFAR-100, CUB-200-2011, VTAB, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, including the retained online and domain-shift settings. New backbone configurations and feature diagnostics use existing coverage. Proposed LLM and reinforcement-learning applications remain future work.

E2.justification: v2 adds InfLoRA, SEMA, and MoE-Adapter to the evaluated comparators in Tables 1, 5, 6, and 8, substantially expanding comparisons to LoRA/adapter methods. Existing comparators remain. The new SDM discussion does not constitute an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: v2 introduces backward-transfer evaluation, experiments using Qwen2.5-VL-7B's vision encoder, and a normalized pairwise-distance diagnostic using 500 sampled CIFAR-100 feature vectors. Additional sensitivity sweeps extend the evaluation design. Existing dataset splits, task schedules, and default hyperparameters remain unchanged; final-stage accuracy was already used in v1.

E4.justification: Appendix B.1 adds an empirical distance-preservation test absent from v1. Appendices C.7-C.8 extend the original CUB/ViT sensitivity analysis to ImageNet-A, longer CUB task sequences, ResNet-50, and projection-dimension sensitivity with Qwen features. These substantially broaden checks of geometric preservation and hyperparameter robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five random seeds and mean plus or minus standard deviation in Appendix E.3. Added results retain this reporting convention; no changed run counts, confidence-interval procedures, or significance tests are stated.

E6.justification: Matched numerical entries in Tables 1-9 are retained, but v2 adds comparator scores, geometric and sensitivity findings, and Tables 10-11. Table 10 reports Fly-CL backward transfer of -3.82, -3.80, and -2.01 on CIFAR-100, CUB, and VTAB. Table 11 adds Qwen-backed accuracies of 95.06%, 94.68%, and 97.45%; these use a different backbone and are not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: Sparse projection, top-k filtering, streaming statistics, GCV regularization selection, and Cholesky-based ridge classification remain unchanged, as do Algorithms 1-2. Section 6 introduces an equivalent Hebbian learning formulation but explicitly retains direct ridge solving rather than implementing those learning dynamics.

P1.justification: The introduction and method explanations receive localized edits. v2 inserts a discussion section, additional appendix subsections, acknowledgments, ethics and reproducibility statements, and a conference header. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence remain intact; the revision is primarily additive rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds a distance-distortion histogram, four sensitivity figures, and tables for final accuracy/backward transfer and backbone comparisons. Tables 1, 5, 6, and 8 gain comparator rows. Existing figures are retained, with original Figures 6-8 becoming Figures 7-9; the new displays substantially expand the visual evidence.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning through LoRA/adapter literature and method descriptions, a dedicated comparison with Kanerva's sparse distributed memory, and cited connections to LLM/RL applications. Hebbian-learning and Qwen references are added, while Ryali et al. (2020) is removed. The FlyLoRA publication update represents the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: New Section 6 derives the ridge stationary solution from supervised Hebbian/anti-Hebbian updates with weight decay, introducing Equations 13-17. Section 4.2 also corrects the thin-SVD orthogonality identities to U^T U = V^T V = I_r. The original sparsity theorems and Appendix B proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by adding adapter competitors, directly measuring forgetting, and testing projection geometry and sensitivity beyond v1's original CUB/ViT analysis. New comparator/backbone implementation details remain limited, and the Qwen experiments establish accuracy rather than an additional latency advantage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Fly-CL work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-H are readable, allowing retained material to be matched across additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original continual-learning evaluations, including accuracy, training time, memory consumption, ablations, and sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Fly-CL: A Fly-Inspired Framework for Enhancing Efficient Decorrelation and Reduced Training Time in Pre-trained Model-based Continual Representation Learning

This broadens the claimed successful training regime, while retaining the central SM contribution and the coding and efficiency-integration claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of ReMDM's diversity-related MAUVE decline, the computational tradeoffs of full-vocabulary feedback, and inference overhead from top-k computation and reduced cache hits. Appendix D also qualifies comparisons across different backbones and evaluation systems. These substantially expand the mechanisms and applicability caveats, although the concluding limitations paragraph is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds inference pseudocode, a code-repository link, and a statement that supplementary materials contain code and environments. These address additional questions about design choices, computational cost, and decoding behavior.

E5.justification: Matched continuation, coding, and math experiments retain five-seed reporting with means and standard deviations; the coding top-k study retains its shared-seed setup. E6.justification: v2 adds substantial scratch, matched-compute, diagnostic, and comparator results. Existing scores also change: Dream-7B MBPP+ at NFE 1/2 changes from 65.0 to 54.7 for SM and 53.7 to 39.6 for the finetuned baseline, changing the reported gain from 11.3 to 15.1 points (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 3). Their cause is unexplained. MAUVE values change under revised sampling settings, so they do not establish same-setting improvements. Math results are retained.

M1.justification: The default top-k feedback, confidence weighting, and training Algorithm 1 are unchanged. Appendix C.3 adds an experimental full-vocabulary variant that propagates gradients through both forward passes, extending the training procedure within an ablation. New Algorithm 2 documents the existing inference approach.

P1.justification: The main section order and much original prose remain intact. Local rewrites revise the abstract, training explanation, experimental narrative, and related work; the appendices gain dedicated inference and concurrent-work sections. P2.justification: v2 adds substantial displays for scratch training, matched-compute results, additional metrics, and concurrent comparisons. New Figures 6, 7, and 9 show runtime components, a decoding trajectory, and comparator tradeoffs; Figure 5 gains ablation curves. Existing tables gain budget information or revised headers, while retained figures and tables are relocated or renumbered.

Section 5 also strengthens the connection to self-conditioning. This is substantial research positioning beyond the numerous publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds the mathematical assertion that feedback makes the marginal distribution analytically intractable and interprets proxy-state training through the existing variational objective. This extends the theoretical rationale without deriving a new bound or proof. The original diffusion equations and interpolation argument remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1's principal training comparisons matched updates despite SM's additional forward pass. v2 materially strengthens the evidence with forward-pass-matched controls across language modeling and coding, plus training-from-scratch evaluations (Tables 1, 2, and 9). Added diagnostics and reproducibility information clarify costs and implementation. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including unexplained MBPP+ revisions and small discrepancies between the runtime totals in Appendix C.4 and Figure 6.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same soft-masked diffusion language modeling work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds training-from-scratch results, matched-compute evaluations, and diagnostic analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original continued-pretraining, coding, mathematical reasoning, and ablation results, including Tables 1–6 and Figures 3–6.

results.title: Soft-Masked Diffusion Language Models

Appendix B also interprets the new 62% versus 65% benign scores as preserving utility.

V1 used AgentDojo attack presentations but did not evaluate its task environment. The existing ten coding and six computer-use CFH-Hard tasks are retained.

E3.justification: Sections 5-5.2 change the reported orchestrator, answer judge, and one LlamaFirewall backing model from o4 to o4-mini. V1's tables already label that LlamaFirewall variant o4-mini, so these edits do not establish reruns. V2 also introduces the custom Slack evaluation setup and a runtime metric averaged only over successful rollouts.

Appendix E adds an empirical runtime comparison. These introduce substantial analysis of operational failures and efficiency beyond the retained graph-generation ablation, now Appendix C.

E5.justification: Existing task experiments retain three trials, and the graph-generation ablation retains five generations per task. The new Slack and timing results follow the existing three-trial averaging practice. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental seed information.

Table 9 adds successful-rollout times of 128 seconds for ControlValve, 51 undefended, and 86-107 for LlamaFirewall. Matched pre-existing result tables retain their numerical values.

The dataset subsection is broadened, appendix results are grouped before task and payload listings, and the publication header is updated. The main section structure and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds compact Slack attack, Slack utility, and runtime tables (5, 6, and 9). Existing benign-result tables are relocated together as Tables 10-11, and some captions are refined. The four figures remain unchanged, and the existing table style and single-column layout are retained.

(2025b): remote agents' API calls cannot be intercepted in the assumed deployment. This modestly sharpens the defense's research positioning.

T1.justification: The context-free-grammar formulation, example CFG, and graph-quality definitions remain unchanged. V2 introduces no new formal assumptions, mathematical derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens evaluation beyond the authors' CFH-Hard tasks through the adapted AgentDojo Slack benchmark, while addressing previously unmeasured execution costs and concrete rule-generation failures. The additions make practical security claims more assessable: zero observed attack success accompanies 62% versus 65% benign success and 128 versus 51 seconds on successful rollouts. These tradeoffs improve transparency rather than merely adding favorable results. Uncertainty estimates remain absent and timing excludes failures, but the broader validation and operational analysis substantially improve the paper's evidential basis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ControlValve research. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, with retained material identifiable across appendix reordering and table renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds AgentDojo Slack experiments, runtime measurements, and observed rule-generation failure modes.

results.title: Breaking and Fixing Defenses Against Control Flow Hijacking in Multi-Agent Systems

The main narrative structure and most existing prose are preserved.

New Figure 7 provides a multipanel timestep visualization, and Figure 2 is revised. Existing sample galleries are retained and renumbered from Figures 7–24 to Figures 8–25.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds original component ablations, diversity measurements, low-NFE experiments, and learned-timestep analyses.

results.title: GAS: Improving Discretization of Diffusion ODEs via Generalized Adversarial Solver

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same knowledge-construction and retrieval contributions. The headline 4.8-point SecurePass@1 improvement and the introduction's 98.7% functionality-retention claim remain unchanged. C2.justification: v2 expands the earlier coverage-based generalization discussion with proposed explanations involving shared vulnerability patterns, transferable guidelines, and pretrained knowledge. It explains differences between vulnerability categories and adds explicit limitations concerning static-analysis errors and function-level applicability (Appendices C.5, C.7, and F). P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained, with local wording and explanatory refinements. v2 swaps the method-details and experimental appendices, expands Section 3.5's roadmap, and adds acknowledgment, ethics, reproducibility, limitations, and LLM-use sections.

P2.justification: New Tables 8 and 10-16 substantially expand the presentation with benchmark comparisons, language and vulnerability breakdowns, and threshold sweeps featuring colored gains and losses. Figure 1's task-analysis panel is revised, and tables and appendix material are relocated. Existing main result displays and Figure 3 retain their substantive content.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds CWEval evaluations, cross-language tests, performance breakdowns, and fusion and threshold experiments in Appendix C.

results.title: RESCUE: Retrieval Augmented Secure Code Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions replace the claim that data and label quantization introduce approximation and separate quantized errors with approximation error attributed to data quantization. They also replace elimination of spectral distortion with preservation of spectral structure and reduced distortion. These materially revise the central characterization of quantization effects.

C2.justification: V2 develops the additive noise-floor and signal-dependent-noise explanations, adds consequences of quantizing master weights, and revises the practical FP-versus-integer bit-width comparison from a half-logarithmic dimension term to one scaled by the spectral exponent a. These change substantive interpretations and applicability guidance.

D1.justification: Appendix G documents the exponential spectrum, Communities and Crime's sources and approximate dimensions, and experiment-specific quantization and batch settings. Reproducibility remains limited: preprocessing, data splits, numerical learning rates, and code-access information are not supplied.
