E1.justification: Coverage expands from Gaussian regression with polynomial-decay covariance to real-world violent-crime-rate regression on Communities and Crime and synthetic regression with exponential-decay covariance. These introduce substantially different populations and feature distributions.

E2.justification: The empirical comparisons retain full precision, additive quantization, and multiplicative quantization. The added experiments reuse these schemes; no additional competing optimizer or quantization method is evaluated.

E3.justification: The original Figure 1 settings remain unchanged. Appendix G adds experiments with B=10 and d=200, fixed quantization error 0.01 for Communities and Crime, and empirical covariance-spectrum measurements. Figure 1's revised population-risk caption clarifies the reported quantity without establishing a changed metric.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained quantization-strength and dimension sweeps, v2 adds a direct examination of covariance-spectrum distortion and sensitivity tests for larger batches and exponential spectral decay. Figures 2(b) and 3 substantially broaden the empirical checks of the proposed mechanisms.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The new figures do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figure 1's plots are unchanged. New Figures 2–3 report that multiplicative quantization stays close to full-precision performance on Communities and Crime, preserves covariance structure better, and retains favorable behavior under larger batches and exponential spectra. These are additional findings under new settings, not improvements to existing same-setting scores.

M1.justification: The main quantized-SGD procedure is retained. Appendix F adds a variant that quantizes the carried master weights, replacing the leading w(t-1) with Qp(w(t-1)) in Eq. (F.1). This is a limited but actual procedural extension.

P1.justification: Substantial passages in the contributions, theoretical explanations, comparisons, and conclusion are rewritten. Additive quantization now precedes multiplicative quantization in Section 4.1, a notation paragraph is added, and the appendix narrative is reorganized around the revised decomposition.

P2.justification: V2 adds two figures containing six experimental panels and substantially redraws the proof-dependency diagram with larger, clearer nodes. Figure 1 retains its plots but receives a revised caption, while the appendix contents and equation layouts are reorganized.

R1.justification: V2 adds Li et al. (2025), Modoranu et al. (2024), and Ozkara et al. (2025), and removes Zou et al. (2021). These modestly update scaling-law and stochastic-quantization context while retaining the overall research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A corrects the sign of a quantization contribution and cancels label terms, supporting a revised three-component bound in Theorem 4.1. Theorems and corollaries receive new bounds and conditions; Assumption 4.1 introduces an isotropic parameter prior; Appendix F adds master-weight proofs. Appendix E also reformulates moment assumptions, although its new Eq. (E.16) appears to omit the label-noise contribution proportional to H.

improvement.justification: Correcting Appendix A's sign error and cancelling label terms repairs a central derivation underlying v1's risk characterization. The master-weight extension and new empirical checks add substantial theoretical scope and support. These gains outweigh a localized apparent omission in v2's Eq. (E.16), although that inequality needs correction and experimental reproducibility remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same quantized-SGD linear-regression research. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and the reorganized proofs can be matched reliably.

after.justification: The original simulations remain, supplemented by Communities and Crime regression, covariance-spectrum measurements, and additional synthetic experiments in Appendix G.

before.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 1 report original Gaussian linear-regression simulations varying quantization strength and dimension.

results.title: Learning under Quantization for High-Dimensional Linear Regression

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the dual-constraint framework, energy-only learning, ELIL benchmark contribution, and claimed greater-than-2.5-fold ESS advantage. New supporting analyses do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 identifies the large gradient-update requirement as a limitation and explains why analytical beta trajectories do not reliably measure the fitted model's closeness to the target (Figure 12). It expands the discussion of small-sample Wasserstein/TICA limitations and computational tradeoffs while retaining the original interpretation of the constraints.

D1.justification: v2 adds project-code and MD-data access information, fuller instructions for generating reference datasets, and dual-optimization timings. Table 11 explicitly lists previously implied CMT annealing-step counts. Conversely, C.4 removes the explicit search procedure and the disclosure of approximately 4–8 hyperparameter-tuning runs per system.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate alanine dipeptide, tetrapeptide, hexapeptide, and ELIL tetrapeptide at 300 K. Regenerated reference samples, additional metrics, and budget comparisons retain the same molecular populations and sampling task.

E2.justification: The principal baselines remain FAB, TA-BG, forward KL, and reverse KL. Appendix B adds a constant-multiplier comparator and a direct CMT-versus-MD comparison. The retained Ram-T-W2 comparison moves from Table 2 to Table 4 without the forward- and reverse-KL rows.

E3.justification: v2 regenerates the MD reference datasets; ELIL changes from a 2 fs timestep and 1 microsecond production to 1 fs and 2 microseconds. TA-BG budgets increase, including ELIL annealed training from 600,000 to 1,350,000 updates. Ram TV gains bin-area weighting, and new TICA, energy-Wasserstein, and MD free-energy-error evaluation protocols are introduced.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained constraint ablations, v2 tests adaptive versus constant multipliers, longer TA-BG schedules, entropy-bound sensitivity, and annealing-parameter trajectories. Energy histograms and TICA comparisons at different sample sizes add diagnostics of distribution quality and metric reliability (Appendix B and Figure 12).

E5.justification: v1 reports four independent runs for all main comparisons. v2 explicitly states that ELIL TA-BG results use only two successful runs because of numerical instability. Mean-and-standard-error reporting otherwise remains unchanged; this revises the reported replicate basis.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 replace many results under revised evaluation settings. For example, ELIL ESS changes from 26.18%/10.14% for CMT/TA-BG to 26.06%/13.75%; these are not same-setting performance gains. The ELIL Ram TV winner changes from CMT to TA-BG. New results include TICA and energy comparisons, dual-optimization timings, and approximately tenfold lower target-evaluation requirements for CMT versus MD in Figure 11.

M1.justification: The constrained objectives, normalizing-flow architecture, importance-weighted forward-KL loss, and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same procedure. The chosen annealing-step notation clarifies an existing fixed budget; the newly tested variants are ablations.

P1.justification: The main section order and Appendices A–D remain intact, with most original prose retained. Localized edits affect the introduction, related work, conclusion, and hyperparameter guidance; affiliations are expanded, and a reproducibility statement and Appendix C.5 are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn using stacked density paths. Six analysis figures are added as Figures 7–12, alongside new Wasserstein/TICA, timing, and annealing-step tables. Existing Wasserstein material is reorganized from Table 2 into Table 4, while v1's Figure 7 is retained as Figure 13.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on mode collapse and mass teleportation, explicitly distinguishing its terminology from Máté and Fleuret's usage. It removes several citations, including Havens, Nam, Plainer, and Guo; the first trust-region/annealing connection is now attributed only to Blessing et al. The overall research positioning remains similar.

T1.justification: The main propositions, Theorem 2.4, Appendix A proofs, and Appendix C.3 derivation remain unchanged. Section D.3.2 revises the Ram TV definition by adding bin area a_ij = (2π/100)^2. The new C.5 path formula also reverses the beta exponents relative to retained Equation (12), introducing an inconsistency.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evaluation weaknesses through corrected Ram TV normalization, regenerated MD references addressing reported bias, and better-matched TA-BG training budgets. Added diagnostics and code/data access information substantially strengthen validation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh remaining inconsistencies: the retained all-metrics superiority claim conflicts with TA-BG's better ELIL Ram TV in Table 1, and the new C.5 formula reverses the annealing exponents.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CMT research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports revised molecular sampling results and additional original schedule, sensitivity, distribution-quality, and molecular-dynamics comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original CMT and baseline experiments on four molecular systems, including quantitative results and constraint ablations in Appendix B.

results.title: Learning Boltzmann Generators via Constrained Mass Transport

C1.justification: The introduction explicitly extends the parity claim to antibody–antigen, protein–nucleic-acid, and RNA structures, and describes sparse long-range interactions. It also narrows the binder sequence-length claim from beyond 800 to beyond 700 amino acids. The central attention-free architecture contribution and headline training/inference efficiency claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 develops the mechanism interpretation from sparse interactions to sparse long-range interactions. Appendices D.1 and D.4–D.6 add a short-training qualification and arguments against performance parity arising only from favorable inputs, diffusion correction, or recycling. Section 5.5 also proposes limited RNA training data as an explanation for the Transformer's RNA advantage; this remains a hypothesis.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability statement and repository link, plus preparation details for the added benchmarks and disclosure of the 64-bin distogram head. The extensive optimizer, hardware, crop-size, architecture, and FLOPs information is retained in renumbered Table 10. The precise additional PoseBusters fine-tuning budget is not specified.

E1.justification: V2 Table 1 and Appendix C.3 add evaluations on 298 PoseBusters protein–ligand complexes, 70 antibody–antigen complexes, 172 protein–nucleic-acid complexes, and 27 RNA-only structures. These substantially broaden the explicitly evaluated populations and structural tasks beyond v1's reported coverage. RCSB, CASP15, binder design, and Match3 remain.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain AlphaFold3, Chai-1, Boltz-1/Pairformer, and the sequence-only Transformer; Match3 retains its second- and third-order attention comparators. The added evaluations reuse existing comparison methods. The new module-removal variants serve as Pairformer ablation controls.

E3.justification: V2 introduces substantial protocols for new experiments: date filtering and deduplication for PoseBusters, longer Pairmixer fine-tuning for that comparison, matched-iteration modality evaluations using ICS/IPS, and 12-layer Pairformer ablations trained for 60 epochs on 3M samples. Locality masking, direct distogram/contact metrics, and accuracy evaluation at 0, 1, 3, and 10 recycles add further procedures. The original main training and evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of local versus long-range interactions (Figure 9), individual Pairformer component removal (Table 6), performance stratified by sequence length and MSA depth (Figure 16), backbone quality independent of diffusion decoding (Table 8), and recycling sensitivity (Table 9). The original mixing/dimension ablations, Match3 experiment, and head-to-head comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for the system-level RCSB/CASP15 comparisons, and the Match3 error-bar figure is unchanged. V2 adds no seed counts, repeated-run information, significance tests, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: RCSB/CASP15 Tables 4–5 are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results. Table 1 reports PoseBusters RMSD<2 of 0.67 for Pairmixer versus 0.68 for Boltz-1, antibody DockQ success of 0.23 for both versus 0.08 for Transformer, and RNA lDDT of 0.59, 0.58, and 0.61 respectively. New diagnostic outcomes appear in Tables 6, 8–9 and Figures 9 and 16. The binder-runtime table also corrects reversed method assignments in the first five rows; its speedup claims are retained.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same incoming/outgoing triangle multiplication and feed-forward updates. The treatment of sequence representations, MSA module, diffusion module, and BindFast integration is unchanged. The new local-dropout intervention is an analysis of the existing model, not a revised proposed architecture.

P1.justification: Targeted editing condenses the main binder-design discussion, moves its detailed treatment to Appendix C.4, and consolidates Match3 discussion in D.3. Appendix material is regrouped into additional results and additional analyses. Most introductory, methodological, related-work, and concluding prose remains intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the displays with the four-part benchmark Table 1, new ablation/distogram/recycling Tables 6, 8, and 9, and locality and stratification Figures 9 and 16. Existing displays are retained but several are relocated or renumbered. The binder-runtime table's method headings and corresponding entries are corrected.

R1.justification: V2 adds Moult et al. (2014) to support contact-prediction evaluation. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to earlier structure predictors and attention-free architectures otherwise remain unchanged; relocated binder-design citations are retained.

T1.justification: Section 6 adds the formal local-interaction mask M(z_ik)=1 when |i-k|≤B and zero otherwise. This is a limited mathematical definition supporting the new diagnostic. Existing architectural equations, Match3 definitions, and FLOPs derivations are retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence for generality and backbone sufficiency. Dedicated biomolecular evaluations address v1's limited modality-specific validation, while direct distogram, component-removal, locality, and recycling tests probe important alternative explanations for its results. Runtime-label and sequence-length corrections also improve accuracy. The extra PoseBusters fine-tuning budget remains underspecified and the RNA explanation is speculative, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger support for the paper's central conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Pairmixer research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds biomolecular benchmark evaluations, component ablations, locality tests, distogram evaluations, and recycling analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-training experiments, RCSB/CASP15 evaluations, inference and binder-design runtimes, architectural ablations, and Match3 results.

results.title: Triangle Multiplication is All You Need for Biomolecular Structure Representations

C1.justification: The introduction now explicitly claims the first RFM framework for text-to-music generation and emphasizes novel music-theoretic controls. The abstract, principal contributions, headline note-accuracy claim, and conclusion otherwise retain their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of prompting–steering complementarity, possible interference in chord control, and the inadequacy of BPM detectors for the observed stylistic differences. It also expands the pooling rationale. Section 7's limitations remain unchanged, while the new claim of monotonic tempo response overstates some reversals in Table 4.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the SONGDESCRIBER prompt source, 250-prompt evaluation set, per-class sample counts, CLAP checkpoint, and FD/MMD reference generations. It clarifies the listening study's 24 clips and participant demographics, adds Appendix F pseudocode, and updates the demo address. These disclosures do not establish reruns or changed participant recruitment.

E1.justification: The demonstrated coverage retains SYNTHEORY's seven concept categories, MusicBench, and the existing single-direction, pairwise, and temporal-control tasks. v2 newly identifies SONGDESCRIBER as the prompt source, but does not establish an added dataset evaluation or a change in the represented musical domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds explicit prompt-only conditioning and Prompt+RFM comparisons across all seven categories, substantially expanding the central steering comparison beyond the RFM-only sweep. The classification and listening-study comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds matched prompting conditions and independent evaluation using chromagram pitch dominance, Essentia chord estimation, and onset event rate. These materially expand how controllability is assessed. Existing splits and steering sweeps remain unchanged; the newly specified prompt and sample counts are disclosures, not demonstrated increases.

E4.justification: New Section 5.3 tests whether control appears in generated waveforms independently of RFM probes. The three-condition comparison also separates the contributions of prompting and activation steering. These substantially strengthen validation, while the pooling, layer-pruning, injection-probability, and temporal analyses already present in v1 are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.3 newly reports Spearman correlations between steering strength and onset event rate, adding a statistical association analysis. Listening-study mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting is unchanged, and no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests are supplied.

E6.justification: The original numerical results are retained, but Tables 2 and 4 add substantial results under new conditions and metrics. For example, v2 reports note probe accuracy of 0.952 for Prompt+RFM at coefficient 0.60 and 0.436 for prompt-only conditioning; the original RFM-only value remains 0.824. These are additional comparisons, not improved same-setting results.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same probe training, AGOP directions, layer weighting, stochastic injection, and temporal and multi-direction steering. Appendix F supplies pseudocode rather than establishing a revised algorithm. Prompt+RFM evaluates the existing text-conditioned procedure with explicit attribute hints.

P1.justification: v2 revises introductory paragraphs, expands the pooling explanation, reorganizes Section 5, and adds an external-evaluation subsection and pseudocode appendix. Most method, limitation, conclusion, and existing appendix text remains unchanged. The publication header is also updated.

P2.justification: Table 2 is expanded into three condition blocks with chance-level annotations and a revised caption. v2 adds the external-evaluation Table 4 and Algorithm 1. Both figures and the remaining table displays are retained, with associated relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds Lilac and strengthens the discussion of fine-tuning costs, alongside references for SONGDESCRIBER, Essentia, librosa, and evaluation metrics. It makes the priority claim more explicit, while retaining the existing positioning relative to activation steering and RFM research.

T1.justification: The AGOP definitions, eigendecomposition, feature updates, kernel-ridge equations, and steering schedules remain unchanged. v2 adds empirical evaluation rules and pseudocode, but no new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central controllability evidence: Table 2 tests the benefit beyond explicit prompting, and Table 4 checks generated audio independently of the RFM probes used for v1's automatic control evaluation. These address an important validation weakness, while added protocol details improve reproducibility. Tempo evaluation remains a rhythmic-density proxy and some monotonicity claims overstate the results, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MusicRFM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and alignable, including Appendices A–E in both versions and the new Appendix F in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds results for explicit prompting, combined prompting and steering, and waveform-based musical-control evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original probing and steering experiments, MusicBench evaluations, a 12-participant listening study, and steering ablations in Appendix C.

results.title: Steering Autoregressive Music Generation with Recursive Feature Machines

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about distributed self-routing, independent self-awareness training, modularity and utility advantages. The added evaluations broaden supporting evidence without redefining these core statements.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations and applicability conditions: tested Qwen models require improved self-awareness, whereas sufficiently self-aware GPT models can route without alignment. It also discusses latency tradeoffs against predictive and cascading routers, and qualifies summarization applicability through metric saturation and dependence on a reliable quality signal.

D1.justification: V2 adds sequential timing details, GPT cost configurations, summarization's DeBERTa-based BERTScore setup and sample counts, and an intrinsic-rejection prompt. Existing training and baseline implementation recipes remain. The new prompt leaves its five example shots unspecified, and no new code or data release is documented.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original ten datasets and adds harder mathematical reasoning evaluations on MATH-500, AIME 2024/2025, AMC 23, JEEBench, OlympiadBench and OlympicArena. It also adds summarization training and evaluation on SAMSum and XSum, extending coverage beyond the original verifiable question-answering tasks.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged, including RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, AutoMix, FORC and GraphRouter where applicable. Added routing studies reuse existing methods or subsets of them. Newly discussed methods such as AgentNet are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: V2 adds GPT and heterogeneous-model configurations, a 100-query latency comparison, and BERTScore-based summarization evaluation with 12,000 training samples. Section 4.3 changes the reported rejected-query procedure from original-model answers to prefix-forced aligned-model answers. Appendix A.8 replaces the relative newly-solved-query metric description with ΔPass@10; identical plotted values do not establish that either retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine cumulative average and worst-case routing overhead, whether native rejection behavior suffices without alignment, and whether self-awareness and scenario adaptability transfer across model families and summarization tasks. These add substantial diagnostics beyond v1's retained modularity, difficulty-discrimination and training-capability analyses.

E5.justification: Figure 9 newly reports a 95% confidence band, Pearson correlation and a significance result for answer rate versus performance: r = 0.97 and p = 9.66e-05. Routing utility tables still lack repeated-run uncertainty reporting. The ten-response capability evaluation was already present in v1.

E6.justification: The original benchmark scores are retained, but substantial new results appear. Table 18 reports GPT-system utilities of 0.76 in-domain and 0.41 out-of-domain; Table 20 reports heterogeneous-system utilities of 0.71, 0.54 and 0.38 across the three scenarios. Additional results cover latency, native self-awareness and summarization. These are new evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The original cascade and binary-task training pipeline remain. However, Appendix A.11.1 adds a substantive adaptation for continuous-quality tasks: SFT rejection thresholds become model-specific score percentiles, and RL uses continuous answer scores and percentile-based rejection rewards.

P1.justification: V2 adds an appendix contents page, reorganizes supplementary sections as A.1–A.12 and moves existing prompts/templates to the end. Selected method, generalization and related-work passages are rewritten; affiliations, publication headers and acknowledgments change. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual evidence with overhead, GPT, heterogeneous-model and summarization tables, plus Figures 9–12 containing correlation and self-awareness diagnostics. Table 6 gains a 14B column, Figure 8 receives revised metric labeling, and existing figures and appendix tables are relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds discussion of capability profiling, decoupled regression, early-abstention cascades and AgentNet's decentralized routing. References also expand for the new datasets, models and evaluation tools. These are focused extensions that retain the central positioning around intrinsic assessment versus external routers.

T1.justification: Appendix A.11 adds a continuous scoring definition, a percentile-based decision threshold in Equation 11 and its corresponding reward definition in Equation 12. The original routing formalization and reward-threshold derivation remain unchanged; the addition does not introduce a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for generality and practical efficiency. V1's routing evaluations used a homogeneous Qwen pool and its overhead argument relied on individual rejection times; v2 adds heterogeneous and GPT routing, summarization diagnostics, and cumulative/comparative latency measurements. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the unreconciled Figure 8 metric change and Figure 10's AIME2025 exception to the claim of consistently higher answered-query accuracy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiSRouter and retain matching core formulations, methods and experiments. The text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison despite reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds latency measurements, intrinsic self-awareness evaluations, heterogeneous-model routing and summarization experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original routing experiments, self-awareness evaluations, model-pool reduction tests and timing measurements in the main text and appendices.

results.title: DiSRouter: Distributed Self-Routing for LLM Selections

C1.justification: The abstract retains the central training-free fusion and segmentation contributions. The conclusion newly claims superiority over training-based methods on ReasonVOS and proposes applicability beyond vision through modality-agnostic attention fusion. These extend the performance claim and outlook without redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: New appendices interpret native-grounding weaknesses, prompt sensitivity, and resilience to similar-object distractors. Appendix I adds a substantive limitation: correctly localized parts can still produce whole-object SAM2 masks because a positive point does not unambiguously specify segmentation granularity. Earlier failure explanations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies alternative prompt templates, native-grounding setup details, and LLaVA-OV Loc-Head adaptation instructions concerning tiling and attention-sink exclusion. It also changes the code-release statement from future availability to stated availability. The core implementation defaults remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The five benchmark datasets remain unchanged. Appendix I adds targeted qualitative evaluation of part-level expressions, contrasting whole-person localization with shirt, face, and glasses targets. The ReasonVOS subset analysis uses retained benchmark data rather than adding a dataset.

E2.justification: Appendix E/Table 9 introduces four evaluated native Qwen2.5-VL grounding baselines combined with SAM2. Table 2 also adds VRS-HQ to the ReasonVOS comparison, where v1 reported no result for it. These substantially expand the comparison beyond the retained attention-based and trained methods.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce frame-wise segmentation, first-frame propagation, reference/key-frame grounding, and matched 16-frame grounding protocols. Appendix F varies the three prompt types, and Appendix H evaluates a specified 187-of-458 ReasonVOS subset. These extend the evaluation design; the original metrics and default thresholds remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds three variants for each of the three prompt types, testing wording and information dependence in Tables 10–12. It also adds quantitative and qualitative similar-object discrimination analyses, part-level failure analysis, and additional implicit-expression case studies. The earlier component ablations and failure examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. SAM confidence and attention-consistency scores are algorithmic quantities, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 revise many benchmark and ablation values. For Qwen2.5-VL-7B DecAF, reported J&F changes from 59.7 to 63.9 on ReasonVOS, 50.3 to 54.2 on ReVOS overall, and 43.5 to 48.1 on MeViS. Tables 9–13 add grounding, prompt, and subset results. The PDFs do not explain the causes of the existing-score revisions.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 retain the same vision-aware rollout, contrastive and complementary fusion, point generation, and SAM2 tracklet scoring. The original prompts also remain unchanged. Appendix prompt variants are experimental ablations, while negative-point prompting is suggested only as future work.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the introduction and conclusion, expands the main qualitative discussion, updates the publication header, and adds Appendices E–J. The existing section order, methodology exposition, and related-work narrative remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 9–13 and substantially expands visual analysis through Figures 10–20, including query points, ground truth, competing masks, and part-level targets. v1 Figures 5–6 are combined and moved into the main text as v2 Figure 4; the other earlier qualitative examples are retained under revised numbering.

R1.justification: The bibliography and Section 2 are unchanged. The introduction more explicitly positions DecAF against joint MLLM–segmentation training costs and generalization limitations, while the new appendices extend its positioning against native Qwen grounding and Loc-Head across backbones.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–8 are retained, including rollout accumulation, vision-aware weighting, point selection, and attention-consistency scoring. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through matched native-grounding controls, systematic prompt ablations, and similar-object subset comparisons in Tables 9–13. Its part-level analysis also clarifies a meaningful SAM2 limitation. Unexplained revisions to existing scores and absent uncertainty estimates remain weaknesses, but the stronger controls and clearer applicability boundaries substantially improve the paper beyond merely reporting higher performance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DecAF research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds native-grounding comparisons, prompt ablations, subset evaluation, and qualitative experiments in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation evaluations, component ablations, model-scaling experiments, and qualitative analyses in Tables 1–8 and the appendices.

results.title: Decomposed Attention Fusion in MLLMs for Training-free Video Reasoning Segmentation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same learning-cliff motivation, hierarchical on-policy scaffolding proposal and broad model-applicability claims. The headline 44.3% relative AIME24 improvement is unchanged. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation through explanations connecting prompt mismatch to clipping instability, selective intervention to faster convergence, and hint-quality ratings to training utility. It also argues that scaffolding enables further learning from an already-converged DeepScaleR checkpoint and distinguishes intervention from DAPO's filtering. The original limitations concerning hint preparation and verifiable tasks remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds the complete hint-judging rubric and prompt, identifies Gemini-2.5-Pro, and reports training time and peak memory. It removes v1's front-page repository link and instead states that source code and scripts accompany the supplementary material; their actual availability cannot be verified from these PDFs. Existing hardware, software and main hyperparameter documentation is retained.

E1.justification: Both use DeepScaleR-Preview training data and the same seven mathematics benchmarks plus GPQA-Diamond. Added backbone, hint-source, sampling and data-mixture experiments remain within this coverage; the hint-quality audit analyzes existing training material.

E2.justification: v2 retains Vanilla GRPO, SimpleRL-Zero, Oat-Zero and LUFFY, while adding evaluated comparisons with Eurus-2-7B-PRIME, rStar-Math-7B and OpenReasoner-Zero in Table 16, DAPO in Table 18, and an explicit off-policy alternative in Table 9. This substantially broadens the comparator set.

E3.justification: The original greedy pass@1 evaluation is retained. v2 adds avg@16 evaluation with temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, graduation tracking over 300 training steps, a Gemini-2.5-Pro hint-rating protocol, additional controlled parameter sweeps and continued training from DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview. These substantially expand evaluation design without establishing changes to the original training settings.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations, v2 adds prompt-conditioning stability tests (Figure 7 and Table 9), exemption-duration and data-mixture sweeps (Tables 11–12), hint-quality/source analyses (Tables 13–14), quantitative skill-graduation tracking, computational-efficiency analysis and sampling robustness checks. These test several previously unexamined aspects of the method.

E5.justification: Appendix I newly averages binary success over 16 sampled responses per problem, adding repeated-sampling performance estimation to v1's single greedy response evaluation. Neither version reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests; the addition does not establish uncertainty across training runs.

E6.justification: The original numerical results are retained, but substantial new results appear. Examples include Qwen2.5-Math-7B avg@16 averages of 48.1% for Scaf-GRPO versus 44.8% for Vanilla GRPO (Table 15), DeepScaleR continued-training averages of 59.1% versus 54.0% (Table 17), and DAPO's 48.5% versus Scaf-GRPO's 50.9% (Table 18). These are additional comparisons or conditions, not improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same guidance exemption phase, incremental knowledge/planning/solution hint search, replacement of one failed trajectory and prompt-conditioned GRPO objective. The new off-policy formulation is an experimental comparator, not a revision of Scaf-GRPO.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. There are targeted rewrites in the experimental discussion and exemption-period appendix, additional ethics/reproducibility/LLM-use statements, revised front matter and a switch to author-year citations. The scientific additions do not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a substantially different conference layout, changing typography, title/abstract presentation and placement of retained figures and tables, including text wrapped around several displays. It also adds the clipping plot, numerous diagnostic and comparison tables, and an expanded GPQA table. The original figures are retained rather than replaced by new scientific content.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for PRIME, rStar-Math and OpenReasoner-Zero, and introduces focused positioning against DAPO's filtering and alongside DeepScaleR continued training. The related-work section and central distinction from prefix-based guidance remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix F.5 newly formalizes the alternative ratio that conditions the current policy on the original prompt and the old policy on the hinted prompt (Equation 13), contrasting it with matched conditioning. The original objectives, algorithm and case analysis remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method. Compared with v1's greedy evaluations and illustrative autonomy case, it adds repeated-sampling evaluation, quantitative graduation tracking, direct stability tests, sensitivity and hint-quality controls, and broader baselines. These address important gaps in evidence for robustness, mechanism and practicality. Some new prose overstates the tables—for example, Table 9's claimed universal superiority excludes its Gaokao result—and training-run uncertainty remains unreported, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Scaf-GRPO work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, equations, figures and tables can be matched despite reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds original stability experiments, sensitivity analyses, hint-quality assessments, repeated-sampling evaluations and continued-training results.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, mathematical reasoning results, GPQA-Diamond evaluation and component ablations, including Appendix F.

results.title: Scaf-GRPO: Scaffolded Group Relative Policy Optimization for Enhancing LLM Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: domain-guided synthetic captions provide complementary supervision and improve biological semantic understanding, classification, and retrieval. Added experiments support and qualify these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v3 removes v1's explicit limitation about untested captioner dependence and adds robustness interpretations from generator comparisons. Appendix E.5 proposes that captions enrich within-species semantics without substantially improving between-species separation, explaining limited few-shot gains. Appendix B.4 adds biological reasoning for genus fallback, while Appendix G proposes conditions for applicability beyond biodiversity.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies two format-example curators, acceptance criteria, and disagreement resolution. Appendix D.3 documents perceptual hashing with distance threshold 10. Existing generation prompts, hardware, training hyperparameters, and code/data access statements are retained; these additions primarily improve procedural documentation.

E1.justification: v3 adds CUB localization evaluation and evaluations on FishNet, NeWT, AwA2, and Herbarium 2019 in Tables 14 and 19. These substantially broaden evaluated data and task coverage beyond the retained classification and retrieval benchmarks. Appendix G discusses other scientific domains without experimentally evaluating them.

E2.justification: The main classification and retrieval comparator sets remain unchanged. New Tables 18–19 add Supervised-IN21K and quantitative comparisons with DINOv3, which previously appeared in embedding visualizations. Table 7 also evaluates Qwen2.5-VL 32B and LLaVA-NeXT 34B as alternative caption generators.

E3.justification: New Appendix D.3 reports overlap filtering, while retrieval-set sizes change from 7,007 to 7,000 Cornell Bird pairs and 2,349 to 2,254 PlantID pairs. Added protocols include one-/five-shot evaluation, bounding-box localization using the energy-based pointing game, and stratification by Wikipedia coverage and the bottom 5% of training-image counts. Existing main training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's prompt, projector, and training-component ablations, v3 tests exemplar count, taxonomic level, independent exemplar generation, and captioner family/size. It adds quantitative localization, Gemini/human verification of behavior labels, underrepresented-species analysis, genus-fallback examples, and caption-quality ablations for few-shot classification. These examine several previously untested design choices and reliability questions.

E5.justification: Tables 18–20 introduce ± reporting for model performance, and Appendix E.3 explicitly describes two independently generated exemplar sets with retraining. However, the meaning of ±, associated run counts, and seeds are unspecified. The existing human-evaluation agreement statistics remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Retrieval values change throughout Tables 2–3; BioCAP's Table 2 mean changes from 52.6 to 53.5 under revised evaluation sets, not an established same-setting gain. Substantial new results include localization scores of 0.47 versus BioCLIP's 0.43 and small average few-shot/visual-task advantages in Tables 18–19. Table 1 remains unchanged. New Table 17 inconsistently reports Rare Species scores of 46.4/37.6 for BioCAP/BioCLIP versus 44.2/37.1 in Table 1.

M1.justification: The proposed method retains shared encoders, separate taxonomy/caption visual projectors, joint label-and-caption supervision, and Wikipedia-guided caption generation with taxonomic format examples. Expanded curation and genus-fallback descriptions document existing steps. Alternative caption generators are tested without changing the adopted InternVL3 38B pipeline.

P1.justification: There are localized introduction and related-work edits, expanded curation explanations, additional appendix subsections, and updated affiliations and conference headers. The limitations appendix is removed and broader-applicability discussion added. The main section sequence and most existing prose, including the abstract and conclusion, remain stable.

P2.justification: Substantial new displays include Tables 6–7, 11, and 14–20 for ablations, annotation agreement, localization, subgroup results, and few-shot/visual-task comparisons, plus Figure 8's genus-fallback examples. Existing main figures are redistributed across pages, and earlier appendix figures are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for alternative caption generators, new benchmarks, localization evaluation, perceptual hashing, and the biological rationale for genus fallback. Appendix G broadens scientific-domain positioning, but Section 2 and Appendix F largely retain the original relationship to biological foundation models and general synthetic-caption methods.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix A retain the same latent-trait/noise assumptions, InfoNCE analysis, and covariance decomposition. No substantive mathematical definition, derivation, theorem, or proof is added or revised.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by reporting removal of detected training–retrieval overlap, testing the captioner dependence explicitly left unresolved in v1, validating automatic behavior labels, and supplementing qualitative localization with quantitative evidence. The added few-shot analyses also clarify limits of caption supervision. Undefined ± statistics and inconsistent Rare Species values in Table 17 weaken parts of the new reporting, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and understanding of applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BioCAP study. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds caption-generator comparisons, localization evaluation, annotation validation, subgroup analyses, and few-shot and biological visual-task results.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification and retrieval experiments, training ablations, qualitative analyses, and a human caption evaluation in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: BioCAP: Exploiting Synthetic Captions Beyond Labels in Biological Foundation Models

C1.justification: The abstract's headline claims and batch-size contribution remain unchanged. Contribution 2 now explicitly claims a connection between optimal clipping and optimization progress. The conclusion replaces an expectation of transfer to full-model tuning with demonstrated LoRA extensions and a full-fine-tuning exception, refining the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: v1 expects the core findings to transfer to full-model tuning; v2 explains that full fine-tuning can favor large clipping bounds in both easy and hard settings, proposing increased parameter count and gradient norms as the mechanism. It also states that operationalizing the optimal-clipping theorem would require additional privacy mechanisms and discusses the small clipping effects observed on the text task.

D1.justification: Table A1 and Appendices G and I substantially expand reproducibility information with optimizer-specific grids, LoRA ranks and placement, trainable-parameter choices, and text sequence length. However, the explicit Opacus implementation attribution and SUN397/Cassava ResNet-50 grid rows disappear. These are documentation changes, not evidence that the underlying implementation or those earlier runs changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds 20 Newsgroups text classification and CIFAR-10 classification in Appendices G.2 and I.1. This substantially extends coverage beyond v1's image transfer-learning datasets. SUN397, Cassava, and both CIFAR-100 data regimes remain represented.

E2.justification: AUTO-S with gamma 0.01 remains the evaluated competing clipping method in Figure 5 and the corresponding accuracy table. The prior batch-size heuristics are also retained. Added architectures, optimizers, and parameterizations test the analysis under different settings rather than introduce competing hyperparameter-selection methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include image LoRA, DistilBERT LoRA with sequence length 512, full-parameter fine-tuning, DP-SGD, and WideResNet training from scratch. Table A3 adds a rank sweep with C fixed to 1. Existing FiLM protocols largely remain. The added scratch experiment's actual budget is unclear: Figure A18's title says 40 epochs, whereas its caption and surrounding text say 8.

E4.justification: v2 adds LoRA-rank sensitivity, per-class clipping analyses across additional training regimes, and investigation of full fine-tuning as an exception to the main trend. Figure 3 and Appendices J and L add gradient-distribution and mean-gradient trajectories during training. Earlier Cassava and CIFAR-100 per-class analyses remain in Appendix K.

E5.justification: New Figure A13 reports medians across three repeats with min–max bands, adding a different aggregation practice from v1's mean-based accuracy comparisons. Existing three- and five-seed reporting and min–max bands are retained; the PDFs do not establish increased replication of the existing experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds accuracy grids for LoRA, text classification, training from scratch, DP-SGD, and full fine-tuning. New Table A3 reports, for example, accuracies of 0.4107 and 0.3800 for LoRA ranks 1 and 16 at epsilon 0.5. Full fine-tuning produces a new exception favoring large clipping bounds in both difficulty regimes. All 15 AUTO-S comparison rows are unchanged between v1 Table A3 and v2 Table A4.

M1.justification: The clipped and noisy updates, joint hyperparameter tuning, and cumulative-noise/minimum-step batch-size rule remain unchanged. LoRA, DP-SGD, and full fine-tuning are additional experimental settings. Section 5.1 explicitly states that the revised optimal-clipping theorem is explanatory and is not used to select clipping bounds during training.

P1.justification: The abstract, main section order, and much existing prose remain intact. Local rewrites clarify problem difficulty, revise the theoretical motivation and conclusion, and expand methodological explanations. The appendices separate the prior bound from proofs and organize the added experiments; publication headers and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a practical-guidance table, a LoRA-rank table, and extensive new heatmaps, per-class plots, histograms, and training trajectories. Figure 3 changes from final-gradient violins to epoch-wise distributions; Figure 5 redisplays unchanged accuracies as differences from the best. Table A1 gains a method column, and Algorithm 1 is relocated and reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LoRA, DistilBERT, WideResNet, scaling rules, and feature-quality research, including discussion of Wang et al. and Zhao et al. It changes the linear-scaling attribution from Tramer and Boneh to Panda et al. and reframes the limitations of Koloskova et al.'s bound. The broader clipping and batch-size positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's inverse-cubic clipping/noise scaling derivation. The revised optimal-clipping theorem adds an explicit bounded-domain assumption and possible optima at individual gradient norms. New Theorem 5.4, Corollary 5.5, and Appendix E connect gradient MSE to a bound on optimization progress under smoothness and step-size assumptions.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important theoretical and applicability weaknesses: it removes v1's invalid inverse-cubic derivation, qualifies the optimal-clipping theorem, and proves a connection to optimization progress. Broader experiments test generality and replace speculative full-model extrapolation with an explicit empirical exception. New reporting inconsistencies, notably the 8-versus-40-epoch discrepancy in Figure A18, limit reproducibility of some additions, but the theoretical repairs and better-supported applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same clipping-bound and batch-size study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained analyses across appendix renumbering. Some new experimental settings are internally inconsistent, but this does not prevent a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds image and text LoRA experiments, training from scratch, DP-SGD, full-parameter fine-tuning, and additional gradient analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original private fine-tuning experiments, accuracy sweeps, gradient distributions, and per-class analyses on SUN397, Cassava, and CIFAR-100, including its 10% subset.

results.title: On Optimal Hyperparameters for Differentially Private Deep Transfer Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: wearable ExG acquisition, DailySense, and task-agnostic PiMT representations outperforming the evaluated baselines. The added co-design wording reframes these existing contributions. The introduction's 87.6% already appeared as 0.876 in v1 Table 1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of pre-training benefits without PiMT, temporal fidelity in tokenization, frozen-feature transferability, reference-device agreement, and free-living versus controlled pre-training. Section 6 also explicitly discusses limited demographic diversity, physiology and placement variability, and excludes full cross-subject generalization from the primary scope.

D1.justification: v2 specifies notch-filter order and Q=30, zero-phase filtering, Butterworth filters, and independent filter-bank branches. It also documents Morlet-wavelet scales and controlled-corpus electrode selections. These improve implementation detail, while most hardware, optimizer, compute, and data-sharing information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: DailySense's six tasks and the four downstream benchmarks remain. Appendix Q adds controlled EEG pre-training coverage through TUAR and a TUSZ subset, substantially extending the training-data domains compared. Appendix D also introduces synchronized NeuroBuds/OpenBCI recordings for direct signal validation.

E2.justification: v2 adds STFT and CWT tokenization comparators in Table 8, EEGConformer to the standardized SEED/BCI comparison in Table 5, and pre-trained Bidirectional-Mamba without PiMT in Table 6. These extend the evaluated alternatives beyond v1's retained comparator sets.

E3.justification: v2 adds standardized EEGConformer-preprocessing evaluations, frozen-encoder testing, and controlled-corpus pre-training with matched electrode selections. Appendix G also changes the stated pre-training amount from 40 to 50 hours and depth from 16 to 8 layers. These revise reported settings and resolve earlier inconsistencies, without establishing that the unchanged original tables were rerun.

E4.justification: v1's backbone, band-count, reconstruction-component, patch-size, scaling, and generalization analyses are retained. v2 adds tests isolating pre-training without PiMT, alternative time–frequency tokenizers, frozen representations, and pre-training sources, plus direct OpenBCI signal validation (Appendices D, I, K, M, Q). These address several previously untested explanations for performance.

E5.justification: Both versions already report three-seed means and standard deviations. v2 adds paired Wilcoxon tests using participant–seed observations, pooling classification tasks for the average comparison (Appendix P/Table 13), and significance reporting for device correlations. No increase in repeated-run counts is established.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–2 and matched ablation/generalization tables retain their numerical results. New results include PiMT F1 scores of 0.971/0.869 under standardized SEED/BCI preprocessing, frozen-encoder F1 of 0.866, and pre-training-source F1 scores of 0.853/0.858 for TUAR/TUAR+TUSZ versus 0.876 for DailySense. These are additional conditions, not same-setting improvements; TUAR yields lower gaze error than DailySense, 5.95° versus 6.00°.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 retain the same 12-band tokenization, Bidirectional-Mamba encoder, token ordering, six reconstruction objectives, and task heads. Appendix G's revised layer count agrees with the eight-layer description already present in v1 Appendix F; it does not establish a new architectural contribution.

P1.justification: Editing and expanded explanations are concentrated in preprocessing, backbone comparisons, and limitations. Discussion moves from Section 5.7 to standalone Section 6; acknowledgments and appendix sections are added, with author-order and publication-header changes. Most existing narrative and method exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven tables covering dataset statistics, new comparisons, ablations, and significance tests, plus Figure 9 comparing synchronized device signals. Figure 8's frequency labels are corrected. Existing displays are retained and often relocated or renumbered, making the principal visual change a substantial expansion of displayed evidence.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for TUAR, TUSZ, TUEG, Neuro-GPT, and NeurIPT, principally to contextualize controlled-corpus pre-training. The main related-work taxonomy and positioning remain largely unchanged; the newly cited foundation models are not newly evaluated baselines.

T1.justification: The mathematical descriptions of filtering, patch embeddings, encoding, and reconstruction remain unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and the added empirical analyses introduce no new formal derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and attribution: alternative-tokenizer comparisons, frozen-encoder tests, pre-training controls, and direct device measurements address important gaps in v1's support for its central claims. Standardized benchmark comparisons and clearer filtering details further improve assessability. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including Appendix P's participant-count conflict with Section 4 and significance tests that pool repeated participant–seed observations without addressing their dependence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NeuroBuds, DailySense, and PiMT research. The text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds reference-device measurements, additional model comparisons and ablations, standardized benchmark evaluations, and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original DailySense experiments, evaluations on four public benchmarks, ablations, generalization tests, and smartphone runtime measurements.

results.title: Beyond Hearing: Learning Task-Agnostic ExG Representations from Earphones via Physiology-Informed Tokenization

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statement and conclusion retain the same claims: benign reasoning training induces self-jailbreaking, increased compliance and reduced perceived harmfulness explain it, and minimal safety reasoning mitigates it while preserving reasoning capability. New experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: Appendix G newly identifies weaker robustness on Wild Jailbreak, motivates incorporating adversarial safety data and acknowledges that the reported results are not best among competing methods. Appendix F adds tentative explanations linking type distributions to training and architecture. These extend the applicability discussion without replacing the central mechanism.

D1.justification: v2 provides more specific training-data provenance for existing models, including RStar-Coder's code data and UniReason's 47K math samples. It also describes the s1 and STAR mixture used for the new Llama experiments. These are limited documentation additions, not evidence that the retained models were retrained differently.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds Wild Jailbreak and evaluates mitigation under adaptive, past-tense and prefilling attacks on StrongREJECT. This substantially extends the mitigation's evaluated input conditions beyond v1's unmodified harmful prompts. v1's separate experiment transferring self-jailbreaking sentences to other models is retained.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 introduces evaluated comparisons against STAR, SafeChain, DAPO and RECAP on StrongREJECT and Wild Jailbreak. v1 discussed related safety-training work but did not provide this comparison against dedicated competing methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds a counterfactual protocol on 102 annotated instances, regenerating self-jailbreaking sentences while holding preceding reasoning fixed. It also introduces manual type-classification sampling across five models and Llama-3-8B training/evaluation configurations. The existing 500-token safety and 8000-token capability evaluation limits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.2 adds a controlled test of sentence-level effects. Appendix F adds rationalization-type frequencies and type-specific activation changes, distinct from the retained prompt-topic distribution. Appendix G adds mitigation generalization to Llama and robustness tests against external jailbreaks.

E5.justification: v1 already reports graphical error bars, which v2 retains. The new ± entries in Tables 1 and 4 accompany additional results without documenting a different uncertainty-estimation practice. Neither version specifies seeds, repeated-run counts, significance tests or the meaning of these uncertainty measures.

E6.justification: v2 Table 1 newly reports compliance/harmfulness changes of 3.1/-2.9 for self-jailbreaking versus -0.2/0.1 for counterfactuals. Tables 4–6 add type-specific, adversarial and baseline results; Table 5 reports StrongREJECT ASRs of 81.7% for Distilled-Llama-8B and 8.1% for SAFE-LLAMA-8B. Original plotted results are retained; these are added comparisons, not improvements to the same v1 measurements.

M1.justification: The activation-direction extraction, steering procedure and minimal safety-training recipe remain unchanged. The Llama experiments apply the existing training mixture; sentence regeneration is introduced as an experimental control, not a revised mitigation algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized explanatory rewrites, adds Appendices F and G, removes the contents page and relabels the retained appendices. The main section sequence and most prose remain intact, so this is not an extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: New Tables 1 and 4–6 present counterfactual effects, type-specific effects, adversarial evaluations and competing-method comparisons; new Figure 13 displays rationalization-type frequencies. These substantially expand the quantitative presentation. Original figures remain, with some relocation and surrounding layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for WildTeaming, past-tense and priming attacks, and training-data sources. Section 4.1.1 more explicitly positions the analysis as extending Zhao et al.'s separation of harmfulness and refusal to reasoning models. The broader positioning remains stable; the adaptive-attack reference is a publication update.

T1.justification: The self-jailbreaking definition, projection normalization and activation-steering equations are unchanged. The counterfactual experiment uses the existing projection quantities and introduces no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: The matched-prefix counterfactual experiment strengthens causal support beyond v1's projection and steering evidence. Type-level analysis and Llama, adversarial and competing-method evaluations address important gaps in the mitigation's validation, while revealing its limits rather than merely reporting successes. Undefined uncertainty summaries and sparse details for the new comparisons remain weaknesses, but the added controls and broader validation substantially improve the paper's evidential foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same self-jailbreaking study and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite appendix renumbering and layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds counterfactual experiments, type-level analyses, Llama safety-training evaluations and adversarial benchmark comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, self-jailbreaking annotations, activation projection and steering experiments, and safety-training results in Sections 3–5 and the appendices.

results.title: Self-Jailbreaking: Language Models Can Reason Themselves Out of Safety Alignment After Benign Reasoning Training

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about prompting-based probabilistic faithfulness, response diversity, theoretical bounds, and reasoning-dependent behavior. The additional experiments support and qualify these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: New Section 7 specifies limitations involving weak reasoning capabilities, biased strings combined with partial-string extraction, and single-answer tasks. Appendix D attributes deterioration with longer strings to arithmetic errors and discusses external-tool failures. Appendix E adds interpretations connecting observed string properties to theoretical assumptions, substantially expanding the applicability and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v3 adds exact simplified and external-randomness prompts, tool function schemas, the seed-length control instruction, and the 24-character printable-ASCII seed specification. Appendix F documents existing NoveltyBench scoring, including the classifier and patience factor p=0.8, plus dataset construction details. These materially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds a limited continuous-sampling extension: Uniform[0,1], Normal(0,1), and Beta(2,5). Existing categorical PIF tasks, Rock-Paper-Scissors, and both NoveltyBench datasets remain. Smaller models and prompt variants expand experimental settings without adding datasets.

E2.justification: Appendix D.6 and Table 11 add Seed Injection and Tool Call comparisons on curated NoveltyBench, substantially strengthening comparison with external sources of randomness. Randomized external seeds previously appeared in PIF ablations, but their participation in the DAG comparison is new. Existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include continuous-sampling evaluation using Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises statistics, requested seed lengths from 2 to 128, six smaller-model configurations, simplified-prompt controls, and external-randomness settings. The original experiments retain their settings; Appendix F supplies additional documentation of existing NoveltyBench evaluation.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's strategy, reasoning-length, and external-seed analyses, v3 adds direct seed-length sensitivity, smaller-model capability checks, simplified-prompt ablations, and a QwQ first-character failure analysis. Appendix E examines 5,000 generated strings through unigram, bigram, and lagged-dependence diagnostics relevant to the theoretical assumptions.

E5.justification: The established mean-and-standard-deviation reporting over ten groups of 100 samples continues in the new sampling experiments. Retained repetition counts and uncertainty practices are unchanged. The new continuous-distribution statistics serve as evaluation metrics; no new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Original results are retained, while Tables 6–12 and the new analyses add substantial findings. Table 7 reports the best tested seed-length result at n=24, with JS divergence 0.019 ± 0.007. Table 8 shows task-dependent regressions for some smaller models. Table 11 adds overall Distinct/Utility scores of 6.00/5.76 for Seed Injection and 5.72/5.33 for Tool Call alongside the retained SSoT score of 6.19/5.92.

M1.justification: SSoT still generates a random string, manipulates it to guide stochastic decisions, and produces an answer. Section 3 and the original Appendix A prompts retain this procedure. The simplified prompts tested in Appendix D.4 preserve the same steps.

P1.justification: The main narrative receives limited wording and grammar edits. A limitations section, benchmark overview, and theoretical-significance explanation are added, and the appendices are reorganized around new material. Most existing prose and its narrative order are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 6–13 and Figures 11–12. Figure 2 is redesigned into two rows with a wider nine-choice panel, and several existing figures and prompt listings are relocated or reformatted. The original strategy Figures 11–12 remain as Figures 13–14, rather than constituting new analyses.

R1.justification: v3 adds Kojima et al. (2022) when discussing smaller models and zero-shot reasoning. Appendix G.3 explicitly positions the existing theoretical contributions relative to the Leftover Hash Lemma and Fourier analysis. The original related-work section otherwise remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The definitions, theorems, and proofs in v1 Appendix D are retained in v3 Appendix G. New Section G.3 explains existing theoretical contributions, and Appendix F states formulas for already-used NoveltyBench metrics. Restoring a missing delta symbol is a typographical correction without a substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence about when and why SSoT works through controlled seed-length and prompt tests, smaller-model evaluations, failure analysis, and external-randomness comparisons. These address important gaps in v1's assessment of robustness and practical alternatives, while explicit limitations and implementation details improve interpretability and reproducibility. Bigram and short-lag diagnostics do not establish the full theoretical assumptions, and tool failures qualify the external-tool comparison, but the overall evidential improvement remains substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same SSoT research work with readable text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably across appendix renumbering and layout changes.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds continuous-sampling experiments, smaller-model evaluations, prompt ablations, external-randomness comparisons, and generated-string analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original PIF, adversarial Rock-Paper-Scissors, NoveltyBench, and reasoning-length experiments, including numerical results and strategy analyses.

results.title: String Seed of Thought: Prompting LLMs for Distribution-Faithful and Diverse Generation

C1.justification: The third introduction contribution changes from claiming state-of-the-art semantic and structural fidelity to emphasizing a balance of semantic fidelity, stability, and speed, with prospective real-time brain-computer-interface applications. The central framework, semantic-fidelity claim, and 4.67× speedup claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about poor one-hour cross-subject transfer, attributed to overfitting, and failures involving materials, counting, text, and identity. Appendix F adds an efficiency explanation based on eliminating refinement and inexpensive coarse stages. Its finding that high-resolution stages dominate latency conflicts with the retained main-text explanation that most computation occurs at low resolutions.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies full CLIP patch-token alignment, MSE weight 2×10^5, temperature 0.005, codebook size 4096, ten autoregressive scales, RTX 4090 inference hardware, and THINGS input padding. These refine existing documentation; the principal optimizer settings, training budgets, pseudocode, and code-release promise remain.

E1.justification: v2 expands beyond NSD reconstruction to THINGS-fMRI with three subjects and different acquisition conditions (Appendix I), VQA on reconstructed images (Appendix G), and held-out-subject transfer (Appendix C). Brain grounding and single-subject one-session experiments already existed in v1.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes both Psychometry variants and adds NeuroPictor and MindTuner. Figure 4 adds MindEye2 to the consistency comparison. New comparisons additionally evaluate MindEye and UMBRAE-S1 for grounding and BrainFlora on THINGS-fMRI, substantially broadening the comparison suite.

E3.justification: New protocols include pooled pretraining followed by held-out-subject finetuning for 40 or 1 hour, N=1 versus N=4 candidate selection, and MindEye2 with 10 versus 38 denoising steps. v2 also introduces quantitative grounding metrics, BLIP-2 top-3 VQA evaluation, and joint-subject THINGS training with 7000-dimensional padded inputs. The original NSD protocol and Table S2 experiment remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds sampling-budget and generation-step controls, component-wise and scale-wise latency analyses, and cross-subject data-scarcity testing. VQA cases and expanded reconstruction galleries support new analyses of counting, material, text, and identity failures. The original encoder, layer-mapping, and guidance ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains the same uncertainty values and reporting format. Neither version specifies additional statistical estimation procedures or training-run counts. The four-trial visual comparison is extended to another baseline, while N=1 versus N=4 concerns candidate selection rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained MindHier NSD scores and Tables 2–4/S1–S2 are unchanged, but substantial new results appear. VQA accuracy is 43.29% versus MindEye2's 41.71%; THINGS CLIP accuracy is 73.1% versus BrainFlora's 57.6%, although Eff distance is worse at 0.900 versus 0.812. New one-hour cross-subject results show MindHier below MindEye2, including CLIP 80.2% versus 80.7%. Grounding, timing, sampling, and qualitative results are also added.

M1.justification: The hierarchical fMRI encoder, MSE/SoftCLIP alignment, two-stage training, and scale-aware autoregressive reconstruction remain unchanged. Added loss-weight and implementation specifications clarify the existing method; the PDFs do not establish a change to its underlying procedure.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose are retained, with local copyediting, clearer two-stage-training explanations, revised contribution wording, and updated affiliations and conference headers. The appendix gains sections F–J, acknowledgments are added, and LLM writing assistance is disclosed; this primarily accompanies new content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables S3–S9 and Figures S4–S9, including four substantial subject-specific galleries. Figure 2 receives clearer feature and mask labels, Figure 4 gains a baseline row, and Table 4's Eff direction arrow is corrected. Existing appendix displays are retained and repositioned.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including THINGS-data, BrainFlora, diffusion foundations, and image/video generation works, while removing UniBrain and BrainGuard. The two related-work narratives and the central positioning against static diffusion guidance remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The alignment equations, token quantization, and autoregressive factorization are retained. Corrections to norm delimiters and feature subscripts are not substantive mathematical revisions. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's NSD-only evaluation through THINGS testing, held-out-subject transfer, sampling and generation-step controls, and downstream grounding/VQA assessments. Explicit failure analyses and missing implementation settings make applicability and reproducibility more assessable. Reporting flaws temper these gains: Appendix F contradicts the retained efficiency explanation and claims stages 0–4 take under 0.1 seconds although Table S7 totals 0.211 seconds. These localized inconsistencies do not outweigh the substantial improvement in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MindHier framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including v2's expanded image galleries.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds cross-subject transfer, THINGS-fMRI, quantitative grounding, VQA, and additional efficiency evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original NSD reconstruction results, component ablations, inference timings, per-subject evaluations, and qualitative analyses.

results.title: Moving Beyond Diffusion: Hierarchy-to-Hierarchy Autoregression for fMRI-to-Image Reconstruction

C1.justification: The central contributions remain chemistry-informed LLM evolution, success/failure memory with multiple islands, constrained multi-objective discovery, and evaluation across fourteen tasks. Both versions claim improved discovery quality, stability, Pareto trade-offs, and reduced memorization. The added studies support these retained claims rather than redefine them; the conclusion is essentially unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of island-count trade-offs, model capacity as a proxy for scientific knowledge, robustness to perturbed oracle feedback, agreement with DFT, and computational cost. These extend the explanation of when and why LLEMA works. The model-scale interpretation attributes gains to domain knowledge without separately isolating that cause, while the conclusion retains the earlier broad limitations.

D1.justification: V2 fills the previously unspecified reward calculation, discloses random sampling of six generation rules, adds a LLEMABench dataset-access link, and provides MatterGen implementation and LLMatDesign feedback details. It also documents Quantum ESPRESSO use, noise parameters, and token/API/runtime costs. These materially improve reproducibility information, although DFT settings are described only as default parameters and some island descriptions remain inconsistent.

E1.justification: The fourteen materials-discovery task families and application domains remain. V2 extends testing to altered prompt formulations and noisy surrogate feedback in Appendices E.2 and E.5, adding input and feedback conditions within the existing domains. Additional model sizes and DFT checks do not themselves introduce new material tasks.
