E2.justification: MatterGen is added as an evaluated comparator across all fourteen tasks in v2 Table 3, using its released base checkpoint. CDVAE, G-SchNet, DiffCSP, End2end, and LLMatDesign remain. Qwen models are LLEMA backbone variants, while MatLLMSearch is discussed without an evaluated comparison.

E3.justification: V2 introduces island-count, prompt-variation, Qwen model-size, Gaussian-noise, 150-candidate DFT-validation, and runtime/token evaluation protocols. Existing settings also change: G-SchNet's stated budget rises from 10,000 to 15,000 iterations, and acousto-optic constraints tighten from 2–9 to 3–9 pC/N and dielectric constants from 8–95 to 8–85. Several other benchmark edits reconcile v1 table–appendix disagreements rather than establish newly executed settings; retained scores are not documented as rerun.

E4.justification: V1's component ablations, search trajectories, memorization analysis, and elemental-diversity studies are retained. V2 adds island-count sensitivity in Appendix B.3 and prompt robustness, model scaling, surrogate-versus-DFT reliability, noisy-feedback robustness, and efficiency analyses in Appendices E.2–E.6. These substantially broaden the questions tested about reliability and practical behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for performance. V2's Gaussian perturbations, prompt variants, and DFT validity percentages add experiments and point estimates, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The LLEMA (GPT) hard, stiff ceramics hit rate changes from 60.99 in v1 Table 2 to 30.99 in v2 Table 3; other pre-existing entries in that table retain their values. MatterGen results and Tables 6–10 add substantial findings on sensitivity, model size, validation, and efficiency. Newly reported DFT checks find 144/150 valid candidates under ordinary guidance and 141/150 under noisy guidance; these are added results, not improvements over corresponding v1 measurements.

M1.justification: The core generation–oracle–memory loop and Algorithm 1 remain. However, the reported evolutionary rule set decreases from nineteen rules in v1 Appendix D.2 to fourteen in v2 Appendix B.4, removing motif replacement, layered intercalation, structural isomer generation, group-based recombination, and phase-diagram extrapolation. V2 also describes hull stability as a separate check rather than v1's explicitly lower-weighted reward component.

P1.justification: Beyond retitling and copyediting, v2 rewrites substantial introductory and fitness-assessment passages and reorganizes the appendices: additional method details move ahead of the benchmark, and baseline descriptions join the implementation appendix. The main memorization and evolutionary-refinement subsections exchange order. This substantially changes document navigation and exposition while retaining the overall research narrative.

P2.justification: V1's benchmark-overview Figure 1 is removed. V2 adds the framework-comparison table and five analysis tables, expands the main results table with MatterGen rows, and redistributes and enlarges appendix heatmaps. Existing framework, Pareto, convergence, and diversity plots are largely retained or relocated rather than newly generated analyses.

R1.justification: V2 adds an introductory framework-comparison table and explicitly positions LLEMA relative to MatterGen and MatLLMSearch. It also adds relevant citations on data scarcity, scientific discovery, Qwen, and Quantum ESPRESSO. The overall research positioning remains; publication updates for already cited works do not constitute additional research coverage.

T1.justification: V1 leaves the normalized reward function unspecified. V2 Appendix B.2 supplies explicit signed, clipped feasibility-margin definitions for lower-bound, upper-bound, and interval constraints, and Equation 2 explicitly includes upper-bound constraints. This adds mathematical specification without introducing a theoretical guarantee or proof.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is stronger validation of the central physical-reliability claim: v1 relies on database/surrogate evaluation and plausibility arguments, whereas v2 adds DFT checks reporting 144/150 valid candidates and 141/150 under noisy guidance. Targeted robustness studies and MatterGen comparisons further strengthen the evidence, while explicit reward definitions improve reproducibility. Sparse DFT settings, absent uncertainty estimates, and unresolved protocol inconsistencies limit these gains, but the new validation substantially addresses an important evidential weakness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LLEMA by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and appendix organization.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds MatterGen comparisons, sensitivity and robustness experiments, DFT validation, and computational-efficiency measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original material-generation experiments across fourteen tasks, component ablations, convergence analyses, and chemical-diversity results.

results.title: LLEMA: Evolutionary Search with LLMs for Multi-Objective Materials Discovery

C1.justification: The introduction narrows the benefit from avoiding information loss inherent in pairwise conversion to mitigating information inefficiency. The abstract explicitly extends its empirical assertion to three model families and both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. The central MLE-unification claim, two representative choice models and conclusion remain.

C2.justification: v1 conjectures that noise may limit gains beyond top-2. v2 substantially expands interpretation through annotation-difficulty, negative-response, batch-capacity, sample-efficiency and pairwise-expansion explanations in Section 4.3 and Appendix F.3. New qualitative examples are explicitly described as illustrative rather than fact-checked. Conversely, the revised cross-model superiority statement drops v1's qualification about LC and overlooks SimPO's Mistral Arena-Hard lead.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies the modified TRL DPO Trainer and DPO Config, states that code and training scripts accompany supplementary materials, specifies the evaluation-generation GPU, supplies the Mistral model identifier and reports training times. These are additional disclosures; the supplied PDFs do not allow verification of the supplementary code.

E1.justification: v2 extends evaluation to an in-distribution UltraFeedback test scenario, alongside the retained AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard evaluations. UltraFeedback was already used for training, so this does not introduce a new domain. Appendix G also replaces equation solving with factual explanation and text simplification. Mistral adds a model configuration rather than a task.

E2.justification: v2 Tables 2 and 10 add DPO-AllPairs, which Table 2 defines as DPO trained on pairwise comparisons implied by top-2 rankings. Existing comparators remain, including those in the unchanged GPT-5-mini comparison. This is a focused addition to the baseline set.

E3.justification: New protocols include evaluating 1,961 UltraFeedback test prompts against their chosen responses using GPT-4.1-mini and training Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2. Section 4.3 and Appendix F.3 introduce ranking-length, assortment-size, training-progress and beta sweeps, together with timing comparisons. These substantially expand the experimental design without establishing revisions to the retained Llama/Gemma benchmark settings.

E4.justification: v1 has cross-judge checks and qualitative examples but no corresponding systematic ablation suite. v2 adds tests of ranking length, assortment size, beta sensitivity, sample efficiency, and pairwise decomposition versus direct ranked training, including computational costs. Appendix G removes the equation-solving case and adds two different cases. The earlier cross-judge analysis is retained, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report AlpacaEval standard errors and Arena-Hard 95% confidence intervals. v2 extends the standard-error convention to its new UltraFeedback results but introduces no new statistical estimation procedure, significance test, seed information or repeated-run count.

E6.justification: Shared Llama/Gemma benchmark scores and GPT-5-mini results are unchanged. Substantial new results include UltraFeedback WR of 68.91% for Mallows-RMJ-PO-Top-2 versus 62.36% for DPO, Mistral outcomes, DPO-AllPairs results, and ablation/efficiency measurements. The new Mistral Arena-Hard results favor SimPO, 19.3% versus 16.9% for Mallows-RMJ-PO-Top-2. Qualitative outputs also change in Appendix G.

M1.justification: The RCPO framework, MNL and Mallows-RMJ training objectives, entropy proxy and final smoothed losses in Table 1 remain unchanged. Appendix C corrects its smoothing description to agree with those losses; it does not establish a different training procedure. Additional models and ranking lengths instantiate the existing method.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract, terminology and explanatory prose, adds the conference header, and introduces experimental subsections. The main conceptual narrative, section sequence and Appendix A–G organization remain recognizable. Most expansion supplies new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting or restructuring.

P2.justification: Tables 2–3 expand structurally to display UltraFeedback, DPO-AllPairs and Mistral results. v2 adds ablation/timing Tables 4, 8 and 10 and learning/sensitivity Figures 3–4, redraws Figure 2a, and replaces one qualitative table with two new examples. This substantially expands the evidence displays; the retained cross-judge table is merely relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds related-work citations for K-order ranking, permutative alignment and multi-level preferences, plus reward-model and evaluation references. It removes Luce and Plackett citations from the MNL discussion and drops the claim that ranked choice was first formally studied by Feng and Tang. Overall positioning remains similar; the additional published LiPO entry represents an already cited work.

T1.justification: Appendix C changes the smoothing approximation from sigma(-beta*x) to sigma(-x), resolving an extra scaling factor relative to the retained Table 1 objectives. The assumptions and Theorems 1–5 remain unchanged. Rewriting the MNL denominators and proofs into equivalent likelihood expressions does not constitute additional theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of empirical justification for feedback-size choices and direct ranked training versus pairwise expansion: Section 4.3 and Appendix F.3 add relevant ablations and cost comparisons. Additional evaluation settings strengthen validation, and removing v1's incorrectly labeled equation-solving success improves qualitative reliability. These gains outweigh limited reporting problems: the new cross-model superiority wording overlooks SimPO's Mistral advantage, and the claimed 9.47-point UltraFeedback gain over IPO conflicts with the 10.47-point difference in Table 2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RCPO research. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–G are readable, and corresponding equations, figures, tables and experiments can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Mistral experiments, UltraFeedback evaluation, ablations, efficiency measurements and qualitative examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original preference-tuning experiments on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-it, including benchmark results, alternative-judge evaluations and generated-response examples.

results.title: Beyond Pairwise: Empowering LLM Alignment With (Ranked) Choice Modeling

C1.justification: The scientific claims in the abstract, four contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same routing, specialization, performance, and scalability contributions. The added experiments expand supporting evidence without redefining those central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking measured costs to methodological efficiency and utilization/GMM results to specialization, while retaining the central redundancy-and-routing explanation. It also removes v1's explicit image-only validation and future multimodality limitation, retaining the FID/IS limitations paragraph.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds substantial text-to-image implementation information, including architecture, encoders, data subset, optimizer settings, hardware, and sampling, plus timing-measurement conditions. The abstract replaces promised future code with a stated availability link. However, the reproducibility statement remains outdated, still describing ImageNet-only experiments and future code release.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates class-conditional ImageNet generation. v2 additionally trains on a LAION-5B subset and evaluates text-to-image generation using GenEval, covering object composition, counting, colors, and spatial relations. Figure 14 adds corresponding prompted samples.

E2.justification: v2 adds GMM-based routing comparisons under top-1 and top-3 activation (Table 15). It also adds DiffMoE to the extended-training comparison previously containing dense DiT and ProMoE (v1 Table 10; v2 Table 12). Existing ImageNet comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: The new text-to-image protocol introduces 3B activated parameters, 400K training steps, GenEval evaluation, and 50-step UniPC sampling at CFG=5.0. Additional protocols include quantitative 2M-step comparisons at CFG=4.0, controlled timing measurements, utilization analysis on two 200-class subsets, and FID10K evaluation for the k-means sweep. Existing ImageNet settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, v2 adds class-dependent expert-utilization analysis (Figure 6), k-means expert-count sensitivity (Appendix D.3), and measured computational-efficiency analysis (Appendix C.7). GMM comparisons under two activation settings additionally test an alternative to the proposed semantic routing (Appendix C.8).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new averaged utilization measurements do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Matched original scores remain unchanged, including the 2M-step rows moved from v1 Table 10 to v2 Table 12. Substantial new results include GenEval overall scores of 0.463 for ProMoE, 0.417 for Token-Choice MoE, and 0.390 for the dense model, plus additional extended-training, GMM, k-means sensitivity, utilization, and timing results.

M1.justification: The two-step router, contrastive loss, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix A adds an MM-DiT-style text-to-image instantiation with joint text/visual self-attention and visual-FFN experts. This variant uses four routed experts and one unconditional expert, without shared experts (Table 6), constituting a limited architectural adaptation.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes terminology from 'standard experts' to 'routed experts,' clarifies selected paragraphs and appendix headings, and adds publication, contact, and acknowledgment text. The existing exposition and overall section organization are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds several substantive tables, expert-utilization panels, and a prompted text-to-image sample grid. Table 5 gains a GFLOPs column, and v1 Table 10 is reorganized into v2 Tables 11–12 with expanded comparison columns and rows. Existing figures are largely retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for GenEval, LAION-5B, Qwen2.5-VL, UniPC, and newer diffusion/tokenization work, and updates the diffusion-related-work paragraph. Its central positioning of explicit semantic guidance against existing implicit MoE routing remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(6) and their mathematical definitions remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs that are added or revised.

improvement.justification: The LAION/GenEval experiment substantially addresses v1's ImageNet-only validation, while new utilization, clustering, extended-training, and timing analyses strengthen evidence about specialization and practical tradeoffs. Expanded implementation details also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the stale reproducibility statement and overbroad efficiency interpretation: Table 14 shows ProMoE remains slower at inference and requires roughly twice the training GPU-hours of dense DiT.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ProMoE work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, with retained material identifiable across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original text-to-image, expert-utilization, computational-cost, and clustering-comparison results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation experiments, routing ablations, scaling results, and token analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Routing Matters in MoE: Scaling Diffusion Transformers with Explicit Routing Guidance

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution statement, and conclusion retain the same central claims about training-free stitching, Diffusion-Forcing compatibility, Omni Guidance, loop closure, and stable camera-guided generation. Explicitly describing the application as offline clarifies the existing predefined-trajectory setting.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly identifies unavailable future camera poses and manually defined spatial windows as applicability limits in Section 5 and Appendix C. It adds interpretations of latency versus throughput and memory, applicability beyond Diffusion Forcing, and consistency versus scene-complexity tradeoffs in sampling-step and chunking ablations. Existing image-conditioning and wide-baseline limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly specifies the shared 459M-parameter backbone size and documents the additional pretrained backbone regimes. Appendix B.5 explicitly states GVS's 50-step default. The overlap convention is clarified without changing the default frame arrangement. These are documentation additions; the PDFs do not establish a changed original model size or sampling budget.

E1.justification: Both versions use RealEstate10K-trained models and the same trajectory benchmarks, impossible and indefinite staircase demonstrations, RE10K-Mini image-conditioning case, and wide-baseline failure scenario. The new experiments vary backbones and sampling configurations within retained coverage. DL3DV and ScanNet++ remain future-work suggestions.

E2.justification: Autoregressive sampling and StochSync remain the comparison algorithms, including in the added backbone experiments. AR+ in v3 Table 4 is the existing autoregressive algorithm evaluated with increased batch size, a setting change rather than a distinct comparison method.

E3.justification: v3 adds evaluations using binary-dropout and full-sequence diffusion backbones, sampling-step sweeps over 25, 50, 100, and 200 steps, and chunk/overlap configurations of (6,2), (4,4), and (2,6). Its new inference-cost protocol measures runtime and GPU memory over 24–120 frames and includes memory-matched autoregressive batching. The original benchmark metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds substantial analyses of backbone dependence, computational scaling, sampling-step sensitivity, and chunking sensitivity. The new experiments also test whether additional denoising steps eliminate the need for explicit loop closure and whether Omni Guidance remains useful with a binary-dropout backbone. Earlier ablations and failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and retain Table 1's averaging over 40 generations, without confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-level variability. v3 averages its new runtime measurements over 40 samples but introduces no different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive inference-cost, alternative-backbone, and sensitivity results in Tables 4 and 6–12. In retained Table 1, GVS's Stairs F2FC/IQ/AQ values change from 0.139/0.635/0.400 to 0.137/0.621/0.401. Table 3's Panorama 1-loop F2FC with Omni Guidance but without loop closing changes from 0.140 to 0.141. Alternative-backbone scores are additional settings, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The stitching procedure, Omni Guidance, cyclic conditioning, and Algorithm 1 remain substantively unchanged. Additional backbone trials introduce no new stitching rule; disabling Omni Guidance was already evaluated in v1. The overlap notation changes, but the default window still contains four target frames and two conditioning frames on each side.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose remain intact. v3 makes localized introduction and method edits, expands and reorganizes appendix subsections, updates the conference header, and removes the acknowledgments. The added scientific material is not accompanied by a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds the runtime/memory plots in Figure 10, backbone comparison montages in Figures 15–17, and Tables 4 and 6–12. Existing displays are also relocated, relabeled, or reformatted. For example, v1 Figures 14–16 are retained as v3 Figures 18–20 rather than newly generated qualitative evidence.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a substantial Camera-Guided Video Diffusion discussion covering methods such as CameraCtrl, VD3D, MotionCtrl, and ReCamMaster, and distinguishes offline trajectory generation from online collision-avoidance approaches. The introduction also adds streaming, interactive-world-model, and exposure-bias literature, substantially expanding the research positioning.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix B.2 and Table 4 add asymptotic time and space analyses for GVS, autoregressive sampling, and StochSync, including their differing dependence on sampling steps. The original compositional distributions and Omni Guidance derivation in Equations 1–8 remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 left backbone dependence, sampling sensitivity, and practical inference costs largely untested. v3 addresses these gaps with Tables 4 and 6–12 and explicitly documents offline-operation and manual-window limitations, substantially strengthening validation and applicability guidance. Some new wording overstates collision avoidance: Appendix B.4 says collision-free despite CA=0.025 in several added backbone cases. This qualification does not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Generative View Stitching, with matching core methods, equations, and experiments. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including identification of retained and relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds backbone comparisons, inference-cost measurements, and sampling-step and chunking ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation comparisons, quantitative ablations, staircase demonstrations, and appendix failure analyses.

results.title: Generative View Stitching

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims: structural learnability through r-score, an easy-to-hard Re-Schedule curriculum, and accuracy gains up to 3.2% on six mathematical benchmarks. Additional evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning preprocessing cost, curriculum ordering, coarse trees at large token intervals, parameter robustness, static scoring sufficiency, and applicability to other models and coding. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix D.5 claims superiority over ACC across all benchmarks, although Table 13 reports lower AMC23 accuracy, 57.6 versus 59.3.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies avg@32 for mathematical evaluation, the default modification budget M = 10, and timing measurements on eight H20 GPUs with an approximately 46-hour, five-epoch training reference. It also documents coding evaluation details. v1's M = 4 was illustrative, so a budget change is not established. The existing implementation appendix and code-access statement are retained.

E1.justification: v1 uses mathematical reasoning data exclusively. v2 retains that coverage and adds code-generation training on ArcherCodeR and evaluation on LiveCodeBench v5 in Appendix D.7, substantially extending the task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: The comparator membership in the original main benchmarks is unchanged, including Eurus-PRIME only for Qwen2.5-Math-7B. New controlled comparisons introduce Reverse Schedule in Table 6 and dynamically refreshed scoring in Table 14. The revised SimpleRL-Zoo scores do not establish a changed comparison method.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Qwen3-4B-Base evaluations and a DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B coding protocol reporting pass@1 and pass@4 using eight samples. It also adds controlled sweeps of token interval, branching factor, depth, and modification budget, plus ordering and refresh-frequency controls. These substantially expand the experimental design without establishing changes to the retained main training recipe.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained analyses, v2 adds computational cost versus performance, easy-to-hard versus reversed ordering, token-interval sensitivity, separately controlled branching/depth sweeps, modification-budget sensitivity, and static versus refreshed scoring. These test important design and robustness questions absent from v1. The original Fix-versus-Pruning ablation is retained as Appendix D.1/Table 7.

E5.justification: Appendix D.2 newly reports repetitions with different random seeds and Table 8 presents six benchmark results as Avg. ± Var. v1 contains no corresponding training-run uncertainty report. The addition is limited to Re-Schedule; run counts, seed identities, baseline variances, and formal significance tests remain unspecified.

E6.justification: SimpleRL-Zoo's numerical rows change in Tables 1 and 2, including averages of 44.0 to 44.6 and 39.8 to 40.0; Re-Schedule's main scores remain unchanged. Substantial new results include Qwen3 averages of 48.8 versus ACC's 46.6 and GRPO's 44.5, coding pass@1/pass@4 of 26.3/37.8 versus GRPO's 25.4/35.4, and the added cost, variance, and ablation results. These additions concern newly evaluated settings.

M1.justification: The default tree construction, r-score calculation, and weighted GRPO procedure remain unchanged. Appendix D.6 adds an experimental dynamic variant that regenerates reasoning trees and recomputes scores three times during training. This is a limited procedural extension; offline scoring remains the default.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Local revisions clarify related work and the motivation example, update affiliations and conference headers, and add acknowledgements. New analysis subsections and an expanded supplementary-experiment hierarchy are introduced, with the original setup and metric-selection material retained under new appendix labels.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evidence displays with a cost-performance plot and ten additional tables covering timing, ordering, variance, sensitivity, model transfer, dynamic scoring, and coding. Existing Figures 1–4 and Tables 1–4 are retained, with limited sizing/caption changes; v1's Table 5 becomes Table 7.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the cited literature, including entropy interventions, reward dithering, LiveCodeBench, and agent/multimodal directions. Section 2.2 also revises LPPO's description from accuracy weighting and online prompts to accuracy gradients, and Seed-GRPO's from token entropy to semantic diversity, sharpening the positioning against outcome-based proxies.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–10, including the reasoning tree, node/query r-scores, and weighting functions, are retained. The MCN definition is also unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the expensive, offline scoring design. Cost measurements, ordering controls, independent sensitivity sweeps, and static-versus-dynamic comparisons address important validation gaps in v1; coding and Qwen3 experiments extend applicability evidence. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, including unspecified repeat counts, inconsistent cost-display labels, and the Table 13 all-benchmarks overclaim. The improvement comes from testing previously unsupported design assumptions and practical tradeoffs, rather than higher headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Re-Schedule research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds computational-cost measurements, sensitivity studies, repeated-seed results, Qwen3 evaluations, and a coding experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original training analyses, evaluations of two Qwen2.5 models on six mathematical benchmarks, and ablations in Section 7 and Appendix C.

results.title: Scheduling Your LLM Reinforcement Learning with Reasoning Trees

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: recommendation requires a distinctive stability/plasticity balance, PESO supplies proximal single-adapter adaptation with direction-wise theoretical guidance, and it outperforms single and cumulative LoRA baselines. Additional evidence and future directions do not redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets intermediate-block forgetting as benign adaptation, explains retraining's weakness through dilution of recent preferences, and attributes full-parameter fine-tuning difficulties to insufficient structural regularization. It also interprets Yelp results as robustness to limited semantic information and discusses prompt-retrieval overhead. These substantially broaden mechanism and applicability arguments.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/documentation repository link, specifies separate A/B groups for attention and MLP modules, revises the documented base learning rate and explains adapter-storage and forward-pass requirements. Repository contents are not established by the PDFs, and the reproducibility statement still retains its future-release wording.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates three Amazon product categories under chronological and pseudo user-disjoint settings. v2 retains these and adds Yelp location/check-in recommendation, extending evaluation beyond e-commerce. Table 3 also separately evaluates dormant returning users and newly arriving users, broadening the populations explicitly examined.

E2.justification: v2 Table 9 adds direct Instruments comparisons against O-LoRA, AM-LoRA, LSAT and LSAT with parameter inheritance. Existing cumulative-adapter and traditional baselines remain. Table 8 separately adds full-parameter fine-tuning and cumulative-data retraining comparisons against Single Evolving LoRA; that table does not include PESO.

E3.justification: v2 adds LC-REC backbone evaluation, final-model user-group tests, logistic-regression/AUC drift measurement, past-block forgetting evaluation and new training-paradigm controls. Appendix C.2 also changes the stated pretraining learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0002 while retaining Figure 4. This establishes a reported setting revision, not that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The original regularizer and hyperparameter analyses remain. v2 adds direct stability/plasticity probes using dormant versus new users, quantified temporal distribution shift, explicit forgetting measurements on previous blocks and robustness testing with LC-REC. These substantially extend the evidence examining PESO's behavior beyond aggregate recommendation accuracy.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or experimental variability estimates. The added tables continue reporting point estimates; averaging over stages or recommendation metrics does not establish repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original Table 2 scores and reported gains are unchanged, as are the original plotted results. New Tables 3 and 7–12 add substantial results. For example, Yelp NDCG@5 is 0.0199 for PESO versus 0.0190 for Single Evolving LoRA. LC-REC Hit@5 instead favors SD-LoRA, 0.0185 versus PESO's 0.0179. These are additional evaluations, not improvements to the original scores.

M1.justification: Both versions use a single inherited LoRA adapter with cross-entropy and proximal regularization toward its previous frozen state. v2 specifies separate A/B parameter groups and expands the autoregressive likelihood description, but does not establish a changed algorithm. The four-token item representation and prompt already appear in v1.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section order remain. v2 clarifies data construction, parameter grouping and proof exposition, adds an intuitive appendix subsection, expands the research-question list and updates publication/contact text. The original prompt and LLM-use appendices move from D/E to G/H.

P2.justification: Document-wide typography and spacing changes, revised display placement and seven additional tables substantially expand the visual presentation. The new tables are v2 Tables 3 and 7–12. Figures 1–4 retain their image content, while the original dataset and traditional-comparison tables persist under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands cited literature and positioning through O-LoRA, AM-LoRA, LSAT, LC-REC and prompt-tuning comparisons. New Appendices E–F discuss prompt pools and connect PESO to broader temporal adaptation, agents and memory research. This extends research positioning beyond the original vision-adapter and continual-recommendation discussion.

T1.justification: The central propositions, assumptions and proof arguments remain. v2 corrects dimensionally inconsistent subspace expressions in Appendix B.1, including theta0+Uv and the tangent-feature gradient projection. It also introduces the AUC-based drift-score definition and explicit storage-complexity reasoning. The new Appendix B.3 primarily supplies intuition for the existing corollary.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through direct user-group and forgetting analyses, relevant additional baselines, and evaluations beyond the original datasets and backbone. These address important gaps in evidence for the stability/plasticity and generality claims. Technical clarifications and reported code access also help. The gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: uncertainty and experimental details remain underreported, and some new superiority wording exceeds the evidence, notably LC-REC Hit@5 in Table 10.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PESO research, with matching authors, core method and original experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison despite reformatting and substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds user-group, distribution-shift, forgetting, additional-baseline, LC-REC and Yelp results.

before.justification: v1 reports original recommendation experiments on three Amazon categories, including baseline comparisons, regularizer ablations and hyperparameter analyses.

results.title: Continual Low-Rank Adapters for LLM-based Generative Recommender Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: Bayesian fusion of explicit and implicit evidence, instantiated with lightweight interpolation and Thompson sampling, improves RFT task selection across domains and model scales. The additional experiments support this retained claim.

C2.justification: V3 corrects the main-text explanation of lambda and emphasizes excessive Thompson-sampling exploration at large values. It adds reference-cost amortization, evidence-based reference-choice guidance, the failure case of identical reference success probabilities, and an interpretation of the Dynamic Sampling comparison. Conversely, much of v1 Appendices F.5–F.7's domain-specific interpretation, including qualifications about competitive baselines and converging performance, is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds step-by-step pseudocode and specifies a default Beta(1,1) prior; Appendix D.3 newly identifies verl as the experimental framework. New figures also specify benchmark averaging and smoothing conventions. Existing hardware and Table 6 hyperparameters remain, so these disclosures do not establish a change of implementation.

E1.justification: V3 adds AMC23 to the 1.5B math evaluations, including Tables 1, 2 and 8. GURU training coverage and the existing math, code and logic benchmarks remain. The retained 7B math evaluation still uses MATH500 and AIME24.

E2.justification: Random, Offline, BOTS-MoPPS and BOTS-DOTS remain in the corresponding comparisons. Appendix G.5 and Figure 11 add an actual evaluation against Dynamic Sampling from Yu et al. (2025) on 1.5B math; v1 discussed oversampling methods without reporting this comparison.

E3.justification: Table 6 retains the main training configurations. New experiments vary reference-model pairs and compare Dynamic Sampling for 55 steps/54.4K tasks with BOTS and Random for 100 steps/25.6K tasks, disclosing approximately 2.5 times greater cost per Dynamic Sampling step. The Offline tie-breaker also changes from Qwen3-8B in v1 Appendix B.6 to 'Qwen3-32B-A3B' in v3 Appendix D.6, conflicting with Section 4.4's retained 30B-A3B description; an actual rerun cannot be inferred.

E4.justification: V1 deferred systematic reference-model ablations to future work. V3 Appendix G.2 tests three reference pairs through both difficulty-prediction quality and downstream training, substantially extending evidence about extrapolation and sensitivity to reference choice. Appendix F.1 adds a noisy, 50-step simulation of the effect of lambda. The posterior-sampling ablation and task-distribution heatmaps are retained.

E5.justification: V3 explicitly reports three-run/seed averages and 95% confidence intervals for central 1.5B math experiments, including Figures 2–3, 7 and 11–14. V1 provides no corresponding run-count or confidence-interval statements. This materially changes uncertainty reporting, without establishing that v1 used only one run; the practice is not extended to all retained experiments.

E6.justification: V3 substantially revises the 1.5B math scores and curves and adds AMC23, reference-choice and Dynamic Sampling results. For example, Table 3's BOTS math TTB(100%) changes from 0.64 to 0.72, but the broader aggregation and newly reported run averaging prevent interpreting this as a like-for-like decline. Tables 4, 7 and 9–13 retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 corrects the maximized utility from positive absolute distance to negative absolute distance, aligning the written selection rule with v1's stated goal of selecting near-target tasks. The Bayesian updates, interpolator and Thompson-sampling design remain; the new pseudocode documents these existing components.

P1.justification: V3 creates dedicated hyperparameter and practical-consideration sections, moves proofs earlier in the appendices, adds a pseudocode appendix and rewrites related-work prose. Most per-domain appendix result narratives are removed in favor of displays and captions. Ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements are also added, producing substantial structural and explanatory revision.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the main math plots, expands Tables 1, 2 and 8 with AMC23 columns, and adds simulation, reference-choice and Dynamic Sampling displays. Expanded appendix panels show individual benchmarks, confidence bands and separately identified smoothed curves. Many other figures are retained and relocated, but the changed displays constitute a substantial visual revision.

R1.justification: V3 adds references connecting discounting to Raj and Kalyani, implementation to Sheng et al., and task selection to DATS, model-predictive sampling and SPO. The rewritten background replaces the Ouyang et al. RLHF reference with the GPT-4 report. The central novelty positioning relative to explicit-only and implicit-only selection remains.

T1.justification: Appendix F.3 adds Assumption 1 and Proposition 3, with a proof claiming an equivalence between exact interpolation and a task-invariant interpolation coefficient. This is a focused formal addition concerning the existing estimator. Propositions 1–2, their proofs and the exponential-family extensions are retained across relocation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical credibility by adding explicit three-run uncertainty reporting, testing previously unexamined reference choices, and evaluating an external oversampling baseline with computational-cost disclosure. Corrected main-text lambda guidance and pseudocode also improve usability. These gains address important weaknesses in v1 and outweigh localized shortcomings: uncertainty reporting remains concentrated on 1.5B math, some settings are inconsistent, and Proposition 3's necessity argument only establishes agreement outside the chosen batch rather than its claimed global condition.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BOTS research. The main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial appendix reorganization.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix G report original experiments, including additional reference-model and Dynamic Sampling comparisons. Appendix F.1 also adds a simulation.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F report original reinforcement-finetuning experiments, hyperparameter ablations, difficulty-estimation results and runtime measurements.

results.title: BOTS: A Unified Framework for Bayesian Online Task Selection in LLM Reinforcement Finetuning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement and conclusion retain the same central claims: compression through reuse-promoting penalties and specialized storage, with comparable predictive performance and reported 4–16-fold compression. New experiments support or qualify these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds qualifications concerning complete versus incomplete trees, random forests' multiclass advantages, and dataset-dependent penalty-search heuristics. It also interprets the measured 5–8-fold prototype slowdown as practically negligible because sensing and communication dominate, although end-to-end latency and energy measurements are not supplied.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the anonymous-code access information with a named repository and specifies release v1.0.0 and LightGBM 4.6.0. It newly documents five-fold validation for the two smallest datasets, validation holdouts for larger datasets, the PALMA II computing resource, and hardware/prototype details and access instructions. These materially strengthen reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: The eight tabular prediction benchmarks in Table 1 are unchanged. Appendix E.1 adds actual deployment tests on XIAO ESP32S3 and Arduino Nano 33 BLE hardware, using randomized inputs to a binary-Covertype model, extending test-environment coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 4 adds array-based, pointer-free LightGBM alongside the retained LightGBM, quantized LightGBM, CEGB and CCP comparators. New Figure 8 additionally evaluates standard random forests and forests pruned using Guo et al. (2018), substantially broadening the comparisons.

E3.justification: The main hyperparameter grid and 80/20 split ratio remain. New protocols include a classification comparison capped at 256 trees and hardware latency evaluation of a 0.5 KB, four-tree, depth-four model using 500 randomized-input predictions per run. Section 4.3 also corrects the stated reuse-factor ratio; newly disclosed validation details do not establish that the earlier protocol changed.

E4.justification: The array-based LightGBM control tests whether benefits extend beyond removing pointers, and Section 4.4 adds a quantitative dominance analysis. Most existing sensitivity analyses are retained, but v1 Figure 25, covering 1,024 iterations and depth 8 in the multivariate analysis, is omitted.

E5.justification: Unlike v1's curves without uncertainty reporting, v2 Figure 4 reports means and standard deviations over 12 train-test splits, with seeds 1–12 specified. Appendix E.1 also reports 20 timing runs and a variance-based stopping rationale. These substantially expand statistical reporting; v1 does not establish its original run count.

E6.justification: Figure 4 replaces the earlier curves with split-averaged results and adds the array-based comparator; Figure 8 adds random-forest results. Table 2 newly reports ToaD versus LightGBM latencies of 137.08 versus 17.63 microseconds on ESP32S3 and 512.89 versus 102.16 on Arduino. Section 4.4 adds the 3.37% dominated-solutions finding, while the final multivariate sensitivity grid is removed. These are revised or additional results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The feature and threshold penalties, modified split gain, pointer-free encoding and shared value arrays remain unchanged. Appendix A retains the same derivation. Parameter renaming and prototype deployment do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. v2 adds a baseline-results subsection, reproducibility statement and acknowledgments, reorganizes the appendices around the new experiments, and updates author information, publication headers and terminology.

P2.justification: Figure 4 gains reordered panels, an expanded legend and uncertainty displays; Figures 5–7 are reformatted. v2 adds Figure 8 and Table 2 and redistributes the retained appendix plots while omitting v1 Figure 25. The method schematics and most sensitivity displays remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 and Appendix C add targeted coverage of FPGA quantization, bit-level GBDT training, forest pruning/refinement and resource-efficient nearest-neighbor models. The central positioning around training-time feature and threshold reuse remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 changes the reuse-factor definition from global values divided by nodes plus leaves to its reciprocal, consistent with the stated reuse interpretation. This corrects a mathematical definition beyond merely renaming RF to ReF. The training equations and Appendix A derivation are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens empirical credibility through split-level uncertainty reporting and a pointer-free LightGBM control that addresses a central comparison weakness. Random-forest comparisons, measured deployment costs and substantially clearer reproducibility information further improve assessability. These gains outweigh the omitted sensitivity grid. The claim that the measured slowdown has negligible overall latency or energy impact remains insufficiently tested.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ToaD research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and relocated or renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: The original empirical study is retained, with additional random-forest comparisons and measured microcontroller inference times in Appendices D and E.1.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original benchmark comparisons and univariate and multivariate penalty-sensitivity experiments.

results.title: Boosted Trees on a Diet: Compact Models for Resource-Constrained Devices

C1.justification: The abstract corrects the claimed GAIA token saving from 29.45% to 29.68%, aligning it with Table 1 and the conclusion already present in v1. The central runtime-supervision, efficiency and general-applicability contributions retain their scope.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly interprets the token–latency tradeoff and attributes most latency overhead to purification. Appendix A.5 adds specific limitations involving very long observations, ineffective guidance and backbone-dependent trigger frequency. These substantially extend v1's more general discussion of overcompression and resource accounting.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Table 5 disclose filter logic and benchmark-specific step intervals and loop windows. Appendix A.3.2 adds OAgents settings and AWorld's MCP invocation/routing details, while A.5 specifies a maximum of two guidance interventions per subtask. These materially expand reproducibility information; the supplied prompts and code-access URL are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GAIA, GSM8k-Hard, AIME 2024, HumanEval, MBPP and DROP. The added analyses use existing GAIA coverage; extending ablations from selected tasks to the full validation set changes sampling scope rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 1, 2 and 4 is unchanged, including the AWorld variants with and without Guard. The expanded ablation retains the same three component-removal variants; token-accounting rows do not introduce new comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds component ablations on the full GAIA validation set alongside the original top-10-token-intensive-tasks-per-level evaluation. It also introduces a purification-threshold sweep over 1000, 3000, 5000 and 7000 characters and latency evaluation in seconds. These substantially expand the evaluation design; existing headline benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's selected-subset ablation, v2 tests component contributions across the full validation set, sensitivity to purification thresholds, supervisor token overhead and each component's latency cost. The original subset ablation survives as Table 8, and the existing case study moves from A.4 to A.6.

E5.justification: The pass@k reporting and token-cost distribution/variance analysis are retained. v2 introduces no seed information, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or statistical tests; its added experiments report point estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Table 3, Figure 5 and Tables 6–7. For example, full-set accuracy is 49.70% without purification versus 50.91% with the full system, while average latency is 233.96 seconds for Smolagent versus 321.15 seconds for SMAS. Tables 1, 2 and 4 remain numerically unchanged, and Table 8 reproduces v1's Table 3; the new ablation values concern different sample coverage, not cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The core supervision strategies, context and action space, intervention pipeline and supplied prompts are retained. The new pseudocode, framework-specific integration descriptions and guidance cap expand documentation of the existing system; the PDFs do not establish an actual implementation change.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording and affiliation/header edits, merges Discussion and Conclusion, and adds acknowledgements, ethics and reproducibility statements. It inserts new appendix sections and renumbers the retained case study and prompts, while preserving most original prose and all supplied prompt content.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with Figures 5–7, Tables 5–7 and Algorithm 1. It redraws Figure 4a for the full-set ablation, presents those results in Table 3, and relocates the original subset table to Table 8. These are substantive display additions and revisions beyond pagination changes.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning against post-hoc failure attribution, architectural optimization and AWorld's Guard are retained. Changes to Gao's author name and the MaAS reference are bibliographic corrections rather than new research positioning.

T1.justification: The SMAS and context-window definitions and context-dependent action space are unchanged. Algorithm 1 documents operational heuristics without adding theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: v1's component evidence was limited to selected high-cost tasks and lacked latency measurements. v2 adds full-set ablations, sensitivity testing and important implementation details, substantially strengthening validation and reproducibility. Reporting the 37.27% latency increase makes the retained token savings more honestly assessable. Although A.4.1 incorrectly describes the denominator of the 15.45% supervisor-overhead share, this localized inconsistency does not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SupervisorAgent research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds full-validation-set ablations, threshold sensitivity, token-overhead breakdowns and latency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, cross-model and cross-framework experiments, and a GAIA case study.

results.title: Stop Wasting Your Tokens: Towards Efficient Runtime Multi-Agent Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contribution list and main conclusion retain the same claims about hierarchical feature construction, heterogeneous manifold alignment, existence and uniqueness of the intermediate optimum, and classification advantages. Additional evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning single-curvature expressiveness, domain shifts, class imbalance and the non-metric distance. Appendix D introduces information-bottleneck and attention-smoothing explanations and an anti-collapse argument, while new analyses support interpretations about approximation robustness, curvature differences and computational costs.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents batchwise estimation of r, weighting coefficients for the no-attention control, alternative label construction and profiling settings. Existing training details remain largely unchanged. The front-page resource link changes from a repository to a project page, without establishing a change in actual code availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR100, SUN, ImageNet and Rare Species for few-shot and base/novel/whole taxonomic classification. Additional backbone, labeling and diagnostic experiments remain within this coverage; the artifact visualizations use already-covered ImageNet classes.

E2.justification: The existing MaPLe, PromptSRC, ProTeCt, MERU and HyCoCLIP comparisons remain. v2 adds squared, squared-log and squared-reciprocal curvature-distance controls in Table 8, and adds ProTeCt to attention-map comparisons that previously showed only the proposed method.

E3.justification: The original training and evaluation settings are retained. New protocols include ViT-L/14 evaluation, hyperparameter sweeps, three clustering-quality metrics, alternative species-label preprocessing, approximation checks using one million vector pairs, and efficiency measurements over 1,000 batches with specified training/inference batch sizes.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations, v2 tests alternative manifold distances, removal of cross-attention, layer/curvature/loss-weight sensitivity, approximation and r-estimation errors, label-concatenation dependence and sample reweighting. It also adds quantitative clustering analysis, artifact attention comparisons, learned-curvature analysis and computational profiling.

E5.justification: Both versions report LA, HCA and MTA averaged over three independent runs in Appendix B.4. Neither reports seed identities, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new approximation-error diagnostics do not introduce uncertainty reporting for repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for the new controls and analyses, including a 5.3% mean Taylor-approximation error and measured computational overhead. Original Table 1 remains numerically unchanged, but some retained harmonic means change: CIFAR100 MaPLe+ProTeCt LA changes from 78.29 to 78.40 in v1 Table 3 versus v2 Table 5.

M1.justification: The main feature-extraction, manifold-alignment and optimization procedure remains intact. Appendix C.12 adds the sample-reweighted Ours-balanced training variant as a preliminary adaptation, without replacing the primary method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and most retained exposition remain recognizable. v2 corrects language and terminology, updates author and conference information, adds acknowledgements, relocates the hyperbolic comparison, and reorganizes appendix topics. Most expansion consists of additional scientific content rather than extensive rewriting of existing prose.

P2.justification: v2 adds numerous diagnostic tables and approximation-error, efficiency and artifact-attention figures. Figure 6 becomes a baseline-versus-method comparison, while earlier animal visualizations are retained in the appendix. The full generalization table moves to the appendix with a shorter main-text display, and the hyperbolic comparison is relocated.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against relative-representation communication, CNN taxonomy classification, latent-hierarchy research and biological vision-language models, including BioCLIP2 and Biotrove. Appendix D adds literature-based distinctions concerning attention suppression and feature fusion. These are substantive positioning additions, not merely bibliography updates.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the c2 update in Equation 18, makes the implicit derivatives in Equation 20 explicit, and states that the proposed distance lacks symmetry and the triangle inequality. The central theorem, propositions and Appendix A proof arguments remain substantially unchanged; Appendix D supplies conceptual justification rather than new formal proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central design choices through direct distance and cross-attention controls, approximation checks, sensitivity tests and alternative-label experiments, addressing important gaps in v1's supporting evidence. Computational profiling and explicit limitations also make applicability easier to assess. The remaining SUN baseline inconsistency between Tables 5 and 7 tempers these gains but does not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidential support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Alignment across Trees. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original sensitivity, approximation-error, labeling, class-imbalance and efficiency experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, generalization and ablation results on four datasets, together with representation and attention visualizations.

results.title: Modality Alignment across Trees on Heterogeneous Hyperbolic Manifolds

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same interaction paradigm, reasoning workflow, two-stage training contributions, and headline 22.5% relative improvement. Added experiments support these retained claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes fewer retrieval iterations from higher total latency and token use, adding a substantive cost trade-off and limitations discussion. It also discusses outcome-reward limitations, dataset-dependent component contributions, and why gains may reflect interaction quality rather than simply larger retrieved contexts.

D1.justification: v2 specifies min-max normalization, entity-term normalization, filter reissuing, concurrent-action execution order, and RL token masking. It also documents settings for the added cost tests and states that source code accompanies supplementary materials. These fill reproducibility gaps; the existing training hyperparameters, hardware, corpus construction, and prompts largely remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds evaluation on MultiHop-RAG, extending the previously Wikipedia-based coverage to news covering technology, health, and business. This materially broadens domain coverage; the original six benchmarks and training datasets remain.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparator set is retained. v2 adds RRF and CombMNZ as fusion alternatives in Table 8 and a Search-R1 best-of-three variant in Appendix C.4, providing limited additional comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation beyond answer accuracy and turn counts: supporting-fact coverage, latency, tool time, token consumption, memory, and best-of-three testing are added. New cost experiments specify Qwen2.5-7B with A100/vLLM, while engine testing uses eight CPU cores and 96 concurrent clients. Existing core evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Table 3 newly isolates the three interaction components. Appendices C.3-C.6 investigate retrieved-evidence coverage, cost versus accuracy, fusion sensitivity, and engine overhead, including a best-of-three control. Appendix D.3 adds training-format error diagnostics. These substantially extend the earlier aggregate ablations, training analyses, and case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run variability, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Best-of-three sampling in v2 is an inference control, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All original main benchmark scores are preserved, including average EM scores of 52.8 for 8B and 47.5 for 7B. Substantial new results include MultiHop-RAG EM scores of 79.4/81.4 for 7B/8B, component and fusion comparisons, evidence coverage, and cost measurements. Table 7 newly reports 36.4-second latency for Interact-RAG-7B versus 17.2 seconds for Search-R1-7B.

M1.justification: The interaction primitives, planner-reasoner-executor workflow, SFT/GRPO training, and reward function remain unchanged. Added descriptions of RL token masking, normalization, filter persistence, and execution order disclose implementation details without establishing a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The original narrative largely survives, with localized rewriting, spelling corrections, an experimental-settings subsection, ethics/reproducibility statements, and reorganized appendices including limitations. Some cross-references deteriorate, notably the unresolved 'Table ??' and references to 'Table 4.3'.

P2.justification: v2 merges the original main and appendix backbone evaluations into an expanded main Table 1 and adds five tables for new evaluations. The training-free table drops parenthetical percentage decreases, Figure 3 receives a more precise caption, and Figure 5 changes bar styling. The original plotted findings and case study are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including MultiHop-RAG, reciprocal rank fusion, proactive multi-agent information seeking, Towards AI Search Paradigm, RankElectra, and RankExpert. The related-work narrative and positioning against black-box retrieval remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds the mathematical observation that the constant -1 reward offset cancels during GRPO group normalization and cannot affect advantages or training, qualifying the earlier penalty rationale. The objective and reward equations themselves remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the retrieval mechanism through component ablations, supporting-fact coverage, and a non-Wikipedia evaluation. It also resolves an important omission in v1's efficiency discussion by measuring latency and token costs and acknowledging their trade-off with accuracy. These gains in empirical substantiation and transparency outweigh localized cross-reference defects, although uncertainty estimates remain absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Interact-RAG work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds news-domain evaluation, component ablations, retrieval-quality measurements, computational-cost comparisons, and other diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original QA benchmark results, training and interaction ablations, training dynamics, and a retrieval case study.

results.title: Interact-RAG: Reason and Interact with the Corpus, Beyond Black-Box Retrieval

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are unchanged, and the introduction retains the same contributions: adjacent-step adversarial self-distillation, first-frame enhancement, improved few-step generation, and one model supporting multiple inference-step counts. The additional evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains four-step parity with Self Forcing through identical DMD supervision, adds a sharpness/detail-preservation rationale for adversarial alignment, and discusses training overhead as a tradeoff for avoiding separately trained models. These refine the interpretation without replacing the original mechanism account.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands reproducibility information with discriminator-head locations and inputs, baseline timestep lists, CFG weight, optimizer settings, learning rates, and update ratio. Appendix G discloses 12 participants and independent randomization; Appendix I reports approximately 20% additional training time and 1.3% additional GPU memory. These are new disclosures, not evidence that the retained experiments changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds explicit complex-object-motion and high-camera-motion scenarios in Appendix C and 20-second continuation tests in Appendix E. These extend temporal and motion coverage within the retained causal text-to-video task; the training prompts and VBench benchmark remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 and the user-study comparator sets are unchanged. New Figure 8 includes both standard and separately retrained Self Forcing at one and two steps in the quantitative comparison, whereas v1's corresponding baseline table included only the retrained few-step variants. This expands that comparison without introducing a new baseline family.

E3.justification: The supplementary evaluations introduce 200-video trajectory analyses per scenario, FVD comparisons against adjacent-step outputs and a 50-step 14B teacher, and 20-second continuation evaluation. The original main benchmark settings remain unchanged. Newly specified baseline-training and user-study settings document existing experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct distribution-gap analysis in Table 3, trajectory-similarity robustness comparisons across scenarios and methods in Figure 9, and generator/discriminator training-dynamics analyses in Figures 13–14. These substantially extend testing of the central distribution-gap, redundancy, and stability arguments. The original component ablations and sensitivity analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Section 3.3 newly states that the similarity finding holds across multiple random seeds, without specifying their count. Appendix I adds training-loss means and variances; these describe fluctuations during training, not uncertainty across independent runs. No confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original preference and sensitivity results are unchanged. v2 adds 16-metric VBench breakdowns, FVD measurements, long-video results, and training/resource measurements. Table 3 reports step-1 FVD of 732 against the adjacent step versus 1836 against the teacher. In new Table 4, ours at 2* steps exceeds Self Forcing at two steps in total score (0.8263 versus 0.8250) but has lower semantic score (0.7998 versus 0.8076). These are additional results, not revisions to the original benchmark scores.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 removes the second timestep draw in line 9, making the stated procedure reuse the timestep sampled in line 7 for the paired outputs. The ASD/DMD framework and FFE inference remain intact. Added discriminator-head specifications document implementation details rather than establish an architectural redesign.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact, with local wording corrections, expanded explanations, author/affiliation updates, and acknowledgements. The appendix gains sections, while the original hyperparameter, user-study, and LLM-use sections move from B–D to F–H.

P2.justification: v2 adds five figures covering metric breakdowns, scenario heatmaps, long-video examples, and training dynamics, plus two new result tables. Figure 1 is revised and Figure 6's axis label is corrected. The original sensitivity plot and study interface are retained as Figures 11 and 12.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to SF-V, autoregressive adversarial post-training, and flow matching. Section 2.2 distinguishes the first two works' real-data alignment from ASD's adjacent-student-step alignment. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Equation (2) corrects the DMD gradient by applying the generator derivative to the entire teacher-minus-student score difference; v1 displayed it multiplying only the second term. The remaining mathematical framework is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 offered little direct measurement for its smaller-distribution-gap and training-stability arguments. v2 substantially strengthens them with FVD comparisons and training-dynamics evidence, while motion-scenario and long-video tests examine the claimed resistance to error accumulation. Detailed baseline and discriminator specifications also improve reproducibility. The gains are substantial despite remaining limits: the long-video two-step semantic score is lower than Self Forcing's, and independent-run uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ASD/FFE video-generation work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison. The original appendix material remains identifiable within v2's expanded appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original distribution-gap measurements, motion-scenario analyses, long-video evaluations, and training-dynamics results.

before.justification: v1 reports original VBench results, ASD/FFE component ablations, a human preference study, and hyperparameter sensitivity results.

results.title: Towards One-step Causal Video Generation via Adversarial Self-Distillation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal claims: compact, interpretable canonical embeddings, correspondence consistency across subjects and views, whole-head coverage, and benefits for matching and tracking. Additional experiments do not revise these headline contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning interview-style training data, backside views, rapid motion, long hair and accessories. It interprets supervision-noise sensitivity and design tradeoffs, and discusses why PRNet can score better on face-focused ArcFace/Met3R measures while losing on PCK. V1's interpretation of volumetrically ordered ear surfaces is removed.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies grid resolution 128, Gaussian smoothing strength 1.5, the default tracker-confidence threshold 0.6, memory requirements, and preprocessing/training details for the new applications. These disclosures do not establish changes to the original settings. Conversely, v1 Appendix A.3's DLT reconstruction, downsampling, consistency tolerances and reprojection-threshold instructions are removed. The promised future code/checkpoint release remains unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 retains CelebV-HQ and Nersemble coverage while adding ShapeNet chair correspondence experiments, head-pose estimation on 300W-LP and AFLW2000-3D, and LPFF evaluations of cross-person matching, synthetic perturbations and challenging appearances. These substantially broaden object domains, tasks and tested input conditions.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CSE and FaRL. CSE also enters Figure 3 and replaces Fit3D in Figure 5, although Fit3D remains in Table 1. New comparisons include PRNet in Table 12 and RGB-based pose regressors in Table 10. The fine-tuned DINOv3 comparator corresponds to the earlier no-canonical-space ablation, rather than an entirely new comparator.

E3.justification: V2 introduces same-person PCK@0.05 and cross-person PCK@0.1, the latter evaluated on 400 LPFF pairs from 30 manually annotated subjects. New protocols include half-budget training for Table 3 and Appendix B, a 90/10 training-validation split for pose regression, and synthetic perturbations of 300 LPFF images. The canonical-space ablation is retained and expanded. V1's pretraining ablation, ear-surface pose analysis and extended stereo-configuration analysis are removed.

This adds variability estimation for one analysis, rather than uncertainty across training seeds or confidence intervals for the main benchmarks.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 scores remain, including DenseMarks MAE 3.68 and RMSE 5.90. V2 adds extensive results: Table 10 reports AFLW2000-3D MAE 5.97 degrees with DenseMarks versus 18.22 with RGB using MobileNet. Table 12 gives DenseMarks higher cross-person PCK than PRNet (0.85 versus 0.76), but PRNet better ArcFace and Met3R scores. Pretraining-ablation and extended stereo results disappear. M1.justification: The central ViT/DPT embedder and canonical-cube pipeline remain. V2 adds a downstream DenseMarks-to-head-pose regressor using MobileNet or a fully connected layer (Appendix F), and adapts supervision to chair keypoints and object masks (Appendix E). These are limited procedural extensions.

P1.justification: The original main narrative is largely retained. V2 consolidates baseline descriptions, brings canonical-space analysis into the main results, reorganizes the appendices, and adds explanatory and limitations paragraphs. Publication headers, acknowledgments and an LLM-use disclosure also change; the revision is not an extensive rewrite of the retained prose.

P2.justification: V2 expands and groups Table 1, revises comparator panels in Figures 3 and 5, reformats the canonical-space comparison, and adds numerous ablation, application and robustness displays. It removes pretraining, ear-surface and extended stereo panels. The lighting illustration is retained and relocated from Figure 12 to Figure 14. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting the new experiments, including ShapeNet, KeypointNet, LPFF, AllTracker and head-pose research, and discusses comparison with face-only PRNet in Appendix I. The main related-work organization and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged. Duplicate CSE and FaRL bibliography entries do not represent additional distinct works.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DenseMarks work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised, relocated and removed content.

after.justification: V2 retains original correspondence and tracking results and reports additional ablations, robustness tests, chair experiments, head-pose estimation and manually annotated cross-person matching results.

before.justification: V1 reports original correspondence measurements in Table 1, tracking and reconstruction demonstrations, and original ablation and consistency analyses in Appendix A.

results.title: Densemarks: Learning Canonical Embeddings for Human Heads Images via Point Tracks
