This narrows the theoretical framing alongside removal of the formal multiclass extension. The central embedding-regularization and superior worst-group-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds a rationale for Gaussian embeddings with shared covariance and explicitly acknowledges the strength of the extreme-correlation assumption. It also interprets the new noisy-environment and visualization results as evidence of robustness beyond accurate group inference and of representation differences from GroupDRO.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly explains training/validation annotation availability and worst-group checkpoint selection, supported by Table 10. It also documents the four-group CivilComments construction and sample counts. Algorithm 1 clarifies the domain-label input; the existing hyperparameter search spaces and code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The six benchmark tasks remain. v2 extends ColorMNIST coverage to 99% spurious correlation and noisier inferred environments, and adds a coarse four-group CivilComments scenario with a broader sample pool. These are extensions within the existing vision and language tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds GroupDRO-ES as an evaluated comparator in Table 16 and includes GroupDRO in the expanded Grad-CAM comparisons. Baselines omitted from the shortened main tables remain in appendix Tables 11–13 and 15, so those omissions are not comparator removals.

E3.justification: New Table 16 uses a separately cited experimental configuration, including a four-group CivilComments split with 269,038 training examples. Table 14 tests approximately 70% accurate environment partitions while retaining other Table 4 settings. The original main experimental budgets, metrics, and splits remain; newly explained annotation and checkpoint-selection practices are disclosures.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends robustness and representation analyses: it adds the 99% correlation stress test, tests degraded environment inference, introduces Waterbirds t-SNE comparisons, and replaces the single Grad-CAM example with comparisons including GroupDRO and additional cases. Existing loss-weight sensitivity, norm ablation, correlation plots, and timing analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three runs with seeds 0, 1, and 2 and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting. However, v2's new Table 16 reports only point estimates for MultiNLI and four-group CivilComments, introducing a limited inconsistency in uncertainty reporting. No increase in runs or new statistical test is stated.

E6.justification: Original benchmark scores are retained, including the full comparisons relocated to the appendix. Substantial new results include SCER's 56.0 ± 2.2 worst-group accuracy at 99% correlation and EIIL+SCER's 65.1 ± 2.8 average accuracy with noisy partitions. Table 16 adds four GroupDRO-ES comparisons under different settings; these are new results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The group-mean directions, alignment losses, combined objective in Equations 1–3, and training updates remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 explicitly adds domain labels d to its input list, documenting information already used in v1 rather than introducing a new procedure.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits the prose, expands explanatory passages and the conclusion, and reorganizes baseline discussion around abbreviated main comparisons and complete appendix results. The main section sequence remains recognizable. Conference-status text, an affiliation, and acknowledgments are also updated.

P2.justification: Main Tables 1, 2, 3, and 5 are condensed, with complete comparisons displayed in appendix Tables 11–13 and 15. v2 adds annotation-availability and experimental tables, a t-SNE figure, and expanded Grad-CAM displays. The original correlation plot is retained as Figure 4. Conference formatting, captions, and page layouts are extensively revised.

R1.justification: v2 adds Seddik et al., Papyan et al., and Lai and Muthukumar to support its theoretical assumptions, and Selvaraju et al. for Grad-CAM. It gives greater attention to early-stopped GroupDRO as a competitive comparator. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain largely intact.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the core-term coefficient in Theorem 1 from 1 to 1/2, revises Proposition 1's class-mean signs, and rewrites the subgroup-error derivation. The ± sign now identifies the worst subgroup rather than an alleged classifier-sign equivalence. v1's multiclass/multidomain Proposition 2, Theorem 2, and associated derivations are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects important coefficient, sign, and subgroup-error mistakes in the central binary derivation and strengthens empirical validation through GroupDRO-ES comparisons and targeted robustness tests. Annotation and model-selection disclosures also improve assessability. Removing the multiclass proof narrows formal coverage, and uncertainty reporting is incomplete in part of Table 16, but the central theoretical repairs and stronger validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SCER. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching despite revisions and relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and reports additional results for extreme correlations, noisy inferred environments, and comparison with GroupDRO-ES.

before.justification: v1 reports original SCER experiments across six benchmarks, including component ablations, environment-inference experiments, visual analyses, and timing results.

results.title: Spurious Correlation-Aware Embedding Regularization for Worst-Group Robustness

C1.justification: v5 extends v1's empirical commonness claim with a theoretical inevitability claim for coordinate-patching divergence. Its introduction also adds an explicit contribution of reducing divergence while preserving intervention accuracy in a 7B language model; v1's mitigation contribution was demonstrated only in synthetic settings. These materially broaden the paper's central contributions.

C2.justification: v5 substantially develops the existing claim-dependence argument: unchanged overall computation can conceal altered sub-computations, and harmlessness cannot be defined independently of the mechanistic claim (Section 4.1). It explicitly states that minimizing divergence does not guarantee elimination of hidden pathways and that the new diagnostic is approximate and vulnerable to dormant behavioral changes (Section 5; Appendix A.3).

D1.justification: v5 adds a public-repository link and instructions for generating exact CL samples for the continuous-feature Boundless DAS task. It newly documents alignment parameterization and initialization, convergence patience, different checkpoint-selection criteria for DAS and CL, and partition-specific training procedures (Appendices A.4–A.5). These substantially extend v1's implementation disclosures without establishing that every newly documented practice changed.

E1.justification: The evaluated coverage remains language-model representation interventions and the synthetic ten-class feature task, including dense/sparse transfer. The new CL experiment reuses the Boundless DAS setting already examined in v1. Revised partitions, noise dimensions, and generation of matching counterfactual samples change settings within this coverage.

E2.justification: The three intervention families in the divergence comparison remain unchanged. However, v5's learning-rate/noise sweeps directly compare CL-only and DAS+CL against behavior-only DAS, whereas the corresponding v1 sweeps contain DAS+CL at different weights, including zero. CL-only was already evaluated separately in v1 Figure 4, so this is a limited expansion of comparator participation rather than an entirely new baseline.

E3.justification: Reported synthetic defaults change from 64 to 16 noise coordinates, MLP learning rate/epochs from 0.005/1000 to 0.01/300, and alignment learning rate from 0.05 to 0.01. Appendix A.1 replaces independently sampled natural baseline vectors with corresponding ground-truth vectors and adds several divergence metrics. These are substantive reported protocol revisions; they do not independently establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v5 adds checks using alternative divergence measures (Figure 4), a language-model CL-weight sensitivity analysis (Figure 3B), and regression relating training divergence to held-out intervention accuracy (Appendix A.6). Synthetic loss-component comparisons are expanded, but v1's mask-size sensitivity analyses and full-dimensional synthetic EMD sweep are removed. The supplementary evidence therefore changes substantially in both directions.

E5.justification: v1 already reports error bars and plus/minus values, but does not specify seed counts or provide inferential tests. v5 newly reports five training seeds and partition averaging, and adds a 30-observation OLS analysis with standard errors, confidence intervals, t/F statistics, and p-values (Appendices A.5–A.6). The seed disclosure does not establish an increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Synthetic DAS/CL feature-EMD means change from 0.043/0.024 to 0.032/0.007, and IIA means from 0.981/0.977 to 0.997/0.9988. These are replacement results under revised settings, not matched-setting improvements. v5 also adds language-model divergence reductions with maintained IIA at suitable CL weights, additional divergence measurements, and an EMD–IIA regression reporting coefficient -0.3424 and R-squared 0.729.

M1.justification: The synthetic alignment changes from orthogonal rotations to an explicitly parameterized invertible linear map. The modified CL objective now compares inverse-mapped causal components and stops gradients through its target, unlike v1's aligned-coordinate objective (v1 Section 5.2; v5 Section 5.2 and Appendix A.5.3). Appendix A.3 also introduces a local-PCA and behavioral-testing algorithm for approximate harmlessness classification.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: Section 3 separates theoretical and empirical arguments, Section 4 rewrites the harmlessness discussion, and Section 5 replaces the synthetic-setting/method/results sequence with language-model and synthetic studies. The appendices are reorganized around proofs, a diagnostic algorithm, experiments, and regression. v5 also adds an LLM usage statement and updates the publication header and affiliations.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are redesigned, including clearer legends, a coordinate-patching illustration, separate natural/intervened EMD bars, and new language-model panels. Appendix sweeps change from dense/sparse paired bars to CL-only/DAS+CL groups with a DAS reference. New divergence plots, an algorithm display, and a regression table substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v5 adds citations to pyvene (Wu et al., 2024) and statsmodels (Seabold and Perktold, 2010) for the new implementation and analysis. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to causal abstraction, problematic patching, and Grant's CL loss remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v5 adds the coordinate-patching proposition and patch-closure theorem with a convex hyperrectangle corollary (Section 3.1; Appendix A.2). It formalizes behavioral null-spaces for general functions and dormant changes across contexts, and revises divergence to use class-specific support. The balanced-subspace example is retained and relocated from Appendix A.1.4 to A.2.1, rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: The language-model CL experiment addresses an important weakness in v1, whose mitigation evidence was confined to synthetic networks. Alternative divergence measurements, fuller implementation disclosures, and more precise applicability limits substantially strengthen the practical case. The gain is tempered by removed mask-size analyses and a source/target-order error in the new Appendix A.2 proof, but these do not outweigh the improvement in empirical support and clarity about the method's scope.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material that was reorganized or relocated.

after.justification: v5 reports original divergence measurements, synthetic experiments, CL regularization of Boundless DAS in a language model, and regression results in Appendix A.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original measurements of representational divergence across three intervention methods and synthetic CL-loss experiments, including generalization and hyperparameter results in Section 5 and Appendix A.2.

results.title: Addressing divergent representations from causal interventions on neural networks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about cancellation's unreliability, informative attention layers, Rank/Vote aggregation, and NDR-based evaluation. The added experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: New discussion hypothesizes that Llama's reduced depth contributes to its weak attribution performance and interprets rank trajectories through persistent noisy outliers. Appendix L also identifies how optimal voting cutoff depends on noise level as unresolved. These refine the existing interpretations and applicability guidance.

D1.justification: Section 7 newly supplies a code-repository link, seed-script information, deterministic PyTorch settings, and server details. Appendix J documents comparator implementation choices and learning rates. These are additional disclosures; the new 40GB-per-GPU statement is inconsistent with the retained A100 80GB description in Appendix A.

E1.justification: Appendix J extends evaluation beyond the retained eight noisy GLUE tasks to Grammar, Math, and Math With Reasoning instruction datasets. These evaluate whether influence rankings recover semantic-category relationships, substantially broadening coverage beyond detecting injected label noise.

E2.justification: The new comparisons in Figures 23–26 evaluate Outlier Gradient, Kronfluence/EKFAC, and RepSim alongside TracIn, Cosine, and DataInf. RepSim includes last-token and mean-token variants. This substantially broadens the evaluated attribution approaches; the original GLUE comparator sets remain intact.

E3.justification: The original GLUE protocol is retained. New protocols include semantic-category AUC and Recall evaluation in Appendix J, a voting-cutoff sweep from 10 to 100 in steps of 10 in Appendix L, and selected Llama Value B modules with k=20 in Appendix M. These are additional experimental designs, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices K–M add substantial diagnostics: tracking benign and noisy sample ranks across layers, testing sensitivity to voting cutoff across LoRA modules, and investigating whether module selection remedies Llama's weak filtering performance. These extend the earlier layer correlations and noise-distribution analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds an explicit Friedman test to Figure 2 and reports 95% confidence intervals over 10 seeds in Figures 27–28. The original ten-seed design and Wilcoxon reporting remain; the PDFs do not establish an increased run count for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 and the original plots retain their results, while Appendices J–M add extensive findings. For example, Table 7 reports rank 6.80 ± 4.10 for Cosine/Vote on v-b-9 versus 9.40 ± 6.00 for Random, with reported Wilcoxon p=0.0072. This is a new selected-module comparison, not a same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The proposed Rank and Vote procedures, including their restriction to correctly predicted validation samples, remain unchanged in Section 3.3 and Equations 9–10. Varying voting parameters and selecting particular modules are experimental settings; the additional attribution techniques are comparators.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 adds a reproducibility section, Appendices J–M, and supporting cross-references, with localized wording and heading changes. The additions do not constitute extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds multi-panel AUC/Recall plots, sample-rank plots, three-dimensional voting-sensitivity displays, and Table 7. The ICLR template also changes margins, headers, sizing, and table placement throughout. Earlier figures remain present, mostly with renumbering and resizing.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through two new discussions: responding to recent evidence of influence-function failures, especially Li et al. (2025), and connecting layer localization and aggregation to ROME, R-ROME, MEMIT, and EMMET. These introduce substantive relationships to prior research beyond additional citations.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, Equations 1–10, cancellation theorem, and Appendix G proof are substantively unchanged. The new empirical analyses introduce no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support was confined to synthetic-label-noise filtering on GLUE. Appendix J substantially strengthens the scope of validation through semantic-category attribution tasks and additional comparators, while Appendices K–M investigate voting sensitivity and the Llama failure case. These additions improve the evidence behind practical layer-selection guidance, alongside new reproducibility disclosures. Table 7's unclear task quantities and inconsistent GPU descriptions introduce reporting weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the substantial empirical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across layout changes and figure renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds autoregressive-dataset evaluations, voting sensitivity experiments, sample-rank analyses, and targeted Llama experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on noisy GLUE datasets, including downstream accuracy, layer comparisons, aggregation experiments, and noise-detection analyses.

C1.justification: The benchmark, descriptor-based evaluation and Global North bias claims persist. These substantially extend the validation design; generation counts and seeds remain unchanged.

The original proposer–refiner and threshold ablations are retained as Tables 4–5, and the descriptor-source experiment remains Table 10; these are not new analyses.

E5.justification: V2 adds ± quantities in Table 1, human-rating standard deviations in Table 13, Krippendorff’s alpha and Cohen’s kappa in Appendix A.4, and a p≤0.0001 statement in Table 3. Table 1 does not explain its ± quantities and leaves FAITH/SDIV uncertainties as placeholders. Additional random-seed runs are not established.

Appendix A.5, Figure 8 and Table 32 also introduce a concrete procedure for converting descriptor feedback into Nano Banana editing instructions, extending the previously suggested application.

P1.justification: The abstract, much of the introduction, related work, methodology and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. V2 adds Section 4.3, reorganizes related-work categories, expands appendix explanations and rewrites prompt documentation. This constitutes substantial editorial restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 2, enlarges Figure 4 into two rows, restructures comparisons by backbone and separates component results into Table 3. It adds Figure 8 and diagnostic/human-score tables. Appendix prompts are reformatted into wrapped, readable blocks, replacing v1’s small monospaced blocks with overflowing lines.

R1.justification: V2 adds OpenBias as methodological inspiration, VIEScore, additional compositional-understanding studies and statistical-reliability references; Culture-TRIP and Liu et al.’s cultural-gap paper disappear. The central positioning around social activities and descriptor-based faithfulness evaluation remains. Several other citation changes merely update publication metadata.

The bipartite-graph and indicator notation otherwise restates existing descriptor matching; no substantial theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central metric-validation evidence through a second backbone, stronger judges, broader human assessment and explicit agreement analysis, addressing v1’s narrower validation. More complete implementation details and readable appendix prompts improve reproducibility. Undefined uncertainty entries and the misleading percentage wording remain, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CULTIVate benchmark and AHEaD framework. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the main text and complete appendices, including corresponding equations, tables, figures and prompts despite renumbering and substantial rewriting.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark results and reports expanded human evaluation, additional metric comparisons, descriptor-coverage assessments and image-editing examples.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of six image generators, human judgments, metric correlations and descriptor-generation ablations in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Culture in Action: Evaluating Text-to-Image Models through Social Activities

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: explaining sparse-embedding overfitting, proposing adaptive regularization, improving single- and multi-epoch performance, and production deployment. C2.justification: V2 supplements the retained norm-growth explanation with an embedding-collapse interpretation, attributes high-frequency-bucket gains to larger norm budgets, and offers sparsity-dependent coefficient guidance. E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same tasks and four datasets: iPinYou, Amazon Electronics, Avazu and LZD. Dataset descriptions move from Section 4.1.1 to Appendix L. New frequency-bucket and architecture analyses use retained data and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds SAM as a comparator in both Adam and Adagrad benchmark comparisons, including Tables 1–2 and the learning-curve analysis. The native optimizers, MEDA and fixed-weight-decay comparators remain, making this a focused expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: The reported benchmark backbone changes from DeepFM to xDeepFM, supported by different citations and CIN configurations. E4.justification: New Section 4.5 isolates frequency-dependent regularization through bucket analysis and progressive replacement of fixed decay. Appendix E adds embedding-size sensitivity and embedding-collapse diagnostics. Weight-decay sensitivity expands from Avazu alone to all four datasets in Appendix I. The original IP-filtering analysis remains.

E5.justification: V1 supplies point scores without run-count or uncertainty reporting. V2 states that Section 4.3 experiments use three different seeds, reports averages in Tables 1–2 and standard deviations in Tables 8–11, and discloses seed matching. E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace many earlier scores with reported three-seed averages; for example, Avazu/DNN/AdamAR epoch-2 AUC changes from 0.7640 to 0.7631. These are revised reported results under changed reporting/settings. SAM adds new rankings, including Amazon/WDL/Adam epoch-1 AUC of 0.8516 versus AdamAR's 0.8496. Bucket, embedding-size, spectrum and expanded sensitivity results are also added.

M1.justification: The clipped interval-dependent regularization rule and AdamAR/AdagradAR update procedures remain unchanged. Section 3.1 clarifies time indices consistently with the existing pseudocode; moving AdagradAR from Appendix B to G does not introduce a new method.

P1.justification: V2 lightly revises the abstract and notation, condenses Section 4.1 into labeled paragraphs, moves dataset descriptions to Appendix L, and reorganizes appendix labels around added material. Most introduction, method explanation and conclusion prose remains intact; the document is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adds bucket and spectrum visualizations, three additional dataset sensitivity figures, ablation/embedding-size/resource tables, and four mean-plus-standard-deviation tables. Existing benchmark tables and Figure 1 gain SAM entries. V1's Avazu sensitivity Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 7, while the feature-statistics table is retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds supporting references for SAM, convergence theory, nonsmooth analysis and embedding collapse. The experimental setup cites Zhang et al. (2024) for the recommendation WuKong architecture instead of Gu et al. (2022), and the DIN citation disappears with shortened dataset discussion. The central positioning against MEDA and uniform decay remains stable.

T1.justification: V2 adds nonconvex convergence assumptions and Proposition 3 in Section 3.3, its derivation and occurrence-interval noise bounds in Appendix B, a Clarke-subgradient treatment of nonsmooth optimality in Appendix C, and an FM-like Rademacher-complexity derivation in Appendix D. These substantially extend the original theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: V1 lacks reported run variability and direct component ablations of frequency adaptation. V2 addresses these important evidential gaps with three-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting and progressive bucket ablations, supplemented by SAM comparisons and embedding-size analyses. Acknowledging SAM's Amazon advantage also improves qualification of the findings. These substantially strengthen validation and transparency, despite minor editing defects such as Figure 1 still saying 'four methods' while displaying five.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive-regularization work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial additions and relocation.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results with three-seed averages and standard deviations, alongside frequency-bucket ablations, embedding-size experiments and singular-spectrum analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original AUC comparisons on iPinYou, Amazon Electronics, Avazu and LZD, plus learning curves, feature-filtering experiments and weight-decay sensitivity results.

results.title: Adaptive Regularization for Large-Scale Sparse Feature Embedding Models

C1.justification: v5 refines the central contribution to generalization from admissions of on-policy mistakes. Its abstract and conclusion explicitly describe training models to make factual errors and then confess them. The principal detection, elicitation, and decoy-robustness claims remain.

C2.justification: v5 adds substantive explanations involving on-policy errors, stronger training updates, and admissions aligned with model belief. It also identifies weakened instruction-hierarchy compliance as a possible contributor to disclosure and explicitly acknowledges that the evaluation confounds this with honesty. These materially qualify the earlier interpretation.

D1.justification: v5 clarifies assistant-message weighting and which turns receive training, documents the new ablation recipes, and replaces the anonymized repository pointer with a named GitHub repository. These improve documentation without proving changes to the original implementation. The instruction-tuning data source remains unresolved as '(?)' in Appendix H.1.

E1.justification: v5 substantially expands auxiliary coverage with a general instruction-hierarchy conflict task, general instruction-tuning data for mixing, and difficult HLE questions used to train admissions under mistaken beliefs. The four stealth tasks and existing capability benchmarks remain; the new held-out factual-QA validation alone does not constitute new task coverage.

E3.justification: New protocols include comparing ablations on common GPT-4.1 trajectories, validating 400 held-out questions and 800 admissions, and evaluating 247 instruction conflicts across eight types. v5 also specifies HLE filtering and controlled data-mixing and admission-corruption conditions. The original stealth-task sampling and principal metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendices A.2, H, and L.1 add substantial tests of training-turn necessity, model belief versus ground truth, benign-data mixing, inaccurate admissions, and instruction-hierarchy side effects. Earlier decoy, auditing-only, and system-prompt analyses remain, including the system-prompt analysis relocated to Appendix K.

E5.justification: v5 first specifies fine-tuning seed 42. Existing interrogation repetition counts and Wilson interval, bootstrap interval, and standard-error reporting practices are retained. The added seed disclosure does not establish additional training runs or rerunning the original experiments.

E6.justification: The headline F1 of 0.98 and 28–100% elicitation results remain unchanged. Substantial new outcomes include zero elicitation for turn2-only training, 61% factual-QA and 96% admission accuracy for SRFT in held-out validation, and hierarchy compliance of 72% for GPT-4.1 versus 61% for SRFT. Figures 5, 17, and 18 additionally report belief-target, mixing, and contamination results.

M1.justification: The primary SRFT procedure retains GPT-4.1, the 770 two-turn training examples, and the interrogation procedure. v5 explicitly documents training both assistant turns, including false first answers; this clarifies the setup rather than establishes an algorithm change. The additional training variants serve as experimental ablations.

P1.justification: v5 regroups the methods subsections, condenses several passages, repairs incomplete wording, and moves the detailed system-prompt analysis into Appendix K. Appendices are reorganized, but much of the introduction, principal results, and retained appendix text remains verbatim or lightly edited.

P2.justification: v5 adds multi-panel ablation, validation, and hierarchy-compliance figures; relocates the system-prompt figure; and redraws the capability plots with explicit numerical labels and revised axes and ordering. It also corrects the training-example illustration and caption. This substantially expands and revises the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v5 removes the related-work paragraph on unexpected fine-tuning generalization and its references to Betley et al. on emergent misalignment, He et al. on benign data breaking safety, and Qi et al. on fine-tuning compromising safety. The broader positioning around auditing, probing, steering, and introspection remains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The F1 and elicitation metric definitions are retained. The new explanations and empirical selection rules do not introduce a formal theory.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens the paper by testing which training ingredients support generalization and examining instruction-hierarchy weakening as an alternative explanation, gaps left largely untested in v1. Clearer training documentation and explicit limitations make the retained headline results easier to interpret. The hierarchy confound remains unresolved, and missing data provenance and small prose–figure discrepancies limit precision, but the added controls and qualifications provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SRFT study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v5.

after.justification: v5 retains these original results and adds training-data ablations, held-out validation, and instruction-hierarchy compliance experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-4.1 fine-tuning and interrogation experiments, Claude prefill comparisons, robustness analyses, and capability evaluations.

results.title: Spilling the Beans: Teaching LLMs to Self-Report Their Hidden Objectives

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: efficient embedder-only reinforcement learning, temporal retrieval reasoning, competitive QA, and strong long-context performance up to 10M tokens.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of retrieval-budget versus noise tradeoffs, premature versus redundant retrieval, and threshold-dependent stopping failures. It also explains which components determine context-length scaling and distinguishes L2 approximation guarantees from stronger uniform guarantees requiring additional assumptions.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code link, statements about data/instructions and checkpoint availability, and detailed dataset-specific retrievers, chunk sizes, retrieval limits, and decoding settings. Appendix G clarifies that Fact EM means covering all supporting facts, allowing extra chunks; this documents the metric without establishing that its implementation changed. V1's optimizer and hardware details are retained.

E1.justification: Table 1 adds RULER single-hop QA alongside the existing NIAH and multi-hop tasks. V2 also explicitly uses MuSiQue in joint training for the new GTE experiment, whereas v1 describes HotPotQA training and MuSiQue out-of-distribution evaluation. The benchmark families remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The new stopping analysis introduces an oracle stopping-policy reference in Figure 5. Evaluated comparator membership in Tables 1–3 remains unchanged. Search-o1 and HippoRAG have only empty rows in Table 7, which do not establish new evaluations.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 introduces a joint-trained GTE configuration, 1,000 HotPotQA examples, retrieval budgets of 2–5, and three Qwen3 answerers. Appendix B adds threshold sweeps and stopping-error metrics, excluding episodes whose full trajectories never recover all supporting chunks. These are substantial new evaluation designs; Appendix G's disclosures alone do not establish changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds retrieval-budget sensitivity, detailed early/late stopping-error analysis, threshold-dependent accuracy and retrieval-length comparisons, ROC curves, and training-convergence curves. The original architectural ablations and temperature/lambda sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same three-seed averages and identical plus/minus values in Table 3. The added experiments introduce no explicit new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises Q-RAG's multi-hop QA scores at 16K/32K/128K/1M from 67/67/62/57 to 64/65/65/61, and Beam Retriever's 4K/16K scores from 28.3/28.3 to 39/35. V2 adds single-hop QA, budget, stopping, in-distribution MuSiQue, and convergence results. Tables 2–3 retain their scores. These are revised and additional results, not evidence of an algorithmic performance gain.

M1.justification: Appendix B adds a simulated Q-value-threshold early-stopping variant; v1 specified only a retrieval budget or generic STOP action. The embedding architecture, soft-Q training, temporal encoding, and existing Plan Q-RAG beam search are retained.

P1.justification: Appendix A is substantially rewritten and reorganized into a real/complex reformulation, reordered lemma and theorem, staged derivations, and a uniform-bound discussion. Elsewhere, v2 promotes ablations to a standalone section, expands appendix organization, adds a reproducibility statement, and corrects terminology and cross-references. The main introduction and conclusion remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures 4–6 and Tables 4–8 for stopping, budget, convergence, additional QA, and configurations. Table 1 gains separate single-hop and multi-hop QA columns. Existing Figures 2–3 retain their plotted content, while Figure 1 is resized.

R1.justification: V2 adds MemUP to the recurrent-memory discussion and cites Malkov–Yashunin and Zhao et al. for approximate nearest-neighbor search. Birman–Solomyak and Novak–Wozniakowski disappear with the replaced proofs. The main positioning against retriever training, LLM training, and recurrent models remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix A replaces the fixed-RoPE density argument with a variable-dimensional complex-diagonal theorem requiring a self-adjoint, point-separating positional algebra. The uniform rate with exponent s/(2dx+2dy+2) is replaced by an L2 rate with exponent s/(dx+dy+1), different assumptions, and new proofs. Separate uniform-bound conditions and Appendix D's complexity derivation are added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves theoretical precision and reproducibility: Appendix A makes approximation assumptions and norm-dependent guarantees explicit, while Appendix G resolves important omissions about retrieval, generation, and Fact EM. Budget and stopping experiments address practical questions left untested in v1. These gains outweigh limited inconsistencies, including Appendix G's blanket QwQ-32B statement despite the Qwen3 answerers in Section 5.1. The improvement concerns evidence and documentation, not a demonstrated advance in the core algorithm.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Q-RAG work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds retrieval-budget experiments, stopping-policy analyses, training curves, and additional QA results.

before.justification: V1 reports original Q-RAG evaluations on BabiLong, RULER, HotPotQA, and MuSiQue, together with architectural ablations and sensitivity experiments.

results.title: Q-RAG: Long Context Multi‑Step Retrieval via Value‑Based Embedder Training

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claims about utility collapse, parameter drift, regularization, and semantic-aware projection. The conclusion now specifically recommends selective fine-tuning plus gradient projection for in-domain and cross-domain retention, refining v1's general statement that the add-ons provide strong baselines.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets anchor-based unlearning as representation replacement, explains how erasure thresholds complicate merging, and argues that excess sequential drift persists beyond optimization-step differences. It also qualifies smoothness as local and identifies unresolved adversarial recovery, architecture, objective, and modality generalization questions. These substantially expand v1's interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly discloses that the original sequential experiments used method-default iteration budgets while simultaneous unlearning used validation checks every 100 iterations and a 99% UA stopping threshold. Appendix B.2 specifies relative UNet perturbations and matched minibatches, diffusion noise, and timesteps. These improve procedural documentation without supplying a comprehensive implementation specification.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates UNLEARNCANVAS style and object erasure. v2 retains this coverage and adds identity-based erasure involving six target celebrities and six held-out celebrities, plus general-generation retention using MS-COCO prompts (Appendix A.2–A.3). This extends evaluation beyond the original concept domains.

E2.justification: SculpMem replaces EraseDiff as the second principal evaluated unlearning method in Section 5 and Appendix A. ESD is newly evaluated for SDXL celebrity erasure. v2 also adds the simultaneous comparator to the ConAbl regularizer comparison in Figure 6, where v1 showed sequential unlearning and its regularized variants.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce the GIPHY celebrity classifier, FID and CLIP Score on 5,000 COCO-prompt images, and SDXL. Appendix B.2 replaces the base-checkpoint perturbation experiment with relative UNet perturbations across base and independently unlearned checkpoints on held-out retention concepts. Appendices D–E add experiments applying 99% UA early stopping to both strategies; these are additional controls, not evidence that all original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Section 8 and Appendices C–E examine anchor-dependent parameter updates, concept-erasure thresholds under model interpolation, drift under matched stopping criteria, and cumulative training costs. Appendix B.2 substantially revises the curvature analysis. These add mechanistic, sensitivity, and optimization-budget investigations absent from v1.

E5.justification: v1's curvature table reports means and standard deviations. v2's Figure 18 instead presents per-model trends, medians, 95% intervals across models, distributions, and Spearman and Mann–Whitney U p-values. This expands statistical reporting for one analysis; neither version establishes repeated training-run uncertainty for the main benchmark comparisons.

E6.justification: EraseDiff results are removed, while SculpMem, celebrity, SDXL, and new diagnostic results are reported. For example, v2 Figure 17 reports harmonic means of 82.6 for model merging, 50.8 for projection, and 87.0 for their combination with ESD/SDXL; these are new-setting results, not improvements over v1 scores. The original ConAbl combination scores in Figure 8 remain 89.6 for styles and 88.3 for objects.

M1.justification: The update-norm penalties, selective fine-tuning rule, TIES merging procedure, and auxiliary-concept gradient projection remain unchanged in Sections 6–7. Evaluating these regularizers with SculpMem and ESD does not introduce a new proposed algorithm component.

P1.justification: Most of the abstract, introduction, and Sections 3–7 preserve their wording and ordering. Local revisions affect related work, the conclusion, captions, and organizational summaries; Section 8 and additional appendix sections are inserted. Conference headers, affiliations, acknowledgments, and an LLM-use disclosure are also added, without a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive celebrity/SDXL plots, an anchor-correlation heatmap, interpolation panels, a controlled-drift heatmap, and a training-cost plot. It replaces the curvature table with distribution plots and introduces an optimization-step table. Existing diagrams, legends, captions, and placements are revised, while v1's Figure 9 normalized-gain plot disappears and the document adopts ICLR formatting.

R1.justification: v2 introduces SculpMem and COCO references and several additional continual-learning, generation, and safety citations. SculpMem replaces EraseDiff as the prominent recent-method example. The broader novelty positioning and detailed discussions of semantic awareness and model merging remain largely unchanged; the latter move from Appendix C to F.

T1.justification: The continual-unlearning definition, projection construction, first-order invariance lemma and proof, and Taylor/Cauchy–Schwarz retention-loss derivation are retained. The revised curvature experiment and interpolation analysis do not change these formal results.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence was confined to style/object erasure on one diffusion architecture and lacked an explicit stopping-budget control for its drift explanation. v2's identity-erasure and SDXL evaluations, controlled drift experiment, and measured training costs substantially strengthen generality and evidential support (Appendices A, D–E). Removing EraseDiff results loses evidence, and celebrity summary-metric captions and cumulative-step terminology remain unclear, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same continual-unlearning study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support comparison despite expanded experiments and conference reformatting.

after.justification: v2 reports original ConAbl, SculpMem, and ESD experiments, including celebrity erasure, SDXL evaluation, and additional analyses of unlearning dynamics.

before.justification: v1 reports original ConAbl and EraseDiff experiments, regularizer comparisons, semantic-similarity analyses, and retention-loss curvature measurements.

results.title: Continual Unlearning for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models: A Regularization Perspective

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: combining verbal and latent forecasting, training reasoning through inverse-MSE Time-GRPO, and conditioning forecasts on reasoning-derived attributes. The principal claims of strong financial forecasting and expert-rated reasoning quality remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds a proposed explanation for resilience to unreliable reasoning, limits the usefulness of reasoning beyond trend extrapolation on ILI/ETTh1, and acknowledges that portfolio alpha is statistically significant only for China A50. Expert criticisms and discussion of the short evaluation horizon further qualify the largely favorable interpretations in v1.

D1.justification: New Appendix A documents training frameworks, learning rates, batches, epochs, forecasting LoRA settings, GPU hardware, memory use and training times. The abstract adds a code-access link, and Appendix C discloses best-run selection for subsequent evaluations. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to the underlying retained experiments.

E1.justification: The four financial datasets remain. Section 5 and Appendix G add actual evaluations on ILI healthcare data and ETTh1 transformer oil-temperature data, substantially extending coverage beyond financial time series.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the retained forecasting, expert-rating and portfolio experiments. The new-domain experiments reuse existing time-series baselines. TimeCAP is discussed but not experimentally evaluated; CAPM and Fama–French are used for portfolio attribution rather than as competing forecasting or trading algorithms.

E3.justification: The original ten-day forecasting and 25-expert evaluation settings are retained. New protocols include indicator-noise and indicator-removal interventions in Figure 4, GPT-4.1 judging of 1,000 sampled reasoning traces in Appendix F, and daily-return risk-factor regressions in Appendix H. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained training-stage ablations and reward curves, v2 tests whether corrupting or removing reasoning inputs harms forecasts. It also adds multiple forecast case studies, qualitative expert feedback, analysis of reasoning limitations outside finance, and CAPM/Fama–French portfolio attribution.

E5.justification: v1 provides no seed counts or significance tests. v2 first reports ten seeded runs with means and standard deviations, one-sided one-sample tests against a fixed CALF reference, paired expert-rating tests, and portfolio-alpha p-values. Figure 5 also adds error bars without defining their statistical meaning. The PDFs do not establish that the run count increased from v1.

E6.justification: The original forecasting, stage-ablation, expert criterion means and portfolio scores are unchanged. Substantial new results include corruption effects, automated judging, seed distributions and factor regressions. Table 9 newly reports VTA ILI MSE of 1.4366 versus TimesNet's 1.0795, and ETTh1 MSE of 0.0346 versus CALF's 0.0361; these are additional evaluations, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The Time-GRPO stages, forecasting backbone and conditional-training procedure are retained. However, v1 Equation 9 combines the conditional prediction with y_phi, the backbone forecast, whereas v2 Equation 10 substitutes y_theta, previously defined as the reasoning-model prediction. Both passages describe conditional/unconditional forecasting, leaving unresolved whether this is a notation error or an inference change.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the original prose remain intact. Local revisions expand the introduction and related work, explain portfolio metrics, move the expert-rating definitions from v1 Appendix B into Section 5, and add appendix navigation, acknowledgements and author-information updates.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column conference format. The expert-rating table becomes a bar chart with error bars and an overall score, while new corruption plots, case-study figures and statistical, cross-domain and financial-analysis tables substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing diagrams and results are also resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 introduces TimeCAP as the closest related approach and distinguishes its auxiliary-context classification from VTA's intrinsic financial signals and trajectory forecasts. It also adds references supporting automated judging, nonfinancial forecasting limitations and conditional image control, while dropping PromptCast. The broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds explicit CAPM and six-factor regression formulations, defining excess returns, alpha, beta and residual terms for the new financial analysis. These are limited formal-model additions; no new theorem or proof is supplied, and the principal VTA training mathematics is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's point-estimate evidence with reasoning-corruption tests, seed variability, expert significance tests and informative domain and portfolio limitations. Training and computational details plus a code-access link also address substantial reproducibility gaps. These gains improve assessment of the central claims despite incomplete new protocol descriptions, testing against a fixed baseline while selecting the best VTA run, and the ambiguous inference equation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VTA research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and can be matched across the formatting changes and expanded supplementary material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds reasoning-corruption experiments, evaluations in other domains, automated reasoning assessments, statistical tests and portfolio factor analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments, training-stage ablations, evaluations by 25 financial experts, and portfolio backtests in Tables 2–5.

results.title: Reasoning on Time-Series for Financial Technical Analysis

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about latent anonymization, multi-task generalization, approximately 35% privacy-leakage reduction and gender-bias mitigation. The additional experiments support or qualify these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges failure against white-box inversion and interprets the tested black-box attack as leaving attribute prediction near chance. It newly restricts current applicability to global-embedding tasks, leaving patch-based tasks for future work, and discusses spatial-information loss in reconstruction. These materially expand the earlier limitations and interpretations.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies CLS versus globally pooled encoder outputs, and the new experiments document decoder and retrieval setup details. Existing training hyperparameters and project-page access remain unchanged. Removing 'linear' from the privacy-evaluation prose reconciles it with the two-layer MLP already documented in both appendices.

E1.justification: v2 adds VP-HMDB51 and VP-UCF101 evaluation using five clip-level private attributes, alongside the retained VISPR and PA-HMDB51 evaluations. It also adds UCF101 action-video retrieval and feature-inversion/video-reconstruction scenarios, substantially broadening task requirements and threat coverage.

E2.justification: New Table 2 evaluates a supervised latent anonymizer trained with private-attribute labels against SPLAVU. This differs from the existing pixel-level VITA comparator. Table 8 also adds random-chance references; the original Table 1 comparator roster remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols specify learned black-box inversion and gradient-based white-box inversion, assessed with predictors trained on raw features. Reconstruction compares four token-input conditions with 10-epoch decoder finetuning; retrieval uses test queries, a training-set gallery and Recall@1/5/10 plus mAP. These are substantial protocol additions, while retained experiments keep their settings.

E4.justification: The original task, loss, architecture and sensitivity ablations remain. v2 adds a substantial security analysis: Table 8 tests embedding recoverability under black-box and white-box attacks, while Figure 4 compares reconstruction from patch and CLS representations with and without anonymization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or run-to-run error bars. The added results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained numerical results are unchanged after matching renumbered tables. New results include SPLAVU privacy cMAP of 70.5/69.6 versus raw-feature 76.4/75.9 on VP-HMDB51/VP-UCF101 (Table 2), inversion outcomes (Table 8), UCF101 retrieval R@1 of 94.9 versus baseline 95.3 (Table 13), and qualitative reconstruction findings (Figure 4).

M1.justification: The frozen encoder, self-attention AAM, three training objectives and Algorithm 1 retain the same procedure. The explicit CLS/average-pooled embedding description clarifies implementation; the added evaluations do not establish a revised SPLAVU algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are retained. Changes include a new embedding-notation subsection, localized explanatory additions, standardized dataset notation, wording corrections and updated affiliations and conference headers; there is no extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 2, 8 and 13 and the reconstruction panels in Figure 4, and expands Figure 2’s caption. Existing diagrams, plots and table designs remain substantially intact; the original runtime Figure 4 becomes Figure 5, with local relocation and layout adjustments.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations on video representations, bias and safety, including Swetha et al. (2021, 2023), Prabhu and Birhane (2020), SAFE-LLaVA and SAFER-CLIP. The central positioning against pixel-level anonymization and the claimed novelty of generalizable latent anonymization remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives and reasoning remain substantively unchanged. Equation (1), dataset symbols and loss-weight naming receive notation cleanup; Appendix B.1 explains standard global-token and pooling representations without introducing a new theoretical argument or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct inversion and reconstruction tests of its central privacy claim. v2 substantially strengthens assessment through these tests, explicit disclosure of white-box vulnerability, clearer applicability limits, clip-level privacy comparisons and held-out retrieval evaluation. The gains concern evidence and transparency rather than higher retained scores. Reconstruction evidence still has limits: non-anonymized CLS inputs also reconstruct poorly, so Figure 4 cannot attribute all resistance to AAM.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPLAVU study. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–D are readable and can be matched reliably despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds video-level privacy comparisons, inversion attacks, video retrieval and qualitative reconstruction experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original privacy–utility comparisons, gender-bias evaluations, ablations, gait-recognition results and appendix experiments on scaling and efficiency.

results.title: Privacy Beyond Pixels: Latent Anonymization for Privacy-Preserving Video Understanding

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same substantive claims about geometric BPE, compression, generalization, data efficiency, downstream transfer, generation and interpretability. The expanded evidence does not redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations separating tokenizer data efficiency from downstream-model underfitting, explaining hyperparameter tradeoffs, and relating reconstruction to fold type and size. The limitations now explicitly frame SSLM as a tokenizer comparison and acknowledge noncompetitive backbone-design quality, while dropping v1's explicit pretrained-PLM-dependence and larger-codebook caveats. New scaling and secondary-structure interpretations substantially broaden the discussion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies explicit unseen-structure tokenization pseudocode, extensive parameter-selection instructions, loss-weight settings, measured CPU runtimes and the larger Transformer's configuration. It also specifies ProteinMPNN with eight sequences per structure and OmegaFold for scTM assessment, where v1 described generic tools. These materially improve procedural documentation without establishing that every retained experiment changed.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds 550,000 Swiss-Prot structures predicted by AlphaFold for tokenization and language-model training, substantially extending the original experimental-structure coverage. Appendix C adds agreement evaluation against eight DSSP secondary-structure classes. The original PDB, CAMEO, CASP14 and downstream benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Appendix F.2 adds explicit designability comparisons with ProtDiff (11.8%) and FoldingDiff (14.2%). These are numerical reference comparisons; the PDFs do not establish fresh runs of those baselines. The existing tokenizer comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds downstream training-fraction controls and a 65.9M-parameter SSLM alongside the 7.3M model. Its scaling evaluation generates 50–128-residue proteins, whereas the original experiment samples an empirical length prior averaging approximately 214 residues. Appendix K also specifies fixed bond lengths for transfer and w_t=1.0 for the updated Pareto evaluation.

E4.justification: V2 extends the existing ablations with downstream-data sweeps (Table 4), reconstruction after 1% tokenizer training (Table 5), secondary-structure agreement (Tables 8–9), and robustness across unusualness, length and fold types (Figure 11). Tables 16–18 and Figure 13 add systematic sensitivity tests of vocabulary resolution, binning, glue optimization and bond-length handling.

E5.justification: Appendix I newly reports per-bin means and standard deviations, distribution boxplots, and Pearson correlations with 95% confidence intervals. These describe variation across proteins and uncertainty in correlations, rather than repeated-training uncertainty. The 1,000-random-partition agreement baseline was already present in v1.

E6.justification: V2 updates the GeoBPE Pareto points and corrects Table 1's functional-site mean from 79.93 to 80.20 while retaining the individual split scores. It adds extensive analysis results, Swiss-Prot reconstruction scores, and scaled-generation results of 0.376/0.405 scTM and 12%/21% designability. The generation additions use different settings from v1's retained SSLM results.

M1.justification: The clustering, Geo-Pair merging, glue-angle optimization, TreeLSTM transfer encoder and autoregressive modeling procedures are retained. New Algorithms 10–11 detail learned-vocabulary tokenization of unseen structures, already described and evaluated in v1. Expanded pseudocode and parameter-selection guidance do not establish an algorithmic redesign.

P1.justification: The methods exposition gains organized notation and an expanded explanation of grounding, quantization, refinement and synchronization. Transfer is distinguished through the GeoBPE-TRANSFER name. The hyperparameter appendix is rebuilt into documentation, application-specific guidance and sensitivity sections, while SSLM framing and limitations are substantially rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adds the toy-geometry diagram, robustness plots, stopping-rule illustration, sensitivity panels and numerous analysis tables. The existing flowchart moves into Methods, and the retained expert-case figures are redesigned as explicit merge trees with arrows and span labels. The Pareto plot is redrawn and the generation table gains scaling rows.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for UniProt, AlphaFold DB, ProtDiff, FoldingDiff and OmegaFold, positioning the scaling experiment relative to diffusion-based generation. The main related-work discussion and positioning against structural alphabets, VQ-VAEs and biological BPE remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the per-link transform's dihedral argument and corresponding glue definition from phi_{i+1} to phi_i. Appendix I defines structural unusualness as 100 times one minus the best-hit TM-score. The principal geometric derivations, tokenizer principles and complexity analysis remain; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence and guidance on practical scalability, parameter sensitivity and unseen-structure encoding. The 550,000-structure benchmark, controlled data and sensitivity studies, robustness analysis, and explicit inference algorithms provide stronger validation and reproducibility. Changed generation lengths limit the scaling conclusions, and secondary-structure score conventions remain unclear, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and procedural clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GeoBPE research. The main text, figures, tables, equations and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across relocation, renumbering and terminology changes.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds predicted-structure tokenization, larger language-model experiments, robustness analyses and sensitivity studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original compression/reconstruction experiments, downstream prediction results, ablations, backbone generation and expert-agreement analyses.

results.title: Protein Structure Tokenization via Geometric Byte Pair Encoding

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the LR-decay incompatibility claim, CMA/CDMA remedies, and reported 1.64% benchmark improvement. The shortened conclusion preserves the central contribution. The new appendix broadens support and implementation scope without revising these headline claims.

C2.justification: Appendix D discusses the difficulty of comparing quality scores across domains and interprets the new Chinese-language gains. It also acknowledges limited mathematics gains and coding regression, suggesting mixture proportions and crude quality proxies as possible explanations. Earlier mechanism interpretations remain intact.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial implementation documentation for the multi-domain experiment: domain token counts and proportions, selection thresholds, quality proxies, rank construction, LR settings, batch size, and checkpoint spacing of approximately 1.67B tokens. The original implementation details and hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds heterogeneous continual pretraining using DCLM, Fineweb-Edu-Chinese-V2.1, StarCoder, and MegaMath. Evaluation newly includes GSM8K, MBPP, CEval, and BoolQ, expanding coverage to mathematical reasoning, coding, Chinese understanding, and reading comprehension.

E2.justification: Existing uniform, reverse-curriculum, folding, and averaging comparisons are retained. The new experiment uses the established uniform-ordering plus WSD baseline; its different training settings do not introduce a new comparison-method family.

E3.justification: The added experiment uses a 3.2B model, a 728.7B-token base phase, and 156.1B-token continual phase. Its protocol specifies batch size 2048, peak LR 0.001, baseline linear decay over the final 84B tokens, and a CDMA endpoint of 0.000367. Existing experiments' settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The LR-decay, folding, alternative-quality-metric, WebOrganizer, and validation-loss correlation analyses are retained. Appendix D adds method and evaluation coverage, without a separate new ablation or sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the 20-run simulation description in Figure 6 and correlation statistics in Figure 7. v2 adds no training-seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: All nine original tables retain their values, with v1 Tables 8–9 becoming v2 Tables 11–12. New Table 10 reports baseline versus CDMA averages of 52.70 and 53.79, including ARC-C and BoolQ gains of 3.39 points each, but MBPP and ARC-E decreases of 0.78 and 0.18 points. These are new-setting results.

M1.justification: Appendix D.1 and Algorithm 2 add a multi-domain extension: independently rank samples using domain-specific quality metrics, rescale ranks by domain size, and globally interleave samples. This substantively extends v1's global or sequential-phase sorting procedure while retaining CMA/CDMA's optimization components.

Equation (5) replaces uniform normalization by T(T-M) with per-step weighting by 1/t followed by averaging over T. T1.justification: Equations (1), (3), and (5) receive substantive mathematical revisions. In Equation (1), multiplying exp(q_t^T k_i) by the binary mask correctly gives evicted tokens zero weight; v1 instead placed the mask inside the exponential, leaving exp(0) weight. The revised retention definition also supports the newly stated additive-logit expression q_t^T k_i + (t-i) log(beta_i). These repair central definitions rather than merely change notation; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Correcting Equations (1) and (3) resolves an important flaw in the paper's central mathematical specification: zero retention previously left nonzero exponential weight, whereas v2's formulation actually suppresses or excludes tokens as intended. The more restrained LongMemEval interpretation also better matches the reported evidence. P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract and introduction, refines terminology, updates the publication header, and adds appendix headings and cross-references, including an LLM-use disclosure. results.title: Synchronizing Probabilities in Model-Driven Lossless Compression

The Gaussian-initialization theorem also changes its first failure-probability exponent denominator from 2 to 4. These substantially revise the mathematical justification.

improvement.justification: V1 repeatedly relies on an unjustified global softmax-Jacobian bound. V2 replaces it with a proved local bound and supplies the logit-range arguments needed to apply it, addressing an important defect in the paper's central theoretical support. Corrected gradients and explicit assumptions further improve rigor. The narrower auxiliary conditions and more conservative probability statement improve precision while the empirical evidence remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching the revised proofs across renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experimental results, including the learned-weight comparisons, Pythia analyses, and appendix interventions.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original TinyStories training experiments, semantic-association analyses, Pythia-1.4B analyses, and interventions removing leading-term components.
